paragraph_context: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Daejeon 34141, Republic of Korea. Email: jwlee1@kaist.ac.kr Owing to the emergence of energy storage and electric vehicles, the desire for safe high-energy-density energy storage devices has increased research interest in anode-free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs). Unlike general lithium metal batteries (LMBs), in which excess Li exists to compensate for the irreversible loss of Li, only the current collector is employed as an anode and paired with a lithiated cathode in the fabrication of AFLMBs. Owing to their unique cell configuration, AFLMBs have attractive characteristics, including the highest energy density, safety, and cost-effectiveness. However, developing AFLMBs with extended cyclability remains an issue for practical applications because the high reactivity of Li with limited inventory causes severely low Coulombic efficiency (CE), poor cyclability, and dendrite growth. To address these issues, tremendous effort has been devoted to stabilizing Li metal anodes for AFLMBs. In this review, the importance and challenges of AFLMBs are highlighted. Then, diverse strategies, such as current collectors modification, advanced electrolytes, cathode engineering, and operation protocols are thoroughly reviewed. Finally, a future perspective on the strategy is provided for insight into the basis of future research. It is hoped that this review provides a comprehensive understanding by reviewing previous research and arousing more interest in this field. advanced electrolytes, anode-free lithium metal batteries, current collectors Since the first commercialization of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) by Sony Corp. in 1991, LIBs have been successfully used in applications ranging from small portable devices to grid energy storage systems.[1,2] In the 21st century, global environmental issues have driven the development of electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy, which require greater energy storage density. However, state-of-the-art LIBs have almost reached the theoretical limit of energy density ( $\approx$ 300 Wh $\mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ ) because of the low theoretical capacity of intercalation-type electrode materials (e.g. graphite and lithium metal oxides).[3,4,5] Therefore, next-generation anodes such as alkali metals (Li, Na,[6-10] K,[11-14]), alkaline earth metals (Mg,[15-19] Ca[20-24]), and multivalent metals (Zn,[25-29] Al[30,31]) are in the spotlight to go beyond LIBs. Among them, Li metal has gained the most attention as a next-generation anode material to overcome the theoretical limitations of intercalation-type anodes.[4,32] Li metal has very promising characteristics for high energy density, namely the lowest reduction potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ vs standard hydrogen electrode, SHE), high theoretical capacity $(3860\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1})$ and being lightweight $(0.53\mathrm{gcm}^{-3})$ . However, thick Li metal anodes $(>250~\mu \mathrm{m})$ are frequently used in lithium metal batteries (LMBs)[33,34] to compensate for the irreversible loss of electrically isolated dead Li[35,36] and solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer generation.[37-39] This configuration extends the cyclability of the cells but significantly lowers the energy density, which is often lower than that of LIBs.[4,39] To overcome the above issue, thin Li metal $(20 - 50~\mu \mathrm{m})$ electrodes have been employed. Recently, an anode composed of a sole current collector without Li metal was used by pairing it with a lithiated cathode, where the negative-to-positive (N/P) ratio is 0. The batteries with this simple configuration are called anode-free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs), which were first developed by Neudecker et al. in 2000 (Scheme 1).[40] Maximum energy density can be achieved because of the ideal environment.[41,42] Despite the considerable advantages of the anode-free configuration, the cycle stability of AFLMBs is too poor because the absence of a Li reservoir in the anode causes rapid degradation of the cycle.[43,44] As shown in Scheme 1, AFLMBs have received significant attention since a breakthrough by Qian et al. in 2016,[45] who initiated an anode-free boom by proving the feasibility of AFLMBs. Even now, more and more advanced strategies are being conducted to extend the cycle stability of AFLMBs.[46] Various efforts have been made to enhance the cyclability of AFLMBs.[44,47] In this review, we categorize the various strategies for high-performance AFLMBs into three types. The first is the rational design of current collectors to enhance the reversibility of Li metal. The construction of elaborate 3D structures,[48] diverse lithophilic sites,[49] artificial layers on current collectors,[50,51] and carbon hosts[52] have been explored to reduce the nucleation energy barrier, lead to uniform deposition of Li, and suppress dendrites. The next one is electrolyte engineering. The SEI layer formed by electrolyte decomposition has the greatest effect on the reversibility of Li metal.[44,47,53-58] Various studies have fabricated high-quality SEI layers, including by adjusting salt concentration,[45] changing solvent characteristics,[47,59] and introducing additives.[54,60] Then, we introduce a strategy through cathode engineering. This is achieved through the unique properties of the $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ cathode system[61-63] or the introduction of lithiated additives into the cathode.[64,65] The last category is operating protocols. Various parameters such as temperature, external pressure, current density, and cut-off voltages dramatically affect the cycle stability.[66-68] The initial cell configuration of AFLMBs is the same as that of general LMBs, except that the anode is composed of sole current collectors without Li metal (Figure 1A). Therefore, lithiated cathode materials are necessary for AFLMBs. Generally, intercalation materials such as lithium cobalt nickel manganese oxide (NMC),[44] lithium iron phosphate (LFP),[45,69] lithium nickel cobalt aluminum oxide (NCA), or conversion-type (e.g. $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ ) cathodes[61,63] are utilized as cathodes for AFLMBs. During the initial charging process, Li-ions are delithiated from the cathode and reduced on the surface of the current collectors in the anode. The subsequent discharge and charge processes progressed similarly to the LMBs.

paragraph_context: The absence of excess Li metal brings not only huge advantages but also causes rapid capacity decay of AFLMBs within a few cycles. Owing to the high reactivity of Li metal, active Li is continuously consumed by the reaction with the electrolytes and the formation of dead Li.[35,76-79] Without excess Li metal, CEs are directly related to the reversibility of the Li stripping/plating process. The correlation between the CE and cycle life is shown in Table 1.[42] High CE ( $>99.978\%$ ) is required for AFLMBs to practically compete with commercial LIBs ( $>500$ cycles), but this has not yet been achieved. Even when CE is highly improved to $99.8\%$ , the cell only exhibits $80\%$ capacity retention after only 100 cycles, which is far below the commercialization. Therefore, even if a high initial energy density is achieved through AFLMBs, it drops rapidly within several cycles.

paragraph_context: In the case of AFLMBs, the direct deposition of Li on the surface of the current collector is inevitable. However, impurities or a non-uniform native oxide layer on the surface of the current collector consume active Li and increase the Li nucleation barrier, resulting in adverse effects on the morphology of the initial and subsequent growth of Li.[80] Furthermore, the uneven surface properties of the current collector can induce preferential growth of Li, causing dendrite formation. Therefore, it is important to maintain the surface of the current collector by removing impurities and storing them to prevent contamination to improve the reversibility of Li.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Li is a very strong reducing agent because of the lowest redox potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ vs SHE). Thus, Li reacts intensely with the electrolytes, forming the SEI layer, which passivates the Li sur face to prevent further consumption of Li and electrolytes.[51] However, the SEI layer is usually cracked owing to the large volume change during the charge/discharge process,[53,81] so that fresh Li is inevitably exposed to the electrolytes, leading to the repetitive loss of Li and electrolytes. A thick and non-uniform SEI layer formed by the repeated formation of SEI interferes with Li-ion conduction and induces uneven and dendritic Li deposition. This unfavorable morphology of Li is susceptible to the formation of electrically isolated dead Li,[35,77,78,79] which accelerates active Li loss.[82] In addition to Li loss from direct contact between the electrolyte and Li, galvanic corrosion of Li occurs during the rest period because of spontaneous electron flow due to the difference in the redox potential.[83] During the initial charge process of AFLMBs, Cu substrates are easily exposed to electrolytes. Because the porous, organic-rich SEI formed on the surface of Cu current collectors cannot prevent the entire surface of Cu, the exposed Cu surface becomes a pathway for electron transfer. The electrons from the oxidation of Li are transported to the electrolyte through the exposed Cu, causing the loss of Li with a pit shape and decomposition of the electrolyte simultaneously. Eventually, dendrites were induced during the charging process. Galvanic corrosion, which can significantly reduce the reversibility of Li during the resting period, has not yet been taken seriously; however, considering the actual operation of AFLMBs, much attention is needed.

paragraph_context: Despite the complicated challenges to overcome, the potential benefits of AFLMBs must be apparent. With tremendous lessons learned from both LIBs and LMBs, there have been rapid developments in extending the limited cyclability of AFLMBs. In this review, we discuss current collector modification, electrolyte optimization, cathode engineering, and regulation of cycling parameters in detail to provide an understanding of its impacts and obtain insights. Finally, we provide perspectives on various strategies emphasizing the practicality of AFLMBs.

paragraph_context: A representative strategy to lower the nucleation overpotential and induce lateral Li growth is to introduce elements capable of forming alloys with Li, such as $\mathrm{Au},^{[90,91]}$ Ag,[92,93] Sn,[94,95] Zn,[96,97] and $\mathrm{Mg}^{[98,99]}$ . Yan et al. investigated the nucleation overpotential of 11 elements (Au, Ag, Zn, Mg, Al, Pt, Si, Sn, C, Cu, and Ni). In the case of Au, Ag, Zn, and Mg, the nucleation overpotential is nearly zero because they can form a solid solution at room temperature, which was confirmed by the phase diagram of Li-Au. In the case of Pt and Al, the nucleation overpotentials were observed to be 8 and $5\mathrm{mV}$ at $10\mu \mathrm{Acm}^{-2}$ , respectively, because both elements have relatively low solubility in Li metal. In contrast, Cu and Ni, which cannot form an alloy with Li, show a clear overpotential of approximately $30\mathrm{mV}$ . C, Sn, and Si can form an alloy with Li metal but cannot be soluble in Li metal, resulting in a nucleation overpotential of $\approx 15\mathrm{mV}$ at the same current density. In this context, researchers have attempted to modify Cu current collectors by introducing lithophilic elements such as $\mathrm{Au},^{[100]}\mathrm{Ag},^{[101-105]}\mathrm{Sn},^{[49,106,107]}\mathrm{Zn},^{[108]}\mathrm{SiO}_x,[69] \mathrm{Te},^{[109]}$ and $\mathrm{GaInSn}^{[110]}$ to enhance the electrochemical performance and Li plating morphology of AFLMBs.

Furthermore, the alloying potential during Li deposition is approximately $0.75\mathrm{V}$ (vs $\mathrm{Li^{+} / Li}$ ), resulting in a large proportion of the LiF-rich SEI layer. To prove the practical application of E-Cu, the authors fabricated a 120-mA h scale anode-free lithium metal pouch cell. Likewise, the ICE and capacity retention after 50 cycles of E-Cu were recorded as $85\%$ and $84\%$ , respectively, but that of bare Cu only exhibited $78\%$ and $66\%$ , and the nucleation overpotential of practical anode-free lithium metal full-cell was highly improved (Figure 3G). paragraph_context: Because of the highly reactive nature of Li metal and the low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) level of the electrolyte, the electrolytes were chemically and electrochemically degraded to generate a non-uniform SEI layer during the charging of the AFLMBs. The in-situ generated SEI layer has inhomogeneity in both chemical species and physical properties; hence, it suffers from uncontrollable Li dendritic growth and rapid cell failure.[35] On the other hand, the ex-situ generated SEI layer, the so-called artificial SEI layer, can sufficiently provide the properties that the SEI layer should have, such as mechanical strength, dielectric constant, ionic conductivity, spatial homogeneity, fast ionic conductivity, and low interfacial resistance. Various materials have been adopted for artificial coating for many different purposes; therefore, we will discuss representative substances among them.

paragraph_context: Carbonaceous materials have also been reported to improve the electrochemical performance of AFLMBs, benefiting from their mechanical strength and flexibility, and Li-ion diffusion ability. Assegie et al. introduced multilayer-graphene (MLG) onto electropolished Cu current collectors via chemical vapor deposition (CVD).[52] The number of layers was carefully controlled to 1-5 layers of graphene by varying the heating temperature, gas flow rate $(\mathrm{CH}_4 / \mathrm{H}_2)$ , and growth time. Both the nucleation and plateau overpotentials were enhanced owing to the interfacial stability and ability to distribute the local current density of the MLG. In addition, the cyclability of the MLG-protected anode was improved compared to bare Cu and single-layer graphene in Li||Cu half-cells and Cu||LFP full-cells. In particular, the discharge capacity of MLG anodes at the 100th cycle was approximately $92.62\mathrm{m}$ Ah $\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ , which corresponds to $61.34\%$ of initial discharge capacity and $\approx 99\%$ of CE, whereas, bare Cu only delivered $46\%$ of initial capacity after 100 cycles. The electrodeposited Li metal on the MLG anodes showed a nondendritic, chunky morphology, while bare Cu had highly dendritic, porous features. Furthermore, spin coating,[50] capillary liquid bridge,[113] and micro-patterning[114] were also adopted to introduce a graphene-like carbon layer for controlling the Li growth morphology to achieve high-performance AFLMBs.

paragraph_context: Meanwhile, a metal oxide nanofilm with high electrical resistance has been proposed to control the Li metal deposition morphology (Figure 4C). Though the structure of SEI is not fully understood yet,[58,76] it is well-known that anion-derived SEI components (i.e. inorganic-based SEI layer) are in favor of reversible Li stripping/plating compared to those solvent-derived ones (i.e. organic-based SEI layer) because of the high (electro)chemical stability and insulating nature of inorganic SEI components, especially LiF.[56,121] In this regard, Li-ion solvation structure engineering is getting tremendous attention.[56,123,124] When Li-ions in the electrolyte electrodeposited on the anode during the charging, desolvation should occur, which involves breaking the interactions between the solute and solvent molecules and FIGURE 5 Schematic representation of high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) and localized high-concentration electrolytes (LHCEs), and their applications. Solvents with strong Li-ion solvation strength, such as 1,2-dimethoxyethane (i.e. DME) or ethylene carbonate (i.e. EC), form solvent-rich solvation shells due to strong interactions with Li ions. The free solvent on the electrode surface that occurs during desolvation reacts with the Li metal to form an organic-rich SEI layer, resulting in poor electrochemical stability. On the other hand, solvents with weak Li-ion solvation strength increase the interactions between Li ions and anions in the solvation sheath rather than the interactions with the solvent, resulting in anion-derived, inorganic-rich SEI layer. This excellent cycle performance of the AFLSBs is attributed to the intrinsic properties of stabilizing the Li metal in the (AF)LSBs.[157] During the charge and discharge processes of (AF)LSBs, intermediate polysulfide $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_x, 2 < x \leq 8)$ species diffuse to the anode and reduce to ionic conductive $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2$ by reacting with Li metal and stabilizing Li deposition.[158] The use of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ as an active material for anode-free systems is not only advantageous in terms of capacity but also greatly stabilizes the stripping and plating of Li metal. Although AFLSBs have shown higher cyclability than AFLMBs with NMC and LFP cathodes, it is still difficult to achieve more than 100 cycles with proper capacity retention without modification. To improve the reversibility of the Li metal of AFLSBs, Manthiram's group incorporated 10 wt% (vs $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ ) of Te as a cathode additive.[63] Anode-free $\mathrm{Ni}||(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S} + 0.1\mathrm{Te})$ full cells at C/5 attained 50% capacity retention after 240 cycles (Figure 8C). On the other hand, in the case of AFLSBs without Te, the capacity retention dropped to $50\%$ after only 34 cycles. The improved cycle stability with the Te additive is attributed to the formation of soluble polytellurosulfides $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Te}_x\mathrm{S}_y)$ , which are derived from the reaction between Te and lithium polysulfides. As illustrated in Figure 8D, these soluble $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Te}_x\mathrm{S}_y$ diffused to the anode and reacted with Li metal, forming $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Te}\mathrm{S}_3$ and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Te}$ on the Li metal anode. The covalence of the Te-S bonds increases the Li-ion diffusivity through the SEI layer. Te additives are advantageous for improving the stability of Li metal by simply mixing Te with $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ without complex modifications of the anode or cathode owing to the unique characteristics of LSBs. To realize high-performance AFLSBs, not only the stability of the anode, but also the problems of the cathode, such as the low electrical conductivity of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ , low kinetic shuttling of lithium polysulfides, and low utilization of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ must be solved simultaneously.[62,159,160] In this regard, He et al. synthesized an $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ /electrocatalysts $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}/\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8)$ nanoparticle composite via the carbothermal reduction reaction of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$ and $\mathrm{CoSO}_4$ (Figure 8E).[161] Nano-sized Co-based catalysts in intimate contact with $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ accelerate the polysulfide conversion reaction and suppress the shuttle effect, resulting in a high $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ utilization ratio. Finally, they introduced $\mathrm{Te}^{[63]}$ into the $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8/\mathrm{Co}$ cathode to stabilize the anode ( $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8/\mathrm{Co}-\mathrm{Te}$ ). With high $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ loading ( $4\mathrm{mg~cm}^{-2}$ ) at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ , they compared the performance of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8/\mathrm{Co}-\mathrm{Te}$ to $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{C}$ (without electrocatalyst and $\mathrm{Te}$ ) and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8/\mathrm{Co}$ (without $\mathrm{Te}$ ) cathodes (Figure 8F). As expected, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8/\mathrm{Co}-\mathrm{Te}$ cathode delivered a high initial capacity of $1025\mathrm{mA~h~g}^{-1}$ and low capacity decay ( $84\%$ capacity retention after 100 cycles). Surprisingly, anode-free lithium-sulfur pouch cells modified with $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{Co}_9\mathrm{S}_8/\mathrm{Co}-\mathrm{Te}$ under practical conditions ( $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}, 4\mathrm{mg~cm}^{-2}$ and lean electrolyte $4.5\mu\text{l~mg}^{-1}$ ) achieved promising results with a high energy density of $221\text{W~h~kg}^{-1}$ . To enhance the cyclability and capacity of AFLSBs, it is necessary not only to stabilize the anode, but also to prevent the dissolution of polysulfide and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ occurring at the cathode at the same time.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Although irreversible Li loss caused by dead Li and SEI formation occurs in the same manner for AFLMBs and LMBs, replenishment of Li loss does not occur in AFLMBs, resulting in a significant difference in cyclability between LMBs and AFLMBs. To compensate for the initial irreversible loss of Li, pre-lithiation strategies have been widely used in LIBs[162] to compensate the Li loss during the initial charge. Similarly, Wang's group demonstrated an in situ-built Li reservoir during the initial charge.[163] They combined a Li-rich $\mathrm{Li_2CuO_2}$ (LCO) additive with NCM811, $(80 - x)\mathrm{NMC - }x\mathrm{LCO}$ . LCO delivered an irreversible capacity of $321\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ within a potential window of $3.2 - 4.2\mathrm{V}$ . As shown in Figure 9A, the Li reservoir was successively built by incorporating LCO; the reservoir size increased as the amount of LCO increased. With two formation cycles at $0.1\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ for the formation of the Li reservoir, the cycle stability of the Cu/NMC-LCO cells was largely extended. In 2021, motivated by the sacrificial Li compound strategy, Qiao et al. incorporated lithium oxide $\mathrm{(Li_2O)}$ as a sacrificial agent in the cathode for AFLMBs.[64] It should be noted that $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ has been studied extensively in metal-air batteries and as a sacrificial additive for LIBs because of its high theoretical capacity $(\mathrm{O}_2 + 4\mathrm{Li}^+ + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}, 1793\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1})$ .[164,165] By mixing $25\mathrm{wt}\%$ $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ with NCM811, an irreversible capacity of $320\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{NCM}}^{-1}$ attributed to the oxidation of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ appeared during the initial charging process. TTE additives were used to inhibit the oxygen evolution reaction. The nucleophilic reaction of TTE and the superoxide anion $(\mathrm{O}_2^-)$ prevents oxygen evolution and produces a CEI layer composed of LiF, which further increases the oxidative stability of the ether electrolyte. When fabricated as anode-free pouch cells with $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ additive, not only a high energy density of $320\mathrm{W}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ was achieved, but also no significant capacity decay was observed over 200 cycles, and $80\%$ of initial capacity was maintained after 300 cycles. The Li donor reacts irreversibly during the first charging process to form a Li reservoir, and it is very effective in increasing the lifespan of AFLMBs by supplementing Li loss. Huang et al. used lithium oxalate (LO) as an additive in the cathode as the sacrificial Li source.[65] During initial charging, LO irreversibly oxidizes at $4.7\mathrm{V}$ to form Li reservoir and carbon dioxide (Figure 9B). As synthesized $\mathrm{CO}_2$ diffused to the anode and formed a $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ -rich SEI layer on the Li metal.[166] Furthermore, Dong et al. reported $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ additive in AFLMBs. In addition to the formation of a Li reservoir from $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ incorporated into the cathode during the initial charge process, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ coated on the anode reacts with $\mathrm{PF}_5^-$ resulting in a LiF-rich SEI layer. The dual function of the additive resulted in anode-free $\mathrm{Cu@Li_2CO_3/NCM811@Li_2CO_3}$ cells delivering high capacity retention ( $81.60\%$ ) at $1/3\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles.[167] However, the additive takes up weight, which lowers the energy density after the first charging reaction. Therefore, additional additives improve the cycle stability while simultaneously sacrificing the energy density. In the absence of additives, Lin et al. synthesized Li-rich $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{NCM811}$ ( $\mathrm{Li}_2[\mathrm{Ni}_{0.8}\mathrm{Co}_{0.1}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.1}]\mathrm{O}_2$ ) to build a Li reservoir in the anode.[71] When additional Li ions are introduced into NCM811, they are partially stored in tetrahedral sites and the NMC811 is transformed into P3ml type $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{NCM811}$ (Figure 9C). After delithiation, the structure reversibly changed to R3m NCM811. With a partially over-lithiated $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{NCM811}$ cathode, the anode-free pouch cell composed of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.37}[\mathrm{Ni}_{0.8}\mathrm{Co}_{0.1}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.1}]\mathrm{O}_2$ cathode enabled high capacity retention of $84\%$ at 100th cycle and achieved high energy density ( $447~\mathrm{Wh~kg}^{-1}$ ) in the lean electrolyte ( $2\mathrm{g}\left[\mathrm{A}\mathrm{h}\right]^{-1}$ ) and high loading system ( $25\mathrm{mg~cm}^{-2}$ ) in Figure 9D.

Dahn et al. investigated the effects of pressurized conditions on anode-free pouch cells with two different electrolytes ( $1\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ dissolved in FEC:DEC and FEC: bis(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl) carbonate, TEFC).[67] Surprisingly, the cyclability of cells containing FEC:DEC was greatly improved to 100 cycles at $1725\mathrm{kPa}$ in Figure 10A. However, a higher pressure (above $1725\mathrm{kPa}$ ) did not further enhance the cyclability because of electrode degradation by polarization growth. In contrast, the cycle life of cells with FEC:TEFC was saturated at a relatively low pressure of $795\mathrm{kPa}$ . In addition, as shown in Figure 10B, the morphology of the plated Li at high pressure ( $485\mathrm{kPa}$ ) with more fluorinated solvents (FEC:TFEC) was more compact than that with FEC:DEC because of the contribution of fluorinated solvents to form LiF-rich SEI layer. Therefore, although higher pressure is beneficial to Li deposition, proper pressurized conditions should be set considering electrolyte properties.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: In addition, the current density seriously affects dendritic growth as Li-ions are depleted near the surface of Li under a higher current density. In 2020, Louli et al. investigated the effects of symmetric and asymmetric charge/discharge rates.[137] They showed that an asymmetric slow charge benefits cyclability more than an asymmetric fast charge or a symmetric charge and discharge (Figure 10C). This was because the slow charge induced a low concentration gradient of Li-ions near the electrode surface, leading to uniform Li growth. Conversely, fast discharge is beneficial for preferential Li stripping owing to the high localized current density of the protrusions.[172,173] Therefore, a flat uniform surface of Li metal was built by an asymmetric faster discharge. However, a slower discharge results in dendritic and tortuous Li metal with high Li-ion gradients on the electrode surface, which deteriorates the cycle life. As shown in Figure 10D, a high-capacity throughput was delivered by the asymmetric slower charge.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Also, adjusting the depth of discharge (DoD) affects the cycle stability of the AFLMBs. The Li reservoir could be formed by controlling the discharging cut-off voltage because Li was not completely removed from the anode owing to the slow kinetics of the cathode during the discharge process (Figure 10E).[137] In situ built Li reservoirs are favorable for extending cycle stability until depletion, as in general Li excess LMBs or Li reservoir strategy of ALFMBs. Louli et al. investigated the correlation between the lower cut-off voltage and the cycle life of anode-free $\mathrm{Cu}||\mathrm{NMC}532$ cells. After fully charged to $4.5\mathrm{V}$ , various cut-off voltages were set to investigate the effects of DoD (Figure 10E). As the lower cut-off voltage is set from $3.0\mathrm{V}$ ( $90\%$ of DoD) to $4.05\mathrm{V}$ ( $23\%$ of DoD), $1.7 - 11.5\mu \mathrm{m}$ of excess Li reservoir is built. As shown in Figure 10F, the low DoD protocol is effective in improving cycle stability and capacity throughput. However, since the discharge capacity is very limited, it must be recharged frequently, and practical applications may be difficult. Therefore, it is important to precisely set the cut-off voltage while carefully considering the balance between cycle stability and discharge capacity. Furthermore, temperature is an important parameter for electrochemistry because it affects the diffusion, viscosity, and rate of the decomposition reaction of the electrolyte.[169,174] In particular, Li becomes softer as the temperature increases, inducing lateral and compact morphologies.[66] However, decompo sition of salts could be accelerated resulting in unsatisfactory cycle performance. Genovese et al. used a hot formation protocol to preserve the electrolyte and benefit from high temperature.[66] As shown in Figure 10G, the capacity retention of the anode-free pouch cell improved when operated at $40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; in contrast, a large capacity decay occurred for the cells operated at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . However, the cycle stability of the cell operated at low temperature was improved dramatically by two initial cycles at $40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with asymmetric charge and discharge (C/10 and D/2) between 3.6-4.5 V. This significant improvement in the hot formation protocol comes from the beneficial SEI layer through active $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ gas generation by the decomposition of LiDFOB during hot formation cycles. Combined with high pressure, anode-free Cu||NMC532 batteries with hot formation protocols operated at low temperatures achieved over 200 cycles with $80\%$ capacity retention (Figure 10H).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Despite numerous efforts dedicated to the research of AFLMBs, there are still many challenges to overcome, including their extremely low cyclability. As a result, in this section, we focus on the broad issues and prospects for future research on AFLMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Commercial carbonate-based electrolytes for LIBs are not applicable to practical AFLMBs because of their higher reactivity with Li metal. Even at high operating pressures, the discharge capacity of pouch cells containing commercial carbonate-based electrolytes reached zero in approximately 30 cycles. In this context, ether-based electrolytes have attracted considerable attention owing to their compatibility with Li metal. As mentioned earlier, the low oxidation stability, which is considered a major disadvantage of ether-based electrolytes, was alleviated by HCEs, LHCEs, or fluorination of solvent molecules. In particular, fluorination of solvent molecules not only improves their oxidative stability but also increases the proportion of LiF in the SEI layer, resulting in state-of-the-art anode-free lithium metal pouch-cell performance. On the other hand, these strategies have a trade-off relationship between electrochemical performance and high contents of fluorine elements in electrolytes, which causes severe cost and environmental issues.[47,125] As a result, fluorine-free or low-fluorine electrolytes have been gaining immense attention in the research field of alkali metal anodes.[6,175] In Section 2, various fabrication processes have been discussed to enhance the electrochemical reversibility of the Li plating/stripping process on Cu current collectors, including ALD,[176] CVD,[52] spin coating,[50,51] and doctor-blade coating.[105,112,177] However, most papers do not clearly state if these methods are practical for large-scale production. The current collectors for AFLMBs should be designed to meet the demands of large-scale production and automatic operation, just like how cathodes and anodes for LIBs are optimized for roll-to-roll processes.[178] Adopting the roll-to-roll process of current LIB production lines to AFLMBs would ensure economic feasibility, which is crucial for commercialization. For example, the silver-carbon composites,[105] which we introduced earlier, can be easily applied to the roll-to-roll process, as it is similar to producing graphite anodes for LIBs. Conversely, thin-film manufacturing processes such as ALD and CVD can be adapted for roll-to-roll processes,[179,180] but they differ significantly from the current LIB manufacturing processes. Therefore, new production lines are necessary for practical applications. On the other hand, the spin coating technique can only be utilized in batch processes, making it unsuitable for roll-to-roll processing. In summary, while there are various approaches to modifying Cu current collectors, only few are applicable to large-scale production and automated processes. Therefore, in-depth research on fundamental understandings of current collectors and practical research on achieving high-energy AFLMBs through modification of current collectors should be carried out simultaneously. Finally, various electrochemical evaluations for the modification of the current collectors should be performed under strict conditions to confirm their feasibility in large-scale cell.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: AFLMBs meet the social need for high energy density, which can maximize the range of electric vehicles and expand their applications. Accordingly, a low E/C ratio (amount of electrolyte to the capacity of the cathode, under $3\mathrm{g}\mathrm{Ah}^{-1}$ ) and high areal capacity of the cathode (over $3.8\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ ) should be satisfied to achieve a high energy density AFLMBs.[181] However, many papers have recently reported the fabrication of anode-free lithium metal full cells with low-loading cathodes and flooded electrolytes. In such cases, assessments of the practical application of the strategy may be doubted because the cyclability of AFLMBs under harsh conditions is completely different from that under mild conditions. For instance, when $4\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ of the cathode is operated at $0.25\mathrm{C}$ , a current density of $1\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ is applied to the anode (if the sizes of the cathode and anode are equal), but in the case of $1\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ an equal current density is applied at $1\mathrm{C}$ . In addition, electrolyte drying due to the reaction with Li metal increases dramatically with Li utilization. Consequently, the test protocol and conditions should be carefully established to demonstrate the practical application of this strategy.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: The inherent limitations of the AFLMBs are obvious. With zero excess Li, even if a CE of $99.9\%$ is achieved, only $80\%$ of the initial capacity can be maintained for 223 cycles (Table 1). Therefore, sacrificial cathode additives, such as $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}^{[64]}$ and Lithium oxalate (LO)[65] which provide excess Li at the cathode, should be introduced to extend the cycle life of AFLMBs. Because an LMB with a thin Li anode suffers from (1) high production cost, (2) energy-intensive, repetitive rolling process, and (3) thickness control limit,[182,183] sacrificial cathode additive in AFLMBs is considered to be a better option for excess Li. Moreover, the introduction of sacrificial additives slightly reduces the energy compared to the typical AFLMBs, but it is believed that a high energy density and cyclability can be achieved simultaneously by investigating the optimal point for the capacity of the sacrificial additive. Finally, it is anticipated that by simultaneously implementing the various fundamental approaches outlined above, many issues with AFLMBs can be resolved.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In conclusion, AFLMBs are regarded as promising systems because of their unique cell configuration, in which the energy density is maximized. Furthermore, the absence of highly reactive Li metal for initial cell fabrication gives rise to significant advantages, such as easy processability, reduced cost, and high safety. However, the rapid capacity degradation and low cyclability by parasitic reaction of Li and low reversibility are major concerns for AFLMBs. In this review, fundamental issues and major challenges are presented, and recently reported major strategies are summarized. To overcome the challenging nature of metallic Li, many efforts have been devoted to suppressing dendrites, dead Li, and electrolyte consumption by focusing on developing beneficial layers through the artificial coating on current collectors and electrolyte modification. In addition, cathode engineering and various protocols are proven to be effective in extending the cycle life of AFLMBs. To cope with the limitation of the limited inventory of Li, these strategies should be combined to give a synergistic effect in enhancing the reversible reaction of Li. Finally, as we provide in perspective, practical electrolytes and current collector modifications should be considered and tested with practical testing conditions and the impact of various sacrificial agents should be explored for future AFLMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The upsurging demand for electric vehicles and the rapid consumption of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) calls for LIBs to possess high energy density and resource sustainability. The former requires the usage of electroactive materials with high capacity and the maximum amount within the fixed electrode volume. The latter essentially creates a closed-loop circulation scenario for electroactive materials. In all aspects, binders are of practical significance in bonding electroactive materials, maintaining electrode integrity and detaching electrode slurry from the current collector. Currently, the key role of binders in enhancing the electrochemical behavior of sustainable high-capacity electroactive materials has been recognized. Meanwhile, binders that are designed for easy and cost-effective recycling of electroactive materials are gradually reported. Herein, recently developed binders that hold promises in establishing sustainable high-energy-density LIBs are summarized. The role of binder in facilitating easy separation of electroactive materials are first highlighted. Subsequently, special attention is paid to conductive binders, contributing to less battery chemistries and higher energy density of electrode. Additionally, progress of emerging binders in high-capacity electroactive materials are also reviewed. It is believed that the advances in binders will open up opportunities for establishing a sustainable high-energy-density battery economy.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been well recognized as the primary power source for electric vehicles (EVs) due to their inherent advantages in energy density, cycling properties, and manufacturing cost.[1] According to the estimation from International Energy Agency (IEA), there will be over 145 million EVs in use in 2030. The rapid uptake of EVs has further propelled the accelerated growth of the power LIB market.[2,3] Thus, this scenario also triggers raised concerns among LIBs regarding energy density and resource sustainability.[4-6,7] On the one hand, LIBs are regularly required to possess higher energy density to mitigate the "range anxiety" of EVs.[8] On the other hand, the production capacity of LIBs reaches over 1000 GWh. Considering their 6-8 years' service life, these will usher in a wave of end-of-life LIBs.[9] How to environmentally friendly dispose of spent LIBs is raising increasing attention.[10,11] In this context, the urgent demand of modern society is to develop high-energy-density LIBs with desirable sustainability.[12] The innovation of battery materials is instrumental in achieving sustainable high-energy-density LIBs.[13] For example, electroactive materials attract the Among inactive materials within the LIBs, polymeric binder plays an important role in bonding electroactive materials with Figure 1. Reproduced with permission.[37] Copyright 2020, The Royal Society of Chemistry. conductive additives on the surface of the current collector as well as maintaining electrode integrity during the repeated charging/discharging procedures.[21] In recent decades, the progress of binders is frequently highlighted in their contribution to the energy density of LIBs, which are specifically manifested in two aspects.[4] First, the functional groups introduced into or grafted on the polymeric binders can confer stronger adhesion, which efficiently deals with the volume effect of high-capacity electroactive materials including Si and S.[22] Second, the use of conductive binders allows the electrode to free conductive additives in the electrode fabrication, contributing to a further increased energy density.[23,24] Moreover, an emerging benefit of binders is their potential for sustainability.[25] Binders with reversible adhesion ability are promising in assisting fast liberation of electroactive materials from the current collector. These collected electroactive materials can then be directly recycled or regenerated for reuse in new LIBs, creating a closed-loop circulation scenario of battery materials.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Herein, we review the recent progress in the binders for sustainable high-energy-density LIBs. Begin by addressing the main obstacles and challenges in separation pretreatment technology, we emphasize the role of binders in facilitating easy separation of electroactive materials. A series of pioneering works are highlighted to showcase the effectiveness of binders in this regard. We then delve into the importance of electrically conductive binders, which simplify battery chemistries and enable a significant increase in the amount of electroactive materials within the limited electrodes. Subsequently, conductive binders tailored for high-energy-density electroactive materials, such as Si and S, are essentially summarized. Finally, we conclude by providing a perspective on the potential of conductive binders and their further contribution to the realization of high-energy-density LIBs with enhanced resource sustainability.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Recycling spent LIBs is an ideal solution to not only establishing resource sustainability of battery materials but also guaranteeing the ecological safety of human beings.[26,27] Further, efficient recycling technologies of spent LIBs are highly desired toward a closed-loop development scenario.[28] The existing challenges remain in the separation of battery components. Normally, a typical LIB has at least 12 components with different physical and chemical properties. Such a complex matrix within the LIBs fundamentally brings difficulties in recycling valuable electroactive materials. State-of-the-art technologies related to spent LIB recycling typically rely on a combination of pyro-, and hydrometallurgical processes (Figure 1a).[29] Specifically, pyro-metallurgy applies high temperatures to directly refine the spent LIBs, extracting valuable metal resources in the form of metal alloy. This undifferentiated treatment of various battery materials undoubtedly leads to low recycling efficiency.[5] In comparison, hydrometallurgical technologies consist of a series of separation, dissolution, and purification processes to extract metal elements separately.[30] Massive spent LIBs are first crushed into powder. Subsequently, the essential separation based on the particle size, material density, magnetic susceptibility, electrical conductivity, and chemical properties (such as gravity, magnetic, eddy current,electrostatic, and froth flotation separation) is employed. For example, the removal of the Fe and steel casing is readily achieved by magnetic technologies. Meanwhile, magnetic separation is further used to sieve the Co-based materials from the powders. The Cu and Al foils are also separated by gravity separation due to the density differences.[7] Low-density substances, such as plastics and graphite, are also separated by the flotation process. After a series of physical separation, the collected powder is the so-called "black powder". These black powders are further soaked in the acid solution for the extraction of high-value metal elements.[31] Although the above-mentioned recycling techniques have been industrialized, profitable recycling routes tailored for spent LIBs remain elusive,[11] especially for the less-valued LFP cathode that lacks valuable metal resources within, such as Cobalt (Co) and Nickel (Ni) elements.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: More recently, direct recycling or direct regeneration that aims at structurally restoring electroactive materials with minimal chemicals and energy inputs holds great promise in fulfilling a sustainable recycling scenario (Figure 1a,b).[32,33] The succeeding challenge is that either direct recycling or direct regeneration essentially requires a prerequisite of obtaining high-purify electroactive materials.[34] However, current battery chemistry restricts the fast and effective separation of high-purify electroactive materials. Specifically, the liberation of electroactive materials from the polymeric binder and conductive additive is not a simple matter. The strong adhesion of polymeric binder makes electroactive particles tightly bonded to the conductive additive and current collectors (Figure 1c). For example, commercial LIBs normally implement poly(vinylidene difluoride) (PVDF) as binders and carbon black as conductive additives. PVDF is a highly non-reactive fluoropolymer with a chemical formula of $(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{F}_2)_n$ . Such an extremely hydrophobic characteristic together with excellent resistance to chemicals unavoidably makes its elimination difficult.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Currently, two strategies are used to decouple the PVDF and cathode. One route to liberate the cathode from the binder is a solvent-based solution. Dipolar aprotic solvents, including $N$ -methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and $N,N$ -dimethylformamide (DMF), are normally applied to dissolve PVDF. Although the use of organic solvent exhibits high efficacy in separating cathode and the recycling of partial PVDF, the management, use, and disposal of these volatile organic solvents pose ecological risks. Therefore, stricter regulations have been released on limiting the industrial applications of these solvents.[38] Compared with the solvent-based solution, pyrolysis is a more preferential approach for PVDF removal in the industrial sector. In an inert atmosphere, high temperature enables the PVDF decomposition into amorphous carbon and fluorocarbons. More studies are focused on temperature controlling.[39,40] The decomposition temperature of PVDF starts at $\approx 475^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . If the decomposition temperature is insufficient, the incomplete removal of PVDF and toxic gas products is undesirable for the industrial sector.[41] If the thermal treatment is over $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the decomposition of cathode materials also occurs in this process.[42] Generally, the efficient removal of the PVDF has been optimized at the pyrolysis temperature of $500 - 700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .[40] Even if the thermal treatment is the most straightforward method to liberate electroactive materials from the PVDF, stricter requirements are also placed on the post-treatment section to minimize the environmental impacts. For example, the formed HF gas is essentially absorbed by alkali solutions. Meanwhile, other fluorocarbons generated from the pyrolysis process also pose a great threat to the environment.[40,41] Although fruitful strategies, such as organic dissolution and heat treatment, have been reported to efficiently remove the binder from recycled electrodes, the use of high energy consumption, chemical inputs, and toxic solvent inevitably reduces the sustainability and economic feasibility of battery recycling. Moreover, researchers also attempted to delaminate the electroactive material by using ethylene glycol but the results showed that only the bonding between the PVDF and current collector was inhibited and most of the PVDF remains in the delaminated electroactive materials.[32] In this context, binders that possess better solubility in non-toxic organic/inorganic solvents, or even water demonstrate better simplicity and sustainability regarding separation.[5] Therefore, separating electroactive materials in a green and effective manner will open up opportunities for establishing a sustainable and closed-loop battery economy at the raw-material level.

paragraph_context: Recently, the design of a reversible binder in sulfur (S) electrodes has shown promise in separating electroactive materials in an environmentally-friendly and effective manner. Specifically, a dissolvable ionic crosslinked polymer (DICP) has been prepared as a binder by crosslinking polyacrylic acid and polyethyleneimine through carboxy-amino ionic interaction,[25] which is pH-controlled and allows the crosslinked binder network to be readily dissociated under basic conditions. The DICP binder can be promptly dissolved in basics, enabling the successful recycling of electroactive materials from spent batteries using a simple water-washing method (Figure 2a). The discharge capacity of refabricated cells is comparable to that of fresh materials. Similarly, a hydrogen bonding crosslinked multi-functional binder has been explored based on lithiated polyacrylic acid-co-vinylphosphonic acid (AA-VPA) and phosphorylated soy protein (P-SPI). More interestingly, such a hydrogen bonding crosslinking between AA-VPA and P-SPI can be readily dissociated under acidic conditions, thus allowing the S-C composite to be easily recycled through an acidic treatment (Figure 2b). These studies provide a promising approach for developing eco-efficient and sustainable large-scale energy storage systems through the use of reversible crosslinked polymer binders, offering guidance for green chemistry and future circular economy.

paragraph_context: Besides the binder, the role of conductive additives primarily ensures fast electric migration between electroactive materials and the current collector since most of the polymeric binders and electroactive materials are isolated. However, the use of conductive additives is inevitably adverse to the energy density of LIBs and makes its elimination difficult in the recycling process. Streamlining battery components smooths the efficient recycling of high-purified electroactive materials. As a recent development, the use of conductive binders is expected to enable conventional cathodes to function without the need for conductive additives.

The conductive process of carriers in the polymer can be directed to form a current, making the electronically conductive premise dependent on having a conjugate structure of the conductive polymer binder. The intrinsic state of a polymer molecule contains $\pi$ -bonded molecular orbitals with a certain energy level difference.[44] This difference impedes the complete freedom of $\pi$ -electrons to migrate across the conjugated system. To enable electron migration within the polymer, it is necessary to overcome this energy level difference, which can be achieved through doping. The purpose of doping is to pull out electrons (p-type) from the empty orbitals of polymers, such as polyaniline,[45] polypyrrole,[46] PEDOT:PSS,[47,48] etc.; or to add electrons (n-type) from the occupied orbitals such as polyfluorene.[49] In turn, the energy level of the existing $\sigma$ -electron energy band is changed and a half-filled energy band with centered energy appears, which reduces the energy differ ence between energy bands and makes the free electrons or holes migrate with less obstructive force, thus leading to a greatly improved conductivity. Generally speaking, p-type conductive polymers such as polyaniline, polypyrrole, PEDOT:PSS can be typically utilized as conductive binders in the positive electrode. For the negative electrode, considering the strong reductive environment, n-type conductive binders such as polyfluorene are applicable.

Such a conductive film also acts as a binder to hold the electroactive materials together. Due to the use Figure 3. paragraph_context: Subsequently, this attempt has also been extended to the $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ (LFP) cathode. Eliseeva and co-authors have successfully proven the feasibility of using the PEDOT:PSS binder for LFP electrode fabrication. At 0.2 C, LFP electrode with PEDOT:PSS delivered a specific capacity of up to $165\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , which substantially exceeds that of the LFP electrode using the conventional compositions. Similarly, Pratik et al further reported the LFP electrode free of carbon black when directly using PEDOT:PSS as the binder.[52] As the PEDOT:PSS content is increased to $8\%$ , the specific capacity, cycling stability, rate capacity, and operation overvoltage of the composite electrode are comparable to those of a conventional composite electrode based on a PVDF binder and carbon additives. In addition, the solid loading of the LFP slurries was further optimized.[53] The optimal electrochemical performance was achieved using slurries with a solid loading of $40\%$ This is likely due to the improved connectivity of polymer chains and inter-chain hopping, resulting in more effective conductive bridges in the 3D electrode compared to a composite of carbon black and insulating binder. In this context, the electrical conductivity, ionic conductivity, and aqueous treatment properties of PEDOT:PSS make it the preferred conductive polymer binder for other cathode and anode active materials (e.g., LCO,[23] LTO[54] and Si[55]).

paragraph_context: PEDOT:PSS can be employed as a conductive binder in combination with conventional binders such as carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), to design a 3D structured conductive binder (PEDOT:PSS/CMC) for the LFP electrode.[56] With CMC component contributing to enhanced adhesive force and the PEDOT:PSS establishing a conducting pathway, the binder amount for the LFP electrode can be substantially reduced to $4\mathrm{wt}.\%$ . Moreover, the introduction of PEDOT:PSS successfully allows the LFP electrode free of conductive additives. The resultant LFP electrode, therefore, establishes a maximized volumetric energy density with 96 wt.% active materials, exhibiting reversible capacity of 148 $\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ and $126\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at rates of $0.2\mathrm{C}$ and $5\mathrm{C}$ respectively, and demonstrating excellent cycling stability with less than $1\%$ decay after 100 cycles. In addition, Zhong and co-authors reported a water-soluble conductive composite binder consisting of carboxymethyl chitosan (CCTS) and PEDOT:PSS,[48] which provided the dual role of adhesive bonding and electronic conduction to enable long cycling lifespan of the electrode at the acceptable rate. Specifically, a 10 Ah LFP pouch cell using PEDOT:PSS/CCTS binder displayed stable cycling performance of over 1000 cycles with a capacity retention of $89.7\%$ at a $1\mathrm{C} / 2\mathrm{C}$ (charge/discharge) rate. Even without carbon additives, the PEDOT:PSS/CCTS binder assured a higher rate capability of the LFP electrode than that with commercial PVDF binder. Similarly, PEDOT:PSS has been implemented in combination with co-binding polymers such as poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) or sulfonated poly(phenylene oxide) (SPPO),[57] resulting in LFP electrode exhibiting a high specific capacity of up to $120\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ and areal capacity of up to $2\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ at 1 C, even at a thicker electrode, with excellent cycling stability. For now, the PEDOT:PSS binder offers a strong candidate to replace conventional binders and conductive additives, as evidenced by the above studies exhibiting rather satisfactory electrochemical values that exceed those of LFP electrodes fabricated with conventional methods under the same conditions.

paragraph_context: Apart from the PEDOT:PSS polymer, massive conductive polymers, such as polyetheramines,[58] polyetherthioureas,[59] and ionic copolymers[60] have also been applied to LFP electrodes. For example, the 3,4-propylenedioxythiophene-2,5-dicarboxylic acid (ProDOT) has been explored by Lin et al combining with sodium alginate (SA) to form SA-PProDOT composite polymer,[50] as shown in Figure 3b. Due to its various functional groups such as carboxyl, hydroxyl, and ester moieties, the SA-PProDOT binder exhibits remarkable chemical bonding between LFP particles and binder, as well as between binders, indicating an enhanced mechanical adhesion within the electrode. The conjugated structure of PProDOT enabled the formation of an electric-conduction network, allowing the LFP electrode to function without the use of conductive additives. The resultant LFP electrode delivered theoretical specific capacities of $120\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ over 400 cycles. Meanwhile, poly(furfuryl alcohol) (PFA) conductive binder was also proposed by Liu and coauthors to replace PVDF and conductive additive.[51] This PFA binder has a long-range ordered structure of conjugated diene, which allows electronic conductivity and leads to a conductive additive-free electrode fabrication process (Figure 3c). The number of conductive binders added was decreased to below 5 wt.% which would be beneficial for increasing the energy densities of electrodes. The resultant LFP electrode achieved a high electrode density of $2.65\mathrm{gcm}^{-3}$ and therefore the highest volumetric energy density of 1551 Wh $\mathrm{L}^{-1}$ . The LFP electrode using PFA binder exhibited an impressive capacity retention of $\approx 80\%$ and a Coulombic efficiency of over $99.9\%$ after cycling for 500 times.

paragraph_context: Silicon (Si)-based materials are the oft-studied anode due to their high capacity and resource abundance, making Si-based anodes a promising and sustainable option for targeted LIBs.[2,20] However, large volume variation caused by electrochemical Li insertion/extraction process destroys the mechanical integrity and electric transfer of the electrode.[17,61] The practical application of Si-based anode is thus hindered by the volume effect and interfacial instability, which are known to be the root causes of insufficient electrochemical performances.[62] In this context, polymeric binders have had many significant contributions and improvements to the practical applications of Si-based anodes.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Reviewing the development of binders for stable Si-based anodes, conventional PVDF binders are hardly applied for Si-based anodes because of their weak van der Waals interactions with Si-based particles.[63] Since 2011, the conception of hydrogen bonding between binders and Si-based particles has been proposed to significantly arouse the binder design for the satisfactory stable Si-based anode.[19] This is attributed to the stronger mechanical adhesion enabled by an additional bonding ability of binder to defend the volume variation of Si-based particles. The most representative example is the use of sodiated alginate (SA).[19] Moreover, the higher the hydrogen bonding density and the stronger the bonding ability of the binders for the Si-based anode. Following this conception, considerable natural polymers are proposed as the new binders instead of conventional PVDF for robust operation of Si-based anode. For example, gum arabic (GA), naturally composed of polysaccharides and glycoproteins (Figure 4a), has abundant hydroxyl groups to enable strong bonding to Si nanoparticles.[64] Along with enhanced mechanical tolerance to large volume variation of Si nanoparticles, the resultant Si anode delivered a stable cycling performance with a reversible capacity of $\approx 2000\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ In addition, different polymers tend to have different viscoelasticity. The hydrogen bonding is also responsible for generating the network binder based on the mixture of two or more polymeric constituents.[65] For example, in situ cross-linked 3D network binder (c-PAA-DS) based on polyacrylic acid and d-sorbitol was proposed to maintain structural/electrode integrity of S-based anode.[66] The resultant anode exhibited a reversible capacity of $696\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ with tiny capacity decay after 500 cycles. Such a binder design strategy is further explored for the Si microparticles, which are more easily pulverized by the volume variation during the Li uptake and release process as compared with nanoparticle counterparts. For instance, the network binder consisting of ring-slide polyrotaxane and conventional polyacrylic acid (PAA) possessed a robust reversible elastic ability to keep the pulverized Si particles coalesced and maintained the electrode morphology,[63] as shown in Figure 4b. Consequently, with an areal capacity of up to $2.67\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ , the Si anode still preserved $2.43\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ after 150 cycles. Similar manipulation of this network binder is evidenced by combining partially lithiated polyacrylic with partially lithiated Nafion.[62] The resultant Si anode exhibits not only a stable cycling performance for 500 cycles at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ but also a high initial Coulombic efficiency of $93.18\%$ . Therefore, the contribution from the network binder fundamentally enables the feasibility of the Si anode at commercial-level areal capacities.

paragraph_context: Besides the enhanced bonding ability, the development of Si-based binders is evolving towards multi-functional, such as electrical conduction and ionic transfer. Typically, Huo and co-authors grafted $\mathbb{D}$ -sorbitol and vinyl acetateacrylic (VAA) onto electrically conducting polymer poly(3,4- ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) chains.[55] This novel stretchable conductive glue (CG) composite polymer possessed electric conductivity, robust stretchability, and mechanical ductility. When applied as a binder for the Si-based anode, the CG-coated Si nanoparticle during Li uptake and release displayed the reversible volume variation, as shown in Figure 4d. Meanwhile, the conductive CG coating makes Si anode free of the use of conductive additives, maximizing the volume energy density of the Si anode. Similarly, the ability of ionic transfer in the polymer is enabled by the lone-pair electrons on the oxygen of the ether groups, resulting in the movement of complex Li ions between complexation sites assisted by the segmental motion of the polymer matrix. Guided by this strategy, a novel binder (GG-g-PAM) with high ionic conductivity was constructed by grating polyacrylamide (PAM) onto ion-conductive guar gum (GG) backbone.[27] The GG backbone provided abundant oxygen heteroatoms for Li complexation sites to construct the Li-ion pathways for enhancing Li diffusion within the Si anode. Consequently, even at a commercial-level areal capacity of over $3\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ , the Si anode based on GG-g-PAM binder has shown a stable cycling performance. Furthermore, in order to enable these conductive binders low cost and solvent processable, the continuous exploration of conductive binders has been done in polymer research. Unlike the above conductive binders relying on either closely packed, well-aligned structure through $\pi-\pi$ stacking or organic functionalities, a well-organized 3D architecture is proposed by Liu and coauthors to directly achieve the desired functionality (Figure 4e). The hierarchically ordered structures (HOS) with well-defined nanocrystalline morphologies are developed by a thermal process to reduce primary structural complexity. When applied for Si-based anode, this binder successfully enables the stable cycling and high-capacity retention at high-loading condition.

paragraph_context: Sulfur (S) is an extremely rich element in nature.[68] When applied as the electroactive materials for Li storage, the S materials can provide a theoretical specific capacity of over $1600\mathrm{mAh}$ $\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ , relying on the two-electron reaction.[16] However, their practical application is severely hindered by the inherent large volume variation ( $\approx 76\%$ ) between S and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ components in conjunction with the "shuttle effect" stemming from the dissolution/diffusion of long-chain Li polysulfide (LiPS). This is in fact quite akin to the case of Si-based anodes. Considerable studies have also clarified that the binder design substantially contributes to improving their cycling lifespan,[21,51,69] which shares comparable efficacy to the structural modifications of the S-based materials.

paragraph_context: In the recycling process of spent LIBs, the direct regeneration and reuse of recycled electrode materials are well recognized as the most low-carbon and environmentally friendly method compared with metallurgical methods. This is attributed to reduced energy and chemical agents consumption, as well as the shorter processes involved in the structural restoration of electroactive materials. Naturally, the field of battery recycling has a shift of research to develop efficient electrochemical restoration as an alternative technology, aiming at coping with the issues of spent LIBs. However, direct regeneration calls for the precise separation of each component within the LIBs as a prerequisite. This is because the residues of polymeric binder and attached conductive additives can lead to impurities in recycled cathode materials, making the regeneration process challenging. Regretfully, there are few reported cases of mentioning this pre-treatment in the removal of polymeric binder and conductive additive. In nearly all cases regarding direct regeneration, removing these inactive materials within the electrode is critical for the high-purity collection of recycled cathode materials from spent LIBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: For the case of designing recyclable LIBs, the binders are expected to provide various abilities including robust adhesion, reversible elasticity, electric transfer, and chemical inertness. Presently, cases, where conductive binders enable the cathode materials to function without using conductive additives, can be referred to inspire the design of conductive binders for easy recycling. Next, development of conductive binders for robust and recyclable electrodes may be surfaced as a highly researched topic. Due to the use of conductive binders, the resultant electrodes are free of conductive additives and gradually evolve to have binary components instead of ternary components in conventional design. If such a conductive binder is water-soluble, the electroactive materials are readily separated through an aqueous treatment. Moreover, the recyclability of binders integrated into the Si or S electrodes should be investigated to pave the way for future sustainable and easy recycling.

The adhesive failure of the binder allows the electrode slurry to be separated from current collector. Moreover, when using conductive binders for electrode fabrication, the benefits not only are highlighted in the easy separation of electrode materials stemming from no conductive additive but also in the increased energy density of LIBs by filling more electroactive materials in limited volume. Furthermore, along with the alternative of Si- and S-based materials to conventional electrode materials, together with the development of conductive binders made from natural materials, the LIBs trends to achieve a true ecologically compatible product.
