paragraph_context: As the global energy structure transforms and renewable energy rapidly develops, rechargeable batteries are increasingly focus on high energy density, rapid charge/discharge rates, and enhanced safety performance, particularly in extreme environments. Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have emerged as a significant research area in recent years owing to high capacity and low electrochemical potential of lithium (Li). However, challenges, uncontrolled Li dendrite growth, unstable solid electrolyte interface and separator puncture/interface incompatibility, greatly impact battery life and lead to battery failure, thus impeding commercialization. This review presents a thorough analysis of the key challenges facing stable LMBs from multiple perspectives, alongside potential regulatory strategies. The methods include Li anode, Li metal interface, solid/liquid electrolytes, separators, pressure and artificial intelligence. An in-depth discussion on operational mechanism, advantages/drawbacks of methods is provided. Additionally, it offers a succinct overview of anticipated future trends and potential challenges. A comprehensive review of numerous documents and studies has been conducted to summarize the number of published papers and unique characteristics of corresponding strategies. This review provides valuable recommendations for the practical application of other high-energy-density metal batteries (Sodium, Potassium, Magnesium, Zinc), thereby contributing effectively to the implementation of national strategic planning in the new energy sector.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Amid the global energy transition, lithium (Li)-ion $(\mathrm{Li^{+}})$ batteries (LIBs), integral to core technologies, have experienced a steady increase in market demand.[1] These batteries, omnipresent in our daily lives, power everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to wearable devices.[2] The performance of LIBs, particularly their energy density and safety, largely depends on the choice of anode materials.[3] Graphite anode materials, traditionally used in LIBs, have reached a performance plateau.[4] As technology advances and market demands increase, there is a growing interest in superior anode materials. Lithium metal anodes (LMAs), owing to their high specific capacity and working voltage, are gaining prominence as a promising direction for future LIBs anode material development.[5] The theoretical specific capacity of an LMA reaches an impressive $3860\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ [5a,6] This is notably ten times greater than that of the graphite anode currently used in commercialized LIBs. The use of lithium metal as an anode could, therefore, potentially enhance the energy density and overall performance of the battery.[7] Additionally, LMAs offer cost benefits both in terms of raw materials and processing, reducing total costs by $14\%$ compared to traditional liquid LIBs. Nevertheless, the industrialization of the LMAs presents significant challenges.[8] The challenges including production costs, technical barriers, and safety concerns persist. Particularly in the conventional liquid battery system, the stability of the LMAs remains a significant issue.[9] This manifests through uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth, loss of active Li, an unstable solid electrolyte interface (SEI), significant volume expansion, flammability and slow lithium-ion transport kinetics within the electrolyte, low coulombic efficiency and energy density.[10] The ease of separator puncture and its incompatibility with the electrode interface further limit the commercial application of lithium metal batteries (LMBs).[11] The advent of solid-state batteries offers new potential for LMAs.[12] However, the substantial resistance caused by the solid-solid contact between the solid electrolyte and the electrode interface impedes its development.[12,13] In order to improve the performance and safety of lithium metal rechargeable batteries, a variety of strategies have been implemented. These strategies include modifying the Li anode (encompassing quality, structure, and conductivity), the SEI film, the liquid/solid electrolyte, ionic liquids, and separators.[14] Despite these efforts, when operating at high rates or in particularly harsh environments, LMBs confront amplified safety hazards, diminished performance, significantly curtailed battery life, and outright failure.[15] As battery technology continues its rapid advancement and industrialization accelerates, the application prospects for LMBs are expanding.[16] It is crucial to continually explore innovative approaches and incorporate multidisciplinary knowledge to improve performance of LMBs. Concurrently, enhancing the monitoring and management of battery storage and usage environments is crucial to mitigate potential risks.[17] A comprehensive and in-depth review is urgently needed to guide the future research and development of stable LMBs with high safety, high energy density, industrialization ability to work under harsh environments (such as polar, deep sea, etc).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Herein, we survey the key challenges and latest advances in the development of LMBs with high-safety and high-rate, offering valuable insights for relevant industries and researchers, which is complementary to other recent existing reviews.[1,8,10a,c,13b,18] Initially, we review working mechanisms and analyze the critical challenges associated with stable LMBs. Subsequently, we review the most recent representative strategies of cell components for achieving stable LMBs, focusing on LMAs regulation, Li metal interface engineering, electrolyte adjustment, advanced separators, emerging solid electrolytes/solid-state interface engineering, pressure, and artificial intelligence. The mechanisms, challenges, performance, and applications of these strategies are thoroughly discussed. Finally, we summarize and forecast the future development of LMBs. We believe that in the coming years, LMBs will usher in a new era, making significant contributions to the global energy transition and the advancement of a green economy.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Research on LMBs dates back to the 1970s when Whittingham et al. at ExxonMobil invented the first rechargeable lithium-based battery.[19] These first-generation LMBs, comprised of a lithium-aluminum anode and a $\mathrm{TiS}_2$ cathode, demonstrated high energy density and rapid charging rates.[20] The working principle of LMBs is mainly based on the deposition and stripping process of lithium ions.[21] During the charging process, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ is reduced to metallic Li on the surface of the anode by gaining electrons, gradually resulting in the formation of a plating layer on the anode.[19] Conversely, during discharge, the metal is oxidized to $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and reinserted into the cathode.[17a] This deposition/stripping process is influenced by the thermodynamics and kinetics of heterogeneous nucleation.[17a,19] Various factors, including the composition of the electrolyte, temperature, current density, and the properties of the anode collector, and so on, determine the efficiency and deposited morphology of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and influence the performance and lifespan of the battery.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In LMBs, the various challenges, such as unstable and irreversible passivation SEI, infinite relative volume change, the uncontrollable growth of Li dendrites, low coulombic efficiencies (CEs), and formation of "dead Li" faced by Li anodes are not independent of each other, but are interrelated and affect the cell performance of LMBs together (Figure 1a).[10b] The high reactivity and low potential of lithium anode cause them to react immediately with the electrolyte, forming an interfacial SEI film.[22] The SEI film, composed of organic and inorganic compounds such as Lithium oxide $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O})$ , Lithium fluoride (LiF), Lithium chloride (LiCl), Lithium carbonate $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)$ , Lithium carboxylate $(\mathrm{LiCO}_2\cdot \mathrm{R})$ , alkoxides, and nonconductive polymers, varies depending on the electrolyte composition.[23] Specifically, the side adjacent to the electrolyte exhibits a porous architecture, while the side near the electrode is designed to be dense.[23d] The SEI film enables the passage of lithium ions while blocking electrons, preventing further depletion of lithium ions and electrolyte decomposition and ensuring an efficient charge/discharge cycle.[23f,24] This functionality enhances the overall cycling lifespan of batteries.[24,25] While the SEI can maintain stability within organic electrolyte solutions, its stability is affected by various factors such as the composition of the electrolyte, the formation current, temperature, and the specific type of anode material used.[26] The composition, structure, thickness, and stability of the SEI film are critical to LMBs performance.[26b] Therefore, optimizing these factors is essential for developing safe, high-rate batteries with improved SEI functionality.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: During the charging/discharging process, lithium deposition leads to volume expansion.[27] Due to the unique conversion-type mechanism of metallic lithium anode, which alternates between presence and absence, its volume expansion during deposition can be infinite. This substantial volume changes generates mechanical stress, leading to the fracture of the SEI film over repeated electrochemical cycles.[14b,28] The resulting microcrack creates low-diffusion-barrier sites, promoting preferential $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ deposition and dendrite formation through the tip effect.[29] Additionally, fresh lithium exposed during this process accelerates electrolyte consumption, causing capacity loss and reduced CEs.[23b] To address these issues, minimizing volume expansion is critical for extending the cycle life of LMBs.[9a,30] Effective strategies include constructing 3D host structures and developing alternative metal anodes.[3,31] This will be discussed in detail later.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The growth of Li dendrite can cause failure of LMBs.[32] The uniform deposition of Li is closely related to the spatial distribution of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and electrons on the surface of Li anode.[5b,6] This distribution is influenced by several factors, including the anode materials (crystal structure, surface morphology, chemical composition), electrolyte properties (composition, concentration, viscosity, conductivity), and charge-discharge conditions (rate, temperature, voltage).[27,29,33] Charge density is inversely proportional to the surface's radius of curvature, meaning that sharper protrusions have a higher surface charge density and a stronger local electric field.[34] The accumulation of charges promotes the growth of lithium deposits, ultimately leading to the formation of dendrites.[34] Defects caused by repeated SEI fracture and formation, as well as nonuniform voids in the separators, can cause an uneven electric field and ionic current, further accelerating the uncontrollable growth of dendrites.[14c,23d,34] Additionally, the lower temperatures lead to a reduced diffusion rate of lithium ions,[35] while a higher charging rate leads to more severe dendrite formation. Li dendrites primarily deposit in three modes: moss-like, dendritic, and granular.[36] Their thickness can reach tens to hundreds of microns, potentially penetrating the separators and resulting in a short circuit or even an internal explosion of batteries.[9a] Furthermore, some dendrites may detach from the lithium anode due to their fragile structure after multiple plating/stripping cycles.[9a] Once encapsulated by the isolated SEI layer, they become "dead Li", reducing the actual capacity and cycle life of LMBs.[5b,9a] The emergence of lithium dendrites amplifies the risk of side reactions within the battery.[29] This not only depletes the valuable active lithium metal but also results in electrolyte loss, thereby diminishing the battery's coulombic efficiency.[30] To maintain battery operation, it is imperative to increase the amount of electrolyte added, however, this inevitably compromises the energy density of the battery.[37] Furthermore, the fragile structure of the lithium dendrites makes them susceptible to breakage, which produces dead lithium.[6] This dead lithium, separated from the collector, is unable to continue participating in the electrochem- ical reaction, further reducing the battery's coulombic efficiency and posing a threat to its energy density and cycle stability.[29] As electric vehicle technology continues to evolve, the demands for enhanced battery performance intensify, particularly concerning cycle stability under conditions of high rate and large current density. High rates and large current densities can lead to an increase in resistance and the occurrence of polarization phenomena. They also can result in capacity degradation and a decline in cyclic stability. This presents a significant challenge to the durability and operational lifespan of electric vehicles.

paragraph_context: The limited specific surface area and atomic-level flatness of the conventional Li anodes not only hinder the establishment of a uniform electric field but also negatively impact the uniform Li nucleation. In contrast, Li anodes with high surface area can provide more nucleation sites and reduce the local current density, which helps achieve more uniform ionic flux and electric field distribution.[38] Meanwhile, a porous electrode structure is beneficial to improve the penetration of electrolytes and increase the ion diffusion kinetics, realizing the efficient utilization of the Li anodes.[39] Therefore, the design and optimization of Li anode structures have broad prospects for tailoring Li deposition behavior. paragraph_context: Mechanical processing is a simple, processable, and cost-effective method to achieve a dendrite-free electrochemical process.[43] Highly ductile metals can be readily molded or deformed to create large mechanical strains on the surface patterns. The patterned surface can reduce the current density on the surface of Li metal by expanding the surface area of the Li metal and reducing the formation of Li dendrites during battery operation.[44] Stamping is an effective method of mechanical processing. Ryou et al.[43] first applied skin needling to surface roughening to construct a large-surface-area Li metal anode with an abundance Li plating sites. The anode showed high electrochemical performance compared with bare Li. Inspired by this simple but effective methods, Park et al.[40] investigated the use of surface-patterned Li that was pretreated with a commercial microneedle roller (Figure 3a,b). The relationship between the pattern size and Li deposition behavior was systematically verified with finite element analysis and postmortem examination. After stamping, the anode exhibited reversible plating and stripping without dendrite growth in the surface-patterned holes. To further improve the interface lithophilic of the electrode, Zhu et al.[41] fabricated a hierarchically porous Copper (Cu) with lithophilic $\mathrm{Cu}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{O}$ (HPCu-Cu $_{\mathrm{x}}$ O) via a simple femtosecond laser method. The HPCu-Cu $_{\mathrm{x}}$ O possessed a unique hierarchical porous architecture that facilitated homogeneous Li nucleation and deposition while also offering ample space to counter volume expansion, thus preventing damage (Figure 3c,d). As a result, the HPCu-Cu $_{\mathrm{x}}$ O@Li based cell exhibited significantly decreased overpotential, high Coulombic efficiency, and exceptional plating/stripping behavior. Cui et al.[42] presented a stretchable Li metal anode demonstrating stable mechanical characteristics and electrochemical performance (Figure 3e,f). The anode featured single-entity 3D patterned Li metal micro-domains linked by highly elastic polymer rubber. Remarkably, the entire electrode was constructed using a single Cu wire, making the fabrication process simple and economical. This novel design of the Li metal anode not only imparted high stretchability to the electrode but also significantly improved the cycling stability of the Li anode. 3D stainless-steel mesh and a Cu net-modified Li metal anode were also employed in LMAs.[45] The capacity of deposited lithium was often significantly larger in rapid-charging or large-scale energy storage devices. When this exceeded the capacity of the storage medium, the lithium grew out of the pores, leading to the formation of dendrites.

paragraph_context: Compared to the 2D Li anode, the 3D Li anode significantly increases the specific surface area, provides more storage space, and promotes the even distribution of localized current density and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ .[46] It also offers sufficient nucleation sites for $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ adsorption. Moreover, 3D porous configuration anodes allow for diverse geometries and compositions, thereby surpassing the structural constraints of 2D Li foils. They also effectively modulated the lithiophilic of the anode and the solvation structure of the electrolyte.[47] This leads to precise control over ion distribution and ion deposition energy, fostering a dendrite-free and side reaction-minimized Li anode.[48] The composition of the supporting current collector mainly comprises metal-based, carbon-based, and conductive polymer materials. Specially, the reported metal based 3D Li Metal materials had Cu mesh,[49] nickel (Ni) foam,[50] Cu wires,[51] and porous titanium (Ti),[52] gold (Au),[53] silver (Ag),[54] tin (Sn),[55] silicon (Si),[56] zinc (Zn),[57] magnesium (Mg),[58] aluminum (Al),[59] and platinum (Pt)[60] with lithiophobic properties, metal oxides, metal sulfides (copper sulfide),[61] nitrides (such as copper nitride ( $\mathrm{Cu}_{3}\mathrm{N}$ ),[62] nickel(III) nitride),[63] phosphides (copper phosphide), fluorides (such as magnesium fluoride[64] and aluminum fluoride (AlF3)),[55] selenides (cobalt selenide),[65] bromides (copper bromide)[66] and boride[67] with lithiophilic natures. The carbon-based materials had CNTs, carbon cloth, graphene, and carbon fiber, porous carbon.[68] Heteroatom-doped carbon, composite materials of carbon with above metal/metal-based compounds, along with gradient 3D materials, had been employed in LMBs. More importantly, crystal forms, structures, electrical conductivity, and the combinations form of metals, polymers, carbon or composite materials significantly impact the deposition morphology of Li. Future research necessitates a comprehensive exploration of all potential preparation methods to achieve high-performance anodes. So far, the development and application of materials have received extensive attention from researchers.

paragraph_context: SEI formed when Li contacts with the electrolyte is primarily composed of lithium compounds and exhibits brittleness, coupled with limited adhesion to the Li surface.[34] As a result, during the Li deposition, the film surface frequently cracks due to volumetric expansion, exposing fresh lithium metal for further side-reactions.[33b] This leads to the dissolution of Li, forming pits and crevices.[10b,23f] Li ions traverse these defects, prompting the rapid proliferation of metal filaments and dendrites.[17a] Consequently, there is a need for an ideal interfacial protective layer, which should have: 1) uniformity and chemical stability: no adverse reactions occur; 2) high electronic insulation and ionic conductivity to suppress the decomposition of the electrolyte and ensure that $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ can smoothly insertion and extraction; 3) sufficient mechanical strength to withstand stress changes without breaking or collapsing; 4) highly flexible to accommodate the volumetric expansion of lithium deposition without mechanical damage; 5) control the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flow to ensure uniform lithium deposition. A variety of protective layers have been suggested for application on the Li surface, which including organic materials,[79] inorganic,[80] MXene/MOF/COF,[81] and hybrid materials.[82] Inorganic compounds have inherent advantages. They possess high dielectric constant, high Young's modulus, high ion conductivity, and low cost, which make them as superior candidates for facilitating uniform deposition of Li.[17a] Moreover, these inorganic materials effectively mitigated undesired side reactions.[23d] A wide range of inorganic materials (Figure 6) can be used as interfacial interfaces, including metals, alloys, oxides, nitrides, chalcogenides, halides, polyanion, and carbon. Metals, including $\mathrm{Ag(Au)}$ [53] Cu,[83] Al,[84] Sn,[85] etc; alloys, including $\mathrm{AlLi}$ [84] $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{Bi}$ [86] $\mathrm{LiIn}$ [86,87] $\mathrm{LiHg}$ [88] $\mathrm{Li}_{15}\mathrm{Si}_4$ [89] $\mathrm{Li}_{22}\mathrm{Ge}_5$ [90] $\mathrm{LiZn}$ [88] $\mathrm{LiMg}$ [91] etc; oxides, including titanium oxide,[92] aluminum oxide,[93] zinc oxide,[94] Silicon dioxide $(\mathrm{SiO}_2)$ [95] Zirconium dioxide $(\mathrm{ZrO}_2)$ [96] Magnesium oxide $(\mathrm{MgO})$ [97] and $\mathrm{Li}_{6.4}\mathrm{La}_3\mathrm{Zr}_{1.4}\mathrm{Ta}_{0.6}\mathrm{O}_{12}$ [98] etc; nitrides, including $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{N}$ [38] boron nitride (h-BN),[99] $\mathrm{Cu}_3\mathrm{N}$ $\mathrm{Mo}_3\mathrm{N}_2$ [80b] Lithium phospho-oxynitride (LiPON),[100] zirconyl nitrate $(\mathrm{ZrO}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2)$ [101] etc; chalcogenides, including $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ ,[102] Lithium selenide $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Se})$ ,[102] Molybdenum disulfide $(\mathrm{MoS}_2)$ ,[103] and Lithium thiophosphate $(\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{PS}_4)$ ,[104] etc; halides, including lithium fluoride (LiF),[105] LiBr,[106] LiI,[107] etc; polyanion, including Lithium phosphate $(\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{PO}_4)$ ,[108] Lithium niobate $(\mathrm{LiNbO}_3)$ ,[109] etc; and carbon, including graphene,[110] carbon nanotubes (CNTs),[111] and activated carbon (AC),[68] etc. The preparation methods of these materials include chemical vapor deposition (CVD), physical vapor deposition (PVD), in situ reaction, drop coating, blade coating, and spin coating. Suitable materials can be selected according to specific needs and the corresponding advantages/disadvantages. By adjusting the type, structure, crystal form and composition of materials, the electronic structure and electrical conductivity of SEI can be regulated, which is conducive to improving the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux efficiency. A threshold of ionic conductivity the and Young's modulus for the SEI need above $1.5\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{Scm}^{-1}$ and $4.0\mathrm{GPa}$ for the SEI to effectively eliminate stress concentrations, producing smooth Li deposition and suppressing of SEI breakdown.[112] Specifically, Choi et al.[113] assessed Li plating kinetics of a series of conversion-type metal fluorides $\mathrm{(MF_x}$ , M=Ag, Sn(II), In, Zn, Bi) (Figure 7a). $\mathrm{MF_x}$ with Li produced lithium fluoride (LiF) following which metal M proceeds to form the lithium-metal alloy (Li-M). Hence, the anode was protected by LiF while the metal serves as a nucleation seed. Study found that the Li plating kinetics and behavior were largely affected by the Li-M reaction mechanism. According to this metric, Silver fluoride (AgF), Tin fluoride $(\mathrm{SnF_2})$ , Indium fluoride $(\mathrm{InF_3})$ , Zinc fluoride $(\mathrm{ZnF_2})$ , and Bismuth fluoride $(\mathrm{BiF_3})$ based electrodes had nucleation overpotentials of 0.92, 3.1, 2.6, 3.4, and $10\mathrm{mV}$ , respectively, implying that AgF was the most efficient in terms of nucleating the Li-M alloy. Zhang et al.[114] prepared a multi-functional protection layer by a one-step spin coating of Copper chloride $(\mathrm{CuCl_2})$ , Aluminum chloride $(\mathrm{AlCl_3})$ , Zinc chloride $(\mathrm{ZnCl_2})$ solution. SEM indicated surface morphologies were nanorose, nanosheet, and nano-bubble, respectively (Figure 7b). Atomic Force Microscope (AFM) indicated a smoother surface and the overpotential showed a decreasing tendency $(\mathrm{CuCl_2 > AlCl_3 > ZnCl_2})$ . Tour et al.[115] have outlined a simple, solvent-free brushing technique, which facilitates the transformation of powders into films atop Li foils (Figure 7c). This method strategically leveraged the reactivity of Li metal with the powder films to fine-tune the surface energy, effectively suppressing parasitic reactions. The $\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{S}_5-$ Li anodes demonstrated a more consistent Li electrodeposition and dissolution during cycling, maintaining ultralow polarization in symmetric cells for over $4000\mathrm{h}$ , which was approximately eight times longer than that of bare Li anodes. The optimal Li protection interlayer should not only maintain an intact structure throughout the initial lithiation process, but also demonstrate robust electron-blocking capabilities to prevent electrolyte decomposition. Thus, Peng et al.[116] discovered that preventing electron escape to the electrode surface was a more critical strategy for suppressing electrolyte decomposition than controlling Li plating morphology in LMB performances (Figure 7d). The study involved a Li-intercalated interlayer, derived through the lithiation of an orthorhombic niobium pentoxide $(\mathrm{Nb}_2\mathrm{O}_5)$ precursor layer with disproportionate $\mathrm{Nb}^{4+}/\mathrm{Nb}^{5+}$ components, as the model Li protection structure. This structure exhibited high structural integrity, rapid Li conducting channels, and most notably, a strong electron withdrawing ability. The performance of the Li anode, enhanced by this advanced interlayer, significantly surpassed that of the conventional lithiophilic interlayer. In addition to the components and structure, the thickness of the SEI film also had an impact on the performance of LMBs. Gong et al.[117] developed 2D $\mathrm{g - C_3N_4}$ layers with varied thicknesses to evaluate the thickness effects of artificial SEI on Li metal deposition (Figure 7e). It was demonstrated that a thin $\mathrm{g - C_3N_4}$ layer ( $\approx 2\mathrm{nm}$ ) was rapidly decomposed and fractured under the impact of Li-ion flux, while a thick $\mathrm{g - C_3N_4}$ layer ( $\approx 50\mathrm{nm}$ ) impeded the transport of lithium ions and electrons simultaneously, hindering the Li meta deposition underneath. Notably, a $\mathrm{g - C_3N_4}$ layer with moderate thickness ( $\approx 10\mathrm{nm}$ ) dominated in situ generation of stable $\mathrm{g - C_3N_4 / Li_3N}$ hybrid artificial SEI and enabled fast Li-ion transport, which induced low overpotential and uniform Li deposition. Furthermore, Yang et al.[118] taken advantage of the simpler approach to produce an inorganic nanocrystal dominant interphase by preimmersing the Li in molten lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (Figure 7f). Cross-sectional focused ion beam-scanning electron microscope (FIB-SEM) images showed that a flat layer of $\approx 2\mu \mathrm{m}$ thick. Corresponding 3D images constructed from Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) measurements confirmed that the interphase is principally composed of F (represented by $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{F}^+$ and $\mathrm{LiF}_2^-$ fragments), S ( $\mathrm{LiSO}_4^-$ and $\mathrm{SO}_2^-$ ), and N ( $\mathrm{NSO}^-$ ) species, and other inorganics ( $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{O}^+$ ). This excellent ion conduction was predominantly caused by the large number of nano-sized domains and the derived interfaces in the SEI. The mean moduli of bare-Li and SEI-coated lithium (AS-Li) probed by Atomic force microscopy (AFM) were $1.7\mathrm{GPa}$ and $18.6\mathrm{GPa}$ , which enabled uniform deposition by mitigated the stress distribution, faster local deposition rate of the SEI and improved the Li electrodeposition.

paragraph_context: In situ-formed protective layers offer a significant advantage over ex situ-created layers due to their superior adhesion properties, which eliminate the need for additional binders.[17a] These in situ coating layers are typically formed through chemical reactions between Li anode and various materials. For example, Lemmon et al.[121] developed a dense organic layer with controllable thickness via spin-coating carboxylic acid solution (Figure 8h). The presence of oxygen atoms in the lithium carboxylate layer significantly amplified the Li adsorption energy to $2.66\mathrm{eV}$ . This can be attributed to the robust interaction between the Li atom and the carboxylic acid/Li. The organic layer, which formed in situ, provided an effective shield for the Li, protecting it from electrolyte corrosion and inhibiting the growth of dendrites. This process enhanced lithophilicity and reduced the deposition overpotential. However, the elastic strength of the lithium carboxylate layer was insufficient to resist lithium dendrites during extended cycling. To avoid this shortcoming, a self-healing, adhesive supramolecular copolymer was developed, featuring pendant poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) segments and ureido-pyrimidinone (UPy) quadruple-hydrogen-bonding moieties (Figure 8i).[122] This was applied as a protective layer to the Li anode using a straightforward drop coating method. The in situ-formed LiPEO-UPy SEI layer significantly enhanced the protection performance of the Li anode due to the strong binding and increased stability resulting from a spontaneous reaction between the UPy groups and Li metal (Figure 8i). This layer provided protection to the Li foil, with minimal changes observed even after $30\mathrm{min}$ in air, compared to the Li foil turning black within just one minute. Furthermore, the LiPEO-UPy@Li construct demonstrated its robustness by with-. standing the weight of $50\mathrm{g}$ . It also facilitated a homogeneous ionic flux, leading to a flat, smooth plating/stripping surface, and only a slight increase in thickness as observed from scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Consequently, the LiPEO-UPy layer contributed to stable, dendrite-free cycling at high current densities of $20\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ at $1\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ for $400\mathrm{h}$ , and $1\mathrm{mA}$ $\mathrm{cm}^{-2} / 10\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ for $1000\mathrm{h}$ (Figure 8j). Besides, Fu et al.[123] reported a fatigue-free dynamic supramolecular ion-conductive elastomericinterphase (DSIEI) as artificial SEI layers (Figure 8k). The poly(propylene glycol) backbone, characterized by its flexible $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -O coordination, facilitates rapid ion transport. Concurrently, the supramolecular quadruple hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) in the harder phases provide mechanical reinforcement to the elastomeric interphase. Importantly, gradient H-bonds can effectively dissipate strain energy through sequential bond cleavage. The DSIEI@LiLiFePO4coin cell exhibited enhanced cycling and rate performance than LiLiFePO4coin cell (Figure 8l,m). Cao et al. Cao et al.[124] synthesized an ultra-stretchable, ionic conducting chemically crosslinked pressure-sensitive adhesive (70cPSA) through the copolymerization of 2-ethylhexyl acrylate and acrylic acid (Figure 8n). Poly(ethyleneglycol)dimethacrylate worked as a crosslinker among the process. The 70cPSA@Li/70cPSA@Li cell demonstrated an impressively extended lifetime of $1500\mathrm{h}$ with an overpotential of $\approx 50\mathrm{mV}$ compared to a Li/Li cell at $2.0\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2} / 1\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ (Figure 8o).

paragraph_context: Numerous studies have been conducted to date on the utilization of Metal-Organic Framework (MOF) and Covalent Organic Framework (COF) based materials as protective layers for Li anodes.[125] These materials present several advantages. They boast high porosity and a plethora of active sites that significantly enhance the transmission of lithium ions and the impregnation of electrolytes.[126] The structure can be fine-tuned by manipulating the types and ratios of metal ions and organic ligands, as well as adjusting the synthesis conditions.[127] This level of control ensures the precise composition of the SEI. Furthermore, the chemical properties can be tailored to meet the specific requirements of individual battery systems by incorporating various functional groups.[128] MXene is a class of transition metal carbides or nitrides with a 2D structure.[129] It possesses high conductivity, excellent mechanical properties, and a rich abundance of surface functional groups.[129a] It can significantly enhance the stability and mechanical strength of the SEI, preventing the crushing and regeneration. For example, Zeng et al.[130] synthesized a novel 3D COF with abundance of lithophilic sites and a heteroatom weight content of $32.32\mathrm{wt}\%$ (Figure 9a). Within this COF, both phosphazene and porphyrin rings functioned as electron-rich and lithophilic sites, facilitating a consistent $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux in a 3D direction and leading to compact Li deposition. Notably, the associated $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ full cells demonstrated a lifespan of up to 200 cycles (Figure 9b). Song et al.[131] documented a tris(4-aminophenyl)amine-pyromeleptic dianhydride COF (TPCOF) (Figure 9c). The structure, characterized by a strong donor-acceptor unit, induced local charge separation, leading to electron depletion and subsequently enhancing its affinity to bisfluorosulfonimide anion (FSI). Moreover, FSI expedited the decomposition processed and formed a stable LiF-rich SEI and extended battery life (Figure 9d). Zhang et al.[81] developed a MOF polycrystalline membrane based on HKUST-1 through in situ epitaxial growth (Figure 9e). A significant charge density was observed in the $\{\mathrm{Li - O}_4\}$ region, indicating that lithium tends to bond with HKUST-1, resulting in a stable lithium-rich film (Figure 9f). Following Li stripping, a new peak emerged at $57\mathrm{eV}$ , indicated of a remarkably low lithium electron cloud density, attributed to the capture of lithium by the $\{\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{O}_{10}\}$ unit of HKUST-1. This process effectively exposed the active planes and lithophilic sites, leveraging the benefits of MOFs for directed Li deposition. In addition to those introduced above, many other COF/MOF containing functional groups had been reported, such as Zr-BDCF,[132] EB-COF:NO,[133] Additionally, MXene or its hybrid with COF also had been used as SEI layer for Li anode.

paragraph_context: The liquid electrolyte is commonly composed of solvents and salts. As noted earlier, Li metal anodes frequently react with the electrolyte, leading to the formation of a thick SEI layer that has limited stability. Numerous studies have been undertaken to refine the constituents of the electrolyte, including the solvent, Li salt, various electrolyte additives, and electrolyte salt, with the aim of improving the stability of LMAs for high-rate applications.

paragraph_context: Li Salt: Lithium salts are pivotal in the functioning of lithium-ion batteries, influencing both energy density and charging rate. Moreover, they are intrinsically linked to the battery's cycle life and safety. Predominantly, these salts serve as electrolytes, dissolved in organic solvents to create conductive solutions for lithium-ion transfer.[139] The ideal lithium salt should possess the following properties: high ionic conductivity to achieve fast charging, chemical, and thermal stability, anti-oxidation and anti-reduction properties, low cost and environmental friendliness, and safety.

paragraph_context: Salt concentration: The salt concentration is a key parameter that directly affects the performance, safety, and cost of the battery. The ionic conductivity, viscosity, and side reactions with the Li metal anode of the electrolyte are all influenced by the concentration.[37] In most electrolyte systems, the concentration that corresponds to the maximum ionic conductivity is typically $1\mathrm{M}$ .[9a] The formation of solvated complexes, primarily in the form of solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIP), contact ion pairs (CIP), and aggregates of cations and anions (AGG), is directly affected by the competition in the electrolyte between the cation-anion coulombic interaction and the ion-dipole interaction $\mathrm{(Li^{+}}$ -solvent).[9] As the concentration of lithium salt increases to a level above $3\mathrm{M}$ the solution becomes nearly devoid of free solvent molecules.[7] Consequently, the anions of the lithium salt penetrate the solvation sheath, predominantly coexisting with the cations and solvent molecules in the form of AGGs and CIPs.[37] In this context, the LUMO energy of the anion decreases, and the inorganic SEI derived from the anion becomes dominant.[161] Simultaneously, the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -solvent coordination causes the HOMO energy of the solvent to decrease, thereby exhibiting greater oxidation stability than free solvent molecules and reducing the inherent volatility of the solvent.[161] Consequently, the electrochemical window of the electrolytes was significantly expanded.[162] However, excessively high lithium salt concentration can lead to increased electrolyte costs and increased system viscosity.[163] To address the aforementioned challenges, research has introduced the concept of "Localized High Concentration Electrolyte" (LHCE).[164] This approach entails adding diluents to a high-concentration electrolyte, creating a localized state of lithium salts that is highly concentrated.[14e] This balances the dichotomy between interface stability and ionic conductivity, significantly reducing the cost of the electrolyte.[165] The optimal diluent for LHCE should exhibit several essential properties: a low dielectric constant and minimal complexing ability; low viscosity and high wettability; it should not dissolve lithium salts, yet remain miscible with solvents; it must not disrupt the unique coordination structure of the salt-solvent in the native high-concentration electrolyte.[166] Non-solvating and low-dielectric co-solvents inherently bolster the interaction between anions and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ by establishing a low-dielectric environment.[167] The introduction of these co-solvents leads to a prevalence of positively charged anion-cation aggregates, which are drawn to the surface of the negatively charged Li anode.[168] As a result, an anion-derived, inorganic-rich SEI is induced. This not only effectively stabilizes the Li anode but also suppresses the formation of lithium dendrites and augments interfacial reaction kinetics. Nevertheless, the LHCE exhibits inferior ionic conductivity due to the encapsulation of the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation sheath by the diluent, which restricts its migration speed.[14e] Alongside high-concentration electrolytes (HCE) and LHCE, the Weak Solvating Electrolyte (WSE), alternatively termed Low Solvating Electrolyte, presents another viable solution.[169] In the solvation sheath of WSE, both the solvent and anions are coordinated to $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ with weak interactions.[170] Compared to HCE, WSE achieves an anion-rich solvation structure under diluted conditions, resulting in a decrease in viscosity.[171] Unlike LHCE, all solvents in WSE participate in the solvation process, eliminating the use of non-solvating diluents and thereby improving ionic conductivity.[172] Figure 13 provides a graphical depiction of the solvated structure.

The selection and proportioning of these combinations must be tailored to the specific battery system, electrode materials, and desired performance criteria. Different combinations can significantly influence battery performance. In conclusion, the quest for efficient solvents is a crucial and widely applicable strategy in advancing development.

paragraph_context: Organic solvent additives have also been explored to stabilize LMAs for high-rate applications.[178] Among them, FEC and VC were the most widely used electrolyte additives. FEC was given preference over other solvents for reductive decomposition, resulting in the formation of a LiF-rich SEI film characterized by high mechanical strength.[172] This process markedly improved the cycling stability of LMBs. The SEI film, formulated by VC, primarily comprised polymers, inorganic salts, and other compounds.[168] It is noteworthy that these constituents could decrease the concentration of soluble organic components within the SEI film, thereby leading to a thinner and more stable SEI film.[168] In an effort to enhance the electrochemical performance of LMBs, the researcher assessed a range of electrolyte additives.[161] Fluorinated flame retardant solvents (FEC, FEMC, Ethyl difluoroacetate (DFEA), 2,2,2-trifluorodiethyl ether (HFE), etc.) and cyclic phosphonitrile solvent molecules (such as 1,3,5,2,4,6-Triazatriphosphorine (FPPN), 1,3,5,2,4,6-triazatriphosphorine (PFPN), Tetrafluoroterephthalonitrile (TFPN), etc.) could serve as effective flame-retardant additives.[37] While an increase in F content in fluorinated solvents enhanced flame retardancy, it simultaneously and significantly escalated the economic cost of the electrolyte. Furthermore, the existing utilization of cyclic phosphonitrile solvents entailed high expenses and generated environmentally detrimental halide constituents upon combustion, thereby impeding their pragmatic employment. Conversely, traditional phosphorus compounds like trimethyl phosphate (TMP)[186] and triethyl phosphate (TEP),[162] as well as Dimethyl methylphosphonate (DMMP),[187] were extensively employed due to their cost-effectiveness and environmental friendliness. Presently, studies focusing on the addition of sulfate esters and sulfonate esters were predominantly characterized by the use of ethylene sulfate esters (DTD)[188] and 1,3-propanesultone (PST)[189] as primary representatives. They possessed the capability to generate protective SEI films, which were enriched in both $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{SO}_3$ and $\mathrm{ROSO}_2\mathrm{Li}$ . The investigation into novel sulfur-containing additives, each possessing unique functional groups, was progressively advancing. Examples included dimethyl sulfite (DMS)[190] and 1,3-propane sultone (1,3-PS).[191] etc. Redox shuttle additives were a subset of electrically-active molecules that could serve as electrolyte additives, providing reversible overcharge protection. It was important to note that traditional electrolytes underwent considerable oxidative decomposition ( $>4.3~\mathrm{V}$ ), and thus couldn't align with the high-voltage cathode.[162] To address this issue, the integration of high-pressure resistant solvents such as 2,2-difluoroethyl methyl sulfone (FS),[192] 2,5-dioxahexanedioate (DMDOHD)[193] and bis(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl) ether (BTFE),[162] etc was proposed. The use of various dual-additive electrolyte additives or salt-solvent hybrid additives, along with the adjustment of components and ratios, also can expand the voltage and temperature range of electrolytes.

paragraph_context: The non-flammable solid-state electrolytes have become a research hotspot because of their excellent safety performance compared to the flammable organic electrolytes.[13a,194] So Solid-state lithium metal batteries represent a promising advancement in technology. The Coulombic efficiency, power performance, and cycling stability of solid-state Li metal batteries are still limited and face some key challenges.[195] Predominantly, these challenges stem from the limited ionic conductivity of solid-state electrolytes, their compromised interfacial stability, and their solid-solid contact with Lithium. The elevated internal resistance and interfacial impedance detrimentally affect the battery's cycle longevity and power efficiency. The numerous defects present in solid-state electrolytes, such as cracks, bubbles, holes, or grain boundaries, can readily induce and accelerate the growth of lithium dendrites. Furthermore, the stress generated at the interface due to the rigidity of the solid-state electrolyte can impact the mechanical stability and cyclic performance of the battery.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Solid-state electrolytes are categorized based on their composition into inorganic solid-state electrolytes (ISEs), organic polymer electrolytes (OSEs), and organic-inorganic composite electrolytes (OICEs).[12] ISEs include a variety of options such as oxide, sulfide, halide, glassy, and ceramic electrolytes, among others.[12] OSEs are derived from polymers and their ionic conductivity is enhanced through doping with lithium salts and other modification methods.[10c] Meanwhile, OISEs combined the advantages of both inorganic solid-state electrolytes and polymers, enhancing ionic conductivity via the creation of a 3D network structure.[13b] ISEs possess several key advantages including excellent conductivity $(0.1 - 10\mathrm{mScm}^{-1})$ , a wide operating temperature range $(-50$ to $200^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ , and high mechanical strength with a shear modulus exceeding 6 GPa.[13b] However, ISEs also present significant limitations. Issues such as holes created from non-conformal solid-solid contact, low compaction density, and conductivity differences between grains and their boundaries can all promote Li dendrite growth.[196] Furthermore, the operational current $(0.01 - 3\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2})$ and capacity $(0.0025 - 3\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2})$ for Solid-State Lithium Metal Batteries are markedly lower compared to those in non-aqueous electrolytes $(0.1 - 10\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}, 0.5 - 10\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2})$ used in practical cells.[13b] Although most oxide electrolytes demonstrate exceptional oxidation stability, they can potentially cause undesirable chemical side reactions.[13a] Ensuring optimal interfacial contact between rigid oxide electrolytes and electrodes necessitates the use of high temperatures. However, these elevated temperatures may lead to mutual element diffusion and structural reorganization.[197] In comparison, sulfide SEs present low grain boundary resistance and exceptional mechanical deformation capacity.[198] Additionally, they ensure optimal contact with the electrode and permit scalable cold-pressed fabrication. These attributes position sulfide SEs as the foremost SEs candidate for all solid-state lithium batteries. However, sulfide SEs are sensitive to air and will decompose due to toxic gases in the air, which presents serious safety problems.[199] The four typical crystalline solid electrolytes with high ionic conductivity include $\mathrm{Li}_7\mathrm{P}_3\mathrm{S}_{11}$ , $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{PS}_4$ , $\mathrm{Li}_{10}\mathrm{GeP}_2\mathrm{S}_{12}$ , and $\mathrm{Li}_6\mathrm{PS}_5\mathrm{X}$ .[12] The electrochemical performance of sulfide SEs can be enhanced by optimizing the size and implementing element doping techniques to improve their crystallinity. Halide electrolytes, which can undergo phase transitions at various temperatures and are prone to hydrolysis in air, are expensive to synthesize.[200] Their conductivity is significantly affected by these phase transitions.[201] Depending on the anionic sublattice and spatial groups, halide elec trolytes can be categorized into monoclinic, orthorhombic and trigonal halide SEs. A general trend observed in ionic conductivity is $\sigma_{\mathrm{monoclinic}} > \sigma_{\mathrm{orthorhombic}} > \sigma_{\mathrm{trigonal}}$ .[197] Furthermore, the particle size, micro-morphology, and mechanical properties of these halide electrolytes substantially influence the performance of halide SEs.

paragraph_context: Building upon prior research on the challenges of solid-state lithium metal batteries, here we propose three effective solutions: 1) the development of novel solid electrolytes and the refinement of existing ones. Factors such as ionic conductivity, crystal type, particle size, relative compactness, and macroscopic defects in the electrolyte influence its resistance to lithium dendrites. Composite or deformable electrolytes can be designed, leveraging the strengths of each component to enhance battery performance. 2) the introduction of an interfacial protection layer. Solid-solid interfacial contact and reactions can result in significant interfacial resistance and the growth of lithium dendrites. A protective layer at the Li/SEs interface can expedite interfacial Li-ion transport, inhibit the interdiffusion of interfacial elements, and prevent adverse reactions. Parameters such as ionic conductivity, electrical insulation, electrochemical stability toward SE and Li metal, wetting properties with Li metal and SE, and layer thickness should be carefully considered. 3) The modification of the LMA. Strategies developed for liquid LMBs can be adapted and refined for solid-state LMBs, offering potential enhancements in the performance of solid-state LMBs.

paragraph_context: Separators serve as inert components that offer a pathway for ion migration while preventing direct contact between the cathode and the anode. Damage to the separator, whether caused by external impacts, punctures, local overheating, or internal and external short circuits, can trigger thermal runaway, potentially leading to explosions in LMBs.[213] Therefore, improving the safety of separators is a major obstacle in the quest for superior performance in LMBs. Commercially available separators in the laboratory including polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE), or their composites, polymer-based nonwoven membranes for rechargeable LMBs due to their chemical stability in common organic solvents and cost-effectiveness. These separators, due to their low melting point (PP: $165^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , PE: $135^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and ionic conductivity (0.37–0.65), have their applications constrained under particular working conditions, such as extreme cold and underwater environments.[214] By altering the composition and structure of the separator, the distribution and transmission properties of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ can be effectively regulated, thereby effectively suppressing the nucleation and growth of lithium dendrites.[213] Current strategies for the design of highly safe separators include the following aspects: i) composite ceramic materials or organic polymers to improve thermal stability, ii) modified polymers and composite structures to enhance mechanical strength, iii) designing new and functional separators to regulate ion transport and lithium deposition to mitigate lithium dendrites, and iv) intelligently controlling thermal runaway with flame retardant and thermal shut-off functions.

paragraph_context: Specifically, Chen et al.[215] reported on a quasi-continuous strategy to prepare separators that employed in situ enamel mineralization engineering, followed by thermal treatment (Figure 18a). This approach facilitated the straightforward development of a large-area, 3D interlaced hydroxyapatite nanosheet array (HAP-NA)-reinforced polyethylene (PE) nanocomposite separator. This separator boasted robust mechanical properties and exceptional resistance to thermal shrinkage. Notably, the nanocomposite, when heated to $120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , demonstrated superior breaking stress and ultrahigh toughness, with a value of $\approx 434.4\mathrm{MJm}^{-3}$ . Tang et al.[213] developed a thermally conductive, graphene-coated separator to mitigate local temperature "hotspots" (Figure 18b). The graphene layer promoted efficient diffusion of local heat produced by irregular lithium growth and initial dendrite formation, thereby ensuring stable and uniform lithium deposition to inhibit further degradation. SEM images showed many dendrites could be observed on the Cu substrate cycled with PP separator, while relatively uniform surface could be observed on the Cu substrate cycled with graphene nanosheets coated PP separator (Figure 18c). Zhang et al.[216] combined microencapsulation and electrospinning technologies to develop a multifunctional composite separator (P@AS, silica microencapsulated ammonium polyphosphate (APP) particles anchored in polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fiber matrix). The P@AS separator employed a condensed phase flame retardant mechanism to create a dense charcoal layer, leading to the internal separator being deprived of oxygen. Furthermore, it guaranteed the steady flow of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , formed a highly ion-conductive SEI, and encouraged stable lithium deposition via active $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ seed points. The Li symmetric cells exhibited stable cycling for over $400\mathrm{h}$ with lower polarization potential $(96.8\mathrm{mV})$ (Figure 18d). $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}\| \mathrm{Li}$ cell with P@AS-10 separator exhibited initial discharge capacity of 140.80 mAh $\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ with capacity retention rate of $93.56\%$ after 300 cycles (Figure 18e). Meanwhile, the $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}\| \mathrm{Li}$ cells demonstrated outstanding rate performance. The discharge capacities were 161.16, 155.78, 147.12, 138.23, 124.27, 99.97, and $66.56\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8C, respectively (Figure 18e). The modifying polyolefin separators (PP) with covalent organic polymer networks (TPE) developed by Zhang team.[217] The TPE@PP separator exhibit excellent e thermal stability and thermal distribution (Figure 18f). The Li||Li cell TPE@PP showed excellent rate performance (Figure 18g). In situ optical microscopy techniques demonstrated mossy dendrites formed for PP separator, while even distribution and the effective suppression of dendrite could be realized for TPE@PP separator (Figure 18h). Liao et al.[218] developed a novel nanofibrous covalent organic framework (COF) separator, featuring a meticulously designed hierarchical porous channels (Figure 18i). Through computational fluid dynamics simulations, it was demonstrated that this hierarchical structure effectively regulates both the ion flow and flux rates (Figure 18j). This design guaranteed a steady flow rate and an overall high flux rate, thereby upholding stable, swift charging and fairly consistent lithium deposition. As a result, this novel approach eliminated dendrite-related problems in LMBs systems. Lu et al.[219] described a composite separator incorporating poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) and heterometallic metal-organic frameworks. This design offered a greater density of open bimetal sites, enhanced complexation with anions, a more porous structure, as well as improved electrolyte wettability. Notably, the use of such separators significantly boosted $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ conductivity and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number. The Li symmetric cells with ZHP separator (PVA containing $60\mathrm{wt.\%}$ UiO-66(Zr/Hf)) maintained $400\mathrm{h}$ with low overpotential of $79 - 50\mathrm{mV}$ (Figure 18k). The cycled Li/Li cells with ZTP (PVA containing $60\mathrm{wt.\%}$ UiO-66(Zr/Ti)) and ZHP showed smaller electrochemical resistance than that of the cells with PP (71, 78 vs $199\Omega$ ) (Figure 18l).

For solid-state batteries, factors such as internal stress, external deformation, and operational pressures can alter interfacial contact and material porosity, thereby impacting the electrochemical characteristics of these batteries.[229] The ionic conductivity of the solid electrolytes (SEs) and the growth of lithium dendrites are profoundly influenced by applied pressure.[230] As stacking pressure escalates, the surface of SEs becomes smoother, and the proportion of voids and defects diminishes notably. High-density electrolytes offer more continuous ion transport channels, enhancing ionic conductivity.[228,230] Research indicates that within a moderate pressure range (e.g., $30 - 50\mathrm{MPa}$ ), the ionic conductivity of SEs is markedly enhanced without risking material failure from excessive pressure.[231] However, when pressure surpasses a specific threshold, the solid electrolyte might experience plastic deformation. This can lead to the degradation of the internal structure or the emergence of electronic percolation paths, subsequently reducing ionic conductivity and potentially causing a short circuit.[231] The impact of external pressure is intimately tied to the mechanical properties of electrolytes.[228] For example, in the case of electrolytes with a lower elastic modulus, a minimal pressure $(1 - 5\mathrm{MPa})$ can result in a significant enhancement in Li-deposition behavior.[228] On the other hand, for electrolytes with a high modulus, a greater pressure is necessary to achieve an equivalent effect. Through the strategic design of the mechanical properties of the electrolytes and optimization of the applied pressure, the uniformity of Li-deposition can be substantially improved.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: In SSBs, the absence of wetting characteristics in liquid electrolytes necessitates the application of stack pressure to mitigate contact loss between electrodes and the SEs. A uniform external pressure enables smooth and close interface contact, effectively reducing interface resistance and improving the transport efficiency of ions and electrons.[232] Effective "face-to-face" contact minimizes current density per unit area and mitigates the tip effect, thereby facilitating uniform Li deposition.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: External pressure plays a pivotal role in enhancing interface contact and optimizing lithium deposition behavior. Nevertheless, the choice of pressure necessitates a thorough examination of the mechanical properties of electrolyte, battery design, and operational conditions. Future research endeavors should 1) improve the mechanical strength, internal density and purity, and surface integrity of SEs to prevent the formation and penetration of lithium dendrites; 2) reasonably establish the standard for applying external pressure for each type of SSBs component according to its characteristics; 3) qualitatively and quantitatively analyze the effects of pressure on electrochemical processes by multi-scale characterization and modeling (such as time scale, space scale, and kinetic factor), clarify the structure and performance changes of SSBs components during cycling and predict the optimal pressure for certain application scenarios. These efforts aim to provide robust theoretical and technical foundations for the commercialization of high-performance LMBs.

paragraph_context: Traditional electrolyte development relies on experimental trial-and-error and theoretical calculations, which are time-consuming and costly. The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in materials science is driving innovation in battery technology at an unprecedented rate, particularly in new electrolytes, SEI layers, and anode designs. Through high-throughput screening, molecular design, and performance prediction, AI can significantly accelerate the discovery and optimization of new materials, providing a robust foundation for the development of next-generation batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: AI technology, through machine learning and high-throughput computational methods, provides efficient and precise tools for the screening and design of solid-state electrolytes (SEs) with excellent properties and specific performance requirements.[233] Open-source databases (such as Materials Project, and AFLOW) and proprietary databases provide rich material information for the screening and design of electrolyte molecules.[234] AI quickly evaluates millions of molecular structures to select candidate electrolyte molecules. The AI model, combined with known electrolyte performance data and combined with quantum chemical calculations, can rapidly generate physicochemical property data for electrolytes.[235] In the optimization of the SEI layer, AI helps design a more stable artificial SEI layer by analyzing the interfacial reaction mechanisms under different combinations of electrolytes and electrode materials, thus prolonging the cycle life of the battery and improving safety.[235,236] Additionally, AI can simulate the dynamic growth process of SEI through deep learning models, providing theoretical guidance for interface engineering.[237] In anode design, AI optimizes the microstructure of Li anodes (such as porosity, and surface morphology) through multi-scale simulation and machine learning, inhibiting the growth of lithium dendrites and alleviating volume expansion problems.[235] For example, an AI-based composite material screening method can rapidly develop high-stability Li anode materials.[237] At the same time, an AI-driven multi-objective optimization framework can simultaneously optimize multiple per formance indicators of the battery (such as energy density, cycle life, and safety), reducing experimental trial and error costs.[237] By enabling rapid screening, precise prediction, and rational design of novel materials, AI is accelerating the development of next-generation batteries with enhanced performance, safety, and longevity. As AI technologies continue to evolve, their integration with experimental and theoretical approaches will unlock new possibilities for battery innovation, ultimately driving the commercialization of high-performance energy storage systems. 1) Focus on lithium stripping and detailed mechanism. It is crucial to recognize that Li stripping markedly affects the surface morphology of the Li anode, which in turn influences subsequent depositions. More sophisticated technologies are needed in the future to elucidate the underlying mechanisms.  2) Exploration of new solid-state electrolytes. We should optimize their structure, and mechanical strength and modify the interface to ensure a perfect match with the Li anode. Necessitating concerted efforts and further research to enhance the current density of SSBs $10\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ threshold, which is typically seen in liquid electrolytes. Formulating the criteria for applying appropriate external pressure based on the characteristics of each type of SSBs component.  3) Tailoring electrolytes and separators. Further exploration can be conducted on self-healing electrolytes, overcharge protection electrolytes, heat-resistant SEI layers, and flame-retardant electrolytes to address the various stages of thermal runaway. The current industrialized polymer separators have limited heat resistance and anti-dendrite performance and the development of new separators with high temperature resistance and adequate toughness is urgently needed.  4) Application of Artificial intelligence and machine learning. They significantly augment the efficiency of battery components material screening. The utilization of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations allows for a deeper exploration of the structure-performance relationship. Employing phase-field simulations for the distribution of lithium ions and current density.  5) Development of new multi-characterization techniques. Synergizing these advanced methods with conventional techniques, to delve deeper into the detailed mechanism.  6) Adopting of advanced monitoring platform to facilitate real-time intelligent surveillance and diagnostics of battery components. 7) Improving the energy density of LMBs. Efforts should be made to construct new lightweight Li anodes, reduce the N/P ratio, find strategies for forming stable and thin SEI layers, and use of thin separators and lean electrolytes (E/S ratio $< 3\mathrm{g}$ $\mathrm{Ah}^{-1}$ ) without affecting the electrochemical performance.  8) Industrialization. Future endeavors should focus on the development of soft-packaged batteries for large-scale industrial applications, rather than merely concentrating on small-scale button battery configurations.  9) Widening multiple perspectives. Future research must delve into the multiple physical fields (including ion concentration, electric, temperature, and stress fields) and interdisciplinary collaboration (including materials science, chemistry, physics, and engineering).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In summary, the synergistic optimization of LMB components, cost reduction, enhancement of intelligent control, development of soft-package and solid-state battery design and manufacturing processes to promote the industrialization of LMBs, leveraging artificial intelligence and integrating multidisciplinary technologies can overcome the challenges faced by high-rate LMBs, significantly improve battery performance and safety. This approach aligns with national strategic planning in new energy sectors. These advancements and the above insights also provide valuable ideas for other alkali metal batteries (Na, K, Mg, Zn), and expand the application possibilities of power equipment under extreme conditions (polar exploration, underwater, military, and defense).

paragraph_context: To meet the demand for high-energy-density batteries, alloy-type and conversion-type anode materials have attracted growing attention due to their high specific capacity. However, the huge irreversible lithium loss during initial cycling significantly reduces the energy density of the full cell, which limits their practical applications. Fortunately, various anode prelithiation techniques have been developed to compensate for the initial lithium loss. At the same time, the cathode prelithiation has been proposed and demonstrated remarkable enhancement in the electrochemical performance, along with excellent scalability and compatibility with the existing battery production processes. Here, recent advances are reviewed in the prelithiation of both anodes and cathodes, and the key challenges are discussed in front of their practical applications. It is aimed to provide better recommendations and assistance for its large-scale practical applications.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Recently, the average temperature of some parts of the Antarctic and the Arctic has far exceeded the level of the same period in the past. The unprecedented global warming and the depletion of fossil fuels are making people more attentive to developing and storing renewable energies, and have promoted the expansion of various battery technologies.[1-15] Among various battery systems, lithium-ion battery was regarded as one of the most promising secondary batteries because of their high operating voltages, long cycle life, safety, and environmentally friendly.[7,16,17] Since first commercialization in 1991, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used in various portable devices and electric vehicles.[18-21] However, with the development of society, the current commercial LIBs are unable to meet the ever-increasing demand for high energy densities due to the limited specific capacity of the graphite anode,[7] it is thus urgent to develop ultra-high energy density batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To date, various high-specific-energy materials (for example, alloy-type,[6,22,23] conversion-type[24]) have been used as the anodes for next-generation LIBs.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: However, these materials usually exhibit massive active lithium lossin initial cycles due to the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), the missing of electrical contact caused by the lattice expanding and disintegrating during the lithium-ion intercalation, and the severe side reactions during the cycles (e.g., $\mathrm{Si} \approx 300\%$ ),[25-34] which causes a severe energy density decay.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To make full use of these high-specific-energy anode materials, the lithium loss issue in the initial cycles must be tackled. Various strategies have been proposed to solve the problem, such as controlling the properties of particles,[23] and designing surface protection coatings.[35,36] Although these methods have been further developed, the application of these high-specific-energy anode materials still needs to be improved. Based on this, studies on prelithiation technologies are sparkly emerging (Figure 1), especially after the year 2014 (from Figure 2a). The prelithiation techniques can be viewed as providing additional lithium sources with specific materials or reagents. To increase the internal lithium reserve of the entire lithium-ion battery system, prelithiation techniques can be introduced to electrodes,[37-39] separators,[40,41] or electrolytes.[42] At present, various prelithiation methods have been developed, which can be mainly divided into the cathode prelithiation technology and the anode prelithiation technology. The anode prelithiation technology is the most common and relatively facile route, including the lithium foil prelithiation, the lithium-metal powder prelithiation, the chemical prelithiation, and the electrochemical prelithiation. The anode prelithiation technology faces a key challenge, the inherently Figure 2. The numbers of publications and citations related to prelithiation, by year in the Web of Science core collection from 2014.01 to 2022.12. a) Topic words: “Prelithiation” or “Prelithiation” and “Lithium-ion batteries”. b) Topic words: “Prelithiation cathode” or “Prelithiation cathode” and “Lithium-ion batteries”. high reactivity of lithium metal with the solvents and binders, resulting in undesired byproducts. In addition, the low safety of lithium-metal during the processing of the battery assembly greatly hinders its large-scale application. On the contrary, the cathode prelithiation materials show excellent chemical stability and high open circuit voltage, which provides another route. The cathode prelithiation technology has been widely studied since 2014 (Figure 2b). Compared with the anode prelithiation technology, the cathode prelithiation technology matches better with the existing production process of LIBs, which shows advantages of low safety risk, less investment in equipment modification, easily to be scaled up. However, there are still some challenges with regard to the practical application. In this paper, the critical research progress of anode and cathode prelithiation technologies are reviewed. We summarized the challenges in the practical application of anode and cathode lithium-supplement materials and corresponding modified methods. Furthermore, the bottleneck of prelithiation technology and the prospect of prelithiation technology are also proposed.

paragraph_context: Alloy-type and conversion-type anodes are very promising to replace the conventional graphite anode for next-generation LIBs, with a specific capacity 2-10 times higher than that of the graphite (Figure 3a).[43-47] The graphite-type graphite $(\mathrm{Li^{+} + e^{-} + 6C\leftrightarrow LiC_{6}})$ exhibits high reversibility and excellent cycling performance due to its layer structure not severed or de stroyed during the lithium-ion intercalation. For alloy-type anodes $(\mathrm{M} + n\mathrm{Li}^{+} + n\mathrm{e}^{-}\leftrightarrow \mathrm{Li}_{n}\mathrm{M},\mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Sn},\mathrm{In},\mathrm{Ge},\mathrm{Sb},\mathrm{Bi},$ etc.) and conversion-type anodes $(\mathrm{M}_a\mathrm{X}_b + (b\cdot n)\mathrm{Li}\leftrightarrow a\mathrm{M} + b\mathrm{Li}_n\mathrm{X},\mathrm{M} =$ transition metal, $\mathbf{X} =$ anion, $n =$ oxidation state of X) (Figure 3b),[48] continuous formation of SEI due to cracks during lithium-ion intercalation and deintercalation, and the trap of lithium-ions caused by side reactions continuously consume active lithium, which leads to lower columbic efficiency of alloy-type anodes and conversion-type anodes than graphite anodes.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Forming a uniform SEI on the anode surface is critical to constructing high-performance LIBs, promoting homogenizing lithium deposition and high coulombic efficiency. The graphite anode exhibits a relatively high initial coulombic efficiency of $85 - 95\%$ owing to the formation of a uniform and dense SEI passivation layer containing several inorganic and organic components, such as $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ , LiF, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ , $\mathrm{LiCO}_2$ -R, and lithium trifluoromethane.[50] However, the surface cracking and surface exposure of active alloy-type and conversion-type anode materials are caused by the continuous volume expansion and contraction during cycling, which keeps consuming active lithium to generate the SEI, leading to a lower columbic efficiency than that of the graphite anodes.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Generally, electrode materials such as alloy-type and conversion-type anode materials experience significant volume changes during the cycling process. For example, the volume expansion of the typical Si anode after the complete lithiation is about $300\%$ (the Sn anode is greater than $260\%$ , and the Sb anode is greater than $200\%$ ).[43,51] In order to adapt to chemical changes, the conversion-type anode undergoes intense structural reorganization, resulting in huge changes in volume.[49] In addition to the continuous SEI generation, the fragmentation and pulverization of the anode active material due to the volume expansion will cause electrical contact loss between the active material and the current collector, increasing the internal resistance of the battery. While the breakdown of the conductive network results in the lithium trapping phenomenon, which brings a greater lithium loss.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: For the alloy-type and conversion-type anodes, the lithium-ion plating/stripping process is theoretically reversible. However, the enormous volume change of both types of anode materials during the cycling will lead to the formation of crystal defects on the anode materials. A certain amount of lithium can be stored in the crystal defects on the anode materials and cannot be released reversely.[52] For the conversion-type anode materials (for instance, $\mathrm{Co}_3\mathrm{O}_4$ , $\mathrm{CoS}_2$ ), lithium-ions will also form some side products, for example, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ , which will lead to further irreversible lithium loss. More severely, the electron-insulating nature of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O} / \mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ leads to a hindered electrochemical activity of the anode active material.

paragraph_context: Prelithiation via the direct contact with lithium powders is applied to provide additional Li source to the anode materials, which requires less prelithiation time and degree of control than the lithium foil approach. However, raw lithium powder is incompatible with the ambient environment, solvent, and the binder.[37] Therefore, the stabilized lithium metal powder is widely investigated by researchers to provide additional lithium source.[8,79,101-115] The stabilized lithium metal powder (SLMP) consists of $97\%$ lithium and $3\%$ protective layer (mainly $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ ) (Figure 6a), which has a high specific capacity of $3623\mathrm{mAh}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ .[79] There are some advantages of using SLMPP to eliminate the irreversible capacity loss of the anode.[112] First, the degree of anode prelithiation can be controlled more precisely. Second, the SLMP is evenly distributed at the anode electrode. Thirdly, the SLMP can be placed in the dry air. Fourthly, there is no residual lithium metal if the prelithiation process is well controlled. Typically, there are two methods to use SLMP for the anode prelithiation, one is to directly distribute the SLMP on the surface of anode, and another is to prepare the uni formly distributed SLMP slurry. However, it is regrettable that the SLMP cannot be used in the common solvents (such as 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP), $N,N$ -dimethylformamide (DMF), $N,N$ -dimethylacetamide (DMA)). SLMP can only be dispersed in some hydrocarbon solvents (such as hexane, toluene, and xylene). The usual methods of distributing the SLMP on the anode surface are spraying[111,116] and dropping.[109] Li et al. sprayed SLMP/p-xylene slurry onto graphite and HC anode using painting technology (Figure 6b), and the SLMP was activated after the anode rolling crushing. The prelithiated graphite and HC were assembled with a $\mathrm{LiMnO}_2$ cathode to construct a full-cell battery, which shows and improved initial coulombic efficiency (the graphite anode was increased from $82\%$ to $91\%$ , and the HC anode was increased from $61\%$ to $92\%$ ).[111] Forney et al. suspended the $3\%$ of SLMP in toluene and dropped suspension onto the silicon-carbon nanotube anode (Figure 6c-e). And then manual press was used to pressure-activate the SLMP, eliminating the $20 - 40\%$ initial cycle irreversible capacity loss. They are generally prepared by reacting powders with the molten lithium or a salt of lithium.[80,117-127] Similar to the SLMP, lithium alloy powders exhibit a high chemical reactivity. Therefore, improving the chemical stability is the key for the lithium alloy to be used as ideal prelithiation materials. Zhao et al.[117] synthesized $\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Si}$ nanoparticles (NPs) by mixing the Si NPs and lithium foil at $200^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in a glove box. The $\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ NPs are stable under the dry environment, which is compatible with the manufacturing environment of commercial LIBs. The $\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Si}-$ $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ NPs are readily mixed with various anode materials, both Si and graphite anodes are successfully prelithiated to achieve high initial cycle coulombic efficiencies of $94 - 100\%$ .
