label: 概述
paragraph_context: Organophosphorus compounds are key flame-retardant additives for improving the safety of Si-based lithium batteries, functioning mainly through a dual mechanism: [122-124] in the gas phase, phosphorus-containing radicals (e.g., PO-) generated from their thermal decomposition can efficiently capture H-/HO- radicals necessary for combustion chain reaction, rapidly interrupting flame propagation; in the condensed phase, some compounds can catalyze the formation of an intumescent carbon layer, which covers the surface of electrodes or separators, acting as a physical barrier for heat insulation and oxygen isolation [125, 126]. For Si anodes, this carbon layer can also alleviate structural damage caused by volume expansion and inhibit side reaction to a certain extent. However, the core challenge of flame-retardant additives lies in balancing flame-retardant efficiency and electrochemical performance, specifically reducing their reductive loss on Si anodes, optimizing the dynamic stability of SEI, minimizing the impact on ionic conductivity, and ensuring their oxidation resistance under high voltage. Developing novel phosphorus-based flame retardants through molecular engineering (e.g., fluorination modification, multi-functional group design) to achieve synergistic improvement of safety and electrochemical performance is a key pathway for the practical application of Si-based batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are widely recognized as a key technical pathway to enhance battery thermal safety due to their non-flammable property. Nevertheless, SSEs face a series of unique challenges when matched with Si-based materials [131, 132]. The primary issues include: dynamic volume expansion/contraction of Si-based anodes, which induces microcracks in SSE layers, impairs interfacial continuity, and causes localized resistance surges with heat accumulation [133-136]; and exothermic reactions at elevated temperatures — for instance, certain inorganic SSEs (e.g., sulfides) react with Si-based materials to form high-resistance phases, while the brittleness of some SSEs (e.g., oxides) leads to structural collapse under severe volume change, risking short-circuiting and thermal runaway [135-137].

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: To address these, researchers have developed targeted adaptation strategies. For polymer electrolytes, Pan et al. [127]. Designed elastic solid electrolytes (comprising a soft copolymer matrix and a deep eutectic mixture of N-methylacetamide and LiFSI) with high room-temperature ionic conductivity $(2\times 10^{-13}\mathrm{Scm}^{-1})$ , flame retardancy, and self-healing ability (Figure 8a,b). When paired with a $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode (without external pressure), this electrolyte enabled stable cycling over 300 cycles, and full cells ( $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ /elastic electrolyte/LiFePO $_4$ ) retained $98.3\%$ capacity after 100 cycles (Figure 8c). For sulfide electrolytes (valued for near-liquid ionic conductivity and mechanical deformability), Meng's team [128] integrated a 99.9 wt.% micro-silicon anode with sulfide SSEs, forming a stable SEI layer that allowed $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -NMC811 full cells to cycle stably at $5\mathrm{Ma cm}^{-2}$ ( $80\%$ capacity retention after 500 cycles) and operate across $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}-80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 8d). Wu et al. [129]. Further paired sulfide SSEs with hard-carbon-stabilized Li-Si anodes, achieving 5000 stable cycles for NMC811-based full cells (Figure 8e).

paragraph_context: In terms of safety, all-solid-state batteries with SSEs are not absolutely risk-free. Rui et al. [133] found that sulfide SSEs exhibit distinct thermal runaway (TR) mechanisms with NMC811 cathodes: glass-ceramic SSEs (e.g., $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{PS}_4$ ) react with cathode-released oxygen at $200^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (releasing $\mathrm{SO}_2$ and intense heat), while crystalline SSEs (e.g., $\mathrm{Li}_6\mathrm{PS}_5\mathrm{Cl}$ ) react with cathode decomposition products (e.g., transition metal oxides) at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 8f). More critically, at temperature $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the interface formed between Si and sulfide-based SSEs undergoes a vigorous chemical reaction, generating semiconductor products (e.g., Si-P compounds). These products significantly degrade the insulating property of SEI, triggering the continuous growth of the SEI and thereby leading to a dramatic increase in interfacial resistance. Meanwhile, the volume expansion of Si during charge-discharge processes induces transverse cracks in the composite electrode, which not only destroys the conductive network inside the electrode but also ultimately results in battery capacity decay (Figure 8g) [130].

However, the interfacial reaction mechanism of the system under high-temperature condition and specific impact of this reaction on battery performance have not been clearly clarified. Furthermore, the thermal safety performance of such sulfide-based solid-state electrolyte silicon-based electrode systems still requires further systematic evaluation.

paragraph_context: High-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) generally refer to electrolytes with a lithium salt concentration exceeding $3\mathrm{mol}\mathrm{L}^{-1}$ , and their breakthroughs in thermal safety are particularly notable [141-143]. Due to the significant increase in lithium salt concentration, solvent molecules are largely encapsulated in ionic aggregates, resulting in extremely low free solvent content (Figure 9a,b). Solvents are often the core combustible agents that contribute to battery combustion at high temperatures. This structural characteristic directly reduces the flammability of the electrolyte; even when the battery encounters extreme conditions such as puncture or short circuit, the amount of combustible gases released during thermal runaway is significantly reduced. Meanwhile, the SEI formed by HCEs is not only dense but also rich in inorganic substances derived from anion decomposition, thus exhibiting excellent thermal stability. Chang et al. [139]. Constructed a HCE composed of propylene carbonate (PC) and LiFSI. In this high-concentration electrolyte, PC and $\mathrm{FSI^{-}}$ form a specific structure through $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ complexation, which facilitates the formation of a self-limiting SEI. Compared with dilute electrolytes, the evolution of particle morphology and the expansion of electrode cracks are inhibited, and the cycling stability of nano-silicon is significantly improved.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: However, high-concentration electrolytes suffer from high cost, high viscosity, and restricted lithium-ion mobility. Therefore, the design of locally high-concentration electrolytes (LHCEs) has been proposed [144, 145]. Without significantly increasing the overall lithium salt concentration, locally high-concentration electrolytes utilize the regulatory effect of fluorinated solvents or diluents to create a solvation environment similar to that of HCEs at the electrode/electrolyte interface, precisely targeting the interfacial issues of Si-based anodes. Chae et al. [139]. Designed a LHCE using 1H,1H,5H-octafluoropentyl 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (OTE) as a diluent, tailored to the required molecular structure range for Si anodes operating over an extensive temperature range. This LHCE features an optimized ion solvation structure and achieves better cycling stability of Si anodes over a broad temperature range. Within the new electrolyte, cycled silicon anodes show a thinner SEI and a well-preserved compact structure (Figure 9c). Full cells with Si/graphite composite anodes and $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.3}\mathrm{Co}_{0.2}\mathrm{O}_2$ cathodes retained $80\%$ of their capacity after 500 cycles in $1.74\mathrm{M}$ lithium bis (fluorosulfonyl) imide in dimethyl carbonate with OTE, with enhanced thermal stability. Jia et al. [146]. Developed a non-flammable LHCE for Si-based anodes. Compared with conventional carbonate electrolytes with a high content of FEC, LHCE enables Si anodes to exhibit significantly enhanced electrochemical performance. paragraph_context: In contrast to the previously mentioned passive approaches for enhancing electrolyte safety, thermally responsive solidifying electrolytes represent a novel electrolyte system that establishes an active thermal safety mechanism. Under normal operating temperatures, these electrolytes maintain a liquid state or favorable liquid-solid interface characteristics, exhibiting high ionic conductivity to meet regular battery charge/discharge requirements. However, when encountering thermal safety risks (i.e., when temperature rises beyond a certain threshold), they rapidly transform into a solid or gel state through either self-polymerization reactions or interface polymerization reactions with the anode [149-152]. This transformation effectively blocks ion transport channels, prevents lithium-ion migration between electrodes, and suppresses high-temperature-induced gas crossover, thereby significantly improving the intrinsic safety of batteries [153].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Compared to graphite, Si-based material have attracted significant attention due to their higher specific capacity. However, substantial volume expansion during lithiation/delithiation processes has hindered their practical implementation. Through persistent efforts by researchers, the application of Si-based material in lithium-ion battery anodes has demonstrated promising breakthroughs. Nevertheless, safety concerns remain a critical challenge for lithium batteries. This review systematically addresses three key aspects: classification of Si-based mate rial, reaction mechanisms among components during thermal runaway, and strategies for enhancing thermal safety. While Si-based materials show bright prospects in LIBs, current research on their thermal runaway behavior remains insufficient, with numerous critical issues requiring further investigation. The following aspects may represent priority research directions for future Si-based thermal safety studies.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The current research on the thermal safety of Si-based batteries lacks depth. The high-temperature failure mechanism of Si-based interfaces during the cycle aging process remains unclear, especially the lack of systematic analysis of the dynamic correlation between the evolution of SEI components and gas generation. The action mechanisms and reaction principles of inactive components (e.g., binders, conductive agents) in the thermal runaway process are insufficiently studied. Quantitative models for gas migration paths during electrode crosstalk and cathode degradation have not yet been established. Future research should focus on developing high-temperature in situ characterization technologies (e.g., in situ high-temperature XPS, SEM) to enable real-time tracking of the thermal decomposition process of aged interfaces. Meanwhile, efforts should be made to construct multi-physics field coupling models to systematically simulate the chain reaction kinetic characteristics of "gas crosstalk-cathode oxygen release-thermal accumulation".

label: 概述
paragraph_context: A comprehensive and systematic comparative analysis of the thermal runaway mechanisms between graphite and Si-based materials is lacking, which restricts the safety design of Si-based anodes. Significant discrepancies exist in the conclusions from existing studies. There is also controversy regarding the evaluation index for the heat release of lithium-silicon alloys in the fully lithiated state (e.g., the use of $\mathrm{Jg^{-1}}$ vs. $\mathrm{JmAh^{-1}}$ ). Future work needs to systematically compare the reactions of Si-based materials and graphite with various battery components at high temperatures and establish a more scientific evaluation system.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The differences in thermal safety among different types of Si-based materials (e.g., nano-silicon, pre-lithiated silicon oxide, CVD silicon-carbon composites) and their underlying mechanisms are not yet clear. Systematic comparative research and mechanistic analysis are urgently required. Simultaneously, there is a gap in understanding the correlation mechanism between material-level test results (e.g., DSC exothermic peaks) and cell-level characteristic temperatures $(\mathrm{T}_1,\mathrm{T}_2,\mathrm{T}_3)$ in ARC tests. Targeted research is urgently needed to establish a cross-test platform data analysis system.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Existing coating layers are difficult to simultaneously meet the multiple requirements of high integrity, strong toughness, high thermal stability, and ionic conductivity. The impact of modification strategies on thermal runaway characteristic temperatures lacks a quantitative evaluation system. In the future, emphasis should be placed on developing gradient composite coating layers and self-healing interface materials, and quantifying their modification effects by combining technologies such as ARC/DSC. Meanwhile, the performance balance of electrolyte systems faces severe challenges. Electrolyte innovation needs to focus on multifunctional additives (e.g., fluorinated phosphorus compounds) to balance flame retardancy and electrochemical performance, optimize solid electrolyte interfaces (e.g., by introducing buffer layers or flexible composite solid electrolytes), and promote the synergistic application of LHCEs and temperature-responsive self-polymerizing electrolytes.

paragraph_context: Research on thermal safety at the full-cell level is seriously insufficient. Most studies ignore the synergistic thermal runaway mechanism between high-nickel cathodes and Si anodes, and the exothermic reaction path between sulfide electrolytes and cathodes in all-solid-state batteries has not been analyzed. In the future, it is necessary to construct a thermal runaway database for Si-based full cells (covering different cathode types and Si contents) to systematically verify the safety characteristics of multi-component systems. For all-solid-state batteries, it is necessary to distinguish the failure paths of different types of sulfide electrolytes and develop interface passivation technologies to provide theoretical support for the safety design of Si-based full cells.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Abstract: Lithium and sodium metal batteries continue to occupy the forefront of battery research. Their exceptionally high energy density and nominal voltages are highly attractive for cutting-edge energy storage applications. Anode-free metal batteries are also coming into the research spotlight offering improved safety and even higher energy densities than conventional metal batteries. However, uneven metal nucleation and growth which leads to dendrites continues to limit the commercialisation of conventional and anode-free metal batteries alike. This review connects models and theories from well-established fields in metallurgy and electrodeposition to both conventional and anode-free metal batteries. These highly applicable models and theories explain the driving forces of uneven metal growth and can inform future experiment design. Finally, the models and theories that are most relevant to each anode-related cell component are identified. Keeping these specific models and theories in mind will assist with rational design for these components.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In the necessary transition away from fossil-fuelled power, it is likely that solar and wind energy technologies will make up a large portion of power generation.[1-2] Additional grid stabilisation, such as large-scale energy storage, is required to support these variable renewable energy sources. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are currently the go-to option for grid-scale batteries.[3] However, LIBs have been specifically developed for portable applications (such as electric vehicles) so their use for stationary storage is suboptimal.[4-5] Alternatives to LIBs include sodium metal batteries (NMBs) and lithium metal batteries (LMBs) which offer greatly increased energy density and nominal voltages compared to ion batteries.[6-7] However, these metal batteries carry safety and lifetime concerns due to inadequate efficiencies, dendrite growth, and parasitic reactions.[8-12] Solving these challenges is the focus of metal battery research and has led to the development of new metal battery types such as the "anode-free" battery (where the metal anode is omitted during construction).[13] Despite the ongoing efforts, the challenges of metal batteries are yet to be solved in either conventional or anode-free configurations.[13-15] [+] E. Improving nucleation quality can be highly effective in improving battery performance by suppressing dendrites and minimising solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation.[9,13-19] Present approaches to improve nucleation include solid electrolytes,[14] modified liquid electrolytes,[20-21] artificial SEI layers,[22-23] novel current collectors,[9,11,24] and optimising cycling and construction parameters.[25-27] However, the nuances of nucleation and growth in metal batteries are not yet fully understood which is hampering the rational design of nucleation-focused investigations, though great strides have been made in recent years owing to the growing popularity of this field.[28-33] This review aims to take a more fundamental approach to metal nucleation and growth by collating and contrasting several prospective nucleation models and theories relevant to Na and Li metal batteries. Section 2 introduces the metal nucleation process in CMBs and anode-free batteries. Then Section 3 focuses on nucleation-relevant models and theory, and Section 4 concerns the growth process, following the outline below.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Section 3 Outline - Nucleation: The early nucleation process involves the establishment of metallic nuclei on the electrode surface, the thermodynamics of which can be explained using Gibbs free energy theory. Nucleation thermodynamics can also be explained by the wetting angle of the metal nucleus on the electrode surface, which may be affected by the lattice matching of the two materials. Later in the nucleation process, the distinction between progressive and instantaneous nucleation modes becomes clear, where the Scharifker-Hills model will be explored. This model is rather simplistic considering the complex environment of a metal battery; however recent extensions of the model have been developed such as the mixed nucleation model and the SEI fracture model, both of which are readily applicable to metal battery systems.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Section 4 Outline - Growth: Once the nucleation process has proceeded, the growth process begins (potentially in competition). This section explores growth-related models and theories, beginning with the highly influential Sand's time theory. The morphology of the deposited metal can also shift significantly due to its own surface diffusion which is the final collection of models discussed in this section.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The later sections of this review then assess the application of these models and theories to metal batteries noting their accuracy, relevance, and potential to further experimental findings.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Metallic batteries differ from ion batteries in the storage of the active material on the anode. Note, in literature it is common for the "negative" electrode to be referred to as an anode, a convention that has been adopted from the primary battery. However, in secondary batteries the "negative" electrode is the anode during discharging and is the cathode during charging. Here, "anode" will be used to refer the Na or Li metal electrode (for CMBs).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In metal batteries, rather than intercalating into a host material (e.g. graphite in LIBs), the metal cations are reduced directly on the anode surface forming metallic nuclei (see Figure 1). In CMBs, a piece of metallic foil (e.g. Na or Li) is used as the anode and during charging additional metal nucleates on the surface. In anode-free batteries the anode is omitted during fabrication, which means the metal will nucleate and electroplate directly onto the current collector.[13-15] The omission of the anode material in anode-free batteries improves energy density and safety; however, the only active material source is the cathode.[15,18] The inability to replace lost material can lead to rapid capacity loss and is the most significant challenge in anode-free metal batteries.[13,15,20] The differences between Li and Na are also important when considering their nucleation and growth. While it is assumed that they nucleate via identical fundamental stages, there are several inherent differences that can impact ion and atom behaviour in theoretical and practical applications. As summarised by Wang, et al. the larger atomic radius and weaker Lewis acid nature of Na compared to Li can lead to drastically different chemical and electrochemical behaviours.[30] Additionally, ion mobility through the electrolyte and SEI varies due to Stokes radius, which is larger for Li than Na in carbonate electrolytes.[34] The models and theories covered in this review generally use parameters such as the diffusion coefficient which are specific to each element, however it is still worthwhile to consider the impact of these qualities when planning practical investigations.

paragraph_context: Figure 1. From left to right, a solvated metal cation approaches the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and travels to the electrode surface (either a current collector or metal anode). Electron transfer is completed and the metal adatom diffuses across the surface to aggregate. Once sufficient in size, the nucleus is stable and is attractive to other incoming cations.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: A thorough understanding of the nucleation process in metal batteries is critical to solving their remaining challenges as it determines metal morphology, and therefore the development of dendrites and SEI formation.[35] A simple place to begin is the two major nucleation modes of electrodeposition: instantaneous and progressive.[36] The dominant nucleation mode is important in cell performance as it impacts metal morphology and surface coverage, as will be discussed later.[35] In instantaneous nucleation, nuclei are rapidly formed at the onset of deposition. Once initial nuclei have formed only the growth process occurs which results in metal deposits emerging from the nuclei as shown in Figure 2.[33] Intuitively, the instantaneous nucleation process results in good crystalline structures of the deposited material.[37] However, the surface of the deposited material may be rough if certain areas are prioritised for growth over others.[38] As the name implies, progressive nucleation involves the development of nuclei over time. The additional nuclei may form on the substrate or on top of previously deposited material (Figure 2). New nuclei formation occurs in competition with the growth of existing nuclei.[33] Progressive nucleation can lead to more dense, less crystalline, or smoother deposits in comparison to instantaneous nucleation.[35,37,39] The varied morphology and local deposition rates caused by instantaneous and progressive nucleation also has knock-on impacts on surface ion flux and SEI formation and vice versa. This relationship can induce or suppress the formation of dendrites and so controlling nucleation mode is desirable in metal batteries, however the criteria for inducing specific nucleation modes is still unclear. Several investigations observed switching between nucleation modes as potentials, temperature, electrolyte, and pH change.[35,39-40] In a recent work by Feng, et al. the nucleation of Li on Cu (mimicking a Li anode-free battery) was observed in situ using a reflection interference microscope (RIM).[41] They identified a transition in nucleation mode from progressive to instantaneous as the SEI was formed. Initially, SEI formation reactions decreased Li nucleation rate, inducing progressive nucleation. Over time this transitioned to instantaneous nucleation as SEI formation completed, then standard metallic growth once all nucleation sites were occupied. The impact of nucleation mode on long-term battery performance was further explored by observing Li removal during stripping. The areas where Li had most recently deposited were stripped first before areas which had "older" deposits. This was attributed to the structure of the SEI on these areas, but the morphology of the Li, and therefore Li flux would also play a significant role.[41] The method developed by Feng, et al. may be valuable for observing in situ nucleation and stripping of a range of metals and should be applied to other systems to confirm if the nucleation mode switching behaviour observed is common. Nucleation mechanisms can clearly impact the morphology of an electrodeposited metal and therefore dendrite formation. However, general understanding of when a switch in nucleation mode will occur is still not clear and further systematic investigations are needed for varied systems.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The following section discusses several models and theories which can identify instantaneous and progressive nucleation modes, and some others which cannot. The models and theories that cannot identify nucleation mode (those that are independent of time) are still highly useful for understanding the thermodynamic drivers of nucleation.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: To begin broadly, classical nucleation theory (CNT) provides a description of heterogeneous solid nucleation and can be applied to many systems.[42-43] However, the earliest definitions of CNT do not fully account for the complex electrostatic environment of a battery.[42,44-45] Because of this, a range of additional models and modifications to CNT have been proposed, which will be discussed.[46-47] Nonclassical nucleation theories are also noteworthy as they allow for multi-step nucleation processes through meta-stable intermediates. Analysing intermediate species provides more detail to the driving forces of nucleation, as opposed to CNT being based on the net change in Gibbs free energy.[48] Meta-stable intermediates are particularly important for nucleation and crystallisation of complex species such as protein, polymers, and minerals, which nonclassical nucleation theories are targeted towards.[42,49] However, given metallic nucleation in metal batteries is direct, and the nucleating species is simple, it is rational to apply CNT rather than nonclassical theories.[30,42-43,48,50-51] This section discusses several models that use CNT including their fundamental principles, state of development, and applicability to battery systems. Finally, discrepancies between the models are discussed.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: CNT originates from condensation and precipitation in supersaturated systems and uses the change in Gibbs free energy to assess nuclei formation (Equation 1). An energy barrier must be overcome for successful nucleation, which can be altered by the battery environment and operating parameters.[30,42-43,48,50-51] Importantly, this analysis of metal nucleation does not consider time, and so cannot discern whether instantaneous or progressive nucleation will occur. $$ G = - \frac {4}{3} \pi R ^ {3} \left(\Delta G _ {\mathrm {V}} + \frac {F \eta}{V _ {\mathrm {m}}}\right) + 4 \pi R ^ {2} \gamma_ {\mathrm {M E}} \tag {1} $$ Equation 1 calculates the total change in Gibbs free energy from nucleation by using a volumetric free energy term (left in Equation 1) and a surface-related term (right). In Equation 1, $R$ represents nuclei radius, $\Delta G_{\mathrm{V}}$ change in Gibbs free energy per unit volume, $F$ Faraday constant, $\eta$ overpotential, $V_{\mathrm{m}}$ metal molar volume, and $\gamma_{\mathrm{ME}}$ surface energy of deposited metal and the electrolyte interface.[30] During early nucleation, metallic "embryos" (clusters of 10s to 100s of atoms) are deposited on the electrode as shown in Figure 1. These embryos are not stable and some will redissolve into the electrolyte while others continue to collect metal atoms and grow until a stable critical radius $(R_{\mathrm{crit}})$ is reached.[30] Reaching $R_{\mathrm{crit}}$ demands an activation energy that must be overcome for nucleation to proceed (see Figure 3). This energy barrier is realised in the nucleation overpotential of the cell.[30,52-53] Improving the wettability of deposited Li or Na metal on the electrode can also improve nucleation thermodynamics and is measured via wetting angle $\theta$ .[53-55] $\theta$ is dependent on the interfacial energies between the deposited metal, electrolyte, and electrode as shown in Figure 4. Young's equation in Figure 4 then connects $\theta$ to the Gibbs free energy theory, with a small $\theta$ improving nucleation thermodynamics. Note that Young's equation is only applicable after $R_{\mathrm{crit}}$ has been reached so the system is in equilibrium.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Following Figure 4, the wetting angle $\theta$ can be reduced by using electrolytes and metal anodes (in CMBs) or CCs (in anode-free batteries) that have high interfacial energies against one another $(\gamma_{\mathrm{CE}})$ , or by decreasing the interfacial energy between the anode or CC and the deposited metal $(\gamma_{\mathrm{MC}})$ .[43,50,53-54] Strategies to increase $\gamma_{\mathrm{CE}}$ have been explored in rigorous experimental works.[56-58] For example Cheng, et al. observed a decrease in Li dendrite formation when using a ZnO/LiF dual layer interphase that had a high interfacial energy with the anode $(\gamma_{\mathrm{CE}})$ in a solid-state CMB.[58] Additionally, the low electronic conductivity of LiF hindered ongoing reactions between the anode and solid electrolyte. The resulting full cell, using a $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ cathode and $\mathrm{Li}_{10}\mathrm{GeP}_2\mathrm{S}_{12}$ solid electrolyte, exhibited a high reversible discharge capacity of $80\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ over 500 cycles.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: A possible technique to reduce $\gamma_{\mathrm{MC}}$ in anode-free batteries is to improve the crystallographic matching $$ \theta = \arccos \left(\frac {\gamma_ {\mathrm {C E}} - \gamma_ {\mathrm {M C}}}{\gamma_ {\mathrm {M E}}}\right) $$ between the metal and CC as will be discussed.[11,59-60] Understanding phenomena in metal batteries using a crystallographic perspective is emerging as a topic of interest in metal batteries, leading to a variety of theoretical and experimental investigations including anode preparation[61-63] and CC modification.[11,64-65] Gibbs free energy theory and wetting angle models consider the thermodynamic impacts of the applied overpotential and interfacial energies of the nucleus, electrode, and electrolyte/SEI species on the nucleation process. While they do not discern the mode of nucleation, these equations are useful in analysing the consequences of changing electrode materials and SEI or electrolyte makeup in metal batteries.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The crystal planes of the electrode surface impact metal nucleation according to Young's equation ( $\gamma_{\mathrm{MC}}$ in Figure 4) and may also influence the diffusion of cations near the electrolyte interface. These phenomena contribute to the thermodynamics of nucleation and influence the morphology of the deposited metal.[61,66-67] This is particularly relevant in anode-free batteries as the metal must nucleate on a different material, which imposes additional energy barriers.[31] Compatibility calculations and modelling have been used to screen potential current collector (CC) materials that will encourage metal nucleation in anode-free batteries.[31,65,67-71] A 2021 review by Bao, et al. and 2022 review by Olsson, et al. captures this interest well and discusses recent progress in understanding the impact of substrate crystal planes in Li, Na, Mg, K, and Zn battery systems, however some additional details are discussed here.[61,72] The interaction between two crystalline materials (such as a nucleating metal and anode (in CMBs) or CC (in anode-free batteries)) can be considered through "edge-to-edge" matching and "plane-on-plane" matching as shown in Figure 5.[31,68-69,73-74] For example, the edge-to-edge matching model proposed by Zhang et al. assesses the compatibility of close packed planes and assumes that the relationship is controlled by the minimisation of strain along these interfaces.[73] This model has become quite popular in light metal and alloy systems, particularly for assessing grain refinement.[73-76] Recently, models like the edge-to-edge matching model have been applied to a range of anode-free battery systems to assess the compatibility between the metal and current collector.[31,69] Cai, et al. (2022) assessed the deposition of Cu onto different CCs in an aqueous Cu battery. Ni, Pt, Au, and Ti were screened as potential CC materials and from the simulations Ni was the best material as shown in Figure 6a.[31] In-operando optical microscopy was used to evaluate surface evolution during deposition (Figure 6b). Images of these surfaces show nonuniform Cu deposits on Pt, Au, and Ti substrates within 10 minutes, however Cu on Ni remained relatively smooth.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Poor compatibility between the nucleating metal and electrode increases the lattice distortion of initial nucleating layers of metal (Figure 7) which increases the nucleation energy barrier.[31,68-69] Therefore, good matching between both materials may be necessary to facilitate mass nucleation across the electrode. However, identifying the best electrode material based on planes and rows is a complex process because: (i) certain rows/planes will be more effective for nucleation, (ii) these rows and planes are present in different proportions on the material surface, and (iii) they have different electron transfer capabilities.[31,38,68-69] An ideal electrode material will have an abundance of planes and rows with small misfit against the active metal for increased likelihood of favourable interactions.

paragraph_context: Sand's time theory, first described by Henry Sand in 1901, is a classical theory used to describe the evolution of metallic growth in diffusion-limited systems.[84] Bai, et al. summarised the core concepts of Sand's time theory well in their work relating to Li batteries.[85] Applying a current to a rechargeable battery induces a concentration gradient in the electrolytic salt near the surface of an electrode subject to a governing diffusion equation. If the applied current is significantly large, the salt concentration at the electrode surface can be driven to zero, preventing uniform deposition.[85] The time where the surface concentration reaches zero is defined as "Sand's time". After this time, deposition will be prioritised on surface protrusions which reach into areas of higher salt concentration, which directly leads to dendritic growth.[84-85] Sand's time theory clearly has large relevance to metal batteries and has been applied in several works.[85-89] Bai, et al. observed rapid onset dendritic growth and a spike in potential in capillary Li cells which corresponded to Sand's time when the current density was sufficiently high (see Figure 14a and b).[85] The apparent diffusion coefficient of the electrolyte $(D_{\mathrm{app}})$ was calculated following Equation 11 below, where $t_{\mathrm{sand}}$ is Sand's time, $z_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the charge number of the metal cation, $c_{0}$ is the bulk salt concentration, $F$ is Faraday's constant, $J$ is the current density, and $t_{\mathrm{a}} = 0.62$ is the transference number of anions in the system.[85] $$ t _ {\text {S a n d}} = \pi D _ {\text {a p p}} \frac {\left(z _ {\mathrm {c}} c _ {0} F\right) ^ {2}}{4 \left(J t _ {\mathrm {a}}\right) ^ {2}} \tag {11} $$ The group converted Sand's time into "Sand's capacity" by multiplying it with current density. This created a logarithmic curve which separated mossy and dendritic Li growths (Figure 14d).

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Compared to other Li battery literature (marked in Figure 14d), the curve does an adequate job in dividing dendritic and stable mossy Li deposits however some exceptions do appear.[90-92] These exceptions originate from changes in the SEI (either by the addition of an artificial SEI or changing electrolytes). This fundamentally alters the diffusion coefficient and current density experienced at the surface of the anode in CMBs, which will impact $t_{\mathrm{Sand}}$ . For this reason, the impact of SEI formation and makeup on Sand's time needs further exploration. The Sand's capacity curve generated by Bai, et al. could be very valuable in determining appropriate operating conditions for a battery, but only if the system is well understood through extensive testing.

paragraph_context: Surface diffusion models aim to describe how the morphology of metal deposits evolve over time due to diffusion of adatoms along the surface. This can directly decrease dendrite growth if the diffusion of adatoms away from the dendrite is sufficiently fast.[93-94] Surface diffusion is also critical in early nucleation stages as shown in Figure 1. By developing a surface diffusion model, Jäckle and Groß explained why Li regularly forms dendrites but Mg does not.[95] It was determined that Mg had a low surface diffusion barrier and tended to form agglomerates (due to its highly coordinated hcp arrangement). It was hypothesised that this low diffusion barrier was the consequence of strong interactions between Mg adatoms and lower adsorption energies than Li or Na.[96] Importantly, this early model could not consider SEI interactions with the adatoms as at the time it was "not possible to model dendrite growth atomistically in a realistic electrochemical environment".[96] Ozhabes, et al. screened the surface diffusion of Li on Li halide salts often present in SEI layers using DFT simulations.[96] They concluded that salts using moderately sized anions such as $\mathrm{Cl}^-$ and $\mathrm{Br}^-$ had the lowest diffusion barriers as these created multiple viable diffusion pathways.[96] While this is useful for comparing SEI species, it does not capture the full environment of a CMB anode (e.g. Li adatoms diffusing across the anode while interacting with SEI species). Ozhabes, et al. suggested that anode materials with high surface energies and surface mobilities are favourable due to the enhanced surface diffusion effect. This agrees with a surface diffusion model from Aogaki and Makino, however conflicts with concepts from the Gibbs free energy theory where increased surface energy between the metal and SEI $(\gamma_{\mathrm{ME}})$ has a negative impact on even metal deposition.[93,96] A 2D kinetic Monte Carlo simulation completed by Vishnugopi, et al. (2020) showed Li, Al, Mg, and Na self-diffusion in a liquid electrolyte. Their focus was on how different surface diffusion pathways impact overall morphology, which was achieved by controlling the activation energies for certain transitions.[97] Li, Na, Mg, and Al deposition was simulated at 0.6 and $0.8\mathrm{V}$ potentials (see Figure 15). At $0.6\mathrm{V}$ , Li developed into a porous network while all other metals were solid, albeit rough. At $0.8\mathrm{V}$ the Li deposits were dendritic and Na displayed some protrusions that could develop into dendrites. Both Mg and Al did not show obvious protrusions, but their surfaces had more noticeable peaks and valleys compared to $0.6\mathrm{V}.$ [97] According to the authors, $\mathrm{Mg}$ did not form dendritic structures due to its low energy barrier for diffusion across a step (0.01 eV). This means that the deposited metal quickly diffused away from the site of deposition and into more coordinated positions in valleys on the surface.[97] This rationale aligns with the other investigations discussed previously.[94-95,97] However, the lack of dendritic growth in the Na system reveals the limitations of this simulation, given the tendency of Na to form dendrites due to the influence of the SEI.[30,61,98-100] The impact of the SEI is known to be critical for metal deposition, and so future simulations must attempt to consider the SEI and anode material (in CMBs and anode-free batteries) together for a holistic perspective and more accurate results.

paragraph_context: Surface diffusion models highlight the importance of considering metal self-diffusion when describing metal growth. Specifically, how morphology can naturally evolve due to fundamental properties of the deposited metal. However, the impact of SEI species on self-diffusion needs to be better understood to make the surface diffusion model sufficiently robust for predicting metal morphology in battery research.

paragraph_context: The reviewed models represent diverse approaches to modelling and understanding metal nucleation and growth processes in batteries. All these models and theories are applicable to CMBs and anode-free metal batteries, however those that consider side reactions and make minimal assumptions regarding nucleation have higher relevance that those which neglect realistic features such as concentration gradients or side reactions. Table 1 presents a summary of models and theories related to nucleation, and Table 2 those that are growth-related. No single model or theory encompasses everything for metal nucleation and growth in complicated battery systems, rather a combination is needed to get an accurate representation.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: For example, the Gibbs free energy theory (and by extension the lattice matching model) has very strong theoretical foundations however neither consider side reactions or concentration gradients at a battery electrode. Introducing the SEI fracture model adds this consideration and allows for the identification of nucleation mode. However, in isolation this model (and all other Scharifker Hills-based models) cannot assess the favourability of nucleation on one material compared to another. Further extensions of the Scharifker Hills model are also still under development. To be robust it is critical that they are applied to diverse systems and shortfalls and limitations are identified.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Growth-related models are useful in explaining and simulating the evolution of metal morphology over time. Given that the nucleation and growth process can occur simultaneously, it would be wise to consider at least one growth-related model in conjunction with nucleation-related ones. Sand's time theory is robust and highly relevant to metal batteries, although the amount of experimental work required to thoroughly understand each unique battery environment is a downside. Surface diffusion models have also proven valuable for explaining the passive evolution of metal surfaces, particularly where a lack of dendritic growth is observed. To date, these computationally diffusion models have considered adatoms diffusing across the electrode surface or SEI species separately as considering both is too computationally expensive. However, it seems feasible that interactions between the SEI and electrode together could interfere with adatom surface diffusion, suggesting a gap in present literature.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Applying a smart selection of nucleation and growth-related models and theory is likely to provide an in-depth and comprehensive perspective into metal nucleation in batteries. Further development will require better understanding of the impact of the SEI and side reactions on the nucleation and growth processes.

paragraph_context: Metal nucleation and growth in batteries depends on the diffusion of ions through the electrolyte. Highly ionically conductive electrolytes will allow rapid and even diffusion to the electrode (promoting uniform nucleation and growth as illustrated in Figure 16c). Diffusion coefficients and electrolyte salt concentration are key drivers of ionic conductivity and also tie into SH-based models and Sand's time theory.[82,101-102] In recent years, solid-state electrolytes for Li and Na metal batteries have increased in popularity due to promises of higher energy density with improved safety.[8,14,103] As with liquid electrolyte batteries, in solid-state batteries it is important to consider the nucleation and growth steps separately. Because metal nucleation occurs in contact with the SEI, not the electrolyte, the state of electrolyte matter does not directly impact the nucleation process.[16,104] However, there are other factors such as internal pressure exerted by a solid-state electrolyte, that should be considered in Li and Na growth investigations.[105-106] Solid-state electrolytes appear to propagate dendrites differently to liquid electrolytes, particularly through grain boundaries.[107-108] It is important to understand how solid-state electrolytes should be considered in comparison to liquid electrolytes, which many of the previous models and theories are based on. Several reviews discuss this, particularly the differences in ion diffusion and SEI formation.[109-112] Sand's time theory has been directly applied to many electrolyte studies and is a useful tool for analysing the potential for dendrite formation, including solid-state electrolytes.[102,113-121] In one example, Song, et al. (2022) observed a $>10$ times increase in time to short-circuit when using PEO doped with LLZTO, FEC, and succinonitrile compared to a regular PEO solid-state electrolyte.[123] Both polymers had similar transference numbers and ion concentrations, however the doped polymer had $>30$ times greater ion diffusivity, which lead to greatly increased cycle lifetime according to experimental data and Sand's time theory.[122] Sand's time (Equation 11) can be strikingly accurate given the variability of battery systems.[123] Xu, et al. (2020) assessed the time required for the surface salt concentration at a Li electrode to reach zero - much the same as the Sand's time theory - at varied temperatures, concentrations, and current densities as shown in Figure 16a.[101] The relationships (see Figure 16b) between applied current density and electrolyte salt concentration to the depletion time (approximately reciprocally squared, and squared respectively) were similar to those predicted by Sand's time theory.[101] Additionally, while temperature is not explicitly considered in Sand's time theory, it does influence the ion diffusion coefficient through the Stokes-Einstein relation which is then applicable.[123] The impaired diffusion of ions due to viscosity is also not directly considered in Sand's time, but does have an impact on diffusivity and ion conductivity. While they did not employ Sand's time theory, Liu, et al. demonstrated a locally concentrated ionic liquid electrolyte (LCILE) (an ionic liquid electrolyte (ILE) diluted with a co-solvent) had decreased viscosity and improved ionic conductivity, leading to excellent battery performance.[124] The goal of LCILEs is to maintain the high transference numbers and non-flammability of ILEs, while decreasing viscosity and maintaining good solvation structure to enhance ion conductivity. Sand's time theory is incredibly valuable in electrolyte investigations, but the impact of features such as temperature and viscosity must also be taken into account.

paragraph_context: The overlap between the SH model and Gibbs free energy theory should not be overlooked. For example, a large critical radius can lead to instantaneous nucleation as the nucleation energy barrier is only overcome during initial deposition. Kim, et al. (2019) observed a similar phenomenon when introducing presodiated carbon nanotube (CNT) composites to Na metal batteries.[125] The presodiated CNTs provided ample sites for Na nucleation and a low nucleation energy barrier which changed the instantaneous nucleation in the Na symmetric cells to progressive as shown in Figure 17. The CNTs also reduced the formation of the SEI, as supported by reduced deviation from the SH curves and discussed in Section 3.3.

paragraph_context: Sand's time theory and the SH model (including components of Gibbs free energy theory) are highly relevant to electrolyte-based battery studies. However, it is important to note that while the diffusion of ions through the bulk electrolyte is influential, the solid electrolyte interphase plays perhaps a larger role in the diffusion of ions to the electrode surface. This, in combination with the high complexity of the interphase leads to more research interest in this field.

paragraph_context: The electrolyte in a metal battery decomposes upon exposure to Li or Na and under the applied potential, forming the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).[12,126] The SEI is critical in shielding the remaining metal from the electrolyte and therefore has a major influence on cell lifespan. The SEI also impacts metal nucleation and growth by interfering with local ion diffusivity.[82,127] The composition and morphology of the SEI is therefore critical for cell health and can be modified by changing the electrolyte and cycling parameters.[82,128-130] Artificial SEI layers are an alternative, which avoid initial metal consumption required to form the SEI.[12,126,131-132] Artificial SEIs are commonly based on species found in conventional SEIs, which for Li and Na batteries is often halide salts owing to their high ionic conductivity and mechanical hardness which may suppress dendrites.[127,132,134] However, other artificial SEIs which capitalise on the freedom offered by external synthesis use alternative materials such as silica, polymers, and alloys.[135-137] Both conventional and artificial SEI layers receive extensive research attention, given their significant role in individual cycle performance and overall cell lifespan.[6,10,12,127,131,133,137] Several of the models and theories covered in this review consider the influence of the SEI, namely the SEI fracture model, mixed nucleation model, and Sand's time theory. The combination of these three can be powerful as they cover the impact of SEI formation processes on over- potential as well as the change in diffusion of metal cations to nucleation sites. The direct application of Sand's time theory in SEI investigations is uncommon, however it can partially explain performance improvements observed in SEI experiments. For example, multiple studies have observed an improved SEI makeup and suppressed dendrite formation when using high concentration electrolytes in Na and Li batteries.[138-140] The SEIs in these systems feature a high proportion of Na- or Li-based salts, which effectively increases $c_{0}$ in the Sand's time equation (Equation 11) thus directly increasing Sand's time.[128] In addition to salt concentration, Sand's time theory also quantifies the importance of $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusivity through the SEI and local current densities which highlights the need for a homogeneous SEI. As an example, Pang, et al. (2017) introduced $\mathrm{Li_2S_6 - P_2S_5}$ (LSPS) to the electrolyte in a Li-S battery. The additive became a homogeneous and amorphous $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{PS}_4$ SEI layer with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ conductivity around $5\times 10^{-4}$ $\mathrm{Scm}^{-1}$ .[137] The advantage of the homogeneous and ionically conductive SEI was apparent in the greatly reduced impedance of the LSPS cell compared to one using the blank electrolyte (Figure 18 A versus B). High $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusivity across the electrode surface in the LSPS cell also reduced local current densities ( $J$ in Equation 11) by facilitating $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion over the whole electrode and slowing $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ depletion. This directly improves Sand's time, leading to an eightfold increase compared to the blank electrolyte as shown in Figure 18C.[137] SH-based models including the mixed nucleation and SEI fracture models are related to nucleation mode. As mentioned earlier, the original SH model does not consider side reactions during metal deposition and so modified versions can be more applicable in Li and Na metal batteries. Despite this, many papers focusing on SEI design have directly applied the original SH model.[29,81-82] In these studies it is common for data to deviate from the SH model curves due to SEI formation processes.

paragraph_context: The current collector (CC) has a significant role in both anode-free and conventional metal batteries (CMBs). In both types, the CC moves electrons between the connected electric circuit and electrode materials. In anode-free batteries the CC also facilitates metal nucleation, whereas in CMBs nucleation occurs on the metal anode. A sufficiently high electronic conductivity is required to ensure electron transfer is not a rate-limiting step, however this is easily achieved by metallic CCs and anodes. Instead, improving the thermodynamics of metal nucleation on the CC or anode surface is a challenge.[30,44,119] Good crystallographic compatibility between the metal and CC in anode-free batteries is important for favourable nucleation thermodynamics according to Gibbs free energy theory and lattice matching models.[11,70,141] An excellent example of this was developed by Foroozan, et al. who used graphene-modified (Gr-modified) Cu CCs in anode-free Zn metal batteries.[142] Graphene has a low $(\approx 8\%)$ lattice misfit with Zn and both have hexagonal packing. It was suggested this induced compact and uniform Zn deposits and reduced dendritic Zn growth. The graphene coating also shielded the Cu CC from the aqueous electrolyte, preventing parasitic side reactions and improving efficiency.[143] The influence of graphene on Zn deposition was further explored with grazing incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD) on the bare Cu and Gr-modified Cu surface. On the bare Cu, a range of Zn crystal planes such as (0002), (101 2), and (101 0) had similar intensities. However, on the Gr-modified CC the (0002) plane was clearly dominant.[142] This highlights the impact of CC lattice compatibility and its influence on the crystallographic orientation of electrodeposited metals in anode-free batteries. Further applications of Gibbs free energy theory and lattice matching models should be further explored in other anode-free and CMB systems.

paragraph_context: Electrochemical testing using charge and discharge cycles is a cornerstone of secondary battery research. However, there is no standardisation of cycling parameters (such as C rate, initial "preconditioning" cycles, rest times, or depth-of-discharge) and indeed the accuracy of these parameters (e.g. current density across a non-smooth electrode surface) is almost impossible to determine. Cycling parameters ultimately influence metal growth, CE, cell temperature, and side reaction kinetics so their selection is non-trivial.[16,148] It is therefore difficult to accurately compare experimental findings from cells tested with differing cycling parameters and this can be further explained by understanding the impact on the discussed models and theories.

paragraph_context: For example, the overpotential applied in chronoamperometry tests directly alters the profile of the current transients (as seen in Figure 12) used in SH-based models. A high current density also affects the kinetics of side reactions which can complicate the SEI component in the SEI-fracture model. According to Equation 11, Sand's time can be altered by changing current density and anion transference number (which is affected by the electrolyte and SEI composition). High current density can also lead to the rapid depletion of cations from near the electrode surface, bringing the onset of dendritic growth sooner.

paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have the potential to exceed the energy density of current lithium-ion batteries. Achieving this requires a thick positive electrode, a thin Li metal negative electrode, and minimal electrolyte-loading. Despite their promise, high energy density LMBs with high-loading positive electrodes, thin Li, and low electrolytes face significant challenges. A key issue is the high reactivity of Li metal with nonaqueous electrolytes, leading to the consumption of both during each cycle. This reaction causes insulating Li compounds to accumulate, increases electrode porosity and thickness, depletes the electrolyte, raises cell impedance, and reduces capacity. Therefore, understanding the interphase evolution of In response to the escalating energy demands of modern society, it is essential to develop high-performance energy storage systems to achieve sustainable energy solutions.[1] For decades, rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have proven effective for powering portable electronic devices and have recently emerged as the primary technology for electric vehicles. Nonetheless, the need for batteries with greater energy density is growing to enable electric vehicles to travel longer distances at reduced costs.[2,3] A promising strategy to increase the energy density of LIBs is to substitute the graphite electrode, which has a theoretical specific capacity of $372\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , with a lithium metal (Li) electrode.[4] Li metal electrode provides an exceptional theoretical specific capacity of $3860\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , low redox potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ versus the standard hydrogen electrode), and low density $(0.534\mathrm{gcm}^{-3})$ . the Li metal electrode is crucial to addressing cell failure. While various ex situ and in situ techniques have been used to study these interphases, they often involve non-practical cell configurations and sample-damaging preparation processes. In this regard, noninvasive methods like X-ray and neutron-based imaging are beneficial as they do not damage samples, can be used both in situ and ex situ, employ practical cell configurations, and enable long-term data collection. This review explores recent advancements in X-ray and neutron-based techniques for characterizing high-energy LMBs, emphasizing their potential to improve understanding of interphasial dynamics and advance robust high-energy-density batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Despite the promise, the commercialization of lithium metal batteries (LMBs) faces significant challenges, primarily due to low Coulombic efficiency (CE) and the formation of needle-like Li dendrites, which can penetrate the separator and cause short circuits.[5-7] Although recent advancements in electrolyte formulations have significantly mitigated the dendrite issue, the low CE remains a critical concern due to the high reactivity of Li metal.[7-12] Typically, the surface of Li metal is coated with a native film, and upon contact with a nonaqueous electrolyte, a new layer called the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) forms.[13,14] Ideally, this SEI layer should protect the Li metal surface from further reactions and stabilize the interphase. However, in practice, the SEI is mechanically unable to withstand the significant volume changes during Li plating and stripping cycles. Consequently, the SEI cracks, exposes fresh Li surfaces, and triggers continuous SEI formation.[15] This repeated SEI formation depletes active Li, resulting in lower CE and reduced cycle life. Additionally, the formation of electrically disconnected Li, or 'dead Li', also reduces the CE and cycle life.[16,17] The accumulation of insulating SEI compounds and 'dead Li', causing electrode volume expansion, increased electrode porosity, and entrapment of liquid electrolyte on the porous electrode surface, leads to increased cell impedance, voltage polarization, and premature cell failure.[18-21] Therefore, understanding the interphasial evolution of the Li metal electrode is crucial to addressing the interconnected problems of low CE, significant volume expansion, impedance growth, and short cycle life.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To investigate the interphasial processes on Li metal electrodes, both qualitatively and quantitatively, various analytical techniques have been applied. These include transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), optical microscopy (OM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and titration- based techniques etc.[22-35] Postmortem analyses using SEM and TEM offer high-resolution, site-specific insights into the interphasal morphologies of Li metal electrodes. However, the sample preparation required for these techniques often results in physical damage to the electrode surface, leading to potential inaccuracies. Furthermore, ex-situ methods cannot deliver time-resolved information. While in situ SEM and TEM studies can provide real-time visualization of electrode processes, they typically require cell configurations that differ significantly from actual batteries.[36-39] Additionally, the electron beams used in SEM and TEM can cause substantial damage to the sample under observation. In situ OM, although less invasive to the electrode surface structures, lacks sufficient spatial resolution.[24,40,41] Moreover, the cell configuration used for in situ OM, which often involves large quantities of electrolyte and physically separated electrodes without stack pressure, does not represent practical battery cells. Moreover, the microscopic techniques fail to provide any quantitative correlation between active Li loss due to interphasial changes and capacity fade in the cell. XPS, on the other hand, provides quantitative estimations of the SEI composition but is limited by its shallow penetration depth of only a few nanometers from the surface. Titration-based techniques, in this regard, have emerged as more precise quantitative tools for estimating Li loss due to SEI formation and dead Li accumulation.[26] Although each of these techniques has its own limitations, their combined application can complement one another and provide a comprehensive analysis. However, despite the utility of these techniques in characterizing the interphase of Li metal electrodes, their applicability is generally restricted to the initial few cycles. This restriction hinders their ability to provide information on the evolution of the interphase over prolonged cycling periods. Furthermore, given the fragility of Li metal electrodes under extended cycling, it is crucial to avoid any physical damage to the electrodes. This necessitates the introduction of noninvasive characterization techniques to ensure accurate and reliable analysis.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In this context, the characterization of the interphase using noninvasive techniques such as X-ray and neutron-based imaging techniques is highly beneficial.[18,42-51] These techniques offer several advantages: they do not damage the samples, can be employed both in situ and ex situ, closely resemble the actual cell configuration, and allow data acquisition over extended cycling periods. In this review, we discuss recent progress in non-destructive analytical methods for the characterization of high-energy-designed liquid electrolyte-based LMBs, focusing on their potential to enhance our understanding of interphasial dynamics and to drive the development of more robust high-energy-density batteries. Given the extensive number of review articles that discuss the application of various in situ and ex situ analytical techniques, this article specifically highlights the use of non-destructive methods in the study of LMBs.[34,52-54] Despite significant advancements in all-solid-state LMBs and the broad application of cutting-edge analytical techniques, the scope of this review is limited to liquid electrolyte-based LMBs. The primary rationale for this focus is the distinct degradation mechanisms between liquid electrolyte-based and solid-state LMBs. By focusing on LMBs with liquid electrolytes, this review aims to enhance the understanding of interphasial evolution at the Li electrode due to its complex interactions with liquid electrolytes and the subsequent impact on the stability and performance of LMBs.

Cross-sectional SEM revealed an expanded porous SEI layer on the electrode surface, with unused Li underneath, indicating that electrolyte depletion was the primary cause of cell failure. In high-energy pouch cells, the limited Li and electrolyte, combined with significant cell swelling, result in inadequate wetting of newly exposed Li surfaces during cycling. Ensuring proper wetting of these surfaces is essential for continuous electrochemical reactions.

paragraph_context: In high-energy-density LMBs designed with suitable technological parameters, the significant volume expansion of Li metal electrodes is a key factor in determining cycle life. Most studies analyzing the structural changes in Li metal electrodes rely on ex situ SEM analysis. However, this method inevitably damages the electrodes during cell disassembly, cleaning, and drying processes, preventing a clear identification of their actual condition. Particularly for Li metal electrodes that have undergone repeated charge/discharge cycles under practical cell conditions, they become very fragile due to increased porosity, and their structure easily collapses when released from the cell constraints. Therefore, non-destructive analytical techniques are essential to accurately monitor and understand structural changes in Li metal electrodes. In the following sections, we will discuss the potential and recent advancements of X-ray and neutron-based imaging techniques for high energy density LMB analysis.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: X-ray computed tomography (XCT) is widely recognized in medical and scientific fields as a non-destructive imaging technique that derives contrast from the absorption coefficients of different materials. The X-ray beam, attenuated by its interaction with the sample, is collected and processed using advanced algorithms to generate cross-sectional and three- dimensional (3D) images. Since its initial application in 1971, laboratory-based XCT technology has seen significant advancements, particularly in achieving spatial resolutions at the nanometer scale.[59-61] As a result, XCT has proven to be an invaluable tool for evaluating batteries and related materials.[51] In particular, the use of synchrotron-based XCT with high-brilliance beamlines enables faster imaging and greater sensitivity compared to that of laboratory-based XCT. This translates to faster image acquisition, enhanced sensitivity, and the ability to achieve higher spatial and temporal resolutions. Such powerful synchrotron-based XCT offers several distinct advantages for the analysis of LMBs.

paragraph_context: Unlike X-rays, which primarily interact with the electron clouds of atoms, neutrons are uncharged particles that interact with atomic nuclei. This fundamental difference gives neutron-based imaging techniques several unique advantages. While X-ray attenuation is significantly affected by the atomic number, with heavier elements causing greater attenuation, neutron attenuation is largely independent of atomic number. As a result, neutron imaging (NI) is a highly effective tool for analyzing LMB components, owing to the high neutron sensitivity to low-Z materials, such as Li and hydrogen, which are difficult to visualize by X-ray-based imaging techniques (XIs).[63] Additionally, because the nucleus is much smaller than the electron cloud, neutrons are only weakly absorbed by many common materials. As a result, NI can effectively probe structures hidden within dense metallic environments. Another significant advantage of NI is its sensitivity to isotopes, which allows for isotopic labeling—a powerful technique where specific isotopes within battery components are selectively reported.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Although NI complements XI by excelling at visualizing materials and features that are challenging for X-rays, this advantage is counterbalanced by certain limitations. The interaction between neutrons and atomic nuclei is inherently weak, resulting in lower neutron fluxes compared to X-ray sources. Consequently, NI often experiences lower counts reaching the detector, leading to higher noise levels and lower signal-to-noise ratios in the images. This necessitates longer exposure times to achieve comparable image quality to XI. In terms of spatial resolution and temporal resolution, neutron-based analysis cannot compete with X-ray-based analysis simply from the viewpoint of structural analysis of metallic Li electrodes.

paragraph_context: In this review article, we overview the applications of non-invasive characterization techniques used to study the degradation of LMBs. These techniques aim to address key issues such as the morphological evolution of Li metal, interphase growth, and quantitative assessment of cell degradation without causing physical damage to cell components. Non-invasive tools have successfully captured the microstructures of Li, revealing the heterogeneous growth of Li metal in three dimensions. Both laboratory-based and synchrotron XCT techniques have provided detailed insights into complicated structural changes of Li electrodes. These observations help us understand Li growth behaviors and interphase formation, which are crucial for identifying the root causes of cell failure, such as Li depletion or electrolyte consumption. However, lab-based XCT suffers from low resolution, while synchrotron XCT, though resolving this issue, faces the challenge of limited beamtime availability in many cases. Moreover, XCT techniques struggle with detecting low atomic number elements. NI is a highly effective tool for analyzing the degradation mechanism of LMB, owing to the high neutron sensitivity of low-Z materials, such as Li and hydrogen. Although the NI technique requires longer measurement time compared to the XI technique. NI can provide complements of XI by excelling at visualizing materials and features that are challenging for X-rays, such as concentration change of Li ions and movement of the electrolyte.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Despite the promising potential of Li metal electrodes, practical LMBs face several challenges, including an insufficient understanding of degradation mechanisms. Recent advancements in state-of-the-art techniques have shed light on some of these mechanisms. Each technique has its limitations, but collectively, they have significantly enriched our understanding of Li metal electrodes. To develop high-energy-density LMBs, focusing on non-invasive characterization techniques using practical cell configurations is essential. Complementary use of multiple tools can provide a more comprehensive understanding of cell processes, overcoming individual technical limitations.

paragraph_context: Lithium metal, with its high theoretical capacity and low redox potential, is the most promising next-generation high-energy-density battery anode material. However, the formation of uneven surface layers and dead lithium, significant volume changes in the electrode, and dendrite growth lead to rapid capacity degradation, low cycling stability, and safety issues, limiting the commercialization of lithium metal batteries (LMBs). As a strategy to improve the stability of LMBs, introducing three-dimensional (3D) structure with a large surface area can accommodate lithium (Li) inside the structure and homogenize Secondary batteries, which can be recharged and used continuously, have found applications ranging from small devices to various fields of energy storage systems. Recently, the market for Electric Vehicles (EVs) and their most crucial component, rechargeable secondary batteries, has experienced explosive growth due to the repercussions of climate policies. In line with this trend, there is also a significant increase in interest in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), which dominate the secondary battery market.[1-4] Alongside the market growth, the demand for high energy density and rapidly rechargeable batteries is also increasing. However, commercial graphite anodes fail to meet the performance requirements for the next generation due to their low theoretical capacity $(372\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1})$ and poor rate performance.[5-6] As an alternative to the graphite anode, a lithium metal battery (LMB) using lithium (Li) metal with high theoretical capacity $(3860\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1})$ and low electrochemical potential (standard hydrogen electrode, SHE vs. $-3.04\mathrm{V}$ ) as an anode material is an attractive anode system for high energy density batteries (Figure 1A).[7-8] Furthermore, Li metal anodes are considered essential materials for maximizing energy density in next-generation energy storage systems such as Li-sulfur and Li-air batteries.[9-12] The LMBs operate differently from conventional LIB systems, providing capacity through the plating/stripping of Li metal,[13] in contrast to materials such as graphite, silicon which respectively provide capacity through intercalation/deintercalation[14] and alloying/dealloying[15-16] reactions. local current density. Also, as a current collector and host material, free-standing carbon materials, with the advantages of lightness, low cost, electrochemical and mechanical stability, and excellent electronic conductivity, can effectively enhance energy density and cycle performance. In this review, we first discuss the chemical properties of carbon, and then summarize recent research progress related to the 3D structuring and chemical modification of carbon materials as a Li metal host. Finally, we present perspectives on future research for the practical application of free-standing carbon materials for LMBs.

paragraph_context: (1) The uneven solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer and the rough Li surface induce uneven charge distribution across the entire surface, leading to non-uniform nucleation and growth processes.[17] Furthermore, charge density accumulates around areas such as tips on the rough Li metal surface, resulting in the concentration of Li. This can lead to the preferential nucleation and growth of Li, promoting the formation of dendrites.[18] When sharp dendrites continue to grow, they may penetrate the separator, leading to internal short-circuiting upon reaching the cathode and causing safety issues.  (2) Li metal can undergo infinite volume changes during cycling processes. The stress resulting from these volume changes can lead to the destruction of the original anode structure, generation of cracks in the SEI, and acceleration of electrolyte depletion as the exposed Li metal surface reacts with the electrolyte.[19-22]  (3) During the stripping process of Li, inactive dead Li is formed, which is mechanically separated from the current collector and cannot participate in further reactions due to the broken electrical contact. The dead Li accumulated on the surface during the cycle slows the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport dynamics together with the thickened SEI layer due to repeated formation. The limited diffusion of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ increases the nonuniformity of Li electrodeposition, consequently increasing the possibility of dendrite growth. Moreover, the significant increase in interfacial resistance caused by the dead Li layer leads to a considerable decrease in Coulombic efficiency (CE), rate performance, and cycle life, resulting in battery failure.[23-25] To address this issue, numerous studies have been conducted mainly to modify the interface of Li metal. Various approaches, including electrolyte salt modifications,[26-27] electrolyte additives,[28-30] and the introduction of artificial layers,[31-33] have enabled fast Li movement while forming a robust electrolyte-anode interface. While these approaches have had a beneficial effect on enhancing the cycle stability of LMBs, they have not yet provided a fundamental solution for achieving stable operation of LMBs under high current density and high capacity conditions, as the improvements are still limited to the surface. In addition, in order to provide high energy density at the full cell level, control of the negative to positive capacity (N/P) ratio is also a key factor.[34-35] Although the thickness of Li metal foil can be controlled through the calendaring process, and the amount of Li in the anode can be adjusted, the utilization of Li metal foil still faces limitations from a commercial standpoint due to the complexity and increased cost associated with the production processes required for thin Li metal foils.[36-37] Therefore, an alternative system to the Li metal foil anode was needed, and the concept of anode-free LMBs has been proposed, gaining significant attention in recent times. In anode-free LMBs, the anode part does not contain active materials such as graphite, silicon, or Li metal. Instead, only a copper foil, serving as the current collector, is present in the anode part (Figure 1B). Li metal directly plating/striped on the Cu surface in anode-free LMBs, providing capacity without the presence of active materials. With only a thin current collector, this design enables the maximization of energy density and simplification of the electrode manufacturing process.[38-39] However, simply plating Li metal on the bare Cu foil can lead to uneven Li metal nucleation reactions on the surface due to the lattice mismatch between Cu and Li.[40] The non-uniform Li nucleation step and the limitation of surface area provided by the two-dimensional (2D) plane of the Cu foil result in the concentration of local current density. The increase in the local current density shortens the sand's time, defined as the time when the cation concentration reaches zero, and from this time, a local spatial charge is generated on the electrode surface, resulting in the growth of Li dendrite. The mentioned Sand's time can be expressed as formula (1).[41,42] $$ \tau = \pi D \left(\frac {C _ {0} e}{2 J}\right) ^ {2} \left(\frac {\mu_ {a} + \mu_ {c}}{\mu_ {a}}\right) ^ {2} $$ Where $\tau$ represents the sand's time, $D$ is the ambipolar diffusion coefficient, $C_0$ is the initial Li-ion concentration, e is the charge of an electron, J is the effective current density, and $\mu_{a},\mu_{c}$ denote the mobility of anions and cations, respectively.
