paragraph_context: As mentioned above, carbon materials have gained significant attention as strong candidates for Li metal plating. However, bare graphitic carbon materials exhibit lithiophobic characteristics due to the nonpolar structure of $\mathfrak{sp}^2$ carbon and the large lattice mismatch between graphene and Li metal.[58-59] These characteristics make carbon can only have weak interactions with Li, causing significant energy barriers for nucleation and a high possibility of uneven nucleation and dendrites formation on the surface. For this reason, Li and carbon form a large contact angle between them, making it difficult for Li to uniformly growth on the surface. It also restricts the application of pre-lithium infusion processes such as molten Li infusion. According to Young's equation, the contact angle of a metal nucleus is determined by the interfacial energies between Metal-Substrate $(\gamma_{MS})$ , Metal-Electrolyte $(\gamma_{ME})$ and Substrate-Electrolyte Electrolyte $(\gamma_{SE})$ , and it can be expressed as follows.[60] $$ \theta = \arccos \left(\frac {\gamma_ {S E} - \gamma_ {M S}}{\gamma_ {M E}}\right) $$ That is, since contact angle can be reduced by reducing the interfacial energy $(\gamma_{MS})$ between the carbon host material and Li metal by modifying the characteristics of carbon. Therefore, to utilize carbon substrate as an LMBs host, it is considered necessary to adjust the surface characteristics of carbon substrate in a form favorable to Li plating by introducing lithophilic seed particles or adjusting the chemical properties of the carbon itself.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: When assessing the suitability of a substrate material as a Li host material for LMBs, lithophilicity, and surface diffusion barriers are mentioned as the most representative factors from a chemistry perspective. Lithophilicity significantly contributes to the nucleation step, and surface diffusion barriers are closely associated with the subsequent deposition behavior of Li. In the typical charging process, under the electric field, solvated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ approach the SEI layer on the anode side. Subsequently, solvated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ undergoes desolvation, and only the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ pass through the SEI layer to reach the electrode surface. Afterward, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ is reduced to Li atoms on the electrode surface, aggregated through surface diffusion until reaching a stable critical size, forming nuclei, and then grow further. When reviewing the entire process of Li plating, the Li nucleation step depends on the surface chemistry of the structure. In other words, the binding energy between Li and the substrate, indicative of the interaction strength at the atomic level, serves as a crucial indicator associated with the lithophilicity of the substrate. $$ E _ {\text {b i n d}} = E _ {\text {t o t a l}} - E _ {\text {L i}} - E _ {\text {s u b s t r a t e}} $$ $E_{\mathrm{bind}}$ , $E_{\mathrm{total}}$ , $E_{\mathrm{Li}}$ , $E_{\mathrm{substrate}}$ represent the binding energy, total energy of the adsorbed Li atom and the bound substrate, energy of the Li atom, and substrate bound energy, respectively.[61] Substrates capable of strong interactions with Li atoms are known to reduce Li nucleation overpotential, thus substrates with moderately high negative binding energy are preferred. Graphitic carbon typically exhibits low binding energy, so this means is that for the successful application of carbon as a host in LMBs, modification of carbon properties is required.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: However, during the synthesis and adjustment of surface chemistry in carbon materials, defects are almost inevitably generated in carbon. The defects in carbon can be divided into intrinsic defects and extrinsic defects. Intrinsic defects include topology, vacancy, and edge defects, while extrinsic defects include heteroatom doping and defects arising from their binding sites.[62] Defects in carbon typically enable stronger interactions with other reactants and act as electrochemical active sites. Thus, carbon defect engineering is of interest in various energy storage fields.[63] When applied to LMB, defects in carbon not only form sites with charge and spin density, enhancing the interaction capability with Li and reducing nucleation energy barriers but also lower the diffusion barriers of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and Li atoms. However, excessive defect concentrations can disrupt the C-C sp<sup>2</sup> conjugated structure, impairing its electrochemical activity.[64] Therefore, precise defect control based on a comprehensive and deep understanding of defect chemistry is essential for the rational design of carbon materials for LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The topological defects refer to the distortion of the carbon lattice into one or more unconventional polygonal forms or the manifestation of dangling bonds, accompanied by the redistribution of asymmetric electrons. Vacancy defects are characterized by the absence of carbon atoms in the hexagonal carbon lattice, while edge defects result from the loss of carbon atoms in a fixed orientation, leading to high spin and high charge density.[64] Intrinsic carbon defects inevitably occur, but carbon materials can have different characteristics depending on the intrinsic carbon defect structure. The surface chemistry of the defect structure is an element that must be understood and utilized because it is directly related to the ability to interact with Li metal.

Carbon atoms at the typical C6 site form three $\sigma$ bonds with nearby neighboring carbon atoms and delocalized $\pi$ bonds. paragraph_context: One of the challenges when using carbon-based materials in battery systems is the increase in side reactions. The formed uneven SEI further promotes the uneven initial Li nucleation and dendrite growth in Li systems where surface chemistry plays a crucial role. To address this, H. Kwon et al. introduced multivacancy (MV) defect sites on the surface of carbon paper to adjust the Fermi level of carbon as shown in Figure 3F, forming a thin and uniform SEI and inducing uniform Li nucleation.[67] Experimental results show that pristine carbon paper $(\mathsf{p} - \mathsf{CP})$ forms an irregular mosaic SEI with randomly dispersed organic and inorganic particles. In contrast, defective carbon layer-coated carbon paper $(\mathsf{d} - \mathsf{CP})$ exhibits improved CE and a uniform, thin SEI. They interpreted this phenomenon through the Fermi level. The defective structure exhibits a lower Fermi level of the electrode surface than that of $\mathsf{p} - \mathsf{CP}$ in all lithiation state regions (Figure 3G). The reduced Fermi level on the Carbon surface due to MV defects inhibits electron transfer to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of the electrolyte, preferring to accept electrons from Li at electron-deficient MV defect sites, thereby suppressing side reactions. Furthermore, according to quantum mechanical tunneling theory, decreasing the Fermi level increases the tunneling barrier. This allows electrical insulation to be reached at lower SEI thicknesses, mitigating electrolyte decomposition and restricting the growth of the SEI. To investigate nucleation behavior on the surface, Li atom cluster arrays on bilayer graphene (BLG) and MV defects were calculated via density functional theory (DFT). The results indicate that Li grows vertically on the $\mathsf{p} - \mathsf{CP}$ surface. On the other hand, Li nucleation on d-CP involves the continuous adsorption of five Li atoms due to strong orbital hybridization between Li and MV defects, leading to their growth along the defect side. Therefore, the combination of lithiated MV defects with lithiophilic properties, along with a thin and dense SEI providing a uniform $\mathsf{Li}^{+}$ flux, promotes homogeneous nucleation (Figure 3H). During additional deposition processes, Li nuclei undergo lateral growth and merging with nearby nuclei, allowing for flat Li deposition on the carbon substrate (Figure 3I).

paragraph_context: Heteroatom doping involves substitution of some carbon atoms with heteroatoms, which integrate into the $sp^2$ -centered network or defect sites of carbon, serving as an easy and effective method to modify carbon properties. The formed heteroatom-carbon bonds can modulate charge distribution and electronic properties, altering localized chemical reactivity. Depending on the characteristics of the dopant, carbon exhibits different properties such as lithophilicity, wettability, and electronic conductivity. Introducing appropriate dopants can effectively enhance electrochemical activity.

paragraph_context: X. Chen et al. summarized the calculated binding energy between various heteroatom-doped carbons and Li atoms (Figures 4A-B). Then, demonstrated that the lithophilicity of doping sites is correlated with the electronegativity, local dipole, and charge transfer with Li of the dopant. Subsequently, they provided comprehensive guidelines for the design of lithophilic doped carbon.[68] The relatively electronegative N (3.04) and O (3.44) compared to carbon (2.55) can strongly interact with the electropositive Li atom (0.98) through Lewis acid-base interactions. Doping with B (2.04), which has a lower electronegativity than carbon, can render adjacent C electronegative, leading to enhanced Li adsorption. Additionally, considering the actual effective electronegativity is crucial as the interaction capabilities between the dopant and Li may vary depending on the chemical state of the doped site. For example, The N, O, and F atoms all form $\sigma$ bonds with adjacent carbon and withdraw electrons through inductive effects. Among them, N and O atoms can contribute additionally to the negative charge state due to their participation in the delocalized $\pi$ system. On the other hand, the F atom forms $p-\pi$ conjugation with the carbon plane, feeding electrons back to C from its filled p orbital. As a result, despite having the highest electronegativity, the F site exhibits low effective electronegativity, leading to low Li adsorption energy. Thus, the limitation of comparing different dopants solely based on electronegativity led this research group to consider additional factors. They additionally considered the local dipole defined as dipoles formed by doped atoms and adjacent carbon atoms. As a result, an implicit linear correlation between binding energy and factors associated with the sum of electronegativity and local dipole has been proposed.

paragraph_context: The introduction of metal atoms into carbon materials can significantly enhance the electrochemical activity of the material. Among them, Single Atom Catalysts (SACs) utilizing metal atoms as catalysts provide highly dispersed individual active sites fixed on a support. By doping a single atom metal into the carbon matrix, agglomeration of metal species can be prevented and atom utilization efficiency can be maximized. Recently, there has been an increasing effort to utilize materials where metal atoms are anchored in a Metal-N-C configuration through strong interactions with coordinating atoms possessing lone pairs of electrons, such as N, as hosts for Li metal.[75-76] Adding the SA catalyst improves lithiophilicity, reduces Li metal nucleation overpotential, and enables uniform Li deposition. They performed MD simulations and experimental tests to demonstrate the enhanced lithophilicity achieved through the introduction of single atoms.[77] Furthermore, T. Liu et al. explored the priority of Li deposition behavior on the carbon surface induced by N and $\mathrm{Cu}_{x}\mathrm{N}$ doping using in-situ Raman spectroscopy.[78] As the Li plating time increased, both the intensity of the D-band and G-band gradually decreased. However, it induces too strong adsorption with Li atoms and side reactions between Li and nitrogen, resulting in structural damage to the $\mathrm{Zr - N_x - C}$ configuration and leading to a low cycle life. SAMn@NG shows little change of bond length and bond angle between the metal atom and surrounding coordinating N atoms in the processes before and after Li deposition, functioning as a reversible site with minimal chemical structural changes during Li plating/stripping. This contributed to more stable cycling. In conclusion, it is essential to design SA-doped host materials with appropriate binding energy for Li, and a sophisticated design considering various factors such as binding energy with multiple Li atoms and chemical stability is necessary.

paragraph_context: In this section, we discussed the reaction characteristics and effects related to various defects and dopants. Controlling the intrinsic defect sites of carbon is an effective approach. However, forming and precisely distributing specific defects that are favorable for Li plating/stripping still requires further research. Doping with heteroatoms is also an effective strategy that can significantly enhance the affinity with Li. However, for practical success in LMBs, it is essential to be able to control the doping elements and amounts. Furthermore, it is important to understand the interaction of Li at the bulk level, rather than solely at the atomic scale, to ensure that doping can induce uniform reactions even in high-current density and high-capacity deposition systems. Moreover, screening for effective dopants that not only reduce the nucleation barrier of Li metal but also improve surface diffusion kinetics is essential for achieving uniform Li deposition during rapid charging. Lastly, while discussions on the characteristics of carbon itself have been extensive, there is a lack of exploration into how such doping influences the structuring and architecture of carbon. Therefore, future designs should also consider the synergistic effects of carbon doping with carbon building blocks and the final structure.

paragraph_context: Various carbon materials such as carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, and carbon fibers have been utilized to produce freestanding carbon materials for applications in the field of energy storage. In this section, we categorize the conducted research into building block structures of 1D, 2D, and 3D in the fabrication process of free-standing films. Additionally, we aim to explore approaches for modifying the properties of carbon and film formation to apply these building structures as hosts for LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: CNTs have a high aspect ratio (length to diameter ratio) and possess a one-dimensional (1D) cylindrical structure, similar to rolling up a graphene sheet.[84-85] CNTs are lightweight and have good mechanical and chemical stability, as well as a high surface area and excellent electrical conductivity, making them suitable materials for use as current collectors. Furthermore, the entangled network structure of CNT bundles is easily assembled into free-standing films with a high surface area. This makes it straightforward to manufacture CNT films using various methods, rendering them promising materials in various energy storage applications.[86-87] Recently, efforts have been made to leverage the advantages of these CNT substrates for use as Li metal plating hosts. This includes adjusting the carbon surface chemistry or forming composites with other lithophilic particles to overcome the inherent lithiophobic limitations of CNTs. In addition, efforts are being made to address the issue of the high irreversible reaction in CNTs by developing a prelithiation process for a 3D structure.

These results suggest that, in terms of Li storage capacity, the number of graphitic layers has a more significant impact than the specific surface area. The walls of MWNT also enable reversible storage/release of Li-ions and promote more uniform and stable Li deposition compared to DWNT. When applying CNTs as Li metal hosts, some of the Li-ions are stored between the walls at the initial stage of Li deposition, and the interface of the lithiated CNT scaffold can promote uniform Li deposition. paragraph_context: Graphene is a material characterized by a hexagonal 2D planar structure formed by chemically $\mathfrak{sp}^2$ hybridized carbon atoms. It has gained attention in various energy fields due to its advantages such as high thermal/electrical conductivity, mechanical properties, and chemical stability.[101-102] Graphene oxide (GO) is functionalized with oxygen, imparting a negative charge and enabling the formation of stable colloidal suspensions. This makes it advantageous in modification or processing, allowing for easier composite with other materials and fabricating graphene films. Additionally, GO possesses lithophilic properties that allow it to absorb Li, and reduced graphene oxide (rGO), with stronger binding energy with Li compared to pure graphene due to its carboxyl and alkoxy groups, exhibits enhanced surface lithophilicity compared to bare graphene.[103] For this reason, when applying a graphene-based material as a host for LMBs, a method of fabricating a mechanically stable and flexible film with functionalized graphene and then injecting Li into the structure is drawing attention.

paragraph_context: Chen et al. attempted to maximize the energy density of LMB by developing an ultra-thin structure based on graphene.[104] First, a graphene oxide (GO) solution was blade-coated onto a substrate using a doctor blade to obtain a GO film, and through the ultrafast self-expansion and reduction (USER) reaction, the GO film was transformed into a porous, expanded, and reduced graphene oxide film (eGF). The obtained eGF was calendered through a roller to adjust the thickness to $0.3 - 20\mu \mathrm{m}$ . Afterwards, molten Li was injected between the internal channels of eGF using capillary action to design a thin Li electrode (Li@eGF) with a 3D host structure. The lithophilic 3D rGO structure inhibits inhomogeneity of local current density, provides high mechanical strength, and the low weight ratio and high conductivity of rGO play an excellent role as a current collector. As a result, the cycle stability and energy density of the battery using Li@eGF as the anode were improved. In a pouch cell manufactured with lithium iron phosphate $(\mathrm{LiFePO}_4,$ LFP) as the cathode, it maintained $81\%$ of its capacity after 200 cycles, providing a nine-time higher cycle life than when using pure Li metal as the anode.

paragraph_context: LMBs are considered ideal battery systems for high energy density applications due to the high theoretical capacity of Li and its low negative electrochemical potential. However, despite these advantages, the uneven nucleation and growth of Li dendrites during the growth process, along with the formation of dead Li, pose safety concerns and lead to low cycling performance, becoming significant obstacles for practical applications. Among various strategies, utilizing free-standing carbon materials as a Li metal host is a promising option to address these issues. 1) The inherent excellent conductivity of carbon, along with a superior three-dimensional conductive network, provides fast electron conduction pathways, 2) and the lightweight characteristics of the porous carbon framework can maximize the specific energy density. 3) The large surface area provided by the aligned or interconnected three-dimensional structures can reduce local current density and provide a uniform $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux, inducing uniform Li nucleation and growth, ultimately suppressing dendrite formation. 4) Lastly, the wide spaces within the structure alleviate the stress of volume changes caused by the growth of Li metal and can stably accommodate Li metal.

paragraph_context: To design high energy density full-cell, it is crucial to consider compatibility with other parameters, and there are still unresolved challenges to practically apply free-standing carbon materials as the anode of LMBs. Several key issues to be addressed in the future and additional factors to consider when designing free-standing carbon materials are as follows.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: (1) The use of high surface area and defects of carbon frameworks can lead to high irreversible reactions, resulting in decreased CE, which can negatively impact the cycle life and overall energy density. This could be a significant obstacle to commercialization. Therefore, an effective prelithiation process for carbon needs to be established. The method used in previous studies, manufacturing cells followed by electroplating and disassembly, results in a complex process and increased costs. The molten Li infusion method also has limitations in terms of quantification of infused Li quantity, scalability, and universality. Therefore, for considering the DOD and N/P ratio, it is essential to establish a sophisticated and scalable pre-lithium infusion method that can control the amount of Li.  (2) Carbon with excessively large surface area can undergo excessive irreversible reactions. To prevent additional side reactions, the SEI layer can be pre-formed during pre-processing steps such as Li infusion, or artificial layers can be introduced.  (3) Unlike copper-based substrates, an additional Li insertion reaction occurs in carbon materials, but there is a lack of understanding of the effects of this lithiation process. However, many studies utilizing carbon as an LMB host focused on only improving the lithophilicity of carbon. Therefore, comprehensive carbon chemistry engineering is required, taking into account lithophilicity, carbon surface diffusion kinetics, bulk $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion, and interfacial layers, after understanding the nucleation and growth processes of Li on carbon materials through in-depth experimental and theoretical analysis.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: (4) It is important to design a substrate that considers practical utilization and fabrication process. The produced film should be flexible, and the process should be simple, cost-effective, and capable of large-scale production.  (5) The uncontrolled thick thickness of the 3D framework can impede volumetric energy density, so a technology that can control the thickness of the substrate according to the required capacity is needed. At this point, methods to effectively utilize the space within the 3D structure should also be considered.  (6) Testing should be conducted in a practical environment, considering the high loading mass of commercial cathode material; in other words, test conditions that utilize the high areal capacity of the Li anode.  (7) Extensive analysis has been conducted on the electrochemical behavior of free-standing carbon materials as hosts for Li metal. However, many studies have been limited to laboratory-scale coin cell tests. To evaluate commercial viability, analysis at the pouch cell level is necessary. Differences between pouch cells and coin cells, such as cell components, and scale can lead to gaps in pressure and current density distribution, areal resistance of electrodes, electrolyte content, cell design, and other factors. Recently, there has been a recognition of this importance, and evaluations of electrochemical performance at the pouch cell level are also being provided. But still, most of these evaluations are limited to cycle test results. Therefore, conducting an in-depth analysis of operational principles in pouch cells and designing free-standing carbon materials suitable for pouch cells, including multi-stack cell configurations is essential.  In an ideal scenario where these requirements are met, freestanding carbon materials have the potential to maximize energy density and improve cycle performance, making the development of these materials highly promising. Therefore, in-depth research from multiple perspectives on free-standing carbon hosts is expected to offer significant promise in the realization of practical LMBs for next-generation energy storage devices.

paragraph_context: Finally, the roll-milling-included procedure has been adopted as one of the most remarkable concepts for designing dry battery electrodes. The shear force created by the calender gap, pressing, and rotation ratio between rolls causes the dry-mixed power to experience additional mixing and dispersion, resulting in a smooth electrode film. In industry, Maxwell-Tesla selected a roll-milling-based dry coating process to fabricate freestanding electrode films by using two roll mills, and Fraunhofer IWS recently patented DRYtraec® technology consisting of multiple roll mills toward cost-saving electrode production (Figure 4d). Achieving homogeneity demands substantial energy input due to the difficulty in thoroughly mixing these components. Consequently, relatively simple processes result in uneven material distribution, similar to wet electrode fabrication, thereby adversely affecting cell performance. Uneven distribution causes several issues, including 1) disruption of electron- and ion-transport pathways, increasing internal resistance; 2) localized high stress or insufficient adhesion, leading to poor electrode performance and potential mechanical failure; 3) fluctuations in the charge-storage capacity and cycling stability due to uneven active material loading; and 4) over- or underutilization of specific electrode areas. Therefore, meticulous attention is necessary in material mixing for dry electrodes, especially when compared to wet processes and strategic approaches are suggested such as hot-melt mixing, secondary mixing to realize well-mixed composites and uniform distribution in electrode. Design factors such as the mixing equipment, mixing strength, mixing protocols, and material properties significantly impact the electrode characteristics. paragraph_context: Recently, it has become imperative to develop high energy density as well as high safety lithium-ion batteries (LIBS) to meet the growing energy demand. Among the anode materials used in LIBs, the currently used commercial graphite has low capacity and is a safety hazard due to the formation of lithium dendrites during the reaction. Among the transition metal oxide (TMO) anode materials, TMO based on the intercalation reaction mechanism has a more stable structure and is less prone to volume expansion than TMO based on the conversion reaction mechanism, especially the niobium-based oxide in it has attracted much attention. Niobium-based oxides have a high In recent years, the rapid depletion of non-renewable resources such as oil, natural gas and coal has brought about a huge hazard to the natural ecological environment as well as an energy crisis.[1-3] As a result, there is a surge in demand for effective alternatives to fossil energy sources. Among the many new energy sources, LIBs are typical of secondary batteries with high energy density and excellent cycle stability.[4-7] LIBs have become an indispensable capability component for electronic devices such as cell phones and computers, as well as the energy source of choice for electric vehicles, due to their powerful portability and safe high energy storage. LIBs also have great potential in lighting systems and can be used to provide reliable power by combining them with solar cells. LIBs consist mainly of cathode and anode materials, diaphragms, electrolyte and a casing. LIBs work by embedding and deembedding $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ back and forth in the anode and cathode materials. During the discharge of LIBs, the cathode material is the oxidizing element, which receives electrons in the external circuit and is reduced; the anode material acts as the reducing element, which releases electrons to the external circuit and is oxidized. Thus, LIBS is capacity reversible and constantly enables the conversion of chemical and electrical energy.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Any material that can reversibly store lithium ions and has a suitable potential window can be used as a cathode material, so the cathode material has a wide range of options. Currently, a wide variety of cathode materials for LIBs are available in the market, including $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ , $\mathrm{LiMn}_2\mathrm{O}_4$ , $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ and Ni-Co-Mn.[8,9] In terms of anode materials, the main materials include carbon, alloy type and TMO. The main carbon material currently used in the market is graphite. However, the multiplicity performance operating potential to inhibit the formation of lithium dendrites and lithium deposits to ensure safety, and have stable and fast lithium ion transport channels with excellent multiplicative performance. This review summarizes the recent developments of niobium-based oxides as anode materials for lithium-ion batteries, discusses the special structure and electrochemical reaction mechanism of the materials, the synthesis methods and morphology of nanostructures, deficiencies and improvement strategies, and looks into the future developments and challenges of niobium-based oxide anode materials. of graphite can no longer meet the current requirements for fast-charging anode materials for LIBs, and because graphite has a low embedded lithium potential, it is prone to lithium deposition and lithium dendrite generation during charging and discharging, which leads to certain safety hazards. Alloy materials mainly include silicon-based and tin-based materials. Silicon-based materials have higher theoretical specific capacity and voltage plateau than conventional carbon materials, and have good safety performance. Alloy materials all have the disadvantage that during the reaction process, the volume will undergo huge expansion, material shattering and structural destruction, leading to battery performance decay. Compared with carbon materials with lower theoretical specific capacity and alloy materials with severe volume expansion, TMO has better structural advantages to solve the above problems. TMO is abundant in nature and has low development cost, according to the reaction mechanism, TMO can be divided into two types: intercalation reaction and conversion reaction. The conversion reaction mechanism of TMO has a high specific capacity, but its volume expansion during the reaction is large. The intercalation reaction mechanism has a stable structure and is less prone to volume expansion, but its theoretical capacity is low and its electrical conductivity is poor. Therefore, in order to optimise the multiplicity performance of anode materials for LIBs to meet the increasing demand, it is urgent to find new safe and high multiplicity anode materials.

paragraph_context: Niobium-based oxides have attracted a lot of attention as an anode material in recent years. paragraph_context: $\mathrm{Nb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ is a typical semiconductor metal oxide material, with a typical trimmed edge $\mathrm{ReO}_3$ structure, its shear surface is composed of a large number of $\mathrm{NbO}_{6}(\mathrm{n}\times \mathrm{m})$ octahedral, the octahedron connection through the sharing of edges and corners, which makes the material maintain a stable lattice structure in the process of lithium intercalation and insertion, so the material can have good cycle stability, and this layered structure of A-B-A provides a large number of lithium ion transport channels, providing a structural basis for the rapid transport of lithium ions inside the material.[11] The reaction process can be represented by the following equation: $$ \mathrm {N b} _ {2} \mathrm {O} _ {5} + \mathrm {x L i} ^ {+} + \mathrm {x e} ^ {-} \leftrightarrow \mathrm {L i} _ {\mathrm {x}} \mathrm {N b} _ {2} \mathrm {O} _ {5} $$ Although the three crystal forms of $\mathrm{Nb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ can undergo reversible intercalation of lithium ions, their mechanisms are somewhat different. Kodama et al. tested $\mathrm{O - Nb_2O_5}$ (tetragonal crystal system) and $\mathrm{T - Nb_2O_5}$ in different states by in situ technology, and the results showed that the crystal structure of $\mathrm{Nb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ remained unchanged during intercalation and delithiation, and the volume expansion of unit cells did not exceed $1\%$ , indicating that it had good structural stability.[18] The number of $\mathrm{Nb}^{5 + }$ and $\mathrm{Nb}^{4 + }$ ions is continuously converted with the amount of lithium ions, which indicates that the intercalation and delithiation removal process of $\mathrm{O - Nb_2O_5}$ and $\mathrm{T - Nb_2O_5}$ is a simple single-phase solid solution reaction. Although the intercalation and delithiation processes of the two are similar, $\mathrm{T - Nb_2O_5}$ has better electrochemical intercalation and delithiation removal performance due to the different internal lithium ion storage locations. B. Dunn et al. found that $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ preferentially passed through (180) and (001) crystal planes through testing. No new diffraction peaks were observed after electrochemical cycling, confirming that the redox reaction of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ with $\mathrm{T - Nb_2O_5}$ occurs in a single system.[19] When $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ is embedded in $x = 1.8$ in $\mathrm{Li_xNb_2O_5}$ , the lattice parameter of the c axis increases to $4.02\AA$ . The diffraction peak shifts towards a lower diffraction angle, which indicates that the crystal plane spacing increases due to the larger radius of the $\mathrm{Nb}^{4+}$ cation (0.83 Å) than the $\mathrm{Nb}^{5+}$ cation radius (0.78 Å). These phenomena indicate that the material forms a channel that promotes $\mathrm{Li}^+$ migration during the reaction. Thus, the special crystal structure of $\mathrm{T - Nb_2O_5}$ provides two-dimensional $\mathrm{Li}^+$ channels with minimal crystal structure change during $\mathrm{Li}^+$ embedding. $\mathrm{T - Nb_2O_5}$ has the ultrafast dynamics of Li storage because of the special $\mathrm{Li}^+$ storage mechanism.

paragraph_context: Niobium-titanium oxides are generally prepared by various methods for different contents of niobium oxide and titanium oxide. The niobium and titanium atoms have similar radii and chemical properties, and the $\mathrm{Ti}^{4+}/\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}$ redox corresponds to an lithiation-delithiation platform nearly identical to that of $\mathrm{Nb}^{5+}/\mathrm{Nb}^{4+}$ . The main niobium-titanium oxides reported for LIBs anode materials are $\mathrm{TiNb}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ , $\mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Nb}_2\mathrm{O}_9$ , $\mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Nb}_{10}\mathrm{O}_{29}$ , etc. Among them, the most studied and the best performance is $\mathrm{TiNb}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ .

paragraph_context: $\mathrm{TiNb_2O_7}$ belongs to a monoclinic crystal system with space group $C2 / m$ [42] Its structure can be described as a $\mathrm{ReO}_3$ configuration with $\mathrm{TiO_6}$ octahedra and $\mathrm{NbO_6}$ octahedra sharing edges and corners. As shown in Figure 7, with Nb atoms and Ti atoms at the center of the octahedra, where Nb atoms and Ti atoms are arranged in a disordered manner.[43] Each layer plane of TNO consists of a large number of shear plane units, each containing $3\times 3\mathrm{MO}_6$ (M=Nb, Ti) octahedra, and the shear planes form an A-B-A laminar structure between them for lithium ion storage; moreover, in the process of lithiation-delithiation, a 5-electron transfer can occur, corresponding to a redox reaction of 5 electric pairs $(\mathrm{Ti}^{4 + } / \mathrm{Ti}^{3 + },\mathrm{Nb}^{5 + } / \mathrm{Nb}^{4 + },\mathrm{Nb}^{4 + } / \mathrm{Nb}^{3 + })$ ,with a theoretical capacity of $387.6\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , while the "shear surface $\mathrm{ReO}_3$ structure" of $\mathrm{TiNb}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ is more suitable for the embedding and exfoliation of lithium ions than the simple $\mathrm{ReO}_3$ structure, during which the structure remains largely unchanged.

paragraph_context: Similar to $\mathrm{Nb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ , $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}$ is a broadband compound (2.9 eV),[45] which is commonly used in photocatalysis.[42] In 2011, the electrochemical properties of $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}$ were first investigated by Goodenough's group,[46] who prepared $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}$ , carbon-coated $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}$ ( $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}/\mathrm{C}$ ) and Ti (10%) doped $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}$ ( $\mathrm{Ti}_{1.1}\mathrm{Nb}_{1.9}\mathrm{O}7$ ). The first reversible capacity of $\mathrm{TiNb}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}/\mathrm{C}$ at a multiplicity of 0.1 C was 285 mAh g $^{-1}$ , and the capacity did not decay after 30 cycles; when the multiplicity was increased to 2 C and the charge/discharge interval was 1.4–2.5 V, the reversible capacity of the material was 150 mAh/g, which showed better multiplicity performance than that of lithium titanate. $\mathrm{Ti}_{1.1}\mathrm{Nb}_{1.9}\mathrm{O}_{7}$ shows a better multiplicative performance, with a charge capacity of $\sim 170$ mAh g $^{-1}$ for 3 min, $\sim 115$ mAh g $^{-1}$ for 20 s, $\sim 90$ mAh g $^{-1}$ for 10 s, and $\sim 75$ mAh g $^{-1}$ for 5 s at a fixed discharge rate of 2 C. The authors also assembled TiNb2O7 with $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Mn}_{1.5}\mathrm{O}_{4}$ , and found that when the conventional positive limit capacity was used, $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.5}\mathrm{O}_{4}$ was overcharged at the end of charging ( $\sim 3.3\mathrm{V}$ ), resulting in a significant decay of the total battery capacity with the increase of charge and discharge times; when the anode dosage was used to limit the capacity, the full battery showed excellent cycling stability, and the capacity basically did not change in 50 cycles. This indicates that the unreasonable positive and anode electrode dosage has been used to limit the capacity. This indicates that the unreasonable capacity matching of cathode and negative electrode will lead to a more likely side reaction between cathode material and electrolyte, resulting in the reduction of active lithium ions inside the battery, which will lead to the degradation of battery performance. Therefore, when niobium-based oxide is used as anode material, its adaptation character- istics in the battery are different compared to graphite and need special attention.

paragraph_context: Niobium-based oxides have excellent performance and high safety as anode materials for lithium-ion batteries. Its high working potential prevents the formation of lithium dendrites and SEI films, and almost no volume expansion occurs during the reaction. However, they all suffer from problems such as low electrical conductivity, which hinders research on the application of electrochemical energy storage. Although optimization strategies such as structural nanosizing have been compounded with carbon materials to improve the multiplicity and cycling performance, there are still some problems and challenges in the future research of niobium-based oxide lithium-ion battery anode materials. 1. There is no definite theory on the kinetic control of the electrochemical reactions in niobium-based oxide materials. In particular, there is a lack of corresponding calculations for the mechanism of intercalation pseudo capacitance, which leads to an insufficient number of experimental projects that can be practically applied, and a more in-depth study of the $\mathsf{Li}^{+}$ embedding/detachment mechanism through theory is needed.  2. For issues such as the conductivity of niobium-based oxides, compound modification with carbon materials remains the main avenue for future research. However, the introduction of carbon materials during the modification process brings about an overall loss of battery capacity. Therefore, a preparation method that incorporates the smallest amount of carbon to obtain the optimal performance needs to be discovered in future research on anode materials for lithium-ion batteries.  3. Although the multiplicity and cycling performance of niobium-based oxides are excellent, their low theoretical specific capacity limits practical applications to some extent. Therefore, considering the synergistic effect, it is promising to compound niobium-based oxide anode materials with some high-capacity cathode materials. On the other hand, half-cells can be used to analyze the electrochemical properties of electrode materials, but to use the materials for practical applications, the full cells of which they are composed need to be tested. For this reason, in-depth research on niobium-based oxide full electrodes must be intensified in order to expand the industrial application of niobium-based oxide electrode materials.

paragraph_context: The urgent demand for high-energy-density storage systems evokes the research upsurge on the alkali metal batteries with high theoretical capacities. However, the utilization of alkali metal anodes, including Li, Na, and K, is significantly hindered by notorious dendrite growth, undesirable corrosion, and unstable solid electrolyte interface. In order to resolve these issues, the carbon materials for the rational design of current collector/host that can regulate the plating/stripping behavior of alkali metal have been exploited. These carbon-based current collectors/hosts are featured with many pivotal advantages, including mechanical integrity to accommodate the volume change, superior electronic/ionic conductivity, large available surface area, and rich functionalization chemistries to increase the affinity to alkali metal. In this review, the recent progress on various dimensional carbon-based current collectors/hosts with different chemical components in stabilizing the alkali metal anodes through the regulation of initial deposition and subsequent growth behavior during plating/stripping process is provided. The nanostructured carbon scaffolds with self-affinity to alkali metals, as well as the carbon frameworks with internal/external affinitive sites to alkali metals, catalogued by various dimensions, are discussed in this review. Therefore, these appealing strategies based on the carbon-based current collectors/hosts can provide a paradigm for the realization of high-energy-density alkali metal batteries.

paragraph_context: The commercial Li-ion batteries (LIBs) based on intercalation chemistry are approaching their energy limit, which can hardly meet the high- Institute for Health Sciences and Technology (SAIHST), Sungkyunkwan University, 2066, Seoburo, Jangan-gu, Suwon 440-746, Korea University, 2066, Seoburo, Jangan-gu, Suwon 440-746, Korea energy-density demand for the tremendous development of portable electronics and electric vehicles in recent years.[1] This limitation triggers the research upsurge for the next-generation battery chemistries beyond the conventional LIBs. Among electrochemical energy storage devices, the rechargeable Li metal batteries (LMBs), utilizing Li metal as the anode, have drawn ever-increasing attention owing to the ultrahigh theoretical capacity $(3860\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1})$ and the lowest electrochemical potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ vs SHE).[1-4] Benefiting from the employment of Li metal anodes (LMAs), more options of high-capacity cathodes, such as sulfur and oxygen, are available to further boost the specific energy instead of conventional Li-containing inorganic compounds.[5-8] It has been known that the utilization of LMAs was firstly pioneered by Stanley Whittingham at Exxon in the 70s of last century.[1] Unfortunately, the research concerning LMAs became depressed for decades due to the significant safety concern caused by the notorious Li dendrite growth. The achievements enabled by nanotechnology over the years have reawakened the focus on LMAs owing to their potential capability to tackle the severe issues of Li dendritic The major hurdles of LMAs for practical application can be addressed to be unrestrained dendrite growth and high chemical reactivity between Li metal and electrolyte.[1,2,9] The uneven initial nucleation of Li metal can induce the nonuniform deposition and subsequent dendrite formation, whose aggregation might penetrate the separator to cause the short circuit of the battery and terrible safety issues. Meanwhile, the fragile solid electrolyte interface (SEI) generated on the Li metal surface, arising from the contact between electrolytes/additives and Li metal, might be also pierced by the dendrites with large specific surface area, leading to the formation of isolated inactive "dead" Li during stripping process and the remarkable reduction in Coulombic efficiency (CE). The newly exposed Li metal near SEI cracks can result in the formation of substitutional SEI, accelerating the continuous consumption of electrolyte and Li itself. Moreover, the infinite relative volume change during cycling can also contribute to the failure of the LMAs. Therefore, regulation of the initial nucleation, suppression of Li dendrite growth, and accommodation of the volume fluctuation are all prerequisites to fully boost the performance of LMAs while avoiding safe concerns.

paragraph_context: It is worth noting that the rapid evolution of LIBs and LMBs relies heavily on the availability of Li resources in the Earth crust. However, due to the low nature reserves and continuous consumption, the cost issue of Li-containing materials is becoming more serious in the recent years. Both Na and K are regarded as ideal alternatives to Li owing to their high natural abundance and similar physicochemical properties to Li (Figure 1).[1-3,10-16] Thus, sodium/potassium metal batteries (SMBs/KMBs), based on the utilization of Na/K metal anodes (SMAs/KMAs), have been receiving significant attention owing to their high theoretical capacity $(1166\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ for Na anodes and $685\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ for K anodes) and low electrochemical potential $(-2.71\mathrm{V}$ vs SHE for Na anodes and $-2.94\mathrm{V}$ vs SHE for K anodes), as well as natural abundance. In a similar manner to the LMAs, the employment of SMAs and KMAs is also facing the similar challenges, especially for the abominable dendrite growth. Besides, the direct utilization of pristine foils of these alkali metals with excessive capacity fails in achieving the expectation from the safety and economic perspective. In order to alleviate this problem, one viable approach is to employ the electrodeposited metal with limited capacity rather than these pristine foils. The thicknesses of electrodeposited metallic Li, Na, and K with an areal capacity of $1\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ are 4.85, 8.86, and $16.92~{\mu\mathrm{m}}$ respectively, which is also beneficial for the subsequent regulation of ratio of negative to positive electrodes (N/P ratio). Thus, it is of great importance to guide the Na/K nucleation and deposition during the plating/stripping process.

paragraph_context: As an important component of the battery system, the current collectors are used to support the active materials and to collect electrons. For alkali metal anodes, the modification or functionalization of current collectors/hosts could be an appealing choice to inhibit the dendrite growth during cycling.[15-17] According to classic Chazalviel's diffusion model, the initial time of dendrite growth is correlated with "Sand's time" $(\tau)$ .[20-22] $$ \tau = \pi D \left(1 + \frac {\mu_ {c}}{\mu_ {a}}\right) ^ {2} e ^ {2} C _ {0} ^ {2} / 4 J ^ {2} \tag {1} $$ where $D$ is the diffusion coefficient; $e$ , the electronic charge; $C_0$ , the initial electrolyte concentration; and $J$ , the effective current density. $I_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $I_{\mathrm{c}}$ represent the mobilities of anion and cation, respectively; namely, one viable solution for the postponement of dendrite occurrence is to reduce the effective current density, which can be realized by the employment of nanostructured current collectors/hosts with large specific surface area. Generally, in order to fully activate the potential of current collectors/hosts, several features should be endowed: 1) lightweight to achieve the high specific capacity; 2) electronically and ionically conductive to allow the electron/ion transport; 3) mechanically robust to tolerate the volume fluctuation; 4) chemically stable to avoid the electrochemical corrosion; 5) low cost to meet the urgent demand of industrial scale-up; and 6) rich functionalization chemistry to realize various modification. The carbon-based current collectors or hosts have been demonstrated to become strong candidates to satisfy these requirements (Figure 2).[16-20,23,24] Recently, many efforts have been devoted to develop excellent current collectors/hosts for high-performance alkali metal anodes.[16,25] Up to now, several reviews have been presented to summarize the advances of current collectors for LMAs and SMAs.[16-20,23,24] Some of the literatures mainly focus on three-dimensional (3D) current collectors for LMAs/SMAs,[17,18] while others pay great attention to the utilization of porous carbon materials in LMAs/SMAs.[23,24] However, the systematic and comprehensive review about current collectors/hosts based on carbon materials for advanced alkali metal anodes (LMAs, SMAs, and KMAs) is timely needed. Since the electrochemical properties and functionality of carbon materials are mainly determined by their structures and compositions, the delicate control in the structural dimension and the desirable regulation of chemical structures of the current collectors/hosts is required for achieving homogeneous plating/stripping of alkali metal ions, which results in realizing high-performance dendrite-free alkali metal batteries. Thus, the elaborate chemical strategies for the rational design of carbon-based current collectors/hosts from the perspective of different structural dimensions and chemical components are critical for the future development of advanced alkali metal batteries. Herein, we aim to provide a comprehensive review on the recent advances in carbon-based current collectors/hosts for alkali metal anodes based on the different dimensions and chemical functionalities of carbon materials. Generally speaking, the various nanostructured carbon frameworks with affinity to alkali metals, as well as the robust carbon network with internal/external decoration to attract the alkali metals, are summarized in this review. We believe that these strategies mentioned below will shed light on the research of the next-generation high-energy-density alkali metal batteries.

paragraph_context: The development of LMAs has been plagued by the dendrite growth problem for decades.[1,2,17,18,24,26-28] Recently, tremendous efforts have been devoted to regulating the Li deposition at the initial stage and alleviating the Li dendrite growth during repeated plating/stripping cycles. Among the various strategies, the employment of carbon-based materials as current collectors/hosts has proven to be effective approaches.[1,17,18,23,24,27] With the merits of low density, high flexibility, large surface area, high electrical conductivity, and tunable properties, carbon-based materials have been intensively investigated as either the nucleation agents or the accommodation scaffolds/hosts for metallic Li.[23,24] The volume change of LMAs during cycling can be reduced by the employment of carbon frameworks with large interior space. The large surface area and high conductivity of carbon-based materials are also beneficial for the establishment of uniform charge distribution and homogeneous Li-ion flux. The functionalization or doping of carbon substrates also enables to improve lithophilicity to guide the Li deposition at early stage to prevent the dendrite nucleation.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: From the structural point of view, the commonly used carbon materials can be divided into zero-dimensional (0D) carbon materials such as carbon particles/spheres, one-dimensional (1D) ones such as carbon fibers/nanotubes, two-dimensional (2D) ones such as carbon sheets/graphene, and 3D ones such as carbon frameworks/skeletons. The structural dimensions hold a great impact on the functionalities and properties of the carbon-based current collectors/hosts. For instance, 2D carbon-based current collectors/hosts possess sheet-like nanostructure with ultrahigh specific surface area and preferable mechanical toughness to regulate the Li electrodeposition and physically suppress the dendrite puncture. In a contrast to 2D planar current collectors/hosts, the 3D lithophilic carbon-based nanostructures with intrinsic large internal space can deliver a rapid electrochemical reaction kinetics with a low interfacial resistance and stabilize the deposition of metallic Li by lowering local ion flux near the anode. To realize the abovementioned functionality, the favorable affinity of these carbon materials to the metallic Li is the prerequisite. Thus, the chemical modification of those carbon nanomaterials to increase the lithophilicity is also important. In the following sections, we will mainly review the recent progress concerning different dimensional carbon-based materials with self-lithophilicity as current collectors/hosts for LMAs, and the electrochemical properties of the mentioned studies are listed in Table 1.

paragraph_context: Carbon materials can be utilized as substrates for metallic Li deposition due to the lithiation capability.[29-31] However, the intercalation of Li ions might result in severe exfoliation and pulverization of carbon substrates. In order to address this issue, Yang et al. introduced the ball milling method upon natural graphite to reduce the particle size and yield micropores with surface defects, realizing the suppression of pulverization during the Li deposition process and the stability improvement for Li plating/stripping cycling.[30] Thus, to some extent, minimizing (nano-sizing) the carbon particle or damaging the graphitic structure to introduce the defects could be conducive to enhancing the lithium plating/stripping cyclability. In order to further understand the key factors to determine the cell performance, the electrochemical performance of representative carbon hosts and chemically functionalized carbon materials for LMAs in different electrolytes was recently evaluated by Liu's group.[31] Their results demonstrated that the interaction between electrolytes and the carbon materials was more important than other factors such as the host structure types and surface chemistries. However, common carbon materials, such as graphene, usually suffer from unavoidable aggregation, which is unfavorable for the Li accommodation. Pan and coworkers developed a tough graphene framework comprising 3D periodic hollow carbon spheres to serve as a freestanding host to stabilize LMAs.[32] This specific 3D periodic hollow structure rendered the framework high robustness under pressure caused by battery assembly.

S-doped carbon nanospheres with ordered mesoporous channels (SMC) can be utilized as the functional scaffold for stable LMA.[35] The regulated local current density, homogeneous nucleation sites, and facilitated mass transport enabled by large surface area, S-doping, and ordered mesoporous structure of the carbon spheres, respectively, can induce uniform lithium nucleation and the subsequent dendrite-free growth.

paragraph_context: 2D carbon materials possess a huge potential for in situ or ex situ surface modification due to their layered structure with abundant exposed sites, which makes them ideal candidate as scaffolds or hosts for LMAs.[20] As the most common 2D materials, raw graphite has been investigated to accommodate Li by increasing the porosity and prelithiation.[58,59] Another attractive choice is graphene, which confronted with research boom due to its unique physiochemical properties since its advent. The rGO with large surface area and great lithophilicity guaranteed the initial homogeneous Li injection and later deposition even after cycling. Besides, the top cap layer of rGO can also serve as a robust artificial interface to stabilize the SEI. For further investigation, Wang and coworkers demonstrated bending-tolerant LMAs by integrating metallic Li into bendable rGO.[62] The severe Li dendritic growth and loss resulted from the bending stress can be remarkably circumvented by the employment of flexible rGO films. This improvement can be ascribed to the fact that the proposed scaffolds provided increased available surface for homogeneous plating of metallic Li and minimized the volume fluctuation of Li composite anode during cycling. Heteroatom doping is considered as a feasible strategy to realize the improvement of lithophilicity for carbon materials. First principle calculations and experimental verifications were adopted by Zhang's group to examine the effect of the lithophilicity chemistry of heteroatom-doped carbon on the nucleation behavior of Li metal.[64] The characteristics containing electronegativity, local dipole, and charge transfer were proposed to reveal the lithophilicity of doping sites. Their results demonstrated that O-doped and O/B-codoped carbons possessed the best lithophilicity among those single-doped and codoped carbons, respectively. This finding would afford a mechanistic guidance to construction of heteroatom-doped current collectors/hosts for LMAs.

In sharp contrast, the straight, direct, and inward ion transport paths enabled by the vertically aligned rGO with ultralow tortuosity gave rise to uniform delivery of metallic Li (Figure 5b). paragraph_context: Wang's group developed a 3D cross-linked porous polyethylenimine sponge (PPS) with enhanced lithophilicity on the conventional Cu current collector to mitigate the dendritic growth issue.[85] As shown in Figure 6a, the self-concentrating feature of PPS resulting from its high Li-ion affinity can guarantee the higher local concentration of Li ion than that in the bulk solution. Moreover, the electrokinetic surface conduction and electro-osmosis can also be promoted by the interfacial electric double layer (EDL) with the strong Li-ion affinity, which can be denoted as the electrokinetic pumping feature (Figure 6b). These abovementioned two features can facilitate the regulation of ion concentration in the deionization area and thus enable a uniform Li-ion distribution by synergistically reducing the concentration polarization and overcoming the diffusion-limited current. The sponge-like porous structure of the PPS@Cu host, confirmed by the SEM investigations (Figure 6c), demonstrated the superiority of accommodating large amounts of deposited Li (as high as $74.6\mathrm{wt}\%$ ). In order to gain a further understanding of the deposition behavior, the simulation of morphology, as well as Li-ion concentration and current density within the 3D PPS, was also presented. As shown in Figure 6d, for the bare Cu foil, a large concentration polarization and uneven current density distribution gave rise to the obvious dendritic morphology. In sharp contrast, the employment of 3D PPS would significantly reduce the concentration polarization and induce the uniform local current density distribution, which was favorable for the homogeneous morphology of Li plating. The electrochemical performance superiority of the 3D PPS@Cu to the bare Cu foil further confirmed the dendrite-free characteristic of the modified current collector. As shown in Figure 6e-g, the asymmetric cell configurations based on 3D PPS@Cu foils can deliver an inspiring cycling stability for Li plating/stripping. paragraph_context: Cui's group has done a series of groundbreaking work on LMAs. They ever conducted a pioneered research work on the exploration of nucleation pattern of Li metal on various metal substrates and unraveled that the metal with strong binding energy with Li can significantly reduce the nucleation barriers.[87] Based on this finding, they thereafter designed a nanocapsule structure with lithophilic metal seeds located in the hollow carbon spheres. As expected, the Li metal was inclined to grow inside the hollow carbon spheres, which eliminated the Li dendrite formation. Some further work of their group also followed this principle. For instance, they replaced the hollow carbon spheres with wrinkled graphene cage (WGC), since the latter possessed highly improved mechanical stability and better Li-ion conductivity.[88] As shown in Figure 7a, the Li metal can be preferentially deposited into the hollow cage through the defects/pinholes of the graphene shell due to the fact that the Au NPs embedded on the inner surface can remarkably reduce the nucleation overpotential. Notably, benefiting from the well-defined structure of WGC, the SEI will be maintained even after the full stripping of the metallic Li (Figure 7b). The cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) images shown in Figure 7c,d further confirmed the formation of stable SEI in two kinds of carbonate-based electrolyte systems. The SEI layer comprising the $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ outer layer and polymerized inner layer exhibited excellent stability to prevent the solvent leakage into the hollow cage and continuous corrosion of Li metal. The deposition can be separated into two stages based on the SEM investigation. As shown in Figure 7e, at the stage 1 with lower deposition capacity $(0 - 5\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2})$ , the Li metal was more inclined to alloy with the inner Au NPs to fill each cage. Afterward, the outer pore spaces of the WGC electrode would be filled the deposited Li. The dense and homogeneous feature of the WGC electrode can accommodate high loading of Li metal without volume fluctuation and dendritic growth, which was conducive for high CEs at higher capacities. As shown in Figure 7f, in the common carbonate electrolyte with additives, the bare Cu foil can only deliver a short cycling life for only $\sim 40$ cycles with a low $\mathrm{CE}\sim 93\%$ at $0.5\mathrm{mA cm}^{-2}$ and $1\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ . In stark contrast, the employment of WGC can remarkably prolong the life span to nearly 90 cycles with a higher CE $97.5\%$ . Further rate performance test also demonstrated the outstanding properties of WGC electrodes under higher capacities (Figure 7g). In another high-concentration electrolyte, the WGC can also function well to give a stable high CE of $99.0\%$ for over 140 cycles under $1\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and $1\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ (Figure 7h). At the lower current density of $0.5\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ but high capacity of $3\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ , the WGC electrode still outperformed the bare Cu electrode (Figure 7i). As shown in Figure 7j, the full cells using prestored Li in the WGC electrodes coupled with high loading of $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ also showed superior cycling life to those with bare Cu foils, especially in the high-concentration electrolyte (340 cycles).

paragraph_context: As mentioned above, 1D carbon-base materials have been widely used as the current collectors/hosts for LMAs. Thus, it is reasonable to introduce metal/semimetal-based sites to reinforce the lithophilicity of 1D carbon scaffolds/substrates. As early as 2012, Stucky's group ever introduced a carbon fiber paper (CP) decorated with a thin $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ layer or $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ -derived SiC layer to generate anisotropic spatially heterogeneous current collectors.[95] The spatially heterogeneous insulating/conducting properties of the CP were crucial for the dendrite-free deposition of Li metal on the $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ -CP or SiC-CP current collectors. Moreover, the large porous volume of the current collectors can effectively tolerate the volume change during deposition. Similar coating strategy was then adopted by Liang and coworkers.[96] A thin Si layer coated on electrospun carbon fiber network via chemical vapor deposition (CVD) can raise the lithophilicity and assist the infusion of molten Li. Alternative approach to modify the carbon materials is the utilization of noble metals, such as silver (Ag) and gold (Au).[97-99] Yang et al. introduced ultrafine Ag nanoseeds anchored on the carbon nanofibers to significantly reduce the nucleation overpotential of Li and direct the uniform deposition of Li inside the 3D carbon matrix.[97] Later on, Zhang and coworkers electroplated Ag particles onto the carbon fiber (CF) to construct Li composite anode (CF/Ag-Li).[98] The lithophilic Ag sites were conducive for the regulation of Li nucleation and growth during plating. Consequently, the proposed CF/Ag-Li electrode can deliver an improved cyclability with dendrite-free morphology even at the ultrahigh current density $10\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ and ultrahigh capacity of $10\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ .

paragraph_context: Unlike the conventional uniform distribution of lithophilic sites on 1D carbon, the ingenious design for controllable Li deposition realized by partially decoration of lithophilic metal/semimetal is also attractive. Inspired by the Chinese legend "King Yu Tamed the Flood," Huang's group devised a new strategy of combing dredge and block to control the Li-ion migration (Figure 8a).[99] For the conventional Li anode or the CFs-Li anode, the dendritic Li growth cannot be prevented during the repeated plating/stripping cycles due to the aggravated inhomogeneity. This issue can be effectively addressed by the employment of CFs@Au anode. Due to the alloying capability of Au with Li, a much lower nucleation barrier could be obtained on the buffer layer. The Li ion will pass through the front surface regularly and finally deposit on the back side of CFs@Au. Benefiting from this "bottom-to-up" deposition behavior, high space utilization can be realized since the metallic Li grown on the adjacent CFs would fill the space between the CFs, which was conducive for obtaining the excellent electrochemical performance. Moreover, the selective modification of Au on one side of the carbon fiber matrix can induce the selective and homogeneous Li deposition on the bottom of the current collector, which was far away from the separator and thus increased the cell safety. As shown in Figure 8b, Au NPs were magnetron-sputtered and coated on one side of conventional CFs to increase the affinity with Li, which can successfully induce the preferential deposition of metallic Li at the lithophilic site. However, random distribution of Li deposition around the bare CFs can only lead to the unbridled dendritic Li growth. Further, CE values during the galvanostatic deposition/dissolution process of the metallic Li on different electrodes shown at Figure 8c,d further verified the outstanding performance of the CFs@Au composite. At the current density of $2\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and the capacity of $4\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ , the LMA based on CFs@Au can deliver a high CE of $99.0\%$ and a stable cycling for over 300 times (Figure 8c). Notably, the CE of the LMA based on CFs@Au can still maintain a high value of $98.0\%$ even after 100 cycles when the current density and capacity were increased to $5\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and $5\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ , respectively, further revealing the efficiency of the selected Au decoration on suppressing the Li dendrite growth (Figure 8d).

paragraph_context: The employment of base metals instead of noble metals also exhibited comparable performance to the aforementioned work, significantly reducing the cost for the preparation of current collectors/hosts for LMAs.[100-102] As the research moves along, the metal-based compounds, such as oxides and nitrides, are demonstrated to serve as viable lithophilic sites on nanofibers to attract the injected or deposited Li.[103-108] For instance, carbon nanofiber matrix could deliver a smooth Li morphology under the decoration and assistance of lithiophilic nitride $\mathrm{(Mo_2N}$ or $\mathrm{CrO_{0.78}N_{0.48})}$ .[103,104] Interestingly, when the exterior decoration of lithiophilic components was replaced by interior encapsulation, their function seemed to be not affected. paragraph_context: The delicate gradient structure design has also been demonstrated to contribute to the regulation of Li-ion flux and resulting suppression of Li dendrite growth, especially at high current density and capacity.[106,115,153,154] The unique conductivity gradient structure proposed by Hong and coworkers can guide the nucleation sites of Li metal to be directed during the electrochemical plating process.[154] As shown in Figure 10a, for the conventional Cu foil, the direct Li nucleation and dendritic growth were inclined to take place on the top surface, due to the intrinsic high electrical conductivity and the predominantly vertical electrical field in the sandwich-structured cell configuration. Besides, the simulation indicated the formation of hot spots (shown in red on the nucleation spots), which would increase the Li-ion flux and further accelerate the Li dendrite growth. Unlike conventional Cu foil, the commonly used hosts can improve the life span by reducing the current density and accommodate the volume change during Li plating/stripping by their active area. Nevertheless, the high ion flux on the top surface cannot be effectively alleviated due to the high electrical conductivity in the vertical direction. In order to address the issue of top-surface nucleation, the authors adopted the electrical conductivity gradient (CG) system to suppress the Li plating on the top surface. The layer with highest electrical conductivity was located at the bottom of the host; thus, the local reaction flux would be preferentially concentrated from the bottom. Meanwhile, the hot spots in the top layer were significantly reduced due to its least electrical conductivity. Besides, the generated "dead" Li can also be captured by the middle layer with well-tailored conductivity. This structural uniqueness with conductivity gradient endows the proposed cells with excellent electrochemical performance at high current densities. As shown in Figure 10b, the employment of Cu nanowire (CuNW) membrane can deliver a much better cycling life with a lower hysteresis voltage than the bare Cu foil. However, the life span was still less than 50 cycles. In stark contrast, the proposed CG host cell can be stably plated/stripped for as many as 250 cycles with the smallest hysteresis. As shown in Figure 10c, at the current density of $0.5\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ , the CG host can deliver a stable cycling life for 120 times of plating/stripping with a high CE of $\sim96\%$ . The bare Cu foil and CuNW membrane could only by stably cycled for 50 and 80 times, respectively. As shown in Figure 10e, the full cell with bare Cu foil showed a fast capacity fading after 20 cycles. paragraph_context: Due to the similarity between Li and Na, the strategies adopting the carbon-based materials as current collectors/hosts for LMAs can be also applicable for SMAs. The sodium insertion and storage in carbon revealed by recent literature further validate the potential of carbon-based materials as sodiophilic current collectors/hosts for metallic Na electrodes.[168] Motivated by this conjecture, Pint's group investigated the utilization of carbon nucleation layer to enable highly efficient and stable sodium plating/stripping for over 1000 cycles with an average CE of $99.8\%$ .[169] Their further work demonstrated that the conventional sodium-ion anode materials, including nongraphitized carbons and sodium-alloying metals, could serve as nucleation layers to facilitate stable electroplating of sodium metal, which held an impressive impact on the subsequent research work on SMAs.[170] Just like aforementioned LMAs, 1D carbon materials, including carbon nanofibers[171-174] and carbon nanotubes,[175-177] can also be utilized as current collectors/hosts to accommodate the metallic Na. For instance, Kim's group prepared the hollow and mesoporous carbon nanofiber (HpCNF) with abundant defects and nitrogen functional groups to realize the compact and uniform Na deposition, yielding an outstanding plating/striping cyclability with an average CE of $99.7\%$ after 1400 cycles at $3\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and $6\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ .[172] The excellent performance can also be realized by adopting an oxygen-functionalized carbon nanotube networks $\mathrm{(O_f - CNT)}$ , which concurrently facilitated the homogeneous sodium nucleation at the initial plating stage and the subsequent dendrite-free growth behavior to finally render the obtained $\mathrm{Na@O_f - CNT}$ electrodes an ultrahigh capacity $1078\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ and ultralong cycle life up to 3000 cycles.[175] As one of the most common carbon materials, graphene has been intensively studied as a component of current collectors/hosts for LMAs, and their utilization in SMAs is also greatly appreciated. Wang and coworkers reported a processable and moldable composite Na metal anode comprising metallic Na and $4.5\%$ reduced graphene oxide (r-GO) with improved hardness, strength, and stability to environmental corrosion. Due to the less dendrite formation, this $\mathrm{Na@r - GO}$ composite anode exhibited superior plating/stripping cycling stability to Na metal in both ether and carbonate electrolytes.[178] Yan et al. further developed a porous reduced graphene oxide (PRGO) film with outstanding sociophilicity and flexibility, to support dendrite-free Na nucleation in the initial electroplating stage, contributing to high-performance Na metal batteries.[179] The Na-carbon composite electrodes can also be prepared by employing other carbon source with special structural features, such as carbon cloth,[180,181] carbon microlattice comprising reduced graphene oxide/carbon nanotube,[182] and oxygen-doped carbon foam (OCF) derived from starch.[183] Moreover, the utilization of the wood-derived carbon materials in LMAs also triggered the interest of their potential in SMAs.[184,185] The high-surface-area, conductive, mechanically stable skeleton of proposed Na carbonized wood (Na-wood) composite anode fabricated via a rapid capillary melt infusion ( $\sim 5$ s) reported by Luo et al. can remarkably lower the effective current density, ensure a uniform Na nucleation, and restrict the volume change over cycling.[184] Another feasible approach to modifying the sociophilicity of carbon hosts is to introduce additional sodiophilic sites into carbon framework. Many literatures have demonstrated that metal oxides are commonly used as the sociophilic elements to ensure the impregnation of metallic Na into the carbon-based current collectors/hosts.[186-190] For instance, Xu and coworkers introduced 3D carbon cloth scaffold covered by $\mathrm{SnO}_2$ quantum dots $(\mathrm{SnO}_2 - \mathrm{CC})$ to gain the affinity to molten Na, as $\mathrm{SnO}_2$ could spontaneously initiate alloying reactions with Na and thus provide low nucleation barrier for Na deposition.[190] The combination of sociophilic $\mathrm{SnO}_2$ and CC substrates delivered almost 400 plating/stripping cycles at an ultrahigh current density of $20\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ in Na symmetric battery. Besides, nanostructure metals can be also utilized as sociophilic nucleation sites as they possessed similar sociophilicity as aforementioned metal oxides.[191-199] Recently, we have conducted a series of investigations on nucleation buffer layers consisting of sodiophilic metal and supporting carbon frameworks for high-performance SMAs.[196-199] A well-designed core-shell C@Sb NPs comprising interior porous Sb cores and exterior carbon protective shell enabled the homogeneous Na deposition through regulating the initial nucleation (Figure 11a).[196] The different deposition behaviors on bare and modified Cu foils were investigated by optical photographs and SEM images. As shown in Figure 11b, mossy and patchy Na was found to deposit on bare Cu foils. Further SEM investigation demonstrated that these bulk deposited Na was consisting of anisotropic Na dendrites and fiber-like aggregates. However, the employment of C@Sb NPs made a great impact on the Na deposition behavior. Uniform and progressing plating would be established. The island-like seeding of Na metal at lower plating capacity would finally coalesce mutually into an entire block with a smooth surface along with the increasing loading of metallic Na. As depicted in Figure 11c, benefiting from the nucleation layer, the assembled cells can be stably plating/stripping for nearly $6000\mathrm{h}$ at a high areal capacity of $4\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ with an average CE $99.7\%$ . The voltage hysteresis on cycling was as low as $14\mathrm{mV}$ at the initial stage and finally increased to $50\mathrm{mV}$ , indicating the good kinetics during plating/stripping (Figure 11d). In this work, the inner porous Sb cores served as the nucleation sites to reduce the nucleation barrier, while the external carbon shell was introduced to ensure the functionality after the long-term cycling by avoiding the structure breakage and aggregation of Sb cores. These synergistic effects endowed the proposed cell with dendrite-free morphology and significantly prolonged life span.

paragraph_context: Recently, Wang's group reported a composite based on defect-rich N-containing MXene (DN-MXene) and carbon nanotube (CNT) to serve as a freestanding scaffold for KMAs (Figure 11g).[212] As schematically shown in Figure 11h, for the K@CNT anode, the random nucleation and plating of K atoms onto the CNTs during the repeated plating/stripping process would result in porous deposition and dendritic growth outside the scaffold, which was detrimental to the CE and life span of the cells. Benefiting from the highly electronically conductive feature, the DN-MXene sheets with potassium-philicity can serve as "seed points" to lower the nucleation barrier and regulate the ionic flux during cycling, delivering a uniform K metal deposition without dendrite formation. The density functional theory (DFT) calculations further confirmed the potassium-philic characteristic of MXenes in comparison with other substrates. As depicted in Figure 11i, the binding energies between K atoms and DN-MXene with different terminal functional groups were 2.27, 2.10, and $2.04\mathrm{eV}$ , respectively. However, the Cu foil, Au foil, and CNT scaffold can only deliver much smaller binding energies. This result indicates that the K atoms are more inclined to nucleate on the K-intercalated DN-MXene sheets rather than the conventional current collectors or CNT scaffold. The nucleation overpotential comparison shown in Figure 11j further validated this conclusion. The K nucleation overpotential for Cu, Al, and CNT is 65, 103, and $33\mathrm{mV}$ , respectively. In sharp contrast, the value of DN-MXene/CNT is as low as $6\mathrm{mV}$ . This rational design of the freestanding DN-MXene/CNT scaffold can endow the KMAs with dendrite-free feature, which is crucial for the high-performance K metal batteries.
