paragraph_context: Alkali metal batteries are regarded as promising alternatives to conventional LIBs owing to their high theoretical energy densities. Nevertheless, the improvement of their electrochemical performance is significantly plagued the uncontrolled dendritic growth of alkali metal anodes. Inspiringly, many efforts have been devoted in recent years to tackling these severe issues obsceding the practical deployment of alkali metal batteries. Among the various approaches to inhibiting the dendritic growth, the elaborate design of current collectors/hosts for alkali metal anodes have demonstrated to be an appealing strategy. Apparently, the structural dimensionality has a great impact on the performance of proposed current collectors/hosts. Compared with 0D and 1D substrates, the high specific surface area of those current collectors/host with higher dimensionality (2D and 3D) endows them with abundant surface chemistry. For the 2D substrates/hosts with planar structure, their superior mechanical strength can physically prevent the penetration of dendrites. Apart from those merits, the unique framework structure enables those 3D hosts/scaffolds to accommodate the volume expansion during plating/stripping of the alkali metal anodes. The reduction in the local current density is also beneficial for the suppression of the dendritic growth. Notably, the effective diffusion of electron and ion within the 3D hosts/scaffolds might also promote their electrochemical performance under higher current density and capacity. Nevertheless, the large surface area of those current collectors/hosts with higher dimensionality will inevitably cause the consumption of both electrolyte and alkali metal anodes, lowering the Coulombic efficiency of the batteries. Besides, the volumetric and gravimetric capacities of those battery systems will be also reduced by employing the 2D and 3D current collectors/hosts, especially for those 3D metal foams. Briefly, those carbon-based current collectors/hosts with different dimensionality all have their own pros and cons. The final employment of the appropriate current collectors/hosts need to take various factors into consideration.

Many efforts, such as molten metal infusing, mechanical rolling, and in situ plating, have been devoted to addressing these issues. However, the poor wettability of molten metal can hardly allow its spread across the surface of substrates with less affinity. Thus, the wettability regulation of the current collectors/hosts with the infused molten metal is the priority for the large-scale production. Nevertheless, the excess of alkali metals in these abovementioned strategies will not only reduce the energy density of the batteries but also bring additional safety hazards for practical applications. paragraph_context: Dendrite formation is a commonly observed phenomenon for metallic elements during the electroplating process, referring to the growth of typically unwanted needle-like, moss-like, whisker-like, or branch-like morphologies. As a consequence of the simultaneous electrolyte decomposition and Li-ion reduction, the SEI layer is formed over the metal surface during the initial cycling. During repeated cycling, particularly during the charging process, Li nuclei begin to form on the surface of the anode. Due to the surface curvature of the nuclei, a potential difference is generated between the base and tip of these nuclei (referred to as the base potential $(\varphi_{\mathrm{b}})$ and tip potential $(\varphi_{\mathrm{t}})$ , respectively). It follows that a Li nucleus with a smaller radius of curvature would have a higher tip potential $(\varphi_{\mathrm{t}})$ . Moreover, the tip of the nucleus has an unusually high density of steps and kinks, which can result in a higher exchange-current density for the Li deposition. This, in turn, leads to a lower activation energy and, consequently, a lower overpotential on the tip than on the plane, which continuously promotes the preferential growth of Li on the tips. The persistent potential difference $(\Delta \varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{t}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{b}})$ between the base and the tip, driven by the localized electric field, leads to the continuous growth of dendritic Li preferentially along the direction of protrusion. Eventually, these dendrites can penetrate through the separator, causing an internal short circuit and posing a thermal runaway hazard (Figure 2A).

paragraph_context: In Section 3.1, we described various factors and fabrication methods required for producing ultra-thin LMAs for next-generation high energy density LMBs, aiming to achieve a near $1:1\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{P}$ ratio. The aforementioned strategies relied on enhancing the lithophilicity of a given substrate to increase Li-ion conductivity, plating Li metal uniformly to the surface of the current collector/host matrix or depositing molten Li in an extremely thin form on the current collector to manufacture ultrathin LMAs. Differently in this part, we introduce various approaches involving a protection layer that is deposited on the surface of the LMA. The protection layer regulates reactions on the Li surface, controls Li volume expansion, and increases the uniformity of Li-ion conductivity, thus addressing the root cause of Li dendrite growth. Such strategies can be applied regardless of Li thickness and are highly effective in stabilizing electrochemical reactions occurring on the Li metal surface, making them a valuable approach for enhancing the longevity of next-generation batteries utilizing LMAs. The protection layer should possess the following four characteristics: (i) it should be able to transfer Li-ions and electrolytes through the layer; (ii) it should be compatible and miscible with the native SEI layer; (iii) it should provide sufficient mechanical strength; and (iv) it should not introduce critical structural defects by decomposing during electrochemical reactions. On top of that, it is important to ensure that the interfacial layer does not reduce the electronic conductivity of the entire LMA.[14,57] Various studies have been conducted using materials that satisfy these characteristics, such organic polymers with various lithophilic functional groups, lithophilic metals and metal oxides, and metal chlorides/fluorides/sulfides as protection layers. Herein, we aim to provide a case-by-case discussion on the role of the protection layer, with a specific focus on the material type.

paragraph_context: Polymers often serve as effective protective layers for LMAs due to their low electrical conductivity and physicochemical stability in harsh environments. The wide variety of polymers and organic ligands with respectively unique functionalities has allowed several different designs for the protection layer, as is discussed herein. Zhao et al.[66] fabricated PVA-coated Li foils by simply drop-coating a polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) solution onto the surface of Li metal foil. The PVA protection layer was very thin $(1 - 2\mu \mathrm{m})$ and could smooth out the rough surface of the bare Li foil. Notably, the PVA-coated Li anode was used to operate a Li-S battery as well as Li-LFP and Li-NCM full cells, from which a significant improvement in life characteristics could be observed compared to when using a bare LMA, confirming the increased electrochemical stability of the anode from the PVA protection layer. Yu et al.[67] placed a Li metal foil on a bed of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) powder and performed hot pressing at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to create a Li metal electrode coated with a protection layer composed of approximately $20\mu \mathrm{m}$ thick LiF/F-doped carbon (denoted as PTL) (Figure 6A). Specifically, when the Li metal is heated at high temperatures, it reacts with the fluorine in PTFE to form LiF, and the remaining carbon byproduct reacts with PTFE to form F-doped carbons. In this process, F-doped carbon is abundant in the upper part of the protection layer that is in direct contact with PTFE, and LiF becomes relatively more abundant as it goes downward. The C-F bond in F-doped carbon acts as an effective Lewis base site, adsorbing Lewis-acidic $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and providing a uniform Li-ion flux, serving as a protection layer to suppress dendrite formation (Figure 6B). On a different approach, Zhao et al.[68] proposed a strategy of coating a Li-affinitive and electrochemically active 2D covalent organic framework (COF) film on the surface of Li metal as an artificial SEI layer (Figure 6C). The LiF formed through the conventional SEI layer formation plays a significant role in facilitating a uniform Li-ion flux, but its size and distribution could be usually uncontrolled since it was formed by electrolyte decomposition during the charging and discharging processes. The flexible COF layer proposed therein not only serves as a protection layer to protect Li metal from volume expansion but can also uniformly accommodate LiF particles within its microporous channels, while simultaneously acting as a fast Li-ion transport channel. Based on these advantages, a full cell test using LiCOF-LiF@Li (Li coated with uniform distribution of LiF grains throughout the lithiated COF film) and NCM based cathode achieved stable operation for over 150 cycles with a high capacity of $10.6\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ . Recently, Bae et al.[69] used an initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD) process to deposit a polymer nanolayer onto the Li metal surface, which strengthened the existing SEI layer and stabilized the interface (Figure 6D). In a standard process, authors deposited poly(dimethylaminomethyl styrene) (pDMAMS) at a thickness of $100\mathrm{nm}$ on the Li metal surface (Figure 6E). The resulting pDMAMS layer swelled 2.64 times in a carbonate electrolyte, forming a soft scaffold on the Li surface filled with the electrolyte (Figure 6F), facilitating excellent Li-ion transport. The usage of polymer-based protective layers for LMAs highlights the potential of leveraging the unique properties of these materials for improved safety and performance. This approach offers the potential for tailormade solutions, considering the diverse functionality of various polymers and organic ligands, thereby opening up a plethora of innovative opportunities for future research in this field.

The symmetric cell using $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ -coated Li was stably operated for more than $750\mathrm{h}$ , showing more than three times enhanced stability compared to using a bare Li metal symmetric cell. This gas-phase process can also be expanded as a Li protection layer with a large-area technology by simply increasing the size of the heat treatment chamber. Liu et al.[78] utilized the unique properties of $\mathrm{SeS}_2$ , which has an extremely low boiling point of $118^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , to devise a method for depositing Se and S on the Li metal surface. $\mathrm{SeS}_2$ powder was placed in a container with Li metal and heated to $150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , at which point Li, which has a melting point of $180^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , maintains its metallic state while $\mathrm{SeS}_2$ is vaporized and reacts with Li to form a composite layer of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Se}$ on the Li metal surface. The resulting $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S} / \mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Se}$ layer uniformizes the Li-ion flux and inhibits dendrite growth, serving as a protective layer for high-performance LMAs. Furthermore, halide perovskites exhibited great potential as protection layers for Li metal. Yin et al.[79] used thin films of halide perovskites containing methylammonium (MA), such as $\mathrm{MASnCl}_3$ (MSC) or $\mathrm{MAPbCl}_3$ (MPC), as an interfacial layer between Li metal and liquid electrolyte. As shown in Figure 7E, they fabricated MSC-Li and MPC-Li anodes by depositing the perovskite film on a substrate and then placing Li metal on top using a solid-state transfer process. When operated at a very high C rate of 5 C using an $\mathrm{Li}_4\mathrm{Ti}_5\mathrm{O}_{12}$ (LTO) cathode, both electrodes demonstrated stable cell operation for more than $500\mathrm{h}$ , indicating that the perovskite film improved the stability of the LMA. This simple deposition method has the potential to be developed into a roll-to-roll process, making it applicable to large-area LMAs. Lastly, Zhang et al.[80] deposited a Fe-based valence gradient protection layer on the surface of a Li foil anode by dripping a mixture of $\mathrm{FeF}_3$ and $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ onto the surface and evaporating the solvent on a hot plate. The protection layer gradually changed from $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ , $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ , to $\mathrm{Fe}^0$ from the outer layer to the inner layer, creating a buffer region capable of storing Li and preventing corrosion from the carbonate electrolyte, as well as suppressing dendrite and dead Li formation. When $1\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ of plating was performed on both protected and bare Li, dendrite growth was inhibited in protected Li due to the uniform Li-ion flux on the surface (Figure 7F). Thanks to these characteristics, a symmetric cell using protected Li was able to operate stably for over $100\mathrm{h}$ with a capacity of $1\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ under high current density conditions of $10\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ . In conclusion, each of these innovative strategies brings unique advantages to LMA design, from improved performance and stability to potential scalability. However, each approach also presents specific challenges, whether related to complexity, energy use, safety, or the stability of materials. Future research in this field should strive to balance these considerations, all the while seeking ways to further optimize the design of LMAs for higher performance and broader practical application.

Unfortunately, precautionary measures usually degrade the specific energy density of the battery in an unavoidable trade-off. To overcome this dilemma, the concept of AFLMB has been proposed, which eliminates the conventional anode material (e.g., graphite, Li metal) in its entirety in the manufactured product.[94,95] During the first charging step of the AFLMB, Li-ions migrate from a lithiated cathode to the current collector and undergoes in-situ electroplating to form a layer of Li metal that transiently serves as the anode.[96] Here, by incorporating the current collector with a lithiophilic host material, the nucleation and growth of Li can occur in a uniform manner.[97] During subsequent cycles, Li-ions are stripped through electrochemical dissolution, then again deposited and plated on the current collector in a reversible process. Adopting the anode free battery system, which physically lacks the weight of the anode, offers maximization of the specific energy density. In addition, the absence of Li foil fabrication and handling steps greatly simplifies the cell assembly and lowers the overall cost and manufacturing expenses.[98] It follows that, for the design of AFLMBs, the rational synthesis of the lithophilic current collector and the lithiated cathode are of critical importance.[94,99,100] On one hand, in organic liquid electrolyte systems, several lithophilic species such as polar functional groups like carbonyl,[101] fluorinated[102] and hydroxyl groups[66] could be decorated on the Cu current collector to reduce the overpotential of Li nucleation and growth, facilitating the reversible in-situ Li plating and dissolution processes. paragraph_context: As discussed in the introduction, current LIBs are reaching their theoretical limit in terms of energy density. $^{111,112}$ As such, the more energy-dense Li metal is being considered as a "holy grail" anode material for the next generation of rechargeable batteries. However, despite promising developments in stabilizing the LMAs, there are still significant challenges to overcome before LMBs can be used for consumer electronics or large-scale operations in any practical capacity. In this section, we will discuss the various challenges that must be addressed in order to deploy LMAs for the successful development of LMBs.

paragraph_context: Small-scale laboratory cells, such as coin cells, are often used for academic research, but their performance is not always representative of larger format cells, such as pouch, cylindrical, or prismatic cells, which are used in industrial products.[32,113] There are several reasons for this discrepancy in cell performance between small and large format cells. The performance of Li metal pouch cells is far outpaced by that of coin cells in many aspects such as rate responses and cycling lifespan. This indicates that there are more challenges at the large format cell level. For one, as mentioned in the previous chapter, the amount of electrolytes in a typical coin cell fabricated in lab are as high as $75\mathrm{g}\mathrm{Ah}^{-1}$ ( $75~\mu \mathrm{L}$ electrolyte per cathode capacity of $1\mathrm{mAh}$ ), which is significantly higher ( $\sim 57$ times) compared to a commercial LIB (Figure 9A).[32,33] Also, while laboratory-scale coin cells often utilize thick LMAs ( $>250~{\mu\mathrm{m}}$ ) with an effectively limited surplus of Li, real-life pouch cells cannot involve thick Li, leading to further constraints on their performance. Therefore, to meet the commercial level criteria of energy density along with the thinner and lighter designs, such dead weight from excessive electrolyte and Li metal should be decreased. Simply, every component of the battery cannot be scaled up proportionally along with the increased size/thickness of electrodes. Furthermore, typical coin cell cathodes usually contain conductive agents and binders in the electrode slurry that take up around $20\%$ of the total weight, making it completely suboptimal from a commercial standpoint unless both can be significantly reduced.[34,114] In addition, large-area electrodes with thick Li metal have more complicated and aggressive interfacial reactions as well as nonconformal current distribution, respectively due to the large contact with the electrolyte and harsh operational conditions (e.g., high areal/mass current density). As a result, the depletion of the electrolyte, which is already in a limited supply in a large format cell, is accelerated to generate even more dead Li and mossy Li along with continuous and irreversible side reactions on the metal surface. This ultimately results in significant cell swelling, large impedance/polarization, and faster decay of the metal anode (Figure 9B).[115] Therefore, to ensure a smoother and a more facile transition of battery technology to the industry, battery researchers must concentrate on bridging the discrepancy between lab-scale and commercial-level cells. To achieve this, it is crucial to evaluate larger format cells in addition to small-scale laboratory cells during the research and development of functional electrode materials.

paragraph_context: Unfortunately, poor repeatability and variation of cell performance between multiple samples have been chronic issues in battery research. Generally, incorporating more electrolytes, increasing the LMA thickness, and decreasing the mass/area of the cathode can lead to higher cell capacity and energy. The amount of electrolyte is dependent on the porosity of the electrode, which can be regulated by the calendaring process to some extent.[32] However, it is impossible to quantifiably normalize the intrinsic porosity of electrode materials, which makes it difficult to define a generalized value for the amount of electrolyte to be used. Therefore, a more specific and detailed metrics considering the intrinsic property of electrode materials, together with a facile yet simple measurement protocol, should be proposed and developed by the research community. For example, the electrolyte weight relative to capacity/intrinsic porosity/packing density of electrode can serve as a standard. On the Li metal side, the ambiguous interface kinetics between each electrode and electrolyte/ion diffusion dynamics under practical and realistic operation conditions should be explored in depth. Along with that, the N/P ratio, the presence of current collector (usually Cu foil), and the thickness are also important factors for consideration. A clear description of whether the cathode loading mass encompasses all the electrode components, including the binder, active materials, and conductive agent is highly critical to accurately assess the full cell performance when paired with LMAs. Additionally, the voltage window, initial discharge capacity and CE, capacity retention of cathode materials should be also described in detail. For the quick screening of materials, evaluation with a coin cell is of priority to validate the electrochemical properties of cells in a cost- and resource-effective way with limited Li use ( $\leq 100\mu \mathrm{m}$ or $\leq \sim 6\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ ). After corroborating the intrinsic and fundamental electrochemical properties of proposed materials/cell components, large format cells such as pouch type cells should be fabricated to demonstrate their practical viability. The weight and thickness of the separator and packaging foil are also important metrics, which should be included in the battery weight. To this end, several journals have introduced some kind of checklist to fill in the detailed specifications of each battery component and operating condition, with recommendations for reporting multiple data points noted with standard deviations. They provide guidance for data curation and visualization for fair comparison between reported cells. Along with these efforts, the establishment of a generalized testing protocol would reduce errors and data inconsistencies between cells.

paragraph_context: The manufacturing of thin and stable LMAs as well as their passivation layers with a high degree of regularity and uniformity, while possible over lab-scale developments, remains a grand engineering challenge over a large, industrially-relevant scale. The thickness of the coating layer can be controlled with various levels of precision from nanometers to micrometers depending on the coating method, often in an inverse correlation with the rate at which it is manufactured. Gas phase methods, such as physical vapor deposition (PVD), $^{76,119}$ chemical vapor deposition (CVD), $^{120}$ atomic layer deposition (ALD), $^{121,122}$ and molecular layer deposition (MLD), $^{123}$ enable the formation of nanometer-thick coatings, but they are critically limited by the need for a rigorous operating condition, restricted synthesis area, and cumbersome machinery, making it difficult to build in a glove box or dry room. $^{124}$ Solution-phase methods are simpler to implement, but achieving nanometer-thick control is not yet feasible, making it unsuitable for the fabrication of thinner LMAs. To achieve delicate control of the thickness of the coating layer, gas phase methods can be a promising and effective approach. While solution phase methods can take advantages for simplicity, productivity, and economical viewpoints over gas phase methods. Therefore, we would need to go forward in a way to develop air/operating condition insensitive gas phase methods or to enable nanometer-thick coating available solution phase methods. Meanwhile, ultrafast flash-assisted methods such as carbothermal shock or intense pulsed light can also be applicable to generate multielement particles and metallophilic overlayers within very short processing time even in just a few seconds. $^{125-127}$ However, these flash-based technologies are in their infancy with restricted synthesis areas and difficulties with integrating highly susceptible Li metals in the synthesis, but they have the potential to make a breakthrough in designing thin and stable Li metal. Additionally, attention should be directed toward automated or semi-automated manufacturing processes with continuous production that remove manual control processes as much as possible. Ultimately, a powerful synthetic technology with short processing time, simple operation steps, high production rate, compatibility with the existing battery production system, and nanometer-level control over the thickness would be able to decisively empower the practical application of Li metal pouch cells. As also highlighted in an earlier section, the work by Bae et al.[69] offers a promising path toward developing such a synthetic technology. The authors have passivated the LMA with an ultrathin electrolyte-swellable polymer nanolayer by (Figure 9C). This iCVD enables uniform polymerization and conformal coverage of polymers with nanometer level thickness directly onto the Li metal surface without any heating of the metal electrode. The $100\mathrm{nm}$ iCVD pDMAMS layer, which can swell under electrolyte, provided a record-high Li-ion transference number (0.95) and $600\%$ extended cycle life in full cells (paired with NCM622) compared to bare Li metal (Figure 9D). Moreover, iCVD technique allows for the ultrathin polymer coatings, with thicknesses as low as $10\mathrm{nm}$ .[128] Note that the vast array of iCVD monomers enables the synthesis of various homo-/copolymers, showing potential for versatile and expandable coating materials.[129-131] Furthermore, this process can be easily scaled up by utilizing a larger stationary substrate or implementing a roll-to-roll process, where uncoated substrates are continuously fed into the reaction chamber.[132,133] Consequently, the development of large-area coating technology at a nanometer-thick controlling level, combined with roll-to-roll processing, has the potential to enhance production rates and reduce manufacturing costs. This technological advancement will facilitate the production and commercialization of thin and wide LMAs with a substantial impact on the battery industry.

paragraph_context: Compared to the other major components of batteries, such as the separator, cathode, and the electrolyte (which also require protection from moisture/humidity), LMAs are much more susceptible to air (e.g., $\mathrm{O}_2$ , $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{CO}_2$ , $\mathrm{N}_2$ ) and can even become explosive when exposed to excessive moisture, making it challenging to fabricate cells in an open environment.[134-136] As a result, Li must be handled in a dry room or glove box, the maintenance costs as well as time-rated usage fees add to the cost of manufacturing and impedes industrial production.[137] Therefore, simple and effective methods to stabilize the Li metal against ambient air and water must be developed with equal emphasis as suppressing dendritic growth/dead Li/unstable SEI layer. The production of environmentally insensitive and stable Li metal will ultimately enhance battery safety and longevity, while also increasing the efficiency of manufacturing costs per unit of the device.

paragraph_context: Two potential materials-based approaches can be conceived: (i) a dense insulating layer with a selective $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ conduction path and (ii) a hydrophobic layer. This phenomenon becomes more severe as the area of the cell increases. Also, thick metal sheets incur large variations in dimension and thickness which could lead to critical failure, necessitating a thin Na and K metal anode.[10] Moreover, from a practical research point of view, Na and K are not commercially available as rolled foils at the present, and it is difficult to cut out thin sheets of Na and/or K from ingots with the necessary precision and accuracy. Therefore, the synthesis of thin metal foils through techniques such as electrodeposition, infusion of metals on the host scaffold, and cutting or pressing of larger ingots of metal should be developed at the same time.[155-157] Safety issues are also of concern for Na and K metal electrodes in rechargeable batteries, just as much as for Li metal. As a result, aqueous-based rechargeable batteries, such as Zn-metal batteries, have emerged as one of the most promising alternatives, especially for large-scale energy storage that prioritizes safety. $^{158,159}$ However, as Zn dendrites can easily pierce through separators due to its high Young's modulus compared to Li and Na, the dendrite growth issue is a much greater challenge in Zn-metal batteries. $^{111}$ This property makes it easier for the metal to short-circuit, orphan, and cause cell death. Additionally, developing a more stable and thinner Zn metal that maximizes the utilization is important for further advancement of Zn-based batteries. One effective approach is to design a thin zincophilic matrix to host the Zn metal. It is crucial to modify the surface of the matrix to have a matching lattice with that of Zn. For example, Zheng et al. $^{160}$ proposed the epitaxial electrodeposition process to form a coherent or semicoherent lattice interface with the host matrix and Zn metal. Specifically, they covered well-aligned graphene sheets with [0001] graphene facets over the substrate, achieving high CE ( $>99.7\%$ ) at high current densities. Interestingly, this epitaxial coating with low lattice mismatch with the metal of interest showed broader utility to other metals, such as aluminum. $^{161}$ This strategy would also be useful for the preparation of current collector in anode free systems. Like alkali metals, integrating a thin but robust protective layer on the Zn metal is another promising approach to stabilize thin Zn metal. Inorganic layers such as $\mathrm{ZnO}$ , ${}^{162}\mathrm{ZrO}_2$ , ${}^{163}\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3$ , ${}^{164}\mathrm{TiO}_2$ , ${}^{165}$ montmorillonite, $^{166}$ and Au nanoparticles, $^{167}$ have been introduced, while organic layers such as nafion, $^{168}$ polypyrrole, $^{169}$ polyamide, $^{170}$ carrageenan film, $^{171}$ fluorinated porous framework, $^{172}$ and hydrophilic but water-insoluble gelatine $^{173}$ have also been proposed. Furthermore, Yang et al. $^{174}$ reported a zincophilic polyanionic hydrogel, which serves not only as a protective layer to suppress Zn dendritic growth but also as an anti-catalyst to alleviate the undesired hydrogen evolution reaction. They can widen the operating voltage window and enhance redox reversibility of aqueous based batteries by reducing the side reactions involving water. This multi-functional single layer can eventually minimize the thickness of additional layer to coat on metal, promising as future research direction. Furthermore, the engineering strategy proposed in this review can be adapted to the design of anodes for all-solid-state batteries, which have the potential to significantly increase energy density by eliminating the use of liquid electrolytes. By integrating a compact solid electrolyte with the metal surface, dendrite formation can be prevented and fast ion-conducting pathways can be created.

paragraph_context: As countries transition to sustainable energy and mobility strategies, EV technology has made rapid progress, and demand for EVs has increased significantly.[175,176] With it, the demand for large-capacity and high-performance batteries have skyrocketed, with the majority of today's battery manufacturers primarily target EVs as their research and development objective. However, consumers are hesitant to purchase EVs due to various reasons, including unreliable performance at different temperatures, which is considered a critical issue.[177] Consumers have noticed that harsh winters and scorching summers can degrade battery performance and raise safety concerns. For reference, current LIBs are recommended to operate within a temperature range of $15 - 35^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (or $0 - 45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ).[176] In particular, thin Li metal anodes with limited Li sources are more sensitive to temperature effects, which must be addressed to advance the development of lightweight, compact, and energy-efficient batteries for EVs.

paragraph_context: When temperatures drop below $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the battery capacity decreases due to increased electrolyte viscosity, large polarization, and slow interfacial kinetics, leading to shorter driving distances and battery failure. Some popular models of EVs have been found to show a depreciation in their range by $10\% - 12\%$ due to temperature alone.[178,179] This indicates that the actual CE of the battery becomes very limited over cycling. However, this phenomenon can be partially concealed when using thick Li metal anodes with high N/P ratios. In other words, the CE in thick Li metal cells can only be high due to the excessive Li that compensates for Li loss, securing longer cycling life to some extent. However, this situation is different for thin Li metal anodes. Moreover, thin Li metal has lower mechanical strength and is prone to forming surface cracks compared to thick anodes. These cracks can be exacerbated in low-temperature regimes due to the embrittlement of the Li metal, leading to rapid ruptures, discrete ion gradients, and disconnection of active Li metal. Therefore, a more reliable strategy is needed to support thin Li metal anodes for the development of reliable EVs in low-temperature operations. Recently, Cai et al.[180] have proposed a promising approach to address this issue by integrating a very thin metal organic framework (MOF)-polymer membrane integrated with liquified gas electrolyte (e.g., fluoromethane) as quasi-solid-state electrolytes.

paragraph_context: On the other hand, elevating the temperature above $45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ can result in degradation of cycling stability due to the increased reactivity of electrode materials and side reactions such as SEI formation.[181,182] For example, when temperatures exceed $55^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ salt begins to decompose into HF with the presence of trace levels of water or protic impurities, causing significant deterioration in battery performance. $^{183}$ Above $65^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the SEI starts to break down, leading to gas evolution within the battery that could potentially cause catastrophic failure. $^{184}$ All these phenomena accelerate the consumption rate of Li, depletion rate of electrolyte, and accumulation rate of unwanted materials including the SEI, massive Li dendrites, and dead Li, which increases the risk of thermal runaway and cell death. $^{185}$ These issues are far more significant in thin Li metal anodes with confined Li sources. However, higher temperatures can also promote larger Li particle nucleation which can potentially decrease the electrode/electrolyte contact area. Given this circumstance, large Li particles could inhibit side reactions and SEI formation. $^{176}$ Note that the large Li particles should secure their robustness that not to be cracked or fissured from the vigorous ion kinetics at an elevated temperature. Such promotional founding on increased particle size with increased temperature imposes great potential to realize the cell performance even at high temperature. All in all, optimized Li metal thickness coordinated with a suitable metal protection strategy are needed to balance Li consumption rate and high energy efficiency (e.g., high CE and high degree of Li utilization without excessive Li) under a wide temperature regime for realistic high-energy LMBs for successful adoption in EVs.

paragraph_context: With the widespread usage of portable electronic devices and electric cars, it has become increasingly important for customers without expert knowledge to be able to self-manage or monitor their battery performance.[186] As previously mentioned, thin Li metal anodes can experience more severe degradation and rapid failure under realistic constrained operating conditions, making self-diagnosis crucial for the safety of the driver if future batteries are to become even thinner and even more lightweight. On the basis of the above discussion, a scalable and commercialization process of thin and stable Li meal anodes for next generation rechargeable batteries along with fundamental analysis, metal surface modulation/thinning strategies, some critical challenges and opportunities is proposed (Figure 10).

paragraph_context: Industries are increasingly turning to electric power as an alternative to fossil fuels in an effort to mitigate global warming. While the development of rechargeable batteries has advanced significantly over the past few decades, their power and energy storage capacity remain limited in light of the advent of large-scale high-power applications such as electric vehicles. To address this issue, current research is focused on high-capacity electrodes such as Li metals, which has a theoretical capacity over 10 times higher than that of graphite electrodes. However, the practical implementation of Li metal anodes faces significant challenges. Thick Li metal can result in poor performance for large-format cells due to increased weight and volume, as well as vigorous interfacial reactions during cycling. As such, the next generation of LMBs must have lithium metal electrodes that are thinner, lighter, wider, and more stable. This review highlights in-depth analyses of lithium failure mechanisms and state-of-the-art research in LMA structural engineering and surface modifications, with a focus on thickness control methods and interface stabilization strategies. However, several scientific and technical challenges must be overcome before LMBs meet industrial standards. These include reducing discrepancies between coin-cell and large format cells, regulating interfacial kinetics over large electrode areas, developing scalable and eco-friendly manufacturing processes, and creating air/water-stable lithium metal electrodes. The structuration and functionalization strategies discussed in this review could also be adapted to stabilize other types of rechargeable metallic batteries, including Na, K, and aqueous-based Zn metals, as well as all-solid-state batteries. The proposed future opportunities and prospects, including all-temperature stable batteries, battery self-monitoring systems, and AI-orchestrated non-destructive analysis, can guide the design of practical Li metal anodes and advance their commercialization. To this end, although there are formidable obstacles to the fabrication of practical Li metal anodes, including the lack of suitable fabrication methods with manufacturability and desirable interface stabilization strategies, we believe that as these challenges are addressed, LMBs will achieve high energy densities while remaining safe, positioning them as viable commercial products in the near future.

paragraph_context: Keywords: active lithium loss | anode free lithium metal batteries | deposition mechanism Anode-free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs), also known as lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with zero excess lithium, have garnered significant attention due to their substantially higher energy density compared to conventional lithium metal anodes, improved safety characteristics, and lower production costs. However, the current cycling stability of AFLMBs faces formidable challenges primarily caused by significant lithium loss associated with the deposition of lithium metal. Therefore, this review focuses on the crucial aspects of lithium metal nucleation and growth on the anode side. Respectively, aiming to provide an in-depth understanding of the deposition mechanisms, comprehensively summarize the corresponding scientific influencing factors, and analyze specific strategies for addressing these issues through the integration of relevant exemplary cases. Importantly, this review endeavors to offer a profound explication of the scientific essence and intricate mechanisms that underlie the diverse modification strategies. This review possesses the inherent capacity to greatly facilitate the progress and enlightenment of research in this field, offering a valuable resource for the researchers.

paragraph_context: Nevertheless, under the condition that the lithium source in the anode-free battery system is limited (originating from the cathode), AFLMBs face more severe challenges in terms of cycling stability compared to conventional lithium batteries, making it difficult to fully leverage the advantages in high energy density for practical applications [11]. Figure 1C represents the comparison between LMBs and AFLMBs in terms of safety, cost, assembly, energy density and cycle stability. In the Cu CC side, the initial plating of high surface area lithium metal morphologies, such as dendritic and mossy structures, give rise to the formation of a thick solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) with high specific area [12], which consumes active lithium and electrolyte, resulting in low initial Coulombic efficiency. Moreover, the continuous irregular deposition of lithium metal during plating leads to volumetric expansion, exerting stress on the native SEI and making it prone to rupture and subsequent reformation. And the non-compact plating morphologies not only aggravate the formation of dead lithium but also exacerbate the deterioration of the anode interface, thereby resulting in a repetitive cycle of active lithium and electrolyte consumption [6, 13, 14].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: It is unmistakably clear that the depletion of active lithium in AFLMBs is intricately intertwined with three pivotal factors: the nucleation of deposited lithium metal, the stability of SEI, and the extent of volumetric expansion accompanying the deposition of lithium metal. We systematically summarize the crucial modification directions relevant to the anode side for enhancing the performance of AFLMBs. The morphology of lithium metal plating, primarily determined by the nucleation process, hinges significantly on the properties of the CC, which serves as the crucial substrate for nucleation. The purposes of CC design primarily focus on reducing the nucleation overpotential to optimize the nucleation process of lithium metal. After initial nucleation, the subsequent growth morphology of lithium metal is also controlled by the stability of the SEI. Optimizing properties like ionic conductivity and mechanical stability of SEIs involves constructing an artificial solid electrolyte interface (ASEI) or adjusting the components, concentration, and morphology of the electrolyte, effectively extending the cycle life of AFLMBs. Furthermore, variations in testing conditions can significantly impact the morphology and growth process of lithium plating, consequently influencing the energy density and lifetime of AFLMBs. In contrast to other reviews concerning anode-free systems that predominantly concentrate on comprehensive summaries of specific modification methodologies, this review places emphasis on providing an in-depth elucidation of the scientific essence and mechanisms underlying various modification strategies as seen in Figure 2. By incorporating concrete examples, it aims to illustrate the scientific coherence behind the diverse modification schemes, offering readers a concise and clear direction for anode-related modifications in AFLMBs. Ultimately, the primary objective of this review is to stimulate the progress and innovation of emerging designs for AFLMBs.

paragraph_context: Cu foil has been extensively employed as a CC for anode in LMBs due to its high electrical conductivity, excellent mechanical stability, and cost-effectiveness [15-17]. Cu and Li belong to a heterogeneous system. And for AFLMBs, it is necessary to deposit lithium metal directly onto the Cu foil rather than lithium itself [18]. Therefore, it is crucial to accurately understand the nucleation and growth mechanism of lithium on Cu as well as its influencing factors.

paragraph_context: Nucleation of a new solid phase involves an associated free energy barrier, which is related to the thermodynamic energy demand of forming a critical cluster of atoms [19]. The homogeneous nucleation rate $J$ for liquid-solid systems is described by the Arrhenius chemical reaction rate equation within the classical nucleation theory framework [20-22]: $$ J = K \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {\Delta G ^ {*}}{k _ {\mathrm {B}} T}\right), \tag {1} $$ where $K$ is the pre-exponential factor, $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann's constant, $\Delta G^{*}$ is the change in Gibbs free energy required for critical cluster formation, and $T$ is the nucleation temperature [23]. The Gibbs energy $\Delta G^{*}$ for forming a spherical nuclei of radius $r$ is the sum of its bulk free energy and surface free energy [24]. $$ \Delta G ^ {*} = - \frac {4}{3 \pi r ^ {3} \Delta G _ {\mathrm {v}}} + 4 \pi r ^ {2} \gamma , \tag {2} $$ where $\Delta G_{\mathrm{v}}$ is the free energy change per volume and $\gamma$ is the surface energy of the Li-electrolyte interface [19]. And the deposition overpotential $\eta$ is related to $\Delta G_{\mathrm{v}}$ : $$ \Delta G _ {\mathrm {v}} = \frac {F | \eta |}{V _ {\mathrm {m}}}, \tag {3} $$ where $F$ is the Faraday constant, $V_{\mathrm{m}}$ is the molar volume of Li. The critical radius for nucleation is [25] $$ r _ {\mathrm {c r i t}} = \frac {2 \gamma V _ {\mathrm {m}}}{F \eta_ {\mathrm {n}}}, \tag {4} $$ where $\eta_{\mathrm{n}}$ is the nucleation overpotential.

paragraph_context: The design of 3D structured CCs has become a hotspot in AFLMBs, which provide larger specific surface areas to effectively reduce local current density and ensure uniform lithium nucleation with large size [38-44]. Commonly used 3D CCs include porous Cu [45], layered graphite oxide [46], and dendritic three-dimensional Cu [47]. In addition to the 3D structure of CC, augmenting the surface of CC resistance is also being explored as a method to decrease current density. Increasing the surface resistance of the CC, such as with $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ coatings, reduces available nucleation sites for Li-metal, promoting sparse nucleation of Linuclei [48]. Besides, modifying the Cu surface with high dielectric coatings also can effectively reduce the overpotential. For example, combining high dielectric constant materials like $\mathrm{BaTiO_3}$ with 3D CC structures effectively reduces current density and uniforms local electric field gradients as presented in Figure 3C [26]. Kim et al. proposed an approach involves adopting a multi-vacancy defect-rich carbon 3D CC design concept [27]. This design not only reduces current density, but also effectively mitigates the side reactions between lithium and the electrolyte via lowering the Fermi energy level (Figure 3D). However, it is worth pointing out that the challenge of inherent side reactions between lithium metal and the electrolyte persists in these 3D CC structures. Achieving a balance between reducing local current density via 3D CC design and avoiding the more electrode interface side reactions induced by the high surface area the electrode itself remains a challenge which requires further research.

paragraph_context: A weaker affinity between the substrate and lithium leads to a higher deposition overpotential [49-51]. Broadly speaking, at room temperature, Cu exhibits poor affinity with lithium. The deposition of lithium onto Cu surface necessitates overcoming a high nucleation barrier [52, 53]. Alternatively, metals that alloy with lithium exhibit minimal nucleation barriers. For instance, Au not only reacts with Li to form multiple $\mathrm{Li_xAu}$ alloy phases as shown in Figure 4A, but also has a solubility zone of Au inside Li metal when the atomic ratio of Li is near $100\%$ , giving a solubility of $\sim 0.7$ at.% [19]. The surface layer of this solid solution shares an identical crystal structure with pure lithium metal ( $\beta$ Li), thus acting as a substrate for subsequent lithium plating and effectively diminishing the nucleation resistance. Therefore, the modification of the CC by establishing a lithophilic layer represents a strategy to enhance the cycling stability and longevity of AFLMBs.

paragraph_context: There are a variety of materials that have reduced nucleation overpotentials due to their significant lithophilicity as outlined in Figure 4B [58]. Researchers have strategically deposited Sn onto Cu surface to establish the affinity with lithium metal [59], facilitating the deposition of thicker lithium layers that adhere firmly to the substrate, contrasting sharply with lithium detachment observed on bare Cu surfaces as presented in Figure 4C [55]. paragraph_context: In addition to metallic layers, various lithophilic composite materials and compounds have been utilized in CCs. Multi-stage potential reduction typically refers to a process in which the potential is not decreased to the target value in a single step but rather is gradually lowered through multiple distinct stages. paragraph_context: As a pivotal interface located on the anode, SEI often experiences significant mechanical stress when subjected to continuous deposition of lithium metal, due to the volumetric changes associated with lithium metal. Thus, the mechanical stability is of paramount importance to a stable interface [86-88]. According to Griffith's theory of fracture: $$ \sigma = \frac {E \cdot \gamma}{\sqrt {\pi \alpha}}, \tag {5} $$ where $E$ is Young's modulus, $\gamma$ is the surface energy, and $\alpha$ is the crack length.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Notably, critical stress refers to the stress level at which a material will fracture and fail due to crack propagation, and it is an important parameter for assessing the mechanical strength of a material. Griffith's theory of fracture provides an intuitive explanation of the relationship between critical stress and Young's modulus of a material. The higher Young's modulus, the higher the critical stress that the material can withstand. Consequently, in the AFLMB, when subjected to the same stress resulting from the deposition of lithium metal with equivalent capacity, SEI with a higher Young's modulus and surface energy is less prone to fracture, indicating better interface stability. It is worth pointing out that the ruptured SEI cannot inhibit lithium dendrite penetration, leading to uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth, exacerbating the loss of active lithium and triggering a series of side reactions.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The rigid inorganic SEI with high fracture toughness and the flexible organic polymer SEI with excellent deformability are currently widely reported as effective in mitigating issues of battery short circuits and active lithium loss caused by lithium dendrites. It is worth discussing that both have their own advantages and disadvantages, necessitating comprehensive consideration in practical applications. The inorganic SEI, under the precondition of membrane integrity, can achieve the full protection of deposited active lithium metal. However, once localized stress exceeds its critical threshold due to uneven deposition of lithium metal, the membrane is highly prone to rupture, losing its ability to inhibit dendrites and secondary reactions. Furthermore, the inorganic SEI imposes strict requirements on membrane quality (thickness uniformity, compositional uniformity, and membrane density), with inherently high fabrication difficulty and relatively stringent preparation conditions, often requiring various physical thin-film deposition techniques such as atomic layer deposition and magnetron sputtering, leading to higher practical application costs. Conversely, artificial SEIs composed of various organic polymers possess the advantages of easy implementation and low cost. Nevertheless, due to the inherent properties of polymers, it is challenging to effectively block the penetration of electrolytes within the range of SEI thickness requirements (generally in the nanometer scale, to ensure efficient ion transport at the interface), thereby providing only partial insulation and protection against interfacial side reactions. Besides, the inorganic SEI films exhibit excellent electrochemical stability, while organic SEIs predominantly composed of polymers require consideration of their electrochemical stability window and compatibility with the current battery system.

paragraph_context: The ionic conductivity of the SEI profoundly influences lithium plating during charging. In an experiment conducted by Liu et al. At very low conductivities $(\Gamma = 0.001)$ , lithium ions in the SEI are depleted, resulting in low current density on the substrate surface. As conductivity increases, lithium-ion depletion in the SEI decreases and the concentration gradient between the liquid electrolyte and SEI diminishes. Beyond $\Gamma = 0.1$ , only little changes are observed, with high current densities concentrated at the top of the column. At low SEI ionic conductivities, electrodeposited lithium shows a tooth-like morphology with low electrodeposition probability as highlighted in Figure 6A. Conversely, at high conductivities $(\Gamma \geq 0.1)$ , lithium exhibits a bulb-like morphology with higher electrodeposition probability. In summary, lithium-ion depletion probably leads to a reduction in current density on the substrate surface, as current density depends on the availability and mobility of lithium ions. Simply put, the fewer lithium ions available, the lower the current generated, resulting in reduced current density. These findings suggest that a higher ionic conductivity of the SEI is necessary to achieve efficient and uniform lithium plating on substrates covered with ASEI [15].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The previous sections mainly discussed the crucial influence of SEI on lithium deposition morphology. However, in addition to that, unlike liquid-based battery systems [129], the mechanical stability of the SSE itself in solid-state batteries (SSBs) systems also affects the deposition morphology (dendrite) of lithium metal [130, 131]. It was proposed that the dendrite formation and the dendrite induced short-circuiting process in SSBs into two distinct stages: initiation and propagation [132]. The initiation of dendrites occurs through the deposition of lithium at near-interface pores (defects) connected to the lithium metal/ solid electrolyte interface. During the process of lithium extrusion after pore filling, high current densities cause significant internal stress in lithium as a viscoplastic fluid, leading to the fracture of the electrolyte. High current densities can result in the rapid deposition of lithium on the electrode surface, often leading to inhomogeneous growth such as dendrites or other irregular structures. These uneven deposits cause localized volume expansion and deformation, generating internal stresses within the lithium metal. On the one hand, the expansion process of lithium dendrites involves the wedge opening of the SSE by a growing dendrite from the tail of the dendritic crack during deposition. The initiation of dendrites depends on the local fracture strength of the grain boundaries in the SSE, the size and distribution density of the pores, and the current density. On the other hand, the expansion process of dendrites is influenced by the macroscopic fracture toughness of the SSE, the distribution of dendrites within cracks, the current density, and the areal capacity during the charging process [133]. Thus, the mechanical stability of the SSE itself plays a crucial role in the growth behavior of dendrites in SSBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In the practical application of AFLMBs, the influence of pressure on electrochemical properties warrants consideration [139, 141]. During battery cycling, from the perspective of anode, factors that predominantly influence the variation of internal pressure encompass the reversible expansion induced by lithium plating and stripping during the cycling process, as well as the irreversible expansion arising from SEI growth and the accumulation of dead lithium. Remarkably, substantial research has demonstrated that the performance of batteries which is closely related to the lithium deposition behavior can be modulated by controlling the applied pressure. Moreover, the magnitude and uniformity of mechanical pressure markedly affect the deposition morphology and distribution of the lithium metal on the anode side, thereby determining the lithium loss in the battery [142]. Given that there exist certain distinctions between solid-state and liquid-state systems, this section will delineate the influence mechanisms of pressure separately in these two systems.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: It is clearly reported that the uniformity of mechanical pressure applied to the liquid electrolyte based AFLMBs battery significantly influence the distribution and morphology of lithium deposition. Taking coin cell as an example, when a single spacer is used and the internal pressure is non-uniform, the lithium metal tends to be deposited in the central region of the Cu CC [139]. However, by using two spacers to improve the uniformity of pressure, a uniform deposition morphology distributed on the surface of the Cu foil can be achieved [142]. The phenomenon of pressure affecting lithium distribution has also been demonstrated in pouch-cells. It was observed that Li-ions (from cathode) tend to electrochemically deposit in the central region of anode during the charging process, leading to a faster increase in the spontaneous pressure generation rate in the central region. Ideally, the electrochemical deposition of Li (from cathode) should follow a process of uniform distribution. However, influenced by pressure, some $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ that should have deposited at the edges now bypass to the central region of the anode and deposit there, resulting in a thicker deposition layer covering the central region of anode as demonstrated in Figure 7A [143]. Researchers also have conducted in-depth analyses based on solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques and found that the formation of dead lithium at low pressure is primarily associated with dendritic lithium. On the other hand, at high pressure, the formation of dead lithium may be related to mossy lithium morphology. This reveals the differences in the evolution of dead lithium in LMBs under different pressure conditions and sheds light on the reasons for the variation in cycling performance between high and low pressures [147]. A comprehensive analysis suggests that increasing the pressure aids in enhancing deposition compactness can reduce associated lithium losses and optimized the cycling performances [148]. As empirically demonstrated in practical pouch LMBs, the performance of these batteries improve gradually as the initial average mechanical pressure increases from 75 to $2200\mathrm{kPa}$ [149]. It is noteworthy that, as reported, higher pressure does not necessarily equate to superior performance. Excessively high pressure can instead lead to the deterioration of battery performance. This phenomenon may be attributed to variations in the amounts of electrolyte retained within the electrodes under elevated pressures or inducing-deformation of the polymer separator [142].

paragraph_context: The cycling performance of AFLMB exhibits a significant correlation with the charge-discharge rate. Professor Dahn conducted a comparative study on the performance of AFLMB under different charge-discharge cycling conditions. The study concluded that the relative rate of charge and discharge is more important than the absolute current density. During lithium plating, the concentration gradient at the anode is directly proportional to the applied current. Therefore, under fast charging conditions, significant concentration gradients are formed on the lithium surface. Additionally, the unavoidable convection further interferes with ion diffusion, resulting in uneven distribution of lithium ions and the non-uniform localized current density. This leads to rapid growth of high surface area lithium. On the contrary, lower current density results in the formation of denser, low surface area lithium morphologies as shown in Figure 7F [146]. During lithium stripping, lithium in an environment with extremely low concentration gradient is uniformly stripped from the surface. It worth noting that the isolated inactive lithium may be formed due to the stripping of the bottom of lithium during the uniform stripping process. In contrast, at faster discharge rates, significant concentration gradients occur on the lithium surface. These concentration gradients increase the current density at the tips of lithium, leading to preferential stripping of the tips.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The current strategies for CC design primarily involve material selection and optimization, as well as surface modification and interface engineering. While these approaches can significantly enhance performance, they also inevitably increase costs and complicate manufacturability. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the commercial viability of these advancements. Efforts should be directed toward reducing research and development costs, optimizing material synthesis and processing techniques, and ensuring that the modified collectors are feasible for large-scale industrial applications. In terms of SSEs, inorganic composite electrolytes are widely employed to address the challenges posed by unstable interfacial chemistry and volume changes at the solid-solid interface, owing to their excellent ionic conductivity and robust mechanical properties. However, the fabrication of high-quality inorganic composite electrolytes and the development of methods to produce them in thin-film form remain critical areas of focus for future research. Leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) for the screening of battery materials is poised to become a critical trend in the evolution of AFLMBs. By compiling comprehensive data on electrolyte properties—such as ionic conductivity, electrochemical stability window, and viscosity—unique models can be developed to optimize electrolytes. Advanced techniques, including the use of encoder-decoder frameworks, can compress high-dimensional discrete chemical spaces into low-dimensional continuous representations, thereby streamlining the selection of optimal candidate materials. Such methodologies, which are already widely employed in biological and medical small molecule screening, can be adapted for AFLMB development. These technological advancements not only contribute to improved energy density and cycle life but also hasten the commercialization process, enabling earlier real-world applications. In addition, we summarize the importance of various testing conditions for optimizing the lithium metal deposition morphology on the anode side. In summary, this review provides a systematic and organized presentation of the current key strategies and approaches for optimizing anode-free batteries by summarizing the scientific mechanisms related to various factors influencing lithium metal deposition and nucleation, along with typical case analyses. AFLMBs face numerous opportunities and challenges and represent an important opportunity for the development of advanced energy storage technologies. This article aims to provide ideas and inspiration for the development of next-generation AFLMBs with high energy density, long cycling stability, and high safety.

paragraph_context: Anode-free batteries (AFBs) are emerging as a safer and more energy-dense option for next-generation energy storage. Their simple design, lower material costs, and compatibility with current lithium-ion battery (LIB) manufacturing processes make them a potential game-changer. Unlike traditional LIBs, AFBs—often referred to as “Li-free” or “anode-less”—use a bare current collector (CC) as the negative electrode, which theoretically enables significantly higher energy density. However, challenges remain, including low Coulombic efficiency (CE) (often $< 90\%$ ), quick capacity loss due to dendritic lithium (Li) growth, and formation of “dead” Li. This review overviews surface engineering techniques for CCs aimed at overcoming these challenges. The focus is on coatings that encourage homogeneous Li deposition, reduce nucleation overpotentials, curb dendrite formation, and stabilize the chemistry at the interface. Various coating methods are critically assessed, including inorganic, polymeric, and carbon-based layers. With mechanistic understanding and comparative analysis, this review highlights engineered surface modifications as a key enabler of uniform Li deposition and prolong cycle life. This review bridges the gap between materials science, focusing on surface chemistry, morphology, and interface design with electrochemical engineering principles such as cell design, ion transport, and interfacial kinetics, thereby guiding the development of next-generation AFBs.

paragraph_context: With the increase in the global demand for clean and sustainable energy, the development of an advanced energy storage system is paramount. The largest part of the current energy storage market is dominated by LIB technology, particularly in portable electronics and in the electric vehicle (EV) market.[1-3] However, commercial LIBs with graphite anodes have typical energy densities of 200–250 Wh kg $^{-1}$ , which is insufficient to meet the increasing requirements of EVs (>500 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ).[4-7] Lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) with Li-foil anodes offer an alternative battery chemistry that can increase the energy density by 50% at the cell level.[8-10] Primarily due to the exceptional properties of Li metal as an anode material. While graphite can host only one Li-ion per six carbon atoms, forming $\mathrm{LiC}_6$ , Li metal can directly store Li-ions without the need for a host structure, allowing for a theoretical specific capacity of 3860 mAh g $^{-1}$ , about ten times higher than that of graphite ( $\approx$ 372 mAh g $^{-1}$ ). In addition, Li metal has a very low electrochemical potential (-3.04 V vs the standard hydrogen electrode), contributing to specific energy densities of up to $\approx$ 440 Wh kg $^{-1}$ in LMBs.[11,12] Nonetheless, the practical applications of LMBs are challenging due to the dendrite formation, accumulation of dead Li, and parasitic reactions between the Li metal and the electrolyte; all of these issues contribute to the capacity degradation, safety issues (fire risk), and reduced cycle life.[12,13] AFBs, also referred to as anode-less batteries (ALBs), are an innovative cell design that marks a significant step toward next-generation energy storage technologies. AFBs have attracted considerable attention for their potential to deliver exceptionally high energy densities. They are capable of delivering a volumetric energy density exceeding $900\mathrm{WhL^{-1}}$ and a gravimetric energy density exceeding $500\mathrm{Whkg^{-1}}$ , higher than those of traditional LIBs $(\approx 500 - 700\mathrm{WhL^{-1}}$ and $200 - 300\mathrm{Whkg^{-1}}$ respectively).[3,14-18] In AFBs, the traditional anode material is eliminated, and Li metal is directly plated onto the bare CC during charging, while it is stripped during discharging. Thus, the AFB is regarded as a special kind of "LMB" in which the negative to positive aerial capacity ratio $(\mathrm{N / P})$ is close to zero.[15] This innovative design not only simplifies the cell manufacturing process but also increases the energy density by eliminating the need for anode materials such as graphite. The elimination of the anode reduces both the mass and volume of the cell, thereby maximizing the energy density on a cell level. In the literature, AFBs and ALBs are often used interchangeably; however, they represent different concepts in terms of how they operate. A truly AFB system consists of only a bare CC (typically Cu foil) without any pre-existing Li or active anode material. In this case, Li is directly plated onto the current collector during the first charge from the cathode, making the system highly energy dense. In contrast, an ALB employs a current collector modified with lithiophilic coatings, alloying layers, or functional interlayers. These modifications can provide an initial capacity by reversibly interacting with Li, thereby distinguishing ALBs from truly anode-free systems.[19] The concept of AFBs was introduced to advance LIB technology and was first demonstrated by Neudecker et al. in 2000.[20] They developed Li-free thin-film batteries using copper (Cu), a solid electrolyte, and lithium cobalt oxide $\mathrm{(LiCoO_2)}$ , successfully achieving in-situ Li plating on Cu during charging, laying the foundation for AFB technology. Building on this, in 2016, Qian et al. reported a rechargeable AFB using a Cu CC and a $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ cathode, showcasing the practical feasibility of this architecture.[16] Subsequent advances aimed at improving cycle life include the development of dual-salt LiDFOB/LiBF electrodes by Weber et al., highlighting the role of electrolyte modifications in enhancing cycling stability.[21] These developments, particularly the high energy density and simplified design, have significantly accelerated global interest in AFB technology. Additionally, AFBs offer potential cost advantages over conventional LIBs by eliminating the anode materials and associated processes, such as slurry preparation and electrode coating, reducing manufacturing difficulties and material costs. This simplified production process results in more economical battery systems, making AFBs an attractive option for large-scale applications, including EVs and grid storage.

paragraph_context: Nonetheless, the low CE and poor cycling stability due to dendrite formation on the CC and accumulation of dead Li remain critical challenges that hinder the commercial viability of AFBs.[22] Non-uniform Li plating on the CC results in the growth of dendrites, which are needle-like metallic Li structures.[23] These dendrites can penetrate the separator and cause internal short circuits, posing serious safety risks. Additionally, dendrites can break off and form dead Li. Dead Li refers to Li that is no longer electrically connected and, therefore, cannot participate in the electrochemical reactions responsible for charging and discharging.[24] This contributes to capacity loss during cycling, a phenomenon known as capacity fade. The CE (which indicates how efficiently the battery can cycle Li) is typically low, especially in the initial cycles. This results from Li consumption due to side reactions and solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation.[25] If the SEI is unstable and continues to degrade with each cycle, more Li is consumed to reform it. This further reduces the number of effective cycles and leads to poor interfacial stability. Altogether, these challenges result in capacity fade, limited cycle life, and safety concerns, which need to be addressed to enable the commercial viability of AFBs.[22] Several strategies have been explored to address these issues, including surface treatment of the CC, optimization of the electrolyte, and the development of optimized operational protocols.[22,26] The electrolyte is a critical component in determining AFB performance, as it helps in the formation of a stable SEI on the surface of CC. This SEI layer serves a dual purpose: it prevents further decomposition of the electrolyte by acting as a protective barrier, while simultaneously allowing efficient Li-ion conduction across the interface.[27] Additionally, modifications to the CC significantly enhance AFB performance by controlling the morphology of the deposited Li. The CC plays an essential role in this process, as its surface properties influence the nucleation overpotential (the energy barrier associated with initiating Li deposition) and growth of Li during cycling. Specifically, tailored CC surfaces can lower the nucleation overpotential during the Li plating and stripping processes, which promotes more uniform Li deposition, mitigates dendrite formation, and enhances the overall cycling stability of AFBs. paragraph_context: This review article outlines recent progress in surface engineering approaches for CCs in AFBs, with particular focus on the design, synthesis, and implementation of protective coatings to enhance electrochemical performance and cyclic stability. Although there have been some reviews addressing coating techniques and surface treatments for CCs, these have largely focused on Li metal and LIBs.[28,29] The role of surface engineering of CCs specifically for AFBs has not yet been systematically reviewed. The present study emphasises exclusively how surface coatings help to improve Li plating/stripping reversibility, minimize dendritic growth, and enhance overall cycling stability in AFBs. We have critically assessed various coatings, including inorganic, polymeric, and carbon-based layers, all designed to manage Li nucleation, lower interfacial resistance, suppress dendritic growth, and maintain stable interfacial chemistry.
