paragraph_context: Abstract: Recycling useful materials such as Ag, Al, Sn, Cu and Si from waste silicon solar cell chips is a sustainable project to slow down the ever-growing amount of waste crystalline-silicon photovoltaic panels. However, the recovery cost of the above-mentioned materials from silicon chips via acid-alkaline treatments outweights the gain economically. Herein, we propose a new proof-of-concept to fabricate Si-based anodes with waste silicon chips as raw materials. Nanoparticles from waste silicon chips were prepared with the high-energy ball milling followed by introducing carbon nanotubes and N-doped carbon into the nanoparticles, which amplifies the electrochemical properties. It is explored that Al and Ag elements influenced electrochemical performance respectively. The results showed that the Al metal in the composite possesses an adverse impact on the electrochemical performance. After removing Al, the composite was confirmed to possess a pronounced durable cycling property due to the presence of Ag, resulting in significantly more superior property than the composite having both Al and Ag removed.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Key words: waste solar panels; recycling; Si-based anodes; lithium-ion batteries Over the past three decades, solar photovoltaic (PV) modules have been widely employed to harvest clean energy around the globe [1 − 3]. In 2009, the total installed capacity of PV power was estimated to be about 99.1 GW. Over the next 5 years, the cumulative installed capacity had then surged 4-fold to 404.5 GW where the demand will statistically anticipate to soar up exponentially to 4500 GW by 2050 [4]. The current conventional PV production relies on the crystalline silicon panels (c-Si), which have gained a total of $9 2 \%$ market share in 2014 [4] with an expected lifespan of $2 5 -$ 30 years [5 − 6]. However, the ever-growing PV demand directly translated into a surge in waste and retired PV modules. It is estimated that 1.7 million tonnes of PV waste will likely be generated by 2030 and the number will exponentially increase to 60 million tonnes by 2050 as a result of the utilization of PV devices [7]. Due to its dominance in the PV industry, the c-Si panels are estimated to produce an enormous amount of waste materials after its first 25-year journey. Consequently, the management and recycling of waste c-Si panels have become not only an essential issue, but also a topic to the environmental sustainability in humanity.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: A typical c-Si solar panel consists of Al alloy frame, ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant, crystalline silicon chips, Ag bar line [8], glass, Al coating film, etc. [9]. The removal of the junction box, frame, back sheet, EVA, and glass from the panel is effortless and affordable which can be realized by mechanical and thermal methods. However, the recovery of silicon and other precious metals from silicon chips $( \mathrm { S i } { > } 9 0 \%$ , $\mathrm { A l } { > } 6 \%$ , Ag about $1 \%$ , and $\mathrm { S i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ about 0.1 wt% ) can be economically intractable and costly. During the recovery process, strong acids, and bases such as $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ , $\mathrm { H N O } _ { 3 }$ , HF, $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ , NaOH, and KOH are the essential chemical agents operating under heating, stirring, and ultrasonic conditions. It is also important to note that the commercial value of a recovery product depends on its purity and recovery rate, therefore the added value is generally low. Accomplishing a higher recovery rate and product purity remains the highest priority and requires rigorous and complicated recovery steps, which directly compromises its commercial value and profitability of recovering elemental products from crystalline silicon solar cells. The commercially viable options for sustainability remain to optimize the recycling protocol, reduce the cost of the recycling process, increase the value of the product, and find novel alternative recycling processes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In recent years, silicon-based anode in lithiumion batteries (LIBs) has been widely studied and regarded as the next generation anode material due to its high theoretical capacity $( 3 5 6 0 \mathrm { \ m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { h } / \mathrm { g }$ for $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 5 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 4 , }$ ), suitable lithiation potential (about 0.37 V (vs Li+ /Li)) as well as the abundant reserves [10 − 12]. Unfortunately, the intrinsic semiconductor property of Si particle reveals low electronic conductivity, leading to impeded electrons transfer and unsatisfactory rate performance. Besides, the lithiation/delithiation process of Si electrode generates tremendous volume change, resulting in Si particle pulverization, instable solid state interphase, and inferior cycling performance [13 − 14]. Many strategies have been proposed to address the aforementioned shortcomings, namely constructing Si-based anode with nanostructures (nanoparticles, nanoarrays and hollow nanospheres), combining Si particles with conductive agents (carbon, Ag and conducting polymer), and prelithiation of Si/C electrode [15 − 17]. On top of this, element doping (such as boron and phosphorus) in silicon has been concluded to be another crucial tactic to enhance the electronic conductivity of Si-based anodes and thus improve its electrochemical properties [18−19]. Presumably, the c-Si as an active material possesses a superior electronic conductivity than the traditional Si anode due to its doping nature and the presence of Ag.

paragraph_context: Here in our work, we propose a novel concept by recycling waste solar silicon chips as highperformance Si/C anodes. As a kind of onedimensional nanomaterial, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) have many excellent mechanical, chemical and electrochemical properties [20]. Nanostructured waste silicon particles were prepared with high energy ball milling and the electrochemical properties of these nanoparticles were enhanced through CNTs and N-doped carbon coating. More importantly, the electrochemical properties of Al and Ag in the carbon-coated nanoparticles were studied in the preliminary test where it was concluded that the Al metal in the composite possesses an adverse effect on the electrochemical performance. After removing the Al, the composite presented a higher initial columbic efficiency and a more durable cycling performance attributed to the presence of Ag. Meanwhile, the composite having both Al and Ag removed exhibited the same electrochemical properties as the pure Si@C composite. This implies that high performance of c-$\mathrm { S i } @ \mathrm { C }$ anode can be achieved by eliminating Al from the carbon-coated composite. This method not only eluded the complex recovery processes involving a toxic etchant to etch the surface of the solar cell chips but also reduced the cost in the element recovery of crystalline silicon solar cells. At the same time, a decrease has been observed in energy consumption for high-purity silicon Preparation of waste silicon nanoparticles (WSNPs). The waste solar panels in large rectangular fragments where the frames and ethylene/vinyl acetate (EVA) copolymer layers have been preliminarily removed, were acquired from JinkoSolar Holding Co., Ltd. The remaining components of these waste solar panels were crystalline silicon chips, containing four major chemical constituents of Si $( 9 1 . 9 ~ \mathrm { ~ w t \% }$ ), Al $( 7 . 0 ~ \mathrm { w t \% }$ ), Ag (1.0 wt% ) and $\mathrm { S i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ (0.1 wt% ). For granulation, the crystalline silicon chips were milled into nanoparticles by high energy ball milling to obtain WSNPs.

paragraph_context: Removal of Al in WSNPs (W-rAl). WSNP was dispersed into NaOH solution. The Al element was removed by magnetically stirring, filtration, washing, and drying. Then the Al removed sample was labeled as W-rAl.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: Removal of Ag in W-rAl (W-rAlAg). The Ag metal in W-rAl was removed by the ${ \mathrm { H N O } } _ { 3 }$ solution. Detailed process was the same as removed Al. The sample with Al and Ag removed was marked as WrAlAg. Given that the negligible amount of $\mathrm { S i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ in the W-rAlAg and the formidable chemical stability of $\mathrm { S i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ itself, no further treatment was taken to remove the $\mathrm { S i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ component.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: Preparation of carbon hybrid composites. Herein, to enhance the electrochemical performances of the three above-mentioned samples, carbon materials were introduced into these samples (WSNPs, W-rAl, and W-rAlAg) as follows. In the first step, WSNPs and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) were dispersed with N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) to obtain a solution. The solution was then ultrasonicated for $3 0 ~ \mathrm { \ m i n }$ and transferred into a $\mathrm { Z r O } _ { 2 }$ cup with $5 \ \mathrm { m m } \ Z \mathrm { r O } _ { 2 }$ balls (in diameter) to ball milling. Following that, the resultant slurry was dried in an oven to obtain WSNPs-CNTs composite. In the subsequent step, WSNPs-CNTs and dopamine hydrochloride were added into deionized water and magnetically stirred to acquire mixture. The mixture was then dried. Finally, the dried mixture was annealed in argonatmosphere. The dopamine hydrochloride in the anneal condition was carbonized into N-doped carbon and coated onto the particle surface of WSNPs-CNTs. The resultant sample was therefore coined $\mathrm { W S N P s } @ { \mathrm { C } }$ . Likewise, W-rAl@C and W-rAlAg@C were prepared in the same manner by substituting W-rAl and W-rAlAg for WSNPs, respectively. paragraph_context: This study has revealed the feasibility of converting the waste solar cell materials to highperformance silicon-based anodes. The strategy in the present study was to bypass the inefficient and low-return metallurgical recycling steps in the element recycling process and it circumvented the smelting and purification of the silicon metallurgical process. Instead, large fragments of waste c-Si chips were ground into nanoparticles followed by CNTs and N-doped carbon coating to improve the electrochemical performance of nanoparticles. The electrochemical properties of Al and Ag in the carbon-coated nanoparticles were comprehensively studied where the results have demonstrated that the absence of Al in the silicon nanoparticles is beneficial to a higher capacity and a more durable cycling performance. Meanwhile, the composite having both Al and Ag removed exerted similar electrochemical properties with the pure Si@C composite.

paragraph_context: HUANG Shao-zhen(黄绍祯) 1, 2 , HE Pan(贺盼) 1 , YU Hua-ming(于铧铭) 1 , LI Hui-miao(李卉淼) 1 , CHEN Li-bao(陈立宝) 1, 2 * Abstract: Lithium metal stands out as an exceptionally promising anode material, boasting an extraordinarily high theoretical capacity and impressive energy density. Despite these advantageous characters, the issues of dendrite formation and volume expansion of lithium metal anodes lead to performance decay and safety concerns, significantly impeding their advancement towards widespread commercial viability. Herein, a lithium-rich Li-B-In composite anode with abundant lithophilic sites and outstanding structural stability is reported to address the mentioned challenges. The evenly distributed Li-In alloy in the bulk phase of anodes act as mixed ion/electron conductors and nucleation sites, facilitating accelerated Li ions transport dynamics and suppressing lithium dendrite formation. Additionally, these micron-sized Li-In particles in LiB fibers framework can enhance overall structural integrity and provide sufficient interior space to accommodate the volume changes during cycling. The electrochemical performance of Li-B-In composite anode exhibits long-term cyclability, superior rate performance and high-capacity retention. This work confirms that the synergy between a 3D skeleton and hetero-metallic lithiophilic sites can achieve stable and durable lithium metal anodes, offering innovative insights for the practical deployment of lithium metal batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Key words: lithium metal anodes; lithiophilic sites; intermetallic phase; enhanced structural stability; fast ion diffusion In recent years, with the rapid development of electrified transportation and the widespread demand for portable electronic devices, there is an urgent need to develop new anode materials to meet the demands of new types of energy storage with high energy density [1 − 4]. Although traditional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have achieved tremendous success in commercial applications, their limited energy density has become a bottleneck for further development [5 − 8]. In this regard, lithium metal with high theoretical specific capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { \ m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { h } / \mathrm { g } )$ and the lowest reduction potential (3.040 V vs the standard hydrogen electrode), has become the most promising anode material. However, the lithium metal anode faces rampant dendrite growth and significant volume expansion during the cycling process, which inevitably brings safety issues and low cycle stability to its practical application. Specifically, during the repeated lithium deposition/stripping process, the large volume change of lithium metal leads to the repeated breaking and repairing of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer. This not only causes the consumption of active materials and electrolyte but also promotes the formation of inactive Li (namely dead Li) [9 11]. The construction of an artificial solid-state electrolyte layer at the interface can effectively alleviate the failure of the lithium metal anode and prolong the service life of the lithium metal battery [12, 13]. The instability of SEI will cause the overall performance of the battery to decline rapidly [14 − 16]. Simultaneously, the stacking of lithium dendrites during the cycling process may eventually puncture the separator and cause a battery short circuit, leading to serious safety issues [17, 18]. Therefore, it is crucial to design a new type of lithium-based anode material that can suppress volume expansion and dendrites extension during battery cycling.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Constructing a composite anode with a threedimensional (3D) skeleton structure is an effective strategy to mitigate the challenges faced by lithium metal anodes. The 3D skeleton structure can suppress lithium dendrites and volume expansion by reducing local current density and ensuring uniform lithium-ion flux. However, most of the reported 3D composite lithium anodes to date involve a complex and costly fabrication process which involves infiltrating or rolling lithium metal into the 3D skeleton [19, 20]. Moreover, many of the introduced 3D skeletons have poor wettability for Li, which can lead to difficulties in achieving dense filling of lithium metal within the structure or exhibit poor structural stability during cycling. Therefore, using the uniformly distributed alloy phases in some special lithium alloys as an internal skeleton to construct a 3D composite anode has become a new option. As early as 1989, SANCHEZ et al [21] proposed the possibility of using Li-B alloys to replace Li for electrochemical research. The LiB alloy anode is composed of free lithium and LiB compound. The LiB compound with fiber structure intersperses between free lithium, making it an ideal skeleton for constructing complex 3D frameworks [22]. However, the LiB fiber network gradually collapses during repeated cycling, leading to a decrease in electrode stability [23, 24]. Therefore, it is still necessary to further enhance the lithiophilicity and conductivity of the Li-B alloy anode to strengthen Li ion diffusion-deposition kinetics, ultimately achieving an improvement in the cycling stability of the anode.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Based on the above consideration, a lithiumrich Li-B-In composite anode which possesses rich lithophilic sites and superior mechanical stability was synthesized by a simple vacuum smelting method. The prepared Li-B-In anode is consisted of free-Li, Li-B compound, and Li-In intermetallic phase. The fibrous LiB compound forms the fundamental framework of the anode; the Li-In intermetallic phase is uniformly distributed throughout the fibers; and the excess lithium metal effectively occupies the remaining interstitial spaces within the material, thereby creating a robust and stable 3D composite skeletal structure. The LiB fibers which serve as a skeleton can enhance the mechanical strength of the lithium metal anode. Meanwhile, the uniformly distributed Li-In alloy within the anode bulk phase provides a multitude of lithiophilic sites, thereby accelerating the diffusion and deposition kinetics of ions on the electrode surface and inside the anodes. As a result, the alloy composite anode is able to suppress lithium dendrite growth while also mitigating the volume change, thus maintaining a stable electrode structure. Li-B-In composite anode combines the advantages of a 3D skeletal material and hetero-metallic lithiophilic alloy. These effects have been verified by a series of characterization and electrochemical tests. As expected, the constructed Li-B-In composite anode achieves an ultralong lifespan (over 700 h) at $2 { \mathrm { m A } } / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 }$ and an excellent cyclic stability of $1 3 0 0 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ even at a large capacity of 5 $\mathrm { m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { h } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . Furthermore, the assembled full cell with Li-B-In composite anode shows an excellent capacity retention of close to $8 7 . 2 \%$ after 300 cycles. This work opens an approach with easy operation and broad applicability to design advanced composite anode materials for exploring next generation lithium metal batteries.

paragraph_context: The Li-B-In composite anode was synthesized by vacuum melting method. The melting points of Li and In are close ( $1 8 0 . 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for Li vs $1 5 6 . 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for In). During the heating process of preparing composite materials, Li and In will solidify at similar temperatures to form an intermetallic phase. This characteristic ensures that the resulting phases are distributed uniformly within the material. During the preparation, a precise mass ratio of lithium blocks, boron powder, and indium nanoparticles was uniformly heated and mixed in an iron crucible under rigorous stirring conditions. The use of heterometallic lithiophilic sites in the 3D Li metal anode could continuously accelerate the diffusion and deposition of lithium ions in the bulk phase, which helps to maintain good structural integrity during repeated stripping and electroplating processes.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, a hetero-metallic lithiophilic alloy was introduced as a nucleation site into the LiB fiber electrode to construct a Li-B-In composite anode by a simple melting method. A large amount of Li-In alloy compounds serving as hetero-metallic lithiophilic sites, can accelerate the diffusion and deposition of lithium ions at the interface and within the bulk, and achieve a dendrite-free and dense lithium plating layer. The addition and dispersion of the alloy phase significantly enhance the mechanical strength of the composite anode, preventing structural collapse during the cycling process. Furthermore, this unique composite anode can provide a larger specific surface area and abundant internal space after delithiation, not only effectively reducing the local current density but also suppressing the significant volume changes of the electrode during prolonged deposition/dissolution processes. Due to the synergistic effects, the prepared Li-B-In composite anode further leads to a remarkable elevation in the performance of symmetric cells (670 h at $2 \mathrm { \ m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } - 1 \mathrm { \ m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { h } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , 1300 h at $1 \ \mathrm { \ m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } { - } 5 \ \mathrm { \ m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { h } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , respectively). Additionally, the full cell matched with Li-B-In composite anode and the $\mathrm { L i F e P O } _ { 4 }$ cathode demonstrates superior capacity retention of $8 7 . 2 \%$ after 300 cycles and outstanding rate performance. ABSTRACT Lithium (Li) metal is promising for high energy density batteries due to its low electrochemical redox potential and high specific capacity. However, the formation of dendrites and its tendency for large volume expansion during plating/stripping restrict the application of Li metal in practical scenarios. In this work, we developed reduced graphene oxide-graphitic carbon nitride $\bf ( r G O - C _ { 3 } N _ { 4 } ,$ GCN) with highly elastic and wrinkled structure as the current collector. Lithiophilic site $\mathbf { C } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N } _ { 4 }$ in GCN could reduce the nucleation overpotential. In addition, this material effectively inhibited electrode expansion during cycling. At the same time, due to its high elasticity, GCN could release the stress induced by Li deposition to maintain structural integrity of the electrode. Limetal anodes with GCN exhibited small volume expansion, high Coulombic efficiency (CE) of $9 8 . 6 \%$ within 300 cycles and long cycling life of more than $\mathbf { 1 7 0 0 6 }$ . This work described and demonstrated a new approach to construct flexible current collectors for stable lithium-metal anodes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: lithium-metal anode, 3D current collector, high elasticity In recent years, there have been rapid developments in electric vehicles and portable electronic products, but lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) can hardly meet the high energy densities required in future applications. Therefore, new battery systems with high energy densities are needed [1,2]. Lithium metal (Li) is regarded as the nextgeneration anode material due to its high energy density $( 3 8 6 0 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and low electrochemical redox potential $( - 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } \nu s $ . standard hydrogen electrode) [3–5]. However, the dendrite formation and volume expansion of Li restrict its potential application [6,7]. Firstly, uncontrolled growth of Li dendrites leads to the formation of non-active Li, which causes irreversible capacity loss and low Coulombic efficiency (CE). Furthermore, dendrites can pierce the separator, which can cause shortcircuit and lead to safety issues [8–10]. Unlike the electrode materials in LIBs that undergo intercalation, the plating/stripping of Li is a phase-conversion reaction, which results in infinite volume expansion in the electrodes. This leads to their fragmentation and pulverization and deteriorates their cycling performance [11–13].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Therefore, several strategies were developed to resolve these issues [14–17], which can be classified as follows: construct artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [18], optimize electrolyte [19], and use three-dimensional (3D) current collectors [20,21]. A 3D current collector, when used as the substrate for Li deposition, has great impact on Li nucleation and growth processes. The porous structure with abundant active sites of 3D current collector can facilitate Li-ion flux and nucleation, reduce the local current density, and inhibit Li dendrites. These structures have high application prospects in Li-metal batteries [22]. The main strategies to optimize 3D current collectors are as follows: (1) design the pore structure to facilitate Li-ion migration [23,24] and (2) modify the lithiophilic sites to reduce Li nucleation overpotential and promote uniform electrodeposition [25,26]. However, the incorporation of non-active frameworks in the electrodes decreases the intrinsic capacity advantages of Li metal. To ensure high volumetric/gravimetric energy density of Limetal anodes, the constructed 3D current collectors should have small volume and low weight. Because carbon nanomaterials have the advantages of low weight, high pore volume, and high electrical conductivity, they are promising candidates for 3D current collectors. Such porous structures with no tensile strength can accommodate only limited amount of Li. They fail at high current density and capacity. In addition, Li dendrites can form beyond the pores and volume expansion can take place (Fig. 1a). Moreover, the stress produced on the substrate during Li deposition cannot be released effectively, which damages the integrity of current collectors.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: To solve these issues, in this work, we prepared reduced graphene oxide-graphitic carbon nitride $\mathrm { ( r G O - C _ { 3 } N _ { 4 } , }$ denoted as GCN) with highly elastic wrinkled structure as a 3D current collector. We constructed this structure based on our earlier report [27]. Dicyandiamide (DICY) was polymerized into $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ on the graphene layer. In this case, the wrinkles were formed in the material at micron level during the calcining process as the thermal expansion coefficients of $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ and graphene were different. At the same time, according to the tip-charge concentration dendrite formation model [28], Li was mainly deposited in the convex part of the wrinkles. The wrinkles were stretched apart because the stress was generated by Li deposition on the substrate. Therefore, GCN provided more space for volume expansion in Li-metal anodes during cycling (Fig. 1b). In this way, the elastic material released the stress, maintained the structural integrity of the electrode, and improved the electrochemical performance of Li-metal anodes [29]. Lithiophilic $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ effectively reduced the nucleation overpotential and ensured uniform Li deposition [30–32]. As demonstrated in this study, Li-metal anodes with GCN exhibited small volume expansion, high CE $( > 9 8 . 6 \%$ over 300 cycles), and long cycling life of more than $1 7 0 0 \mathrm { h }$ .

paragraph_context: GCN was synthesized according to the previously report [27]. Briefly, DICY solution $\left( 4 0 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { m L } ^ { - 1 } \right)$ ) was added to a GO dispersion at a mass ratio of 3:5 and the mixture was ultrasonically dispersed for $3 0 \mathrm { \ m i n }$ and then freeze-dried to obtain a GO/DICY aerogel. Finally, the GO/DICY aerogel was heated at $5 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $1 { - } 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ in Ar atmosphere to reduce GO and produce $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ .

paragraph_context: The morphological differences between rGO and GCN were further characterized by SEM (Fig. 2c and d). While the surface of rGO was flat and smooth (Fig. 2c), GCN exhibited homogeneous wrinkled structure (Fig. 2d and Fig. S3). To verify that this wrinkled structure has high elasticity and good resilience, cyclic mechanical tests were conducted (Fig. 2e). The area of the hysteresis loop over 100 cycles was small, indicating that energy loss during the loading-unloading process was negligible and the material underwent elastic deformation. After cycling, there was no large deviation in the strain and the overlap between the curves was relatively high, indicating good resilience in the material [35–37]. As shown in the SEM images, there were no wrinkles on the rGO surface, and it was not elastic. Therefore, the rGO electrode was unable to support the stress caused by volume expansion during Li plating/stripping and can suffer from the structural failure (Fig. 2f). In contrast, GCN could release the stress effectively and maintain structural integrity after cycling (Fig. 2g).

paragraph_context: A 3D current collector with highly elastic, lithiophilic sites, and wrinkled structure was developed in this study for Li-metal anodes. This highly elastic structure effectively released the stress caused by Li deposition on the substrate, thus ensuring the integrity of the structure and limiting its volume expansion. Because $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ was lithiophilic, it reduced the nucleation overpotential and led to uniform deposition of Li. Li-metal anodes with GCN as the current collector exhibited high CE of $9 8 . 6 \%$ after 300 cycles and long cycle life of more than $1 7 0 0 \mathrm { h }$ at $\mathrm { i } . 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Meanwhile, the capacity-retention rate of the cells assembled with LFP was $9 8 . 1 5 \%$ after 100 cycles at 1 C. The insights gained from this study offer a simple and practical method to effectively enhance the performance of Li-metal batteries and suggest a new approach for 3D current collector development.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT The pursuit of high-mileage models results in the recurrence of lithium metal batteries (LMBs) to researchers’ horizon. However, the lithium (Li) metal anode for LMBs undergoes the uncontrollable formation of Li dendrites and infinite volume change during cycling, impeding its practical application. To overcome these challenges, we developed a metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived pathway to construct lithiophilic three-dimensional (3D) skeleton using different substrates (e.g., carbon cloth (CC) and Cu mesh) for dendrite-free lithium metal anodes. As a typical example, the MOF-derived ZnO/nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) nanosheet-modified 3D CC was well-constructed as a lithiophilic hierarchical host $\mathbf { ( C C } @ \mathbf { Z n O / N C } @ \mathbf { L i } )$ for molten Li infiltration. Benefiting from the lithiophilic N-functional groups and LiZn alloy, the synthesized CC@ZnO/NC@Li composite anode promoted the uniform distribution of Li, resulting in a dendrite-free morphology. Meanwhile, the 3D conductive carbon skeleton enhanced the reaction kinetics and buffered the volume change of the electrode. The $\mathbf { C C } @ \mathbf { Z n O } /$ NC@Li composite anode presented a prolonged lifespan of over 1000 cycles at $5 \mathbf { m } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a low overpotential of $\mathbf { 1 9 m V }$ . Coupled with a $\mathbf { L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ cathode, the CC@ZnO/ NC@Li composite anode also exhibited superior electrochemical properties in the full-cell system. This versatile strategy may open up the channel of designing multi-functional lithiophilic 3D hosts for the Li metal anode.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: dendrite-free lithium anode, 3D lithiophilic host, MOF-derived, ZnO/NC nanosheets, lithium metal batteries Since their discovery in the 1990s, the demand for commercial lithium ion batteries (LIBs) in energy storage devices has dramatically increased, and LIBs are now applied in a wide range of fields, such as electric vehicles, portable electronics, and aviation [1–4]. Meanwhile, given the confined theoretical specific capacity of graphite anode $( 3 7 2 \mathrm { m A h g } ^ { - 1 } )$ ), the increased rate in the energy density of LIBs is gradually lagging behind social needs [5]. Among the currently emerging anodes, the Li metal anode with a theoretical specific capacity of $3 8 6 0 \mathrm { m A h g ^ { - 1 } }$ is a promising contender; it can significantly raise the energy density of batteries and meet the $5 0 0 \mathrm { \bar { W } h k g ^ { - 1 } }$ design requirement for nextgeneration high-energy-density devices [6–9]. However, the Li metal anode normally has certain disadvantages. The “hostless” nature of lithium deposition can result in unstable solid electrical interface (SEI) films on the active lithium surface and infinite volume expansion during cycling, which will cause a series of issues, such as low coulombic efficiency (CE), poor cyclic stability, and safety hazard [10,11]. The appearance of dendrites in the irregular Li plating/stripping process may cause severe safety problems, thereby posing grave challenges for the commercialization of Li metal anodes [12,13].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: A series of strategies have been exploited to settle the abovemotioned problems. The stabilization of SEI films by adding beneficial components to the electrolyte and the application of solid electrolytes with high elastic modulus can impede Li dendrites from penetrating the membrane and thus causing a short circuit [14–17]. Additionally, the introduction of a dense and stable artificial SEI film at the Li interface can inhibit the constant formation of Li dendrites to a certain extent [18–22]. Nevertheless, the aforementioned modifications did not effectively solve the problem of volume change in the Li electrode due to its “hostless” property.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Therefore, the construction of a three-dimensional (3D) stable “host” for Li metal is a promising strategy to simultaneously address the Li dendrite and infinite dimension change. The special 3D host provides a sufficient space to store Li and mitigate electrode size changes and possesses a high specific surface area for lowering the local current density and preventing the growth of Li dendrites [23,24]. To date, a series of 3D Li skeletons, such as 3D metal-based (e.g., Cu mesh (CM) [25–27], Cu nanowires [28,29], and Cu foam [30,31]) and carbon-based materials (e.g., carbon nanotubes [32], graphene [33], and carbon cloth (CC) [34]), have been exploited to effectively alleviate the double problems of volume change and Li dendrites in Li metal anodes. Among these 3D skeletons, CC is most promising due to its lightweight, high surface areas, superior mechanical properties, and good corrosion resistance.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Electrochemical deposition is widely used for Li prestorage, but its complex operation and uneven Li distribution during the electrodeposition process are not conducive for practical applications [35]. A molten Li infusion technology proposed by Lin et al. [33] can achieve high manufacturing efficiency and uniform Li distribution during the Li prestorage process. However, the hosts require sufficient lithiophilicity to induce the automatic absorption of molten Li and maintain a low Li nucleation barrier during cycling. The challenge is that most 3D skeletons, except for reduced graphene oxide, cannot meet these requirements. Therefore, appropriate surface modification strategies must be explored to significantly enhance the affinity between the Li and 3D skeletons. The decoration of 3D skeletons with lithiophilic substances is one of the most effective ways, and a reasonable design of micro/nanostructured lithiophilic layer on 3D skeletons facilitates the improvement of the wettability of Li metals, resulting in uniform Li deposition [36–40]. The present metalorganic framework (MOF)-derived pathway is an effective strategy to grow controllable hollow/porous structures and easily introduce lithiophilic N-functional groups or precursors for the conversion to lithiophilic metal oxides [41–43]. Therefore, using the MOF-derived method to construct a tunable microstructured lithiophilic layer on the 3D skeleton is a promising approach to prepare dendritic-free lithium composite anodes.

paragraph_context: Herein, CC modified with ZnO nanosheets and nitrogendoped carbon (CC@ZnO/NC) was first synthesized as an example and employed as the 3D skeleton to accommodate molten Li for the dendrite-free composite Li anode. With the synergistic effect of the induced lithiophilic ZnO and N-doped carbon, CC@ZnO/NC skeleton possessed high Li affinity to realize the rapid infusion of molten Li into the host forming a dense CC@ZnO/NC@Li composite anode. Furthermore, the flexible 3D framework structure of CC served as a soft snubber to mitigate the dimension change of the anode during cycling. In addition, the LiZn alloy obtained via the chemical reaction of ZnO and Li can facilitate electron/ion diffusion and regulate Li in uniform plating/stripping. Given the above-mentioned merits, the synthetic $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ composite anode presented a prolonged lifetime with a low hysteresis voltage, and its skeleton exhibited a high CE after long cycling. Furthermore, the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C @ L i } | | \mathrm { L i F e P O } _ { 4 }$ (LFP) full cells also achieved an improved cycling performance and rate capability.

paragraph_context: Fig. 1a shows the detailed process diagram of CC@ZnO/NC@Li. First, ZIF-L were uniformly grown on the CC by a facile water bath deposition. Then, the uniform ZIF-L-decorated CC was annealed in air to obtain the lithiophilic $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ host. Finally, the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ host was infused with molten lithium to form the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ composite anode. The morphology of the CC@ZIF-L precursor and the derived CC@ZnO/NC intermediate were measured via SEM. The ZIF-L appeared as uniform nanosheets and grew perpendicularly on the surface of CC to form a self-supported nanoarray structure (Fig. 1b). After the growth of ZIF-L, the color of the CC skeleton turned light gray (Fig. S1), but the flexibility of the CC skeleton was not affected. Further, the XRD result of CC@ZIF-L (Fig. S2) agreed with the standard ZIF-L sample in previous literature [44], confirming the successful synthesis of ZIF-L on the CC. Moreover, the XRD pattern of the annealed $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z I F - L }$ precursor (Fig. 1d) was in accordance with the ZnO standard PDF card (ICSD 06-5119), except a bulge diffraction peak that originated from CC, which indicates that the lithiophilic $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ was successfully obtained. Fig. 1c shows that $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ well inherited the interconnected nanosheet structure of the ZIF-L precursor. The TEM image (Fig. 1e) illustrates that a single $Z \mathrm { n O } /$ NC nanosheet was composed of numerous ultrafine nanoparticles embedded in the carbon framework. The high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 1f) exhibits lattice spacings of 0.247 and $0 . 2 8 1 \mathrm { n m }$ on the nanoparticles, which can be assigned to the (101) and (100) planes of cubic ZnO, respectively, and all nanoparticles were connected by the amorphous carbon originating from the pyrolytic organic groups. The TEM elemental mapping signals of ZnO/NC nanosheet (Fig. 1g and Fig. S3) demonstrate the co-existence and homogeneous distribution of Zn, O, C, and N, revealing that a considerable amount of Ndoped carbon was present in the ZnO/NC nanosheet. The XPS results are provided in Figs S4 and S5. The XPS spectrum of $\mathtt { Z n 2 p }$ (Fig. S5a) exhibits two typical signal peaks at 1022.5 and $1 0 4 5 . 8 \mathrm { e V }$ , belonging to $\mathrm { Z n ~ } 2 \mathsf { p } _ { 3 / 2 }$ and Zn ${ 2 \mathrm { p } _ { 1 / 2 } } ,$ respectively. The XPS spectrum of O 1s (Fig. S5c) reveals the presence of ${ \mathrm { Z n } } { - } \mathrm { O }$ , which further verifies the complete conversion of ZIF-L to ZnO. Moreover, the peaks at 284.4, 285.2, and $2 8 5 . 9 \mathrm { e V }$ in the C 1s XPS spectrum confirm the existence of C–C, C–N, and C–O–C (Fig. S5b), respectively. Meanwhile, the peaks at 398.3, 399.3, and $4 0 0 . 2 \ : \mathrm { e V }$ in the N 1s XPS spectrum (Fig. S5d) correspond to the doping of N elements in the carbon substrate in the form of pyridinic, pyrrolic, and graphitic N, respectively. The N-doped carbon was lithiophilic and strongly bonded to Li [45,46]. Thus, this modified 3D CC combines the strong synergistic of lithiophilic ZnO nanoparticles and N-doped sites, which might promote the rapid and even adsorption of molten Li liquid on the CC@ZnO/NC skeleton.

paragraph_context: Fig. 2a shows the detailed process of melting and entrapping Li onto CC@ZnO/NC skeleton. The molten Li metal gradually covered the CC@ZnO/NC skeleton, and the color of the skeleton changed to shiny silver. For a more accurate and intuitive observation, a video clip of the lithium entrapment process was offered. As presented in Movie S1, once the edge of the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ skeleton was immersed in molten Li, the liquid Li rapidly and automatically adsorbed onto the host along the skeleton network. After 5 s, the whole $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ skeleton was completely covered with the silver-colored molten Li (Fig. 2a and Fig. S6). However, in the contrast experiment of the CC, the molten Li cannot be adsorbed on the CC skeleton (Movie S2), which strongly verifies that the MOF-derived $Z \mathrm { n O } /$ NC nanosheets significantly improve the lithiophilicity of the CC skeleton. Fig. 2 illustrates the morphology of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O } /$ NC@Li. Evidently, the surface of the CC@ZnO/NC@Li composite anode is smooth, and the thickness of the Li metal is ${ \sim } 2 9 2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . A mass of white particles appeared on $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O } /$ NC@Li. This phenomenon was further investigated via elemental mapping (Fig. 2e), and the results confirmed that this white-particle region was enriched with Zn element. The XRD pattern of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ (Fig. 2d) verifies the formation of LiZn alloy after entrapment of Li metal. Thus, the white particles may be identified as LiZn alloy, which was formed because of the reaction between molten Li and ZnO during the entrapment process. The LiZn alloy particles facilitate the diffusion of Li metal and electrons, given that the potential difference between Li metal and LiZn alloy can provide a driving force for lithium diffusion, thus inducing the uniform dissolution and deposition of lithium [47]. In addition, the XPS result of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ identifies the presence of Li, Zn, C, O, and N elements (Fig. S7). The high-resolution spectrum of Li 1s can be divided into three different signal peaks, which were located at 54.9 (Li), 55.3 $\mathrm { ( L i C O _ { 3 } }$ or $\mathrm { L i N } _ { 3 }$ ), and $5 5 . 9 \mathrm { e V }$ $( \mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } )$ [28,45]. Therefore, except for LiZn, lithium compounds, such as $\mathrm { L i C O _ { 3 } / L i N _ { 3 } }$ and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , were observed in $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ . The areal mass loading and the mass ratio of Li on the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ composite anode were about $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { m g c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $5 1 . 9 \%$ , respectively, corresponding to a high areal capacity of $5 3 . 8 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a specific capacity of ${ \sim } 2 0 0 1 . 5 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { \bar { h } g ^ { - 1 } }$ (Table S1). Distinctly, this $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O } /$ NC@Li composite anode possesses a higher mass loading than the commercial Li disk $( 2 1 . 7 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ) $ ) accompanied by sufficient flexibility and binder-free features, which are promising for applications in flexible high-energy-density batteries.

paragraph_context: To explore whether the CC@ZnO/NC@Li composite anode can maintain stable Li stripping/plating and inhibit the formation of lithium dendrites, we characterized the electrodes at different stripping/plating stages disassembled from symmetric cells using ex-situ SEM measurements. Fig. 3 displays the surface morphological change in CC@ZnO/NC@Li. When stripped with $2 0 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ capacity of Li, the originally filled molten Li was largely peeled off, and the spaces among carbon fibers reappeared (Fig. 3a). After the initial stripping process, Li was replated with $5 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ capacity, and the corresponding SEM image is displayed in Fig. 3b. Li filled the free space between CC fibers. With the plating capacity raised to $1 0 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (Fig. 3c), the deposited Li appeared on the surface of the CC. With the continuous increase in the Li deposition capacity to $2 0 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (Fig. 3d), the CC was completely covered with Li metal, and a dense surface reemerged without dendrites. These results confirm that the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ composite anode effectively confines the deposition behavior of Li and guides the uniform plating of Li on its skeleton, thereby avoiding the formation of Li dendrites.

The rate capability of the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ i electrode was also better than that of the bare Li electrode. The overpotential of the Li electrode was related to the Li dendrites formed by uneven Li plating/stripping and associated with the electrode pulverization due to the accumulation of loose “dead Li” at the same current densities [52]. The $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ electrode with MOFderived lithiophilic skeleton has several characteristics, such as a large specific surface area, extensive N-doped active sites, and high lithiophilicity, which facilitate the uniform distribution of Li in the electrode, suppress the formation of Li dendrites, and alleviate volume expansion, thereby obtaining excellent electrochemical performance, which is better than that of the bare Li and other reported ZnO-decorated Li electrodes (Table S2). These outstanding electrochemical results prove that the Li metal anode was significantly improved by adopting a ZIF-Lderived method to grow lithiophilic ZnO/NC nanosheets on CC and form a hierarchical $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ .

paragraph_context: For further exploration of the dynamic behavior of the CC@ZnO/NC@Li electrode, EIS test was conducted for the CC@ZnO/NC@Li and bare Li electrodes before and after 100 cycles (Fig. 4e, f). Fig. S13 illustrates the equivalent circuit. The first semicircle in the high-frequency range was used to estimate the SEI interfacial resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ , and a low interfacial resistance means that the electrode has a stable interface that can facilitate fast ion transport at the interface. Before cycling, given the highly reactive nature of Li, a native SEI layer formed on the surface of the Li anode surface in contact with the electrolyte. After 100 cycles, the interfacial resistance of the bare Li electrode decreased from ${ \sim } 4 6$ to ${ \sim } 8 \Omega$ , probably due to the rupture of the SEI layer and formation of lithium dendrites, which greatly increased the working surface area of the Li metal [53]. However, the $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ composite anode consistently presented low $R _ { \mathrm { f } }$ values before and after cycling, ${ \sim } 3 1 \Omega$ before cycling and ${ \sim } 5 \Omega$ after 100 cycles, demonstrating that $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O } /$ NC@Li possessed desirable interfacial stability. In addition, the charge-transfer resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { c t } } )$ of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C } @ \mathrm { L i }$ i was lower than that of the bare Li before cycling and after 100 cycles, which illustrates that the unique design of the CC@ZnO/NC@Li electrode reduced the continuous interface reaction and formed a stable SEI film to achieve a low charge-transfer resistance at the electrode-electrolyte interface. CE is also a vital argument related to the reversibility of the repeated Li plating/stripping, and it was measured in half cells (Li vs. $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ and Cu foil) at $2 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with the charging cutoff voltage of 1 V. As shown in Fig. 4g, the initial CE of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ $( 6 1 . 6 \% )$ 1 was lower than that of Cu foil $( 7 6 . 0 \% )$ , which may be ascribed to the reaction of lithiophilic ZnO nanosheets with the deposited Li, forming the irreversible $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and then consuming a superfluous amount of Li. Subsequently, the CE of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ rapidly increased to $9 4 . 0 \%$ in the $2 ^ { \mathrm { n d } }$ cycle, exceeding the CE of Cu foil $( 9 0 . 4 \% )$ . The average CE of $\mathrm { C C } @ \mathrm { Z n O / N C }$ remained around $9 9 . 7 \%$ for over 500 cycles, whereas the CE of Cu foil dropped sharply after 200 cycles. This result proves that the CC@ZnO/NC skeleton can promote beneficial effects on stabilizing Li plating/stripping processes to improve cyclic reversibility.

In the initial plating profile, the potential gap from the lowest voltage to the subsequent voltage plateau is the nucleation overpotential, which reflects the heterogeneous nucleation barrier required for Li plating on the host. The CM/NC NWA electrode showed a reduced nucleation overpotential of $4 4 . 9 \mathrm { m V }$ , which implies a small nucleation barrier on its surface, facilitating the uniform deposition of Li and suppressing Li dendrites. The corresponding deposition morphology evolution of Li metal on the CM/NC NWA electrode was characterized by SEM (Fig. 6a–h). The plated Li existed between the interstices and on the surface of the NWA. With the augmented plating capacity of Li, the initial carbon nanowires increased in diameter due to the embedding of the deposited Li, whereas the number of coarse whisker-like Li deposited on the surface increased. These surface-deposited whisker Li gradually fused together and spread into the pores until they filled the entire Cu network, which formed a uniform and flat Li deposition plane with no dendrite. Fig. S17 shows the morphological evolution of CM with the same amount of Li deposition, and the results show that the deposition of Li on CM is not uniform, and several Li dendrites exist at the junctions of the Cu network, which exacerbate the subsequent inhomogeneous stripping/plating of Li. The CE values of the CM and CM/NC NWA electrodes were measured in half cells at $2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $1 0 \mathrm { m A h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and the comparative results are illustrated in Fig. 6j. paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Lithium (Li) metal anodes have the potential to stimulate the development of secondary batteries due to their high theoretical specific capacities and low redox potentials among all possible solid secondary anode compounds. However, the growth of Li dendrites during repeated Li stripping/ plating processes leads to low coulombic efficiencies (CEs) and safety hazards, which significantly hinders their practical application. In this work, commercial Cu foil was modified in situ by $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N }$ nanowires $( \mathbf { C u _ { 3 } N } \ \mathbf { N W s } / \mathbf { C u } )$ and used as the current collector for a Li anode. In addition to decreasing the true current density of the anode and alleviating the volume change during the cycles, $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N }$ reacted with Li during the initial cycle $( 3 \mathbf { L i } + \mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N } \mathbf { L i } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N } + 3 \mathbf { C u } )$ , which enabled the formation of a $\bf { L i } _ { 3 } N$ -rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). This $\bf { L i } _ { 3 } N$ -rich SEI with a high ionic conductivity not only boosted Li ion transport but also promoted the homogeneous deposition of Li via increased Li nucleation sites. The improvements in both mass transport and deposition dynamics restrained dendrite growth. As a result, the $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N }$ NWs/Cu anode had stable Li plating/stripping over 270 cycles with a high average CE of $9 8 . 6 \%$ at $\mathbf { 1 } \mathbf { m } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , with Li capacities of 1 mA h $\mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . A long cycling lifespan of 430 cycles was achieved using a full cell with a high-load $\mathbf { L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ cathode (mass loading: $1 0 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ ) and a $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N N W s } / \mathbf { C u }$ –Li anode (N/ $P = 2 . 3 5 )$ ), demonstrating the effectiveness and practicality of the $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } \mathbf { N }$ NWs/Cu current collector in stabilizing the Li anode.

paragraph_context: Keywords: $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ nanowires, current collectors, lithium anode, lithium metal batteries Lithium (Li) metal is an ideal anode for next-generation secondary batteries because of its high specific capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { \dot { m A } h \ g ^ { - 1 } ) }$ and low redox potential (−3.040 V vs. a standard hydrogen electrode) [1–3] compared with other solid secondary anode compounds. However, the practical application of Li metal anodes (LMAs) suffers from Li dendrite growth, volume expansion, and severe side reactions between Li and the electrolyte [4–6]. These limitations cause low coulombic efficiencies (CEs) [7,8] and shortened cycling lifespans [9–11]. Li dendrites may also pierce the separator, causing a short circuit and thermal runaway [12,13].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To improve the rechargeability of LMAs, studies have focused on restraining the growth of Li dendrites, intensifying the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) in the anode/electrolyte interface, and accommodating the volume expansion of the Li during the stripping/plating cycles. A wide variety of components such as poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMs) [14], Li polyacrylic acid [15], $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ [16], $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ [17], and $\mathrm { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } ,$ /poly(vinylidene fluoride-cohexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) [18] have been used to construct artificial SEIs on the surface of Li anodes. Compact artificial SEIs with significantly improved chemical/electrochemical properties or mechanical strengths can prevent Li dendrite growth and suppress further side reactions. Several other electrolyte additives (e.g., $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ [19], $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ [20], ${ \mathrm { C s P F } } _ { 6 }$ [21], $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ [22], and fluoroethylene carbonate [23]) can also boost the in-situ formation of a stable and compact SEI. During the initial electrode process, additives are easily reduced by Li and generate inorganic phases such as $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ and LiF, which can enhance the chemical stability and compactness of the SEI.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Although an optimized SEI can restrain dendrite growth and prevent side reactions, intrinsic volume expansion can destroy the integrity of the SEI, especially when the cells operate at high current densities and a low Li excess [24]. If the in-situ-formed or pre-constructed SEIs are not completely uniform, they can cause ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ flux at the interface, leading to the formation of Li dendrites [25,26]. Therefore, constructing an ideal matrix for Li deposition while optimizing the SEI is an effective method to improve the rechargeability of the Li anode. Cu is the most commonly used current collector for anodes [27]. Threedimensional (3D)-structured Cu has been studied as a current collector for Li anodes as it provides a host for deposited Li and effectively homogenizes local current densities. The energy density of these cells is largely reduced due to the thickness and high mass fraction of the anode system [28,29]. Cu foils with hybrid structures modified by 3D submicron skeletons are attractive materials due to their lightweight nature. Several chemically active materials such as CuO [30], ${ \mathrm { C u } } _ { 2 } S$ [31], and $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ [32] have been used to modify Cu foil. The 3D submicron structure provides a skeleton for Li deposition, reducing the volume change caused by Li plating/stripping. These chemically active materials with lithiophilic elements can react with Li and solid products such as $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ , $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } ;$ , and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , provide nucleation sites for Li plating, and contribute to the formation of an SEI with greater stability.

paragraph_context: In this work, $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ nanowires (NWs) were grown on the surface of a commercial Cu film via simple chemical reactions. The obtained hybrid microstructure $\mathrm { ( C u _ { 3 } N \ N W s / C u ) }$ $\mathrm { \ C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ acted as an ideal host for Li deposition. For the bare Cu foil, both the high nucleation barrier on the lithiophobic Cu and the uneven Li flux near the interface accelerated the growth of Li dendrites (Fig. 1a). For the Cu NWs/Cu system, the 3D NW structure uniformly affected the Li ion flow and electric field distribution. This structure suppressed dendrite growth, but the lithiophobicity of the Cu led to a disordered and loose Li deposition (Fig. 1b). In the $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } \mathrm { N W } s / \mathrm { C u }$ system, in addition to improving mass transport and lowering the true current density, the $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ reacted with Li during the initial Li plating process $( 3 \mathrm { L i } + \mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ $ \mathrm { \ L i _ { 3 } N ~ + ~ 3 C u ) }$ ), forming $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ -rich channels with high ionic conductivities on the Cu foil, which guided a homogeneous distribution of the Li ion flux. The lithiophilic $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ resulted in uniform Li nucleation, which led to dense Li deposition (Fig. 1c). $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ also contributed to a high-performance SEI. $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ has a high room-temperature ionic conductivity of $6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { S } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and a high Young’s modulus [33]. Therefore, the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ -rich SEI could bear the volume change caused by the Li plating/stripping, preventing side reactions between Li and the electrolyte by minimizing cracks in the SEI layer [34]. As a result, the Li anode with a $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ NWs/Cu current collector achieved a high average CE of $9 8 . 6 \%$ for ${ > } 2 7 0$ cycles $( 1 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ; $1 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ) and $9 8 . 9 \%$ for ${ \scriptstyle > 1 0 0 }$ cycles $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \prime } 1 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ; 4 mA h cm−2 ). The $\mathrm { L i F e P O _ { 4 } } |$ Li full cell also demonstrated a high capacity retention ratio of $9 0 \%$ after 430 cycles, indicating the potential of this current collector for practical applications.

paragraph_context: 摘要 在二次电池的所有固态负极中, 锂金属负极因其极高的理论比容量和极低的还原电位对促进二次电池的进一步发展具有很大的潜力. 然而, 锂负极在不断脱锂/嵌锂的过程中因锂枝晶的生长导致低库伦效率并存在安全隐患, 严重阻碍了锂金属负极的实际应用. 该研究通过化学方法在商业化的铜箔集流体表面原位修饰 $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 纳米线得到复合微结构型集流体 $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ NWs/Cu). 引入的 $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 纳米线具有三维结构,不仅可以增大集流体的比表面积、降低集流体表面的电流密度, 还可以容纳锂负极在沉积/脱嵌过程中发生的体积变化. 此外, 在首次锂沉积的过程中, $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 与锂金属反应生成 $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } ( 3 \mathrm { L i } + \mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } \mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } + 3 \mathrm { C u } )$ ,可以促进稳定的富含 $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 的固态电解质膜(SEI)形成. 富含 $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 的SEI既能增强锂离子的传输, 又能给锂的沉积提供充足的形核位点, 促进锂金属的均匀沉积, 从而抑制了锂枝晶的生长. 在锂沉积/剥离循环过程中,这种经过 $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 纳米线修饰的铜箔集流体在电流密度为 $1 \ \mathrm { m A } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , 锂沉积量为1 mA h $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ 的条件下可以稳定循环270圈, 平均库伦效率为$9 8 . 6 \%$ . 将沉积锂金属后的 $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ NWs/Cu–Li复合负极与LiFePO 正极(正极活性物质载量: $1 0 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ; $N / P = 2 . 3 5$ )组装成全电池, 该全电池能稳定循环430圈. 研究表明经 $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ 纳米线修饰的铜箔集流体在提高锂金属负极的循环稳定性方面具有良好的应用前景.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Lithium metal anode possesses a high theoretical capacity and the lowest redox potential, while the severe growth of Li dendrite prevents its practical application. Herein, we prepared a structure of Li P nanosheets and Ni nanoparticles decorated on Ni foam (NF) as a three-dimensional (3D) scaffold for dendrite-free Li metal anodes $( { \bf L i - L i _ { 3 } P } /$ Ni@Ni foam anodes, shortened as L-LPNNF) using a facile melting method. The $\mathbf { L i } _ { 3 } \mathbf { P }$ nanosheets exhibit excellent Li-ion conductivity as well as superior lithiophilicity, and the 3D nickel scaffold provides sufficient electron conductivity and ensures structure stability. Therefore, symmetric cells assembled by L-LPNNF possess lowered voltage hysteresis and improved long cycle stability (a voltage hysteresis of $\mathbf { 1 0 4 . 2 \ m V }$ after 500 cycles at a high current density of $2 0 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a high capacity of $1 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ ), compared with the cells assembled with Li foil or Li-NF anodes. Furthermore, the full cells with paired L-LPNNF anodes and commercial LiFePO cathodes suggest a specific capacity of $\mathbf { 1 2 4 . 6 \ m A \ h \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and capacity retention of $9 0 . 8 \%$ after 180 cycles with the Coulombic efficiency (CE) of $\sim 1 0 0 \%$ at a current rate of 1 C. This work provides a potentially scalable option for preparing a mixed electronic-ionic conductive and lithiophilic scaffold for dendrite-free Li anodes at high current densities.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: lithium metal anodes, dendrite-free, mixed ionic/ electronic conductivity, 3D lithiophilic scaffold With the rapid development of energy storage equipment, commercialized lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) cannot meet the increasing demand for high energy density in energy storage devices. Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) take advantage of lithium metal’s high theoretical capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } ) \ ,$ , lowest redox potential (−3.04 V vs. $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + } ]$ ), and low gravimetric density $( 0 . 5 3 4 \mathrm { ~ g ~ c m } ^ { - 3 } )$ ) to provide high operating voltage and specific storage capacity [1–3]. Beyond LIBs, they are expected to become the next-generation battery system with higher energy density [4]. Nevertheless, due to the high reactivity of lithium metal, LMBs inevitably possess various problems, especially the growth of Li dendrites, hindering their practical application [5]. Nonuniform Li-ion flux and charge allocation aggravate uncontrolled Li deposition, resulting in Li dendrites that can destroy the electrode structure, cause a short circuit, electrolyte consumption, and serious safety accidents.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Several strategies have been adopted to inhibit the growth of Li dendrites, including the use of three-dimensional (3D) scaffold (e.g., a Ni foam (NF) [6–8] and a porous Cu collector [9– 11]), the construction of a stable artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) or artificial protective layer (e.g., $\mathrm { S r F } _ { 2 }$ -rich artificial SEI [12], lithium-rich antiperovskites artificial SEI [13], a novel $\mathrm { L i _ { 6 . 4 } L a _ { 3 } Z r _ { 1 . 4 } T a _ { 0 . 6 } O _ { 1 2 } }$ interface [14] and Li-Sn alloy $/ \mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ electrolyte composite interface layer [15]), the optimization of electrolytes (e.g., 1,2-difluorobenzene [16] diluent solvent in the electrolyte, an octaphenyl polyoxyethylene [17] electrolyte additive, and 3D network gel polymer electrolyte [18]). Among them, incorporating a 3D scaffold with lithiophilic sites into the lithium metal matrix is an efficient and facile method for inhibiting the Li dendrites, which can not only effectively reduce the local current density, but also provide a large contact area between the electrolyte and substrates, contributing to uniform Li deposition. Until now, a large number of conversion materials (e.g., $\mathrm { C u } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ [19], ZnO [20], $\mathrm { V } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 }$ [21], $\mathbf { M o S } _ { 2 }$ [22], and AlN [23]) have shown to obtain excellent lithiophilicity via chemical reactions with Li. However, these incorporated lithiophilic sites commonly possess intrinsically poor Li-ion conductivity, and the resulting inert $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ or $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ may be harmful to the transportation of Li-ion flux and results in an uncontrollable dendritic Li formation. As an ideal candidate for modifying 3D scaffolds, $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ possesses excellent lithiophilicity and has a low ion and electron transport barrier, facilitating rapid and uniform Li deposition to avoid dendrites. However, the moisture sensitivity of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ makes it unstable in the environment of materials synthesis [24]. Therefore, the in-situ conversion reaction of metal phosphide and molten lithium is feasible for preparing Li3P as reported in recent work [25]. Furthermore, the consistency of the generated Ni metal particles and the introduced 3D NF is beneficial to avoiding the interference of foreign metals on the performance of Li metal anodes.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Herein, we used the in-situ conversion reaction between $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ and molten Li to combine the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ and Ni scaffold for dendritefree Li $- \mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P } / \mathrm { N i } @ \mathrm { N F }$ anodes (L-LPNNF). In-situ $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ nanolayers have a good electronic conductivity and high $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conductivity of $1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { S } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ [25,26], which endow the anode with a mixed electronic-ionic conductive scaffold to ensure the uniform distribution of charge and Li-ion in the subsequent electroplating/ stripping process. The 3D skeleton of the NF and the generated Ni nanoparticles during the melt impregnation process can withstand the stress and strain caused by the volume change during the electroplating/stripping process, thereby ensuring the stability of the structure. Benefitting from the above advantages, symmetric cells assembled by L-LPNNF suggest a low voltage hysteresis of $1 0 4 . 2 \mathrm { m V }$ after 500 cycles at a high current density of $2 0 \mathrm { \ m A \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ with a high capacity of $1 0 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { \bar { A } } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Furthermore, by pairing with commercial $\mathrm { L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ (LFP) cathodes, L-LPNNF|LFP exhibits high-rate performance and long cycle stability at a current rate of 1 C with a specific capacity of $1 2 4 . 6 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and capacity retention of $9 0 . 8 \%$ after 180 cycles, indicating the merits of L-LPNNF for practical applications.

paragraph_context: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP). The calculation adopted the projector augmented-wave (PAW) [27,28] pseudopotentials and Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation functional [29]. The planewave energy cutoff was set to $4 0 0 ~ \mathrm { e V } ,$ . The $T -$ -centered $k$ mesh density by Monkhorst-Pack method [30] was set to be $0 . 0 3 \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 }$ for all the calculations. The optimization process was repeated until the total energy change of the system was less than $1 0 ^ { - 6 } \mathrm { e V }$ , and the atomic position was fully relaxed until the maximum force on each atom was less than $\dot { - } 0 . 0 1 \mathrm { e V } \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 }$ . We used the slab containing $2 \times 2 \times 1$ supercell models with a thickness greater than $1 0 \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ to simulate the anode surfaces, while relaxing the first two layers of Li (1 1 0), Ni (1 1 1), $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ (1 −1 0), and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ (0 0 1). A vacuum space of $1 5 \textup { \AA }$ was inserted along the $z$ -direction to avoid any interactions between the periodically neighboring structures [31]. The adsorption energies $\left( E _ { \mathrm { a d s } } \right)$ of a Li atom on different surfaces were calculated as follows: $$ E _ {\mathrm {a d s}} = E _ {\mathrm {L i} / \mathrm {s l a b}} - E _ {\mathrm {s l a b}} - E _ {\mathrm {L i}}, \tag {1} $$ where $E _ { \mathrm { { L i / s l a b } } } ,$ $E _ { \mathrm { s l a b } } ,$ and $E _ { \mathrm { L i } }$ are the total energies of different surfaces with a Li atom, different surfaces, and a Li atom, respectively.

After the hydrothermalphosphating process, $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ nanosheets composed of a pile of rod- Figure 1 (a) Schematic illustration of the synthetic procedure of L-LPNNF. label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: In order to understand the changes in the surface of the scaffold, lithium metal was removed from L-LPNNF by stripping at the current density of $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (named LPNNF). Besides the obvious Ni peak, the peaks at $2 3 . 4 ^ { \circ }$ and $2 6 . 8 ^ { \circ }$ correspond to the (002) and (101) crystal facets of $\mathrm { P D F } \# 8 7 \mathrm { - } 0 7 1 2 \ \mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ , respectively (Fig. 1c). The $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P } / \mathrm { N i }$ suggests a nanosheet structure on the surface of NF (Fig. 1d). The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image (Fig. 1e) shows Ni metal nanoparticles $\dot { d } _ { 1 } = 0 . 2 0 5 \ : \mathrm { n m }$ , $d _ { 2 } = 0 . 2 0 4 \ : \mathrm { n m }$ , Fig. S8) corresponding to Ni (1 1 1) crystal facet are distributed in LPNNF, which helps the occurrence of the conversion reaction of $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ and Li. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping images further suggest the distributions of Ni and $\mathrm { P }$ elements are inconsistent across the LPNNF nanosheets (Fig. 1f). In the HRXPS spectrum of Li 1s for LPNNF, two peaks at 55.3 and $5 4 . 6 \mathrm { e V }$ indicate the existence of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and Li metal (Fig. 1g), and the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ peak may be induced by the existence of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ [33]. In the high-resolution Ni 2p spectrum of LPNNF, there are two sharp peaks at 852.6 and $8 6 9 . 9 \mathrm { e V }$ that correspond to Ni $2 \mathsf { p } _ { 3 / 2 }$ and Ni $2 \mathsf { p } _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 0 }$ , respectively [34], instead of $\mathrm { N i } ^ { \delta + }$ of Ni–P and Ni–P–O in NPNF [35–37], indicating the disappearance of $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ and further illustrating the complete conversion of $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ to $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ (Fig. 1h, Fig. S3e). In the P 2p spectrum, the changes from the Ni–P bond at $1 2 9 . 5 \mathrm { e V }$ $( \mathrm { P } 2 \mathsf { p } _ { 3 / 2 } )$ and $1 3 0 . 4 \ : \mathrm { e V }$ $( \mathrm { P } 2 \mathsf { p } _ { 1 / 2 } )$ to two peaks at 129.0 eV $( \mathrm { P } 2 \mathsf { p } _ { 3 / 2 } )$ and 130.0 eV $\left( \mathrm { P } ~ 2 \mathsf { p } _ { 1 / 2 } \right)$ of the Li–P bond also indicate the existence of the conversion reaction between $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ and Li (Fig. 1i, Fig. S3f) [26,38,39]. Another two peaks at 134.0 and $1 3 3 . 1 \mathrm { e V }$ are assigned to the P–O bond due to the oxidation of surface P on metal phosphide by air [40]. As a result of the abundant contact surfaces and the in-situ chemical reaction, $\mathrm { N i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P }$ nanosheets can improve the wettability of NF and lithium metal. Furthermore, the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ formed on the surface of scaffolds during the melt impregnation process is a key factor determining the subsequent electroplating/stripping.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: To clarify the lithiophilicity during the electroplating process, the nucleation overpotentials of three different types of anodes were characterized. In addition to its excellent affinity for Li, LPNNF exhibits a $2 2 . 6 \mathrm { m V }$ nucleation overpotential at a deposition current density of $2 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , indicating that it has the lowest Li-ion nucleation barrier among the three candidates (Fig. 2a). We further analyzed the reaction kinetics by EIS to study the Li-ion conductivity of LPNNF. For fresh symmetric cells, the resistance of charge transport at the interface $( R _ { \mathrm { c t } } =$ $9 0 . 1 \ \Omega )$ and the resistance between electrolyte and electrode $R _ { \Omega }$ $= 3 . 2 \Omega )$ ) of L-LPNNF|L-LPNNF are significantly lower than that of Li and L-NF, indicating the lowest charge transport barrier of the surface passivation layer and better connection between the electrolyte and electrode (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, in the lowfrequency region, the Warburg factor (δ) can be obtained using the slope of the fitting curve referring to real parts of the impedance $( Z )$ and the reciprocal square root of the angular frequency (ω), which has the relationship with Li-ion diffusion efficiency $( D _ { \mathrm { L i } } )$ , as shown in Equation (2): $$ D _ {\mathrm {L i}} = \frac {R ^ {2} T ^ {2}}{2 A ^ {2} n ^ {4} F ^ {4} C ^ {2} \delta^ {2}}, \tag {2} $$ where $R$ is the gas constant, $T$ is the absolute temperature, $A$ is the surface area of the electrode, $n$ is the number of electrons per molecule during oxidization, $F$ is the Faraday constant, and $C$ is the concentration of the Li-ion. The smallest $\delta$ value for L-LPNNF reflects the fastest Li-ion diffusion process compared with Li and L-NF (Fig. 2c).

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Owing to the abundance and low price of sodium, researches on sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) as a lithiumion battery (LIB) alternative are emerging as a consensus. It is crucial to develop electrode materials suitable for sodium storage. In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) layered transition metal disulfide compounds (TMDs) have trigered interest in the realm of energy and environmental fields. In particular, $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ is thought to be a suitable material for SIBs due to its wide original layer spacing and high conductivity. Herein, N-doped dual carbon-coated $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ with multichannel paths $( \mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 } /$ multichannel carbon nanofibers $( \mathbf { M C F s } ) @ \mathbf { N C } )$ is fabricated via electrospinning, followed by a selenation and carbonization process. The existence of a 3D conductive network, abundant void spaces, and sufficient electron transportation pathways are conducive to rapid and fast charge transfer kinetics under volume expansion stress. When applied in SIBs, the $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 } / \mathbf { M C F s } @ \mathbf { N C }$ shows a high capability $( 3 1 9 \mathrm { \ m A \ h \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ at $\mathbf { 1 0 A \ g ^ { - 1 } } )$ ), as well as good cycling stability $( 3 0 3 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { \ h \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ after 1100 cycles at $\mathbf { 1 0 \ A \ g ^ { - 1 } } .$ ). Furthermore, coupled with the $\mathbf { N a } _ { 3 } \mathbf { V } _ { 2 } ( \mathbf { P O } _ { 4 } ) _ { 2 } \mathbf { O } _ { 2 } \mathbf { F }$ cathode, the full cell also exhibits excellent performance. The theoretical calculation of the $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 } / \mathbf { M C F s } @ \mathbf { N C }$ confirms that the superiority of its SIB performance is owing to the strong interaction between the double-doped carbon and $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ . This scheme provides a wide space for preparing high-performance electrode materials for SIBs.

paragraph_context: Keywords: dual carbon-coated, multichannel paths, sodium-ion batteries, full batteries, theoretical calculation Due to the increasing energy crisis, clean energy has attracted extensive attention [1,2]. In recent years, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been commonly used in mobile electronic devices and electric vehicles as efficient energy storage devices [3–5]. However, Due to the lack of lithium resources, LIBs will not meet the market demand in the long term [6–8]. Due to the low cost and abundant storage of sodium, sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), which have a similar energy storage mechanism with LIBs, have been regarded as a promising candidate [9–11]. Even though lithium and sodium belong to the same group and have similar physicochemical characteristics, the large sodium ion radius shows slow diffusion dynamics during the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (de)sodiation in the electrode materials, resulting in sluggish kinetics and large structural changes of the active materials during the cycling [12–14]. Because conventional graphite structures cannot be directly applied to SIBs, designing and developing suitable anodes for practical application in SIBs are desired.
