paragraph_context: Transition metal disulfides (TMDs) have gained great attention in the field of power supply and conversion devices [15–19]. TMDs are more stable with a unique defect structure due to the existence of lone pair d electrons and empty d orbitals that are easy to bond, as well as the high charge/radius ratio of atoms or ions. Among them, ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ possesses several appealing features, including a large interlayer distance $( \sim 0 . 6 4 \ \mathrm { n m } )$ ), a high theoretical capacity $( 4 2 2 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ ), and a small bandgap $( \sim 1 . 5 \mathrm { e V } )$ 1 [20–22]. The van der Waals (vdW) forces between Mo–Se bonds are comparable to those between Mo–O or Mo–S bonds, favoring kinetic conversion reactions for SIBs [23]. However, the poor cycling stability of ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ derived from the structural collapse during the repeated extraction and insertion of sodium ions is a mountain ahead of its application in SIBs. Improving the sodium storage performance of ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ by rational design is an effective way to enhance the performance of SIBs. The hybridization of ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ and carbon-based materials can improve the overall performance of SIBs. Liu et al. [24] designed an encapsulation-type structured $\mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } @$ hollow carbon nanosphere material, which showed a high capacity of 471 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ over 1000 cycles at $3 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ~ } ^ { - 1 }$ . Wu et al. [25] produced $\mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } @$ NPC/rGO composites with a few layers of $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ encased by $\mathrm { N } / \AA$ P co-doped carbon and reduced grapheme oxide (rGO), which had a high specific capacity of $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \ h \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ even at $5 0 \mathrm { A g ^ { - 1 } }$ . Ultrathin two-dimensional (2D) ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ nanosheets can grow on 3D ordered macroporous carbon by a simple hydrothermal reaction, displaying an outstanding rate capability $( 2 7 9 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $1 0 \mathrm { A } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ ) [26]. Although a composite of ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ and conductive carbon material can improve the conductivity, it cannot buffer more than $3 0 0 \%$ of its volume change during the cycle [27–29]. Therefore, it often shows a low-rate performance when used as the anode of SIBs. It is particularly important to build continuous and connected multichannel with plentiful voids to adapt to its stress relief through simple design methods. In parallel, the electronic transportation capacity of $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ is improved to further enhance the comprehensive performance of SIBs. The multistage distribution also could inhibit the aggregation of active substances and make the electrode material in full contact with the electrolyte.

paragraph_context: Herein, a designable structure of N-doped dual carbon-modified ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ is reported. Multichannel carbon nanofibers (MCFs) were prepared via electrospinning followed by subsequent coupling with ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ and carbonization $\mathrm { ( M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C ) }$ . As nanofillers, the MCFs and carbon coating can inhibit the ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ re-stacking, enabling the formation of homogeneous ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ nanosheets with an extended (002) crystal plane layer spacing structure $\left( 0 . 6 8 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ . In addition, the $\mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C }$ has many structural features that are favorable for sodium-ion (de)embedding: (1) ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ loading on MCFs and carbon coating improve the charge transfer kinetics and reduce the charge transfer resistance; (2) increased $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ layer spacing promotes the diffusion of sodium ions; (3) the N-doped carbon nanosheets strengthen the contact of active substances during the cycling process and buffer the volume expansion of ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ . The $\mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } /$ MCFs@NC anode for SIBs has an outstanding rate performance of $3 1 9 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $1 0 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ and good cycling performance $( 3 0 3 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $1 0 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ after 1100 cycles). An energy density of 104 W h $\mathrm { k g ^ { - 1 } }$ can also be achieved in the full batteries at a power density of $2 2 6 \mathrm { W } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ $\mathrm { k g ^ { - 1 } }$ , showing the practical application of $\mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C }$ in SIBs. The good SIB performance of the $\mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C }$ electrode is verified by theoretical simulation and reaction kinetics analysis.

paragraph_context: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to obtain the adsorption and diffusion performance of sodium ions. Within the framework of generalized gradient approximation, the study of electronic exchange and correlation effects was based on the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional (GGA-PBE) and the double numerical atomic orbital with polarized pfunction (DNP) [30]. Grimme’s dispersion correction (DFT-D2) [31] was included to account for the vdW interactions. During geometry optimization, the threshold values were established at $1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } \mathrm { H a }$ for convergence of energies, $1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { H a } \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 }$ for gradient, and $5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ for displacement. The $1 3 \times 1 3 \times 1$ and $1 7 \times 1 7 \times 1 ~ k$ -point meshes of $2 \mathrm { H } { - } \mathrm { M o } \mathrm { S e } _ { 2 }$ and carbon unit cells, respectively, were used for lattice optimization. The carbon nanofibers $/ \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ heterostructure $( \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { M C F s } )$ was modeled with the carbon $4 \times 4$ and $\mathbf { M o S e } _ { 2 } \boldsymbol { 3 } \times \boldsymbol { 3 }$ supercell. And one of the carbon atoms was replaced by a nitrogen atom to obtain the nitrogen-doped $\mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { M C F s }$ heterostructure $( \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } /$ MCFs@NC). It should be pointed out that the position of the doped N in carbon has a negligible influence on the total energy of $\mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C }$ according to our results. The bilayer ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ $\left( \mathrm { B L } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } \right)$ with $3 \times 3$ supercells was used. The $4 \times 4 \times 1$ $k$ -point mesh was used during the calculations of the BL- $. \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ $3 \times 3$ supercell and the heterostructures. The adsorption energy $( E _ { \mathrm { a d s } } )$ for a single Na atom was defined as: $$ E _ {\mathrm {a d s}} = E _ {*} + E _ {\mathrm {N a}} - E _ {\mathrm {N a} ^ {*}}, $$ where $E _ { * }$ is the adsorbent’s energy and $E _ { \mathrm { N a } }$ is the energy per atom in bulk Na. The total energy of the optimized adsorption system is $E _ { \mathrm { N a ^ { * } } }$ . The diffusion barriers $( E _ { \mathrm { b } } )$ of the inserted Na in different inter surfaces were determined via transition state searches employing the full linear synchronous transit/quadratic synchronous transit (LST/QST) technique [32].

The intercalation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ layers to generate $\mathrm { N a } _ { x } \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ is the first reduction peak at $0 . 7 6 \mathrm { V }$ , while another peak at 0.57 V corresponds to the further reduction of $\mathrm { N a } _ { x } \mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 }$ to metallic Mo and $\mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S e } _ { 3 }$ , as well as the formation of the solid electrolyte interface (SEI) film [21,25]. The strong peak located near $_ { 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ is caused by the ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ embedded in the multichannel carbon fiber [43–45]. In the subsequent anodic sweep (charge process), the reversed conversion reaction of Mo to ${ \bf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ is responsible for the oxidation peak at $1 . 6 6 \mathrm { V }$ [46]. In the next cycles, the almost overlapping cathode and anode curves suggest good electrochemical reversibility of $\mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C }$ . The GCD was performed to understand the storage capacity of the $\mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } /$ MCFs@NC electrode at a current rate of $1 \mathrm { A g ^ { - 1 } }$ . paragraph_context: 摘要 由于钠资源储量丰富且价格低廉, 钠离子电池(SIBs)可作为锂离子电池(LIBs)的有效替代品已成为共识. 基于此, 开发适合钠存储的电极材料是钠离子电池发展的关键. 近年来, 二维层状过渡金属硫属化物在能源和环境领域受到广泛关注. 其中 ${ \mathrm { ~ \bf ~ M o S e } } _ { 2 }$ , 由于其宽的层间距和较高电导率, 被认为是一种具有潜力的SIBs负极材料. 本工作中, 我们通过静电纺丝, 硒化及碳化过程, 设计制造了具有多通道电子传输路径的氮掺杂双碳壳层MoSe 纳米材料 $( \mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C } )$ ). 此结构具有三维连通的导电网络, 丰富的空隙和足够的电子传输路径, 有助于适应钠离子脱嵌带来的体积膨胀应力, 并加快电荷转移动力学. 作为钠离子电池负极材料时, $\mathrm { M o S e _ { 2 } / M C F s @ N C }$ 表现出高的比容量 $( 1 0 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ 电流密度下为319 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ )和优异的循环稳定性 $1 0 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ 的电流密度下可循环1100圈). 此外, 该材料在与 $\mathrm { \Delta N a _ { 3 } V _ { 2 } ( P O _ { 4 } ) _ { 2 } O _ { 2 } I }$ F正极材料组成的钠离子全电池中也表现出了卓越的性能. 理论计算进一步验证了双碳壳层和MoSe 之间的强相互作用, 对于提升MoSe /MCFs@NC的钠离子电池综合性能具有重要意义. 本研究为制备高性能钠离子电池电极材料提供了新思路.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Molybdenum oxide $\mathbf { ( M o O } _ { 3 } )$ is an attractive anode material for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs); however, its low electrical conductivity, large volume expansion after lithiation, and slow Li-ion diffusion kinetics severely limit its practical applications. Here, ultrafine $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ nanoparticles (NPs) $\left( \mathbf { 1 0 - 1 5 \ n m } \right)$ are synthesized from heavily Mo/N-doped carbonaceous precursors, resulting in $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ NPs confined in an N-doped carbon network. This design allows fast electron conduction and short Li-ion diffusion paths; meanwhile, abundant N species and O vacancies on the $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ surface lower the Li-ion adsorption barrier and together contribute to the durable Li-ion storage at high current rates. Notably, the obtained nanocomposite $\mathbf { N C } \mathbf { - M o O } _ { 3 }$ exhibits a high capacity of 1362 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ (0.1 A $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } .$ ) and maintains a reversible capacity of 394 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $\mathbf { 1 0 . 0 \ A \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ . A coin-type full $\mathbf { L i F e P O _ { 4 } } / / \mathbf { N C } \mathbf { - }$ $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ -400 cell obtains a large specific capacity of 81 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 5 C. Our work inspires the design and confinement synthesis of other transition metal oxides embedded in conducting carbon networks for practical LIB applications.

paragraph_context: Keywords: carbon materials, nanocomposites, molybdenum oxide, Li-ion battery With the continuous depletion of fossil energy sources and the accelerated evolution of the energy crisis, the development of clean and sustainable energy sources has become an urgent issue for human society [1]. Among all the energy storage technologies, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), because of their merits of high operation voltage, large specific energy, and long cycling stability, have been widely implanted in electric vehicles and portable electronic devices [2–4]. Graphite is currently the commercialized LIB anode material; however, its inherent low theoretical capacity largely hinders future high-energy LIB applications [5,6]. Therefore, the design and development of new cathode materials with large reversible capacity, large energy density, and long cycle life have been urgently pursued. Anode materials with large capacities, such as Si [7–9], Sn [10–12], and transition metal oxides (TMOs) [13–18], have received worldwide attention, yet still do not meet expectations in terms of practicality due to their large volume change during lithiation/delithiation Among all the TMOs, molybdenum oxide $\left( \mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } \right)$ ) has gained tremendous attention due to its high theoretical capacity $( 1 1 1 7 \mathrm { m A h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } . $ ), good chemical stability, low cost, and environmental benignity [21,22]. However, $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ has its limitations, such as poor electrical conductivity and large volume expansion after lithiation, leading to unstable cycling stability and rapid capacity decay [23–25]. Many strategies have been adopted to improve cycling stability, particularly at high current rates. For instance, adjusting the nanostructure and morphology of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ has been realized, including nanoparticles (NPs) [26], nanorods [27,28], nanobelts [29,30], nanosheets [31,32], and nanowires [33], to increase the specific surface area of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ materials, exposing more open edges or shortening the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion path. Meanwhile, heteroatom doping [31,34,35] and compositing with conductive carbon materials [36–38] have been developed to improve the electron conductivity of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ and the overall composites, respectively. For instance, Li et al. [39] developed an efficient method for constructing highly dispersed ultrasmall $\mathrm { M o O } _ { x }$ NP-anchored N-doped three-dimensional (3D) porous carbon, and the delicately designed $\mathrm { M o O } _ { x } /$ /carbon composite delivered high specific capacities of $7 4 2 \ \mathrm { m A } \ h \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A g ^ { - 1 } }$ and $4 3 1 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $1 . 0 \mathrm { \bar { A } g ^ { - 1 } }$ after 1000 cycles. Despite fruitful achievements by architectural and heterodoping design, the Liion storage performance of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ at high rates is still far from practical expectations.

paragraph_context: In this work, an in-situ conversion method is developed to bottom-up synthesize ultrafine N-doped $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ NPs (10–15 nm) strongly coupled in a highly N-doped carbon network. A unique Mo/N-doped carbon (NC) precursor (termed f-Mo-NC) with atomically dispersed Mo $( 6 . 2 \mathrm { a t \% }$ , in atomic dispersion) was synthesized by solvothermal treatment of Mo salts in formamide (FA) and heavy N doping $\left( 3 1 . 8 \mathrm { a t \% } \right)$ ). The target product was obtained by annealing the f-Mo-NC precursor in air. The thermally driven transition behavior of f-Mo-NCs was investigated: at $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , the product exhibited a similar texture of f-Mo-NC in Mo/N co-doped carbon; at $4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ it showed a typical structure of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ embedded in an N-doped carbon network; at 500 and $6 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ carbon-free $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ nanocrystals were obtained. The lithium-ion storage properties of the obtained products at 400 and $5 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ were comparatively studied to confirm the importance of in situ constructing an N-doped carbon network, which are represented by the $\mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { N C }$ nanocomposites (product at $4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ named $\mathrm { N C } { \cdot } \mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } { \cdot } 4 0 0$ ) and the N-doped $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ nanocrystals (product at $5 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ). Notably, ${ \mathrm { N C } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { M o O } } _ { 3 }$ -400 shows a larger Li-ion diffusion coefficient and lower Li-ion adsorption/ plating overpotential due to the small size of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ NPs and the presence of a conductive carbon network. Therefore, ${ \mathrm { N C } } { \mathrm { - M o O } } _ { 3 }$ - 400 exhibits an excellent reversible capacity of $1 3 6 2 \mathrm { m A h g ^ { - 1 } }$ at $0 . 1 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ , high rate performance (e.g., $3 9 4 { \mathrm { ~ m A ~ h ~ g ^ { - 1 } } }$ at $1 0 . 0 \mathrm { A } \ \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ , and superior cycle life $7 9 \%$ , capacity retention after 200 cycles at $5 0 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { \dot { \Omega } } ,$ ). Our work may open new avenues for the efficient synthesis of TMO materials for alkaline ion batteries.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, we developed an in-situ conversion method for constructing strongly coupled N-doped $\mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 }$ NPs (10–15 nm) in a highly N-doped carbon network. A unique Mo/NC material (f-Mo-NC) with highly dispersed Mo $( 6 . 2 \mathrm { a t \% }$ , atomically dispersed) and heavy N doping $( 3 1 . 8 \mathrm { a t \% } )$ ) was developed as the precursor. paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Lithium (Li) metal, with the highest theoretical capacity, is considered the most promising anode in lithium metal batteries (LMBs) despite the undesirable growth of Li dendrites and large volume change during long-term cycling. Although three-dimensional (3D) hosts such as graphene aerogels are usually used to accommodate the Li metal, pure graphene aerogels can barely withstand large volume changes during the charge/discharge process. Herein, a polyimide (PI) nanofiber-interlocked holey graphene (HG) composite aerogel (CA) with self-adapting mechanical resilience, denoted as PI-HGCA, is prepared as a hierarchically porous host to accommodate Li metal. The HG nanosheets with in-plane nanopores can effectively regulate Li-ion flux and provide highly directed ion transfer pathways. Furthermore, the 3D CA host, constructed with horizontally aligned HG layers and interlocked PI nanofibers, exhibits highly reversible self-adapting compression resilience to large volume change during long-term cycling. Consequently, the lithiated PI-HGCA anode shows a relatively low overpotential of $4 6 \mathrm { m V }$ with a long lifespan of 1300 cycles in the symmetrical cell and displays an ultrahigh capacity retention of $\mathbf { 8 1 . 2 \% }$ after 800 cycles at 1 C coupled with a $\mathbf { L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ cathode, demonstrating the great potential of the interlocked aerogels in high-energy-density LMBs.

paragraph_context: Keywords: polyimide nanofiber, composite aerogel, hierarchically porous host, self-adapting mechanical resilience, Li metal anode The demand for high-energy-density electric vehicles $( > 5 0 0 \mathrm { ~ W ~ h ~ k g ^ { - 1 } } )$ ) and portable electronics has far exceeded the theoretical limit of commercial lithium (Li)-ion batteries [1–3]. Li metal is considered the most promising anode for next-generation lithium metal batteries (LMBs) because of its ultrahigh theoretical capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } ) $ ) and lowest electrochemical potential $- 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { V }$ versus the standard hydrogen electrode) [4– 8]. Unfortunately, the use of Li metal anodes is restricted by the growth of Li dendrites and large volume change during the Li plating/stripping process [9,10]. Moreover, the accumulation of dead Li is always accompanied by continuous reactions between electrolyte and fresh Li, which inevitably leads to a thicker solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and decreased coulombic efficiency (CE) [11–14].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Tremendous efforts have been dedicated to studying the formation mechanism and inhibition of Li dendrites, including substituting Li alloy for Li metal [15–17], constructing an artificial SEI [18–21], engineering solid electrolyte systems [22–28], and fabricating functional separators [29–32]. Compared with these strategies, the most effective approach to achieving dendrite-free Li metal anodes is to integrate Li into conductive hosts to construct composite anodes and redistribute the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux [33,34]. Most studies focus on one-dimensional (1D) or 2D hosts, such as copper oxide nanosheet-modified Cu networks [35], hollow carbon nanofibers (CNFs) [36–38], and crumpled graphene balls [39]. Despite the inhibition of Li dendrites to some extent, these hosts are always accompanied by a more severe problem of large volume change during the cycling process. The Li metal anode exhibits an infinite volume expansion due to its host-less property, which not only causes internal stress in the battery but also results in a fluctuational interface and a fragile SEI. In contrast to the 1D or 2D hosts facing large volume change during cycling, the 3D conductive hosts [40–43] can provide a large surface area with more vigorous nucleation sites to efficiently reduce local current density and regulate Li nucleation behavior based on the Sand’s law, thus accommodating a considerable amount of Li metal [44,45]. Furthermore, the 3D conductive hosts can even cope with large volume fluctuation under high current density and capacity [46].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Among various 3D porous conductive frameworks, carbon nanomaterials such as graphene aerogels hybridized with labile organic molecules [47] and carbon nanotubes [48] have been constructed as the hosts in LMBs for their excellent conductivity [49], stable chemical properties [50], and appropriate lattice matching [51] to guide uniform Li deposition. However, an aerogel simply constructed by graphene layers cannot provide abundant channels for Li ions and electrons to pass through the 2D carbonaceous layers, leading to an incomplete and nonuniform deposition of Li metal. Furthermore, pure graphene aerogels usually endure large volume fluctuation with difficulty due to their unsatisfactory mechanical resilience. Consequently, a porous aerogel structure can hardly restore its original structure and morphology after several cycles, losing its advantage as a host to accommodate Li metal. This irreversible hostdestruction process finally leads to the sprouting of dendrites and eventually damages batteries.

paragraph_context: Herein, we propose a polyimide (PI) nanofiber-interlocked holey graphene (HG) composite aerogel (CA) with self-adapting mechanical resilience, denoted as PI-HGCA, as a hierarchically porous host for Li metal anodes through a bidirectional freezedrying strategy. The simulations of the current density and Liion concentration (Fig. 1a, b, and Fig. S1) indicate that the horizontally aligned HG nanosheets with in-plane nanopores in PI-HGCA provide more homogenized transfer channels for electrons and Li ions during Li deposition compared with the PI nanofiber-interlocked pure graphene aerogel (designated as PI-GCA). Furthermore, PI nanofibers acting as the interlayer columns between HG nanosheets (Fig. 1c) can guarantee the excellent self-adapting compression resilience of the macroscopic CA against a large volume expansion instead of the irreversible mechanical property of the HG CA without PI nanofibers (denoted as HGCA) in Fig. 1d. Given the above advantages, the hierarchically porous structure with a large specific surface area possesses more vigorous nucleation sites to effectively induce bottom-up deposition of Li metal directly into PI-HGCA. Therefore, the symmetric cell based on a PI-HGCA host displays the substantially improved electrochemical performance of an ultralow overpotential of $4 6 \mathrm { m V }$ and a super long lifespan of over 1200 cycles. In addition, the full cell coupled with a lithiated PI-HGCA (designed as PI-HGCA@Li) anode and a $\mathrm { L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ (LFP) cathode displays a high CE of $9 9 . 6 \%$ and retains a capacity of $8 7 . 4 \%$ over 800 cycles. The 3D nanofiber-interlocked CA host with self-adapting mechanical resilience provides a new path for efficiently constructing dendritefree Li anodes and other types of metal anodes.

paragraph_context: CE, defined as the proportion of discharge capacity to charge capacity in each cycle, is a vital parameter for evaluating the reversibility of Li metal plating/stripping. The half cells with different hosts and Li metal were assembled to assess CE (Fig. 3i and Fig. S11). Theoretically, according to the formula for Sand’s time $( \tau )$ : $$ \tau = \pi D \frac {e C _ {0} \left(\mu_ {\mathrm {a}} + \mu_ {\mathrm {L i} ^ {+}}\right) ^ {2}}{2 J \mu_ {\mathrm {a}}}, \tag {1} $$ where $\tau$ is described as the time when dendrites begin to sprout, $C _ { 0 }$ is the initial concentration of Li ions, $\mu _ { \mathrm { a } }$ and $\mu _ { \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ are the mobilities of anion and Li ions, respectively. The 3D hierarchically porous structure of PI-HGCA with horizontally aligned HG layers supported by interlayer PI nanofibers can effectively increase the diffusion coefficient $( D )$ and decrease the local current density $( J )$ , leading to an extension of Sand’s time. Because PI-HGCA has a larger specific surface area than PI-GCA owing to the in-plane pores on HG nanosheets, PI-HGCA exhibited a more stable and higher average CE of $9 8 . 4 \%$ for 350 cycles than PI-GCA $( 9 7 . 5 \%$ for 100 cycles) and PI-HGCA hosts with a lower mass ratio of HG nanosheets of $3 3 ~ \mathrm { w t \% }$ $( 9 8 . 0 \%$ for 120 cycles) and $5 0 ~ \mathrm { w t \% }$ $9 4 . 2 \%$ for 200 cycles) at $1 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ for $1 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , respectively. The porous interlayer structure of HGCA without the support of interlayer PI nanofibers is irreversibly decreased after compression, leading to incomplete Li stripping in each cycle and eventual damage to the battery, which finally leads to the poor CE performance of HGCA $( 9 7 . 0 \%$ for 100 cycles). As the current density increases to $3 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , PI-HGCA still demonstrates the highest and most stable CE of $9 5 . 0 \%$ for 102 cycles among various hosts, proving that HG nanosheets provide more transport channels for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , and thus Li metal can gradually and completely deposit into the aerogel from bottom to top.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, we have proposed a 3D hierarchically porous aerogel host with self-adapting mechanical resilience features through a bidirectional freeze-drying strategy to accommodate the uniform deposition of Li metal. The horizontally aligned HG nanosheets with in-plane nanopores effectively provide excellent transfer pathways for electrolyte and Li ions, which can effectively regulate the Li-ion flux to induce homogeneous Li deposition into the aerogel from bottom to top. Furthermore, PI-HGCA with an ultrahigh self-adapting mechanical compression feature contributed by interlayer PI nanofibers can avoid structural collapse from large volume expansion, making it easily recover to the original thickness during cycling. All these merits endow PI-HGCA with a relatively high CE of $9 8 . 4 \%$ at $1 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ in half cells and approximately $8 7 . 4 \%$ capacity retention for 800 cycles under 1 C coupled with an LFP cathode in full cells. Hence, this work proposes a new strategy for constructing self-adapting 3D hierarchically porous hosts for potential applications in highly reversible and dendrite-free Li metal anodes and other types of anodes. lithium deposition for lithium metal batteries. paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Because of its high capacity, availability, and environmental friendliness, copper oxide (CuO) is a desirable anode material for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). However, due to low intrinsic electrical conductivity and enormous volume expansion during cycling, the capacity utilization and cycle stability of the CuO anode remain insufficient for battery applications. In this study, we design and fabricate a threedimensional (3D) porous carbon@CuO composite $( \mathbf { C } @ \mathbf { C } \mathbf { u } \mathbf { O } )$ by in situ synthesis of CuO nanosheets directly on the internal and external walls of chitin-derived carbon microspheres. Benefiting from the hierarchical conductive framework of the carbon microspheres and a rational distribution of CuO nanosheets, the capacity utilization and structural stability of the CuO nanosheets are substantially improved during the charge/ discharge process. Therefore, this study innovatively constructs carbon microspheres with a hierarchical structure accompanied by self-growing CuO nanosheets as the anode material for LIBs, which may provide a new idea for the rational design of 3D carbon/metal oxide hybrids.

paragraph_context: Keywords: chitin-derived carbon, microspheres, CuO nanosheets, hierarchical pore structure, anode material At present, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) continue to dominate all battery systems because of their distinct features of long cycle life, high operating voltage, environmental compatibility, and high energy density [1–3]. Graphite is used as a commercial anode material for LIBs because of its chemical stability, abundance, and low cost [4]. However, because of the poor rate performance and the low theoretical capacity $( \sim 3 7 2 \ \mathrm { \ m A } \ \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ of graphite, the rising requirements in next-generation energy storage devices are difficult to fulfill [5,6]. Consequently, new anode materials with high energy storage potentials urgently need to be developed for LIBs. Much effort has been devoted to searching for ideal anode materials to enhance the reversible storage capacity of lithium ions. Transition metal oxides, such as $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ [7,8], $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ [9–11], $\mathrm { M n O } _ { 2 }$ [12,13], NiO [14,15], $\mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ [16–18], $\mathrm { S n O } _ { 2 }$ [19,20], and CuO [2,21–24], are considered very attractive anode alternatives for high-performance LIBs and are being intensively studied because of their superior theoretical lithium-ion storage capacity compared with commercial graphite. In particular, CuO has gained considerable interest as a potential anode material to replace traditional graphite because of its reasonable cost, environmental friendliness, abundance, and high theoretical capacity $( { \sim } 6 7 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \ \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ ) [25–27]. Nevertheless, CuO still has many difficulties to overcome, including its large and uneven growth of volume while charging and discharging and its low intrinsic conductivity, which leads to poor cycle stability and substantial capacity loss [28,29].

paragraph_context: To solve these problems, modifying the morphology of particles, optimizing their size, and creating carbon hybrids with acceptable nanostructures are considered effective methods. Several studies have demonstrated that the effective design and tuning of CuO morphology, such as nanosheets [30,31], nanorods [2,32], nanofibers [33], nanoflakes [34], nanowires [35,36], nanoparticles [5,22], and nanoplates [37], can help enhance the utilization of CuO and inhibit the volume expansion during the lithiation and de-lithiation processes. Nevertheless, most CuO-based anodes exhibit mediocre performance because of their poor electrical conductivity. In contrast, combining CuO with nanostructured carbon materials can increase the electrical conductivity of the electrodes, enhancing their electrochemical performance. Three-dimensional (3D) constructed porous carbon materials are considered the most promising substrates for LIBs because of their unique features, including a large specific surface area, a rich porous structure, and a modifiable pore size distribution [38]. The hierarchical porous structure (e.g., micro/meso/micropores) facilitates the penetration of electrolytes and the contact between the electrolyte and the electrode surface. In addition, the 3D interconnected pore network facilitates electron transfer along its backbone while promoting lithium-ion transport through interconnected nanopores and increasing the transfer rate of electrons and lithium ions, and this mixed charge conduction channel ensures high-rate performance [39,40]. Furthermore, the 3D interconnected pore network can improve the cycling stability of LIBs by buffering the volume expansion of electrodes during the charge/discharge process [28]. For example, Pu et al. [41] reported the reduced graphene oxide (RGO) loaded with CuO ultrathin nanosheets as an anode for LIBs and confirmed that wrinkled RGO layers combined with CuO nanosheets via interfacial coupling exhibited excellent rate capability and high reversible capacity. Chen et al. [5] successfully prepared activated tubular carbon loaded with ultrafine CuO nanoparticles as an anode material for LIBs. The obtained carbon/CuO nanosheet electrode exhibited enhanced rate capability and cycling stability due to the co-effect of the unique microporous structure, large specific surface area, and the abundant oxygencontaining groups of the activated tubular carbon. However, the weak contact between the conductive additive and the CuO nanostructures leads to their segregation during the lithiation and de-lithiation processes, particularly resulting in low electrochemical activity at high current densities [42,43]. Therefore, constructing reasonable CuO morphologies while combining them with conductive carbon remains a difficult task.

paragraph_context: In terms of sustainability, biomass pyrolysis has become one of the most extensively used, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly methods for producing porous carbon-based materials for energy storage [44–47]. Chitin, which has a high proportion of N/O functional groups, is the second most prevalent source of biomass on the planet. The direct pyrolysis of chitin enables the uniform integration of heteroatoms into a carbon structure, resulting in N, O self-doped carbon. Chitin has enormous promise as an ideal precursor to produce nanostructured carbonbased anode materials for LIBs [48]. In this study, we inventively built a porous carbon microsphere (CM) derived from chitin with a dense growth of CuO nanosheets as a highly efficient anode material in LIBs. First, the obtained CMs, coated with nearly vertically aligned and interlaced CuO nanosheets, exhibit a unique structure, which can lead to excellent electrochemical properties. The multiscale porous structure and the effective space between adjacent CuO nanosheets not only enable a large electrode/electrolyte interface for rapid reactions but also can accommodate the volume change during cycling. Second, the interlaced CuO nanosheets formed directly on the carbon substrates are structurally stable, thereby reducing the pulverization during cycling, which is advantageous for structural integrity. Finally, the nitrogen-doped carbon substrate and CuO nanosheets may promote the uniform nucleation and homogeneous growth of Li, hence enhancing the cycling stability of the electrode. With the co-effect of the hierarchical structure of CMs and the interlaced CuO nanosheets, the hybrid materials exhibit extraordinary potential in LIBs, delivering high reversible capacities and excellent long-term cycling stability and rate capabilities. This study developed a method for achieving homogeneous mixing between chitin chains and copper hydroxides, obtained homogenous carbon/copper hybrids after carbonization, and finally performed oxidation to CuO using a hydrothermal reaction to obtain carbon/CuO composite microspheres. The obtained carbon/CuO microspheres can ensure strong bonding between CuO and the substrate, providing a new idea for preparing carbon-based hybrid materials.

According to the above analysis, the corresponding reactions can be expressed as follows: $$ \begin{array}{l} 2 \mathrm {C u O} + 2 x \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} + 2 x \mathrm {e} ^ {-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm {C u} _ {1 - x} ^ {\mathrm {I I}} \mathrm {C u} _ {x} ^ {\mathrm {I}} \mathrm {O} _ {1 - x / 2} + x \mathrm {L i} _ {2} \mathrm {O}, \\ \begin{array}{l}2 \mathrm {C u} _ {1 - x} ^ {\mathrm {I I}} \mathrm {C u} _ {x} ^ {\mathrm {I}} \mathrm {O} _ {1 - x / 2} + 2 (1 - x) \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} + 2 (1 - x) \mathrm {e} ^ {-} \rightarrow \mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O} +\\(1 - x) \mathrm {L i} _ {2} \mathrm {O},\end{array} \\ \mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O} + 2 \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} + 2 e ^ {-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm {C u} + \mathrm {L i} _ {2} \mathrm {O}. \\ \end{array} $$ After the second cycle, the cathodic potentials were increased to approximately 0.82 and 1.36 V. Likewise, the anodic potential was moved to 2.58 V. This process is typical of structural alterations in metal oxides during charging and discharging, and the decrease in intensity and integral area of individual peaks reflects capacity loss and the creation of SEI layers during the first cycle [62]. Thus, the highly overlapping CV curves, excluding the first cycle, demonstrated high reversibility of the redox reaction at the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode and excellent cycling stability due to the hierarchical pore structure. Fig. 4b shows the GCD profiles measured between 0.01 and $3 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ at a current density of $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A g ^ { - 1 } }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ . In the first discharge curve, four potential ranges are observed at 0.8–0.9, 1.0–1.1, 1.2–1.4, and $2 . 0 { - } 2 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ , which can be attributed to the reaction of ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ insertion into CuO and the irreversible formation of the SEI film. paragraph_context: EIS experiments were performed to evaluate the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion kinetics and charge transfer behavior of the electrode materials. Fig. S7 shows the EIS curves of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ cells after 1, 5, and 15 cycles. In the high- and medium-frequency regions, all EIS curves exhibit a semicircle, which is due to a re-equilibration corresponding to charge transfer and SEI film resistance. In addition, in the low-frequency region, all EIS curves exhibit a linear Warburg tail, which may be ascribed to the solid-state diffusion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ in the electrode material [66]. Using the equivalent circuit model in Fig. S8 [67], the semicircle in the medium to high frequency range was divided into SEI resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ and charge transfer resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { c t } } )$ , and the corresponding results are summarized in Table S2. The $R _ { \mathrm { c t } }$ decreases from $4 9 . 2 \Omega$ in the cell after 1 cycle to $1 1 . 3 \Omega$ in the cell after 15 cycles, indicating a more rapid charge transfer in the cell after cycling, which may reduce polarization. Equation (5) can be used to analyze and determine the diffusion coefficient of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions $( D _ { \mathrm { L i + } } )$ for the electrodes [66]. $$ D _ {\mathrm {L i} ^ {+}} = R ^ {2} T ^ {2} / 2 A ^ {2} n ^ {4} F ^ {4} C ^ {2} \sigma^ {2}. \tag {5} $$ The parameters and constants in this equation are T (absolute temperature), R (gas constant), C (concentration of lithium ions), n (number of electrons involved in the reaction), $\sigma$ (Warburg factor), A (surface area of the electrode), and $F$ (Faraday constant), where $\sigma$ is related to $Z _ { \mathrm { r e } }$ in the low-frequency region and can be determined using Equations (6) and (7): $$ Z _ {\mathrm {r e}} = R + \sigma \omega^ {- 1 / 2}, \tag {6} $$ $$ \omega = 2 \pi f, \tag {7} $$ where $\omega$ is the angular frequency and $f$ is the corresponding frequency. Plots of $Z _ { \mathrm { r e } }$ versus $\omega ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ for $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ cells after 1, 5, and 15 cycles are shown in Fig. S9, which depicts a linear rela- tionship between $Z _ { \mathrm { r e } }$ and $\omega ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ . The $D _ { \mathrm { L i + } }$ of the 15-cycle $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode is approximately 2.0-fold and 1.3-fold larger than that of the one-cycle $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode and the five-cycle $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode, respectively. The EIS curves of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ , CMs, and bare CuO cells after 15 cycles are shown in Fig. 4h. Similarly, the equivalent circuit model in Fig. S8 can be used to obtain the $R _ { \mathrm { c t } }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { f } }$ of the electrodes, which are also collected in Table S2. The $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ cell has the lowest $R _ { \mathrm { c t } }$ value $\left( 1 1 . 3 \Omega \right)$ compared with the CMs $\left( 6 5 . 8 \Omega \right)$ and bare CuO $\left( 3 8 8 . 1 \Omega \right)$ cells, suggesting that it has the highest charge transfer rate. Fig. 4i shows the relationship between $Z _ { \mathrm { r e } }$ and $\omega ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ for the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ , CMs, and bare CuO electrodes. The $D _ { \mathrm { L i + } }$ of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode is approximately 6.3- and 2.1-fold larger than that of the CMs and bare CuO electrodes, respectively. Equations (5)–(7) indicate that the lower the value of $\sigma$ is, the higher the value of $D _ { \mathrm { L i } } ,$ indicating a faster transport of ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ in the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode [68]. Obviously, the unique structure of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode is favorable for electron/ion charge transport.

paragraph_context: The cycling performance of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode was evaluated at a current density of $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A g ^ { - 1 } }$ (Fig. S10). We evaluated the results of the CM and bare CuO electrodes under identical test conditions for comparison. The discharge capacity of the CM electrode decreases mildly and then increases gradually throughout the cycling process. Notably, the initial coulombic efficiency of the CM electrode is only approximately $5 2 \%$ because of the generation of the SEI film. The initial coulombic efficiency of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ anode can be improved by pre-lithiation, and the initial irreversible capacity loss can be compensated for by introducing a lithium supplement additive into the anode [69]. However, except for the initial two cycles, the coulombic efficiency of CMs exhibits a rapid increase and could eventually be stably maintained at approximately $9 9 \%$ , proving the excellent capacity retention of the CM electrode. In addition, the specific capacity of the bare CuO electrode initially shows an obvious gradual increase, followed by rapid, cliff-like decay throughout the cycling process. The gradual increase in the reversible capacity of metal oxide anode materials during charging and discharging is a common phenomenon, and it is most likely caused by the gradual activation process of the metal oxide electrode and the reversible reactions between the electrolyte and metal particles [2]. On the other hand, the inherent disadvantages of CuO lead to poor cycling stability, exhibiting rapid capacity fading. The $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microspheres combine a multiscale pore structure with a rational distribution of CuO nanosheets. The $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode still has a high reversible capacity of $6 2 6 \mathrm { m A h g ^ { - 1 } }$ and a capacity retention of ${ \sim } 9 3 \%$ after 200 cycles. The long-term cycling curves are shown in Fig. 5a to assess the cycling stability of the electrodes. The specific capacity of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode first mildly decreases to ${ \sim } 4 7 2 \ \mathrm { \ m A } \ \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and then gradually increases to ${ \sim } 5 5 3 \mathrm { m A h g ^ { - 1 } }$ after 600 cycles. The same phenomenon is presented in the charge/discharge cycles of the CM electrode. The specific capacity of the CM electrode remained stable at ${ \sim } 2 1 2 \ \mathrm { \ m A } \ \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 50 cycles. From 150 cycles onward, the specific capacity of CMs gradually increased and eventually remained stable. The specific capacity of the CM electrode after 600 cycles remained at ${ \sim } 2 6 1 \ \mathrm { m A } \ h \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , accompanied by a capacity retention of ${ \sim } 1 0 2 \%$ . The increased capacity of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ and CM electrodes is due to the expansion of the interlayer distance of the chitin-derived carbon during the charge/discharge process [70]. The bare CuO electrode delivered lower discharge and charge capacities. label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: To investigate the mechanism of capacity increase with cycling, first, XRD tests were performed to analyze the change in carbon interlayer distance after long cycling (Fig. S11a). The (002) peak of $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ after 600 cycles (completely delithiated) is broad, confirming its amorphous nature. The calculated interlayer distance of the (002) peak was $0 . 4 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ , larger than $0 . 3 7 { \mathrm { n m } }$ for the original electrode, demonstrating that the repeated charge/discharge processes increase the interlayer distance. The enlarged carbon interlayer distance not only enhances ion transport but also accommodates more $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , thus increasing the capacity of the carbon material. Second, to examine the effect of the high-rate charge/discharge process on the carbon structure, a cycled $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode (completely delithiated) was investigated using Raman spectra (Fig. S11b). The results reveal no apparent alterations in the D- and G-bands even after 600 cycles, demonstrating that the chitin-derived carbon can maintain its structural integrity during prolonged cycling. The intensity ratio of $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { G }$ bands $\left( { I _ { \mathrm { D } } } / { I _ { \mathrm { G } } } \right)$ of the electrode after 600 cycles was considerably lower than that of the original electrode, indicating that the long cycling resulted in a better alignment of the graphitic carbon layers [72,73]. Better-aligned graphite layers not only facilitate the transport of lithium ions between carbon layers but also provide better transport paths for electrons, leading to faster charge transport [74]. On the basis of the foregoing findings, we can outline the reasons for the excellent cycling stability and the increase in capacity after the long cycling of the electrodes, and the corresponding schematic is shown in Fig. 5b. The robust and interconnected multiscale pore structure can mitigate the volume expansion of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode after cycling, thereby maintaining its structural integrity. Thus, based on the above properties, the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode can ensure fast lithium storage from the surface-induced capacitive process, which explains the increase in capacity.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The excellent cycling stability of $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ is due to its unique structure. The nitrogen-doped carbon derived from chitin used as a lithium plating substrate can regulate the nucleation of lithium metal and limit dendritic crystal formation [75]. The low nucleation overpotential of CuO and the uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ion flux induced by CuO nanosheets on the carbon substrate can effectively prevent the generation of Li dendrites and lead to uniform Li nucleation [31,76,77]. The mechanism of the Li nucleation and deposition process on bare CuO and $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ is shown in Fig. 6. For the bare CuO electrode (Fig. 6a), during the lithiation process, Li particles usually aggregate into irregular island-like shapes with the presence of dendritic Li and mossy Li on the surface. After repeated lithiation and de-lithiation processes, isolated lithium and dead lithium are continuously generated on the electrode surface, forming an unstable interface that greatly limits $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer and leads to poor coulombic efficiency and rapid capacity decay [78]. In contrast, as shown in Fig. 6b, the nitrogen-doped carbon substrate and the uniformly grown CuO nanosheets provide abundant Li nucleation sites. Therefore, Li can be nucleated and grown on the surface of carbon substrates and CuO nanosheets, promoting the uniform deposition of Li. The $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microspheres possessed a multiscale porous structure with uniformly distributed CuO nanosheets as the anode material for LIBs, which not only has excellent structural stability during cycling but also can reduce the local effective current density, thus forming a uniform electric field for uniform Li deposition. Finally, the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode was obtained with homogeneous Li deposition and dendrite-free morphology. Fig. 6c, d show the SEM images of the bare CuO and $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrodes, respectively, in the half-cells after cycling. As depicted in Fig. 6c, after 200 cycles at $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A g ^ { - 1 } }$ , a rough island-like Li aggregate is observed on the bare CuO electrode and has randomly dispersed mossy Li on its surface. This morphology of Li deposition arises from the inhomogeneous lithiation and delithiation occurring on the bare CuO electrode [75,76]. Importantly, the nitrogen-doped carbon substrates and CuO nanosheets provided plentiful Li nucleation sites on the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode, facilitating the subsequent Li deposition process. As shown in Fig. 6d, after 200 cycles at $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A g ^ { - 1 } }$ , Li was deposited almost uniformly on the surface of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode, forming a relatively smooth Li layer. In addition, the nucleation overpotential was used to quantitatively assess the degree of lithiophilicity on the electrode surface. The Li nucleation overpotential is a key parameter for evaluating the barrier to heterogeneous Li formation by electrochemical plating, and it is defined as the difference between the initial Li plating mutation potential and the subsequent Li deposition stability potential [75]. As shown in Fig. S12, a sharp voltage drop to $- 0 . 2 0 5 \mathrm { V }$ was recorded at the beginning of the Li plating process on the bare CuO electrode, which was associated with the nucleation process of metallic Li. After nucleation, a plateau corresponding to Li growth was observed near $- 0 . 0 8 6 \ \mathrm { m V } ,$ , thus giving a nucleation overpotential of $0 . 1 1 9 \mathrm { V }$ . In contrast, the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode exhibited an inclined voltage drop to $- 0 . 0 7 4 \mathrm { V }$ and stabilized at $- 0 . 0 2 8 \mathrm { V }$ , achieving a lower nucleation overpotential of $0 . 0 4 6 \mathrm { V }$ compared with the bare CuO electrode. The above results show that the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode can reduce the nucleation overpotential and achieve the uniform nucleation and growth of Li.

paragraph_context: As summarized in Fig. S13 and Table S3, the electrochemical performance of the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microspheres was compared with those of other reported CuO and CuO-based electrodes with various morphologies. The $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode prepared in this study exhibited high reversible specific capacity and remarkable cycling stability capability in lithium-ion storage, being one of the best performances among all CuO-based anode materials for LIBs. This performance benefits from the co-effect between porous CMs and uniformly dispersed CuO nanosheets. First, the interpenetrating micro/meso/macroporous structure of $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microspheres has a high specific surface area, which not only ensures the effective penetration of the electrolyte and improves the contact area between the electrolyte and electrode but also shortens the ion transport length. Second, the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microsphere, with a multiscale porous structure and adequate space between the CuO nanosheets, can alleviate the volume expansion caused by the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ insertion and extraction reactions and prevent the nanostructures from agglomerating. Third, the high specific surface area of nitrogen-doped CMs and uniformly distributed CuO nanosheets not only provide a substantial amount of nucleation sites for Li but also contribute to the uniform nucleation and homogeneous growth of Li. Thus, the $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ electrode exhibits outstanding electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: In summary, we developed CMs with hierarchical structures and self-grown CuO nanosheets as anode materials for LIBs. The prepared $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microspheres exhibit an interconnected multiscale pore structure, which facilitates the diffusion of electrolyte, increases the contact area between the electrode and electrolyte, promotes the charge transfer, and buffers the volume expansion of the electrode during charging and discharging. Moreover, the nitrogen-doped chitin-derived carbon substrates and CuO nanosheets not only provide abundant lithium nucleation sites but also induce the homogeneous nucleation and growth of Li. This excellent electrochemical performance ensures that $\mathrm { C @ C u O }$ microspheres are potential anode materials for LIBs. paragraph_context: 摘要 氧化铜(CuO)具有高理论容量、丰富的资源以及生态友好等特点, 被认为是一种理想的锂离子电池负极材料. 然而, 由于CuO本身的低导电性和循环时巨大的体积膨胀, 它在电池应用中的容量利用率和循环稳定性仍然存在不足. 本工作中, 我们通过在甲壳素衍生的碳微球的内外壁上直接原位合成CuO纳米片, 构造出一种三维多孔碳@CuO复合材料. 得益于碳微球的三维多孔导电框架和CuO纳米片的合理分布,CuO的容量利用率和结构稳定性在充电/放电过程中得到明显改善, 所制备的电极具有优越的循环稳定性和出色的可逆容量. 本工作为合理设计三维碳/过渡金属氧化物杂化体并用作电池负极材料提供了新的思路.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Lithium metal is one of the most promising anode materials for use in the next generation of high-energy lithium batteries. However, uneven Li deposition and large volume changes severely restrict the practical use of lithium metal anodes. Here, a dendrite-free three-dimensional (3D) composite Li anode (Li-B-Sn) with dual-skeletons was produced by a simple melting method. The unique dual-skeleton structure was composed of LiB fiber phase and $\mathbf { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathbf { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase, which enabled even Li stripping and plating processes and reduced the volume variations to improve the performance of the Li-B-Sn anode. The Li-B-Sn anode exhibited a long lifespan of 1100 h during cycling operating under a large areal capacity of 10 mA h $\mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ in a symmetrical cell. In addition, full batteries assembled with the high mass loading LiFePO4 cathode $( \sim 1 1 \mathrm { \ m g \ c m ^ { - 2 } } )$ and the Li-B-Sn composite anode showed superior electrochemical performance, with a high capacity retention of $9 2 . 5 \%$ at 2 C after 430 cycles. Li-S pouch cells based on the Li-B-Sn composite anode survived over 30 cycles, which constituted better cycling stability than that of the Li-B anode. This work describes new 3D skeletons for practical use in lithium metal batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: lithium metal anode, dual-skeletons, 3D skeleton With the rapid development of the new energy industry, lithium-ion batteries have gradually been used in energy storage devices such as mobile phones, computers, and new energy vehicles [1–4]. However, commercial lithium-ion technology is largely limited to batteries with mass energy densities of $< 2 5 0$ W h kg−1 and volume energy densities of $< 6 5 0 \mathrm { W } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ , and current lithium-ion batteries cannot meet the needs of industrial development [5,6]. Meanwhile, it is difficult to improve the energy densities of lithium-ion batteries by optimizing the battery process, which is limited by the theoretical capacities of existing commercially available electrode materials. Surprisingly, the lithium metal anode has an ultrahigh theoretical specific capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } ) ,$ ) and ultralow electrochemical potential $_ { - 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ vs. standard hydrogen electrodes), which greatly improves the energy density of the entire battery system [7,8]. Therefore, lithium metal anodes are among the most promising anode materials for future use. However, the practical application of lithium metal anodes has always faced many technical problems. The first is the large volume change of the lithium metal anode, which inevitably leads to pulverization of the electrode and failure of the battery [9]. The second is the formation of lithium dendrites, which results in low coulombic efficiency and poor cycling life [10]. In addition, side reactions between lithium and the electrolyte also consume large amounts of lithium and electrolyte [11]. Overall, the application of lithium metal anodes faces great challenges.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: At present, many breakthroughs have been made in the research on lithium metal anodes, which may bring about a revival of lithium metal battery technology. In recent decades, optimized electrolytes and artificial solid electrolyte interface (SEI) layers have often been used to protect the lithium metal from direct contact with the electrolyte or to inhibit the growth of lithium dendrites [12,13]. Liu’s group [14] reported a novel ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ flux distributor realized by making an electroactive polyvinylidene fluoride/polymethyl methacrylate (PVDF/PMMA) composite nanofiber interlayer and inducing uniform lithium deposition to mitigate the dendrite problem. In addition, Shi’s group [15] designed a catalyst-derived artificial SEI layer with an ordered polyamide-lithium hydroxide (PA-LiOH) biphase structure to modulate ion transport and enable dendrite-free Li deposition. However, because the volume of the lithium metal expands during cycling, the surface SEI layer continues to crack and rebuild; this makes the surface SEI layer unstable and uneven, places the active lithium on the surface in continuous contact with the electrolyte and leads to consumption of the electrolyte [16,17]. In addition, the introduction of a threedimensional (3D) skeleton to support the lithium metal anode is also a promising strategy [18,19]. Chen et al. [20] prepared Li-$\mathrm { A u L i } _ { 3 } @$ carbon fiber (CF) electrodes by the infusion of molten Li into CF paper modified with nonporous gold (NPG), which was converted to $\mathrm { A u L i } _ { 3 }$ after infusion. The Li- $\mathbf { \Delta A u L i _ { 3 } @ C F }$ electrode was then subjected to the “pre-stripping” (PS) process in which a fraction of Li metal was stripped from Li-AuLi3@CF in order to expose the upper porous $\mathrm { A u L i } _ { 3 } @ \mathrm { C F }$ structure. The as-designed PS-Li-AuLi @CF electrodes maintained structural stability at the whole-electrode level to accommodate the large volume changes occurring during Li plating/stripping. Compared with surface modifications, the 3D skeleton of lithium metal inhibited the growth of lithium dendrites due to surface structure damage arising from drastic fluctuations of the matrix by reducing the volume changes of the anode and maintaining interface stability. In other words, even if dendrite-free lithium metal is achieved, the volume change of lithium metal still poses a considerable challenge and is a more serious issue for the safe operation of lithium metal batteries, and thus, emphasis should be placed on using efficient 3D structural scaffolds to suppress the volume change of lithium metal [21,22]. Li-B alloys have been used in many skeletal structures due to their unique LiB fibrous shapes and excellent lithiophilicities [23,24]. Therefore, many researchers have used LiB fibers as 3D frameworks to improve the structural stabilities of electrodes. However, due to collapse and aggregation of the LiB fibers after the removal of the free lithium around them, they cannot function as 3D skeletons [25]. Recently, a Li-rich alloy, which consisted of metallic Li and $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 }$ phases, was shown to inhibit the volume changes and enable conformal deposition of Li due to the good electrical conductivity, fast lithium ion diffusion rates and superior lithiophilicity of the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ skeleton [26]. However, the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ particles were loosely packed, and there was no tight binding between them, so the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase alone could not form a stable self-supporting skeleton.

paragraph_context: In this work, a composite lithium metal anode, named the Li-B-Sn composite, with a Li:B:Sn mass ratio of 8:1:1 was fabricated by vacuum melting and was composed of LiB, $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 }$ and free Li. First, the composite dual-skeleton comprising $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase and LiB phase improved the structural stability of the lithium metal anode by suppressing the volume changes of the anode. Second, the superlithiophilicity and fast lithium-ion diffusion rates of the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase inhibited the formation of lithium dendrites and promoted uniform Li plating/stripping. The Li-B-Sn composite exhibited a long lifetime of $1 1 0 0 \mathrm { h }$ at $1 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ in a symmetrical battery. In addition, the full battery based on the Li-B-Sn anode and a $\mathrm { L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ cathode $( 1 1 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ ) showed superior electrochemical performance, and its capacity retention rate was as high as $9 2 . 5 \%$ at 2 C after 430 cycles. The Li-B-Sn composite anode also exhibited good cycling stability when used in Li-S pouch cells.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: The Li-B-Sn composite was fabricated via a simple melting reaction in a glove box filled with Ar gas. Lithium (ingots), boron (powder) and tin (powder) were put into an iron crucible with a mass ratio of 8:1:1. First, mechanical stirring was carried out between 200 and $4 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to evenly disperse the boron powder and tin powder. Then, the sample was kept at $6 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 min to allow full reaction and finally cooled to room temperature. The obtained composite was rolled into $1 5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick foils, from which $1 6 \mathrm { - m m }$ -diameter disks were punched for use as electrodes in the LMBs. Li-B and Li-Sn control samples were prepared in the same way. Table S1 shows the mass ratios of the raw materials.

The sample structures and morphologies were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and microcomputed tomography. paragraph_context: To explore the effects of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ on lithium stripping and plating at the Li-B-Sn composite anode, a discharge capacity of $\mathrm { \bar { 1 0 } \ m A \ h \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ was used to remove lithium from the Li-B-Sn composite anode and Li-B composite anode at $0 . 5 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , as shown in Fig. 2a, b. During stripping, lithium was preferentially removed from around the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase of the Li-B-Sn composite, and planar stripping is shown in Fig. 2a. After lithium stripping, the exposed LiB fibers were tightly interwoven with the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase, as shown in Fig. S2. However, due to the nonuniform SEI film on the Li-B surface, many corrosion pits were formed on the surface of the Li-B anode (Fig. 2b), and the LiB fibers in the pits were significantly fractured, causing uneven charge distribution and an aberrant Li-ion flux over the edges of the pits. Further investigation was conducted on the lithium deposition process of Li-B-Sn, and Fig. 2c shows the image of the Li-B-Sn composite anode after stripping $1 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and replating $0 . 5 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ Li. Due to the excellent electrical conductivity and fast lithium-ion diffusion in the $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase, lithium was first deposited on the $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase, indicating that Li was uniformly nucleated and grew on the surface of the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase. With increasing amounts deposited from 0.5 to $1 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , as shown in Fig. 2d–g, lithium deposition started from the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase and continued toward the surrounding areas while maintaining a uniform and dense deposition morphology throughout. In contrast, for the Li-B composite anode, as shown in Fig. 2h–k, lithium was first deposited on the surfaces of pits and presented a dendritic deposition morphology. Since the LiB fibers broke after stripping lithium, a charge concentration was easily generated at the fracture site, resulting in the deposition of Li metal at the fracture site and the formation of long strips of Li dendrites. As the deposition capacity was increased, the lithium metal was gradually deposited over the entire surface but maintained the morphology of loosely packed particles. Additionally, Li metal was deposited more uniformly on the surface of the Li-B-Sn electrode than on the Li-B electrode, as shown in Fig. S3. This suggested that the $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase effectively improved the morphology of the deposited Li metal and facilitated dense deposition. Moreover, after stripping 5 mA h lithium from both Li-B-Sn and Li-B composite anodes, they were individually assembled with the lithium metal into button cells for CV experiments. The stripping and deposition behavior of lithium is extremely important in lithium-sulfur batteries, as the lithium anode experiences the Li stripping process first. The Li-B-Sn composite anode effectively improved the striping and plating morphology of the lithium, which is important for optimum performance of lithium-sulfur batteries.

paragraph_context: To investigate the structural stability of the Li-B-Sn composite anode, 10 mA h lithium was removed from the Li-B-Sn anode at $1 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , as shown in Fig. S5. The thickness of the pristine Li-B-Sn composite anode was $1 5 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . After 10 mA h Li was stripped from the composite, the thickness of the composite plate had decreased by only $8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , which was less than the theoretical thickness reduction of $2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ calculated for removing 10 mA h Li from the Li metal anode (the calculation is shown in the Supplementary information). This suggested that the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ and LiB skeletons effectively mitigated the structural changes occurring during plating/stripping. Additionally, the Li-Sn and Li-B-Sn composite electrodes were compared. The XRD patterns of the synthesized Li-Sn anode are shown in Fig. S6. The assembled Li||Li-B-Sn and Li||Li-Sn cells were charged to $0 . 2 \mathrm { V }$ so that all of the free Li in the Li-B-Sn and Li-Sn anodes was removed. A digital photograph of the composite anode stripped of all free Li is shown in Fig. S7. The Li-B-Sn composite still formed a complete electrode after the removal of all free Li, but the Li-Sn anode was a collection of scattered particles adhering to the cell case and was thus unable to form a complete structure. The stability of the composite structure composed of the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ skeleton and LiB fibers was better than that of the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ skeleton structure alone. Thus, the dual-phase structure formed by crosslinking the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase with the LiB fibers greatly improved the structural stability of the Li anode.

paragraph_context: In this work, a Li-B-Sn composite with a dual-phase skeletal structure was successfully produced with a simple melting reaction. The Li-B-Sn composite contained three phases, namely, free Li metal, LiB and $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 }$ phases. On the one hand, the LiB fibers exhibited light weight and high strength, and after compounding them with the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase, they formed a lithiophilic composite skeleton with high strength; this maintained structural stability and mitigated the volume changes of the electrodes. On the other hand, due to the superb lithiophilicity and conductivity of the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ phase, the skeleton was capable of inducing conformal deposition of Li and inhibiting the formation of Li dendrites. The Li-B-Sn composites produced by the simple melting method have the advantages of low cost, feasibility for large-scale production and practical applications. Therefore, the Li-B-Sn composite is a promising candidate for use as the anode in Li metal batteries.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Two-dimensional conductive metal-organic frameworks (2D c-MOFs) are emerging as promising electrode materials for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). However, 2D c-MOFs with binary redox-active organic ligands are rare and suffer from complicated synthesis procedures. Herein, a facile one-step method is developed for the synthesis of a dual-ligand-based 2D c-MOF Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) (HHTP = 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene, $\mathbf { T H Q } =$ tetrahydroxy-1,4-benzoquinone) by using the ethylenediamine regulator. The resulting $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } ( \mathbf { H H T P } ) ( \mathbf { T H Q } )$ possesses good conductivity, abundant active sites, and excellent chemical stability. As an anode material for LIBs, $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } ( \mathbf { H H T P } ) ( \mathbf { T H Q } )$ exhibits high specific capacity, good rate performance, and long-term cycling stability. Comprehensive experimental studies and theoretical calculations reveal that $\mathbf { C u O _ { 4 } }$ units and aromatic benzene rings in $\mathbf { C u } _ { 3 } ( \mathbf { H H T P } ) ( \mathbf { T H Q } )$ are involved in lithium storage, thereby optimizing the lithium storage performance. This work provides a new way for the construction of dualligand 2D c-MOFs and high-performance LIB electrode materials.

paragraph_context: Keywords: conductive metal-organic frameworks, redox-active sites, dual-ligand, lithium-ion batteries Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have attracted increasing attention due to their extensive use in advanced electronic equipment, electric vehicles, grid-scale energy-storage systems, etc. [1–4]. However, commercial LIBs made using graphite anodes and transition-metal compound-based cathodes are approaching their performance limits [5]. Particularly, graphite anodes possess a low theoretical capacity of $3 7 2 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , which cannot meet the ever-growing demand for high-capacity LIBs [6,7]. Therefore, the exploitation of advanced electrode materials is highly desirable for the development of high-performance LIBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Two-dimensional conductive metal-organic frameworks (2D c-MOFs), as a class of emerging porous crystalline 2D materials comprised of $\pi$ -conjugated organic linkers and metal nodes, have been shown to exhibit great potential as electrode materials for rechargeable batteries in recent years [8,9]. 2D c-MOFs integrate the advantages of traditional MOFs in terms of structural tunability and channel variability. The designable and predictable structures give rise to substantial opportunities for integrating distinct multi-functional redox components into the target network, thereby improving the lithium storage performance [10,11]. Furthermore, 2D c-MOFs exhibit an unprecedented degree of high electrical conductivity and porosity, which enables them to provide efficient electron/ion transport pathways and fast charging rates [12]. Besides, their rigid and robust frameworks render excellent stability in organic electrolytes, guaranteeing the electrochemical durability of electrodes [13]. These advantages enable the rapid development of 2D c-MOFs in the field of lithium storage. In 2018, Nishihara and coworkers [14] reported the first 2D c-MOF-based electrode for LIBs, NiDI $\mathrm { { . D I } = }$ hexaiminobenzene), in which $\mathrm { N i } ( \mathrm { L } ^ { \mathrm { i s q } } ) _ { 2 }$ $\operatorname { T } ^ { \mathrm { i s q } } =$ $o$ -diiminobenzosemiquinonate) centers can serve as redox active sites demonstrated by series spectroscopic techniques. Since then, a series of 2D c-MOF-based electrode materials have been developed and widely used in rechargeable batteries [15–17]. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art 2D c-MOF-based electrodes are still limited to systems with a single redox-active organic ligand, which restricts their maximum potential in the field of electrochemical energy storage. In contrast, dual-ligand-based 2D c-MOFs possess abundant chemical compositions and tunable topological structures [18,19], which not only overcome the limitation of the few kinds of 2D c-MOFs’ ligands but also provide more opportunities for improving the electrochemical performance of 2D c-MOF-based electrode materials. However, due to the competitive coordination effect between different ligands, the construction of dual-ligand-based 2D c-MOFs in one step is very challenging.

paragraph_context: To explore the lithium storage mechanism of $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } ( \mathrm { H H T P } )$ - (THQ), ex-situ FT-IR and XPS measurements were conducted at different discharge/charge states to monitor the composition variation in the Cu (HHTP)(THQ) electrode (Fig. 5a). As illustrated in Fig. 5b, the FT-IR spectrum of the pristine Cu (HHTP)(THQ) anode shows characteristic peaks at 1654 and $1 5 8 5 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , attributed to the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { O }$ and the aromatic $\mathrm { C = C }$ groups, respectively [44,45]. These peaks gradually weaken with continuous discharge to $0 . 0 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , corresponding to the insertion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ at the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { O }$ and aromatic $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C }$ sites, forming the C–O–Li and C–C–Li species [45]. Significantly, after again charging to $3 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ , the intensity of these characteristic peaks can recover to the initial state, demonstrating high reversibility of the interaction between the active sites and $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ . Moreover, a similar reversible variation of the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { O }$ group can also be observed in the XPS spectra of O 1s. As shown in Fig. 5c, the HR-XPS O 1s spectrum for the Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) electrode at the initial state exhibits two peaks at 533.0 and $5 3 1 . 4 \ : \mathrm { e V }$ , which are assigned to the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { O }$ and C–O bonds, respectively [46–48]. When the electrode is gradually discharged to $0 . 0 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , the ${ \mathrm { C } } { = } \mathrm { O }$ peak intensity significantly reduces while the C–O peak intensity gradually increases. In the following charging process, the intensity of ${ \mathrm { C } } { = } \mathrm { O }$ gradually recovers. These results further confirm that the ${ \mathrm { C } } { = } \mathrm { O }$ group in the $\mathrm { C u O _ { 4 } }$ unit is the redox-active site for lithium storage. In addition, the valence variation of the central metal in the $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 } ( \mathrm { H H T P } ) ( \mathrm { T H Q } )$ structure during the discharge/charge process was also investigated. As displayed in HR-XPS Cu 2p spectra, the ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ signals at 934.6 and $9 5 4 . 6 \mathrm { e V }$ in a pristine state entirely vanish after full discharge to 0.01 V (Fig. 5d), suggesting the reduction of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ . In the subsequent charging process, the opposite evolution did not occur due to the oxidation of $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ requires a voltage higher than $3 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ [17].

paragraph_context: 尹佳成1 , 张印强2 , 李志刚1 , 程明仁1 , 刘明1 , 李伟1 , 李娜2* ,卜显和1,2* 摘要 基于双氧化还原活性有机配体的二维导电金属-有机框架(2D c-MOFs)是极具潜力的锂离子电池(LIBs)电极材料. 然而, 双配体竞争配位导致该类材料合成具有极大挑战性. 本文以乙二胺为调节剂, 发展了一步法合成双配体基2D c-MOF $\mathrm { C u } _ { 3 }$ (HHTP)(THQ) (HHTP $=$ 2,3,6,7,10,11-六羟基三亚苯, THQ $=$ 四羟基-1,4-苯醌). 所得${ \mathrm { C u } } _ { 3 }$ (HHTP)(THQ)具有良好的导电性、丰富的活性位点和优异的化学稳定性, 其作为LIBs负极材料展现出高比容量、良好的倍率性能和长循环稳定性. 实验结果和理论计算表明, Cu (HHTP)(THQ)中CuO 活性位点和苯环单元均参与了锂存储, 从而优化了储锂性能. 该工作为构筑双配体基2D c-MOFs和高性能LIBs电极材料提供了新的途径.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT As electrode materials, transition metal oxides (TMOs) exhibit poor electrochemical performances owing to their inherent low electronic conductivity and considerable volume expansion and contraction during charge/discharge cycles. Designing TMOs with unique nanostructure and combining them with conductive carbon substrates are effective strategies to address the inherent issues. In this work, we designed C/Cu porous microspheres and grew $\mathbf { { C o } _ { 3 } } \mathbf { { O } _ { 4 } }$ nanosheets (NS) vertically on the carbon walls using an in situ synthesis route. As a conductive substrate, the C/Cu microspheres provide a hierarchical pore network and an electrode/ electrolyte contact interface with large area, which can substantially enhance electron and ion diffusion kinetics. The in situ synthesized $\mathbf { { C o _ { 3 } O _ { 4 } } }$ NSs are firmly anchored on the carbon walls, thereby increasing the structural durability of the composites in long-term cycling. Due to their unique structural characteristics, when using the $\mathbf { C } / \mathbf { C } \mathbf { u } @ \mathbf { C 0 } _ { 3 } \mathbf { O } _ { 4 }$ composite microspheres as the anode materials for lithium-ion batteries, the batteries exhibit an enhanced rate performance (a high reversible specific capacity of $6 2 2 \ \mathbf { m A } \ \mathbf { h } \ \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at a current density of $\mathbf { 5 0 0 0 \ m A \ g ^ { - 1 } } ,$ ), high charge-specific capacity $( \mathbf { 9 0 } 7 \mathbf { m A } \mathbf { h } \mathbf { \Lambda } \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $\mathbf { 1 0 0 \ m A \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ after 200 cycles, and a stable specific capacity of 944 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ over 800 cycles, even at a high current density of $\mathbf { 1 0 0 0 \ m A \ g ^ { - 1 } } ,$ ), and excellent cycling stability.
