paragraph_context: Keywords: C/Cu microspheres, multiscale pore structure, chitinderived carbon, mesoporous $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ nanosheets, anode materials With the growing interest in sustainable and renewable energy sources, the requirement for low-cost, efficient, and environment-friendly renewable energy conversion and storage technologies has become urgent [1,2]. Currently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) become the primary energy source for portable electronic devices. They are regarded as the most promising energy storage technology for grid applications and electric vehicles [3,4]. However, commonly used graphite anode materials cannot meet the rapidly growing demand for next-generation LIBs with high power and energy densities due to their low rate capability and low theoretical capacity. Therefore, extensive research is being conducted on alternative anode materials with high-rate performance and high capacity to develop a new generation of LIBs [5,6]. In this context, transition metal oxides (TMOs) are considered the most potential candidates for anode materials owing to their low cost, abundant natural resources, and theoretically high specific capacity [6–10]. Among various TMOs, $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ is regarded as one of the most promising anode materials, which can provide a higher specific capacity $( { \sim } 8 9 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ owing to its eight-electron transfer reaction compared with the conventional graphite anode [11,12]. However, $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ has two major drawbacks. One is that during the charge/discharge cycling process, severe volume changes in the active material result in electrode shattering and poor long-cycling stability. The other is that the inherent low electronic conductivity of $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ leads to poor rate performance. These issues seriously impede its practical applications in LIBs [13,14].

paragraph_context: Two effective strategies have been extensively investigated to address the aforementioned obstacles and enhance the lithium storage capacity of $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ -based electrodes. One approach is to design unique $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ nanostructures, such as nanoparticles [15,16], nanotubes [17,18], nanorods [19], hollow nanospheres [20,21], nanoflowers [22,23], and nanosheets (NS) [24,25]. These nanostructures render the active material a larger specific surface area, enlarge the electrolyte/electrode contact interface, shorten the transport distance of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , and consequently enhance the diffusion kinetics. Furthermore, nanostructures, particularly porous or hollow structures, can reduce the volume expansion/ contraction during ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ insertion/extraction to a certain extent [26,27]. However, during the charging and discharging processes, the nanostructured $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ often suffers from severe particle aggregation, large volume changes, and low conductivity, which leads to electrode crushing and rapid capacity decay, thereby presenting poor long-term cycling stability and rate performance [28,29]. The other efficient strategy is to introduce a specific conductive buffer matrix, such as graphene [30,31], carbon nanotubes [32], carbon nanofibers [33], and porous carbon [34,35], to form corresponding $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ composites. Carbon materials can provide a fast electron conduction channel, which improves the conductivity of the active material. Moreover, the carbon material can buffer the volume change during the charge/discharge cycles, and effectively prevent the aggregation of nanoparticals [36]. Thus, stable specific reversible capacity and good rate capability could be achieved. In this context, Zhang et al. [37] prepared a high-density corn-like $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } /$ /graphene hybrid material by direct pyrolysis of $\mathrm { C o } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } { \cdot } 6 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ on graphene NS through self-assembly induced by graphene wrinkles. This composite preserved a high reversible capacity of $1 0 6 0 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 50 cycles at a current density of $5 0 \mathrm { m A } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ . Chen et al. [38] reported a nanocomposite material of $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ nanoparticles grafted onto a three-dimensional (3D) nanotube sponge. The material exhibited an excellent rate capability and a high specific capacity. However, achieving a strong interaction between $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ and carbon substrates and thus avoiding the shedding and aggregation of nanomaterials during repeated lithiation/delithiation processes remain challenging.

paragraph_context: Chitin is the second largest amount of biomass on Earth. Direct pyrolysis is used to uniformly incorporate heteroatoms into the carbon structure of chitin, resulting in N/O self-doping. This material has been reported as an anode material for highperformance electrode materials [33,39,40]. Recently, we developed a dissolution system for chitin based on alkali/urea aqueous solutions and constructed heteroatom-self-doped C/Cu composite porous microspheres using an emulsion method and high-temperature carbonization [41]. The decay of capacity in the early stage is attributed to the volume expansion/contraction caused by the ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ insertion/extraction processes, leading to the continuous formation of SEI films on the new surface. As charging and discharging cycles progress, the SEI films of $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ NS tend to stabilize quickly. However, the reversible capacity of the $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { N S }$ electrode gradually increases after about the 60th cycle, which can be attributed to the gradual activation of the active material and the creation of the polymer gel-like film [58,59]. Fig. S13 shows that the C/Cu electrode shows the specific capacities of only 266 and 173 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 200 cycles at $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A g ^ { - 1 } }$ and 800 cycles at $1 0 0 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively, much lower than those of the $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ NS electrode. The excellent cycling performance of $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ can be attributed to the robust and unique structure of $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ which is responsible for its exceptional cycling performance, where the vertically grown $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { N S }$ is uniformly distributed on the inner and outer carbon walls of the C/Cu microspheres. By the interconnected pore network of C/Cu substrates and the ample space between the vertically grown $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { N S }$ , a consistent $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux can be generated, and uniform electrochemical reactions of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ can occur on the interface of the active material [62]. This unique structure provides numerous diffusion channels, shortens the distance of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion, and enlarges the contact area between the electrolyte and the electrode. The vertically grown mesoporous $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { N S }$ anchored on the porous microspheres provides sufficient pores for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport and prevents the aggregation of $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ NS during the charging/discharging cycles. Simultaneously, the C/Cu matrix considerably improves the conductivity of the electrode materials and facilitates the diffusion kinetics of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ [68].

paragraph_context: As shown in Fig. S15 and Table S3, the electrochemical performance of the $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ electrode is superior to those of reported $\mathrm { { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { { O } _ { 4 } / } }$ carbon materials in various forms. Regarding lithium storage, the $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ electrodes developed in our work exhibit outstanding long-cycle stability, high reversible charge-specific capacity, and excellent rate performance, owing to the synergistic influence of the hierarchical structure of the $\mathrm { C } /$ Cu microspheres and the reasonably distributed $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { N S }$ . First, the multiscale structure of microspheres provides a large specific surface area, which enlarges the contact area between the electrolyte and the electrode and accelerates the diffusion of ${ \mathrm { L i } } ^ { + }$ , thereby accelerating the redox reaction. Second, the network of the interconnected pores of microspheres and the sufficient space between the interlaced $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ NS can buffer the volume expansion/contraction of the electrode during discharge/charge cycles. Finally, due to the strong interaction force between the C/ Cu matrix and $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ NS, the exfoliation and agglomeration of $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ can be effectively impeded during the charging and discharging processes. Therefore, the $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ electrode demonstrates enhanced electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: In this work, composite microspheres firmly coated with vertically aligned and interlaced $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ NS were synthesized using C/ Cu microspheres with a multiscale structure as the substrates. When used as an anode material for LIBs, the interpenetrating porous structure of $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ microspheres facilitates the penetration of electrolyte, accelerates charge transfer, increases the electrolyte/electrode interface, promotes fast reaction, and mitigates the volume expansion/contraction of the electrode during discharge/charge cycles. paragraph_context: 摘要 过渡金属氧化物(TMOs)用作电极材料时, 会在循环过程中产生严重的体积变化, 并且其自身的导电率也较低, 因此它的电化学性能较差. 设计和开发独特的TMOs纳米结构并将其与导电碳基底相结合是改善其电化学性能的有效策略. 本工作中, 我们设计了一种C/Cu多孔微球, 并通过原位合成在碳壁上垂直生长 $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ 纳米片. 作为导电基底,C/Cu多孔微球提供了多尺度孔隙网络和大的电极/电解质接触界面, 显著改善了电子和离子扩散动力学. 原位合成的 $\mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ 纳米片牢牢地固定在碳壁上, 从而提高了复合微球在长期循环中的结构稳定性. 得益于独特的结构特征, 用作锂离子电池负极材料的 $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C u } @ \mathrm { C o } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ 复合多孔微球表现出优异的倍率性能、高充电比容量和出色的循环稳定性.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Jia $\mathrm { K o n g ^ { 1 } }$ , Tianyi $\mathrm { H o u } ^ { 1 }$ , Ting $\mathrm { S h i ^ { \mathrm { 1 } } }$ , Jianbo $\mathrm { L i } ^ { 1 }$ , Xin Deng1 , Dinggen ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { 2 ^ { * } } }$ , Yunhui Huang1* and Henghui ${ \mathrm { X u } } ^ { 1 ^ { * } }$ ABSTRACT The unstable interface between lithium metal anodes and carbonate-based electrolytes is a key challenge limiting the cycling lifespan of high-energy lithium metal batteries. Here, a resilient artificial solid electrolyte interphase (RASEI) was designed by regulating poly(hexafluorobutyl acrylate) (PHFBA) matrix with the benzene-containing bisphenol A ethoxylate dimethacrylate (BAED) crosslinker to address this issue. The rigid BAED molecule can finely tune the flexible PHFBA matrix, enabling superior resilience from $6 0 0 \%$ elongation to $9 0 \%$ compression with a high Young’s modulus of over 2 MPa. RASEI with these characteristics can accommodate large volume changes of lithium metal and ensure the intimate contact between the lithium metal and the RASEI during battery operation. Consequently, it facilitated homogeneous lithium deposition while mitigating parasitic side reactions. Thanks to the tough and resilient nature of the fluorinated RASEI, the long-term cycling of Li||Li symmetric cells can be achieved for over ${ \bf 5 0 0 ~ h }$ at $\mathbf { 1 } \mathbf { m } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and 1 mAh $\mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The following post-mortem of cycled Li metal reveals that Li dendrite growth is effectively inhibited. Furthermore, the NCM811 pouch cell with a high cathode loading of $2 0 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ exhibits a capacity retention of over $8 5 \%$ after 200 cycles at 1 C.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: lithium metal anode, carbonate electrolytes, resilient ASEI, high cathode loading Lithium metal anode, with a high theoretical specific capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A h \ g ^ { - 1 } } . $ ) and the lowest redox potential $_ { - 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ vs. the standard hydrogen electrode), has been considered as the “holy grail” of higher energy density batteries [1,2]. In addition, carbonate electrolytes demonstrate anodic stability at high potentials, which makes them promising candidates for matching with high-voltage cathodes, such as $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { x } \mathrm { M n } _ { y } \mathrm { C o } _ { 1 - x - y } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ , to achieve higher energy density [3,4]. However, studies have delineated that conventional carbonate electrolytes may not be apt for lithium metal batteries, as they readily undergo reactions with lithium metal anodes, engendering unstable solid-electrolyte interphases (SEIs) [5–7]. Unstable SEIs lead to uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth and limited Coulombic efficiency during repeated plating/stripping processes, which remain key challenges limiting their practical application [8–10].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Up to now, plenty of strategies have been proposed to solve the issue of lithium dendrites, such as electrolyte modification [11–13], separator modification [14–16], and artificial solid electrolyte interfaces (ASEIs) [17–20]. Among these strategies, ASEIs have been extensively explored to enhance the stability of lithium metal anodes. ASEIs can be categorized into inorganic and polymeric interphases [21–23]. Inorganic ASEIs such as LiF [24,25], LiPON [26], $\mathrm { { A l } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { { O } } _ { 3 }$ [27], and others [28–31] exhibit high mechanical strength or excellent ionic conductivity, which can effectively prevent the growth of dendrites. However, their brittle nature makes them prone to fracturing and delamination during lithium stripping/plating, especially under bending and stretching. Loss of contact with the lithium anode leads to uncontrolled dendrite growth and rapid capacity fading. Meanwhile, conventional polymeric ASEIs with narrow elasticity limit typically undergo plastic deformation, which cannot sustain conformal interfacial contact with lithium metal anodes. In contrast, high elastic artificial solid electrolyte interfaces using rubbery polymer matrices exhibit superior flexibility and fracture resistance under large deformation [32–36]. The elastic ASEIs accommodate huge volume changes of lithium metal, ensuring sustained intimate contact with the lithium substrate. Resilient ASEIs (RASEIs) have great potential for lithium metal protection, but there are still few relevant reports.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: RASEIs necessitate not only favorable mechanical properties but also specific characteristics including the resistance to electrolyte degradation and facilitation of ion transport at interfaces. A common approach to obtain elastic materials is by introducing an appropriate quantity of multifunctional cross-linking agent into the monomer and achieving cross-linking. By carefully designing the monomers, cross-linking agents, and reaction conditions, it becomes possible to precisely control the physical and chemical properties of the final polymer to better meet diverse application requirements. Extensive investigations have established that fluorinated acrylates exhibit superior electrochemical and thermal stability compared with their non-fluorinated counterparts, thus making them as promising monomers [37–39]. Moreover, the incorporation of fluorine induces the formation of interfacial LiF, which effectively reinforces the integrity of the electrode–electrolyte interface and contributes to extending the battery’s lifespan [40,41]. Among various fluorinated acrylates, hexafluorobutyl acrylate offers the advantages of being readily available and cost-effective. Furthermore, the inclusion of benzene rings in the cross-linking agent significantly enhances the strength, stiffness, and corrosion resistance of the polymer network.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: In this study, we propose a RASEI coating layer on lithium metal (RASEI@Li) to improve the interfacial stability of lithium metal anodes against carbonate-based electrolytes. The RASEI was synthesized by cross-linking hexafluorobutyl acrylate (HFBA) by the bisphenol A ethoxylate dimethacrylate (BAED) via an instant photocuring process. The inclusion of a benzenecontaining crosslinker regulated the mechanical properties of poly(hexafluorobutyl acrylate) (PHFBA). Remarkably, the RASEI with only $2 \%$ BAED content exhibits exceptional resilience, capable of withstanding elongations of up to $6 0 0 \%$ and compressions of up to $9 0 \%$ , while maintaining a high Young’s modulus exceeding 2 MPa. On the one hand, the elasticity of the RASEI coating allows it to stretch and deform alongside the expansion and contraction of lithium metal, thereby minimizing the cracking and delamination. On the other hand, the RASEI coating effectively hinders the dendrite formation by mechanically obstructing the lithium penetration. Thus, the elastic coating with a unique combination of strength, flexibility, and stability, makes it a highly suitable protective layer for highperformance lithium metal anodes.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Carbon-based anode materials are widely used in various battery energy storage systems due to their low cost, wide source, high conductivity and easy morphology control. However, current commercially available anode materials as active materials for lithium-/sodium-ion batteries generally suffer from large volume changes and poor rate performance. In response, we synthesized defect-rich N, S co-doped two dimensional (2D) nanosheet-assembled porous carbon microspheres (N, S-PCS) via simple hydrothermal, carbonization and etching process based on the principle of Schiff base reaction. The N, S-PCS structure is thus constructed by removing $\bf { F e } _ { 7 } \bf { S _ { 8 } }$ nanoparticles from the carbon skeleton to form porous microspheres with N, S doping. Therefore, the micromorphology characteristic, pore structure and electroconductivity of carbon materials are effectively optimized via heteroatom doping and surface engineering. As expected, the prepared N, S-PCS electrodes exhibit excellent electrochemical performance in both lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. For lithium-ion batteries, it achieves reversible capacities of 1045 and 237 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.1 and $2 0 \mathrm { \bf ~ A } \mathrm { \bf ~ g } ^ { - 1 } ;$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively. For sodium-ion batteries, it shows good cycling stability with a capacity of 157 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 500 cycles at 1 A $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ . Experimental and theoretical calculation results confirm that the N, S co-doping strategies help to improve the structural stability, shorten the ion diffusion paths, and promote the reaction kinetics, thus achieving excellent electrochemical performance. This work is instructive for the practical application of nonmetal doping functionalized porous carbon structures for metal-ion batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: porous carbon microspheres, element doping, lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion batteries, electrochemical performance With the strong impetus from the global secondary energy grid and electric vehicle industries, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely used due to their high energy density and other advantages [1–9]. Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), a new generation of batteries, are a favorable alternative to lithium-ion batteries due to their abundant source, lower cost and environmental friendliness [10–19]. Finding and designing low-cost anode electrode materials with high energy density, high electrochemical performance and long cycle life are crucial to advancing the commercialization of LIBs and SIBs [20–25]. Among the various electrode materials, carbon-based materials are considered to be highly promising anode materials for LIBs and SIBs due to their wide source, low cost, good electrical conductivity, high mechanical strength and environmental friendliness [26–28]. However, the low energy density and poor rate performance of carbon-based materials as battery electrodes generally hinder their practical applications.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In recent years, carbon-based materials based on structural and dimensional optimization have been the main focus of research into anode materials in LIBs and SIBs [29–31]. We have effectively tuned many aspects of carbon materials such as structure, surface interfaces and pores [32–35]. Building carbonbased materials into nanostructures can relieve mechanical stress, shorten the diffusion paths of electrons and ions during cycling, enhance reaction kinetics and thus improve electrochemical performance. Heteroatom doping is also an effective way to improve the structure of materials [36]. Element doping can increase the defects and active sites of the material and increase the storage sites for storing lithium/sodium ions. The design of porous structure increases the contact area between the electrolyte and the electrode material, shortens the diffusion channels for ions and enhances the diffusion kinetics. Strategies such as heteroatom doping and porous structure design can modulate the microstructure of carbon-based materials and promote ion diffusion and electron transfer.

paragraph_context: In this paper, we successfully synthesized N, S co-doped porous carbon microspheres embedded with $\mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } \mathrm { S } _ { 8 }$ nanoparticles using a simple hydrothermal and carbonization process, and then removed the $\mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } \mathrm { S } _ { 8 }$ nanoparticles by a simple one-step etching method to form porous carbon microspheres composed of N, S co-doped 2D nanosheets (N, S-PCS) [37–40]. The large number of honeycomb porous structures increase the contact area with the electrolyte and shorten the diffusion paths of electrons and ions, thus facilitating the reaction kinetics. In addition, the N doping not only improves the electrical conductivity of the carbon material, but also provides a large number of active sites, allowing more binding sites for Li/Na ions and thus increasing the specific capacity. S doping increases the specific surface area of the carbon materials, providing enough space to enrich the diffusion and storage channels for Li/ Na ions, thus providing superior diffusion kinetics. Due to the structural and compositional characteristics of the materials, the N, S-PCS exhibits excellent electrochemical properties in both LIBs and SIBs. For lithium-ion batteries, after 300 cycles at a current density of $5 \mathrm { A } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , the N, S-PCS electrodes still have a reversible capacity of up to $2 6 3 \mathrm { \ m A h \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , and have a reversible capacity of 237 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at a high current density of $2 0 \mathrm { A g } ^ { - 1 }$ , showing excellent long cycle stability and high performance. In sodium-ion batteries, an impressive reversible capacity of 157 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ is also achieved after 500 cycles at a current density of $1 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ . The unique spherical morphology of the N, S-PCS and the N, S co-doping engineering provide important references for the practical application of porous carbon structures in Li/Na batteries.

paragraph_context: Fig. 1 shows the preparation process of N, S-PCS. Firstly, during the hydrothermal synthesis process, since thioacetamide contains both amino and sulfur carbonyl groups, based on the Schiff base reaction, they can self-condense to form imine bonds $\scriptstyle ( \mathrm { C = N } )$ ) under the high-temperature and high-pressure environment of the reactor, accompanied by the escape of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } .$ . In addition, the free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ will coordinate with the lone pair of electrons in the imine group and chelate with the remaining sulfur carbonyl group to form $\mathrm { F e S } _ { 2 }$ , and the formed $\mathrm { F e S } _ { 2 }$ nanodots will be embedded in the 2D nanosheets. Finally, polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP)-K30 as a plasticizer and surfactant contributed to the gradual assembly of the 2D nanosheets into porous spherical structures (called $\mathrm { F e S } _ { 2 } @ \mathrm { P P S } )$ . Subsequently, porous carbon microspheres with $\mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } \mathrm { S } _ { 8 }$ nanoparticles $( \mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } \mathrm { S } _ { 8 }$ $\textstyle { \ @ \mathrm { P C S } }$ ) were formed by carbonization. Further after aqua regia etching, $\mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } S _ { 8 }$ nanoparticles were removed and porous carbon microspheres assembled from nitrogen-doped and sulfur-doped 2D nanosheets were synthesized.

paragraph_context: Due to the advantages of N, S-PCS in terms of porous structure, it has significant advantages in terms of lithium storage capacity and $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ transfer kinetics. The lithium plates were assembled as reverse electrodes into a CR2032 coin cell and the lithium storage performance of the prepared samples was evaluated. Fig. 5 shows the lithium storage performance of N, S-PCS in a button half battery. Fig. 5a shows the first five cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves between 0.01 and $3 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ (vs. $\mathrm { L i / L i ^ { + } }$ ) at a sweep speed of $0 . 1 ~ \mathrm { m V } ~ s ^ { - 1 }$ . Two irreversible reduction peaks were observed near 0.6 and $1 . 2 7 \mathrm { V }$ , respectively, in the first lap of the discharge, which were associated with the formation of the captured $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) membranes as well as the decomposition of the electrolyte. Notably, the reduction peaks formed by the SEI membrane disappeared in the next cycle, while two pairs of less pronounced redox peaks, located at 1.55 and $0 . 7 5 \mathrm { V }$ for the cathodic scans and at 1.85 and $2 . 1 5 \mathrm { V }$ for the anodic scans, appeared, which was attributed to the multistep reversible redox reaction of $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ in the N, S-PCS. In addition, since the reduction peak formed by SEI film irreversibly disappeared from the second cycle, the cyclic voltammetry scanning curves of the last four cycles were well coincident, indicating that no other side reactions occurred in the subsequent cycles, which proved that the structure and composition of N, S-PCS were relatively stable in the process of lithium storage. In order to understand the reaction kinetics of the N, S-PCS samples, the lithium-ion diffusion coefficients of the N, S-PCS electrodes during the second discharge/charge were evaluated using the galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) method (Fig. S6). The $D _ { \mathrm { L i ^ { + } } }$ value can be determined by: $$ D = \frac {4}{\pi \tau} \left(\frac {m _ {\mathrm {B}} V _ {\mathrm {M}}}{M _ {\mathrm {B}} S}\right) ^ {2} \left(\frac {\Delta E _ {\mathrm {S}}}{\Delta E _ {\tau}}\right) ^ {2}, \tag {1} $$ where m , $V _ { \mathrm { { M } } } ,$ and $M _ { \mathrm { B } }$ are the mass, molar volume, and molar mass of the active substance, respectively; S is the surface area of the electrode; and $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { S } }$ and $\Delta E _ { \tau }$ are the change in the opencircuit voltage during the relaxation period and the total change in the cell voltage during the pulse time, respectively. Its $D _ { \mathrm { L i ^ { + } } }$ value varied stably in the order of magnitude of $1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ – $1 0 ^ { - 1 4 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \thinspace s ^ { - 1 }$ , demonstrating excellent electrochemical reaction kinetics.

paragraph_context: In summary, we used the Schiff base reaction principle to insert $\mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } \mathrm { S } _ { 8 }$ nanoparticles into nitro-doped carbon porous microspheres by the hydrothermal method combined with the carbonization process, and then removed $\mathrm { F e } _ { 7 } \mathrm { S } _ { 8 }$ nanoparticles by etching, and successfully synthesized porous carbon structures composed of two-dimensional sheets with N and S doping. paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Lithium (Li) metal anodes (LMAs) have garnered significant attention due to their exceptionally high theoretical capacity and low redox potentials. However, the uncontrolled growth of Li dendrites and substantial volume expansion severely undermine their cycling stability, particularly at elevated current densities. Herein, we develop a lithiophilic 3D Li host by incorporating ZnO/ZnSe heterostructures onto brass fibers (ZnO/ZnSe@Brass), designed to enhance the fast-charging capabilities of Li metal batteries. This hierarchical structure effectively mitigates volume expansion and reduces local current density during lithiation. The uniformly distributed ZnO/ZnSe functions as a lithiophilic skin for the Li anode, facilitating smooth and dense Li deposition. Notably, the in situ formed solid electrolyte interphase, enriched with $\mathbf { L i } _ { 2 } \mathbf { S } \mathbf { e }$ and $\mathbf { L i } _ { 2 } \mathbf { O } _ { 3 }$ , provides high ionic conductivity and superior mechanical strength, thereby accelerating ion transport and charge transfer kinetics. Benefiting from the synergistic effects of the ZnO/ZnSe@Brass host, the resulting Li symmetric cell exhibits robust cycling performance exceeding 10,000 cycles (20 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } /$ $\mathbf { \bar { l } \ m A \ h c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ $\mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and supports fast charging rates at an ultra-high current density of $8 0 \ \mathbf { \hat { m } } \mathbf { A } \ \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . When paired with LiFeP $\bf { { O } _ { 4 ) } }$ the full-cell demonstrates excellent cycle life $\mathbf { 5 5 0 0 }$ cycles at 2 C) and outstanding rate performance. This finding of $\mathbf { Z n O } /$ ZnSe@Brass as a Li host sheds light on the design of advanced LMAs for fast-charging Li metal batteries.

paragraph_context: Keywords: fast-charging, dendrite-free, ZnO/ZnSe heterostructure, 3D lithiophilic current collector, lithium metal batteries With the rapid development of energy storage technologies in the 21st century, the demands for advanced batteries have steadily increased across various fields, including electric vehicles, electric aircraft, and portable devices [1–3]. Among these demands, high energy density, fast-charging capability, and long cycle life have emerged as key research priorities [4–6]. Although traditional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with graphite anodes have undergone rapid development and widespread application, their energy density is progressively approaching its theoretical limit. Consequently, they are becoming inadequate to meet the growing demand for high-energy-density storage solutions in modern society [7]. In contrast, lithium (Li) metal anode has a high theoretical capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } ) \ ,$ ), far exceeding that of graphite, and exhibits the lowest redox potential $_ { - 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ vs. standard hydrogen electrode) [8]. These properties make Li metal as one of the most promising anode materials and open up new avenues for enhancing energy density of LIBs. However, several challenges must be addressed to realize the commercial application of Li metal batteries (LMBs), particularly in fastcharging applications such as electric vehicles [9–11]. One major challenge is the infinite volume expansion during Li deposition, leading to continuous rupture and reforming of the solid electrolyte interface (SEI) film. This consumes both the electrolyte and Li, resulting in low Coulomb efficiency (CE) and shortened cycling life [12]. Additionally, uneven Li deposition triggers the rampant growth of Li dendrites, especially at high current densities [13]. The formation of dendrites not only compromises battery safety by increasing the risk of internal short circuits and potential explosions but also severely degrades the battery’s cycle life and fast-charging performance [14]. Therefore, addressing these challenges is critical for the development of stable and fastcharging LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Considerable efforts have directed towards the advanced architectures of Li hosts for addressing the challenges associated with infinite volume expansion and dendrite formation in Li metal anodes (LMAs). Among these strategies, the introduction of three-dimensional (3D) current collectors has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the electrochemical performance of LMAs [15]. The porous structure of a 3D current collector provides a large specific surface area, effectively reducing local current density and optimizing the electric field distribution to delay Li dendrite growth, while also offering buffer space for volume expansion during cycling [16]. Consequently, various 3D current collectors have been developed as Li hosts, primarily focusing on metal-based frameworks, such as Cu foam [17], and Ni foam [18], alongside carbon-based collectors, including carbon fiber cloth [19], graphene foam [20], and carbon nanofiber scaffolds [21]. Among these options, commercial Cu mesh has demonstrated significant advantages as a current collector, particularly in enhancing the electrochemical performance of LMAs. In addition to mitigating volume expansion, its fiber-oriented growth mode and porous structure effectively inhibit the formation and growth of Li dendrites [22].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: However, due to the lithiophobic nature of Cu, the nucleation overpotential for Li on Cu-based LMAs significantly increases. This leads to higher hysteresis voltage and uneven Li deposition. To reduce nucleation overpotential while promoting homogeneous Li deposition and suppressing dendrite formation, active materials such as metal oxides [23], phosphides [24], sulfides [25], and selenides [26] are typically incorporated as modifiers for 3D current collectors. Among these, zinc-based materials (e.g., ZnO and ZnSe) are particularly attractive due to their natural abundance, low cost, and facile synthesis. However, when employed independently as frameworks for LMAs, both oxides and selenides present distinct limitations. ZnO despite demonstrating moderate lithiophilic properties (lithiophilicity), suffers from inadequate Li storage performance, especially for long-term cycling stability. Conversely, ZnSe provides remarkable electrochemical performance but is constrained by its inherent low conductivity and significant volumetric change during Li insertion/extraction processes [27,28]. Moreover, these 3D lithiophilic host strategy requires additional Li storage processes such as electrodeposition and molten infusion, which increase experimental complexity, material cost, and challenges for scalable production. To enhance charge/discharge capabilities in LMBs, it is crucial not only to design 3D current collectors with optimized lithiophilicity to improve Li deposition behavior and suppress dendrite formation, but also to facilitate the rapid migration of $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ within interfaces of the electrolyteanode/cathode. Crucially, this must be coupled with cost-effective LMA fabrication at industrial scale [29].

paragraph_context: In this work, we demonstrate a novel 3D Li host based on ZnO/ZnSe heterostructures grown on 3D brass fibers $( Z \mathrm { n O } /$ ZnSe@Brass) through facile air annealing and subsequently high-temperature selenization by using commercial brass mesh as substrate. This innovative design of ZnO/ZnSe@Brass host combines flexibility, porosity, lithiophilicity, and ion conductivity, which endows LMAs with smooth Li deposition and high reversibility under high current density. The $Z \mathrm { n O } /$ ZnSe@Brass configuration offers following advantages. (1) The hierarchical structure with enriched pores and high specific surface area effectively mitigates volume expansion and reduces local current density, respectively. (2) The uniform distribution of $\mathrm { Z n O } / \mathrm { Z n S e }$ endows Cu framework with excellent lithiophilicity, ZnO/ZnSe heterostructure not only incorporates the advantages of ZnO and ZnSe but also features abundant interfacial defects and active sites (including built-in electric fields and vacancies), which effectively regulate Li deposition kinetics and reduce the $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ nucleation barrier, thus enabling smooth and dense Li deposition under low overpotential. (3) The in situ formed SEI layer enriched with $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } e$ and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , provides high ionic conductivity, superior mechanical strength and robust chemical stability, which accelerate the transport kinetics of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and enhance the interfaces between electrolyte and anode. paragraph_context: Mechanical fracture is a critical failure mode in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), with crack propagation—central to the fracture mechanism—posing significant challenging in control. This issue is particularly pronounced in alloytype anodes, which exhibit limited stress tolerance, constraining advancements toward higher energy densities in LIBs. Herein, we introduce a biomimetic laminated structure alloy-type foil anode by compositing Sn foil with single-walled carbon nanotubes that enables cyclic stability and high energy density. By modulating the crack propagation mechanism at multiple length scales, the biomimetic structure effectively raises the energy release threshold and facilitates the delocalization of electrochemically induced stress concentration, significantly delaying the onset of mechanical fracture during cycling. Consequently, the full-cell paired with LiFePO4 and LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 cathodes achieve stable hundreds of cycles at practically relevant areal capacities. In particular, the full-cell with $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ at high loading of 10 mAh cm− 2 delivers a volumetric energy density of 1127.2 Wh L− 1 , offering a promising pathway for advancing alloy-type foil anodes in high-energy LIBs.

paragraph_context: As the demand for rechargeable batteries continues to grow, the development of advanced lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with higher energy density and long lifespan faces new challenges [1,2]. Numerous studies have focused on understanding the failure mechanisms of these advanced LIBs to identify potential modification strategies. Among these, mechanical fracture emerges as a primary cause of LIBs failure from a materials perspective. The cyclic stress accumulation that occurs during the charge-discharge process ultimately results in crack initiation, propagation, and eventual fracture, whether within the bulk phase or at the interfaces of electrode materials [3–5]. This issue is especially critical in alloy-type anodes, which are essential for next-generation high energy density LIBs due to their significantly higher specific capacity (ranging from 3 to 10 times that of graphite) [6,7].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Alloy-type foils, such as aluminum (Al) and tin (Sn), represent a significant advancement in battery technology. They generally offer high electrical conductivity, high density and, consequently, greater volumetric energy density. Meanwhile, the use of foil eliminates the costs associated with casting, additives and solvents typically required in conventional anode slurries. These advantages make alloy-type foil anodes particularly promising for practical applications in advanced LIBs (Fig. 1a) [8–15]. However, during the lithiation/delithiation process of alloy-type foil anodes, grain boundaries (GBs) serve as fast diffusion pathways. The limited number of GBs in conventional alloys results in highly uneven lithiation rates. Typically, the Li concentration at GBs is higher than in surrounding regions, leading to non-uniform advancement of the phase transition front. Due to kinetic barriers, lithium cannot be fully extracted during delithiation, resulting in the formation of "dead lithium" regions that further exacerbate phase inhomogeneity. The volume expansion associated with the lithiation-induced phase transition increases local stress. When this stress exceeds the yield strength of material, it initiates plastic deformation. Moreover, the combination of uneven lithiation and inhomogeneous phase transition amplifies the development of localized plastic strain. In summary during the lithiation/delithiation process, challenges arise from disproportionate lithiation rates, inhomogeneous phase transitions, and localized plastic deformation. These factors complicate the management of electrochemically induced stress concentration, reducing the stress tolerance of foils, and leading to rapid mechanical pulverization during cycling (Fig. 1b, c).

paragraph_context: To improve the structural stability of alloy-type foils during cycling, current research is focusing on strategies such as grain boundary engineering [16,17], alloying design [12,18–20], and interface modification [21,22]. For example, Xu et al. suggested that $\mathrm { L i _ { x } } 3 \mathrm { A g 0 . 5 C u 9 6 . 5 S n }$ alloys, with abundant GBs, facilitate additional sliding systems that help alleviate stress and reduce the likelihood of deep fractures12. Tan et al. proposed using a high-concentration ether-based electrolyte to form a fluorine-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, which boosts superior structural modulus and high ionic conductivity, thereby enhancing the durability of Al foil anodes [22]. However, despite these advances, results have been suboptimal. A key issue often overlooked is the crack propagation process, which governs the fracture mechanism of the foil anode. This process is difficult to control and remains a significant challenge. Li et al. emphasized that the intrinsic material properties play a crucial role in the battery reaction process, underscoring the need to link material characteristics with electrochemical performance [23]. Thus, characterizing the foil before lithiation is just as critical as evaluating its properties post-lithiation. Both aspects must ensure the material exhibits suitable mechanical properties and enhanced electrochemical activity. The development of structure-function integrated alloy-type foils is therefore essential for advancing next-generation LIBs.

Additionally, Bio-Sn-2 exhibits a stable voltage plateau and reduced voltage polarization during cycling compared to Sn foils (Fig. 3d). This indicates a strong correlation between the properties of the biomimetic structure and enhanced electrochemical performance, significantly improving electrode stability. Furthermore, the tested current densities also confirm high-rate capability, achieving 4 C performance, thereby supporting the potential for practical applications of alloy-type foils in high-performance batteries.

paragraph_context: To further confirm the practical applicability and energy density advantages of the biomimetic foils, theoretical calculations were performed using NCM811 as the cathode (4 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ and prelithiated Bio-Sn-2 (70 µm) as the anode in a pouch cell configuration $( 5 5 \times 7 2$ $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } )$ . In this setup, double-sided NCM811 provides a capacity of 3.16 Ah when paired with 10 layers of Bio-Sn-2. The resulting pouch cell has an approximate thickness of 2.5 mm, with Bio-Sn-2 comprising only 27.4 % of the whole cell, eliminating the need for a heavy Cu current collector. In contrast, a traditional graphite anode would increase the cell thickness to 3.5 mm due to its 43.4 % greater thickness and the requirement for a 2.9 % Cu current collector. Thus, Bio-Sn-2||NCM811 configuration achieves a 29 % reduction in cell thickness (Fig. 3f and detailed calculation information is provided in Supplementary Tables 2, 3). Under these conditions, the Bio-Sn-2||NCM811 pouch cell would achieve a high volumetric energy density of 1001.1 Wh $L ^ { - 1 }$ (Fig. 3 g, detailed calculation information is provided in Supplementary Table 4). To validate these calculations, a Bio-Sn-2||NCM811 pouch cell was assembled with a prelithiated Bio-Sn-2 anode and single-sided NCM811 cathode, achieving stable cycling over 100 cycles (Fig. 3h, i). These results demonstrate that Bio-Sn-2 exhibits excellent cycling stability at practically high areal capacities, underscoring its significant potential for high-energy-density, long-life alloy-type foil LIBs. It is worth emphasizing that the biomimetic foils are prepared through a simple, scalable process involving spraying, cold pressing, and rolling—making this approach commercially viable. The ease of large-scale production further supports its potential for practical application in next-generation high-energy-density LIBs (Supplementary Fig. 22).

paragraph_context: The enhanced cycling performance of alloy-type foils is fundamentally tied to their fracture tolerance. The evolution of cracks at different areal capacities after the first cycle indicates that during the lithiation reaction, inhomogeneous alloying and significant volume expansion generate a stress field. This stress, when released, initiates cracks near stress concentration points. As lithiation proceeds, cumulative surface damage on the electrode leads to internal crack growth and eventually to the foil anode’s pulverization. However, in the Bio-Sn-2 anode, damage progresses more slowly, effectively suppressing electrochemical failure (Supplementary Fig. 23). The cross-sectional structure evolution of Sn and Bio-Sn-2 under various cut-off areal capacities was illustrated in Fig. 4a. At an areal capacity of 1 mAh cm− 2 , cracks in the Sn foil initiate at the surface and propagate vertically. With further lithiation, the crack tips become destabilized, allowing for further penetration and expansion in the absence of barriers to crack movement. By 10 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ,$ , these cracks intersect, pulverizing the intact electrode into weakly connected fragments, which severely hinders Li⁺ and electron transport. In contrast, the Bio-Sn-2 anode maintains structural integrity during lithiation, showing only minor micro-cracks dispersed within the bulk and no major penetrating cracks (Supplementary Fig. 24). This stability stems from its biomimetic structure, which dissipates lithiation stress, slowing crack initiation. Additionally, the SWCNT-bridged interface within micro-cracks increases the energy threshold for fracture while preserving conductive paths (Supplementary Fig. 25). These features collectively reinforce the structural stability of the Bio-Sn-2 foil.

paragraph_context: Micro computed tomography (micro-CT) offers a non-destructive 3D imaging approach with sub-micron spatial resolution, allowing assessing material morphology, composition and 3D crack distribution [49, 50]. In this study, micro-CT was used to examine Sn and Bio-Sn-2 at an areal capacity of 5 mAh cm− 2 during the first cycle. The reconstructed 3D images reveal crack segmentation within the materials, allowing visualization of their distribution. As illustrated in Fig. 4b, the Sn foil exhibits pronounced plastic deformation with extensive, uncontrolled cracks penetrating to the backside, with the widest reaching nearly 18 µm and an average width around 10 µm. In contrast, Bio-Sn-2 foils display a smooth surface with only a few, narrower cracks, typically less than 10 µm wide (Fig. 4c), underscoring the structural integrity of the Bio-Sn-2 anode.

paragraph_context: Further cross-sectional analysis highlights this difference. In the longitudinal section, the Sn foil shows deep, penetrating cracks originating from the regions of high plastic deformation, whereas Bio-Sn-2 exhibits a notably lower crack density (Supplementary Fig. 26), consistent with the SEM results. The transverse section of the Sn foil displays a dense crack network along the grain boundaries, extending with depth. Conversely, Bio-Sn-2 shows a sparse micro-crack network, with cracks nearly disappearing at a depth of 50 µm (Fig. 4d). This difference can be attributed to the dynamic morphology of the biomimetic structure, which disperses stress across multiple length scales through mechanisms such as crack initiation, deflection, pinning, and annihilation, thereby enhancing electrode toughness.

paragraph_context: Quantitative analysis confirms these findings (Fig. 4e, f): crack percentage in Bio-Sn-2 is just 0.89 %, compared to 4.72 % in Sn foil—5.3 times higher. In Sn foil, crack percentage decreases with depth but slightly increases near the backside due to unrestricted propagation and plastic deformation. In contrast, Bio-Sn-2 rapidly reduces crack formation through efficient stress dispersion. Micro-CT results thus provide clear evidence that Bio-Sn-2 inhibits crack propagation via mechanisms like deflection, splitting, and pinning, substantially enhancing fracture tolerance and preventing electrode failure during cycling.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: To elucidate the advantages of the biomimetic structure, we examine the macro- and micro-mechanical behavior of the foils before and after lithiation. Soft metals like Sn foils struggle to withstand stress from electrochemical processes. This results in plastic deformation due to volumetric expansion, and lithiation progresses easily to the backside of the foil, driven by thermodynamic and kinetic factors, which accelerates electrode breakage and fracture formation. In contrast, the biomimetic structure substantially enhances microhardness. After the first cycle at an areal capacity of 2.5 mAh cm− 2 , both the surface and backside of the Bio-Sn remain relatively flat compared to the Sn foil, greatly mitigating crack initiation and propagation (Supplementary Fig. 27).

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Micro-indentation tests further confirmed the improved mechanical properties of Bio-Sn-2. The indentation area of Bio-Sn-2 remains consistently smaller than that of Sn across various loads (Supplementary Fig. 28), demonstrating greater resistance to plastic deformation. To better understand energy dissipation mechanism of Bio-Sn-2, crosssectional EBSD analysis of the subsurface region under indentation reveals a more uniform stress distribution and efficient stress storage at grain boundaries or layer boundaries in Bio-Sn-2 (Fig. 5a-c). Kernel average misorientation (KAM) analysis highlighted that this structural arrangement increases fracture energy threshold of Bio-Sn-2, enhancing fracture resistance. The micro-indentation test, which simulates compressive forces from restricted volumetric expansion during cycling, shows that lithiation further reinforces resistance to deformation of Bio-Sn-2 (Fig. 5d, e). Under a 100 mN load, cracks appear and expand in the Sn foil, while Bio-Sn-2 shows no significant cracking. This behavior is attributed to biomimetic structure, which absorbs a substantial amount of indentation energy (0.22 nJ mm− 3 , compared to Sn: 0.16 nJ mm− 3 ) and dissipates additional energy through microcrack formation (Supplementary Figs. 29–31). Bio-Sn-2 consistently displays a lower indentation depth than Sn, requiring less inelastic deformation to counteract the applied force. Overall, the biomimetic structure in Bio-Sn-2 enhances the toughness of the alloy-type anode via multi-scale energy dissipation mechanisms, improving mechanical robustness and mitigating rapid battery failure due to electrochemical stress.

paragraph_context: To further elucidate the electro-mechanical coupling mechanism, we employed COMSOL finite element simulations that integrate lithiation/ delithiation kinetics with elastic–plastic large deformation behavior. Fig. 6a presents time-resolved simulation snapshots of lithium concentration in both Sn and Bio-Sn-2 foils. In pure Sn, which features large grain sizes, lithium migrates preferentially along fast-diffusion pathways such as GBs, resulting in highly non-uniform lithiation. In contrast, the biomimetic Bio-Sn-2 foil contains a denser network of GBs and welldefined layer boundaries, which promote more homogeneous lithium distribution throughout the bulk. Since lithiation-induced stress is directly correlated with lithium transport behavior, severe stress localization occurs near GBs in pure Sn. When the accumulated strain energy exceeds the GB binding energy, rapid energy release leads to the formation of penetrating cracks. Bio-Sn-2, with its hierarchical structure of layer boundaries and fine GBs, effectively disperses lithiation stress under the same degree of lithiation (Fig. 6b). As cycling proceeds, energy is gradually released through the formation of microcracks along GBs and interfaces, while the overall structural integrity of the electrode remains intact. This structural design enables Bio-Sn-2 to simultaneously enhance electrochemical performance and mechanical stability through a synergistic electro-mechanical coupling mechanism.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Importantly, the repeated accumulation and release of lithiation/ delithiation stress over cycles govern crack evolution and ultimately determine electrochemical failure. After 50 cycles at an areal capacity of 2 mAh cm− 2 and a current density of 1 mA cm− 2 , the 30 µm Sn and Bio-Sn-2 foils exhibit markedly different structural evolutions (Supplementary Fig. 32). The pristine Sn foil expands to 97.7 µm in thickness, primarily due to uncontrolled crack propagation. This leads to extensive fragmentation and the formation of porous void regions, which not only amplify volume expansion but also disrupt the structural integrity of the active material. These voids facilitate subsequent non-uniform lithiation and localized stress accumulation, while isolated domains tend to trap lithium irreversibly, forming "dead lithium" zones that cannot be contracted during delithiation. The interplay of these effects results in nearly 200 % volume expansion and rapid mechanical degradation of the Sn anode. In contrast, Bio-Sn-2 demonstrates superior lithiation kinetics and stress dissipation capability, limiting thickness expansion to just 63.5 µm—approximately half that of pure Sn. paragraph_context: Mechanical fracture is a major obstacle to the performance of LIBs, especially in alloy-type anodes, where maintaining stable cycling at high areal capacities remains challenging. Our study demonstrates that structural-functional integration for alloy-type foils can be achieved effectively through a biomimetic structure design (Fig. 6c). This approach enabled a notable energy density of 1127.2 Wh $L ^ { - 1 }$ in alloytype foil anodes with stable cyclic performance. By enhancing mechanical properties in tandem with lithiation kinetics, we establish a framework for electro-mechanical coupling via multi-scale microstructural modulation. Toughening features of crack-resistant biomaterials introduce an additional energy threshold against fracture through mechanisms such as crack bridging, pinning, deflection, and splitting. These mechanisms absorb electrochemically induced stresses, enhance stress tolerance, and prevent mechanical rupture (Fig. 6d). The Bio-Sn-2 anode, in particular, demonstrates exceptional cycling stability at a thin thickness of 30 µm. The Bio-Sn-2||LFP cell, with a high areal capacity of 2.6 mAh cm− 2 , completed over 260 cycles, while the assembled pouch cell sustained stable cycling for more than 100 cycles, marking a significant advancement in alloy-type foil anodes. This innovative structural design strategy offers a new pathway for optimizing alloy-type anodes and lithium metal electrodes, with promising potential for future performance breakthroughs.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: The 50 μm Sn foil was cut into regular squares measuring $5 0 \times 5 0$ mm. It was then placed on a heating table set to $7 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ A 0.15 wt. % aqueous dispersion of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) was evenly sprayed onto the surface of the heated Sn foil using an air spray pen, allowing the water to evaporate. This process resulted in a Sn foil with SWCNT content of 0.058 wt. %. This operation was repeated to ensure uniform coverage. Subsequently, the Sn foil with SWCNT was stacked in different configurations, specifically with 100, 200, 300, and 500 layers. A biomimetic structural foil was obtained by applying a load of 500 kN at a loading speed of 2.5 kN s⁻¹ using a cold press. This load was stabilized for 300 s. Afterward, the stacked material was wire cut into regular blocks and rolled at room temperature through multiple passes using a rolling mill.

paragraph_context: Standard CR2025 coin-type cells were assembled for electrochemical measurements. Celgard 2400 was used as the separator, and the electrolyte comprised 1 M LiPF dissolved in a 1:1 vol ratio of ethylene carbonate (EC) and diethyl carbonate (DEC), supplemented with 10 % fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and 1 % vinylene carbonate (VC). For the half-cell configuration, the foil (30 μm thickness) was punched into discs with a diameter of 10 mm. Metallic lithium foil served as both the counter and reference electrode. In the full-cell assembly, the anode underwent mechanical prelithiation prior to assembly. The cathode was prepared by coating a slurry containing 80 wt. % $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811), 10 wt. % carbon black, and 10 wt. % polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) onto an aluminum (Al) current collector. The electrode was then dried at $1 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 12 h. To evaluate volumetric energy density, a cathode was produced using a slurry composed of 97 wt. % NCM811, 0.5 wt. % SWCNT, and 2 wt. % PVDF. In the pouch cell test, the NCM811 cathode exhibited a higher mass loading of $2 2 . 7 ~ \mathrm { m g ~ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ (mass ratio of NCM811: 94 %) and had dimensions of $5 5 \times 7 2 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ . The operating voltage window and rate were set at 2.8–4.2 V and $0 . 3 \mathrm { C } ,$ respectively. The electrochemical performance of the assembled half-cells was assessed using the BTS4000 NEWARE battery test system (NEWARE, Shenzhen, China) with galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) procedures. The galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) was performed at a pulse current of 0.5 mA cm $^ { . 2 } \mathrm { f o r } 0 . 5 \mathrm { h } ,$ followed by a relaxation period of 0.5 h. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were conducted using the American AMETEK Princeton Versa STAT electrochemical workstation.

paragraph_context: Micro-CT was performed using the Nano Voxel-3000 system. The Xray tube was operated at a voltage of 90 kV and a current of $3 0 \mu \mathrm { A }$ . The scanning mode was set to High Resolution, with a total scan time of 150 min. The scanning pixel size was 0.5 µm, and the field of view measured $0 . 9 \ \times \ 0 . 9 \ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ . A total of 1080 projections were acquired for each tomogram, evenly distributed over a 360-degree rotation. The distance between the focus and the object was maintained at 2.5 mm, while the distance from the focus to the detector was 250.8 mm. Tomographic reconstruction of the projections was conducted using the Voxel Studio Recon routine, and data analysis was performed using the Dragonfly software. Specifically, an adaptive threshold segmentation method was applied to binarize the crack regions, utilizing the density contrast between the cracks and the surrounding electrode material. The binarized images were then reconstructed into a 3D dataset by stacking pixel points, with the resolution determined by the pixel size. The software subsequently calculated the crack volume, length, and thickness by quantifying the number of corresponding voxel points.

paragraph_context: Phase structure analysis of the samples was performed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 Discover). Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images were acquired with a JEOL JSM-7100F at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV and a working distance of 10 mm. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) patterns were obtained using a TSL OIM system attached to the same scanning electron microscope, operating at a voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 500 nm. Field emission transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was conducted on a FEI Talos F200X. FIB specimen preparation via lift-out technique was performed on a FEI Helios G5 UX focused ion beam operating at 5–30 kV. Element distribution was analyzed using an electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA, JXA-8530F). Tensile experiments were carried out using dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA, Q800), and micro-indentation tests were performed using a dynamic ultra-microhardness tester (DUH-211S). Before XRD measurements, samples were placed on a glass slide and covered with Kapton tape within an Ar-filled glove box to prevent reactions with ambient air. Samples for SEM and TEM analysis were also sealed in the Ar-filled glove box prior to transfer to the equipment chamber. Additionally, the samples for characterization were rinsed with dimethyl carbonate.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the rapid development of electric vehicles (EVs) and other electronic devices, there is an increasing demand for high energy density batteries, driving the development of anode materials with higher energy density than graphite. Silicon, as the most promising candidate for the next generation of lithium-ion battery anodes, has a theoretical specific capacity nearly ten times that of graphite. Among these materials, nano‑silicon has been widely studied because of its small particle size and ability to adapt well to its drastic volume changes during the lithiation/delithiation process. However, there are relatively few articles that systematically summarize the research progress on the structural design of nano‑silicon-based anodes. This review provides a detailed overview of advancements in the structural design of nano‑silicon and summarizes the advantages of various dimensional structures, shell, pore nanostructures and surface modification of silicon-based nanomaterials. Finally, the future development trends and prospects for the large-scale application of nano‑silicon-based anodes are discussed.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Fossil fuels are a finite resource that will inevitably be depleted in the foreseeable future, necessitating the search for alternative clean energy sources. [1,2] Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) currently dominate the energy storage market and are widely utilized to power portable electronic devices and EVs/hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs). [3–6] Driven by national policies and commercial advancements, the development of EVs has significantly progressed [7–9]. The power battery as a crucial component determining the cruising range of EVs, must evolve into a high energy density rechargeable system to overcome the mileage limitations of current EVs. [10–12] Among the various components of LIBs, electrode materials are the most significant factor influencing their energy density. However, conventional graphite anode materials, with a theoretical capacity of 372 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , are unable to meet the growing energy density demands of LIBs. [13,14] Thus, it is imperative to explore alternative anode materials such as silicon-based materials, which offer significantly higher energy density and are naturally abundant, making them a promising candidate for next-generation LIBs.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Silicon-based anodes offer numerous advantages and are regarded as one of the most promising alternative anodes for high density energy LIBs. Silicon is abundant in nature and delivers a theoretical capacity exceeding 3500 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ (corresponding to $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 5 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 4 }$ observed in roomtemperature electrochemical cells), which is approximately ten times higher than that of graphite. [15–17] Furthermore, silicon exhibits a relatively low lithiation potential of \~0.37 V (vs. Li/Li+), ensuring the normal operation voltage of the battery and a high output energy density. Additionally, the lithiation potential of silicon is slightly higher than that of graphite (\~0.1 V vs. Li/Li+), reducing the likelihood of “lithium dendrites” formation during the charging process. [18] Hence, silicon-based anodes hold great potential for significantly extending the driving range of VEs and are expected to serve as commercial anodes for next generation LIBs. They are also well-suited for energy storage applications in everyday electronic devices. [19–21] However, the silicon particles undergo more than 300 % volume expansion during the lithiation process. [22–25] The repeated contraction and expansion of silicon during lithiation/delithiation cycles can cause the active material to fracture and disintegrate, leading to the loss of contact between the electrode material and the current collector. This ultimately results in reduced cycling stability. [26–33] Different strategies have been implemented to address these challenges. Liu et al. [34] discovered that silicon particles do not fracture or pulverize during the lithiation/delithiation process when their size is reduced to below 150 nm. Consequently, the design of nanostructures has been extensively explored to accommodate the volume expansion of silicon particles. Silicon nanoparticles (0D), [35] silicon nanowires (1D) (Si-NWs) and silicon nanotubes (Si-NTs), [36] silicon thin films (2D) (Si-TFs) [37] and porous silicon (3D) [38] have been widely studied. These structural designs aim to mitigate the issues of volume expansion, low electron conductivity, and limited ion transport in silicon-based anodes. However, nano‑silicon also presents challenges due to its high specific surface area, which leads to parasitic reactions with the electrolyte during cycling, ultimately compromising the cycle life of battery. To address this issue, various surface modification strategies have been proposed. Modifying the surface of nano‑silicon can effectively alter its physical and chemical properties. For instance, coating nano‑silicon with a carbon layer has been widely investigated. [39] A highly conductive carbon layer not only enhances the electrical conductivity of the electrode materials but also serves as a dense barrier, preventing direct contact between nano‑silicon and the electrolyte. This significantly reduces excessive electrolyte consumption and improves cycling performance. [40] Despite these advancements, comprehensive reviews that summarize the latest research progress and future prospects of nano‑silicon anodes from the perspective of structural design remain scarce. Addressing this gap is essential for guiding the development of next-generation silicon-based anode materials.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: This review systematically summarizes the various structural designs and the functional properties of nano‑silicon as anode materials for LIBs in Fig. 1. First, the preparation methods for 0D nanoparticles, 1D nanowires and nanotubes, and 2D nanosheets through direct nanosizing of silicon are described. Second, to shield the nano‑silicon cores from direct interaction with the electrolyte and to facilitate the formation of a stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, the strategically designed core-shell structures are summarized. Third, the design and advantages of pore structure is introduced. Fourth, as the stability of the SEI layer plays a decisive role in cycling performance, modifying the physical or chemical properties of the nano‑silicon surface to form a stable electrode interface is examined. This section primarily introduces three types of modification media: carbon-based materials, metal/metal compound materials, organic polymer materials, as well as other materials. Finally, this review provides a concise summary of the different structural designs of nano‑silicon and discusses the future development prospects of nano‑silicon anodes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Silicon is the second most abundant element on Earth, widely distributed in rocks, sands, and soils as various forms of silicon dioxide or silicates. Nanostructured silicon can be fabricated using a variety of methods, typically relying on either expensive, high-purity silicon sources or toxic silanes. Recently, various low-grade Si (untreated or initially treated raw silicon materials) and natural sources have been explored as cost-effective alternatives for producing nanostructured silicon. [41,42] The design of nanostructures for silicon-based anode materials primarily follows two main approaches. The first approach involves directly reducing silicon particles to the nanoscale using physical or chemical methods. For instance, physical methods such as high-energy ball milling (HEBM) can directly reduce the size of silicon particles to the nanometer scale, [43] while chemical methods such as laser pyrolysis can convert silanes into single-crystal nano‑silicon. [44] The second approach involves modifying or decorating the primary structure of nano‑silicon, including nanoparticles, nanowires, nanotubes, and thin films. Silicon-based anodes with diverse nanostructures generally exhibit larger specific surface areas, facilitating better electrolyte penetration and yielding improved electrochemical properties. This review highlights the characteristics of the three main nanostructure designs—silicon nanoparticles, silicon nanowires and nanotubes, and silicon thin films—and discusses their influence on electrochemical performance in detail below.

paragraph_context: Hwang et al. [43] used HEBM to mechanochemically mix cheap micron-sized Si with amorphous $\mathrm { { S i O _ { 2 } } }$ powder. As shown in Fig. 2a, nanoscale silicon particles were impregnated into the silica substrate after 24 h of HEBM treatment, resulting in a reversible capacity of 1270 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ in the first cycle, with a capacity retention rate of 83.5 % after 100 cycles. As illustrated in Fig. 2b, Kim et al. converted $\mathrm { { S i H } _ { 4 } }$ into nano‑silicon particles using laser pyrolysis with $S \mathrm { F } _ { 6 }$ as a photosensitizer, achieving a conversion rate of 97.1 %. [44] Fig. 2c presents a synthesis method for nano‑silicon particles using diatomaceous earth as raw material. A molten salt-assisted low-temperature reduction method was employed to prepare Si nanospheres. This approach reduces the reaction temperature and preparation cost, while the use of diatomaceous earth as the starting material further lowers the cost of raw material acquisition. The resulting novel nano/micro-structure of Si microspheres, assembled from Si nanoparticles, effectively disperses the stress changes in silicon during lithiation/delithiation due to localized nano-sizing. As a result, the prepared nano‑silicon microspheres maintain a high specific capacity of over 1300 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 200 cycles at $0 . 2 \mathrm { A g } ^ { - 1 }$ . [45] Fig. 2d demonstrates an in-situ adaptive electrochemical grinding (ECG) strategy that uses $\mathrm { M g H } _ { 2 }$ as a grinding aid for the electrochemical reduction of micron-sized silicon. The expansion of silicon induces significant internal stress changes, and the lithiation products of $\mathrm { M g H } _ { 2 }$ migrate into the cracked Si particles, gradually transforming into a conductive matrix consisting of ionically conductive LiH and electron conductive components by partial reversible lithiation of Mg. This process preserves the electrochemical activity of the silicon particles even after rupture, effectively grinding micro‑silicon into nano‑silicon to accommodate the significant stress changes during lithiation/delithiation. The materials prepared using ECG strategy demonstrated a high specific capacity of 3228 mAh ${ \tt g } ^ { - \bar { 1 } }$ and maintained a capacity retention rate of 91 % after 200 cycles. paragraph_context: Si-NWs exhibit strong strain resistance, enabling them to maintain structural stability during repeated expansion and contraction. Additionally, Si-NWs possess high electrical conductivity, a short lithium-ion diffusion path, and an extremely high specific surface area. [47–49] These structural advantages allow the electrolyte to fully infiltrate the Si-NWs electrode, thereby accelerating lithium-ion diffusion and providing more reaction sites, which collectively enhance the lithium storage performance of Si-NWs. [50,51] In flexible electronic devices, conductive nanowires are widely utilized, and their application in energy storage materials has been extensively studied by incorporating functional materials such as silicon (Si) and carbon (C) into nanowires. [52] The size of silicon plays a critical role in determining its performance. When the particle size of Si is reduced to less than 150 nm, it can effectively accommodate the significant stress caused by volumetric expansion and contraction of silicon volume. Similarly, studies have demonstrated that Si-NWs with diameters smaller than 300 nm can adapt to stress changes without structural failure. [53] In 2007, as shown in Fig. 3a, Cui et al. reported a gas-liquid-solid (VLS) method for growing silicon nanowire (Si-NWs) anode materials directly on stainless steel current collectors. Compared with traditional micron-scale silicon, smaller-diameter Si-NWs could better accommodate volume changes during lithiation and delithiation. Each Si-NW was electrically connected to the current collector, and all the nanowires contributed to the capacity without requiring conductive agents or binders. Additionally, Si-NWs exhibit a direct 1D electron transport pathway, enabling efficient charge transport behavior. [36] Cui’s group also synthesized silicon amorphous-crystal core-shell nanowires through a vapor-solid (VS) mechanism in a single step. The resulting products could be directly grown on stainless steel current collectors without binders and conductive agents. [54] The crystalline silicon core served as a stable mechanical support and an efficient electrical conduction pathway, while the outer amorphous silicon shell contributed more than 98 % of the capacity during the cycle. As illustrated in Fig. 3b, another method for fabricating Si-NW anodes involved promoting the growth of Si-NWs from densely intertwined seeds by in situ growing copper silicide (CS) network films on copper foils. This approach achieved a binder-free electrode structure with a thickness of less than 10 μm and a surface load of \~1.04 $\mathrm { m g \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ . This electrode demonstrated an average coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.6 %. [48] Si-NTs are emerging materials characterized by inner and outer membranes that can be directly exposed to the electrolyte. The thin walls of Si-NTs shorten the lithium-ion transport path, thereby reducing both ohmic and polarization impedance. Additionally, the hollow structure of Si-NTs provides sufficient buffer space to accommodate volume expansion and contraction during the alloying and dealloying processes, enabling the material to adapt to stress changes and maintain structural stability. However, due to their hollow structure, Si-NTs exhibit a relatively low tap density, which in turn results in a reduced volumetric energy density. [55–57] The expansion of Si-NWs during lithiation can thin or rupture the SEI film, exposing the Si surface to the electrolyte and triggering further reactions to form new SEI layers. Repeated lithiation and delithiation cycles ultimately result in the formation of a thick SEI film on the silicon surface. Similarly, the outer layer of Si-NTs also forms a thick SEI film during cycling. To address this issue, Cui’s group designed a confined coating on hollow Si-NTs. As shown in Fig. 3c, a double-walled $\mathrm { S i } { - } \mathrm { S i O } _ { x }$ nanotube (DWSi-NT) anode has been synthesized using the electrospinning nanofiber template method. The inner wall consists of active silicon, while the outer wall is composed of $\mathrm { S i O } _ { x } ,$ , which is permeable to lithium ions. This design ensures that the electrolyte contacts only the outer surface and does not infiltrate the hollow interior. During lithiation, lithium ions penetrate the outer SiOx wall to react with the inner silicon, preventing outward silicon expansion. This confinement stabilizes the SEI film, making it thinner and more robust, thereby significantly enhancing the electrochemical performance of Si-NTs. [56] As illustrated in Fig. 3d, Ma et al. [58] fabricated coaxial hollow nanotube CNTs@Si (HNCSi), which served as a model material to investigate the SEI growth process on hollow silicon structures. In this design, silicon nanotubes act as shells for lithium storage, while multiwalled carbon nanotubes enhance conductivity. The hollow nanotube structure also provides sufficient space for SEI growth. Due to the combined effects of the hollow structure and SEI confinement, the prepared HNCSi exhibited excellent electrochemical performance. paragraph_context: Silicon thin films (Si-TFs) can effectively accommodate the volume expansion and contraction of silicon-based anode materials during cycling, owing to their two-dimensional structure. Si-TFs also shorten the lithium-ion transport pathway and exhibit higher electrical conductivity compared to other silicon nanomaterials, because of their superior electrical contact with current collectors. [59] Thus, the unique structure of Si-TFs significantly enhances their cycling stability. [60–62] Si-TFs are primarily fabricated using chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and fused salt development (FSD) methods. [63,64] In the CVD process, gaseous silicon precursors undergo chemical reactions at high temperature and are subsequently deposited onto a substrate to form Si-TFs. This method typically requires high reaction temperatures, which impose stringent requirements on the equipment. Additionally, the unstable nature of silicon precursors can pose safety concerns under the harsh reaction conditions. Common silicon precursors used in CVD include silanes and trichlorosilanes. Si-TFs synthesized via the CVD method are generally polycrystalline.
