paragraph_context: Nanoscale silicon anodes possess a large specific surface area, which can react with the electrolyte during cycling to form excessive SEI layers. This reaction consumes a significant amount of electrolyte and can lead to the formation of multiple SEI layers that hinder lithium-ion transport, thereby increasing the charge transfer impedance of the electrode and adversely affecting the cycling performance of battery. To mitigate the over-reaction between the nano‑silicon and electrolyte, various strategies involving the design of core-shell structure have been widely explored. In these structures, the core typically consists of silicon nanomaterials, while the outer shell is generally a carbon layer. The carbon shell, with its high conductivity, serves as a conductive agent. Furthermore, the dense carbon layer prevents direct contact between the silicon nanocore and the electrolyte, thereby reducing excessive electrolyte consumption. [67–69] This section discusses the design of four distinct core-shell structures: yolk-shell, pomegranate-shaped, multicore-shell, and cage-like structures.

paragraph_context: The yolk-shell structure typically consists of Si-NPs as the yolk, surrounded by an outer shell structure, usually composed of a carbon layer. As illustrated in Fig. 5a, [70] the Si@void@C was synthesized using a room temperature solution method. The yolk-shell structure, comprising nano‑silicon particles (\~100 nm) as the yolk and an amorphous carbon shell (5–10 nm), was specifically designed to address the challenges associated with nano‑silicon anodes. The carbon shell includes a void between its self-supporting skeleton and the central nano‑silicon particles, providing sufficient space to accommodate the volume expansion of nano‑silicon during lithiation. Additionally, the dense outer carbon shell reacts with the electrolyte to form a stable SEI film while effectively preventing the electrolyte from penetrating the shell and reacting with the inner nano‑silicon particles, thereby reducing excessive electrolyte consumption. Lithium ions can diffuse through the carbon shell to the internal silicon core, facilitating lithium storage. The Si@void@C yolk-shell electrode demonstrates an excellent specific capacity of 2800 mAh ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ and an average CE of up to 99.84 % at 0.1C after 1000 cycles (1C = 4200 mAh $g ^ { - 1 } )$ .

paragraph_context: As a high-performance anode material for LIBs, nano‑silicon holds significant potential for a wide range of applications. However, several challenges remain to be addressed, including the loss of electrical contact between nanoparticles, excessive electrolyte consumption caused by the high specific surface area of the particles, low intrinsic conductivity, and high manufacturing costs. To systematically address the issue of poor cycling performance in nano‑silicon anodes, it is essential to focus on multiple aspects, such as the preparation of active materials, the design of novel binders and electrolytes, and the selection of suitable conductive agents. These efforts aim to enhance the cycling stability of nano‑silicon-based electrode structures. In this review, the research progress in the structural design of nano‑silicon anodes is presented. The relevant preparation methods are categorized into the following four approaches: (1) Nanostructured design: Nanostructures such as nanoparticles, nanowires, nanotubes, nano thin films enable silicon to accommodate the significant stress changes during the lithiation/delithiation process, thereby maintaining structural stability. However, designing intricate structures like nanowires and nanotubes often complicates the synthesis process, making them unsuitable for cost-effective, large-scale applications. Therefore, future developments are expected to focus on nanostructured designs derived from raw micro-sized silicon particles using electrochemical processes, due to the lower cost of raw microsized silicon.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: (2) Shell structure design: Shell structures, including core-shell, yolkshell, multi-core-shell, and cage-like configurations, serve primarily to prevent direct contact between the silicon core and the electrolyte. This isolation reduces the continuous consumption of the electrolyte, thereby improving the cycling performance of the electrode material.  (3) Porous Structure Design: Porous structures provide buffer space to accommodate the substantial volume expansion of silicon particles during lithiation/delithiation. Additionally, the presence of pores facilitates effective contact between the active material and the electrolyte, thereby reducing lithium-ion transport distances and ultimately improving the electrochemical performance of the material.  (4) Interface Modification: Interface modification is critical for improving the cycling performance of the material. Modifying the surface of nano‑silicon alters its physical and chemical properties, enabling the formation of a relatively stable SEI layer between the electrode material and the electrolyte during electrochemical cycling. Common modification agents include carbon-based materials, metal and metal compound materials, as well as organic polymer materials.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: These four strategies are not mutually exclusive, and many examples discussed in this review simultaneously incorporate two or three of them. For example, in the section on Shell Structure Design, the shell is often combined with other materials, aligning with the introduction of heteroatoms discussed in Interface Modification to enhance the properties of nano‑silicon. Similarly, the design of porous nano‑silicon structures (Section 4) frequently involves the integration of carbon materials, as the surface coating layer of the porous silicon anode helps stabilize the interface. While the stable cycling of nano‑silicon anodes has been achieved in laboratory settings, commercialization remains a significant challenge. The current production costs of nano‑silicon anodes are too high to meet commercial requirements. Although silicon‑carbon composite anodes have been commercialized, the silicon content in these anodes is extremely low, resulting in limited improvements in the energy density of the entire battery. To enable the largescale commercialization of high‑silicon-content anodes, it is essential to develop simpler preparation methods and lower manufacturing costs while ensuring stable cycling performance. For instance, previous work developed a straightforward electrode synthesis strategy that begins with a conductive polymer binder mixed with active silicon. After carbonization, the conductive polymer is converted into a carbon layer. The resulting electrode demonstrated a reversible capacity of 2100 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and an average coulombic efficiency of 91.85 % [18]. This approach provides a new perspective for designing high-performance siliconbased anode materials, suggesting that complex structural design may not always be necessary. It also represents an innovative direction for designing macroscopic electrode structures in silicon-based anodes. In the future, the development of silicon-based anodes will definitely shift to simpler and cheaper synthesis methods based on the whole electrode components, rather than just the active materials.

paragraph_context: Among various technologies that go beyond lithium-ion batteries, lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have been intensively studied as the next generation of high-energy battery technology. However, achieving scalable production of dendrite-free lithium metal anodes (LMAs) for practical application is still a formidable challenge. Herein, we propose a simple and feasible method to modify lithium foil with graphene coatings, which is expected to be used in practical applications on a large scale. Graphene has a high specific surface area and excellent electrical conductivity, which can disperse current density, induce uniform Li deposition, and reduce the generation of dendrites and dead lithium. Meanwhile, the porous graphene coating layer is beneficial to the continuous compensation of irreversible active Li loss by the Li foil underneath the graphene coating. As a result, pouch cells using graphene coated Li anode display superior cyclic stability comparing to the cell with bare Li anode. The cell with a high areal capacity of 4 mAh cm− 2 reaches a high capacity retention of 76% after 470 charge/discharge cycles at a current density of 0.1C.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: With the development of advanced energy storage applications, rechargeable batteries with ultrahigh energy density and safe operation have gained increasing attention. Lithium-ion batteries are approaching the upper limit of energy density, thus secondary batteries with higher energy density have attracted widespread attention [1–3]. Lithium metal is considered a promising candidate anode for high-energy-density batteries because of its high specific capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ), low electrochemical potential (3.04 V vs. SHE), and low density (0.59 g cm− 3 ) [4–6], which has the potential to double or triple the stored energies in rechargeable Li batteries [7,8].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: However, lithium metal anode suffers from short cycling lifetime and low coulombic efficiency, which is due to the parasitic reaction between lithium metal and electrolyte [9,10]. The SEI formed on the surface of lithium metal is unstable, causing dendrite growth, volume expansion, dead lithium accumulation, and other problems, all of which give rise to short cycle life and even safety risks of short circuit and explosion, seriously hindering the wide-scale application of high-energy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs) [11–13]. Dendrite growth arises intrinsically from the uneven lithium electroplating process, whereas a definitive suppression could be hardly realized [13,14]. In the past decades, various strategies from both academia and industry have been proposed to improve the lifetime of LMBs, such as adjusting the composition of liquid electrolytes and additives to form more robust SEI [15–18], and introducing robust artificial protection layers on the lithium metal anode surface [19–21], which can inhibit the growth of dendrites and improve the coulombic efficiency. Another attractive way is to construct a three-dimensional current collector to accommodate electroplated Li, such as copper foam [22] and nickel foam [23]. Other methods such as using modified separators [24,25], and introducing solid-state-electrolytes [26–28] have also been proposed to solve the problem of lithium metal anode to extend the cycle life and improve the safety of LMBs. All of these strategies have shown effectiveness, however, considering practicability, these strategies still have some difficulties in large-scale production. These research efforts are generally based on laboratory-grade coin-type cells. The experimental parameters and working environment of coin cell are very different from practical batteries, which cannot provide direct guidance for large-scale application of actual lithium metal batteries in a comprehensive and detailed manner [29]. At the same time, many modification strategies reported in literature involve complex processes and harsh experimental conditions which are generally limited to the laboratory level. Achieving large-scale production of dendrite-free lithium anodes for LMBs applications still remains a formidable challenge [30].

paragraph_context: Carbon materials, including carbon nanotubes [31–33], carbon cloth [34], graphene [35,36], etc, possess the advantages of good conductivity, chemical stability, and structural diversity. Carbon materials have a widespread application in the field of lithium metal batteries due to their lightweight and distinct advantages in raising energy density [37–39]. In previous research, three-dimensional carbon materials with self-supporting structures have been extensively used to construct three-dimensional lithium anode [40–43]. Carbon skeletons not only decrease the local current density owing to their large specific surface area, but also alleviate the volume change during lithium metal deposition by their three-dimensional structure, thus extending the cycle life of the battery [44,45]. However, the large pore volume of three-dimensional carbon skeleton will absorb too much electrolyte that exacerbates electrolyte depletion in a practical cell with lean electrolyte during cycling and causes rapid battery failure. Therefore, it is necessary to design carbon substrates with reduced specific surface area to avoid excessive consumption of electrolyte, while still keeping the function in guiding reversible Li plating/stripping. Graphene is a two-dimensional material that exhibits high electrical conductivity and large specific surface area [46]. Moreover, graphene nanosheets are easy to be assembled with diverse structures for various applications.

paragraph_context: In this work, a thin graphene coating layer was constructed on the surface of lithium metal by slurry coating to form a composite anode (G@Li) with a double-layer structure. Due to the high electrical conductivity of graphene, the deposition position of lithium metal is transferred from the lithium foil to the graphene layer. Benefiting from the large surface area of graphene coating that reduces the local current density, uniform deposition of lithium metal is induced, and generation of dendrites and “dead $\mathbf { L } \mathbf { i } ^ { \ast }$ is reduced. At the same time, the graphene coating layer possesses a loose and porous structure, which is conducive to the stripping of lithium metal underneath it simultaneously, facilitating compensation for the irreversible lithium loss during the cycle by the lithium foil underneath the graphene coating. Thus, the G@Li composite anode exhibits outstanding electrochemical performance and extended lifespan comparing with that of bare Li anode. The G@Li|| NCM811 pouch cell delivers a high capacity retention of 76% after 470 cycles, showing significantly improved cycling stability. The facile preparation method enables large-scale production of graphene coated Li anodes, which offers the prospects of practical applications in lithium metal batteries.

paragraph_context: In lithium-metal batteries, electrochemical side reactions are the main reason for the poor reversibility of lithium. The SEI formed by side reactions between lithium metal and electrolyte and the dendrite growth caused by inhomogeneous deposition reduces the reversibility of the cells [48]. Coulombic efficiency (CE) is a key indicator to evaluate the reversibility of Li plating/stripping in half cells without additional lithium sources. Hence graphene was coated directly on Cu foil (named G@Cu) using the same procedure as that on Li foil (G@Li), and the CE and the cycling stability of Li||G@Cu half cell was measured and compared with that of Li||Cu half cell with no graphene coating on $\mathrm { C u } .$ . As shown in Figs. S4a and S4b, at the current density of 0.5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and capacity of 1 mAh cm− 2 , a high average CE of 95.37% was achieved on Li||G@Cu half cells, while the average CE Li||Cu half cell was merely 89.37%. Meanwhile, the CE of Li||Cu half cell decreased rapidly and fluctuated sharply after 30 cycles. At a higher current density of 1 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and capacity of 1 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (Figs. S4c and S4d), the CE of Li||Cu half cell fluctuated sharply only after 20 cycles with an average CE of 86.30%, and the CE of Li||G@Cu half cell kept steady within 60 cycles with an average value of 96.0%. During the cycling, the irreversible capacity loss mainly comes from the proliferation of SEI, which is ascribed to uneven deposition of lithium metal. Therefore, the above data suggest that deposition reversibility on graphene layers is significantly improved. The deposition morphology of Li plating on copper and G@Cu was also characterized (Fig. S5). Lithium metal deposited on Cu foil was less uniform than deposited on graphene. The surface of Cu foil was covered with dendrites, while only paucity dendrites could be observed on G@Cu at the deposition capacity of 2 mAh cm− 2 .

paragraph_context: To investigate the influence of the micro-structure of graphene coatings on the lithium metal plating/stripping behaviors, the original G@Li anode was roll-pressed to densify the graphene coating, and the as-prepared electrode was named dG@Li. Fig. 3a and b displays that the porous graphene coating in G@Li was transformed to a dense layered structure after compressing, and the thickness of the coating shrunk considerably. Then the Li, dG@Li, G@Li symmetric cells were assembled and a continuous stripping process was applied at a current density of 1.0 mA cm− 2 on these cells. As shown in Fig. 3c, the stripping voltage profile of the dG@Li cell is significantly different from that of the Li and G@Li symmetric cells, which exhibits extremely high polarization voltage of \~0.5 V at the beginning of stripping along with the substantial fluctuation of the voltage throughout the whole stripping process. By replacing the graphene coating with a completely nonporous commercial graphite paper with a thickness of about 20 μm (GP), which is composed of parallel graphene sheets with a dense stacked structure (Fig. S6a), similar voltage curves as that of dG@Li were obtained under the same current density as shown in Fig. S6b. In sharp contrast, the stripping profiles of G@Li and Li exhibit a normal and stable voltage plateau with much lower polarization of \~50 mV. Fig. S7a compares the electrochemical performances of the dG@Li and G@Li symmetrical cells. The symmetric cell with G@Li exhibits more flat voltage profiles and smaller voltage hysteresis, while the dG@Li cell shows serious voltage polarization and cannot work normally. The dG@Li||NCM811 full cell was also assembled, whose discharge capacity rapidly decayed to 0 after 40 cycles (Fig. S7b). Stable plating/stripping voltage hysteresis is observed in the G@Li cells (Fig. 3d and e), the polarization voltages are 28 mV and 30 mV at the 10th and 50th cycle, respectively, presenting a stable lithium metal deposition/stripping process. In contrast, the voltage of the dG@Li cell is extremely unstable and the voltage hysteresis even exceeds 1.0 V. The above results clearly manifest that densification of the graphene coating layer brings about severe polarization to the electrode, as the densely stacked graphene sheets kinetically obstruct electrochemical stripping of lithium metal underneath the graphene layer. Thus, it can be concluded that the threedimensional porous structure is of significant importance to the graphene coatings, which facilitates the stripping of lithium, hence continuous compensation to the irreversible loss active Li can be realized to prolong the cycle life of LMBs (Fig. 3f).

paragraph_context: In summary, a feasible and simple fabrication strategy has been proposed to obtain graphene-coated lithium metal anode with a double layer structure in this work. First, the large surface area of graphene disperses the current density, improves deposition uniformity, and reduces the accumulation of dead lithium. Besides, the porous threedimensional structure of the graphene layer is beneficial to the transport of lithium ions, so that the lithium foil continuously replenishes the irreversible lithium loss during the cycle. Benefiting from the dendritefree and ultra-stable Li plating/strippping on G@Li anode, the corresponding cells show improved electrochemical performances including long cycling life, low voltage hysteresis, and high coulombic efficiency. A practical application of the G@Li has also been realized in pouch cells. The full cells show extraordinary cycling stability and prolonged lifespan over 470 cycles with capacity retention of 76% when matching the NCM811 cathode with a high mass loading of 4 mAh cm− 2 . This strategy offers a promising and efficient way of utilizing graphene in LMAs, showing great application potential of graphene coated lithium metal anode in high-energy and long-life Li metal batteries.

paragraph_context: Reasonable design of light-weight carbon-based current collector is a promising strategy to enable high-energydensity lithium batteries. Herein, carbon-coated ZnO nanotube arrays with good lithiophilicity are constructed on carbon cloth, which is used as anode current collector to construct hybrid lithium ion/lithium metal battery. The modified carbon cloth effectively promotes the formation of robust and inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase, which consists of mixed ionic-electronic conductive (MIEC) interface with ion-conductive $\mathrm { L i _ { 2 } O / L i C _ { 6 } }$ and electron-conductive LiZn alloy. Rapid electron/ion transportation during repeated lithium plating/stripping is realized by the Li2O/LiZn/LiC6 MIEC arrays, which homogenizes the lithium deposition and ensures uniform dendrite-free Li deposition. The three-dimensional structure of the current collector also provides enough space to constrain the lithium deposition and avoid the huge volume change. As a result, continuous anode-electrolyte interfacial side reactions and active lithium loss are effectively suppressed. Uniform Li deposition and high average Coulombic efficiency are achieved in the hybrid lithium ion/lithium metal cell. The capacity retention of full cell with carbonate-based electrolyte maintains 47.0 % after 600 cycles, and the full cell also shows superiority in rate performance and energy density. This work provides a promising alternative for light-weight anode current collector to enable high-energy-density lithium batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The rapid development of mobile electronic terminals and electric vehicles expedites the urgent demand for high-energy-density energy storage devices. Lithium-ion battery (LIB) is the most successful commercial energy storage and power generation equipment because of its comprehensive advantages in energy density, cost and safety [1]. In order to pursue higher energy density, lithium metal, which is a very light metal (0.534 g cm− 3 ) with ultra-high specific capacity (3862 mAh⋅g− 1 ) and low potential (− 3.040V vs standard hydrogen electrode), is considered as an ideal alternative for graphite anode $( 3 7 2 \mathrm { m A h } . \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ in the LIB [2]. However, lithium metal anode faces greatly challenges in the practical application, including formation of lithium dendrites during cycling, excessive usage of lithium metal, severe side reactions with electrolyte and corresponding successive consumption of active lithium/electrolyte [3–6].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The initial anode-free lithium metal battery comes into being to meet the increasing requirements of high energy density, low cost and high safety for the utilization of lithium metal anode [7,8]. By pairing the fully lithiated cathode with bare current collector on the anode side, the capacity ratio of the anode to the cathode (N/P) is initially "0", avoiding excessive usage of lithium foil and other anode electrode materials [9, 10]. Lithium ions extracted from lithium-containing positive electrodes (such as $\mathrm { L i F e P O _ { 4 } , L i C o O _ { 2 } , L i N i _ { x } M n _ { y } O _ { 1 - x - y } O _ { 2 } , }$ etc.) are electroplated on the surface of anode current collector along with the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) during the cycles [11]. Such cells, however, often degrade fast with low Coulombic efficiency and capacity retention due to the active lithium loss, continuous SEI reconstruction and "dead lithium” formation [12]. Hybrid lithium ion/lithium metal batteries are proposed to tackle the problems of low-energy-density in lithium-ion battery and low cycling efficiency in lithium metal battery at once [13]. Rational design of anode current collector is the most straightforward strategy to regulate the lithium behavior at the anode side, which has been demonstrated to be one of the most efficient approaches for the battery performance improvement [14–16]. Copper foil, the commonly used commercial anode current collector, is lithiophobic, which easily induces the formation of lithium dendrites and cell failure. Cui et al. [17] emphasized the importance of overpotential in lithium nucleation and growth based on the classical nucleation theory. The phase field simulation reported by Wang et al. [18] shows that dendritic lithium deposition on planar copper current collector has large concentration polarization and uneven current density distribution. The three-dimensional (3D) microstructure of current collector can change the diffusion path of lithium ions from two-dimensional plane to three-dimension, and the high specific surface area of electroactivity can reduce the actual surface current density. The uniform electric field distribution makes it easy for lithium ions to deposit on the whole surface instead of on the tip or edge, and the electrolyte also penetrates into the skeleton more easily [19]. Meanwhile, the 3D skeleton can avoid stress concentration and evenly disperse stress, and the large internal space can accommodate the large volume expansion and contraction of lithium metal, thus reducing the formation of "dead lithium".

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Although the electrical conductivity and mechanical properties of metal-based 3D skeleton current collector are reasonable, the high weight and instability of 3D microstructure greatly reduces the actual energy density of the battery. Also, the large surface area may induce severe interfacial side reactions between lithium and electrolyte. Carbon materials crosslinked by covalent bonds possess low density, good electrical and thermal conductivity, high structural stability, rich surface functional groups, and so on, which are promising to improve the energy-density and cyclability of lithium batteries [20]. The introduction of lithium-loving sites can directionally induce lithium deposition and inhibit the formation of lithium dendrites [21–23]. Kwon et al. [24] designed an electronic defective carbon paper current collector, in which polycrystalline defects induced uniform SEI formation and homogeneous Li nucleation/growth on the current collector, resulting in increased cycle life of anode free cells. Besides, constructing metal/- metal oxide-based lithiophilic sites in carbon scaffolds can also effectively regulate the deposition of lithium and achieve improved electrochemical performance. For example, Cui et al. [25] explored the lithium nucleation on various metal substrates, and found that metals with strong binding energy with lithium can significantly reduce the nucleation barrier. Although some modification methods have been proposed, it is still challenging to develop appropriate anode current collectors with light weight, high lithiophilicity and controllable lithium deposition.

paragraph_context: Herein, we construct lithiophilic carbon-coated ZnO nanotubes on carbon cloth (C@ZnOnts@CC) by hydrothermal method and it is used as anode current collector without extra active materials in the lithium battery. This design has the following three advantages: (1) Mixed ionicelectronic conductive (MIEC) interface composed of ion-conductive $\mathrm { L i _ { 2 } O / L i C _ { 6 } }$ and electron-conductive LiZn is in-situ formed on the nanotube arrays during the activation process, which ensures fast charge transfer and provides lithiophilic sites to effectively regulate the Li plating/stripping. (2) The carbon-coated ZnO nanotubes can constrain the volume change of lithium metal to reduce the huge volume change during cycling. The channels among the nanotube arrays homogenize the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ distribution, promote uniform lithium deposition and inhibit the growth of lithium dendrites. (3) The 3D skeleton of carbon cloth with high mechanical strength can adapt to the volume change of the battery during cycling and reduce the local current density. The synergistic effect of these three aspects ensures uniform lithium nucleation/plating along with lithiation in carbon cloth, inhibits dendrite growth and volume expansion, and enables hybrid lithium ion/lithium metal battery with excellent electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: The carbon cloth (CeTech WOS1011) was soaked in acetone solution for 24 h in order to remove the sizing agent on the surface of the carbon fiber. The carbon cloth was activated with a mixture of $\mathrm { H _ { 2 } } S \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { : H N } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 } =$ 3:1 (v/v) to provide uniform growth sites for the growth of ZnO. 0.5 M zinc nitrate hexahydrate $\mathrm { ( Z n ( C H _ { 3 } C O O ) _ { 2 } { \bullet 2 H _ { 2 } O ) } }$ and 0.5 M sodium hydroxide were dissolved in anhydrous ethanol respectively to get the ZnO seed layer solution. Then, the two solutions were mixed, vigorously stirred for 30 min at the speed of 500 r/min and stood for 24 h to obtain ZnO seed layer. The carbon cloth was soaked in the seed layer solution for 10 min, then taken out and dried in an oven at ${ 1 0 0 } ^ { \circ } { \bf C } ,$ and soaked three times repeatedly. Hydrothermal growth of ZnO: The carbon cloth impregnated with the seed layer was placed in the ZnO growth solution at $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 h. Growth solution configuration: the concentration of Zn $( \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ) _ { 2 } { \bullet } 6 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ was 36 mM, and the concentration of hexamethylenetetramine was 36 mM. The pH of the growth solution was adjusted to 9 with ammonia water, and ZnO nanorods were grown on the surface of carbon cloth to obtain ZnO nanorods current collector (ZnOnrs@CC). Carbon coating: 70 ml of ethanol, 10 ml of deionized water, and 10 ml of ammonia-water mixture were mixed and stirred magnetically for 10 min. Afterwards, 0.7 g of m-aminophenol powder was added and stirred for 15 min, then 0.49 ml of formaldehyde (37 wt%) was added dropwise. The temperature of the solution was controlled at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (heated in a water bath) and stirred for 12 h, then centrifuged and washed with ethanol and deionized water until neutral, and then dried. Then it was pyrolyzed in Ar at $7 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 2 h to obtain a carbon-coated ZnO nano nanorods current collector (C@ZnOnrs@CC). After cooling, part of the ZnO was partially removed with 1 M HCl, washed to neutrality, and dried at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to obtain a carbon-coated ZnO nanotube current collector (C@ZnOnts@CC). Similar procedure was carried out to prepare C@CC by 0.7 g of m-aminophenol powder and 0.49 ml of formaldehyde.

paragraph_context: Carbon cloth (CC) possesses good mechanical strength and flexibility, and can still maintain integrity after being curled and folded into different shapes (Fig. 1a–b). A strand of carbon fiber (consisting of hundreds of fibers) is tightly woven together, ensuring interconnection between fibers and good integrity of CC. Besides, the density of carbon cloth is much lower than Cu foil and makes it promising for high-energydensity system. Fig. 1c schematically shows the three-step procedure (hydrothermal、carbon coating and etching) to prepare the modified carbon cloth. Firstly, carbon cloth with woven fibers (Fig. 1d) was immersed in the solution of $\mathrm { Z n ( N O _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } { \bullet } 6 H _ { 2 } O , }$ , and ZnO nanorods were grown on bare carbon cloth fibers by hydrothermal method (ZnOnrs@CC, Fig. 1e). Then, ZnO nanorods were coated with resorcinolformaldehyde resin layer as carbon source by alkali-catalyzed aldol condensation, and then annealed in Ar to pyrolyze resorcinolformaldehyde resin and carbonize it into amorphous carbon. The carbon-coated ZnO nanorods (C@ZnOnrs@CC) with diameter of 30\~100 nm were obtained (Fig. 1f). Finally, part of ZnO was etched away by 1 M HCl to get the carbon-coated ZnO nanotubes (C@ZnOnts@CC) on carbon cloth (Fig. 1g). Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) on the C@ZnOnts@CC was collected to further understand the composition and structure. As shown in Fig. 1h–k, O and C are uniformly distributed in the structure of C@ZnOnts@CC. Although the content of zinc is reduced after etching, Zn can still be detected in the structure of C@ZnOnts@CC (Fig. 1j). It shows that C@ZnOnts@CC is mainly composed of O, Zn and C. The carbon content originated from C@ZnOnts is 3.7 % (Fig. S1).

paragraph_context: The bare CC and C@ZnOnts@CC current collectors were assembled into half cells with Li reference electrode to evaluate their electrochemical performance. The initial discharge curve of Li|| C@ZnOnts@CC shows four plateaus around 0.2–2 V (Fig. 4a, Regime I) with extra reaction plateaus compared to that in Li||CC cell. For bare CC, the voltage curve consists of a \~1V solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation plateau following by the slope corresponding to the reaction between Li ions and carbon in CC. For C@ZnOnts@CC, in Regime I, the first SEI formation plateau appears at \~1.65 V (vs. Li+/Li), earlier than that in CC. On one hand, the increased specific surface area of C@ZnOnts@CC (Fig. S3b, 87.85 $ { \mathbf { m } } ^ { 2 } \ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { - 1 } )$ compared to that of CC (Fig. S3a, 18.56 $\mathbf { m } ^ { 2 } ~ \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ will result in increased SEI formation due to extra interfacial side reactions. Also, the defects and heteroatoms introduced by the modification, as revealed by Raman in Figs. 2f and $^ { 3 , }$ could also induce more side reactions at high potentials. [48]. On the other hand, the electronic insulation, which is essentially important to inhibit the transfer of electrons at the interface and reduce the occurrence of side reactions [49] is influenced after the carbon-coated zinc oxide nanotube structure was constructed on carbon cloth, especially at the beginning of the cycling. The dipole moment induced by the coating layer could attract electrons from the substrate to the solution environment [50] which results in more electron transfer. Excessive electron transfer leads to the decomposition of TFSI in the electrolyte, thus promoting a LiF-rich SEI layer. The second plateau appears at \~0.9 V (vs. Li+/Li), which correlates to the reduction reaction between ZnO and $\mathrm { L i , i . e . 2 L i ^ { + } + Z n O + 2 e ^ { - } \mathrm { Z n + L i _ { 2 } O } }$ (Equation (1)). The disappearance of this plateau after the first cycle (Fig. 4c) suggests that this reaction is irreversible. The third plateau appears at \~0.5 V (vs. $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } / L i ) }$ , which represents the alloying reaction between lithium and zinc: $\mathrm { \bf x L i } + \mathrm { \bf Z n } $ LixZn (Equation (2)). The formed LiZn alloy is not only lithiophilic but also electron conductor, which could promote the lithium deposition and the charge transfer in the current collector [51]. Afterwards, the plateau at lower potential around \~0.2 V is related to the lithiation of active carbon in the current collector to generate $\mathrm { L i C } _ { 6 }$ which is also lithiophilic and a good ion conductor [52]. As a result, a mixed ionic-electronic conductive (MIEC) interface is in-situ formed during the initial lithiation in C@ZnOnts@CC. There is a transition regime around 0–0.2 V from lithiation (Regime I) to lithium metal plating (Regime III), which is considered as simultaneous lithium plating and lithiation (Regime II). The complete lithium metal plating (Regime III) is represented by a distinct platform (Fig. 4a), which maintains stable (\~40 % capacity contribution) after the initial cycle (Fig. S4), demonstrating the successful construction of hybrid lithium ion/lithium metal battery.

paragraph_context: The transport kinetics of lithium ion at the electrode/electrolyte interface is highly dependent on the quality of SEI and charge transfer process. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurement was carried out to further study the transport behavior of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ at the electrode/electrolyte interface. In the fresh state, the charge transfer resistance of bare CC is 158.7 Ω, which is about twice that of C@ZnOnts@CC (79.3 Ω, Fig. 4h). The linear slope of C@ZnOnts@CC in the low frequency region is obviously larger than that of bare $\mathrm { C C } ,$ indicating fast mass transfer in the C@ZnOnts@CC cell as well. This may be related to the good conductivity and lithiophilicity of LiZn/Li2O arrays formed on the nanotubes in C@ZnOnts@CC, which promotes the diffusion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ . After 50 cycles at 1 mA cm− 2 /4mAh⋅cm− $^ { - 2 } ,$ with the formation of stable SEI, there are two typical semicircles and one slope corresponding to the interfacial impedance of SEI $( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { S E I } } )$ at high frequency regime, charge transfer resistance $\scriptstyle ( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { C T } } )$ at middle frequency regime, and mass transfer at low frequency regime (Fig. 4i). The $\mathtt { R } _ { \mathtt { S E I } }$ of bare CC (7.5Ω) is higher than that of C@ZnOnts@CC (3.1Ω), which could originate from the side reactions between lithium and electrolyte and the accumulation of resistive SEI and dead lithium in the Li||CC cell. The $\operatorname { R } _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ of both samples decreases after cycling due to the formation of conductive SEI. However, the bare CC still shows higher $\operatorname { R } _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ (59.3 Ω) than C@ZnOnts@CC (15.7Ω), further demonstrating the superiority of the modified current collector in constructing beneficial interface for accelerated interfacial charge transfer. In addition, the modified layer on C@ZnOnts@CC also effectively improves the mass transfer kinetics during cycling. These improvements by the carbon-coated ZnO nanotubes on carbon cloth contribute to the stable Li plating/stripping, and prolong the cycle stability of the half cells.

paragraph_context: In summary, carbon-coated ZnO nanotube arrays with good lithium affinity were constructed on carbon cloth (C@ZnOnts@CC) by simple hydrothermal method and thermal treatment, which is used as the anode current collector in hybrid lithium ion/lithium metal batteries. The modified current collector can effectively promote the formation of robust and inorganic-rich SEI, which consists of mixed ion and electron conduction (MIEC) interface composed of ion-conductive $\mathrm { L i _ { 2 } O / L i C _ { 6 } }$ and electron-conductive LiZn alloy. This significantly facilitates the rapid electron/ion transportation during repeated lithium plating/stripping. The nanotubular arrays homogenize the lithium deposition and ensure uniform dendrite-free Li deposition. Additionally, the three-dimensional structure of C@ZnOnts@CC provides enough space to limit the lithium deposition and avoid the huge volume change. As a result, continuous interfacial side reactions with electrolyte and active lithium loss are successfully suppressed and high average Coulombic efficiency of 98.54 % is achieved after 150 cycles in the Li||C@ZnOnts@CC half-cell. In addition, the capacity retention of 47 % over 600 cycles is realized for the NCM811||C@ZnOnts@CC full cell with carbonate-based electrolyte. The cell also shows superiority in rate performance. This work opens up a new prospect for developing light current collector to improve the energy density as well as the lifetime of lithium batteries for the nextgeneration energy storage devices.

paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries represent potential candidates for high-energy–density batteries. However, non-uniform Li deposition and dendrite growth limit the practical applications of Li anodes in solid-state and liquid-phase battery systems. This report investigates the conversion mechanism of an aluminum coordination compound (Al(MMP)3) at the interface of a lithium metal anode. Based on the proposed mechanism, a novel dual alloy comprising a LixAl-LixP hybrid interphase is designed to promote interfacial charge balance. Under the synergic effect of a fluoropolymer, the organic/inorganic protective layer containing the dual lithiated alloy exhibits short-term Li storage and rapid Li+ transport, thereby limiting the accumulation of inactive lithium and decreasing the Li+ migration barrier. Upon implementing the hybrid anode, the electrochemical life span of the Li metal battery exceeds 2000 h. Moreover, pairing with a Ni-rich cathode leads to excellent capacity retention and stable coulomb efficiency. The developed strategy can guide future advancements in lithium metal batteries with long cycle lives.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the increasing demand for electronic devices and electric vehicles, high-energy–density rechargeable batteries have emerged as a critical technology. Lithium metal batteries are regarded as one of the most promising high-energy–density batteries owing to the low electrode potential (–3.04 V vs. SHE) and relatively high theoretical capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ) of lithium metal [1–6]. The lithium metal anode is an attractive alternative to other Li-based batteries, such as Li–air [7] and Li–S batteries [8]. However, because of undesirable interface compatibility [9–11], the formation of Li dendrites upon cycling [12–13], and fast depletion of the electrolyte [14–15], lithium metal batteries are generally inefficient in many practical applications.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Recently, significant research efforts have been devoted to constructing stable lithium anode interfaces by addressing these issues, e.g., by introducing functional liquid electrolyte additives [16–18], an artificial solid-electrolyte interface (SEI) layer [19–21], or a hybrid lithium metal anode [22–23]. To a certain extent, these strategies can suppress the growth of lithium dendrites, reduce electrolyte consumption, and improve cycling performance. However, the derived ionic conductor protective layer still causes lithium accumulation after long-term cycling because the anisotropic morphological characteristics facilitate the migration of lithium ions [3] and promote local cracking of the SEI. Additionally, the continuous side reaction between the electrolyte and exposed fresh lithium may generate inactive lithium and a thicker SEI. All of these issues can be attributed to the structural anisotropy of the SEI layer, which leads to non-uniform charge distribution and Li+ migration. Therefore, the development of an interface layer with balanced charge distribution and ion conduction is crucial. The formation and evolution of such a layer are related to the interface stability between the electrolyte and the electrode [24–25]. Lithium metal alloying is an effective approach for mitigating the infinite consumption of the lithium meal anode [26–27]. The alloying reaction, which is different from intercalation chemistry, allows the alloyed lithium anode to participate in a valence transformation, thus leading to high conductivity [28]. The alloy phase with high conductivity is beneficial for charge distribution, which prevents non-uniform ion migration. However, most lithium alloy phases in SEIs cannot exhibit valence transformations because of the weak electron tunneling effect in the SEI layer. As a result, the lithium alloy interphase layer generally cannot regulate interfacial Li deposition or control the charge distribution unless it is combined with a conductive material, such as graphene oxide [29]. Therefore, an interphase capable of charge regulation is crucial in high-energy–density battery systems with lithium metal anodes. However, the rational design of an interphase layer that promotes uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ migration is a major challenge because the Li+ migration is driven by electric field forces that are closely related to charge distribution.

paragraph_context: In the present study, a unique hybrid protective film was prepared on a lithium metal anode to minimize side reactions and regulate the electrochemical lithium deposition behavior by introducing an aluminum coordination compound $( \mathrm { A l } ( \mathrm { M M P } ) _ { 3 } )$ . This hybrid film comprised a flexible fluoropolymer (TGD) and $\mathrm { { A l } ( M M P ) _ { 3 } , }$ which together were converted in situ to a polymer/dual alloy of $\mathrm { L i _ { x } A l - L i _ { x } P }$ hybrid interphase. This hybrid interphase exhibits several advantages. First, trifluoroethyl methacrylate (TFEMA) in a fluoropolymer with a large HOMO–LUMO gap [30] is an excellent alternative for creating films because it can relieve the volume expansion of lithium metal during cycling, and it can generate an LiF-rich phase through the defluorination of terminal C–F functional groups. Second, the aluminum coordination compound reacts with the Li metal anode to build a dual lithiated alloy interphase that exhibits short-term $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ storage and fast $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport, which can regulate charge distribution and ensure uniform electrodeposition. Finally, the hybrid interphase can accelerate significant planar crystalline grain growth instead of small vertical growth during cycling, and this interphase does not crack easily, even after long-term cycling. Owing to the modified TGD/Al(MMP)3 interphase layer, Li deposition adopted a dendrite-free morphology, which prolonged its cycle life. Moreover, pairing with a Ni-rich NCM811 cathode led to excellent capacity retention at high current density. This work enables uniform Li deposition in typical commercial electrolytes and provides a reliable strategy to support the practical application of lithium metal anodes.

The Al (MMP)3 exhibits the lowest LUMO (–2.03 eV) energy among the main species in the hybrid film; this result rationalizes its high electron affinity and confirms that the Al(MMP)3 can be preferentially reduced on a lithium metal anode. In addition, the relatively high LUMO energy of DMMP suggests that the reducibility of DMMP solvent on the surface of the lithium anode is weaker than that of Al(MMP) . Furthermore, the LUMO energy of the TGD polymer (–0.51 eV) was between that of poly-1,3-dioxolane (PDOL; –0.14 eV) and TFEMA (–1.89 eV) owing to the effects of electron withdrawing groups. The TGD polymer had a larger gap HOMO–LUMO energy gap (7.25 eV) than the electrolyte-derived SEI [21,30], which justifies its excellent stability. The LUMO energies of $\mathrm { i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P }$ (–0.41 eV) and LiP (–3.62 eV) indicate that the Li P is relatively more stable on the lithium metal anode compared with LiP. However, a phase transition occurs between Li P and LiP, suggesting that the ionic/electron mixed conductor in the interface layer plays a key role. Owing to the negatively-charged nature of the Li metal surface, any species in direct coordination with positive charges can be preferentially reduced to construct a sustainable SEI on the lithium metal anode surface [33]. paragraph_context: The conversion of an aluminum coordination compound (i.e., Al (MMP)3) at the interface of a lithium metal anode enabled the construction of a polymer/dual alloy of $\mathbf { L i } _ { \mathbf { x } } \mathbf { A l - L i } _ { \mathbf { x } } \mathbf { P }$ hybrid interphase layer. The $\mathrm { { A l } ( M M P ) _ { 3 } }$ coordination compound with a low LUMO energy level formed a dual lithiated alloy hybrid interphase comprising $\operatorname { L i } _ { \mathbf { X } } \operatorname { A l }$ and Li P/LiP after cycling; this interphase was beneficial for Li deposition because it promoted uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ migration by regulating charge redistribution. The $\operatorname { L i } _ { \mathbf { X } } \operatorname { A l }$ supports electron transfer, which allows for in situ conversion from LiP to Li P. The high ionic conductivity of Li P facilitates short-term $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ storage and fast $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transmission, which allow Li+ to rapidly and uniformly pass through the interphase layer and deposit on the Li anode. In addition, the $\mathrm { \bf A l { ( M M P ) } _ { 3 } }$ also could trigger the crosslinking of fluoropolymer (TGD), the TGD polymer can reinforce the flexible and rigid hybrid interphase. Owing to the synergistic action of a flexible TGD polymer, the accumulation of inactive lithium can be avoided after long-term cycling. In the $\mathrm { T G D / A l ( M M P ) _ { 3 } \mathrm { - } L i | | C u }$ cell, a dense and uniform Li deposition morphology was observed on the anode surface. The Li||Li symmetrical cell exhibited ultralow overpotential (\~20 mV over 2000 h). These results confirmed that the TGD/Al (MMP) -modified interphase exhibited excellent shelter and charge balance capabilities. Moreover, the Li||NCM811 cell demonstrated outstanding capacity retention (>70% after 500 cycles) and stable CE, which further verified that the TGD/Al(MMP) -modified interphase can promote uniform Li deposition. Overall, the developed method provides a guiding reference for Li metal anode protection in high-energy–density batteries.

paragraph_context: Keywords: Quasi-metallic Li Subnanopore Confinement effect Hybrid anode Li metal anodes The commercial application of Li metal anodes (LMAs) has been impeded by the irreversible side reactions, uncontrolled dendrite growth, and large volume changes. In this work, we utilize sub-nanometer confinement to address these challenges by encapsulating quasi-metallic Li (denoted as QM–Li) in the subnanopores of hard carbon (HC). The sub-nanometer pores can effectively prevent the contact between electrolyte and QM–Li, provide large pore volume for QM–Li storage, and restrain the dendrite growth. Therefore, the HC hybrid anode realizes a high Coulombic efficiency of 99.7% in half cell over 240 cycles in ester electrolyte. When coupled with LiNi Co Mn O (NCM811), the assembled full cell exhibits good cycling stability over 200 cycles with 0.1% capacity decay per cycle. The sub-nanometer confinement effect provides new route for practical LMAs.

paragraph_context: Based on the high reversibility of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ion insertion/extraction reactions, graphite is the current commercial anode material in Li–ion batteries (LIBs) because of its high stability and low cost. Unfortunately, the energy density of graphite-based anode is approaching its theoretical limit (372 mAh ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ [1–3]. Among the candidates, metallic Li is quite promising owing to its high theoretical capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ) and the lowest electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V vs RHE) [4,5]. However, the application of Li metal anode (LMA) suffers from the irreversible side reactions between Li and electrolyte, uncontrollable dendrite growth, and inevitable large volume changes, resulting in the low Coulombic efficiency (CE), short circuit, “dead Li” and safety issues. To address these issues, various strategies including three-dimensional (3D) current collectors or host [6–10], artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers [11–16], electrolyte optimization [17–21] have been developed.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Among these available strategies, 3D porous carbons have been considered as promising hosts to guide the Li plating by regulating the electric filed [22–25]. In addition, lithiophobic surface of 3D porous carbon can be further modified to regulate the Li nucleation behavior [26–28]. Nevertheless, the high surface area of 3D porous carbon is favorable to sides reactions between deposited metallic Li and electrolyte. Many sagacious researchers explore new strategies to construct graphite-based Li hosts with low surface area [29–33]. With the help of localized high concentration electrolyte for the robust SEI, the CE of Li plating/stripping on the lithiated graphite can reach the high value of 99% and maintain over 100 cycles [34]. Cui and coworkers employed artificial graphite (AG) with internal macropores to achieve the preferential Li-metal deposition inside, reducing direct contact with organic electrolyte [35]. However, the intrinsic side reactions between plated Li and electrolyte are still challenging for LMAs, especially in the ester electrolyte. Coincidentally, the Li can nucleate and grow on the surface of graphite during overcharging process in LIB, which is the intricate safety hazard for LIBs. Surprisingly, hard carbon (HC) anode can effectively reduce the Li nucleation and growth phenomenon on its surface during overcharging process in LIB because its microstructure which can accommodate a certain amount of quasi-metallic Li (denoted as QM–Li). Therefore, chemical state and reversibility of QM–Li in HC deserve indepth study, which is crucial to both the LIBs and LMAs.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, we demonstrate that the sub-nanometer confinement can significantly improve the performance of HC based hybrid LMA. HC possesses abundant subnanopores for the encapsulation of QM–Li $\mathrm { ( L i C _ { x } , }$ $2 \leq x < 6 )$ . The limited pore size of sub-nanometer structure of HC could effectively prevent the contact between QM–Li and electrolyte for reduced side reactions. paragraph_context: Lithium powder is a suitable candidate for anode material to suppress the formation of dendritic lithium and alleviate the volume changes. Here, a novel strategy for designing the lithium powder anode stabilized by electrospun membrane (LP@EM LPA) is reported. The lithium powder prepared via a middle-temperature emulsification method is embedded into electrospun membrane to obtain stable three-dimensional network structure that can enhance the interface stability between separator and lithium metal anode, thus leading to improve electrochemical performance for lithium metal batteries (LMBs). The LP@EM LPA can guide the regular lithium-ion distribution and uniform lithium deposition. As a result, the Li//Li symmetric cells present a superior inhibition of dendritic lithium with good long-term cyclic stability for 800 h at current density of 0.2 mA cm− 2 . Furthermore, the Li//LiCoO and $\mathrm { L i } / / \mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ asymmetric cells deliver an outstanding cycle performance and rate capability. This methodology may be useful in designing high specific energy anode for nextgeneration LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In the past several decades, the shortage of fossil fuels and carbon emissions are driving reasons for developing renewable electrochemical power source [1–3]. Recently, rechargeable batteries including zinc-air batteries, sodium-ion batteries, and lithium batteries have been reported by Yasin and Zhao [4–7]. In particular, rechargeable lithium batteries have been widely studied owing to their high energy density and high voltage, such as lithium ion batteries (LIBs), lithium metal batteries (LMBs), lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, and so on [8–11]. Thereinto, LMBs become one of the most promising lithium secondary batteries because of their lowest redox potential (-3.04 V vs H /2H+) and superhigh theoretical specific density (3860 mAh $g ^ { - 1 } )$ [12–16]. However, conventional LMA with a plain foil exists severe volume change and inevitable lithium dendrites growth during cycling process, resulting in poor Coulombic efficiency (CE) and even safety issues [17–19]. To overcome these shortcomings, many strategies were designed and developed, such as using functional electrolyte, polymer electrolytes, inorganic electrolyte, modified separator, LMA interphase engineering, and so forth [20–26]. For example, Yasin et al. [27] systematically introduced the suppress strategies toward stable LMA. Du et al. [28] prepared silver nanowire/Li composite anode material to obtain dendrite-free LMA, which can achieve uniform lithium deposition during lithium deposition and stripping. Hu et al. [29] constructed an artificial hybrid LiF/Li Sb layer in stabilizing the LMA under practical high-rate condition for Li-S batteries. Another approach for using the LMAs is to transfer the lithium foil anode into lithium powder anode (LPA), thus leading to obtain a high surface area, which can effectively reduce the current density during lithium electrodeposition and electrodissolution [30–32]. The cavity structure among particles within LPA can also alleviate volume change during cycling process. Moreover, the lithium powder can be compatible with electrode preparation process and it also has the convenience to easily mix with functional additives [33–35].

paragraph_context: In recent years, the preparation of lithium powder (LP) and the modification of LPA have been reported. For example, Li et al. [33] prepared LP by using top-down method. Subsequently, the LPA was fabricated by mixing 80 wt% LP and 20 wt% CNT and then pressing into a pellet. Compared with the lithium metal foil anode, the obtained LPA can enhance electroactive surface areas, alleviate the volume changes, and further improve the cycling performance. Jin et al. [36] fabricated LPA by using 97 wt% stabilized Li-metal powder (SLMP) and 3 wt% polyimide (PI) polymeric binders. Their results showed that PI binders can generate a uniform protective layer on the exposed Li-powdercoated surfaces and act as a three-dimensional buffer layer, which can alleviate volume change and improve the cohesion among lithium powder particles. Pu et al. [37] fabricated the LP with nano-scale by using a cryomilling approach in liquid nitrogen atmosphere. The asprepared LPA delivers extraordinarily low overpotential at current density of 10 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (about 50 mV, 30 mAh cm− 2 ) and excellent cycle life (1200 h). After assembling with $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811) cathode, the LPA//NCM811 full cell remains a high specific capacity of 180 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and a capacity retention of 92.7 % after 350 cycles. Moreover, the LPA//NCM811 full cell also exhibits superior rate capability. Lee et al. [38] prepared LP by using a droplet emulsion technique and the LPA was formed by compacting the LP on a stainless steel mesh collector. In comparison with Li-metal foil anode, the LPA cells present higher capacities for Li-graphite and $\mathrm { L i } { - } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ cells. The capacity enhancement is attribute to the high Li-ion flux between the cathode and the anode. However, these preparation methods of LP are generally relative harsh, which are not conducive to large-scale production. Therefore, the development of fabrication methodology of LP and corresponding LPA has currently become exceedingly in demand for carrying out the next-generation LMBs.

paragraph_context: Commercial graphite hosting excessive Li is a promising hybrid Li-ion/Li metal anode for high energy battery. Nevertheless, the issue of Li plating on the top surface of the graphite anode (Gra) is not well tackled, resulting in the uncontrollable growth of Li dendrites and accumulation of “dead Li”, as well as the deactivation of graphite particles. In this work, an insulating ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer (EVOH) layer is head-mounted covered on the graphite anode surface (Gra-OH) via a simple spray coating method. Due to the electron retarding ability of EVOH film, the top surface of the graphite host is passivated and the excessive Li can be well accommodated inside the porous structure of graphite host. Meanwhile, the lithiophilic –OH group of EVOH can regulate the Li+ flux and render the uniform Li plating behavior. Featuring these, the Gra-OH anodes with a Li storage capacity of 600 mAh/g show high Coulombic efficiencies (CEs) in both coin-cell and pouch cell even under carbonate electrolyte condition. When operating in Li-ion working mode, higher capacity retentions are readily achieved in the half-cell, full-cell and 5 Ah NCM811 pouch-cell, further demonstrating the application compatibility of this surface passivated Gra-OH anode.

paragraph_context: The excessive consumption of fossil energy and the widespread installed renewable power facilities have promoted the prosperity of electrochemical energy storage systems, including lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), in the energy market [1–6]. By virtue of easy processibility and low cost, graphite has emerged as a dominant anode material for LIBs [7]. Theoretically, it is well-known that the intercalation of Li+ into the graphite materials can deliver a low theoretical specific capacity (<372 mAh/g) when the operating potential of the graphite anode is located above 0 V [8–11]. Such limited intercalation capacity currently cannot meet the increasing demand for electrochemical energy storage systems with high energy density [12,13]. On the other hand, especially for thick electrode at high current rates, the real potential of the graphite anode easily falls below the threshold of Li plating (0 V vs. Li/Li+) owing to the enlarged ohmic drop, concentration gradient overpotential and charge transfer overpotential [8,14,15]. Thus, Li ions shall be reduced to metallic Li instead of intercalated into the layered graphite [16]. In light of the uneven Li+ concentration distribution and shorter ion diffusion path, Li+ prefers to be reduced and deposited on the surface of the conductive graphite anode [17–19]. Similar to Li metal anode (LMA) [20–24], the uneven Li deposition can form some protrusions and gradually evolve into Li dendrites. The uncontrollable dendrite growth would inevitably produce the “dead Li” and thus deactivate the graphite particles during the repeated cycling process, lowering the Coulombic efficiency (CE) and safety threshold of the cell [25–27]. Meanwhile, the large volume changes accompanied with the excessive breakdown/ buildup of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) occurs frequently, further deteriorating the cyclic stability [8,28,29]. Therefore, the uncontrollable Li deposition in graphite anode is obnoxious, regarding the commercial application [30,31]. Improving the safety performance of graphite anode and exploring the graphite based high-capacity anode materials are of great significance.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Currently, the composite of graphite and high-capacity silicon can not only enhance the energy density of the commercial graphite in LIBs, but also buffer the dimensional expansion of silicon active material [32–34]. However, a pre-lithiation treatment is generally required, as the specific capacity of the graphite/silicon composite is higher considering the intrinsic low CE of silicon active material. Alternatively, Dahn et al. proposed a novel anode system by using commercial graphite as the host for Li plating, calling as hybrid Li-ion/Li metal anode. In terms of both Li-ion intercalation and Li metal plating reactions, this hybrid anode accompanied with a dual-salt electrolyte can provide 20 % higher energy–density than conventional LIBs [35]. Meanwhile, the fabrication process of this hybrid Li-ion/metal anode is highly compatible with that of commercial LIB anode. Moreover, the graphite host can in-situ transform into the lithiophilic $\mathrm { L i C } _ { 6 }$ with high ion diffusion rate [36], thus rendering the smooth Li growth in hybrid anode[19,36]. These factors can result in the wide concerns on this hybrid anode for accelerating its commercial application [30,36–38]. Li et al. fabricated a porous graphite layer (PGL) on Cu foil for hybrid Li-ion/metal anodes. Due to the abundant inner space, 30 % amount of excess Li can be well accommodated in the PGL host [36]. Zhang et al. systematically investigated the boundary of Li plating in graphite electrodes with the localized high concentration electrolytes (LHCE) for battery safety, realizing a highly reversible Li plating/stripping process, even with a 25 % capacity increasement [8]. Wang et al reported a graphite-Li metal hybrid anode by combining an optimized SEI and preset void in the composite electrodes. As a result, the accumulation of dead Li was retarded and the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ insertion channels was retained, contributing a high average CE of \~ 98.5 % for 85 cycles [38]. While the conventional conductive hosts (such as Ni foam, Cu foam, Cu mesh and porous carbon) of LMBs always need to be decorated with the additional lithiophilic species, due to the inherent lithiophobic or weak lithiophilic nature [39,40], making the handling and manufacturing process more challenging. Moreover, the benefits of ultrahigh specific capacity of the hybrid anode are often negated owing to the high mass density and large volume of these conventional porous hosts (as illustrated in Fig. 1a) [41,42]. Noteworthy, as shown in Fig. 1b, the “top-depositing” of Li frequently occurs on the surface of these hosts including graphite, resulting in the underutilization of inner space of host scaffold and uncontrollable growth of Li dendrites. It is inevitable to further improve the safety and electrochemical performance of the hybrid Li-ion/Li metal anode towards practical applications. Moreover, the deep insight on the deposition/stripping behavior of Li in this hybrid anode is also lacked.

paragraph_context: In this work, through a simple spray coating method, the insulating ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer (EVOH) film is head-mounted coated on the graphite anode surface (Gra-OH). As schematically illustrated in Fig. 1c, the insulating EVOH film can passivate the surface of the graphite host by retarding the electrons migration. Owing to the headmounted architecture, the inner electric/ionic conducting pathways of graphite anode was undisturbed and the inherent porous structure of graphite host was well-preserved for the subsequently Li accommodating. Consequently, the surface deposition of metallic Li was forbidden and the reduced Li was allocated in the porous Gra-OH host, leading to high host space utilization and the reduced volume variation. Besides, the inherent lithiophilic functional groups of –OH of EVOH can further regulate the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux distribution and facilitate the uniform Li deposition behaviour [43,44]. Meanwhile, the initial CE was improved due to pre-formation of an artificial solid electrolyte interface (SEI). Benefiting from these merits, the issues of uncontrollable growth of Li dendrites and accumulation of “dead Li”, as well as the deactivation of graphite particles were readily addressed. Under the carbonate electrolyte condition, the Gra-OH/Li hybrid anode with a Li capacity of 600 mAh/g (\~3 mAh cm− 2 ) can show a high average CE of 98. 9 % for 140 cycles in coin cell, with the good reversibility of Li plating/stripping over the successive 55 cycles in pouch cell. When paired with high mass loading LFP cathode $( 1 0 . 5 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ , the hybrid Gra-OH/Li|LFP full cell endows outstanding capacity retention of 77.4 % over 270 cycles. Moreover, the industrial application compatibility in Li-ion working mode was investigated. Both of the half-cells and LFP-full-cells based on the Gra-OH anodes exhibit higher capacity retentions and enhanced rate performances, while the 5 Ah Gra-OH|NCM811 pouch cell also confirms improved cycling stability than that of pristine Gra anode.

paragraph_context: Commercial graphite powder was purchased without further treatment. The pristine graphite electrode (Gra) was fabricated via a typical cast-coating method by mixing the graphite powder, super P, and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder (8:1:1, mass ratio) in N-methyl-2- pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent. Cu foil was selected as the current collector, and the average mass loading of active material was about 5.0 mg⋅cm− 2 . After blade-casting, the as-prepared electrode was vacuum dried at 80 ◦C for 12 h. For the surface passivation treatment, a certain amount of the insulative polymer of EVOH was firstly dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) solvent at $6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to form a 1 wt% homogeneous solution. Subsequently, the as-formed EVOH solution was sprayed onto the graphite anode. After drying quickly in the oven at $6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ the Gra-OH electrode with head-mounted coating layer was successfully prepared. In addition, the conventional LFP cathode was also fabricated by the same slurry blade-casting method, without subsequent spray coating. Specially, the mass ratio of LFP powder, super P, and PVDF binder was 8: 1: 1 and the areal loading of active material was about 10.5 mg cm− 2 .

paragraph_context: The microstructures of the pristine graphite electrode and the EVOH head-mounted coated electrode were investigated by SEM imaging from top view and cross-sectional view, as illustrated in Fig. 2a–f. The graphite particles stacked together to form a porous structure with the abundant microscale pores (Fig. 2a-c), serving as the host to provide enough space for Li plating. The small particles, adhering to the graphite particles were attributed to the conductive additives (Fig. 2b). In Fig. ${ \displaystyle 2 \mathbf { c } } ,$ the thickness of the graphite layer on Cu foil was around 50 µm. After spray coating, the surface of the micro-sized graphite particles becomes smoother, with the contour easily identified (Fig. 2d and e). Moreover, the porous structure of the electrode was fully preserved without the obvious change in thickness (Fig. 2f), suggesting the thin coating layer was conformally covered on the anode surface without filling up the inner voids. In order to determine the coverage area of the coating layer, EDS element mapping was conducted. Since the graphite particle and EVOH shared the same carbon element, $\mathrm { \bf A g N O _ { 3 } }$ was chosen as staining agent and mixed in the EVOH solution for spray coating. As exhibited in Figure S1, C, F and O elements were dispersed homogeneously in the whole electrode while Ag element was mostly distributed in the upper part of the electrode, demonstrating the EVOH layer was successfully head-mounted coated on the graphite anode rather than infiltrating the whole electrode.

paragraph_context: XPS analysis was implemented to visually demonstrate the successful coating of EVOH. As shown in Fig. S2a, the C 1 s spectra displayed two fitting peaks at the binding energy of 284.5 and 290.5 eV, assigned to C = C & C-C bond and $\pi { - } \pi ^ { * }$ excitation, respectively. paragraph_context: For the hybrid Li-ion/metal anode, hosting excess Li was inevitable to realize high capacity via Li-ion intercalation and Li metal plating working mechanism. In order to balance the relationship between the capacity and cycling life, and further validate the improvement of Li plating/stripping behaviors under this novel head-mounted coating layer, Gra anode and Gra-OH anode with different amounts of Li deposition and dissolution were characterized by SEM. As shown in Fig. 3a and $\mathbf { b } ,$ when lithiated with a specific capacity of 400 mAh/g, the surface morphology of the Gra-OH electrode was still porous, without obvious change, as compared with the pristine Gra-OH electrode. With the capacity of Li plating increased to 500 mAh/g, the voids among the graphite particles became smaller and the conformal deposition of Li layer on the graphite particles was clearly observed. When the lithiated capacity was promoted up to 600 mAh/g, the graphite particles become wrapped up and the pores of Gra-OH were uniformly filled with Li metal. Remarkably, the pristine contour of graphite particles was unrecognized, suggestive of the maximum allowed capacity. As exhibited in Fig. 3g and ${ \mathrm { h } } ,$ some tubular-shaped species were gradually evolved and aggregated, when plating with 700 mAh/g of Li, ascribed to the growth of Li dendrites due to the inadequate internal space for Li deposition. Therefore, 600 mAh/g of lithiated capacity was used as the standard testing condition for subsequent electrochemical tests of Gra-OH electrodes, to balance capacity and lifespan. As a comparison, even though the pristine graphite electrode was lithiated with a limited capacity of 400 mAh/g (Fig. S5a and b), the deposited Li metal was significantly inclined to accumulate on the electrode surface. This tendency became obvious, while some tubular-shaped dendrites were observed with the lithiated capacity up to 500 mAh/g (Fig. S5c and d). Further increasing Li capacity to 600 and 700 mAh/g, it’s illustrated in Fig. S4e-h, the dendrites were evolved and unevenly agglomerated into porous chunks, and ultimately conglutinated on the surface of the electrode. Such random Li plating behavior can accelerate the production of a large amount of dead Li or side reaction sediments, further deactivate the Li intercalation into graphite and reduce the cyclic reversibility [15].

paragraph_context: The uneven Li plating behavior and the poor cycling reversibility of Gra electrode were further confirmed by the side perspectives. As exhibited in Fig. S5i and ${ \bf j } ,$ for the Gra electrode with a 600 mAh/g capacity of Li, a large amount of Li chunks with dendrites were formed, preferring to deposit on the top surface. The pore structure inside the electrode was still visible, indicative of the underutilization of inner space in the host scaffold. After Li atoms were fully stripped, the apparent Li residuals adhering and stacking on the surface of graphite anode were identified (Fig. S5k and l). On the contrary, even loading with 600 mAh/g capacity of $\operatorname { L i } ,$ the GRA-OH anode delivered the homogeneous and tightly packed cross-section morphologies, with almost unchanged overall thickness of the electrode (around 51 μm). Metallic Li was well hosted inside the pores of the Gra-OH electrode, instead of growing on the top surface (Fig. 3i and j). Under the stripping to cut-off voltages, the dead Li residues can be hardly observed and the porous structure of pristine Gra-OH electrode was recovered (Fig. 3k and l). These results suggest the electric insulative EVOH protective layer can passivate the electrode surface and avoid Li preferential deposition on the graphite electrode surface, thus endowing high Li accommodation ability of the internal pore space of the graphite host. On the other hand, graphite without surface modification is always regarded as a lithiophobic material, which can show super lithiophilic after intercalated with Li+ [47,48]. Therefore, combining with the lithiophilic –OH group of EVOH, the lithiophilic Gra-OH anode can not only facilitate $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer and regulate $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux, but also reduce the nucleation barrier of Li and smooth the Li plating process. Benefiting from the Li confinement effect of the host and the dendrite-free plating behavior, high Li reversibility would be achieved during cycling.

paragraph_context: To further evaluate the compatibility of this novel designed headmounted coated anode, the as-prepared anodes were operated in lithium-ion battery mode. Fig. 7a-b illustrate the related CEs of the Gra and the Gra-OH based half cells during the initial two cycles. As expected, the head-mounted coating layer of EVOH can not only passivate the surface of the electrode, and thus induce the deposition of Li inside the host, but also provide as an artificial SEI film attached on the upper surface of the electrode, leading to the reduced electrolyte consumption and the improved reversibility of Li intercalation/de-intercalation reaction. Therefore, the EVOH modified graphite anode showed higher CEs of 84.5 % and 98.1 % than pure graphite anode during SEI formation cycles. We also purchased commercial graphite anodes (5.8 mg cm− 2 ) for surface passivation modification and tested the related electrochemical performances in Li-ion batteries. As shown in Fig. 7c, when cycled at low current density of 0.1, 0.2 and $0 . 5 \mathrm { C } ( 1 \mathrm { C } = 3 4 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ , the specific capacities of Gra-OH anode were only slightly higher than that of pure graphite anode. This could be originated from the thin headmounted insulating coating layer, which prevents the Li nucleation on the electrode surface and has little effect on the conductivity inside the electrode, thus leading to the less formation of Li metal and the complete intercalation of Li ions into the graphite. Thereby, these two anodes delivered minor irreversibility of Li consumption, revealing the same intercalation capacity contribution at low current densities. Nevertheless, inferior rate performances were observed in Gra anode when the current density was increased to 1 and $^ { 2 \mathrm { C } , }$ which should be assigned to the emerged Li depositing since the high current rate can induce the plating on the electrode surface preferentially, resulting in severe side reactions. Fig. 7d assesses the cycling performances of these two electrodes at 1C. Benefiting from the artificial SEI formation and the surface passivation, the Li plating behavior is modulated and suppressed for the Gra-OH anode. Hence, the Gra-OH anode realizes a prolonged cycling life of over 200 cycles with a superior capacity retention of 89.7 %, observably outperforming the Gra anode (dropped dramatically after 150 cycles).

In contrast, the Gra-OH electrode harvested an outstanding cycling behavior with a higher capacity retention of 74.5 %. The corresponding voltage-capacity curves under diverse cycles were also summarized in Figures S13c and d. Unlike the hybrid Li anodes assembled full cells (Fig. 8c and d), all the charge/ discharge curves represent only a pair of charge/discharge plateaus, manifesting the typical Li-ion working mechanism. Obviously, all the discharge/charge plateaus of the Gra|LFP were deducted with a larger voltage hysteresis gap in contrasted to Gra-OH|LFP, suggesting the intensified dendrites growth on the bare electrode surface induced the accumulation of dead Li, resulting in the increased polarization and accelerated degradation of the graphite particles. To evaluate the practical performance of Gra-OH anode in pouch cells, two different types of pouch cells were assembled separately. As shown in Fig. 8e, a 5 Ah pouch cell was assembled by a spray-coated commercial graphite anode and a high mass loading NCM811cathode (23.8 mg cm− 2 ). Notably, with the increasement of the current, the uneven Li precipitation and aggravation on the surface of the electrode would be exacerbated. However, due to the passivation of the EVOH coating layer, the surface Li deposition can be greatly reduced. Therefore, the Gra-OH| NCM811 pouch cell exhibits a boosted capacity retention, as compared to the Gra|NCM811 even over 400 cycles. The Gra-OH|Li pouch cell was assembled by using Li metal as counter electrode to measure the Li plating/stripping reversibility (Fig. 8f). Significantly, the Gra-OH|Li pouch cell showed a higher CE with over the successive 55 cycles, whilst the Gra|Li pouch cell presented an inferior CE and a rapid decay.
