paragraph_context: In summary, an electric insulating EVOH copolymer film was headmounted coated on the graphite anode surface (Gra-OH) via a simple spray coating method for Li-ion/Li metal hybrid batteries and Li-ion batteries. Remarkably, this head-mounted coating method revealed negligible impact on the inner electric/ionic conducting pathways of graphite host. Owing to the passivation effect of EVOH layer, metallic Li was fully accommodated inside the porous structure of the Gra-OH host rather than the preferential plating on the top surface of the graphite anode, thereby realizing high space utilization and alleviating the volume change during repeated cycling. Meanwhile, the lithiophilicity –OH group of EVOH can effectively regulate the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux and render even Li plating behavior. Besides, the ICE (initial Coulombic efficiency) was improved due to the prior formation of an artificial SEI. Therefore, the issues of uncontrollable growth of dendrites and accumulation of “dead Li”, as well as the deactivation of graphite particles are successfully addressed in hybrid Li-ion/Li metal batteries and Li-ion batteries. As a result, the Gra-OH/Li hybrid anodes with a reversible capacity of 600 mAh/g presented high CEs in both coin cell and pouch cell under carbonate electrolyte condition. Remarkably, when paired with high mass loading LFP cathode (10.5 mg cm− 2 ), the hybrid Gra-OH/Li based full cell delivered outstanding capacity retention of 77.4 % even after 270 cycles. When operating in Li-ion working mode, the improved cycling stabilities were harvested in coin half-cell, coin LFP-full-cell and even 5Ah NCM811 pouch cell. This work sheds a new light on the development of the practical Li-ion batteries and hybrid Li-ion/Li metal batteries with significantly promoted safety and electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: Silver and silver‑lithium (Li–Ag) alloys have been widely applied in both liquid and solid-state lithium metal batteries for their exceptional ability to enhance negative electrode stability and regulate lithium deposition. However, the underlying mechanisms governing silver–lithium interactions vary significantly across different application scenarios, necessitating deeper fundamental investigation. In this work, we conduct a combined experimental and computational study to elucidate the behavior of silver during cycling, to uncover mechanistic insights that guide the rational design of composite negative electrode. Leveraging these insights, we develop a feasible and straightforward strategy to fabricate a robust lithium metal composite negative electrode. This architecture provides effective nucleation sites and facilitates uniform lithium deposition throughout cycling. The resulting composite negative electrode demonstrates excellent electrochemical performance, with enhanced stability and reversibility. Our findings offer a promising pathway toward next-generation high-performance lithium metal negative electrode.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium metal is a the highly promising negative electrode materials for next-generation lithium-ion batteries due to its exceptionally high theoretical capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ) and relatively low electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode) [1–3]. However, its high reactivity leads to the formation of an unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) with the electrolyte. During lithium stripping and plating processes, the uneven distribution of lithium-ion flux causes repeated fracturing and regeneration of the SEI, leading to continuous interfacial side reactions and excessive electrolyte consumption [4–7]. These issues contribute to low Coulombic efficiency (CE), short cycle life, and substantial volume changes [5,8–10]. Moreover, lithium dendrites can grow through cracks in the SEI and eventually penetrate the separator, leading to short circuits and serious safety concerns.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Various strategies have been explored to improve the electrochemical stability of lithium metal negative electrodes, including tailored electrolyte additives, solid-state electrolytes, artificial protective layers, and lithium metal hosts [11–15]. All these strategies aim to engineer the interface to minimize side reactions, suppress dendrite growth, ensure even charge distribution, and accommodate volume changes [16–28]. Among recent advances, lithiophilic interlayers composed of metals such as gold, silver, zinc, tin, and magnesium have shown promise in improving wettability and regulating lithium deposition [28–31]. Among these, silver is particularly advantageous due to its excellent electronic conductivity and chemical stability. More importantly, its high solubility in lithium allows it to form a Li–Ag alloy, which reduces nucleation overpotential and promotes uniform lithium deposition [30,32,33]. As a result, Li–Ag alloys, or silver itself, are commonly employed to stabilize the negative electrode in both solidstate and liquid electrolyte lithium-metal batteries, as well as in anodefree batteries [34–36].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Despite widespread empirical success, the fundamental mechanisms, particularly the kinetic aspects, of Ag’s role in Li stabilization remain contested. For example, when silver is applied to the copper (Cu) current collector in an anode-free battery, there are differing opinions on how silver distributes and contributes to performance during the lithium stripping and plating cycles. Niu et al. claim that the silver layer remains at the bottom of the copper current collector, inducing pure lithium metal deposition on top, while Zhang et al. suggest that silver undergoes upward diffusion from bottom to top and Shin et al. suggest that all silver reacts with lithium instead of forming a distinct layer on the copper [34,36,37]. Similarly, in solid-state systems, divergent models have been proposed. For instance, Cho et al. claim that to suppress volume expansion, the Li–Ag alloy must be fully delithiated during the lithium stripping process, meaning that the Li–Ag alloy must be reversible, whereas the pure silver‑lithium alloy is too stable to achieve this [32]. Conversely, Li et al. claim that lithium will plate underneath the silver layer and above the current collector based on Coble creep mechanism in solid-state electrolyte batteries, which differs from the lithium plating behavior on the silver layer observed in liquid electrolyte systems [38,39]. Given these complexities and inconsistencies in the mechanisms of silver‑lithium interactions, it is essential to conduct further fundamental investigations into silver and lithium deposition behavior during cycling to develop a more comprehensive understanding of their performance, ultimately enabling their effective application In this work, we present a feasible and effective approach to create a silver-rich protective layer by reacting a silver fluoride (AgF) layer with molten lithium metal. AgF can react with lithium metal to form a Li–Ag alloy and LiF, facilitating molten lithium absorption, with AgF serving both as a silver source and as a fluoride source to provide dual protection. The high interfacial energy of LiF enables uniform Li deposition, while its mechanical strength and electronic insulating nature prevent electron tunneling and suppress dendrite growth during charge–discharge processes [33,35]. Beyond demonstrating dramatic interfacial stability, we investigate the underlying the Ag-mediated mechanisms by integrating advanced characterizations and calculations. We uncover how reversible transformations between Li-rich and Ag-rich alloys, by studying their favorable formation, adsorption, and migration energetics, enable continuous SEI stabilization, uniform Li flux, and dendrite suppression. The integrated results illustrate that the Li–Ag alloy mechanism tends to remain on the surface rather than forming pure lithium deposition during the stripping and plating process, which is dynamic and kinetically favorable. The outstanding reversibility of the $_ { \mathrm { L i - A g } }$ alloy helps reduce dendrite growth and ensures an even distribution of lithium during electrodeposition, leading to a more stable lithium stripping and plating process. By coupling these mechanistic insights with comprehensive electrochemical validation, symmetrical cycling at 1 mA cm− 2 for more than 3000 h, and full cell/pouch cell tests with high mass loading positive electrode maintaining high CEs over hundreds of cycles, this composite negative electrode platform delivers both fundamental understanding and a practical pathway toward high energy density lithium-metal batteries as well as other SEI chemistries in both kinetics and durability.

paragraph_context: Fig. 1a illustrates the fabrication process of the Li-based composite negative electrode. Commercial carbon fiber was selected for this project due to its high mechanical strength, cost-effectiveness, ready availability, and suitability for producing robust, commercially viable composite negative electrodes. In this study, Toray T300 carbon fiber fabric (plain weave) was selected, as its medium-modulus grade has been shown in previous studies to exhibit superior electrochemical performance to high-modulus fibers when used as a current collector or electrode in lithium batteries [40,41]. The carbon fiber is first de-sized to remove surface epoxy, as shown in Fig. 1b, ensuring better interaction in subsequent steps. When immersed in an AgF solution, $\mathsf { A g F }$ particles attach uniformly to the carbon fiber surface, as confirmed by EDS analysis in Fig. S1 and illustrated in Fig. 1c. The AgF-modified carbon fiber readily absorbs molten lithium, forming a composite negative electrode with a shiny surface (Figs. 1d, S2), while the untreated fiber shows significant difficulty in lithium uptake. Lithium infusion also fills the inter-fiber spaces, effectively binding individual carbon fibers, and significantly increasing the mechanical integrity of the structure. As a result, the originally flexible carbon fiber transforms into a mechanically robust composite. The reinforcement is further evidenced by three-point bending tests, which show that pouch cells incorporating the composite negative electrode exhibit nearly twice the bending strength compared to those with pure lithium negative electrode. The composite negative electrode enhances both structural integrity and overall safety of the battery [42,43], as shown in Fig. S3.

paragraph_context: To investigate the interface dynamics during the lithium stripping/ plating process, the composite negative electrode was analyzed using EDS and XPS after 100 cycles at 1 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a capacity of 1 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ in a symmetric cell. Compared to bare lithium, which exhibit significant lithium dendrite growth after 100 cycles, the composite negative electrode maintains a dense and relatively smooth surface, indicating more regulated lithium flux during cycling (Fig. 2a, b). EDS results $( { \mathrm { F i g . ~ 2 c , d , } }$ and S7) show that $\mathbf { A } g$ and F elements remain evenly distributed across the electrode surface in symmetric cells, suggesting that silver element diffuses up to the surface rather than being fully covered by newly plated pure lithium metal. The cross-sectional SEM image in Fig. S8 of the composite electrode after cycling further confirms that no dendritic growth occurred. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) also confirms that no significant mechanical decomposition occurred after cycling, as shown in ${ \mathrm { F i g . } }$ S9⋅In-depth XPS analysis from 0 to 150 nm (Fig. 2e) reveals the formation of a lithium-rich Li–Ag alloy on the plating side of the composite negative electrode, evidenced by the $\mathbf { A } g$ peak shift from 373.6 eV before cycling to 371.4 eV, where the lower binding energy indicates higher lithium content [45,46]. The $\mathbf { A } g$ peak position and intensity remain relatively constant as the depth increases from 0 nm to 150 nm, indicating a uniform distribution of the $\mathtt { L i \mathrm { - } A g }$ alloy. On the stripping side, $_ { \mathbf { A } g }$ 3d peaks around 373.7 eV observed in Fig. S10; these peaks shift back to a higher binding energy compared to the plating side, and to a slightly higher value than that of the uncycled composite negative electrode (373.6 eV), further confirming the transformation of the silver-rich layer into a relatively lithium-rich alloy [45,47]. Additionally, the F1s peak at 685 eV in Fig. 2f demonstrates a uniform distribution of LiF in the SEI layer after 100 cycles. The retention of silver and LiF on the surface of the composite negative electrode provides a dual protective effect, enhancing interfacial stability during cycling and ultimately leading to improved electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: To further elucidate the mechanism of silver diffusion and alloy transformation during lithium stripping and plating, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to further provide insights into the mechanism of silver diffusion and alloy transformation during lithium stripping and plating. As shown in Fig. 3a and further supported by Fig. S11, the lower formation energy of $_ { \mathrm { L i - A g } }$ alloys compared to pure silver or lithium, together with the consistently negative formation energies of all $_ { \mathrm { L i - A g } }$ alloys derived from AgF and molten Li, confirms that alloy formation is a spontaneous process and thermodynamically stable. Fig. 3b presents the adsorption energy, showing that all $\mathtt { L i \mathrm { - } A g }$ alloys have more negative adsorption energy than pure lithium. This indicates a stronger interaction between Li–Ag alloys and lithium ions in the electrolyte, helping to prevent the formation of unstable pure lithium deposits on the surface. The Li adsorption energy of LiF was simulated to be − 7.43 eV (Fig. S12), confirming its role as a protective layer with favorable Li adsorption that enhances Li affinity at the interface, promotes uniform and dense Li plating [48,49]. Fig. 3c, together with the migration pathways shown in Fig. S13, demonstrates that pure silver exhibits a significantly higher lithium migration barrier compared to both lithium metal and Li–Ag alloys. The lower migration barrier allows for smoother lithium-ion movement, and enabling faster and more uniform lithium deposition and removal, significantly reducing the risk of dendrite formation. In addition, Fig. 3d and Fig. S14 show that pure silver has a larger work function than lithium metal, while $_ { \mathrm { L i - A g } }$ alloys exhibit relatively lower values compared to pure silver and close to pure Li metal. The lower work function of the $\mathtt { L i \mathrm { - } A g }$ alloy facilitates interfacial electron transfer by reducing the energy barrier for electron emission compared to pure silver, helping to lower overpotentials during cycling $[ 5 0 , 5 1 ]$ . Although pure silver exhibits lower adsorption energy than $_ { \mathrm { L i - A g } }$ alloys, its high formation energy and limited lithium diffusion capability prevent it from effectively forming and remaining on the composite negative electrode’s surface during cycling. In contrast, Li–Ag alloys provide a well-balanced combination of properties, including lower lithium migration barriers and improved adsorption energy compared to both pure lithium and silver. These characteristics collectively enhance the alloy’s ability to facilitate efficient lithium transport during stripping and plating. Furthermore, the lower formation energy of Li–Ag alloys also indicates that the phase transformation within the Li–Ag alloy, rather than the formation of pure lithium or silver on the negative electrode surface, is both thermodynamically and kinetically favorable.

paragraph_context: Based on the simulation and characterization results, the mechanism of the composite negative electrode can be proposed as illustrated in Figs. 3e, f. During the plating process, lithium-rich alloys with a relatively low silver ratio are formed, while during stripping, relatively silver-rich alloys are generated. The relatively lower migration barrier allows lithium ions to pass through and integrate into the Li–Ag alloy rather than accumulating on the surface. As a result, the alloy remains on the surface and leverages its thermodynamic advantages, such as favorable lithium adsorption energy, to stabilize negative electrode throughout the entire cycling process and suppressing dendrite formation. In addition, the reduced energy barrier for electron emission contributes to improved charge transfer kinetics and helps regulate lithiumion flux and alleviating overpotential. Consequently, the negative elec trode surface undergoes continuous and reversible transformations between Li–Ag alloys, rather than forming isolated regions of pure lithium or pure silver. These controlled transitions significantly enhance lithium cycling behavior by mitigating dendrite growth, preventing uneven lithium deposition, and improving cycling stability. This dynamic alloying mechanism helps maintain a stable electrode–electrolyte interface, thereby enhancing the overall electrochemical performance of the composite negative electrode and preventing dendrite formation and dead lithium accumulation which are commonly observed in bare lithium negative electrodes.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, this work reveals that Li–Ag alloys undergo reversible phase transformations during lithium plating and stripping, indicating a dynamic and kinetically favorable process. The favorable kinetics facilitate efficient migration of lithium ions into the Li–Ag alloy rather than accumulation on the surface, while the dynamic stability of the alloy ensures that the Li–Ag phases remain at the interface, continuously stabilizing the negative electrode throughout cycling. This reversible alloying–dealloying behavior, driven by both thermodynamic stability and low diffusion barriers, ensures the Li–Ag alloy to effectively stabilize the lithium metal negative electrode, which has the potential to be extended to broader lithium battery systems. Our investigation highlights the potential of silver-based strategies to enhance lithium battery performance through improved interfacial regulation and structural stability. Building on these insights, we developed a simple and effective method to fabricate a robust carbon fiber–lithium composite negative electrode. The integration of silver and fluoride components lowers the nucleation barrier and promotes uniform lithium deposition, thereby significantly enhancing the electrochemical stability of the negative electrode during cycling. As a result, the composite negative electrode achieves stable galvanostatic chargedischarge cycles for up to 3000 h at 1 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - \bar { 2 } }$ in symmetric cells, along with a full cell cycling over 500 cycles at 1C. Furthermore, its compatibility with high-mass-loading and its successful operation in pouch cell configurations demonstrate strong potential for practical deployment. Taken together, these findings underscore the promise of Ag-based composite negative electrodes as a viable pathway toward high-performance, durable lithium-metal batteries suitable for commercial applications.

paragraph_context: Efficient fabrication and practical application of thin lithium (Li) anodes are critical for commercializing highenergy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs). However, scaling up production of such anodes with excellent electrochemical performance remains an enormous challenge, which is mainly from the fragile mechanical properties, high reactivity, and rapid active Li depletion during cycling of pristine Li. To tackle these issues, we proposed an alloy-sulfide co-engineered strategy to construct a thin composite Li anode (LAS) with controllable thickness (10–50 μm), produced by adding Ag2S precursors to molten Li and then applying an industrially mature mechanical rolling process. The in situ-constructed LixAg-Li2S mixed ionic/electronic conductive framework balances ion diffusion and electron transport, suppressing the dead-Li formation and achieving uniform, dense Li deposition. The full cells exhibit markedly improved rate capability and stable cycling performance using highmass-loading LiFePO (LFP) and LiNi Co Mn O (NCM811) cathodes at low negative/positive (N/P) ratios of 2.7 and 2.4, respectively. More importantly, a 10 μm-thick LAS||NCM811 full cell cycles stably for 100 cycles at a low N/P ratio of 1.0. Furthermore, the pouch cell delivers a high energy density of 347 Wh kg− 1 . This alloysulfide co-engineered thin Li anode provides valuable guidance for the design, fabrication, and practical deployment of high-energy-density LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The increasing demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries is being fueled by the expansion of electric vehicles, intelligent robotics, and electric aircraft, all of which necessitate enhanced battery endurance capability [1–3]. Despite the significant progress achieved in this technology, the intrinsically limited capacity of graphite anodes continues to hinder further enhancements in overall energy density [4–6]. To achieve breakthroughs in energy density, lithium (Li) metal has emerged as the most competitive candidate for anodes, which offers the highest theoretical specific capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ) and the lowest electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode) [7,8]. However, Li metal anodes (LMAs) face numerous technical challenges in practical applications. Owing to their high reactivity, LMAs continuously react with the electrolyte, forming an unstable and nonuniform solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) that readily triggers random surface nucleation and subsequent Li-dendrite growth. Moreover, the effectively unbounded volume expansion of LMAs during cycling accumulates stress, causing repeated SEI rupture and regeneration, which further exacerbates dendrite growth and consumes the active Li inventory. These issues could easily cause rapid deterioration of battery cycle life and even lead to a series of safety hazards [4,9,10]. To address the above challenges, the scientific community has proposed many different solutions such as electrode structure design [11–14], electrolyte engineering [15–17], and the construction of high-strength artificial SEI [18–20]. Although these schemes have achieved a series of enhanced performance, most of the modification strategies are based on thick Li anodes (\~400–750 μm), whose areal capacity commonly varies from 80 to 150 mAh cm− 2 , 20 to 100 times more than that of commercial cathode typically ranging from 1.5 to 4 mAh cm− 2 . Excessive Li leads to extremely low utilization rate of active Li in the battery, masking their true performance limits. This wastes Li resources and may even make the actual specific capacity of LMAs lower than that of graphite ones, thus failing to fully exploit their inherent advantages. Therefore, to promote the practical application of LMBs, it is crucial to investigate the advanced manufacturing techniques and electrochemical performance of thin Li anodes with the thickness of less than 50 μm [21–23].

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: However, commercializing thin Li anodes faces significant challenges, requiring a synergistic approach integrating fabrication processes with structural design. Among these, the preparation process must prioritize cost control and scalability. Moreover, given the extremely limited active Li in thin Li anodes, minimizing its loss is critical for superior cycling performance. Thus, rational structural designs should be comprehensively considered to suppress dead-Li formation, stabilize interfaces, mitigate volume expansion, and guide uniform Li deposition/stripping. From the perspective of manufacturing technology, the fragile mechanical properties and poor electrochemical stability of thin Li anodes seriously restrict their efficient preparation, posing significant challenges to their industrial production and application research. Compared to other preparation techniques such as liquid-phase coating, physical vapor deposition, or electrodeposition, the solid-phase mechanical rolling method at room temperature is simpler, cheaper, and scalable, making it the most promising approach for industrializing thin Li anodes production. However, pure Li foil is prone to damage or adhesion to rollers due to its poor mechanical properties and extremely high reactivity, making large-scale production of thin Li via rolling challenging [24]. In industry, alloy design plays a crucial role in improving the machinability of metallic materials. Alloying can enhance the mechanical strength of composite materials, reduce the reactivity of Li, and thus facilitate direct contact with rollers for large-scale production [25]. Additionally, from an electrochemical stability perspective, lithiophilic Li alloy structure can not only act as functional skeleton to mitigate volume expansion during cycling, but also serve as uniform nucleation sites to guide uniform Li deposition and suppress dead-Li formation. Moreover, substrates forming solid solutions with Li (such as Ag, Au, and Mg) have lower phase transition energy barriers during repeated alloying/dealloying, leading to minimal structural changes, which can better ensure structural stability and continue lithiophilicity [26]. While most alloy materials exhibit excellent electronic conductivity, their presence in the artificial interface layer causes preferential accumulation of ions and electrons on electrode surfaces, rapidly depleting near-surface $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and driving Li to nucleate preferentially on the surface [27]. Therefore, alloying strategies combined with further interface optimization are crucial. Till now, numerous interface fluorination strategies have been reported, including the introduction of various fluorine-containing electrolyte additives [28,29], or the displacement reaction between Li and metal fluorides to generate LiF $[ 2 5 , 2 7 , 3 0 - 3 2 ]$ , with the aim of increasing the content of LiF in the SEI. However, LiF has low ionic conductivity $( \sim 1 0 ^ { - 1 2 } \mathrm { { S c m } ^ { - 1 } ) }$ and a relatively high $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion barrier (\~0.73 eV), making it hard to ensure excellent rate performance under high areal capacity and high-rate charge/discharge conditions [33–36]. Sulfides, with their unique advantages in $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ regulation and stable interface construction, have become one of the key materials for optimizing the interface and cycling stability of LMAs. In particular, sulfurization engineering incorporating thermodynamically stable $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } S$ components has been proven to be a highly promising technical route $[ 3 7 - 3 9 ]$ . $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } S$ exhibits a high ionic conductivity of approximately $1 0 ^ { - 5 } \mathrm { { S c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ at room temperature [39], enabling $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ deposition within the constructed framework. Furthermore, Li2S phases can adsorb $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and form stable bonds with them, its excellent lithiophilicity can also mitigate uneven ion flow, facilitating the redistribution of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ within the framework [40]. Accordingly, an alloy-sulfide co-engineered strategy is proposed, which consists in constructing a LixAg-Li2S collaborative structure. Such a strategy is expected not only to introduce solid-solution and secondphase strengthening, thereby enabling highly feasible large-scale production of thin Li anodes [25], but also to promote uniform, dense Li plating/stripping, which is expected to suppress dead-Li formation and enhance the cycling stability of thin Li anodes.

paragraph_context: Herein, we propose an alloy-sulfide co-engineered strategy to design a multifunctional composite anode (LAS) containing Li-Ag alloy and Li2S phases in the Li matrix by adding silver sulfide $( \mathsf { A } \mathsf { g } _ { 2 } \mathsf { S } )$ powder to molten Li. The cooled composite material was then thinned using mechanical rolling, enabling the efficient and scalable preparation of thin Li anodes with controllable thicknesses ranging from 10 to 50 μm. The in situconstructed lithiophilic Li-Ag alloy phases with a stable structure provide abundant Li nucleation sites, reducing the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion energy barrier. While the $\mathbf { L i } _ { 2 } \mathbf { S }$ phases with excellent electronic insulation and ionic conductivity can provide a fast $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transmission pathway and homogenizing $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux, accelerating $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport and suppressing the rapid depletion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ on the electrode surface. Therefore, the in situconstructed 3D $\mathrm { L i } _ { \mathrm { x } } \mathrm { A g } { \cdot } \mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } S$ mixed ionic/electronic conductive framework achieves a balance between ionic diffusion pathways and electronic transfer pathways inside the electrode, suppressing the formation of dead-Li. The resultant LAS symmetric cells exhibit excellent rate performance and cycling stability, capable of stable cycling with a high Li utilization rate of 51.9 %. By paring with high mass loading LiFePO4 (LFP) and $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (NCM811) cathodes, the obtained full cells deliver significantly improved rate and cycle performance at low N/P ratios. paragraph_context: The Ag atoms dissolved in the Li metal can introduce the solid solution strengthening to the matrix, while the uniformly dispersed Li2S particles can introduce the second phase strengthening, which can significantly enhance the composite's mechanical processability [25], enabling scalable production of LAS thin foils with controllable thicknesses ranging from 10 to 50 μm (Fig. S1, Supporting information). However, bare Li cannot be directly thinned by rollers due to its fragile mechanical properties and stickiness, it can only be thinned using polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film through physical isolation between the film and the rollers. Furthermore, severe adhesion and damage are likely to occur during the gradual thinning process of bare Li (Fig. S2, Supporting information), rendering it extremely difficult to thin below 30 μm. In sharp contrast, the LAS foil and the LA foil (prepared by adding Ag powder to molten Li) show minimal adhesion to the rollers during direct-contact rolling and yield significantly smoother, flatter surfaces than bare Li foil (Fig. S3, Supporting information). Moreover, as shown in Fig. 1e, the 20 μm-thick LAS foil shows no visible wrinkles or fractures even at areas ${ > } 3 0 \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } .$ . The maximum attainable area is mainly limited by the 8 cm-wide rollers of the processing equipment rather than the material properties. The 20 μm-thick foil also exhibits excellent flexibility, retaining its shape after rolling (Fig. S4, Supporting information). Furthermore, the LAS foil maintains a dense structure and smooth surface even when thinned to 10 μm (Fig. 1f).

paragraph_context: In summary, an alloy-sulfide co-engineered strategy is proposed by introducing the Ag S precursors into molten Li matrix to in situ form a 3D $\mathrm { L i } _ { \mathrm { x } } \mathrm { A g } { \cdot } \mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } S$ mixed conductive framework. Through mechanical rolling, scalable multifunctional LAS composite anodes with controllable thicknesses of 10–50 μm can be prepared as required. The Li-Ag alloy phases provide abundant nucleation sites, reducing $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion barriers. The $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 } s$ phases, with excellent ionic conductivity and electrical insulation, suppresses surface $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ depletion while enabling fast transport, ensuring rapid diffusion and uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux. This 3D LixAg-Li2S framework helps to achieve a balance between ion diffusion and electron transport, thereby suppressing the dead-Li formation, alleviating electrode volume expansion and promoting uniform and dense Li deposition within the electrode. The resultant symmetric cell with LAS electrodes demonstrates superior electrochemical performance at high Li utilization rate of 51.9 %. The NCM811 full cell assembled with a 10 μm-thick LAS composite anode delivers high reversible capacity and excellent cycling stability at a low N/P ratio of only 1.0. More importantly, the assembled pouch cell with good flexibility delivers a high energy density up to 347 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ . This alloy-sulfide co-engineered strategy sheds lights on developing high performance thin Li anodes for practical LMBs.

paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) face critical challenges including uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth and inferior cycling stability. Traditional electrolyte additives represent a robust strategy to mitigate these issues, yet they are predominantly monovalent or divalent compounds. This work overcomes this valence limitation by employing high-valent metal chlorides as multifunctional electrolyte additives, with $\mathbf { M o C l } _ { 5 }$ selected as the primary candidate. Attractively, this additive constructs an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) comprising an ultrafast ionic conductor matrix (LiCl, Li3N) embedded with Mo nanocrystals (NCs), which synergistically optimizes interfacial mechanical strength, ionic conductivity, and charge distribution. Rigid inorganic components (LiF, Li2O) effectively suppress dendrite penetration, while Mo NCs facilitate dense lithium deposition by homogenizing the electric field and providing uniform nucleation sites. Consequently, this strategy enables Li||Li cells to achieve exceptional cycling stability for over 4000 h. LMBs paired with LiFePO4 cathodes deliver excellent cycling performance, retaining 95.8% of their capacity after 200 cycles even under lean electrolyte and limited lithium conditions. Meaningfully, our work here elucidates the working mechanism of highvalent metal chloride electrolyte additives, broadens the exploration scope and design space of additive valence states, establishes fundamental principles and practical design strategies for advanced electrolytes toward nextgeneration LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) are key contenders for nextgeneration high-energy-density energy storage systems due to the high theoretical specific capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ) and lowest electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode) of the involved lithium metal anodes (LMAs) [1–4]. They hold promise for applications in electric vehicles, low-altitude economy, and drone equipment [5–7]. However, LMAs still encounter significant challenges in practical applications, including uncontrollable lithium dendrite growth, unstable solid electrolyte interface (SEI), ongoing interfacial side reactions, and low Coulombic efficiency (CE) [8,9], which severely limit the cycle life and intrinsic safety of LMBs, posing critical bottlenecks for their commercialization [10,11].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To tackle these issues, researchers have developed innovative strategies such as creating artificial protective layers, designing threedimensional current collectors, and optimizing electrolyte compositions [12–15]. This optimization involves the fine exploration of novel solvents [16–22], additives [23–27], and lithium salts [28–30]. Among these approaches, electrolyte additives have garnered significant interest due to their simplicity, high efficiency, and excellent compatibility with existing manufacturing processes [31–33]. Generally, ideal additives should preferentially react or adsorb at the anode interface, contribute to forming a stable SEI with high ionic conductivity, promote uniform lithium nucleation and deposition, and suppress continuous electrolyte decomposition [34,35]. The primary objective of additive engineering is to construct a robust and stable SEI, which is especially crucial for achieving high-performance LMBs [36–38].

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Emerging stable and inorganic-rich SEIs hold great application prospects owing to their remarkable chemical and electrochemical stability [39]. However, incorporating inorganic components into SEIs involves an inherent trade-off between performance metrics [32]. For example, LiF possesses an exceptionally high Young's modulus that effectively suppresses dendrite penetration, yet its high Li+ diffusion barrier results in low ionic conductivity [19]. In contrast, Li N offers outstanding ionic conductivity but suffers from poor long-term stability due to its high oxidation susceptibility [23]. Li2O strikes a balance between mechanical strength and ionic conductivity, but its formation is often contingent upon specific, highly reactive chemical pathways, leading to poor controllability [40]. In this context, the unique advantages of LiCl become prominent. Compared with LiF, LiCl has been shown to exhibit a lower $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion barrier, which is expected to diminish interfacial impedance, alleviate concentration polarization, and suppress localized ion-transport inhomogeneity [41–44]. In the composite SEIs, LiCl synergizes with high-strength LiF, $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ,$ , and highconductivity $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ to form a rigid and ion-conductive multifunctional matrix [45,46]. Here, Cl-containing halide regions can act as lowerbarrier $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ -migration pathways that bridge transport across rigid inorganic domains, thereby improving overall ionic connectivity without sacrificing the protective nature of an inorganic framework. By strategically incorporating LiCl, a high-performance ionic conductor, into SEIs through chlorinated compounds, the intrinsic limitation of sluggish ionic transport in conventional inorganic-rich SEIs can be effectively addressed.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To date, numerous studies have focused on electrolyte additives for LMBs, with recent advances centered on nitrogen- [47,48], fluorine-[49,50], and some chlorine-based functional groups [51]. Notably, chlorine-based additives exhibit unique advantages in constructing high-performance interphases for LMBs. Unlike conventional approaches, chlorine-containing species support the formation of a LiCl component that integrates exceptionally high ionic conductivity and moderate mechanical properties, resolving the core trade-off between ionic transport and mechanical strength in SEI design. Ma et al. demonstrated that a chlorobenzene-derived LiF-LiCl composite SEI enables stable operation of lithium-rich manganese-based oxides at 4.8 V, highlighting the high-voltage compatibility of chlorine-modified interfaces [52]. Similarly, Fan et al. utilized 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE) as an additive to mitigate the low $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux of LiF, forming a binary halide $\mathrm { ( L i F _ { 1 - x } C l _ { x } ) }$ composite SEI that homogenizes $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ distribution and facilitates uniform lithium deposition [41]. Beyond organic chlorine sources, low-valent metal chlorides (typically $\mathbf { M C l } _ { 2 } / \mathbf { M C l } _ { 3 } )$ have also been extensively explored to construct LiCl-involved protective interphases on Li metal. For instance, CuCl2, $\mathrm { Z n C l _ { 2 } } ,$ and $\mathrm { L n C l } _ { 3 }$ have been employed to generate hybrid interphases composed of LiCl and metallic/alloy domains, which effectively regulates the Li deposition and enhances interfacial stability [53–55]. Despite these advances in low-valent metal chlorides, studies on high-valent metal chloride additives remain remarkably scarce, even though they can provide more Cl− ligands per metal center and enable more tunable solvation structure and interfacial chemistry. Thus, the strategic integration of chlorine addresses the inherent trade-off in traditional SEI design, thereby reconciling conductive yet fragile and robust yet ionically resistive components. Unfortunately, reports on high-valent metal chloride additives remain scarce, motivating our exploration of this untapped field.

paragraph_context: Herein, we demonstrated the unique synergistic potential of highvalent metal chloride additives in regulating the electrolyte and interphase of LMBs. Different from the previously reported chloride additives, the key innovation of this work lied in employing MoCl5 as a highvalent metal chloride additive to simultaneously regulate $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation chemistry and interphase composition in ether-based electrolytes. Unlike conventional single-function additives, high-valent metal chlorides provided dual functionalities. Their reducible metal centers and chloride ligands jointly regulated the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation structure and participated in interfacial reactions. Based on previous findings, we selected the base electrolyte (BE) which was formulated with 0.5 M lithium bis (trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) and 0.5 M lithium nitrate $\left( \mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 } \right)$ dissolved in a 1: 1 (v/v) mixture of 1, 3-dioxolane (DOL) and dimethoxyethane (DME). To validate the proposed dual functionalities, we designed a modified electrolyte by incorporating 5 mmol $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ MoCl into BE, denoted as MC5E. Combined computational and experimental studies substantiated that both of its cationic and anionic components synergistically enhanced $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport kinetics and interfacial stability. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirmed the incorporation of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ into the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation shell, while sputtered X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of Li foil verified the involvement of Mo NCs in SEI formation. This optimized electrolyte enabled the $\mathrm { L i } | | \mathrm { L i F e P O } _ { 4 }$ (LFP) cells to achieve a per-cycle capacity decay rate of merely 0.021% under stringent test conditions. Collectively, these findings bridge the knowledge gap concerning high-valent metal chloride additives and provided valuable guidance for designing high-performance electrolytes for advanced LMBs.

The equations for the motion of all atoms were integrated using a classic Verlet leapfrog integration algorithm with a time step of 1.0 fs. paragraph_context: XPS depth profiling offers the direct evidence of the distinct chemical composition of the SEI formed by MC5E, revealing a composite interface composed of $\mathrm { M o } ^ { 0 } ,$ , LiCl, Li3N, LiF, Li2O, and MoO3 (Fig. 4g, h; Fig. S20). The inorganic components LiF, LiCl, and Li N facilitate $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conduction and create efficient transport pathways, while LiF, $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ,$ , and $\mathbf { M o O _ { 3 } }$ form a robust framework that impedes lithium dendrite penetration. Correspondingly, the improved deposition morphologies and superior interfacial properties are observed with MC5E. SEM after the first lithium deposition at 0.2 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ presents the pronounced inhomogeneity for BE, whereas MC5E produces uniform, continuous lithium coverage (Fig. 4i, j; Fig. S21). This difference persists after 30 cycles at 0.5 mA cm− 2 with MC5E forming a dense deposit layer and BE displaying a porous morphology (Fig. 4k, l; Fig. S22). Crosssectional SEM analysis confirms the distinct lithium deposition structure and thickness. Notably, BE exhibits loose, dendritic lithium deposition with a thicknesses of about 21 μm, whereas MC5E enables dense and uniform lithium deposition with a thickness of 16.5 μm (Fig. 4m, n). Furthermore, MC5E keeps the superior uniformity and dendrite suppression even under harsh conditions of 2 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $2 \mathrm { m A h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ for 30 cycles (Fig. 4o, p; Fig. S23). To further elucidate the lithium volume expansion, thickness evolution, and dead-Li accumulation, crosssectional optical microscopy was employed to characterize the Li electrode after Li plating under conditions identical to those used in Li||Li electrolytic cell cycling (effective area $\sim 0 . 1 8 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } ; 1$ mA for 1 h, corresponding to 5.56 mA cm− 2 and 5.56 mAh cm $^ { - 2 } ) .$ . paragraph_context: SEI as a composite interfacial layer with solid electrolyte feature, is recognized to enhance ionic conductivity via rational interfacial design. Given the low bulk ionic conductivity of inorganic SEI components, the interface serves as the dominant pathway for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conduction. paragraph_context: Thus far, limited studies have investigated the solvent chemistry of high-valent metal chlorides to date. This work highlights one irrefutable fact that high-valent cations do not exist independently in solution but instead exhibit strong solvation. As schemed in Fig. 7h, when $\mathbf { M o C l } _ { 5 }$ is dissolved in the electrolyte, it dissociates into Cl− and MoCl+. The Cl− participates in the solvation structure and undergoes de-solvation at the LMAs to form LiCl within the SEI. The MoCl4+ migrates toward the LMAs, where it undergoes electrochemical reaction with Li. This reaction leads to the reduction of Mo species to form Mo NCs embedded in the Li anode, and the oxidation of Mo to form $\mathbf { M o O 3 }$ that enhances the mechanical robustness of the SEI. Both reactions also generate additional Cl− , which replenishes the dissolved chloride species participating in the solvation structure. Within this SEI, synergistic interactions among components ensure rapid $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport and mechanical stability via the inorganic matrix, while the dispersed Mo NCs provide localized electronic conduction and reduced nucleation barriers. This sophisticated synergy between composition and function is crucial for significantly enhancing the cycling life of LMAs and suppressing lithium dendrite growth. The MC5E fundamentally modifies the interphase chemistry, transforming the fragile, organic-dominated SEI into a robust, inorganicrich layer with high ionic conductivity and mechanical integrity. This inorganic restructuring simultaneously reinforces the CEI, improving its stability against electrolyte oxidation. Collectively, these modifications suppress interfacial side reactions, minimize impedance growth, and directly contribute to the observed improvements in cycling stability and capacity retention.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, this work systematically elucidated the unique synergistic regulatory mechanism and multifunctional value of high-valent metal chlorides as electrolyte additives for LMBs, with MoCl as the primary research target and $\mathrm { w C l } _ { 6 }$ further explored as an extended additive candidate. More specifically, the central contribution of this work was the identification of $\mathbf { M o C l } _ { 5 }$ as a high-valent metal chloride additive that coupled $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation regulation with LiCl-rich interphase construction in ether-based LMBs. In contrast to low-valent additives, highvalent metal chlorides underwent electrochemical reactions with LMAs, generating Mo NCs and Cl− . The formed NCs established a uniform electric field to facilitate dense lithium deposition, while Cl− incorporated into the solvation structure and promoted the LiCl formation within the SEI. Experimental and theoretical analyses revealed that the inorganic-rich SEI and NCs enhanced electrochemical kinetics, effectively inhibited lithium dendrite growth and conferred excellent electrochemical performance. Specifically, the Li||Li and Li||Cu cells demonstrated long cycle lives of over 4000 h and 600 cycles. Furthermore, the Li||LFP cells exhibited stable cycling performance over 700 cycles at 2C and 200 cycles under lean-electrolyte and limited‑lithium conditions, with capacity retentions of 96.8% and 95.8% of their initial capacity, respectively. Consequently, these findings positioned highvalent metal chlorides as a highly promising category of highperformance electrolyte additives and offered valuable insights for advancing next-generation LMBs.

paragraph_context: With the development of lithium-ion batteries, the demand for low-cost and high-performance anode materials is urgent. In this work, an inexpensive porous MnO and pitch carbon composite was synthesized, through a simple solvent-thermal reaction and carbothermal reduction treatment. As an anode material for lithium-ion batteries, the composite exhibits excellent initial capacity (597 mA ${ \textbf { h } } g ^ { - 1 } )$ and remarkable reversible capacity (419 mA h ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.1 $\textbf { A } \ g ^ { - 1 }$ after 150 cycles), which is higher than that of pitch carbon. It also shows outstanding rate performance and long cycling stability. The porous structure is conducive to the diffusion of the electrolyte and activation of the active material. The addition of pitch carbon can improve the conductivity of the composite and alleviate the bulk expansion of MnO, thereby achieving stable electrochemical properties. The proposed simple synthesis strategy is expected to promote the development of low-cost anode materials for lithium-ion batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries are widely used in electronic equipment, electric vehicle and energy storage because of their high energy, stable cycle performance, and non-memory effect, and are considered to be the most attractive energy storage devices (Li et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2018). With the intensification of energy crisis and greenhouse effect, the demand for lithium-ion batteries with higher energy density is becoming urgent. Up to now, the most commonly used lithium-ion battery anode material is graphite with low theoretical capacity (372 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } ) .$ , whereas the price is getting higher and higher, and battery grade graphite has reached about \$6,000/ton (Zhang et al., 2014; Bai et al., 2021). Therefore, it is urgent to develop novel anode materials with high performance and low price.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: In recent years, a large number of new materials have been used in the research of lithium-ion battery anodes, among which transition metal oxides have attracted much attention due to the advantages of high energy density and low price (Xiao and Cao, 2015). In particular, MnO has attracted great attention owing to its high capacity (756 mA h $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } ) , } \end{array}$ environmental friendliness, and abundant resources (Liu et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2019; Ding et al., 2017). However, when MnO is used directly as an anode material, it is limited by poor conductivity and large volume change during charging and discharging, which leads to poor cycle and rate performances (Pei et al., 2019).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To solve these issues, researchers prepared plenty of MnO-carbon composite materials. The introduction of carbon materials can not only improve the conductivity of MnO, but also greatly alleviate the volume expansion of MnO (Zheng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018). Therefore, graphene-MnO (Gao et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), carbon nanotube-MnO (Wang et al., 2018; Bai et al., 2018; Cui et al., 2015), biochar-MnO (Huang et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2019) and other composite materials have been developed to improve the electrochemical performance of the electrodes. Nevertheless, the preparation process of nanomaterials such as graphene is complex and expensive, which is difficult to achieve large-scale application in the short term, and biomass materials also have poor reproducibility and low carbon content.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Petroleum asphalt is one of the products of crude oil processing, with the advantages of low price (\~\$400/ton), rich output and high carbon yield. It can be converted into hard carbon through simple oxidation and carbonization treatment, which is an ideal anode material (Hao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2012). However, if asphalt carbon is used as a negative electrode alone, the specific capacity is only about 250 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } ,$ which is difficult to meet the actual demand (Zhao et al., 2017).

In the first cycle, the reduction peak appeared at 0.7 V and disappeared in the subsequent test, mainly due to the decomposition of electrolyte and the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer (Gao et al., 2019). In the second to sixth cycles, the reduction peaks appearing at 0.35 V is mainly attributed to the conversion of MnO to Mn, as well as the generation of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } \left( \mathrm { M n O } + 2 \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } \right)$ $+ 2 \mathrm { e } ^ { - } \to \mathrm { M n } + \mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } )$ . The sharp reduction peak at a lower voltage can be attributed to the intercalation of Li into the carbon layers (Wang et al., 2017). In contrast, the oxidation peak appears around 1.30 V, corresponding to the reaction of Mn to MnO and the decomposition of Li O $( \mathrm { M n } + \mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } \to \mathrm { M n O } + 2 \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } + 2 \mathrm { e } ^ { - } )$ (Jia et al., 2018). We tested ex-situ XRD of the composite electrode (Fig. S6). As the voltage is discharged to 0.1 V, manganese oxide gradually converts into manganese, and lithium ions convert into lithium oxide. Clear diffraction peaks of LiOH can be seen on the fully discharged electrode sheet. Subsequently, when charged to $^ { 3 } \lor ,$ the diffraction peaks of LiOH gradually disappear, and the diffraction peaks of MnO reappear, which is consistent with the CV test. Furthermore, the peak currents of the oxidation and reduction peaks slowly increase with cycling, which can be attributed to the activation of the electrode material during cycling (Pei et al., 2019).

paragraph_context: In summary, a simple solvothermal and carbothermal reduction method was successfully proposed to prepare manganese oxide and pitch carbon composite materials for lithium-ion battery anode. In order to obtain low-cost negative electrode materials and simplify the process, we used manganese nitrate and petroleum asphalt as raw materials, and realized the porous manganese oxide-pitch carbon composite, which has good electrochemical performance. The initial capacity of MnO/C-3 composite reached 597 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , which was close to the theoretical specific capacity of MnO (756 mA h ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ . After 150 cycles at $0 . 1 \mathrm { \ A g ^ { - 1 } } ,$ , the capacity of MnO/C-3 composite could still maintain 419 mA h $^ { g ^ { - 1 } , }$ which was much higher than that of pitch-C sample. In addition, the composite material has good rate performance which can maintain a stable capacity of more than 250 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ under the high current density $( 1 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ~ } ^ { - 1 } )$ . The porous structure of the composite facilitates electrolyte diffusion and the utilization of active material. The introduction of pitch-C is able to increase the conductivity of MnO, ensuring fast electron transport and efficient utilization of lithium ions. Moreover, the volume change of MnO during charging and discharging can be inhibited, so that the structure and electrochemical stability of the electrode material can be improved. This novel porous MnO/C composite is expected to promote the development and application of a new generation of low-cost high-performance lithium-ion battery anode.

paragraph_context: Converting carbon dioxide $\left( \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } \right)$ into battery materials with high value is an effective strategy to address the problem of excessive $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions. Silicon (Si) anodes provide outstanding lithium storage capacity for lithiumion batteries but face practical limitations due to low intrinsic electrical conductivity and significant volume expansion. Here, we developed an innovative method for ultrafast preparation of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ derived porous micro-sized Si-C anodes, which is achieved by induction heating of commercial alloy. This configuration showed remarkably an enhanced reversible capacity (e.g., 1617.2 mA $\mathbf { \bar { h { g } } } ^ { - 1 } )$ , outstanding rate performance (e.g., 839.6 mA h $g ^ { - 1 }$ at 2 $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { A ~ g ^ { - 1 } } } ) _ { : }$ , and excellent cycling stability $( \mathrm { e . g . }$ , 80.3 % capacity retention for 300 cycles at 1 $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf A \ g ^ { - 1 } ) , } \end{array}$ which exceeds previously reported. In-situ optical microscopy characterization further reveals the structural stability of the porous micro-sized Si-C electrode during lithiation. Based on this excellent performance, we assembled pouch cells with NCM811 cathodes, which achieved 91.8 % capacity retention after 200 cycles at 0.5 $\textbf { A } \ g ^ { - 1 }$ . This effective strategy opens up a new avenue for large-scale and efficient conversion of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ into high-value products.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Due to the global climate change and the intensification of the greenhouse effect, the utilization of CO2 has received extensive attention by the scientific community (Wang et al., 2022). The resource utilization of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ plays an important role in the energy and environmental fields as it is the most abundant and cheapest carbon resource (Jin et al., 2010). Combined with renewable energy, which converts $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ into chemicals, fuels and materials, it is an effective way to achieve carbon neutrality (Hepburn et al., 2019). It not only has the function of storing and utilizing clean energy, but also effectively reduces $\mathrm { C O _ { 2 } }$ emissions, which achieves the purpose of high-value conversion of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } .$ Energy storage technology is very important for solar and wind energy due to the fact that these energy sources are intermittent, which necessitates the storage of excess energy to be used when there is a shortage. Among them, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely used in electronic devices, electric vehicles, hybrid vehicles, renewable energy storage and aerospace due to their high energy density and long cycle life (Hasan et al., 2021; Du et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2023).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Graphite anodes are the main choice for commercial lithium-ion batteries due to their stable electrochemical performance, excellent cycle life and cost-effectiveness (Luo et al., 2009; Du Cao et al., 2024). However, its limited theoretical capacity (372 mA h $g ^ { - 1 } )$ restricts energy density improvements. Silicon carbon (Si-C) composites have emerged as promising alternatives by taking advantage of Si’s theoretical specific capacity (4200 mA h ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and low operating voltage (\~0.45 V vs Li/ Li+), as well as its environmental friendliness and abundance of raw materials (Bitew et al., 2022; Holzapfel et al., 2005). However, large volume expansion and low electrical conductivity of micro-sized Si particles are known as the main drawbacks of its commercialization (Li et al., 2013). Micro-sized Si/C composites are considered a promising strategy for practical applications, which are widely used to improve the electrical conductivity and mitigate volume expansion of Si anodes (Xiao et al., 2022; Man et al., 2023). Although micro-sized Si/C composites have made great progress, there are still two urgent issues that need to be addressed. First, conventional carbon sources (e.g., acetylene, glucose, etc.) produce environmentally harmful gases during the preparation of micro-sized Si/C composites, which is a $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emitting technology (Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). Second, the conventional synthesis methods for micro-sized Si/C composites are complex and time-consuming, which increases their manufacturing cost and limits their commercial production (Xu et al., 2024; Lin and Chen, 2022).

paragraph_context: Here, we developed an innovative method for ultrafast preparation of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ derived porous micro-sized Si-C anodes, which is achieved by induction heating of commercial alloy. The as-prepared Si-C composite has a porous structure and uniform carbon layer, which not only mitigates the huge volume expansion during charging and discharging, but also enhances the electrical conductivity of the composite. This configuration showed remarkably an enhanced reversible capacity $( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { e } } . \boldsymbol { \mathrm { g } } . ,$ , 1617.2 mA h ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ , outstanding rate performance $( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { e . } } \boldsymbol { \mathrm { g . } } ,$ , 839.6 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $2 \texttt { A g } ^ { - 1 } )$ , and excellent cycling stability (e.g., 80.3 % capacity retention for 300 cycles at 1 $\mathsf { A } \mathsf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ , which exceeds previously reported. paragraph_context: In order to test the electrochemical performance of Si/C electrodes, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed on Si/C electrodes at a rate of 0.1 mV $\mathsf { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , which showed highly overlapping redox peaks after the initial activation cycle (Fig. 3a). The cathodic peak appeared at 0.14 $\mathrm { v , }$ corresponding to the alloying reaction between Si and Li, where the structure of Si changed from crystalline to amorphous. There are two anodic peaks at 0.37 V and 0.54 V, corresponding to the separation of Li from Li Si (Ke et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2013). The discharge curve of the first cycle does not completely overlap with some areas of the other discharge curves, and the broad cathodic peak of about 0.7 V disappears in subsequent cycles, which is related to the formation of a solid electrolyte interface (SEI) at the electrode (Tian et al., 2021). The redox peaks of the later charge/discharge curves are highly coincident and the peak area increases, indicating that a stable SEI has been formed and that the volume expansion of Si/C is weak. Fig. 3b shows the first three charge/discharge curves of Si/C electrodes at 100 mA $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ . The initial discharge and charge specific capacities are 2619.52 and 1912.96 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively, with a corresponding Coulombic efficiency of 73.03 $^ { \% , }$ which is mainly attributed to the irreversible formation of the SEI membrane. The Coulombic efficiency increased to 94.93 % in the second cycle and 96.76 % in the third cycle, which indicates that the SEI film has been basically stabilized. The stable SEI can inhibit the side reaction with the electrolyte, which is conducive to enhancing the cycling stability of the electrode (Pan et al., 2022).

All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chempr.2025.102879 THE BIGGER PICTURE Metal anodes offer the promise of high energy density in the corresponding metal batteries, but their uneven growth and unstable surface reactions during electrodeposition have remained longstanding challenges with limited mechanistic understanding. While considerable efforts have been dedicated to tuning electrolyte compositions and designing artificial interphases, one critical factor has been largely overlooked: the irregular and resistive passivation layer, inherently formed on the metal surfaces. Even a sub-nanometer-thick passivation layer can disrupt the pathways of carrier-ion transport and perturb the stability of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, impairing both cycle and calendar life markedly. In this work, we elucidate the overlooked effect of the passivation layer on the SEI evolution and metal deposition behavior using time-sensitive analytical tools. Furthermore, we remove the passivation layer via simple acid-base reactions to facilitate crystallographically coherent, epitaxy-like electrodeposition and thus extend the cycle life drastically for all of lithium, zinc, and magnesium batteries. This work identifies a hidden spot in metal batteries, namely, the surface passivation layer, and demonstrates the significant impact of its removal on the sustainable and reliable operation of a wide class of metal batteries.

paragraph_context: Uniform electrodeposition is vital for long-term operation of high-energy metal batteries, yet early interfacial dynamics related to electrodeposition remain underexplored. While irregular native passivation layers can perturb the uniformity of interfacial ion transport flux, their impact on nucleation and deposition behavior has received limited attention. Here, we reveal that nanometer-scale irregularities along initial passivation and nascent solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers critically govern electrodeposition morphology by affecting its directionality and anisotropy. This correlation demonstrates that early interphasial phenomena are key factors in determining the crystallographic texture and structural coherence of electrodeposits. Consequently, we surface-engineered lithium, zinc, and magnesium foils to promote spatially uniform, structurally seamless electrodeposition for improved cycling performance: 75.5% capacity retention after 800 cycles for a full cell pairing a 1.6 mAh cm− 2 $\mathsf { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathsf { C o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathsf { M n } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathsf { O } _ { 2 }$ cathode with a 20-μm-thick Li foil. This work uncovers the regularity of early interphase structure as a key parameter for sustainable cycling of various emerging metal anode batteries.

paragraph_context: In the rapidly expanding battery landscape, the limitations inherent to conventional intercalation-based chemistries— particularly those relying on graphite anodes and metal oxide cathodes—are becoming evident.1–3 As emerging applications demand higher energy densities, new carrier-ion storage mechanisms that transcend traditional operating principles are required. Among the available alternatives, electroplating and stripping processes with metal anodes are among the most promising, as they offer both low reduction potentials and large specific capacities, without the weight constraints imposed by separate host materials. Extensive research efforts have therefore been dedicated to exploring various carrier cations, including Li+ , Na+ , K+ , Zn2+, Mg2+, Ca2+, and Al3+.4− 7 Despite this broad portfolio, achieving sufficient plating reversibility, critical for practical applications, remains a significant challenge for most metal-based batteries. The primary obstacle lies in the inherent tendency of metals to form porous and filamentous morphologies6,8,9 when plated on the current collector during deposition. In this regard, metal deposits with densely packed morphologies are highly desirable to warrant the reversibility for prolonged cycling. Thus far, extensive research efforts have been made for guiding plating morphologies into forming rounded, large-dimension structures.10 These approaches include electrolyte engineering,11–13 separator modifications,14 and substrate surface treatment.15 Among these strategies, electrolyte engineering specific to each metal-based battery has progressed the most: for example, locally highly concentrated electrolytes (LHCEs) for lithium-metal batteries (LMBs),16,17 hybrid electrolytes composed of water and organic solvents for aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs),18–22 and amine-type electrolytes targeting solvation shell reorganization for magnesium-ion batteries (MIBs).23–26 In parallel, the community has recognized that the components and physicochemical properties of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer are greatly influenced by the electrolyte design. In particular, inorganic-rich SEI compositions, especially those rich in lithium fluoride (LiF),27–30 have been identified as ideal benchmarks for LMBs. Nonetheless, the SEI composition alone does not fully account for the plating morphology and Coulombic efficiency (CE), implying that the current understanding of the SEI is insufficient.31 This rationale, in turn, points to other factors at play, besides electrolyte composition, in determining the CE and other key electrochemical properties.

paragraph_context: The composition of the SEI layer is not the only determinant of the morphology and quality of metal deposits. Rather, its spatial variance—thus, the variance in the interfacial resistance—along the interface at the nanometer scale is even more critical.7,32 Accordingly, ion diffusion within the SEI layer follows the path of minimal ionic resistance, highlighting that uniform metal deposition necessitates the formation and maintenance of an SEI layer with spatially minimal variations in its composition and thickness.6,33–35 However, the realization of a uniform interface is nontrivial with the metal anodes both in their pristine states and during cycling. A non-uniform, inconsistent SEI layer leads to the formation of irregular, fragile junctions, which eventually evolve into porous lithium (Li) layers over cycling (Figure 1).

paragraph_context: This structural drawback of Li deposits is related to the coexistence of diverse types of passivation layers—ranging from the pristine oxide layer to early-stage, thin infant SEI layers to their thickened, mature successors. The uneven resistance levels caused by these diverse interfacial characteristics associated with their varying physicochemical properties give rise to locally distinct deposition kinetics, which lead to preferential irregular deposition at certain ‘‘hot’’ spots. Consequently, achieving a homogeneous interface with minimal resistance variations is greatly desirable for uniform and sustainable metal deposition. Notably, as shown in Figure 1, dense Li can be deposited on an underlying porous Li layer under certain electrolyte conditions (e.g., LHCEs), 36 implying that a comprehensive cross-sectional analysis would be necessary to fully capture the morphology of the Li deposition near the substrate.

paragraph_context: Here, we investigated the relationship between passivation regularities and the metal deposition morphology and drastically extended the cycle life by promoting the ‘‘seamless growth’’ of metal onto the current collector. This was accomplished by eliminating the initial passivation layer and exposing the metal surface to electrolytes designed to promote the formation of a homogeneous SEI layer with moderate resistance and high stability. Specifically, by removing the intrinsic irregular passivation layer, crystallographically continuous and large-dimensional metal deposits, which play a crucial role in maintaining a stable interface, were facilitated. As a result, the (de)plating reversibility of various metals, including Li, zinc (Zn), and magnesium (Mg), was universally improved to significantly extend their cycle lives. This study examines the extent to which local irregularities throughout the passivation and SEI layers critically determine the metal (de)plating characteristics for repeated cycling. Our findings point to passivation-free seamless bonding between the deposit and the substrate as a simple yet effective strategy to maximize the key performance indicators.

paragraph_context: Once Li+ ions successfully nucleate on the current collector, the nucleated Li metal can grow into various morphologies, ranging from filamentous (unidirectional) to isotropic shapes, depending on the cell conditions. The transport of Li+ ions through the SEI layer is a critical step that determines the rate of plating and stripping. During the course of SEI penetration, Li+ ions are preferentially directed to local spots with low SEI resistance. Simultaneously, due to the high reactivity of Li metal, the SEI evolves rapidly during plating or stripping, which significantly affects subsequent metal deposition behavior. The SEI can be classified depending on its evolution stage. The SEI formed directly on the pristine metal surface and is thus in its beginning stage and is referred to as the ‘‘infant SEI,’’ whereas the SEI that develops progressively on the infant SEI over various time scales, even as short as a few seconds, is termed the ‘‘mature SEI.’’ The infant SEI is generally preferred for electrodeposition due to its thinness.

paragraph_context: Building on this understanding, we hypothesized that such temporal variations in passivation—driven by differing SEI thickening rates across the electrolytes—lead to spatial passivation heterogeneity. This heterogeneity, in turn, governs the morphology of metal deposits by inducing different degrees of spatial variation in the interfacial resistance (equally, in SEI aging), varying the growth mode from filamentous growth in conventional carbonate electrolytes (CCEs) to isotropic growth in LHCEs (Figure 2A). Specifically, our research focused on the SEI resistance during the initial stages within the very short timeframe of several seconds, which can indeed influence the Li deposition morphology and ultimately the cyclability of the corresponding cell. This contrasts with previous studies,37 which were primarily concerned with the changes in the SEI after long periods of storage, typically for time scales ranging from 1 h to several days. Such perspectives generally aimed to study the differences between the mature and ‘‘calendar-aged’’ SEI, thus focusing on the aging associated with self-discharge. The SEI dynamics in our scheme (infant SEI vs. mature SEI) over short periods are more closely associated with the deposition behavior in the very beginning of plating.

paragraph_context: As it is difficult to accurately measure the ion conductivity in the SEI layer, particularly in its early stage, intermittent short rest steps were introduced during electrodeposition (Figure 2B). These steps allowed us to measure the dynamic increase in the SEI resistance over a short time frame by monitoring the overpotential before and after each period of rest. The higher plating overpotential (ΔV) upon resumption, a result of the thickening infant SEI during the rest periods, was used as an indicator to comparatively assess the SEI thickening rate for each electrolyte. Using a Li|Cu half-cell setup, Li was plated under constant current (CC) and capacity conditions (1 mA cm− 2 and 1 mAh cm− 2 , respectively) with four distinct rest durations (1, 10, 60, and 300 s). The following six electrolytes were evaluated: 1 M lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF ) in ethylene carbonate/diethyl carbonate (EC/DEC = 50/50 [v/v]), 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DEC (50/50 = v/v) with 10 wt % fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC), 1 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) in 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), 1LiFSI-1.2DME-3 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2, 2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE), 1 M lithium tetrafluoroborate (LiBF ) in DME, and 1 M lithium bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide (LiTFSI) in 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)/DME (50/50 = v/v).

paragraph_context: The overpotential across all electrolytes generally increased after the rest periods, confirming that the SEI thickens during these periods from 1 to 300 s (Figure S1). Importantly, the overpotential profiles over these different rest durations across different types of electrolytes do not necessarily correlate with the presence of certain inorganic or organic components (Figure S2). For example, the cell with the 1 M LiPF6 EC/DEC + 10% FEC electrolyte demonstrated a significant overpotential increase after a brief rest period of 10 s, whereas the cell with the 1LiFSI-1.2DME-3TTE electrolyte largely maintained its overpotential for up to a few minutes of rest. Despite these contrasting behaviors, the types of chemical species in the SEI layers after the first plating were not drastically different for both electrolytes (Figure S2). Instead, the distinct behaviors could be explained by the reactivity of the mother solvents (carbonate vs. ether), as the high lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) level of ether is known to mitigate its severe decomposition and enables a thinner SEI to be sustained during plating. Accordingly, in CCE, the infant SEI rapidly evolves toward a mature state enriched with organic species of higher resistance, whereas in LHCE, the infant SEI is already dominated by inorganic components that persist during growth, leading to a much slower resistance increase.38,39 The increase in the overpotential as a function of the rest time for the different electrolytes (Figure 2C) reveals that the rate at which the SEI resistance evolves is correlated to the morphology (isotropic vs. filamentous) of the Li electrodeposits, as captured by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure S3). Moreover, this pronounced spatial heterogeneity in the SEI resistance can promote filamentous growth, as electrodeposition preferentially occurs at hotspots. By contrast, in the case of 1LiFSI-1.2DME-3TTE, the less rapid increase in the overpotential suggests that, during a few-second pause of the electrodeposition, the SEI layer maintains spatially consistent ionic resistance and thereby facilitates isotropic growth (Figure S3).

paragraph_context: To remove the oxide layer, we used an alkali-halide acid-base reaction, whereupon we created a new passivation layer before nucleation of the corresponding metal (Figure 3A). Specifically, bromine (Br ) completely removed the oxide from Li metal foil within 3 s at room temperature, whereas iodine (I ) was used for the divalent metals (Zn and Mg). $\mid _ { 2 }$ was chosen because the higher solubility of the metal iodides $( Z \mathsf { n l } _ { 2 }$ and MgI2) than ZnBr2 and ${ \mathsf { M g B r } } _ { 2 }$ allows for their complete removal by rinsing before cell assembly. $\mathsf { I } _ { 2 }$ is incompatible with Li metal because the iodization yields unstable intermediates such as $\mathsf { L i l } _ { 3 } ,$ which readily react with the electrolyte. The halide treatment proceeds via penetration through oxide cracks and direct reaction with the underlying metal, producing a stable ultrathin halide layer (Figure S6). paragraph_context: To explore the broader applicability of surface reformation to various metal anodes, the native oxide layers were removed from the Li, Zn, and Mg metal foils, followed by electrodeposition at a current density of 1 mA cm− 2 with a capacity of 1 mAh cm− 2 .
