paragraph_context: Building on these structural observations, our simulation assessment of the thermodynamic stability of newly deposited atoms on Li, Zn, and Mg foils (Figure S13) revealed that the surfaces attained greater stability by positioning the atoms alongside steps, indicating their natural preference for in-plane growth (Figure 4F; Table S1). Furthermore, the low activation energies for atom migration facilitate the natural settling of atoms into stable planes (Figure S14; Table S1). Despite this natural tendency of metals to grow in a compact and aligned manner to minimize their surface energy, dendritic patterns frequently emerge in practice, indicating the presence of additional influencing factors. The dependence of the surface energy on the electrode potential was analyzed and showed that tree-like growth can be initiated in highly electrostatically repulsive environments. According to the simulations, the electrode potentials reach − 0.95, − 2.22, and − 1.81 V vs. M/M+ for Li, Zn, and Mg metal, respectively, at which points the surface energies become negative (Figure S15) to favor fractal morphologies. COMSOL simulations revealed that filamentous growth, triggered by Li-ion depletion, begins at around 300 mV for the Li-ion case (Figures 4G, S16, and S17; Table S2). Yet, these findings, in turn, indicate that dendritic growth in the lower voltage range of 50–200 mV (Figure 4C) during the initial stage of deposition is neither affected by surface charge aggregation nor by carrier-ion depletion, suggesting that other mechanisms play a more significant role. This logical flow led us to consider the passivation layer, particularly its irregularities, as the primary factor responsible for dendritic growth under typical cell operating overpotentials (<200 mV), although this surface passivation was not reflected in the COMSOL simulations. This rationale re-emphasizes the importance of mitigating passivation irregularities to enable stricter control over the metal deposition kinetics and morphology.

paragraph_context: The recent development of electrolytes that form thin inorganicrich SEI layers represents tremendous progress in terms of improving the reversibility of LMBs during cycling. However, despite the use of these innovative electrolytes or the application of substantial stack pressure, as long as the passivation layer on the Li metal electrode is spatially irregular, Li metal nucleation and growth behavior is unlikely to be well controllable over cycling. This lost controllability drives the cell to gradually impair the uniformity of the morphology and reaction kinetics of Li metal deposition. Although the native oxide layer on the Li metal is known to be of nanometer dimensions, the significant effect of its elimination was indeed visualized by crosssectional FIB-assisted SEM after electrodeposition (Figure 6B). paragraph_context: In conclusion, the spatial uniformity of nucleation and growth during metal deposition dictates the deposition morphology and thus determines the lifetime of the corresponding metal batteries. However, this process is affected by various interfacial conditions. We elucidated that the regularity of passivation and the spatial variation in SEI aging both play a decisive role throughout the process. Even minor irregularities in the C  as discussed above, prompting filamentous growth and producing a typical dendritic electrodeposition layer that floats above the substrate. By contrast, when combining the LHCE with the bare Li foil, the formation of a thin inorganic-rich SEI facilitated isotropic Li growth to yield a layer of thick Li chunks. However, this combination still gave rise to a loosely bound interface between the substrate and deposition layer. Remarkably, pairing the SR Li foil with the LHCE resulted in seamless film-like growth with a tightly bound interface that obfuscated the distinction between the electrodeposited layer and the substrate.

paragraph_context: The distinct growth modes were also reflected in the thickness evolution of the electrodeposition layers over cycling (Figure 6C), which was monitored using FIB-SEM analysis after the ${ 3 0 } ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ Li deposition. Until this point, the pristine Li foil with CCE continued developing the porous initial deposition layer, resulting in a thickness increase from 10.9 μm to beyond 15 μm. The pristine Li foil with LHCE exhibited a moderate thickness increase from 5.1 to 7.0 μm after the same number of cycles, with significant porous Li formation. By contrast, the SR Li foil with LHCE maintained the most compact morphology, with a final thickness of only 5.1 μm—close to the theoretical thickness (4.85 μm) of the corresponding Li. Similarly, in the case of the SR Zn foil, the epitaxial morphology was observed after the $1 0 0 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ cycle, mirroring the individual polycrystalline domains on the substrate (Figure S26). X-ray tomographic microscopy (XTM) confirmed the consistent monolithic nature of the Zn deposition (Figure S27). Overall, leveling the passivation irregularities proved to be a universal, intrinsic passivation layers of metal foils disrupt uniform ion transport therein, leading to indiscriminate filamentous growth at hotspots. Surface reformation, achieved by removing the passivation layer and creating an infant SEI layer that supports uniform ion flux, significantly improves the cycle life by enabling spatially uniform or even epitaxy-like electrodeposition. In the case of Li and Zn, the crystalline domains of the epitaxy-like deposition layers mirrored those of the underlying substrates. Additionally, the advanced LHCE effectively abates SEI aging to mitigate the filamentous growth caused by spatial variations in the SEI maturity. This study suggests the usefulness of surface reformation and the subsequent formation of a suitable SEI for metal foil anodes to drive morphologically favorable electrodeposition and, consequently, markedly extend the cycle life of metal batteries.

paragraph_context: The electrode’s material properties have an important role in the efficient performance of metal ion batteries. The possibility of using the two-dimensional AlB monolayer as the negative electrode material of lithium, sodium, and potassium ions was explored by the first-principles calculation in this study. It turns out that the storage capacity of AlB2 for Li, Na, and K ions is superior to that of many reported negative electrodes, which are about 1102, 1102, and 413 mA $\mathbf { h } { \mathbf { \left. g ^ { - 1 } \right. } } ;$ , respectively. The migration barriers for Li, Na, and K ions in the monolayer of AlB2 are 0.428, 0.162, and 0.019 eV, respectively, indicating that the $\mathrm { A l B } _ { 2 }$ monolayer can be charged and discharged rapidly. Therefore, AlB2 is promising as a potential anode material for alkali metal ion batteries.

paragraph_context: The task of enhancing the efficiency of energy storage systems is challenging in advanced electrification and transportation applications. Batteries are one of the most potential options in the current energy storage scheme and must meet the criteria of high energy density, safety, and low cost [1–3]. In 1991, lithium-ion batteries were commercialized for the first time and made remarkable achievements in the market with the advantages of long cycle life and high energy density [4,5]. The theoretical specific capacity of graphite, which is commonly used as the negative electrode of lithium-ion batteries, is only 372 mA h ${ \mathbf { g } } ^ { - 1 } ,$ , which does not meet the requirements of most practical applications [6–10]. At the same time, the lack of lithium reserves limits the use of lithium-ion batteries and increases their price [11,12]. Therefore, the significance of non-lithium rechargeable batteries cannot be ignored [13]. Sodium and potassium are found directly below lithium in the periodic table, so the three elements have similar chemical properties in many respects, but compared with lithium, sodium, and potassium are richer in earth resources and have broad prospects in the next-generation battery system. However, because sodium and potassium have large atomic radii, their electrochemical performance at the negative electrode is somewhat limited, and the storage capacity of sodium and potassium in graphite electrodes is relatively low. Therefore, it is very important to develop new active materials with high energy density and storage capacity that can be applied to three types of alkali metal ion batteries at the same Two-dimensional (2D) materials have important application prospects in the fields of photoelectric devices, energy storage, and biomedicine because of their unique photoelectric and chemical properties [16–19]. The first successful isolation of graphene in 2004 was an important milestone in the field of 2D materials and not only opened up a new field of research for 2D materials but also for 2D electrode materials [20]. Several studies have shown that ion batteries based on 2D materials have excellent electrochemical performance. For example, the energy storage performance of single-layer TiSe in lithium-ion, sodium ion, and potassium ion batteries was reported by Wang et al. The storage capacity of all three batteries reached 422.63 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ with the ion diffusion barriers estimated at 0.29, 0.36, and $0 . 3 3 \ \mathrm { e V } ,$ respectively [21]. Kaviani et al. have studied the application of hexagonal boron oxide $\mathbf { ( B _ { 3 } O _ { 3 } ) }$ monolayer in $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } , \mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ batteries. The theoretical storage capacities of $\dot { { \bf A } } 1 ^ { 3 + } , { \bf C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , and K+ ions reached 1778.25, 1185.50, and 790.33 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively, and they have relatively fast migration rates (the migration energy barriers of $\mathrm { \bar { A l } } ^ { 3 + } , \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions are 0.17/0.05, 0.12/0.35 and 0.22/0.39 eV, respectively) [22]. Of course, there are also many 2D materials, such as ScS2 NiN2, B3S, WC4, SiP, CrB , MoB , B N , and SnSe , which are likely to serve as electrode materials for alkali-metal ion batteries, because of their good storage capacity and ion diffusivity [23–30]. Two-dimensional materials can be categorized into different types according to their structure such as transition metal disulfides, MXenes, transition metal borides, etc.

Among them, there exists a class of two-dimensional materials with a Dirac cone structure, most of which show extremely high Fermi velocities and superb electrical conductivity. It has been found that when such materials are used as electrode materials, they exhibit excellent electrochemical properties [34–36]. For example, when Sun et al. used a 2D Dirac material, BP, with ultra-high Fermi velocities and good stability in Li and Na ion batteries, they found that BP had an ultrahigh storage capacity (1924 mA h $g ^ { - 1 } )$ and a low diffusion barrier (0.16 eV) [37]. paragraph_context: In this paper, the structural parameters, electronic properties, and electrochemical properties of $\mathrm { \ A l B } _ { 2 }$ single-molecule membrane as a negative electrode material of alkali metal ion (Li/Na/K) battery were studied by first-principles calculation method. Calculation results show that the $\mathrm { A l B } _ { 2 }$ monomolecular film has superior thermal stability and conductivity. The migration barriers of Li, Na, and K atoms on $\mathrm { A l B } _ { 2 }$ monomolecular are low, which indicates that $\mathrm { \ A l B _ { 2 } }$ has a good charge/ discharge rate. The ion storage capacity of AlB2 is relatively high, with the theoretical capacities of Li and Na reaching 1102 mA h $\cdot { \bf g } ^ { - 1 }$ , and the theoretical capacity of K atoms reaching 413 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is better than many reported 2D materials. In conclusion, 2D monolayer $\mathrm { A l B } _ { 2 }$ has the potential to be an anode material for alkali metal ion batteries.

paragraph_context: Making anodes from silicon results in various longstanding challenges, including drastic volume expansion, formation of a thick and high-impedance solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), rapid capacity decay, and poor rate performance. The use of these anodes in high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries is thus limited. Herein, an artificial SEI with a self-assembled alkyl sulfonic acid (SAASA) reinforcement structure is deposited onto the surface of Si through an organosilane approach (to obtain a Si-SAASA electrode). A coupling agent, 3-mercaptopropyl trimethoxysilane (MPTMS), was tailored on the surface of Si to produce strong siloxane (Si–O–Si) bonds. The thiol group (-SH) in the MPTMS molecule consequently oxidized into sulfonic acid (-SO3H), resulting in sulfonated artificial SEI reinforcement on the Si surface. With sulfonated MPTMS, the Si anode was improved through the formation of -SO3Li, which enhanced Li+-ion diffusion and ionic mobility. The Si-SAASA electrode has the highest discharge capacity of 1507.1 mAh g− 1 at 0.5 C after 400 cycles with a retention capacity of 74.3%, high rate capability, and a high lithium-ion diffusion coefficient $( 2 . 8 8 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ s ^ { - 1 } )$ . This study demonstrated that the SAASA reinforcement, acting as an artificial SEI, gives the electrode mechanical integrity, meaning that during cycling, expansion of the Si’s volume can be accommodated and the fragmentation of Si particles can be prevented through the strong siloxane bonds. Additionally, the SAASA serves as a protection against parasitic reactions between the electrolyte and active interface, thus preventing the repeated growth of a thick and high-impedance SEI layer. The developed approach will be exceedingly effective and minimize the cost of developing high-performance Si anodes for next-generation lithium-ion batteries.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are being developed to meet demands related to electric vehicles, intelligent electronics, and mobile electronic devices because of their high operating voltage, low weight, small size, high cycling performance, high power capability, and environmental friendliness [1–3]. Some efforts have been made to identify new materials that can eventually replace graphite, which is currently the material most commonly used for the anode of LIBs and has a low theoretical capacity of 372 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ [4]. Silicon substances have proven to be an excellent alternative anode material for high-energy LIBs because of their excellent theoretical specific capacity (4200 mAh $g ^ { - 1 } ) ,$ , attractive discharge potential (0.2–0.4 V vs. Li/Li+), and low toxicity [5–7]. However, Si-based anode materials have not been widely used due to their large volume change (\~400%) during the alloying–dealloying process [8–10]. This volume variation causes particle pulverization as well as repeated growth of a high-impedance and thick solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), which ultimately leads to low initial coulombic efficiency (ICE), rapid capacity fade, and low rate capability of the battery [11–13].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Several strategies for addressing the failure mechanism and enhancing the performance of Si anodes have been investigated. Among these are decreasing the size of the Si by creating nanostructures—such as nanoparticles [14], nanowires [15], and nanocomposites [16]—and by designing multistage structures such as yolk–shell [17] and porous [18] structures. The use of polymeric binders such as carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) [19] and polyacrylic acid [20] can improve mechanical adhesion through covalent bonding with the Si, thereby reducing the volume expansion of Si to some degree [21]. However, the preparation of nanostructures and polymeric binders is both expensive and difficult or fails to provide an adequate solution for Si-based anodes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Another important requirement is interfacial control, which would ensure that a stable SEI layer forms on the Si anode. The SEI is a protective layer that reduces the degree of electrolyte degradation, particularly in the case of an Si anode [22]. Researchers are currently focusing primarily on two basic strategies for stabilizing the SEI layer on a Si anode. These strategies include adding additives to the electrolyte, such as vinylene carbonate and fluoroethylene carbonate [23,24]. Other strategies are the deposition of coating layers that act as an artificial SEI on the Si surface; such layers have been carbon-based [25], metal oxide $[ 2 6 , 2 7 ]$ , and polymer brush core–shell materials [28]. These approaches minimize interaction between the active surface of the Si and the electrolyte, thus inhibiting the electrolyte’s degradation. Because these artificial SEI layers are incapable of accommodating the volume expansion of Si, the structure of the SEI cannot be maintained due to its limited strength. A tailored reinforcement design, in the form of an artificial SEI that can inherently accommodate the volume expansion of Si, would be appropriate. The end of such a reinforcement structure could contain negatively charged functional groups that readily accept $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions through ion exchange during the first alloying–dealloying cycle, resulting in high long-term performance of the anode.

paragraph_context: In this study, a coupling agent of 3-mercaptopropyl trimethoxysilane (MPTMS) consisting of a thiol (-SH) functional group was employed to construct, through an organosilane reaction, a self-assembled alkyl sulfonic acid (SAASA) reinforcement structure for use as an artificial SEI on a Si surface. The MPTMS structure, which contains a methoxysilane group, produces a strong covalent Si–O–Si bond with the surface of the Si. Previously, some works had studied that using MPTMS on metal surface is eligible for forming a high resistance membrane due to its high chemical, mechanical, and electrochemical stability [29,30]. The -SH group in the MPTMS layer at the silanized surface is easily oxidized into a sulfonic acid group $\mathrm { ( - } S \mathrm { O _ { 3 } H ) }$ through peroxide/acidic solution [31]. Consequently, the sulfonic acid group $\mathrm { ( - } S \mathrm { O _ { 3 } H ) }$ , with its negative charge, attracts $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions to the electrode, enhancing ionic mobility. This structure on the Si anode has advantageous mechanical properties because it accommodates volume expansion while preventing, through the strong siloxane linkage, the fragmentation of Si particles during cycling. It also serves as a cover to repress parasitic reactions between the electrode and electrolyte, preventing the formation of a thick and high-impedance SEI layer over numerous cycles, and improves the ICE. As anticipated, the Si-SAASA electrode was discovered to exhibit lower charge transfer resistance, a higher rate, and higher cyclic performance than the Si-OH electrode, which was accredited to the stable SEI and electrode structure. Therefore, the approach developed in this study is effective and minimizes the cost of improving the performance of Si anodes for next-generation LIBs.

paragraph_context: In summary, new SAASA reinforcement served as an artificial SEI on the surface of Si, was synthesized through an organosilane approach. The SAASA reinforcement grafted onto the Si surface through strong siloxane bonds, offers different functions to the Si anode such as (1) an enhanced mechanical property to accommodate volume expansion, (2) a shelter that suppresses a parasitic reaction between the electrode interface and electrolyte, (3) a negatively charged boundary containing $- S O _ { 3 } \mathrm { H }$ groups that can easily accept Li+ ions through ion exchange and enhance ionic mobility, and (4) prevention of the formation of a thick and high-impedance SEI. paragraph_context: Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) is characterized by easy synthesis, high porosity and high nitrogen doping level. It has good application prospects as an negative electrode material for metal-ion batteries. However, graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) cannot be directly used as negative electrode material (NEMs) for lithium-ion batteries due to poor electrical conductivity and poor cycling performance. To solve this problem, in this paper, g-C3N4 is synthesized on the surface of reduced graphene oxide by in situ synthesis method. The prepared rGO-g-C3N4 composites have high surface capacitance process occupancy due to the presence of a large amount of pyridinic-N and pyrrolic-N, and various defects and pores generated during the synthesis process provide a large lithium-ion mobility rate for the rGO-g-C3N4 composites. The rGO-g-C3N4 composites have excellent electrochemical properties and excellent lithium storage performance, the capacity of 1 A/g after cycling 300 laps to maintain a high lithium storage capacity of 708.6 mAh/g, and is still in the rising state, even if the current density of 15 A/g under the cycle of 10,000 laps, the highest lithium storage capacity of up to can still be up to 423.6 mAh/g, and stabilized in the 306.8 mAh/g. This work provides a new idea for the preparation of new negative electrode materials with low cost and high capacity.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries have the advantages of high energy density and long service life[1,2], can be widely used in new energy vehicles and various electronic products as an efficient energy storage system[3–5]. However, improving the energy storage requirements of new energy vehicles and other equipment, fast charging speed and high mileage are the key research directions today. The negative electrode material used in traditional lithium-ion batteries is still graphite as a raw material. The graphite electrode has the disadvantages of low theoretical lithium storage capacity, poor rate performance and large volume expansion, which can no longer meet the development of lithium-ion battery technology and the increasing demand for lithium-ion battery applications[6,7]. Therefore, the search for negative electrode material with high lithium storage capacity, superior multiplication performance, high cycling stability, and possessing superior electronic conductivity is the focus of research. For example, carbon negative electrode materials such as reduced graphene oxide (rGO)[4], fullerene (C60)[8], carbon nanotubes[9], porous carbon spheres, soft carbon and hard carbon, which possess good electronic conductivity, unique structures, and high lithium storage capacity, have been extensively studied. Graphene oxide has been the most widely studied material, with researchers aiming to improve its electrochemical performance through various methods. This includes composites with metal oxides such as (ZnO[10], SnO [11], etc. [12].) and metal sulfide (MoS [13], SnS [14], etc.[15].). Additionally, techniques like the preparation of defective reduced graphene oxide [16], and doping with non-metallic elements such as B, N, S, P, and others have been employed to further enhance its electrochemical properties[17–19]. It has been shown that modifying reduced graphene oxide with elemental N can further improve its electronic and chemical properties. Reduced graphene oxide modified with elemental N has more metal ion storage sites, higher porosity, electronic conductivity and reactivity[19–21].

paragraph_context: There are two traditional methods of nitrogen doping: in-situ nitrogen doping and post-processing doping, where in-situ nitrogen doping utilizes pyrolysis of nitrogen-rich compounds to increase the content of nitrogen atoms in carbon materials. It has been shown that there are four main types of nitrogen atoms in carbon materials treated by in situ nitrogen doping: 1) pyridine-N, 2) pyrrole-N, 3) graphite-N, and 4) oxidized pyridine-N[21]. Among them, there are pyridine nitrogen and pyrrole nitrogen at the edge of the lattice, which can generate lone pairs of electrons to strongly interact with metal ions, resulting in the formation of active centers in the lithium-ion detachment/embedding process, and can also achieve higher lithium storage capacity, which is usually able to have an initial capacity of 1260.0 mAh/g and a cycling capacity of 462.0 mAh/g. On the other hand, graphitic nitrogen has been found to irreversibly bind to lithium ions, resulting in a reduction in lithium storage capacity. Therefore, in the synthesis of nitrogen-doped carbon materials, it is crucial to increase the content of pyridine nitrogen and pyrrole nitrogen and reduce the content of graphitic nitrogen as much as possible. Therefore, it is particularly important to find suitable nitrogen-rich compounds to be used as precursors for the preparation of composites, with low cost, ease of synthesis and good chemical stability being the main focus, as well as having high levels of pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen.

This unique structure allows for the presence of large triangular pores that can be obtained by simply pyrolyzing the inexpensive melamine precursor, advantages that meet our requirements for nitrogen-rich compound precursors. There are two main strategies to overcome the above deficiencies: 1) Complete exposure of pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen by controlling the relative content of graphitic nitrogen. It has been found that the synthesis of self-supporting nitrogen-doped carbon nanosheets using active thermal metal reduction (Mg-thermal, Zn-thermal[25–27]) can effectively increase the content of pyridine nitrogen as well as pyrrole nitrogen, obtain the excellent cycling stability and the outstanding lithium-ion storage capacity. 2) Introducing highly conductive substances, such as carbonized fiber or C60, as carriers of graphitic phase carbon nitride to provide an excellent chemical environment for lithium-ion detachment/embedding [8,28-30].

paragraph_context: a School of Materials Science and Engineering, Ocean University of China, Qingdao 266404, China  b Department of Hospital Infection Management, the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University, No.16 Jiangsu Road, Qingdao 266000, Shandong, China  c Key Laboratory for Liquid-Solid Structural Evolution and Processing of Materials, Ministry of Education, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, PR China  d School of Mechanical, Electrical & Information Engineering, Shandong University, Weihai 264209, China  e College of Textiles and Clothing, State Key Laboratory of Bio-Fibers and Eco-textiles, Qingdao University, Qingdao, 266071, China  f Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Electronic Functional Materials and Devices, Huizhou University, Huizhou 516001, Guangdong, China Lithium metal is expected to be the perfect anode material for the next generation of rechargeable batteries owing to its ultra-high theoretical specific capacity, low density and the lowest redox potential. However, the practical application of lithium metal batteries faces serious challenges, including uneven lithium deposition, negative electrode volume expansion, and short circuits brought by dendritic protrusions. Although the 3D structure of silver nanowires is effective in inhibiting lithium dendrite growth and lithium metal volume expansion, it still suffers from lithium inhomogeneity caused by uneven distribution of silver nanowires and complicated preparation. Therefore, PAN@AgNWs collector was prepared by a simple suction filtration method, and uniform dispersion of silver nanowires and uniform deposition of lithium were achieved. Lithium nucleation overpotential and lithium dendrite formation can be effectively reduced by PAN@AgNWs hosts due to the reduction of local current density by 3D collectors and the improved lithiophilicity of silver nanowires. With low voltage hysteresis, the symmetric battery constructed with its composite anode may cycle steadily for 4500 h at 1 mA cm− 2 and 1 mAh cm− 2 . At the same time, the Li-PAN@AgNWs||LFP full cell still possesses a reversible of 144.18 mAh g− 1 after 500 cycles at 1C. Moreover, due to large specific surface area and high surface energy of 3D silver nanowires, it exhibits excellent antimicrobial properties, with an inactivation efficiency of 96.3 % after contacting with E. coli for 2.5 h. This work shows the possibility of using PAN@AgNWs in a large scale for LMBs, and paves the way for development of high-performance antimicrobial materials.

paragraph_context: Considering the present energy crisis and environmental pollution, the development of renewable energy has been accelerated, causing an increasing demand for energy storage systems [1-4]. The focus has been on lithium-sulfur batteries with extremely high energy densities, lithium-air batteries, and lithium metal batteries (LMBs), because graphite anodes can no longer provide the long-term power needed for electric motor equipment [5-8]. An abundance of investigation has been done on LMBs because of their high energy density and special features [9-14]. However, Li metal anode practical application is extremely difficult due to the uncontrolled volume change of Li during the plating/stripping process [15,16], uneven Li deposition [17-20], Li dendrites, the formation of dead Li [21-24], and even explosion and fire hazards [25,26].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Recently, people have proposed many effective methods to inhibit the growth of lithium dendrites. The key actions are: (1) establishing a relatively stable artificial SEI film to improve the surface stability of lithium metal anodes so as to avoid side reactions [27-29]; (2) adding suitable electrolyte additives to make lithium ions diffuse evenly [30-32]; (3) designing a 3D host structure that can inhibit the growth of lithium dendrites by reducing the local current density [33-35]; and (4) introducing a lithium-friendly matrix to form a lithium-friendly composite anode to control side reactions [36-39]. According to Chazalviel’s model, the lithium ion flux is more stable and uniform when the current density is lower [40]. Conversely, when the current density is higher, the lithium ion flux at the negative electrode decreases more quickly, which causes the lithium dendrites to grow more quickly [41]. Since 3D col lectors can effectively reduce local current density and induce bottom-up deposition of lithium, current research is more inclined to design 3D bulk structures to delay the growth or volume expansion of lithium dendrites [42,43]. The current 3D current collectors mainly include 3D porous copper current collectors [44], 3D nickel foam current collectors [45], graphene current collectors [46], carbon cloth composite anodes [47] and Ag nanowire films [48], all of which have shown excellent cycle stability in lithium metal batteries. However, compared with copper, nickel, graphene, and carbon cloth, lots of lithophilic sites can be provided by the silver nanowires, thus effectively guiding the uniform nucleation and deposition of lithium [49].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Wang et al. proposed a method to incorporate AgNWs into MS frameworks using a self-assembly technique (immersion method). It achieves uniform deposition of lithium metal and adapts to the volume change of lithium anode during plating/stripping process, which significantly improves the performance of LMB [48]. Fan et al. created flexible freestanding porous 3D silver nanowire networks (AgNWs) on Cu substrates co-deposited with lithium alloys, resulting in robust, lightweight and porous AgNWs@Cu structures (drop-in method) [50]. It is obvious that silver nanowires cannot function alone in lithium metal batteries, but must be combined with other substrates to create self-supporting flexible structures. In addition, the current silver nanowire composite host faces serious challenges such as complicated preparation process, poor substrate flexibility, and inability to ensure uniform dispersion of silver nanowires, which limits its practicality and results in a short stable cycle duration. Silver nanowires with high surface energy and large specific surface area not only effectively inhibit lithium dendrites during charge/discharge cycling [51], and it also helps to improve the antimicrobial activity [52].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Moreover, germs are present in all aspects of human life, and there are numerous ways for them to be infected [53]. Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a typical resident of the intestines of warm-blooded animals and is often used as an indicator of fecal contamination in the food industry [54]. Although most E. coli strains are unlikely to cause disease, certain E. coli pathotypes acquire genetic virulence factors that enable them to produce a wide range of diseases and have greater potential to adapt to new environments [55]. In addition, E. coli has been linked to human infections, including diarrhea, urinary tract infections, and meningitis. It can also cause acute enteritis in humans and animals and is a common cause of "traveler’s diarrhea," a dysentery-like disease affecting humans. Consequently, in the face of bacterial infestation, humanity has never given up resistance, and many different antimicrobial agents and antimicrobial materials have been investigated and created one after the other [56]. Metal ion (metal or metal oxide) antimicrobial compounds are typically integrated into carriers and employed as antibacterial materials [57]. However, there are still many problems, such as complex and uncontrollable preparation processes, difficulty in recycling, high cost, and difficulty in large-scale preparation, which hinder the development of antibacterial materials [58].

paragraph_context: In this paper, a unique multifunctional membrane of electrostatically spun Polyacrylonitrile @ Silver nanowires (PAN@AgNWs) was prepared by a simple and controlled filtration extraction method. Silver nanowires can be evenly distributed in the PAN substrate, and the silver nanowires are filled in the PAN spinning gap by suction filtration. Silver is soluble and reacts with lithium to form solid-solution alloys, and silver has excellent electronic conductivity and lithophilicity, the AgNWs can guide the uniform deposition of lithium, which contributes to the rapid transport of lithium ions. As is well known, PAN presents good mechanical strength and has been widely used as a film material [59]. Furthermore, interlayers such as polyacrylonitrile (PAN) fibers with a large number of polar groups (-C––N, C–H and so on) can act as efficient lithiophilic sites to guide even Li nucleation and growth [60]. The PAN spinning as the substrate has excellent shape adaptability to accommodate the volume change of lithium plating/stripping. Therefore, PAN@AgNWs composite anode has the benefit of inhibiting the growth of lithium dendrites, and corresponding symmetric battery can be stably cycled for 4500 h at 1 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and 1mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 , }$ and the full cell coupled with lithium iron phosphate cathode exhibits reversible capacity of 144.18 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ after 500 cycles at 1C. In addition, silver is bacteriostatic and bacterial cell membranes or DNA can be destroyed by the metal ions $( \mathsf { A } \mathsf { g } ^ { + } )$ in PAN@AgNWs film. The silver nanowires show excellent antibacterial properties, the inactivation efficiency of PAN@- AgNWs host reached 96.3 % after contacting with E. coli for 2.5 h, which is much higher than that of other antimicrobial materials reported so far. Therefore, the PAN@AgNWs composite collector not only makes it possible for high energy density Li-metal batteries to be applied in a large scale, but also paves the way for the development of high-performance antimicrobial materials.

paragraph_context: Fig. 1a depicts the PAN@AgNWs composite current collector preparation method. The PAN was first electrostatically spun(Contains a small amount of PANI), and then the prepared AgNWs solution was pumped into the PAN spun wire substrate to create the PAN@AgNWs collector. The lithium plating/stripping of PAN@AgNWs collectors is showed in Fig. 1b. The presence of PAN@AgNWs is beneficial to the uniform deposition of lithium because AgNWs has a strong affinity for lithium, thus greatly reducing the nucleation barrier. After electroplating, lithium metal grows along the linear collector, retaining a resilient void space to release strain during Li-Ag alloying, thus confining the lithium in a compact matrix for a longer cycle life. After cycling, the lithium metal aggregates into a more homogeneous spherical shape without the appearance of dendrites. Thus, the use of PAN@AgNWs as lithium protective structures provides compact interlayer lithium coatings with high reversibility and stable cycling of the lithium metal anode [61]. In contrast, as shown in Fig. 1c, after the repeated cycling process of plating/stripping, the lithium anode undergoes a large volume change which increases its surface area. In addition, the repeated rupture and build-up of its SEI film affects the growth rate of lithium metal, leading to uneven lithium deposition, lithium dendrites, and even the growth of dead lithium.

paragraph_context: Fig. 6a depicts a inactivation diagram of E. coli sterilization. Because E. coli is hydrophilic, it can fully touch PAN@AgNWs in the culture medium. When E. coli’s cell wall and cell membrane come into contact with the edge of the silver nanowires, they are damaged, exposing the cytoplasm and DNA structure and causing apoptosis (e.g. I) [83]. Furthermore, metal ions (Ag+) can kill bacteria by breaking membranes or disrupting DNA (e.g. II) [84]. We performed an E. coli antibacterial test to investigate the bacterial inhibitory capacity of PAN@AgNWs composite membrane. Fig. 6b depicts the growth of E. coli on NA petri dish in contact with film samples at various intervals. When compared to the control group, the number of colonies on the film sample reduces dramatically after 0.5 h of contact, and then decreases more as time passed. The number of colonies in the blank control remains consistent after 6.5 h, whereas the number of colonies in the film sample containing PAN@AgNWs steadily drops with time. The efficiency of inactivation grows over time. The PAN@AgNWs film exhibits obvious antibacterial action, with an inactivation efficiency of 96.3 % within 2.5 h and 98.6 % within 4.5 h (Fig. 6d). The linear fitting diagram of disinfection kinetics in Fig. 6e is based on the Chick classic disinfection model [85]. This demonstrates that the PAN@AgNWs polymer composite membrane has a very high inactivation rate. As a result, it is demonstrated that the composite material has the function of limiting E. coli activity.

paragraph_context: In summary, a unique multifunctional membrane of electrostatically spun Polyacrylonitrile @ Silver nanowires (PAN@AgNWs) was prepared by a simple and controlled filtration extraction method. The nucleation barrier energy of lithium is significantly reduced, due to the superb lithophilic of AgNWs for lithium. Volume changes of Li metal during lithium plating/stripping can be accommodated by the porous structure of the electro-spun film. Because of its large specific surface area and good electrical conductivity, the PAN@AgNWs current collector is useful for lowering the local current density and reducing the formation of lithium dendrites. Impressively, at a current density of 1 mA cm− 2 and deposition capacity of 1 mAh cm− 2 , the Li-PAN@AgNWs cell exhibited stable cycling performance with low voltage hysteresis (\~16.7 mV) for 4500 h. Therefore, silver nanowires prevent E. coli growth significantly, with a sterilizing rate of 96.3 % at 2.5 h. paragraph_context: Lithium metal is considered as the ultimate anode material for next-generation Li based battery chemistries. The constituted lithium metal batteries (LMBs) specialize in high energy density, but the inherent dendritic lithium growth as well as the serious proliferation of native solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) have been impeding their practical application, in particular under the high-rate conditions of a more concentrated Li+ flux. Herein, we report a composite anode design, in which LiF/LiC as the products of the in situ spontaneous reductive defluorination between Li and poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) are uniformly implanted in bulk metallic Li via facile mechanical kneading. The macroscopical composite anode creates a dispersion of lithiophilic nanodomains microscopically in bulk. The built-in LiF/LiC doping of high Li adsorption energy improves the affinity towards Li+ flux and avoids the Li+-adhesion-induced Li aggregation. The construction facilitates a dense while large granular plating as well as the generation of a thin, inorganic-rich SEI to synergistically ensure a dendrite-free Li deposition behavior. The improved plating reversibility and cycling stability are verified in forms of both symmetric cell under harsh conditions up to 30 mA cm− 2 @30 mAh cm− 2 and high-areal-capacity Li||LiFeO4 full cell for 500 cycles at 3 C. This not only expands the state-of-the-art LMBs under high-loading and power-intensive scenarios, but also preliminarily evidences its scalable and industry-adaptable potential.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The state-of-the-art graphite anode in conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) is reaching its theoretical limit and the development of alternatives with higher energy densities is desired to satisfy the continuously increasing energy demand in various applications and energy storage devices [1,2]. In this regard, lithium (Li) metal anode and the built Li metal battery (LMB) have become the most promising pairs in enhancing the energy density of batteries by both academic and industrial researchers [3,4]. This is attributed to the highest theoretical specific capacity of 3860 mAh g− 1 for lithium metal combining with its lowest redox potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode) [5,6]. Despite such striking advantages, to realize the practical implementation of LMBs, several great technological challenges require to be timely identified and tackled. Though excessive amount of Li is commonly used [7], the continuous loss of active Li in LMB is still the most dominant problem, as it would fatally deteriorate the long-term cycling stability and degrade the overall cell performance [8]. In a cycling Li metal anode, the irreversible Li consists of the electrically isolated metallic Li (inactive Li or “dead” Li) evolved from dendritic Li and the electrochemically and chemically generated Li+ compounds in the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [9]. SEI species are derived from the undesirable parasitic reactions between the metallic lithium of high chemical activity and electrolytes [10], and such parasitic reactions are easily exacerbated by the notorious dendrites, which expose fresh active Li to electrolyte [11].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Guiding even Li nucleation/growth to inhibit dendrite growth and passivating the Li/electrolyte interface to suppress SEI proliferation are crucial for battery performance improvements [12,13]. Considerable efforts have been devoted to regulating the anode side interface from the perspective of electrolyte engineering (including fluorinated ether solvents [14–16], localized highly concentrated electrolyte (LHCE) [17], and functional additives [18]), and interface engineering (including artificial SEI coating [19] and nanoscale interfacial layer [20,21]). These efforts effectively alleviate certain problems and achieve a better understanding of the interface evolution and protection [8,22,23]. Strategies and approaches that decrease energy barriers, create lithiophilic interphase and enhance the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ mobility to homogenize the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux on Li surface are favored [22]. This implies that the surface/bulk composition tailoring should be equally emphasized. It necessitates the development of rational doping recipe and proper technological processing, which is capable of fine-tuning the Li/electrolyte interfacial environment to unlock the electroplating behaviors and parasitic reactions.

paragraph_context: In this work, we developed a Li/LiF/LiC composite anode, which was fabricated via a facile mechanical kneading operation. An in situ reductive defluorination reaction between Li and poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) was triggered, which spontaneously implanted the produced LiF/LiC into both the bulk and surface of the metallic Li. Compared to bare Li, the high Li adsorption energy of LiF/LiC improved the overall affinity towards $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux, which directed a dense while large granular plating morphology to suppress the parasitic reactions between Li and electrolyte, forming a thin and inorganic-rich SEI. This composite Li anode demonstrated a stable cycling even under an extremely harsh condition of 30 mA cm− 2 @30 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a greatly enhanced cycle stability for high-areal-capacity full cell (500 cycles at 3 C). This work offers a new strategy for constructing composite Li metal with high stability and improved deposition reversibility, manifesting great potential for future high-performance Li metal and high-energy-density LMBs.

paragraph_context: In connection with primary lithium batteries, the electroreduction of fluorographites (polycarbon fluorides, $( \mathrm { C F } _ { x } ) _ { \mathfrak { n } } \left( x \leq 1 \right) )$ has been extensively explored since 1968 [24]. Such electrochemical carbonization process is initiated in reductive circumstance, and it is applicable for various fluoropolymers and low molecular weight perhalogenated hydrocarbons. Since then, past experimental study has demonstrated the decomposition of PTFE in contact with Li-amalgam [25] in 1970s, forming metal fluorides and defluorinated polymers including polyene or/and unsaturated fluorocarbon species. A step further, the detailed reductive decomposition mechanism of PTFE by Li was revealed [26]. On the one hand, PTFE itself has a very negative energy for the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), suggesting the natural tendency of PTFE towards reductive reactions. On the other hand, based on calculations using density functional theory (DFT), PTFE would undergo continuous cleavage of C–F bond to produce LiF and defluorinated carbon.

paragraph_context: Inspired by such attempts, the in situ spontaneous reductive defluorination between Li and PTFE was firstly involved for the modi fication of Li bulk, instead of the routine synthesis of the electrochemical carbons. Fig. 1a presents the conceptual preparation process of the composite anode. Upon repeat calendaring, PTFE powder dilutes and uniformly disperses into the Li matrix to promote the mechanical energy-induced defluorination of PTFE as well as the fluorination of Li. As the results, electrochemical carbon was intermediately formed, followed by a further lithiation with flood lithium to generate LiC. Thus, via facile mechanical kneading, LiF–LiC hetero-interface is implanted in bulk metallic Li.

paragraph_context: It has been confirmed that the adsorption energy of Li atom on substrate $( E _ { a d s } )$ should be higher than the intrinsic cohesive energy of Li atom of − 1.61 eV to favor a laminar lithium deposition manner against dendrite [27]. A negative adsorption energy means that the free energy change of the adsorption process is negative, that is, the adsorption process is spontaneous. The magnitude of the adsorption energy determines the adsorption strength, a diminished negative value of the adsorption energy corresponds to heightened adsorption energy, while conversely, an increased negative value results in attenuated adsorption energy. Fig. 1b− d illustrate the stable configurations and the corresponding charge density differences of Li atom on Li (110), LiF (110) and LiC (110) facet, respectively. The blue and yellow regions represent charge loss and accumulation. The absorption of Li atom has a significant impact on the electronic state and charge distribution of the surrounding area, leading to an electron transfer from Li to F and C atoms surrounding the region. On the basis of our DFT calculations in Fig. 1e and Fig. S1, the $E _ { a d s }$ values on Li (110), (200) and (211) are − 1.55, − 1.58 and − 1.83 eV, respectively. This verifies that the $E _ { a d s }$ on metallic lithium approaches the cohesive energy of lithium, indicating an easy aggregation of Li. The introduced LiF $( - 2 . 8 0 ~ \mathrm { e V } )$ and LiC (− 6.30 eV) would significantly enhance the overall $E _ { a d s }$ level. Stronger Li atom adsorption facilitates the crystal facet growth on LiC and LiF, thus inducing an oriented Li deposition and growth on the composite anode. Moreover, LiF specializes in interface Li diffusivity instead of bulk ionic conductivity as determined by the huge difference in carrier concentration [28,29]. Specifically, the low carrier concentration of bulk LiF $( < 1 . 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 } )$ drives down its bulk ionic conductivity, while the high carrier concentrations in LiF involved interfaces (i.e. LiF/Li of 0.2 mol $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 } )$ contribute to its ultrahigh overall ionic conductivity reaching $1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { S c m } ^ { - 1 }$ level [28,29]. Therefore, it is rational to speculate that the abundant LiF/Li and LiF/LiC interfaces would further accelerate the transport of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , promoting a homogenous $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux and ultimately mitigating the dendrite growth.

paragraph_context: To gain deeper insights into the underlying factors contributing to the substantial differences in lithium compatibility, both the surface and bulk morphology as well as the SEI composition of lithium deposits on both bare Li and PTFE@Li electrodes were explored. Cross-sectional views of the electrode deposition morphology can quick elucidate the difference. After plating 20 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 ^ { - } }$ of Li, a thicker surface proliferation layer is observed in bare Li than in PTFE@Li (Fig. 4a, d). The proliferation is a mixture of the products of the parasitic reactions between the electrolyte and Li (i.e. the native SEI), as well as large amount of mossy Li and “dead” Li that inlaid within the layer [33]. PTFE@Li exhibits a relatively high deposition density of lithium. This was manifested by a dense, compact, and flat morphology comprised of micron-sized particles (Fig. 4b). In contrast, in the case of bare Li, the deposited lithium layer exhibits a highly non-uniform distribution (Fig. 4e), characterized by loose and uneven deposits. Further observations conducted via FIB (Fig. 4c, f) reveal the cross-sectional morphology evolution upon cycling. After 10 cycles under 10 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } @ 5 \mathrm { m A h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , the interior of PTFE@Li (Fig. 4c) remains a dense morphology. In contrast, for bare Li, large amount of mossy Li and a thick surface layer are observed. The growth of mossy Li promoted the formation and densification of a crust layer comprising passive sediments as the results of the parasitic reactions between active Li and electrolyte, both chemically and electrochemically. And this proliferation layer would obstruct charge transfer to the underlying lithium, leading to the diminished lithium utilization, “dead” Li and the eventual battery failure [34].

The doped LiC/LiF of high Li adsorption energy serves as the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ capture site to homogenize $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux. paragraph_context: High-energy-density batteries using high mass loaded silicon (Si)-based anode are of great interest to battery manufacturers as a transition toward next-generation storage technology. However, the huge volume expansion and insufficient cation utilization accompanied by low initial Coulombic efficiency of the anode limit the battery performance. Herein, a cost-effective and controllable clinging prelithiation strategy for high-loaded dry Si-based electrodes is proposed to achieve a homogeneous prelithiation process with improved structural stability and higher initial Coulombic efficiency. The sufficient interior space enabled by dry electrode technology and uniformly distributed lithiated alloy phases can tolerate large volume changes and avoid irreversible capacity loss, thereby improving Li utilization and enhancing cycle stability. With this prelithiation strategy, initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) can be improved by 22.3%-25.1% to around 100% even under a high-loading Si-based anode of 16.51 mg cm-2 with reduced open circuit voltage. Therefore, the assembled full cell paired with both electrodes fabricated via dry electrode technology further exhibits an improved ICE of 98.73% with high capacity retention of 88.15% over 300 cycles, suggesting that dry electrode technology combined with the prelithiation method is suitable for optimizing high Si loading anode for next-generation high energy density batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the continuous breakthroughs in lithium-ion battery (LIB) technology, high-energy-density LIBs will drive the continued development of the entire technology in the following decades, where the operating voltages and specific capacities mainly determine the energy density [1]. Since there is little room for further improvement in research on adhesives, separators, outer cases, and basic electrolyte components, current research hotspots are mainly focused on active materials and manufacturing technologies of electrodes, especially for the anode [2]. Some new anode coating technologies are designed to improve the energy density of batteries, such as dry coating technology [3–5]. As an energy-efficient, low-operating-cost, and environmentally-friendly electrode manufacturing process [6–8], dry coating technology can maximize the active material loading threshold of electrodes with a thickness ranging from 20.0 to 100.0 μm. Such a high mass loading strategy is a promising way to improve the energy density of LIBs by reducing the proportion of inactive component ratios and maximizing the proportion of active materials in limited spaces of overall cell devices [9–12]. As for anode active materials, graphite is the most mainstream commercial anode material today [13], accounting for more than 95% of the market share. For the next-generation anode materials towards high-energy-density LIBs, Si-based anode has been considered as one of the most promising alternatives [14–18], with attractive operating voltage and gravimetric capacity 10 times higher than that of graphite.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Many design strategies have been devoted to improving the performance of Si-based anode by employing unique nanostructures and forming composites with electrochemically inactive materials, all of which require the consumption of a large amount of lithium (Li) ions to form stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, thereby impairing energy density [19,20]. Moreover, for ultrahigh-loading electrodes, the Li loss becomes more serious due to the presence of more active materials. Fortunately, various prelithiation methods, which introduce additional active Li ions into anode materials before assembling batteries, can effectively address this problem and improve energy density [21]. Based on different protocols and mechanisms, the prelithiation strategies can be mainly divided into two categories: electrochemical methods and chemical methods [22]. Electrochemical methods are widely used on a laboratory scale by constructing a half-cell structure consisting of Li metal anode [23,24], but require multistep complex reassembly and disassembly processes, which is not conducive to large-scale production. The chemical method refers to immersing the Si-based materials in a Li-containing solution [25–27], which requires strict reaction and storage environments. Unfortunately, both electrochemical and chemical prelithiation methods are limited by their significant complexity and low industrial feasibility, which require the optimizations of the prelithiation strategy with a deep understanding of their mechanism.

paragraph_context: Herein, we proposed a controllable, cost-effective, and industryadaptable clinging prelithiation method to optimize high Si-loaded anode fabricated by dry electrode technology. A conventional Si-based anode that underwent a prelithiation process was prepared as a comparison. Taking advantage of the contact-type spontaneous lithiated alloy reaction, the lithiated dry Si-carbon-based anode (LDSC) is successfully prepared with a stable SEI layer, which can compensate for active Li-ion loss during the initial cycle and tolerate large volume changes, resulting in a high initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) and improved cycling performance. With this homogeneous prelithiation strategy, 22.3%-25.1% improvements in ICE are achieved for half cells with a high Si-loaded anode of 16.51 mg cm-2, and the prelithiated dry electrode enables a high ICE of 98.73% in full cells with excellent cycling retention of 88.15% after 300 cycles, which achieve a breakthrough in solving the challenges of low ICE and huge volume changes for high capacity anodes, further accelerating the application of high-energydensity batteries.

paragraph_context: It is well known that the lithiation mechanism of Si-based anode is based on the reversible Li alloying/dealloying process, in which a series of alloy phases will be formed corresponding to the phase transition from crystalline Si to amorphous Li-Si alloy during the discharging processes. With the help of the density functional theory (DFT) calculations, a LixSi phase is spontaneously formed during the roll-to-roll prelithiation process when the crystalline Si reacts with Li ions. As shown in Fig. 1 c, the lithiated Si is formed primarily as an amorphous phase, and the binding energy of the LixSi phase decreases with the increase of Li ions. The binding energies for LiSi, Li Si, and Li Si phases are -1.24 eV, -2.68 eV, and -3.61 eV (Table S1), respectively, further demonstrating that the prelithiation process of Si-based materials can proceed spontaneously. Si-based materials act as the reservoir compensating for Li trapping to store additional active Li ions before battery packaging. From the cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images, the thickness of the DSC electrode is increased from the initial 51.25 μm to 70.21 μm after the prelithiation process with a flat surface (Figs. 1 d and S2), corresponding to the formation of the $\operatorname { L i } _ { \mathbf { X } } S \mathbf { i }$ phase and SEI layer with the corresponding volume change rate of 36.90%. The PTFE binder still exhibits a fibrous structure, further maintaining the integrity of the electrode during the large volume change caused by the lithiation process (Fig. S4). The obtained LDSC with open pores can tolerate large volume changes during longterm charging-discharging cycles. The corresponding energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) images clearly show that Si, O, and C are evenly distributed in the electrode (Fig. 1 e). The uniformly distributed LixSi phase helps to maintain structural integrity and reduces the irreversible consumption of Li ions during long-term cycling. Furthermore, the surface of the LDSC electrode remains flat after prelithiation even with SEI formation and large volume change (Figs. S5 and S6). Furthermore, due to the advantages of the dry electrode preparation method, the surface of the LDSC electrode remains flat after prelithiation even in the presence of large volume changes (Figs. S5–S7). In sharp contrast, the wet Si-carbon-based anode (WSC) made by conventional electrode preparation methods using polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder and poisonous N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent exhibits a bumpy and rough surface, where some cracks on the surface can be observed after prelithiation process, further demonstrating that conventional electrode preparation method cannot maintain structural integrity due to the large volume change during the prelithiation process (Figs. S8 and S9). However, our prelithiation method can still obtain prelithiated WSC electrodes and replenish Li ions in the anode before assembling the battery, which is bound to improve the electrochemical performance of the battery to a certain extent.

paragraph_context: In summary, a controllable, cost-effective, and industry-adaptable clinging prelithiation strategy was adopted by introducing a contacttype spontaneous lithiated alloy reaction in a dry Si-based anode to enable better electrochemical and mechanical properties. The formation of homogeneous Li Si alloy phases can compensate for the irreversible Li-ion loss in the initial cycle, and the abundant open pores in the high dry Si-loaded electrode can tolerate large volume changes, further resulting in an improved cycling performance. The half cells with lithiated high Si-loaded anode up to 16.51 mg cm-2 deliver an ICE of around 98.42%-100.09%, and all dry electrode-based full cells show over 98.73% of ICE with a capacity retention of 88.15% for 300 cycles. Within this context, the dry electrode technology combined with the prelithiation strategy stands out as a promising solution for the scalable manufacturing of various high-capacity anodes and serves as a suitable candidate for next-generation high-energy-density batteries.

paragraph_context: Lithium (Li) metal has been extensively regarded as the ultimate choice for the anode in rechargeable high energy density Li-based batteries to meet the ever-increasing demands for electric vehicles and gridscale energy storage [1], because it possesses the highest theoretical capacity (3860 mAh⋅g-1, or 2061 mAh cm-3) and lowest electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode) among all possible candidates [2,3]. Nevertheless, Li metal anode realizes the reversible release/storage of Li ions based on a conversion mechanism, which will inevitably trigger the irregular dendrite-like deposition and uncontrollable volume change due to the imperfect substrate and “frameless” nature [4–6]. The growth of dendrites is considered to be the primary cause of internal short circuits in batteries, leading to thermal runaway and explosion hazards [7]. Furthermore, the volume variation of the “frameless” Li metal electrode also causes repeated breakage and reconstruction of the fragile solid electrolyte interface (SEI) during cycling, accompanied by continuous depletion of active Li and electrolyte, consequently leading to low Coulombic efficiency (CE), fast performance degradation, and ultimately short cycle life of the batteries [8].

paragraph_context: In order to tackle the issues of Li metal anode, various strategies have been proposed, including advanced electrolyte design [9,10], electrode-electrolyte interface engineering [11,12], and three-dimensional (3D) framework manufacturing [13–17]. Through these approaches, the suppression of Li dendrites growth or restriction of large volume change can be realized, but there are very few of both can be achieved simultaneously. On one hand, the electrolyte design and electrolyte-electrode interface engineering are usually used to construct a dense SEI by adding novel additives or introducing an artificial SEI on the Li anode [18–20] to suppress the growth of Li dendrites. However, the planar Li metal anodes still undergo large volume change during the cycling process, especially at large area capacities, which severely limits the use of Li metal anodes. On the other hand, 3D frameworks are generally adopted as hosts in anodes to accommodate Li and reduce volume change, yet most of them, such as Cu foams [21–24], Ni foams [25–28], and carbon frameworks [29–31], etc. possess poor wettability to Li, resulting in large Li nucleation overpotential and uneven Li deposition during the Li plating process, which requires further modification and treatment during the electrode preparation process. Moreover, as the thickness of the anode is closely related to that of the 3D hosts, the volumetric energy density of these 3D Li metal composite anodes will be limited due to the large volume fraction of the scaffolds. Therefore, it is greatly desirable to design a thin Li metal-based anode that can simultaneously inhibit the growth of Li dendrites and address the volume change induced by Li stripping/plating.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: By doping heteroatoms in the molten state of Li, Li-M alloy phase (M: Ag, Mg, Al, Zn, etc.) conductive frameworks have been constructed inside Li metal foils recently to facilitate planar Li deposition and electrode structural stabilization [32–36]. However, the adhesive nature and poor mechanical processability typically lead to thick Li metal anodes [37–39], forestalling applications of the strategy from the laboratory to commercialization, as the large thickness of the anodes may not only undermine the energy density of the batteries, but also aggravate the waste of Li resources. To meet the requirements of practical cells for high-energy-density LMBs $( > 3 5 0 \mathrm { w h } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ with an areal capacity (e.g., $4 . 0 \ \mathrm { m A h \ c m ^ { - 2 } ) }$ of the state-of-art industrial cathodes, the thickness of a reliable Li metal foil anode should be ≤ 60 μm in consideration of the low negative/positive capacity ratio (N/P ratio < 3) [40]. Whereas, the failure mechanisms of the batteries become more complex as the thickness of Li metal electrodes decreases [41,42]. Therefore, it is of vital strategic significance to explore a facile and scalable strategy to fabricate thin Li-based electrodes with optimized electrochemical performances and tunable thickness. Fortunately, the mechanical roll-to-roll manufacturing method offers a much safer, more feasible, and extra cost-effective way than the co-melting method to produce Li metal-based alloy foils, on the premise that the co-rolled heterogeneous metal foils, such as $\operatorname { I n } , \operatorname { S n } ,$ , and Ag, possess excellent ductility and can alloy with Li spontaneously [43–46]. As different Li alloys exhibit varying properties in terms of texture structure, ionic conductivity, mechanical strength, etc., a binary Li-M alloy phase is not sufficient for durable Li metal-based anodes sometimes, and a multi-element hybrid strategy may contribute to a better performance of the electrode [47–49]. In this regard, Sn-In eutectic alloy with excellent ductility and small grains as a host of Li might hold the promise for preparing and stabilizing Li anode [50–53].

paragraph_context: Herein, by repeatedly calendering and folding the In Sn eutectic alloy foil with Li metal foil, Li-rich Li-Sn-In alloy (LSI) composite electrodes are constructed via a facile mechanical kneading strategy. The spontaneous reaction between the $\mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } S \mathrm { n } _ { 4 8 }$ and Li metal during the rollto-roll kneading process can lead to the generation of Li alloys with low interfacial energy, including InLiSn, $\mathrm { I n } _ { 3 } \mathrm { L i } _ { 1 3 } ,$ and $\operatorname { L i } _ { 2 2 } \operatorname { S n } _ { 5 } ,$ which endow the LSI composites with modulated ductility and mechanical properties, contributing to the LSI electrode as thin as 10 μm. As revealed by both experimental characterizations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the stable interpenetrated InLiSn skeleton in the LSI electrode produced with 20 wt % In52Sn48 alloy (LSI-20) can not only help to supply enough space to accommodate volume change, stabilizing the whole electrode structure, but also provide rich lithiophilic sites to guide homogeneous and planar Li stripping/plating, benefiting to the enhancement of long-term cycling stability and rate capability. As a result, the symmetrical cell with 50 μm thick LSI-20 composite electrode displays a long cycle lifespan of 2700 h with a negligible overpotential increase at 1 mA cm-2 and 1 mAh cm-2 in carbonate-based electrolytes. With the increment of the current density to 3 mA cm-2, the LSI-20||LSI-20 cell still survives over 500 h. Moreover, when paired with a $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 5 } C o _ { 0 . 0 2 } M n _ { 0 . 0 3 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM95) cathode with a mass loading of \~18 mg $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , the NCM95||LSI-20 coin-type full cell exhibits a high capacity retention of 89.2 % after 200 cycles at 0.5 C (1 C = 214 mA $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } ) _ { : } } \end{array}$ , far outperforming the NCM95||Li cell that fails after only 45 cycles. Furthermore, the assembled NCM95||LSI-20 pouch cell with a low N/P ratio of \~ 2.0 can deliver an impressive energy density of \~ 495.5 $W \mathrm { h } { \cdot } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.2 C based on the mass of both cathode and anode, and maintain stable cycling with a high capacity retention of 91.7 % for 100 cycles, suggesting the promising practical application perspective of the LSI anode in the next-generation high-energy LMBs.

paragraph_context: As shown in Fig. 1a, compared with the pure Sn and In phases, the finely dispersed Sn-In phases in the In52Sn48 alloy can not only pin down grain growth to refine the initial grain size, but also facilitate a more uniform alloying with Li [54]. Additionally, the Li-In phases belong to a unique class of inherently low second Damkohler ¨ number materials that exhibit high Li reversibility at ethylene carbonate (EC) based electrolyte system [55]. Moreover, the three-dimensional $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 5 }$ skeleton with high hardness and strength can strengthen the structural stability of the electrode [47]. Therefore, the distinct properties of Li, Sn, and In might work synergistically to improve the electrochemical performances of the LSI composite anode. Fig. 1b shows the schematically comparison of the Li stripping/plating processes of the LSI and pure Li electrodes. For the LSI composite electrode, the stable interpenetrated InLiSn skeleton can not only help to supply enough space to accommodate Li stripping/- plating but also provide rich lithiophilic sites to guide homogeneous and planar Li stripping/plating [56]. However, due to the absence of lithiophilic skeleton, the pure Li electrode suffers from severe volume change accompanied by disordered dendrite growth during cycling. To systematically investigate the electrochemical performances of LSI composite anodes, a facile mechanical kneading strategy was employed herein to produce them, as schematically illustrated in Fig. S1. Compared with the pristine $s \mathtt { n } ,$ the much smaller grains and higher proportion of grain boundaries in the adopted Sn-In eutectic alloy $\mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } S \mathrm { n } _ { 4 8 }$ (Fig. S2) can facilitate the spontaneous reaction between the $\mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } S \mathrm { n } _ { 4 8 }$ and metallic Li during the kneading process, generating uniform LSI composite foil. Based on the weight ratios of the $\mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } S \mathrm { n } _ { 4 8 }$ alloy used for constructing the $\mathrm { L i } | \mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } \mathrm { S n } _ { 4 8 } | \mathrm { L i }$ i sandwich-structured foil, i.e. 10, 20, and 30 wt %, the obtained LSI composite foils are denoted as LSI-10, LSI-20, and LSI-30, respectively. Benefiting from the excellent ductility and mechanical processability of the $\mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } S \mathrm { n } _ { 4 8 }$ foil, the LSI-20 composite foil, as an example, can be processed into 10 μm, but still exhibits a smooth and dense surface structure (Fig. 1c). It can undergo large deformations of curving and flattening, manifesting good mechanical flexibility and stability that are beneficial for subsequent materials processing and battery fabrication. In contrast, even though under the protection of plastic films, a much thicker Li foil (60 μm) still cannot be processed successfully (Fig. S3). Nanoindentation tests further confirm that the LSI-20 exhibits an enhanced Young’s modulus of 17.78 GPa (Table S1), significantly higher than that of the pure Li (3.37 GPa), demonstrating the superiority of the as-prepared LSI composites in the aspect of mechanical processability.

paragraph_context: Material phase compositions and the surface electronic state of the LSI composite foils were then characterized. Surface morphologies and elemental distributions of LSI foils were observed and analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and time of flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS). Fig. 1d and Fig. S4 display the surface morphology and the elemental mapping images of the obtained LSI foils. Both the LSI-10 and LSI-20 possess relatively flat and homogeneous surface morphology, with the surface In and Sn elements exhibiting uniform distribution patterns. However, the surface of LSI-30 exhibits obvious white bumps corresponding to the concentrated heterogeneous elements, accompanied by irregular pits. Moreover, the SEM-EDS line scan analysis and the obtained TOF-SIMS images for the 3D spatial distributions of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } } , \mathrm { S n ^ { + } }$ , and $\mathrm { I n } ^ { + }$ in the LSI-20 foil further manifest that the In and Sn elements are uniformly scattered in the bulk material and wrapped by Li (Fig. 1e and Fig. S5), indicating that the well-dispersed Li-Sn-In, Li-In, and Li-Sn species in the metallic Li matrix are closely connected with metallic Li to form a compact and stable LSI composite structure, which is favorable for the fast and uniform Li diffusion. Besides, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra of the LSI-20 composite foil were measured (Fig. 1f). The high-resolution XPS spectra in Fig. S6 reveal distinct peaks: three at 54.2, 55.2, and 55.6 eV in the Li 1 s spectrum; two at 444.1 and 451.7 eV in the In 3d spectrum; and three at 485.4, 487.8, and 494.4 eV in the Sn 3d spectrum. Furthermore, according to the measured X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the LSI-10, LSI-20, and LSI-30 composite foils (Fig. 1g and Fig. S7), the three diffraction peaks at 23.1◦, 38.1◦, and 68.8◦ can be assigned to the (111), (220), and (422) planes of the InLiSn (PDF#65–9300), verifying the formation of the LSI composite. In addition, two obvious diffraction peaks of metallic Li at 36.2◦ and 52.0◦ (2θ) (PDF#15–0401) still clearly appear in the XRD patterns of different LSI composites, indicating that only partial Li in the metal Li matrix reacts with $\mathrm { I n } _ { 5 2 } S \mathrm { n } _ { 4 8 }$ alloy when they get contact with each other during the mechanical kneading process.

paragraph_context: To investigate the electrochemical performances of the LSI composite electrodes with thicknesses of 10 μm and 50 μm, symmetrical LSI||LSI coin cells were assembled. For comparison, Li||Li symmetrical coin cells were also constructed based on the pure Li foil (50 μm, as commercially received). Unless otherwise specified, all the compared electrochemical testing results of the LSI and pure Li are based on the electrodes with the same thickness (50 μm). For each coin cell, 60 µL 1 M LiPF in EC/DEC (1:1 in volume) with 10 wt % FEC and 1 % VC additives was used as the electrolyte. It is worth noting that using carbonate electrolytes in LMBs is a very challenging task because it has a relatively positive reduction potential and is prone to forming a fragile SEl layer, aggravating the growth of Li dendrites [57–59]. However, since carbonate electrolytes have widespread practical applications in commercial Li-ion batteries, it is still of great interest to study the electrochemical performances of LSI and Li metal in carbonate environments [60,61]. Using the above carbonate electrolyte, the electrolyte wettability of the LSI-20 and pure Li electrodes was studied. As displayed in Fig. S8, rather than maintaining a droplet shape on the surface of the pure Li electrode, the adopted carbonate electrolyte easily spreads out to wet the whole surface of the LSI-20 electrode, which can effectively enlarge the electrochemical contact area and promote the uniform stripping/plating reaction.

paragraph_context: Based on the assembled symmetrical coin cells, galvanostatic Li stripping/plating cycling tests were conducted to investigate the electrochemical performances of the LSI electrodes. Due to the significant difference in relative molecular mass between Li $( 6 . 9 4 \mathrm { \ g \ m o l ^ { - 1 } ) }$ and In₅₂Sn₄₈ $( \sim 1 1 6 . 6 9 \ \mathrm { g \ m o l ^ { - 1 } } ) ,$ a fine mass gradient (5 wt %) has a negligible impact on analyzing compositional effects (Fig. S9). Consequently, a larger mass increment (10 wt %) was selected to more effectively capture the impact of In₅₂Sn₄₈ content on the electrochemical performances of the system. Fig. S10 shows the time evolution voltage profiles of the symmetrical cells with different LSI electrodes that undergo galvanostatic Li stripping/plating cycling at a current density of 1 mA $\mathrm { c m ^ { - 2 } }$ with a capacity of 1 mAh cm-2, indicating that the LSI electrode prepared with moderate content of In52Sn48 (LSI-20) possesses a much more stable cycling behavior than the other two cases constructed respectively with low (LSI-10) and high (LSI-30) contents of In52Sn48. The SEM characterizations of the surface morphologies of the LSI electrodes after 50 cycles (Fig. S11) reveal that the LSI-10 electrode exhibits a rough surface structure with chunky Li deposits, indicating that the low contents of In and Sn cannot effectively guide the uniform deposition of Li (Fig. S11a). However, when the contents of In and Sn are too high, the uneven initial surface of the LSI-30 with not well-scattered In and Sn would inevitably lead to highly nonuniform Li deposition and even cracks during Li stripping/plating (Fig. S11c). In distinct contrast, with moderate contents of In and Sn, the LSI-20 electrode maintains a flat and dense surface with little Li dendrites, suggesting the uniform Li stripping/plating, which is favorable for the long-term cycling stability (Fig. S11b).
