paragraph_context: To disclose the superiority of the as-prepared LSI-20 electrodes, the electrochemical performances of 50 μm thick LSI-20 and pure Li electrodes were compared. Fig. 2a shows the time evolution voltage profiles of the LSI-20||LSI-20 and Li||Li symmetrical cells cycling at 1 $\mathrm { \ m A \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ and 1 mAh cm-2. At the onset of the first cycle, the pure Li electrode displays a nucleation overpotential of \~158 mV for the formation of Li nuclei. Then, the overpotential decreases rapidly to \~45 mV due to the increment of actual surface area caused by the deposition of Li. As the stripping/plating process proceeds, the voltage polarization increases, which can be attributed to the activation of previously unused fresh Li beneath the surface and the accumulation of “dead Li”. After cycling for 700 h, the overpotential grows dramatically beyond 600 mV, which could greatly accelerate the growth of Li dendrite on the Li electrodes, causing the occurrence of the micro-short circuit with the voltage fluctuating dramatically and eventually leading to the failure of the battery. In contrast, the LSI-20 electrode exhibits a much lower nucleation overpotential (\~78 mV) initially, indicating a superior charge carrier transport through the LSI-20 electrode. With further activation of the electrode, the overpotential of the LSI-20 electrode gradually decreases to \~26 mV and then stably maintains there during the following over 2700 h cycling. The detailed comparisons of the voltage profiles of the Li||Li and LSI-20||LSI-20 symmetric cells in $\mathrm { F i g . }$ 2a at the 1–20th, 100–120th, 200–220th, 300–320th, and 380–400th cycles further indicate that the LSI-20||LSI-20 cell retains a steady voltage profile with a negligible overpotential increment even after 800 h, whereas the Li electrode exhibits large voltage fluctuations with the overpotential increasing rapidly (Fig. S12). As shown in the insets of Fig. 2a, the pure Li electrode of the Li||Li symmetrical cell shows obvious delamination and pulverization, while the LSI-20 electrode still maintains an integrated structure after cycling 400 cycles. Such distinct electrochemical cycling performances of the LSI-20 electrode can be ascribed to the InLiSn interpenetrated conductive frameworks distributed inside the electrode that can not only accelerate the conduction of $\mathbf { L i } ^ { + } ,$ , but also provide inner space for Li plating, thus alleviating the structure damage caused by Li plating/stripping. Additionally, symmetric cells assembled with 50 μm-thick electrodes exhibits stable cycling performances for over 500 h, while the one with a 10 μm-thick electrode maintains a stable operation for more than 300 h at a high current density of 3 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ( \mathbf { F i g . } s 1 3 )$ . In contrast, the voltage of the Li||Li cell increases swiftly in the early stage of cycling and then fluctuates severely until the failure of the cell after 105 h (Fig. 2b). Such poor cycling behavior of the Li||Li cell can be attributed to its inferior structural stability, uneven Li deposition, and accumulation of dead Li [62,63].

When the current density returns from 5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ to 0.5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } { \mathrm { ; } }$ , the polarization voltage drops significantly to a value much lower than that observed in the initial stage. paragraph_context: As the change of electrode structure can exert a prominent influence on its cycling stability during the Li stripping/plating process, especially with large capacity, the morphological evolutions of the LSI and pure Li electrodes during charging/discharging were further investigated. Fig. 3a and b show the surface morphologies of the LSI-20 electrode after first stripping Li to 3 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and then plating Li back to 3 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ at 1.0 mA cm-2, respectively. For comparison, the counterparts of the pure Li, LSI-10, and LSI-30 electrodes are displayed in Fig. 3c–h. As can be observed in Fig. 3a, the LSI-20 electrode presents a homogeneously porous surface after the first Li stripping, indicating the uniform striping of Li from the surface of the electrode with the continuous InLiSn skeleton left there. From the local magnified SEM image in Fig 3a, it can be observed that the InLiSn skeleton displays a compact crosslinked network structure, which is conducive to the maintenance of the electrode structure integrity during long-term cycling. The presence of the InLiSn skeleton is further confirmed by the SEM images of the LSI-20 electrode after stripping Li to 1 mAh cm-2 at 1 mA cm-2 (Fig. S18), in which the In and Sn elements are concentrated where the skeleton exists. With Li plating back to 3 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ,$ , a compact and smooth surface is reconstructed on the LSI-20 electrode (Fig. 3b). Such surface evolution of the LSI-20 electrode demonstrates that the InLiSn skeleton embedded in the composite can effectively guide homogeneous Li stripping/ platting around the skeleton, thus regulating electrode surface structure and improving Li utilization. In contrast, the pure Li and LSI-10 electrodes show highly irregular surface structures with deep cavities after Li stripping (Fig. 3c and e). The LSI-30 electrode exhibits a similar but much larger and more heterogeneous particle skeleton than the LSI-20 electrode (Fig. 3g). After plating Li back to 3 mAh cm-2, uneven mossy dendrites can still be observed and they form independent islands on the surface of the pure Li electrode, indicating that Li preferentially deposits in the direction that is perpendicular to the electrode surface rather than grows in the surface plane (Fig. 3d). For the LSI-10 and LSI-30, with the increment of lithiophilic sites in the electrodes, the compactness of Li deposition increases accordingly (Fig. 3f and h). Moreover, the top-view and the cross-sectional morphologies of the LSI-20, pure Li, LSI-10, and LSI-30 electrodes after 100 cycles at 1 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and 2 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ were also examined. As depicted in Fig. 3i, the surface of the LSI-20 electrode remains uniform and compact, whereas the pure Li electrode exhibits a loose surface structure characterized by numerous cracks (Fig. 3j), which further indicates that the uniform implantation of InLiSn phases within metallic Li can stabilize the interphase structure and regulate the deposition/dissolution behavior of Li during cycling. However, an insufficient number of lithiophilic sites in the LSI-10 fails to prevent crack formation (Fig. 3k), while an excessive number of these sites that nonuniformly distributed in the LSI-30 hinders the formation of a smooth Li deposition on the surface (Fig. 3l). Consistently, as shown in the SEM images in Fig. S19, a similar trend can also be observed in the cross-sectional morphologies of the different electrodes. The LSI-20 electrode exhibits a flat, uniform, and dense surface structure after Li plating (Fig. S19a), indicating that the conductive InLiSn framework can help to accommodate large-capacity Li via planar deposition to alleviate the relative dimensional change of the electrode [71]. Nevertheless, much thicker reaction layers with whiskery Li dendrites on them and lost contact with the substrate can be observed in the cross-sectional SEM images of the pure Li (Fig. S19b) and LSI-10 electrodes (Fig. S19c), which will inevitably consume active Li and electrolyte, causing detrimental effects on Li diffusion and ultimately leading to poor cycling performances. The heterogeneous InLiSn skeleton in the LSI-30 electrode is also detrimental to the uniform deposition of Li during cycling (Fig. S19d). Therefore, the distinct structure evolution behavior of the LSI-20 electrode during Li stripping/plating reveals that an appropriate introduction of InLiSn could facilitate the fast and homogeneous Li diffusion and stabilize the electrode structure [72].

paragraph_context: To evaluate the Li migration kinetics in different electrodes, temperature-dependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests of the Li||Li and LSI-20||LSI-20 symmetric cells were conducted. Fig. S20aand b present the fitted Nyquist plots of different symmetric cells at the temperature varying from 263 to 288 K, based on the equivalent circuit models shown in the insets. The temperaturedependent evolutions of the impedance for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ passing through the SEI, $R _ { S E I } .$ , which corresponds to the high-frequency semicircles in the Nyquist plot, are plotted in Fig. S20c. With the decrement of temperature from 288 to 263 $\mathrm { K , }$ the $R _ { S E I }$ of the LSI-20 electrode exhibits only a slight increment (from 42.5 Ω at 288 K to 354.1 Ω at 263 $\mathrm { K } ,$ remaining consistently lower than that of the pure Li electrode which increases significantly from 118.3 Ω to 1752.0 Ω. Such small $R _ { S E I }$ of the LSI-20 electrode, especially in the low-temperature region, suggests the better charge transport of the LSI-20 electrode. Furthermore, according to the Arrhenius formula [73–75], the activation energy $\left( E _ { a } \right)$ of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion can be assessed with the following simplified equation: $$ R _ {S E I} ^ {- 1} = \mathrm{A} \exp (- E _ {a} / \mathrm{RT}) $$ where, A is the pre-exponential factor, R is the gas constant, and T is the Kelvin absolute temperature. By linearly fitting $\mathrm { l n } R _ { S E I } ^ { - 1 }$ with $\mathrm { T } ^ { - 1 }$ , the values of the $E _ { a }$ for Li+ diffusion in the pure Li and LSI-20 electrodes are calculated. As shown in Fig. 4a, the value of $E _ { a }$ for the LSI-20 electrode (36.10 kJ mol-1) is much lower than that of the pure Li anode (67.93 kJ mol-1), which demonstrates that the introduction of the InLiSn skeleton could effectively reduce the activation energy for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ passing through the SEI and thus facilitate the rapid transport of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ . Moreover, EIS measurements for the Li||Li and LSI-20||LSI-20 symmetric cells after different resting periods were conducted to compare the electrode interface stability in the carbonate electrolyte. According to the Nyquist plots shown in Fig. S21, the fitted $R _ { S E I }$ reveals that the pure Li electrode experiences a more severe parasitic reaction at the interface between electrode and electrolyte, with the value of $R _ { S E I }$ increases significantly from \~94.8 Ω after 8 h resting to \~187.9 Ω after 16 h resting (Fig. 4b). In contrast, when the resting period changes from 8 to 16 h, the RSEI of the LSI-20 electrode only increase slightly from \~39.8 to \~59.5 Ω. Even after 24 h resting, the $R _ { S E I }$ of the LSI-20 electrode (\~92.2 Ω) is still much smaller than that of the pure Li electrode (\~205.1 Ω). Furthermore, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests were also conducted with a scan speed of 0.1 mV $s ^ { - 1 }$ and a scan voltage range of − 0.13 to 0.13 V. As illustrated in the obtained Tafel curves in Fig. 4c, the LSI-20 electrode shows a larger exchange current density (0.480 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ compared to the pure Li counterpart (0.033 mA cm-2), indicating its much faster $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer kinetics.

paragraph_context: To disclose the underlying mechanism that leads to the superior performances of the LSI-20 electrode, DFT calculations were conducted using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). By calculating the binding energy of Li atoms on various potentially exposed crystal planes of pure Li, Li₁₃In₃, Li₂₂Sn₅, and InLiSn, we identified that the InLiSn (111) facet terminated by In atoms exhibits the strongest Li binding affinity among all possible crystal planes (Fig. S22). Therefore, we further investigated the Li deposition process on the Li (110) facet and the InLiSn (111) facet terminated by In atoms. Fig. 4d and Fig. 4e show the simulated Li(110) and InLiSn(111) slabs with 6-layer Li atoms adsorbed on their facet planes, respectively, and the corresponding binding energies are summarized in Table S2. It can be observed that the adsorbed Li atoms on the surface of the InLiSn slab exhibit a more condensed structure than that on the surface of the Li slab. The binding energies of the first layer of Li atoms adsorbed on the Li (110) and InLiSn (111) are calculated to be 1.68 and 2.51 eV, respectively. Such strong interaction between the Li atom and InLiSn facilitates the adsorption and nucleation of Li on the InLiSn conductive frameworks, which can well explain the low nucleation overpotential and voltage polarization observed in Fig. 2a. With the increment of the Li deposition layers, the binding energy of Li atoms on Li(110) remains constant with no significant fluctuations, while the binding energy for the adsorption of Li atoms on the InLiSn(111) keeps decreasing in the first three layers but is still higher than that on the Li(110) (Fig. 4f), indicating that a new Li layer cannot be formed until the underlying layer is fully covered by the planar Li deposition, which can contribute to the uniform and dense Li deposition observed through experiments (Fig. 3) and is beneficial for the suppression of Li dendrite growth [76,77]. As the number of adsorbed Li layers further increases, the influence of the InLiSn substrate on the newly adsorbed Li atoms becomes weak enough that the binding energy approaches the value of Li atoms adsorbed on the Li slab gradually with slight fluctuation. Moreover, Bader charge analysis was also conducted to further reveal the interactions between Li atoms and different substrates. Fig. S23 displays the evolutions of Bader charges of Li atoms on the top surfaces of Li(110) and InLiSn(111) with the increment of Li deposition layers, with the corresponding data provided in Table S3. In contrast to the Bader charge value of Li atoms on the Li (110) which is only 0.63 e/atom in the first layer and then fluctuates around 0 e/atom, the Bader charge value of Li atoms on the InLiSn(111) in the first four layers is around 0.82 e/atom and it decreases gradually to 0.41 e/atom for the 6th layer, indicating excellent charge transfer ability between the Li atoms and InLiSn interface.

paragraph_context: In summary, we construct the Li-rich LSI composite electrodes with good mechanical processability via a facile mechanical kneading strategy. As revealed by both experimental characterizations and DFT calculations, the stable interpenetrated InLiSn skeleton generated by the spontaneous reaction between the In Sn and Li metal in the LSI-20 electrode can not only help to accommodate the volume expansion, but also provide rich lithiophilic sites to guide homogeneous and planar Li stripping/plating. Therefore, as expected, the obtained LSI-20 electrode with a thickness of 10\~50 μm possesses high ionic conductivity and negligible potential polarization, contributing to significantly extended cycle lifespan and improved rate capability in comparison to the pure Li metal electrode. The symmetrical cell with a 50 μm thick LSI-20 composite electrode displays a long cycle lifespan of 2700 h with negligible overpotential changes at 1 mA cm-2 and 1 mAh cm-2. With the increment of the current density to 3 mA cm-2, the LSI-20||LSI-20 cell still survives over 500 h. Moreover, when paired with an NCM95 cathode with a mass loading of \~18 mg cm-2, the NCM95||LSI-20 coin-type full cell exhibits a capacity retention of 89.2 % after 200 cycles at 0.5 C $( 1 ~ C = 2 1 4 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ , significantly outperforming the NCM95||Li cell that fails after only 45 cycles. Furthermore, the assembled NCM95||LSI-20 pouch cell with a low N/P ratio $\mathbf { o f } \sim 2 . 0$ can deliver an impressive energy density of \~ 495.5 Wh⋅kg-1 at 0.2 C based on the mass of both cathode and anode and maintain stable cycling with a high capacity retention of 91.7 % for 100 cycles. The facile fabrication, good mechanical processability, stable electrochemical performances, and potentially low cost endow the ultrathin LSI composite foil with great competitiveness in Li metal-based electrodes. The strategy presented herein also sheds light on the construction of ternary Li alloy-based anodes for the next-generation high-energy LMBs with improved electrochemical performances and low N/P ratio simultaneously.

paragraph_context: The practical application of high-energy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs) is severely limited by dendritic lithium (Li) growth and low Coulombic efficiency (CE). Herein, we developed a flexible host consisting of equimolar AlMnCoNiFe high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) uniformly embedded within carbon cloth (HEA-NPs-CC) to address these challenges synergistically. The resulting HEA-NPs-CC achieves a high average CE of 99.1 % over 560 cycles and enables dendrite-free cycling for >4700 h at an ultrahigh current density of 50 mA cm− 2 . When paired with a high-lo ading NCM811 cathode and ultra-low N/P ratio of 1, full cells retain 85.8 % of their capacity after 260 cycles at 1 C and maintain stable performance over 100 cycles at 5 C. Additionally, the pouch cell maintains a highcapacity retention rate of 83.1 % after 100 cycles. Anode-free full cells also show stable cycling over 180 cycles. In-situ transmission electron microscopy (in-situ TEM) was conducted to visualize the structural evolution of HEAs during lithiation and delithiation at the micro–nano scale, revealing negligible volume expansion and indicating robust structural stability. The formation of Li-Al alloys during cycling effectively reduces the nucleation overpotential of lithium, promoting uniform Li deposition. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with COMSOL simulations further reveal that HEAs reduce the surface adsorption energy barrier for lithium, thereby homogenizing local current density and electric field distribution to facilitate uniform lithium plating. These findings provide new insights for the design of LMBs with enhanced structural stability and fast-charging capabilities.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have been regarded as a cornerstone of the next-generation high-energy storage systems due to their ultrahigh theoretical specific capacity (3860 mA h g⁻¹), low redox potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode), and low density (0.53 g cm− 3 ) [1,2]. However, their commercialization is severely hindered by two critical electrochemical challenges: (1) Unregulated Li deposition forms needle-like structures, causing short circuits and consuming active Li due to "dead Li" formation, and (2) Repeated volume fluctuations (300 % swelling/shrinkage) during plating/stripping degrade electrode/electrolyte interfaces, leading to low Coulombic efficiency (CE) in long-term cycling $[ 3 , 4 ]$ . These issues demand innovative strategies to engineer stable Li-metal interfaces and mitigate morphological instability.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To address these challenges, researchers have proposed numerous strategies, including the optimization of electrolyte formulations [5–8], the design of solid-state electrolytes [9–11], the construction of artificial interfacial protective layers [12–15], and the optimization of current collectors or 3D hosts [16–19]. Among these, considerable efforts have been devoted to modifying Li metal anodes and their supporting substrates. Carbon materials, as substrates for Li metal anodes, can be utilized to fabricate carbon/Li metal composite anodes to enhance the average CE and suppress Li dendrite growth [2,20–22]. Therefore, the introduction of lithiophilic sites on the anode carrier is essential for achieving battery stability. Consequently, pure carbon cloth (CC) has been modified through atomic doping, surface defects, and Li alloying. Previous reports have confirmed that 3D structures with uniformly distributed lithiophilic sites can effectively promote the uniform deposition of Li metal and suppress the growth of Li dendrites [23–26].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), homogeneous solid solutions composed of multiple elements, have been extensively applied in the fields of catalysis and energy storage [27,28]. Unlike traditional binary alloys, HEAs leverage the high-entropy effect to stabilize single-phase solid solutions with tunable multi-element synergies [29,30]. Their complex lattice structures induce significant lattice distortions, leading to a high density of dislocations and defects. Meanwhile, the uniform distribution of the constituent elements increases configurational entropy, triggering the high-entropy effect. In LMBs, the adsorption and diffusion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ on the anode surface affect the uniformity of Li deposition. The multiple-atomic synergistic effect of HEAs can regulate such inherent lithiophilic properties, thereby enhancing the adsorption and diffusion capabilities. Therefore, it is necessary to gain an in-depth understanding of the lithiophilicity of HEAs, the role of HEAs in ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ kinetic transport processes, as well as the structural stability or phase transition that occur in HEAs during slow and fast lithiation processes. This will provide more theoretical basis for the design of HEAs for Li metal anodes.

paragraph_context: Herein, we reported a three-dimensional (3D) porous framework composed of equimolar FeCoNiMnAl high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) uniformly embedded within carbon cloth (HEA-NPs-CC). This multifunctional host promotes uniform Li deposition via multipleelement synergistic effects, effectively improving $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport kinetics. DFT calculations reveal strong Li⁺ adsorption on the HEA-NP surface $( - 2 . 6 3 \mathrm { \ t o \ } - 2 . 1 4 \mathrm { \ e V } )$ , which combines with the homogenized electric field and reduced local current density as indicated by COMSOL simulations, synergistically promotes uniform lithium deposition. Insitu transmission electron microscopy (in-situ TEM) captures the dynamic phase transitions of HEAs during lithiation and highlights their ability to guide uniform Li deposition during fast charging conditions. The 3D porous structure further accommodates volume expansion during cycling and effectively mitigates dendrite growth even under ultrahigh current densities. As a result, the HEA-NPs-CC host delivers stable cycling over 4700 h at $5 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a high areal capacity of 50 mA h cm− 2 . Paired with an NCM811 cathode at a low $\mathrm { N } / \mathrm { P }$ ratio of 1, the full cell maintains cycling stability over 260 cycles at 1C, and retains 80.2 % capacity after 100 cycles at 5 C. The anode-free LMBs assembled with the HEA-NPs-CC anode and NCM811 cathode exhibit an average CE of 99.5 % after 180 cycles at 1 C. A 77 mA h pouch cell maintains stable performance over 100 cycles $^ { \mathrm { ~ a t ~ 1 ~ C , ~ } }$ maintaining a high-capacity retention rate of 83.1 %, further highlighting the practical viability of the HEA-NPs-CC host for high-performance LMBs.

paragraph_context: Fig. 1a illustrates the synthesis process of the HEA-NPs-CC. The fabrication involves a two-step process: first, immersing CC in a mixed transition metal precursor solution, followed by a thermodynamically driven phase transformation via calcination at 1000 $^ \circ \mathrm { C }$ under $\mathrm { N } _ { 2 }$ atmosphere. Fig. 1b depicts the hydrophilic-treated CC with a smooth, impurity-free surface, providing a clean substrate for metal precursor adsorption. Subsequently, during the temperature-programmed carbonization, the five mixed metal precursors $( { \mathbb A } ^ { 3 + } , \ { \overline { { { \bf M } } } } { \bar { \bf n } } ^ { \bar { 2 } + } , \ { \bf C } { \bf 0 } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { N i ^ { 2 + } }$ , and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ undergo decomposition. The ample kinetic energy causes the metal atoms to diffuse vigorously, thereby forming a highentropy phase. As shown in the SEM images in Fig. 1a and Fig. 1d, a large number of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) are successfully, densely, and uniformly embedded in the 3D CC matrix.

paragraph_context: Structural characterization via TEM reveals distinct microstructural features. The TEM image of HEA-NPs-CC reveals a uniform nanoparticle morphology with a radius of approximately 50 nm (Fig. S2). It is worth noting that the HEA layer is only \~20 nm (Fig. S3). Additionally, the HRTEM image also shows some amorphous regions. Fig. 1a–f displays an interface twin structure composed of (111) coherent boundaries. The observed lattice fringes exhibit a double-peak dislocation (Fig. S1); the results of the fast Fourier transform (FFT) in this region are shown in Fig. S4. The two overlapping patterns from the two observed crystallites are indicated by the indexation of the FCC phases with two different colors. For the growth of the HEA-NPs’ FCC structure, the segregation of metal atoms on the (111) crystallographic plane proceeds with a twin fault packing sequence (-‘A-B-C’-D-‘C-B-A’), where A, B, and C represent different kinds of atomic stacking sites, and the twin faulted plane $" \mathrm { D } ^ { \ast }$ separates the twinned lattice “-C-B-A”. Fig. 1h shows that HEA nanoparticles are monodisperse with uniform particle size, clear lattice fringes and lattice constants of 2.050 $\mathring { \mathsf { A } } ,$ the slightly larger lattice constant measured, compared with that of the FeCoNi phase (2.046 $\mathring { \mathrm { A } } ) ,$ , is consistent with the slightly larger atomic radius of Al and Mn relative to Fe, Co, and Ni.

paragraph_context: Elemental distribution analysis via EDS mapping (Fig. 1i) reveals the homogeneous distribution of Al, Mn, Co, Ni, and Fe elements throughout the 3D CC matrix, with no observable elemental segregation. In addition, the scanning transmission electron microscopy energy dispersive X-ray (STEM-EDX) elemental mapping (Fig. S5) further confirms a uniform distribution of multi-elements distribution in a single AlMn-CoNiFe alloy nanoparticle. The composition of HEA-NPs-CC is determined by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS, Fig. S6). The result indicates that HEA-NPs-CC is composed of equiatomic composition, validating the high-entropy nature of the alloy. According to the definition of statistical thermodynamics, the configurational entropy $( \Delta S _ { \mathrm { c o n f } } )$ of HEA-NPs-CC is calculated to be 1.598 R using Equation S1. According to the entropy concept, HEAs are quantitatively defined as having a configurational entropy larger than 1.5R in their random solution state [31,32]. Therefore, taking into account the single crystal phase observed, the large atomic percentage of each element, and the high entropy calculated, the HEA-NPs-CC produced here is probed to be a HEA.

As shown in Fig. 2a, the CC and Cu substrates exhibit nucleation overpotentials of 23.1 mV and 47.3 mV, respectively, at a current density o $\bar { 0 . 5 } \mathbf { m A } \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . In contrast, the Cu substrate’s CE significantly decreases after only 50 cycles, while the CC substrate maintain stability for up to 136 cycles. This indicates that unmodified Cu foil and pure CC are inadequate substrates for Li metal anodes. Notably, when the current density is increased to 5 mA cm− 2 , the HEA-NPs-CC substrate exhibited excellent cycling performance, maintaining an average CE of 99.0 % after 160 cycles. paragraph_context: To further elucidate the dynamic Li deposition mechanism, two finite element models—HEA-NPs-CC and CC were constructed to simulate Li deposition behavior. Specifically, the HEA-NPs-CC model features an ultra-smooth layer with high ionic conductivity (≈ $1 0 . 4 \mathrm { S } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ loaded with nanoparticle arrays (Fig. S16a, S16b). A conventional carbon model with ionic conductivity $( \approx 2 . 2 \ : \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } } )$ was established to simulate the actual distribution of Li on the carbon surface (Fig. S16c, S16d). Simultaneously, to better identify the changes in surface details during the deposition process, the entire deposition process was divided into four stages (Fig. 3d, 3f). Due to the nanoscale alloy arrays in HEA-NPs-$\mathrm { C C } ,$ the initial HEA-NPs-CC model surface has minimal height differences at nucleation sites, which facilitates uniform Li deposition (Fig. 3d (I)). In stages II-IV (Fig. 3d), metallic Li is uniformly deposited on both the surfaces of the nanoscale HEA alloy arrays and interstitial sites. In contrast, the CC model’s lower ionic conductivity results in reduced initial local current density, while its lithiophobic surface promotes Li accumulation and the formation of high-concentration regions in subsequent stages (Fig. 3f (II-IV)). During the Li deposition simulation, Li⁺ preferentially deposits at high local current density sites rather than uniformly across the surface (Fig. S17).

S18, and S19). In Figs. S18, when the capacity reaches 1 mA h cm− 2 , the HEA-NPs-CC surface gradually becomes coated with Li metal, which diffuses uniformly (Fig. S18a (II)). paragraph_context: Uniform Li deposition critically depends on interfacial stability, as Li dendrite growth remains a primary determinant of battery failure. To characterize the evolution of impedance and Li-ion diffusion kinetics during electrochemical cycling, in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements and distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis were performed (Fig. 5(a–d)). A typical EIS profile exhibits two semicircles: the high-frequency semicircle corresponds to bulk impedance, while the low-frequency semicircle reflects interfacial impedance [47,48]. Fig. 5(d-g) illustrates the impedance evolution of HEA-NPs-CC||Li and CC||Li half-cells under identical cutoff voltage conditions. For HEA-NPs-CC||Li, the semicircular impedance continuously shrank during discharge, decreasing from 45 to 19 Ω. During charging, the anode’s ionic conductivity declined gradually due to continuous stripping of the Li metal surface, causing the HEA-NPs-CC|| Li interfacial impedance to increase from 22 to 39 Ω. In contrast, the CC||Li interfacial impedance exhibited erratic behavior without consistent trends.

paragraph_context: To dissect the Li kinetic processes across different time scales, the EIS data were analyzed using DRT methodology. DRT results during discharge revealed four dominant peaks—labeled D1, D2, D3, and D4 (Fig. 5a , 5c ). Notably, the D1 peak at a relaxation time of $1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ s was associated with solid–solid contact resistance $\left( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { i n t e r } } \right)$ . The minimal variations observed during cycling indicate intimate interlayer–electrolyte contact and high interfacial compatibility, which are critical for stable Li plating/stripping. Peak D2 corresponds to the ion transport across the interfacial solid electrolyte interface (SEI) resistance $( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { S E I } } ) ,$ , while peak D3 reflects charge transfer during the redox processes of Li metal [49]. During subsequent discharge, peak D2 gradually shifted to the high-frequency region and stabilized, attributed to uniform interfacial charge transfer at the anode surface. Conversely, peak D3 shifted to the low-frequency region and stabilized, which can be attributed to uniform interfacial charge transfer at the anode surface. Notably, the low-frequency peak D4 was associated with interfacial Li diffusion: as Li deposition increased, both the charge transfer resistance $\mathrm { ( R _ { c t } ) }$ values and peak magnitudes of D4 exhibited a downward trend.

The content of the inorganic component Li2O (528.7 eV) increases from 4.95 % in CC to 6.68 % in HEA-NPs-CC. The presence of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ promotes the formation of an inorganic-rich SEI, which not only ensures the stability of the SEI but also effectively suppresses side reactions [52,53]. In the F 1 s spectrum, the content of Li fluoride (684.9 eV) in the SEI increases from 85.09 % in CC to $9 2 . 8 1$ % in HEA-NPs-CC. Li fluoride, characterized by high Young’s modulus and relatively low ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ diffusion barrier, can significantly enhance the mechanical strength of the SEI, making it more stable. The presence of Li-F and Li-N, as indicated by the N 1 s and Li 1 s spectra, suggests that TFSI⁻ anions and adsorbed ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ promote the formation of a LiF/Li₃N SEI [54]. The inner layer is primarily composed of Li, N, and metal atoms, with their stoichiometric ratios remaining unchanged. For the S 2p spectrum (Fig. S25), the enhanced XPS signals of sulfur compounds (mainly SO₂F and SOₓ) indicate that the inner layer of the SEI in HEA-NPs-CC is rich in inorganic components derived from the decomposition of TFSI⁻ anions [55]. Metallic bonding features in the N 1 s and $\mathrm { L i } \ 1 \ s \ \mathrm { X P S }$ spectra confirm the existence of an alloy layer beneath the SEI. These results validate the in-situ formation of an inorganic-alloy bilayer SEI at the HEA-NPs-CC interface, where the underlying HEAs promote the uniform distribution of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , while the inorganic components enhance the toughness of the SEI, ensuring the cycling stability of the Li metal anode. SEM-EDS and XPS analyses of the HEA-NPs-CC interface after Li plati ng/stripping show consistent elemental composition and crystalline structure, indicating no significant structural degradation (Figs. In the correlation matrices, darker colors indicate higher correlations between selected secondary ion fragments, while lighter colors denote lower correlations. Notably, we also analyzed the cathode CEI film composition corresponding to different anodes (Fig. S29), with detailed descriptions in the Supplementary Information. paragraph_context: a State Key Laboratory of Fire Science, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China  b CETC Lantian Technology Co., Ltd, Tianjin 300384, China Incorporating silicon into graphite anodes effectively increases the energy density of lithium-ion batteries but also raises critical thermal safety concerns. Here, the electrochemical-thermal behavior of silicon-graphite (SiOx/ Gr) composite anodes is systematically investigated by combining cell-level experiments, thermal runaway tests, and an electrochemical-thermal coupling model. The results reveal that battery heat generation is dominated by the anode and strongly coupled to the depth of discharge. Graphite delithiates preferentially at early stages with limited heat generation, whereas silicon governs the later stage and produces substantially higher irreversible heat, reaching approximately seven times that of graphite at 20 % silicon content. Increasing silicon content or discharge rate markedly intensifies temperature rise, while reducing silicon particle size mitigates irreversible heat generation; however, this benefit diminishes below \~300 nm due to the dominance of interfacial and side reactions. Furthermore, thermal runaway tests demonstrate that higher silicon content lowers the onset temperature of self-heating and significantly exacerbates thermal runaway severity, while low-rate overcharging promotes extensive lithium plating and violent heat release. These insights provide quantitative guidance for balancing energy density and thermal safety in high-silicon lithium-ion batteries.

paragraph_context: With the popularization and use of electric vehicles (EVs), the demand for high mileage drives the urgent development of high-specificenergy lithium-ion batteries (HELIBs) [1,2]. Emerging battery technologies, including silicon-based lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), lithium metal batteries, and solid-state batteries, have attracted significant research attention [3,4]. Among them, silicon-based LIBs exhibit the strongest applicability and have been mass-produced recently [5,6]. The silicon electrode can reach a high theoretical capacity of 4200 mAh/g, more than ten times as much as graphite (375 mAh/g) [7]. As the lithiation and delithiation processes of silicon anode suffer great volume change and heat production [8], silicon oxide $\mathbf { ( S i O _ { X } ) }$ coupled with graphite is a practical and effective choice to release the volume expansion problem and has been applied for long-range electric vehicles and aircraft. Battery energy density can be increased to 350 Wh/kg, even higher with 20 % silicon doped into the graphite anode. However, the thermal safety of LIB with SiOx/Gr composite electrode cannot be ignored [9–12]. It is verified that with the increase of silicon content, the thermal runaway temperature increases obviously [13,14]. The optimal operating temperature range for lithium-ion batteries is generally accepted as 25 - 45 ◦C [15]. Cold work conditions would result in capacity fade [16]. High work temperature leads to material decomposition and even thermal runaway [10,17]. Therefore, it is important to investigate the thermal behavior of ${ \mathrm { S i O } } _ { \mathrm { x } } / { \mathrm { G r } }$ composite HELIB during the electrochemical process.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The electrochemical and thermal mechanisms in the silicon graphite composite electrode are complicated, since the different properties of silicon (alloying material) and graphite (intercalation material). To explore the thermal behavior of a high energy density battery with silicon-graphite composite anode, many pouch cells and coin cells microcalorimetry experiments were carried out [18,19]. Bai et al. [20] calculated the reversible and irreversible heat of a 0.55 Ah pouch cell with NCA cathode and silicon-graphite anode. Irreversible heat, which domains the overall heat generation, is the main safety concern of the battery during the electrochemical process compared with reversible heat. To further investigate the thermal performance of silicon-graphite anode in the practical application of large-format batteries, Qi et al. [21] took a 57.4 Ah high-energy density battery as the research object. By measuring the entropic coefficients and internal resistance of the battery under different state of charge (SOC), the real-time heat generation and release characteristics were unveiled during battery discharging. At a SOC below 0.25, the heat generation rate was greatly increased because of the mismatched voltage windows of $\mathrm { { s i O } _ { x } }$ and graphite. However, there is still a lack of understanding regarding the mechanism of the impact of silicon and graphite on the heat generation of batteries. For the heat generation of silicon anodes, the thermal behavior of silicon anodes based on the Si/Li half-coin-cell was tested by isothermal microcalorimetry [22]. Parasitic reactions heat, polarization flow, and entropic heat flow of the half-coin-cell were clarified during the lithiation and delithiation process. The parasitic reactions heat caused by the phase evolution of crystalline silicon to amorphous and SEI formation, play an important role in total heat generation of the first cycle. The heat generation of silicon is also affected by electrolytes, as a less stable solid electrolyte interface results in lower parasitic reactions enthalpies [23]. Compared with silicon, the heat generation of graphite has been studied for a long time [24]. Liang et al. [25] have tested the heat generation of full-cell and half-cell, using a multi-model calorimeter. It is found that graphite anode contributes much during battery charge, while NCM cathode generates more heat during discharging. The reversible heat of graphite is of great importance to the total heat flow curve of the discharging process. Temperature rise during LIB discharging can be divided into three phases, initial rapid rise stage (0–30 % depth of discharge (DOD)), subsequent slow rise stage (30–70 % DOD), and final rapid rise stage (70–100 % DOD). The higher charge/discharging rate and higher ambient temperature result in more heat generation and higher safety risk [26]. When silicon is incorporated into graphite, the electrochemical interactions between the two phases become significantly more complex [27,28]. Although silicon-graphite composite anodes may exhibit improved low-temperature performance due to enhanced Li⁺ diffusion and suppressed lithium plating [29]. their behavior under thermal exposure is markedly different: coupled electron and ion migration between silicon and graphite has been shown to accelerate calendar aging in such electrodes [17]. These contrasting phenomena indicate that the underlying heat-generation processes arising from silicon-graphite interactions remain poorly understood. More importantly, studies on the thermal runaway characteristics of silicon-containing anodes are extremely limited. Existing work indicates that high-silicon anodes may promote earlier onset of exothermic reactions, elevated gas generation, and stronger reactivity with electrolytes $[ 1 4 , 3 0 ]$ , all of which can exacerbate thermal runaway severity compared with graphite-only systems. Yet, how silicon content influences heat-release pathways, onset temperatures, and reaction kinetics during thermal runaway remains largely unexplored.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Simulation is an important method to study the thermal characteristics of LIBs which can reveal the internal physical field. There are many simulations works focus on the mechanical and electrochemical performance of LIBs with silicon graphite anodes [31–33], but several works pay attention to their thermal behavior, especially for the thermal behavior of LIBs with a high silicon content. Ai et al. [34] developed a composite silicon and graphite electrode model. The interfacial current of each component shows that at high SOC, the graphite phase provides the majority of the lithium, and the silicon phase contributes more at the SOC. Electrochemical-mechanical models were also constructed for the silicon-graphite composite anode [35,36]. The influence of SiO fraction, SiO locations, SiO size, and C-rate on the electrochemical performance and battery stress was discussed, which guides $\mathrm { \mathbf { S i O _ { x } / G r } }$ anode optimization from a mechanical point of view. The thermal model of lithium battery during charging and discharging can be divided into two categories mainly, the lumped heat model and the pseudo two-dimensional (P2D) model. With the input parameters of internal resistance and entropic heat coefficient, a lumped thermal model can accurately predict the temperature rise of the batteries at different discharge rates [37]. Many battery thermal management system researches were carried out based on the lumped thermal model [38]. The P2D model with the merit of scalability and relative accuracy has been used broadly [39, 40]. Recently, several studies focusing on the thermal performance of LIBs with silicon-graphite composite anode have been reported at a cell level. Sturm et al. [41] constructed an electrochemical-thermal model for silicon-graphite-based LIBs with a Si content of 3.5 wt% during fast charging. The tab design and electrode design were optimized regarding their susceptibility to lithium plating. However, the model used in this work considered the silicon phase and graphite phase as one lumped phase. Shao et al. [42] further developed this model to differentiate the thermal characteristics of silicon and graphite for a half-cell. To release the calculated loads, an efficient and high-fidelity model based on a novel equivalent circuit model was established and verified for commercial 18,650 cells with a Si content of 3–4 wt% [43]. Therefore, there is still a lack of research connecting the macroscopic thermal behavior of cells with the microscopic material reactions within the LIBs with silicon-graphite composite anode. This is growing important, nowadays, as the silicon content could even reach nearly 20 wt% with the battery energy density increasing [44].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In summary, although prior investigations have explored thermal behavior in silicon-graphite composite anodes, these studies predominantly treat the composite electrode as a homogeneous entity due to the low silicon content in anodes. As a result, the distinct thermal roles of silicon and graphite during electrochemical operation, as well as the coupled effects of silicon content and operating conditions on battery thermal safety, remain insufficiently understood. In particular, how silicon and graphite separately contribute to heat generation during discharge and thermal runaway has rarely been clarified. In this work, the electrochemical and thermal behavior of high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries with $\mathrm { \mathbf { S i O _ { x } / G r } }$ composite anodes is systematically investigated by combining experiments and modeling. An electrochemical-thermal coupling model that explicitly distinguishes silicon and graphite is developed to decouple their respective thermal contributions during discharge. Moreover, the effects of silicon content, silicon size, discharge rate, and overcharging conditions on battery thermal behavior and thermal runaway are examined through pouchcell, coin-cell, and ARC tests.

paragraph_context: Fig. 4(a) illustrates the lithium-ion concentration evolution of graphite and silicon particles during anode delithiation. From the variation of particle-level lithium concentration, the discharge process can be divided into a graphite-dominated delithiation region (green) and a silicon-dominated delithiation region (orange). Because graphite has a lower working potential than silicon, it is preferentially delithiated. This behavior is consistent with the operando XRD results reported in Ref. [48]. The corresponding heat-generation density of each component is shown in Fig. 4(b). In the graphite-dominated stage, the separator exhibits the highest heat generation due to the large ionic flux through the electrolyte. As delithiation shifts from graphite to silicon, the separator heat generation decreases from $\mathrm { 3 ~ t o ~ 2 ~ W / m ^ { 3 } }$ , consistent with the lower operating voltage of the battery when the silicon phase becomes active. A distinct thermal response is observed for the two anode components. Graphite shows a net heat-absorption behavior during discharge, whereas silicon exhibits the highest heat-generation density, peaking at 14 ${ \mathrm { { W / m } } } ^ { 3 }$ , consistent with the calorimetric trends of standalone graphite and silicon coin cells, as shown in Fig. S3. Statistical comparison indicates that heat generation in the silicon-delithiation stage is approximately seven times higher than that in the graphite-delithiation stage. Fig. 4(c) further breaks down reversible and irreversible heat contributions: for silicon, irreversible heat dominates, whereas for graphite reversible heat is comparable or larger, consistent with their respective reaction kinetics. Based on those findings, the temperature-rise of HELIB with ${ \mathrm { G r } } / { \mathrm { S i O } } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ composite anode can be reasonably divided into two regimes, stage I graphite delithiation (0–0.4 DOD), and stage II silicon delithiation (0.4–1 DOD), as shown in Fig. 4(d). The spatially resolved reaction-rate distributions in Fig. 4 (e)-(F) reveal a clear local current redistribution between graphite and silicon during discharge. Graphite initially carries most of the current owing to its lower overpotential and higher exchange current density, whereas silicon progressively assumes a larger fraction of the local current as it becomes electrochemically active. This redistribution elevates the polarization and irreversible heat generation associated with the silicon phase, thereby increasing its overall thermal contribution despite the homogeneous spatial mixing of the two active materials.

paragraph_context: Fig. 5(e) illustrates the voltage and temperature variation curves of silicon-graphite composite anode lithium-ion batteries with different silicon particle sizes. As the silicon particle size decreases from microsized silicon (9 μm) to nanosized silicon (90 nm), the cell polarization drop gradually decreases, and the maximum temperature during discharge is reduced from 51.37 ◦C to $3 7 . 0 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . Based on the comparison of reversible and irreversible heat of silicon in Fig. $5 ( \mathrm { f } ) ,$ it can be concluded that reducing the silicon particle size shortens the lithium-ion extraction pathway, thereby decreasing the heat generated by solid-state diffusion within silicon particles and leading to a lower peak temperature during discharge. In addition, smaller silicon particles are more uniformly dispersed within the graphite matrix, which forms more continuous electrolyte pathways and slightly reduces local ionic transport resistance in the composite electrode, further contributing to the reduced thermal rise, as reflected in Fig. 5(g). As shown in Fig. S4, once the silicon particle size enters the nanoscale regime, the reversible heat becomes larger than the irreversible heat, indicating that entropyrelated reversible processes start to dominate the overall thermal behavior. Meanwhile, the irreversible heat exhibits a clear turning point around \~300 nm, after which the decrease in total heat generation begins to level off. This transition explains why further size reduction (e. g., from 300 nm to 90 nm) results in only negligible additional decreases in peak temperature. At this nanoscale, the characteristic diffusion length is already sufficiently small that bulk diffusion is no longer the primary contributor to heat generation. Instead, heat production becomes governed mainly by interfacial charge-transfer reactions and electrolyte side reactions rather than lithium-ion transport within the silicon bulk. Because these interfacial processes depend only weakly on particle size, the thermal behavior becomes insensitive to further reductions in silicon particle size. paragraph_context: A higher discharge rate requires larger currents and, consequently, faster electron and ion transfer between electrodes. In this study, we simulated the rate-dependent performance of a LIB using an electrochemical-thermal model, keeping the silicon fraction constant at 20 %. Fig. 6 summarizes the electrochemical and thermal behavior under different discharge rates. The battery used here is a high-energydensity design with a thick cathode layer (80 mm). Therefore, the maximum C-rate is limited to 0.4 C to avoid thermal runaway. As shown in Fig. 6(a), increasing the discharge rate enhances cell polarization, leading to a noticeable drop in terminal voltage. Correspondingly, Fig. 6 (b) shows that the maximum cell temperature rises by $4 1 . 3 4 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ from 33.74 ◦C at 0.1 C to $7 5 . 0 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ at 0.4 C. This peak temperature of $7 5 . 0 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ is sufficiently high to risk triggering thermal runaway in lithium batteries [50]. The heat generation profile, presented in Fig. 6(c), further confirms that maximum heat generation increases significantly, from $7 . 2 \mathrm { ~ k W } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ to $5 8 . 7 \mathrm { ~ k W } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 } ,$ , as the discharge rate rises. The heat contributions of individual components, shown in Fig. 6(d), also shift with C-rate: the anode’s contribution decreases from 62 % to 49 %, while the cathode and separator contributions increase from 34 % and 4 % to 41 % and 10 %, respectively. This is because anode heat is dominated by reversible heat, whose relative contribution decreases at higher currents. In addition, the thin (62 μm) ${ \mathrm { S i O } } _ { \mathrm { x } } / { \mathrm { G r } }$ anode has low interfacial impedance, so its overpotential and additional heat remain limited, whereas the thicker (80 μm) cathode experiences stronger solid-state lithium diffusion limitations, leading to increased overpotential and thermal contribution. Capacity retention, shown in Fig. 6(e), declines with increasing discharge rate, with high-silicon-fraction cells exhibiting more severe degradation. As the discharge rate increases from 0.1 C to 0.4 C, capacity retention drops by 2.75 % for cells with 5 % silicon but by 5.18 % for cells with 40 % silicon. This is attributed to silicon’s higher voltage plateau, which causes the cell to reach its cut-off voltage earlier. Furthermore, Fig. 6(f) and Fig. S5 illustrates that higher discharge rates shorten lithium-ion diffusion paths and limit interfacial reaction kinetics, leading to non-uniform particle discharge depths and increased localized heat generation. Finally, Fig. 6(g) depicts the heat distribution within the silicon-graphite anode. At 5 % silicon content, heat generation is relatively uneven, with about 50 % occurring near the separator and only about 20 % near the current collector. As silicon content increases, the temperature distribution becomes progressively more uniform across the electrode layer, partially mitigating local overheating near the separator.

The temperature and voltage profiles of a 69 Ah pouch cell with 20 % silicon content under overcharging rates of 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7C are shown in Fig. 8(a). For all cases, casing rupture occurred at approximately $9 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ prior to thermal runaway. After casing rupture, the air thermal resistance between the thermocouple and the internal jelly roll was markedly reduced, resulting in a slight temperature jump, followed immediately by violent thermal runaway accompanied by the ejection of a large fraction of the cell materials (Fig. S7). As the overcharging rate decreases, more energy is accumulated before thermal runaway. Specifically, thermal runaway was triggered at 120.8 % SOC under 0.7C overcharging, whereas the cell overcharged at 0.1C reached 156.8 % SOC before thermal runaway. This substantial difference in stored energy directly leads to a pronounced increase in the maximum thermal runaway temperature, rising from 991. $8 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to $1 2 1 6 . 6 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ , as summarized in Fig. 8(b). The visual observations during thermal runaway further reveal that, with decreasing overcharging rate, the duration of the particle jet stage becomes significantly longer and more intense (Fig. 8(d) and Fig. S8). Fig. 8(c) presents the voltage evolution during overcharging. During the incubation stage of thermal runaway, the voltage generally exhibits an initial increase followed by a decrease, accompanied by an abrupt fluctuation immediately prior to thermal runaway. However, the voltage profile under 0.1C overcharging is markedly different from those at higher rates. After the voltage drop, a prolonged secondary voltage rise is consistently observed, which is reproducible across repeated experiments. This secondary voltage rise observed at a low overcharging rate (0.1C) is closely associated with the use of thick electrodes, which induce pronounced through-thickness reaction heterogeneity. Localized lithium plating and side reactions are confined to the near-separator region, while the deeper electrode regions remain electrochemically active, allowing the terminal voltage to rise again under continued overcharging. To further verify this mechanism, ${ \mathrm { S i O } } _ { \mathrm { x } } / { \mathrm { G r } }$ anode halfcells were assembled, and the morphologies of the ${ \mathrm { S i O } } _ { \mathrm { x } } / { \mathrm { G r } }$ anodes overcharged to 130 % SOC at 0.1C and 0.3C were compared, as shown in Fig. 8(e). Under normal charge-discharge conditions, the electrode surface remains relatively smooth with well-defined particle boundaries. In contrast, pronounced lithium plating is observed on all overcharged electrodes. The internal short circuits induced by lithium plating are identified as the primary cause of the voltage drop during overcharging. Compared with 0.3C overcharging, lithium dendrites formed at 0.1C not only accumulate on the electrode surface but also penetrate into the interior of the electrode. The more uniform lithium plating under low overcharging rates delays the onset of internal short circuits, yet results in a larger amount of highly reactive lithium distributed throughout the electrode, which is consistent with the prolonged and intensified particle jet stage observed during thermal runaway.

paragraph_context: A schematic diagram of the heat generation mechanism during the discharge and thermal runaway process of the HELIB with silicongraphite composite anode is shown in Fig. 9. For $\mathrm { S i O _ { x } }$ and graphite, which store lithium through alloying and intercalation, respectively, their delithiation processes exhibit distinct thermodynamic and kinetic characteristics, leading to complex coupling effects on heat generation during discharge. Thermodynamically, the silicon content significantly influences battery heat generation by affecting the entropy coefficient and open-circuit voltage. The entropy coefficient directly determines the reversible heat term, while the slope of the open-circuit voltage impacts the reaction rate. The incorporation of silicon can, to some extent, improve the uniformity of the reaction rate, thereby making overall heat generation more homogeneous. Kinetically, factors such as silicon particle size and discharge rate affect irreversible heat generation by altering ionic diffusion rates, electronic conductivity, and current distribution within the cell. Consequently, higher silicon content reduces and advances the temperature trough on the battery’s temperature profile, while also weakening its staged features. Smaller silicon particle sizes influence the voltage decline in the later stage of discharge, and higher discharge rates lead to an overall temperature rise. The thermal runaway of silicon-graphite anodes is governed by the combined effects of interfacial instability, high reaction enthalpy, and accelerated reaction kinetics. Compared with graphite, silicon-rich anodes form thicker and thermally less stable SEI layers, whose early decomposition lowers the onset temperature of self-heating. Once thermal runaway is triggered, lithiated silicon and Li-Si alloys react violently with electrolyte and adjacent cell components [51], releasing substantially more heat and gas than graphite, thereby leading to higher peak temperatures, faster temperature rise rates, and more severe structural failure. The overcharging rate further modulates the spatial distribution of reactions and the severity of thermal runaway. Under low-rate overcharging, thick silicon-graphite electrodes induce pronounced through-thickness reaction heterogeneity, where lithium plating is initially confined near the separator while deeper regions remain electrochemically active. This heterogeneous reaction regime enables continued energy accumulation and gives rise to a secondary voltage rise prior to failure. Although the delayed internal short circuit temporarily stabilizes the cell, it promotes more uniform and extensive lithium plating throughout the electrode. Upon thermal runaway, the widely distributed and highly reactive lithium acts as an effective fuel, sustaining prolonged particle jet behavior and intensifying heat and material ejection. Consequently, high silicon content amplifies both the thermodynamic driving force and kinetic aggressiveness of thermal runaway, while low overcharging rates exacerbate its ultimate severity.

paragraph_context: Nowadays, various types of electrical facilities and the elevated demand for the wider application of electronic devices in future smart cities are calling for next-generation batteries of higher energy density, superior rate capability, and extended cycling performance. Multi-electron systems, based on related reactions and materials, have been considered as promising battery systems for future applications, and massive attempts have been made to achieve their practical use. Therefore, a comprehensive realization of multi-electron reactions is imperative for the exploitation of innovative multi-electron materials and steps forward to higher battery performances. In this review, the fundamental conception of multi-electron reactions and their application bottlenecks are given from both theoretical principles and practice.

paragraph_context: Massive attempts have been devoted to developing secure, eco-friendly, and cost-effective energy storage systems to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and curtail carbon emissions. Renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, and geothermal, are becoming much more popular alongside technological advancements. However, these sources often exhibit unstable and intermittent characteristics, necessitating the support of a complementary energy storage system.[1] Electrochemical energy Collaborative Innovation Center of Electric Vehicles in Beijing storage systems (ESSs) achieve energy storage through electrochemical reactions, which play an indispensable role in improving the tunability of the power system, integrating renewable energy sources, and balancing supply and demand.[2] On account of its long cycle life, high energy conversion efficiency, eco-friendliness, and other advantages, in recent years, the applications of ESSs have gradually expanded from power system auxiliary services to decentralized power generation, microgrid power supply, home and commercial energy storage, and other fields. Particularly, with the rapid development of science and technology, the future smart city will inevitably require the increased deployment of high-energy-density batteries in various areas, including low-altitude aerophycles, electric vehicles/yachts, wearable electronic devices, photovoltaic buildings, space and deep-sea exploration (Figure 1).[3] The applications of various fields have stimulated the pursuit of high energy density, thereby presenting multidimensional and multifaceted demands for energy storage systems.[4] The secondary batteries are highly efficient and convenient energy storage devices with multiple cycles of energy release and recovery. After the iteration of lead-acid, nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd), nickel-metal hydride (Ni-MH), and lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) over the centuries, secondary batteries have better performance and lower cost.[5] The advantages of long cycle life and no memory effect make LIBs the most widely used secondary battery technology today. However, the large-scale application of LIBs in electric vehicles and energy storage systems has caused a shortage of metal resources such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel and a surge in costs. The energy density of existing lithium-ion batteries, $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ -C or $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ -C system, is close to the limit, which is not enough to meet the demands of higher energy density and longer battery life.[6] Therefore, it is committed to developing high-energy materials for large-scale applications.

When the two sides of the equation are divided by the molar mass (M) of the reactant, the gravimetric energy density (W) of the battery can be expressed as: $$ W = n F E / 3. 6 \mathrm {M} (\mathrm {W h} \mathrm {k g} ^ {- 1}) \tag {2} $$ There are several ways to improve the energy density of the battery system according to Equations (1) and (2): i) Improve the potential difference of the battery by using a higher potential cathode and a lower potential anode. ii) Minimize the molar mass of the active materials in order to achieve a higher energy density per unit mass. iii) Introduce materials that can undergo multi-electron transfer processes in a unit chemical reaction to obtain a multiplier increase in energy density.[7] Based on the above theory, there have been studies calculating the theoretical energy densities of common systems on the basis of thermodynamics to screen the potential energy storage systems.[8] However, it is difficult to find a matching electrolyte system for ultrahigh voltage materials $(>5\mathrm{V})$ , so the energy density increase in voltage is limited.[9] The pursuit of gravimetric energy density can be achieved by using elements with low molar mass, such as materials composed of elements from the first four periods of the periodic table. In addition, multi-electron reactions, which means more than one electron transferred in a specific electrode reaction per formula in general, are effective ways to achieve high energy density. For example, compounds composed of transition metal elements such as Mn, V, Ti and non-metallic elements such as C, N, and Si can transfer two or more electrons.[10] Therefore, under the premise of ensuring the voltage, the use of lightweight electroactive materials with abundant oxidation states can effectively improve the energy density of the system.[11] In our previous work, we tried to give the basic conception of multi-electron reactions and discuss the basic theories and application bottleneck of multi-electron mechanisms from both the thermodynamic principle and the kinetic principle.[12] According to various reaction paths, multi-electron reactions can be generally categorized into the following six types: i) The single-ion intercalation reaction refers to the reversible insertion of metal ions into the host material, accompanied by a series of phase transitions of the host lattice. ii) The dual-ion intercalation reaction refers to that in dual-ion batteries, the anions and cations in the system are stored in the cathode and anode, respectively. iii) The chemical bond reaction is the storage of cations in some organic materials through reversible structural transformation. iv) The conversion reaction could be interpreted as a kind of phase transition that changes transition metal compounds into their simple substances. v) The alloying reaction is the integration reaction involving alkali metal ions and alloyed anodes, progressively generating intermetallic compounds. vi) The conversion-alloying reaction is the combination of the conversion reaction and the following alloying reaction, in which participate more Figure 2. However, limited by the thermodynamic and kinetic intrinsic properties of these materials, the multi-electron materials often have some inherent shortcomings, resulting in large volume expansion, poor rate performance, and low reactivity during charge and discharge, which need to be further optimized by advanced materials and modification methods. paragraph_context: The single-ion intercalation reaction with multi-electron transfer can be described as the transformation of the reactant from the initial phase to another phase during the charge-discharge process, and the storage or release of more than one mole of monovalent cations Li, Na, or K (Figure 2). Due to the great tunability of the intercalated host material, guest ions can enter the lattice of the host material reversibly. Depending on the intercalation reaction, a series of compounds such as $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ , $\mathrm{LiMn}_2\mathrm{O}_4$ , and $\mathrm{NaCrO}_2$ have been widely used as cathodes for secondary batteries. The specific capacity of these compounds is closely related to the number of ions in the intercalation reaction.[14] However, most materials cannot be inserted and extracted by more than one unit ion owing to the limitation of their structures. The compounds mentioned in this section can insert/extract more than one guest ion without destroying their structure reversibly. It should be noted that when multivalent metal ions are used as inserted or extracted cations, and more than $1 / a$ mol of $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{a + }}$ ions are stored or released, they also belong to the multi-electron reaction of single-ion intercalation. During the process, such as $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{V}_3\mathrm{O}_8$ , $\mathrm{Na}_{1.4}\mathrm{Ni}_{1.3}\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6$ , $\mathrm{MgMnSiO}_4$ , and others.[15] We won't dwell on this class of reactions for multivalent metal ions in this paper.

However, when the traditional metal oxides such as $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ $\mathrm{Na_xMnO_2}$ , and $\mathrm{K_xNi_{1 / 3}Mn_{2 / 3}O_2}$ discharge, the number of guest ions is often less than one, and multi-electron transfer cannot be achieved, which also limits their energy density.[16] The use of anion redox activity provides a new way to obtain high-capacity cathode materials. We summarize the anion redox materials in this part since they usually contain a layered phase, and the process is accompanied by the intercalation reaction of alkali metal ions. Lithium-rich manganese-based(LRM) material is a layered cathode material with a general formula of $x\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3$ $(1 - x)\mathrm{LiMO}_2$ ( $\mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Mn}$ , Co, Ni, Fe, etc).[17] Thanks to their ultrahigh capacities ( $>250\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ ) and voltages ( $>4.5\mathrm{V}$ ), these materials have received extensive attention in recent years. There are two viewpoints of single-phase solid solution and two-phase composite about the structure of LRM. are still in debate.[18] The structural formula $x\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3\cdot (1 - x)\mathrm{LiMO}_2$ belongs to the two-phase composite model. This viewpoint holds that the LRM is composed of a monoclinic lithium-rich phase $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3$ and a rhombohedral $\mathrm{LiMO}_2$ phase.[19] The lithium storage mechanism of LRM is that, with $4.5\mathrm{V}$ as the dividing line, below $4.5\mathrm{V}$ , $\mathrm{LiMO}_2$ is responsible for providing capacity during charge, while $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3$ is electrochemically inactive. The oxidation of the transition metal is accompanied by the release of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , showing an inclined platform in the charge-discharge curve (similar to layered ternary materials). The reaction at this stage can be expressed as: $$ (1 - x) \mathrm {L i M O} _ {2} \rightarrow (1 - x) \mathrm {M O} _ {2} + (1 - x) \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} + (1 - x) \mathrm {e} ^ {-} \tag {3} $$ When the voltage reaches $4.5\mathrm{V}$ , the lithium-rich phase $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3$ is activated, and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3$ is also involved in the intercalation reaction. The oxidation state of transition metal and manganese remains unchanged. During this process, the $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3$ phase transforms into the active $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ phase, which transfers more electrons, presenting a longer charge-discharge platform. It is accompanied by the oxidation and release of lattice oxygen. This is an irreversible electrochemical reaction, which can be expressed as: $$ x \mathrm {L i} _ {2} \mathrm {M n O} _ {3} \rightarrow x \mathrm {L i} _ {2} \mathrm {O} + x \mathrm {M n O} _ {2} \tag {4} $$ The precipitation of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and O and the migration of transition metal ions rearrange the crystal structure. Due to the destruction of the crystal structure, the original $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ cannot be completely intercalated into the lattice during the discharge process, resulting in partial capacity loss. The layered structure gradually transforms into a spinel structure in the subsequent cycles and the average discharge voltage continues to decrease.[20] In addition to layered materials, there are also disordered rock-salt structure types in LRM materials. These materials (such as $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Mn}_{2/3}\mathrm{Nb}_{1/3}\mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{F}$ ) show a high theoretical specific capacity, but the cycle performance and operating voltage are slightly inferior, resulting in a lower energy density.[21] At present, there are still many problems in lithium-rich manganese-based cathodes, hence its commercialization is still a long way to go. The fatal shortcomings include low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE), severe voltage decay, and poor rate performance. There are numerous studies on LRM modification. Effective strategies include improving the synthesis method, doping transition metal ions $(\mathrm{Zr}^{4+}, \mathrm{Ti}^{4+})$ or low valence anions $(\mathrm{F}^{-}, \mathrm{Cl}^{-})$ , surface coating, and electrolyte design.[22] For instance, in Wei's study, $\mathrm{Zr(HPO_4)}\cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ (ZHP) solid acid was used to form an interfacial protective layer to regulate the redox activity of the anions in the LRM material (Figure 3a).[23] The protonation reactions of protons in the hydroxyl group between the layers lead to the formation of spinel phases and oxygen vacancies. Between 2.0 and 4.7 V, the material shows an initial discharge capacity of 254.4 mAh g $^{-1}$ and an energy density of 836 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . Ma et al. synthesize double-shell LRLO hollow microspheres with sandwich-like shells (LRLO-500@S@C) (Figure 3b). The calcination temperature of the precursor determines the internal structure of the microspheres. The sandwich-like carbon shells can not only protect the electrode from acid corrosion and reduce side reactions but also promote the rapid transfer of electrons. The oxygen vacancies formed during the carbothermal reduction process will lead to an unbalanced charge distribution, which is conducive to accelerating the insertion/extraction of lithium ions during the cycle, and can also inhibit the oxygen release on the surface of the electrode material. The LRLO-500@S@C cathode shows an initial charge capacity of 312.5 mA h g $^{-1}$ and a high stable discharge capacity of 196.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ after 200 cycles at 5C.[25] Among materials dominated by redox of transition metals, Vanadium oxide is a widely-studied class of cathode materials, owing to their high specific capacity and various structures. As a transition metal element of the VB-family, Vanadium contains abundant oxidation states $(\mathrm{V}^{2+}, \mathrm{V}^{3+}, \mathrm{V}^{4+}, \mathrm{V}^{5+})$ , which can form compounds with different vanadium-oxygen ratios such as VO, $\mathrm{V}_2\mathrm{O}_3$ , $\mathrm{VO}_2$ , and $\mathrm{V}_2\mathrm{O}_5$ .[26] $\mathrm{V}_2\mathrm{O}_5$ is the most stable phase in vanadium oxides with a typical layered structure, which is a traditional cathode material for secondary batteries.[27] It is composed of $\mathrm{VO}_5$ square pyramids connected by common edges/corners, and a large interlayer spacing of 4.37 Å allows multiple alkali metal ions to be intercalated. paragraph_context: Prussian blue(PB) and its analogs are a class of coordination compound materials with a face-centered cubic structure, of which structural formula can be expressed as $\mathrm{R_xM[Fe(CN)_6]\cdot nH_2O(0\leq x\leq 2; R = Li, Na, K; M = Fe, Mn, Ni, Co, etc.)}$ Fe and M (transition metal) in the lattice are six-coordinated with C and N in $\mathrm{CN^{-}}$ , respectively.[33] The open 3D structure of PBAs provides storage space for alkali metal ions. During the charge-discharge process, alkali metal ions are reversibly inserted/extracted from the lattice, accompanied by the redox of transition metals.[34] There are double redox centers in PBAs, and theoretically, each unit compound can accommodate up to two alkali metal ions. The reported PBAs can be divided into two categories, including poor cation and rich cation. Taking sodium ion storage as an example, the sodium content in sodium-poor PBAs is less than one, while in sodium-rich PBAs is greater than one and less than two. Only the latter can produce multi-electron intercalation reactions, and the conversion between the sodium-poor phase and sodium-rich phase occurs during charge or discharge. A variety of sodium-/ potassium-rich compounds, such as $\mathrm{Na}_{3.1}\mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3$ , $\mathrm{K}_{1.84}\mathrm{Ni}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_{0.88}\cdot 0.49\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ , show good specific capacity $(>120\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}})$ and cycle performance as cathodes in $\mathrm{Na}-/\mathrm{K}$ -ion batteries.[35] In recent years, PBAs with long cycle life and high reversible capacity have been developed and commercialized in the field of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). Manufacturers, for example, Natron Energy of the United States and CATL of China have set about mass-producing PB cathodes. However, there is still room for optimization of such materials. The PBA cathodes produced by hydrothermal and co-precipitation methods usually have coordinated water and interstitial water, which will collapse during the cycle, which may cause structural collapse during cycling. Nanostructure, surface coating, metal element doping, and improvement of the synthesis process are effective ways to reduce coordinated water and vacancies.[33a,36] Yang et al. synthesized microcubic PB without coordinated water by heat treatment.[37] The product shows satisfactory electrochemical performance and excellent cycling stability. This is because of the electron exchange between graphene oxide and PB, and the coordinated water is removed from the PB lattice. Fu and his co-workers prepared perylene tetracarboxylic dianhydride amine (PTCDA) coating on the surface of Fe-based Prussian blue through the liquid phase method.[38] The aminated PTCA (PTCA) coating with a filamentous structure (Figure 3c) increases the specific surface area and conductivity while reducing the crystal water and vacancies. The PTCA-coated Fe-PB exhibits a capacity retention rate of $73\%$ after 1000 cycles at a current density of $1\mathrm{A}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ . Although PBAs have no toxic effect on the environment and human beings, they may produce $\mathrm{CN^{-}}$ ions under high temperatures or strongly acidic conditions, which will cause pollution to the environment.
