When $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ substitutes into the Li site in $\mathrm{Li}_{1 + x}(\mathrm{Ni}_{1 / 3}\mathrm{Mn}_{1 / 3}\mathrm{Co}_{1 / 3})_{1 - x}\mathrm{O}_2$ , ferromagnetic clusters centered around $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ occupying the Li site are formed due to $180^{\circ}\mathrm{Mn}^{4+}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ superexchange interaction. Under an applied magnetic field of $30\mathrm{kOe}$ at $4.2\mathrm{K}$ , the Brillouin function for the effective spin of the clusters approaches 1, indicating that the magnetization of the ferromagnetic clusters has reached saturation. Thus, the amount of $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ occupying Li sites can be estimated by the ratio of the saturated magnetic moment of the ferromagnetic component to the theoretical saturated magnetic moment if all Mn and Ni ions were fully ferromagnetically aligned, as shown in Figure 5d.[14] Atomic-scale microscopy provides intuitive information about the presence, extent, and domains of antisite defects through visualization of atomic occupancy. For instance, HRTEM, combined with electron diffraction patterns of layered regions, can detect antisite defects in specific domains. Comparing the SAED patterns from the bulk and surface regions of the Mo and F co-doped $\mathrm{LiNi_{0.92}Co_{0.04}Mn_{0.04}O_2}$ (NCMMF) in Figure 5e,f, the bulk region shows no signal in the Li layer, while the surface region displays faint bright spots in the Li layer, indicating the presence of antisite defects.[15] STEM, on the other hand, allows direct observation of the occupancy of Li and TMs within the layered structure. In HAADF mode, where TMs appear brighter than Li, the brightness of the Li layer serves as an indicator of the degree of antisite defects, whereas the Li in TM layer is observed in ABF mode.[53] Figure 5g represents that the variation in antisite defect levels in $\mathrm{LiNi_{0.8}Co_{0.1}Mn_{0.1}O_2}$ , based on different dopants, was investigated using HAADF-STEM. These differences were visually apparent and further quantified within the unit cell using deep learning.[128] Additionally, Li/Fe antisite defects at the short-range level can be quantitatively analyzed using intensity line profiles.[18] However, careful interpretation of STEM images is required when dopants are introduced into Li sites. For example, in $\mathrm{Na_{0.67}Mn_{0.5}Co_{0.3}Fe_{0.2}O_2}$ , $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ substitution at Na sites increases the signal intensity of the Na layer.[54] Similarly, dopant occupation of Li sites can artificially enhance the Li layer contrast, which should be considered during analysis to avoid misinterpretation. STEM can also complement diffraction analysis in studying the evolution of locally disordered phases. Although diffraction techniques are capable of quantitatively analyzing disordered phases, STEM provides direct imaging of transitions across regions ranging from ordered to intermediate to disordered states, enabling visualization of the interconnected array of these phases.[17] Antisite defect affects the site occupancy of cations and magnetic interactions of neighboring atoms. Although the antisite defects are relatively straightforward in terms of site occupancy, their induced effects on the surrounding structure are critical to the electrochemical reversibility of cathode materials. Consequently, comprehensive interpretation using complementary characterization methods is essential to uncover the impact of antisite defects on performance.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Unlike the ideal case of a perfect crystalline structure, the distribution of ions in cathode materials is often heterogeneous, resulting in distinct short-range arrangements that deviate from a perfect crystal lattice. Earlier studies primarily focused on cathode materials composed of a single TM, exhibiting highly crystalline structures such as $\alpha\text{-NaFeO}_2$ -type LCO. Moreover, due to the lack of advanced analytical techniques then, the effects from nonperiodic atomic arrangement were often neglected. However, recent advances in cathode design have introduced various TMs and off-stoichiometric compositions to enhance energy density, leading to intriguing structural phenomena such as superstructure or atomic clustering. Consequently, various analytical techniques are integrated to investigate the disparity between short-range and long-range structures, contributing to the development of next-generation cathode materials.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: XRD is a conventional method for characterizing the crystal structures of cathode materials but is limited to analyze disordered structures. However, in some cases, the deviation from the XRD pattern of perfect crystal gives indirect evidence of short-range ordering. In Li-rich $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.13}\mathrm{Co}_{0.13}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.54}\mathrm{O}_2$ , even though the diffraction pattern assigned to crystallization with an O3-type stacking of the oxide layers, honeycomb ordering of the TM ions within the TM layers generates weak superstructure peaks in the XRD pattern (Figure 6a,b).[19] Asymmetric broadening of these peaks is commonly observed in honeycomb-ordered materials due to the presence of stacking faults.[21] Furthermore, honeycomb superstructure peaks are observed not only in the XRD patterns of oxide $\mathrm{Li}[\mathrm{Li}_{0.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.6}]\mathrm{O}_2$ but also in those of sulfide $\mathrm{Li}_{0.9}[\mathrm{Li}_{0.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.2}\mathrm{Ti}_{0.6}]\mathrm{S}_2$ .[20] On the other hand, in $\mathrm{LiMnO}_2$ , the highly crystalline zigzag-type layered structure transitions into a DRX phase exhibiting broad cubic rocksalt diffraction peaks after mechanical milling. The resulting weak, asymmetric diffraction peak suggests inhomogeneous $\mathrm{Li / Mn}$ distribution and structural defects or strains.[23] PDF offers structural information of materials from short-range to long-range based on total scattering, which is important to analyze short-range ordering that deviates from long-range structure. In a comparative study of DRX cathode materials $\mathrm{Li_{1.2}Mn_{0.4}Zr_{0.4}O_2}$ (LMZO) and $\mathrm{Li_{1.2}Mn_{0.4}Ti_{0.4}O_2}$ (LMTO), X-ray PDF refinement over the long-range using a structure model with a random cation distribution provided a reasonable fit for both materials, as shown in Figure 6c. However, Figure 6d displays that PDF refinement at the short-range scale did not align well for LMZO. This discrepancy highlights that LMZO demonstrates significantly more short-range ordering compared to LMTO, despite both materials displaying random cation distribution at the long-range scale.[22] To achieve a more accurate investigation of short-range ordering, neutron PDF combined with appropriate structural modeling through first-principles calculations can be notably beneficial.[29] Raman spectroscopy is widely applied to analyze local bonding and short-range ordering through characteristic vibrational modes, which is contrary to diffraction analysis.[129] In R-3 m layered structures, axial $(\mathrm{A}_{1\mathrm{~g}})$ and h)  Figure 6. a) Illustration of in-plane honeycomb ordering in $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.13}\mathrm{Co}_{0.13}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.54}\mathrm{O}_2$ . b) XRD pattern with superstructure peaks (inset) of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.13}\mathrm{Co}_{0.13}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.54}\mathrm{O}_2$ . (a, b) are reproduced with permission from Ref. [19], Copyright 2020 Springer Nature. X-ray PDF refinement with random cation distribution model over c) long-range structure and d) short-range structure of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.4}\mathrm{Ti}_{0.4}\mathrm{O}_2$ (left) and $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.4}\mathrm{Zr}_{0.4}\mathrm{O}_2$ (right). (g, h) are reproduced with permission from Ref. [56], Copyright 2023 Springer Nature. lateral $(\mathrm{E_g})$ vibrations result in distinct Raman bands, with LCO serving as an ideal model compound exhibiting sharp bands. In contrast, TM alloying (Ni, Mn, and Co) in $\mathrm{LiNi_{0.33}Co_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_2}$ (NMC111) broadens these bands due to wider distribution of mode frequencies and contributions from nonF-point modes, reflecting deviations from a perfect crystal. Compared to layered structures, the first-order Raman mode for cubic rock-salt structures is $\mathrm{T}_{1\mathrm{u}}$ , which is Raman-inactive. As a result, ideal cubic compounds such as MgO and LiF do not show Raman-active bands.[41] However, in case of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{VO}_2\mathrm{F}$ DRX cathode, a broad Raman band emerges, indicating that the cation distribution within the DRX structure is not fully random and implies short-range order.[42] Similarly, as shown in Figure 6e, the Raman spectra of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.3}\mathrm{Nb}_{0.3}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.4}\mathrm{O}_2$ and $\mathrm{Li}_{1.1}\mathrm{Nb}_{0.1}\mathrm{Fe}_{0.8}\mathrm{O}_2$ reveal layered-like short-range ordering, as evidenced by bands corresponding to axial and lateral O vibrations, analogous to those observed in NMC333.[41] Meanwhile, the increase of peaks at $450-500~\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{Li}_{1.33}\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_4$ DRX, which are assigned to characteristic vibrational modes in spinel structure, indicates a gradual increase of spinel-like short-range ordering within the structure.[43] NMR spectroscopy is employed to probe atomic clustering in terms of local environments of specific cations. Fermi contact shifts and electron–nucleus dipolar interactions have been extensively studied for $^6\mathrm{Li}$ and $^7\mathrm{Li}$ NMR, providing useful information on Li local ordering, structural defects, and changes in Li environments.[130] For example, the ratio of $\mathrm{LiMn_6}$ and $\mathrm{LiNiMn_5}$ in $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_x\mathrm{Mn}_{0.8 - x}\mathrm{O}_2$ is quantified by fitting the $^6\mathrm{Li}$ NMR spectra.[45] Additionally, $^7\mathrm{Li}$ NMR spectra are collected to detect the presence or absence of $\mathrm{LiMn_6}$ in $\mathrm{Na}_{2/3}[\mathrm{Li}_{1/7}\mathrm{Mn}_{5/14}][\mathrm{Mg}_{1/7}\mathrm{Mn}_{5/14}] \mathrm{O}_2$ and $\mathrm{Na}_{0.78}\mathrm{Li}_{0.26}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.74} \mathrm{O}_2$ across their pristine, charged, and discharged states.[46] In addition to $^6\mathrm{Li}$ NMR, $^{27}\mathrm{Al}$ NMR spectroscopy has been used to elucidate the local lattice environments of Al in pristine $\mathrm{LiNi}_{1-y-z} \mathrm{Co}_y \mathrm{Al}_z \mathrm{O}_2$ (NCA), particularly TM-O-Al coordinations and the evolution of lattice aluminum sites during NCA cycling.[47] For pristine NCA with high nickel content, lattice Al predominantly coordinates with six Ni atoms in $\mathrm{Al_{oct}}$ honeycomb sites, resulting in a distinct $^{27}\mathrm{Al}$ NMR peak at approximately $-1200~\mathrm{ppm}$ . However, as Co content increases, Al site disorder rises up, facilitating the formation of $\mathrm{Al_{oct}}$ -3Ni3Co honeycomb sites, characterized by $^{27}\mathrm{Al}$ resonances at approximately $-600~\mathrm{ppm}$ (Figure 6f). Furthermore, $^{19}\mathrm{F}$ NMR demonstrated LiF-like local domain in cathode materials. The $^{19}\mathrm{F}$ NMR spectrum of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Mn}_{2/3}\mathrm{Nb}_{1/3} \mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{F}$ indicates that most fluoride ions are located in paramagnetic environments, where Mn occupies the first, second, or third metal coordination shell around the $^{19}\mathrm{F}$ nucleus. This results in broad, overlapping NMR signals shifted away from the resonant frequency of pure LiF $(-204~\mathrm{ppm})$ . Nevertheless, sharp signals corresponding to LiF-like environments, with a resonant frequency matching that of pure LiF, are also observed, reflecting the presence of LiF-like local domain within the structure.[48] STEM generates atomic-scale imaging, which is direct evidence for short-range ordering. In the analysis of superstructures in $\mathrm{Na}_{0.75}[\mathrm{Li}_{0.25}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.75}]\mathrm{O}_2$ and $\mathrm{Na}_{0.6}[\mathrm{Li}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.8}]\mathrm{O}_2$ , ADF-STEM revealed distinct atomic contrast, observing direct local cation arrangements.[55] For $\mathrm{Na}_{0.75}[\mathrm{Li}_{0.25}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.75}]\mathrm{O}_2$ , two-atom dumbbells (Mn-Mn) along the [010] direction, as seen in ADF images, are characteristic of the honeycomb ordering superstructure. Conversely, the ADF image of $\mathrm{Na}_{0.6}[\mathrm{Li}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.8}]\mathrm{O}_2$ along the [010] direction exhibits the retention of four-atom (Mn-Mn-Mn-Mn) configurations, indicative of ribbon ordering. Similarly, Figure 6g,h shows that honeycomb ordering was observed in $\mathrm{Li}_{1.1}(\mathrm{Ni}_{0.21}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.65}\mathrm{Al}_{0.04})\mathrm{O}_2$ , where dumbbell-like pairs along the[110] direction were identified through HAADF imaging and line scan.[56] Each analytical method reveals different aspects of non-periodic atomic arrangement, yet they are often neglected so far. Recent cathode materials have developed for high-energy density, and most of them contain local domain which deviates from average long-range structure. Therefore, understanding short-range ordering and its impact on electrochemical performances ultimately takes a significant step toward the development of next-generation cathode materials TM dynamically migrates from their original sites to others within the Li layer (out-of-plane) or TM layer (in-plane) during electrochemical cycling. Although this process initially occurs on a local scale, multiple TM migrations can simultaneously occur and potentially lead to long-range structural rearrangements upon cycling that require not only atomic-scale characterization but also long-range scale analysis.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: Generally, XRD analysis is difficult to detect local TM migration. However, broader-scale structural rearrangements triggered by TM migration can be observed. Figure 7a represents that variation in superstructure peaks during the first cycle, associated with honeycomb ordering, is observed in the XRD pattern of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.13}\mathrm{Co}_{0.13}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.54}\mathrm{O}_2$ . The intensity of this peak decreases upon charging and does not reappear upon discharge, indicating the irreversible loss of honeycomb ordering (Figure 7b).[19] Rietveld refinement of the charged state further confirms that TM migration occurs within the plane, with only a small fraction of TM ions migrating into the Li layer at full charge. Furthermore, quantification of atomic site occupancy by Rietveld refinement using ND provides the amount of Ni migration into the Li layer during charge.[26] Hard-XAS is an effective technique for analyzing TM migration due to its atomic-scale sensitivity, allowing for detailed information about the local atomic environment. In $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Cr}_{0.4}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.4}\mathrm{O}_2$ , Cr migration from $\mathrm{O_h}$ to $\mathrm{T_d}$ sites during cycling has been observed using XANES and EXAFS.[35] Figure 7c displays the pre-edge peak at various charged and discharged states revealing the formation of $\mathrm{T_dCr^{6 + }O_4}$ in the initial charged state, indicated by a high pre-edge intensity associated with $\mathrm{T_d}$ symmetry of $\mathrm{Cr^{6 + }}$ . EXAFS data supported this observation, disclosing that distinct peaks at $\sim 1.0\sim 1.5$ and $\sim 2.5\AA$ each correspond to $\mathrm{T_dCr - O}$ $(\mathrm{Cr - O_{tet}})$ , $\mathrm{O_h}$ $\mathrm{Cr - O}$ $(\mathrm{Cr - O_{oct}})$ , and $\mathrm{Cr - Cr / Mn}$ coordination. paragraph_context: Furthermore, EXAFS fitting quantified the changes in Cr coordination during cycling. Similar to $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Cr}_{0.4}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.4}\mathrm{O}_2$ , hard-XAS was utilized to investigate Mn migration in spinel-type $\mathrm{LiMn_2O_4}$ .[36] The radial distribution function (RDF) profile derived from Fourier-transformed EXAFS spectra exhibited a decrease in both the Mn-O peak (first peak) and the edge-shared Mn-Mn peak (second peak) after cycling, reflecting changes in bond length distribution due to Mn migration. Notably, a shoulder peak appeared near the edge-shared Mn-Mn peak, corresponding to a corner-shared Mn-Mn interaction. This finding indicates that Mn ions migrated from $\mathrm{O_h}$ sites to $\mathrm{T_d}$ sites within the Li layer.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: NMR spectroscopy, which leverages Fermi contact interactions to detect the influence of surrounding TM ions, is another useful tool for analyzing TM migration. In pristine $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.13}\mathrm{Co}_{0.13}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.54}\mathrm{O}_2$ , $^6\mathrm{Li}$ NMR spectrum shows sharp resonances, indicating that Li ions occupy well-ordered, defined sites (Figure 7e).[19] However, in the fully discharged state, the spectrum shows significantly broader resonances and additional signals, reflecting a diverse range of NMR environments. This observation indicates an increased degree of TM disorder around Li ions caused by potential TM migration during charge. Furthermore, a substantial shift in the weighted center of the spectrum between the pristine and fully discharged states suggests that Li environments have become, on average, more diamagnetic. This shift aligns with the clustering of Li into more diamagnetic regions with fewer neighboring TM ions. Thus, NMR gives knowledge of TM migration by revealing changes in the average local environment of Li ions.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: STEM is the most obvious tool for investigating structural changes at the atomic level owing to the direct visualization of atomic arrangements. Various STEM techniques, each with unique capabilities, can be employed to analyze TM migration. For example, in a study of TM migration in $\mathrm{Li_{0.6}Li_{0.2}Ru_{0.8}O_2}$ (LLRO), HAADF-STEM was adopted to confirm Ru migration from $\mathrm{O_h}$ sites in the TM layer to $\mathrm{O_h}$ sites in the Li layer.[57] In the pristine state, Li was clearly observed in the Li layer, while both Li and Ru atoms were located in the TM layer, as verified using integrated differential phase contrast STEM (iDPC-STEM) and ABF-STEM. During the first delithiation process, Figure 7f displays HAADF-STEM image revealing slight Ru migration, along with a reduction in the spacing between two adjacent TM layers (from $0.501\mathrm{nm}$ ) due to significant $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ removal. Upon relithiation, Figure 7g represents HAADF-STEM image showing reversible TM migration, indicated by cation rearrangement in the TM layer and the disappearance of bright dots in the Li layer, accompanied by a slight expansion of the Li layer (to $0.510\mathrm{nm}$ ). Out-of-plane TM migration was also observed in $\mathrm{Li[Li_{0.2}Ni_{0.2}Mn_{0.6}]O_2}$ (LMR) using HAADF-STEM.[58] Analysis of space groups along specific crystal direction zone axis and interatomic distances revealed that LMR undergoes a phase transformation from a layered to a defect spinel-like structure (Fd-3 m) and eventually to a DRX structure (Fm-3 m). In another study, both in-plane and out-of-plane TM migration in $\mathrm{Li_{1.2}Ni_{0.13}Mn_{0.54}Co_{0.13}O_2}$ were visualized using a combination of ADF imaging and electron psychography.[59] Conventional ADF imaging effectively highlights heavier TMs, but the contrast from these atoms often overshadows that of lighter elements such as Li and O. To address this limitation, 4D-STEM electron psychography was applied, utilizing the Wigner distribution deconvolution (WDD) algorithm to reconstruct phase images from 4D-STEM datasets, thereby enhancing sensitivity to lighter atomic species. Focused-probe electron psychography also enabled the simultaneous acquisition of aberration-corrected ADF images, allowing for the identification of all atomic species. Together, ADF and psychographic imaging provided clear visualization of both in-plane and out-of-plane TM migration. STEM remains one of the most reliable and widely used methods for analyzing TM migration, and its accuracy can be further improved by integrating various STEM techniques, each offering complementary insights into TM migration behavior.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: TM migration triggered by delithiation propagates local atomic rearrangement as well as phase transition. Thus, multiscale characterization techniques to analyze structural changes from short-range to long-range are essential for the observation of TM migration. As TM migration is closely related to dynamic redox reaction during charge/discharge, it significantly affects the electrochemical performance of cathode materials, underscoring the importance of comprehensive analysis.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Research on the O redox mechanism is gaining much attention as it has significant potential to enhance the energy density of cathode materials. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, numerous computational studies have been conducted, with extensive efforts toward direct experimental validation of these findings. This validation focuses on characterizing complex structural changes accompanied by O redox, including the formation of O vacancies, O release, and intermediate species. To identify and distinguish these O species, advanced analytical techniques targeting atomic distances, electronic structures, and energy states are actively being developed.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: Although Bragg diffraction is not sensitive to local defects, PDF discloses the short-range structure, making it particularly suitable for investigating O vacancies and intermediate species. For instance, neutron PDF analysis revealed direct evidence of trapped $\mathrm{O}_2$ in Li-rich cathodes.[30] The detection of $1.2\AA$ O-O distances in the charged state corresponds to the bond length of molecular $\mathrm{O}_2$ trapped within the bulk as shown in the left panel of Figure 8a. This observation was achieved by collecting data at temperatures down to $2\mathrm{K}$ , i.e., near absolute zero, without evidence of other O species such as peroxide or superoxide. PDF fitting in the right panel of Figure 8a indicated that approximately 20 at% of the O atoms exist as molecular $\mathrm{O}_2$ , consistent with findings from operando mass spectroscopy.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: O $K$ -edge RIXS is a direct and informative technique for characterizing oxidized O in the lattice during electrochemical cycles. A fingerprint feature of oxidized O in O $K$ -edge mapping of RIXS (mRIXS) is located at 523.7 eV emission energy and 531 eV excitation energy region, indicating excited electrons to unfilled O 2p states. The left panel of Figure 8b represents O $K$ -edge mRIXS data of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.6}\mathrm{O}_2$ (LNMO) with various state of charge states. O oxidation during charge was evidenced by the appearance of a distinct spot with a white arrowhead at 4.8 V first charged state, which was absent in the pristine state.[38] In contrast, for $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Co}_{0.4}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.4}\mathrm{O}_2$ (LCMO) in the right panel of Figure 8b, the feature observed up to $-4.5\mathrm{V}$ during the first charge got weakened at 4.8 V, likely due to the loss of oxidized O species in LCMO as $\mathrm{O}_2$ release. Furthermore, 2D mRIXS data can be plotted with 1D RIXS cuts by integrating signals within a specific emission or excitation energy range, allowing quantitative and comparative analysis regarding oxidized O species. For example, RIXS cuts obtained by integrating mRIXS intensity within the excitation range around 531 eV were used to analyze O redox behavior and the tendency for TM-O hybridization.[39] By normalizing the integrated RIXS intensities to the intensity of peak II, key peaks were identified as peak I and peak III. label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: NMR is also useful to analyze O species, as differences in electron numbers and electronic structures between molecular O and O intermediates result in distinct variations in chemical shift and peak intensity. In $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.13}\mathrm{Co}_{0.13}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.54}\mathrm{O}_2$ , voids generated by O release and O species associated with anionic redox were identified through $^{129}\mathrm{Xe}$ and $^{17}\mathrm{O}$ NMR in Figure 8d, respectively.[49] $^{129}\mathrm{Xe}$ is an inert gas with a highly polarizable electron cloud that interacts with void surfaces. This interaction distorts the electron cloud and causes chemical shifts, informing the presence of open pores. In comparison, $\mathrm{O}_2$ molecules with two unpaired electrons exhibit much stronger paramagnetic relaxation enhancement than oxides. The 100th cycle charged data reveals a well-defined chemical environment centered at $\delta_{\mathrm{cg}} = 2770\mathrm{ppm}$ , corresponding to $\mathrm{O}_2$ resonance. Additionally, the decrease in intensity between the 100th charged and discharged states suggests that $\mathrm{O}_2$ is reduced to $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ , although residual $\mathrm{O}_2$ is still observed. Furthermore, NMR provided detailed information about the void size of $17\mathrm{nm}$ and the neighboring environment of $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ , predominantly surrounded by Li and $\mathrm{Li}-\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ . On the other hand, EPR measures resonance originating from unpaired electrons, enabling the characterization of radical O species during cycling. O intermediates in $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Ru}_{0.75}\mathrm{Sn}_{0.25}\mathrm{O}_3$ were identified through operando EPR in Figure 8e.[52] During charge $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Ru}_{0.75}\mathrm{Sn}_{0.25}\mathrm{O}_3$ up to $4.6\mathrm{V}$ , a new signal with $g = 2.007$ appeared, exhibiting asymmetric broadening and a positive g-shift relative to the free electron spin value of 2.0023. This signal indicated the presence of holes in the O 2p orbital, attributed to a reductive coupling mechanism driven by strong $\mathrm{Ru}$ (4d)-O (2p) orbital interactions. Among O intermediates, $\mathrm{O}_2^{3-} (\pi_{\mathrm{g}}^{*4}\sigma_{\mathrm{u}}^{*1})$ and superoxo $\mathrm{O}_2^-$ ( $\pi_{\mathrm{g}}^{*3}\sigma_{\mathrm{u}}^{*0}$ ) species ( $S = 1/2$ ) are EPR-active. The EPR line could arise from either $\mathrm{O}_2^{3-}$ or superoxo $\mathrm{O}_2^-$ species through the oxidation of peroxo $\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}$ species. During discharge, the signal displayed an overall reversible process with minor variations in reaction pathways. EPR is thus a vital and unique tool for detecting O species with unpaired electrons in cathode materials. Additionally, EPR imaging (EPRI) offers electron-density visualization as microscopy, providing critical information on electron donation mechanisms and the spatial distribution of O species.

paragraph_context: In this review, we emphasize the characterization of disorder within cathode materials for improving the energy density of cathode materials by understanding the disorder-property relationship (Figure 9). Although many characterizations are based on crystallography, we summarized how we can interpret the analyzed data and associated advantages of each characterization regarding structural disorder of cathode materials. First, we categorized the types of disorders from short-range to long-range scale. Each disorder can occur due to various reasons including interplay of atomic size, electroneutrality, and magnetic interactions. Moreover, such interactions often correlate with each other and evolve with external stimuli. Therefore, disorders within cathode materials are generated not only as a result of synthesis but also during charge/discharge as well. Second, we discussed characterization techniques such as diffraction, total scattering, absorption/resonant spectroscopy, vibrational spectroscopy, magnetic resonance, magnetometry, and microscopy with their principles. Moreover, we have summarized the case studies and focused on how structural disorder within cathode materials can be identified based on the underlying principles of each characterization and the distinct phenomena in structure induced by disorder.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Although identifying structural disorder within cathode materials is still challenging due to its complex parasitic reaction and correlation, understanding the disorder-property relationship of the cathode material is important. Furthermore, as research on disordered cathode materials continues to expand, achieving a more comprehensive and time-resolved understanding of disorder is becoming increasingly important. Therefore, emerging characterization techniques require the detailed observation of the temporal evolution of disorder during charge/discharge. For example, femtosecond spectroscopy, which probes ultrafast electronic and structural dynamics incorporated with operando analysis enabling real-time monitoring of cathode material during electrochemical cycling, offers new opportunities to capture the dynamic evolution of disorder across different timescales. Meanwhile, even the most recent and advanced characterizations are based on fundamental principle of characterization methods discussed in this review. Therefore, summarized approaches for characterizing disorder not only provide guidance on how to analyze the structural disorder governing the functionalities for developing high-energy density and high-stability cathode materials but also offer valuable insights into future development direction of characterization techniques especially for disordered cathode materials.

paragraph_context: Lithium metal, with its high theoretical capacity of $3860\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ and low redox potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ vs. standard hydrogen electrode), is a promising anode material.[12-14] However, dendrite growth during charge and discharge cycles leads to the formation of "dead lithium," deterioration of the SEI film, and reduced Coulombic efficiency (CE). Significant volume changes during cycling also pose practical challenges. Optimizing electrolyte formulations, particularly with additives $(< 5\%)$ by volume or weight), can suppress dendrite growth and regulate $\mathrm{Li + }$ ion deposition, enhancing cell performance.[15-18] Solid-state electrolytes also show promise in suppressing dendrite formation and enabling higher energy densities, making their investigation crucial for advancing lithium metal batteries. Computational modeling and simulation can accelerate development by predicting anode behavior and optimizing electrolyte compositions.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Silicon-based anode materials are being extensively researched due to their affordability and high theoretical capacity of $3579\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , nearly ten times that of graphite. Strategies to facilitate their use include synthesizing silicon as periodic nanostructures or nanoparticles and creating silicon-carbon composites with core-shell structures (Figure 3 (c)). Nonstoichiometric $\mathrm{SiO_x}$ $(0 < x < 2)$ is particularly promising for high-capacity lithium-ion anodes.[19] $\mathrm{SiO_x}$ is an amorphous material, often a two-phase mixture of silicon and silicon dioxide nanodomains.[20] The formation of lithium oxide and silicates provides buffer zones that mitigate volumetric changes during (de)lithiation, resulting in significantly higher cycling stability compared to pure silicon.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Germanium (Ge) and tin (Sn) are also strong candidates for anode materials due to their high theoretical capacities $(1600\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ and $984\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , respectively).[22] Germanium boasts 400 times faster lithium-ion conductivity and 104 times higher electrical conductivity than silicon.[23] However, challenges such as volume expansion, mechanical degradation, and the formation of unstable SEI layers remain.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: $\mathrm{Li}_4\mathrm{Ti}_5\mathrm{O}_{12}$ (LTO) is a spinel material and a promising anode for lithium-ion batteries, known for its commendable cycle stability, rate capability, and safety. Despite zero volume change during charge and discharge cycles, its theoretical capacity of $175\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ is insufficient for grid-scale energy storage and electric vehicles (EVs).[24,25] Additionally, LTO production costs are generally higher than those of some other anode materials. Continued research to improve performance and reduce production costs is essential for positioning LTO as the future of energy storage solutions.

paragraph_context: Different oxides and phosphates are the most popular types of cathode materials (Figure 3d), each offering unique advantages and limitations, making them suitable for various applications and performance requirements.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Layered oxides $(\mathrm{LiMO}_2, \mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Ni}, \mathrm{Co}, \mathrm{Mn})$ are commonly used as cathode materials in LIBs due to their favorable electrochemical properties. $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ , first commercialized by Sony Corporation in the 1990s, plays a pivotal role in the history of LIBs. This material exhibits a high theoretical specific capacity of over $270 \mathrm{~mA} / \mathrm{g}$ , a relatively high operating potential ( $>3.6 \mathrm{~V}$ vs. Li), and adequate cycle life.[26] However, it also has limitations, such as thermal stability issues and the high cost of cobalt, which is environmentally damaging to extract. Currently, NMC-type $(\mathrm{LiNi}_{1-x-y} \mathrm{CO}_x \mathrm{Mn}_y \mathrm{O}_2)$ cathodes dominate the market, particularly those with reduced cobalt content, ranging from NMC532 to NMC811.[27] Increased nickel concentration enhances specific capacity, rising from $160 \mathrm{mAh} \mathrm{g}^{-1}$ in NMC111 to $200 \mathrm{mAh} \mathrm{g}^{-1}$ in NMC811.[28] NCA $(\mathrm{LiNi}_{1-x-y} \mathrm{Co}_x \mathrm{Al}_y \mathrm{O}_2)$ cathodes typically have a higher nickel content compared to NMC cathodes, offer improved specific capacity and high energy density, making them suitable for high energy storage applications such as EVs.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Spinel oxides $(\mathrm{LiM}_2\mathrm{O}_4, \mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Mn}, \mathrm{Ni})$ are another paramount class of cathode materials in LIBs. They are less expensive and more environmentally friendly compared to other cathode oxides. The three-dimensional ion arrangement in spinel structures offers advantageous characteristics for electrochemical energy storage. LMO $(\mathrm{LiMn}_2\mathrm{O}_4)$ is the most studied spinel oxide and has entered the EV market. However, its low capacity, energy density, and short lifetime due to structural instabilities during cycling limit its use. Ni-doped spinel oxide $(\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Mn}_{1.5}\mathrm{O}_4)$ is promising due to its strong cycling characteristics and relatively large capacity, with a dominant peak at $4.75\mathrm{V}$ .[29] Despite using a more expensive component (nickel), the increased energy density reduces material costs per kWh.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Olivine structures $(\mathrm{LiMPO}_4, \mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Fe})$ have attracted significant interest as cathode materials due to their high theoretical capacities and redox potentials (3.45 V vs. Li for $\mathrm{LiFePO}_4$ ). However, issues such as poor electronic conductivity and slow lithium-ion diffusion need to be addressed. Current developments focus on overcoming these drawbacks through surface modification approaches like carbon coating[30] and doping with conductive materials.[31] Enhancing the specific capacity and rate capability of olivine cathodes through heteroatom doping and alloying with transition metals has shown promising results. Although $\mathrm{LiFePO}_4$ (LFP) has lower energy density compared to $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ , it compensates with better safety characteristics. Thus, olivine-structured materials present an effective alternative for LIB cathodes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Overall, each type of cathode material, from established ones like lithium cobalt oxide $(\mathrm{LiCoO}_2)$ to emerging candidates like olivine-structured lithium iron phosphate $(\mathrm{LiFePO}_4)$ , has distinct advantages and disadvantages. Transition metal oxides like $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ and nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) are ideal for applications requiring small, lightweight battery systems due to their high specific capacities and energy densities. However, concerns regarding cost, resource availability, and safety, especially related to cobalt supplies, have driven research into alternative compositions. Advanced characterization techniques and computer simulations have expanded our understanding of cathode materials. Future studies will likely focus on more affordable and sustainable options, achieving higher energy and power densities, and addressing critical issues such as resource shortages, environmental impacts, and safety concerns. The battery research community has the opportunity to unlock the full potential of cathode materials, ushering in a new era of advanced energy storage solutions.

paragraph_context: The components of LIB slurries include a combination of solvent-dispersed electrolytes, binders (e.g., polyvinylidene fluoride, or PVDF), conductive additives (e.g., carbon black or graphite), and active materials (e.g., lithium compounds). Solvents are crucial, despite often being taken for granted. They dissolve electrolytes, binders, and conductive additives to create homogeneous slurries, which are then deposited onto electrode substrates to form the active material layers inside the battery. The solvent choice significantly influences the morphology, porosity, and adherence of electrode coatings, as well as the rheological characteristics of the slurry, thereby affecting the performance, stability, and safety of the battery.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) is a widely used polar aprotic solvent in the fabrication of cathodes and some types of anodes for LIBs. NMP dissolves binders like PVDF, promoting good wetting of electrode materials, ensuring proper adhesion, and uniform distribution of active materials on the current collector, which is essential for maximizing the electrochemical performance and stability of LIBs. However, NMP is classified as a reproductive toxicant and poses health and safety risks, especially with improper handling or prolonged exposure. Due to potential health and environmental concerns, there is significant interest in finding NMP substitutes. Alternatives like ionic liquids, deep eutectic solvents, and supercooling solvents are being investigated for their lower environmental impact.[32-34] Water-based slurries offer a viable alternative to conventional organic solvent-based slurries, particularly favored for anode preparation, as some anode materials like silicon are incompatible with NMP. For instance, water has been proposed as a substitute for NMP in electrode fabrication and black mass recovery during battery recycling in green manufacturing and direct recycling approaches. Electrochemical performance of water-processed electrodes has been shown to be equivalent to that of NMP-based electrodes.[35] Wood et al.[36] reported that switching from NMP to water-based solvents could reduce battery pack costs by $2 \%$ and save $3–6 million in capital investment.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Dry processing technologies have emerged as a viable option, offering several advantages over conventional wet processes, including reduced energy consumption and elimination of safety issues related to flammable solvents. Dry processing methods, such as thermal evaporation, sputtering, powder pressing, and dry mixing, reduce or eliminate the need for liquid solvents in battery manufacturing. For example, Wang et al.[38] studied the effects of high-speed and ball mill mixing prior to electrostatic spray deposition (ESD) on dry-made electrodes. These techniques often require lower energy inputs than wet processes since they do not involve solvent evaporation or drying stages. In particular, the energy requirement for manufacturing with NMP is high, at $10.2\mathrm{kWh}$ per kilogram of vaporized NMP and $421\mathrm{kWh}$ per $10\mathrm{kWh}$ battery pack, with the total energy requirement being 45 times the heat required for NMP vaporization.[37] In summary, exploring LIB solvents is crucial for improving the efficiency, safety, and sustainability of energy storage technologies. Through extensive research and innovation, a variety of solvent solutions have been identified, ranging from traditional organic solvents to water-based alternatives. This ongoing investigation holds promise for advancing the performance and environmental compatibility of lithium-ion batteries.

paragraph_context: To produce high-quality battery cells or packs, a lithium-ion battery (LIB) production line typically comprises numerous interrelated processes and stages (Figure 4a). The cell and battery casing types of LIBs can vary based on several parameters, including application, size, performance requirements, and safety concerns. The most common materials for casings are aluminum, plastic, and stainless steel. Typical designs for LIB cells include: (1) Coin Cells: Small with high energy density, these are often used in small electronic devices. Named for their coin-like appearance, they can be identified by standard sizes such as CR2032 or CR2025.  (2) Pouch Cells: Flexible, thin, and lightweight, these are widely used in devices like computers, tablets, smartphones, ebikes, and electric scooters. Pouch cells are economical to manufacture and offer a high degree of design flexibility.  (3) Cylindrical Cells: Known for their high energy density and durability, these cells have a tubular shape that simplifies loading and stacking in battery packs. They are commonly found in large-scale energy storage systems, electric vehicles (EVs), and consumer electronics.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: (4) Prismatic Cells: With a rectangular shape, these cells are easy to stack in battery packs and are used in various applications, including energy storage systems and EVs.

paragraph_context: Various models from fields such as chemistry, physics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are employed in the development and manufacturing of LIBs to enhance productivity, ensure high-quality battery products, and optimize processes. These models are categorized into physics-based, AI and machine learning, and data-driven models. This review will discuss both cell and battery pack levels.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Physics-based models and their mathematical representations (Table 1) are critical for creating intelligent materials and devices for LIBs. These models (Figures 4b, 6) mimic and forecast different processes in battery cells and manufacturing equipment using the principles of physics. If manufacturers incorporate physics-based models into the design, quality, and operation of their manufacturing processes, they may enhance performance, quality, and sustainability throughout the whole Li-ion battery production chain.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Complex lithium-ion diffusion mechanisms and the corresponding electrochemical reactions in electrode materials are crucial for LIB applications. Diffusion-reaction models are valuable for elucidating these fundamental mechanisms and improving battery performance. Fick's diffusion equations govern the flow of lithium ions between the cathode and anode in an LIB. These equations describe the diffusion of lithium ions through complex electrolytes driven by concentration gradients, with the material's diffusion coefficient influencing the diffusion rate. This process can be mathematically represented as a partial differential equation, where the concentration of lithium ions is dependent on both time and space: $$ \frac {\partial c}{\partial t} = D \nabla^ {2} c \tag {1} $$ where $c$ represents the lithium concentration, $t$ denotes time, and $D$ is the diffusion coefficient. Zhang et al.[39] proposed a new reaction-controlled diffusion model with the help of the bond-breaking energy barrier $E_0$ as the key physical quantity.

paragraph_context: Another key method is the Butler-Volmer (BV) equation, derived from the principles of thermodynamics. This electrochemical equation describes the relationship between the potential difference across an electrode and the current flowing through it. The BV equation is also used in simulating battery performance and the kinetics of charge transfer at both cathode and anode interfaces during charging and discharging. Lu and colleagues proposed a modified version of the Butler-Volmer equation to account for the impact of mechanical stresses on electrochemical processes in lithium-ion battery electrodes.[40] They discovered that compressive stress in the active material's surface layer impedes lithium intercalation, requiring an additional electrical overpotential to overcome the stress-induced reaction barrier. The modified equation, incorporating stress effects, was first identified as: $$ i = i _ {0} \left\{\exp \left[ (1 - \alpha) \frac {F \left(E _ {v} - E _ {e q}\right) - \sigma_ {h} \Omega}{R _ {g} T} \right] - \exp \left[ - \alpha \frac {F \left(E _ {v} - E _ {e q}\right) - \sigma_ {h} \Omega}{R _ {g} T} \right] \right\} \tag {2} $$ where $i_0$ is the exchange current density, $R_g$ is the universal gas constant, $T$ is the temperature, and $\alpha$ is the charge transfer coefficient, $\sigma_h$ is the hydrostatic stress and $\Omega$ is the partial molar volume, $F$ is the Faraday constant, $E_v$ and $E_{eq}$ are the electrode potentials at the present state and at the chemical equilibrium state, respectively.

paragraph_context: A frequently used technique in the modeling of LIBs is the pseudo-two-dimensional (P2D) model (Figure 4c). This model strikes a balance between accuracy and computational complexity, making it a superior option for studying battery activity. The battery is represented as a stack of pseudo-two-dimensional layers, allowing for a comprehensive description of electrochemical processes within. Solving a P2D model for LIBs often requires numerically solving coupled differential equations that depict the various physical processes occurring inside the battery. As this is computationally intensive, it is unsuitable for real-time control applications.[41] The model accounts for several transport processes within each layer, including electron transport through the electrodes and lithium-ion diffusion within the solid electrode materials and electrolyte. The kinetics of charge transfer during charge and discharge cycles are described by the Butler-Volmer equation, which also considers mechanical variables. Recently, Laue et al. showed that a threestep procedure combining the classical C-rate test with OCP measurements is insufficient for P2D model identification.[42] In quasi-static settings, highly dynamic tests (such as impedance spectroscopy) are needed to clarify the ambiguity of diffusive and electric processes. A mix of quasi-static and highly dynamic testing, along with experimental data from electrode-resolved experiments, is required for any parameterization of electrochemical models. Utilizing the P2D model, Tulsyan et al.[43] introduced a novel approach for state-of-charge estimation. It was proved that reducing computing complexity by using an unusual strategy called "tethering," yielding precise state-of-charge estimates. This method could potentially be adapted to include state-of-health equations. The predictive ability of a parametrized Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model was demonstrated using a commercial cylindrical (21700 cell) Li-ion cell with an NCA cathode and a $\mathrm{Gr - SiO_x}$ anode.[44] The cell voltage was predicted using the DFN model in two scenarios: (i) a driving cycle with a highly non-uniform current distribution and (ii) a constant current discharge under varying discharge rates.

paragraph_context: Compared to the computationally expensive P2D model, the single-particle model (SPM) offers an attractive alternative for several applications. The SPM simplifies battery representation by modeling each electrode particle as a single entity while retaining key battery features. This approach, developed from comprehensive electrochemical models, involves a limited set of ordinary differential equations, reducing the risk of overfitting and simplifying parameter estimation. Guo et al. extended the SPM to include thermal effects and added an energy balance equation.[45] They solved the solid-phase diffusion equations using the eigenfunction expansion approach instead of a two-term polynomial approximation, increasing the model's accuracy. Identifying primary stress elements is crucial for constructing an appropriate model. For instance, concentration polarization must be included, as the system is significantly affected by temperature and current.[46] Consequently, with a constant current of $\pm 0.5$ C/1 C and a SOC of $2\% -98\%$ , the compensated model's error is within $\pm 40$ mv.

paragraph_context: Integrating several physical processes that happen within the battery at the same time is the complex topic of multiphysics modeling of LIBs.[47-52] The term "multiphysics" in the literature often refers to models that theoretically explain interactions between mechanisms from several physical domains.[53] Most models designed to explain LIB function fall into this category as they must consider at least two distinct physical domains: charge transfer and electrochemistry. Multiphysics models provide critical insights into battery behavior under various operating conditions, aiding the design, development, and management of modern battery systems by combining electrochemical, thermal, mechanical, and transport processes. The first publication on coupled mechanical-electrical-thermal simulation of battery failure at the cell level was introduced in 2015 (Figure 5a).[54] Using a representative-sandwich finite-element model in the commercial program LS-DYNA©, the combined mechanical-electrical-thermal response was simulated. Each component, such as the active material, current collector, and separator, was explicitly represented, predicting their mechanical deformation under quasi-static indentation. The stress-strain relationship was calculated as follows: $$ \sigma = \int_ {0} ^ {\varepsilon} E d \varepsilon = \left\{ \begin{array}{c} \frac {E _ {m a x} \left(e ^ {\beta c} - 1\right)}{\beta e ^ {\beta c _ {p}}} \quad \varepsilon < \varepsilon_ {p} \\ \frac {E _ {m a x} \left(1 - e ^ {- \beta c _ {p}}\right)}{\beta} + E _ {m a x} \left(\varepsilon - e _ {p}\right) \varepsilon \geq \varepsilon_ {p} \end{array} \right. \tag {3} $$ where $E$ denotes the Young's modulus, $E_{\text{max}}$ represents a fully compacted value modulus, $\varepsilon$ is the strain, $\varepsilon_p$ corresponds to the strain when the material is fully compacted and $\beta$ is the fitting parameter.

paragraph_context: To study detailed multiphysics heterogeneity in multiple layers of a 12 Ah large-format pouch cell at varying discharge rates, a new 3D multiphysics model with excellent computing efficiency was created (Figure 5b).[67] The framework consists of two levels: electrode submodels and cell submodels. Therefore, local current density and temperature factors interact with electrochemical performance at high C-rates.

paragraph_context: Stochastic (random) modeling, which involves representing battery behavior using mathematical equations, is a highly effective and versatile technique for creating both anode and cathode structures.[68-70] Stochastic modeling incorporates vari- bility by expressing uncertain parameters as random variables that correspond to certain probability distributions. Understanding the relationship between battery microstructure and characteristics benefits greatly from 3D electrode morphology. For complex, nonlinear systems, advanced approaches like Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods[71] and Bayesian inference[72] can be used to estimate parameters more accurately. Thiedmann et al.[72] created a 3D stochastic simulation model of composite materials based on stochastic geometry and spatial statistics. Stochastic modeling has also been applied to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles,[73,74] for example, the capacity loss and usage time of LIBs with NMC-LMO chemistry were predicted.[73] Using the Gaussian distribution and computing the mean and standard deviation of error, the stochastic component of the capacity fade model yields a mean to characterize the fluctuation of the capacity and resistance relationship. The general model for stochastic life prediction is given by: $$ Q _ {p r e d} = Q _ {r a t i o} \left(R _ {\text {s y n}}\right) + \omega \tag {5} $$ where $\omega$ , or $\omega \sim \mathsf{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ , is the random term with a normal distribution.

paragraph_context: Applications for Monte Carlo (MC) and Kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) have also been identified in LIB manufacturing. These methods work by executing large quantities of random operations to produce outcomes that resemble inherently unpredictable natural systems.[75] A kMC simulation requires a collection of discrete configurations and prior knowledge of a set of transition rate constants describing the transition events between these configurations. Several electrochemical models of lithium plating have been developed under various operational scenarios.[76,77] It is well-known that lithium plating is a primary cause of capacity decline and safety issues in lithium-ion batteries. Zhang et al.[76] demonstrated that rapid charging rates, low temperatures, high states of charge, and high starting concentrations of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ enhance the probability of Li plating. Furthermore, kMC has been frequently employed in research on the kinetics of Li-ion insertion in graphite electrodes.[78-80] These simulations provide atomistic information on the phenomena, making them valuable tools for explaining the electrochemical behavior of $\mathrm{Li}+$ insertion. For example, a unique strategy based on a model was adopted, which uses process models to explain the electrode manufacturing process and a physical-based battery cell simulation to examine the final result. By connecting the two model sections via transferred structural parameters, different parameter levels can be coherently considered, allowing for the study of uncertainty propagation from the manufacturing process to the performance of the LIBs.

paragraph_context: Brownian dynamics is the most elementary type of stochastic dynamics, characterized by a lack of spatial or temporal correlations.[81] Stochastic differential equations, including the simplified Langevin equation, help us understand Brownian dynamics by indicating the limit where there is no average acceleration. Ermak and McCammon developed a technique in 1978 for modeling the Brownian dynamics of $N$ particles with the addition of hydrodynamic interactions, nearly 50 years ago.[82] The aggregation process between LMO and carbon black (CB) was simulated using Brownian dynamics, and the Langevin equation was used to control the particle trajectory.[83] Regarding anodes, dilute suspensions composed of silicon and carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) were analyzed using Brownian dynamics simulations with a coarse-grained model.[84] Using a 3D coarse-grained Brownian dynamics model, the impact of the Damkohler number on morphology and lithium deposition under an applied voltage was investigated.[85] Research has demonstrated that rapid kinetics promote dendritic development, whereas slower kinetic deposition leads to significantly more uniform, dense, and compact deposition.

paragraph_context: The coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) modeling mesoscopic approach is primarily used to analyze the behavior of large molecular systems, such as proteins[85] and nucleic acids.[86] This method reduces computational costs by representing groups of atoms as single particles with fewer degrees of freedom. In the context of batteries, Li et al.[87] employed the CGMD simulation approach to model the working ion diffusion and transmission mechanism in the cathode of lithium-oxygen batteries. Additionally, the drying process of electrodes made from water-based suspensions was studied using CGMD simulations to predict and analyze debonding phenomena and microstructure progression.[88] It was discovered that the water-based electrode did not bind active material-active material (AM-AM) and active material-current collector (AM-CC) as effectively as NMP-based electrodes during the drying process. The ultimate volume of the water-based coating was lower than that of the NMP-based coating, leading to a more compact AM distribution after drying, which increased energy density.

paragraph_context: Over the past several years, AI-based modeling (Table 2) has emerged as a revolutionary technique in the realm in LIB manufacturing. AI technologies (Figure 9) employ advanced algorithms and machine learning techniques to process large datasets and forecast outcomes, thereby enhancing the efficiency and productivity of battery production. For material optimization, this approach is particularly beneficial due to its ability to process vast amounts of data simultaneously while also predicting different scenarios. By utilizing data from sensors and production equipment, AI algorithms can detect inefficiencies and optimize various parameters (e.g., temperature,[89] SOC,[90,91] SOH[90,92]) in real-time, leading to significant improvements in production processes. Through the analysis of historical data and continuous monitoring of equipment performance, AI algorithms can predict potential failures and reduce periods of inactivity. Moreover, substituting manual check-ups with AI not only improves speed but also minimizes human error. Overall, enabling manufacturers to optimize processes, adjust material ratios, and enhance quality control, AI-based modeling paves the way for a new era of efficient and high-yield manufacturing of high-energy density batteries.

paragraph_context: Inspired by the structure of the human brain, neural networks (NNs) are a key component of artificial intelligence algorithms and offer solutions for various battery challenges, including process optimization, quality assurance, and predicting battery lifespan. Layers in NNs can be categorized as input, output, or hidden layers (Figure 7a). NNs learn to organize input information into output predictions through repeated training cycles. Due to their computational efficiency, NNs can be implemented in real-time applications. Wu et al.[93] trained two NNs (the classifier and the calculator) using electrochemical-thermal model simulation results. They selected specific energy and power as outputs and compared the resulting data with finite element simulation estimations. In 2010, a technique for modeling and estimating the state of charge (SOC) of LIBs using the extended Kalman filter (EKF) and NNs was introduced.[94] The full charging cycle was divided into three sections: $70\%$ , $35\%$ , and $20\%$ duty cycles, requiring the NN to be trained under varying charging conditions. The neurons located in the hidden layer are activated by Green functions, which are equivalent to Gaussian functions, and have the following form: $$ \varphi_ {i} = G \left(\left\| r _ {k} - t _ {i} \right\|\right) = e x p \left(\frac {\left\| r _ {k} - t _ {i} \right\| ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}\right), i = 1, \dots , M \tag {6} $$ Where $r_k$ is the input vector, $t_i$ and $\sigma_i$ are the center and the standard deviations of the Gaussian function, and $M$ is the number of neurons in the hidden layer.

paragraph_context: Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) are the simplest form of NNs because of their uni-directional flow. Despite this simplicity, they are versatile and can be employed for various tasks, such as predicting battery properties,[95,96] estimating SOCs,[97,98] and optimizing charging and discharging processes. FNNs trained on historical data can differentiate between high-quality and subpar batteries, assisting in quality control. Additionally, they can be programmed to recognize and prevent manufacturing process flaws by detecting real-time deviations. Recently, an FNN estimator was developed to estimate the SOC of LIBs using MATLAB simulations.[99] The inputs were temperature, terminal voltage, and discharge current; the output was SOC. Prior to developing, training, and validating the FNN network, data had to be gathered and normalized. The proposed model exhibited a low mean absolute error (less than $1.5\%$ ), confirming the method's high accuracy. Dziechciaruk et al. provided a guideline for the training procedure and recommended adapting an easily estimated FNN with dynamic signal preprocessing over the traditional electrical equivalent circuit model.[96] The crucial factors included selecting appropriate training tests, the number of neurons and hidden layers, the quantity of delay filters, measurement accuracy, and sampling periods. Remarkably, the FNN was effectively trained using only three discharge tests, demonstrating that extensive data is not always necessary. Comparatively, the FNN approach outperformed the EEC model, with lower root mean squared errors in most test versions. However, significant error values at deep discharge states were observed for both models, likely due to the steep voltage profile and minor measurement errors.

CNNs are particularly useful for visual recognition applications.[100-102] Regarding batteries, these neural networks have been implemented in SOC,[103] SOH,[104-106] and capacity[107-109] estimations. An accurate (2% of RMSE) and image-based method for battery degradation diagnosis was successfully presented.[110] The model's architecture comprised four types of layers: masking, convolutional, flatten, and dense (Figure 7c). Initially validated using synthetic data and later real data, the CNN model achieved an average error of $2\%$ , significantly lower than FNN, random forest (RF), and 1D convolution models. For commercial high-power graphite/LFP systems, the model considered various degradation forms, including irreversible lithium plating, and produced superior results, opening new avenues for AI and battery research collaboration.

paragraph_context: Some research groups have explored the integration of CNN and long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) techniques.[111-115] LSTM networks are advantageous for handling data sequences by identifying long-term relationships through repeated steps. The integration of CNN and LSTM methodologies facilitates the extraction of spatial and temporal characteristics from input data. While employed similarly to CNNs, some studies have focused on estimating remaining useful life (RUL) using these hybrid networks.[112,115] For instance, Ren et al.[112] suggested an architecture (Figure 10a) where raw data from the battery is retrieved via the autoencoder. The equation for discrete two-dimensional convolution was as follows: $$ A (i, j) = \sum_ {m = - s} ^ {s} \sum_ {n = - s} ^ {s} K (m, n) ^ {*} z (i + m, j + n) \tag {7} $$ The following equations were implemented to determine each gate function and state transfer process in the LSTM process: $$ \boldsymbol {f} ^ {t} = \sigma \left(W _ {f} \cdot \left[ h ^ {t - 1}, x ^ {t} \right] + b _ {f}\right) \tag {8} $$ $$ i ^ {t} = \sigma \left(W _ {i} \cdot \left[ h ^ {t - 1}, x ^ {t} \right] + b _ {i}\right) \tag {9} $$ $$ \bar {C} ^ {t} = \operatorname {t a n h} \left(W _ {g} \cdot \left[ h ^ {t - 1}, x ^ {t} \right] + b _ {g}\right) \tag {10} $$ $$ o ^ {t} = \sigma \left(W _ {o} \cdot \left[ h ^ {t - 1}, x ^ {t} \right] + C ^ {t}\right) \tag {11} $$ $$ C ^ {t} = f ^ {t} * C ^ {t - 1} + i ^ {t} * \overline {{C}} ^ {t} \tag {12} $$ $$ h ^ {t} = o ^ {t} * \operatorname {t a n h} \left(C ^ {t}\right) \tag {13} $$ where $W$ stands for connection weight and $b$ for offset parameters, $C^t$ for the intermediate variable, which was multiplied by the input gate result and sent to the state space. Also, $f$ was for forgetting, $i$ for input, $o$ for output gate outputs; $h^t$ for $t$ moment hidden layer output, and $x^t$ for input at time $t$ .

paragraph_context: Feng et al.[122] trained, verified, and evaluated SVM models for online SOH calculation in commercial LIBs with NCM cathode, having an error of less than $3\%$ in $95\%$ of cases. LSSVMs are especially useful for both classification and regression applications. Li et al. overcame the model's reliance on internal battery variables by utilizing the sliding window method-based LSSVM.[125] They proposed a new LSSVM model with numerous feedback vectors to enhance SOC accuracy. paragraph_context: When combined with SVMs, particle swarm optimization (PSO) may enhance the model global search capability and computation performance.[124,131,133-139] The PSO-SVM model has been demonstrated as the best option for estimating SOH of LFP and NCA cathodes, with an RMSE lower than $2.5\%$ , outperforming other models.[134] This model mitigates the overfitting issue and enhances generalization capacity by using k-fold cross-validation. A novel strategy to increase SOC estimation precision involves incorporating data-driven modeling with an unscented Kalman filter and LSSVM-PSO.[140] This method significantly improves upon previous approaches, maintaining maximum SOC error under different operating conditions at $0.5\%$ .

paragraph_context: Tree-based machine learning algorithms, including decision trees (DTs), random forests (RFs), and other specific models, have become highly successful tools for forecasting characteristics and enhancing LIB performance. These models contribute significantly to LIB development and research by providing accuracy, durability, and scalability. Employing a flowchart architecture and accurately mapping non-linear relationships, tree-based approaches offer strong interpretability, making the linkages relevant to battery manufacturing clear. DTs are straightforward yet effective models that recursively divide data according to attributes to generate predictions.[141-146] In DTs, each internal node represents a feature, each branch represents a choice made based on that feature, and each leaf node represents the final conclusion. However, the structure of DTs is easily modified, which can make them unstable and unsuitable for modeling highly nonlinear battery behaviors.[121] A particularly successful example is the RUBost-based ensemble learning framework, proposed to identify LFP and LTO electrodes based on their half-cell capacity, thickness, and electronic conductivity.[147] In this framework, DTs are used as the weak learners, and adding more DTs can improve classification accuracy. The RUBost-based model includes three primary hyperparameters: the number of decision trees (M), the learning rate (r), and the desired percentage $(\mathbb{P}\%)$ of total samples represented by the minority class. As more DTs are applied, the classification error of conductivity tests decreases progressively, converging to 0.13 after 90 DTs for LFP and to 0.14 after 76 DTs for LTO electrodes (Figure 8b). Remarkable classification results were achieved for electrode capacities, with $94.4\%$ accuracy for LTO and $97.8\%$ for LFP. Notably, only three DTs were used to estimate LFP capacity with an error of $0.02\%$ , suggesting a roughly linear relationship between these formulation factors and electrode capacity.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Random forest (RF) is a powerful machine learning algorithm that leverages the outputs of several decision trees (DTs) to handle both classification and regression tasks effectively (Figure 7b).[148-154] RF offers significant advantages over individual DTs, primarily due to its ability to manage complex datasets with intricate feature relationships and its resistance to overfitting. This technique has been widely utilized in numerous fields related to LIB manufacturing, including of online capacity,[149] SOC,[155] and SOH[152,153] estimations. Moreover, RF serves as an excellent alternative to the commonly used equivalent circuit model (ECM) in battery management systems (BMS) due to its precision and reliability. Leveraging trained random forest regressors, ML analysis of the low rate charge curves produced by the mechanistic model has been carried out for LFP, NMC, and NCA cells with an RMSE of $5\%$ .[156] Li et al.[149] presented a low computational cost RF regression (RFR) method to estimate the battery capacity of NMC cells under various aging scenarios, achieving an RMSE of less than $1.3\%$ . paragraph_context: Lithiated transition metal oxides are the most important cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries. Many efforts have been devoted in recent years to improving their energy density, stability, and safety, as demonstrated by thousands of publications. However, the commercialization of several promising materials is limited due to obstacles like stability limitations. To overcome the limitations of energetically high-voltage or high-capacity cathode materials, unconventional solutions for their surface engineering were suggested; among them, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and zeolites have been employed. MOFs possess favorable characteristics for stabilization goals, The rise in average global temperatures in recent years has compelled scientists and engineers to investigate alternative means of energy production and lessen our reliance on nonrenewable energy sources, namely, massive combustion of fossil fuels for electricity production and transportation. Reducing the use of fossil fuels for transportation and promoting an electromobility revolution requires the availability and full practicality of highly reliable, high-energy density, rechargeable batteries. As a result of the increasing energy density demands, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have emerged as a powerful technology for consumer electronics, power tools, and electric vehicles (EVs).[1] LIBs possess desirable properties such as a high energy density, sturdy constructions, and the capability to satisfy multiple long-lasting performance requirements compared to alternative rechargeable systems.[2,3] Most cathode and anode components used in commercial lithium-ion batteries are considered stable and secure.[4,5] In developing LIB systems, notable advances in components were made to address safety issues and meet the high power density requirements. $\mathrm{TiS}_2$ was one of the first LIB cathodes reported.[6] Still, its commercialization proved ineffective due to low voltage, limited specific capacity, and problems using Li metal anodes in secondary $\mathrm{Li}-\mathrm{TiS}_2$ batteries.[6,7] Additional exploration of diverse cathode materials was initiated, discovering various highly appropriate materials for lithium-ion batteries. The groundbreaking research by Prof. Goodenough and Prof. Dahn laid the foundation for developing lithium cobalt oxide $(\mathrm{LiCoO}_2)$ cathodes. These cathodes proved highly effective and were successfully incorporated into commercial applications, leading to a significant shift including manageable structures, topological control, high porosity, large surface area, and low density. This review article explores promising strategies for improving the electrochemical behavior of favorable cathode materials through surface modifications by using MOFs and zeolites. Investigating the potential of this frameworks-based surface engineering for high energy density batteries' electrodes is essential for optimal control of their surface chemistry. It may be highly effective to upgrade the performance of high-energy cathode materials, thus extending the practical use of very high energy density rechargeable batteries.

paragraph_context: The selection of linkers and metal nodes in MOFs is well-known for its ability to impart functionality. Numerous in-depth evaluations have emphasized the various synthetic approaches available to adjust the framework's chemistry, stability, particle size, and flexibility.[59] Advanced modifications can be made to frameworks through a "post-synthetic modification," which involves exchanging, modifying, or removing linker or node components. Additionally, surface chemistry can be altered by controlling the crystallographic phases and size/morphology of the crystallites. Porous framework materials possess a crucial characteristic in energy storage applications, i.e., the ability to manipulate host-guest chemistry strategically. These materials offer the unique advantage of fine-tuning properties, allowing for precise control over energy storage capabilities. The electrochemical stability of frameworks can be improved by selecting appropriate synthetic parameters. Framework materials (such as MOFs) containing redox-inactive nodes and shorter, more rigid linkers have excellent thermal and chemical stability. However, high porosity and flexibility allow for better ion storage and transport.[59] Besides, the zeolites, which are aluminosilicate compounds with a molecular formula of $\mathrm{A_xB_y(Al_{x + 2y}Si_{n - (x + }$ $2\mathrm{y})O_{2n}\cdot mH_2O)}$ , possess micro/mesoporous structures with 3- Dimensional (3D) networks and are composed of monovalent cations (like $\mathsf{K}^+$ or $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ ) and divalent cations (such as $\mathrm{Ca^{2 + }}$ or $\mathrm{Mg^{2 + }}$ ).[68,69] Through three synthetic strategies, researchers have discovered new zeolite materials with unique structural features over the past decade.[70] These include using pre-designed organic structure directing agents (SDAs) such as quaternary and di-quaternary SDAs, P-containing SDAs, proton sponges, imidazolium derivatives, and metal complexes. Additionally, heteroatom substitutions in alumino-phosphates, silicates, and germanates have been used. Finally, topotactic transformations of 2D-3D, 3D-2D-3D, and 3D-3D structures have been employed. Zeolite materials can exhibit diverse sizes, shapes, and visual characteristics, including membrane formation through seed assembly and secondary growth methods.[71] Control over the pore size and topology of the framework can be achieved with precision by carefully choosing the appropriate linkers and metal nodes. Such modifications with suitable linkers will boost porosity and produce ultra-high surface areas. For example, frameworks with the same structural topology, such as isoreticular metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), are produced using a collection of related organic linkers that vary in length and functionality. The manipulation of pore size and chemical environment within isoreticular metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) allows for the isolated investigation of the structural and chemical elements.[59] Frameworks with both micropores and mesopores offer a hierarchical porous structure that can significantly influence molecular diffusion by providing well-defined channels and pore space.[59] Microporous materials have been limited by diffusion issues, prompting the development of zeolites with hierarchical pores. These types of zeolites possess additional porosity, either meso- or macroporosity, which is categorized according to pore size as micropore (< 2 nm), mesopore (2–50 nm), or macropore (> 50 nm). Including larger porosity into the zeolite framework facilitates mass transfer and boosts catalytic activity.[72] Developing emergent synthetic strategies for enhancing ionic and electronic conductivity in framework materials has yielded new materials useful for charge transport applications.[59] These strategies offer unique molecular insights beyond those provided by porous organic frameworks, thus opening new avenues for material modification pathways. Despite the abundance of newly discovered framework materials over the past twenty years, most materials tend to be insulated because of the prevalent use of metal-oxygen linkages. Researchers have focused on modifying their electronic structures using metal and linker contributions to address the challenge.[59] Such a method, called "through-bond" conductivity, enhances conductivity by altering the electron transfer pathway. Improving electron conduction is achieved by utilizing "through-space" via $\pi-\pi$ interactions or electron hopping to guest molecules, a commonly observed phenomenon in various framework materials.[59] Multiple strategies can be used to regulate ionic and protonic conductivity in these materials. Introducing ionic guest species that aid transport is the easiest way among the methods employed. Spatial and directional control over transport can be achieved by incorporating polar functionalities into the framework post-synthesis. The versatility of framework materials in modifying their chemical, electronic, structural, and mechanical properties is advantageous for electrochemical applications. The distinct priorities for materials properties in energy storage devices can only be comprehended by considering the specific requirements of the storage system. For example, high MOF's porosity permits the storage of active species, which is particularly beneficial for devices that rely on the chemical conversion of small molecules. An investigation was conducted into the ionic conductivity of zeolite frameworks with alkali ions.[73,74] High-alumina zeolites have an abundance of extra-framework cations, which suggests their potential as effective ion conductors. However, further investigation is needed to understand their conductivity properties fully. The electrical conductivity of these materials was unexpectedly low, despite excess alkali cations outside of the framework. The limitations of ionic motion and conduction in zeolites lack a clear rationale. A systematic investigation of these limiting factors has the potential to unlock new opportunities for the design of ion-conducting porous materials. Utilizing ion-conducting zeolites presents a promising approach to achieving high ionic mobility while maintaining defined porosity. Charge-compensating cations overcome potential barriers of varying heights as they move through the voids of the zeolite, and the specific structure and composition of the zeolite material, as well as the electrical charge of the cation used for balancing the charge, influence the process of ionic diffusion.[73,74] In the past few decades, porous coordination polymers or framework materials (MOFs or Zeolites), as explained in the previous section, have become ideal compounds due to their permeable framework structures with pores and channels.[75,76] Their versatile properties have shown significant potential in various applications, such as heterogeneous catalysis, membrane separation, molecular sensing, medical purposes, and energy storage and conversion.[75,76] One of their notable abilities is their capacity to adjust quickly to structure and crystal composition changes, resulting in attaining specific physical and chemical characteristics. Researchers have developed several techniques and methods to alter the surface chemistry of high-voltage cathodes by using many of these framework materials. The predominant techniques employed for these objectives involve chemical coating or standard solid-state mixing methods.[20,33,55-58,67] Detailed discussions related to each coating technique is mentioned in the upcoming sections.
