paragraph_context: The works discussed in this review consolidate the idea that cathode protection and surface engineering are possible using framework materials such as zeolites and MOFs. Although these materials are unconventional, their disruptive impact in stabilizing commercial cathodes, such as NCM, LNMO, LCO, etc., is phenomenal. As explained in various examples throughout our article, the surface of LCO particles has been modified with Prussian blue (PB) nanolayers using a step-by-step approach. Improved electrochemical performance of LCO was demonstrated through the deposition treatment of single-layer PBNL. Similarly, the Mn-MOF modification enhanced Li and Mn-rich NCM layered oxide cathode performance by increasing discharge capacity, initial Coulombic efficiency, and thermal stability while preserving cycle performance and high-rate capability. The Mn-MOF layer provided excellent oxygen storage capability during the first charge. The Co-MOF-74 coating improved the NCM811 cathodes without sacrificing their capacity. Modified electrodes maintained high capacity at high temperatures after 100 cycles and captured Ni ions to mitigate Ni dissolution in prototype cells. A microporous coating was created on Ni-rich NCM cathodes using $\mathsf{Li}^+$ selective MOPAC. It improves Li-ion solid-state diffusion, discharge capacity, and cycle performance while inhibiting electrolyte decomposition and reducing $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and CO evolution. The coating also featured tunable porosity for accelerated $\mathsf{Li}^+$ ions diffusion. Using coatings comprising Li-zeolites improved capacity retention and reduced Mn dissolution in LMO and NCM electrodes at high temperatures. It absorbs trace water, prevents unwanted HF attacks, and thus improves cycle life. The TMA-based coatings improved LNMO cathode behavior in half and full cells by stabilizing their structure and reducing the dissolution of TM cations. They also enhanced thermal stability and enabled smooth Li-ion transport. In addition, the zeolite-based coatings improved the performance of LNMO cathodes in Li-ion batteries. They enhanced capacity retention, rate capability, voltage stability, and redox kinetics while reducing metal dissolution and deposition on anodes. Additionally, they absorbed water molecules and enhanced thermal stability in reactions with electrolyte solutions. The zeolite-based coatings offered a promising option for high energy/high voltage Li-ion batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The increasing demand for new energy sources has promoted the improvement of the energy storage capacity of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that urged the development of higher energy density cathode materials. The enhancement of the classical cathode in the last 30 years has reached a bottleneck, and then the discovery of the lithium-excess disordered materials has greatly expanded the research space of the cathode materials. Compared with the conventional layered oxides, the lithium-excess disordered rock-salt oxides (LEDRXs) with a more stable structure has higher extractable $\mathsf{Li}^+$ content, even though the inactive high-valent transition metals (TMs) were needed to compensate for the excess Li, which would reduce the total TM redox content. In addition, oxygen redox provides additional electron capacity for the materials, which also causes O loss and results in the subsequent poor cycle performance. Herein, a series of studies about LEDRXs and their targeted modification measures are summarized, including the prospect of the materials, in order to provide ideas for the design of high-performance LEDRXs. Finally, the new discoveries and outlook on future research directions of LEDRX cathode materials for LIBs with higher energy density are given.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: With the exhaustion of fossil energy and the severity of environmental pollution, clean energy has exploded in recent years, leading to more concentrated research on electrochemical energy storage.[1-5] As the core components of electric vehicles and portable electronic devices,[6-8] LIBs are required to achieve higher energy density to meet the growing needs.[9-11] The development of highcapacity, high-voltage cathode materials is the key to assembling next-generation highperformance LIBs.[12] The layered $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ cathode was first proposed in 1980 by Goodenough;[13-16] on this basis, a series of cathode materials including spinel, $\gamma \text{-LiFeO}_2$ , and layered oxides were synthesized and developed.[17,18] Recently, there has been an effort to develop disordered rock-salt (DRX)-type oxides or oxyfluorides as high-energy cathode materials. As the performance of the classical layered rock-salt cathode would deteriorate due to the cation disorder, the initial discovery of disordered materials in 2003 did not attract much attention.[19] In DRX oxides, the random distribution of Li and transition metal (TM) in the structure, as shown in Figure 1, prevents the path of conventional $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport, so DRX oxides have always been ignored. $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions in the DRX structures are in octahedral sites $(\mathrm{O_h})$ . Then, Li-migration between two connected $\mathrm{O_h}$ sites occurs through an intermediate face-sharing tetrahedral $(\mathrm{T_d})$ site instead of directly moving through the octahedral edges to avoid high migration barriers.[20-22] Except for the original $\mathrm{O_h}$ site and another $\mathrm{O_h}$ site it will move into, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ion in the activated $\mathrm{T_d}$ site shares faces with two other sites that could be either $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , TM-cations, or vacancy, and the obstacle of the migration is mainly determined by the electrostatic repulsion between the activated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and the latter two face-shared species. For fully DRX, the local environment around the Li diffusion channel (0-TM, 1-TM, 2-TM) is random (Figure 1), and similar to the Li slab distance in the layered oxide, the average height of the tetrahedron (h) in DRX structure can greatly influence the Li diffusion activity. The average Li diffusion barrier increases with smaller h because it makes the activated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ion closer to neighboring octahedral cations, increasing the electrostatic repulsion. In the DRX structure, h is relatively small (2.35-2.42 Å), rendering both 2-TM and 1-TM channels (containing repulsive high-valent TM cations) negligibly active.[22] Meanwhile, the 0-TM channels are surrounded only by Li sites, and for the low valency of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions, the channels can still allow facile Li migration even under small h in the DRX structure. However, for the 0-TM channels to support long-distance diffusion, they must form a percolation network that is not hindered by 1-TM and 2-TM channels. It was proved by Lee et al.[22] through Monte Carlo (MC) simulation that percolating 0-TM network would be created if a DRX material is made with more than $10\%$ excess lithium ( $x > 0.1$ in $\mathrm{Li_{1 + x}TM_{1 - x}O_2}$ ) in its as-made composition. This finding has greatly activated the studies on lithium-excess DRXs (LEDRXs) in recent years. They then summarized the relationship between lithium exchange capacity and cation disorder in the rock-salt structure, and explained the lithium percolation properties in the design of high-performance cathodes through comparison of DRX, layered, spinel-like, and $\gamma$ -LiFeO $_2$ structure.[21] Combined with the effective method of DRX identification proposed by Urban et al.,[23] the exploration of DRXs was accelerated by computation to expand larger composition spaces and the viability of pre-screening.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: By now, the commonly studied TM-based redox centers can be divided into Ni, Mn, Fe, and V groups, etc.[20] New redox couples such as $\mathrm{Mo}^{3+}/\mathrm{Mo}^{6+}$ in $\mathrm{Li}_{9/7}\mathrm{Nb}_{2/7}\mathrm{Mo}_{3/7}\mathrm{O}_2$ have also been proposed and applied to LEDRXs.[24] Achieving high capacity from cathode materials requires a large number of cyclable $\mathrm{Li}^+$ ions, electrons, and a stable structure during charging and discharging.[25] For LEDRXs, TM ions remain in the original sites that maintain the original stable framework after Li extraction, even though $45\%$ of cationic sites are empty.[26] However, high-valent TM ions was needed to be introduced to charge-balance excessive $\mathrm{Li}^+$ in the structure, and Urban et al.[27] showed that the interaction between randomly distributed cations with various ion sizes and valence electrons leads to distortion of an octahedron. While $\mathrm{Li}^+$ without valence electrons have no particular preference for octahedral shape, the filling of the TM d shell almost entirely dominated the disordered tendency of $\mathrm{LiTMO}_2$ compounds. Moreover, the density functional theory (DFT) calculation results have shown that TM without d electrons ( $\mathrm{d}^0$ TM) could accommodate the site distortions with the lowest energy cost, which also meant that $\mathrm{d}^0$ TM could stabilize the structure even the ionic radius differs largely. In this regard, various high-valent electrochemical inactive TM ions (i.e., $\mathrm{Ti}^{4+}$ , $\mathrm{Nb}^{5+}$ , $\mathrm{Ru}^{5+}$ , $\mathrm{Mo}^{6+}$ ) were introduced to obtain excellent cycling stability, but with the compromise of the theoretical TM-based redox capacity of LEDRXs.[28] primary cause of the capacity degradation and voltage fade.[29,30] However, Kwon et al.[31] found that the formed metal densification layer of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.6}\mathrm{Nb}_{0.2}\mathrm{O}_2$ was spinel phase, promoting unimpeded $\mathrm{Li}^+$ transport on the surface. In addition, the exposure of oxidized active oxygen species to electrolyte will generate a resistance layer that blocks $\mathrm{Li}^+$ diffusion,[32] so the regulation of electrolyte composition can also be an effective strategy.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: For most LEDRXs, nanoengineering is necessary to achieve high energy density. In this regard, Lee et al.[33] recently discovered that at a sufficiently small size $(< 150~\mathrm{nm})$ Mn-based DRXs reached a high capacity over $250\mathrm{mAh / g}$ without excess lithium. However, nanoparticles with high porosity are not easy to control and are difficult to apply a uniform coating. Also, the excessive volume and low tap density of nanoparticles reduce the volumetric and gravimetric energy density of cathode materials.[34] To overcome such limitations, Li diffusion dynamics in a larger particle still need to be optimized to catch up with the Li diffusivity of the conventional cathode $(10^{-10}$ to $10^{-8}\mathrm{cm}^2 /\mathrm{S}$ for $\mathrm{LiCoO_2}$ ). Note that the 0-TM percolation theory was originally proposed based on the hypothetical completely random cations. However, recent studies have shown that short-range order (SRO) exists in DRXs that affects the 0-TM percolation network. Jones et al.[35] found that $\gamma \text{-LiFeO}_2$ -type SRO blocks $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport. Then, Lun et al. demonstrated that increasing the number of TM species inhibits the formation of such SRO.[36] In addition to the TM type and oxidation state, the SRO formation is also affected by $\mathbf{F}^{-}$ . The introduction of fluorine to replace oxygen in LEDRXs was shown to increase the proportion of active TM ions, mitigating the adverse effects of oxygen redox.[37] Thus, fluorinated LEDRXs minimize the side effects of oxygen loss and improve the capacity retention rate. Meanwhile, the addition of F changes the redox potential of TMs. For example, for V-based materials, it leads to more overlap between the redox levels of V and O. On the other hand, the stronger bonding tendency between Li and F may change the percolation network to limit the number of cyclable Li in the structure, which becomes a restriction to realize energy density over $900\mathrm{Wh / kg}$ . Moreover, a complete understanding of new local regions (i.e., separated domains,[38] surface structures after cycling[31] ...) that affect electrochemical performance is also essential. Overall, there are critical needs to overcome the limitations in LEDRXs systematically.

However, more oxygen oxidization occurs in Ni-based LEDRXs because of the strong overlap between Ni redox and O-redox states, leading to a poor stability.[20] Mn-based LEDRX materials have received much attention because of the abundance of Mn, while the high charging voltage $(>4.8\mathrm{V})$ is necessary to achieve their high capacity with the risk of electrolyte decomposition.[34] $\mathrm{Li}_{(1 + x)}\mathrm{Ti}_{2x}\mathrm{Fe}_{(1 - 3x)}\mathrm{O}_2$ can show an attractive capacity over $150\mathrm{mAh / g}$ as early as 2003, but its further performance improvement was restricted by the limited redox of Fe.[71] Finally, V-based LEDRXs can exhibit a high capacity based on $\mathrm{V}^{3+} / \mathrm{V}^{5+}$ redox without oxygen redox,[54,55] which may be attributed to the negligible overlap between V and O and their low average operating voltage at $\sim 2.3\mathrm{V}$ . paragraph_context: To establish a guiding framework for the design of LEDRXs, it is necessary to explore the redox mechanism in depth, especially for anionic redox. Lee et al.[29] introduced $\mathrm{Mo}^{6+}$ into the Li-Ni-Ti-O compound to maximize the proportion of $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{4+}$ redox couple. Then, they combined X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) to analyze the redox reaction of bulk and surface, respectively, during the charge and discharge process. The results showed that most $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ only oxidized to $\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}$ during charging, and the additional capacity comes from oxygen loss and/or oxygen oxidation. Oxygen loss occurs on the surface after $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{\sim 3+}$ oxidation, while oxygen oxidation appears together with a slight reduction of $\mathrm{Mo}^{6+}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}^{4+}$ at high voltage. For Ni-based LEDRXs, the redox order during charging is $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{3+} \rightarrow \mathrm{O}^{2-}/\mathrm{O}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni}^{3+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{4+}$ , while in discharging process, it is the opposite, as shown in Figure 2a,b. According to the work of Abdellahi et al.,[75] cation disorder leads to the voltage increases in $\mathrm{LiMO}_2$ (M=Ni, Mn, Cr, V) except for Cr and V; thus, the oxidation potential of $\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{4+}$ in DRXs was increased higher than the oxidation potential of oxygen ( $>4.4\mathrm{~V}$ ). Furthermore, DFT calculation shows that reduction of Ni decreases the anionic redox potential to $\sim 1.5\mathrm{~V}$ ,[44] leading to large voltage hysteresis and resulting in low energy efficiency of Ni-based materials. Incomplete oxidation of Ni is due to the strong overlap between Ni 3d and O 2p redox states or the overlap between Li-O-Li and $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{4+}$ bands (Figure 2c).[41,42,45] It was analyzed that a decrease in lattice parameters by cationic substitution can reduce the overlap to enhance $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{4+}$ .[29,30] $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{NbO}_4$ was introduced to $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Ti}_{0.5}\mathrm{O}_2$ to achieve smaller lattice parameters than the same lithium content Li-Ni-Ti-O compounds,[43] whose capacity is shown in Figure 2d,e. The extension of the plateau at $3.8\mathrm{V}$ during charging proved the increase of $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}^{4+}$ redox activity. $\mathrm{Nb}^{5+}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}^{4+}$ tend not to form covalent bonds with oxidized ions, supporting the reversible oxygen oxidation process to provide additional capacities rather than the oxygen loss. Oxygen oxidation was first proved by the reversible $\mathrm{O}^{2-}/\mathrm{O}^{-}$ redox chemical and the peroxide speciation observed through a series of in situ tests including in situ Raman spectrum.[45] However, although the increase of Li content provides more extra capacities from reversible oxygen oxidation,[41] there are still existing issues of (i) overpotential caused by unstable and slow kinetics of $\mathrm{O}^{2-}/\mathrm{O}^{-}$ redox[42] and (ii) the generation of irreversible $\mathrm{O}_2$ and side reactions between oxidized oxygen species and electrolyte during the first charge. The oxide powder with good uniformity can be obtained by the hydrothermal method, but it faces the challenge of high temperature and high pressure. The spray drying method can make all kinds of cations mixed fully and uniformly, but the particles only stay in micron scale. The ion sputtering deposition method is mainly advantaged in the application of thin-film materials. For the two most commonly used methods, the high-temperature treatment in the solid-state synthesis process causes particle agglomeration accompanied by partial Li evaporation,[17,54,98] while mechanical ball milling does not require heat treatment and the prepared particle size is relatively smaller.[26,37,62,76] For example, because the performance of the obtained DRXs was poorer than theoretically expected, Takeda et al.[70] applied ball milling to reduce the particle size and mix the cathode powder more evenly with the carbon material, which increased the discharge capacity. However, defects and amorphous morphology of materials were formed upon ball milling, and long-term grinding would introduce impurities of the grinding medium.[26] Then, the heat treatment is considered to relieve the strain.[55] Interestingly, Qiu et al.[99] used a gas-solid interface reaction to uniformly create oxygen vacancies on the surface (up to $20\mathrm{nm}$ thick) of layered $\mathrm{Li}_{1.144}\mathrm{Ni}_{0.136}\mathrm{Co}_{0.136}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.544}\mathrm{O}_2$ which activated the surrounding $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and then provided a favorable diffusion environment. These treatments may also be useful for DRX cathodes as they also suffer from oxygen loss during cycling. On the other hand, particle size reduction undoubtedly has a positive impact on the achieved capacity, as it shortens the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion path upon cycling,[102] accompanied by the reduced migration barrier.[103] In addition, the proportion of surface states also increases with the decrease of size, corresponding to larger contact area with electrolyte. The study[33] indicated that lithium-excess in Mn-based DRXs is not even necessary when the particle size is less than $150~\mathrm{nm}$ . Thus, nanostructure engineering is widely used to improve the performance of electrode materials, while the low tap density and more severe side effects in nanomaterials should be take into account.[76] Therefore, synthesis process selection/optimization is an important factor to be considered in the design of high-performance LEDRXs cathode. Nakajima et al.[55] added a heat treatment step in the preparation of $\mathrm{Li}_{1.25}\mathrm{Nb}_{0.25}\mathrm{V}_{0.5}\mathrm{O}_2$ , which effectively changed the cation distribution at nano scale. The heat-treated samples showed stronger resistance to structural strain and better rate capability with reduced impedance. paragraph_context: To date, element doping/substitution has been one of the most common practices to improve the performance of cathode materials as shown in Figure 5b. This is because the introduction of different elements and the adjustment of element proportion can tune the electronic structure and structural stability during cycling to improve the performance of cathode materials. The introduction of dopants into cationic sites was partly discussed in section 2, including the regulation of electroactive elements (i.e., Ni, Mn, Fe, V, Cr) and inactive $\mathrm{d}^0$ TMs (i.e., Ti, Nb, Ru, Mo), as well as the interactions with each other. paragraph_context: In summary, this review introduced the research status of LEDRXs with various electroactive TM-based (Ni/Mn/V-based etc.) and summarized the developed methods to enhance the performance of LEDRXs. Most LEDRXs deliver high capacity $>250\mathrm{mAh / g}$ with contributions of anionic redox, and the combination of multi-electron redox coupled with high-valent $3\mathrm{d}^0$ TM is the most typical representative where inactive TM ions are beneficial to maintain the structural stability during cycling. Although the involvement of O-redox is beneficial in providing extra capacity beyond theoretical TM-redox capacity, the accumulation of O-redox causes oxygen loss, resulting in a cationic densified surface that blocks the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport path and limits cycle performance.[51,69] As recent work has demonstrated, oxygen redox can be divided into reversible $(\mathrm{O}^{2 - } / \mathrm{O}^{\mathrm{n - }}$ redox) and irreversible $(\mathrm{O}_2$ release) processes based on meta-dynamic simulations, and the $\mathrm{O}_2^{-2,6}$ state is considered to be a representative intermediate from reversible to irreversible.[80] Along with more lithium being extracted at the voltage of $4.5 - 4.7\mathrm{V}$ , the structure of LEDRX becomes highly unstable and O more easily escapes from the lattice.[81] In addition, there are cracks/defects formed in the particles on the deep extraction, leading to accelerated capacity fading.[50] To avoid this, the increase of $\mathrm{d}^0$ TM $(\mathrm{Ti}^{4 + })$ comment in the composition is suggested to inhibit the evolution of $\mathrm{O}_2$ ,[80] while the decrease in the average oxidation state of redox center in Ti-rich compositions corresponds to more unstable O-redox.[66] Therefore, the inactive/active TM ratio should be further optimized by theoretical simulation and experiments. Besides, fluorination is also one of the most effective ways to increase the capacity of TM-redox and reduce irreversible oxygen oxidation, which is extensively studied recently. Although the new finding revealed that O-redox can play a positive role in DRX structure,[92] further studies are needed to prove this point. On the other hand, the species evolved from oxygen oxidation on the surface will have side effects with the electrolyte, forming a resistance layer between cathode and electrolyte and also increasing the resistance in the battery.[101] Such electrolyte degradation might be overcome by applying a surface coating to DRXs and adjusting the electrolyte composition.

paragraph_context: Accumulated and profound understanding of DRXs is expected to accelerate the discovery of high-capacity DRX cathodes. As a perspective to promote the new discoveries, developing advanced characterizations is inevitable, especially the operando-characterizations to analyze the dynamic change and synchrotron radiation for in-depth analysis of redox process. So far, Mn-based materials have received the most attention because Mn can provide multiple redox electrons and has a low cost and non-toxicity. For the effect of fluorination on the interface stability of Mn-based LEDRXs, the regulation of composition on surface coating and electrolyte against Mn dissolution needs to be continuously studied. To improve the gravimetric energy density, the introduction of TM ions in higher valence state was considered to reduce the amount of TM ions in DRX materials, but the mass of $\mathrm{d}^0$ TM ions increases with the ascending valence state, so the total weight of the material may not decrease. Moreover, the optimization of binder also has a positive effect on electrochemical performance of battery. Overall, although the current improvement methods are not enough for the LEDRXs to meet the commercial cathode materials, the high reversible capacity and feasibility of modification lay a foundation for the practical application of LEDRXs.

paragraph_context: Sodium-sulfur (Na-S) batteries that utilize earth-abundant materials of Na and S have been one of the hottest topics in battery research. The low cost and high energy density make them promising candidates for next-generation storage technologies as required in the grid and renewable energy. In recent years, extensive efforts have been devoted to the diversity and functionalities of Na-S batteries, aiming to extend their potential applications across multiple temporal and spatial dimensions. Here, we summarize the unconventional designs for the functionalities of Na-S batteries such as flexible batteries, solid-state cells, flame resistance, and operation at extreme temperatures. By highlighting these design strategies that help to realize the functionalities, we hope this review offers a pathway to foster the bright future of Na-S batteries in diverse applications.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Despite their dominant position in powering small electronics, the deployment of Li-ion batteries in vehicles and renewable energy storage has been restrained by the issues of cost and energy density.[1,2] Mitigation of these problems relies on the exploration and development of lithium-beyond battery technologies such as Na-S batteries.[3,4] The operation of Na-S batteries relies on the use of an S cathode and Na anode.[5] During the discharge process, $S_{8}$ molecules are reduced by Na to generate several soluble long-chain polysulfide intermediates of $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}$ ( $4 \leq \mathfrak{n} \leq 8$ ), which further transform insoluble short-chain polysulfides of $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}$ ( $1 \leq \mathfrak{n} \leq 3$ ). Upon the reversal charge, $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}$ is oxidized to S through a series of intermediate phases (Equation 1). This conversion reaction of S leads to a large theoretical capacity of $1672\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , and the stripping and plating of Na metal give a high capacity of $1166\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ .[6,7] The combination of these two high-capacity electrode materials leads to a high specific energy of $1274\mathrm{Whkg^{-1}}$ (based on the product of $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}$ ), which is much greater than that of Li-ion batteries. Current Li-ion batteries in electronics need to recharge at least once each day. However, with Na-S batteries, it would be possible to recharge once 3-4 days. $$ 2 \mathrm {N a} + \mathrm {n} / 8 \mathrm {S} _ {8} \leftrightarrow \mathrm {N a} _ {2} \mathrm {S} _ {\mathrm {n}} (1 \leq \mathrm {n} \leq 8) \tag {1} $$ Historically, Na-S batteries were implemented at a temperature of $\sim 300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ because the high temperature is required to keep the cathode and anode materials in a molten state for battery operation.[8] High-temperature Na-S batteries have already been commercialized. However, the energy efficiency and safety hazards associated with high-temperature Na-S batteries pose a challenge to reducing the operation temperature. To this target, operation of Na-S batteries at room temperature has been demonstrated, although they exhibit limited cycling stability in the early days.[9] The working principle of Na-S batteries, at either high temperature or room temperature, is quite analogous.[10] However, the reduction of operating temperature brings significant challenges in the performance of Na-S batteries, mostly involving the S cathodes.[11] First, S and $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}$ at ambient temperature are both poorly conductive to efficiently transport electrons and ions during the reaction, leading to sluggish charge transfer kinetics. The kinetic barriers related to the S conversion cannot be completely overcome, and the electrochemical reversibility of room-temperature Na-S batteries is much inferior to that at high temperatures. In addition, soluble sodium polysulfides (NaPSs) formed on the cathode side will diffuse to the anode, leading to a so-called shuttle effect. This phenomenon corrodes metallic Na to produce a less-conductive passivation layer on the anode, resulting in low Coulombic efficiency and continuous capacity decay of batteries. The shuttle effect has been considered the most notorious issue affecting the lifespan of S-based batteries. Moreover, the S electrode expands ( $\sim 170\%$ ) and contracts substantially during electrochemical cycling, leading to continuous electrode evolution and finally pulverization, causing rapid capacity decay.[12] The profit of using abundant and cost-effective S and Na electrode materials prompts the rapid development of Na-S batteries. In particular, recent knowledge accumulated for the Li-S technology can be well leveraged for Na-S batteries. As a result, the Na-S system has captured a great deal of attention in the battery community. Great efforts have been devoted to the selection of materials and optimization of systems. Several reviews are available, focusing on the choice and design of S cathode, Na anode, separator, and electrolytes.[13-18] On the other hand, the prospect of Na-S batteries fosters their bright future in diverse applications across multiple temporal and spatial dimensions. For instance, flexible Na-S batteries have been developed to meet the high-energy demands of wearable devices. Non-flammable electrolytes have been introduced to impart flame-resistance functions, while solid-state designs help to realize high safety. In this sense, it is essential to explore and develop their multiple functionalities to adapt for a specific purpose. To this end, we summarize the unconventional designs for the functionalities of Na-S batteries such as flexible batteries, solid-state cells, flame resistance, and operation at extreme temperatures (Scheme 1). We highlight the design principles of how these functionalities can be recognized in Na-S batteries. The challenges and research directions to foster their future potential are also discussed at the end of this review.

paragraph_context: Flexible batteries, which are different from conventional batteries with rigid and fixed shapes, can be changed according to the shape required by the external environment.[19,20] These batteries can resist external forces and bend to a certain angle without the formation and propagation of cracks.[21,22] Therefore, flexible batteries expand the practical application of batteries in wearable devices, folding electronics, and bendable gadgets. At present, flexible lithium-ion batteries are booming toward multiple applications. However, their limited energy density hardly meets the energy needs of flexible devices. In contrast, high-energy Na-S batteries make them one of the most promising competitors for powering wearable devices.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To assemble flexible Na-S batteries, researchers usually adopted flexible substrates to host the electrodes of sodium and sulfur (Figure 1). Carbon-based materials, such as one-dimensional (1D) carbon fiber, two-dimensional (2D) carbon cloth, and three-dimensional (3D) porous carbon, have been broadly applied in flexible Na-S batteries, owing to their lightweight, mechanical robustness, and high conduction.[23,24] Moreover, they are chemically and electrochemically stable, thus avoiding possible structural and performance degradation.

paragraph_context: Because of the low melting point of sodium, it is general to combine the molten sodium with carbon substrate.[25] The electrode obtained has both flexibility and good mechanical properties. As non-polar carbon materials have a relatively weak interaction with polar Na, it is necessary to modify the carbon matrix to strengthen their interaction. For example, Yu's team used a 2D carbon cloth loaded with $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ as a host of molten sodium,[26] and Li et al.[27] introduced $\mathrm{SnO_2}$ arrays with high sodiphilicity onto the carbon cloth. Alternatively, Fang et al.[28] coated carbon cloth with MXene to load Na metal. By utilizing the sodiphilicity of MXene, molten liquid sodium can evenly penetrate the substrate, which alleviates the poor wetting of molten sodium on the surface of carbon cloth.[29] In addition, 3D carbon substrates such as carbon felt can simultaneously improve the mechanical and electrochemical properties of flexible electrodes through the interwoven network structure.[30] The flexible Na electrode can operate at a high current density of $5\mathrm{mAcm}^{-1}$ for many cycles.

paragraph_context: Similarly, flexible S electrodes can be obtained by loading S directly onto carbon substrates. In general, a mild heating of the S powder and the substrate will lead to the deposition of S on the flexible substrate. By this means, both flexible and binder-free features can be realized simultaneously, thus greatly improving the energy density of batteries. For instance, Yao et al.[31] directly loaded $\mathrm{S}_{0.6}\mathrm{Se}_{0.4}$ onto 1D carbon fibers. paragraph_context: Room-temperature Na-S batteries have recently been widely studied with organic electrolytes. Although liquid electrolytes show high ionic conductivity, several obstacles hinder their further applications. One is the dissolution of transient NaPS species, which generally leads to poor Coulomb efficiency and continuous capacity decay during repeated charge and discharge.[12,38] In addition, liquid organic electrolytes face the issues of leakage and the potential formation of Na dendrites, which will cause significant safe concern in energy storage.[39] These stimulate the adoption of solid-state electrolytes to develop solid-state Na-S cells.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The common inorganic solid electrolytes include three types: ceramic, glass-ceramic, and glass. NASICON- (Na superionic conductor-) type oxides and $\beta''$ -alumina are two representative ceramic electrolytes. While $\beta''$ -alumina only operates at high temperatures ( $\sim 300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ), NASICON-type oxides exhibit considerable conductivity at room temperature.[3,40] Generally, solid electrolytes could prevent the growth of Na dendrites due to their high mechanical moduli. However, Hu's group recently observed the propagation of Na dendrites through the NASICON electrolyte.[41] Therefore, additional material strategies should be employed to mitigate this issue. Also, solid electrolytes show much lower ionic conductivity than the liquid ones, often leading to sluggish Na-ion transport across the electrode/electrolyte interphase. The ionic conductivity and working temperature of common solid-state electrolytes are summarized in Figure 2. Note that surface coating, element substitution, and doping have proven capable of enhancing their ionic conductivity. Theoretically, the aluminum secondary battery obtains a higher theoretical specific capacity through the three-electron oxidation-reduction reaction of aluminum. The practical study, interestingly, shows that there are two electrochemical reaction mechanisms in aluminum batteries, namely, the $\mathrm{AlCl}_4^-$ anion in the intercalation reaction mechanism[21-26] and the $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ cation in the conversion reaction mechanism.[27,28] In the early days, aluminum-based batteries only served as primary batteries, with metallic Aluminum as cathode. However, the alkaline electrolyte used at that time would produce a dense oxide layer on the surface of the aluminum cathode, and then the aluminum cathode was severely corroded due to the side reactions, which eventually led to the much lower electrode potential of the aluminum batteries compared with the theoretical value.[29] In past studies, aluminum batteries manifested problems such as low discharge voltage,[28,30] short cycle life,[21,31] rapid capacity decay,[32] coulomb inefficiency resulting from poor reversibility,[21,33] and electrode material crushing off caused by the structure collapse.[34-36] In order to advance aluminum-ion batteries, researchers have tried to use low-temperature molten salt electrolytes or room-temperature organic ionic liquid as electrolytes. Therefore, the proper selection of electrolyte and electrode materials that will work well together is vital to the success of battery technology. In this paper, we have classified the state-of-the-art non-aqueous aluminum ion battery electrolytes, matching with suitable advanced cathode materials to realize excellent electrochemical performances in various aluminum ion batteries. paragraph_context: High-loading electrodes play a crucial role in designing practical high-energy batteries as they reduce the proportion of non-active materials, such as current separators, collectors, and battery packaging components. This design approach not only enhances battery performance but also facilitates faster processing and assembly, ultimately leading to reduced production costs. Despite the existing strategies to improve rechargeable battery performance, which mainly focus on novel electrode materials and high-performance electrolyte, most reported high electrochemical performances are achieved with low loading of active materials ( $<2\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ ). Such low loading, however, fails to meet application requirements. Moreover, when attempting to scale up the loading of active materials, significant challenges are identified, including sluggish ion diffusion and electron conduction kinetics, volume expansion, high reaction barriers, and limitations associated with conventional electrode preparation processes. Unfortunately, these issues are often overlooked. In this review, the mechanisms responsible for the decay in the electrochemical performance of high-loading electrodes are thoroughly discussed. Additionally, efficient solutions, such as doping and structural design, are summarized to address these challenges. Drawing from the current achievements, this review proposes future directions for development and identifies technological challenges that must be tackled to facilitate the commercialization of high-energy-density rechargeable batteries.

paragraph_context: As the demand for fossil fuels persists, the global energy landscape is gradually shifting toward renewable sources like solar energy, wind energy, hydropower, etc.[1] To efficiently harness clean energy, the development of electrochemical energy storage systems (ESSs) is crucial. These systems, including lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), lithium-sulfur batteries, and supercapacitors, have become ubiquitous in modern society, powering portable electronic devices, electric vehicles, and smart grids.[2-5] As the need for such technologies grows, there is a requirement to explore ESSs with higher energy density, improved power density, and longer cycling life.[6-12] The specific energy of a packaged system depends not only on its areal capacity but also on the proportion of active material in the electrode. Consequently, developing novel cathodes, anodes, and electrolytes is essential.[13-15] Additionally, adopting high-loading electrodes is an effective strategy to enhance energy density. Importantly, this approach also contributes to reducing the overall battery processing cost, which can be significantly decreased (by $\approx 25\%$ when the cathode thickness increases to $50 - 100~{\mu\mathrm{m}}$ .[16] The advancements in laboratory-scale research have predominantly focused on batteries employing active materials with low loading levels $(< 2\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2})$ [17,18] These loading levels are considerably below what practical applications necessitate. As such, adopting a high mass-loading electrode strategy becomes pivotal to bridging the divide between laboratory and industrial scales. There is a pressing need for researchers to investigate the optimized utilization and prolonged lifespan of active materials at these elevated loading levels. However, transitioning directly from low to high-loading electrode configurations is not straightforward. Thicker electrodes pose challenges like slow electron/ion transport kinetics, suboptimal utilization of active materials, and substantial volume expansion. Additionally, the formulation of high-loading electrodes presents its own set of challenges. Consequently, the quest to boost the loading of active materials in electrodes without compromising their performance has garnered significant attention in the energy storage domain.[19-30] This study investigates the decline in the electrochemical performance of high-loading electrodes, examining it through the lens of failure mechanisms and potential rectification strategies. Key challenges identified include delayed electrode reaction Figure 1. The proposed strategies to counteract these performance degradations encompass micro-nano structural designs, heteroatom doping, additive enhancements,[31] and refining the electrode fabrication process (Figure 1). In light of recent research advancements, we further suggest potential pathways for the development of high-loading electrodes suitable for industrial manufacturing and commercial deployment.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With an increased loading of active materials, the battery's electrochemical performance tends to decline, manifesting as enhanced polarization, restricted cycle life, and diminished rate capability. From a review of pertinent studies, the performance degradation of high-loading electrodes can primarily be attributed to these five factors: 1) High-loading electrodes necessitate a substantial amount of binder to maintain mechanical integrity. However, the electrically insulating binder curtails electron conductivity and escalates the electron charge resistance of the electrode $(R_{\mathrm{ct}})$ .[33] This results in sluggish electrochemical reaction kinetics, highly polarized, and subpar electrochemical performance.[34-37]  2) Ion transport is impeded in high-loading electrodes. After the active ions inside the thick electrode are consumed, the ions in the electrolyte cannot diffuse and replenish to the inside of the electrode in time. Consequently, slow ion transport kinetics further contribute to amplified polarization, inadequate rate capability, and degradation in electrochemical performance.[38] 3) The volumetric expansion observed in high-loading electrodes is pronounced, at times leading to electrode fracturing and detachment, which in turn results in battery failure.[39]  4) An inevitable consequence of high-loading is the increased electrode thickness, which hinders the electrolyte wetting and penetration thoroughly, leading to reduced utilization of active materials.[40,41]  5) The formulation process of high-loading electrodes presents challenges. Standard slurry-coating procedures can induce electrode cracking and detachment, culminating in battery malfunction.[18,36,42,43] In essence, the degradation of electrochemical performance under high-loading conditions stems from a combination of factors. The interplay of these elements hastens the performance decline. Thus, understanding the underlying causes of this performance degradation in high-loading electrodes paves the way for devising effective improvement strategies.

paragraph_context: During the standard slurry-coating procedure, active materials, conductive agents, and binders are thoroughly mixed. These strategies include: 1) Creating micro-nano structures to establish a cross-linked conductive network, which helps mitigate volume expansion and enhances ion/electron transport. This approach significantly improves redox kinetics, facilitates electrolyte penetration into the electrode, and enhances the utilization of active materials.  2) Implementing heteroatom doping to enhance intrinsic conductivity, stimulate more active sites, and reduce the barrier of electrochemical reactions.  3) Incorporating additive modifications, such as electrocatalysts, functional binders, and other special additives, to reduce the barrier of electrochemical reactions and enhance redox kinetics.  4) Utilizing advanced electrode preparation technologies, such as self-supporting electrode fabrication and 3D printing, to effectively address mechanical failure issues under high-loading conditions.

paragraph_context: The design of a layered structure for high-loading electrodes aims to transform a single thick electrode into multiple thinner ones. This configuration ensures robust connections between each layer through superior affinity and chemical bonding, thus, enhancing electron transport within the high-loading electrodes.[94] Typically, each layer of the electrode material has distinct roles and collaboratively functions with its counterparts.[74] Electrodes constructed from conductive carbon nanomaterials combined with active materials have emerged as a preferred choice. Furthermore, the number of active substances loaded can be modulated by varying the number of layers.[92,95] As an illustration, Huang et al. developed flexible carbon-based film electrodes termed CNC (carbon nanocoils)/PIL (PEDOT:PSS)-nL, where "n" denotes the layers of the high-loading electrodes (exceeding $15\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ ). This CNC/PIL bilayer features a porous composition, shaped by CNCs (as depicted in Figure 2c). Concurrently, the PIL layers act as both adhesives to fortify the film's stability and current collectors to augment electron transfer dynamics. Given its porous nature and plethora of ion transfer pathways enabling rapid electrolyte penetration, the (CNC/PIL)-15L electrode exhibited an impressive areal capacitance of $1402.5\mathrm{mFcm}^{-2}$ at $0.25\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ and a lifespan exceeding 10,000 cycles at a high current density of $50\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ (refer to Figure 2d).[92] In the context of Li-S and Li-Se batteries, the material layer interfacing with the electrolyte often performs physical shielding and barrier functions.[96-100] Qie and colleagues introduced a layer-by-layer technique for high-areal-capacity S electrodes, where commercial sulfur powders are sandwiched between porous carbon nanofiber (PCNF) layers (visualized in Figure 2e). This design allowed for an elevation of the sulfur cathode loading to $11.4\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , yielding a robust discharge capacity of $995\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ [93] Subsequently, they showed the application of a dual-layer lithium polysulfide (LPS) cathode, which improved sulfur utilization and curtailed the diffusion of dissolved intermediates, achieving an exceptionally high areal sulfur loading of $18.1\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ in a separate study.[97] In sum, the strategic hierarchical layered design offers a potent method to elevate electronic conductivity, enhance electrolyte absorption, and provide effective physical shielding and blockage of polysulfides in high-loading electrodes, leading to superior electrochemical outcomes.

paragraph_context: Heterostructures can adsorb active ionic groups and promote their conversion, which can significantly increase the ionic/electronic conductivity, and are widely used in high-loading electrode (especially lithium-sulfur batteries).[151-159] The physical and chemical limitations of carbon or noncarbon hosts have been used to block LiPSs shuttling and accelerate ion transport, but it is difficult to simultaneously promote the LiPS fast conversion, which is extremely limited to improve the kinetic performance of high-loading electrodes. Heterostructures can adsorb LiPSs and promote their conversion to $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ . Yang et al. reported a twinborn $\mathrm{TiO}_2$ -TiN heterostructure, which combines the merits of highly adsorbed $\mathrm{TiO}_2$ and conductive TiN, and realizes the smooth trapping-diffusion-conversion of LiPSs at the interface, achieving high capacity retention at high loading.[160] DFT calculations show that on the $\mathrm{TiO}_2$ (110) surface, the favorable binding sites of the two Li atoms in $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_4$ are the bridge sites of the two oxygen atoms, while sulfur tends to bind to Ti. The good conductivity of TiN is beneficial to the reversible electrochemical conversion of LiPSs during charge/discharge. Under the action of the heterojunction trapping-diffusion-conversion dual function, the capacity retention rates at 1C are $73\%$ (3.1 mg $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ ) and $67\%$ (4.3 mg $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ ) after 2000 cycles.

paragraph_context: Carbon-derived materials, possessing varied micro-nano architectures, can form conductive networks, mitigating the decline in electrochemical performance observed in high- loading electrodes. Such a modification approach finds extensive use in lithium-sulfur batteries,[133,134,137] lithium-air batteries, supercapacitors,[49,164] and lithium-selenium batteries.[71,139] Nonetheless, when the loading reaches a certain threshold, the effectiveness of carbon modification starts to wane noticeably. Additionally, for insulating active components like $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ and S, the prevalent adoption of carbon-based materials at high loading compromises the battery's overall specific capacity. As a response, scholars have delved into heteroatom doping strategies to address the challenges related to lagging electron conduction/ion transport kinetics and suboptimal utilization of active materials under elevated loading scenarios.[165] Doping with non-metallic elements has become a prevalent strategy to enhance the electrochemical performance of high-loading electrodes, encompassing nitrogen, boron, oxygen, phosphorus, and co-doping approaches. Among them, the nitrogen doping (N-doping) strategy is the most widely studied. Specifically, the N-doping carbon has been used to improve the electrochemical attributes of high-loading sulfur cathodes, making it an effective modification method. There are primarily two doping techniques: one through the carbonization of nitrogen-rich precursors and the other via post-carbon surface treatment using a nitrogen source.[166] When carbonizing nitrogen-laden precursors at high temperatures in an inert setting, nitrogen atoms are consistently interspersed within the carbon framework. By judiciously choosing the right nitrogen-containing precursors and refining experimental conditions, one can produce N-doped carbon with a diverse microstructure, facilitating multi-functional attributes. Generally, the carbonization temperature hovers $\approx 800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , a parameter derived from meticulous optimization.[47,48,51,167-169] For instance, N-doped carbon foam, created using cost-effective melamine foam under an argon ambience at elevated temperatures, is extensively employed as a foundational material in high-loading sulfur electrodes.[48,51,168] This N-doped carbon structure establishes a swift ion/electron transport network essential for high-loading sulfur electrodes, further intensifying the chemisorption of lithium polysulfides and substantially curbing the shuttle effect. Even with a loading reaching $14.4\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , the sulfur electrode maintains a specific capacity of $612\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ post 50 cycles.[48] An alternative N-doping method involves calcining intermediates at high heat in the presence of a nitrogen source (like $\mathrm{NH}_3$ , $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CN}$ ). For example, Mai and colleagues crafted a 3D N-doped graphene/TiN nanowires composite (3DNG/TiN) by calcining a blend of 3D graphene and $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{Ti}_3\mathrm{O}_7$ at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $2\mathrm{h}$ in an $\mathrm{NH}_3$ environment.[167] The 3DNG/TiN acts as a robust polysulfide anchor, facilitating the creation of an electrode with a sulfur load of $9.6\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ while showing an impressive rate performance for lithium-sulfur batteries. Notably, the nitrogen percentage in N-doped carbon obtained from both methods seldom exceeds 14.5 atom%, with actual figures typically below 5 atom%.[170-172] For further advancements, it is imperative to thoroughly comprehend the mechanisms underpinning N-doping modifications. The role of N-doped carbon in refining electrochemical attributes can be summarized as follows: 1) Heteroatom doping results in defects and disordered structures, which expedite ion transport and amplify redox kinetics.  2) Nitrogen dopants influence carbon atoms' charge distribution and spin density, facilitating the genesis of functional groups on the carbon exterior. This amplifies the chemical adsorption of active ions and hastens ion mobility.  3) Electron-rich nitrogen atoms supply supplementary lone pair electrons, which speed up electron conduction. Additionally, this boosts the active sites count on the carbon surface, decreases the potential barrier for electrochemical reactions, and enhances the kinetics of these reactions.

paragraph_context: Through the introduction of N-doped carbon, which incorporates added defects and disordered structures, one can establish more active sites, hasten ion transport, and augment the kinetics of electrochemical reactions.[48,51] The electronic configuration of the nitrogen heteroatom can be analyzed by high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The N 1s spectra are typically divided into three peaks within the binding energy range of $398 - 404\mathrm{eV}$ , representing graphitic N $(401.9\mathrm{eV})$ , pyrrolic N $(400.8\mathrm{eV})$ , and pyridinic N $(398.7\mathrm{eV})$ (as depicted in Figure 6a).[11,35,76] Owing to their high electronegativity and available lone pair electrons, pyrrole-N and pyridine-N can lead to copious defects. The nitrogen doping enhancement is majorly attributed to these two species. In the context of lithium-sulfur batteries, both pyrrole-N and pyridine-N can bond with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in polysulfides, forming the $\mathrm{LiS}_{n}\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ -N bond. This bond plays a pivotal role in entrapping polysulfides, curbing the shuttle effect, and diminishing performance falloff at elevated loading (as shown in Figure 6b).[51,76,173,174] The heteroatom, nitrogen, can fashion an -N functional group on the carbon surface, acting as reaction hotspots for electrochemical processes.[85,175] As illustrated in Figure 6c, nitrogen-related active sites are evenly dispersed over the surface of N-doped carbon nanospheres.[85] Such functional groups, stemming from nitrogen doping, speed up ion transport via chemical adsorption, thereby boosting the kinetics of electrode reactions. Moreover, the potent chemical adsorption of ions and functional groups in the electrolyte encourages electrolyte penetration and optimizes the employment of active substances.

paragraph_context: Metal heteroatom doping is anticipated to reduce the inherent resistance of the electrode and enhance electrode reaction kinetics. Both metal doping and metal-nonmetal co-doping strategies have been employed to improve the electrochemical performance of high-loading electrodes. Cobalt-doped,[177,183,184] cobalt-nitrogen co-doped,[76,185,186] and iron-nitrogen co-doped configurations have been investigated. Unlike non-metallic doping, the modification mechanism of metal heteroatom doping mainly involves two aspects: 1) Disordered structures and defects resulting from metal heteroatom doping can generate additional catalytic sites, expedite ion transport, reduce the energy barrier of reactions, and enhance redox reaction kinetics.[186,187] 2) Metal heteroatom doping can adjust the Fermi level of the matrix materials, thereby improving intrinsic conductivity.[177,188] Both cobalt-modified carbon[76] and cobalt-doped electrocatalysts[177,184] have shown improvements in electrochemical performance. For instance, Li et al. synthesized a cobalt-doped $\mathrm{MoSe}_2 / \mathrm{Ti}_3\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{x}}$ bifunctional catalyst as an efficient sulfur host.[177] DFT simulations and experimental results demonstrated that the introduction of Co heteroatom into the $\mathrm{MoSe}_2$ plane can move the Mo-3d orbitals closer to the Fermi level and form shorter Co-Se bonds, thereby enhancing catalytic activity and the intrinsic electronic conductivity of the catalyst. paragraph_context: The decline in performance at high-loading conditions is primarily attributed to sluggish kinetics. Electrocatalysts are widely employed in high-loading studies to enhance reaction kinetics and mitigate the attenuation of electrochemical performance. These electrocatalysts include metal-based materials,[74,189-191] nanometal catalysts (such as Co,[192] Sn,[169] Cu,[193] Fe,[194] and conjugated polymers,[195,196] among others. Conventional metal-based electrocatalysts consist of metal oxides,[72,197,198] sulfides,[73,180,195] carbides,[173,199] and some dual transition metal catalysts.[38,184] More recently, single-atom catalysis[192] has also been explored in high-loading electrode research. These electrocatalysts exhibit different catalytic mechanisms, and their efficiency is influenced by crystal structures.[200] Xie et al. developed polymer tubes (PQT) with anthraquinone as a reactive component, which enables the efficient conversion and immobilization of sulfur species through a reversible lithiation/delithiation process.[196] As depicted in Figure 7a, the oxidation/reduction of sulfur species occurs concurrently with the delithiation/lithiation process of the carbonyl group, creating additional Li-S bonds that promote electron/ion migration between the polysulfide and the polymer. DFT calculations demonstrate that the binding energy of PQT-Li matrix with sulfur species is higher than that of $S_4^{2-}$ , $\mathrm{LiS}_4^-$ , and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_4$ on the PQT monolayer due to the formation of extra Li-S bonds (Figure 7b). This mechanism delays the reduction of polysulfides to $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ ( $\approx 1.90 - 2.05$ V) until after the prelimithiation of PQT at $\approx 2.10$ V during the discharge of the sulfur cathode. The CV curves show that the potential of the PQT/S cathode shifts negatively and positively during the charging and discharging scans (Figure 7c), indicating enhanced kinetics of the electrochemical reactions.

paragraph_context: Furthermore, defect engineering can improve catalytic efficiency and has been applied in the study of high-loading electrodes.[72,180,186,191] Atomic dislocations raise the energy of defect sites, enabling them to serve as catalytic sites for the adsorption of reactant particles and providing a potential driving force for electrochemical reactions.[191] Hence, a reasonable defect concentration and type can boost redox kinetics. In the study of high- loading lithium-sulfur batteries, oxygen, and sulfur vacancies are found to be defect types with high catalytic activity.[63,72,173] Zhang et al. synthesized oxygen defect-rich iron oxide (ODFO) nanoparticles as an electrocatalyst for lithium-sulfur batteries, achieving excellent electrochemical performance under high loading.[191] DFT simulations and electrochemical experiments revealed that the active site of oxygen defects is crucial in promoting sulfur species conversion and reducing the energy barrier for the reaction. The XAS spectrum shows that the reduced electron state of the Fe component in $\mathrm{FO}@\mathrm{3DGC}$ is higher than that in ODFO@3DGC. The presence of oxygen defects induces local charge transfer, enabling mediated electrons to be injected into polysulfides from the conductive matrix. This process facilitates the breakage of long polysulfide chains to form $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_{1-2}$ or lower-order polysulfides (Figure 7d). Furthermore, we calculated the adsorption energy of the discharge product $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ on ODFO and the charge density of the adsorption configuration. The binding energy of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ on ODFO $(3.85\mathrm{eV})$ is much higher than that on FO, leading to a noticeable shift in the electronic density of polysulfides and a decrease in the S-S bond energy. Under the influence of the ODFO nanocatalyst, the diffusion coefficient of lithium ions and the peak current significantly increased (Figure 7e). The ODFO@3DGC@S cathode with a high loading of $11.02\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ delivers a specific capacity of $789\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ .

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: To effectively enhance reaction kinetics in diverse battery systems, it is essential to comprehensively study the macro-micromolecular mechanisms during battery operation and utilize targeted electrocatalysts. In the discharge process of a lithium-sulfur battery, the electrochemical reaction at the cathode can be divided into three steps. Initially, $S_{8}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}_{4}$ at high potential $(>2.1\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ), providing a theoretical capacity of $418\mathrm{mAh}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ . In this step, a solid-liquid reaction occurs, and its reaction kinetics are faster compared to the third step. The second stage is also a solid-liquid reaction but with relatively low dynamics. Here, $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}_{4}$ is further reduced to $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}_{2}$ , contributing $25\%$ of the theoretical capacity. Finally, $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}_{2}$ is reduced to the end product $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ , providing $50\%$ of the theoretical capacity. The last stage involves a solid-state reaction, exhibiting the highest reaction energy barrier and the slowest kinetics. This step controls the overall discharge process rate. Therefore, reducing the energy barrier for $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}_{2}$ reduction to $\mathrm{Li}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ through an electrocatalyst can accelerate the reaction rate and significantly enhance the overall specific capacity.

paragraph_context: Sun et al. synthesized $\mathrm{CoS}_3$ using a Co-based metal-organic framework (Co-MOF) and employed it as an electrocatalyst for lithium-sulfur batteries, achieving excellent performance under high loading.[63] Control experiments were conducted under high loading $(3 - 10\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2})$ . Upon incorporating $\mathrm{CoS}_3$ as the electrocatalyst, the discharge product exhibited an increased ratio of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ to $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2$ , changing from $1 / 1.63$ to $5.60 / 1$ , resulting in a $20\%$ improvement in sulfur utilization. Additionally, we investigated the adsorption mechanism of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2$ on $\mathrm{CoS}_3$ and NCNT surfaces using DFT simulation. Under the electrocatalytic effect of $\mathrm{CoS}_3$ , the dissociation energy $(\Delta E)$ of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2$ decreased from 2.74 eV to $0.93\mathrm{eV}$ , which accelerated the conversion of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2$ to $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ (Figure 7f,g). Therefore, reducing the energy barrier of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2$ reduction to $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ is crucial for the catalyst to improve sulfur utilization under high loading. In addition, catalytic engineering can be combined with other strategies, such as doping[74,130,173,199] and micro-nano structure design.[38,74,193] The majority of binders suffer from poor conductivity, which poses challenges when used in high-loading electrodes that require a large amount of binder to maintain mechanical stability. To address this issue, the development of functional binders has emerged as a promising approach to improve the sluggish kinetics of high-loading electrodes, particularly in cases with significant volume expansion, such as silicon anodes.[201-204] Functional binders leverage interchain entanglement to enhance mechanical strength and preserve the physical integrity of high-loading electrodes, effectively mitigating volume expansion.[202,204] Additionally, certain novel binders exhibit excellent conductivity and resist agglomeration, facilitating the formation of conductive pathways among active materials.[36] Designing binders tailored to specific electrode types and addressing existing challenges is of utmost importance. For example, the recently developed polyacrylic acid $\left(\mathrm{Li}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{PAA}\right)$ binder for silicon anodes has shown remarkable progress in achieving high areal capacity.[205] The presence of -COOH groups in the PAA polymer facilitates pre-lithiation reactions, while the abundant - COOLi groups serve as an additional lithium source, enhancing ionic conductivity and effectively mitigating electrode polarization. As depicted in Figure 8a, $\mathrm{Li}_{0.75}\mathrm{PAA}$ exhibits the highest average adhesion strength in load-displacement curves. Moreover, the polyacrylic acid binder improves the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number and kinetic performance of the silicon anode (Figure 8b,c). Even at a $\mathrm{SiO_x}$ loading of $3.1\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , the $\mathrm{SiO_x@Li_{0.75}PAA}$ electrode demonstrates decent cycle stability, retaining a high areal capacity of $2.7\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ after 170 cycles at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 8d). Furthermore, the research group has reported a robust binder with a 3D interpenetrating binding network (3D-IBN).[202] The 3D-IBN, comprising a rigid poly(furfuryl alcohol) skeleton interwoven with a flexible polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) filler, effectively mitigates the volume expansion of high-loading silicon electrodes. Remarkably, even at a loading as high as $3.8\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , the silicon anode utilizing this binder achieves an areal capacity exceeding $6\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ at a current density of $100\mathrm{mA g^{-1}}$ .

Zhang et al. developed an ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) copolymer and utilized EVA@CNT to co-wrap $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ particles, resulting in the fabrication of the LFP/CN/EVA70 electrode.[50] The EVA@CNT composite offers flexible support and facilitates rapid ion transfer within the ultrathick high-loading electrode. At a $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ loading of $49\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , the LFP/CN/EVA70 electrode demonstrates a specific capacity of $154\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ , showing excellent electrochemical performance under ultrahigh loading conditions. label: 概述
paragraph_context: In conclusion, functional binders for high-loading electrodes must exhibit excellent adhesion to prevent the collapse of the electrode structure during cycling. The specific functions of the binder's functional groups can be fully utilized depending on the characteristics of the electrode system.

paragraph_context: In addition to electrocatalysts and functional binders, researchers have developed other specialized additives with strong compatibility to address challenges in high-loading electrodes.[206] For instance, polysulfide anchors have been investigated for lithium-sulfur batteries to mitigate the shuttle effect during the electrochemical process. [17,43,48,74,138,167,207] By incorporating polar materials like metal oxides (e.g., $\mathrm{MgO}^{[48]}$ ), sulfides (e.g., $\mathrm{NbS}_2$ ,[74] $\mathrm{Co}_3\mathrm{S}_4$ [207]), and nitrides (e.g., VN,[17] TiN[167]), the shuttle effect can be suppressed through strong interactions with polysulfides; thus, facilitating the transport of active ions. Polysulfide anchors in sulfur cathodes often serve multiple functions and also contribute to the creation of a conductive framework.[74] Therefore, this approach is often combined with micro-nano structure modifications to synthesize composite materials. Functional carbon materials like 3D N-doped graphene, carbon foam, and N-doped porous carbon are typically used in combination with this strategy. Additionally, hollow, porous, and sandwich layered structures can be designed. For example, TiN nanowire and N- doped graphene composites serve as polysulfide anchors in high-loading sulfur electrodes, enabling chemical adsorption through strong binding between Li-S and Ti-N.[167] The N-doped conductive graphene network provides efficient pathways for electrons and ions. With a high sulfur loading of $9.6\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , the TiN nanowire and N-doped graphene modified sulfur cathode achieved an ultra-high areal capacity of $12.0\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ at a high current density of $8.03\mathrm{mA cm}^{-2}$ .

paragraph_context: A significant challenge in developing high-loading electrodes is the difficulty in constructing durable electrode structures, necessitating improvements in existing preparation methods. High-loading electrodes produced through traditional coating methods encounter several issues: 1) Poor compatibility between polymer binders and active materials leads to particle aggregation and inadequate electronic conductivity[68,208]; 2) Electrodes often lack interconnected pore channels, resulting in limited electrolyte wettability and slow ion transport[208,209]; 3) The loading of active materials remains restricted even with binders; 4) Conventional methods result in extensive large pores in the electrodes after drying, necessitating rolling to shorten ion transport distance; and 5) The metal foil collector accounts for most of the weight of the entire electrodes, significantly reducing the battery's energy density. Hence, advanced manufacturing technologies like 3D printing, dry pressing, and solution deposition show great promise in the field of high-loading electrode preparation.[2,183] 3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, is a rapid prototyping technology that constructs objects layer-by-layer using digital models and powder-like adhesive materials.[210] Compared to traditional preparation methods, 3D printing offers unique advantages such as customized design, rapid prototyping, and structural optimization, with micron-level accuracy for fabricating complex structures.[211] In the realm of energy storage, researchers have utilized 3D printing for various high-loading electrode applications, including Li-S batteries,[210] lithium-oxygen batteries,[30] Li-Se batteries,[199,210,212-214] lithium metal batteries,[215] supercapacitors,[32] lithium-ion batteries,[216,217] zinc-ion batteries,[211] and nickel-iron batteries.[218] For successful 3D printing, the ink formulation plays a crucial role. The ink must possess suitable rheological properties to ensure uniformity and successful extrusion through the printing device's nozzle. Additionally, it should have high viscosity or a gel-like state in static conditions to prevent the collapse of the printed electrode structure.[30] Current ink formulations primarily consist of traditional coating ingredients, such as LFP, graphite, SP, CNT, etc. In Li-S/Se batteries, some inks may include heteroatoms or electrocatalysts to facilitate fixation or conversion reactions.[199,212] Common 3D printing patterns include square, circular, and grid structures. Wang et al. designed three electrodes with different patterns, demonstrating excellent electrochemical performance, including an ultra-thick $(1500\mu \mathrm{m})$ LFP cathode with a capacity of $7.5\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ (Figure 9a).[216] Wu et al. also customized square and circular electrodes using 3D printing.[188] Moreover, porous 3D printing structures like grid,[217] cube, and block structures[219] have been explored. By combining micro/mesoporous materials in the ink formulation, hierarchical porous structures have been achieved, creating smooth transmission channels for electrons/ions and buffering volume expansion during cycling.[30] Chen et al. utilized digital light processing (DLP) 3D printing to prepare high-loading $\mathrm{SnO}_2$ -based porous electrodes (Figure 9b). DLP 3D printing employs a digital optical processor to form a surface at once, rather than using a point or line, resulting in faster speed and higher accuracy. The thick electrode with a mass loading of $23\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ exhibited a specific capacity about three times that of traditional electrodes at $400\mathrm{mA g^{-1}}$ [220] In addition to 3D printing, researchers have explored various alternative preparation methods for high-loading electrodes, such as dry compressed/cold press/hydraulic techniques,[30,52,75,221,223-225] electrospinning strategy,[222,226] coassembly,[107] bottom-up/top-bottom method,[73,227] and others. Many of these methods do not require the use of solvents or binders.[18,228] Simultaneously, traditional coating processes have also been enhanced by researchers.[36,65,106,229-231] Holey graphene (hG) is widely utilized in the dry pressing preparation method owing to its unique compressibility. Through this approach, hG can be directly molded into dense and porous electrodes with arbitrary shapes without the need for any polymer binder or solvent.[223,224] The outstanding conductivity, surface area, and mechanical strength of hG make it suitable for various energy storage devices.[221] In 2017, Lin et al. introduced the dry pressing method and demonstrated its appli cation by preparing three types of electrodes for lithium-oxygen batteries. These electrodes were fabricated by directly pressing a mixture of hG and active substances, employing sandwich pressing, and using multilayer alternating pressing (Figure 9c). The equivalent areal cycling depths for these ultra-thick electrodes exceeded $4\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ , meeting the requirements for both hybrid electric vehicles (HEV) and electric vehicles (EV). Despite the high thickness of the electrode, it did not hinder the inner reactions of the active materials. The researchers analyzed the electrode under discharge state using SEM, TEM, and XRD and confirmed the presence of discharge products in the internal structure of the electrode.[221] Subsequent reports by the same group further verified the superiority of these ultra-thick electrodes.[30] Furthermore, the researchers extended the application of the dry pressing technique to $\mathrm{S / Se / SeS_2}$ electrodes, constructing a two-layered structure with hG interlayered active materials.[223,225] Electrospinning technology is a process in which a polymer liquid is emitted from the spinneret at high voltage to form nanometer-level fibers on the collector. The structure of nanofibers (core-shell or hollow structures) can be adjusted by modifying the precursors or electrospinning parameters.[226] The conductive fiber sheet produced through electrospinning possesses high porosity, which facilitates the incorporation of a substantial amount of active materials. Moreover, the electrodes prepared by electrospinning eliminate the need for binders, conductive additives, and collectors. Huang et al. prepared composite paper electrodes by combining electrospinning with spraying. PAN nanofibers were electrospun while simultaneously spraying $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ (LFP)/MWNT (Figure 9d). The LFP/MWNT particles were uniformly distributed on PAN fibers, and the intertwining of MWNT and PAN fibers firmly anchored the LFP. This unique staggered structure enabled high-loading electrodes. The LFP electrodes $(13\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2})$ exhibited a charge/discharge capacity of $\approx 120\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ and remarkable cycling stability with capacity decay of only $15\%$ over 300 cycles at $1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . In this method, PTFE particles were sheared to form viscous fibrils; thus, closely combining conductive carbon and active materials (Figure 10a). paragraph_context: Increasing the amount of active materials loaded on the electrode per unit area while minimizing performance decay is crucial for successfully commercializing novel batteries. This review presents a comprehensive overview of recent research on high-loading electrodes in various energy storage systems. The performance decay mechanism involves several factors that synergistically accelerate degradation including ion transport and electron conduction blockage, volume expansion/shrinkage, and uneven deposition of products, resulting in electrode structure collapse. To address these issues, researchers have explored various modi fication strategies, including the design of micro-nano structures, heteroatom doping, the use of additives, as well as the development of advanced electrode preparation technologies.

One major obstacle is the severe performance fading experienced at high currents. As current density increases to higher values, the specific capacity declines rapidly, with the fading ratio even reaching $50\%$ . Another significant challenge is the short cycle life, exemplified by high-loading lithium-sulfur batteries, showing less than 300 cycles with rapid capacity fade.
