paragraph_context: In pursuit of high-energy–density SSBs, metal Li anodes are indispensable. PRPAA (as shown in Fig. 18c) was prepared by Choi and coworkers to integrate with carboxylic acid functionalized CNT (fCNT) networks to regulate the Li deposition process [347]. After the frst Li deposition process of $1 \ \mathrm { m A h \ c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , it can be seen that the CNT networks were still loosely packed and some cracks occurred on the surface due to the stress generated during Li deposition (Fig. 18d1). The $5 \%$ PRPAA meditated fCNT (fCNT-PRPAA) shows a compact cross-section with no cracks (Fig. 18d2), demonstrating the stress dissipation and keeping the network interconnected efect of PRPAA. They proved that the fCNT-PRPAA network could withstand a large amount of Li deposition of 6 Ah $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at current densities up to $6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ( $1 8 \mathrm { A g ^ { - 1 } C N T } )$ , which could efectively support the quick charge of LMBs. Although the authors did not use this concept in SSBs, it is a common sense that the EO groups on PR and PAA are ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ conductive. Meanwhile, the CNT endows the system with high electronic conduction. Therefore, the fCNT-PRPAA network may also be suitable for the solid confguration.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To summarize, after a decade of fast development, some high-quality SE materials are readily produced currently, which lets us see the dawn of SSBs. However, issues also come, e.g., the designs of thin SE flms and high-loading electrodes, their interfacial stability, the compatibility with SOA LIB equipment, the volume/thickness changes on the cell level, etc. Although binders only take a very small share in cells, they can link the particles, endow the electrode/ separator with certain fexibility, and sometimes, suppress the parasitic reactions and even bufer the volume changes on lithiation/delithiation. This makes the relevant research meaningful and important for the SSBs, both in science and technology.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: All aforementioned binders are organic polymers. They realize their adhesive function by physical interlocking or chemical binding, and in most cases, by both of them. Some inorganics could also work as binders, e.g., the $\mathbf { M g O }$ , ${ \bf A l } _ { 2 } { \bf O } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ in thermal battery electrolytes [348, 349], waterglass in high-temperature refractory adhesives [350], etc. Compared with organics, inorganics usually have better thermal stability and higher ionic conductivity due to the delocalized ion cloud, which, however, may also bring about more parasitic reactions especially in the electric feld. Therefore, the research on inorganic binders only started few years ago along with the increasing requirements on battery safety [350–352]. In fact, many relevant patents have been granted in this feld. Their applications can be tracked back to more than a decade ago, and the assignees include large companies such as Dow, Samsung, CATL and LG Chem., [353–356].

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Ammonium polyphosphate (APP, as shown in Fig. 19a) was adopted as a binder for sulfur cathodes in Cui’s work due to its moderate binding strength, fame retardant and water-soluble properties. Moreover, it can also promote the transport of ${ \mathrm { L i } } ^ { + }$ thus enhancing the battery kinetics as evidenced by the improved rate performance [351]. Compared to PVDF, APP has stronger afnity to $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm S _ { x }$ via the interaction between Li and the multiple O atoms on the molecular chains (Fig. 19b); thus, the shuttle efect was suppressed. Meanwhile, the cell with the APP binder showed little selfdischarge within a month, while the open circuit voltage (OCV) of the cell with the PVDF binder dropped from 2.42 to 2.29 V. In a long-term cycling test, APP also demonstrated its feasibility with $6 4 0 \ \mathrm { m A h \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ retained after 400 cycles at $0 . 5 \ : \mathrm { C }$ . As a contrast, it was $3 2 9 \mathrm { \ m A h \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ for the one with PVDF.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Waterglass (sodium silicate as the main component, as shown in Fig. 19c) is a water-soluble earth-abundant inorganic compound that binds to a diverse range of materials with high-adhesion strength and exhibits extreme chemical and thermal stability. Structural ceramic batteries (SCBs) are capable of acting as an electrochemical energy storage system (i.e., batteries) while possessing mechanical integrity [357], thus having higher requirements on electrode modulus, which is usually beyond the capability of polymer binders. Ransil and Belcher trailed the waterglass in SCBs as the binders for LFP electrodes [350]. Impressively, it showed high Young’s moduli of 75–85 GPa under both dry and wet (by electrolyte) conditions. XRD tests proved that the mixture of LFP and waterglass is stable even when heated to $6 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , which greatly enhances the battery safety in use. Paring with a mesoporous carbon microbead (MCMB) anode and a silica modifed separator (high-density ultra-thin fberglass) using the same binder, a full cell was prepared. It demonstrated a satisfying tensile modulus of $1 . 4 \mathrm { G P a }$ and a much higher energy density of 93.9 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ than that in previous works on SCBs.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Both APP and waterglass are polymers, thus it is reasonable for them to show high adhesive ability toward other materials either by physical interlocking or chemical bonding (such as H-bond and Li-bond). Recently, Obrovac and Wei used three kinds of salts [the sodium polyphosphate (SPP), lithium polysilicate $( \mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 5 } \mathrm { O } _ { 1 1 }$ , Fig. 19d) and lithium phosphate monobasic $\mathrm { L i H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ , Fig. 19e)] for Si and Gra. anodes [352]. Surprisingly, all these binders could form good coating layers on Si alloys when the dosage is $1 0 \%$ and show good cycle stability similar to that with PAALi binders. The authors proposed that there might be a hydrolysis-polymerization process between $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 5 } \mathrm { O } _ { 1 1 } /$ $\mathrm { L i H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ and –OH groups on the Si particles. As a contrast, the binders $( 1 0 \% )$ form poor coating layers when being used in graphite due to the lacking of functional groups. Increasing the binder content to $2 0 \%$ could also improve the coating quality, although no reason was given in the paper. The cross-sectional SEM images and EDS mapping illustrated that $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 5 } \mathrm { O } _ { 1 1 }$ takes a larger volume fraction of $\sim 3 0 \%$ in the graphite electrode, 3 times the theoretical value or that of other binders, for which the authors inferred that its hydrate process may form an open structure like sol–gel. Considering the areal capacity of the Si-alloy anode $( 2 . 4 \mathrm { m A h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ), which is close to the commercial level, these inorganic binders especially the small molecular ones (e.g., $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 5 } \mathrm { O } _ { 1 1 }$ and ${ \mathrm { L i H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { P O } } _ { 4 } ,$ may be good choices in the future applications.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Unlike the organic binders’ adhesion that usually resulted from direct chemical reactions, hydrogen bonding or mechanical interlocking [43], the adhesion theory between inorganics in batteries is still lacking of intensive study and far from mature. Although organic binders can fulfll most of the requirements of SOA LIBs, in some special applications such as the ultra-low/-high-temperature operations, structural batteries and space explorations where the irradiation may infuence the organic stability, inorganic binders may provide good chances.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: As a small but indispensable part in cells (usually $< 3 \%$ in SOA battery industry), binders not only infuence the slurry rheology on the coating process and quality, but also keep the electrode integrity during the whole battery life. Most binders in LIB industry form a coating layer on the AM particles and thus infuence the SEI components. For the development of conversion-type electrode materials and SSBs, binders with more functions such as self-healing, ionic/electronic conductive, and forming special shapes (e.g., fbrous PTFE), are required. Although so many binders have been developed and showed enhanced performance within specifc systems in the past years, as the binders are difcult to be distinguished from the CA in the CBD, their detailed working mechanisms are yet to be clarifed. Therefore, future works should emphasize on the following points.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: (1) The development of high-energy LIBs calls for systematic and standardized research on binders. Binder and conductive agent fractions as well as the areal capacity of electrodes have signifcant infuences on the cell energy density. Although some binders demonstrated outstanding cycle stability and rate performance, $1 0 \%$ or even $2 0 \%$ binders and relatively low-loading active materials are typically used, which in fact results in quite limited energy density even at the electrode level.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Therefore, it is of vital importance to test the binders’ performance under restricted fractions and areal AM loadings, so that their feasibility in mass production could be exhibited. Besides, most anode materials including graphite, silicon [181] and their composites have enough electronic conductivity, which could support the CA free design especially when conductive binders are used. In fact, $5 \%$ conductive binders could support the batteries working as reported in several papers. Systematic studies on these binders may promote the applications of high-capacity anode materials. Meanwhile, the environmental infuences of binders should be considered along with the fast development of battery industry and the relevant recycle process. Although the binder can be removed by simply washing or sintering the coating layer, the bio-derived and water-soluble binders might be better choices.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: (2) Novel binders are essential for SSBs. As previously discussed, SSBs are coming to the dawn before applications, and intensive eforts are now being devoted on electrode (particularly, the cathode) and electrode/ electrolyte interface design and optimization. Functional binders can not only form percolating ion and electron passages and targeted porous structures in the electrodes thus reducing the cell volume changes, but also potentially construct integrated interfaces (e.g., using the PEO-based binder when PEO SE is adopted) thus diminishing the space charge layer and enhancing the interfacial stability, which is quite important as the inner resistance of SSBs is usually much larger than that in LIBs. Considering the trade-of between ionic conductivity, electrochemical stability and mechanical processability, organic/inorganic composite binders with higher degrees of freedom might be good choices. Besides, special techniques such as dip coating might be useful here.

Most binders were considered to be inert even in the battery working processes. Along with the development of high-voltage LIBs and functional binders such as the self-healing ones and the conductive ones, more and more works proved that some binders are reactive, either participating in the formation of SEI/CEI or changing their conduction with voltage variations. Therefore, more attention is deserved for the advanced characterization methods of monitoring this small but essential part, so that better battery techniques could be achieved.

paragraph_context: High-nickel layered oxides, like $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811), are promising cathode material candidates for high-energy lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). However, the serious cathode-electrolyte interface reactions and cathode degradation usually lead to poor rate performance and pronounced capacity degradation, especially at high voltages (>4.3 V). Herein, two novel aromatic polyimide (PI) binders integrated with soft and hard functional segments, denoted as PI(OBO) and PI(BBP), were designed and used as NCM811 cathode binders, which possesses excellent thermal stability and provides abundant active sites to ensure excellent adhesion strength, and dramatic ion pathway. The NCM811 half-cells using PI(OBO), PI(BBP) and conventional PVDF binders exhibit rate capability of 138.0, 127.7 and 115.1 mA h g $^ { - 1 } \mathsf { a t } 5 \mathsf { C } ,$ respectively, within the voltage range of 2.5 to 4.3 V. Further test under higher cutoff voltages up to 4.5 V indicates that the NCM811 half-cells depending on PI (OBO) and PI(BBP) binders display remarkable cycling stability with 39% and 62% capacity retention after 100 cycles at $0 . 2 \mathrm { C } ,$ which are much higher than the 25% capacity retention of the PVDF analogues. CV, XPS, XRD, TEM data confirm that the synthesized PI binders form a uniform and continuous coating layer on the surface of NCM811, obviously stabilize the layered structure of NCM811 and inhibits the irreversible phase transformation of the NCM811 to its rock-salt form, consequently achieve superior long-term cycling stability at high-voltage operation. The DSC test indicates that the heat release of fully-charged PI(BBP)-NCM811 and PI(OBO)- NCM811 cathodes is 66.19 and $7 1 . 6 4 \mathrm { ~ J ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ , which is much lower than PVDF-NCM811 cathode $( 1 0 8 . 0 1 \mathrm { ~ J ~ g ~ } ^ { - 1 } )$ during heat treatment to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ demonstrating the superiority of the synthesized PI binders in improving the safety of LIBs. This study gives a valuable insight of advanced novel PI binder materials for high-energy and highsafety LIBs.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have received ever-increasing attention due to their high energy density, which have been widely applied in hybrid (HEV), full electric (EV) vehicles and other large-scale applications [1–5]. However, being limited by the low theoretical power density and energy density, LIBs show insufficient performance when they are used for high-power electronic devices, which encourage researchers to exploit next-generation cathode materials with high capacity and energy density [6–8]. Among diversified active cathode materials, such as $\mathrm { L i M n } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ (LMO), LiNiO₂ (LNO), LiCoO₂ (LCO), LiFePO (LFP), LiNi $\mathrm { C o _ { y } M n _ { z } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM) and $\mathrm { L i N i _ { x } C o _ { y } A l _ { z } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCA) [9–17], the high-nickel NCM materials, such as NCM811, have been the most desirable candidates for manufacturing the new-generation high-energy LIBs because of their high specific capacity up to ≈200 mA h g− 1 (4.3 V vs Li/Li+) and an unique potential of high-voltage operation ability theoretically up to 4.5 V [18–21]. By simply increasing the charge cut-off voltage from 4.3 V to $4 . 5 \mathrm { V } ,$ the energy density could be enhanced about 10% [22,23], which is of great economy and practical feasibility, and thus have gained widespread attentions [24]. The low content of cobalt and manganese in high-nickel NCM materials results in structural degradation and poor cycle stability in the process of battery cycle [25]. Unfortunately, the NCM811 materials are sensitive to $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ in the atmosphere, which inevitably cause certain undesirable reactions during the preparation of the cathode, leading to irreversible phase transition of the material structure, and affecting the rate performance and cycling stability of the battery [26]. Moreover, the NCM811 materials exhibit severely-declined structural stability and side reactions at the cathodeelectrolyte interface, especially at high operating voltage. As a result, the NCM811 cathodes experience inevitable capacity decay, and occasional thermal runaway.

paragraph_context: Pioneering attempts have been carried out to improve the cycle life and safety of the high-nickel layered NCM811 cathode materials, such as doping and surface decorating [3,8,27–32]. Feng [31] et al. modified the NCM811 cathode material by doping ${ \mathsf { C e } } ^ { 4 + }$ and coating $\mathrm { C e O _ { 2 } }$ to improve the cycle performance. Ji [32] et al. employed the LiMn1 ${ 4 } \mathrm { N i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ coating and bulk Mo doping on the surface of the cathode material, which improved the initial coulombic efficiency, cycle performance and rate performance of the battery. Doping and surface decoration methods will engender a large amount of consumption of transition metals and rare metals, which only increase the production process complexity, but also violate the environment-friendly sustainable development concept.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: As an alternative, functional binding materials play an important role in tightly integrating the active NCM811 particle and carbon black together and forming strong binding force to ensure the high cycle stability and high safety. Currently, rare attention has been paid on designing multifunctional binder materials for the NCM811 cathode even though the binder is a key component of battery electrode. The commonly-used PVDF binder, has a quite weaken binding strength and limited tolerance to high voltages and thermal stability for its poor physical binding energy and low melting point (m.p., 140 ◦C) [33,34]. Moreover, the internal temperature of the battery will increase in the long-term cycling, and PVDF and other fluoride binders are easy to react with the electrolyte to generate LiF and other harmful products, which further leads to thermal runaway [35]. Polyimide (PI), one of the polymer materials with the excellent comprehensive performance, outstanding thermal stability, superior adhesive ability and diversified structural designability, has been rarely used as novel binder for LIBs electrode.

paragraph_context: In this paper, two novel polyimide (PI) binders, denoted as PI(OBO) and PI(BBP), were designed with soft and hard functional segments (Fig. 1). The soft functional segment (i.e. ether bond) has the excellent $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ affinity due to the lone-pair electrons on oxygen in ether bond, inducing good coverage of binder around active particle surface and keeping stable ion pathway, the hard functional segment (i.e., biphenyl structure etc.) has outstanding heat resistance, which could provide high thermal stability for the NCM811 cathode. Fig. 1a, b is the fabrication process of PI binders with two steps: first, a poly(amic acid) (PAA) precursor glue was prepared by the condensation reaction; second, the PAA was converted into its final PI form through a heating procedure to 300 ◦C. Particularly, PAA contains a large number of polar groups $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ , –CONH, –COOH) in the molecular chains, forming a high density of active sites among the cathode component during the preparation of cathode slurry, leading to the favorable and stable cathode interface. Furthermore, the final PI binder contains many heterocyclic imide rings and aromatic benzene rings in macromolecular backbones, ensuring the excellent NCM811 cathode stability. The experimental results show that the two kinds of PI (i.e., PI(OBO) and PI(BBP)) binders have the generality of promoting the binding force $( \mathrm { i } . \mathrm { e } . ,$ , 0.644 and 0.525 kN m− 1 , respectively), inhibiting the transformation of NCM811 particles to rock-salt phase and improving the electrochemical performance and thermal stability. The NCM811 cathode using PI(OBO) binder can improve the discharge capacity to 138.0 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ in the high C-rate at ${ \mathrm { 5 C } } ,$ , the NCM811 cathode using PI(BBP) binder can improve the discharge capacity (121.9 mA h $g ^ { - 1 } )$ and discharge retention (62%), after 100 cycles in the high voltage at 4.5 V which are higher than those of the PVDF-NCM811 cathode $( \mathrm { i . e . } _ { \cdot }$ , the discharge capacity to 115.1 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ in the high C rate at 5 $\mathrm { C } ,$ the discharge capacity of 53.8 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and discharge retention of 25% after 100 cycles in high voltage at $4 . 5 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively). This study provides a new insight on designing the functional novel binder structure to realize excellent rate performance and out-performing cycling stability of NCM811 cathode under high voltage.

paragraph_context: In conclusion, two kinds of novel PIs, i.e., PI(OBO) and PI(BBP), have been synthesized and employed as binders for LIBs, which not only promote the electrochemical performance of LIBs charged to 4.3 and 4.5 V, but also improve the safety. The NCM811 cathodes with PI(OBO) and PI(BBP) binders display excellent rate capability (138.0 and 127.7 mA h $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 5C, respectively) in comparison to the NCM811 cathode using PVDF binder (115.1 mA h $\cdot \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 5C). Moreover, PI(OBO)-NCM811 and PI(BBP)-NCM811 cathodes demonstrate superior stability in long-term cycling, and the capacity retention rates after 100 cycles within 2.5–4.3 V (i.e., 86% and 88%, respectively) and 2.5–4.5 V (i.e., 39% and 62%, respectively) are much higher than the PVDF-NCM811 cathode (70% within 2.5–4.3 V and 25% within 2.5–4.5 V, respectively). Due to the unique process of preparing cathode slurry with PAA (PI precursor) and heating in $3 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to transform into PI-NCM811 cathode, the even and compact coating layer were formed on the surface of NCM811 particles, which efficiently inhibit the phase transition and the cathodeelectrolyte interface reactions, as confirmed by EIS, CV, ICP, TEM, XRD and XPS. Besides, compared with PVDF-NCM811 cathode, the binding force and flame retardance of NCM811 cathode with PI(OBO) and PI (BBP) binders are greatly enhanced, and the diffusion coefficient of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ in PI(OBO) and PI(BBP) binders is also better than PVDF binder. More importantly, the heat release of fully-charged NCM811 cathode at 4.5 V is decreased from 108.01 to 71.64 and 66.19 J $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } :$ , respectively, by substituting PI(OBO) and PI(BBP) binders for PVDF binder, showing great advantage to improve the safety of batteries. This study provides a novel and significant design strategy of PI binders to possess an extremely important application potential of high-energy and highsafety lithium ion batteries.

paragraph_context: Lithium (Li) metal is an impeccable candidate anode for satisfying the energy density requirements of nextgeneration Li batteries. However, Li dendritic growth and fragile solid-elecrolyte interphase (SEI) caused by the high reactivity between Li and electrolyte are the primary challenges for its large-scale applications. Herein, a bifunctional lithiophilic hierarchical substrate composed of high-density nitrogen-doped carbon nanotubes and Co nanoparticles encapsulated in graphene (Co@G) decorated carbon fibers (Co-N-CNT-CF) can modulate the structural dimensions and hierarchy of Li nucleation/growth and alleviate Li volume expansion, achieving the homogeneous Li plating/stripping behavior. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and experimental results confirm the highly lithiophilicity of the substrate, which exhibits a low Li nucleation overpotential, enhanced Coulombic efficiency (CE), small voltage hysteresis, and ultrastable lifespan without dendritic formation. As coupled with the thick LiFePO4 and LiCoO2 (\~2 mA h cm− 2 ) cathodes, the Co-N-CNT-CF@Li composite anode (N/P = 3) enables a high reversible capacity, high Li utilization, and improved cycle stability. This work engineers a hierarchical structure of the three-dimensional (3D) lithiophilic carbon substrate for realizing highly reversible, dendritic-free Li metal anodes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The increasing demand for new clean energy has attracted significant attention from rechargeable batteries. Li-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely used as the primary power sources for transport, portable electronics, electric vehicles, and other applications, while their limited energy density is far from meeting future market demands [1,2]. Li metal battery (LMB) is considered to be an impeccable candidate to address the overall energy density requirements of next-generation Li batteries due to the highest theoretical capacity (3860 mA h ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and the lowest negative electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode) of Li metal anode (LMA) [3,4]. However, the Li dendrites caused by the high reactivity of Li continuously consume the electrolyte during cycling, resulting in rapid capacity degradation, which seriously hinders its commercial application [5,6]. Therefore, it is imperative to develop efficient LMA to address the above obstacles rationally.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Tremendous works have proposed effective strategies to enhance the stability of LMA by modifying electrolyte components, employing solid electrolyte, constructing artificial SEI layer, and building 3D Li substrate [7–11]. Among them, the well-designed 3D substrate provides Li metal storage space and homogenizes the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux and interfacial current, thereby effectively mitigating the volume expansion and Li dendritic growth during the plating/stripping process [12–14]. 3D carbon substrate has been considered feasible substrate for stabilizing Li metal to overcome obstacles because of their high conductivity, lightweight, and adjustable physicochemical properties [3,15]. Nevertheless, the unmodified carbon surface is almost lithiophobic, generating in rough Li deposition and rapid Li dendritic growth [16,17]. So far, strategies including heteroatom-doped, Co and $\mathbf { A } g$ nanoparticles, MgO nano-sheet, and metal nitrides have been reported to enhance the lithiophilicity of carbon substrate for smaller Li nucleation barrier and lower nucleation overpotential [3,17–19].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: In recent years, carbon substrate with bifunctional lithiophilic sites has attracted much attention [20,21]. On the one hand, bifunctional lithiophilic sites enrich Li storage sites and reduce the formation barrier of Li on carbon substrate. On the other hand, the difference in forming nuclear barrier of bifunctional lithiophilic sites makes the order of the formation barrier of Li at these sites different, and the first nucleation with small nuclear energy regulates the arrangement direction of Li growth, thus actualizing hierarchy of Li nucleation/growth and suppressing Li dendritic growth. Interestingly, as a one-dimensional structure, N-doped carbon nanotubes (N-CNT) can not only contain abundant N functional groups, excellent electrical, optical, mechanical, and thermal properties, but also modulate the structural dimensions and hierarchical structure on carbon substrate [22,23]. Therefore, it is an important method to use N-CNT to modify the carbon substrate to achieve hierarchy of Li nucleation/growth on the surface of carbon substrate. However, currently, high-density CNTs are mainly prepared by traditional CVD (acetylene gas as a carbon source, etc.) methods, which increases the experimental complexity and insecurity. Therefore, it is important to develop the simple and effective method to obtain high-density N-CNT and gradient lithium affinity layer on carbon substrate.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Encouraged by these findings, we propose the Co-MOF in-situ growth and CVD process (dicyandiamide as carbon source and N source) to introduce a bifunctional lithiophilic hierarchical substrate composed of high-density N-CNT and Co@G decorated carbon fibers, which can accommodate high Li loading and alleviate Li volume expansion during cycling. Meanwhile, the bifunctional lithiophilic sites, Co@G and highdensity N-CNT provide multitudinous lithiophilic sites, reducing the Li nucleation overpotential and achieving homogeneous Li plating/stripping behavior. DFT calculations confirm that pyridinic N, pyrrolic N, graphene-Co, graphitic N-doped graphene-Co, pyridinic N-doped graphene-Co, and pyrrolic N-doped graphene-Co can greatly enhance the lithophilicity of the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate. Ex-situ scanning electron microscope (SEM) reveals Li preferentially nucleates and grows in Co@G and N-CNT to achieve hierarchy of Li nucleation/growth on Co-N-CNT-CF, and then Li uniformly covers hierarchical carbon fibers and 3D voids on Co-N-CNT-CF substrate. The results show that Co-N-CNT-CF exhibits the lowest Li nucleation overpotential in all the prepared carbon substrates. The symmetrical cell of the Co-N-CNT-CF@Li electrode delivers small voltage hysteresis with a long-term stability of more than 1000 h at 3 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - \dot { 2 } } .$ After coupling with the thick LFP and LiCoO2 cathodes, the Co-N-CNT-CF composite anode with low N/P ratio can provide high reversible capacity and excellent cycle stability.

paragraph_context: Fig. 1a illustrates the schematic synthesis of bifunctional lithiophilic hierarchical carbon substrate. Firstly, a self-supporting precursor substrate is fabricated by electrospinning using polyacrylonitrile (PAN)/ lignin/cobalt nitrate hexahydrate mixed solution. Interestingly, the addition of lignin can reduce the carbon source cost and also significantly increase the flexibility of carbon substrate (Figure S1, Supporting Information). Secondly, the precursor substrate is soaked in the imidazolium solution, and the Co ions on the substrate surface gradually coordinate with the organic imidazolium salt ligands to form columnar Co-based metal–organic framework (Co-MOFs), and a purple hybrid substrate is obtained (Co-MOF-PAN/lignin precursor substrate) (Figure S2-S3, Supporting Information). Subsequently, the Co-MOF uniformly dispersed on the carbon fibers are converted into metallic Co nano-catalysts after carbonization (Figure S4a-b, Supporting Information). Simultaneously, the decomposition of dicyandiamide provides carbon and N sources, which promotes the growth of high-density N-CNT by Co nanoparticles on the carbon skeleton, and finally yields Co-N-CNT-CF with hierarchical structure after treatment of diluted nitric acid. This is confirmed by SEM images that high-density N-CNT containing Co nanoparticles grows uniformly on the carbon fibers, extending their structural hierarchy (Fig. 1b-c). Without any modification, the CF exhibits a smooth surface (Fig. 1d), while the Co-doped CF (Co-CF) displays a columnar surface (Fig. S4c-d, Supporting Information). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) images further reveal that the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate contains a high-density N-CNT layer anchored with uniformly dispersed Co nanoparticles and stable Co nanoparticles on the carbon fiber surface (Fig. 1e). Co nanoparticles on the carbon fiber surface are mainly derived from Co precursors added to the spin ning solution. Furthermore, HRTEM analysis vindicates that Co nanoparticles are embedded in graphitic carbon layers to form Co@G clusters (Fig. 1f-g). The energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping shows that the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate is mainly composed of C, O, N, and Co elements, and these elements are also uniformly distributed in the among such Co@G clusters (Figure $\mathbf { h } { } \mathbf { - } \mathbf { h } _ { 4 } )$ . Compared with CF and Co-CF, this structurally hierarchical carbon fibers (Co-N-CNT-CF) can not only provide a larger space for Li storage, but also regulate the Li nucleation/growth through the tentacle-like N-CNT and Co@G clusters.

paragraph_context: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) is used to investigate the structural characteristics of the as-developed carbon substrates. The carbon substrates show a typical hard carbon structure with a broad peak at 25◦ [15,24]. After modification, new diffraction peaks at 44.1◦, 51.4◦, and $7 5 . 8 ^ { \circ }$ are observed for the Co-CF and Co-N-CNT-CF substrates (Fig. 2a), corresponding to the metallic Co phase (Co-PDF#15–0806) [25]. Combined with TEM images of Co-N-CNT-CF and XRD results of uncarbonized Co-MOF-PAN/lignin precursor substrate (Figure S5, Supporting Information), the Co-MOF on the carbon fibers is finally converted into metallic Co after carbonization. The Raman spectra of all carbon substrates show two broad peaks at 1344 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and $1 5 9 1 ~ \mathrm { { c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ , which are attributed to the disordered carbon (D-band) and graphite structure (G-band), respectively (Figure S6, Supporting Information) $[ 2 6 , 2 7 ]$ . The $\mathrm { I _ { G } / I _ { D } }$ ratio of Co-N-CNT-CF $( \mathrm { I _ { G } } / \mathrm { I _ { D } } = 0 . 6 3 )$ is about twice that of $\mathrm { C F } \left( \mathrm { I _ { G } } / \mathrm { I _ { D } } = 0 . 3 1 \right)$ , which illustrates the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate has better graphitization degree than CF and Co-CF substrates. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further detects the chemical state and elemental composition of the surface of carbon substrates. As shown in Fig. 2b, the full survey of XPS exhibits that the primary elements of CF are C, N, and $^ { 0 , }$ while those of Co-CF and Co-N-CNT-CF are C, N, O, and $\mathrm { C o } ,$ , which are consistent with the EDS mapping and XRD results. Notably, the contents of N (10.5%) and Co (1.34%) in Co-N-CNT-CF are higher than those of Co-CF, proving that the N-CNT have a higher N content. In Fig. $2 \mathbf { c } ,$ the Co 2p spectra of Co-CF and Co-N-CNT-CF show two peaks of Co $\boldsymbol { 2 } \mathsf { p } _ { 3 / 2 }$ (778.4 eV) and $\mathrm { C o C } _ { x } \mathrm { N } _ { y }$ (780.5 eV), where the latter is probably formed by the carbon layer covering the decomposed Co-MOF or carbon fibers precursor [28]. Additionally, the N 1 s spectra of Co-CF and Co-N-CNT-CF exhibit four peaks of graphitic N (401.8 eV), pyrrolic N (400.8 eV), $\mathrm { C o - N } _ { x }$ (399.2 eV), and pyridinic N (398.9 eV) (Fig. 2d) [29]. The percentages of different N-functional groups of the carbon substrates are listed in Figure S7 (Supporting Information). To further investigate the state of Co nanoparticles in Co-N-CNT-CF, extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) characterization is conducted, which can evaluate the local coordination environment and the electrical structure variation. Co foil and CoO are used for comparison. The EXAFS spectra (Fig. 2e) show that the pre-edge of Co-N-CNT-CF is similar to Co foil but quite different from CoO, confirming a structural composition similar to Co foil [28,30]. Nevertheless, Co-N-CNT-CF transfers to a higher binding energy compared to Co foil, indicating the oxidation of Co in the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate, which is consistent with the XPS results [28,31]. We then perform the Fourier transform (FT) based on the $\mathrm { k } ^ { 3 } .$ -weighted χ(k)-function curves of the Co K-edge EXAFS spectra $( \mathrm { F i g . ~ } 2 \mathbf { e } )$ . For Co-N-CNT-CF, the R-space spectra show that the peak at 2.1 Å is consistent with that of $\mathrm { C o - C o } ,$ indicating that the Co-Co bond mainly exists [32]. Moreover, Morlet wavelet transform (MWT) is further performed to reveal changes in the local bonding climate of Co in the substrates. All EXAFS signal contributions from adjacent atoms are directly visualized by MWT, an efficient method to identify the local environment of Co in the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate (Fig. 2g-i) [30]. These results indicate that the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate is mainly composed of the $_ { \mathrm { C o - C o } }$ bond. Furthermore, the specific surface area and pore width of carbon substrates are measured by the $\Nu _ { 2 }$ adsorption/desorption (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The results display that the specific surface areas of CF, Co-CF, and Co-N-CNT-CF are 250.0, 208.0, and $2 4 3 . 6 { \mathrm { m } } ^ { 2 } { \mathrm { g } } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively. Besides, Co-N-CNT-CF shows abundant micro-mesoporous structure which is conductive to uniform Li nucleation/growth [33]. According to Sand’s model, the Co-N-CNT-CF can also effectively reduce the local current density and alleviate Li dendritic growth by providing a higher specific surface area [3,34,35].

paragraph_context: DFT simulation is used to explore the effect of high-density N-CNT and Co@G clusters on enhancing the lithophilicity of Co-N-CNT-CF substrate. In Fig. 3a-d, the calculated adsorption energies $\mathrm { ( E _ { a d } ) }$ of Li on pure graphene, graphitic N-doped graphene, pyridinic N-doped graphene, and pyrrolic N-doped graphene are − 1.3, − 0.9, − 2.2, and − 3.9 eV, respectively, revealing that the introducing of pyrrolic N and pyridinic N can enhance the adsorption capacity of Li on the graphene. In addition, the $\mathrm { E _ { a d } }$ of Li on graphene- $^ { \mathrm { \tiny ~ C o , } }$ graphitic N-doped graphene-$\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { C o } , } \end{array}$ pyridinic N-doped graphene-Co, and pyrrolic N-doped graphene-Co are 3.0, − 2.9, − 2.6, and − 2.2 eV, respectively (Fig. 3e-i), indicating that graphene-Co, graphitic N-doped graphene-Co, pyridinic N-doped graphene-Co, and pyrrolic N-doped graphene-Co can also improve the adsorption capacity of Li on the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate. These results suggest that the nucleophilicity of the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate is more effective than that of CF and Co-CF substrates through the synergistic effect of high-density N-CNT and abundant Co@G clusters. Therefore, Li ions can preferentially nucleate and grow on these nucleophilicity sites, inducing uniform Li plating/stripping behavior (Fig. 3j). A simple Li melting method can demonstrate the lithiophilicity of different carbon substrates (Figure S9, Supporting Information) [36,37]. Obviously, the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate quickly contacts the molten Li and ultimately invades the substrate within $^ { 1 5 \ : s , }$ which is higher than the Co-CF (60 s) and CF substrates (the molten Li cannot invade the substrate). Moreover, the Co-N-CNT-CF/Li composite electrode fabricated by the Li melting method shows that Li ultimately enters and fills the gaps in the 3D substrate (Figure S10, Supporting Information), and the theoretical specific capacity achieves 2483 mA h ${ \mathbf { g } } ^ { - 1 } .$ . The Li melting results on different substrates are consistent with the DFT calculated results, that is, high-density N-CNT and Co@-G clusters can effectively ameliorate the lithiophilicity of the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate.

paragraph_context: The nucleation overpotential is stipulated as the discrepancy between the voltage dip and the subsequent platform potential to elucidate the nucleation barrier. Therefore, the nucleation overpotential is a key parameter to evaluate the lithophilicity between the Li nucleus and substrate [15,38]. The smaller the absolute value of the nucleation overpotential, the better the lithophilicity of the substrate, and the more conducive to uniform nucleation on the substrate [38,39]. As shown in Fig. 4a and Figure S11(Supporting Information), the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate delivers the smallest nucleation overpotential of 9.4 mV at 0.5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ among four substrates, representing the fastest and lowest energy barrier for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ migration during the initial Li plating process. Although the two reference samples, CF and Co-CF, exhibit similar crosslinked 3D carbon fibers substrates to Co-N-CNT-CF, their electrochemical behavior for Li deposition is far inferior to that of Co-N-CNT-CF. It is worth mentioning that high-density N-CNT and Co@G clusters can regulate the Co-N-CNT-CF surface to be rich in pyridinic $\mathrm { N } ,$ pyrrolic $\mathrm { N } ,$ graphene-Co, graphitic N-doped graphene-Co, pyridinic Ndoped graphene- $\cdot \mathbf { C o } ,$ and pyrrolic N-doped graphene $\cdot \mathrm { C o } ,$ , thereby effectively improving the lithophilicity of the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate. Especially when Li is electroplated on Cu foil, the nucleation overpotential is as high as 29.7 mV, indicating that the unmodified Cu foil is challenging to be the substrate of Li metal. Moreover, the Co-N-CNT-CF electrode displays an average CE of 98.4 % over 200 cycles at 0.5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with 1 mA h $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ,$ and keeps stable discharge/charge profiles $( { \mathrm { F i g } } .$ . 4b and Figure S12, Supporting Information). In sharp contrast, the CE of the Cu electrode decreases rapidly after 20 cycles. For the CE of CF and Co-CF, they maintain the stability of 50 and 110 cycles, respectively. paragraph_context: The rate performance is explored to reflect the robustness of the electrode against different current densities. As shown in Figure S13 (Supporting Information), three symmetrical cells exhibit an increasing voltage hysteresis with increasing current density. In particular, the Co-N-CNT-CF@Li symmetrical cell shows the smallest voltage hysteresis and the best reversibility at each current density, verifying that the introduction of high-density N-CNT and Co@G clusters can not only improve the lithophilicity, but also enhance the stability of Co-N-CNT-CF during Li plating/stripping. In contrast, Li symmetrical cells exhibit higher voltage hysteresis, with Li dendrites proliferating at 5 mA cm− 2 , leading to coin cell failure. The long-term cycling stability further evaluates the role of carbon substrates in suppressing Li dendrites [40,41]. Fig. 4c shows the Li stripping/plating profiles of the symmetrical cells at 1 mA cm− 2 with 1 mA h cm− 2 . The Co-N-CNT-CF@Li symmetrical cell demonstrates excellent cycling stability with much lower voltage hysteresis, negligible voltage fluctuation, and stable cycling for over 1000 h. Conversely, the Li symmetrical cell displays irregular rise and fall within 750 h, indicating the severe growth of Li dendrites. The Co-CF@Li symmetrical cell exhibits lower voltage hysteresis than the Li symmetrical cell, but still fails after 800 h. Zooming in on the Li plating/stripping profiles, the Co-N-CNT-CF@Li symmetrical cell consistently shows flat plating/stripping profiles, and has the lowest voltage hysteresis compared to the Li and Co-CF@Li symmetrical cells (Fig. 4c1-c3). Increasing the current density to 3 mA cm− 2 , the Co-N-CNT-CF@Li symmetrical cell still shows stable durability and low voltage hysteresis over 1000 h (Fig. 4d). Whereas the Li symmetrical cell fails after only 50 h. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results of the symmetrical cells before and after cycling are shown in Figure S14 (Supporting Information). The EIS of symmetrical cells exhibit two sections before the cycle. One represents the interfacial resistance in the high-frequency region, and the other represents the charge transfer resistance in the low-frequency region [39,42]. Co-N-CNT-CF@Li symmetrical cell displays a lower interfacial resistance (82.6 Ω) than Li symmetrical cell (95.3 Ω) before cycling. paragraph_context: In summary, bifunctional lithiophilic hierarchical Co-N-CNT-CF composed of high-density N-CNT and Co@G clusters is designed via a efficient and straightforward method. The high-density N-CNT and Co@G clusters on Co-N-CNT-CF surfaces provide multitudinous lithiophilic sites for reducing the nucleation overpotential and guiding the uniform Li metal deposition. Abundant Co@G clusters regulate Li to deposit uniformly on the Co-N-CNT-CF substrate from the inside to the outside to achieve a hierarchy of Li nucleation/growth and reversible Li stripping, which is more conducive to long-term Li dendrite-free plating/stripping. As a result, the hierarchical Co-N-CNT-CF substrate exhibits a low Li nucleation overpotential, enhanced Coulombic efficiency (CE), small voltage hysteresis, and ultrastable lifespan without dendritic formation. As coupled with the thick $\mathrm { L i F e P O } _ { 4 }$ and LiCoO cathodes, the Co-N-CNT-CF@Li composite anode enables a high reversible capacity, high Li utilization, and improved cycle stability. This work engineers a hierarchical structure of the 3D lithiophilic carbon substrate for realizing highly reversible, dendritic-free Li metal anodes.

paragraph_context: A series of TMO nanowires were prepared to investigate their structure–property relationships in half-cell and full-cell structures. paragraph_context: School of Chemical Engineering and Pharmacy, Wuhan Institute of Technology, LiuFang Campus, No. 206, Guanggu 1st Road, Donghu New & High Technology Development Zone, Wuhan 430205, Hubei Province, PR China Binders need to exhibit high bonding strength, sufficient mechanical properties, and electrolyte insolubility to help achieve uniform and stable porous structure and conductive network in electrode composites. Traditional binders like polyvinylidene fluoride offer good electrochemical stability but suffer from poor adhesion performance and weak mechanical flexibility, resulting in unstable electrode structures. To address these issues, a cyanoethyl cellulose-based binder was used to prepare a cyanoethyl cellulose-based cathodes with interpenetrating electron transport and ion transport paths via phase inversion method for high energy density lithium metal batteries. The polar groups (C–––N, C-O-C, and –OH) on the cyanoethyl cellulose chains could promote the transport of Li-ions through electrostatic interactions. The interpenetrating electron transport and ion transport paths enabled fast Li-ion and electron transport in the cyanoethyl cellulose-based cathodes, resulting in a higher Li-ion diffusion coefficient of to $3 . 7 4 \ \dot { \times } \ 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } { \cdot } \dot { s ^ { - 1 } }$ . Hence, the cyanoethyl cellulosebased cathodes enabled batteries with an energy density of 419.8 Wh⋅kgcathode− 1 (mass loading of 16.6 mg⋅cm− 2 ). This study provided a new strategy to achieve uniform and stable porous structure and conductive network in electrode composites high energy density batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Binders, controlling the porous structure and conductive network in the electrode, needs to exhibit high bonding strength, sufficient mechanical properties, and electrolyte insolubility [1,2]. Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) is a traditional polymer binder that is widely used as a commercial binder due to its good electrochemical stability [3]. However, due to weak van der Waals forces, its adhesion performance is poor [4], and the inevitable crystallization stage during the drying process leads to poor mechanical flexibility, causing the active material to separate from the conductive agent [5], both of which affect the structural stability of batteries. To solve these problems, polymer binders including chitosan [6], polysaccharides [7,8], sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) [9], and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) [10], which could facilitate strong adhesion to electrode particles or conductive agents have been reported.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: Cellulose was used as a potential binder for the preparation of electrodes [11–15]. Due to their abundant polar groups (C-O-C and –OH), cellulose had ability to transmit Li-ions [16,17]. Phase inversion method has been used to prepare uniform cellulose/inorganic filler composite membranes with porous structure [18]. During the phase inversion process, pores were formed in the solvent-rich region [19]. And the solid particles uniformly dispersed in the cellulose solution were used as nucleation sites to induce desolvation of the solvent-poor phase. Inorganic filler was uniformly immobilized in the cellulose network. Therefore, the electrodes prepared by the phase inversion method might have a continuous and evenly dispersed network of active materials and conductive agents. Additionally, the pores formed in the solvent-rich region could serve as transport channels for Li-ions. Such an interpenetrating electron and ion transport paths could increase the mass loading of active materials to obtained a higher energy density of lithium metal batteries (LMBs).

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Here, a phase conversion method was used to prepare a cyanoethyl cellulose-based cathode with interpenetrating electron transport and ion transport paths to achieve higher energy density of lithium metal batteries (LMBs) (Scheme 1). Grafting cyanoethyl groups onto cellulose disrupted the ordered arrangement of cellulose molecules, resulting in a formation of more amorphous phase. The swelling of the amorphous phase of the cyanoethyl cellulose (CEC) in the electrolyte allowed the polar groups on the chain (C––N, C-O-C, and –OH) to promote the transport of Li-ions through electrostatic interactions. The interpenetrating electron transport and ion transport paths were established during the phase inversion process, which enabled fast Li-ion and electron transport in cyanoethyl cellulose-based cathode. As a result, the Liion diffusion coefficient of cyanoethyl cellulose-based cathode had been improved to $3 . 7 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } { \cdot } s ^ { - 1 }$ . This allowed an increased mass loading of $1 6 . 6 0 \mathrm { \ m g } { \cdot } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ for the LMBs, which exhibited an energy density of 419.8 Wh⋅kgcathode− 1 .

paragraph_context: Cellulose solutions were created in a 7 wt% NaOH/12 wt% urea aqueous solution as per a prior procedure [20]. Cotton linter pulp (6 g) was mixed into the pre-chilled NaOH/urea solution $( - 1 2 . 7 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and stirred at room temperature for 5 min. The solutions were then centrifuged at 4,000 rpm for 10 min to remove any undissolved residue, yielding a clear cellulose solution. Slowly, 4 mL of AN was added to this solution, and the mixture was stirred at $5 \mathrm { - } 1 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 7 h [21]. The equation for the Michael addition reaction between cellulose hydroxyl and acrylonitrile was shown in the supporting information (equation (1). The solutions were then poured into an ethanol solution to precipitate the raw product, which was subsequently washed with pure ethanol to yield the purified CEC. The final product was dried in a vacuum.

paragraph_context: A cathode slurry based on LFP was prepared by mixing 0.8 g of LFP with 0.1 g of Carbon in a solution of NMP. This mixture was then enhanced with the addition of 0.1 g of either CEC or PVDF. For the slurry that incorporated CEC, it was applied as a coating on a glass pane. This coated pane was then immersed in an absolute ethanol bath, triggering a phase inversion mechanism that solidified the slurry. On the other hand, the slurry that incorporated PVDF was spread onto an aluminum foil. Finally, both types of materials were subjected to a drying process in an oven set at $8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 12 h, and then shaped into circular sheets with a diameter of 8 mm. These sheets were labeled as CEC-LFP and Con-LFP, respectively.

paragraph_context: The performance of lithium-ion batteries is highly dependent on the distribution of conductive additives and the formation of an electrical network within the electrode. In particular, in dry electrode processes, the uniform dispersion of conductive additives is challenging, potentially leading to decreased battery performance. In this study, we successfully synthesized a single-walled carbon nanotubes $\mathrm { \langle L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } ( N C M ) }$ composite (SW-SPD) by uniformly coating the NCM surface with single-walled carbon nanotubes using a spray-drying process to address this issue. Despite having 10 times less conductive additive compared to carbon black, the SW-SPD electrode exhibited excellent electrical conductivity and electrochemical performance, maintaining a high capacity of 137.39 mAh/g even at a 2C discharge rate. Additionally, at the high areal capacity of the electrode with 7 mAh/cm2 , the electrode demonstrated significant long-term cycling performance, retaining 89.4 % of its capacity after 100 cycles, and 52.2 % after 500 cycles. SW-SPD offers an innovative solution to the dispersion challenges in dry electrode fabrication processes, presenting significant potential for the development of highperformance batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Due to the climate crisis, the need for energy sources with lower carbon emissions has become more prominent, leading to the explosive growth of the lithium-ion battery market in the electric vehicle (EV) and energy storage system (ESS) sectors over the past decade. Ironically, however, the current lithium-ion battery manufacturing process involves significant energy consumption and carbon emissions.[1] Battery cell manufacturing includes various steps such as raw material production, electrode fabrication, cell assembly, and formation.[2] This study will focus specifically on the electrode fabrication process.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Regardless of the manufacturer, the current standard for fabricating battery electrodes is the slurry-casting method. The process begins with a slurry-mixing stage where the active material, conductive additive, and binder are dispersed in a solvent. The slurry is then coated onto an Al or Cu current collector and passed through a drying zone to evaporate the solvent, using a roll-to-roll process to produce the electrode. According to the research by M. Schütte and H. Walter, the energy consumption associated with coating and solvent evaporation accounts for a substantial 27 % of the entire battery manufacturing process.[3] Moreover, due to the toxicity of 1-Methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP), the solvent used in the cathode slurry, operating a solvent recovery system is essential, and it is estimated that the cost associated with this accounts for 4.6 % of the total manufacturing cost.[1] These are some of the reasons why dry electrode processes, which do not require solvents, are gaining significant attention in both industry and academia, with companies such as LG Energy Solution and Tesla leading the charge.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In addition to reducing the energy and costs associated with battery production, the dry electrode process is evaluated as a technology that can potentially enhance the energy density of batteries. As presented in the literature[4,5], introducing thick electrodes or high areal capacity electrodes can significantly improve the energy density of batteries. Consequently, research on thick electrode coating[6], as well as studies on high areal capacity materials and structures [7–9], are actively progressing. However, the conventional slurry-casting process has the limitation of being difficult to manufacture thick electrodes due to the well-known binder migration phenomenon [10]. In contrast, the dry electrode process does not experience binder migration, making the fabrication of thick electrodes very easy and thus enabling improvements in energy density. Due to these advantages, various types of dry electrode processes, including PTFE fibrillation, powder spraying, and hot pressing, are being actively researched.[11–14].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: However, for dry electrode technology to be successfully adopted, two critical challenges must be overcome: the effective selection of conductive additives and the development of dispersion technologies. The most commonly used conductive additives in secondary batteries include particle-type additives like carbon black and linear additives such as multi-walled carbon nanotubes (mw-CNTs) and single-walled carbon nanotubes (sw-CNTs). [15,16] These materials are typically composed of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } .$ -bonded carbon, providing electron conductivity to the electrode, and are known to significantly enhance battery rate performance and cycle life.[17–19] Notably, SW-CNT exhibits exceptional performance, primarily attributed to its superior electronic conductivity, as highlighted in numerous previous studies[20–22]. The challenge, however, lies in the fact that all conductive additives tend to exist as agglomerates due to the strong π-π interactions between carbon atoms, originating from their $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ orbitals. In the traditional slurry-coating process, the solvent and dispersant play a key role in breaking these interactions, enabling successful dispersion of the conductive additives. [23–25] In contrast, the dry process, which does not utilize solvents, presents a significant challenge in dispersing conductive additives effectively.[26,27] An uneven distribution of conductive additives in the electrode can lead to decreased initial capacity, rate capability, and lifespan performance. This issue is particularly pronounced with carbon nanotubes, which, although more effective than particle-type additives like carbon black in reducing cell resistance and enhancing battery performance, pose greater difficulties in dispersion within dry electrode processes. [28–30].

paragraph_context: To address this problem, research has been conducted to improve the dispersibility of CNT powders by treating their surfaces or applying surfactants to the conductive additives.[31,32] In our study, we successfully introduced spray-drying technology to achieve effective dispersion of conductive additives. Spray drying is a simple and rapid technology that has garnered attention for its ability to produce highquality powder with high productivity [33–35]. It is already widely utilized in industries such as pharmaceuticals and food[36–38]. As S. Poozesh has demonstrated based on various literatures, spray drying technology enables the production of multiple tons of powder per day, making it industrially valuable[39]. Ongoing research on continuous scale-up and mass production is progressing, and the outlook is promising [40–42]. Through this method, we were able to uniformly coat $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (NCM811) active material with single-walled carbon nanotube (sw-CNT), naming the resulting composite material SW-SPD. Using this composite, we fabricated cathodes through the dry electrode process and evaluated the battery cells, confirming improvements in both output and lifespan performance. Notably, leveraging the excellent electrical conductivity of sw-CNT (in the range of $1 0 ^ { 2 }$ to $1 0 ^ { 3 } S /$ cm), we reduced the carbon additive content in the electrode to as low as 0.12 wt%, which is anticipated to contribute to enhancing the cell’s energy density. The introduction of these technologies is expected to integrate with advanced technologies in various energy devices, such as batteries and capacitors, [43–46] leading to greater progress.

paragraph_context: In this study, the active material used was single-crystal LiNi0.8- $\mathrm { C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811, SMLab). The conductive additives were carbon black (CB, Super C65, Imerys) and single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNT, OCSiAl), and the binder used was PTFE powder (Merck). The vibrational modes of NCM and SW-SPD were characterized using Raman spectroscopy (LABRAM HR, Horiba) with a 514 nm wavelength source. Elemental mappings of each electrode were performed using energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). paragraph_context: Fig. 1 presents the core concept of this study, demonstrating the PTFE fibrillation-based dry electrode fabrication process. It highlights the superior electrical network formation of the sw-CNT/NCM composite (SW-SPD) electrodes produced through spray-drying. We synthesized SW-SPD by uniformly dispersing NCM particles and sw-CNT in a solution, followed by spray-drying at a temperature above $2 1 0 \ { ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } } .$ . Spray drying is a powerful technique for creating composite electrode materials, offering several advantages over traditional drying methods. First, it ensures the uniform distribution of conductive additives like CNTs across the dispersed particles due to the atomization and rapid drying stages. This uniformity is crucial for achieving consistent electronic conductivity and enhancing the electrochemical performance of the resulting cathode materials. Unlike other drying methods, spray drying facilitates precise control over particle size and morphology, which are vital for optimizing electrode properties. Furthermore, the mechanism of spray drying inherently promotes the formation of a thin and homogeneous CNT coating on the particle surfaces. This is due to the synchronous evaporation of solvent and deposition of CNTs during the droplet-to-particle conversion phase, as highlighted in both experimental studies and reviews on spray drying techniques. [47–49] The coated CNT layer is anticipated to significantly improve electron transfer by providing conductive pathways while maintaining the structural integrity of the cathode material during cycling.

Cells were assembled using electrodes of CB, SW, and SW-SPD, followed by the formation process. After disassembling the cells, the cathodes were retrieved, prepared as samples, and analyzed. As reported in numerous studies [60,61], cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI) layers were formed on the NCM surface via the oxidative decomposition of the electrolyte (LiF, organic/inorganic compounds) and the dissolution and redeposition of transition metal ions. However, notable differences in layer morphology were observed. While the NCM surfaces of the CB and SW electrodes exhibited uneven and thick CEI layers, the NCM surface of the SW-SPD electrode showed a uniform and thin CEI layer, measuring only a few nanometers in thickness. The thick and uneven CEI layers on the CB and SW electrodes could result in reduced ionic conductivity and increased internal resistance, potentially leading to the degradation of output performance, as confirmed by earlier results. In contrast, the thin and uniform CEI layer on the SW-SPD electrode minimized adverse effects on the output performance of the electrode while retaining the positive characteristics of CEI, such as protecting the cathode surface and enhancing high-voltage stability. Considering the localized nature of TEM analysis, multiple points were analyzed for each sample, and the thickness measurements were statistically compiled, and provided in Fig. S10. The average CEI thickness, calculated from measurements at 20 locations for each sample, was 20.7 nm, 20.9 nm, and 8.5 nm for CB, SW, and SW-SPD, respectively.

paragraph_context: With the advent of long-range electric vehicles, the requirement for driving range per charge has increased to 500 km [1]. However, modern mainstream electric vehicles powered by lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) typically achieve 200–300 km per charge, largely constrained by the limited energy density of commercial LIBs (approximately 250 Wh/kg and 770 Wh/L) [2–4]. Significant efforts have been put into improving the energy density of LIBs [5,6]. One of the strategies is exploring highenergy–density battery systems such as Mn-rich (Li Ni Mn O ) cathode whose mass-energy density is up to 1100 Wh/kg [7]. Besides, optimizing the electrode structure can increase the battery mass loading (almost 100 mg/cm2 ) and have a long life span [8]. Lastly, using battery packing techniques (i.e., blade batteries) to increase the energy density is a practical and effective strategy [9]. Among them, increasing the mass loading of the electrode to enhance the ratio of active material mass to inactive mass holds significant promise for boosting the energy density of the system. This approach is particularly advantageous as it aligns seamlessly with electrode manufacturing processes. For example, with the mass loading of commercial electrode $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 6 } M n _ { 0 . 2 } C o _ { 0 . 2 } O _ { 2 } }$ increasing from 6 mg/cm2 to 20 mg/cm2 , the corresponding battery mass-energy density can be enhanced by roughly 40 % [10]. Whereas, the increase in mass loading can also lead to an increase in electrode thickness, which causes a series of undesirable effects, including the complexity of the coating process [11,12], the difficulty in the regulation of pore structure/tap density [13], and the increase in tortuosity [14,15]. As a result, the capacity fades rapidly in such a high-thick electrode battery system.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Significant progress has been achieved in understanding the battery performance deterioration of thick electrodes [16]. For example, several theoretical models have been developed to simulate the effect of porosity on the ion transport in thick electrodes [17]. These studies reveal that the capacity of thick electrodes declines rapidly at high current rates and that cathode thickness has a pronounced impact on specific energy. Appiah et al. utilized mathematical modeling to simulate the impact of varying electrode thickness and porosity on Li-ions transport [18]. Boyce et al. demonstrated through image-based modeling that increasing the porosity at the interface between the cathode and the separator can significantly enhance high-rate performance.[19] Fu et al. argue that compared to thin electrodes, thick electrodes are more sensitive to parameters such as porosity. Furthermore, they assert that strong dynamic constraints make thermodynamic failure the primary cause of capacity loss [20]. However, simulation methods have notable limitations [21,22]. Most simulation approaches rely on averaged values rather than calculating porosity variations across different electrode depths [23]. Additionally, conventional Butler–Vermer models fail to account for the concentration-dependent Li insertion/withdrawal process at the solid side of the electrode/electrolyte interface, leading to discrepancies in the calculated current density and overpotential [24]. Furthermore, studies have shown that thick electrodes with low porosity significantly reduce a battery’s capacity retention rate, which declines sharply as current density increases [25]. However, the complexity of pore distribution, along with thickness and tortuosity, makes these properties challenging to characterize, as traditional techniques are unable to probe such thick electrodes [26,27]. Consequently, most investigations into their failure mechanisms are limited to theoretical simulations, leaving the precise causes of rapid capacity fading largely unresolved. Therefore, advanced characterization techniques is crucial and urgent for gaining a deeper understanding of the mass transfer mechanisms in thick electrodes.

paragraph_context: The electrochemical performance of Li|LMLE and Li|HMLE cells were investigated. All cells are resting for 24 h to realize a full infiltration state of the electrodes. As shown in Fig. 3a, the gap between the oxidation and reduction peaks in cyclic voltammetry (CV) results of HMLE (0.48 V to 0.31 V) is larger and less symmetrical compared to LMLE, indicating higher polarization and weaker electrochemical reversibility. This supports the hypothesis that the uneven pore structure in HMLE hinders mass transport within the battery, resulting in significant polarization and rapid capacity decay. The cycling performance of Li|LMLE and Li|HMLE cells with flooded electrolyte to achieve a fully wetted state was compared. As shown in Fig. 3b-c, during the first cycle, the Li|LMLE cell delivers a specific capacity of 218.6 mAh/g (areal capacity is \~ 4.4 mAh/cm2 ) at a current density of 0.1C (1C = 274 mA/g), which is close to the theoretical capacity of LCO at 4.6 V (220 mAh/g), while the Li|HMLE cell reaches only \~ 200 mAh/g (areal capacity is \~ 9.5 mAh/cm2 ). The Li|LMLE cell demonstrates stable cycling behavior, retaining 80 % of its capacity after 100 cycles. In contrast, the capacity of the Li|HMLE cell declines rapidly between 20th and 50th cycles, resulting in poor retention of just 14 % after 100 cycles. This can be attributed to the uneven pore structure in HMLE, which restricts ion diffusion, hindering the full participation of the active material in electrochemical reactions and resulting in a lower specific capacity. Cross-sectional analysis after 100 cycles (Fig. S4) shows that the thickness of LMLE increases to 79.9 μm, corresponding to a maximum expansion rate of 17.5 %, whereas HMLE expands to 200 μm with an expansion rate of only 5 %. These findings highlight the lower utilization rate of active material in HMLE, as reflected in its reduced capacity and more pronounced capacity degradation during cycling. For the charge and discharge tests, a different industrial battery operating scenario was simulated with a high current density of 0.5C (Fig. 3d). In these measurements, the first three cycles were conducted at 0.1C for activation but were excluded from the plotted data. The LMLE battery demon strated excellent performance, maintaining a capacity of 191 mAh/g and a specific capacity of 43 mAh/g after 100 cycles. In contrast, the HMLE battery exhibited an initial specific capacity of only 74 mAh/g, which rapidly declined under the high current density. This stark difference highlights that, at high current densities, the rapid charge and discharge processes necessitate efficient mass transfer of lithium ions during lithiation and delithiation. The ion transport in HMLE, due to its complex pore structure, is sluggish and cannot be replenished during high-rate cycling, leading to significant performance degradation compared to LMLE.

Li|LMLE cells deliver discharge capacities of 221, 217.5, 193, 152, 37, and 15 mAh/g at rates of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, and 3C, respectively. As a result, most active materials remain unreacted at high current densities (≥0.5C). However, since the structure remains intact, the capacity recovers when the rate returns to 0.1C. These results indicate that the smaller porosity and higher tortuosity in HMLE significantly limit its rate performance, as its spatial structure cannot efficiently replenish the required amount of Li ions during high-rate cycles, resulting in a considerable reduction in ion transport capacity. In addition, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed on lithium metal half-cells constructed with LCO cathodes. The Nyquist plots exhibit semicircles in the high-medium frequency region, corresponding to charge transfer resistance $( \operatorname { R } _ { \mathrm { c t } } ,$ Fig. S5). As a result, the reaction depth is shallow, leading to a lower degree of lithiation. The cobalt elements in both electrodes appeared fibrous and densely packed. A substantial portion of these materials fails to participate in the electrochemical reaction, leading to a relatively shallow reaction depth. These findings confirm that the slow electrolyte diffusion caused by the uneven pore distribution is the primary reason for the rapid capacity degradation observed in thick HMLE.

paragraph_context: Finally, the key findings are summarized in the schematic diagram shown in Fig. 5. Increasing electrode mass loading inevitably alters the electrode structure, resulting in significantly greater thickness, reduced porosity, and increased tortuosity. These structural changes directly affect mass transport dynamics within the electrode, including intrinsic ion diffusion (D+) within particles and effective electrolyte diffusion $\begin{array} { r } { ( \mathrm { D } _ { \mathrm { e f f } } ) . } \end{array}$ . For both LMLE and HMLE prior to cycling, sufficient electrolyte availability and adequate resting time initially facilitate proper electrode infiltration. However, in thick electrodes $\mathrm { ( L _ { t h i c k } ) } _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , uneven pore distribution and reduced porosity are more pronounced compared to thin electrodes $\left( \mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { t h i n } } \right)$ . These structural deficiencies increase tortuosity and impede electrolyte infiltration, particularly for particles near the current collector. When electrolyte infiltration becomes insufficient and Li ions cannot replenished, LCO particles tend to partially participate in electrochemical reactions, reducing the overall mean diffusion coefficient. This limitation becomes even more pronounced under high-rate cycling or lean electrolyte conditions. Consequently, poor electrolyte wettability significantly accelerates the degradation of cell performance.

paragraph_context: Multi-scale imaging techniques including synchrotron micro-CT, nano-scale TXM-XANES, and ToF-SIMS, were employed to investigate the pore microstructure, mass dynamic transfer in thick $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ electrodes as well as their impacts on electrochemical performance. We demonstrate that poor electrolyte infiltration in thick electrodes, driven by decreased porosity and increased tortuosity, is a key factor in the rapid capacity degradation of cells. In the studied systems, increasing the mass loading of $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ electrodes from \~ 20 mg/cm2 to \~ 50 mg/ $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ raises the electrode thickness from \~ 68 μm to \~ 190 μm, leading to a decline in capacity retention rate from 80 % to 14 %. These adverse effects are particularly pronounced under fast-charge conditions or in lean-electrolyte battery systems. For example, the capacity retention of 68 μm electrodes decreases from 80 % to 23 % when decreasing the electrolyte to 5 μL/mAh. These results demonstrate that optimizing pore distribution, porosity, and tortuosity in thick electrodes to enhance electrolyte infiltration is essential for improving the performance of high-energy–density Li-ion batteries.

paragraph_context: The application of high energy density battery presents challenges for high loading electrode to achieve good performance. Polytetrafluoroethylene fibrillation results in unique advantages including high tap density, nonpollution, and thick electrodes. However, with an increase in electrode thickness, Li + transport within a dry cathode with a low porosity is particularly limited. Additionally, the binder currently used in the dry-film process suffers from poor conductivity and viscosity, resulting in a lithium-ion battery with poor cycling stability and rate performance. In this study, we developed a dry ultra-high-loading cathode using a Li+-carrier composite binder, which facilitated Li+ migration and ensured good interfacial contact between the active material particles (LiNi0.5Co0.2Mn0.3O2). This was attributed to the high dispersion performance of polyacrylonitrile and its interactions with Li+. Density functional theory analysis revealed that the composite binder exhibited a homogeneous electrostatic potential profile and narrow lowest unoccupied molecular orbital-highest occupied molecular orbital energy gap, thus enhancing its effectiveness in facilitating electron mobility. Therefore, the thick cathode fabricated with the composite binder displayed a high discharge capacity of 170.4 mAh g− 1 (200 μm, 9 mAh cm− 2 ) at 0.1C and a stable cycling performance, retaining 80.8 % of its initial capacity after 250 cycles at 0.5C. The single-layer lithium-metal pouch cell exhibited a high energy density of 300 Wh $\mathbf { k } g ^ { - 1 }$ , and 85.5 % of the capacity was retained after 150 cycles at 0.1C.

paragraph_context: Global warming and the resulting environmental regulations have yielded a pressing need for the development of energy storage devices with green fabrication processes and excellent electrochemical performances [1–3]. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs, 200–500 Wh L− 1 ) are the most extensively studied energy storage devices [4–6], but the current limitations of LIBs, such as their safety [7,8], costs [9,10], and energy densities [11,12], must be overcome to integrate high-capacity batteries into electric vehicles. The traditional slurry method of fabricating electrodes contributes significantly to the high costs of LIBs [13,14]. A major cost reduction measure involves increasing the area capacities of the electrodes, which requires thicker cathodes than those currently used in commercial batteries [15,16]. However, increasing the thickness of a composite electrode often leads to cracking, which can compromise battery performance [17]. In addition, the uniform, efficient transfer of electrons and ions throughout the volume must be ensured by optimizing the cathode, thus avoiding the degradation of cell performance [18,19].

paragraph_context: To address these drawbacks, the solvent-free dry-film process may be a promising alternative method because of its low contamination and the resulting inhibition of interfacial reactions and improved electrochemical performance [20–24]. The current representative fibrous binder used in solvent-free (dry) processing is polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), which forms a 3D fibrous backbone that supports the cathode material and facilitates the fabrication of laminate composite cathodes [25,26]. PTFE is electrochemically stable within a certain potential window, and it does not react with the active materials [22]. PTFE exhibits a limited capacity to transport $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } } ,$ and adequate levels of interfacial adhesion between the active materials and conductive carbon are not guaranteed because of its limited viscoelasticity [27–29]. This leads to the formation of voids and gaps during the volume expansion/contraction of the active material, thus reducing the battery capacity/cycle stability [30]. Therefore, exploring approaches for use in improving the viscoelasticity and conductivity to compensate for the limitations of PTFE in the solvent-free dry processing of composite cathodes is urgently necessary.

paragraph_context: Herein, a novel dry Li+-carrier composite polyacrylonitrile (PAN)/ PTFE binder fiber (LCB) was screened and developed. PAN elastomers contain polar side-chain groups, such as nitrile moieties, and they display high flexibilities and mechanical strengths but also the additional advantages of their amorphous natures [35–37]. PAN can interact with $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and the nitrogen single-pair orbital gains $\ " \mathbf { p } \ "$ character, and thus, the $\mathrm { C } { \equiv } \mathrm { N }$ triple bond gains $" s "$ character, resulting in higher force constants and a more negative peak compared to that of free $\mathrm { C } { \equiv } \mathrm { N } .$ . Additionally, acrylonitrile units can be involved in the self-diffusion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ to facilitate higher electrolyte absorption, which indirectly leads to improved ion migration [38,39]. The dry LCB cathode exhibited a unique 3D network structure, and the optimal composite binder provided a high discharge capacity and superior cycle stability (80.8 % capacity retention over 250 cycles). Our study provides novel possibilities for the further optimization of dry electrodes.
