paragraph_context: Binder fibrillation significantly affects battery performance [29,40]. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of PTFE after jet and ball milling are shown in Fig. S1. After jet milling, the PTFE particles are assembled into micron-scale fibers with good tensile strengths, whereas ball milling can only form nanoscale fibers, with numerous particles displaying no fibrosis. Before electrode preparation, we evaluated the oxidation stabilities of the different binders. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed using the different types of binders, and the results are shown in Fig. S2. A schematic of the preparation of the dry composite cathode is shown in Fig. 1a. In dry film processing, the active materials, Super P Li (SP), and binder (the mass ratios of PTFE:PAN used are 3:1, 1:1, and 1:3, denoted LCB-1, -2, and $^ { - 3 , }$ respectively) are mixed uniformly in a dispersing machine and then via high-speed air blowing to form binder fibers. The material is then pressed to the final thickness (200 μm) using a hot roller press at ${ 1 0 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , followed by hot overlaying onto a carbon-coated aluminum foil to yield the dry electrode. The dry composite cathode with the PAN additive exhibits an improved mechanical strength owing to the PTFE fibers, and the nitrile groups also attract $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ for coordination, providing additional rapid ion transfer carriers. The traditional dry process only yields transverse fibers, which can easily suffer longitudinal damage, whereas the cathode film prepared via intersect hot calendering displays good flexibility.

paragraph_context: SEM and cross-sectional SEM images of the prepared dry LCB cathode (Fig. 2a–c) reveal the presence of fibers evenly distributed on the surfaces of the NCM and SP particles and connected to form a dense, complete, flexible mesh bonding structure. This ensures the good mechanical stability of the independent film. The composite cathodes prepared with the other binders display similar morphologies (Fig. S5). Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) indicates that nitrogen and fluorine are uniformly distributed within the fibers of the PTFE/PAN binder throughout the dry cathode (Fig. 2b). The formation of the netlike binding structures of the fibers ensures high stability. Meanwhile, the homogeneous PAN attached to the PTFE fibers facilitates the entry of the electrolyte, avoiding the problem of limited electrolyte infiltration caused by a low porosity. The area capacity of the dry cathode film, with a flat, compact surface, is as high as 9 mAh cm− 2 (200 μm), whereas the area capacities of commercial cathodes generally reach 4 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [16]. The porosity measured via Archimedean method is ≈ 20 % (Fig. 2d and e), which is considerably lower than that of the conventional slurry cathode (≈40 %) [46]. SEM mapping of the electrode cross-section was performed to analyze the distributions of the binder and conductive additive, as shown in Fig. S6–S9. The uniformity of the LCB cathode and coincidence of F and N are good, and thus, the PAN mainly adheres to the PTFE fibers. The PTFE cathode exhibits aggregation of the conductive agent and binder, and thus, PAN is beneficial in the dispersion of the electrode materials, and it improves the mixing integrity. Notably, PAN has a high mechanical strength but poor adhesion; thus, a small amount can improve the dispersion. However, adding excess PAN is inappropriate; LCB-3 cathodes display excessive levels of PAN that fill areas not covered by the PTFE fibers, which may increase the rigidities of the electrodes, but lack structural stability. The material distribution within the LCB-1 cathode was further examined using Raman 2D mapping with a respective scanning step size and area of 2 and 50 × 50 μm (Fig. S10). The results reveal that the PAN particles and PTFE fibers are connected together to the active materials, the distribution of PAN is more uniform, and most of the PAN cover the PTFE fibers, which inhibited the agglomeration.

paragraph_context: Nanoindentation was used to further investigate the mechanical properties of the composite binder and moduli, hardnesses, and elasticities of the composite cathodes. To ensure the reliabilities of the results, seven random locations in each sample were used in evaluation (Fig. 2f) [47]. Fig. $2 g$ shows the load-depth curves of the nanoindentation of the four binders, and their elastic recovery ratios $( \mathrm { h } _ { \mathrm { r } } ,$ the ratio of the restored to the penetrated depth) are 0.074, 0.115, 0.133, and 0.134. The cathode prepared using the composite binder displays a higher elastic recovery rate. Hence, it can withstand the stress change caused by the variation in the volume of NCM during charging and discharging, eventually resulting in a battery with good cycle stability. Fig. 2h shows the data processing and statistical analysis of the results of nanoindentation that adhere to the Oliver and Pharr method [48]. The average standard moduli of the composite binders gradually decrease initially and then increase with increasing PAN content (0.955, 0.658, 0.291, and 0.494 GPa), following the same trend as that of the average hardness (7.568, 7.209, 3.904, and 6.299 MPa). This may be due to the combined effect of the decrease in the number of PTFE fibers and the decrease in the adhesive force of the bonding network caused by the adsorption of PAN on the surfaces of the PTFE fibers. However, when the amount of PAN is excessive, the free PAN exhibits an adhesive effect, leading to increases in the hardness and Young’s modulus. In addition, the variance analysis of the seven groups of hardness data reveals that the smallest error is observed when using composite binder-1, indicating the good uniformity of the composite cathode. The homogeneity and excellent mechanical properties of the composite cathode contribute to the stability of the cathode structure during electrode preparation and electrochemical cycling, thus providing rapid electron transfer and a long-term reduction in cell impedance. Fig. S11 shows the adhesive strengths of the dry cathodes with various binders, and the peel force of the dry cathode with LCB-1 exceeds those of the dry cathodes with the other binders. An appropriate amount of PAN can enhance the interfacial adhesion and reduce the interfacial impedance, whereas an excessive amount can weaken the adhesive strength, which is consistent with the above results. Tensile stress evaluation, as shown in Fig. S12 and Table S8, was conducted to further analyze the mechanical strength of the cathode. The evaluated samples exhibit dimensions of 50.0, 10.0, and 1.0 mm in length, width, and thickness, respectively. The LCB-1 cathode displays a higher tensile fracture strength and break strain (0.124 MPa, 16.056 %) than those of the PTFE (0.046 MPa, 7.761 %) and LCB-2 (0.107 MPa, 10.217 %) cathodes. However, the mechanical strength of LCB-3 is insufficient to support the tensile studies, which may be due to insufficient adhesion with the small number of PTFE fibers. Therefore, the mechanical strength of a cathode can be enhanced by introducing a suitable proportion of PAN.

The large polarization generated by the high current is the main cause of the large difference. The effects of the different types of binders on the electrochemical performance of the cell were determined based on the mechanical strengths, dispersive characteristics, and $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport capacities of the binders. A $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } } .$ -conductive binder that is more easily dispersed is urgently required for use in LIBs. These consistencies are further confirmed by the results of the LIBs shown in Fig. 3c, which indicate that the cell system exhibits high tolerances for current density at low and high current densities. Furthermore, based on the cyclic voltammograms of the LIBs with the samples (Fig. S15), characteristic redox peaks of NCM523, corresponding to $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { N i } ^ { 4 + }$ , are observed in the voltammograms of the LIBs, with deviations (ΔV), which represent polarization. ΔV reflects the reversibility of the battery, side reactions of the cathode and electrolyte, and properties of the cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI). The smaller ΔV is, the faster the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport is, and the better the electronic conductivity is. According to the charge/discharge curves of the 2nd and 3rd cycles, the lowest polarization among those of the LIBs is that of the LIB with the LCB-1 NCM523 cathode of 0.12 V. paragraph_context: The comparative cycling performances of the cells at 0.5C, as shown in Fig. 3d, reveal that the cell featuring PTFE suffers severe capacity loss during cycling. The capacity decay is attributed to the limited mechanical and adhesive strengths of the fiber network structure during the repeated changes in the volume of the NCM material [53]. As the volume expands and contracts repeatedly, the juncture with strong binding is cleaved, and thus, the contacts between the NCM cathode particles loosen after exceeding this limit. paragraph_context: Electrolyte wettability studies were conducted to further verify the mechanism of performance enhancement, and the dynamic contact angle of the electrolyte on the dry cathode surface was recorded. The conventional dry electrode exhibited a contact angle of 20.1◦ after 20 s, whereas the dry LCB electrode displayed no angle, and thus, the electrolyte entered the underlying microstructure beneath the electrode surface. The analysis shown in Fig. 4c indicates that the movement of the electrolyte through the dry LCB electrode is almost linear, whereas the rate of variation in the contact angle of the conventional dry cathode decreases with time. Therefore, PAN facilitates the absorption of the electrolyte, which may be due to the higher requirements of the thick electrode in terms of Li transport throughout the electrode microstructure, particularly those of the dry electrode (lower porosity) [58]. Wetting using the electrolyte was qualitatively analyzed via capillary rise (Fig. S17). The dry LCB electrode displays a rising height of 50 mm, whereas that of the dry PTFE electrode is 20 mm [59], which is related to the PAN-optimized transport of liquid electrolytes within the thick electrodes. The function of the PAN Li carrier is further confirmed, which is conducive to the uniform distribution of the electrolyte and rapid Li+ transport. The wettability with the electrolyte not only supports the presence of Li-carrier fibers within the electrode microstructure but also aids in understanding the potential migration of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ through the electrode during electrochemical charging/discharging (Fig. 4d). In the conventional dry cathode, the insulating properties of PTFE hinder $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer, and the electrolyte is mainly concentrated on the electrode surface. Furthermore, it cannot retain strong levels of adhesion between composite cathode assemblies with high loadings during long-term cycling. Unlike in the conventional dry cathode, the electrolyte is evenly dispersed over the entire dry LCB cathode, and PAN facilitates $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ migration, and thus, the LIB with the dry LCB cathode displays a superior high-rate capability and cycling stability.

paragraph_context: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of the NCM523 surface was performed before and after 250 cycles at 0.5C to further understand the effects of the CEI properties and mechanism of performance enhancement. Based on the standardisation reference peak at 284.8 eV associated with carbon black (C–C), the C 1s spectra of NCM523 with PTFE and LCB before cycling are similar, with peaks representing C─C/C─H (284.8 eV), O─C––O (289.6 eV), and C─F bonds (292.4 eV) [62]. The higher intensity of the peak representing C─F associated with PTFE combined with NCM523 compared to those of the peaks representing C─F associated with the LCB samples combined with NCM523 is attributed to the introduction of PAN (Fig. S23a). In the O 1s core region (Fig. 6i), the intensity of the peak representing the lattice oxygen (529.7 eV) within the cycled PTFE-based NCM523 is considerably higher than that of the peak representing the lattice oxygen within the cycled LCB-based NCM523. Therefore, the CEI of the PTFE-based NCM523 is not formed well, whereas the surfaces of the LCB-based NCM523 particles bear a stable CEI that fully covers the cathode surface, as shown in Fig. S30. The surface LCB forms a thin, uniform CEI layer, and the lattice oxygen is gradually exposed via the stripping of the CEI layer during Ar+ etching. At a depth of 10 nm, the strength of the peak representing P–F–O within PTFE displays a large attenuation, and thus, the electrolyte is not fully absorbed within the PTFE. This is consistent with the results of the contact angle measurements (Fig. 6j).

paragraph_context: To improve the thermal management and temperature uniformity of lithium-ion batteries, this study proposes and evaluates a novel liquid cooling plate structure featuring gradient porous metal foam (GPFM). A fully integrated three-dimensional electrochemical-thermal coupled model was developed to accurately capture the battery's internal thermal behavior and assess the cooling plate's performance. The numerical simulations for this model were conducted using COMSOL Multiphysics. The study systematically investigated the influence of key input parameters—specifically, four distinct porosity gradient variations (defined by the gradient index n) and discharge rates (e.g., 2C, 5C, 7C)—on the primary output parameters: the battery's peak temperature and maximum temperature difference $( \Delta T _ { m a x } )$ . The results indicate that the designed GPFM cooling plate effectively lowers the peak temperature while markedly improving thermal uniformity. The enhancement was most evident when the gradient variation index ${ \mathfrak { n } } = 2 .$ . The impact of the gradient design varied with the discharge rate. The maximum temperature reduction peaked at 13.5% under a 7C discharge rate. Conversely, the temperature difference achieved its highest percentage reduction of 58.1% at a 2C discharge rate. This study demonstrates that optimizing the porosity gradient design is an effective approach to enhancing tem perature uniformity in lithium-ion batteries, particularly offering significant benefits under highdischarge-rate conditions.

paragraph_context: Lithium batteries, as one of the main energy storage methods of new energy sources, have been extensively studied because of their benefits, including enhanced safety, superior energy density, and affordability. The lifespan of electric vehicles affects their social acceptance and ecological sustainability, particularly in terms of secondary use applications. The understanding of degradation mechanisms remains insufficient, despite the influence of C-rate, depth of discharge, state of charge range, and temperature on battery cycle aging. Battery performance relies on internal temperature, with an optimal operating range between ${ } ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ and ${ 3 5 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C } ,$ a maximum threshold of $5 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , and an ideal temperature of approximately $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } [ 1 ]$ ]. External cooling can reduce internal heating but may create temperature gradients; at high C-rates, the temperature difference within the battery can exceed 10K [2].

paragraph_context: In the study of temperature uniformity of lithium batteries, the electrochemical-thermal coupled heat generation model has received widespread attention because it can simultaneously consider the electrochemical reaction and heat transfer process inside the battery [3]. Despite numerous studies on managing the heat in Li-ion batteries, there are two main challenges. First, the complex and computationally intensive electrochemical-thermal model needs more efficient and accurate solving methods. Second, factors like surrounding temperature, charging speed, battery design, and more impact Li-ion batteries in real-world use, and their effects on thermal management require deeper exploration [4,5]. Newman et al. [6] proposed for the first time an electrochemical model to estimate the discharge behavior by combining the micro/macro parameters (e.g., Li + concentration, current, and potential), respectively, simplifying the anodes, diaphragm, and cathodes as three spaced intervals in the thickness direction. This model is widely adopted because of its exceptional accuracy and fast computation time. Li et al. [7] proposed this 3D hierarchical electrochemical model to visualize the spatial and temporal distribution of lithium-ion battery electrochemical properties. There are two common treatments in 3D hierarchical thermal modeling: one selects the unit cell as the geometrical basis and divides it into several layers, including the anode collector, anode active material, diaphragm, cathode active material, and cathode collector [8]. In order to simplify the battery structure by dividing it into anode, cathode, and diaphragm layers, which are not actual thicknesses (micrometers) but roughly fitted values (millimeters) based on the cardinality of laminated components [9]. This model is typically integrated with a one-dimensional electrochemical model or an electrical model that can be either two-dimensional or three-dimensional. The three-dimensional non-stratified model [10], commonly known as the lumped thermal approach, is the most widely used thermal model and is typically combined with a one-dimensional electrochemical model. In this model [11,12], the cell is characterized as an anisotropic thermal material, which means it exhibits varying thermal properties in different directions, ignores the internal layered structure, and has a shorter computational time. Wang et al. [13] devised a model integrating a one-dimensional electrochemical method and a three-dimensional thermal analysis. Their findings highlighted that the anode's electrochemical parameters notably influence the overall electrochemical behavior. Tang et al. [14] examined how the conductivity of solid and liquid phases affects the distribution of reaction current density through a coupled 1D electrochemical and 3D thermal model. They discovered that these conductivities significantly influence the current density distribution. Xu et al. [15] comprehensively investigated the thermal behavior of cylindrical $\mathrm { L i F e P O } _ { 4 }$ cells during discharge using a two-dimensional electrochemical-thermal coupling model. Their findings indicate that cylindrical cells exhibit more favorable voltage distribution compared to square cells.

paragraph_context: Traditional thermal management systems for lithium batteries primarily depend on air cooling. However, as battery energy density increases, the efficiency of air cooling alone is increasingly insufficient to meet the required demands. Typically, the focus of thermal management for liquid-cooled lithium batteries is primarily on optimizing the design of the cooling plate's runner structure. Su et al. [16] examined how the thickness, wall thickness, coolant inlet temperature, and flow rate of a U-shaped liquid-cooling plate influence the thermal and pressure profiles within a battery. Jarrett et al. [17] utilized a serpentine-shaped runner channel design to optimize the temperature and pressure drop as the optimization objectives and analyzed the flow channel width and layout through simulation. Optimization of runner width and layout. The study revealed improvements in average temperature and pressure drop, albeit with a slight rise in temperature difference. Su et al. [18] developed a double-inlet and -outlet serpentine runner and examined how various design configurations impacted the temperature difference. Their findings indicated that the placement of the inlets and outlets, as well as the flow orientation, significantly influenced the temperature gradient. Zhao et al. [19] designed a honeycomb liquid cooling plate, significantly increasing the heat transfer surface area between the coolant and the plate. Bhattacharjee et al. [20] compared air-cooled and liquid-cooled battery thermal management systems (BTMS) and developed an immersion liquid-cooled BTMS for kilowatt battery packs. Their findings indicated superior cooling efficiency in the liquid-cooled system compared to the air-cooled system. Seyed et al. [21] designed three unique configurations of liquid-cooled plates (LCPs) and showed that increasing the coolant's pressure drop (ΔP) or the number of cooling channels significantly improves temperature uniformity in LCPs. Nieto et al. [22] integrated the heat generation characteristics of lithium batteries (LiBs) into simulations of heat dissipation in Li-ion battery modules, thereby identifying optimal coolant flow rates and temperature parameters. In recent years, due to advances in modern manufacturing techniques, considerable technology exists to make materials such as open-cell foam metals with good heat transfer properties available for industrial applications [23–28]. These materials are capable of boosting heat transfer in forced convection scenarios, thanks to their elevated surface area density for heat transfer, effective fluid mixing capabilities, and excellent permeability. Owing to its superior heat and mass transfer properties, it has been widely adopted by numerous researchers in the thermal management of electric vehicle batteries. Bai et al. [29] explored the thermally developing forced convective flow within a channel containing metallic foam that exhibited an axial gradient in porosity, employing a local thermal nonequilibrium approach. Their findings indicated that porous foam aluminum, with its porosity changing along the axial gradient, significantly influenced the development of wall temperature in the axial direction. Li et al. [30] investigated a passive thermal management approach for high-power lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) using copper-metal foam embedded with phase change material (PCM). This method can substantially reduce the battery's surface temperature while improving temperature distribution uniformity. Moreover, the battery's surface temperature is affected by the porosity and pore density of the metal foam. Wang et al. [31] employed a composite phase change material made of paraffin and aluminum foam to maintain the battery temperature in an optimal range for maximum performance. Their study concluded that while aluminum foam can substantially boost the thermal conductivity of the phase change material (PCM), it also suppresses local natural convection. Developed a thermal management system for lithium-ion batteries by employing phase change materials saturated with graphene-coated nickel foam. The permeation of paraffin into the foam metal increased the thermal conductivity by nearly 23 times compared to the pure phase change material. Mehdi et al. [32] designed a thermal management system integrating phase change materials into a copper foam matrix, achieving superior thermal performance for the battery pack over extended operating periods. Recent studies have explored advanced cooling media such as ice slurry and microencapsulated phase change slurry (MPCS) for lithium-ion battery thermal management. Yoon et al. [33] investigated MPCS in immersion cooling systems, demonstrating improved temperature uniformity and reduced thermal gradients due to the latent heat of encapsulated phase change materials. Zhou et al. [34] provided a comprehensive review of liquid cooling technologies, highlighting the potential of slurry-based coolants to outperform traditional methods under high thermal loads. Li et al. [35] conducted simulation analysis on immersion liquid cooling systems, confirming the feasibility of integrating phase change slurries into energy storage battery packs for enhanced thermal control. These findings suggest that slurry-based cooling media, including ice slurry and MPCS, offer promising pathways to improve temperature uniformity and mitigate thermal stress in high-performance battery systems. However, a potential issue in these studies is that excessive thermal load on the LIB may cause the PCM within the metal foam to melt completely. When the solid phase change material in the foam metal fully transitions to a liquid state, its cooling performance becomes inferior to that of direct air cooling. At lower thermal loads, lithium-ion batteries with pure PCM and those with metal-foam-PCM composites exhibit nearly identical surface temperatures. Wang et al. [36] performed a numerical study on aluminum foam-cooled columnar lithium-ion batteries. Reduced porosity results in a lower average cell temperature, while simultaneously intensifying the temperature gradient.

paragraph_context: Operating temperatures significantly influence the performance and lifespan of lithium batteries, which generate substantial heat during operation. Uneven temperature distribution will not only lead to the imbalance of chemical reaction inside the battery, but also may cause localized overheating problems, which will shorten the battery's lifetime and even bring serious safety hazards. To address this challenge, a gradient porous foam metal liquid cooling plate with porous foam aluminum as the substrate and water as the cooling fluid was designed in this study. The gradient porous foam metal liquid cooling plate enhances lithium battery temperature uniformity via its unique gradient porosity structure. To assess the impact of the design scheme, numerical simulation analysis is employed to evaluate how various schemes influence lithium battery temperature uniformity, using the maximum temperature $\mathrm { ( T _ { m a x } ) }$ , minimum temperature $( \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m i n } } ) _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and maximum temperature difference $\left( \Delta \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m a x } } \right)$ as key parameters.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In this study, a gradient porous foam metal liquid-cooled plate with four different porosity gradient variation schemes, which corresponded to ${ \mathbf { n } } = 0 , 0 . 5 { \mathrm { , } }$ , 1 and 2, respectively, and one ordinary hollow liquid-cooled plate without porous foam metal, were compared under same conditions. We assessed the performance of a gradient porous foam metal liquid cooling plate in enhancing lithium battery temperature uniformity by analyzing temperature distribution, maximum temperature, temperature difference, effective thermal conductivity, and coolant flow rate across five solutions. The findings indicate that this novel gradient porous foam liquid cooling plate design significantly improves temperature uniformity in lithium batteries.

paragraph_context: To enhance the study of battery temperature uniformity and more intuitively observe the impact of porous foam metal on temperature distribution, the analysis prioritizes the surface temperature of the cell, focusing on the central region where heat concentration is highest, without delving into the detailed temperature distribution of the entire battery. This approach simplifies the research process while effectively revealing the influence of various cooling schemes on temperature uniformity. Fig. 8 presents a temperature distribution map of the porous foam metal plates on both sides of the central cell under four gradient porosity schemes, using a 5C discharge rate as an example. Comparative analysis of these distributions provides valuable insights into the role of porous foam metal in improving temperature uniformity in Li-ion batteries and its potential for optimization.

paragraph_context: Fig. 8 illustrates that positioning a gradient porous foam metal liquid-cooled plate under the lithium battery alters the heat distribution significantly. Instead of concentrating near the tabs, the heat spreads more uniformly across the battery's bottom. The peak temperature is identified at the center of the battery's base. Under a 5C discharge rate, the gradient porosity's optimization effect is markedly enhanced, with a substantial decrease in the maximum temperature difference between the n = 2 and n = 0 cases. Under high discharge rates, non-uniform heat generation is exacerbated. By matching the heat flux density distribution through gradient porosity $( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { e } } . \boldsymbol { \mathrm { g } } . , \ \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } = 2 )$ , local thermal saturation can be avoided. The channel design of the gradient porous structure effectively eliminates local flow stagnation zones and enhances the overall heat transfer coefficient by promoting fluid flow. This indicates that the gradient porous structure enhances local heat transfer efficiency by optimizing the coolant flow path, especially in areas with high heat flux density (near the electrode tabs), where the increase in thermal conductivity significantly improves the heat dissipation capability. The excellent temperature uniformity observed in Fig. 8 is fundamentally due to the gradient design (n = 2), which optimizes the flow field and effective thermal conductivity, as will be analyzed in detail in Sections 3.4 and 3.5.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The temperature distribution cloud diagram in Fig. 8 clearly shows that heat is more concentrated at the cell's center, particularly at the middle and lower ends, while temperatures are significantly lower on both sides. This temperature distribution characteristic is closely related to the design that the porosity of the liquid-cooling plate of porous foam metal shows a two-dimensional gradient decrease along the flow direction, and the gradient change of porosity effectively guides the conduction and distribution of heat. The gradient porous metal foam mitigates the concentration of hot spots, particularly those near the positive electrode lugs, which typically exhibit elevated temperatures during battery discharge. Implementation of a gradient porous foam metal liquid cooling plate results in a more uniform temperature distribution across the battery cell surface, reducing localized overheating. This enhanced uniformity is most pronounced when the gradient parameter n = 2. Consequently, the gradient porosity design effectively minimizes the risk of electrolyte decomposition due to uneven temperature distribution under high discharge rates, thereby enhancing battery safety.

To comprehensively understand and optimize temperature uniformity in lithium batteries, it is crucial to analyze the maximum temperature difference and variation throughout the battery. A thorough evaluation of temperature differences will identify inconsistencies and optimize cooling system design and material selection, improving temperature uniformity and overall battery performance and safety.

paragraph_context: While the gradient structure effectively optimizes flow velocity for heat transfer, it also introduces additional flow resistance. A key metric for evaluating the operational ‘cost’ of the LCP is the pressure drop (ΔP) from inlet to outlet, which is shown in Table 6. Our simulations show that the hollow liquid-cooling plate (without foam) has a pressure drop of 85.7 Pa. In contrast, the foam-filled plates exhibit a higher pressure drop. The uniform foam (n = 0) has a ΔP of 92.0 Pa, while the best-performing n = 2 gradient design has the highest pressure drop at 97.6 Pa. This represents a \~14% increase in pumping power cost, which is a necessary trade-off for the significant improvements in thermal uniformity and peak temperature reduction. We use the thermal performance evaluation criterion (TPEC) to evaluate the effectiveness of different options. The TPEC formula is as follows [40,41]: $$ T P E C = \frac {\left(1 / \Delta T _ {m a x}\right) / \left(1 / \Delta T _ {m a x , 0}\right)}{\left(\Delta P / \Delta P _ {0}\right) ^ {1 / 3}} \tag {36} $$ $\Delta T _ { m a x }$ is the maximum temperature difference, and ΔP is the pressure drop. $\Delta T _ { m a x , 0 }$ and $\Delta P _ { 0 }$ are the maximum temperature difference and pressure drop at the baseline, with the no porous metals selected as the baseline. The calculation results are shown in Table 7. The results show that even the lowest n = 0 scheme achieves a TPEC of 1.741 at $7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C }$ . This clearly demonstrates that the temperature uniformity benefits brought by the introduction of porous media far outweigh the penalty from fluid resistance. Furthermore, regardless of whether the temperature is increased to 2C or 7C, the TPEC with $\mathbf { n } = 2$ consistently shows the highest value in its row. This indicates that within the scope discussed in this paper, the gradient parameter ${ \mathbf n } = 2$ yields the best results.

paragraph_context: An increasing demand for long-lasting endurance devices impels us to develop lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with high energy density [1–4]. In order to improve energy density of LIBs, the utilization of outstanding cathode materials with high capacity and high operating voltage is one of the most feasible strategies [5,6]. In this respect, Ni-rich layered oxides $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { x } \mathrm { C o } _ { y } \mathrm { M n } _ { z } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \left( x + y + z = 1 , x \ge 0 . 7 \right.$ , denoted as NCM) is attracted great interest owing to the high practical capacity (> 200 mA h $g ^ { \mathrm { ~ - ~ } 1 } )$ ) with a charging cut-off voltage of 4.2 V in half-batteries [7,8]. However, the increment of specific capacity of Ni-rich NCM cathode is accompanied by sacrificing in cycling stability and thermal stability due to the weaker Ni− O bonds destabilizing the crystal structure, as well as increasing the anisotropic volume change upon Li-extraction/insertion [9,10]. Particularly, at high voltage state, Ni-rich cathode materials suffers from large anisotropic volume variations, compromising the mechanical stability and generating intergranular cracks among the primary-particles [11]. As a result, the crystal structure degradation further leads to a sharp drop in electrochemical performance. These issues make it difficult for conventional Ni-rich cathode materials to be adopted in large-scale practical application [12].

paragraph_context: Generally, increasing the charging cut-off voltage is an effective strategy to promote the energy density of layer-structure oxide cathode materials. However, the serious capacity fading at high oxidation state is an intractable issue for the practical application of Ni-rich oxide cathode materials since the high charging cut-off voltage will trigger the phase transition and layer-structure collapse. Hence, we expand the charging cut-off voltage to 4.5 V to inspect the electrochemical performance of core-shell $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } @ L i N i _ { 0 . 5 } M n _ { 1 . 5 } O _ { 4 } }$ composites under high charging cut-off voltage. In contrast, the CS-0.1 sample has a satisfactory capacity retention of 86% after 100 cycles at 0.5 C within the charge-discharge voltage ranging from 2.8 V to $4 . 5 \ \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ as illustrated in Fig. 7b-c. Additionally, even expanding the charging cut-off voltage to 4.5 V, the initial Coulombic efficiency of CS-0.1 cathode (80.9%) still is higher than that of pristine one (78.8%). Vividly, such significant improvement in cycling stability under high charging cut-off voltage condition is mainly attributed to the remarkable electrochemical stability of $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 5 } M n _ { 1 . 5 } O _ { 4 } }$ shell. Furthermore, Fig. 7d compares the rate performance of pristine sample and CS-0.1 sample. Although their reversible discharge capacities both are declined with increasing current density, the CS-0.1 sample exhibits the greatly enhanced rate capability, in which the reversible discharge capacities of CS-0.1 sample are 231.1, 219.1, 206.3, 189.9, and 162.5 mA h $g ^ { \mathrm { ~ - ~ } 1 } ,$ respectively, under 0.2 C to 5.0 C. Additionally, when the current density is switched back to 0.2 C, the CS-0.1 sample still delivers a remarkable discharge capacity of 219.9 mA h ${ \it g } ^ { \mathrm { ~ - ~ } 1 } .$ . paragraph_context: To better validate the remarkable cycling stability of core-shell $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } @ L i N i _ { 0 . 5 } M n _ { 1 . 5 } O _ { 4 } }$ composites, the microstructure evolution of CS-0.1 sample is inspected by SEM tests. As shown in Fig. 9a-d, no obvious cracks can be detected in the surface or interior of CS-0.1 sample, whereas a conspicuous crack is vividly observed in the inner sider of pristine $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ sample. This result indicates that the $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 1 . 5 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ shell is responsible for the significantly enhanced structure stability of $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } } .$ Additionally, even at high charging cut-off voltage of 4.5 V, compared to pristine $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ sample (Fig. 9e), no obvious crack can be found in the surface of CS-0.1 sample (Fig. 9f). However, huge cracks can be clearly seen on the surface of pristine $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 9 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ sample. Generally, at the high delithiation state, Ni-rich layered NCM cathodes often generate intergranular cracks among the primary-particles [14]. These intergranular cracks will propagate along the particle grain boundaries, causing the spalling of secondary microspheres and their subsequent pulverization, eventually resulting in the unexpected degradation of mechanical integrity and cycling retention [12, 44]. In this work, due to the spinel phase has superior microstructure stability, CS-0.1 sample could maintain the integrated structure after cycling to achieve a better electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: To accurately predict the lifetime of commercial cells, multi-physics models can be used, however the accuracy of the model is heavily reliant upon the quality of the input thermodynamics and kinetic parameters. The thermal properties and the variability of the transport and thermodynamic properties with temperature and stateof-charge (SoC) in a high energy 21700 cylindrical cell were measured. The parameters are used in a DFN and 0D thermal model, and the model was tested against experimental data from the commercial cell. The results demonstrate an improved model fit by 27% when including the parameter dependency upon SoC and temperature, compared to without. The maximum power is limited by the negative electrode, which has lower diffusion coefficients and current exchange density over the full SOC window compared to the positive electrode, particularly at 50 and 80% SoC (x = 0.45 and 0.85), reflected in high activation energies of up to 60 kJK− 1 and low diffusion coefficients of 5 × 10− 13 cm− 2 s − 1 at 25 ◦C. At 45 ◦C, the reaction rate increases to greater than that of the positive, diffusion also increases, 2 $\times 1 0 ^ { - 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } s ^ { - 1 }$ , but is still limiting. This work provides for the first time an electrochemical and thermal experimental dataset for a high energy cell, and provides insights into the rate limitations and prediction errors.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries are becoming a preferred technology for energy storage, particularly within the automotive industry due to a transition towards electric vehicles [1,2]. Significant improvements in battery technology have been made, including reducing cost and increasing energy density [3]. However, improving battery performance has an impact upon safety considerations due to increased heat generation inside the cell, which in turn increases the probability of thermal runaway [4,5]. Therefore, the thermal characteristics of a cell are an important consideration during cell and pack design [6]. Models can aid this design process by simulating the heat generation and electrochemical behaviour of a battery [7]. Increasingly, physics-based models are being used for predictive purposes, providing insights into the internal states of a battery and more accurate predictions compared to equivalent circuit models [8]. Through the porous electrode theory introduced in the work of Newman and Tiedemann, physics-based electrochemical models became popularised for predicting the internal states of a battery [9,10]. These predictions can be further improved by coupling to a thermal model to capture the thermal-dependency [11, 12].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Higher energy density materials have been developed to meet the automotive specifications for lower cost vehicles, these include nickelrich layered oxides and silicon-doped graphite electrodes [13,14]. The development of new materials and cell types means that these systems need to be parameterised to enable accurate model predictions for these applications. This is because electrodes vary in composition and microstructure, factors that have significant influence on the resulting electrochemical and thermal properties [15]. Commonly used parameter sets for commercial cells are not for high energy systems and do not include the information required to extend to a 3D thermal model [16–18]. Recent parameterisations of commercial cells only considered batteries with electrodes less than 55 µm [17,19].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Previous work has compared differences in energy vs power cells and their physical and electrochemical properties, these differences identified a need to parameterise high energy cells as literature has focussed on high power [20,21]. Additionally, research that has parameterised thermal-electrochemical models has not involved measuring the specific heat capacities and thermal conductivities of the individual materials needed to describe thermal performance beyond 0D (Table 1) [18,22]. The requirements of the different thermal model definitions are as follows (the electrochemical parameters also need to be defined): • 0D Thermal: Activation energy, entropic term, and lumped (volumetric) heat capacity.  • 1D Thermal: Thermal conductivity, heat capacities, and 1D cell geometry.  • 2D Thermal: 2D cell geometry.  • 3D Thermal: 3D cell geometry, tab locations, and inner structure.

paragraph_context: In this paper we parameterise the LG M50, a cell that with a very high energy density 267 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ , attributed to high electrode coat weight and its composition of $\mathrm { L i } [ \mathrm { N i _ { 1 - x - y } M n _ { x } C o _ { y } } ] \mathrm { O _ { 2 } }$ (NMC) and graphite-SiOy materials. To our knowledge, this is to date the highest energy cell reported in literature, for which parameterisation has been performed, and the only cell to have the thermal characteristics for the electrodes and cell (267 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ . The parameterisation provides the modelling community with the data to predict thermal inhomogeneities within the cell by detailing the cell anatomy and the thermal transport properties required to extend to 3D. Including the information allows better predictions about battery performance to be made, therefore allowing more efficient thermal management systems to be designed.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The M50 has become popular in the academic battery modelling community. The thermal parameters for this cell have not been outlined, meaning research has neglected the thermal behaviour or used properties not specific to the M50 [23,25,26]. Presently, the influence of temperature on the electrochemical behaviour has not been included or these properties required have been taken from a different cell [27]. This work details the complete experimental design for a thermal-electrochemical parameterisation of a 21700 cylindrical cell to evaluate the geometric, electrochemical, and thermal properties of the electrodes, separator, and current collectors. In addition to providing the information necessary for a 3D thermal model, the lithium concentration and temperature parameter dependencies are documented to enable more accurate model predictions by accounting for the local variability in performance during cell operation. Models often neglect the effect of lithium concentration and temperature on cell properties [28,29], despite the parameters being significantly influenced by these variables [17]. This includes the experimental methodology and the mathematical analysis to assess these parameter-dependencies, which can be applied to commonly used NMC and graphite materials.

paragraph_context: Simulations were conducted in the Python Battery Mathematical Modelling (PyBaMM) software package (using v0.4.0) [32]. The equations for the thermal-electrochemical model are summarised in Tables S2 and S3. In order to solve the model a finite volume scheme was used, with 30 grid points for each electrode and the separator, and 150 grid points for each particle; resulting in a system of 9092 ODEs and 150 algebraic equations. An exponential mesh was used to help with the convergence of the solver. In order to solve the system, a CasADI solver was used [33]. Each simulation of discharge plus relaxation takes 10 to 20 min using an Intel Core i7-7660U (2.50 GHz) processor and 16 GB RAM. This is because the nonlinear diffusion takes the solver many iterations to converge. The computational time could be reduced by using more sophisticated numerical methods, but this is out of the scope of this work. It should be noted that reduced models such as the Thermal Single Particle Model with electrolyte (TSPMe) [25] yield very similar results with a significant reduction of the computational time.

The thermal properties of the components should be considered with the presence of electrolyte as the commercial cell is comprised this way and the electrolyte significantly effects thermal transport [19,36]. However, due to the volatility of the electrolyte, ex situ measurements could not be carried out for the separator or electrode and in situ measurements do not allow the deconvolution of the thermal properties of individual components—this is needed to enable physics-based models to predict thermal inhomogeneities. paragraph_context: The specific heat capacity describes the heat energy required to raise a material by a unit of energy, this relates to how easily the temperature rises within a cell and helps the model to predict temperature gradients. Selection of materials with a high specific heat capacity means more energy is needed to raise the internal temperature of a cell reducing the presence of internal gradients. paragraph_context: To capture the change in specific heat capacity due to temperature in the model a function is needed to describe this relationship. The Debye theory of specific heat states that the specific heat of solids is proportional to $T ^ { 3 }$ if the temperature is below the Debye temperature, which is reported to be 141 $^ \circ \mathrm { C }$ for graphite and between 136 and 204 ◦C for the transition metals in NMC [39]. We can therefore fit the specific heat capacity against temperature data using third order polynomial according to Debye theory, it is important to capture these phenomena using scientifically-robust descriptions rather than arbitrary functions. The fits for the electrode powders and separator are illustrated in Fig. 3 with the comparison to raw data in Fig. S3.

Therefore, the thermal conductivity perpendicular to the electrode can be written as [4]: $$ \lambda_ {t o t a l} = \frac {L _ {e 1} + L _ {c c} + L _ {e 2}}{\left(\frac {L _ {e 1}}{\lambda_ {e 1}} + \frac {L _ {c c}}{\lambda_ {c c}} + \frac {L _ {e 2}}{\lambda_ {e 2}}\right)} = \frac {2 L _ {e} + L _ {c c}}{\left(\frac {2 L _ {e}}{\lambda_ {e}} + \frac {L _ {c c}}{\lambda_ {c c}}\right)}. \tag {5} $$ The thickness of the electrode $L _ { e }$ and current collector $L _ { c c } ,$ the conductivity of the current collector $\lambda _ { c c }$ and the total conductivity λ are known, therefore the conductivity of the electrode laminate $\lambda _ { e }$ can be calculated. paragraph_context: In this section, the temperature dependencies of the parameters were outlined to capture the influence of temperature on electrochemical behaviour, batteries undergo self-heating even at moderate C-rates so this information is essential to accurately predict these changes. The activation energy can be evaluated by finding the slope c of plot ln(n) vs. 1/T: $$ c = E _ {n} ^ {\text { act }} / R. \tag {7} $$ To describe the heat generation of the cell, the entropic coefficients were measured to capture the reversible heat and the irreversible heat is accounted for in the DFN model definition. The effect of voltage hysteresis is often not considered in models, these properties are therefore evaluated during cell discharge only $\mathrm { i . e . , }$ positive electrode lithiation and negative electrode delithiation. paragraph_context: The activation energy of solid-phase diffusion can be calculated by repeating GITT at different temperatures [18,48]. This enables us to find the concentration/temperature dependency of solid-phase within the active material. The diffusion coefficients were analysed from the transients and steady-phase regions during GITT. The analytical approach involves evaluating changes in lithium concentration at the particle surface as a function of time. This can be described by an expression relating to the Sand equation[49]: $$ D _ {s} = \frac {4}{\pi} \left(\frac {I}{F S c _ {s} ^ {\text { max }}} - \frac {\frac {\partial U}{\partial x}}{\frac {\partial V}{\partial \sqrt {t}}}\right) ^ {2}. \tag {8} $$ Here I is the applied current, F is the Faraday constant, S is the effective area of the porous electrode-electrolyte interface, and $c _ { s } ^ { m a x }$ is the maximum concentration in the electrode. S can be calculated from the total number of particles in the electrode and the average surface area of a particle: $$ S = n \cdot S _ {\text { particle }} = \frac {\varepsilon_ {\text { act }} \cdot V _ {\text { electrode }}}{V _ {\text { particle }}} S _ {\text { particle }}. \tag {9} $$ $\varepsilon _ { a c t }$ is the active material volume fraction, $V _ { e l e c t r o d e }$ is the electrode volume, $V _ { p a r t i c l e }$ is particle volume, $S _ { p a r i c l e }$ is the particle surface area. For this the average particle sizes of 5.22 µm and 5.86 µm were used for the positive and negative electrode, respectively, these parameters were measured previously using SEM [23]. For the analysis of the positive electrode diffusivity it is assumed S remains unchanged as NMC volume expansions is negligible, but for the negative electrode we account for the volume expansion of the graphite-SiO [23,50,51]. This involves applying a linear scaling factor across the diffusivity to capture the 4x volume expansion across the SOC range of the battery [23]. The expansion of silicon and graphite during battery operation and its effect on the construction and implementation of the Newman model has been outlined by Ai et al. [52] This code is available in PyBaMM to investigate volumetric expansion and electrodes with silicon-additives.

The three-electrode set-up probed a limited stoichiometric range for each electrode, which was near equivalent to that observed under operation in the cylindrical cell. The diffusion coefficients vary significantly with lithium concentration, distinct regions can be identified in these profiles and attributed to distinct thermodynamic phases [53]. For the positive electrode these phases relate to the different crystal structures of $\mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } M n _ { 0 . 2 } C o _ { 0 . 2 } O _ { 2 } }$ e. $g .$ hexagonal and monoclinic [47,54]. For the negative electrode active material, the lithium insertion stages of graphite are responsible for the changes in solid-phase diffusivity e.g. I to IV [53,55]. For the temperature range $5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to $4 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , the diffusivity of the positive electrode active material was approximately $1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } s ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { t o } 1 0 ^ { - 1 1 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } s ^ { - 1 }$ and for the negative electrode active material it was 10-14 cm2 s− 1 to 10-10 cm2 s− 1 , $1 0 ^ { - 1 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } s ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { t o } 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } s ^ { - 1 }$ see Figs. S4 and S5, respectively, for the raw data. paragraph_context: Eq. (10) was used to account for the dependency of solid-phase diffusivity on stoichiometry, this equation is illustrated in Fig. 6. The equation is a linear combination of Gaussian functions and captures the features of the profile accurately, meaning non-linear solid-phase diffusivity can be captured by the simulations (the fitting parameters can be found in Table S7): $$ \begin{array}{l} \log_ {1 0} D _ {s} (x) = a _ {0} \cdot x + b _ {0} + a _ {1} \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {(x - b _ {1}) ^ {2}}{c _ {1}}\right) + a _ {2} \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {(x - b _ {2}) ^ {2}}{c _ {2}}\right) \\ + a _ {3} \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {\left(x - b _ {3}\right) ^ {2}}{c _ {3}}\right) + a _ {4} \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {\left(x - b _ {4}\right) ^ {2}}{c _ {4}}\right). \tag {10} \\ \end{array} $$ These fits are later used in the model and shown in Figs. S4 and S5. Fig. 6 also describes the change in diffusivity across the measured stoichiometric range as a function of temperature, demonstrating the Arrhenius-type behaviour of this parameter. The average value of solidphase diffusivity of the ‘fitted’ curves for the negative electrode active material is lower than the experimental average for about a factor of three, because we are fitting to the $l o g _ { 1 0 } ( D )$ rather than D. The reason not to fit to D directly is because that would not capture the features in low diffusivity zones, plus adds the risk of obtaining negative values for diffusivity. Fitting to the $l o g _ { 1 0 } ( D )$ ensures diffusivity is always positive and captures the features at different orders of magnitude, at the expense of underestimating the average diffusivity (especially in the negative electrode). Therefore, a scaling factor of 3.03 for the negative electrode active material diffusivity was introduced in the diffusivity used in the final model so the fitted average diffusivity matched the experimental average diffusivity across all temperatures, as shown in Fig. 6 (bottom right).

paragraph_context: There are several sources of heat generation in batteries [37]. The irreversible and reversible heat components are considered important as the active materials’ dominating heat generation [69]. For high C-rates (most scenarios) more than half of the heat generation can be ascribed to irreversible heat, known as ohmic heat loss [70]. At low C-rates (1C or less) the reversible heat contribution from the material phase changes becomes more significant, this heat generation is due to the entropy changes that occur as a result of intercalation reactions, and this property depends on the internal temperature and OCV of the system. The entropy change can account for over half the total heat generated at the rates typically used in electric vehicles [71,72]. Parameterisations that outline activation energies do not characterise the reversible heat of the battery, this is important to predict temperature and the influenced electrochemical performance correctly [16,18].

paragraph_context: The change in entropy ΔS can be determined through the slope of the OCV with temperature:[73] $$ \Delta S = \frac {- \Delta G}{T} = n F \left(\frac {E}{T}\right). \tag {15} $$ The entropic term is measured using a potentiostatic method which involves measuring the dependency of OCV on temperature (Fig. 12) [74]. The temperature is changed three times at each lithium concentration. This provides four OCVs at the different temperatures; the entropic term can be calculated from the gradient of a line through the points. This process is repeated to map the stoichiometric range of the electrodes. It can take many hours to attain OCV at a particular SOC and temperature, therefore the thermal stability of the electrolyte needs to be considered when choosing the temperature regime. This is because at high temperatures due to electrochemical instability, particularly at the graphite interface, it is more difficult to attain OCV [75]. Choosing a lower temperature regime avoids instabilities, while allowing the thermodynamic behaviour to be measured.

paragraph_context: As a core component of transportation electrification, lithium-ion batteries need to address two critical challenges: achieving high energy density and enabling fast charging. However, changes in electrode thickness could result in a trade-off between these two characteristics. Herein, the impact of electrode thickness on the electrochemical performance, thermal behavior, as well as energy and power density of LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2(NCM)/ graphite batteries are investigated through mathematical modeling. Underutilization of active materials of the thick electrode is identified as the primary limitation on rate capability, which can be attributed to the slow solidstate diffusion and poor electrolyte transport within the electrode, especially the enlarged concentration gradients in the solid phase and the lithium depletion in the electrolyte phase during high-rate charging. Evolutions of local current density and heat generation rate along the electrode thickness are compared, identifying the underlying mechanism of inducing uneven reaction kinetics inside the battery. The trade-off between the energy and power density as a function of electrode thickness is investigated based on the limitations of charge transfer and mass transport. Furthermore, the rate-limiting factors under various application requirements are elucidated. This study will provide guidance for the electrode design of high-energy-density batteries with fast-charging capabilities.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries are currently the most competitive powertrain candidates for electric vehicles or hybrid electric vehicles, and the advancement of batteries in transportation relies on the ongoing pursuit of energy density and power density [1]. High-energy-density power batteries contribute to increasing driving range or reducing weight, while high-power density implies the convenience of fast charging and excellent acceleration performance. Various approaches can enhance the energy density of Li-ion batteries, including improvements in electrode active materials, electrode structure design, and development of battery architectures [2–5]. One effective method to improve the energy density at the cell level is to increase the electrode thickness, thereby reducing the proportion of electrochemically inactive materials [6]. However, increasing electrode thickness will exacerbate the diffusion limitations within the battery, thus hindering Li-ion mobility [7,8]. Therefore, achieving high energy/power density simultaneously is challenging, and it is significant to explore the trade-off between thick electrodes and fast charging capabilities [9].

paragraph_context: To accurately describe the electrochemical and thermal reactions occurring during the operation of Li-ion batteries, it is necessary to construct a model to capture the battery’s internal states. The pseudotwo-dimensional (P2D) model proposed by Doyle and Newman et al. provides a method for studying electrochemical reaction processes and optimizing battery design parameters [23]. The P2D electrochemical model description of Li-ion batteries is depicted in Fig. 1. Specifically, the model rests on the porous electrode and the concentrated solution theory, and it is applied to sandwich structures consisting of porous electrodes, separators, and current collectors. Based on the assumptions above, the P2D model needs to analyze electrochemical reactions from three principles: charge conservation, mass conservation, and electrochemical kinetics.

paragraph_context: In addition to the Li intercalation/deintercalation reaction at the solid/solution interface, lithium plating on the negative electrode surface should also be taken into account to accurately describe the reaction kinetics under fast charging conditions [24]. Essentially, lithium plating is triggered when the driving overpotentials become negative $\left( \eta _ { \mathrm { L i ^ { + } / L i } } < 0 \right)$ , and the rate of lithium plating also follows the Butler-Volmer equation [25]. On the other hand, the heat generated inside the battery can be categorized into reversible heat and irreversible heat. Reversible heat is generated by reversible chemical reactions, while irreversible heat originates from polarization heat or ohmic losses. In this study, the electrochemical model is coupled with the thermal model, where the heat generated by electrochemical reactions determines the cell temperature. Correspondingly, the temperature variation in the thermal model will affect the temperature-sensitive parameters in the electrochemical model. The governing equations and boundary conditions of the model are summarized in Table 1, and the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 is used to solve the equations.

paragraph_context: and electrode thickness. Typically, thin electrodes (<40 μm) attain low active material loading. Regardless of the charging rate, the limited active material reduces the number of lithium ions that can be intercalated into the active particles. Consequently, the specific capacity of thin electrodes is low and slightly decreases with increasing charging rates. Conversely, thick electrodes can accommodate more active materials. When charging at low rates (<1C), ions and electrons have sufficient time to transfer within the electrode, allowing for higher charge capacity despite slight diffusion limitations. Low-rate charging corresponds to a slower migration rate of lithium ions, and the charging capacity is primarily determined by the number of sites available for lithium intercalation. Therefore, thick electrodes deliver a higher capacity than thin electrodes during low-rate charging. Notably, the thick electrode experiences capacity reversal when charged at high rates, and the capacity loss is more significant with the rate. Compared to 1/2C charging, the capacities of electrodes with thickness of 20 μm, 40 μm, 60 μm, 80 μm, 100 μm and 120 μm at 9C charging are reduced by approximately 16.4 %, 30.4 %, 48 %, 76.7 %, 95 % and 97.5 %, respectively. This suggests that thick electrodes may experience significant charge transfer and diffusion resistance during high-rate charging, resulting in the underutilization of electrode active materials and diminished efficiency of electrochemical reactions. Although increasing electrode thickness can significantly improve capacity, it simultaneously limits the rate performance, which hinders the arbitrary combination of high storage capacity and fast charging capability.

paragraph_context: The energy and power density of Li-ion batteries are two important indicators for evaluating their performance, which can be used to measure the ability of the battery to store energy and to fast charge, respectively. Evaluating the impact of electrode thickness on rate performance is a prerequisite for optimizing batteries to achieve fast charging while maintaining high energy density.

paragraph_context: Essentially, rate-limiting steps of Li-ion batteries during the charging process are typically classified into two types: 1) Charge transfer, involving the desolvation of solvated $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions upon reaching the electrode/electrolyte interface and the naked Li+ diffuses through the interfacial film into the anode; 2) Mass transport, which includes the Liion transport through electrolyte-filled pores and the solid-state diffusion of Li-ions within active material particles. These electrochemical processes determine the charging performance of batteries, and the energy density is a function of electrode thickness and charging rate. Therefore, it is necessary to understand the differences in rate-limiting mechanisms corresponding to different electrode thicknesses.

paragraph_context: To accurately assess the evolution of battery performance, Eqs. (1) and (2) are used to calculate the gravimetric energy/power density of the battery, respectively. $$ E = \frac {1}{M} \int_ {0} ^ {t} I (t) V (t) d t = \frac {I (t)}{M} \int_ {0} ^ {t} V (t) d t \tag {1} $$ $$ P = \frac {1}{M t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} I (t) V (t) d t = \frac {I}{M t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} V (t) d t \tag {2} $$ Since only the thickness of the positive electrode is considered as a variable, the volume or density of other components remains constant. Therefore, the battery mass (M) can be converted based on the proportion of electrode thickness using the test battery as a reference. For electrodes with constant porosity and particle size, the mass loading of active material is proportional to the electrode thickness. Correspondingly, the energy density of thick electrodes increases by decreasing the fraction of inactive materials. Fig. 12 illustrates the evolution of the battery’s gravimetric energy density with electrode thickness and charging rate. On one hand, the overall energy density decreases with the charging rate. On the other hand, the energy density initially increases and then decreases as the thickness increases. It should be noted that when the electrode thickness exceeds a certain value, the battery’s energy density starts to decline. For 1/10C-9C charging, the electrode thicknesses approaching the maximum energy density $\left( E _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } \right)$ are successively 120 μm, 100 μm, 80 μm, 60 μm, 60 μm, 50 μm, 40 μm, and 30 μm, demonstrating the contradiction between rate performance and electrode thickness. Furthermore, the relationship between the corresponding $E _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ under different electrode thicknesses is fitted, revealing an approximate linear variation between the two, indicating that $E _ { \mathrm { m a x } } =$ $1 . 3 L _ { \mathrm { p o s } } $ 113. The thicker the electrode, the higher the $E _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ that can be obtained. It is noteworthy that this linear relationship is established under the premise of charging at different rates. For thin electrodes (20–40 μm), the overall energy density of the battery tends to increase with the charging rate, benefiting from excellent charge transfer kinetic. Due to the shorter interparticle diffusion pathway in thin electrodes, the reduction in resistance mitigates the charge transfer limitations during high-rate charging. However, in thick electrodes, the long $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion pathway in liquid-phase pores and solid-phase active materials leads to mass transport limitations dominating the overall reaction kinetics, which is particularly prominent at high rates. Therefore, thick electrodes are not conducive to fast ion transport. It can be argued that thin electrodes have limited energy density but are suitable for fast-charging requirements, while the advantages of thick electrodes with high energy are typically confined to low-power applications.

paragraph_context: To illustrate the impact of electrode thickness on attainable energy and power density, Ragone plots are depicted based on test results. Fig. 13(a) shows the relationship between gravimetric energy density and corresponding power density. The curves are primarily distributed in the upper-left and lower-right regions, corresponding to high energy density and high power density, respectively. In the upper-left region, increasing the electrode thickness can enhance the energy density, which will be beneficial for portable electronic devices for low-power applications. As the thickness increases from 20 μm to 120 μm, there is a corresponding rise in energy density from approximately 172 Wh/kg to 260 Wh/kg. On the contrary, thin electrodes are beneficial for highpower applications with fast charging. In the high-power range, power density decreases with increasing thickness. Meanwhile, energy density also decreases significantly. The longer migration paths for ions and electrons within the electrodes are the primary factors that limit the battery’s ability to achieve high power output in a short time. It should be noted that there is a trade-off between energy and power density, with energy density decreasing as power density increases and vice versa. There are also inflection points in the curve, signifying the onset of a decrease in energy density when initiating high-power applications, and this phenomenon is more pronounced in thick electrodes. Therefore, electrode thickness is considered to have dual effects on the energy/ power density of Li-ion batteries. While the majority of research aims to achieve high energy density, for electric vehicles requiring both high energy and short-term high power applications, optimizing electrode thickness is crucial for batteries to approach maximum power density while maintaining high energy density.

paragraph_context: The product of energy/power density is referred to as the "energypower density product (E × P)," representing the overall performance of the battery in storing or releasing electrical energy. A larger product implies that the battery possesses both higher energy storage capacity (high energy density) and excellent fast-charging performance (high power density). In electrode thickness optimization, the optimal combination of energy and density can be achieved by seeking the maximum energy-power density product. As shown in Fig. 13(b), the energy-power density product of batteries with different electrode thicknesses (20–120 μm) during charging at different rates (1/10C-9C) can also be divided into two regions dominated by charge transfer limitation and mass transfer limitation, respectively. At moderate rates (<3C), E × P increases with both the rate and thickness, benefiting from uniform electrode utilization. However, the extended transport pathways and increased resistance in thicker electrodes do not significantly impact the rate performance. At high rates, E × P exhibits significant differences with increasing thickness. The product for thin electrodes (20–50 μm) continues to increase with the charging rate, although the rate of increase has slowed down. This indicates that increasing the charging rate can further improve the energy storage capacity of thin electrodes, with charging performance dominated by charge transfer limitations. However, the $E \times P$ of the thick electrode (60–120 μm) gradually decreases during high-rate charging, attributed to the mass transfer limitation that dominates the charging process. Moreover, the increased internal resistance and exacerbated polarization effects limit the battery’s ability to store electrical energy. Hence, it can be considered that the energy storage capacity of the battery is strictly dependent on the electrode thickness and charging rate. Thicker electrodes are less conducive to fast charging, and specific charging conditions correspond to different ratelimiting factors. In this study, it is assumed that positive electrodes with a thickness of 40–50 μm can maximize the energy-power density product under various charging rates, thereby enabling the battery to maximize energy acquisition.

paragraph_context: With the growing demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries, layered lithium-rich cathode materials with high specific capacity and low cost have been widely regarded as one of the most attractive candidates for next-generation lithium-ion batteries. However, issues such as voltage decay, capacity loss and sluggish reaction kinetics have hindered their further commercialization for decades. Intensive investigations have been devoted to developing high-performance lithium-rich cathode materials, highlighting the importance of improvement strategies as a potential approach. Herein, we summarize various strategies for improving performances of layered lithium-rich cathode materials for next-generation high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries. These include surface engineering, elemental doping, composition optimization, structure engineering and electrolyte additives, with emphasis on the effect and functional mechanism of corresponding techniques. In the subsequent section, we illustrate opportunities and challenges for designing high-performance lithium-rich cathode materials and bridging the gap between the laboratory and practical applications.

paragraph_context: With the rapid development of our modern society, the massive consumption of fossil fuels causes severe climate change and global warming [1,2]. Electrification of road transport can effectively alleviate carbon dioxide emissions. Electric vehicles (EVs) using lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) as power sources are being produced with rapidly increased scale annually [3-5]. A typical LIB comprises a cathode, an anode, a separator and the corresponding electrolyte. Such a kind of “rock chair” battery enables the reversible insertion and extraction of lithium ions (Li+) in electrode materials during the operation of LIBs [4,6]. Although the worldwide commercial market for LIBs continues to proliferate, the challenge is the development of LIBs with a significantly extended life span and much-increased energy density. The Li+ storage capability and operation voltage of electrode materials determine the energy density of LIBs, which makes electrode materials playing crucial roles in the entire battery system [7-9]. In 1980, Goodenough and co-workers [10] accurately predicted the high potential of transition metal oxides and reported layered $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ as a suitable cathode material for LIBs. After SONY Corp. commercialized LIBs with $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ as cathode materials and graphite as anode materials in 1991, research interests in discovering new electrode materials with higher energy densities have been accelerated. After almost 30 years of development, graphite anode materials still dominate the market today. Whereas, a series of cathode materials, including $\mathrm { L i M n } _ { 2 } { \sf O } _ { 4 }$ [11], LiFePO4 [12] and $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ [13], were intensively investigated and applied in large-scale LIBs to replace $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ [14]. However, the development of the above-mentioned cathode materials has encountered a bottleneck for electric vehicles because of the low specific capacity (< 250 mAh $g ^ { - 1 } )$ ) and energy density, which cannot meet the requirement of the automotive market to achieve longdistance drive (> 300 miles) and low cost [15,16].

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Driven by the request for high-energy-density LIBs, researchers are quickly moving forward to strive for next-generation cathode materials with high specific capacities. To this end, layered lithium-rich cathode materials (LRCMs) have garnered much attention owing to their low cost, high specific capacity $( > 3 0 0 \ \mathrm { m A h } \ \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and energy density (> 1000 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ [8,17-20]. Nevertheless, efforts of pursuing ideal cathode materials have always been a game of compromise, which comes at the expense of other merits. In addition to the high specific capacity, LR-CMs still face severe challenges. These include: (i) A low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE). Most of LRCMs are suffering from low ICE in the first charge/discharge process. (ii) Serious voltage decay. LRCMs show a continuous decrease in discharge voltage upon cycling, leading to the loss of energy density. (iii) Significant capacity loss. The severe capacity degradation of LRCMs is another technical challenge to achieve a long service life. (iv) Poor rate capability. The sluggish reaction kinetics and poor electronic conductivity of LRCMs induce poor rate performance. (v) Transitional metals (TMs) dissolution. LRCMs undergo severe capacity degradation due to the lattice distortion and dissolution of $\mathrm { M n ^ { 2 + } }$ caused by the Jahn–Teller effect.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Until now, it remains a tough challenge to overcome the above technical hurdles and improve the performance of layered LRCMs as well [19,21-23]. In light of this, strategies for the improvement of LR-CMs have been proposed and intensively investigated. Many pioneering strategies based on other Li+ insertion-type cathode materials have been applied to develop LRCMs [24-29]. In the past decade, various strategies have been explored for improving the electrochemical performance of LRCMs. Their significance is highlighted by the increasing number of publications every year (Fig. 1a and b). As the fundamental knowledge and reaction mechanisms of these improvement strategies are still not entirely understood, revesting the strategies for the design of high-performance LRCMs should be given the priority and attention towards broad prospective applications [30,31]. Herein, in this review, we begin with a brief description of distinct electrochemical features of layered LRCMs. Then, the improvement strategies aiming to handle the technical challenges of layered LRCMs are summarized and discussed in detail. Finally, we propose perspectives and outlooks for the future commercialization of layered LRCMs in high-energy-density LIBs.
