paragraph_context: Since the advent of LRCMs, researchers have strived to understand their fundamental reaction mechanisms and figured out strategies on the material structure design. In this section, we summarize representative electrochemical characteristics of LRCMs. These “fingerprints” are served as powerful indicators for LRCMs, and many theoretical knowledge and frameworks established early are based upon these factors.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: One of the fingerprint-like features of LRCMs is a long and irreversible voltage plateau at approximately 4.5 V during the first charge process. Specifically, the initialcharge capacity is contributed by the oxidation of TM species, such as Ni and $\mathbf { C o } ,$ along with the continuous extraction of $\operatorname { L i } ^ { + } \mathrm { a t }$ low charge voltage (< 4.5 V). However, this situation may be different once these cations have reached their highest oxidation state. In this regard, additional $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ extracted from LRCMs further activates the oxygen-based anionic redox $( 0 ^ { 2 - } { } 0 _ { 2 } )$ on the surface to compensate for the substantial charge capacity during the first voltage plateau, which is ended with the form of the $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ evolution at the high working voltage (> 4.5 V). The release of portion of surface oxygen from LRCMs is irreversible and cannot be restored in the subsequent discharge process, which is the main reason for low ICE [32- 35]. Moreover, this gaseous oxygen is very unstable and trivially easy to escape into the electrolyte. Therefore, the decomposition of carbonate electrolyte is accelerated when encountering trapped or freed oxygen species, as evidenced by the generation of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ collected from differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) analysis [36-38]. Some researchers also pointed out that $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ could be generated from the decomposition of residual $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 }$ [39,40]. The cumulative effect of gas evolution would cause safety hazards like gas bubbling and expansion of pouch cells. Meanwhile, oxygen loss instigates the migration of TM species to lithium sites, accelerating the layered-to-spinel transformation and, consequently, the notorious voltage decay [33,35,41].

paragraph_context: The origin of the very high specific capacity of LRCMs is still a contentious question and needs further experimental evidence. Indeed, such an anomalous specific capacity cannot be interpreted by the traditional reaction mechanism. For instance, TM cation is the main redox center in traditional $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ insertion-type cathode materials. However, for LRCMs, only half of the capacity can be obtained if considering a special case that all TM cations are fully oxidized to their highest oxidation states. Recently, many research groups confirmed the presence of peroxo-like ${ \mathrm { O } } ^ { \mathrm { n - } }$ and its contribution to the overall capacity [23,42-46]. Hence, it becomes clear that the reversible anionic redox activity is responsible for the extra capacity at high charge voltage (> 4.5 V). Generally, the reversibility relies on the correlation between the Coulomb interaction term U and the chargetransfer term Δ [47]. As shown in Fig. 2a, if $U { < } { < } \Delta$ , the whole system is highly ionic and undergoes the traditional cationic redox scenario. However, if $U { > } > \Delta ,$ this situation gives rise to the formation of highly active ${ \mathrm { O } } ^ { \mathrm { n - } }$ species and thereby leads to the irreversible anionic redox. In the intermediate range of $\mathrm { U } / 2 \approx \Delta ,$ , the system has both the TM-O∗ d-band and the O 2p available in theFermi level and undergoes the reversible anionic redox reaction.

paragraph_context: Moreover, the overlap between p orbitals (oxygen) and d orbitals (transition metal) in the band structure of LRCMs results in TM–O bonding and TM–O∗ antibonding bands, manifesting both metal and ligand characteristics [23]. The electronic configuration of $\scriptstyle \cdot _ { 0 ^ { 2 ^ { - } } }$ contains one 2 s (inactive) and three 2p (active) doublets. Normally, all three 2p orbitals in the classic layered cathode materialsare participating in TM-O band formation. While in the layered lithium-rich structure with a high O/TM proportion, one of the O 2p orbitals (towards Li in the TM layer) that is weakly bonded and behaves as peroxo-like ${ \cal O } ^ { \mathrm { n - } }$ (O non-bonding state, n<2), is situated above the TM-O bonding band. Such an oxygen-based anion is able to reversibly engage in redox reactions and contributes to more than half of the total capacity. Through using $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { R u } _ { 1 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { y } } \mathrm { S n } _ { \mathrm { y } } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { I r } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } .$ , Tarascon’s group confirmed the presence of oxygen-based anionic redox reactions within LRCMs [42,48]. Eum et al. [49] found that the anionic redox occurs reversibly at the high working voltage and can be well persevered in O2-type LRCMs. Hong et al. [50] suggested that the oxygen redox reaction is more likely to be stabilized in local coordination environments generated by local structural defects. House et al. [51] also indicated that the molecular $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ trapped in the bulk lattice and lost from the surface region is responsible for the reversible anionic redox. Although the appearance and vanishment of oxidized ${ \mathrm { O } } ^ { \mathrm { n - } }$ species increase the specific capacity of LRCMs, the sluggish anionic redox is kinetically slower than the cationic one, leading to poor rate capability. Meanwhile, the structural collapse and voltage hysteresis are highly related to the anionic reaction, which requires fundamental insights into the reaction mechanism.

paragraph_context: In the first activation process, many vacancies are generated as a result of the irreversible oxygen release. Meanwhile, the presence of a large amount of $\mathrm { M n ^ { 3 + } }$ induces the Jahn–Teller distortion, which causes the irreversible dissolution of manganese species. Under such a circumstance, the stability of TM ions is reduced and, therefore, further triggers the migration of TM ions to the octahedral sites left in Li layers throughthe adjacenttetrahedral sites [19,52,53]. Such cation reorganization relating to TM migration takes place at the surface and then propagates to the center of the particles of LRCMs, in the form of the irreversible layered-to-spinel transformation, resulting in severe voltage decay and capacity loss. When this occurs, some cationic species like Ni and Co preferentially migrate at selective surface regions, causing the obvious chemical gradient (Fig. 2b and c) [54]. This elemental densification process is always rich in the surface but poor in the bulk region, and forms a high diffusion barrier, which significantly slows down the diffusion and transport rate of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ [55,56]. Furthermore, elemental segregation at the atomic level weakens the interaction of different TM ions, leading to continuous reduction of cationic species. As the TM migration and reduction proceed, a surface reconstruction layer (SRL), which is recognized as a kinetic barrier for Li+, is formed and causes the polarization and voltage decay of LRCMs [57,58]. A recent study also indicates that the gradual reduction of TM species shifts the Ni/O to Mn/Co redox couples during cycling, which is responsible for irreversible voltage decay [59].

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: The nucleation and propagation of structural defects upon cycling is also an important characteristic of LRCMs. Although the presence of some structural defects is likely to activate the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ phase and delivers a high discharge capacity, it simultaneously facilitates the irreversible structural transformation from the layered to the spinel phase [60]. Furthermore, these structural defects could accelerate the noncrystallization process with the emerge of disorder in the crystal periodicity and quickly deteriorate the electrochemical performance of LRCMs. For example, the occurrence of microstrain enables the propagation of microcracks and distortions after the electrode is initially charged to a relatively high voltage (> 4.5 V), and hence shows an adverse impact on the structural stability of LRCMs [61,62]. Meanwhile, the generation and propagation of dislocation in LRCMs are also revealed through the in situ Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI) technique, as illustrated in Fig. 2d [63]. Obvious dislocations were generated in the bulk material after charging to 4.3 V. Furthermore, the dislocation density increases with the increase of the working voltage. The formation of the dislocation network not only leads to voltage decay but also reduces the structural stability of LRCMs.

paragraph_context: Despite many compelling features, currently, LRCMs are far behind the requirement for next-generation LIBs with practical high-specificcapacity and long-cycle-life. The evolution of oxygen gas naturally leads to volume expansion when fabricating prototype lithium-ion pouch cells [43,59]. Furthermore, the side reaction is another issue considering the complex redox reaction of LRCMs. Additionally, voltage decay is one of the toughest challenges. The energy density of LRCMs could decrease from 1000 to 500 W h $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 100 cycles due to the uncontrollable voltage decay, which could not be fully explained by capacity fade alone [21,64,65]. Moreover, the poor-rate performance and deteriorated cycling stability make LRCMs more difficult for commercial production. Although the degradation of LRCMs is unpredictable, efforts to overcome obstacles for practical applications have never been stopped for years. Inspired by previous research achievements in intercalation-type cathode materials for LIBs, nowadays, we can tackle these challenges by employing various improvement strategies for LRCMs. These approaches include composition optimization, structure engineering, and electrolyte additives, etc. (Fig. 3).

paragraph_context: Surface engineering involves surface coating or chemical and physical surface treatment on LRCMs. The surface coating strategy has been regarded as one of the most promising and reliable methods to improve electrochemical performances of LIB cathode materials [66]. Since Cho and co-workers [24] first illustrated the effect of the $\mathrm { z r O } _ { 2 }$ coating layer on $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ cathode materials, many investigations have been conducted in this area [67,68]. An ideal coating material should possess high ionic conductivity while maintain electrochemical inactivity during cycling. For LRCMs, introducing a surface coating layer on the cathode material is beneficial to suppress the lattice-constant change and undesired oxygen loss during cycling, thereby restricting the irreversible layered to spinel-like phase transformation and enhancing the structural stability as well. Moreover, a surface coating layer prevents the accumulation of by-products on the cathode surface that leads to rapid capacity degradation [19]. Recent reports demonstrated that the surface coating strategy is effective to improve the electrochemical property of LR-CMs as summarized in Table 1. Zheng et al. [69] reported the use of the ${ \mathrm { A l F } } _ { 3 }$ material as a coating layer on LRCMs. The ${ \mathrm { A l F } } _ { 3 }$ -coated LRCM shows negligible capacity loss after 100 cycles. Meanwhile, voltage decay and rapid capacity degradation have been significantly mitigated after cycling. The ${ \mathrm { A l F } } _ { 3 }$ protective layer could minimize the occurrence of adverse side reactions between the electrolyte and electrode, restricting oxidation of the electrolyte and avoiding the generation of a thick cathode electrolyte interface (CEI). This outer shield layer can protect the cathode material against further corrosion and etching by corrosive species and reduce the generation of the oxygen-deficient surface. Moreover, the irreversible phase transformation has been suppressed to a certain extent, which maintains the structural integrity (Fig. 4a). However, the layered to spinel-like structure evolution cannot be eliminated as indicated by the drop of the average operating voltage. The authors employed electron energy-loss spectroscopy line scan (EELS) to further demonstrated that the average Mn valence in the $\mathrm { A l F } _ { 3 }$ -coated cathode material is higher than that in the pristine one after cycling, which could alleviate the disproportionation of $\mathrm { M n ^ { 3 + } }$ and increase the structural durability.

paragraph_context: Although the surface coating strategy has been proven to effectively improve the electrochemical property of LRCMs, there are still many technical challenges to obtain high-quality coating layers on LR-CMs. Many coating techniques such as solid-state routes, wet-chemistry routes, and nanoengineering routes have been introduced in preparation of high-performance LRCMs, as shown in Table $ { 2 } [ 7 1 , 7 2 , 7 6 - 7 9 ]$ ]. For example, solid-state coating technology is productive and efficient for large-scale applications. However, the uniformity of the coating layer’s thickness is poor. Moreover, the wet-chemistry coating strategy is often limited by its multi-step reactions and may lead to residual water molecules remained during the preparation procedure Although nanoengineering routes like chemical vapor deposition (CVD), molecular layer deposition (MLD) and atomic layer deposition (ALD) achieve promising results such as the uniform coating layer and adjustable coating thickness, these cutting-edge techniques are often expensive and would be not suitable for large-scale production.

paragraph_context: In addition to surface coating, surface treatment is also an effective approach to improve electrochemical performances of LRCMs [94-96]. This strategy is intended to make cathode materials more resistant to chemical corrosion and improves structural stability. $\mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } S _ { 2 } O _ { 8 }$ aqueous solution has been identified as an effective surfactant for the surface treatment of LRCMs [97]. After treated by 40 wt.% $\mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } S _ { 2 } O _ { 8 }$ solution, the modified cathode material shows a high initial discharge capacity (285 mAh ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.1 C) and enhanced ICE (93.2%). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results indicate that the lattice oxygen near the surface of particles is oxidized to form ${ 0 _ { 2 } } ^ { 2 - }$ − species with the extraction of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ from the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M O } _ { 3 }$ region, rather than being oxidized to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ at the pristine particle surface. In most cases, the release of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ causes the formation of vacancies and triggers the structural evolution from layered to defect-spinel phase on the surface. Therefore, this surface modification strategy is beneficial to increase the rate performance and cycling stability of LRCMs. Qiu et al. [98] reported the gas-solid interface reaction in enhancing the electrochemical property of LRCMs. They achieved the control of the cumulative oxygen activity and the interface reaction by creating an appropriate number of oxygen vacancies. Fig. 5a and b show thereaction mechanism of the pristine and activated LRCMs before and after the first full charge process. Before cycling, the pre-activated cathode material contains numerous oxygen vacancies, which can alleviate the partial pressure of oxygen release and prevent the oxygen evolution at the high working voltage $( > 4 . 5 \ : \mathrm { V } )$ . Subsequently, owing to reduced adverse reactions occurring at the interface, a thinner CEI layer is generated on the surface of the cathode material and, therefore, reducing the electrochemical resistance upon cycling. Furthermore, the increased number of oxygen vacancies enables intensive reversible oxygen-based anionic redox reactions, which ensures high $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusivity within the bulk material, together with the minimal structural change. The modi- fied LRCM delivers a high specific capacity of 301 mAh ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.05 C without obvious capacity degradation after 100 cycles.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In summary, surface engineering provides an effective and practical approach to prevent cathode materials from chemical etching caused by harmful intermediates or by-products, and thus enhances the structural stability of LRCMs. Meanwhile, the irreversible structure evolution has also been suppressed via surface modification. However, there are still some drawbacks that need to be solved. The electrically insulating nature of many coating materials brings an inactive component into the cathode material and thus lowers the energy density of LRCMs. Furthermore, the currently available surface coating techniques are unable to achieve pure and homogeneous coating layers at a low cost. More importantly, surface engineering merely postpones the progress ofcathode material degradation. As cycling proceeds, the mechanical stress and irreversible structural transformation continue to build up inside the particles and eventually degrade the electrochemical performance of LRCMs. Therefore, advanced surface modification techniques need to be combined with other strategies to preserve structure stability under long-term operation.

paragraph_context: Heterogeneous ions doping in the crystal structure of cathode materials is a common approach to improve the Li+ diffusion kinetics and structural stability of the bulk phase. With the introduction of stabilizing dopants, the modified local environment can tolerate cationic disorder and structural change to a certain extent. Meanwhile, the doping ions can expand the interplanar spacing of LRCM’s lattice without damaging their original layered structure, thereby significantly enhancing the rate performance and reinforcing the structural integrity [103].

paragraph_context: Cation-doping has been widely employed to improve the electrochemical property of LRCMs. Many metal cations such as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } [ 1 0 4 ]$ , K+[105], Mg2+ [106], Al3+ [107] and $\mathrm { C r ^ { 3 + } }$ [108] have been employed in term of this strategy (Table 3). Wang et al. [103] introduced a facile Sn-doping approach in the $\mathrm { L i _ { 2 } M n O _ { 3 } \bullet L i M n _ { 0 . 5 } N i _ { 0 . 5 } O _ { 2 } }$ cathode material. XRD results confirm that the Sn-doped structure has a relatively larger interplanar spacing of (003) planes compared with the pristine material. The expanded (003) spacing unlocks the lithium diffusion path among different lithium layers and dramatically reduces the energy barrier for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion and transport. Consequently, the Sndoped cathode material delivers a much better rate performance and faster Li+ diffusivity than the pristine material. paragraph_context: According to the previous discussion on the elemental segregation section, a selective surface area with preferential segregation of cations has been discovered in LRCMs, which serves as a dynamic barrier for Li+ diffusion. The synthesis process shows a great influence on the distribution of TM ions. The impact of the synthesis route on $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 . 2 } \mathrm { N i } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 6 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ was investigated by Zheng and co-workers [58]. They found that the electrochemical performances of LRCMs are affected by synthesis routes, including co-precipitation (CP), hydrothermal assisted (HA) and so-gel (SG) methods. X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (XEDS) mappings in Fig. 8a illustrate that the cathode material synthesized via a HA method shows an improved homogeneous distribution of Ni within the material, thereby increasing Ni-Mn interaction and improving the structural stability. Scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) characterization reveals that the HA method facilitates to generate a solid solution dominated by the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ type monoclinic C2/m phase (Fig. 8b). This feature is different from other LRCMs that consist of both trigonal $\mathrm { L i M O } _ { 2 } \ \mathrm { R } { - } 3$ m and monoclinic $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ C2/m components. Meanwhile, it plays a positive role in against oxygen loss and unexpected side reactions during cycling. Consequently, the HA cathode material exhibits the best rate performance (119 mAh ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 5 C) and the lowest average voltage decay (0.15 V after 200 cycles) among three samples. In addition, the pH condition during the synthesis process has a significant influence on the electrochemical performance of LRCMs [128]. The relatively low pH value (< 7.5) normally results in high residual Mn and Ni concentrations in precursors, which could lead to undesired chemical stoichiometry and distribution. However, when pH reaches a comparatively high value (> 8.5), it gives rise to a continuous increase of theresidual Ni concentration and formation of nickel hydroxide, which is detrimental to the quality of LRCMs. A moderate pH range between 7.5 and 8.5 effectively minimizes the residual TM concentration in solution and provides the optimized condition tosynthesize LRCMs, thereby improving the electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: Furthermore, the synthesis process also determines the primary particle size of LRCMs. It is well known that the cathode material with smaller particle size has higher ionic conductivity owing to its shorter $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion pathway in particles. Hence, optimizing the synthesis process is beneficial to control the primary particle size and, therefore, improve the electrochemical performance of LRCMs. Liu et al.[129] confirmed the primary particle size of LRCMs is correlated with the calcination temperature. The particle size of materials changes to 80 nm, 200 nm, and 500 nm at the elevated temperature (800 ${ } ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } ,$ 900 °C and 1000 °C). The sample with the smallest particle size shows the highest discharge capacity (237 mAh ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.1 C) and ICE (75.1%), which is ascribed to the small dynamic barrier for Li+ intercalation owing to the size effect. Apart from the sintering temperature, other conditions such as the preparation method [130] and the lithiation process [131] also remarkably influence the primary particle size of LRCMs.

paragraph_context: Substitution with high-valent cation in the cathode material is another useful way to improve the electrochemical performance of LR-CMs. A key step of this substitution strategy is to reduce the Mn valence $\scriptstyle ( \mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 4 + } )$ to a lower valence state by introducing high oxidation state cation species $\mathrm { ( N b ^ { 5 + } }$ and $\mathrm { T i } ^ { 4 + } )$ in the lithium-rich manganesebased cathode material [132]. Through this method, oxygen can only participate in the redox reaction when charging to above 4.7 V, as indicated by a distinguishable voltage plateau in the galvanostatic chargedischarge profile. By controlling the charge voltage to 5 V, the revisable capacity (>300 mAh ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ is higher than the theoretical capacity of the cationic $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 4 + }$ double redox reaction (270 mAh ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ . The involvement of the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 4 + }$ reaction minimizes the sluggish anionic redox activity and enables rapid Li+ diffusion. Meanwhile, reducing the contribution from the excessive oxygen-based anionic redox upon the charge-discharge process also considerably enhances the structural stability and rate capability. Liu and co-authors reported a new type of $\mathrm { T i } ^ { 4 + }$ -substituted LRCM, $\mathrm { L i _ { 1 . 2 } T i _ { 0 . 2 6 } N i _ { 0 . 1 8 } M n _ { 0 . 1 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 8 } O _ { 2 } }$ , where Ti ions present in both Li and TM layers [133]. As we can see from $\mathrm { F i g . ~ } 8 \mathrm { c } ,$ a native Li–Ti cation mixing structure with strong Ti-O bonding restricts migration of TM ions and, therefore, inhibits the irreversible structural transformation from layered to spinel. Moreover, both of $\mathrm { M n ^ { 4 + } }$ and $\mathrm { T i } ^ { 4 + }$ are electrochemically inert and keep stable during charging and discharging, which contributes to enhanced structural stability. The voltage decay of the $\mathrm { T i } ^ { 4 + }$ -substituted LRCM is only 90 mV after 100 cycles, while the capacity loss is also inhibited to a large extent (3% after 182 cycles). Additionally, the presence of Li–Ti cation mixing also lowers oxidation potential and thereby ensures the reversibility of the oxygenbased redox activity.

paragraph_context: Although the oxygen-based anionic redox activity gives rise to a high specific capacity of LRCMs, it also results in significant voltage decay and sluggish reaction kinetic. Replacing oxygen with more electronegative fluorine in LRCMs holds great promise because both the working voltage and cycling stability are enhanced via substituting ${ 0 ^ { 2 - } }$ for $\mathrm { F ^ { - } } .$ . House et al. [135] demonstrated the partial substitution of ${ 0 ^ { 2 - } }$ with F− in $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 . 9 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 9 5 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 . 0 5 } \mathrm { F } _ { 0 . 9 5 }$ . The F−-substituted cathode material exhibits a high discharge capacity of 283 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - \mathrm { i } }$ 1derived from both the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 3 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 4 + }$ and anionic redox reactions. paragraph_context: Another approach is to substitute less electronegative sulfur for oxygen, which can initiate the reversible anionic redox reaction. Saha et al. paragraph_context: A deep delithiation state always comes along with irreversible loss of oxygen species within LRCMs. Therefore, the lithium content also influences electrochemical performances of LRCMs. Recently, lithiumdeficient layered LRCMs have shown excellent electrochemical properties [136]. paragraph_context: The formation of a stable and conductive passivation layer on the surface of cathode materials through adding additives into the electrolyte has been proved to be a promising strategy to resolve problems such as voltage decay and structural instability. Indeed, the high cut-off voltage (> 4.6 V) usually causes drastic decomposition of carbonate-based electrolytes, which deteriorates the electrochemical performance of LR-CMs. A stable passivation layer can prevent direct contact between electrode materials and electrolytes, which efficiently inhibits the decomposition of electrolyte at the high working voltage and thus ensures struc- tural integrity. Therefore, using electrolyte additives is expected to enable carbonate-based electrolytes thermodynamically stable under the high voltage operating condition. Based on this mechanism, Abouimrane et al. [140] studied the role of 3-hexylthiophene (3HT) as an additive in the electrolyte of 1.2 M $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ in ethylene carbonate/ethyl methylcarbonate (EC/EMC = 3/7). The cell with 5 wt% 3HT in the electrolyte exhibits distinguishable redox peaks in the CV measurement, which is ascribed to the generation of poly (3HT) on the surface of the LRCM. Furthermore, the lithium-ion cell with 0.1 wt% 3HT in the electrolyte shows the best cyclability and the highest CE among other cells with different 3HT contents in electrolytes at both room temperature and 55 $^ \circ \mathrm { C } .$ . Adding 3HT in the electrolyte reduces the interfacial resistance and assists the formation of a protective layer against corrosive acid species such as HF and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 }$ .

paragraph_context: Furthermore, selected electrolyte additives can trap active oxygen species and minimize the negative impact of oxygen loss from the crystal lattice. Zheng et al. [143] introduced tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane $( ( \mathsf { C } _ { 6 } \mathsf { F } _ { 5 } ) _ { 3 } \mathsf { B } _ { : }$ , TPFPB) as an electrolyte additive for the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 . 2 } \mathrm { N i } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 6 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ cathode material. The highly active oxygen species $( { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } { } ^ { - } / { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } { } ^ { 2 - } )$ released from the $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ component are detrimental to the stability of the crystal structure and induce the decomposition of the electrolyte. Under such a circumstance, TPFPB is expected to capture these oxygen species and avoids their further reaction with the electrolyte (Fig. 11c). In addition, other parasitic products are also soluble in TPFPB. Therefore, the interfacial stability is enhanced. Benefit from these advantages, carbonatebased electrolytes with 0.2 M TPFPB can significantly contribute to the improvement of the discharge capacity and cycling stability of LRCMs (Fig. 11d).

paragraph_context: Apart from the afore-mentioned improvement strategies, there are still other approaches to overcome the current and forthcoming challenges of LRCMs. Binders play important roles in determining the overall electrochemical performance of LRCMs in LIBs. Yang et al. [156] applied polyacrylic acid (PAA) as a binder for LRCMs. Unlike the commonly used polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) binder, PAA can form a tight and uniform protection film based on its carboxyl groups and, therefore, prevent the cathode material from being attacked by corrosive by-products. Meanwhile, it also introduces $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ into the crystal lattice via $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / L i ^ { + } }$ exchange to suppress TM ions migration. Benefiting from this surface/interface modification method, the dissolution of TM species, especially for Ni, has been greatly restricted compared with the traditional PVDF binder (1.65% for PAA and 5.93% for PVDF, respectively). Moreover, the presence of carboxylate groups in PAA inclines to bond with both cathode materials and current collectors, thereby enhancing the structural stability and exhibiting a good capacity retention rate of 88% over 500 cycles. Liu et al.[157] prepared a binder-free heterostructured spinel/layered LRCM through the electrospinning technique. The obtained one-dimensional (1D) nanofibers consist of many uniform LRCM nanoparticles, which ensures high $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion and good structural stability. The as-synthesized cathode material was directly used as an electrode for LIBs without any additives, showing very high ICE (≈100%), excellent rate performance (150 mAh ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 5 C), and outstanding cycling stability (> 80% after 70 cycles). Moreover, in situ XRD and Raman investigations demonstrate that the introduction of the spinel phase in the primary layered structure can effectively utilize oxygen vacancies without causing obvious structure evolution. Meanwhile, the spinel structure on the surface promotes the diffusion and transport of Li+. The absence of conductive agents and binders also lowers the charge transfer resistance and reduces the weight of electrodes.

paragraph_context: Annealing is also an effective and facile method to overcome disadvantages such as voltage decay and structural defects for LRCMs. Singer and co-workers [63] demonstrated voltage decay that occurs in LRCMs could be recovered by high-temperature calcination. The superstructure in LRCMs gradually disappears upon cycling, further triggering the phase transformation and the severe voltage decay. Nonetheless, the high-temperature heat treatment allows for the recovery of the superstructure and the oxygenstacking sequence, which facilitates to restore the voltage decay. Electrochemical pre-cycling treatment is also a promising method to improve the electrochemical performance of LRCMs [158]. Generally, LRCMs experience significant capacity loss when cycling at high voltage (> 4.6 V). However, this problem can be greatly mitigated if the cell is pre-cycled at the relatively low voltage $( 4 \sim 4 . 5 \ : \mathrm { V } )$ . Moreover, such effects could be further improved if the cell is treated with a stepwise pre-cycling strategy, i.e., cycles at various potential windows for several times.

paragraph_context: The pursuit of high-energy-density LIBs stimulates the development of next-generation cathode materials with superior specific capacity and high working voltage. Meanwhile, the ever-increasing demand for gridscale batteries also highlights the safety and cost issues for mass production. In recent years, LRCMs show attractive features, including their outstanding specific capacity $( > 3 0 0 \ \mathrm { m A h \ g ^ { - 1 } ) }$ , high energy density (> 1000 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and low cost, which enable them as promising candidates for next-generation LIBs. However, the complexity of crystal structures and reaction mechanisms of LRCMs leads to many severe unresolved problems and hinders their practical applications.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the aid of cutting-edge technologies, recent studies on reaction mechanisms have achieved significant progress [159]. An ideal LRCM must have high specific capacity, good electronic and ionic conductivity, excellent electrochemical stability, small interfacial resistance and minimal side reactions. To meet these standards and address the existing gaps in practical applications, many approaches have been proposed and investigated during the development of LRCMs. Surface engineering has been extensively studied as one of the most effective methods to cope with these drawbacks. The effect of surface engineering has been proven by restricting the irreversible structure evolution and oxygen loss during the charge/discharge process. Moreover, elemental doping is also found to be useful when facing the situation of cationic disorder and structural change. Heterogeneous ions with large radius can expand the interplanar spacing of LRCMs without destroying the primary layered structure, which could endow the cathode material to tolerate long-term cycling. Compositional optimization is an effective method to improve the electrochemical performance of LRCMs. These include synthesis strategy, cationic/anionic substitution and lithium content adjustment. Structure engineering,such as the employment of different structural compositions, is expected to optimize the material component and govern redox kinetics of LRCMs. Furthermore, electrolyte additives play critical roles in determining the overall electrochemical performance of LRCMs. The addition of electrolyte additives facilitates the formation of a stable passivation layer on the surface of cathode materials, which can significantly suppress voltage decay and structural instability.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: From a commercial point of view, surface modification and elemental doping strategies have unparalleled advantages owing to the simple and low-cost process. Although these strategies may be suitable for large-scale production, their negative aspects are equally notable. For example, both of these two techniques only decelerateperformance degradation. As the cycling goes $_ { \mathrm { o n , } }$ the irreversible structural transformation and microstructural defects still exist and eventually worsen the electrochemical performance of LRCMs. Structural and compositional optimization seems to be more promising to avoid structural transformation. However, these strategies are quite time-consuming, and the result is hard to predict. Electrolyte additives and binders are effective in some conditions, but these approaches are suffering from the high cost, toxicity, and uncertainty to other battery components.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: As for the research on improvement strategies of LRCMs, an ideal modification method should not only minimize the irreversible structure evolution but also govern the sluggish and uncontrollable anionic redox activity. Therefore, the exploration of improvement strategies must fulfill these requirements: (1) Suppressing the irreversible anionic redox to stabilize the interface between the electrode and electrolyte, preventing parasitic reactions and decomposition of the electrolyte. Oxygen loss triggered by the irreversible anionic activity is a leading reason for the reduced interfacial stability and should be avoided, especially at the high working voltage. This is the basic requirement for safe and longterm cycling. (2) Enhancing the electronic and ionic conductivity while maintaining the electrochemical stability of LRCMs. The poor rate performance and sluggish diffusion kinetics, which is the main concern for practical applications, are attributed to the low electronic and ionic conductivity of LRCMs. (3) Optimizing the proportion of cationic/anionic redox reactions and thereby attaining the maximal capacity contribution. TM-based cationic redox reactions lead to the unsatisfactory specific capacity and energy density, while high-yielding anionic redox activities usually result in sluggish reaction kinetics and structural degradation during cycling. Therefore, how to balance the contribution from both cationic and anionic aspects is an essential prerequisite for high performance and long cycle life LRCMs. (4) Maintaining the crystal structural integrity of LRCMs without sacrificing their original advantages. The introduction of foreign components (surface coating and elemental doping, for example) should not break the consistency of the primary layer structure and keep the inherent advantages such as high specific capacity and operating voltage. This goal will not be achieved through improving electrode materials alone. Other factors, such as the electrode manufacturing process and the battery assembly process, also ultimately determine electrochemical performances of LRCMs [19].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: For practical applications of LRCMs, many aspects need to be considered and further developed, including operating conditions such as temperatures, pressure and humidity. Meanwhile, the functional mechanisms of many improvement strategies are still unclear and need further discussion [21,25,160]. It should be noted that the tap density of LR-CMs $( 1 . 5 { - } 1 . 8 ~ \mathrm { g } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )$ is still lower than commercial LiNi $\mathrm { _ { \it { x } } C o _ { \it { y } } M n _ { \it { z } } O _ { 2 } \left( 2 - \right. }$ $2 . 5 \ \mathrm { g \ c m ^ { 3 } , N C M , } \ x + y + z = 1 ) , \mathrm { L i _ { 2 } C o O _ { 2 } ( 2 . 4 \mathrm { - } 3 . 2 \ \mathrm { g \ c m ^ { 3 } ) } }$ and $\mathrm { L i M n } _ { 2 } { \sf O } _ { 4 }$ $( 2 { - } 2 . 4 \ \mathrm { g } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )$ cathode materials, which will result in an unsatisfactory volumetric energy density [159,161]. Therefore, strategies such as the optimization of calcination temperature, the construction of hierarchical microspheres, and the control of the particle size distribution, are recommended to solve this problem. When it comes to practical applications, critical issues to obtain high-density LRCM electrodes should be addressed. These include: (1) an increase of reactive surface areas and corresponding side reactions due to the particle-fracture under high pressure calendaring. (2) The formation of a thick CEI layer onto the cathode resulting rapid energy degradation upon cycling [162,163]. These issues are easily to be ignored in lab research conducted commonly using low-density LRCM electrodes and set higher demands for the electrodes manufacturing process [19]. Moreover, the high working voltage of LRCMs could cause decomposition of carbonate-based electrolytes. In the long run, coupling LRCMs with lithium metal anodes and solid-state electrolytes could achieve higher-energy-density LIBs with long service life.

paragraph_context: Flexible lithium ion batteries (FLIBs), considered as the most promising energy source for flexible planar electronic devices especially for portable phones and laptops, have attracted great attention. However, it is a critical challenge to achieve high energy density and high flexibility simultaneously. Herein, we demonstrate a novel and rational rigid-supple integrated FLIB inspired by crocodile skin. The thick, rigid parts for storing the most energy correspond to the osteoderm of crocodile skin, while the thin, supple parts are regarded as dermis of crocodile skin, providing outstanding bidirectional flexibility for planar flexible electronics. The fabricated battery, containing LiNi Co Mn O -based cathode and graphite-based anode, shows a record-setting volumetric energy density of 400.3 Wh L−1. More importantly, it can maintain stable electrochemical performance with 92.3% capacity retention and 0.038% capacity decay per cycle even undergo 30,000 times bending and after 200 charge/discharge cycles. Furthermore, the electrochemical property of the battery is confirmed by the tough dynamic bending test, including over 13,000 bidirectional bending times. Meanwhile, mechanical simulation results reveal its flexible mechanism. Accordingly, the reported bidirectional FLIB provides great promise for future practical applications in flexible devices.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Flexible electronics have captured growing interests in wide applications, including sensors [1–3], flexible displays [4], and health monitoring devices [5]. As one of the energy storage components in these electronics, lithium ion batteries (LIBs) show plenty of advantages, including lightweight, long cycle life, and higher power output [6]. To make the entire electronics flexible, the flexibility of the LIBs is highly needed. However, the critical issue in limiting the further application of flexible lithium ion batteries (FLIBs) is that the repeated large deformation of FLIBs will accelerate mechanical failure and destroy the battery components. For instance, in the battery electrodes, the yield and cracks of the active layer, the interface delamination between the active layer and current collector would happen during battery deformation, finally leading to the fluctuation of the power out, short circuit and other battery degradation and safety issues [7,8]. Recently, various efforts have been made to develop robust FLIBs [9–14]. Several evaluation standards of flexibility and stretchability on flexible energy storage devices are proposed [15–17]. A figure of merit for a flexible battery is reported, considering the flexibility and electrochemical performance comprehensively [18]. Several studies focus on the development of battery materials with intrinsic soft, elastic, and even stretchable mechanical properties [19–26], such as super slim electrodes [27], solid electrolytes [28,29], incorporate carbon-based current collectors [30], etc. Besides, the battery structure design is a more practical and efficient solution to making LIBs flexible only with the use of conventional battery materials. A thin film structure with an anode-separator-cathode stack was first used to obtain bidirectional or multi-directional flexibility [31– 37]. Further, novel flexible battery architectures have also been proposed, including texture-like [38], 2D wavy-like [39], self-similar soft serpentine structure [40], origami, and kirigami structure [41–43]. Most of these FLIBs are bidirectionally flexible, bendable, and even stretchable. Nevertheless, their energy density is remarkably sacrificed showing a low active material load compared to prismatic LIBs. In general, high energy density and flexibility are often in conflict with each other in these structures [44], since the pursuing of flexibility often sacrifices the electroactive part and adds the redundant inactive components into the limited battery space for releasing strain during deformation.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lately advance in FLIBs structure design has provided a promising solution for this challenge. The core idea of these strategies is dividing the battery configuration into two parts that hold the function of energy storage and deformability separately. Battery structure designs such as accordion-like [45], spine-like [46], zigzag-like [47], human-joints-like shape [48] are developed. These batteries possess a great commercial promise with a suitable trade-off between high energy density and superior flexibility. However, none of these designs can achieve a function of bidirectional deformability, which is only confined in a single direction. Complex and harsh deformation such as folding, stretching, and winding in multiple directions cannot be avoided in practical battery working conditions. FLIBs with both high energy density and multi-directional flexibility are highly needed especially for portable and wearable planar electronics.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Rigid-supple integrated structure strategy is widely used in flexible electronic designs and nature as well. For instance, island-bridge design can protect the functional components by putting them at the lowstressed inland position, the connected bridges work for electric conduction and large deformation [49]. In nature, Crocodile skin is rough but flexible. The prominent part in the skin contains scales called ‘scute’, which is bony and solid. Arrays of rigid scutes are connected by soft epidermal, occurring mostly around the shoulders and hips, where multidirectional flexibility and defense are both needed during movement.

paragraph_context: Here, inspired by the crocodile skin, we demonstrate a novel and scalable rigid-supple integrated FLIB configuration that can simultaneously achieve bidimensional bending/folding and high energy density. The rigid-supple integrated FLIBs can be directly coiled from a tailored and stacked electrode sheet by the use of a winding machine. The diagonal joint connects two adjacent electroactive parts in the row direction, while suitable interspace exists between adjacent electroactive parts in another column direction. With the assistance of Al-plastic packaging, rigid-supple integrated FLIBs allow more bending ability bidirectionally compared with previous high energy density FLIBs. Meanwhile, the arrayed thick winding electroactive parts offer superior energy storage capability, showing an energy density of 400.3 Wh $L ^ { - 1 }$ (see calculation details in Supporting Information, Fig. S1, S2) and reaching 91.76% of the conventional prismatic LIB with the same materials and geometric volume (Fig. S3). The battery also performs well under 200 cycles of charge/discharge at 0.5 C, the retention of battery capacity is 92.3% under multiple deformations, including over 30,000 times bidirectional bending/folding. Besides, the discharge capacity of the battery remains above 151.9 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ steadily after over 13,000 cycles of dynamic bending test. Finite element analysis (FEA) is also carried out to reveal the electrode protection mechanism in our robust battery structural design. The results show that supple interconnected joints are suffering most of the stresses during the deformation, the max principal stresses of our proposed cell are much smaller than the conventional prismatic cell while in the same bent state. In addition, the bioinspired rigid-supple integrated design has excellent customization capability, since the geometric parameters, including the position of connected joints, the length of the interspace can be adjusted to satisfy different working conditions. Enabled by a bioinspired rigid-supple integrated strategy, the FLIBs reported here are expected to attract great promise in the applications of soft robotics, flexible displays, and wearable electronics.

paragraph_context: Noticeably, the capacity loss rate for the rigid-supple FLIB is only 0.038% per cycle after 200 cycles with over 30,000 times bent load, which is extremely low compared to the previously reported cell-scale flexible batteries (Fig. 5e and Table S1). As shown in Fig. 5f and S17, Considering the bending times, energy density, and overall bending radius of the reported cell-scale flexible battery, the rigid-supple FLIB in the present study holds excellent mechanical durability, and competitive flexibility as well as record-setting volumetric energy density. With the optimized choice of high energy density electrode material (NCM523) as well as novel structure design, the rigid-supple FLIB demonstrates high volumetric energy density (400.3 Wh L−1) which is compatible with most of the power-supporting requirements in commercial portable electronics. The figure of merit fb, considering both the flexibility and energy density into consideration, is also demonstrated in Supporting Information. Besides, The crocodile skin inspired rigid-supple integrated battery has promising extensibility on flexibility, multidirectional deformability, and energy density. On the one hand, it can easily be extended to an arrayed structure with N rows × N columns electroactive parts, that can offer a novel flexible energy storage strategy for flexible large-scale planar LIBs (Fig. S18). By changing the key geometrical parameters including the length ratio, winding numbers, the tradeoff between energy density and flexibility could be balanced for meeting the requirements in various practical flexible working conditions. For instance, the multiple length ratio can be customized in a rigid-supple FLIB, so it could approximately conform to the curve surface with different curvatures (Fig. S19). On the other hand, the stacked electrode sheet can be tailored into various kirigami 2D electrode sheets. After winding these sheets periodically, the as-fabricated battery cell can suffer bending and folding not only in two directions but also in multiple directions (Fig. S20). Finally, the energy density of the battery can also be promoted by introducing the double side cathodes and anodes. Additional electrode stacked methods are shown in Fig. S21. It is believed that the design of rigid-supple integrated FLIBs with excellent electrochemical performance as well as mechanical durability combined with the easy scaled fabrication process, could offer a broad scope for building robust and high-performance FLIBs.

paragraph_context: In summary, inspired by the crocodile skin, we have proposed a novel rigid-supple integrated FLIB to achieve superior bidirectional flexibility and high energy density simultaneously. Much simple manufacturing process only involved a few cutting and winding procedures for batteries are developed. The as-fabricated battery with periodic winding energy storage arrays could deliver a superior energy density of 400.3 Wh L−1. More importantly, the battery remains 92.3% of discharge capacity after 200 cycles with an average Coulombic efficiency higher than 99.9% even withstanding over 30,000 times harsh bidirectional bending loads at the same time. More importantly, after suffering 13,000 times of continuously dynamic bending, the battery prototype exhibits a robust electrochemical performance with 93.4% capacity retention, ultra-stable charge/discharge curves, and voltage plateau. Meanwhile, the FEM analysis also investigates the underlying mechanism of rigidsupple battery structure for protecting the electrode materials from large deformation, like bending and folding conditions. The competition between effective stiffness and relative energy density is quantitively revealed for the rational design of rigid-supple batteries. The excellent electrochemical and mechanical properties of our designed rigid-supple integrated FLIBs promised that wide practical application in flexible and wearable electronics.

paragraph_context: Fabrication process of the battery: Customized single coated NCM523 cathode (Canrd Corp.) and single coated graphite anode (Canrd Corp.) were utilized. After cutting electrodes and separator (CELGARD 12 ??m) into the required shape, the cathode/anode/separator stacked films were divided into several connected segments and winding segments. Then, each winded segment was folded in half and coiled to an elliptic unit. Next, elliptic units (rigid part) were fixed by polypropylene tapes (Canrd Corp.). Then, the battery cell was covered by the aluminized polyethylene package (Japan Showa Denko) with the three sides sealed. Subsequently, commercial electrolyte (Canrd Corp. KLD-1230C) was added into the aluminized polyethylene package in the argon-filled glove box $( 0 _ { 2 } < 0 . 1$ ppm, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } < 0 . 1$ ppm). The last side of the battery was sealed by a vacuum heat sealing machine. Then, the battery was charged/discharge at low current density of 0.1C for two cycles as battery activation. Subsequently, the battery was degassed and underwent secondary vacuum encapsulation.

paragraph_context: Finite element modeling: The deformations of the crocodile skin inspired rigid-supple integrated FLIBs were simulated in the commercial software ABAQUS 6.13 by using 8-node linear brick with reduced integration (C3D8R) element (see details in supporting information). In the battery geometrical model (Fig. S22 and S23), the rigid part unit was considered as multi-layer winding electrodes stacks, while the supple part was built from a single electrode stacked strip. Since the strain in the rigid part is close to zero during the bending process, the stress in the rigid parts is also very small, the rigid parts are assumed to have an effective bending stiffness in the modeling. The electrode strip contains three detached cathode (or Al current collector)/separator/anode (or Cu current collector) layers. The geometrical parameters were listed in Table S2. The elastic-plastic materials properties were used in the models (Table S3), in which all the material parameters were obtained by experimentally measuring stress-strain curves (Fig. S24).

paragraph_context: a Honda Research Institute USA, Inc., San Jose, CA 95134, United States  b Department of Mechanical Engineering Mechanics & Computation, Stanford University, United States  c NanoSynthesis Plus, Ltd., Columbus, OH 43212, United States The rapidly growing battery market demands both high energy density and waste-management solutions for the anticipated global annual battery waste of about two million metric tons. To address the energy-environment dilemma, we developed self-standing composite electrodes for Li-ion batteries without electrochemically inactive metal current collectors, additives, and binders, increasing energy density by up to 40%. The electrodes were prepared via in situ mixing of as-grown single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) with aerosolized electrode active materials, leading to adequate electrical conductivity and mechanical robustness. The SWNT scaffold exhibits a piezoresistive effect, with resistance depending on the voltage-weighted number of inter-nanotube contacts. We exploit this intrinsic piezoresistance of SWNT network for operando self-monitoring of battery structural health. The proposed solution-free battery fabrication technology and architecture eliminates environmentally harmful components and enables recycling by simple mechanical separation, aiming at safety and circular economy.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: An imperative need to protect the vulnerable and limited resources of Nature while meeting the growing energy demand of the world makes the sustainable development of renewable energy a mission of central importance [1–7]. The success of this mission depends on the advances in storage technologies such as rechargeable batteries. In addition to recent worldwide renewable energy commitments, advances in electrical vehicle technologies, flexible electronics, smart wearable devices, and internet of things, have contributed to the increasing demand for batteries with a wide range of electrochemical and electromechanical properties [8–13]. In response, the battery industry has launched intensive research and development efforts in search of new materials, technologies, and concepts. However, these rapid developments give rise to a growing concern about the impact of this industry on Nature. This entails the abundance and safety of the utilized materials, selection of chemistries and fabrication processes, battery management systems, and waste treatments [4,5,14]. One way to resolve this energy and environment dilemma is by revising the conventional battery architec ture to assure both high energy density and efficient recyclability aiming at circular economy [4]. This involves developing more potent and longer-lasting battery architecture, leading to not only more new applications of the batteries, but also reducing the number of components in them and longer lifespan. For example, energy densities of the batteries can be increased by eliminating or modifying electrochemically inactive components of the battery, such as metal foil-based current collectors, binders, and conductive additives (Fig. S1); this also reduces the amount of materials required for battery production. Ensuring proper function of the batteries during their operation by operando monitoring of the battery health is also an important aspect of increasing the safety of battery users. Preferably such monitoring would be done by using intrinsic properties of existing structure(s) of the battery without additional component(s) in or on the battery. Hence, there is a wide range of opportunities to address the aforementioned challenges by altering the design and fabrication technologies of Li-ion batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The metal current collectors in batteries play a dual role by providing mechanical support for the electrode active materials and enabling electron transfer. However, they account for over 40% of the battery weight [15,16], thereby reducing the energy density. Therefore, one way to increase the energy density is to eliminate the metal current collectors. To this end, the fabrication of self-standing composite electrodes consisting of a mixture of carbon nanotubes (CNT) and the active material via solution processing is widely explored [17–27].

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: However, this approach comprises intense treatments of CNTs postsynthesis that affect their unique intrinsic properties, thereby diminishing their advantages, such as high aspect ratio, electrical and thermal conductivities, and mechanical robustness. To overcome this challenge, we developed a novel solution-free method for the fabrication of selfstanding composite electrodes by utilizing as-grown pristine singlewalled nanotubes (SWNTs). SWNTs were used since they have higher electrical conductivities than multi-walled CNTs and they tend to have more chemically active surface and higher specific surface area that provides a better interface with the active material. We use in situ gasphase mixing of as-grown floating SWNTs [28] with aerosolized $\mathrm { L i } { \bf - N i } _ { 0 . 5 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 3 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (LiNMC 5:3:2) and graphite (Gr) particles as active materials for the cathode and anode, respectively. The apparatus comprises a reactor for SWNT synthesis that is in fluidic communication with the chamber containing the aerosolized active material, followed by a co-deposition chamber [29,30], (Fig. S2a). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images confirm that the obtained self-standing cathode and anode sheets consist of a finely dispersed three-dimensional SWNT network, in which the active material particles (LiNMC or Gr) are embedded (Figs. 1a, S3 and S4). This method can be easily adapted for the production of self-standing electrodes from 0.05 mm to \~2 mm thick (Fig. S3) containing other commonly used powdered electrode materials including, but not limited to $\mathrm { S i , \ S i O _ { x } / C , \ L i C o O _ { 2 } , \ L i N i _ { x } M n _ { y } C o _ { z } O _ { 2 } , }$ etc. (Fig. S4). The Raman spectroscopy and temperature programmed oxidation (TPO) studies confirm the preservation of high quality (G/D>20) of SWNTs (Fig. S2b–f). This solution-free method makes it possible to produce much thicker electrodes (up to 2 mm) than the traditional slurry-based technologies. This enables unprecedented areal loadings of the electrodes. Therefore, cells with very high capacity densities and specific capacities can be produced for the active materials used in this work. However, with increase of thicknesses of electrodes, diffusion of Li ions will gradually become a limiting factor, and in very thick electrodes a fraction of the active material might be underutilized in charge-discharge processes, thereby reducing the practical cell capacity; or require reduction of the current density, limiting the power of the battery. Another practical challenge in producing very thick electrodes is to ensure uniformity of the electrodes.

paragraph_context: For our electrodes to be a viable solution in practice, they need to be mechanically robust to withstand strains that the battery undergoes during charge-discharge cycles. Furthermore, the flexible nature of our SWNT-supported electrodes makes them promising candidates for the wearable electronics market, if they can sustain even larger strains. To test the mechanical robustness of the electrodes, we examined the deformation behavior of the self-standing electrode sheets as a function of SWNTs concentration and electrode densities. We found that our electrodes tolerate a bending diameter of as low as 2 mm, twisting angle higher than $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ and stretching up to 12% (Fig. 1b–e) in the evaluated concentration range of SWNTs (0.8–5.0 wt%). Compared to aluminum and copper foils [21,31,32], which are used as current collectors in conventional batteries, our electrode sheets tolerate about twice as much tensile strain (Fig. 1e). The Young’s modulus of our free-standing electrode sheets is estimated to be in the range of 0.2-72.7 MPa for the SWNT concentration and density being in the range of 0.8–3.6 wt%, and of 0.4–2.15 g/cm3 (Fig. S5), respectively. Fig. 1f shows the cyclic stress-strain curves of the self-standing cathodes of density 1.3 $g / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 3 }$ between zero strain and a peak stress of 0.15 MPa. A hysteretic behavior similar to the elastic-plastic behavior of ductile materials [33–37] is observed. The stress at zero strain is negative after unloading (Fig. 1f) because the sheet has been irreversibly stretched to a longer length during the first loading cycle. The area of the hysteresis loop is much smaller in subsequent loading cycles (Fig. 1f). However, the hysteresis loop shifts to the right with increasing cycle number, indicating further plastic strain. However, the nominal stress stays constant during a significant portion of the unloading phase because the electrode sheets buckle under the compressive load.

paragraph_context: We hypothesize that the observed stress-strain behavior arises because of the Van der Waals interactions within the fiber network and microstructural changes caused by the deformation. To test this hypothesis, we constructed a coarse-grained molecular statics (CGMS) model, in which each SWNT is represented by a series of nodes connected by straight segments. Nodes on the same SWNT have bonded interaction with their neighbors to represent the stretching and bending stiffness, whereas nodes on different SWNTs have Van der Waals interactions with each other represented by a Lennard-Jones potential[37, 38]. The NMC particles interact with each other and with the SWNTs through an integrated Van der Waals interaction (Section S.6 in SI).

paragraph_context: Our CGMS model provides mechanistic insights into the microstructural changes of the SWNT network that is responsible for the observed stress-strain behavior. First, the increase in sheet stiffness at higher density can be explained by the increased level of connectivity of the SWNT network (Fig. S7). As the density increases from 1 $g / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 3 } \tan 2$ $\mathrm { { g } / \mathrm { { c m } ^ { 3 } } } ,$ , the average number of contacts an SWNT makes with the others increases by a factor of ${ \sim } 1 . 4 5 ,$ which results in the increase in the stiffness by a factor of \~2 observed in our simulations. Second, the plastic deformation (increase in the “rest length”) of the electrode sheet during loading can be explained by the sliding between SWNTs in contact with each other (Section S.8.3). Third, the sliding between SWNTs during loading is often accompanied by a slight increase in bundling (Section S.8.1), in which the average overlap length between two SWNTs in contact increases by \~5%. This is consistent with the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) measurements showing a \~6% decrease in the surface area after irreversible structural deformation (Fig. S11c–f).

Therefore, the composition of the self-standing electrodes can be tuned to the desired energy density and mechanical robustness demanded by the application. It is worth noting, that the conductivity of LiNMC 5:3:2 based free-standing cathode sheets even with 0.25 wt% of nanotubes $( \sim 3 5 ~ \Omega ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { m } ^ { - 1 } )$ is higher than the conductivity of LiNMC 5:3:2 based cathode material of commercial electrodes $( \dot { 0 } . 1 { - } 1 0 ~ \Omega ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , which contain 4 wt% of a conductive additive (Fig. 3b, SI Section S.2.2, and [39]). Remarkably, the measurements reveal a piezoresistive effect and a resistance-strain hysteresis, which varies with the composition and density of the electrode. The slope of resistance-strain curve and the extent of its hysteresis increase substantially as the electrode density increases from $0 . 4 ~ \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ to 1 $g / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 3 }$ and then $\mathsf { t o } \ \mathsf { \Omega } 2 \ \mathsf { \ g } / \mathsf { c m } ^ { 3 } \ \mathsf { \Gamma } ( \mathrm { F i g . } \ \mathsf { \Omega } 3 \mathsf { c } ) ,$ . paragraph_context: Our CGMS model qualitatively captures the resistance-strain $\left( R - \varepsilon \right)$ hysteresis observed in the experiments, as shown in Fig. 2c. A higher gauge factor is observed during unloading (and re-loading) than that during initial loading. The behavior observed in the free-standing film here is opposite to what was observed in quasi-2D films [40] in which the resistance remains nearly constant (i.e., smaller gauge factor) during unloading (Fig. S6h). The difference in the R − ε hysteresis between the two types of films is successfully captured by our CGMS model, suggesting that it is caused by the microstructural differences in the two SWNT networks. paragraph_context: The change of electrical resistance ΔR during the loading/unloading cycles can be explained in terms of the inter-nanotube contacts, weighted by the square of the open-circuit potential defined below. Given the initial configuration (at ε = 0), the calculation of its resistance also provides the voltage Vi of every node i in response to an external potential $\Delta \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { e x t } }$ applied across the periodic simulation box in x. The open-circuit potential between nodes i and j not in electrical contact is simply the voltage difference between them, $\Delta V _ { i j } ^ { \mathrm { o p e n } } = \Delta V _ { j } \ - \ \Delta V _ { i } .$ . If nodes i and j are in electrical contact in the initial configuration, the open-circuit potential is the voltage difference between them in the configuration (at $\varepsilon > 0 )$ where this contact is broken (Fig. S8c). The open-circuit potential defined above provides a measure of how important a given contact is to the change of total resistance ΔR. For example, if $\Delta V _ { i j } ^ { \mathrm { o p e n } } = 0$ , then forming a new contact between nodes i and j would not change the total resistance at all, i.e., such a contact would be redundant. For each configuration, we can compute the voltageweighted change of contacts relative to the initial configuration as follows, $$ \Delta \widetilde {N} = \sum_ {(i, j)} \left(\Delta V _ {i j} ^ {\text { open }}\right) ^ {2} \cdot \Delta \sigma_ {i j} $$ where the sum is over all node pairs (i, j) whose contact condition has changed relative to the initial configuration, and Δσ is the corresponding change of local contact resistance (positive for contact formation, negative for contact breaking). The magnitude of open-circuit potentials for all such contacts has a distribution that looks approximately exponential (Fig. S7d–e). Fig. 2d shows that the evolution of ΔÑ with ε exhibits a hysteresis behavior mirroring that of ΔR. Fig. 2e shows that the simulation data exhibits a linear relationship $\Delta R \propto - \Delta \widetilde { N } .$ . These results suggest that the piezoresistive behavior observed during both the loading/ unloading cycles is caused by the change of the voltageweighted number of contacts between nanotubes. The greater gauge factor observed during unloading is caused by the rapid formation of inter-nanotube contacts, as nanotubes bundle (elongated by initial loading) and buckle (Fig. S8).

paragraph_context: We have established that calendared and pre-strained self-standing electrodes have suitable electromechanical properties for use in batteries. Next for battery fabrication we have developed methods for attaching tabs to self-standing electrodes [41,42] (Section S.3 in SI), which are critical for performance of batteries based on such electrodes. Full pouch cell batteries were assembled using these electrodes, as shown in Fig. 4a, and described in SI Sections S.1.2 and S.3, and their performance was evaluated. Fig. 4b shows the performance of a typical pouch cell battery with 1.4 wt% SWNT. Our batteries exhibit excellent discharge capacity retention up to 1C rate for all cathodes with a nanotube concentration ≥1 wt% (thickness of 0.1-0.3 mm), as shown in Fig. 4c. The batteries also exhibit a high C-rate tolerance and retain about half of their capacity (compared to that at 0.2C) at 5C and retain some capacity up to 20C (Fig. 4b). A higher SWNT concentration appears to be beneficial for higher C-rate tolerance, while a lower SWNT concentration leads to higher energy density. The Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) shows that our electrodes are well suited for high power applications (Section S.3 in SI) by exhibiting higher charge transfer kinetics (in the 0.1 Hz to 1000 Hz range) in comparison to commercial batteries; however, our electrodes can have marginally higher Ohmic resistance (Fig. S9). According to estimations, our battery architecture enhances the energy density by up to 40% and specific energy by up to 70% due to the elimination of the metal current collectors, 5–10 wt% binder, and 5–10 wt% carbon-based additives (SI Section S.1.1, Fig. S1b). Fig. 4d–e indeed demonstrates \~35% increase in capacity density and up to \~70% increase in specific capacity over a traditional battery with identical dimensions at 0.2C (SI Section S.1.2, Tables S1 and S2, Fig. S10). Fig. 4f demonstrates good long-term performance of our batteries based on self-standing electrodes. The performance of the battery tolerates the mechanical disturbances as demonstrated by the bending-unbending (down to 8 mm diameter) cycling test with 0.2C charge/discharge rates (Fig. 4g). We also find a good performance of our pouch cell battery in stacked configuration, in which two anodes share a cathode to create an elementary block. Since our electrodes are naturally two-sided, it simplifies the creation of stacked and folded configurations of the batteries. This paves way for using such batteries for high energy demanding applications, specifically for electrical vehicles, which require stacked or folded cells.

paragraph_context: Currently, there are no widely available prognostic methods to perform in situ/operando monitoring of the battery health [5]. The existing approaches include the use of the sensors embedded in the electrode or battery cell, or attached to the battery surface, which introduces additional components into the battery architecture and can interfere with electrochemical reactions [43,44]. On the other hand, since our self-standing electrode demonstrates the piezoresistive effect (Fig. 3c–f) introduced by the embedded SWNTs network, it can operate as an intrinsic strain sensor providing information about the structural changes [45,46]. Indeed, the slopes of the resistance-strain curves correspond to a gauge factor of 1.2–6.32 (Fig. 5a) for cathodes with different densities at the given nanotube concentration (1.12 wt%), which have been measured by adding one more tab on each electrode (see insert in Fig. 5a). To test whether this effect can be leveraged for operando monitoring of battery health, we intentionally prepared a relatively low-density electrode in which structural defects can be easily introduced by deformation (bending/unbending). The additional tabs allow independent operando monitoring of the spatial variation of the potential along the electrodes Fig. 5b. Figs. 5c and S11a and b show the variations of difference of potential between the two tabs of the cathode when the battery is subjected to bending/twisting cycles, while the battery powers the device. The mechanical disturbances are sensed as the sharp changes in the potential difference, although the BET surface area and pore size distributions measurements did not reveal noticeable differences after mechanical impacts (Fig. S11c and f). Hence, the SWNT network can inherently provide useful information by in situ/operando self-monitoring of electrode health.

paragraph_context: We developed a coarse-grained molecular statics (CGMS) model to simulate the morphology change of the self-standing SWNT/NMC composite system under cyclic loading with increasing strain. We use LAMMPS [47,48] for the parallel implementation of the CGMS model. The composite system was simulated by a collection of SWNTs interacting with each other and incompressible NMC particles. Each SWNT was represented by a series of nodes connected by linear segments. The interactions between the nodes were modelled to mimic the stretching and bending stiffness of the SWNTs and the interaction between a pair of SWNTs was modelled as Van der Waals interactions. The interaction between the SWNTs and the NMC particles was modelled as an integrated Van der Waals interaction (SI, Section S.6). Periodic boundary conditions were applied in all three directions. The initial configuration is randomly generated by solving the Frenet-Serret equations by using arbitrary torsion and curvature inputs to avoid initializing planar fibers that might not provide the electrical connectivity across the simulation box (SI, Section S.7). This structure was then relaxed to a local energy minimum using the conjugate-gradient algorithm. $H _ { x } , \ H _ { y }$ and $H _ { z }$ are the simulation box sizes in the x, y and z direction, respectively. The initial simulation cell size is $H _ { x } = H _ { y } = H _ { z } = 4 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ . We begin with anisotropic compression to obtain the desired initial density after which the loading-unloading cycle is simulated. The simulation box is stretched in the x direction, while compressing the y and z directions to obtain an almost zero-stress in these directions. The simulation box is stretched in small increments, allowing the configuration to relax a local energy minimum at the end of every step. The net resistance is computed by first calculating the voltage at each discretized SWNT node by balancing the current through each node. A periodic boundary condition for the potential drop across the box is implemented to deal with nodal connections across the periodic boundary conditions. The resistance can then be computed as the current/flux across the periodic boundary due to a unit drop in potential difference across the box (See Section S.7.2).

paragraph_context: Energy storage through additional anionic redox can deliver ultrahigh specific capacities of Lithium-rich manganese-based oxides cathode materials (LRMO). The commercial application of LRMO is hampered by several drawbacks, including structure degradation, continuous capacity and voltage decay, sluggish kinetics and severe irreversible oxygen release, stemming from generation of O2n− $( 0 \leq n < 2 )$ species during deep oxidation. Notably, relying solely on a single modification strategy only partially address the problems of LRMO materials. Herein, one-step phosphatizing-assisted interface engineering strategy was successfully implemented, simultaneously fabricating oxygen vacancies, spinel-like structure and an ionic conductor $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } }$ capping layer on the surface. Among them, the formation of oxygen vacancies is accompanied by the production of a spinel phase buffer layer, which inhibits the generation of O–O dimers and oxygen loss, contributing to the stability and reversibility of anionic redox reactions. The lithium ions conductive protective layer of $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } }$ accelerates Li+ diffusion rate while suppressing harmful interfacial side-reactions between the electrode and electrolyte. More importantly, the incorporation of P into the subsurface lattice regulates the local electron configuration and activates oxygen redox. As a result, the modification LRMO demonstrates an impressive reversible capacity of 312.9 mAh $\stackrel { \textstyle \cdot \ } { g ^ { - 1 } }$ , with excellent capacity retention of 91.87 % at 1 C and 82.43 % at 2 C after 500 cycles, respectively. The mult-ianionic redox mechanism provides an effective and straightforward method to stabilizing LRMO for next-generation high-energy lithium-ion batteries.
