paragraph_context: The rapid advancement of contemporary energy storage systems and conversion fields has substantially fueled the escalating demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with high energy density and long lifespan [1–3]. Amidst this trend, the development of advanced cathode materials is considered as a key factor. The Li-rich Mn-based layered oxides (LRMO) with the general formula of xLi MnO ⋅(1-x)LiMO ((0 < x < 1), transition metal (TM) = Mn, Co, Ni) are recognized to be the most competitive cathode candidates materials with high energy density (> 1000 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and cost-effectiveness [4,5]. Massive research has demonstrated that the LRMO possesses reversible specific capacity over 250 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ arises from the distinctive anionic redox, which far surpasses that of conventional cathode materials [6,7]. The unique Li–O–Li configuration of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ phase generates isolated oxygen electrons (nonbonding O 2p bands), enabling reversible redox reductions between lattice oxygen and peroxide ions $( 0 ^ { 2 - } / 0 _ { 2 } ^ { \mathrm { n - } } , ~ n ~ < ~ 2 )$ during the charge-discharge process [8–10]. Nevertheless, the involvement of anionic redox for charge compensation concurrently causes irreversible oxygen evolution, exacerbating the severe corrosion of interface electrolyte and migration/dissolution of TM during cycling [11]. These results trigger the transition of LRMO phase structure from layered to spinel/rock-salt, ultimately resulting in electrochemical performance attenuation including capacity degradation, decreased cycling stability, severe voltage hysteresis and undesirable rate performance, etc. [12–15]. The issues mentioned above pose tremendous obstacles to the practical applications LRMO as cathode materials.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Consequently, it is urgent to find an efficacious strategy to stabilize the lattice oxygen structure, activate reversible oxygen redox, and simultaneously expedite electrochemical kinetics of LRMO. The interfacial engineering is frequently deemed to be a direct and efficient strategy, with feasible methods encompassing surface defect engineering, element doping, and surface coating. Surface defects, such as Li/O vacancies enable modulation of the local electronic structure or TM ions coordination environment, thereby facilitating greater anion participation in oxidation–reduction reactions, inhibiting irreversible oxygen loss and mitigating structural deterioration [16–18]. When oxygen vacancies are generated through surface treatment, the formation of surface spinel layer is invariably observed, in which Li-poor spinel phase plays a key role in stabilizing surface lattice oxygen [19]. Doping modification can be categorized into cation doping, anion doping, and co-doping based on the states of doping ions. The introduction of elements (Al, Ti, Nb, Ta, F, etc.) is conducive to decrease Li/Ni cation mixing and sustain the structural stability of cathode materials [20–24]. Specifically, element doping promotes the formation of stronger TM–O bond to anchor lattice oxygen, thereby preventing the irreversible migration of TM ions into the Li layer. However, doping usually results in a reduction in specific capacity because of the incorporation of inactive dopants. In addition, surface coating has been proposed as a straightforward method to create a protective layer, serving as a buffer structural stress to avoid direct interaction between the active mass and electrolyte, inhibiting TM dissolution and alleviating the Jahn-Teller effect [25,26]. Surface coating, such as $\mathrm { L i T a O _ { 3 } , L i _ { 4 } M n _ { 5 } O _ { 1 2 } , L i _ { 4 } P _ { 2 } O _ { 7 } , e t c . }$ , not only mitigate side reactions, but also enhance the diffusion kinetics of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ at the electrode/electrolyte interface [27–29]. Alternatively, for better tackling the challenges of Li-rich Mn-based oxides, it is not sufficient to rely solely on a single modification. Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop a comprehensive strategy to effectively address the aforementioned problems, which is essential for facilitating the broad application of LRMO materials.

The underlying mechanisms by which interfacial modification improve structural stability, electrochemical performance and kinetic properties are elucidated through various characterization techniques. Specifically, the formation of oxygen vacancies provides active sites for TM migration to build a spinel phase transition layer, which is advantageous for reducing oxygen release and enhancing reversible oxygen redox. As a physical protective layer, the $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } }$ capping layer serve to mitigate the electrolyte decomposition and structural phase transformations during cycling. More significantly, under the oxygen vacancy-assisted ions conductive surface capping layer, more anions in $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ phase are stimulated to participate in oxidation–reduction with increasing fast Li+ diffusion kinetics. This study offers a feasible pathway for the advancement of high-performance LRMO cathode materials.

paragraph_context: Raman spectroscopy can be employed to reveal fine structural changes by applying its sensitivity to short-range order. As expressed in Fig. 2(a, b), two apparent peaks at 597 and $4 8 8 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ correspond to $\mathbf { A } _ { 1 \mathbf { g } }$ stretching and $\operatorname { E } _ { \mathbf { g } }$ bending of the R-3 m phase, respectively [33]. The weak peak at 424 cm− 1 is associated with the C2/m symmetry structure. Notably, a shoulder peak of LRMO and 25P-LRMO at about $6 7 5 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ was detected, which belong to the cubic spinel phase with Fd-3 m space group [34]. It was difficult to identify by using XRD measurements due to the low crystallinity. Based on the fitting data of peak area percentages, the spinel phase in 25P-LRMO increased compared to that in LRMO. This finding suggests that the surface of 25P-LRMO has reconstructed from initial layered to spinel structure. Additionally, the position of $\mathrm { E _ { g } }$ and $\mathbf { A } _ { 1 \mathbf { g } }$ peaks of 25P-LRMO exhibit a red shift compared to those of LRMO, indicating $\mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { 3 \cdot }$ − group is introduced around the TM-O bond [35] (Figure S4). To further clarify the surface components and elemental valence states of both samples were investigated and compared through X-ray photoelectron spectra (XPS). The full XPS spectra shown in Figure S5 manifested the presence of Li, Mn, Ni, Co, O, and P. As shown in Fig. $2 \mathrm { c } , \mathrm { d } ,$ , the P 2p spectra was confirmed existence of P element in the surface and bulk of 25P-LRMO. In Figure $^ { S 6 , }$ the asymmetric stretching P–O vibrations in PO43− polyanion at about 1074 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ are detected by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) [36]. These above results demonstrated that $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } }$ indeed exists in the 25P-LRMO materials. Additionally, the valence state of Mn decreased compared to LRMO (Figure $s 7 ) ,$ implying that 25P-LRMO provided more electron transfer, thus enhancing the energy density. The binding energy of Ni 2p and Co 2p spectra remains relatively unchanged. The O 1 s spectra (Fig. 2e) were separated into three distinct peaks at 529.5, 531.5 and 532.8 eV, corresponding to lattice oxygen, oxygen vacancies and surface oxides, respectively [37]. The proportion of oxygen vacancies has increased (reaching 42.7 %) compared with LRMO, revealing the fabrication of more oxygen vacancies on the 25P-LRMO particles surface. Meanwhile, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra corroborate these results (Figure 2f, S8). The plentiful of oxygen vacancies on the surface layer promotes the activation of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ component and initiates mult-ianionic redox, accordingly increasing the specific capacities of LRMO.

paragraph_context: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images depicted in Figure S9 manifest that 25P-LRMO still maintains original morphology and size of approximately 200 nm after integrated modification. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was employed to further elucidate the microscopic crystal structure of material. In Fig. $^ { 2 g , }$ the bare LRMO particles present a smooth crystalline surface. Internally, LRMO possesses a well layered crystal structure, with a lattice spacing of 0.470 nm conforming to the typical (003) plane of $\mathrm { L i T M O _ { 2 } }$ phase or the (001) plane of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M n O } _ { 3 }$ phase (Figure S10). From the high-angle annular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images (Fig. 2i), it is evident that the surface is enveloped with an amorphous layer \~ 5 nm thick, which it speculated to be lithium phosphate oxides. The measured spacing between the internal lattice stripe is 0.471 nm (Fig. 2j), suggesting that 25P-LRMO samples exhibit a well-defined layered structure. This result shows that the $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } }$ capping layer was merely present on the particles surface and did not disrupt the layered crystal structure of LRMO. Besides, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping was performed to disclose uniform distribution of Mn, Ni, Co and P elements within the particles, demonstrating that P ions were successfully doped into the samples (Fig. 2k).

paragraph_context: Various electrochemical characterizations were employed to evaluate the impact of interfacial engineering on the electrochemical performance. In accordance with the intrinsic characteristics of LRMO, the voltage window of all electrochemical assays was ranged from 2.0 to 4.8 V. Fig. 3a illustrates the initial charge-discharge curves for all samples at 0.1 $\mathrm { C } ,$ where a sloping region below 4.5 V and a high-voltage plateau region above 4.5 V, correspond to the cationic oxidation o ${ \bf \ddot { N i } } ^ { 2 + / }$ $^ { 4 + }$ and $\cos ^ { 3 + / 4 + }$ [38] and the anionic oxidation process [39], respectively. Furthermore, the LRMO, 20P-LRMO, 25P-LRMO, and 30P-LRMO electrodes exhibit initial discharge capacities of 276.0, 288.4, 312.9, and 295.1 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively. The addition of P initiates anion-induced oxidation–reduction reactions at high voltages, significantly increasing the discharge capacity. Due to the generation of extra oxygen vacancies and an amorphous phase capping layer during cathode preparation, which reduce the amount of lattice $\mathrm { O } ^ { 2 - }$ on the surface, thereby suppressing irreversible oxygen escape. Nevertheless, as the P-doping amount increases, the initial charge capacity decreases in this case. The reduction of lattice oxygen concentration destroys the original layered structure of LRMO. Moreover, the higher the addition amount of P, the thicker the inactive phase surface capping layer, which impedes the electrochemical reaction kinetics and leads to a lower theoretical specific capacity. The Coulombic efficiency of 20P-LRMO, 25P-LRMO, and 30P-LRMO are improved (85.02 %, 82.17 % and 82.88 %, respectively) (Fig. 3b). As shown in Fig. 3c, the 25P-LRMO still maintains a higher capacity of 125.66 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ at 10 C in contrast to LRMO (92.92 mAh $g ^ { - 1 } ) _ { : }$ , and its excellent rate performance can be attributed to the fast Li+ diffusion kinetic and enlarged $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ insertion spacing. Subsequently, the cycling stability was verified by measuring the capacity decay at 0.1 C, 1 $\mathrm { C } ,$ and 2 C. After 50 cycles at 0.1C (Figure S11), the 25P-LRMO retains a capacity retention rate of 98.86 %, whereas it is only 85.07 % for LRMO. The initial discharge capacity of 241.10 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ at 1 C for 25P-LRMO, higher than 197.06 mAh $g ^ { - \mathrm { i } }$ of pristine LRMO. Compared with LRMO (65.17 %), 25P-LRMO exhibits superior cyclic stability with capacity-retention of 91.87 % after 500 cycles at 1 C, indicating that P-modification was beneficial for improving anionic redox, thereby leading to strengthened electrochemical properties. From the discharge curves of the LRMO and 25P-LRMO samples (Figure S12), the voltage fading and polarization of 25P-LRMO electrode are substantially alleviated. After 400 cycles, the mid-point voltage retention for 25P-LRMO electrode can reach 81.1 $^ { \% , }$ implying an enhancement in structural stability after modification. Furthermore, 25P-LRMO still is capable of maintaining steady cycling at $^ { 2 } \mathrm { C } ,$ achieving a high capacity retention rate of 82.43 % (Fig. 3e). The specific capacity of LRMO rapidly decayed, which is attributed to spinel phase transition caused by excessive oxygen vacancies during cycling processes, leading to the structure collapse. Especially, to the best of our knowledge, the P-LRMO cathode exhibits superior electrochemical performance, surpassing most previously reported Li-rich metal oxides in the literature (as listed in Table S3).

paragraph_context: Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were utilized to examine the electrochemical reaction kinetics of all cathode materials. Figure S13 demonstrates that the $\mathrm { O } ^ { 2 - } /$ $0 _ { 2 } ^ { \mathrm { n - } }$ anodic oxidation potential of 25P-LRMO is lower than that of LRMO during the initial cycle, further stabilizing the lattice oxygen and improving reversibility of anionic redox [40]. Figure 3f, S14 exhibit the CV curves of all samples at different scan rates. The voltage peak shift of LRMO is large, whereas the voltage peak shift of 25P-LRMO is smaller, which implies the lower overpotential and better electrochemical reaction reversibility. Figure S14d show linear fitting plots of peak current versus square root of scan rate, where the slope is associated with the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion coefficient. Notably, the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion capability of 25P-LRMO is larger than LRMO, confirming that improved $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion rate elevates rate performance. The dQ/dV curves of the LRMO (Figure S15) show that the two oxidation peaks at 3.5 and 4.0 V gradually evolve into one peak as cycling progresses, accompanied by irreversible structural transitions from the layered to spinel/rock-salt phase. In contrast, the 25P-LRMO exhibits three distinct pairs of redox peaks, corresponding to the redox processes of $\mathrm { M n } , \mathrm { N i } / \mathrm { C o } ,$ and $^ { 0 , }$ respectively. The $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 3 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 4 + }$ redox peak potential difference of 25P-LRMO is lower than that of LRMO, further confirming that 25P-LRMO manifests electrochemical polarization and higher reversibility [41]. As illustrated in Fig. 3g, the EIS curves perceived that modification samples have better charge transfer kinetics. The semicircles in the mid-to-high and the mid-to-low frequency regions represent the solid electrolyte interface resistance (Rse) and the charge transfer resistance (Rct), respectively, while the inclined line reflects the diffusion dynamics of Li+ ions within cathode material. In Fig. 3h, the coated composite material illustrates a higher diffusion coefficient than that of the pristine LRMO, indicating that the encapsulation of $\mathrm { \Delta L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } }$ accelerates the transport of Li+ and slows down polarization phenomenon. These results collectively highlight the enhanced $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion kinetics of modification samples, ascribed to the spinel heterostructure featuring three-dimensional Li+ transport pathways and a more stable cathode/electrolyte interface.

paragraph_context: To investigate the phase transition of LRMO and 25P-LRMO material for the initial charge-discharge process, in situ XRD measurements were performed to detect crystal structure evolution. As displayed in Fig. 6, the evolution of (003), (101) and (104) peaks for LRMO and 25P-LRMO are presented in the form of 2D-contour maps, respectively. The (003) peak gradually shifts to a lower angle before the voltage reaches to 4.5 V, which is ascribed to increased electrostatic repulsive force from the $\mathrm { L i T M O _ { 2 } }$ phase with the expansion of crystal plane spacing after $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ extraction. The peak subsequently reaches an opposite point and begins to move toward higher angles caused by the activation of Li MnO -like crystal domain with oxidation of anions, resulting in shrinkage of the (003) plane. Conversely, the (101) and (104) peaks shift to higher angle, reflecting a contraction in the interlaminar spacing along the a-axis owing to the smaller ionic diameters of $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { N i } ^ { 3 + }$ and ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 3 + }$ after oxidation. During subsequent discharging process, the (003), (101) and (104) peaks shift to the opposite direction as the intercalation of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , implying the structural evolution is largely reversible. Nevertheless, irreversible $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ escape and TM ions migration/dissolution lead to the intrinsic structural transitions of LRMO from layered to spinel/rock-salt phase, rendering it difficult for the peaks restore to its original positions. The 25P-LRMO always exhibits much smaller peak shifts than LRMO, which manifests reduced $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ release and more effective reversible oxygen redox chemistry. The shifts of (003) and (101) peaks are associated with the evolution of lattice parameters a and c that control $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion, respectively [47]. paragraph_context: The global transition to electrification is driving the demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with higher energy density, lower cost, and reduced environmental footprint. Conventional slurry-based electrode manufacturing, which relies on toxic solvents and energy-intensive drying processes, poses significant economic and environmental challenges. Solvent-free dry electrode technology has emerged as a transformative alternative to overcome these limitations. This review provides a comprehensive and critical analysis of the dry process from three pivotal perspectives: economic advantages, environmental benefits, and performance superiority, conducting a multidimensional comparative analysis with slurry-process electrode manufacturing. The scientific principles behind these advantages are elucidated through microstructural and electrochemical characterization. Meanwhile, comparative life cycle assessment (LCA) data are employed to demonstrate the significant advantages of dry electrodes in terms of energy consumption and carbon emissions. Regarding application potential, leveraging Tesla’s successful industrial application case, we explore the broad prospects of dry electrodes in LIBs, solid-state batteries, and other domains. Finally, in the context of the rapidly advancing dry electrode technology, we highlight the severe challenges that remain before truly achieving industrial-scale application. This work offers a holistic theoretical foundation and practical guidance for adopting dry electrode technology as a core strategy for sustainable battery manufacturing.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) prevail in energy storage facilities owing to their superior energy density, robust power, extended cycle life, and proven reliability [1,2]. The cost-effectiveness and operational capacity of LIBs are intimately dependent on the electrode manufacturing process [3,4]. Most battery manufacturers currently utilize conventional slurry processing to produce battery electrodes; however, there are some drawbacks associated with this processing method [1], particularly in terms of environmental pollution and production costs (Fig. 1) [5,6]. As the primary solvent in the drying process, the utilization of N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) raises toxicity concerns, and the solvent drying process generates volatile emissions that cause serious environmental pollution [7,8]. This necessitates the incorporation of a solvent recycling apparatus, in addition to the slurry electrode manufacturing unit. The slurry process is characterized by long durations, which require the construction of additional facilities. This in turn leads to higher investment costs, and the electrode drying and solvent recovery also require large amounts of electricity, resulting in significant energy consumption in the slurry electrode manufacturing [9]. Beyond cost and environmental considerations, electrode manufacturing technologies still stand as the primary governing factor for electrode thickness, which directly governs energy density.

It is found that most of the production costs in the electrode manufacturing process and potential threats to ecological and environmental benefits come, to a large extent, from the use of solvents. Consequently, the groundbreaking concept of eliminating solvents from electrode manufacturing processes has been proposed, which has prompted substantial research advancements in solvent-free electrode (also commonly referred to as dry-processed (DP) electrode) processing technology and catalyzed the emergence of transformative technological innovations, specifically dry electrode technology $[ 1 0 , 1 1 ]$ . Bypassing the slurry coating process, this method eliminates a massive drying phase allowing the manufacturing of higher mass-loading electrodes [12,13]. The prominent advantages of DP electrodes can be systematically delineated into two critical dimensions: the harmonious amalgamation of economic feasibility and ecological compatibility, alongside enhanced performance characteristics in product functionality. This dual-aspect superiority manifests specifically through: (1) Reduced costs and pollutions [14]. The elimination of all solvent-involving manufacturing steps not only achieves significant production cost reduction but also prevents potential contamination risks associated with solvent utilization. (2) Electrode performance breakthroughs [10]. The DP procedure approach completely avoids electrode delamination caused by solvent evaporation while breaking through traditional thickness limitations, demonstrating significant advantages in manufacturing high energy density electrodes [2,15].

paragraph_context: Slurry processing is a well-established method, but there are many disadvantages associated with this method, which can be summarized in the following four points [6].

paragraph_context: (1) Elevated expenses [9]. The electrode slurry mixing necessitates substantial NMP consumption, thus the implementation of a reclamation system is necessary to capture and recycle volatilized NMP throughout the dehydration cycle in industrial manufacturing, which requires large equipment with extensive drying infrastructure and a further increase in capital expenditure (CAPEX) of about 20 %, thus reducing the economics of the process, particularly given the exponentially increasing requisition for electrochemical cells in electromobility and stationary storage systems. Additionally, the equipment footprint of the slurry process is significantly larger due to the required solvent recovery systems and multiple drying stages, which are necessary to handle large volumes of hazardous solvents such as NMP. These systems increase the physical production space required to set up a manufacturing plant, as well as increase production costs. In terms of energy costs, the drying process is notably energy-intensive in slurry electrode fabrication, this high energy demand not only increases the operating expenditure (OPEX) associated with production cost, with NMP solvent in cathode production alone accounting for 11.5 % of the production costs (Fig. 3a) and over 46 % of the energy consumption (Fig. 3b) [28,32].

paragraph_context: With the emergent recognition of DP processing merits, diversified DP-based electrode architectures have been orchestrated for advanced LIB manufacturing. The manufacturing process of dry electrodes has also been simplified compared to the slurry-based electrode fabrication. There are six typical DP electrode fabrication processes (Fig. 4a), such as dry spraying deposition [23,39–41], vapor deposition [42–44], melting and extrusion [45], 3D printing $[ 9 , 1 0 , 4 6 - 4 9 ]$ , direct pressing $[ 5 0 , 5 1 ] ,$ , and polymer fibrillation [52–54]. Specifically, the implementation methods of these six processes are as follows [6,11]: (1) dry spraying deposition: this method employs electrostatic spraying to deposit pre-mixed powder granules onto a current collector followed by hot pressing, offering uniform distribution and comparable electrode performance to slurry methods, yet remains limited by low active loading, inhomogeneity, and poor scalability for commercial use; (2) vapor deposition: this method is a vacuum-based atomic-level film formation process, unlike dry spray deposition which operates at atmospheric pressure through mechanical deposition, enabling the production of high-performance micro-batteries with superior energy density and cycle life, albeit at high cost and low areal capacity; (3) melting and extrusion: this method involves pre-mixing active materials, conductive agents, and binders, followed by twin-screw compounding, extrusion into a self-supporting film, and final calendering onto a current collector, enabling scalable production of thick electrodes with high active loading and energy density, but it requires precise control of processing parameters and faces challenges such as high polymer consumption and complex manufacturing steps; (4) 3D printing: this method is an extension of melt extrusion technology that enables customized electrode manufacturing through modeling, but it faces limitations in production scalability and requires relatively high equipment investment; (5) direct pressing: this method compacts dry powder mixtures into electrodes or bilayers in a single step, providing a simple, solvent-free, and scalable process, but typically yields thick and brittle structures incompatible with high-energy-density cells or roll-to-roll (R2R) production; (6) polymer fibrillation: this method produces self-supporting electrodes through shear-induced binder fibrillization and lamination, enabling low-binder, high-strength, and scalable manufacturing, but requires specific binder properties and may lead to side reactions that impair electrode performance. Although each method exhibits multivariate process identifiers, the fundamental workflow retains consistency, and mainly includes dry mixing, electrode film fabrication, calendering, laminating, and slitting. Notably, the dry electrode fabrication involves three subsequential steps (Fig. 4b): (1) powder homogenization to achieve dispersion uniformity of AM, carbonaceous conductor, and elastomeric polymer binder; (2) calendering, wherein mixed powders are consolidated through precision-gap counter-rotating rolls to fabricate separate, continuous electrode film; (3) thermocompression bonding integrating electrodes onto current collectors [55,56].

This substantial energy demand not only elevates production costs but also compounds the environmental impact of battery technologies. The DP procedure aims to reduce the risk of solvent emissions, waste generation, and potential safety hazards by eliminating the need for solvents, which aligns with a growing emphasis on sustainable and environmentally friendly manufacturing practices [28]. The cornerstone of the DP procedure is its eco-friendliness, which eliminates the need for toxic solvents and thus significantly reduces the environmental impact by minimizing the generation of most hazardous wastes such as NMPs $\mathrm { [ 1 0 , 8 0 , 8 1 }$ ]. A 10 kWh battery production line emits about 1000 kg of CO2 during the coating and drying process. With the demand for LIBs in electric vehicles expected to exceed 1 TWh by 2030, it is expected that 100 million tons of $\mathrm { C O _ { 2 } }$ emissions could be reduced if all batteries are produced by drying process, eliminating the coating and drying process. Researchers have developed a LCA model to evaluate the environmental impacts of dry electrode technology, revealing that the DP method achieves 47.5 % reduction of environmental impacts in 12 out of 13 categories, which compared with slurry processes [82]. In summary, the dry electrode method has advantages over the traditional slurry process from both economic and environmental perspectives, and the main differences between the two are briefly summarized in Table 3 [28,30].

paragraph_context: DP electrodes exhibit superior structural and electrical characteristics, demonstrating reduced tortuosity relative to conventional slurry electrodes while maintaining lower resistance, which facilitates the electrochemical performance (Fig. 6a) [90]. Specifically, the optimized microstructure of DP electrodes enhances electrolyte permeability and minimizes lithium-ion diffusion tortuosity, thereby improving rate performance at high current rates [91]. Both half-cell and full-cell configurations of the DP high-loaded graphite anodes $( 6 . 6 \ \mathrm { m A h } . \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ and NMC cathodes $( 6 . 0 \mathrm { \ m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ demonstrate robust electrochemical performance. Full cells employing DP electrodes exhibit superior rate capability versus conventional slurry counterparts, with capacity retentions of 74.1 % (400 cycles) and 63.6 % (800 cycles), respectively [90]. The PTFE binder in DP electrodes forms a hierarchical fibril network composed of primary and secondary fibrils with sizes up to the nanometer sizes, which is very different from the “moss-like” polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) domains in SC electrodes [92]. The DP electrodes minimize the masking of the NMC particle surface without pore blockage, which reduces the charge transfer resistance and improves the ionic mobility (Fig. 6b). Electrochemical tests show that DP electrodes perform better than SC ones, especially at higher charge-discharge rates. They exhibit a 150 % increase in capacity at a 2 C rate. DP electrodes exhibit 40 % slower capacity fade versus SC counterparts, maintaining 96 % initial capacity retention after 200 cycles at C/3 rate.

paragraph_context: Elevated volumetric energy density proves critical for volumeconstrained applications including electric vehicles and consumer electronics. In the SC process, solvent evaporation leaves a large number of pores inside the electrode, and the compact density after low calendering [11]. Commercial LIBs generally maintain electrode porosity at 30–45 %, whereas elevated porosity detrimentally compromises volumetric energy density. DP procedure enables higher compaction density than slurry methods via reduced porosity, exemplified by LFP-based electrodes achieving 1.6-fold greater density compared to slurry counterparts [39]. Engineered DP electrode fabrication process integrating high-speed pneumatic deposition, thermal calendaring, and lamination achieves 120 μm thick electrodes with 1.6 times enhanced density versus conventional slurry-coated counterparts. The system achieves an areal capacity of 1.4 $\mathbf { m A h { \cdot } c m ^ { - 2 } }$ and a volumetric energy density of 95 ${ \mathrm { { W h } } } \cdot \mathbf { L } ^ { - 1 }$ , doubling the performance of conventional slurry-coated counterparts (Fig. 6c). Comparative studies reveal DP-LFP electrodes exhibit enhanced rate capability and reduced charge transfer resistance relative to SC-LFP counterparts, originating from optimized PTFE fibril-LFP particle interfacial contact [93]. DP NCM and NCA electrodes consistently outperform slurry-processed counterparts in areal capacity and energy density, due to higher active material loadings, increased electrode density, and a more homogeneous conductive network without solvent-induced binder migration. For instance, dry NCM electrodes achieve areal capacities up to 17.6 mAh⋅cm⁻² and full-cell volumetric energy densities of 701 Wh⋅L⁻¹, compared to only 4 mAh⋅cm⁻² typical of slurry-processed electrodes [10,94]. Similarly, dry NCA cathodes reach volumetric energy densities up to 858 Wh⋅L⁻¹, aided by optimized binder distribution and thick, crack-free structures [95,96]. These improvements highlight the general advantages of the DP method for both commercial cathode systems.

paragraph_context: The DP procedure can also be used to produce high-loading, fastcharging graphite anodes with improved mechanical and electrochemical properties compared to slurry-processed electrodes [97]. Graphite powder and PTFE binder are mixed in the DP process and the mixture is then kneaded, rolled, and pressed into individual electrode sheets. The resulting electrode is laminated onto a copper current collector [98]. An ultrathin adhesive interlayer is interfaced between the electrode and current collector, optimizing interfacial adhesion. This DP technique allows the fabrication of high-loaded electrodes with a PTFE binder content of 2.0 wt. %, ensures uniform binder distribution, and improves mechanical strength. The DP electrode exhibited a uniform PTFE distribution and a mesh structure, which favor the direct interaction of lithium-ion with the graphite surface. The conductivity test (Fig. 6d) of the electrodes shows a significant difference between dry and slurry electrodes, with the dry electrodes providing excellent ion and electron transport capabilities. The DP graphite anodes demonstrate superior performance with 88.2 % retention of discharge capacity after 300 cycles at 0.5 C [99]. Hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) methodology rigorously assesses DP electrodes under practical operating conditions (Fig. 6e). At all levels of depth of discharge (DOD), the DP cell exhibits higher available power than the SC batteries during both the discharge and regen processes, confirming the better rate capability of the DP electrodes under different test conditions. In fast-charging tests, the DP anodes show significantly less lithium plating than traditional slurry-processed anodes [39]. The unique PTFE fibrillate structure of the DP electrode enhanced Li+ diffusion and low internal resistance for the DP anodes demonstrate fast-charging capability at 6 mA⋅cm− ² current density while retaining superior capacity retention during cycling, surpassing conventional slurry electrodes. Comparative galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) analyses of DP and TSC full cells (0.05–1 ${ \mathsf { A } } { \cdot } { \pmb { g } } ^ { - 1 }$ , 0.1–2.7 V) reveal dry electrodes’ superior capacity retention versus slurry counterparts, particularly at 50 mA $\cdot { \bf g } ^ { - 1 }$ (Fig. 6f).

SEM analysis demonstrates increased NMC particle cracking in dry electrodes from intensive calendering required to match slurry electrode porosity. Dry electrodes exhibit superior specific capacity at ≤1 C rates, while slurry counterparts demonstrate enhanced high-rate performance at >2 C attributed to optimized carbon-binder homogeneity and mitigated cracking. Both types of electrodes in the full cells perform similarly in long-term cycling, despite the initial cracking observed on the dry electrodes. Full-cell evaluations demonstrate achieving 174 mAh $\cdot { \bf g } ^ { - 1 }$ initial reversible capacity with 64 % retention after 500 cycles, while the slurry electrodes have a capacity retention of 71 %. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy indicates that the dry electrodes have a higher charge transfer resistance after cycling, which could be attributed to the increased surface area exposed by calendering-induced cracks. Cold plasma process-powder coating (CPC) LFP electrodes exhibit 10-fold higher peel strength $( 1 . 6 9 ~ \mathrm { \ v s . } ~ < 0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { N } { \cdot } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ than slurry-cast counterparts, demonstrating enhanced interfacial adhesion and mechanical integrity (Fig. 6h) [23]. In addition to the above studies, the team of scientists quantified the key factor “coverage”, i.e., the percentage of the area of the surface of AMs covered with electrolyte, by digitally processing the images. Dry electrodes achieve 67.2 % active material coverage, outperforming pellet-processed (30.6 %) and slurry-coated (33.3 %) counterparts, thereby enhancing rate performance and cycle stability. In the slurry-processed electrodes, the binder is coated onto the AM surface as the solvent evaporates, while the carbon black (CB) conductor forms aggregates [101]. In contrast, DP electrodes have limited binder coating on the AM surface due to the absence of solvent and the simultaneous application of shear.

paragraph_context: In terms of micro-characterization, SEM analysis shows that dry electrodes have a denser surface (Fig. 6i) and different binder distribution compared to the porous structure of slurry electrodes [101]. Dry electrodes exhibit higher porosity (67 %) versus slurry counterparts (63 %). This higher porosity contributes to longer cycle life but may reduce volumetric energy density. SEM analysis confirms DP cathode (DC) and anode (DA) electrodes exhibit defect-free surface morphology with comparable thickness and porosity to reference SC counterparts [99]. DP electrode fabrication initiates with powder blending, where SEM analysis reveals ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 6 5 }$ and PVDF particles partially form uniform surface coatings on AM particles while others create loosely bound micrometer-scale agglomerates. Distinct interparticle pores facilitate electrolyte infiltration while promoting Li⁺ transport kinetics across AM-electrolyte interfaces. DC-DA full-cells demonstrate superior capacity retention at high rates (78.24 % at 3 C, 69.37 % at 4 C), exceeding SC counterparts by 11.2 % and 17.4 %, while hybrid DC-SC/SC-DA configurations demonstrate transitional performance metrics, confirming DC electrodes’ superior rate capability compared to conventional SC counterparts.

paragraph_context: In addition to investigating performance comparisons, some studies have attempted to elucidate the underlying principles. A study presents high-loading (thick) NMC electrodes fabricated using DP dry powder electrostatic spray deposition (ESD) and conventional slurry processes [39]. Dry electrodes demonstrate equivalent or superior performance within 0.05–1 C rate ranges, attributed to enhanced AM utilization via calendering-induced particle cracking. Dry ESD-processed NMC electrodes exhibit comparable full-cell cycling stability to conventional electrodes, despite particle cracking caused by calendering, validating the manufacturability of high-loading electrode even with non-optimized PVDF binder systems. Moreover, ultra-thick DP electrodes (3D-DEs) are compared to SC electrodes to assess differences in charge transport, mechanical properties, and cycling stability (Fig. 7a) [102]. 3D-DEs achieve 101.4 mg⋅cm− ² electrode loading with 242 % enhanced energy density versus conventional LIBs, retaining 92.6 % capacity after 20 charge-discharge cycles (0.1 C) and demonstrated thickness-tolerant stability, while their ultrathin CEI layers enable efficient Li⁺ transport compared to thick, resistive CEI in slurry-cast electrodes. Micro-computed tomography analysis reveals DP electrodes form denser conductive networks through surface energy-driven particle cohesion, contrasting with slurry systems where solvent-dispersed binders encapsulate active materials [103]. This microstructural advantage enables optimized binder-AM interfacial bonding exceeding binder-conductive agent interactions, establishing robust percolation pathways critical for enhanced ion transport and electrochemical performance.

paragraph_context: Slurry-based electrode fabrication exhibits significant limitations in both economic viability, environmental impact and electrode performance. The CAPEX for equipment and facilities, coupled with OPEX from energy-intensive drying processes, can be substantially reduced through DP manufacturing. Furthermore, the substantial $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions and inherent risks of toxic solvent leakage impose non-negligible ecological burdens on SC technologies. From a performance perspective, SC electrodes inevitably suffer from delamination and thickness constraints. In contrast, DP electrode manufacturing demonstrates tripartite advantages encompassing economic, environmental, and electrode performance aspects: it minimizes infrastructure costs and eliminates solvent and energy-related OPEX; eradicates solvent-related contamination risks at the source; and crucially overcomes inherent thickness limitations to achieve synergistic enhancements in both electrochemical metrics and mechanical robustness.

paragraph_context: As a critical tool for quantifying environmental impacts and economic value, life cycle assessment (LCA) plays an indispensable role in battery manufacturing. Current LCA analyses for batteries increasingly cover expanded scopes, ranging from raw material extraction through production and use to recycling, offering considerable flexibility depending on assessment objectives. Research on the electrode manufacturing process has been extensively conducted, with the current research focus shifting towards SC electrodes, revealing their significant environmental burdens and economic constraints. Due to current commercial adoption barriers, LCA investigations of DP electrodes are scarce. Recent comparative LCAs of slurry compared with DP techniques demonstrate the superior ecological and environmental performance of DP technology.

These investigations are primarily categorized into four main scope categories (Fig. 7b) [104]: (1) Cradle-to-grave [107]. As a conventional full LCA methodology, it encompasses processes from resource extraction through the use phase to disposal, quantifying energy and material inputs and outputs at each stage. Widely applied in product design for comprehensive lifecycle evaluation, this approach particularly includes electrode material extraction and manufacturing processes, offering critical insights for scaled electrode production. (2) Cradle-to-cradle [108,109]. As an emerging LCA methodology building upon conventional approaches, it is tailored to specifically include waste recovery and recycling processes. paragraph_context: Given the central role of electrode manufacturing in the entire LIB life cycle assessment, the aforementioned diverse choices of system boundaries provide crucial theoretical support for the whole industry chain from production to recycling. The diverse selection of system boundaries provides significant theoretical support for the entire industrial chain of LIBs, spanning from production and use to recycling. The cradle-to-gate and gate-to-gate perspectives are currently the most frequently applied [106]. The End-of-Life (EoL) stage, whether viewed through cradle-to-grave or cradle-to-cradle perspectives, has also gained attention. Furthermore, beyond system boundaries, LCA can also be classified according to organizational levels, which is essential for understanding the impact of decision-making at different levels on electrode manufacturing. In addition to system boundary categorization, LCA for LIBs can also be classified based on organizational levels into four types[104,113]: (1) Product-level [114]. Product-level LCA serves to evaluate and improve specific products, encompassing eco-design, process optimization, supply chain management, marketing, and strategic decisions. For electrode manufacturing, this level of analysis primarily functions by providing feedback from battery product performance, which is important particularly under the urgent demand for high-energy-density batteries, to optimize material selection and process parameters during electrode fabrication. (2) Organization-level [115]. Organizational-level LCA analyzes the environmental impacts of an organization’s products and proposes holistic solutions. For electrode manufacturing, this tier of analysis places greater emphasis on product environmental impacts, thereby promoting greener manufacturing practices. (3) Consumer-level [116]. Consumer-level LCA predicts future consumption trends by analyzing specific consumers’ purchasing information and lifestyles. This level focuses on market analysis. Within the battery manufacturing industry, the currently noteworthy sector is the power battery market for electric vehicles. Ultimately, consumer demands propagate to the electrode manufacturing stage, especially the demand for high-range and low-energy-consumption batteries consequently guides technological innovation. (4) Regional-level. Regional-level LCA aims to identify critical sectors and environmental impacts within specific countries and regions. With the rapid global expansion of battery production, electrode manufacturing is emerging as a key industry for nations worldwide. Different LCA methods have distinct scopes and objectives. Within the electrode manufacturing industry, product-level LCA is the most frequently employed level due to its direct links to product development, upgrades, and risk assessment.

paragraph_context: In recent years, the LCA research of battery production demonstrates that carbon emissions receive significant attention, with electrode manufacturing being a key focus [108,117,118]. Extensive research consistently identifies battery production as the principal source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and key environmental burdens throughout the full life cycle of LIBs [119–122]. Extensive evidence indicates that substantial energy consumption and emissions arise from the production of cathode, aluminum casings, and electrolytes, as well as drying processes during battery manufacturing, with electrode production accounting for the predominant [123]. Using NCM batteries as an illustrative case, their production process is examined. During cathode material production, electrical power and natural gas serve as energy inputs, while raw material inputs include lithium carbonate, nickel sulfate, cobalt sulfate, manganese sulfate, oxygen, and ammonia. Process outputs comprise air pollutants, water pollutants, and the cathode material itself [124,125]. As quantified in Table 4 for GHG emissions across battery production stages, cathode production emerges as the predominant emission source, especially for NCM batteries. This reflects the dominant role of electrode manufacturing processes in determining both the energy footprint and environmental impact of battery production [104].

paragraph_context: widespread adoption in engineering contexts for technological innovation [105]: 1) LCA requires comprehensive primary data on all inputs and outputs throughout a product system’s life cycle. Consequently, it imposes stringent requirements for both data quality and quantity. For emerging and cutting-edge technologies, limited data availability makes it difficult to meet these requirements. For such technologies, data must often be generated through simulations or process-based calculations, which typically yield lower data quality compared to primary LCA datasets [132]. 2) Within innovation-driven dynamic environments, assumptions and estimations undergo frequent revisions. Consequently, continual recalibration of the entire product system becomes necessary, requiring support from Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) databases or fundamental material and energy flow models. 3) Traditional LCI databases represent static snapshots of production systems at specific states. These inventories embed implicit interactions within the product system, exemplified by connections between material design and process design, as well as interactions across the life cycle, illustrated by recyclability linkages extending from material production to end-of-life stages. Due to the lack of precise modeling of the aforementioned relationships, adaptation to innovation-driven changes remains challenging. Concurrently, given the rapid development of the LIB industry and imperatives such as technological optimization and energy mix restructuring, LCA for the battery sector must adopt a broader scope, richer analytical perspectives, and enhanced adaptability to emerging changes. Particular emphasis should be placed on electrode manufacturing, which accounts for the majority of energy consumption and environmental impacts in battery production.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Current LCA analyses of electrode manufacturing processes have been extensively investigated, with the large-scale industrial adoption of SC electrode technology leading to a predominant research focus on SC manufacturing. Key factors influencing environmental impacts in SC electrode production include electrode materials, production scale and energy mix, electrode thickness, and component categories, which can be systematically examined through different LCA system boundaries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: From a cradle-to-grave perspective, the significant environmental impact of electrode manufacturing stems primarily from the materials introduced at the beginning of the process chain, as their extraction and processing dominate energy consumption and emissions [133,134]. Different materials lead to different CO₂ emissions and land occupation. It has been adequately demonstrated that lower CO₂ emissions occur during the extraction and processing phases of materials in the life cycle of LFP batteries, which are approximately 10 % lower compared with NCM batteries. The largest total environmental burden, including land occupation, was created in the extraction and processing of LFP battery materials (1875.73 m²a), 68 % more than NCM and 41 % more than Li-ion [105]. A large share of the impacts in most categories is caused by these battery materials. Furthermore, dry room energy consumption, which is attributed to equipment footprint during drying steps, exemplifies how SC electrode manufacturing impacts become embedded within material-related assessments [108].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Within the cradle-to-cradle framework, increasing emphasis on circular economy principles highlights the importance of waste recovery and recycling processes [108]. This approach is particularly relevant given that material and energy flows are inherently incorporated into process step categories, meaning environmental impacts from both raw material production and electrode manufacturing processes are accounted for when materials enter the production system. The cathode-active material (CAM) contributes significantly to the total global warming potential (GWP) of the battery cell and even more to terrestrial acidification potential (TAP-80 %) and metal depletion potential (MDP-83 %) (Fig. 7c) [105]. Other impact categories like freshwater eutrophication, ecotoxicity, and human toxicity are dominated by the anode coating process, primarily through copper foil, underscoring the need for recycling and material recovery strategies.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: From a cradle-to-gate viewpoint, which focuses on resource extraction to factory output, production scale and energy structure of electrode manufacturing modulate LCA outcomes by altering cumulative resource inputs and emission profiles across interconnected unit processes [106]. Significant heterogeneity in per-cell energy demand emerges when examining production volumes, revealing a distinct inverse correlation: larger scales consistently demonstrate reduced average energy requirements [106,118]. This scale-efficiency relationship aligns with established literature, exhibiting particular prominence at pilot-scale operations where volumetric increases yield substantial efficiency gains [105,108]. The environmental impact of energy structures is primarily attributed to high energy consumption during manufacturing processes, particularly the drying phase in SC electrode production [105]. At the laboratory scale, dry room operations, the most energy-intensive process, predominantly govern environmental impacts across multiple categories (Fig. 7d), contributing approximately 56 % to acidification, 79 % to climate change, and 48 % to particulate matter emissions [105]. Climate change impacts are predominantly determined by carbon dioxide emissions originating from the electricity generation mix. Regarding particulate matter formation, key causative agents include fine particulates and sulfur dioxide emissions from copper processing (anode current collector), emissions from cathode active material supply chains, and combustion residues during fossil-based power generation [105]. Electrode thickness also influences cradle-to-gate environmental performance, revealing complex interrelationships between material utilization, manufacturing energy dynamics, and structural design imperatives [135]. Increased electrode thickness introduces multifaceted effects: although absolute energy consumption rises in high-intensity operations such as electrode drying, this is counterbalanced by enhanced cell-specific energy throughput [105]. Thickness-driven reductions in inactive material constituents, especially copper foil, drive benefits in human toxicity potential (HTP), freshwater eutrophication (FEP), and ecotoxicity (FETP) indicators. LCA of cylindrical LFP batteries reaffirms electrode manufacturing as the predominant environmental hotspot in LIB production, accounting for 41.36 % of the total cradle-to-gate burden, with production energy contributing 71.42 % of total carbon footprints in NCM batteries [136,137]. Environmental burdens partition asymmetrically between electrode components due to divergent material chemistries and processing pathways [136].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Through a gate-to-gate lens, which specifically targets the battery manufacturing process, the influence of production scale is evident. Significant heterogeneity in per-cell energy demand emerges with production volume, showing an inverse correlation where larger scales reduce average energy requirements [78]. This variability is most prominent at pilot-scale operations, diminishing at industrial volumes. Material consumption dynamics mirror this pattern, as expanding production capacity enhances process efficiency, reducing material waste and net resource utilization per functional unit [78]. The cell battery production process (CBPP) manifests its influence by exceeding component impacts in multiple categories, and electrode design parameters, particularly architectural morphology and thickness, serve as critical environmental levers [136]. Increased thickness enhances material efficiency by reducing inactive constituents but introduces energy consumption trade-offs, such as elevated drying energy, yet enables net burden reduction through higher specific energy output [136]. Thick electrodes necessitate micro-structuring innovations to maintain ionic conductivity, adding process steps whose environmental trade-offs depend on methodological implementation [138].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: SC electrode manufacturing constitutes a critical environmental focal point within LIB production systems, with life cycle assessments consistently identifying it as the dominant contributor across different system boundaries, including cradle-to-grave, cradle-to-cradle, cradleto-gate, and gate-to-gate—due to the convergence of materialintensive upstream processes and energy-dependent manufacturing operations that collectively amplify environmental footprints. These LCA perspectives provide complementary insights and reveal that four interconnected factors govern this environmental profile: material selection dynamics, wherein raw material extraction and processing serve as primary environmental vectors, with cathode active materials and anode copper foils driving distinct impact pathways; production scale effects, which manifest through non-linear relationships between manufacturing volumes and environmental efficiency, particularly during pilot-to-industrial transitions; energy infrastructure interdependencies arising from thermal-intensive drying operations that link geographical energy structures to environmental outcomes; and electrode architecture implications, notably thickness, which introduces complex trade-offs between material efficiency and process energy demands. The synthesis of current LCA research underscores that sustainable electrode manufacturing requires simultaneous optimization of material supply chains, industrial scaling strategies, renewable energy integration, and geometric design innovations, recognizing their synergistic influence on environmental outcomes across the battery value chain.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The entrenched first-mover advantage of SC electrode manufacturing has precipitated extensive LCA research documenting its environmental footprint, yet this methodological dominance coexists with persistent technical, environmental, and economic limitations, including energy-intensive drying stages exacerbating global warming potential, volatile organic compound emissions posing occupational hazards, solvent recovery inefficiencies inflating costs, and throughput constraints impeding scalability, which prompting the emergence of DP electrode technology as a solvent-free alternative that fundamentally reconfigures fabrication paradigms through binder-fibrillation powder processing. While this disruptive innovation demonstrates industrial viability through applications like Tesla’s 4680 battery manufacturing technology, where it eliminates energy-intensive drying and solvent recovery infrastructure, comprehensive environmental evaluation via standardized LCA frameworks remains critically underdeveloped despite its technological maturation. This knowledge gap persists amid accelerating deployment, creating a methodologically isolated landscape where peer-reviewed comparative cradle-to-gate assessments against SC benchmarks are exceptionally scarce, process-specific inventories lack standardization, and environmental verification lags behind production scaling, an untenable disconnect given DP procedure’s triple imperative: to quantitatively validate purported ecological advantages like thermal energy reduction and solvent emission elimination; to identify and mitigate unforeseen trade-offs in novel material supply chains or pulverization energy demands; and to establish sciencebased benchmarks guiding sustainable infrastructure expansion during this formative phase. Consequently, advancing rigorous LCA research constitutes both a scientific priority and industrial necessity, demanding methodological focus on developing granular inventories capturing DP parameters, conducting scenario analyses of renewable energy integration sensitivities, establishing performance-adjusted functional units accounting for electrochemical variances, and quantifying circularity potentials through end-of-life material recovery pathways, thereby enabling evidence-based optimization while ensuring environmental considerations evolve in synergistic alignment with this transformative technology’s progression.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The fundamental divergence between DP and SC electrode manufacturing necessitates paradigm-shifting adaptations in life cycle assessment methodologies. Solvent elimination inherently omits process steps intrinsically tied to solvent management, primarily energyintensive drying operations and solvent recovery systems, thereby eradicating their associated energy expenditures and environmental burdens. This operational simplification, however, introduces compensatory environmental trade-offs through reconfigured material processing demands. Specifically, the absence of liquid-phase carriers imposes substantially heightened requirements for powder homogeneity during mixing, necessitating higher-shear blending equipment with elevated energy intensity. Furthermore, subsequent forming operations such as calendering exhibit amplified environmental footprints due to increased pressure requirements and thermal inputs for binder activation, contrasting with SC deposition mechanics. These diametrically opposed process characteristics generate fundamentally distinct environmental vectors that invalidate direct methodological transfer from SC LCA frameworks. Conventional impact allocation models, calibrated to solvent-related energy penalties and drying emissions, become structurally misaligned with DP systems where binder fibrillation energy and hot-roll compaction emerge as new critical hotspots. Consequently, comprehensive assessment demands holistic recalibration: analytical boundaries must expand to encompass specific DP procedures like electrostatic deposition; impact accounting requires reformulation to address altered material-intensity ratios and novel auxiliary energy demands; and functional unit definitions necessitate adjustment to accommodate differential electrode performance characteristics. Such methodological transformation ensures environmental evaluations accurately reflect this technological transition’s ecological trade-offs rather than perpetuating SC analytical inheritances.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The life cycle assessment of DP electrode manufacturing necessitates a distinct methodological framework from conventional SC approaches due to fundamentally divergent process configurations and environmental burden distributions. This analytical paradigm shift is exemplified through modeled process chains incorporating DP dry mixing with optimized binder formulations, electrostatic deposition eliminating liquid-phase carriers, and hot-pressing consolidation requiring heated rollers [139]. Within this configuration, dry mixing retains similarities to SC baseline procedures but critically excludes solvent-related infrastructure while modifying binder systems for powder-based compatibility. The most significant environmental transformation emerges from the complete elimination of thermal drying operations, where conventional systems consume substantial natural gas for drying-line heating, an energy demand rendered obsolete in solvent-free manufacturing. Consequently, DP energy profiles shift exclusively toward electrical consumption sources. Subsequent hot-pressing operations, conceptually approximated through calendering mechanics but with distinct thermal requirements, incur a 10 % energy premium for roller heating yet remain environmentally inconsequential due to constituting under 3 % of total electrical demand [82]. This reconfigured manufacturing sequence delivers substantial systemic advantages: GWP declines by 15.1 % to 49.3 kg CO₂-eq/kWh, while fossil depletion potential (FDP) decreases by 19.4 % to 19.0 kg oil-eq, primarily attributable to dual mechanisms, which the removal of solvent management burdens and energy conservation in mixing/drying stages for both anode types. Crucially, the minor environmental penalty from hot-pressing energy intensification is offset by order-of-magnitude savings elsewhere, culminating in a 37 % aggregate energy reduction across the entire process chain relative to solvent-based benchmarks. Thus, DP electrode manufacturing fundamentally reconfigures environmental impact profiles through solvent-phase elimination, redirecting energy expenditures toward targeted electrical applications while achieving substantial multi-category impact reductions, albeit requiring specialized assessment protocols to account for compensatory thermal demands in consolidation stages.

paragraph_context: Recently, a research presents the first comprehensive cradle-to-grave LCA model specifically developed to evaluate the environmental impacts of Maxwell-type, which as a typical dry electrode manufacturing for LIB, providing a critical comparison against conventional NMP-based slurry process [82]. This detailed, process-based, attributional LCA framework is constructed to quantify the environmental burdens associated with the PTFE-based DP method across the entire product life cycle [90,140]. The analysis meticulously tracks the cradle-to-grave primary energy consumption for both NMP-based and DP electric vehicle (EV) battery packs, as comprehensively illustrated, with the contribution of each distinct manufacturing process clearly delineated for the two methodologies (Fig. 8a). The total primary energy demand calculated for the NMP-based pack is 2.30 GJ⋅kg− ¹, compared to 2.19 GJ⋅kg− ¹ for the DP pack. This energy consumption is systematically divided into four principal life cycle stages: material extraction and processing, battery manufacturing, battery use, and EoL recycling. Notably, the battery use stage overwhelmingly dominates the energy profile for both technologies, consuming $1 . { \overset { - } { 9 } } { \overset { - } { 5 } } \ \mathbf { G J } { \cdot } \mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ in each case, reflecting the significant operational energy requirements of the vehicle during its service life. Within the material extraction and processing stage, the NMP-based pack consumes 124.4 MJ⋅kg− ¹, slightly higher than the $1 2 2 . 0 ~ \mathrm { M J } { \cdot } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ required for the DP pack; this difference primarily originates from the energy embodied in the production of the NMP solvent necessary for the conventional slurry method. The most substantial divergence between the two electrode fabrication routes emerges during the battery manufacturing stage. Here, the primary energy requirement plummets to 90.2 MJ⋅kg− ¹ for the DP pack, representing a marked 41 % reduction from the 152.9 MJ⋅kg− ¹ consumed by the NMP-based approach. This dramatic decrease is directly attributable to the inherent characteristics of the DP method. In the NMP-based manufacturing sequence, the energy-intensive dry room operation, essential for maintaining low humidity to prevent solvent absorption, constitutes the largest single energy consumer at 44.0 % of the total manufacturing energy. This is closely followed by the drying step, required to evaporate the NMP solvent after coating, accounting for 41.0 % of the energy consumption. The DP method fundamentally eliminates the need for both solvent usage and the subsequent drying step. Consequently, the dry room operation, while still necessary for powder handling and electrode formation, becomes the predominant energy consumer within this stage, responsible for 74.7 % of the total manufacturing energy. It is significant to observe that although the DP method incorporates calendering and laminating steps conducted at elevated temperatures of 50 degrees Celsius and 120 degrees Celsius respectively, the energy demands of these specific thermal processes are comparatively minor. Calendering contributes only 0.41 % and laminating merely 0.91 % to the total manufacturing energy consumption of the DP pack, indicating that the thermal energy requirements for these forming operations are efficiently managed and do not negate the overall energy savings. Further energy savings are realized during the end-of-life recycling stage. The NMP-based battery pack consumes 76.3 MJ⋅kg− ¹ for recycling, whereas the DP pack requires significantly less energy, only 29.5 MJ⋅kg− ¹. The key disparity during EoL recycling arises predominantly from the preprocessing step, specifically the separation of electrode materials from the current collectors. The conventional method relies on NMP to dissolve the PVDF binder, a process demanding considerable energy for solvent recovery due to NMP’s high boiling point. In contrast, the DP pack utilizes trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) solution for binder dissolution during separation. TFA possesses a substantially lower boiling point compared to NMP, resulting in markedly reduced energy consumption during its recovery and regeneration phase within the recycling infrastructure. Beyond energy analysis, the cradle-to-grave environmental impacts of the battery pack produced via the DP route were rigorously benchmarked against the baseline NMP-based pack across thirteen distinct impact categories, normalized for a reference flow of one kilogram of battery pack. The results demonstrate that the DP battery pack exhibits slightly lower environmental impacts in twelve out of the thirteen categories evaluated. The sole exception is human toxicity potential (HTP), where the DP method shows a marginally higher value of 39.656 kg 1,4-DB eq. compared to 39.648 kg 1,4-DB eq. for the NMP-based method. This negligible increase in HTP for the DP procedure can be reasonably attributed to the utilization of TFA during the preprocessing stage of end-of-life battery recycling. Crucially, although the DP method achieves a substantial 41 % reduction in energy consumption during the battery manufacturing stage, this advantage does not translate into an equivalently dominant benefit across the entire life cycle. This limitation occurs because the primary contributors to the majority of the impact categories are overwhelmingly the material extraction and processing stage and, most significantly, the battery use stage, which are largely comparable between the two technologies. Detailed analysis of the impact contribution from individual components throughout the cradle-to-grave cycle highlights a noteworthy finding: significant contributions, particularly evident in the large green bars representing GWP and ozone depletion potential (ODP), are linked to the PTFE binder used in the DP procedure. A parallel pattern is observable for the PVDF binder within the NMP-based system, confirming that the fluorinated polymer binder, whether PTFE or PVDF, consistently emerges as the top contributor to GWP among all battery pack components. It is pertinent to recognize that the practical application of Maxwell-type DP method for manufacturing LIB electrodes remains a relatively nascent technology. Certain technical challenges, such as achieving comparable production line speeds to established slurry casting methods and optimizing performance specifically for graphite anodes, which can currently exhibit limitations, necessitate further research and development efforts for widespread industrial adoption [74,90,141]. Nevertheless, the demonstrable advantages of this solvent-free approach, particularly its significant reductions in manufacturing energy demand, lower overall life cycle primary energy consumption, and favorable environmental impact profile across most categories, solidify its position as a highly promising and strong alter native to the conventional, solvent-intensive NMP-based electrode manufacturing technology. While this technology offers clear and quantifiable reductions in manufacturing energy and overall life cycle primary energy demand, along with marginal advantages in most environmental impact categories, the dominance of the battery use phase and the significant impact of fluorinated binders temper the magnitude of the whole-life-cycle environmental benefits when compared to conventional NMP-based electrode manufacturing.

paragraph_context: A modular methodology for modeling material and energy flows (MEF) in battery cell production is presented, generating LCI data for engineering-oriented LCA [105]. This approach integrates modularity at process and process-chain levels to dynamically configure material/energy flows across varying product specifications, production parameters, and innovative process chains (Fig. 8b). Through morphological analysis of core stages (electrode production, cell assembly, finishing), it identifies variability nodes (e.g., new process insertion, existing process adaptation, sequence reconfiguration) while accommodating production system adjustments (e.g., dry room scale), material properties, and cell design parameters [76]. Linked to Brightway2, the model quantifies LCI for six innovations (Fig. 8c): 1) extrusion-based slurry preparation; 2) water-based electrode processing; 3) dry electrode coating; 4) thick electrodes; 5) active material substitution; and 6) combined innovations. For dry electrode coating, the reconfigured process chain comprises dry mixing, electrostatic deposition, and hot pressing [73,139]. Mixing adapts the baseline by eliminating solvents and modifying binders, with the key distinction being removal of the drying step (dominant natural gas consumer in baseline), leaving only electrical energy. Results demonstrate that DP method significantly reduces environmental impacts by omitting energy-intensive coating/drying and solvent use.

paragraph_context: LCA holds significant importance for the high-quality development of the battery industry. Currently, various system boundaries and levels are available for battery LCA studies. Battery manufacturing, as a crucial segment in battery LCA research, has been extensively explored. Electrode manufacturing, being the source of most energy consumption and environmental impacts within battery manufacturing, plays a vital role. Considerable research has analyzed the electrode manufacturing process, particularly providing detailed studies on the well-established slurry electrode manufacturing process, which holds a first-mover advantage. Studies reveal that the dominance of electrode manufacturing in the energy consumption and environmental footprint of battery manufacturing primarily stems from electrode materials, production scale and energy structure, electrode thickness, and electrode components, encompassing the entire process from raw material production to electrode fabrication. Dry electrode manufacturing technology, as one approach to overcome the economic, environmental, and performance limitations of slurry processing, is a key enabler for producing high-energy-density batteries. The industrial application of dry electrodes represents a future trend in electrode manufacturing, making LCA studies on this technology both necessary and inevitable. However, as industrial-scale dry electrode manufacturing remains in the early exploration phase, corresponding LCA studies are still scarce. A recent study conducted the first LCA analysis specifically on Maxwell-type dry electrode manufacturing technology, comparing it with slurry processing. The results indicate that dry electrode manufacturing has relatively lower environmental impacts. In summary, due to the fundamental differences between dry and slurry electrode manufacturing technologies, continuous exploration of dry electrode LCA is required. Future research needs to develop widely applicable analytical approaches, such as modular system design, based on technological optimization and industrial development progress, thereby supporting the high-quality development of the electrode manufacturing industry.
