paragraph_context: DP electrodes demonstrate multifaceted advantages that define their pivotal role in advancing high-energy-density batteries while exhibiting broad application prospects. Currently, as an alternative to SC electrodes, they show significant potential in LIBs, prompting battery enterprises worldwide to conduct in-depth research and explore scaled-up production. In the long term, DP electrodes are expected to play a crucial role in the industrialization and application of all-solid-state batteries (ASSB), enabling genuinely solid-state manufacturing across the entire supply chain. For lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, which are also a key focus in next-generation batteries, DP technology will overcome the inherent limitations of slurry processing, enabling the production of thick electrodes with high energy density. Therefore, from a temporal perspective, whether driving continuous upgrades to existing widely deployed LIBs or achieving industrial-scale application of nextgeneration batteries with high energy density advantages and future potential, dry electrode manufacturing technology that has been validated both theoretically and practically will profoundly influence the future landscape of battery manufacturing.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Extensive research on DP electrode production has been conducted at the laboratory scale, with comprehensive investigations into electrode performance. However, numerous considerations and improvements remain necessary for industrial-scale implementation. To date, Tesla stands as the globally recognized entity implementing large-scale industrialization of DP electrodes, primarily represented in the 4680 batteries for its Model Y vehicles [142]. Compared to previous Tesla battery models, the 4680 series achieve significant cost reduction and substantial performance enhancement, wherein DP electrode manufacturing technology plays a key role, while still presenting multiple areas pending further refinement [76]. The structure of the Tesla 4680 battery is very unique (Fig. 9a) [143]. Unlike other cylindrical batteries, it adopts a tabless design connected via hexagonally symmetric electrode discs to reduce internal resistance and polarization heat, thereby improving charging performance and temperature management [144–148]. Analysis of the electrode structure (Fig. 9b), reveals the thickness profiles of the electrodes and separator within the 4680 battery, indicating that the electrode thickness, particularly for the cathode which critically determines battery performance, still has significant potential for enhancement [143]. Furthermore, overvoltage analysis indicates thermal dissipation deficiencies inherent in the large-format structure of this battery [149–151]. The low radial thermal conductivity leads to significant internal-to-surface temperature differences, causing non-uniform current distribution and accelerated aging risks, specifically manifested by accelerated solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) thickening and exacerbated lithium plating [142,152]. The tabless design also results in approximately 25 % cathode and 30 % anode area containing notches, extending current paths and adversely affecting electrical and thermal transmission efficiency [143]. Addressing 4680 battery defects involves continuous optimization through improved materials (e.g., housing, current collectors, separators) or structural redesigns to enhance radial thermal conductivity while reducing peak temperatures or thermal gradients, upgrading cooling architectures to mitigate temperature inhomogeneity, and developing advanced battery thermal management systems integrating high-thermal-conductivity materials with active cooling strategies [18,142,145,153,154]. Tesla’s successful large-scale DP application demonstrates considerable potential in LIB manufacturing. Future efforts, based on current temperature sensitivity and electrode defect issues, should focus on synergistic optimization of material and management system factors to overcome these technical bottlenecks.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: As the most successful commercial case of DP technology, analysis based on Tesla’s practices and existing technical challenges indicates that the commercialization of DP electrode manufacturing still faces numerous obstacles. Among these, electrode thickness, a critical factor limiting electrode energy density, is a primary consideration. Furthermore, as one of the most promising DP techniques, binder fibrillation technology is essential for the production of Tesla’s 4680 batteries. However, the most commonly used binder for this technology, PTFE, can cause side reactions during electrode operation that compromise performance. Therefore, exploring alternative binder systems that meet fibrillation requirements without adversely affecting electrode performance is a highly worthwhile consideration. Beyond the design of the electrode itself, the successful commercialization of dry electrodes relies on supporting systems. This can be achieved by optimizing battery structure and thermal management systems to improve temperature uniformity. In summary, the successful commercial adoption of dry electrodes depends not only on optimizing materials and processing techniques but also on integrated system design. Both aspects collectively determine the feasibility of large-scale commercialization.

paragraph_context: ASSBs mitigate safety risks by replacing liquid electrolytes with solid-state alternatives (solid electrolytes, SEs), eliminating vapor pressure and flammability hazards [155]. However, fundamental challenges persist regarding manufacturing costs, environmental impact, and interfacial stability, hindering commercial viability [29]. Consequently, dry electrode technology is crucial for overcoming these bottlenecks (Fig. 9c). The critical role of the DP procedure is first evident in resolving chemical compatibility issues in electrode manufacturing. Distinctive SE properties demand novel manufacturing approaches. Sulfide-based SEs, core materials for sulfide ASSBs, exhibit severe vulnerability to moisture and polar solvents [156]. Exposure degrades ionic conductivity and impairs battery performance, necessitating dry electrode processes for ASSB production [155,156]. Sulfide electrolytes present interfacial instability and reactivity toward conventional slurry solvents, raising interfacial degradation and environmental concerns [157–159]. Furthermore, DP technology is crucial for enabling optimal electrode microstructure design. Primary kinetic limitations stem from poor electrode microstructure design and high interfacial resistance [157,158]. Achieving high performance requires homogeneous distribution of active materials, conductive additives, binders, and SEs to establish efficient ionic and electronic pathways (Fig. 9d) [29]. Polar solvents (e.g., NMP) used in the slurry process react with SEs [160,161]. The adoption of non-polar and low-polarity solvents with binders like nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) preserves SE stability, but their poor binder solubility compromises homogeneity and causes poor slurry dispersion [160,162]. The DP procedure eliminates solvents, preventing SE decomposition and binder migration while reducing energy and costs. It is essential for developing high-rate and high-loading electrodes with structural stability, as high energy density demands thin SE separators, high current density, and high active material loading, all complicated by the need for intimate active material and inorganic SE contact [27,25,163]. paragraph_context: Dry electrode manufacturing technology has demonstrated signifi cant advantages in the fabrication of Li–S battery electrodes, particularly in terms of high sulfur loading, electrical conductivity, structural stability, and scalability [166,167]. This technique enables the production of electrodes with sulfur loadings of 7 mg⋅cm⁻² or higher, and can even achieve ultrahigh loadings such as 25 mg⋅cm⁻² [167]. Recent studies emphasize that high sulfur loading is essential for attaining higher energy densities [13]. Compared to slurry processing, dry electrodes significantly reduce cracking and delamination, thereby enhancing structural stability [166]. It has been widely reported that DP methods offer multiple benefits for Li–S electrodes. For instance, cathodes produced via the DP procedure exhibit superior performance in terms of electrode stability [166]. Furthermore, the use of PTFE fibrillation and R2R-DP procedure improves the conductive network and ion/electron transport, enabling high-sulfur-loading electrodes to maintain high specific capacity and stable cycling performance [13]. As an example, at a sulfur loading of 8.3 mg⋅cm⁻², the electrode delivers an initial capacity of 1363.6 mAh⋅g⁻¹ and retains 71.2 % after 100 cycles and even with a sulfur loading of 12.5 mg⋅cm− 2 , the initial capacity achieved is 966 mAh⋅g− 1 , demonstrating an excellent capacity retention of 88 % [167]. Dry electrodes also perform well under low electrolyte-to-sulfur (E/S) ratios, with pouch cells achieving an initial areal capacity of 14.2 mAh⋅cm⁻² and maintaining an energy density of 462 Wh⋅kg⁻¹ [13,167]. These advantages make dry electrodes particularly suitable for all-solid-state Li–S batteries (ASSLSBs), as the solvent-free process reduces reactivity between solvents and solid electrolytes, thereby improving safety [168]. DP cathodes with ultrahigh sulfur loading (up to 12 mg⋅cm⁻²) using fibrillated PTFE binder were assembled with an Al-mesh current collector and Li-metal anode into multilayer pouch cells (Fig. 10a) [169]. The cell with a total sulfur loading of 14 mg⋅cm⁻² delivered an initial areal capacity of 11.6 mAh⋅cm⁻² (equivalent to 829 mAh $\cdot g ^ { - 1 } )$ and exhibited stable performance over 40 cycles. The combination of dry electrode processing and an Al-mesh current collector effectively ensures robust cycling stability under high sulfur loading. However, despite these advantages, dry electrodes still face challenges related to swelling upon electrolyte wetting, which leads to a reduction in volumetric energy density. DP electrodes are prone to swelling, resulting in a 42 % decrease in volumetric energy density [170]. Further studies highlight that swelling in the DP procedure considerably undermines volumetric energy density in large-scale applications [171]. The same research also indicates that semi-dry electrodes can be optimized to improve conductivity and cycling stability, demonstrating enhanced performance at sulfur loadings such as 9 mg⋅cm⁻² and under high C-rate conditions [171]. In summary, dry electrode technology offers considerable benefits for Li–S battery electrode production, including high sulfur loading, enhanced conductivity, improved structural integrity, and good compatibility with ASSBs. Nevertheless, challenges such as swelling and reduced volumetric energy density remain and require further optimization to meet the demands of large-scale and high-performance applications. Additionally, PTFE-based dry electrode technology enables the scalable production of sulfur cathodes with exceptional ionic/electronic conductivities and mechanical resilience through its unique fibrous binder network, achieving high sulfur loading (2 mg⋅cm⁻²) and ultrathick electrodes (93 μm) with only 1 wt.% binder content [172]. This technology endows ASSLSBs with outstanding rate capability, cycling stability, and safety, demonstrating a high capacity of 9.2 mAh.

paragraph_context: Building upon its well-documented benefits in electrode fabrication, dry electrode technology further demonstrates significant advantages in the manufacturing of SEs by eliminating solvent usage, thereby avoiding decomposition of SEs and binder migration, while reducing energy consumption and cost. A key factor influencing the performance of DP SEs is the choice of binder and its fibrillation behavior. PTFE is widely employed due to its ability to fibrillate under shear mixing and hot calendering, forming a network that binds SE particles without solvents [25,173,174]. For instance, PTFE contents as low as 0.1–0.2 wt.% have been shown to yield mechanically stable and ionically conductive membranes [175,176]. Calendering loops significantly enhance PTFE fibrillation, improving interfacial contact and mechanical strength without severely compromising ionic conductivity [174]. Moreover, bilayer SE structures fabricated via the DP procedure can enhance both electrochemical stability and mechanical durability [174,175]. The DP procedure also enables the production of thin SE membranes (e.g., 15–50 μm) with high ionic conductivity—up to 6.5 mS⋅cm⁻¹ for sulfide-based SEs and 4.5 mS⋅cm⁻¹ for slurry-processed counterparts, indicating less degradation in DP films [25]. Oxide-based SEs like LLZO have also been successfully integrated into DP membranes, benefiting from their high mechanical and moisture stability [177]. Additionally, hybrid approaches involving ionic liquids or reconstructed surface layers (e.g., LLZTO@LiBF₄) further enhance ionic conductivity by converting insulating surface phases into conductive layers (Fig. 10b) [177]. However, the DP procedure faces challenges related to the non-conductive nature of binders like PTFE, which can impede Li-ion transport and react with Li-metal anodes to form electronically conductive interphases, accelerating side reactions and leading to cell failure [25,175]. The compatibility of PTFE with high-voltage cathodes and Li-metal anodes remains a concern, necessitating further optimization of binder chemistry and processing parameters [174,175]. Furthermore, although the DP procedure reduces binder content and avoids solvent-induced degradation, achieving uniform particle-to-particle contact and scalable production remains challenging due to the need for specialized equipment and precise control over fibrillation parameters [173,174]. In summary, while dry electrode technology presents a promising route for fabricating high-performance, solvent-free SEs with enhanced interfacial and mechanical properties, issues related to binder stability, ionic transport, and scalability must be addressed to enable widespread industrial adoption.

paragraph_context: From a theoretical perspective, dry electrode manufacturing tech nology has been extensively demonstrated to possess significant advantages in terms of environmental friendliness, economic efficiency, and performance. Furthermore, leading global enterprises, notably Tesla, are continuously expanding their investments in DP electrode manufacturing. The technology has already been validated through large-scale commercial application in Tesla’s 4680 batteries. Multiple factors indicate that dry electrode technology, as one of the key nextgeneration battery manufacturing technologies, is poised to capture a substantial global market in the future. However, despite numerous cases demonstrating its feasibility, achieving broader industrial-scale manufacturing still faces several challenges. Overall, the current bottlenecks in dry electrode technology involve material selection and optimization, equipment and parameter adjustments, as well as auxiliary systems and facilities. Among materials, the most critical aspect is the development of binder’s indispensable for dry-process electrode manufacturing, particularly the PTFE binder used in the mainstream fibrillation-based production technology. In terms of equipment, the most challenging component is the dry mixing equipment, as the uniformity of dry mixing directly determines electrode performance. Finally, regarding auxiliary systems and equipment, against the backdrop of rapidly advancing AI technology, computer-assisted optimization of dry-process electrode production is also crucial for the rapid industrial-scale manufacturing of this technology.

paragraph_context: The dry mixing process is critically important in dry electrode manufacturing as it fundamentally dictates downstream electrode fabrication and ultimate electrochemical performance. Unlike solventassisted methods, the DP dry mixing environment inherently constrains material distribution homogeneity, necessitating the blending of active materials (AMs), conductive agents, and binders in solid states [181]. This complex procedure is influenced by multiple variables, and insufficient homogeneity compromises electron/ion transport paths, increases internal resistance, and adversely affects charge storage capacity and cycling stability. Key challenges include particle segregation, the difficulty of achieving uniform distribution without substantial energy input, and the risk of performance variability exacerbated by powder handling [6,182]. Inherent limitations of mixing equipment manifest in four aspects (Fig. 10c): (1) under-explored material-equipment compatibility mechanisms; (2) elevated energy costs from high-intensity mixing; (3) severe material wear and tear in high-shear mixers or ball mills; and (4) a lack of a standardized analytical framework for the regulatory influence of equipment parameters in continuous systems. Optimization strategies focus on the coordinated control of multiple key process parameters in the dry mixing process. These parameters are interrelated and collectively determine the dispersion state and interaction effects of the three-phase components (active materials, conductive agents, and binders) during solid-state mixing. The core challenge lies in achieving an optimal balance between conductive network construction and binder fibrillation kinetics through precise regulation of these parameters, which is crucial for electrode functionality [72,74]. Specifically, systematic optimization is required for key variables affecting mixing energy input, shear force distribution, and material residence time. For instance, by adjusting equipment operating parameters and structural configuration, the fibrillation state of PTFE and dispersion of CB can be effectively regulated, both being critical determinants of electrode functionality [72,183,184]. Insufficient parameter settings lead to non-uniform component dispersion and increased interface resistance, while excessive processing may cause material degradation, over-dispersion of active materials, and capacity decay, ultimately compromising the overall electrochemical performance and mechanical integrity of the electrode [185–187]. Additionally, the spatiotemporal sequence of material introduction significantly affects the distribution pattern and interface characteristics of multiphase components, requiring optimization through systematic experimental design or mesoscale computational modeling approaches [188, 189]. Future development of dry powder mixing necessitates achieving coordinated regulation across multiple stages within an integrated process. Research should prioritize material-equipment interface engineering, intelligent systems integrating digital twins with machine learning, and hybrid processing strategies combining shear-impact mechanisms to enhance efficiency and sustainable manufacturing. Furthermore, to fulfill diverse industrial application requirements, it is imperative to establish systematic analytical models. These models will provide theoretical simulation support tailored to varying needs, thereby shortening the pathway from lab to scale-up. The continuous refinement of production technologies is essential in response to the urgent need for continuous production development.

paragraph_context: PTFE remains the predominant binder in DP electrode manufacturing due to its exceptional mechanical robustness, high postsintering crystallinity (>97 %), and inherent fibrillation capability, which structurally reinforces both AMs and conductive additives [16, 54]. Its unique fibrous network formation under minimal shear stress enables superior dimensional stability and aligns well with the requirements of stretch molding in dry electrode fabrication [52]. PTFE facilitates effective binder lean formulations (as low as 0.5 wt. %), enhancing electrode formability and minimizing active material fracture during calendering [190]. Moreover, its nanofibrillar structure improves electrolyte wettability via capillary action, contributing to enhanced battery performance [191]. Despite its advantages, PTFE exhibits significant drawbacks (Fig. 10d). Its nonpolar nature and low surface energy result in poor adhesion, leading to electrode delamination and inadequate wettability with electrolytes [24,192]. More critically, PTFE undergoes reductive defluorination at \~1.2 V vs. Li/Li⁺, producing LiF and causing irreversible capacity fade and mechanical degradation in anodes [54,178,193]. This degradation negatively impacts the SEI: the generated LiF compromises SEI stability, increases interfacial impedance, and exacerbates continuous capacity loss [54,74,194]. This side reaction is exacerbated during lithiation, compromising Coulombic efficiency and structural integrity. Although PTFE demonstrates relative stability in cathodes, it still participates in parasitic reactions, degrading the CEI and increasing impedance [141]. For instance, LiPF₆-based cells show thicker CEI layers than those with LiClO₄, indicating adverse interfacial reactions. Furthermore, PTFE’s fluorine-rich chemistry raises environmental concerns related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), necessitating careful consideration of its lifecycle impact [28]. To address these issues, future binder development must focus on reducing fluorine content to mitigate PFAS risks while maintaining mechanical and electrochemical performance. Optimized pre-fibrillation control and the integration of advanced processing techniques are essential for scalable production [23]. Emerging binder systems—such as bio-based alternatives (e.g., sericin) and functionalized polymers (e.g., carboxylated nitrile rubber, XNBR)—show promise in enhancing adhesion, cycling stability, and environmental compatibility [56,195]. Diversified binder systems can also mitigate the side reactions induced by PTFE that impair electrode performance. The addition of fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) facilitates the formation of a pre-protective SEI layer in graphite-PTFE systems, enabling the achievement of ultrahigh energy density while maintaining cycling stability and electrochemical performance [196,197]. The PVP/PTFE binder system not only helps mitigate the irreversible decomposition of PTFE and enhances mechanical properties to preserve electrode integrity, but also facilitates the formation of a robust PVP-induced Li N-rich SEI, leading to fast Li-ion kinetics and outstanding interfacial stability [198]. Moreover, binder-free technologies and sacrificial binders offer pathways to eliminate parasitic mass and improve ionic transport [199, 200]. Future efforts should also establish unified standards for binder-electrode compatibility across DP procedure and promote interdisciplinary approaches combining material innovation with eco-design principles.

paragraph_context: Computer-aided techniques significantly enhance the efficiency and performance of dry electrode manufacturing. By leveraging artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and high-throughput virtual screening (HTVS), these approaches optimize electrode microstructures, predict material properties, and accelerate the discovery of novel components (Fig. 10e) [9,179,201]. Generative AI models (e.g., Polaron tool) rapidly predict optimal 3D electrode microstructures from limited data and integrate Bayesian optimization loops to identify manufacturing parameters (e.g., porosity, active material ratio) that maximize cell-level energy density [179]. ML models (e.g., CATNet graph neural network) pre-trained on large molecular datasets enable efficient screening of functional materials (e.g., plasticizer FBN), improving ionic conductivity and interfacial stability in solid-state electrolytes [180]. These technologies address critical challenges in DP procedure, which reduces energy consumption by >46 % and costs by \~11.5 % but faces issues such as binder decomposition, particle fracture, and interfacial incompatibility [9,74]. Computer-aided tools overcome these limitations by predicting material behavior, optimizing process sequences, and designing multifunctional components (e.g., binders, electrolytes). Current limitations include data scarcity (for novel materials), high computational costs for high-fidelity simulations, and gaps between lab-scale demonstrations and industrial implementation [9,74,179]. Future progress relies on robust data-efficient algorithms and collaborative efforts to standardize datasets.

paragraph_context: This review systematically contrasts the core differences between conventional slurry-based electrode technology and the emerging dry electrode technology, emphasizing the significant advantages and substantial application potential demonstrated by dry electrode technology in the contemporary battery field. These advantages are concentrated in environmental sustainability, economic viability, and electrode performance. These technological advancements not only signify a shift towards greener and more environmentally friendly manufacturing paradigms in battery production but also suggest its potential to profoundly reshape the entire economic landscape of battery manufacturing. A deeper analysis of the application potential of dry electrode technology reveals its profound impact on the development of next-generation LIBs and the promising solid-state batteries. As clearly demonstrated by the industry benchmark Tesla through its successful large-scale implementation in the 4680 batteries, the achievement of industrial-scale production with dry electrode technology represents an inevitable strategic pivot in battery manufacturing. Comparative LCA research of the two electrode manufacturing routes further confirm that dry electrode technology excels in significantly reducing the overall environmental footprint of the production process. Its environmental benefits far surpass those of the traditional slurry-based process, particularly in the two critical dimensions of substantially lowering greenhouse gas emissions and effectively reducing energy consumption. Concurrently, LCA methodologies also need to be adapted and diversified to account for the unique manufacturing processes to meet the growing needs of industrialized dry electrode manufacturing.

Email: cuigl@qibebt.ac.cn Potassium (K)-based batteries are viewed as the most promising alternatives to lithium-based batteries, owing to their abundant potassium resource, lower redox potentials $(-2.97\mathrm{V}$ vs. SHE), and low cost. Recently, significant achievements on electrode materials have boosted the development of potassium-based batteries. However, the poor interfacial compatibility between electrode and electrolyte hinders their practical. Hence, rational design of electrolyte/electrode interface by electrolytes is the key to develop K-based batteries. In this review, the principles for formulating organic electrolytes are comprehensively summarized. Then, recent progress of various liquid organic and solid-state $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ electrolytes for potassium-ion batteries and beyond are discussed. Finally, we offer the current challenges that need to be addressed for advanced K-based batteries. fundamentals of organic electrolytes, liquid electrolytes, potassium-based batteries, solid-state electrolytes The clean and sustainable energies could relieve the environmental pollution and fossil fuel crisis. However, these generated energies are intermittent depending on the geographic location and weather conditions. Therefore, it is necessary to seek a large-scale energy storage systems (ESSs) for efficient storing and outputting the variable energy (such as, wind, tidal, and solar energy). Rechargeable batteries are the most efficient ESS to store and convert chemical energy into electrical energy. Lithium-based batteries, as one typical rechargeable battery, have dominated the markets of portable electronic devices, and electric vehicles in the past few decades.[1] Nevertheless, the scarce reserves and uneven distribution of lithium together with the increasing cost of cobalt also raise the concerns over sustainable supply, simultaneously, accelerate the research of alternative rechargeable battery. Potassium (K)-base batteries and sodium (Na)-based batteries provide an alternative solution, owing to abundant reserves of K and Na (2.3 and 1.5 wt%, respectively).[2] Moreover, the price of potassium and sodium carbonate $(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{CO}_3, \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)$ are considerably less expensive than $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ . Since both K and Na do not alloy with aluminum, the aluminum foil is employed as the anodic current collector, replacing the costly and dense copper in lithium-based batteries.[3] However, potassium-based batteries potentially offer numerous advantages over sodium-based batteries. First, K-based batteries are expected to provide a higher work voltage than sodium-ion battery (SIB). The lower redox potential of $\mathrm{K} / \mathrm{K}^{+}$ electrode $(-2.93\mathrm{V}$ vs. $E_0)$ than that of Na $(-2.71\mathrm{V}$ vs. $E_0)$ , which guarantee high-energy density. In addition, it has been confirmed the voltage of the $\mathrm{K} / \mathrm{K}^{+}$ in propylene carbonate (PC) is lower than $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ .[4] Then, K-based batteries could realize high-rate performance due to the high diffusion coefficient of $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ ions. Although potassium has the large atomic radius $(1.38\AA)$ , $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ has the smallest Stokes' radius (3.6 Å) in propylene carbonate (PC) solvents owing to weak coulombic interactions of $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ .[5] The first-principles molecular dynamics simulations also have proved that the diffusion coefficient of $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ in EC is three times than that of $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ .[6] In addition, it also revealed that $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ has the lowest solvation energy of $(397.5\mathrm{kJ mol}^{-1})$ in ethylene carbonate (EC), which favors a higher rate capability compared to $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ .[7] Furthermore, $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ could reversibly intercalate/deintercalate into or from graphite, which is the most used anode material for lithium-ion batteries.[8] On the basis of the advantages mentioned above, K-based batteries are most possible alternatives to lithium-ions batteries (LIBs).

paragraph_context: Recently, considerable progress has been achieved on K-based batteries. Specifically, these strategies are focused on designing high-performance cathode and anode materials, electrolyte, interface engineering, and electrode/battery configurations, etc. At present, vast electrode materials have used in K based batteries. For anode materials, carbon-based materials,[9] alloy negative,[10] transition metal oxides/chalcogenides and K or Na-K alloy anode[11] have intensively studied. Among the anode candidates, K metal has higher work voltage and specific capacity $(\approx 687\mathrm{mAh}$ $\mathrm{g}^{-1})$ . Moreover, K metal anodes can enable the application of potassium-free cathodes battery systems, such as, potassium metal batteries (KMBs), potassium superoxide (K $\mathrm{O}_2)$ , and potassium-sulfur batteries (K-S). Cathode materials for K-ion batteries involve four categories: Prussian blue (PB) and its analogues,[12] layered transition metal oxides,[13] organic redox-active molecules, and polyanionic compounds.[14] However, high-compatible electrolyte and optimization of interfaces are still in its infancy.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In battery systems, an electrolyte should possess high ionic conductivity, compatible interface, high chemical stability, large electrochemical stability window, ability to inhibit dendrites, and high electronic resistance.[15] Up to now, the reported electrolytes for K-based batteries can be divided into liquid and solid-state electrolyte (Figure 1A). As for liquid organic electrolyte, the most mature one for K-based batteries, the compositions are continuously optimized to cater new battery electrodes. For instant, the $\mathrm{KClO_4 / PC}$ solutions was first explored for the potassium-ion batteries (PIBs) applications.[16] Recently, $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ and KFSI salts are also widely investigated in PIBs. However, one of the main concerns of such organic electrolyte is narrow electrochemical stability window, leading to some undesirable side reactions at electrode/electrolyte interfaces along with the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).[17] The ideal SEI could prevent further side-reactions, and promoting uniform $\mathrm{K}^+$ diffusion, which is a recognized prerequisite for a metal or insertion/conversion anode. However, there are still several major problems for organic electrolytes, such as, lack of suitable salts and additives, unstable SEI, serious side reactions, high flammability, and K dendrites growth. To address the problems, various electrolytes such as, inorganic electrolytes, ionic liquid (IL) electrolyte, gel polymer, and polymer electrolytes are proposed. Nevertheless, these novel electrolytes suffer from low ionic conductivity at room temper ature, and their electrochemical performance for K-based batteries are almost blank. In brief, the booming development of K-based batteries will depend on the exploration of matching electrolytes, as well as, in-depth understanding of interface.

paragraph_context: As observed, organic electrolytes are the most widely used electrolytes in $\mathrm{Li / Na / K}$ -based batteries, owing to their unsurmountable advantages, such as, high ionic conductivity, good compatibility with electrodes.[18] Most organic potassium electrolytes are based on solutions of one or more potassium salts in mixed solvents, with a small fraction of functional additives. The solvents have two sides. On the one hand, organic solvents with high dielectric constants and low viscosity enable faster ion mobility and better interfacial wetness. On the other hand, the active reaction, the high volatilization and flammability of organic solvents pose a major safety hazard. Thus, the major challenge of organic electrolytes design is the option of solvents, additives and appropriate concentration. Accordingly, it is of great significance to reduce the amount of solvent for batteries. Gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs) could be considered as the special variation of liquid-type electrolytes, in which only a small fraction of polymer is employed as the mechanical host, and essentially swollen by liquid electrolytes.[19] Although they show improved properties in ionic conductivity and compatibility, the growth of dendrites still remained the serious safety concerns. Ionic liquid (IL) electrolytes exist as liquid state, and consist of organic anions and cations, coupled with soluble K salt.[20] The opposite ions are achieved by the thermal melting rather than solvation by solvent. They are demonstrated to possess excellent electrochemical and thermal stability, low volatility, and fire resistance. However, IL electrolytes have lower $\mathrm{K}^+$ conductivity at room temperature (RT) because of higher viscosity and charge transfer numbers.

paragraph_context: The effect of solvents on anode electrode performance has been widely explored. EC become indispensable ester solvent for a number of electrolyte properties. Meanwhile, the EC/PC-based electrolytes show more stable and compatible with graphite at low voltage. Wang et al. investigated the effect of three mixed ester solvents: EC/PC, EC/DMC, and EC/DEC on the electrochemical performance of graphite in K-ion batteries.[58] As shown in Figure 4A,B, the $1\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ in EC/PC electrolyte showed high coulombic efficiency and long cycle life. The authors inferred that the worse performance was related with the poor stability of DEC and DMC at low voltage, which also confirmed by Ponrouch and Kang.[59] Moreover, new battery electrodes would incur new electrolyte compositions. Guo et al. compared the electrochemical performance of red phosphorus (RP/C) alloy anode in EC/DEC and DME solvent, and demonstrated EC/DEC based electrolyte stabilized both K metal and RP electrodes for highly stable PIBs (Figure 4C).[60] Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicated that moderate solvation energy of KFSI based EC/DEC complex could facilitate $\mathrm{K}^+$ ion diffusion and desolvation on RP/C anode surface, and alleviate side reactions of electrolyte (Figure 4D). While Mai's group confirmed $\mathrm{Sb}_2\mathrm{O}_3$ -RGO composite using DME electrolyte exhibited lower energy exchange and migration barrier than other PC, or EC for K ions (Figure 4E).[61] Except for the traditional ester/ether-based electrolyte mentioned above, the new nonflammable phosphate ester electrolytes have been explored. For example, Guo et al. developed a new moderately concentrated KFSI/TEP electrolyte, in which K metal achieved a high average coulombic efficiency of $99.6\%$ and small plating/stripping overpotential.[62] An ideal salt for ambient rechargeable potassium batteries should meet the following minimal requirements, such as, high solubility, good electrochemical/chemical/thermal stability, low-cost, and non-toxic. Unfortunately, the kinds of K salts reported so far are rare. The common salts in K-based batteries include $\mathrm{KBF}_4$ , $\mathrm{KClO}_4$ , $\mathrm{KPF}_6$ , $\mathrm{KN(SO_2F)_2}$ (KFSI), $\mathrm{KN(CF_3SO_2)_2}$ (KTFSI), and $\mathrm{KCF_3SO_3}$ ,[39] and more research is focused on the applications of $\mathrm{KPF}_6$ , and KFSI.

paragraph_context: For $\mathrm{KBF_4}$ and $\mathrm{KClO_4}$ salts, the poor solubility $(0.05\mathrm{M})$ in typical aprotic solvents lead to the low conductivity of the electrolyte, limiting their potential in potassium based batteries.[63] In addition, $\mathrm{KClO_4}$ is rarely applied due to its strong oxidation. The high thermal stability and the passivation to Al foil make $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ based electrolyte be extensively studied. The major objective of $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ based electrolyte is adjusting functional solvents and additives, due to its moderate concentration $(0.5 - 1.5\mathrm{M})$ . Lu et al. significantly improved the cycling stability of graphite anodes applied a high-temperature precycling step to regulate the solvation structure of $\mathrm{K}^+$ -solvents in $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ based electrolyte.[64] However, $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ is extremely sensitive to oxygen and water, and easy to be decomposed HF, $\mathrm{PF}_5$ ,and $\mathrm{POF}_3$ . Imides (KFSI, KTFSI) as new-type potassium salts, are considered as the most advantageous for negative electrodes.[65] Specifically, Komaba et al. demonstrated the $3.9\mathrm{M}$ KFSI/DME realized the smallest polarization of $25\mathrm{mV}$ [66] KFSI/DME electrolyte could significantly improve the electrochemical performance of such kinds of electrodes, that is, carbonaceous material, alloy, and sulfide anodes by building highly stable SEI.[67] However, low concentration KFSI based electrolytes exhibit Al corrosion at potential of $\approx 4.0\mathrm{V}$ versus $\mathrm{K} / \mathrm{K}^{+}$ [68] Therefore, there is a long way to design optimal electrolyte for potassium based batteries.

paragraph_context: Currently, there are no specific potassium ion electrolyte additives. Fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) can improve the stability of solvent under high voltage, and at the same time, FEC can effectively improve the interface stability of hard carbon,[70] alloy anode with large volume expansion (such as, Si),[71] and high-voltage cathode[72] in LIBs and SIBs. Thus, the influence of FEC on cathode and anode in PIBs has also been studied. In 2017, the different effect of FEC on Prussian blue analogue (PBA) cathode in K half cells was investigated by Komaba et al.[73] The 2 vol% FEC additive based electrolyte could improve the initial coulombic efficiency of K-MnHCFe (from 61% to 90%), but the capacity retention was still low. Nazar et al. reported the similar conclusion that FEC enhanced the coulombic efficiency because it could not completely prevent electrolyte side reactions with successively consuming upon cycling.[74] Moreover, FEC additives play a negative role in most anode electrodes. In $\mathrm{K} / \mathrm{Sn}_3\mathrm{P}_4$ half cells, FEC accelerated the decomposition of the electrolyte, leading to greatly increased the polarization during cycling.[75] Similar electrochemical behavior also exists in graphite and $\mathrm{GeP}_5$ anode.[73,76] Apart from FEC, Komaba et al. systematically concluded the negative influence of well-known additives on K metal plating, including fluoroethylene carbonate (DFEC), vinylene carbonate (VC), and ethylenesulfite (ES).[66] For safer PIBs, Ming et al. first discovered that ethylene sulfate (DTD) was a promising additives, which made the electrolyte of $1.0\mathrm{M}$ KFSI in TMP more compatible with graphite anode.[77] It was concluded that the DTD had a stronger coordination capability compared to that of TMP solvent. Thus, the DTD could replace one proportion of TMP solvent and participate in constructing the first solvation shell of central $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ ions, thereby determine the interfacial behaviors of $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ -solvent on electrode interface, and affecting the graphite performance. In addition to these solvent-based additives, small amount of potassium difluorophosphate and blending salts have been developed recently.[78] Potassium-based batteries work in a similar rocking-chair mechanism that $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -based batteries do. In PIBs, generally, potassiated transition-metal compounds work as cathodes, and carbonaceous materials, such as, hard carbon, graphite, as anodes for charge storage (Figure 5A). The research of PIBs much fell behind the Li/Na based batteries due to the larger size of $\mathrm{K}^+$ and high activity of K metal. Until 2010, Yang et al. discovered the phenomenon of $\mathrm{K}^+$ intercalation in graphite based on molten KF electrolyte at high temperature.[79] Then, in 2013, Wu et al. developed the first potassium-oxygen batteries $\mathrm{(K - O_2)}$ (Figure 5D) in $0.5\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{KPF}_6 / \mathrm{DME}$ electrolyte with low charge-discharge polarization. The development of $\mathrm{K - O_2}$ is earlier than the discover of graphite anodes. In 2014, K-S batteries were discovered with ordered mesoporous carbon (CMK-3)/sulfur compounds as cathode paired with K metal anode.[80] In 2015, the storage performance of graphite in carbonate ester (EC/DEC) electrolyte was demonstrated by Komaba et al. and Ji et al.[81] Since then, various alloying, conversion anodes, and Prussian blue (PB), layered metal oxides, polyanionic compounds have been intensively investigated. In addition, there are numerous original works committed to designing advanced electrolytes and optimizing the electrode/electrolyte interface. These instructive works will discuss in the following sections. So far, KMBs (Figure 5A), potassium-sulfur/selenide (K-S/Se) (Figure 5C) have emerged as promising candidates for EES due to low costs and high specific energy density. However, during electrochemical processes, intermediate products are soluble and can shuttle across the cells, leading to low columbic efficiency, high self-discharge rate, and sharp capacity decay (Figure 5).

At present, most researches focus on either single cathode or anode materials in PIBs with potassium as reference electrodes. Second, the unstable SEI would accelerate parasitic reactions, then, lead to short low capacity retention and cycle life. Finally, the type of electrolyte limited. Therefore, the development of electrolytes is urgently needed. Graphite is the most used anodes for PIBs, thus, we review recent findings on it to understand the development of electrolytes.

paragraph_context: The electrolytes and interphases are inseparable, and closely interweave by electro/chemical reactions. As an indispensable part, the interphases on cathode and anode play a vital role in K based batteries, including the initial capacity fading, low coulombic efficiency, short cycle life, and safety. Therefore, the understanding of SEI formation, and dynamic change over cycles help solve the challenge of dendrite formation. For liquid organic electrolyte, a handful of solvents and salts including ethers, nonflammable phosphate, KFSI, etc., have emerged as promising for their ability to form stable inorganic SEI on the anodes. A drawback is that these components typically exhibit low coulombic efficiency and short cycle life. The LHCEs and perfluorinated electrolytes have been demonstrated as effective ways to improve the cycling performance, but highly fluorinated solvents and salts are deficient. Optimizing the electrolyte formulation, and artificial SEI, are effective ways to solve the challenge of SEI instability. For solid-state electrolyte, the poor interface compatibility and ionic conductivity should be given priority. Understanding the mechanism of formation, and dynamic features of the interphases are the guide for designing stable layers.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs), due to their ultra-high energy density, are attracting tremendous attentions. However, their commercial application is severely impeded by poor safety and unsatisfactory cycling stability, which are induced by lithium dendrites, side reactions, and inferior anodic stability. Electrolytes, as the indispensable and necessary components in lithium metal batteries, play a crucial role in regulating the electrochemical performance of LMBs. Recently, the fluorinated electrolytes are widely investigated in high-performance LMBs. Thus, the design strategies of fluorinated electrolytes are thoroughly summarized, including fluorinated salts, fluorinated solvents, and fluorinated additives in LMBs, and insights of the fluorinated components in suppressing lithium dendrites, improving anodic stability and cycling stability. Finally, an outlook with several design strategies and challenges will be proposed for novel fluorinated electrolytes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Over the past decades, rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have overwhelmingly dominated the energy storage fields, including electrical vehicles, wearable electronics, and aerospace since their commercialization in 1990 by Sony.[1,2] However, their unsatisfying energy density can hardly meet the increasing demands for high-performance rechargeable batteries.[3] Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have been considered as the "Holy Grail" due to the ultra-low redox potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode), ultra-high specific Science and Technology on Advanced Ceramic Fibers and Composite Laboratory capacity $(3860\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1})$ and low density $(0.534\mathrm{gcm}^{-3})$ [4-7] It is worth noting the LMBs was successfully constructed M. Stanley Whittingham in 1970s, which was about two decades earlier than that of LIBs, and commercialized by Moli Energy based on $\mathrm{LiI / MoS_2}$ in 1985. However, their further massive applications had been severely hindered by the safety issues resulted from lithium dendrites, which could penetrate through separators, leading to short-circuit, resulting into thermal runaway inside LMBs. Meanwhile, progressive reactions between Li and electrolyte lead to low Coulombic Efficiency (CE). Even today, the notorious lithium dendrites and inferior CE have not been effectively addressed, although tremendous efforts in modification of current collector modification, design of functional separators, and construction of composite lithium metal anodes, have been devoted.[8,9] Moreover, the energy density of LMBs is up to both the specific capacity of the electrode and the working voltage window according to the following equation:[10] $$ E = \int_ {V _ {\text {l o w}}} ^ {V _ {\text {u p}}} Q d v \tag {1} $$ Where $E$ represents the energy density of rechargeable LMBs, $V$ is the working voltages, and $V_{up}$ and $V_{low}$ represents the cut-off voltages during charging and discharging process, respectively. Improving the upper cut-off voltages during charge process not only induces additional specific capacity, but also broadens the operating voltage windows. However, high voltage brings about consistent decomposition of electrolytes, progressive dissolution of transition metal ions from cathode-electrolyte interphases, phase transformation near the surface of cathodes, and cracks or pulverization of the bulk cathodes, which are the main reasons for the degradation of LMBs at high voltages. Various surface coating and heteroatoms doping strategies have been widely adopted to engineer the cathodes for enhanced electrochemical performances, which improved the structural stability.[11-13] Electrolytes, sandwiched between anode and cathodes, are necessary as the media to transporting $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and pivotal in broadening the electrochemical stable potential window (ESPW), engineering stable electrode-electrolyte interphases, suppressing growth of lithium dendrites, and inhibiting the degradation of cathode at high voltages. However, commercial ethylene carbonate (EC)-based electrolytes show poor compatibility with both lithium metal anode and high-voltage cathode. To tackle the issues in LMBs, different solid-state electrolytes, polymer electrolytes, and liquid electrolytes have been widely explored, among which fluorinated liquid electrolytes exhibit huge potentials in high-voltage LMBs.[4,14-16] Introduction of F atoms into electrolytes not only highly improves their anodic stability at high-voltages, promoting the formation of LiF-rich electrode-electrolytes interphases, effectively suppressing the formation of lithium dendrites and decomposition of electrolytes at the surface of both anode and cathode, but also alleviates desolvation barrier of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , facilitating the homogeneously deposition of Li and enhanced electrochemical kinetics.[17-21] As a result, fluorinated electrolytes could significantly improve the performances of LMBs. To our best knowledge, there is no specific review comprehensively summarizing strategies of designing fluorinated electrolytes and insights on the fundamental understanding of their roles in high-voltage LMBs. Thus, in this review, we systemically reviewed the progress of the effect and beneath mechanism of fluorinated electrolyte, including various fluorinated solvents, lithium salts, and functional additives in LMBs. Specifically, this review focuses on the significant role fluorinated electrolytes play in lithium anode and high-voltage cathode. Furthermore, electrochemical kinetics and temperature adaptability of LMBs using fluorinated electrolytes are also included (Figure 1).

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Different from the intercalation/de-intercalation of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in/from graphite for LIBs, the electrochemical process of LMBs is based on the stripping/platting of Li via $\mathrm{Li^{+} + e^{-}\leftrightarrow Li}$ . Theoretically, the volume variation during the stripping/platting process is infinite, which is much higher than that ( $\approx 10\%$ ) in LIBs with graphite as the anode. Because of the ultra-low redox potential, almost all organic molecules are prone to be reduced by Li, forming organic-rich solid-electrolyte interphases (SEI) with poor ionic conductivity and inferior mechanical properties in LMBs using commercial EC-based electrolytes. Moreover, during the plating process, lithium dendrites form due to the low surface energy, which could penetrate the SEI, exposing fresh Li to electrolytes again, triggering the constant decomposition of electrolytes. The constant reaction between electrolyte and Li further result in inferior CE and inhomogeneous and thick SEI, exacerbating the lithium dendrites. In addition, during the stripping process, lithium dendrites may lose contact with the bulk anode, becoming "dead Li". All these issues are responsible to the unsatisfying performance of LMBs. It is crucial to fundamentally understand the mechanism beneath these issues before effectively overcoming these challenges.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Due to the ultra-low potential of lithium metal, organic electrolytes are prone to be reduced on the surface of the anode, forming a quasi-solid passive film, which was defined as solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) by Peled as early as 1979.[22] In LIBs, though Propylene carbonate (PC) has a wider liquid window than EC, EC, instead of PC, is widely used as the main solvent in the electrolytes because stable SEIs are constructed in EC-based electrolytes, inhibiting the co-intercalation of solvent into graphite, which is highly related with the exfoliation of graphite and the further rapid capacity fading. SEI is not only indispensable and necessary in LIBs, but also pivotal in suppressing the formation of Li dendrites, low CE, and poor cycling stability in LMBs.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: The ideal SEI need meet the following standards: high ionic conductivity, excellent mechanic properties, and high surface energy, all of which are highly associated with the structure and components of SEI. In order to describe the structural and component of SEI, several models, including vacancy, mosaic, multilayer, and monolithic models, have been proposed during the last decades.[22,25-27] Most of the model are proposed by speculation based on results derived from indirect characterizations, such as X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), Fourier Transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). It was not until in 2017 when Cui et al. adopted cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to directly observe the morphology of deposited Li and SEI outside Li.[24] It is worth noting that SEI in different LMBs using various electrolytes exhibit different morphologies or/and components. As shown in Figure 2a,b, based on extensive studies, Aurbach proposed the multilayer SEI model in alkyl carbonate-and DOL-based electrolytes.[23] In 2007, Cui and colleagues investigated the SEI in the commercial EC/DEC electrolytes using cryo-EM, and found that EC-based electrolytes are easily reduced by lithium metal, forming organic-rich SEI, including partially soluble semi-carbonates and polymers, forming a mosaic SEI (Figure 2c,d).[23] The fragile organic-rich SEI cannot stand the huge volume variation in the long-term Li stripping/ depositing processes, exposing refresh Li metal to electrolytes, resulting into the constant decomposition of electrolytes, which further lead to inferior CE, poor cycling stability and inhomogeneous and thick SEI. paragraph_context: conductivity and mechanical properties than that of inorganic components.[31,32] Moreover, the abundant grain boundary formed between inorganic components facilitated the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion, highly improving the ionic conductivity of SEI and therefore inhibiting lithium dendrite formation.[33] Recently, fluorinated electrolytes are overwhelmingly investigated in LMBs due to their excellent compatibility with both lithium anode and high-voltage cathode. These fluorinated electrolytes are susceptible to the reduction induced by lithium, forming LiF-rich SEI. LiF has both high surface energy and shear module (Table 1), guiding the deposition of lithium parallel to SEI, effectively suppressing the formation of lithium dendrites. Moreover, LiF has a high bandgap of $8.9\mathrm{eV}$ effectively separating electrolyte from lithium, avoiding the constant decomposition of electrolyte and thickness of SEI. Besides, the abundant grain boundaries in LiF-rich SEI facilitating the diffusion of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ,highly improving the electrochemical performance of LMBs.[8] On the cathode side, due to energy levels of Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO) commercial electrolytes are higher than those of cathode, cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI) is formed by reaction of electrolytes and cathodes, which prevent further decomposition of electrolytes.[34] Similar with SEI, the property of CEI is crucial to electrochemical performance of LMBs, especially at high voltages. At high voltages, both electrolytes and fragile CEI are vulnerable to the transition metal (TM) ions at high oxidative state, resulting into the excessive dissolution of TM ions, constant decomposition of electrolyte, and phase transformation and crack. LiF not only has excellent mechanical properties, but also shows superior anodic stability (up to $6.5\mathrm{V}\mathrm{Li}^{+} / \mathrm{Li}$ ), highly enhancing the stability of CEI. Thus, fluorinated electrolytes have also attracted increasing attentions in high-voltage rechargeable batteries.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: As mentioned above, lithium dendrite are the main obstacles hindering the practical application of LMBs. Therefore, fundamental understanding of the growth behavior of lithium dendrites is pivotal and the prerequisite to suppress lithium dendrites. Generally, there are two processes, i.e., nucleation and growth of Li, in the deposition of Li. The inhomogeneous deposition of Li usually leads to the formation of Li dendrites. Up to now, there are several models proposed to describe the formation process of Li dendrites, including surface nucleating and diffusion model, heterogeneous nucleation model, space-charge model, and Li-SEI model, among which space-charge model is widely accepted and applied to explain the growth process of lithium dendrites.[35-37] In the space-charge model, a rectangle cell consisting of two electrodes using same metal and dilute electrolytes was adopted as the model to investigate the growth of lithium dendrites (Figure 3a). In the steady state, the concentration of cation $(C_{\mathrm{c}})$ Figure 3. a) Schematic of the cell. b) Profile of ion concentration and voltage in the cells. c) Profile of ion concentration and voltage in the cells with different deposition times (solid line $100\mathrm{~s}$ , dashed line $10^{3}\mathrm{~s}$ , dotted line $10^{5}\mathrm{~s}$ ), Reproduced with permission.[35] Copyright 1990, American Physical Society. d) Profile of voltage at a current density of $2.61\mathrm{mA cm}^{-2}$ . e) Images of lithium during the deposition process in (c). f) Plot of the experimental Sand's times at different current densities. Reproduced with permission.[38] Copyright 2016, Royal Society of Chemistry. and anion $(C_{\mathrm{a}})$ decreased linearly with the distance and voltage remained constant in the main domain of the cell. Near the electrode (cathode), the concentration decreased to nearly zero along with the plunge of voltage (Figure 3b). The rapid decrease of voltage was ascribed to the depletion of ions, which induced a large space charge, leading to the inhomogeneous distribution of surface potential, resulting into the formation of lithium dendrites (Figure 3c).[35] The appearance of lithium dendrites is related with deposition time, that is, the "sand time $(\tau_{\mathrm{s}})$ " (Figure 2c), which was defined as follows: $$ \tau_ {\mathrm {s}} = \pi D \left(\frac {C e}{2 J t}\right) ^ {2} \tag {2} $$ Where $D$ is the diffusion coefficient, $C$ is the primary concentration of cation, $e$ is charge of cation (1 for $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ), $J$ is the current density, and $t$ is the transport number of anion. When $\tau > \tau_{\mathrm{s}}$ , lithium dendrites begin nucleating and growing. Moreover, $\tau_{\mathrm{s}}$ is invisibly proportionated with the square of current density, that is, the larger the current density, the smaller the $\tau_{\mathrm{s}}$ , the severer the lithium dendrites. In LMBs, the limit current density $J_{\mathrm{lim}}$ can be derived as follows: $$ J _ {\lim } = 2 D \frac {C}{L t} \tag {3} $$ When $J > J_{\mathrm{lim}}$ , lithium dendrites are prone to grow when the deposition time is larger than sand time, due to the additional space charge induced by the depletion of cations near lithium metal.[39,40] Bai et al. visualized lithium dendrites by optical microscope and proved the sand's behavior in lithium dendrites (Figure 3d-f).[38] Both sand time and limit current density are highly related with the electrolytes: on the one hand increasing the concentration of lithium salts leads to the improvement of the concentration of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in the electrolytes, resulting into larger sand time and limit current density; on the other hand, reducing viscosity of electrolytes and the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -solvent binding energy, and/or constructing conductive and stable electrode-electrolyte interphases by electrolyte design facilitate $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion, which also have a significant effect on sand time and limit current density, all of which can be achieved by design novel fluorinated electrolytes. Therefore, design novel fluorinated electrolyte is an effective strategy to alleviate the lithium dendrites in LMBs. Although great progresses on lithium dendrites have been made during the last decades, more investigation are also needed to elucidate the fundamental mechanism due to their complexity.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: As one of the indispensable components in electrolytes, solvents have significant effect on the properties of electrolytes: $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transfer kinetics, electrochemical stable potential window, operating temperature window, side reaction, and/or redox mechanism are all highly associated with the physiochemical properties of solvents.[41] In the commercial lithium-ion batteries, EC-based electrolytes have been widely used. Carbonate, including EC, Dimethyl carbonate (DMC), Ethyl Methyl Carbonate (EMC), and Diethyl carbonate (DEC) are prevailing due to their excellent overall performance in LIBs. However, these solvents show poor compatibility with lithium metal, which is the same for other solvents as such carboxylate ester, phosphate, etc. Moreover, some solvents, although show good compatibility with lithium metal, suffer from severe decomposition under high voltage $(\geq 4.3\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li^{+} / Li})$ . According to the frontier molecular orbital theory, for molecules, the lower their energy levels of HOMO are, the better the oxidation stability, and the lower the energy levels of Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital (LUMO) are, the easier to be reduced.[42,43] It is found that the introduction of F atoms into solvent molecules decreases their energy levels of HOMO and LUMO simultaneously.[37,44-45] As a result, fluorinated solvents are widely investigated to regulate EEI and strengthen the electrochemical performance under high voltages. Moreover, electrochemical kinetics and environment adaption can be highly improved due to fluorinated solvents. Given these advantages, in this section, we will comprehensively summarize the development of fluorinated solvents in LMBs.[46] Since carbonate (including cyclic and linear carbonate) are widely used recently, we first discussed fluorinated carbonates in LMBs. The molecules of popular carbonates and some of their typical fluorinated solvents are shown in Figure 4.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: One of the most representative fluorinated solvents is FEC. Aurbach and his co-workers found that FEC-based electrolyte not only improved stability of lithium metal stripping/plating at high areal capacity, but also largely enhanced the electrochemical performance of high-voltage cathodes in LMBs due to stable FEC-derived SEI.[47] Amine et al. further investigated the effect of FEC ratio on stabilizing lithium metal anode, and found that when the solvation number of FEC is $< 1$ , it is not enough to maintain the stability of the negative electrode, a reasonable ratio is still crucial though reducing the number of solvent molecules in the solvation sheath can improve the cycle performance of the battery.[48] To further address the issue of unsatisfied oxidation stability, Dong et al. added FEC to $1\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI/tetramethoxysilane (TMS) and discovered that by adjusting the addition ratio, the capacity retention of LiNMC811 cell was $86.1\%$ after 500 cycles with at high cut-off voltage of $4.4\mathrm{V}.$ [49] Later, Amine et al. investigated the effect of F atoms in cyclic carbonates on the electrochemical performance of high-voltage LMBs. As shown in Figure 5a, they found that, compared with EC, FEC alleviated the capacity retention of Li|NCM622 cells during long-term cycling. Moreover, difluoroethylene carbonate (DFEC)-based electrolytes delivers better electrochemical performance due to the more stable SEI with higher content of LiF.[45] Wang et al. not only investigated the effect of DFEC on regulating EEI, but also its function in improve the electrochemical kinetics, especially at low temperatures. As shown in Figure 5b, compared with other solvents, DFEC shown lower energy levels of LUMO and HOMO, indicating that it was PFPN  Figure 4. paragraph_context: As the source of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , lithium salts also have great influence on the performance of electrolytes. An ideal lithium salt should have the following merits: 1) high oxidation stability, 2) good solubility, easy dissociation, and high ion diffuse rate 3) anion itself is nontoxic and harmless and the reaction product is nontoxic, 4) chemical stability, 5) low cost. Lithium salts, such as lithium hexafluoroarsenate $(\mathrm{LiAsF_6})$ and lithium tetrafluoroborate $(\mathrm{LiBF}_4)$ alone cannot meet the needs of high-voltage LMBs, while lithium salts with balanced or outstanding performance have gained increasing attention recently, such as lithium hexafluorophosphate $(\mathrm{LiPF_6})$ , lithium bis (fluorosulfonyl) imide (LiFSI), lithium bis (trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI), lithium difluoro oxalate borate (LiDFOB), etc. The structures of lithium salts are shown in Figures 11 and 12a.[1,101-103] $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ has become a commercially lithium salt in LIBs due to its advantages of balanced oxidation resistance, ion migration rate and dissociation constant.[1] However, its further application of $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ in EC-based electrolytes in high-performance LMBs is limited due to poor low-temperature resistance, thermal and humidity sensitivity, inferior compatibility with lithium metal anode and high-voltage cathodes.[104-106] It was found that combination of $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ with different solvent systems, such as MTFP/FEC and FEC/HFDEC could improve the flame retardancy and oxidation stability of electrolyte by changing the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ [61,109] By dissolving $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ in the FEC/EFA mixed solvents, Yang obtained the electrolyte with good flame retardancy and low temperature performance. Due to the synergistic effect of solvents and salts, a uniform and compact F-rich CEI layer was formed (Figure 12b,c), which effectively reduced the decomposition of electrolytes. The capacity of the Li|NCM811 cells using $\mathrm{LiPF_6 / FEC / EFA}$ electrolyte was $74\%$ after 150 cycles (Figure 12d).[107] LiTFSI and LiFSI are imide-based lithium salts with excellent chemical stability, outstanding thermal stability, and good solubility, but with high reactive ability with Al foil current collector under high voltages.[1,110] Recently, LiFSI has attracted extensive attentions because of the overwhelming research on highly concentrated electrolytes, localized high-concentrated electrolytes, and weakly solvating electrolytes in LMBs. For instance, Yu dissolved LiFSI in FDMB with weakly solvating ability to construct electrolyte with a unique solvation structure (Figure 12e), which greatly improved the stability of Li metal anode and cathode. After 420 cycles at a cut-off voltage of $4.2\mathrm{V}$ the average CE and capacity retention of the Li|NMC cells was $99.98\%$ and $90\%$ respectively (Figure 12f).[87] Since LiTFSI and LiFSI are widely used in highly concentrated electrolytes, localized high-concentrated electrolytes, and weakly solvating electrolytes, which were discussed in the following section, in this section our discussion will not emphasize on them.

By regulating the concentration of lithium salts $(2\mathrm{M}$ LiDFOB+ $1.4\mathrm{M}$ LiBF $_4$ ), the life was extended to 200 cycles with a capacity retention of $80\%$ . Moreover, the nail tests showed that the safety of pouch cells using dual-salt electrolytes was better than those using other electrolytes (Figure 16b,c). However, the continuous consumption of LiDFOB eventually led to the failure of LMBs. Thin and stable LiF, $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{N}$ -rich SEI and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{SO}_3$ -rich CEI were obtained in the LMBs, resulting in enhanced cycling stability of NCM622||Li cells with capacity retentions of $80\%$ after 430 cycles at cut-off voltage of $4.4\mathrm{V}$ and $83\%$ after 100 cycles at high cut-off voltage of $4.5\mathrm{V}.$ [123] Meanwhile, Liu et al. developed a ternary-salt electrolyte composed of LiTFSI-LiPF6-LiFSI salts and poly (1,3-dioxolane) (PDOL) by in-situ polymerization. Consequently, Li|Cu cells delivered an average CE of $99.1\%$ during 450 cycles, and Li||LFP cells exhibit a capacity retention as high as $92\%$ after 500 cycles.[125] Besides introducing different lithium salts, researchers found that increasing the concentration of lithium salts in electrolyte had the following advantages: 1) promoting the coordination of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and reducing the number of free solvent molecules, inhibiting the side reactions; 2) improving the flame retardancy; 3) inhibiting dendrite growth.[126-128] However, the large-scale application of high-concentration electrolyte is limited due to the problems, such as increased viscosity, low ionic conductivity, high cost, and poor low temperature performance.

paragraph_context: Although the addition of diluents reduces the overdose of lithium salts, the prices of some diluents are even higher than those of lithium salts. In order to further reduce the whole cost of the electrolytes, low-concentration electrolytes (LCEs) and ultralow-concentration electrolytes (ULCEs) have emerged recently. It is worth noting that, due to the high molar ratio of solvents to lithium salt, there are usually high percentage of free ions and solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIPs) in their solvation structures, which is totally different with those in HCEs or LHCEs, exacerbating the corresponding electrochemical performance in LMBs.[134] To overcome the challenge, Wang, etc., prepared a novel ULCEs $(0.1\mathrm{M})$ by dissolving LiDFOB in $N$ -methyl- $N$ -methoxyethyl-pyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl) imide ([MEMP][TFSI]) ionic liquid and HFE (1:2, by volume). FTIR spectra and MD simulation results showed that the weak interaction between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and HFE led to the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ with obvious decrease of SSIPs (Figure 18a). The preferential decomposition of TFSI $^-$ and DFOB $^-$ resulted in formation of B-O/B-F, $-\mathrm{CF}_x$ , and N- species, enhancing the mechanical strength of SEI. Moreover, due to the good wettability brought by low concentration of lithium salts, the rate performance of the cell was also improved (Figure 18b). Consequently, NCM622||Li cells using this ULCE not only demonstrated a high capacity retention of $96\%$ after 100 cycles at voltage profile of $2.8 - 4.5\mathrm{V}$ , but also exhibited excellent environmental adaptability with a wide temperature range from $-60$ to $70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 18c).[135] Besides single-salt LCEs, Zheng, etc., reported a dual-salt low-concentration electrolytes (D4B) composed of $0.1\mathrm{M}$ LiDFP + $0.4\mathrm{M}$ LiBOB in EC/DMC (3:7, w/w), which led to the formation of LiF, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{BO}_x$ -rich SEI with increased the mechanical strength and flexibility. As a result, lithium dendrites were effectively inhibited with uniform and compact Li deposition (Figure 18d), and the Li||LFP cells using D4B provided an average CE of $99.8\%$ and a capacity retention of $95.4\%$ after 300 cycles at 1 C $(2.0\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2})$ (Figure 18e).[136] Later, a study on the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in LCEs demonstrated that by constructing a weakly solvation environment, the proportion of aggregates (AGGs) and contact ion pairs (CIPs) still dominated the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ even at low concentrations. Therefore, a low concentration dual-salt electrolyte composed of $0.3\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI and $0.2\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI in 1,4-dioxane (DX) was obtained by Pham DT, etc., Due to the increased proportion of AGGs and CIPs, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number $(t_{\mathrm{Li + }})$ reached to 0.72, and the content of conductive inorganics in the SEI layer was also highly increased, improving the ionic conductivity and alleviating the anode expansion caused by the decrease of concentration (Figure 18f). Consequently, LiLFP cells maintained $\approx 78.5\%$ of the initial capacity $(\approx 152\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{h}\mathrm{g}^{-1})$ after 400 cycles (Figure 18g).[134] Lithium fluoride salts have achieved great progresses in LMBs, though there are still no single lithium salts which can meet most of the requirements in LMBs. Thus, more work needed to be done via the following effective strategies: 1) develop new lithium fluoride salts, 2) study the synergistic mechanism between different salts, 3) explore the influence of salt concentration on solvation.

paragraph_context: Besides optimizing the solvents or solutes in the electrolytes, functional additives, known as 'vitamins' in batteries, also play a key role to boost the electrochemical performance with small content in the electrolyte (weight or volume ratio $< 5\%$ ).[137] Introduction of additives have profound effects on stable EEI construction, inhibition of lithium dendrites, improving cycling and rate performance, without obviously changing the properties or cost of the whole electrolytes. Thus, functional additives have been widely investigated in various types of rechargeable batteries, which were considered as an effective and facile strategy in constructing high-performance LMBs.

paragraph_context: In this review, we summarize the development of fluorinated solvents, fluorinated salts, and fluorinated additives in LMBs. In general, the effects of different fluorinated electrolytes on suppressing lithium dendrites, regulation electrode-electrolyte interfaces, improving high-voltage stability and broadening the operating temperature ranges are summarized and discussed in this article. First, in the section of fluorinated solvents, the design strategies, their working mechanism, and their effect on LMBs of fluorinated esters, including carbonates, carboxylate esters and phosphates, fluorinated ethers, including non-polar fluorinated ethers and weakly solvating fluorinated ethers, and other fluorinated solvents, including fluoroamide (sulfonamide), fluorosilane, fluorosulfone, fluorobenzene, and fluoroalkane, their working mechanism are thoroughly reviewed. Second, in the section of fluorinated salts, the recent advances of single-salt, dual-salt, triple-salts-based electrolytes, and fluorinated electrolytes with different salt concentrations are critically summaries. Moreover, various fluorinated additives, including of film-forming additives and deposition-regulating additives and their functions in LMBs are reported. This review not only provides the latest development about fluorinated electrolytes in LMBs, but also sheds light on the further design of high-performance in LMBs, which is indispensable for the commercial application of LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Generally speaking, compared with the traditional electrolyte, the oxidation stability and flame retardancy of the electrolyte can be effectively improved by fluorination of the components in electrolytes. Moreover, the electrochemical performances of LMBs are enhanced due to the robust LiF-rich interfaces generated during the cycle. Although fluorinated electrolytes have made great progress, further development still faces huge challenges: 1) Fluorinated electrolytes with satisfying properties for massive application of LMBs are still lacking. These reported fluorinated electrolytes still cannot address some common scientific problems traditional electrolytes face in LMBs, such as lithium dendrites, unsatisfying cycling stability in LMBs with limited lithium metal and electrolytes. These problems may be solved by reasonable molecular design, changing the electrolyte ratio, mixing a variety of solvents or solutes, and adding additives. But, new electrolyte systems also needed to be developed. Moreover, nowadays, design of new electrolytes mainly based on "trial and error" paradigm, which is time-consuming and inefficient, new paradigm based on artificial intelligence or big data seems more intriguing in designing new electrolytes. 2) Controversial reaction mechanism of lithium fluoride in electrolyte. In addition to the reaction mechanism of $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ , which was unanimously recognized as an earlier lithium salt, the reaction mechanism of other current lithium fluoride salts is controversial, which affects the selection of lithium salts in electrolyte configuration. The study of the reaction mechanism is helpful to further select the type and content of lithium salts in the electrolyte to obtain better performance LMBs.  3) The structure-property relationship between molecule structure of electrolyte, solvation structure, electrode-electrolyte interfaces and electrochemical performance has not been clearly explained. The significant influence of solvation structure on battery performance has been continuously mentioned in recent years, but it has not been widely explained. Moreover, the molecule structure of components in the electrolytes on the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , the effect of solvation structure in the electrolytes on the electrode-electrolyte interfaces, and the influence of electrode-electrolyte interfaces on the electrochemical performance, including cycling stability, rate performance, performance at low or high temperatures, have not been fully understood.  4) Commercial application of electrolyte. In the previous reports, only the effects of fluorinated electrolyte on the electrochemical performance, including cycle performance, safety issues have been taken into consideration. Cost and environmental issues during the production and usage process are negligible in most works, which is the key factors that limit the commercial applications.
