paragraph_context: Silicon has emerged as a pivotal candidate for next-generation high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) due to high specific capacity $(3579\mathrm{mAh}\cdot \mathrm{g}^{-1})$ , natural abundance, and cost-effectiveness. Compared to nano-Si, micro-sized silicon ( $\mu$ Si) anodes have historically struggled with significant challenges owing to more severe volume expansion. However, $\mu$ Si has recently regained substantial research attention owing to superior tap density and lower production costs. Electrolytes are pivotal in alleviating volume expansion and stabilizing the electrode-electrolyte interface, making their tailored design indispensable for addressing the inherent challenges of $\mu$ Si anodes from liquid to solid-state systems. This review first examines the intrinsic challenges confronting $\mu$ Si anodes and their corresponding electrolytes, proposing targeted design principles. Subsequently, recent advancements and optimization strategies from liquid to all-solid-state electrolytes in $\mu$ Si anode systems are comprehensively summarized. In contrast to liquid electrolytes, research on solid-state electrolytes remains limited and faces more pronounced challenges. Finally, the development prospects of different electrolyte systems for $\mu$ Si anodes are critically discussed, outlining persistent challenges and proposing comprehensive countermeasures. This review delivers insightful perspectives for accelerating the commercialization of $\mu$ Si anodes in high-energy-density LIBs, while also serving as a valuable reference for advancing other micro-sized anode material systems.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The rising global energy demand and diminishing fossil fuel reserves have intensified the transition to renewable energy systems. However, environmental intermittency challenges in hydropower, wind, and solar technologies highlight the critical requirement for advanced energy storage solutions.[1-5] Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), distinguished by their high specific energy, elevated operating voltage, and extended cycle life, have progressively found widespread applications in consumer electronics, telecommunications, electric vehicles, and grid-scale energy storage.[6-10] The energy storage mechanism of LIBs operates through reversible $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport and (de)intercalation processes between cathode and anode materials, enabling electrochemical energy storage and conversion (Figure 1a). A conventional LIB architecture comprises essential components: cathode, anode, electrolyte solution, porous separator, Cu current collector (Cu CC), Cu current collector (Al CC), and other elements (Figure 1b). Commercial graphite anodes are approaching their theoretical capacity limit $(372\mathrm{mAh}\cdot \mathrm{g}^{-1})$ , while the rapid proliferation of portable electronics and EVs demands LIBs with superior energy density and extended cycle life.[11-15] This has driven intensive research into alternative high-capacity anode materials.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Compared to other anode materials in LIBs (graphite, lithium titanium oxide (LTO), Sn), silicon (Si) stands out as one of the most promising anode candidates due to its exceptional theoretical capacity $(3579\mathrm{mAh}\cdot \mathrm{g}^{-1}$ for $\mathrm{Li}_{15}\mathrm{Si}_4)$ , tenfold higher than graphite.[16-19] Additional advantages include natural abundance, environmental benignity, and low electrochemical potential ( $\approx 0.4\mathrm{V}$ vs $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ).[20-23] However, Si anodes confront critical challenges including extreme volumetric fluctuations ( $>300\%$ ) during lithiation/delithiation cycles, resulting in particle pulverization, electrode structural degradation, and accelerated capacity decay.[24-26] Additional limitations arise from the intrinsically low electrical conductivity of Si, which impedes efficient charge transfer kinetics and compromises rate capability (Figure 1c).[27-30] Among Si-based anodes, micro-sized silicon $(\mu \mathrm{Si})$ has recently regained research momentum due to its higher tap density, reduced specific surface area, and lower synthesis costs, Figure 1. a) Schematic diagram of a typical battery system. b) Percentage by weight of each component of LIBs. c) Overview of basic properties of different types of anode materials in LIBs. d) Publications and cited frequencies result for topic keywords "micro/micron/micro-sized/microparticles silicon (μSi) anode & LIBs" and "Electrolyte & μSi anode & LIBs" on the Web of Science. offering greater industrial scalability.[31-33] Figure 1d demonstrates a surge in publications about the "μSi anodes and LIBs" keywords, reflecting their growing promise as next-generation high-capacity materials. Concurrent advancements in μSi anode and electrolyte studies underscore the pivotal role of tailored electrolyte engineering in unlocking their electrochemical potential. Despite these merits, μSi anodes face amplified challenges compared to nano-sized silicon (nano-Si) counterparts: intensified mechanical stress from larger volume expansion induces severe electrode cracking and particle disintegration, while the micron-scale dimensions hinder lithium-ion diffusion kinetics.[34,35] These problems collectively limit their practical implementation of μSi in LIBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To address these limitations and enable $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ commercialization, researchers have proposed multifaceted solutions, mainly focusing on the following aspects: First, structural engineering of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ : Designing 3D porous $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ architectures provides internal void space to accommodate volume expansion while enhancing lithium-ion diffusion pathways, thereby improving cycling stability and rate capability.[35-39] Second, elemental doping: Introducing metal or nonmetal dopants modifies crystal structure and electronic properties, boosting electrical conductivity and electrochemical reversibility.[40-42] Thirdly, functional binders: Advanced binders such as conductive polymers (e.g., polyaniline),[43,44] self-healing polymers,[45-48] ion-conductive polymers,[49] and bio-inspired polymers[50] enhance electrode integrity, reduce additive content, and mitigate mechanical degradation. Fourth, interface modification: Coating $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ particles with carbon layers,[51-54] flexible polymers,[55] or metal oxides[56] improves electrical contact, buffers mechanical stress, and suppresses parasitic reactions. Fifth, current collector modification: Surface-modified or conductive-coated current collectors strengthen electrode adhesion, preventing active material detachment during cycling, improving the stability and cycle life of the electrode.[57-59] Sixth, electrolyte design: Optimizing conventional electrolytes (solvents, lithium salts, additives)[60-62] or developing novel systems[63] (ionic liquids,[64-66] gel polymer electrolyte,[67-69] solid-state electrolytes,[70-72] etc.) stabilizes the electrode/electrolyte interface, mitigates parasitic reactions, and enhances ionic conductivity (Figure 2).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Electrolyte design exhibits complementary yet distinct characteristics compared to other optimization strategies, such as structural and interfacial. As a core chemical modulation approach, electrolyte engineering directly governs ionic transport efficiency and interfacial stability, with costs primarily concentrated in material development and formulation iteration.[39] The unique advantage of electrolyte design lies in its systematic compatibility – synergizing with elemental doping to regulate intrinsic material properties and enabling mechano-electrochemical coupling via binder-current collector innovations. However, its effectiveness is inherently limited by electrolyte physicochemical properties, necessitating integration with other strategies to overcome single-dimensional bottlenecks. Future advancements require balanced cost-performance integration: electrolyte-driven rapid performance iteration combined with structural/interface strategies for reliability assurance, forming a hierarchical multidimensional collaborative framework. This approach will propel high-capacity battery systems toward commercial viability through optimized performance breakthroughs and economic equilibrium.[82] Figure 2. label: 概述
paragraph_context: When serving as anode materials for LIBs, $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ and nano-Si exhibit fundamentally distinct interfacial behaviors due to size effects, necessitating differentiated electrolyte design strategies. Ultrahigh surface area of nano-Si induces severe electrolyte decomposition, addressed via high-concentration or solvent-selective electrolytes to limit free solvent contact and form ultrathin, dense SEI balancing ionic/electronic transport.[83] Nanoparticle agglomeration further necessitates electrolytes with molecular lubrication. Conversely, $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ suffers from bulk fracture during volume expansion, demanding electrolytes that rapidly generate mechanically robust, inorganic-rich SEI using reduction-stable solvents to suppress pulverization.[84] Fundamentally, nano-Si systems emphasize precise interfacial chemistry control through SEI stabilization, whereas $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ systems prioritize dynamic repair capabilities through mechanically robust electrolyte components. This difference is essentially driven by the interfacial kinetics and mechanical behavior determined by the material scale.[31] In liquid electrolytes, rationally designed electrolytes facilitates the formation of a robust SEI layer on $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ surfaces,[85,86] which effectively buffers the volume change of silicon, reduces the side reaction between the electrode and the electrolyte, and improves the cycle stability of the batteries.[87,88] Concurrently, optimized liquid electrolytes enhance ionic conductivity, thereby boosting rate capability.[21,60] For solid-state electrolytes, tailored architectures including polymer-ceramic composites and sulfide-based designoffer mechanical reinforcement to suppress electrode pulverization while enabling intimate interfacial contact for efficient ion transport. Such designs underscore the necessity of electrolyte optimization to unlock the full potential of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes from liquid to solid-state systems.

paragraph_context: In this work, we present a systematic review of electrolyte design engineering and optimization strategies for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes from liquid to solid-state systems. We initiate with analysis of the fundamental challenges confronting $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes and their compatible electrolyte systems, establishing targeted electrolyte design principles. Then we comprehensively summarize recent advancements in liquid, quasi-solid-state, and all-solid-state electrolyte technologies for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes. The challenges and optimization approaches for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes and their corresponding electrolytes evolve significantly when transitioning from liquid to all-solid-state battery systems. Additionally, we elucidate the commercial prospects, potential challenges, and strategic perspectives for achieving $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode compatibility with diverse electrolyte systems. This review provides fundamental insights and practical guidance for overcoming the practical implementation barriers of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes in different battery architectures, while offering valuable references for the development and application of other micron-sized anode materials.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Among silicon-based materials, $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ emerges as a promising candidate for next-generation anode applications due to its cost-effectiveness, superior tap density, high mass loading capacity, and exceptional theoretical capacity, collectively positioning it as a strategically advantageous alternative for high-energy-density lithium-ion battery systems.[31,89,90] Generally, the initial lithiation potential plateau for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes typically occurs at $0.1\mathrm{V}$ (vs $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ), corresponding to the coexistence of crystalline Si (c-Si) and amorphous $\mathrm{Li}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{Si}$ (a- $\mathrm{Li}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{Si}$ ) phases during lithiation. As the potential decreases below $50\mathrm{mV}$ , a- $\mathrm{Li}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{Si}$ undergoes phase transformation into crystalline $\mathrm{Li}_{15}\mathrm{Si}_4$ . During delithiation, crystalline $\mathrm{Li}_{15}\mathrm{Si}_4$ first converts to amorphous $\mathrm{Li}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{Si}$ , which subsequently dealloys to form amorphous Si (a-Si). Subsequent cycling involves reversible lithiation of a-Si and delithiation of crystalline $\mathrm{Li}_{15}\mathrm{Si}_4$ , as schematically represented by Equations (1)-(4).[91,92] Lithiation process $$ \mathrm {S i} (\text {c r e s t a l l i n e}) + x L i ^ {+} + x e ^ {-} \rightarrow L i _ {x} S i (\text {a m o r p h o u s}) \tag {1} $$ $$ \mathrm {L i} _ {x} \mathrm {S i} (\text {a m o r p h o u s}) + (3. 7 5 - x) \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} + (3. 7 5 - x) e ^ {-} \rightarrow \mathrm {L i} _ {1 5} \mathrm {S i} _ {4} $$ $$ \text {(c r e s t a l l i n e)} \tag {2} $$ Delithiation process: $$ \begin{array}{l} \mathrm {L i} _ {1 5} \mathrm {S i} _ {4} (\text {c r y s t a l l i n e}) \rightarrow \mathrm {L i} _ {x} \mathrm {S i} (\text {a m o r p h o u s}) + (3. 7 5 - x) \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} \\ + (3. 7 5 - x) e ^ {-} \tag {3} \\ \end{array} $$ $$ \mathrm {L i} _ {x} \mathrm {S i} (\text {a m o r p h o u s}) \rightarrow \mathrm {S i} (\text {a m o r p h o u s}) + x \mathrm {L i} ^ {+} + x \mathrm {e} ^ {-} \tag {4} $$ In recent years, the development of electrolytes for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes has attracted increasing attention. However, $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes and their compatible electrolytes still face critical challenges in practical applications. Below are the primary challenges and their analyses: 1) Intrinsic Limitations of Micro-Silicon Anodes: Micron-sized silicon anodes inherit the well-documented challenges of Si-based materials while introducing amplified complexities due to their larger particle size. During lithiation, anisotropic expansion arises from crystallographic plane-dependent $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion rate disparities spanning three orders of magnitude.[93] The local stress concentration caused by this is characterized by surface circumferential tensile stress and crack propagation.[94-96] Repeated cycling fragments micron-silicon into subcritical nanoparticles, accelerating active material delamination and persistent solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) growth.[97,98] Additionally, the extended $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion pathways within micron-scale particles, combined with silicon's inherently low diffusion coefficient ( $\approx 10^{-14}~\mathrm{cm^2\cdot s^{-1}}$ ), exacerbate polarization effects. This leads to fast-charging capacity decay rates over $40\%$ higher than nano-silicon systems, severely limiting high-rate performance.[99-101]  2) Electrolyte Compatibility Challenges: Conventional carbonate-based electrolytes (e.g., EC/DMC) form brittle SEI layers dominated by $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ and LiF, which fracture under silicon's volume fluctuations, resulting in Coulombic efficiencies (CE) below $90\%$ and cycle lives under 50 cycles. Ether-based electrolytes (e.g., DME/THF) address SEI flexibility through polymeric components, achieving CE values exceeding $99\%$ , but their low oxidative stability ( $<4\mathrm{V}$ vs $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ) precludes compatibility with high-voltage cathodes such as NMC811. Furthermore, their high volatility and flammability raise safety concerns.[87] Current electrolyte formulations struggle to reconcile competing requirements for $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ solvation structures: mechanically robust LiF-rich SEI, elastic polymer layers for strain mitigation, and suppressed hydrogen activity to prevent LiH-induced pulverization.[102,103] While additives like fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ partially mitigate these issues, they introduce cost escalation and parasitic side reactions.[104]  3) Full-Cell Integration Hurdles: The low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE: 70–85%) of Si anodes necessitates prelithiation strategies to offset lithium inventory loss, complicating manufacturing processes and increasing costs. Full-cell integration further requires electrolytes capable of withstanding oxidative decomposition at high-voltage cathodes ( $>4.3$ V for NMC811) while stabilizing the reductive silicon surface—a dual stability requirement unmet by existing formulations.[105–107] Although micron-silicon theoretically enables energy densities exceeding $340\mathrm{Wh}\cdot \mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ , practical full-cell cycling suffers from rapid capacity fade, typically retaining less than $80\%$ capacity after 500 cycles, significantly underperforming commercial graphite anodes ( $>1000$ cycles).[27]  4) Commercialization Barriers: Electrolyte strategies for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes exhibit significant disparities in production costs and environmental risks, critically influencing commercialization sustainability. Liquid electrolytes, dominated by carbonate solvents (EC/DMC) and $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ offer the lowest short-term manufacturing costs but carry hidden environmental burdens: Moisture sensitivity of $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ demands energy-intensive dry-room processing, while flammable/volatile solvents pose storage risks and potential soil/water contamination.[108,109] Hydrolysis-generated toxic HF further exacerbates ecological threats. Quasi-solid-state systems incorporating gel polymers or inorganic fillers increase material costs by $20 - 30\%$ but maintain compatibility with existing production lines. Residual volatile solvents and fluorinated polymer degradation products, however, complicate end-of-life management. All-solid-state electrolytes face higher costs from inert-atmosphere processing (sulfides) or high-temperature sintering $(>1200^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for oxides).[110,111] $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}$ emission risks of sulfides demand stringent encapsulation, while oxide production involves ecologically disruptive rare-earth mining. Though solvent-free, complex multilayer architectures hinder recycling, potentially creating novel e-waste streams.[90] In view of the above major challenges faced by $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode electrolyte, we need to carry out a reasonable design of the electrolyte to make up for its deficiencies, and promote the large-scale application of micron silicon anode in high-energy-density, long-cycle batteries. According to the characteristics of micron silicon anode, the design of electrolyte should follow the following core principles: Electrolyte design should prioritize the formation of self-adaptive composite interfaces to balance mechanical robustness and dynamic flexibility. By tailoring electrolyte components (e.g., salts, solvents, and additives), high-modulus inorganic layers should be preferentially formed to counteract expansion-induced stress, while elastic polymers or dynamically cross-linked structures should be integrated to accommodate volume variations.[112,113] This approach mitigates repetitive SEI layer fracture and active lithium loss.[104,114] Additionally, optimizing interfacial reaction pathways from thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives is critical to suppress brittle byproduct formation, ensuring long-term chemical and mechanical stability of the interface.[115] To address the large particle size of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ , solvation structure engineering is essential to minimize interfacial side reactions. For example, asymmetric solvation strategies can enhance lithium-ion transport efficiency while inhibiting solvent-induced surface corrosion. Rational regulation of electrolyte concentration and solvent polarity reduces direct contact between free solvent molecules and silicon surfaces.[116,117] Synergistic incorporation of functional additives further modulates interfacial chemistry, achieving a balance between efficient ion transport and side reaction suppression.[118-120] Electrolytes must exhibit mechanical responses compatible with silicon particle expansion behavior. For instance, In-situ polymerization or self-assembly techniques can be employed to construct conformal electrolyte layers that adapt to microstructural deformations, preserving electrode integrity.[121] Coupled with electrode pre-engineering (e.g., pore reservation or coating structures), electrolytes should synergize with electrodes to form stress-buffering networks, alleviating anisotropic expansion-induced interfacial damage while maintaining continuous electron/ion pathways.[122,123] While pursuing high energy density, electrolyte systems must align with the cost advantages of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ . Simplified film-forming processes and universal solvent systems should be developed to reduce scale-up complexity. Furthermore, compatibility with high-voltage cathodes (e.g., Ni-rich NMC) must be addressed through synergistic solvent/additive designs under wide voltage windows,[124,125] optimizing both energy density and cycle life in full-cell configurations.

paragraph_context: Beyond liquid electrolytes, developing compatible solid-state electrolytes for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes requires strategic design. Quasi-solid-state systems should balance "solid-liquid synergy" through gel polymer matrices with moderate crosslinking and nanoceramic fillers to simultaneously restrict silicon expansion and maintain ion transport.[126] Residual liquid components synergize with preformed LiF-rich SEI via solvation structure control and stress buffering. All-solid-state designs should employ rigid-flexible interfaces: sulfide electrolytes utilize gradient interlayers, while composites such as oxide-polymer combine viscoelastic adaptation with surface-functionalized nanoparticles to enhance interfacial stability.[127] Electrolyte design must transition from lab-scale research to practical application scenarios, emphasizing full-cell validation. Key evaluations include performance under high areal capacity electrodes, wide temperature ranges, and extended cycling conditions.[72,128] And safety engineering challenges require targeted solutions. Comprehensive optimization of multidimensional metrics (e.g., cycling stability, rate capability, safety) is imperative to bridge the gap between fundamental research and industrial deployment.[27] Electrolyte design for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes should adopt a multidimensional optimization strategy centered on interface engineering, supported by solvation regulation, grounded in mechanical adaptability, and guided by application requirements.[129-131] Future research may explore dynamic self-healing interfaces, novel solvent/salt combinations, and green fabrication technologies, providing theoretical insights and technical breakthroughs for high-energy-density, long-cycle-life lithium-ion batteries.

paragraph_context: Currently, commercial LIBs predominantly employ lithium hexafluorophosphate $(\mathrm{LiPF}_6)$ dissolved in carbonate-based solvents, which offers high ionic conductivity $(>10^{-3}\mathrm{S}\cdot \mathrm{cm}^{-1})$ and favorable electrochemical stability.[145] $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ is widely used in electrolytes for Si anodes due to its high ionic conductivity, moderate oxidation stability $(\approx 4.5\mathrm{V}$ vs $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+})$ , broad electrochemical window, and compatibility with organic solvents.[146] The $\mathrm{PF}_6^-$ anion serves dual functions as both a fluorine source and solvation structure regulator. Fluorine ions generated through $\mathrm{PF}_6^-$ decomposition combine with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ to form LiF (melting point $1040^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , elastic modulus $\approx 120\mathrm{GPa}$ ), which constitutes a critical rigid framework in the SEI to mitigate fracture caused by Si expansion. Concurrently, $\mathrm{PF}_6^-$ reacts with solvents to yield P/O/F containing inorganic compounds (e.g., $\mathrm{LiPO}_3\mathrm{F}_2$ , $\mathrm{LiPF_4O_2}$ ) that enhance SEI stability and ionic conductivity while alleviating internal polarization within $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ particles, thereby improving rate capability.[147] However, its poor thermal stability leads to decomposition at elevated temperatures ( $>60~^\circ \mathrm{C}$ ) or in the presence of moisture, generating corrosive HF that damages electrodes and current collectors, accelerating capacity fade and posing safety risks.[148-150] Moreover, conventional low-concentration $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ electrolytes form organic-dominated SEI layers prone to repetitive fracture/reconstruction during cycling, leading to continuous electrolyte depletion, lithium inventory loss, and impedance growth that severely limit battery lifespan.[151] To address these challenges, composite additives such as fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and vinylene carbonate (VC) are often combined with $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ to synergistically optimize the SEI composition, forming an organic-inorganic composite film to buffer volume stress.[152] For instance, FEC preferentially reduces to form an elastic polymer layer, which enhances SEI flexibility when combined with LiF derived from $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ .[153,154] Alternatively, employing concentrated $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ electrolytes forces increased $\mathrm{PF}_6^-$ participation in SEI construction, generating thicker LiF and $\mathrm{LiPO}_3\mathrm{F}_2$ layers that enhance SEI mechanical resilience against expansion while maintaining acceptable ionic conductivity despite elevated viscosity.[155] Although high-concentration electrolytes and additives partially mitigate these issues, practical implementation remains constrained by cost considerations, process complexity, and unresolved challenges in long-term stability - particularly under high-temperature operation or extreme cycling conditions.

paragraph_context: Common flame-retardant additives for lithium-ion battery electrolytes include: (1) Organophosphorus compounds: Acting through gas-phase radical scavenging and condensed-phase char formation. Representative examples include trimethyl phosphate (TMP), triethyl phosphate (TEP), and triphenyl phosphate (TPP).[230] (2) Nitrogen-based additives: Releasing inert gases (e.g., $\mathrm{NH}_3$ , $\mathrm{N}_2$ ) to dilute oxygen concentration. Typical materials include melamine (MA), melamine cyanurate (MCA), and ammonium polyphosphate (APP). While environmentally friendly, nitrogen-based additives exhibit poor electrochemical stability under high-voltage conditions. (3) Fluorinated solvents/additives: Reducing electrolyte volatility and radical activity through fluorine's high electronegativity and the main examples include FEMC, DFEA[231] and PFPE, etc. Perfluoropolyethers (PFPE) require blending with polar solvents due to low dielectric constants. (4) Composite systems: Synergistic combinations of multiple additives to balance ionic conductivity, interfacial stability, and flame retardancy.[125,209,213,232] At present, the addition of a single flame retardant additive may increase the interfacial impedance, so it is necessary to develop a composite flame retardant system. Not only that, flame retardant additives often need to be coupled with film forming additives (e.g., FEC) to balance recycling and safety. Jia et al. designed a non-flammable localized high-concentration electrolyte (LHCE) using TEP, LiFSI, and FEC (Figure 11a).[233] The electrolyte forms $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -TEP coordination structures and FSI-derived LiF-rich SEI layers, enabling $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes to achieve capacity retention of $>90\%$ after 600 cycles at C/2 rate (Figure 11b). STEM-HAADF revealed disordered layers and rock-salt phase formation in conventional electrolyte cycled NMC333 particles after 50 cycles. In contrast, LHCE-cycled NMC333 electrodes exhibited enhanced structural integrity with well-preserved layered morphology and suppressed rock-salt phase generation, attributable to stabilizing LiFSI-TEP polymerization at cathode interfaces (Figure 11c). Consequently, the electrolyte system achieved exceptional cycling stability under high-temperature and high-loading conditions. Yamada et al. have rationally designed a nonflammable cyclo-phosphate-based electrolyte system, with $0.93\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI in a solvent mixture of TFEP, FEMC and HFE (1:3:1 vol%).[234] By strategically controlling the reduction of cyclic phosphate compounds and lithium salts, this approach enables precise regulation of electrode-electrolyte interphase composition. This innovative approach facilitates the formation of a highly elastic yet mechanically robust inorganic-polymer hybrid interface on $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes, effectively accommodating severe volume fluctuations during cycling (Figure 11d). The TFEP-derived polymeric network synergizes with LiFSI-derived inorganic components to create a dual-functional SEI architecture combining elastic buffering and rigid support, while HFE suppresses solvent co-intercalation and parasitic reactions. Furthermore, the simultaneous establishment of a stable polymeric interphase on cathode surfaces empowers SiO||NMC622 full cells to achieve remarkable electrochemical performance, delivering an exceptional energy density of $\approx 590~\mathrm{Wh\cdot kg^{-1}}$ while maintaining capacity retention of $71.4\%$ and Coulombic efficiency of $99.9\%$ over 300 cycles (Figure 11e).

paragraph_context: In addition to the flame retardant additives described above, a number of other compounds have been reported as electrolyte flame retardant additives because of their flame retardant properties. Ionic liquids have extremely low vapor pressure, are nonvolatile, eliminate flammable gases from the source, can decompose and absorb large amounts of heat at high temperatures, and have high thermal stability and non-flammability, which enhances electrolyte safety. Polymerizable phosphate ionic liquids (PPILs) developed by Yi et al. form flame-retardant protective layers on $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ surfaces during lithiation (Figure 11f), demonstrating $92\%$ reduction in exothermic heat flow and showing significantly improved thermal stability.[235] Moreover, Fang et al. introduced (ethoxy)pentafluorocyclotriphosphazene with maleic anhydride additives, achieving non-flammable electrolytes for $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2 / \mu \mathrm{Si}$ graphite pouch cells with $78\%$ capacity retention after 300 cycles at 1 C (Figure 11g).[236] Flame retardant additives for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode electrolytes need to balance non-flammability, SEI compatibility and ion transport efficiency. Current research prioritizes phosphorus-based additives (e.g., TMP) and fluorinated solvents combined with other compounds to construct composite systems. Future directions should focus on multifunctional additives integrating flame retardancy, SEI self-healing capability, low toxicity, and cost-effectiveness, ultimately achieving synergistic enhancement of safety and electrochemical performance in $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based batteries.

paragraph_context: In lithium-ion battery electrolyte additives, conductive additives primarily serve to enhance ionic conductivity by increasing the free $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ion concentration in the electrolyte or optimizing the solvation structure, thereby reducing charge transfer resistance. They also mitigate the impact of volume expansion in $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes: during repeated expansion/contraction of silicon particles, these additives help maintain the integrity of the SEI layer, minimizing interfacial impedance growth. Consequently, selecting high-ionic-conductivity additives is critical for improving the overall performance of LIBs. Currently, typical conductive additives for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based anodes primarily include film-forming additives and lithium salts that simultaneously function as conductivity enhancers. For instance, film-forming additives such as fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and vinylene carbonate (VC) are widely employed.[237-239] Notably, VC alone exhibits inferior protective effects on $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes compared to FEC and is often used in combination with FEC. Additionally, lithium salts like lithium bis(oxalato)borate (LiBOB) and lithium difluoro(oxalato)borate (LiDFOB) not only participate in SEI formation by generating boron-containing compounds but also improve the ionic conductivity and thermal stability of the SEI layer.[223,240,241] In electrolytes, the incorporation of overcharge protection additives enhances the battery's resistance to overcharging, partially alleviating safety risks such as thermal runaway or explosion during overcharge conditions.[242] These additives operate via redox shuttle mechanisms, where they undergo oxidation at the cathode during overcharging, diffuse to the anode for reduction to dissipate excess charge, and/or decompose to release gases that activate internal current interrupt devices (CIDs). Furthermore, certain additives can undergo electrochemical polymerization at excessively high cathode potentials, forming a high-impedance film on the cathode surface to block electron transport. Commonly used overcharge protection additives include: (1) Biphenyl (BP): During overcharging, BP undergoes oxidative polymerization on the cathode surface, forming a passivation layer to inhibit further $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ intercalation. (2) Cyclohexylbenzene (CHB): With a high oxidation potential, CHB remains inert during normal cycling but consumes excess charge via oxidation at the cathode under overcharge conditions.

paragraph_context: Despite increasing research on $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode electrolytes, additive development faces technical challenges requiring innovative solutions. The inherent volumetric expansion of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ demands additives combining mechanical resilience with self-healing capabilities, while simultaneously addressing conductivity optimization, wide-temperature adaptability, and safety considerations. Future research directions emphasize synergistic additive combinations and practical evaluation in full-cell configurations to achieve dual objectives of high energy density and enhanced safety.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: In recent years, lithium-ion batteries have emerged as the dominant energy storage technology, with applications expanding into electric vehicles and grid-scale energy storage systems. However, conventional liquid electrolytes, despite their high ionic conductivity, face intrinsic limitations such as high volatility, flammability, and thermodynamic instability under thermal/mechanical abuse or overcharging conditions, which pose significant safety risks. In lithium-ion battery systems employing $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes, the dynamic interfacial incompatibility between conventional liquid electrolytes and silicon materials has become a critical bottleneck limiting the realization of their high-energy-density potential. While liquid electrolytes exhibit high ionic conductivity, their low viscosity, high fluidity, and intrinsic thermodynamic instability render them incompatible with the severe volume fluctuations ( $>300\%$ ) and dynamic interfacial evolution demands of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes.[245-247] First, the liquid electrolyte solvents fail to impose physical constraints on the expansion-contraction cycles of silicon particles, leading to repetitive fracture and regeneration of the SEI. The process triggers irreversible electrolyte decomposition and persistent lithium inventory loss. Second, continuous infiltration of liquid components (e.g., carbonate-based solvents, $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ into fresh cracks on silicon surfaces exacerbates parasitic reactions, catalyzing gas evolution, heat generation, and transition metal dissolution—a cascade of degradation mechanisms.[248,249] Moreover, the coupling effect between unrestricted lithium-ion migration in liquid systems and the heterogeneous deformation of silicon matrices induces localized current density distortion and lithium dendrite growth, compromising the intrinsic safety of batteries. The inherent "mechanicochemical mismatch" between liquid electrolytes and silicon anodes has become a critical bottleneck for realizing the high-energy-density potential of silicon-based systems.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To address these issues, researchers are transitioning from liquid electrolytes to quasi-solid-state electrolytes (QSSEs), which combine the mechanical robustness of solid matrices with the ionic transport efficiency of residual liquid phases.[250] This hybrid design enables adaptive interfacial stabilization while suppressing deleterious side reactions.[251] The solid-phase framework (e.g., polymer networks or inorganic scaffolds) physically constrains silicon volume changes and stabilizes SEI components through chemical bonding, whereas the residual liquid plasticizers maintain interfacial wettability and ion transport channels. Such synergistic mechanisms not only mitigate parasitic reactions but also regulate uniform lithium deposition, thereby enhancing cycling stability and safety. Furthermore, the development of QSSEs establishes a strategic synergy with the high-energy-density attributes of silicon-based anodes. The inherent solid-like characteristics of QSSEs enable compatibility with wider voltage windows and broad temperature-range operation, while their modular-designed matrix architectures allow flexible adaptation to the multiscale architecture design of $\mu$ Si-carbon composites.[252-254] As the degree of solidification is progressively enhanced, the electrolyte system transitions from passively enduring silicon's volume effects to actively regulating interfacial evolution dynamics.[255] This paradigm shift provides foundational technical support for achieving long-term cycling stability, intrinsic safety, and scalable manufacturing of silicon-based batteries, marking a pivotal technological inflection point that accelerates the transition of $\mu$ Si anode systems from laboratory prototypes to industrial applications.

paragraph_context: Song et al. pioneered a cyanoresin organogel electrolyte without the need of initiator or cross-linking agent via in polymerization of cyanoethyl polyvinyl alcohol (PVA-CN) with EC/DEC/FEC-based liquid electrolytes.[256] Compared to liquid electrolytes, the gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) demonstrated a certain buffering capability against $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ volume changes, facilitating the formation of a thinner and more homogeneous SEI layer and provided additional cohesion between silicon particles to maintain the integrity of the electrodes, even after pulverization (Figure 13a). The substantial volume fluctuations of silicon-based materials during lithiation induce pronounced particle displacement and electrode thickness expansion. Such irreversible structural damage during cycling leads to electrode integrity loss, unstable SEI layers, and active material detachment from current collectors. To mitigate particle migration and electrode cracking, Wang et al. engineered a supremely elastic GPE as an internal buffering strategy, which reduces electrode swelling during lithiation and facilitates structural recovery during degradation (Figure 13b).[257] The GPE comprises a copolymer of soft poly (tetramethylene ether glycol) (PTMG) segments and rigid $4,4^{\prime}$ -methylenediphenyl diisocyanate-ethylenediamine (MDI-EDA) cyclic domains, exhibiting exceptional elasticity (elongation at break $>2300\%$ , Young's modulus of $0.7\mathrm{MPa}$ ) and high ionic conductivity (Figure 13c). paragraph_context: Inorganic solid-state electrolytes (ISEs) represent a class of ion-conducting media entirely composed of non-liquid inorganic materials, such as crystalline or glassy frameworks, which enable efficient lithium-ion transport through well-defined migration pathways within their atomic structures. Based on the chemical composition and structural characteristics, the mainstream types of these electrolytes include oxides (e.g., garnet-type LLZO, perovskite-type LLTO, NASICON-type LATP), sulfides (e.g., LGPS, argyrodite-type $\mathrm{Li}_6\mathrm{PS}_5\mathrm{Cl}$ ), and other systems including halides.[296] The electrolytes exhibit distinct crystal architectures, ion conduction mechanisms, and physicochemical properties tailored for diverse electrochemical scenarios. paragraph_context: Oxide solid-state electrolytes (OSEs) exhibit core advantages in their exceptional chemical/electrochemical stability and wide electrochemical window ( $>4.5\mathrm{V}$ ), coupled with outstanding thermal stability evidenced by decomposition temperatures reaching $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which significantly enhances battery safety.[299] Their rigid crystalline lattice structure provides superior mechanical strength to suppress lithium dendrite penetration, while their air stability surpasses sulfide and halide counterparts, facilitating more manageable environmental control for scalable production. Nevertheless, oxide SSEs still face critical technical limitations. Primarily, their room-temperature ionic conductivity generally ranges from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-3}\mathrm{S\cdot cm^{-1}}$ .[300] Although certain crystalline materials (e.g., doped garnet-type LLZO) can achieve $10^{-3}\mathrm{S\cdot cm^{-1}}$ levels, this remains inferior to liquid electrolytes and sulfide SSEs. The brittle nature of oxides complicates fabrication of ultrathin electrolyte layers ( $<50~\mu \mathrm{m}$ ideal thickness), while conventional thick layers ( $>200~\mu \mathrm{m}$ ) compromise volumetric energy density.[301] Additional challenges include interfacial side reactions with silicon-based anodes (e.g., uneven lithium metal deposition), necessitating optimization through interfacial coatings or chemical bonding strategies.[302,303] Due to these mechanical limitations and interfacial compatibility issues, oxide SSEs currently find primary application in thin-film battery systems tolerant to volumetric strain. All-solid-state thin-film lithium batteries demonstrate promising prospects, characterized by extended cycle life, high energy-power density, low self-discharge rates, and versatile applications across specialized fields.[304] Within this developmental context, $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based materials have received comparatively less attention compared to their nano-Si counterparts in composite anode configurations with oxide SSEs, leaving the application of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based materials in oxide solid electrolyte as an area for further exploration and research.

Despite the advantages of thin-film silicon anodes, their production typically involves expensive and low-throughput vacuum technology, limiting their current use to niche applications such as miniature batteries and integrated circuits.[311] In SSEs, carbon is detrimental to the stability of the sulfide electrolyte since it promotes sulfide decomposition. Meng's group exploited the interfacial passivation properties of sulfide solid electrolytes to achieve stable operation of $99.9\mathrm{wt}\%$ carbon-free $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes (Figure 16f).[71] The fully lithiated $\mathrm{Li}_{3.75}\mathrm{Si}$ phase exhibits low hardness (1.3-1.5 GPa), enabling sufficient plastic deformation to form dense, low-porosity alloys while maintaining effective interfacial contact between the SSE layer and the porous delithiated Li-Si structure. The chemical-mechanical compatibility between sulfide electrolytes and Li-Si alloys facilitates effective dispersion of expansion stress, substantially reducing particle fracture. Quantitative analysis of volume and surface evolution confirmed the suppression of continuous interfacial growth and irreversible lithium loss. ASSBs incorporating these anodes demonstrated high areal current density, wide operating temperatures, and elevated areal loading, achieving $80\%$ capacity retention after 500 cycles with an average CE of $99.9\%$ (Figure 16g). The performance stems from optimized $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ /sulfide electrolyte interfacial compatibility and the unique chemo-mechanical behavior of lithium-silicon alloys, which mitigate stress concentration.

McDowell et al. correlated stress evolution with structural changes in alloy-based SSBs, revealing that particle size critically governs stress magnitude—smaller particles induce lower stress, thereby mitigating mechanical degradation (Figure 17a).[312] T. To address this, innovative electrode designs must simultaneously ensure fast lithium-ion conduction and strong bonding between Si and conductive coatings. Han et al. developed a self-integrated monolithic Si/MXene electrode with interfacial nitrogen engineering (Si-N-MXene), where nitrogen-functionalized layers promote stable SEI formation.[327] Applied to a PEO@LATP composite solid electrolyte (Figure 18c), the Si-N-MXene anode exhibits strong adhesion to the electrolyte with $\mu$ Si particles encapsulated by amorphous carbon and MXene featuring robust N-bonding. Consequently, Si@MgO@C anodes in SSBs exhibit smaller volume expansion compared to liquid-electrolyte systems (Figure 18i), achieving high initial Coulombic efficiency, elevated capacity, and extended cycling durability over 200 cycles. paragraph_context: CSEs integrate chemical compatibility and physical confinement to resolve $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode limitations. Chemically matched CSEs promote LiF-rich stable SEI formation, while multicomponent synergy buffers volume expansion stress to suppress particle fracture. Hierarchical architectures combining rigid fillers with flexible polymer matrices construct multidimensional ion transport channels, achieving high ionic conductivity.[284] CSEs support high-loading $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ electrodes and exhibit wide temperature adaptability $(-30$ to $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C})$ . paragraph_context: ASSEs fundamentally address $\mu$ Si expansion challenges but face amplified industrialization barriers at micron scales. Sulfide systems require nanoscale buffer layers (Li $_2$ S-Si composite interphases) on $\mu$ Si surfaces, where rough particle morphology (Ra >1 $\mu$ m) reduces atomic layer deposition process efficiency by 50%, escalating interfacial treatment costs to $15/kWh (vs <$2/kWh for liquid systems).[275] Oxide all-solid-state systems avoid sulfide sensitivity but demand electrolyte sintering temperatures (>1000 °C) incompatible with $\mu$ Si's oxidation threshold (400 °C), forcing multi-step low-temperature sintering with equipment investments exceeding $20 M. Even polymer-oxide composites suffer from interfacial delamination under $\mu$ Si expansion stresses, necessitating gradient modulus electrode architectures (surface-hardened treatments) that complicate manufacturing. Current all-solid-state $\mu$ Si cells cost ~$800/kWh (vs <$150/kWh for liquid systems), limiting deployment to niche applications like aerospace.[184] The application of all-solid-state electrolytes in $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode systems presents a dual landscape of promise and challenge. The integration of ASSBs with $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes theoretically enables dramatic energy density enhancement while leveraging the mechanical rigidity of solid electrolytes to mitigate silicon's volume expansion, thereby extending cycle life. Concurrently, the intrinsic safety of ASSBs (eliminating flammable liquid electrolytes) aligns with the demands of high-energy-density systems. However, the practical application of all-solid-state electrolytes in $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based anode still faces many challenges. The high interfacial impedance due to poor solid-solid interface contact severely restricts the ion transfer efficiency, especially under the high-volume change of the Si-based anode, the interface is prone to peeling or cracking, which exacerbates the capacity degradation.[252,309,318] In addition, process complexity (e.g., high-precision deposition technology, high-temperature sintering conditions) and cost in large-scale production limit the commercialization process.[335] Future progress hinges on breakthroughs in polymer-, oxide-, sulfide-, and composite-based electrolyte systems, coupled with advancements in interfacial engineering, ionic conductivity optimization, and scalable manufacturing. As material innovations and industrial ecosystems mature, ASSBs integrating $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes are poised to transition from lab-scale prototypes to commercial applications, emerging as a cornerstone technology for next-generation energy storage solutions that harmonize ultrahigh energy density with intrinsic safety.

paragraph_context: Therefore, we posit that persistent scientific exploration and technological innovation will soon enable the large-scale implementation of high-energy-density and safety-enhanced LIBs employing $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes. However, the practical deployment of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes across liquid, quasi-solid-state, and all-solid-state electrolyte systems continues to confront challenges of Si-based materials. Substantial research efforts remain imperative to advance optimization strategies for $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anode-compatible electrolyte designs in these three distinct systems. Future breakthrough directions should strategically focus on the following critical dimensions: 1) In liquid electrolyte systems, it is crucial to achieve innovative breakthroughs through synergistic integration and optimization of electrolyte components. This involves constructing a robust yet flexible composite SEI membrane by coordinated regulation of lithium salts, solvents, and functional additives. The strategy should be combined with interfacial optimization approaches including electrode architecture design and pre-lithiation techniques, to address the persistent SEI fracture caused by volumetric expansion of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes. Simultaneously, it must control the uncontrolled interfacial side reactions induced by liquid electrolyte fluidity. Achieving an optimal balance between electrochemical safety and extended cycle durability through these coordinated efforts will pave the way for industrial deployment of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based LIBs.  2) Quasi-solid-state electrolytes, which employ gelation strategies to strike a balance between liquid and solid-state characteristics, face multidimensional and intricately intertwined challenges that require systematic optimization approaches. A critical priority lies in achieving synergistic optimization of ionic conductivity and mechanical robustness through rational integration of functional components with complementary properties. Particularly noteworthy is the pronounced process compatibility challenge between QSSEs and $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes.[261] In addition to the electrolyte design, it is also necessary to combine advanced electrolyte formulation with interfacial engineering innovations, novel processing tech nologies, and electrode architectural modifications to achieve the process compatibility between the $\mu$ Si-based anodes and the QSSB systems. Once breakthrough advancements are achieved in addressing the interfacial challenges between ASSEs and $\mu$ Si anodes, the commercialization of $\mu$ Si-based ASSBs could be rapidly realized. 3) The exploration of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes in all-solid-state electrolytes remains at an early developmental phase, confronting multifaceted challenges that surpass those encountered in conventional liquid electrolyte systems. The critical issue stems from inadequate interfacial contact between ASSEs and $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes, leading to substantially elevated interfacial resistance and universally lower ionic conductivity compared to liquid-based counterparts.[280,317] Additionally, the intricate fabrication processes and technological complexities of ASSEs result in prohibitively high manufacturing costs for all-solid-state $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ -based batteries, hindering their near-term commercial viability.[272] Future advancements should concentrate on these interconnected research thrusts including interfacial engineering optimization, development of composite electrolytes integrating inorganic and polymeric components, and discovery of novel electrolyte materials with superior ionic transport properties.  4) The practical breakthrough of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes relies on the systematic coordination of electrolyte design and multidimensional modification strategies, with the core being the construction of a hierarchical "material-structure-interface-process" compatibility system. For example, the coupling of structural design and elastic composite electrolytes guides lithium-ion flux at mesoscale while dispersing volumetric stress. Elemental doping combined with interface pre-treatment techniques synergizes with electrolyte additives to optimize interfacial chemistry, forming dynamically stable SEI/CEI composite layers.[93] Simultaneously, integrated binder-current collector innovations enhance electrode mechanical integrity and coordinate with electrolyte transport networks to address mechanical-electrochemical coupling challenges during cycling. This collaborative paradigm extends to other micron-sized high-capacity anode materials such as Sn/Ge-based materials.[338] Through cross-material strategy transplantation (artificial interface engineering) combined with customized electrolyte components, micro-sized anode materials can overcome single-modification bottlenecks, achieving multi-objective optimization in energy density, cycle life, and safety.[272,339]  5) The synergistic industrialization of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ anodes and advanced electrolyte design represents a deep integration of material modification strategies and system architecture compatibility, requiring systematic solutions across material-interface-process-structure dimensions. In liquid and quasi-solid-state systems, interfacial stability between $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ and electrolytes is the primary challenge. However, compatibility with existing liquid battery manufacturing enables relatively clear industrialization pathways. Practical applications in pouch/cylindrical cells can be achieved through surface carbon coating, porous architecture design of $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ , combined with binder and electrolyte engineering, enabling breakthroughs in energy density. In contrast, ASSBs demand comprehensive system reengineering. While theoretically enabling energy density leapfrogging through high-compaction electrodes and $\mu \mathrm{Si}$ 's high capacity, practical implementation requires overcoming solid-state-specific challenges with interfacial resistance, stress accommodation, and manufacturing bottlenecks. Maintaining $>300\mathrm{MPa}$ constant pressure in pouch/cylindrical cells remains technically prohibitive with current encapsulation technologies. Current ASSBs development mainly focuses on prototype laminated cells, with structural designs relying on theoretical models and lab-scale validation. Scale-up requires breakthroughs in low-cost solid electrolyte synthesis and precision electrode-electrolyte integration. Future development may adopt dual-track evolution: short-term commercialization through liquid/quasi-solid systems with Si anodes and high-nickel cathodes, while all-solid-state batteries require collaborative research to resolve interface engineering and structural compatibility challenges, ultimately achieving lab-to-industry translation.

paragraph_context: Abstract: Non-flammable ionic liquid electrolytes (ILEs) are well-known candidates for safer and long-lived span lithium metal batteries (LMBs). However, the high viscosity and insufficient $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport limit their practical application. Recently, non-solvating and low-viscosity co-solvents diluting ILEs without affecting the local $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure are employed to solve these problems. The diluted electrolytes, i.e., locally concentrated ionic liquid electrolytes (LCILEs), exhibiting lower viscosity, faster $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport, and enhanced compatibility toward lithium metal anodes, are feasible options for the next-generation high-energy-density LMBs. Herein, the progress of the recently developed LCILEs are summarised, including their physicochemical properties, solution structures, and applications in LMBs with a variety of high-energy cathode materials. Lastly, a perspective on the future research directions of LCILEs to further understanding and achieve improved cell performances is outlined.

paragraph_context: Li metal, with a high theoretical capacity $(3860\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ $2061\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-3})$ and the most negative redox potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ vs. SHE), is a promising anode material for the next-generation high-energy-density batteries, i.e., lithium metal batteries (LMBs).[1] However, the lack of sufficiently protective solid electrolyte interphases (SEIs) on lithium metal anodes (LMAs) leads to low lithium stripping/plating Coulombic efficiency (CE) and lithium dendrite growth, which limits the lifespan of LMBs.[2,3] Moreover, the heat generation from the side reactions and internal short circuit, together with the conventionally used flammable electrolytes, result in safety concerns.[4,5] Among the strategies proposed to mitigate these issues, modulating the electrolyte design by selecting specific electrolyte components and adjusting their concentrations have been considered the most relevant, as it can tune the SEI formation, lithium deposition morphology, and electrolyte flammability.[6,7] Ionic liquid electrolytes (ILEs), i.e., mixtures of lithium salts and ionic liquids (ILs) consisting of bulky organic cations and anions, are well-known candidates for high-safety and long-livedspan LMBs.[8,9] A subclass of ILEs can be chosen from specific organic cations and anions that exhibit non-volatility and high thermal stability, greatly reducing the flammability for the corresponding ILE, thus enhancing the safety profile for high-energy applications.[10] The SEIs [∗] Dr. X. Liu, Dr. A. Mariani, Prof. Dr. S. Passerini Helmholtz Institute Ulm (HIU) derived from the organic cations and anions allow stable cycling of LMAs.[11-13] Moreover, the chemical diversities of the organic cations and anions offer multifarious choices of the ILEs enabling highly reversible LMBs with different high-energy cathode materials, e.g., Ni-rich layered/spinel oxides,[14,15] lithium-rich oxides,[16] cation-disordered rock-salt oxides,[17] sulphur,[18] and even oxygen.[19] Nevertheless, the insufficient $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport and high viscosity of the conventionally used ILEs with lithium salt mole percent of $\approx 10 - 20\%$ limit the operation of LMBs under practical conditions of high current density, e.g., $0.5\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ and high mass loading cathodes, e.g., $10\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , at room temperature (RT).[14,20] Despite the increased electrolyte viscosity, concentrated ionic liquid electrolytes (CILEs) containing higher lithium salt mole percent $(\approx 30 - 50\%)$ are reported to allow the operation of LMBs at higher dis-/charge rates, which results from higher $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ concentrations and improved $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference numbers caused by fewer organic cations and free anions.[21-24] Even though, the rate capability delivered with such CILEs is still inferior to those with conventional carbonate-based electrolytes,[16,22] due to the sluggish $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ mobility limited by the high viscosity. Moreover, the increased viscosity of the CILEs caused by the elevated formation of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -anion complexes severely hampers the wettability toward thick electrodes.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: The addition of low-viscosity co-solvents is an effective strategy to mitigate the high viscosity and sluggish $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ mobility of ILEs.[25-28] However, the early adopted co-solvents are involved in the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation and/or are unstable towards LMAs. Their coordination with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ releases more free anions, which decreases the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number and therefore, lead to unsatisfying rate capability at RT.[26,27] The instability of the co-solvent, e.g., dimethyl carbonate (DMC), towards LMAs lowers lithium stripping/plating CEs, particularly when they are involved in $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation.[29,30] Recently, non-solvating fluorinated ethers and aromatic molecules have been employed as new co-solvents to resolve the aforementioned issues,[30,31] which is inspired by a similar approach for concentrated electrolytes based on conventional organic solvents.[32-40] The strong electron-withdrawing effect of the fluorinated groups weakens the solvating ability of the co-solvents towards $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , and the consequent nonsolvating feature allows the dilution of CILEs with the local $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ coordination and elevated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number preserved.[29-31,41-44] The non-solvating co-solvents could promote the formation of more protective SEIs kinetically enhancing the stability of LMAs against the electrolytes.[30,31,41,45,46] As a result, the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport and fluidity of CILEs are promoted without compromising the CE of Li stripping/plating.[29-31,41-43,45,46] Electrolytes consisting of CILEs and the non-solvating co-solvents are named as locally concentrated ionic liquid electrolytes (LCILEs).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Compared with the locally concentrated electrolytes based on conventional organic solvents, e.g., carbonate esters,[40] ethers,[39] sulfones,[47] and phosphate esters,[34] LCILEs exhibit lower flammability and better compatibility toward LMAs.[31,45,48] On the other hand, the interaction of the positively charged organic cations with the other species in LCILEs is different from that of molecular, i.e., neutral, organic solvents in their locally concentrated electrolytes,[49-51] requiring extra attention for the design of LCILEs. Up to now, several rationally designed LCILEs with thoroughly improved $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport and decreased viscosity have been developed, allowing stable cycling of LMBs with high-mass-loading insertion-type cathodes, lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, and lithium-oxygen $(\mathrm{Li - O_2})$ batteries at elevated current densities.[30,31,42,45,46,52] Despite the remarkable progress and ever increasing attention, the research on LCILEs has not been reviewed to the best of our knowledge.

paragraph_context: Herein, this minireview summarises the recent progress of LCILEs to promote their further development for high-energy-density LMBs. Firstly, the influence of the non-solvating co-solvents on LCILEs' physicochemical proper ties that are critical for practical application is introduced. The ion-ion and ion-diluent interactions associated with the physicochemical properties in LCILEs are then classified and presented. The progress of LCILEs designed for LMAs and a few specific cathodes is also summarised. Lastly, a comment and perspective on future research directions is presented. The names and acronyms which will be used in this review for the organic cations, anions, and non-solvating co-solvents of the reported LCILEs are shown in Table 1 along with their respective chemical structure shown in Figure 1.

paragraph_context: Apart from the qualitative ignition tests, more precise determination of the flammability is given by the flashpoint tests. The American Occupational Safety and Health Standards defines that any liquid having a flashpoint at or below $93^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is a flammable liquid.[53] The occurrence of a flash requires enough vapour of the combustible liquids to be mixed with air for ignition. ILEs exhibit nearly zero vapour pressure, so a flash does not occur during the tests of their flashpoints, i.e., ILEs are non-flammable liquids. On the contrary, most of the co-solvents of the reported LCILEs exhibit flashpoints much lower than $93^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . According to the suppliers, the flashpoints of TTE, BTFE, OTF, dFBn, and mFBn are 27.5, 1.0, 45.0, 1.0, and $-12.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively. Surprisingly, despite the high content of flammable BTFE (around 30 wt.%) no flash was detected for $\left[\mathrm{LiFSI}\right]_{1}-\left[\mathrm{EmimFSI}\right]_{2}\left[\mathrm{BTFE}\right]_{2}$ and $\left[\mathrm{LiFSI}\right]_{1}\left[\mathrm{Pyr}_{14} \mathrm{FSI}\right]_{2}\left[\mathrm{BTFE}\right]_{2}$ in the temperature range of $25-300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .[48] But this is not the case for all the LCILEs. For example, the flashpoints of $\left[\mathrm{LiFSI}\right]_{1}-\left[\mathrm{EmimFSI}\right]_{2}\left[\mathrm{mFBn}\right]_{2}$ containing only 20 wt. % of flammable co-solvents was determined to be $98^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . This value is still above the threshold flashpoint $(93^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ for flammable liquids, so this LCILE is still classified as a non-flammable liquid.[45] But the occurrence of the flash indicates the necessity of flashpoint measurements to assess the flammability of the developed LCILEs.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: The most promising ILEs for LMBs usually employ $\mathrm{FSI}^{-}$ and/or $\mathrm{TFSI}^{-}$ anions, but these electrolytes exhibit poor wettability towards the commercially available separators based on polyolefin, e.g., polyethylene (PE) and/or polypropylene (PP).[54,55] The separators used for the early investigation of ILEs for LMBs were mostly made of glass fibre with large pores, leading to the formation of porous lithium depositions that easily penetrate across the porous separator and cause short circuit.[29,54] It is demonstrated that such an issue is effectively solved when the non-solvating co-solvents are introduced to ILEs. For example, Wang et al. reported that the contact angles of $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[Pip_{13}FSI]_2}$ and $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[Pip_{13}FSI]_2[TTE]_4}$ on commercial PP separators were $85.7^{\circ}$ and $24.9^{\circ}$ , respectively (Figure 2b).[41] The improved wettability has been also reported for TFSI- based LCILEs and PE separators.[30] The use of the well-wetted commercial polyolefin separators with more uniform micro-pores benefits the reported long-term dendrite-free cycling of LMAs in LCILEs.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: In addition, the wettability toward electrodes is also promoted possibly due to the decreased electrolyte viscosity in the presence of low-viscosity diluents. For example, Cai et al. reported that the contact angle of $\left[\mathrm{LiTFSI}\right]_{0.8}-$ $\left[\mathrm{DEMETFSI}\right]_{1}[\mathrm{OTF}]_{4}$ and $\left[\mathrm{LiTFSI}\right]_{0.8}[\mathrm{DEMETFSI}]_{1}$ on $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ electrodes were $51.3^{\circ}$ and $19.4^{\circ}$ (Figure 2c),[42] respectively, which is relevant for the use of thick electrodes.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: The viscosity of CILEs is effectively decreased when low-viscosity co-solvents are added. For example, the viscosity of $\left[\mathrm{LiFSI}\right]_{1}\left[\mathrm{EmimFSI}\right]_{2}$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is $67.5\mathrm{mPa}$ s, which decreases to $24.7\mathrm{mPa}$ s for $\left[\mathrm{LiFSI}\right]_{1}\left[\mathrm{EmimFSI}\right]_{2}\left[\mathrm{dFBn}\right]_{2}$ containing $22.9\mathrm{wt.}\%$ dFBn (Figure 2d).[31] Moreover, a higher mole fraction of the co-solvent leads to even lower viscosities. Nonetheless, it is not possible to indefinitely add a nonsolvating co-solvent to a CILE, differently from the solvating co-solvents which are miscible with ILEs.[28] The systems based on non-solvating co-solvent tend to reach a saturation concentration, and further addition of the co-solvent will lead to a liquid-liquid phase separation.[29,43] Among the currently reported LCILEs, $\left[\mathrm{LiFSI}\right]_{1}\left[\mathrm{Pip}_{13}\mathrm{FSI}\right]_{2}\left[\mathrm{TTE}\right]_{4}$ exhibits the lowest viscosity of $6.8\mathrm{mPa}$ ,[41] which is comparable to conventional carbonate electrolytes for LIBs.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: The room-temperature ionic conductivity of CILEs, fully consisting of ions, is mainly limited by the high viscosity. The decreased viscosity due to the addition of non-solvating co-solvents to CILEs is accompanied with increased ionic conductivity. For example, the ionic conductivity of $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1}$ $\mathrm{[EmimFSI]_2}$ and $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[EmimFSI]_2[dFBn]_2}$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is 5.28 and $8.84\mathrm{mScm}^{-1}$ (Figure 2e), respectively.[31] However, it should be noted that all the ionic species including $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , organic cations, and anions contribute to the ionic conductivity, while only the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport accounts for the operation of the LMBs. To estimate the contribution of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport to the ionic conductivity, i.e., the transference number of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , the Bruce-Vincent method combining the DC polarisation and AC impedance of Li/Li symmetric cells are frequently used.[56] In general, the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number of LCILEs is not lower than the corresponding CILEs,[29,30,41,46] which, together with the higher ionic conductivity of the LCILEs, indicates a faster $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ mobility of LCILEs than the corresponding CILEs. Nonetheless, the interfacial resistance is one order of magnitude higher than the ohmic resistance in the reported AC impedance spectra for the measurement of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number,[29,30,41,46] which could lead to high deviation.

paragraph_context: PFG NMR is also adopted to discriminate the contribution of the ions to the ionic conductivity. The self-diffusion coefficients of the ions in the electrolytes are directly obtained with PFG NMR, which already reflect the mobility of these ions. For instance, Figure 2d displays the measured self-diffusion coefficient of all the ionic charge carriers in $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[EmimFSI]_2}$ and $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[EmimFSI]_2[dFBn]_2}$ . [31] All the ions exhibit higher self-diffusion coefficients in $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1}$ , $\mathrm{[EmimFSI]_2[dFBn]_2}$ than in $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[EmimFSI]_2}$ . The concerned $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ self-diffusion coefficient increases from $1.39\times 10^{-11}$ to $3.48\times 10^{-11}\mathrm{m^2s^{-1}}$ , proving the enhanced translational mobility of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ . Such improvements are also observed for other LCILEs.[30,45,48,57] With the mole fractions and the measured self-diffusion coefficients of the ionic charge carriers, the apparent $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number can be calculated. The values for $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1[EmimFSI]_2}$ and $\mathrm{[LiFSI]_1}$ , $\mathrm{[EmimFSI]_2[dFBn]_2}$ are 0.13 and 0.12, respectively.[31] Therefore, introducing the non-solvating co-solvents to LCILEs does not significantly affect the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number. When this ratio changes, the transference number should be different. Since the non-solvating co-solvent has limited influence on the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number, the enhanced ionic conductivity indicates the faster mobility of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in LCILEs with respect to the corresponding CILEs.

paragraph_context: The solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ is not only relevant to the physicochemical properties of the electrolyte but also the interfacial properties, e.g., desolvation process and SEI formation.[58-60] When a co-solvent is added to an ILE, the mixture will contain $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , organic cations, anions, and co-solvent molecules. $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ could be solvated by the other three species. paragraph_context: Optimisation of LCILEs for superior battery performance is one of the core directions for further investigation of LCILEs, which includes selecting suitable electrolyte components and adjusting their concentrations. Different electrode materials manifest distinct interactions with electrolytes, imposing diverse requirements on the electrolytes. Therefore, the optimisation of advanced LCILEs depends on the specific cathode material, while considering the compatibility toward LMAs. Previous studies on the application of ILEs for different cathode chemistry for LMBs is insightful for the primary selection of organic cations and anions for LCILEs. Nonetheless, it is probable that the addition of non-solvating co-solvent may alter the findings of the study of ILEs via participating/affecting the formation of electrolyte/electrode interphases (EEIs). For example, $\mathrm{Pyr}_{14}^{+}$ is more stable than $\mathrm{Emim}^{+}$ toward LMAs in ILEs,[71] but the $\mathrm{Emim}^{+}$ -based LCILE shows improved lithium stripping/plating CE.[48] Therefore, revisiting the vast choices of organic cations and anions is expected to result in interesting outcomes that can inform on the design of ILEs. The ratio of lithium salts, ILs, and co-solvents has significant influence on the viscosity, $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ transport, and EEI formation. The enhancement of these electrolytic mediums relies on balancing these properties. However, current cells are studied/operated in far from practical conditions. Further development of electrolyte formulas for the cells under operando conditions, e.g., Ah-level cells with high areal capacity, lean electrolyte, and low negative/positive (N/P) ratio, are essential to attain practical application.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Apart from the electrolyte optimisation, studies exploring the electrolyte structure, dynamics and mechanisms as well as how their concentrations affect the electrolytes' physicochemical properties and EEI formation is equally important as this will guide the rational engineering of stable mediums. Although some physical determinations of LCILEs' solution structure have been obtained, how the mole ratio of lithium salts, organic cations, and co-solvents affect the ion-ion and ion-solvent interactions remains unknown. The strong interactions between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and anions can be sensitively characterised using Raman spectroscopy, but this is not the case for the weaker interactions, e.g., organic cations-solvents, and particularly, organic cations-anions. NMR can provide some insights, yet the observed signals need the support of theoretical methods including MD simulations to offer complementary explanations. Importantly, the rate capability of LMBs is not only influenced by the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport in the bulk electrolyte, but also the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport across the electrode/electrolyte interface/interphase. The former is intensively studied and its relation to the solution structure has gained some important insights, while the interfacial/interphasial $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport is much less understood. Further experimental and computational efforts to discriminate the respective contribution of the bulk and interfacial resistance, and to understand the interfacial transport process, including the de-/solvation process of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , migration across the EEIs, are required and could further promote the rate capability of the LMBs employing LCILEs. In addition, the difference of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation in LCILEs and their corresponding CILEs is very limited, but the resultant generated EEIs are likely unique. In this context, the combination of theoretical methods (e.g., density functional theory and ab initio molecular dynamics) and experimental techniques (e.g., XPS, differential electrochemical mass spectrometry, soft X-ray adsorption spectroscopy) can be utilised. Computational approaches that describe the complete electronic structure at the atomic scale can explicate the intricate interactions (including van der Waals, dispersion, hydrogen bonding, etc.) of LCILEs. The results can be made more intelligible when used in synergy with operando experiments such as neutron scattering which utilise non-destructive probes with high material penetration depth offering energy/frequency range along with spatial-temporal resolution. The formation, composition and evolution of interfacial dynamical processes at the EEI can be captured utilising in situ neutron scattering techniques (quasi-elastic, inelastic, etc.) which are sensitive to light elements (H & Li). Towards real-time determinations of LCILEs under operating conditions, neutrons could probe the relationship between structure and electrochemical performance in battery materials under operation. Such methodologies that combine theoretical and advanced experimental techniques will elucidate the functional behaviour of LCILEs for the development of the next generation high-energy-density LMBs.
