paragraph_context: The new energy market is growing rapidly, lithium batteries (LBs) as the most important source of energy supply in the energy storage and power market, has higher requirements for fast charge and long life, so it is necessary to improve the cell voltage and energy density of LBs. However, LBs with high voltage and high energy density will face serious challenges of electrolyte decomposition and electrode corrosion in high voltage environment. Herein, this review summarizes the effects of a series of sultones as electrolyte additives in high voltage electrolytes. It is found that DTD, ES, 1,3-PS, PES, PCS, MMDS, BDTD, BDTT, DTDph, ODTO, FPS, VES and other sultones have excellent properties on stabilizing SEI/CEI formation, inhibiting Generally, high-voltage lithium batteries (LBs) are distinguished by their upper-limit charging voltage, which varies according to different cathode materials. For example, nickel-rich ternary cathode materials can be classified into high-voltage (4.35/ 4.4 V) and normal voltage $(< 4.2\mathrm{V})$ LBs. The normal voltage batteries have a nominal voltage of 3.6 or $3.7\mathrm{V}$ , with a typical upper-limit charging voltage of $4.2\mathrm{V}$ . In contrast, high-voltage LBs have nominal voltages of 3.8 and $3.85\mathrm{V}$ , with corresponding upper-limit charging voltage of 4.35 and $4.4\mathrm{V}$ .[1] For ternary high-nickel or ultra-high-nickel materials, as well as binary materials, ultra-high voltage can sometimes exceed $4.6\mathrm{V}$ and even reach above $5.0\mathrm{V}$ .

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The notable advantage of high-voltage LBs lies in their high energy density, which extends the runtime by $15\%$ to $25\%$ compared to conventional batteries. However, under high-voltage conditions, the decomposition of cathode materials and the cathode-anode cross-talk become more severe, affecting the battery's lifespan and safety.[2] Therefore, high-voltage LBs have significantly different requirements for cathode and anode materials, electrolytes, and separators compared to conven- gas production, and good high temperature resistance. The preferential oxidation/reduction of sultones can protect the electrolyte from decomposition, and the uniform and dense SEI/CEI can also promote $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport, protect the electrode from corrosion, prevent the growth of lithium dendrites, and promote the insertion and removal of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , so as to improve the cycle life of the high-voltage battery. Therefore, sultones are very suitable as high-voltage LBs electrolyte additives to improve the performance of cells. This review can provide theoretical support for the design of high voltage and high energy density LBs electrolyte and selection of additives in the future. tional LBs, necessitating improvements and innovations in these areas.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the adjustment of energy structure, electric vehicles have gradually come into people's view, with pure electric vehicles (EVs) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) progressively occupying the market.[3] In recent years, the rapid development of EVs has placed significant demands on the performance of lithium-ion power batteries. The energy density of the battery determines the single-charge driving range and lifespan of the vehicle, while the safety performance determines the vehicle's operational safety. Direct evidence suggests that the development of high-voltage LBs is an important way to increase the energy density of batteries, as shown in Equation 1.[4] Where $E$ is energy density, $V$ represents operating voltage, and $q$ is battery capacity. Therefore, the development of high-voltage lithium power batteries with high-safety has become a crucial issue for the widespread adoption of EVs. $$ \Delta E = \int V \times q d q \tag {1} $$ Currently, the most frequently used high voltage cathode materials are lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxides (NCMs). Depending on the content of Ni/Co/Mn, NCM cathodes can be divided into two categories: low-nickel content materials such as $\mathrm{LiNi}_{1 / 3}\mathrm{Co}_{1 / 3}\mathrm{Mn}_{1 / 3}\mathrm{O}_2$ (NCM111) and $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Co}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.3}\mathrm{O}_2$ (NCM523), and high-nickel content materials such as $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.6}\mathrm{Co}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.2}\mathrm{O}_2$ (NCM622) and $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.8}\mathrm{Co}_{0.1}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.1}\mathrm{O}_2$ (NCM811). Another one is the spinel-type transition metal-doped compounds $\mathrm{LiNi}_x\mathrm{M}_{2 - x}\mathrm{O}_4$ among which the most typical one is $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Mn}_{1.5}\mathrm{O}_4$ with an operating voltage of up to $4.7\mathrm{V}$ and a specific energy density of $686\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ . Additionally, lithium-rich manganese-based cathodes such as $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_3\mathrm{-LiMO}_2$ (M=Co, Ni, Fe) also exhibit advantages of high voltage, high capacity, and good safety, etc.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The main components of electrolyte for high-voltage LBs are displayed as follows. (1) Lithium Salts: The common lithium salts include lithium hexafluorophosphate $(\mathrm{LiPF}_6)$ and lithium tetrafluoroborate $(\mathrm{LiBF}_4)$ , etc. Lithium salts are often used as a key component in electrolytes to provide ionic conductivity. (2) Organic Solvents: Common organic solvents include carbonates, esters, polyethers, and polymer electrolytes, etc. Organic solvents can effectively dissolve lithium salts, regulate the viscosity and solubility of the electrolyte, and also provide good ion transport properties thereby increasing the energy density and power density of the battery.[5] (3) Additives: to improve the properties and safety of high-voltage electrolyte, some auxiliary components are usually added to improve the performance of electrolyte. These additives can increase the stability of the electrolyte, prevent overpotential mutation, and inhibit side reactions on metal lithium electrodes. Different components and formulations are required for specific applications to adapt to particular battery designs and requirements.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In those existing NCM cathode systems, when the anode capacity reaches $1000\mathrm{mAh / g}$ , further improvements in the anode material yield minimal enhancements in energy density. In this case, increasing the battery's energy density can only be achieved by raising the cut-off voltage, which leads to the development of high-voltage batteries. However, conventional electrolytes do not perform well under high voltage like short lifespan and poor safety. Therefore, it is necessary to develop specific electrolyte formulations for high-voltage applications. The improvement of cut-off voltage is constrained by the oxidative stability of traditional commercial ethylene carbonate (EC) ester-based electrolytes. EC acts like a double-edged sword, while it forms an excellent solid electrolyte interface (SEI) film on the graphite anode side, it is also the most easily oxidized component in the electrolyte matrix which greatly limits the development of high-voltage LBs.[6] Fortunately, the battery performance can be enhanced at high cut-off voltages by regulating the solvation structures of the electrolyte or adding film-forming electrolyte additives to create superior CEI(cathode electrolyte interphase)/SEI films. These measures help to suppress side reactions of the electrolyte during operation, thereby improving the battery's performance under high cut-off voltages.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Sultones have known as esters that simultaneously possess $S = O$ and $S - O$ functional groups. There are many types of sultones, and to date, various sultones have been added to battery electrolytes as additives. The $S = O$ and $S - O$ bonds contained in sultones can undergo reduction or oxidation at the anode or cathode during battery cycling, forming SEI and CEI layers. Most sultones can alter the solventized structures of lithium ions, generating a dense and smooth interfacial layer. This leads to reduced internal resistance, faster charge transfer rates, and higher capacity retention. In general, sultones molecules can be categorized as monoester sultones, bis-sultones, side-chain sultones, etc., as displayed in Figure 1.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Ethylene sulfate (DTD), is one of the earliest monoester sultones used as an additive in electrolytes of high-voltage batteries. DTD can significantly improve the SEI interface and enhance the stability of anode. Although DTD has the advantages of accelerating ion transport, reducing internal resistance, inhibiting the growth of lithium dendrites, enhancing cycling stability, and improving battery capacity retention rate, DTD is more prone to discoloration and has insufficient safety performance.

paragraph_context: With the development of EVs and HEVs, the demand for high output power and endurance of lithium batteries continues to increase, and correspondingly the requirements for battery energy density continue to increase. In addition to choosing high energy cathode materials, it is also an effective way to improve energy density by making the power battery work at high voltage. The performance of high-voltage lithium batteries is mainly determined by the structure and performance of their electrode materials and electrolytes, of which electrolytes are very important. In general, with the increase of energy density, the compaction density of cathodes and anodes will increase, the insertion ability of electrolyte will become worse, and the retention rate of the liquid will be reduced, resulting in poor cycling and storage performance in the battery. In high voltage operating environments, there will be higher requirements for the electrolyte of power battery, so some special electrolytes with better oxidation resistance are needed. The electrolyte is often called the blood of the lithium battery, for one thing, the electrolyte is the bridge between the cathodes and anodes; Second, it is also a transport medium for ion migration. It is well known that additives are crucial to the development of high voltage electrolyte systems, and the solvation structure of the electrolyte can be changed by introducing some additives.

paragraph_context: Since 1996, sultones have been reported in the literatures as electrolyte additives. Because the sulfonic acid groups in the electrolyte can preferentially reduce and decompose to form an excellent SEI layer, they play an important role in the insertion ability of the electrolyte, the liquid retention rate, the transmission ability of lithium ions, and the protection ability of the solvent. In this review, all the sultones reported have excellent modification of high voltage or high temperature batteries based on their SEI/CEI formation ability, which can protect the solvent from decomposition under high voltage conditions, inhibit the formation of lithium dendrites and improve the battery life, and promote the insertion and migration cycle of lithium ions in the electrode, and improve the capacity retention rate under high voltage conditions. Therefore, this series of sultones can be used as a high voltage electrolyte to improve the performance of the battery, are particularly good high voltage electrolyte additives.

paragraph_context: Keywords: aqueous zinc-ion battery | iodide cathode | redox kinetics | zinc anode | zinc-iodine batteries Aqueous rechargeable zinc-iodine $(\mathrm{Zn - I_2})$ batteries have emerged as a promising energy storage solution, offering benefits such as affordability, high energy density, and enhanced safety. However, challenges like the thermodynamic instability of the iodine cathode and undesirable interfacial reactions at the zinc anode lead to issues such as slow redox kinetics, multiple iodide shuttles, and zinc dendrites. This paper reviews the basic working principles of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries, describes the scientific problems within the iodine conversion and zinc stripping-plating processes, and details specific strategies to solve the $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ battery problems with a focus on the electrolyte optimization. In view of the fact that aqueous $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries are still in their infancy, the review aims to provide insights for optimizing their design and advancing their real-world applications.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Serious environmental pollution problems and rapidly growing energy requirements have motivated extensive studies on electrochemical energy storage and conversion systems, targeting the applications in electric vehicles, portable electronics, and large-scale energy storage [1] (Figure 1A). Lithium-ion batteries, owing to their superior energy density and excellent cycling stability, have emerged as the dominant technology for energy storage applications. [3]. However, cost and safety challenges have severely hindered their further application. Currently, zinc serves as a key component in multiple battery systems, such as zinc-ion, zinc-air, $\mathrm{Zn - CO_2}$ , zinc-based flow, and flexible zinc batteries [2]. Compared with lithium-based batteries, zinc-based batteries exhibit superior cost-efficiency along with enhanced safety characteristics [4] (Figure 1B).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Within the family of zinc-based batteries, rechargeable aqueous $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries have become increasingly prominent in energy research due to their fundamentally secure nature, fast redox chemistry, and low cost [5, 6]. Iodine demonstrates competitive material costs in battery applications because of its abundant reserves in the oceans. Compared to bromine, iodine exhibits significantly reduced volatility, corrosivity, and toxicity. Notably, it significantly boosts the electrochemical performance by improving the conversion efficiency and reaction kinetics. Iodine can exhibit higher capacity with higher output voltage than previously reported materials of $\mathrm{MnO}_x$ , $\mathrm{VO}_x$ , organic compounds, or Prussian blue analogs [7].

paragraph_context: Numerous strategies have been developed to enhance the performance of zinc-iodine batteries, encompassing cathode framework engineering, separator modification, electrolyte optimization, FIGURE 1 | (A) Forecasted energy storage requirements (GWh) across energy storage systems, mobile electronics, and electric vehicles between 2020 and 2030. Reproduced with permission [2], Copyright the Royal Society of Chemistry 2024. (B) Comparison of zinc-based and lithium-based batteries in terms of multiple metrics. Reproduced with permission [2], Copyright the Royal Society of Chemistry 2024. and anode protection approaches, with substantial progress achieved in recent years. Despite tremendous efforts and achievements, the $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ battery system remains in the exploratory phase of research. The uncontrolled migration of soluble polyiodide $(\mathrm{I}_3^-)$ during charging process leads to a number of notorious side effects [8]. The redox products $(\mathrm{I}^{-} / \mathrm{I}_{3}^{-} / \mathrm{I}^{\circ})$ generated during electrochemical processes exhibit high solubility and migrate from the cathode-electrolyte interface into the bulk electrolyte, causing both excessive charge accumulation and diminished charge transfer efficiency [9]. Furthermore, $\mathrm{I}_3^-$ can autonomously and efficiently migrate across the diaphragm toward the $\mathrm{Zn}$ electrode, resulting in significant electrode material loss, deteriorating the storage capability, and self-discharge [10]. Therefore, such drawbacks hinder the practical deployment of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ battery systems (Figure 2).

paragraph_context: Various methods have been applied to inhibit the uncontrollable self-shuttling of $\mathrm{I}_3^-$ and the side effects at the zinc surface, such as confining polyiodide into porous matrix materials of functionalized porous carbon, graphene, and MXenes [11], which can facilitate redox reaction dynamics to a certain extent. Wang et al. introduced an exceptionally stable $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries with monatomic Fe-N-C embedded high specific surface area carbon (HC@FeNC) as a core-shell anode material [12], which can promote the $\mathrm{I}^{-} / \mathrm{I}_3^{-} / \mathrm{I}^{\circ}$ transition. $\mathrm{Fe - N_4}$ moieties establish dual chemical coordination and physical adsorption with polyiodides, significantly mitigating iodine shuttle effects through strong interfacial interactions (Figure 3A), resulting in a significant increase in Coulombic efficiency (Figure 3B,C). Hydrogel electrolytes or highly concentrated electrolytes can also be constructed to solve such problems. Ji et al. developed an advanced $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ electrochemical storage system based on hydrothermally reduced graphene oxide (rGO) and a salt-packed aqueous electrolyte with a high concentration of zinc chloride [13]. The three-dimensional microporous structure and excellent electrical conductivity of rGO synergistically enhance iodine utilization efficiency. The salt-packed aqueous electrolyte effectively mitigates triiodide diffusion as shown by the UV spectra (Figure 3D), enabling stable electrochemical cycling over 2000 cycles at $50\mathrm{mA}$ $\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ (Figure 3E).

paragraph_context: This article offers an in-depth survey of advances in $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries, focusing on the electrochemistry and operation mechanism of iodine conversion. The fundamentals of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries operation are first presented, and the cathodic iodine redox transitions, the electrochemistry of the zinc negative electrode, and the scientific issues facing $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries are discussed in detail. This analysis aims to establish a foundational framework for $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ battery optimization via electrolyte design, while inspiring innovative approaches toward high-energy-density $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ battery configurations [14].

paragraph_context: The redox processes in lithium-iodine and sodium-iodine batteries exhibit notable distinctions. paragraph_context: Generally, the kinetics of iodine redox reactions are slow, which can be attributed to the two dominant factors: sluggish charge transfer kinetics and impeded mass transfer [35]. Most studies have used carbon-based materials as the $\mathrm{I}_2$ body. paragraph_context: As sustainable energy storage candidates, aqueous $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries have recently garnered substantial scientific interest due to their inherent advantages in safety and cost-effectiveness. However, this technology still faces many challenges in its commercial application, which greatly restricts its further development. For example, zinc anodes are prone to dendrite growth [70], HER [71], corrosion, and passivation. During the charging and discharging cycle, the zinc-related issues not only affect the cycle stability and battery charge-discharge efficiency, but also may cause battery short circuit and safety hazards [72]. At the same time, iodine cathodes also have a series of problems, such as poor thermal stability [73], insufficient conductivity [74], and polyiodine shuttle effect [75]. This phenomenon detrimentally compromises the battery's energy density and long-term cycling stability. In recent years, to overcome the above problems, researchers have been committed to comprehensively regulating and optimizing different components such as positive electrode [76], negative electrode [77], separator [78], and electrolyte [79]. In these studies, the optimization of electrolytes is considered to be a key breakthrough because it directly affects the ion transport in the electrolytes and the kinetics of electrode reactions. Furthermore, strategic modulation of electrolytes' ionic composition and transport characteristics enables interfacial stabilization between active materials and ionic conductors, which synergistically enhances the cell's electrochemical efficiency and functional durability.

paragraph_context: The introduction of additives has been shown to significantly improve the performance of zinc batteries, especially in inhibiting zinc dendrites. Inorganic additives (such as specific metal salts, oxides, and acidic substances) usually inhibit dendrite growth by enhancing electrolyte polarizability, regulating electric field distribution, and controlling zinc deposition morphology; while organic additives optimize electrolyte performance by constructing electrostatic shielding effects, adjusting solvation structures, and reducing zinc ion diffusion rates. For instance, some organic molecular additives can improve the solvation configuration of zinc ions through chemical reactions, while inhibiting HER, reducing the generation of side products and improving the overall performance of batteries. Inorganic additives are often used to increase electrolyte stability, slow down zinc anode corrosion, and enhance zinc deposition quality.

paragraph_context: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled data analytics has revolutionized the discovery path for high-performance electrolyte additives since 2018, with machine learning (ML) algorithms reducing screening cycles from months to days in advanced battery systems. By analyzing the correlation between molecular structure and performance, candidate substances with dendrite inhibition potential can be quickly pre-selected, significantly reducing the blindness of experimental verification; at the same time, concentration prediction models based on machine learning can optimize the additive ratio and balance the synergistic relationship between dendrite inhibition and battery internal resistance.

paragraph_context: However, the type and concentration of additives need to be precisely controlled to avoid introducing new side effects, for example, although some inorganic additives can inhibit dendrite formation, they may lead to uneven zinc deposition or increase the internal resistance of the battery. By establishing an additive concentration-performance mapping relationship, the matching window between the critical micelle concentration (CMC) and the viscosity threshold can be optimized to achieve the synergistic goal of "inhibiting dendrites-reducing internal resistance." The role of electrolytes in zinc-iodine batteries far exceeds that of ordinary ionic conductive media. It determines the uniformity of zinc electrodeposition, the suppression of zinc dendrites, and the cycle stability of batteries. Although the electrolyte of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ battery usually adopts water-based solution, different components, concentrations, and additives of electrolyte will significantly affect the performance of battery. Electrolyte optimization is closely linked to both enhancing battery charging/discharging efficiency and achieving prolonged cycle life alongside high energy density. The main function of electrolyte is to promote the efficient conduction of zinc ions, while reducing the growth of zinc dendrites and the appearance of electrolyte side reactions. Therefore, how to design and optimize electrolyte to solve these problems has become one of the core problems in the research of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries.

paragraph_context: Electrolyte concentration is another key factor affecting the performance of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries. High-concentration electrolytes can provide more zinc ions, thereby promoting the increase of battery energy density and updating the quality of zinc electrodeposition to a certain extent. High-concentration electrolytes help to optimize the compactness of zinc deposition, prevent the growth of zinc dendrites, and reduce the corrosion of the zinc anode. However, too high electrolyte concentration also brings some negative effects. For example, too high a concentration increases the viscosity of the electrolyte, reduces the diffusion rate of zinc ions, decreases ionic conductivity, which is not conducive to a fast charge or discharge process. Therefore, how to ensure the ionic conductivity and fluidity of the electrolyte while increasing the zinc deposition density has become a major challenge in the optimization of electrolyte concentration. Future research can explore how to balance these factors by adjusting the electrolyte formulation to further improve the overall capability of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries.

paragraph_context: With the deepening of understanding the working principle of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries, the application of In-Situ characterization technology in electrolyte optimization research is becoming increasingly important. By real-time monitoring of the zinc electrodeposition process, In-Situ characterization technology can not only provide dynamic data on the zinc anode electrodeposition behavior but also reveal the role of electrolyte composition on zinc deposition. For instance, In-Situ optical microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), SEM, and atomic force microscopy (AFM) have been extensively employed to investigate the formation and growth of zinc dendrites. Moreover, In-Situ Raman spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) are capable of tracking the real-time interaction between the electrolyte and the zinc anode. They can also explore how the electrolyte composition impacts the morphology of zinc electrodeposition, the alterations in the solvation structure, and the occurrence of side reactions. The application of these In-Situ characterization techniques provides valuable data support for the development of new electrolytes and helps to discover more effective electrolyte formulations.

paragraph_context: In the future, as the application demand of zinc-iodine batteries in energy storage systems, wearable devices, and smart electronics increases, the development of new electrolyte systems will become the focus of research. In addition to traditional aqueous electrolytes, the development of gel electrolytes and solid electrolytes will become the key to improving the energy density and cycle stability of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries. Solid electrolytes can effectively improve the safety of batteries and avoid the volatility problem in liquid electrolytes, thus providing the possibility for the application of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries under high temperature and extreme conditions. In addition, with the in-depth study of the zinc battery electrodeposition process, more efficient electrolyte designs may appear in the future, which can maximize the inhibition of zinc dendrite formation and achieve a more uniform and stable zinc electrodeposition process. Through the comprehensive optimization of electrolyte composition, concentration, and additives, future $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries are expected to achieve elevated energy density, prolonged service lifespan, and higher charge and discharge efficiency. Despite substantial progress achieved in experimental research, the large-scale implementation of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries continues to encounter significant obstacles, particularly regarding electrochemical stability optimization, cost-effective production management, and manufacturing process scalability. How to transform laboratory research results into large-scale production technology always remains a key issue in promoting the widespread application of $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries. With the continuous advancement of materials science, battery engineering, and manufacturing technology, $\mathrm{Zn - I_2}$ batteries are expected to play a pivotal role in advancing next-generation energy storage systems and flexible electronics.

paragraph_context: In recent years, due to the increasing demand for high energy density, nickel-rich ternary cathode material $\mathrm{LiNi_xCo_yMn_zO_2}$ (NCM, $x > 0.6$ , $x + y + z = 1$ ) has been widely developed and applied. Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with lithium metal as the anode have also received significant attention. Currently, commercial electrolytes mainly consist of carbonate-based systems with lithium hexafluorophosphate ( $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ ), which possess advantages such as high ionic conductivity, strong resistance to high voltage oxidation, and low cost. However, $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ undergoes thermal decomposition at high temperatures ( $\mathrm{LiPF_6} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiF} + \mathrm{PF_5}$ ). Furthermore, $\mathrm{PF_5}$ , as a strong Lewis acid, reacts with traces of water in the electrolyte ( $\mathrm{PF_5} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{POF_3} + 2\mathrm{HF}$ ), causing accelerated decomposition of $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ . The generated HF can damage the structure of nickel-rich cathode materials, dissolve transition metal cations, and corrode the electrode-electrolyte interface. Moreover, the decomposition of $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ produces insulating by-products [such as $\mathrm{POF_3}$ , $\mathrm{POF(OH)_2}$ , and $\mathrm{POF_2(OH)}$ ], which increase the impedance of the battery and ultimately lead to rapid capacity decay. Within the ester structure, trimethylsilyl groups can effectively reduce the impedance of the battery and improve cycling performance by virtue of the ease of breaking silicon-oxygen bonds and their reactivity.[85] Currently, methods to mitigate the detrimental effects of trace water and HF on battery systems mainly include strict control of water content during production and the introduction of functional additives such as film-forming additives to create robust interface films that suppress the corrosion of the SEI film by HF.[94,95] Among these methods, extensive research has demonstrated the effectiveness of trimethylsilane in eliminating $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} / \mathrm{HF}$ from the electrolyte, as shown in Table 1. Wang et al.[87] designed an additive called 2,2,2-trifluoro-N-methyl-N-(trimethylsilyl)acetamide (MSTFA), which connects multiple functional groups using amide units. Among many similar compounds, MSTFA stands out with its rational molecular structure and the synergistic complementarity of amide, trifluoromethyl, and trimethylsilane groups. Experimental evidence has shown that the trimethylsilane group in MSTFA can indeed remove $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} / \mathrm{HF}$ , leading to the formation of a high-quality electrode-electrolyte interface, thereby improving the battery's cycling stability, safety, and tolerance to harsh operating conditions (high/low temperatures, high pressure). paragraph_context: The incorporation of additive molecules with dual polarities, especially those containing fluorine elements, has been proven to be an effective strategy for improving film formation. Fluorination can increase the reactivity of open rings and reduce the reactivity of some cyclic and short-chain additives, enhancing the effectiveness of film formation. The addition of fluorine can further improve the compactness and flexibility of the SEI film, allowing for the volume changes of the anode. Fluorinated carbonates, fluoroacetonitrile, and fluoroborate salts are excellent cathode film-forming additives that can stabilize catalytic sites on the cathode surface. As auxiliary additives, perfluorinated chains and anionic cyclic compounds modify the interfacial film. Additionally, film-forming additives that improve the electrochemical performance of lithium-ion batteries should facilitate the film formation process. A rapid and uniform film formation process should favor the formation of dense and stable interfacial films. High $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ migration further stabilizes the structure of the interfacial film. This suggests that film-forming additives with fast kinetics and high reactivity have reactive groups that convert into homogeneous and controllable films. Elucidating the working mechanism of fluorinated additives will greatly facilitate the development of more effective functional electrolytes. However, it should be noted that the mechanism of fluorination additives is still unclear due to the complexity and stability of the SEI layer and battery reactions. The main issue lies in understanding the relationship between the composition, structure, and evolution of the SEI layer and its electrochemical performance. Currently, the study of film-forming additive mechanisms mainly focuses on FEC, and effective research methods include in-situ liquid NMR and solid-state NMR. However, in battery systems, the SEI film is constantly evolving dynamically. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop comprehensive and reliable characterization techniques to understand the SEI layer, in order to design and develop better functional electrolytes. Additionally, theoretical calculations can also help propose the correct reaction pathways based on experimental evidence.

paragraph_context: Substantial efforts are being made not only in designing and synthesizing new electrolyte additives, but also in making use of already existing components in an innovative manner. According to different work mechanisms, these developed additives can be classified into several categories: film-forming, inducing solvent decomposition, removing $\mathrm{HF / H_2O}$ and electrostatic shield mechanisms, which could effectively improve the performance of the battery. The novel $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -coordinated or affecting the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure additive is a new viewpoint to understand the connection among thermodynamics, kinetics, SEI structure, and battery performance. One example is that the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -coordinated FEC exhibit a completely different reduction mechanism accompany by significant change in the electronic structure during the production of LiF-rich SEI, whereas the VEC tended to generate $\mathrm{Li_2CO_3}$ -rich SEI.[109] Also, recruiting anions from electrolyte additives into the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure is a promising concept. The planar DMP molecular layer absorbed on the surface of the Li metal can suppress side reactions and modify the Li deposition behavior via steric hindrance, inducing homogeneous Li deposition, and the DMP leveler does not participate in the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase.[111] Therefore, in the future, novel additives that change the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure will be different from traditional sacrificial additives, paving the way for exploring the direct structure-performance relationship between additives and electrolyte.

paragraph_context: This article starts with the structure and different functions of electrolyte additives, and provides a detailed introduction to the principles of selecting additives in different battery application environments. The focus is on the structure-effect relationship and mechanism of action between the characteristic functional groups and electrochemical performance of additives. Until now, unsaturated carbonate derivatives, ester-based, boron-based, silicon based, fluorinated and alkali metal ions additives have been proven to be good strategies for improving of batteries' performance. Fluorination can increase ring opening and reduce the reactivity of some cyclic and short chain additives, and improve the effectiveness of film formation. The fast and uniform film forming process of film-forming additive is conducive to the formation of dense and stable electrolyte-electrodes interphases, and high lithium mobility further stabilizes the structure of the interfacial layers. Therefore, clarifying the working mechanism of different component/structure additives will contribute to the development of more effective functional electrolytes. But we must also be aware that due to the complexity and stability of the SEI layer and battery reactions, the action mechanism of electrolyte additives is still unclear. The main issue lies in the relationship between the composition, structure, and evolution of the SEI layer and its electrochemical performance. At present, research on the mechanism of film-forming additives mainly focuses on FEC, and the most effective research methods are in-situ liquid NMR and solid-state NMR. However, in battery systems, SEI films have always been in a dynamic evolution process. paragraph_context: The research of electrolyte additives has always accompanied the development of materials, and as one of the most widely studied cathode materials, ternary layered oxides have unique structural properties. It can be seen that the research system of electrolyte additives has gradually transitioned from LCO to NMC, from low-nickel ternary to high-nickel ternary, from low voltage to high voltage, from low temperature to high temperature, and from single to composite. In general, although the content of additives is small compared to the total volume of the electrolyte, their unique chemical structures can undergo chemical or electrochemical reactions, which effectively improve battery performance. Similar to the structure of the solvent EC, VC, in which C-C changes to C=C, improves film-forming properties. FEC, in which F replaces one hydrogen atom of EC, not only enhances oxidative stability but also retains the characteristics of EC. New additives such as lithium salts without F or with higher thermal stability, as well as additives that decompose to eliminate HF, containing P, B, S, and quinoline compounds, can enhance the ionic conductivity and stability of the electrode-electrolyte interface. Composite additives take advantage of the synergistic effects between different substances, greatly enhancing the overall electrochemical performance of batteries. Furthermore, various new structural additives have emerged successively, improving the battery's comprehensive electrochemical performance under harsh conditions of high-energy-density electrode chemistries.

paragraph_context: At present, the selection of additives is focused on function orientation. In order to solve the problem of the structure collapse during the high nickel cathode cycle, and the performance degradation caused by the destruction of the interphases by various by-products of LiPF6's water oxygen sensitivity, the trace additives can improve the performance of the battery in high voltage, high loading, and wide temperature range, and additives with different structures play different roles. Although there are many additives and categories currently being studied with good performance, there are still some issues worth paying attention to: firstly, ternary cathode materials with different Ni contents have different surface physicochemical properties, especially the catalytic or complexation reaction mechanisms between Ni, Co and additives have significant similarities and differences; Secondly, the interface properties between the electrodes and electrolyte jointly determine the performance of the battery, while additives have different mechanisms for the formation of CEI and SEI films, and there is also a cross-linking reaction between them. Therefore, when selecting additives, it is necessary to consider both their oxidation and reduction properties, and it is necessary to propose more specific screening conditions, such as acidity coefficient (pk), performance index (FOM), etc.; Thirdly, at higher temperatures and voltages, electrolyte oxidation and increased impedance are the main factors leading to battery capacity degradation. Therefore, the research on new electrolyte additives should start from the correlation between material structure and the above three factors. In the process of searching for additives, it is necessary to expand research methods. Ionizing radiation testing links the radiation yield of $\mathsf{H}_2$ with the efficacy of additives, and can be completed within a few hours, which to some extent improves the efficiency of screening electrolyte additives. However, accurate selection of additives still requires electrochemical experimental verification. This requires researchers to continue exploring the reasons why additives improve battery performance, from the perspective of solvation structure, film-forming properties of interfaces and the decomposition behavior of induced solvent molecules, in order to better match high nickel cathode materials. In summary, the development direction of new electrolyte additives in the future requires the combination of electrode materials, electrolytes, even separators, and the design of substances with closely related structures and properties to further promote the development of Li ion batteries.

paragraph_context: The ever-growing pursuit of high energy density batteries has triggered extensive efforts toward developing alkali metal (Li, Na, and K) battery (AMB) technologies owing to high theoretical capacities and low redox potentials of metallic anodes. Typically, for new battery systems, the electrolyte design is critical for realizing the battery electrochemistry of AMBs. Conventional electrolytes in alkali ion batteries are generally unsuitable for sustaining the stability owing to the hyper-reactivity and dendritic growth of alkali metals. In this review, we begin with the fundamentals of AMB electrolytes. Recent advancements in concentrated and fluorinated electrolytes, as well as functional electrolyte additives for boosting the stability of Li metal batteries, are summarized and discussed with a special focus on structure-composition-performance relationships. We then delve into the electrolyte formulations for Na- and K metal batteries, including those in which Na/K do not adhere to the Li-inherited paradigms. Finally, the challenges and the future research needs in advanced electrolytes for AMB are highlighted. This comprehensive review sheds light on the principles for the rational design of promising electrolytes and offers new inspirations for developing stable AMBs with high performance.

First, alkali metal ions tend to deposit on the current collector unevenly. With the continuous nonuniform plating/stripping of alkali metals, dendrites gradually form and grow. They can penetrate through the separator, causing terrible short circuits, fire, or even explosions when flammable liquid electrolytes are used. Second, the hyper- Technology, Inner Mongolia Electric Power (Group) Co. Ltd, Hohhot 010020, China reactivity of alkali metals gives rise to their spontaneous redox reactions with conventional organic electrolytes and the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers. It consumes alkali metal ions and decreases the coulombic efficiency (CE). paragraph_context: To address the abovementioned challenges in AMBs, researchers have proposed various strategies, including electrolyte formulation,[9-12] separator modifications,[13-17] solid-state electrolyte design,[18-21] artificial SEI construction,[22-24] and anode structure fabrication.[25-29] As is typical for novel rechargeable battery technologies, a rational design of advanced electrolytes is a prerequisite for constructing practical AMBs. Various types of electrolytes have been developed, including solid-state electrolytes,[30] polymer electrolytes,[31-33] and liquid electrolytes. Carbonate solvents employed in commercially available LIBs usually demonstrate low plating/stripping efficiencies for alkali metals as well as dendritic morphologies in anodes, resulting in poor cycling stabilities. Ether solvents, such as 1, 2-dimethoxyethane, display relatively better compatibility with alkali metals. However, the derived CE values are still not satisfactory and show high fluctuation during high-voltage operations owing to the poor oxidation stability. The recent decade has witnessed a gradual increase in studies with a focus on exploring novel electrolytes for stabilizing alkali metals. These include 1) the concentrated electrolytes that reduce the number of free solvents and alleviate parasitic reactions; 2) the fluorinated solvent-based electrolytes that are more resistant to oxidation due to the high electronegativity of F; and 3) functional additives in novel electrolytes that preferentially react with the alkali metal ahead of solvents and alkali metal salts to produce more favorable SEI layers (Figure 1).[34-36] In this review, we first present the fundamentals and chemistry of AMB electrolytes, which include the solvent-solute interaction and characterization of the SEI and the cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI). We then discuss the recent research progress in the development of concentrated electrolytes, perfluorinated electrolytes, and functional electrolyte additives to improve the reversibility of alkali metal anodes. Special focus was placed on the structure-composition-performance relationship. Electrolyte recipes, wherein $\mathrm{Na} / \mathrm{K}$ did not follow Li-inherited paradigms, are also highlighted. Finally, we shed light on the current limitations and the future scope for the study of liquid electrolytes, aiming to inspire the development of novel advanced electrolytes for practical applications of AMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: An electrolyte is an essential ionic conductor and medium that mediates the ion transferring between the cathode and the anode in a battery cell. The electrolytes for AMBs are generally composed of high-purity solvents, alkali metal salts, and functional additives. Liquid electrolytes were preferred and first commercialized in the battery industry owing to their easy preparation, high conductivity, low viscosity, and excellent wettability on electrode surfaces.[37] An ideal liquid electrolyte has the following merits: 1) a high ionic conductivity; 2) electrochemical stability over a wide potential range; 3) good thermal stability; 4) stable chemical properties to ensure no parasitic reactions with electrodes; and 5) good safety, a low cost, and nontoxicity.[38] In AMBs, a more careful selection of liquid electrolytes is required, considering the hyper-reactivity of metallic anodes and the dendritic growth issue. The spontaneous reaction between alkali metal anodes and the electrolyte at low potentials generates a well-known SEI layer, whose possible formation mechanism was proposed by Goodenough et al.[39] As shown in Figure 2a, when the electrochemical potential, $\mu_{\mathrm{A}}$ is above the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), the electrolyte will be reduced by the anode, except that a protection layer (i.e., SEI) prevents the electron transfer from the anode to the LUMO of electrolyte. Likewise, a cathode with an electrochemical potential, $\mu_{\mathrm{C}}$ below the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) will oxidize the electrolyte, unless a passivation layer (i.e., CEI) produces a barrier for the electron transfer from the electrolyte HOMO to the cathode.

paragraph_context: Ethers and organic carbonates are two of the most important solvents used for AMB electrolytes. Conventional carbonate-based electrolytes employed in LIBs normally result in poor coulombic efficiencies of the alkali metal plating/stripping (generally $< 80\%$ for Li-Cu cells and $< 20\%$ for Na/K counterparts), leading to a very poor cycle life of AMBs. Therefore, they cannot sustain a stable operation of Li/Na metal anodes. Ethers are of significant interest because their high intrinsic energy of LUMO endows them with good electrochemical stability against alkali metal reductions. In addition to solvents, the anions of salts may also be reduced at low potentials to constitute mainly the inorganic components in SEI. The electrochemical reduction potential was found to be varied with salts.[40] The solvent-solute coordination structures and compositions in electrolytes play a critical role in determining the charge storage behavior of AMBs. Recently, great advances have been made in probing the structure of liquid electrolytes for AMBs by numerous advanced experimental techniques. Typically, the small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) is a highly efficient and nondestructive approach for identifying nanostructures in liquids, even at the atomic scale. It provides comprehensive information on anion-cation pairs, solvation sheaths, molecular clusters, and percolating networks of electrolytes.[41] For instance, Aguilera et al. employed SAXS to investigate Li bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI)-tetraglyme (G4) mixtures with various concentrations.[42] As shown in Figure 2b, the intermolecular distances of the G4 solvent was resolved by SAXS, showing a broad peak at $1.5\AA^{-1}$ . The distance of $\sim0.95\AA^{-1}$ between $\mathrm{Li^{+}/G4}$ complexes and TFSI anions was also detected as the electrolyte concentration gradually increases from 0.1 to 0.6 (the molar fraction of LiTFSI to that of LiTFSI/G4).

paragraph_context: Vibrational spectroscopy has also been proven to be a powerful technique for probing ion-molecule and intermolecular interactions through changes in frequency, intensity, and band properties.[43-46] Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR), Raman spectroscopy, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopies are the most commonly used approach for analyzing structural characteristics of liquid electrolytes. FTIR is typically used to study the composition of liquid electrolytes. Bands of different absorption wavenumbers are indicative of the polar group structure and identify the electrolyte and product information, cation solvation numbers, and solvation structures of electrolytes.[47] Raman spectroscopy can help us infer polar functional groups and other structural information of the electrolyte according to different band positions of the absorption wavenumbers. These clues are favorable for analyzing the electrolyte behaviors and understanding the battery reaction and failure mechanisms.[48] For instance, Yang et al.[49] systematically analyzed the Raman spectra of various solvents and electrolytes used for AMBs, as shown in Figure 2c. In particular, they observed an additional peak at approximately $880~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ in the Raman spectra of the LiTFSI electrolyte with the mixed solvent of dimethoxyethane (DME) and tetraethylene glycol dimethyl ether (TEGDME) as compared to that of the pure solvents. They ascribed this peak to the typical Raman active mode of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ co-coordinated with DME and TEGDME. Their observation is also supported by the enhanced intensity of this Raman peak as increasing the concentration of LiTFSI due to the improved coordination of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ with free solvent molecules. NMR can quantify the coordination strength and structure between Li and solvents by analyzing chemical shifts of ${}^{7}\mathrm{Li}$ , ${}^{1}\mathrm{H}$ , ${}^{17}\mathrm{O}$ , and ${}^{13}\mathrm{C}$ .[50] Dahn et al. captured the anion effect of Li salt and the solvent friction on the coordination structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ over prolonged cycling by NMR. paragraph_context: The intrinsic properties including the electrochemical stability, ionic conductivity, and solvation structure of liquid electrolytes are also very important for AMBs. Generally, cyclic and linear sweep voltammetry are explored to evaluate the electrochemical stability window (ESW). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) can be used to evaluate the ionic conductivity of electrolytes and the interfacial compatibility between the electrolyte and the electrode.[53] Moreover, many other electrochemical characterization methods have been applied to study the physicochemical properties of liquid electrolytes for AMBs. For example, based on evaluating the open circuit potential in an LMB cell with symmetric electrodes and asymmetric electrolytes, Cui's group reported the use of potentiometric technique to quantify the effects of the concentration, anions, and solvents on the solvation energy of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in various electrolytes (Figure 2f).[54] Accordingly, they found that the cycling performance of LMBs can be significantly improved by using solvents with lower cell potentials and higher solvation energies of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ .

paragraph_context: In addition to the experimental techniques, theoretical modeling that likes the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is an effective approach for understanding microstructures and properties of the electrolytes at molecular level.[55] An in-depth understanding of the chemical origin for the dielectric constant of a solvent is favorable for regulating the macroscopic properties of electrolytes through modulating the intermolecular interaction at the molecular scale. Typically, Zhang and co-workers achieved the evaluation of dielectric constants of various electrolytes at different temperatures by high-throughput and low-cost MD simulations.[56] Besides, other physicochemical properties such as the viscosity[57] and the diffusion coefficient[58] can also be readily obtained using MD simulations. These data will be very helpful for design-advanced electrolyte for on-demand AMBs.

The SEI formed on metallic anodes shows more complexities because of the low reduction potential of the alkali metal. To obtain satisfactory electrochemical performance, an ideal SEI layer for AMBs should possess the following features (Figure 3a): 1) an electronic insulation to avoid short cut; 2) smooth and uniform ionic conduction pathways; 3) being favorable for ion desolvation; and 4) good mechanical robustness to accommodate the large volume fluctuation during the metal plating/stripping.[59] It is of note that there are significant differences among SEI layers formed on different alkali metals. paragraph_context: The composition and properties of SEI are largely affected by the temperature as the kinetics of parasitic reactions between alkali metals and electrolytes are temperature dependent. Wang et al.[66] well resolved the nanoscopic change of the SEI formed at various temperatures via cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The SEI formed in the electrolyte of $1\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI/ 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)-DME (1:1 by vol.) with $1\mathrm{wt}\%$ lithium nitrate $(\mathrm{LiNO}_3)$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is composed of an amorphous and polymeric interphase (Figure 3d). The dissolution of such thin SEI $(\sim 20\mathrm{nm})$ in the electrolyte may be responsible for the poor passivation capability of the anode. In contrast, the thicker SEI ( $\sim 35 \mathrm{~nm}$ ) formed at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ shows a distinct two-layer structure with an inner layer of amorphous/polymeric layer and an outer layer of large crystalline $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ grains (thickness $\sim 10 \mathrm{~nm}$ ). The thicker SEI layer at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is ascribed to the accelerated parasitic reaction kinetics at elevated temperatures.

paragraph_context: Given the experimental challenge to exactly characterize the dynamically changed SEI, theoretical simulations play critical roles in predicting the properties. Brownian dynamics simulations showed that the radial diffusion of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ results in an anisotropic growth and suppresses the dendritic electrodeposition by thinning the SEI layer to a sub-nanometer scale (Figure 3e).[67] Nagaoka et al.[68] confirmed that the reduction products of Li salts constitute the main body of the SEI using the Red Moon method, a hybrid Monte Carlo (MC)/MD reaction method, to simulate the formation mechanism of SEI at the atomic level.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Compared to SEI, CEI at the cathode side attracts less research attention in AMBs. Although the CEI is thinner than the SEI at the anode, it is still quite complex in structure and composition. A CEI, usually rich in inorganic compounds, can inhibit the parasitic reaction between the electrolyte and the cathode and the phase transition at room temperature, which contributes to the improved cycling performance. More importantly, an ideal CEI should exhibit electrochemical, mechanical, chemical, and thermal stabilities.[69] Wang et al. studied the formation mechanism of CEI in Li-S batteries by determining the chemical composition. They discovered two key roles of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in controlling the CEI formation by using one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) liquid-phase NMR spectra, in a combination with chemical reaction model and density functional theory calculations. They also found that the preferential solvation of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ for EC in a mixed carbonate electrolyte makes EC the main participant in the CEI formation. The coordination of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ with EC carbonyl is attributed to the change of the activation barrier and reaction pathway. Meanwhile, lithium ethylene carbonate was determined to be the main component of the CEI layer in the S cathode, indicating the presence of a highly ordered electrochemical double layer at the interface of the S cathode (Figure 3f).[70] The typical electrolyte for a battery contains salts and aprotic solvents. The intrinsic coordination between solvent molecules, anions, and cations determines the solvation structure of the electrolyte. Generally, there are three main types of ion pairs in an electrolyte: a solvent-separated ion pair (SSIP), contact ion pair (CIP), and aggregate (AGG) in the electrolyte. As shown in Figure 4a, the dilute electrolyte usually comprises SSIP, free solvent molecules, and free anions.[71] As the concentration of salt increased, the dominant ion-pairing gradually changed from SSIP to CIP and AGG. In particular, when the mole ratio of the electrolyte salt to the coordinating solvent increases from 1 to larger than 3 or 4, the amount of free solvent decreases abruptly.[72] In high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs), solvates exist mainly in the form of CIP and AGG. Such a unique solvation structure almost without free solvent molecules improves the oxidation stability of the electrolyte.[73] The changed solvation structure results in the altered LUMO composed of anions, which enhances the reduction stability of the HCE system. Meanwhile, the interface chemistry will be dominated by anion other than solvent. As such, the anion will be preferentially reduced and decomposed to form an SEI with a higher content of inorganic species.[74] Moreover, when the electrolyte concentration exceeds a certain threshold value, some new physicochemical and electrochemical properties are endowed to the electrolytes, such as high thermal stability,[75] inhibition of current collector corrosion,[76] and suppression of lithium polysulfide dissolution.[77] To be more concise, we will focus on discussing the function of HCE in stabilizing Li metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes for LMBs.

paragraph_context: The ether solvents demonstrated good compatibility with alkali metal anodes. For example, a high CE $(>98\%)$ and an evident dendrite suppression were achieved in LMBs owing to the formation of oligomers with good flexibilities and strong binding affinities to the Li surface.[78] The use of a high concentration of ether-based electrolytes can further improve the interface stability between the ether-based electrolyte and Li anodes and effectively alleviate the decomposition problem of ether solvents at high voltage.[79] Zhang's group firstly reported the use of HCE consisting of $4\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI in DME solvent to enable stable cycling of LMAs.[80] A high Li plating/stripping efficiency close to $99.1\%$ was achieved at an areal current of $0.2\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ , without Li dendrite formation. Even at a rather high areal current of $4\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ , the LMAs delivered an average CE of $98.4\%$ over prolonged 1000 cycles. Such an outstanding performance was attributed to the unique solvation structure of the HCE with CIPs and AGGs, where almost all the solvent molecules and anions are coordinated by $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ (Figure 4b). As for the metal anodes based on HCEs, the inorganic rich SEI layer is mainly derived from the reductive decomposition of anions in Li salts. Such a dense and highly conductive SEI layer largely reduces the anion degradation in the extended cycles. Meanwhile, compared with the lithium deposition in conventional carbonate-based electrolyte showing dark gray dendrites, the plated Li in concentrated LiFSI-DME electrolyte demonstrates the dense nodular structure and silver-white luster (Figure 4c). The significantly reduced side reaction between Li and electrolyte is favorable for the much enhanced CE of Li plating/stripping.

paragraph_context: To further improve the compatibility between the ether-based electrolyte and Li metal anode, researchers further introduced functional Li salts that can induce a synergistic effect in HCEs. For instance, Kang et al.[81] developed a dual-salt ether-based HCE by adding $2\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ into $2\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI-DME (denoted as 2LF2LN). The participation of $\mathrm{NO}_3^-$ anions in solving $\mathrm{Li}^+$ gives rise to the formation of a robust $\mathrm{LiN_xO_y}$ -LiF-rich SEI on the Li surface, which is favorable for preventing the growth of Li dendrites. As such, both the half and full cells based on such 2LF2LN electrolyte displayed significantly improved capacity retentions. Similarly, Liu et al.[82] found that SEI layer on Li metal formed in a dual-salt concentrated electrolyte ( $1\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI + $2\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI and $2\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI + $1\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI in DOL/DME) is more compact and thinner than that generated in the single-salt ( $3\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI) electrolyte. LiF content increases with the addition of LiFSI in the dual-salt electrolytes, suggesting that the preferential decomposition of the $\mathrm{FSI}^-$ anion produces a more robust SEI layer.

paragraph_context: Despite the good compatibility of ether-based electrolytes to alkali metal anodes, the poor oxidation stability limits their wide applications in high-voltage batteries. Another advantage of HCEs is that they have a broader electrochemical window against high-voltage oxidation reactions compared with conventional dilute ones. For instance, Ren et al.[83] optimized the electrochemical window of a single-salt concentrated ether electrolyte of LiFSI-DME by adjusting the molar ratio of Li salt to solvent. Due to the good electrochemical stability of the optimized HCE for both Li metal anode and $\mathrm{LiNi_{1 / 3}Mn_{1 / 3}Co_{1 / 3}O_2}$ (NMC333) cathode, the LillNMC333 battery achieved stable cycling at a high voltage of $4.3\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li / Li^{+}}$ . The LillNMC333 battery also maintained $\sim 92\%$ of the initial capacity after 500 cycles at a charge rate of $0.53\mathrm{mA cm^{-2}}$ and discharges rate of $1.6\mathrm{mA cm^{-2}}$ . They revealed that the as-produced high-strength, uniform, and compact CEI layer containing inorganic species can stabilize the cathode and isolate the contact between the NMC333 surface with high activity and free DME molecules, thus inhibiting the dissolution of transition metal ions.

paragraph_context: Ether electrolytes are the preferred choice for next-generation LMBs because of their high stability with the Li metal. However, their low anodic decomposition potential of $< 4\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li^{+} / Li}$ limits their applications.[85] Increasing the cut-off voltage is an effective approach to improve the energy density of the battery cell. Carbonate solvents normally exhibit better antioxidative properties than ethers; thus, it is intriguing to explore carbonate-based HCEs that can be compatible with cathodes for operating under high voltage, such as $4.6\mathrm{V}$ $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.6}-$ $\mathrm{Co}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.2}\mathrm{O}_2$ (NMC622) and $4.9\mathrm{V}$ $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Mn}_{1.5}\mathrm{O}_4$ (LNMO). Doi et al. developed an HCE of $4.27\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ -propylene carbonate (PC) for LNMO cathode operated at $5.0\mathrm{V}$ .[86] The electrochemical stability of PC molecules against oxidation is enormously enhanced in the concentrated electrolyte. Consequently, the LNMO cathode achieved a high initial CE of $90.3\%$ and maintained a high discharge capacity of $122.8\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ after 50 cycles at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ , corresponding to a high-capacity retention of $92.3\%$ . Later, the same group reported a PC-based HCE with a higher concentration ( $7.25\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiBF_4}$ -PC) since $\mathrm{LiBF_4}$ has a higher solubility in PC.[87] Despite the higher viscosity and lower ionic conductivity compared with those of $4.27\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ /PC, the polarization remained very small ( $\sim 30\mathrm{mV}$ at C/10). They ascribed the improved electrochemical performance to the suppressed decomposition and rapid charge transfer kinetics of the HCE electrolyte.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: While the HCEs based on PC solvents facilitate the stable operation under high voltages, their high viscosities result in unsatisfying lithium storage kinetics and poor wettability with electrodes, thus restricting their practical applications. Low-viscosity dimethyl carbonate (DMC) is a promising alternative solvent in HCE. For instance, Wang et al. reported an advanced HCE of $5.5\mathrm{M}$ lithium bisfluorosulfonyl)amide (LiFSA)/DMC. The moderate ion mobility was maintained even at high concentrations.[88] The LiFSA salt is stable yet dissociative even at such a high concentration. The MD modeling reveals that as-prepared HCE with a peculiar three dimensions (3D) network structure can significantly suppress the dissolution of transition metal and Al current collector. As such, the capacity retention of the LMB with this HCE after 100 cycles was over $95\%$ and the CE was close to $100\%$ . Notably, the $5.5\mathrm{M}$ LiFSA/DMC also exhibits superior thermal stability and flame-retardant property, which remarkably improves safety for LMBs.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Mixed EC-based electrolytes have been the dominating electrolytes in the LIB industry owing to the combined merits of each individual. For example, DMC owns a low viscosity as stated above, and EC possesses good stability against oxidative decomposition at high voltage.[89] As such, the mixed EC solvent has been also explored for HCEs. Recently, an HCE of $10\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI in EC/DMC mixture was developed by Wang et al.[90] The preferential oxidation of $\mathrm{FSI}^{-}$ leads to the formation of fluorine-rich CEI on the cathode; this passivates the cathode surface and stabilizes the electrolyte solvent, thus inhibiting the parasitic reaction. Moreover, LiF-enriched SEI was produced on the lithium metal anode, effectively suppressing the growth of Li dendrite. As a result, this HCE based on EC/DMC not only improves Li plating/stripping CE to as high as $99.2\%$ but also enables superior anodic stability over $5.5\mathrm{V}$ (Figure 4e). The as-constructed NMC622llLi cell with this HCE achieved $86\%$ of the initial capacity over 100 cycles at a high cut-off voltage of $4.6\mathrm{V}$ .

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: To further extend the electrochemical voltage window of HCEs, fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) was employed as the solvent in HCE since the SEI derived from the decomposition of FEC usually exhibits superior interfacial compatibility.[91] Suo and co-workers developed a high-concentration perfluorinated organic electrolyte $(7\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI-FEC) to enable the stable operation of a $5\mathrm{V}$ LillLNMO battery.[92] The ductility of the LiF-rich SEI formed in this HCE electrolyte can effectively suppress the Li whisker formation, which facilitates highly reversible lithium plating/stripping. The decomposition of FEC not only benefits the formation of the LiF-rich SEI for stabilizing the anode but also increases the oxidation potential of electrolytes for the cathode. A high concentration of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ gives rise to extensive Li cation coordination, enhancing the stability of electron lone pair of anion and solvent. As for the FEC-based HCE, the minimal distance between solvent molecules and Al current collector is enlarged due to the enwrapped solvent by salt instead of the conventional solvation shell structure, thereby reducing the electron tunneling current to the solvent. Moreover, LiF generated on the cathode surface shows a large bandgap $(13.6\mathrm{eV})$ and a fast tunneling decay rate, thus stabilizing the electrolyte and protecting Al current collector from corrosion (Figure 4f). As such, a dual-salt concentrated electrolyte in mixed carbonate solvents of FEC and DMC (i.e., $4\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI $+0.5\mathrm{M}$ LiDFOB in FEC/DMC) designed by Wang's group enables the LillLNMO and LillNCM batteries to show excellent cycling stabilities even at a high charge cut-off voltage of $4.9\mathrm{V}.$ [93] The unique solvation structure and interface stabilization strategy of the HCE offers opportunities for many other irregular solvents. For example, sulfone solvents exhibit excellent oxidation stabilities, even at an ultrahigh voltage of $5.5\mathrm{V}$ . However, the poor compatibility with anode materials results in an unfavorable SEI. The stable solvation structure in the HCE system is likely to address this issue. An HCE obtained by dissolving LiFSI in sulfolane (SL) at a high concentration developed by Maeyoshi et al.[94] enables a stable lithium plating/stripping cycling of LMB with an average CE of $98\%$ for over 400 cycles at $1.0\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ . Nitrile solvents also show poor compatibility with lithium metal anodes. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation revealed that, in acetonitrile (AN) solvent, the electron affinity of the TFSI anion gradually increases with the increase of LiTFSI concentration. At a certain concentration, the electron affinity to TFSI anion will be stronger than that of AN.[95] As a result, the interaction between $\mathrm{TFSI}^{-}$ and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ increases gradually, and the TFSI would be sacrificially decomposed. The as-generated products on the anode surface contribute to the formation of a stable SEI film, which effectively prevents further decomposition of AN and improves the reduction stability of HCE based on AN. Recently, Peng et al. have reported an HCE of $10\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI-AN/vinylene carbonate (VC) enables LMB to deliver a high CE of $99.2\%$ at a current density of $0.2\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ . [96] Stable cycling of LilNMC622 cells with a high cathode loading of $4\mathrm{mAh}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ was also achieved. Y. Yamada et al. [71] also demonstrated that a highly concentrated LiTFSI/AN electrolyte can improve the plating/stripping efficiency of lithium metal and reduce the growth of lithium dendrites and dead lithium.

label: 材料制备
paragraph_context: As mentioned above, the unique solvation structure of HCEs has been proven to effectively improve the stability of the SEI and extend the cycle life of AMBs. However, HCEs have several disadvantages, such as high cost and viscosity and poor ionic conductivity and wettability between the separator and the electrode. These shortcomings hinder their applications in Li metal batteries, especially at high charge/discharge rates. To solve the abovementioned dilemmas, the idea of a localized high-concentration electrolyte (LHCE) was proposed by Zheng et al. in 2018.[97] Normally, the strategy of LHCE introduces a nonsolvating co-solvent, which was used as a diluent in HCEs, to reduce the salt concentration (Figure 5a). Ideally, the diluent should have the merits of low viscosity, low cost, good wettability, low dielectric constant, and coordination properties, sufficient stability against LMA, and good compatibility with the solvent in HCEs. Four main diluents that meet the above requirements have been explored, including 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl-1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (HFE), bis(2,2,2-Trifluoroethyl) ether (BTFE), 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE), and tris(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl)orthoformate (TFEO) (Figure 5b).

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: HFE is the most commonly used fluorinated ether diluent. In 2013, Dokko et al.[98] firstly introduced HFE to an HCE composed of LiTFSI-G4 for use in Li-S batteries. HFE reduces the viscosity and increases the ionic conductivity of the HCE electrolyte. Owing to the low polarity and low donor capacity of HFE, it does not alter the solvation structure of LiTFSI-G4; meanwhile, it inhibits the dissolution of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}$ , thereby improving the cycle life of the Li-S battery. Similarly, Qi and coworkers subsequently added HFE into an HCE of LiTFSI-(AN)2 for reducing the viscosity and facilitating the reaction kinetics of Li-Se batteries.[99] The LiTFSI-(AN)2/HFE greatly suppressed the "shuttle effect" of Se and promoted the conversion between Se and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{Se}$ , achieving a high utilization of Se (97%). Benefiting from the above advantages of LHCE, the Se utilization, CE, and cycling stability of Se cathodes were significantly improved. Even at a high rate of 2 C, a high discharge capacity of $476\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ was retained, corresponding to $70.5\%$ of the theoretical value.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: LHCE is also favorable for enlarging the output voltage and thus increasing the energy density of AMB. For example, Lin et al. reported the use of an LHCE consisting of $1.2\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6} + 0.15\mathrm{M}$ LiDFOB in a mixed solvent of FEC, DMC, and HFE for LMBs under stable cycling at a high voltage of $4.5\mathrm{V}$ . The LiDFOB additive not only promotes the formation of B-containing components such as $\mathrm{B - F}$ and $\mathrm{B - O}$ but also enriches the LiF and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ contents on CEI. This is critical for maintaining the stability of such LHCE under a high operating voltage of $4.5\mathrm{V}$ . Moreover, a favorable SEI could be produced on the lithium metal anode in such LHCE. As a result, the fabricated $\mathrm{LillLiCoO_2}$ batteries present a superior electrochemical performance, with $84\%$ capacity retention over 300 cycles at a high voltage of $4.5\mathrm{V}$ (Figure 5c).

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Normally, BTFE is more favorable for extending the electrochemical window in comparison with HFE. For instance, Chen et al.[101] developed a novel BTFE-based LHCE by dissolving $1.2\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI in a mixed solvent of DMC/BTFE $(1.2\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI-DMC/BTFE). As shown in Figure 5d, a thinner but more uniform and denser Li film of $10~{\mu\mathrm{m}}$ was deposited in $1.2\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI-DMC/BTFE compared with that produced in the conventional carbonate electrolyte $(1\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6 - EC}/$ EMC). In addition, the LiF-rich SEI layer derived from FSI in LHCE can reduce the interface reaction with this LHCE electrolyte, resulting in a high CE of over $99.3\%$ . This BTFE-based LHCE shows a large electrochemical window over $4.5\mathrm{V}$ as well as keeping the unique characteristics of HCE. As such, it can be used to sustain the stable working of cathode under a high voltage over $4\mathrm{V}$ . The as-constructed LilNCM333 full battery shows excellent cycle stability over 700 cycles as well as the capacity retention rate higher than $80\%$ . The excellent electrochemical performance of LMB can be attributed to the unique solvated structure of LHCE. DFT calculation and Raman results showed that the coordination energy between LiFSI and BTFE is much weaker than that between LiFSI and DMC. Therefore, LiFSI is more likely to form a solvated structure with DMC, while BTFE solvent exists relatively independently. It is worth noting that BTFE slightly weakens the binding strength between lithium-ion and $\mathrm{FSI^{-}}$ , which enhances $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion and improve the ionic conductivity and kinetic properties of the electrolyte (Figure 5e).

paragraph_context: Carbonate-based LHCE has been also developed to enhance the cyclic stability of the lithium metal anode. For example, Yu et al.[102] reported a novel carbonate-based LHCE by employing LiDFOB as an additive and replacing DMC with an EC/ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC) mixture. The decomposition of EC molecules, LiDFOB, and BTFE diluent gives rise to the formation of a dense LiF-rich SEI layer covered on the surface of lithium metal. This SEI can effectively inhibit the formation of lithium dendrites and improve the interface stability of lithium metal. As such, this carbonate-based LHCE significantly improves the cyclic stability of Li metal anode and simultaneously prolongs the cycle life of Lill NMC333 batteries.
