paragraph_context: Another promising diluent for LHCE is TFEO. It has excellent thermal stability, which can greatly improve the operation safety of LMBs. As TFEO has a strong electron absorbing group $\mathrm{(CF_3)}$ and very low HOMO, the oxidation stability is very good. Moreover, the TFEO molecule does not contain any (electro)chemically unstable functional groups such as cyano group $(-C\equiv N)$ , carbonyl group $(-C = O)$ , or sulfonic group $(-S(=O)-)$ , which are highly reactive with metallic Li. It only consists of ether groups (C-O-C), ensuring good stability against lithium metal. The viscosity of TFEO is quite low, enabling a promising diluent in LHCE.[108] Zhang's group systematically studied the electrochemical performance of three dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-based LHCE based on different fluorination diluents in lithium-oxygen batteries (LOBs), namely TTE, TFEO, and 1H,1H,5H-octafluoropentyl1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (OTE).[109] Electrochemical measurements, postmortem characterizations, and DFT calculations revealed the dependence of the LOB performance with LHCEs on the physicochemical properties of diluents including volatility, viscosity, $\mathrm{O}_2$ solubility, and the reaction energy with singlet oxygen. They found that the use of TFEO-based LHCE (1 M LiFSI-DME/TFEO) achieves the highly efficient lithium plating/ stripping. The conventional electrolytes generally produce mosaic- or multilayer-type SEI that leads to continuous consumption of electrolytes and gradually decreased CE. By contrast, the SEI formed in this TFEO-based LHCE electrolyte exhibits a monolithic feature (Figure 5f). The as-generated amorphous and highly uniform SEI layer effectively avoids lithium dendrite growth, alleviates the electrolyte depletion, and well accommodates the volume fluctuation during Li plating/striping. In addition, this electrolyte largely inhibits the phase change of the NCM811 cathode from a layered structure to rock salt (Figure 5g). The as-fabricated high-voltage LillNMC811 cell demonstrates both excellent cycling stability and high-rate capability.[110] To better understand the formation mechanism of the abovementioned monolithic SEI, they presented a theoretical simulation on the reactivity of the LHCE system composed of 1 M LiFSI/DME + TFEO. The simulation results reveal that the early formed interphase is mainly originated from the decomposition of $\mathrm{FSI}^{-}$ anions and TFEO. The resultant decomposed products gradually migrate to the surface of the Li metal slab, leading to the production of a multicomponent atomically dispersed SEI layer (Table 1).[111] F is a bipolar element with a strong electronegativity and a weak polarity. F-containing electrolyte components have an excellent kinetic reactivity and are likely to generate stable SEI films and uniform CEI films for effectively promoting the electrochemical performance of AMBs. F-containing electrolyte components can also be used as flame retardants to improve safety. Owing to the electron absorption-induced effect of F atoms, F-containing organic solvents usually have lower LUMO and HOMO levels, meaning that fluorinated solvents have higher oxidation resistance and worse reducibility. However, owing to the high reduction potential of the fluorinated solvent, it is easier to construct dense LiF-rich interphases on anode and cathode surfaces. This can prevent the continuous decomposition of the electrolyte and further expand the available ESW (Figure 6a).[112] In this section, we summarize the current research progress of F-containing electrolytes, including the fluorinated esters, ethers, and ester/ether co-solvents. At the end of this section, we discuss the controversial role of LiF in the SEI of LMBs.

paragraph_context: Owing to their low viscosity and high solubility for Li salt, ether-based solvents are promising alternatives to rechargeable LMBs. Nevertheless, ether-based electrolytes still face challenges of producing unsatisfied electrolyte/metallic electrode interfaces and Li dendrites during the cycling. Moreover, ether-based electrolytes have low oxidative stability (around $4\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ), which is not compatible with high-voltage cathodes.[85] HFE is a typical fluorinated ether showing good compatibility with $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Na}$ metal, enabling the formation of F-rich interphases at both the cathode and anode sides. Moreover, it can significantly improve the oxidative stability of ether-based electrolytes. For instance, Wang's group reported the introduction of HFE solvent with a high content of fluorine into $1\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI-DME electrolyte and applied it to the Li-S battery. Due to the low donor capacity and dielectric constant of HFE, HFE does not dissolve lithium salts or participate in the solvation process. Therefore, almost all DME molecules are bonded with $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{FSI}^{-}$ in the co-solvent system, and the dissolution of polysulfides can be effectively inhibited. Meanwhile, the decomposition of HFE with a high content of fluorine on the anode surface gives to the formation of a compact and LiF-rich SEI, which ensures efficient Li plating/stripping and protects the lithium metal anode from polysulfides corrosion.[117] Fluorine has a strong electron absorption effect. Therefore, the donation number (DN) value of the solvent will be reduced after fluorination and the solubility of the solvent to lithium salt will be greatly reduced. Despite its wide application as fluorinated ether, HFE can only be paired with high dielectric constant solvents to afford a substantial ionic conductivity. To address this issue, Bao's group developed the fluorinated 1,4-dimethoxylbutane (FDMB) as a sole solvent by selectively functionalizing the lengthened ether backbones with $-\mathrm{CF}_2$ functional group.[118] As shown in Figure 6d, the distance between Li $\mathrm{F_{DMB}}$ (2.935 Å) is close to that of Li- $\mathrm{O_{FDMB}}$ (2.023 Å), indicating the presence of weak interaction between Li and F atoms on FDMB. Therefore, different from the linear coordination structure of DME or DMB, the coordination structure of LiFSI-FDMB presents a five-member ring structure, and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ is coordinated with $\mathrm{O_{FDBM}}$ and $\mathrm{F_{FDMB}}$ simultaneously. The different coordination structure further causes the increase of anion content in the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvated sheath in 1 M LiFSI-FDMB, which is conducive to the formation of inorganic and dense SEI derived from anion for protecting metallic lithium. As a result, 1 M LiFSI-FDMB promotes highly efficient Li plating/stripping with an average CE of $99.52\%$ . Moreover, $\mathrm{FSI^{-}}$ binds closely to solvent molecules, thus enabling a superior and over 6 V oxidation stability of 1 M LiFSI-FDMB.

paragraph_context: In contrast to the wide existence and the important role of LiF in battery passivation, some researchers reported that LiF is absent or not the major component in the as-generated SEI layer. Impressively, Cui et al.[127] quantified the spatial distribution of LiF, and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ components in the Li metal anode SEI layer using cryogenic scanning transmission electron microscopy (cryo-STEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). They revealed that the compact SEI interfaced with the anode material is devoid of LiF, while it contains rich $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ nanocrystals due to its poor solubility in the electrolyte (Figure 7f). They also found that LiF nanoparticles $(100 - 400\mathrm{nm})$ may deposit as an indirect SEI component on a conductive substrate like the current collector, or anchor sparsely on lithium metal surface. Although the LiF deposited on the current collector may promote uniform lithium plating to a certain extent, they do not play a critical role in Li metal passivation nor the smooth $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion through SEI without incorporating into the compact and thin SEI layer. Based on studying the dynamic process of SEI formation based on liquid secondary ion mass spectrometry (liquid SIMS), Xu and co-workers also revealed that the inorganic and compact inner layer of SEI on Li metal anode is dominated by $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ -rich but LiF-depleted interphase.[128] In addition to design advanced solvent-salt systems discussed above, the introduction of additives into the electrolyte is also considered to be a simple and effective method to improve the performance of LMBs. This common approach is also widely used in the LIB industry. Normally, the role of additives can be categorized into two types: modifying the physicochemical properties of SEI layers to suppress the growth of Li dendrites and facilitating favorable $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux toward smooth electrodeposition on the Li metal anode. Specifically, for the former type, the behaviors like the polymerization, decomposition, or adsorption of additives on the Li metal surface could change the microstructure and/or composition of the interphase and further affect the Li deposition. For the latter, additives do not participate in the formation of SEI but mainly influence the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux distribution.[129] The SEI film between the Li metal and the bulk electrolyte is usually generated from the decomposition of electrolytes, mainly the Li salt and solvents. However, as the LUMO energy of the introduced additive is lower than those of the salt and the solvent, the additive could be preferentially decomposed ahead of Li salts/solvents. In this case, the composition and properties of SEI layers could then be manipulated by optimizing the used additives to improve the Li plating/stripping efficiency.[130] FEC is one of the most widely used film-forming additives in LMBs, which is conducive to the formation of stable SEI on lithium metal anode. For example, Zhang et al.[113] verified the much lower LUMO energy of FEC than those of EC and DEC by first-principle calculation. A uniform, dense, and LiF-enriched SEI layer that is related to the FEC gives rise to the long-life cycling of LMB in the $1.0\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ -EC/DEC/ FEC. As the SEI components are mainly derived from the solvation sheath of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in liquid electrolytes, Zhang et al.[131] employed FEC/ DME as co-solvents and $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ as a functional additive in the electrolyte to effectively regulate the composition of SEI. As shown in Figure 8a, their MD simulations reveal that both FEC and $\mathrm{NO}_3^-$ are present in the solvation sheath of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ . First-principle calculations also demonstrated the minimized binding energy of $-0.1\mathrm{eV}$ of FEC, which is favorable for the desolvation process and preferential decomposition. As a result, rich LiF and $\mathrm{LiN_xO_y}$ are formed in the SEI with good uniformity. The dynamic growth process of Li deposition recorded by in situ optical microscopy (Figure 8b) revealed that uniform Li deposition is achieved in $\mathrm{FEC / LiNO_3}$ electrolyte while the dendritic morphology is produced in EC/DEC electrolyte.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: In addition, Aurbach et al. studied the influence of $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ additive on the surface chemistry of lithium anode for the first time. In particular, they optimized the $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ added in the ether-based electrolyte to boost the performance of Li-S batteries.[132] They revealed that the insoluble $\mathrm{Li_xN_yO_z}$ produced from the reduction of $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ specifically absorbed at the lithium metal surface reacts with dissolved polysulfides to form a dense $\mathrm{Li_xSO_y}$ layer that could inhibit further polysulfide shuttling. Richard May et al.[133] also revealed that the as-generated $\mathrm{Li_xN_yO_z}$ layer facilitates rapid $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transfer through the SEI layer, thus contributing to forming uniform Li deposition. Moreover, Zhang et al.[134] disclosed the capability of $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ in catalyzing the conversion of polysulfides to elemental sulfur near the end of the charging process.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: Despite the tremendous progress on $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ additive in improving the cycling stability of lithium metal anode, the $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ additive could be continuously consumed throughout the charge/discharge cycling process. Moreover, the as-formed SEI does not possess enough mechanical strength to withstand the large volume fluctuation on lithium plating/stripping. Defects including pits and cracks are easily generated, where $\mathrm{Li}^+$ is preferentially deposited to form lithium filaments and dendrites. Interestingly, Cui's group demonstrated that the parasitic reaction between lithium polysulfide and Li can be utilized to address the above issue.[135] In their study, both $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_8$ and $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ were employed as functional additives, enabling a synergetic effect and the formation of a stable and uniform SEI layer. Fewer lithium nucleation sites are produced at the beginning of Li plating, and subsequent Li deposition results in a pancake-like morphology (Figure 8c). Consequently, Li dendrites were not observed even at a practical current density of $2.0\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and a high areal capacity of $6.0\mathrm{mAh}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ . Hong et al. further conducted an in-depth investigation on the mechanism of this improvement. They found that $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ and polysulfides are reduced simultaneously and deposited on the Li metal at the beginning of cycling. Subsequently, polysulfides in electrolyte are oxidized to be lithium sulfates by $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ and deposit above the previous layer. As a result, the SEI film contains two sub-layers, with the top layer composed of oxidation products of polysulfides $(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{SO}_4,\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3)$ and the bottom layer formed by the reduction products of polysulfide and $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ $(\mathrm{LiN_xO_y},\mathrm{Li_2S},\mathrm{Li_2S_2})$ (Figure 8d).[136] Such smooth and compact layered structure well suppresses the continuous reaction and electrolyte consumption on the Li metal surface.

paragraph_context: Film-forming additives can also play critical roles in boosting the cycle life of LMBs based on transition metal halides as cathodes. As for these LMBs, metal ion dissolution, active material loss, and lithium metal corrosion are among the major concerns. The HOMO energy of proper additives can be higher than that of solvent molecules, leading to a lower oxidation potential and the preferential decomposition ahead of solvent molecules on the cathode surface. The as-generated protective CEI layer can effectively inhibit the dissolution of transition metal ions. Up to date, there are a variety of cathode film-forming additives reported, including solvents and salts. The reported solvents include fluorides (FEMC),[137] perfluorooctyl-substituted EC (PFO-EC),[138] FEC,[139] and nitriles or succinonitrile (SN).[140] The typical salts are LiBOB,[141] LiDFOB,[142] lithium fluoromalonate borate (LiFMDFB),[143] and lithium difluorophosphate $(\mathrm{LiPO}_2\mathrm{F}_2)$ .[144] We will selectively discuss the roles of these additives as follow. For example, Li et al. revealed that the FEMC additive can be decomposed into C-F compounds and metal fluorides $\mathrm{(NiF_2}$ , $\mathrm{CoF}_2$ , and $\mathrm{MnF}_2$ in the CEI layer, giving rise to the unchanged surface valence of metal elements and effectively passivated cathode surface.[137] Zhao et al. found that $\mathrm{LiPO}_2\mathrm{F}_2$ additive can effectively improve the high-voltage cycling stability of LillNMC532 cell. This is attributed to the significantly reduced surface impedance and the inhibited decomposition of electrolyte enabled by the formation of a CEI film with rich LiF and $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{PO}_4$ from the decomposition of $\mathrm{LiPO}_2\mathrm{F}_2$ .[144] A synergistic effect can be realized by the cooperation of organic-inorganic co-additives due to several merits like neutralizing the weaknesses of each individual and improving the overall electrochemical performance of the battery.[145] The resultant hybrid CEI layer not only shows a robust texture but also has a high ionic conductivity. Simultaneously, the CEI layer can effectively buffer the volume fluctuation, lower the interfacial resistance, and boost the stability of the cathode. For instance, Peng et al. explored $\mathrm{LiPO}_2\mathrm{F}_2$ and FEC as co-additives to produce an organic/inorganic hybrid CEI for LMBs.[146] As shown in Figure 8e, the thin and dense CEI layer contains a variety of favorable organic/inorganic species (LiF, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ , and $\mathrm{Li_xP_yF_z}$ ), which effectively inhibit oxidative decomposition of electrolyte and dissolution of transition metal ions. Even at a high current rate of $5\mathrm{C}$ , the LillNMC cell with such electrolyte shows an excellent capacity retention rate of $88.7\%$ over 500 cycles.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: To date, most of the reported film-forming additives in the electrolytes only work for the cathode or the Li metal anode. It is highly desirable to introduce multifunctional additives to simultaneously optimize the composition and structure of both SEI and CEI for comprehensively improving the performance of LMBs. Recently, Ma and co-workers achieved this by introducing the qua-functional heptafluorobutyric anhydride (HFA) in $1.0\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ -EC/DMC.[147] The HFA can be served as a surfactant to enhance the wettability of the separator with electrolyte and thus increase Li-ion flux. More importantly, the C-F bond formed on the surface of SEI is conducive to the homogeneous adsorption of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ for uniform Li deposition. The electrolyte containing $1.0\%$ HFA can also promote the formation of uniform and dense CEI with much less thickness ( $16~\mathrm{nm}$ ). Besides, the presence of HFA additive is favorable for inhibiting the dissolvation of transition metal in the cathode, as confirmed by the absent of the M-O species ( $530.3\mathrm{eV}$ ) for the O 1s XPS spectrum of CEI (Figure 8f).

paragraph_context: Compared with film-forming additives, the deposition-regulating additives do not directly react with the Li metal anode or the electrolyte to participate in the construction of interface layers. Instead, they affect the diffusion and electroplating behaviors of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and help to improve the electrochemical performance of LMBs.

They proposed a self-healing electrostatic shielding mechanism (SHES) to explain the critical roles of the cation effect.[148] As shown in Figure 9a, as the reduction potential of alkali metal cations $\mathrm{(Cs^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Rb^{+}}$ is lower than the standard reduction potential of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , they will not be deposited during lithium deposition. However, once lithium dendrites are produced, $\mathrm{Cs^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Rb^{+}}$ could aggregate near the Li dendrite tip through electrostatic attraction to form an electrostatic shielding layer. paragraph_context: Cationic long-chain surfactants, like hexadecyltrimethylammonium chloride (CTAC), can also afford the charge shielding function to alter the distribution of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux for achieving uniform lithium deposition.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Typically, Dai et al. applied CTAC as an additive to regulate Li deposition in LMBs.[150] As shown in Figure 9b, during Li plating, $\mathrm{CTA}^+$ could be adsorbed around the lithium tip through electrostatic interaction with nonpolar groups. Compared with the smooth electrode surface, more CTAC molecules can be adsorbed at the convex tip to form a cross-linked lithium hydrophobic protective layer due to the higher surface free energy of the lithium tip. The repulsive force of the lithium hydrophobic layer is conducive to the transfer of solvated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ by polar solvent to the adjacent areas, forming a smoother Li surface.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: An inadequate and nonuniform $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ concentration near the lithium metal surface always brings about dendritic lithium deposition, particularly under a high rate. Yan et al. proposed an effective strategy to address this issue by introducing montmorillonite additive into the bulk electrolyte to modulate the surface $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ concentration and promote dendrite-free Li plating.[151] Lithium ions are preferentially adsorbed on the surface of montmorillonite because of the higher binding energy of lithium ions on the surface of montmorillonite than that on the crystal surface of Li (001). Thus, montmorillonite shows a pumping feature for self-concentrating $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , which accelerates the transfer of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ at the lithium metal/electrolyte interface. Such $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ redistribution effectively compensates for the adverse impact derived from inhomogeneity on the copper surface, leading to stable lithium nucleation and subsequent uniform deposition instead of Li filament or dendrite formation (Figure 9c).

paragraph_context: Lithium dendrites are essentially originated from the abrupt decrease of anion concentration on the surface of Li metal upon $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ deposition, resulting in a huge space charge effect.[152] Lai et al. reported a novel electrolyte additive of cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) with the planar molecular structure to well address the above issue.[153] CoPc can be tightly adsorbed on the surface of lithium metal anode to form a dense molecular protecting layer. It can not only be coordinated with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ to reduce the space charge effect and increase the transfer number of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ but also inhibit the side reaction between anode and electrolyte. paragraph_context: The functional additives may also provide more active nucleation sites for dendrite-free lithium deposition. Up to date, a variety of carbon-based nanomaterials have been reported as deposition-regulating additives to guide the nucleation and subsequent deposition of Li, such as nitrogen, sulfur-codoped carbon dots (N, S-CDs),[155] nitrofullerene,[156] 2D vermiculite sheets,[157] and graphene quantum dots (GQDs).[158] As a typical case, Cheng et al.[159] reported the exploring of nanodiamonds (NDs) to guide the uniform deposition of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions. NDs with robust lithium-ion adsorption could be evenly dispersed in the bulk electrolyte. Because of the low diffusion energy barrier of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ on the surfaces of NDs, they can be further served as heterogeneous nucleation seeds to enable uniform deposition of the adsorbed $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions.

label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: Additives based on alloying with Li for co-deposition have also attracted intensive research attention. Alloying metal elements including $\mathrm{Mg}$ ,[160] $\mathrm{In}$ ,[161] and $\mathrm{Ga}$ [162] have been reported. When these metal ions are (electro)chemically reduced and deposited on the Li metal surface, a thin Li-alloy film could be generated. The reduced irregularity of the interphase by the lithiophilic Li-alloy layer offers a more homogeneous $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ flux distribution and inhibits the lithium dendrite formation. For instance, Sun et al. introduced $\mathrm{Mg(NO_3)_2}$ as a bifunctional additive into an ester-based electrolyte.[160] The strong coordination capability of $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{NO}_3^-$ with solvated $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ makes the Li-solvent complex more prone to be desolvated. As a result, the SEI formed in the $\mathrm{Mg}$ $(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ modified electrolyte is mainly composed of inorganic components, as confirmed by the strong signal of $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{F}^+$ and weak signal of $\mathrm{CH}^{3+}$ in the time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOFSIMS) 3D-rendered image (Figure 9d). By contrast, the signals are converse for the SEI formed in the electrolyte without $\mathrm{Mg(NO_3)_2}$ . Meanwhile, Li-Mg alloys can be formed due to the electrochemical reduction of $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ by lithium metal. Due to the low solubility of $\mathrm{MgNO}_3$ in such an electrolyte, the reduction of $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ is quite limited and a favorable thin Li-Mg alloy layer can thus be generated.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ additive has been widely used in ether electrolytes for LBMs. However, the low solubility of $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ in carbonate solvents limits its application in high-voltage LMBs. To solve this concern, Huang et al. proposed to introduce a trace amount of $\mathrm{CuF}_2$ as a dissolution accelerator.[163] The addition of $\mathrm{CuF}_2$ leads to a new solvation structure in the electrolyte. As shown in Figure 9e, the interaction between $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{NO}_3^-$ is stronger than that between $\mathrm{Li}^+$ and $\mathrm{NO}_3^-$ , resulting in the dissociation of $\mathrm{Cu - F}$ and $\mathrm{Li}^{+} - \mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$ . The as-formed $\mathrm{Cu}^{2 + } - \mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$ complex can be well dissolved in EC/DEC solvent. Thanks to the presence of this complex in the electrolyte, a stable SEI film with $\mathrm{LiN_xO_y}$ and $\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{N}$ compounds could be formed on the Li metal surface during cycling, leading to a uniform lithium deposition morphology. This unique film protective Li metal anode from further reacting with carbonate electrolyte, enabling an excellent cycling performance when paired with the high-voltage NCA cathode. In addition, Lu et al. recently reported $\mathrm{LiBF_4}$ as another promoter for promoting the dissolution of $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ due to its Lewis acidity.[164] The solvated structure $\mathrm{BF}_4^-$ - $\mathrm{NO}_3^-$ of the electrolyte is beneficial to both lithium metal anode- and nickel-rich cathode. The $\mathrm{LiBF_4}$ additive promotes the formation of CEI protective film containing F and B, improving the structural stability of NCM811 under $4.4\mathrm{V}$ . It also helps to produce a robust and highly conductive SEI for chunky lithium metal deposition. Except for well-known $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ , other additives like 3-propane sultone,[165] 1,3,2-dioxathiolane-2,2-dioxide,[166] and ethylene sulfite[167] have also been reported due to their contribution to the formation of beneficial components in the SEI layer.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Very recently, a monomer and effective additive of acrylonitrile (AN) has been reported by Zhang's group.[168] AN is cathodically electropolymerized on a lithium metal surface before the electrochemical decomposition of the salts and solvent in the electrolyte. The resultant polyacrylonitrile layer enormously alleviates the side reactions and enables uniform Li nucleation and subsequent growth. Many other additives besides $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ have been introduced in the electrolytes for LiS batteries. For instance, Wang et al. introduced thionyl chloride $(\mathrm{SOCl}_2)$ as an electrolyte additive to construct a stable protective layer on Li metal to inhibit lithium dendrite growth.[169] A commercial organometallic salt, nickel chloride dimethoxyethane adduct (NiDME), was added as the homogenous catalyst to conquer the polysulfide shuttling issue by Lv's group.[170] It not only facilitates the conversion reaction from polysulfides to elemental sulfur but promotes rapid and even $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{S}$ deposition. Zhao et al. reported the $\mathrm{InI}_3$ additive to serve as both a redox mediator and an anode protector.[171] Fu et al. proposed a dual-functional electrolyte additive, 1,3,5-benzenetrithiol (BTT) to participate in constructing SEI/CEI on both lithium metal anode and sulfur cathode by in situ organothiol conversion, which relieves the shuttling of polysulfides and lithium dendrite formation.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: High-energy-density sodium metal batteries (SMBs) and potassium metal batteries (PMBs) also have attracted increasing attention owing to the high theoretical specific capacities (Na: 1166 mAh g $^{-1}$ ; K: 687 mAh g $^{-1}$ ) and low redox potentials (Na: -2.71 V; K: -2.93 V, vs. SHE) of metallic Na and K anodes.[172] Similar to LMBs, the electrolyte composition plays a crucial role in determining the electrochemical performance and safety of SMBs and PMBs. Since their development falls slightly behind LMBs, the design rules of advanced electrolytes for SMBs and PMBs generally are based on those for LMBs. In this section, we will highlight the representative studies, including those in which Na/K does not follow the Li-inherited paradigms.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: It is well accepted that the ultrahigh reactivity of Na metal anodes (SMAs) based on the conventional carbonate electrolytes at a low concentration usually results in an unstable SEI, causing a short cycle life and severe Na dendrite growth. In this regard, ether-based electrolytes with higher LUMO levels have been widely explored for highly reversible Na plating/stripping. As for a common ether-based electrolyte, the electrolyte salt will be generally reduced prior to solvent, thus leading to an anion-derived SEI with high $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ conductivity and good mechanical properties. As a pioneering study, Cui et al. reported a moderate-concentration ether electrolyte, i.e., $1\mathrm{M}\mathrm{NaPF}_6/$ diglyme, which is capable of plating/stripping Na reversibly.[173] They achieved a high average CE of approximately $99.9\%$ over 300 cycles at $0.5\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ with this electrolyte (Figure 10a). Notably, the anion in the salt has a significant impact on the composition and property of SEIs, which accounts for distinct Na plating/stripping morphologies. When a small-size anion $(e.g.,\mathrm{PF}_6^-)$ was employed, more uniform Na deposition was observed. However, a broken or nonuniform Na deposition appeared for salt with large-size anions, such as $\mathrm{ClO_4^-}$ , $\mathrm{OTf^{-}}$ , and $\mathrm{TFSI^{-}}$ . It is worth mentioning that almost the same Na plating/stripping performance was obtained when monoglyme and tetraglyme were used as solvents (Figure 10b). In another study, Jiao et al. developed a variety of low-concentration ether-based electrolytes containing $0.5\mathrm{MNaBF_4}$ in various glyme solvents, such as diglyme, triglyme, and tetraglyme, for highly reversible and dendrite-free SMBs.[174] They found that $\mathrm{NaBF_4}$ has a relatively low solubility in ether solvents, such as THF, DME, and diglyme. The saturated $\mathrm{NaBF_4}$ /diglyme shows a concentration of around $0.64\mathrm{M}$ . Although the 0.1, 0.25, and $0.5\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{NaBF_4}$ /diglyme electrolytes exhibit similarly high CE at the current density of $0.5\mathrm{mA cm}^{-2}$ , the more concentrated one $(0.5\mathrm{M})$ delivers superior cycling stability and longevity, as well as lower plating/stripping overpotential as compared to those in the low-concentration counterparts due to the higher ionic conductivity. Compared with the $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ -based electrolytes, the $\mathrm{NaBF_4}$ -based electrolytes show pronounced solvent effect. The $\mathrm{NaBF_4}$ /diglyme exhibited the best performance in view of good wettability, high ionic conductivity, and stable plating/stripping efficiency. Owing to the ultrathin and robust SEI layer containing a large amount of NaF and B-O species, the assembled NallCu cell using the $0.5\mathrm{MNaBF_4}$ /diglyme operated steadily over 400 cycles, accompanying by an ultrahigh average CE of $99.93\%$ .

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Recently, Hu et al. proposed an ultralow-concentration electrolyte to produce organic-dominated SEI for Na-ion batteries by taking advantage of the smaller Stokes radius and lower desolvation energy of $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ compared to those of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ .[175] However, such SEI derived in the ultralow-concentration electrolyte cannot solve the issue of Na dendrite growth because the modulus of organic species is far behind that of inorganic components. Until recently, Xiang and co-workers reported the introduction of an acetamide additive, N,O-bis(trimethylsilyl) trifluoroacetamide (BSTFA), into an ultralow-concentration electrolyte composed of $0.3\mathrm{M}\mathrm{NaPF}_6$ in EC/PC (1:1 in volume), for effectively stabilizing the SEI and favoring uniform Na deposition/dissolution.[176] Their theoretical and experimental results demonstrated that the BSTFA additive not only scavenges HF and $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ in the electrolyte to generate more stable and uniform CEI but also inhibits the rapid consumption of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ salt. As a result, the $\mathrm{NaIINa_3V_2(PO_4)_3}$ battery using this novel ultralow-concentration electrolyte containing $2\%$ BSTFA shows remarkable capacity retention of $92.63\%$ after 1955 cycles at $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and an impressive rate capability of $105\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . As the ultralow salt concentration can greatly reduce the cost and viscosity of electrolytes, new electrolyte recipes with an ultralow concentration of salt deserve more research efforts.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: In addition, novel electrolytes enabling stable K plating/stripping for PMBs have also been devised in recent years. For example, Wu et al. reported a potassium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (KFSI)/DME electrolyte for generating uniform SEI on the surface of K metal.[177] Without any surface coating or separator modification, the K metal can be plated and stripped over 200 cycles with a high CE of over $99\%$ in this electrolyte. A further increase of the salt concentration enhances the initial K plating/stripping CE and the oxidation durability of KFSI/DME electrolytes due to the fewer content of free DME molecules. Besides, Guo's group developed a KFSI salt-based carbonate electrolyte for both K metal and alloying anodes.[178] The DFT calculation results revealed that the higher solvation energy of KFSI-based electrolytes than that of $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ related electrolytes gives rise to a higher degree of solvent molecules and fewer side reactions between K metal and electrolyte. They also revealed that a preferable reduction of KFSI dissolved in EC/DEC (1:1) as compared to $\mathrm{KPF_6}$ due to the lower LUMO energy. Consequently, the $1\mathrm{M}$ KFSI/EC+DEC (1:1, v/v) electrolyte facilitated the formation of a robust SEI layer for protecting K metal from corrosion. Aside from the carbonate and ether-based electrolytes, an intrinsically nonflammable electrolyte comprising triethyl phosphate (TEP) as the solvent was widely explored for KMBs.[179] Unlike the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ counterparts, the weak solvation of $\mathrm{K^{+}}$ cations in TEP enables a low viscosity and high ionic conductivity, thereby achieving superior K plating/stripping kinetics. A uniform and robust anion-derived SEI containing S, N, and F-based inorganic compounds was enabled in a moderately concentrated KFSI/TEP electrolyte (2 M). In addition, such a KFSI/TEP electrolyte shows the intrinsic advantages of low cost, low viscosity, and enhanced nonflammability (Figure 10c). As such, nondendritic K metal plating/stripping with an average CE of $99.6\%$ for more than 500 cycles was achieved, which is superior to that in conventional flammable organic liquid electrolytes (Figure 10d).

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: As discussed in Section 3.1, the increased concentration of HCEs is practicable to improve the performance of LMBs owing to the optimized solvation structure. In HCEs, almost all solvent molecules are coordinated to cations, thus forming a huge array of AGGs and CIPs instead of SSIPs commonly existing in the dilute electrolytes (normally, $\leq 1\mathrm{M}$ ). As such, HCEs normally have low volatility, wide voltage windows, and good electrochemical stability against alkali metals. Anions play a pivotal role in preparing HCE. Electrolyte salts with $\mathrm{TFSI}^{-}$ and $\mathrm{FSI}^{-}$ anions are the most commonly used. For example, Cao et al. formulated a $4\mathrm{MNaFSI / DME}$ electrolyte for reversible Na metal plating/stripping with high efficiencies of $>99\%$ at 0.5 and $1.0\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ . In a recent study, Lee et al. designed an ultraconcentrated electrolyte based on $5\mathrm{MNaFSI / DME}$ . This HCE enables a high cycling stability and excellent Na plating/stripping reversibility.[180] Komaba et al. improved the electrochemical reversibility of K plating/stripping in an HCE consisting of $3.9\mathrm{M}$ KFSI in DME based on the same strategy. The symmetric cell display a small and stable polarization of $25\mathrm{mV}$ for more than $300\mathrm{h}$ at $25~\mu \mathrm{A}$ $\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ . [181] Similar to that in LMBs, the poor wettability, high viscosity, and high costs also limit the practical applications of HCEs for both SMBs and PMBs. To maintain the favorable solvation structure as HCEs in an electrolyte with a lower overall concentration, Zheng et al. pioneered a novel electrolyte system by adding inert diluent (mainly hydrofluoroether) into conventional HCEs to reduce their viscosity and improve ionic conductivity. For example, a $2.1\mathrm{M}$ NaFSI salt in a mixed solvent of DME and BTFE at a molar ratio of 1:2 was designed for SMBs.[97] As shown in Figure 10e, the viscosity of the $2.1\mathrm{M}$ NaFSI/DME+BTFE electrolyte is substantially decreased due to the incorporating of BTFE diluent, showing a comparable value to that of the conventional carbonate-based electrolyte. Thanks to the high ionic conductivity and low viscosity, this LHCE enables the prolonged stripping/plating of Na with a high CE of over $99\%$ at $1.0\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ (Figure 10f).

paragraph_context: Room-temperature ionic liquids (ILs) have been widely explored as promising electrolytes for SMBs and PMBs due to their nonflammable nature, high ionic conductivity, good thermal stability, and excellent chemical inertness. However, the reversibility and stability of Na plating/stripping in ILs are still not satisfactory, even with additives. Recently, Dai's group reported an novel IL electrolyte comprising $\mathrm{AlCl}_3 / 1$ -methyl-3-ethylimidazolium chloride ([EMIm]Cl)/NaCl, as well as two important additives of ethylaluminum dichloride (EtAlCl₂) and 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (referred as 'buffered Na-Cl-IL electrolyte') for highly rechargeable SMBs (Figure 11a).[182] The buffered Na-Cl-IL electrolyte shows a high oxidation stability potential of $\sim 4.56\mathrm{V}$ , a high ionic conductivity of $\sim 9.2\mathrm{mS}\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ at $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and excellent thermal stability without apparent weight loss until $\sim 400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 11b). The Na plating/stripping CE of a NallPt cell using the buffered Na-Cl-IL electrolyte increases from $\sim 72$ to $\sim 91\%$ during the first 5 cycles and then reach $\sim 95\%$ at $0.5\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ under a plating capacity of $0.25\mathrm{mAh}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ . They further extended this concept to prepare a KCl-buffered $\mathrm{AlCl}_3 / [\mathrm{EMIm}]$ Cl IL electrolyte with the addition of $\mathrm{EtAlCl_2}$ and KFSI.[183] The above electrolyte shows an ionic conductivity of $\sim 13.1~\mathrm{mS~cm^{-1}}$ , enabling a maximal K plating/stripping CE of $\sim 95.3\%$ on Ni current collector for 200 cycles. It is worth mentioning that the Na and K plating/stripping CEs in IL-based electrolytes are still much lower than expected for practical applications. In addition, the high viscosity and extremely high cost of ILs are two main obstacles to commercial utilization.

paragraph_context: To further improve the plating/stripping CE in IL-based electrolytes, Li et al. recently employed 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate $\left(\left[\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{C}_{1} \mathrm{im}\right]\left[\mathrm{BF}_{4}\right]\right)$ as a co-solvent to prepare a composite electrolyte for deeply cycled sodium metal anodes at low temperature.[184] The composite electrolyte is made up of $1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaPF}_{6}$ in a mixture solvent of $\left[\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{C}_{1} \mathrm{im}\right]\left[\mathrm{BF}_{4}\right]$ and diglyme (1:4, v/v), which is abbreviated as ether- $\left[\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{C}_{1} \mathrm{im}\right]\left[\mathrm{BF}_{4}\right]$ in the following. As displayed in Figure 11c, the ether- $\left[\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{C}_{1} \mathrm{im}\right]\left[\mathrm{BF}_{4}\right]$ electrolyte has a relatively stable and high ionic conductivity of $\sim 42 \mathrm{mS} \mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ even at $-20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for $70 \mathrm{~h}$ , while the ionic conductivity of $1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaPF}_{6}$ /diglyme electrolyte dramatically drops from 60 to $2 \mathrm{mS} \mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ under the same condition. As shown in Figure 11d, precipitates in the ether for ether- $\mathrm{[C_4C_1im][PF_6]}$ and ether- $\mathrm{[C_4C_1im]}$ [OTF] electrolytes were observed after storage at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for six days, while the case for ether- $\mathrm{[C_4C_1im][BF_4]}$ are transparent without sediment. This ensures sufficient $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ conductivity for operation at low temperatures. In addition, the NMR and XPS results confirmed that the introduction of $\mathrm{[C_4C_1im][BF_4]}$ effectively suppresses the decomposition of the electrolyte. The Ar-ion sputtering tests revealed that the SEI formed in the ether- $\mathrm{[C_4C_1im][BF_4]}$ is thinner ( $\sim 7\mathrm{nm}$ ) than that in pure ether electrolyte ( $\sim 10\mathrm{nm}$ ). Due to the fast ion transport, superior desolvation capability, and high electrochemical stability of the electrolyte at low temperature, the SMA can be stably cycled at $2\mathrm{mA}\mathrm{m}^{-2}$ with a reversible capacity of $50\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ for $500\mathrm{h}$ at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ under a lean electrolyte condition of $1.0\mathrm{mL}\mathrm{mAh}^{-1}$ (Figure 11e). Considering the pros and cons of ILs, the hybridization of ILs with the conventional ester and/or ether electrolytes will synergistically improve the performance of alkali metal batteries.

paragraph_context: Electrolyte additives have frequently been used as SEI-stabilizing agents. Implantation of electrolyte additives is simple yet effective for improving the plating/stripping reversibility of rechargeable SMBs and PMBs. In this subsection, the electrolyte additives are simply categorized into two types: 1) film-forming additives to alleviate side reactions; and 2) electrostatic shielding additives to homogenize the cation flux.

paragraph_context: As mentioned before, carbonate-based electrolytes are typically unstable against alkali metals, especially for Na and K. By introducing proper additives in the electrolyte, the CE of Na deposition/dissolution can be substantially improved. Among various additives, FEC is a well-established additive to improve the cyclic stability of alloying and $\mathrm{Na} / \mathrm{K}$ metal anodes owing to its low LUMO energy. The FEC can be preferentially reduced and decomposed on the surface of the $\mathrm{Na} / \mathrm{K}$ metal, accompanied by the formation of a metal fluoride-rich SEI layer. With the participation of FEC in $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ solvation, a robust NaF-rich SEI was generated, thereby contributing to homogeneous Na deposition.[185,186] Besides, a nitrofullerene $(\mathrm{C}_{60}(\mathrm{NO}_2)_6)$ additive that is compatible with both carbonate and ether electrolytes was adopted to enable dendrite-free plating/stripping of SMAs.[187] As illustrated in Figure 11f, the nitro groups anchoring on the $\mathrm{C}_{60}$ cage trigger the formation of the desired SEI layer enriched in $\mathrm{NaN_xO_y / Na_3N}$ species, meanwhile, the $\mathrm{C}_{60}$ cages preferentially deposit on the Na metal surface to govern the uniform, compact, and smooth Na deposition. Consequently, the NallNa symmetric cells with $\mathrm{C}_{60}(\mathrm{NO}_2)_6$ additive displayed low-voltage hysteresis, high-rate capability, and impressive cycle life in both carbonate and ether electrolytes. Moreover, the NallCu half cells utilizing $\mathrm{C}_{60}(\mathrm{NO}_2)_6$ containing ether electrolyte show an ultrahigh CE of $>99.4\%$ at $1.0\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ with a deposition capacity of $1.0\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ and remarkable cyclic stability at a high current density of $5\mathrm{mAcm}^{-2}$ for 450 cycles. In another study, Huang et al. incorporated a small amount of $\mathrm{SnCl}_2$ additive in common carbonate electrolyte to spontaneously induce a Na-Sn alloy layer and a compact NaCl-rich SEI.[188] The as-formed SEI allows for uniform Na deposition, achieving a dendrite-free morphology instead of a dendritic or mossy Na structure. In addition, $\mathrm{NaAsF_6}$ ,[189] $\mathrm{InI}_3$ ,[190] and $\mathrm{Na_2S_6}$ [191] have also been examined to enhance the stability of SEI by generating highly ionic conductive and mechanical robust inorganic species, thereby allowing the stable operation of SMAs. To improve the safety of the SMBs battery, Huang et al. recently designed an intrinsically nonflammable, highly fluorinated electrolyte consisting of $1.0\mathrm{MNaPF_6}$ in FEC/PC/TTE/perfluoro-2-methyl-3-pentanone (PFMP).[192] The TTE is served as the "bridge solvent", enabling the temperature-sensitive all-fluoride PFMP to better dissipate the surrounding heat and promote the formation of passivated NaF-based interphases on both Na anode and cathode simultaneously (Figure 11g).

paragraph_context: Few additives were explored to stabilize K anodes. Very recently, Kang et al. proposed the use of potassium nitrate $\mathrm{(KNO_3)}$ additive in $2.3\mathrm{M}$ KFSI/DME to promote dense K deposition and prevent Al corrosion.[193] They found that the $\mathrm{KNO}_3$ additive can regulate the deposition morphology of K metal from whisker-like filaments to small nodule-like aggregates. The reason needs to be further explored in future. More efforts are required to develop new additives and uncover their working mechanisms for PMBs.

Since the redox potential of $\mathrm{Li^{+} / Li}$ is also lower than that of $\mathrm{Na^{+} / Na}$ , Zhang[195] and Chen[196] reported the use of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ cations to establish the electrostatic shielding layer for uniform Na deposition.

paragraph_context: Advanced AMBs have attracted increasing research attention owing to the ever-growing demand for energy storage systems with boosted energy density. Electrolytes, which insulate electrons but conduct ionic currents between the cathode and anode, are regarded as the key components for enabling new chemistries and functions. An ideal electrolyte should have the features of high safety, rate performance, thermal and electrochemical stability, low cost, and most importantly, good capability to form a favorable electrode/electrolyte interface, especially on the hyper-reaction alkali metal surface. State-of-the-art electrolytes in LIBs can no longer sustain the desired technological trajectory. A variety of novel electrolytes have been developed in recent years and have been comprehensively reviewed in this paper.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: HCEs have several merits, including a relatively low resistance and uniform interface of the SEI for a dendrite-free Li deposition, an extended work voltage window for a high-energy density, and a good flame retardancy toward high operational safety. Furthermore, HCEs are favorable for suppressing the dissolution of transition metal ions in the cathode. Nevertheless, their high viscosity and high cost are major obstacles to their wide application. Diluting HCEs into LHCEs can effectively address the above issues while maintaining all the intrinsic features of HCEs because the introduced diluents usually will not change the overall solvation structure of the Li salt in the HCE electrolytes. To ensure good safety, low volatility and nonflammable diluents are commonly screened and utilized.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Fluorinated compounds are usually necessary components in the electrolytes for promoting thermal and electrochemical stability, alkaline metal ionic conduction, as well as low- and high-temperature performances. They are also favorable for producing better SEI/CEI, the stabilization of Al current collectors, inhibition of transition metal dissolution, and improving inflammability and safety. Proper fluorination of the anions in Li salts can reduce their interaction with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ to enhance the solubility of salts and the anti-oxidation capability at high operating potentials. The fluorinated solvents exhibit reduced HOMO and LUMO levels, resulting in improved anodic stability and/or deteriorated cathodic stability. They can withstand higher work voltages and improve the flame retardancy of the electrolytes.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Functional electrolyte additives have been widely used and are regarded as the most feasible, economic, and efficient strategy for addressing the major issues in AMBs. Even with a small dose, the use of additives can effectively prevent the electrolyte from decomposition, anode dendrite formation, and cathode degradation toward high-energy, stable, and safe AMBs. The film-forming additives alter the microstructure and/or composition of the SEI to promote Li deposition and inhibit dendrite growth. Deposition-regulating additives do not participate in the formation of SEI, while they are effective for the favorable $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ flux distribution toward smooth electrodeposition on the alkali metal anode.

paragraph_context: SMBs and PMBs are promising alternatives to replace LMBs owing to the natural abundance and low cost of sodium and potassium, as well as the inspiration from the successful commercialization of rechargeable sodium batteries. As demonstrated in LMBs, the development of advanced liquid electrolytes is critical for achieving the satisfactory electrochemical performance and safety of SMBs and PMBs. While the rich experience learned from designing advanced electrolytes for LMBs, particularly the (localized) HCEs, the introduction of functional additives etc., the unique design principles of electrolytes for SMBs and PMBs do not always follow the Li-inherited paradigms. The normal concentration of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ in ether solvent enables an ultrahigh Na plating/stripping efficiency of $99.9\%$ and $1\mathrm{M}$ KFSI/DME electrolyte can also achieve a high CE of $\sim 99\%$ , which is far superior to those of LMBs. More impressively, a low-concentration electrolyte $(0.3\mathrm{M}\mathrm{NaPF}_6$ in EC/PC) with an acetamide additive $(2\mathrm{wt}\%)$ in SMBs can also achieve stable cycling operation of SMBs. Such an impressive cycling performance in electrolytes with such a low concentration of salt is never realized in LMBs owing to the smaller Stokes radius and desolvation energy of $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ than those of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ .

Email: caiyun@uow.edu.au The performance of Li batteries is influenced by the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure, which can be precisely adjusted by the components of the electrolytes. In this review, we overview the strategies for optimizing electrolyte solvation structures from three different perspectives, including anion regulation, binding energy regulation, and additive regulation. These strategies can optimize the composition of the electrode-electrolyte interface, enhance the anti-oxidative stability of electrolytes as well as regulate the behaviors of anions, solvents, and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ during the cycling process. Moreover, we also provide our insights into these aspects as well as present perspectives on high-performance Li batteries. anion solvation, electrolyte additives, electrolytes, lithium batteries, solvation structures Currently, Li-ion batteries (LIBs) have received great attention due to their excellent comprehensive performance from the cost to electrochemistry. $^{1-4}$ However, the issues of capacity degradation, slow charging speed, poor low-temperature performance, and safety need to be addressed for the development of high-performance Li batteries with using Li as the high-capacity anode. $^{5-12}$ Different strategies have been applied to ameliorate the above-mentioned issues, such as doping and coating of electrode materials, modification of separators, optimization of binders, and electrolyte engineering. $^{13-17}$ Compared with other measures, electrolyte engineering has attracted increasing interest from academia and industry due to the unchanged procedure of battery fabrication. Ideal electrolytes should have higher safety, lower cost, wider working temperature range, and stronger anti-oxidative stability. $^{18,19}$ Various strategies have been designed for advanced electrolyte systems, e.g., additive regulation, solvent regulation, anion regulation. $^{6,7,20-23}$ Among them, the regulation of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure in electrolytes can cause different de-solvation behavior of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ at the electrode/electrolyte interface and solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) compositions.[24,25] The interactions among anions and cations, solvents, co-solvents, and additives can be changed dynamically in the whole complex electrolyte system, which brings great difficulties for us to analyze the behavior of the electrolytes.[26,27] Fortunately, advanced characterization methods and computational simulations have been developed to analyze the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure for studying the behavior of electrolytes.[28-31] As a function of Li salt in solvents with additives, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure could determine many properties of the electrolytes, and especially the structural model $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ [solvent]x [additive]y[anion] has been proposed to explain battery performance. $^{30,32}$ The precise control of solvation structure can eliminate the adverse effects of some solvent molecules. $^{33-38}$ For example, Ming et al. $^{38}$ found that the formed $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -EC complex in EC-contained electrolyte was crucial to stabilizing the electrolytes. High-concentration electrolyte (HCE) and others could greatly reduce the number of solvent-separated ion pair (SSIP) structures and free solvent molecules, which is mainly composed of contact ion pair (CIP) and aggregates (AGGs). $^{29,39-41}$ CIP and AGGs are the complexes of oppositely charged $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and anions associated due to coulomb interaction, in which AGGs have more than two $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ using the same anion as the center to count the coordinating $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ number. $^{42}$ As reported, $^{43,44}$ due to the interfacial electric double layer (EDL) generated by the dissolution of Li on the electrode surface, only the anions in the solvated structure can participate in the construction of sustainable SEI together with other electrolyte components. In addition, these structures have higher anti-oxidative stability than free molecules due to the lowered highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level. $^{45-48}$ Highly polar solvents preferentially solvate $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and show higher binding energy with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , leading to a sluggish de-solvation process, especially at low temperatures. $^{1,38,49}$ Therefore, weakening the binding energy between the solvent and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ is an effective way to promote the low-temperature performance of Li batteries. $^{7}$ Besides, additives can impact the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure from multiple aspects, such as changing the behavior of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in the electrolyte through special groups in the molecular structures, regulating the electrode-electrolyte interphase compositions, and promoting the interaction between anions and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ , etc. $^{3,21,41,50,51}$ Therefore, it is capable to adjust the performance of Li batteries by manipulating the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure. $^{32,52,53}$ At present, there are some excellent reviews on the electrolytes of Li batteries, such as high-voltage electrolytes,[54] additive modifications,[55] and solvent optimization.[56] Different from them, this review will focus on the structural regulation chemistry of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation for Li batteries.

paragraph_context: CIP and AGGs structures can be generated by weakening the solvability of solvents. Zhang's group $^{96}$ prepared a weakly solvating electrolyte (WSE) dominated with CIP and AGGs structures in 1,4-Dioxane (1,4-DX)-based electrolyte with 1 M LiFSI (Figure 3A), in which free ions, CIP, and AGGs could account for $15.6\%$ , $49\%$ , and $35.4\%$ by Raman spectrum, respectively, which was consistent with the ${}^{17}\mathrm{O}$ Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) analysis result (Figure 3B). As demonstrated in Figure 3C, the $\Delta E$ of 1,4-DX was higher than $2\mathrm{eV}$ , while the conventional solvent was around $0\mathrm{eV}$ , which led to the involvement of a larger number of anions in the coordination according to the rule of thermodynamic enthalpy reduction. In addition, the Li|graphite battery displayed excellent performance due to the stability of SEI by adding $2\%$ ethylene carbonate (EC) (Figure 3D). Pham et al. $^{97}$ found that AGGs and CIP in the weakly solvating electrolyte based on 1,2-diethoxyethane (DEOE) were significantly higher than those in conventional DME-based electrolyte, as shown in Raman spectroscopy (Figure 3E). The study by Cui's group $^{98}$ displayed that the performance difference between DEOE and DME stemmed from steric hindrance. The large ethoxy group of DEOE weakened its coordination ability compared with methoxy, making it a weaker solvated molecule than DME. paragraph_context: The $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ intercalation undergoes three processes. Firstly, it diffuses from the bulk electrolyte to the electrode/electrolyte interphase, and then de-solvates. paragraph_context: The significant reduction of Li-battery capacity at low temperatures greatly limits its application in military and defense, space exploration, and high latitude regions. For low-temperature Li-battery electrolytes, it is critical that the electrolyte has a wide temperature operating range. The PC/DEC-based electrolyte described above could provide a capacity of $62\%$ at low temperature, which was attributed to the low melting point of PC (Figure 8A).<sup>105</sup> The carboxylate with a lower melting point could decrease the lower limit of the operating temperature of the electrolyte.<sup>113,114</sup> As demonstrated in Figure 8B, Xia's group<sup>49</sup> reported a low-temperature battery based on ethyl acetate (EA) that could make the battery operate at $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ due to the low freezing point of $-84^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the conductivity of $0.2\mathrm{mScm}^{-1}$ at $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , whereas the limited voltage window of EA hindered the application in high-voltage batteries. Inert dichloromethane (DCM) was used as a co-solvent to eradicate this shortcoming (Figure 8C).<sup>115</sup> The 5 M EA electrolyte containing DCM could significantly widen the electrochemical window $(1.5 - 4.85\mathrm{V})$ , increase the capacity and conductivity, as well as decrease the viscosity of the electrolyte at low temperature (Figure 8D,E). This is due to the structure similar to the LHCE, in which DCM played as a diluent. Fluorine atoms have a strong electron-withdrawing ability, the fluorination of ethyl acetate amends its stability at high voltage and controls the affinity between solvent and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ . In another work, they prepared an ethyl trifluoroacetate (ETFA)-based low-temperature electrolyte that could reach an oxidation potential of $4.73\mathrm{V}$ .<sup>116</sup> Benefiting from the low polarizability and high electronegativity of fluorine atoms, the binding energy of ETFA with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ was much lower than that of EA, DMC, and EC (Figure 8F). Zhou's group used zeolite molecular sieves to modify the surface of cathode to produce a unique zeolite sieving electrolyte. When weakly coordinated molecules with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ passed through the molecular sieve membrane, the narrow channel (3 Å) of zeolite molecular sieve made them squeeze out, causing only molecules with strong coordination with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ to reach the electrode surface with greatly increased antioxidative stability (Figure 10A,C). In addition, they used CuBTC metalorganic frameworks (MOF) with modified channels to achieve this "de-solvation" process (Figure 10D). The saturated LiTFSI-PC $(\mathrm{Li(PC)}_4, 10.5\AA)$ cannot enter the $6.5\AA$ pore in the modified MOF material. paragraph_context: In short, the de-solvation process has a significant impact on battery performance. As a quantitative criterion of de-solvation, the binding energy between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and electrolyte components is a crucial factor that needs to be considered for electrolyte design. Although the solvent with high polarity attains high conductivity, its strong binding energy with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ causes a slower de-solvation process. Everything has two sides, the strongly solvated molecules with $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ have excellent anti-oxidative stability, sieve out weakly solvated molecules significantly bettering the high-voltage performance of electrolytes.

Changes in any component of the electrolyte, including but not limited to the decreasing of solvent polarity, the enhancing of anion coordination ability, and the introduction of coordination additives, all affect the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ . Adjusting the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation structure can optimize the composition of SEI/CEI, accelerate the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ de-solvation process, enhance the antioxidative stability of the electrolyte, and regulate the behavior of electrolyte components to better the high voltage, low-temperature, and fast charging performance of the electrolyte. paragraph_context: Ziqi Zeng and Jia Xie, State Key Laboratory of Advanced Electromagnetic Engineering and Technology, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, 430074 Wuhan, China. Email: ziqizeng@hust.edu.cn and xiejia@hust.edu.cn Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have monopolized energy storage markets in modern society. The reliable operation of LIBs at cold condition $(<0^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ , nevertheless, is inevitably hampered by the sluggish kinetics and parasite reactions, which falls behind the increasing demands for portable electronics and electric vehicles. The electrolyte controls both $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport and interfacial reaction, dictating the low-temperature performance substantially. Therefore, the rational formulation of electrolytes is significant for realizing superior low-temperature performance and broadening application niches of LIBs. Herein, we first discuss the kinetic limitations of low-temperature LIBs, highlighting the importance of electrolyte structure and interfacial chemistry. Then, the advancements for formulating subzero-temperature electrolyte are summarized with in-depth discussions about electrolyte formulation, solvation structure, interfacial chemistry, and low-temperature behaviors. Moreover, some opportunities for lithium metal batteries and the corresponding low-temperature electrolyte are covered. Finally, the major challenges and future perspectives are outlined for low-temperature LIBs. electrolyte, lithium-ion batteries, low temperatures, solvation structures Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) featuring high energy density, long cycle life, and environmental friendliness have dominated the energy storage areas ever since their commercialization in 1991.[1-4] The great success and advancements of LIBs stimulate potential applications for emergency rescue, military defense, submarine exploration, and space travel, which possibly involve extremely cold conditions even below $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Nevertheless, the inevitable performance decay of LIBs (e.g., capacity fading, cycling instability, and parasite reactions) proves emergent when confronted with cryogenic operations (typically below $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ). Furthermore, the tendency for detrimental Li deposition causes cell failure and safety issues.[5,6] Resultantly, both the temperature-related performance decay and safety concerns restrict the application niches of LIBs in cold conditions.[7] To satisfy the normal functions of LIBs at cold scenarios, thermal management systems (BMS) are equipped indispensably to stabilize local temperature $(0 - 40^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ , however, at the expense of suppressed portability and additional costs,[8,9] which impedes the pursuit for higher energy density. Moreover, the reliability of BMS is threatened by the local heat accumulation and possible mechanical failure during whole service life. Several studies have summarized the existing BMS for low-temperature operations and concluded that preheating LIBs in cold condition is still challenging despite the considerable progress in BMS.[10,11] For this reason, formulating LIBs with intrinsic low-temperature tolerance and reliable operation without ancillary heating devices is absolutely urgent to further widen the application scope of LIBs.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: The degradation of LIBs at a cold environment is mainly reflected by the energy loss and deteriorated service life, in which the former is linked to inferior electrochemical kinetics and the latter is correlated with unfavorable interfacial protections. Each step of the electrochemical process, including inferior electrolyte conduction, hampered charge transfer and sluggish solid-state diffusion might be responsible for the rate-limiting kinetics once the temperature drops blew $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .[12,13] Fortunately, the solid-state diffusion can be easily circumvented via proper surface modification and nanocrystallization (e.g., heteroatomic doping and carbon coating).[14,15] The electrolyte conduction, nevertheless, poses a bigger threat than electrodes since increased viscosity and detrimental solidification, which slows down $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport within the electrolyte and cuts off the electrochemical process. As for service life of LIBs, the electrolyte involves in different reduction pathways as ambient temperature and hence dictate solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). The as-obtained SEI influences reversibility, stability, and $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ deposition. Therefore, the direct innovations and advancements from electrolytes are effective for ensuring efficient $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion and desirable interfacial chemistry simultaneously. As a result, the desirable low-temperature electrolyte should afford high energy (80% of capacity at ambient temperature) and reliable cycling at least below $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Given the ever-growing demands for LIBs operated at low temperature, it is significant to provide a timely review about the challenges and advancements for low-temperature electrolytes. Recently, Sun et al.[16] summarized the critical barriers of ions transport for electrochemical devices, highlighting the significance of mass transfer for reliable low-temperature applications. Zhang et al.[17] discussed the critical factors and strategies for optimizing low-temperature lithium-based batteries from the perspective of the whole system. Despite the electrolyte-related strategies are outlined by many works,[18-20] the underlying relations among electrolyte formulation, electrolyte properties and low-temperature behaviors are seldom revealed systematically. In this article, we first discuss scientific and technological barriers of LIBs under subzero temperature in terms of solid-state diffusion, interfacial chemistry and electrolyte microstructures, elucidating the rate-limiting steps of low-temperature operation. Given the critical importance of electrolytes, we further survey the advancements of low-temperature electrolytes, highlighting electrolyte formulation, electrolyte structure, electrolyte chemistry, interfacial chemistry, and low-temperature performance (Figure 1). On the basis of the above, the general principle for designing low-temperature electrolyte is proposed. In addition, the opportunity and progress for lithium metal batteries (LMBs) at low-temperature are also covered. This review aims to provide a comprehensive and in-depth understanding on the challenges, advancements and prospects of low-temperature electrolyte.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: LIBs exhibit energy loss and limited service life at low temperature, which can be ascribed to the following aspects: (1) the sluggish solid-state diffusion within lattice and intrinsic grain-boundary resistance for electrodes; (2) the decreased conductivity and blocked ion transport in electrolyte originated from increased viscosity and solidification upon cooling; (3) the formidable barrier for $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ desolvation and slow $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ migration across SEI on electrode surface; (4) the kinetically hampered SEI formation and unfavorable interfacial protection; (5) the detrimental Li dendrites formation together with safety considerations during charging. The above limitations and issues are illustrated in Figure 2 and the underlying mechanisms will be discussed sequentially in the following section.

paragraph_context: As reported, only $12\%$ of the ambient-temperature capacity can be obtained for Li//graphite cells operated at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ due to the sluggish kinetics for $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion within graphite lattice.[21] Moreover, the severe degradations from energy density (from 100 to $5\mathrm{WhL}^{-1}$ ) and power density (from 800 to $10\mathrm{WL}^{-1}$ ) are observed in 18,650-type Li-ion batteries as the temperature decreases from $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .[22] These results indicate the detrimental effects of sluggish mass transport within layered graphite under low temperature. Huang et al.[23] first determined the decisive role of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion in carbon anode. As shown in Figure 3A, the delithiation process for lithiated graphite ( $\mathrm{LiC_6}$ ) can be proceeded at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a reasonable capacity retention up to $87\%$ (current density is $0.285\mathrm{mA cm}^{-2}$ ), while the lithiation process for graphite is kinetically sluggish with limited capacity even at lower current density ( $57\%$ of capacity at $0.00095\mathrm{mA cm}^{-2}$ ) (Figure 3B). In addition, the lithiation of graphite is relatively inferior to that of coke ( $5.4\%$ and $42.3\%$ of capacity for graphite and coke, respectively) since the hampered solid-state diffusion ( $10^{-11}$ and $10^{-9}\mathrm{cm}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ for graphite and coke, respectively). The performance decay of LIBs is also correlated with sluggish kinetics in cathode materials in some cases.[24-26] The commonly adopted $\mathrm{LiFePO_4 / C}$ suffers from low diffusion coefficient $(10^{-11} - 10^{-10}\mathrm{cm}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1})$ at subzero temperature, indicating the incompatibility of $\mathrm{LiFePO_4 / C}$ for low-temperature operations.[27] Moreover, the $\mathrm{LiMn_{0.8}Fe_{0.2}PO_4 / C}$ composite, featuring one-dimensional diffusion path as $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ , also exhibits limited coefficient $(10^{-13}\mathrm{cm}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1})$ at ambient temperature.[28] Apart from olivine-type phase, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion in layered cathode is also studied. paragraph_context: Fortunately, there have been numerous methods for improving solid-state diffusion within electrodes (cathode and anode). For instance, the introduction of in-plane defects proves effective for accelerating $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ diffusion in graphene.[39] Exfoliated graphite sheets with through holes are also developed to create more intercalation sites,[40,41] leading to fast $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ migration through in-plane direction $(10^{-7} - 10^{-6}\mathrm{cm}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1})$ . Given the kinetically impeded two-dimensional diffusion path in graphite, researchers switched to electrodes with three-dimensional channels to satisfy the low-temperature performance.[42] The low-temperature behaviors of typical anode materials are compared.[31] Noticeably, Si-C and graphite reach the cut-off potentials $(0.01\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+})$ prematurely when discharging at $-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 3D). $\mathrm{Li}_4\mathrm{Ti}_5\mathrm{O}_{12}$ possesses higher operating potential but suffers from low capacity. Only $\mathrm{SnO}_2$ is capable of delivering both high capacity $(780.7\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1})$ and safe operating potentials (above $0.01\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+})$ at cold condition. These results indicate that anode based on conversion mechanisms might be promising at cold conditions. As for cathode, numerous strategies, including optimizing calcination temperature,[14] controlling particle sizes,[43] improving purity,[44] and surface modifications,[15,45] have been developed to boost electrochemical dynamics.[46] Zheng et al. elucidated the blocking effects of ion transport within the crystal lattice (Figure 3E). The amorphous electrode, featuring abundant active sites and diffusion channels, exhibits remarkably improved performance even at $-80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 3F).[32] Zhang et al. demonstrated the nickel surface doped $\mathrm{LiMn}_2\mathrm{O}_4$ with facilitated interfacial processes and suppressed capacity decay upon cooling, underlining the effectiveness of cationic doping to solve interfacial issues.[47] Alternatively, Ni-based Prussian blue is tentatively employed as low-temperature cathode based on the intercalation pseudocapacitive mechanism, realizing a high capacity retention of $82\%$ even at ultralow temperature of $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .[48] On the basis of the above, great successes have been made towards electrode failure at cold environment, which in turn underlines the importance of electrolyte and interface for subzero-temperature operations.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Ji et al. revealed that the performance decay for LIBs lies in $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport within the electrolyte.[49] Noticeably, the overriding consideration is how to remain in liquid state and maintain sufficient conductivity for low-temperature electrolyte. Typically, the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ conductivity $(\sigma)$ , as a function of temperature, relies heavily upon ion's number $(n_i)$ , ion's mobility $(\mu_{i})$ , unite charge $(e)$ , and charge valence $(z)$ as expressed below: $$ \sigma = \sum_ {i} n _ {i} \mu_ {i} z e, \tag {1} $$ where ion's number is mainly linked to Li salts concentration while ion's mobility is correlated with both viscosity and radius of solvated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ . As revealed, the viscosity of pure solvent increases as temperature decreases (Figure 4A), which is even exacerbated after dissolving Li salts, leading to sluggish ion mobility and low conductivity (Figure 4B).[50,51] Recently, the transport properties in LP57 (1 M $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ in ethylene carbonate [EC]/ethyl methyl carbonate [EMC], 3:7 by volume) were investigated, corroborating the detrimental roles of increased viscosity upon cooling.[52] Moreover, the dielectric constant, reflecting polarizing capability of molecules towards electric field, also affects conductivity. The solvent with a higher dielectric constant enables sufficient Li salt dissociation and higher conductivity. Nevertheless, high dielectric constant typically means strong intermolecular attractions and might lead to high viscosity.[53] The dielectric constant of solvent decreases as temperature increases since facilitated molecular thermal motions (Figure 4C). Therefore, the compromise of viscosity and dielectric constant on $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ migration should be considered.[54] By comparing varied electrolytes over a wide-temperature range (Figure 4D),[55] it is reasonable to conclude that: (1) the ternary and quartenary solutions exhibit higher low-temperature conductivity than binary EC-DMC mixing. (2) $\mathrm{LiClO_4}$ and lithium bis(oxalate)borate (LiBOB)-based electrolyte exhibit poor conductivity compared with $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ and lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI)-based counterpart due to their inferior solubility. (3) Linear alkyl carbonates decrease viscosity and improve conductivity over a wide-temperature range $(-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ .
