paragraph_context: The solvation chemistry is critical for which determines desolvation at the interface. In bulk electrolytes, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ exerts strong colombic attractions towards polar solvents, forming a 4-6-coordinated solvation sheath. The as-formed solvation shell is thermodynamically stable and hard to be stripped off, leading to sluggish lithiation of graphite at low temperature.[78] As reported, dielectric constant decreases with temperature increasing since the boosted thermal motion and weakened intermolecular dipole-dipole interactions.[53,79] As a result, the number of coordinating carbonates in the first solvation shell increases with a decreased population of the contact ion pair (CIP) at cold condition, which dictates both ionic transport and desolvation.[80] The carbonate-dominated solvation shell is hard to strip off completely at low temperatures, leading to solvent cointercalation and detrimental Li plating. Moreover, the electrolyte even gets solidification below freezing points and the dynamic solvation structure, which involves solvent's exchange between inner and outer solvation shell, might be frozen since the enhanced periodicity after crystallization.[56,81] The solidification of electrolyte blocks ionic transport and leads to cell failure. Recently, Lei et al. constructed a weakly solvating electrolyte (WSE) (2 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl) imide [LiFSI] in acetonitrile [AN]/fluorobenzene [FB]) to elucidate the significance of balancing solvation/desolvation for fast-charging and low-temperature operations.[65] The designed electrolyte exhibits high conductivity for efficient $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport (Figure 5D). Furthermore, the weakly solvating chemistry accelerates desolvation on graphite surfaces with the help of FB-derived SEI. In addition, Yao et al.'s group revealed the dominated ion pairs and aggregates (AGGs) in the solvation structure for WSE despite low Li salts concentration of 1 M.[66] The nonpolar solvent of 1,4-dioxane (1,4-DX) shows relatively lower binding energy towards $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ (Figure 5E), which is beneficial for the break-up of solvation shell before intercalating into electrodes. However, these weakly solvating solvents typically exhibit limited Li salt solubility and low conductivity, which in turn hinders viable applications.[82,83] Ming et al. developed a solvation model to qualitatively predict the interfacial behaviors of Li-solvent.[67] Specifically, the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -solvent with lower binding energy is easy to be stripped off and a higher B value (the half distance between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and solvent molecular) usually means looser stack form and incompatibility with graphite (Figure 5F,G). In addition, some additives alter coordination states and influence desolvation process. For example, Huang et al. incorporated $\mathrm{FSI^{-}}$ species and solvent molecules (FEC) into the solvation shell concurrently. The entered $\mathrm{FSI^{-}}$ is helpful for facilitating desolvation and thus optimizing Li surface chemistry, ensuring reversible Li plating/stripping at both ambient and low temperature $(-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ (Figure 5H).[68] For this reason, regulating solvation chemistry and adjusting affinity between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and solvents pose a new direction for low-temperature electrolyte.

Moreover, aggravated internal stress and particle pulverization require higher mechanical stability for SEI during repeated $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ intercalation/deintercalation at low temperatures.[85] Guo et al. compared dimethyl sulfite (DMS) and 1,3,2-dioxathiolane-2,2-dioxide (DTD) as the major contributor to interfacial chemistry (Figure 6A).[86] The single-electron reduction of DMS and DTD both facilitate conductive interphases in baseline electrolyte ( $1\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ in EC/EMC, 1:2 by weight). paragraph_context: Metallic lithium is typically absent in LIBs under normal conditions. Nevertheless, the detrimental lithium deposition poses a great threat once LIBs are operated at high current density and low temperature (below $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ), in which both charge transfer and mass transport limitations are aggravated, leading to irreversible Li plating in preference to $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ intercalation on graphite surface (Figure 7A).[96,97] First, Li deposition is closely related to the graphite structure. paragraph_context: Most electrolytes are formulated by dissolving Li salts (e.g., $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ , LiFSI, $\mathrm{LiBF}_4$ , and LiBOB) in aprotic solvents (e.g., DMC, DEC, EMC, EC, and propylene carbonate [PC]), in which EC is indispensable linked to the excellent disassociating capability and film-forming ability. Nevertheless, some works have revealed that transition metals dissolution and electrode cross-talks contribute to performance decay in EC-based electrolyte.[113-115] Moreover, the lower-temperature application of EC is inevitably plagued by its high melting point $(38^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ and high viscosity, leading to easy solidification and hampered ionic transport upon cooling. Smart and Ratnakumar demonstrated that excessive EC in electrolytes could contribute to thick SEI and unwanted Li plating.[99] At subzero temperature, the SEI derived from EC is extremely resistive and thus hampers electrochemical kinetics. The anion-derived SEI, by contrast, exhibits efficient dynamics for EC-free electrolyte.[116] In addition, the relatively strong coordination between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and EC also leads to sluggish desolvation upon cooling, both of which deteriorate the cold-climate behaviors and in turn highlight the significance of EC-free electrolyte.[78] Liner carbonates are widely introduced into EC electrolytes to formulate eutectic solutions to get superior performance. For example, Li et al. successfully optimized the formulation of $1.0\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF_6}$ in EC/PC/EMC (1:1:8 by weight), enabling decent capacity retention (68% of capacity compared with the ambient temperature) even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 8A).[117] Moreover, cyclic carbonate (e.g., PC) is tentatively introduced into pristine electrolytes, showing beneficial effects for dissociating Li salts, lowering freezing point, and even optimizing SEI.[118] However, particular attention should be paid to the content of PC in electrolyte since excessive PC leads to graphite exfoliation.[119,120] Recently, EC-free electrolyte shows great promising for low-temperature application since the simple elimination of EC can expedite ionic transport and widen liquid range. Nevertheless, poor interfacial compatibility with graphite should be resolved. For this reason, Liu et al. developed a PC-DEC-based electrolyte without EC solvent.[121] The electrolyte chemistry is intelligently tailored to bring abundant anions into the solvation shell to ensure a compatible interface. The strategy of combining low-coordination-number (low-CN) solvents and high-CN solvents is expanded to other systems (e.g., PC-DMC and PC-EMC) and called as the CN rule (Figure 8B).[122] As a result, the PC-DEC electrolyte could sustain a high capacity retention of 63% even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . paragraph_context: Fluorinated carbonates are promising since the high-voltage stability and film-forming capability. Various fluorinated carbonates (e.g., methyl-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl carbonate, ethyl-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl carbonate, and di-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl carbonate) are introduced in carbonates and show improved performance in carbon//LiNi $_{0.8}$ Co $_{0.2}$ O $_{2}$ cells.[133] Fluorinated carbonates can construct passivating films on electrodes and promote electrochemical kinetics at low-temperature conditions. It affords decent cyclability over 200 cycles at -20°C.[85] However, most fluorinated carbonates are employed as additives or cosolvents in electrolytes for the high cost and high viscosity. paragraph_context: Recently, the highly concentrated electrolyte (HCE) was widely studied because of improved interfacial compatibility and unique properties. For example, Wang et al. dissolved $4\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiN(SO_2F)_2}$ in DMC, forming three-dimensional aggregated structure.[130] As shown in Figure 8J, the common electrolyte (1M) suffers from solidification or evaporates beyond liquid range. The HCE, nevertheless, forms a stable coordinated network, ensures stable solvation structure and behaves like ionic liquid over a wide-temperature range $(-80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ . Localized highly concentrated electrolytes (LHCE) is followed to overcome the high cost and high viscosity of HCEs by introducing inert cosolvents. For example, Jiang et al. employed FB as diluent for its low melting point and low density.[134] The electrolyte (LiFSI/DMC/FB molar ratio of 1:1.2:3) enables reliable operations for Li/NCM622 full cells at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . As reported, FB, acting as nonsolvating cosolvent, is benign for constructing optimized interfacial chemistry and suppressing parasite reactions.[135] The diluted low concentration electrolyte is promising for low-temperature applications since its low cost and low viscosity. paragraph_context: Linear carboxylate solvents (e.g., MA, ethyl acetate [EA], MP, and EB) are widely employed in low-temperature electrolyte for their relatively low viscosities and low melting points.[138-140] For example, methyl formate (MF) is blended with EC to formulate a electrolyte (1 M $\mathrm{LiAsF_6}$ in MF/EC, 3:1 by volume) with a high conductivity of $8.4\mathrm{mScm}^{-1}$ at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ .[141] The graphite//Li cells with above electrolyte, nevertheless, still present unsatisfied performance since poor compatibility between graphite and carboxylates. paragraph_context: In ether solvent, DME and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) possess both low viscosities (0.59 and $1.1\mathrm{mPa}$ for DOL and DME, respectively) and low freezing points $(-95^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $-58^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for DOL and DME, respectively), making them promising for cold-climate applications. paragraph_context: Though ether falls out of favor in LIBs, the resurgent LMBs contribute to their success since their superior compatibility with Li metal. As reported, the mixture of DME and DOL is widely employed for Li-S and LMBs, exhibiting satisfied cycling stability and enhanced Coulombic efficiency compared with the carbonate-based one.[155-157] Nevertheless, the low oxidation stability (typically lower than $4.0\mathrm{V}$ vs. $\mathrm{Li} / \mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ) still plagues their application for high-voltage batteries (e.g., $\mathrm{LiNiO}_2$ and NCM811). For this reason, HCE, LHCE, and fluorinated electrolyte are developed to widen the application areas. Holoubek et al. investigated the correlations between ion pairs and low-temperature performance.[81] It was found that electrolytes with lower DME/Li molar ratios could enable reversible Li plating at cold conditions, which is opposite to the ionic transport (superior transport for electrolyte with higher DME/Li molar ratios). As reported, ion pairs in local solvation structure could balance the inner-sphere and outersphere reorganization energies, which is defining features to the improved low-temperature behaviors. Park et al. elucidated the critical factors in HCE (1 M LiTFSI in DME/TTE, 1:2 by volume) for LMBs within a wide-temperature range.[158] Specifically, tetrafluoroethyl tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE) proves indispensable for maintaining original solvation chemistry and enhancing $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport. Additionally, the involvement of TTE for constructing stable interphase ensured the thermal stability within wide temperature $(5 - 60^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ . Jiang et al. first modified traditional localized concentrated electrolyte (LiFSI:DME:TTE, 1:1.2:3 by molar) with the combination of LiTFSI and DOL, generating a hybrid interface and fast $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport in Li-S pouch cells, realizing a high energy density up to $325\mathrm{Whkg^{-1}}$ at ambient temperature.[159] To further improve the energy density, Han et al. replaced TTE by FB (Fluobenzene), a low cost and low density cosolvent, formulating an advanced electrolyte featuring lower density $(1.16\mathrm{g}\mathrm{cm}^{-3})$ , lower viscosity $(1.84\mathrm{mPa}\mathrm{s})$ and higher conductivity (Figure 10C).[160] The Li-S cell filled with FB-modified electrolyte exhibited superior rate capability and cycling stability than that of TTE-based electrolyte (Figure 10D). Apart from constructing a stable interface, the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -solvent binding strength was tentatively tailored. The diethyl ether was used as a solvent in 1 M LiFSI electrolyte to regulate the solvation structure and tailor $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -solvent strength (Figure 10F), leading to homogeneous lithium plating even at ultra-low temperature.[162] As a result, improving oxidation stability and optimizing interfacial chemistry still pose long-standing challenges for developing ether-based electrolyte.

paragraph_context: Gaseous molecules can be employed as solvents because of liquidation at low temperature or under moderate pressure. paragraph_context: Electrolyte additive plays three critical roles in electrolyte despite the limited mass fraction of less than $5\%$ : (1) participating in SEI formation and dictating interfacial kinetics; (2) altering solvation structure and affecting electrolyte properties (e.g., ions migration, CNs, and solvation conformation); (3) endowing electrolyte with special properties (e.g., nonflammability, inhibiting Li plating, and fast-charging capability). The effects of additives were systematically investigated in mesocarbon microbead (MCMB)/ $\mathrm{LiNi}_x\mathrm{Co}_{1-x}\mathrm{O}_2$ cells.[199] Specifically, the interfacial chemistry (e.g., composition and structure of SEI/CEI) changes a lot based on different additives. Moreover, additive-containing electrolyte enables better performance than the baseline formulation, indicating the generally beneficial effects of additives for enhancing interfacial kinetics. In addition, molecular-scale design of additives supplies another strategy to optimize electrolyte. For example, different polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)-based additives are introduced into carbonate electrolyte. A high conductivity of $0.5\mathrm{mS}$ $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ is obtained at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by properly tailoring PDMS main chain and grafting functional groups (acrylate, phenyl, and ethylene oxide).[200] Despite the widespread adoption of different additives in LIBs, it is reasonable to realize that these additives increase the complexity of electrolyte, rendering it too difficult to control the interfacial chemistry.[201] Inorganic species, such as lithium difluorophosphate $(\mathrm{LiPO}_2\mathrm{F}_2)$ , is employed in $\mathrm{LiNi}_{0.5}\mathrm{Co}_{0.2}\mathrm{Mn}_{0.3}\mathrm{O}_2//$ graphite cells to promote low-temperature performance.[111] The sacrifice of $\mathrm{LiPO}_2\mathrm{F}_2$ results in a conductive SEI featuring high content of LiF and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ . paragraph_context: Organic additives are also added to the electrolyte. For example, FEC is widely studied for its excellent film-forming ability. label: 概述
paragraph_context: Electrolyte engineering poses great promising for low-temperature batteries. Despite the thermal management system provides a benign temperature range for LIBs, the additional cost and decreased energy density plague LIBs in scenarios requiring both high energy density and low-temperature tolerance (e.g., electric vehicles and space explorations). As a result, designing low-temperature electrolyte for LIBs with intrinsic cryogenic tolerance is the most convenient and reliable strategy. Here, we discussed the critical issues of low-temperature batteries (LIBs and LMBs) from the aspects of solid-state diffusion, electrolyte structure, and interfacial chemistry, highlighting the significance of interface and desolvation. On the basis of the thorough survey of solvents, Li salts and additives for cold-climate electrolyte, several key points are proposed for designing superior low-temperature electrolyte. 1. High conductivity, low viscosity, and low freezing point are the prerequisites for low-temperature electrolyte, which are intimately related to the electrolyte formulation (e.g., solvents, cosolvents, Li salts, and additives). The employment of linear carbonates with low viscosity and freezing point is conducive for optimizing electrolyte chemistry. In addition, the superior conductivity normally lies between 0.8 and $1.2\mathrm{M}$ of Li salts' concentration for that excessive Li salt results in high viscosity while insufficient Li salt leads to limited $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transference number. Note that additives play complex roles to conductivity and viscosity, which is correlated with its functional groups, electronegativity, and dielectric constant. 2. Solvation structure has been a matter of increasing concern, even prevailing over SEI in recent years. First, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ coordinates with solvents, forming solvent-separated ions, CIPs and AGGs, which is dictated by temperature and thus determines $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ migration within electrolyte. In addition, the desolvation of solvents before intercalating into electrodes, evolving as rate-determining step and typically controlling the faradic reactions. Fortunately, the solvation structure (e.g., CN, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -solvent binding energy, and coordination conformation) can be finely tuned. For example, the weakly solvating solvent can balance Li salts' dissociation and desolvation. The HCEs featuring anion-rich solvation shell typically exhibit decreased Li-solvent binding strength. Additionally, some solvating additives are also capable of entering solvation structure, resulting in varied solvation structure. 3. Excellent interfacial chemistry and electrode protection are required for stable cycling in a cold climate. First, an ionically conductive but electron-insulation SEI is a basic requirement for reliable operation of LIBs, which inhibits parasite reactions between electrolyte and electrode. More importantly, the interphase should be robust and protective to encounter surface degradations and volume expansion/shrinkage. There are several strategies for regulating SEI, including tailoring electrolyte decomposition and electrodes modifications. Additionally, some SEI-forming additives are used to modify the electrode surface. 4. Other properties of electrolytes should be considered for practical applications. For example, the electrolyte should possess excellent physicochemical and electrochemical stability to eliminate detrimental interactions between electrolytes and other parts of cells (e.g., separator, current collector, binder, and packaging shells). Moreover, the electrochemical window should be wide enough to ensure proper reductive and oxidative stability, which is significantly required for achieving high energy density and long-term stability. Additionally, the safety, reliability, cost, and environmental friendliness should also be considered when formulating next-generation electrolyte.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Note that the optimization of LIBs in cold environments is a complex and systematic process, which not only relies on the electrolyte but also intimately correlates with other parts. For example, reliable separator, light current collector, and rational design of battery structure are all indispensable for advanced energy storage devices. Given the increasing demand for advanced energy storage devices and emergent strategies for formulating low-temperature electrolytes, the LIBs (or LMBs) will make progress in the future with superior temperature tolerance and broad energy markets.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: High-voltage nickel (Ni)-rich layered oxide-based lithium metal batteries (LMBs) exhibit a great potential in advanced batteries due to the ultra-high energy density. However, it is still necessary to deal with the challenges in poor cyclic and thermal stability before realizing practical application where cycling life is considered. Among many improved strategies, mechanical and chemical stability for the electrode electrolyte interface plays a key role in addressing these challenges. Therefore, extensive effort has been made to address the challenges of electrode-electrolyte interface. In this progress, the failure mechanism of Ni-rich cathode, lithium metal anode and electrolytes are reviewed, and the latest breakthrough in stabilizing electrode-electrolyte interface is also summarized. Finally, the challenges and future research directions of Ni-rich LMBs are put forward. electrode-electrolyte interface, electrolyte modification, failure mechanisms, high voltage, lithium metal anode, nickel-rich layered oxide cathode Energy storage devices have attracted great attention since the discover of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in 1991, $^{1-3}$ which have been used in various fields due to their advantages of large capacity, high voltage and long cycling life. $^{4-6}$ However, the improvement in the energy density and security performance of LIBs is highly desirable with rapid development of electric vehicles (EVs).<sup>7-9</sup> Therefore, it is necessary to explore new battery systems in greater depth. According to the national power battery technology planning route, to achieve the specific energy density of a single battery close to $300\mathrm{Whkg^{-1}}$ in 2025, $^{10}$ the combination of a theoretical specific capacity of up to $200 - 250\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ nickel (Ni)-rich cathode and $3680\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ lithium metal anode (LMA) is an ideal choice, compared to other electrode materials, such as $\mathrm{LiCoO_2}$ , $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ , $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{MnO}_4$ , and so on. $^{11,12}$ The commonly used Ni-rich cathodes are mainly ternary materials in the form of $\mathrm{LiNi_xCo_yMn_{1 - x - y}O_2}$ , such as $\mathrm{LiNi_{0.6}Co_{0.2}Mn_{0.2}O_2}$ (NCM622), $\mathrm{LiNi_{0.8}Co_{0.1}Mn_{0.1}O_2}$ (NCM811), and $\mathrm{LiNi_{0.9}Co_{0.05}Mn_{0.05}O_2}$ (NCM90). $^{13,14}$ The use of Ni-rich cathode can increase the capacity of the battery while it also reduces the use of Co for lowering the costs and reducing the harm to the environment. However, with the increase of Ni content, Ni-rich cathodes bring capacity advantage at the expense of its stability, mainly in the form of irreversible capacity and voltage attenuation.[15,16] In detail, these results derive from cation mixing, further structural phase transitions, material surface reconstruction, and microcracks caused by internal stress accumulation due to anisotropic volume changes during cycling.[10,17-20] Besides, problems such as volume expansion and uncontrolled Li dendrites growth for LMA during cycling also hinder the commercial development of Ni-rich LMBs.[21,22] Especially under extreme voltage conditions, the case can be worse. It is worth noting that these problems arise at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Therefore, it is urgent to construct a strong and stable electrode-electrolyte interface to realize the long cycle life of Ni-rich LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To solve the interface problem of Ni-rich cathode and LMA under high-voltage, many modification methods have been employed. The most effective and simple way is to modify the electrolytes. Although there are some reviews which are associated with the electrolytes,[23-26] there is no review which just focuses on high-voltage nickel-rich layered oxide-based lithium metal batteries. Thus, it is necessary to write one review for making researchers understand this field more clearly. In this progress, the degradation mechanism of Ni-rich cathode, LMA, and electrolyte is introduced, and the reliable strategies for obtaining stable interface through electrolyte engineering in recent years are summarized. Lastly, we propose new insights into the design of more stable Ni-rich cathode and electrolyte interfaces.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Although Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes have the advantages of capacity and voltage, the increase of Ni content will lead to some unavoidable defects during cycling, such as cationic mixing and surface reconstruction, intra- and intergranular cracks, and poor thermal stability. In addition, side reactions in LMA and electrolytes can also accelerate battery degradation. Thus, a thorough understanding for the degradation mechanism of Ni-rich layered oxide-based LMBs is a prerequisite to build a more stable and robust electrode-electrolyte interface.

paragraph_context: The modification strategies for high-voltage Ni-rich layered oxide-based LMBs aim to improve battery performance and cycle life.[52] This includes surface coating to increase the stability and oxidation resistance of the positive electrode[53]; Optimize the electrochemical performance of the electrode by regulating the crystal structure and particle size distribution of the positive electrode material[54]; Increasing the $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ storage capacity and conductivity of positive electrode materials through alloying modification[55,56]; By utilizing interface engineering to adjust the interface structure and properties between the positive electrode and the electrolyte, the lithium ion transfer rate and interface stability can be improved. The selection and application of these modification strategies need to be based on specific battery needs and optimization objectives. Among them, modifying the electrolyte is the most economical and convenient strategy, including solvents and additives modification.[57] Because traditional EC-based electrolytes have poor anode stability, this makes them very unstable for high voltage nickel-rich cathodes ( $>4.5\mathrm{V}$ ). Therefore, researchers are trying to partially or completely replace the EC-based electrolyte solvent with other high-voltage resistant solvents. Usually, the replacement solvent is divided into fluorinated solvent, sulfone solvent, and nitrile solvent, ionic liquids, and so on.

paragraph_context: In recent years, the pursuit of EVs has driven the development of higher energy-density LIBs. Thus, Ni-rich layered oxides have been considered as advanced cathodes for large-scale applications due to their relatively high working voltage and theoretical specific capacity. However, with the increasing voltage, Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes are facing various challenges, such as cationic mixing, surface reconstruction, microcrack generation and electrolyte decomposition. In order to cope with these challenges, the research on the modification of electrolyte engineering interface has received extensive attention. In this progress, the failure mechanism of Ni-rich layered oxide LMBs is reviewed, and the recent studies on improving battery performance through electrolyte modification strategies are further overviewed.

paragraph_context: The selection criteria for high-voltage electrolytes can be classified as: (i) To choose solvents with high oxidation potential and wide electrochemical window to replace traditional commercial carbonate solvents, such as sulfones, fluorinated solvents, and nitrile solvents, and so on. (ii) To choose the cathode film-forming additive to inhibit the reaction between cathode and electrolyte interface. (iii) To choose a new high voltage resistant Li salt as an additive to prevent the side reaction between electrolyte and electrode material. In terms of economic benefit, the development of appropriate additives is the core of the electrolyte, but also the key to improve the performance. The future development of electrolyte additives will have the following trends: i. More in situ characterization techniques are used to explore the reaction process at the electrode-electrolyte interface and determine the effect mechanism of additives.  ii. The evaluation standards of electrolyte additive are established by combining theoretical simulation with experiment.  iii. The electrolyte additive is combined with other positive electrode modification methods to improve the performance of high-voltage LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries have permeated every aspect of modern production and daily life due to their outstanding performance. However, in the face of continuously rising performance demands and emerging application scenarios, existing commercial lithium-ion batteries can no longer meet current demands. As a novel battery system, lithium metal batteries demonstrate higher energy density compared to traditional lithium-ion batteries, yet still face challenges such as lithium dendrite growth, unstable SEI formation, electrolyte consumption, and high safety risks. Although strategies like electrolyte modification, artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation, and current collector modification have improved the performance of Li-ion and Li metal batteries, they still struggle to balance characteristics like energy density, rate capability, cycle life, wide temperature range, and safety. In recent years, the high-entropy concept has been introduced into liquid electrolyte-based lithium-ion and lithium metal batteries, achieving preliminary progress. This mini-review focuses on the application of high-entropy effects in liquid electrolytes for lithium-ion and lithium metal batteries. In this review, we summarize methods for modulating electrolyte mixing entropy and configuration entropy. Furthermore, the structure-property relationships between entropy-driven lithium-ion solvation environments and battery performances such as high rate capability, wide voltage window, and temperature range adaptability are discussed. Through a series of characterization studies and theoretical simulations, the regulatory mechanisms are elucidated. Finally, based on existing researches, this review proposes perspectives for future studies and practical development of liquid high-entropy electrolytes, aiming to accelerate technological iteration in novel lithium-ion batteries and high-energy-density lithium metal batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the global demand for clean energy and sustainable development growing steadily, lithium batteries have become a game changer in energy storage solutions, permeating every facet of economic and social progress. From portable electronics to electric vehicles and large-scale grid storage systems, their applications are expanding rapidly while their importance continues to grow [1]. In the transportation sector, the surge in electric vehicle adoption is fueling explosive growth in the lithium battery market. Commercial lithium-ion batteries come in various types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, ternary lithium battery, and lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) battery and so on. However, with current technological advancements, these batteries are approaching their performance limits, significant improvements in energy density, cycle life and safety remain challenging [2]. Therefore, to meet growing market demands, innovative technical strategies and development pathways must be proactively explored.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In current technological applications, lithium-ion batteries urgently require enhanced stability to ensure efficient and reliable power output across diverse operating environments. In addition, accelerating charging speeds has become a critical challenge, as modern users increasingly demand rapid charging in fast-paced lifestyles [3]. Furthermore, safety issues are drawing more attention to the fast-growing application of Li-ion batteries in electrical vehicles and the emerging electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) vehicles [4, 5]. To further break the energy density limit, the lithium metal anode is used to pair with different cathode to form lithium metal batteries [6, 7]. For Li metal batteries, lithium dendrite and SEI vulnerability limit the battery cycle life far less than that of the Li-ion batteries, and even cause safety hazards, thus the practical application is hindered [8]. Although other rechargeable energy storage devices using aqueous electrolyte such as Zinc, Magnesium batteries can eliminate the safety concerns, their energy densities are far less than Li metal batteries [9-11]. The origin of lithium dendrites primarily includes non-uniform surface physicochemical environments [12, 13], high desolvation barriers [14, 15], and heterogeneous SEI compositions [16], which lead to non-uniform nucleation of lithium and trigger deposition hot-spots, resulting in dendrite formation [17]. This dendrite growth further causes localized rupture of the fragile SEI layer, exposing new high-reactivity lithium metal surfaces that react with the electrolyte, leading to electrolyte drying [16]. Although solid-state-electrolyte may be the ultimate solution for Li metal batteries [18-20], there are still lots of intractable problems which need more time to resolve for further application verification [21-23]. Therefore, current studies for practical Li metal batteries are focusing on the liquid type systems. During lithium stripping, the root deposition mechanism causes the SEI layer near the surface of anode to become thinner and faster in $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ transport [24]. To address these issues, existing strategies mainly focus on three approaches: artificial SEI formation modified three-dimensional collectors, and electrolyte modification [25]. The artificial SEI strategy employs chemically induced SEI layers with controlled compositions to replace spontaneously formed SEI during battery charging/discharging, typically by increasing beneficial inorganic components like LiF while reducing unstable organic components from solvent decomposition [8]. The three-dimensional collector strategy utilizes porous conductive materials to expand conductive area, reduce equivalent surface current, and introduce lithium-affinity sites within the collector, thereby lowering deposition barriers and guiding uniform nucleation/deposition of lithium [26]. Last but not the least, the electrolyte modification strategies have long dominated the research field, as they only require screening and combining lithium salts, solvents, and additives in the electrolyte. This approach offers simpler development processes compared to artificial SEI and modified three-dimensional collectors, making it more suitable for largescale practical applications [27]. However, current electrolyte modification strategies primarily focus on altering individual components to influence battery electrochemical performance [28, 29]. Although the mechanism of electrolyte modification enhancing lithium metal battery stability has been increasingly understood, it still fails to fully balance key performance metrics such as cycle life, energy density, rate performance, and safety. This persistent challenge has hindered the transition of lithium metal batteries from laboratory research to commercialization.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Electrolytes (HEEs), as the emerging design strategy, increase the molecular diversity and the configuration entropy of electrolyte systems, providing new ideas for solving the above problems. The concept of high entropy originated in the field of materials science, characterized by the formation of high entropy alloys through alloying of multiple principal components, exhibiting excellent mechanical properties and corrosion resistance [30, 31]. This concept was later extended to electrolyte design by introducing various lithium salts, solvents, and additives, significantly increasing the molecular diversity and disorder of the electrolyte, thereby regulating the solvation structure and interfacial behavior of lithium ions.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The role of entropy plays in the phase stability in an electrolyte system with multiple components can be elucidated based on the Gibbs free energy of mixing $(\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}})$ as: $$ \Delta G _ {\text {m i x}} = \Delta H _ {\text {m i x}} - T \Delta S _ {\text {m i x}} \tag {1} $$ where $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the mixing enthalpy, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the mixing entropy, and $T$ is the absolute temperature [32]. Generally, the configuration entropy $(\Delta S_{\mathrm{conf}})$ contributes to the most of $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ , which is defined in an ideal solid solution as [33]: $$ \Delta S _ {\mathrm {c o n f}} = - R \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} x _ {\mathrm {i}} \ln x _ {\mathrm {i}} $$ where $R$ is the ideal gas constant and $x_{\mathrm{i}}$ is the component mole fraction. Typically, for high-entropy alloy, at least five elements should be included with an atomic percentage between $5\%$ and $35\%$ for each element [34]. Another definition for the high-entropy alloy is that the ΔSconf should be greater than $1.5R$ [34]. Different from the materials with fewer elements, the high-entropy alloys possess unique properties due to the entropy stabilization effect, lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion and the cocktail effect [35].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: In liquid-based electrolyte systems, the situation is more complicated without a stable and semi-stable lattice or phase. First, the entropy stabilization effect works on the anion/cation solvation structure instead of the solid solution phase. Second, unlike the lattice distortion in the solid solution system, the solvation sheath of anions and cations in the electrolyte changes due to the different molecular radius, polarity and stereo configuration of the electrolyte components. Third, the sluggish diffusion due to the low diffusion and phase transformation rates from the fluctuation of lattice potential energy no longer exists, while the diffusion mechanism in high entropy liquid electrolyte systems is yet to be explored. And finally, the cocktail effect still plays a critical role, which may contribute to more aspects such as electrochemical stability window, wide-temperature performance and non-flammability in liquid electrolyte-based Li-ion and Li metal batteries (Figure 1).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Previous reviews have summarized the general progresses of the high entropy materials for rechargeable lithium batteries, including electrode materials, solid-state electrolytes and non-aqueous electrolyte [36, 37]. Specially, high entropy materials have been used in Li-S batteries to suppress the Li polysulfides (LiPSs) shuttle effect, accelerate the redox kinetics of active materials, improve the electron/ion transport, improve the structural and interfacial stability, and so on [38]. HEEs are also studied in water-based battery systems such as Zn batteries [39]. Here in this mini review, we focus on the lithium batteries based on liquid form non-aqueous electrolytes, especially for high-energy density lithium metal battery systems. Through this review, we aim to systematically analyze existing research on high-entropy electrolytes for lithium-ion batteries and Li-metal batteries, comprehensively evaluating their strengths and limitations in performance enhancement and stability improvement. Building upon in-depth analysis of current studies, we propose forward-looking perspectives and recommendations for future research directions to accelerate the transition of high-entropy electrolytes from laboratory research to practical applications, and establish a solid foundation for the further development and widespread adoption of lithium battery technology.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Current lithium-ion battery technology still faces significant challenges in practical applications. Firstly, existing systems struggle to achieve efficient fast charging capability, which not only compromises user experience but also limits their use in scenarios requiring rapid power replenishment [40]. Secondly, performance under low-temperature conditions remains problematic, as lithium-ion batteries tend to experience capacity degradation and reduced discharge efficiency in cold environments, severely affecting reliability in cold regions [41]. Additionally, the flammability of electrolytes poses a critical safety hazard, with current materials prone to combustion or even explosions when exposed to high temperatures or impacts, creating substantial risks to battery safety [42]. These challenges not only hinder technological advancement but also impede the expansion of related application fields.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: The challenges in fast-charging lithium-ion batteries primarily involve lithium plating, electrode polarization, overheating, and structural material damage [43]. Under ideal slow charging conditions, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions smoothly intercalate into graphite interlayers. However, during high-current fast charging, excessive $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions flow to the negative electrode at excessive speeds. When the intercalation rate lags behind their arrival speed, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions gain electrons at the electrode surface and directly reduce to metallic lithium instead of intercalating into graphite, which is known as "lithium plating" [44]. Different from lithium plating, electrode polarization refers to the deviation of actual electrode potential from equilibrium potential, essentially representing the "additional pressure" required to drive the ion migration [45]. During fast charging, Ohmic polarization, electrochemical polarization, and concentration polarization all intensify significantly. Regarding overheating, the Joule's law ( $Q = I^2 R$ ) indicates that heat generation is proportional to current squared [46]. Therefore, the massive current during fast charging causes instantaneous thermal spikes. If the cooling system fails to dissipate this heat promptly, battery temperature will surge dramatically [47]. Additionally, high temperatures accelerate the electrolyte decomposition and SEI film rupture/regeneration. Conversely, the reduced SEI film stability exacerbates side reactions, making lithium plating more likely and creating a vicious cycle that may ultimately lead to thermal runaway [48]. Last but not the least, fast charging causes structural damage to active materials of both positive and negative electrodes. During fast charging, the rapid intercalation/deintercalation of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ ions in the cathode generates significant lattice stress. This stress may induce cracks or fragmentation in cathode material particles, increasing internal resistance and disrupting ion/electron conduction pathways [49]. In the anode, graphite undergoes approximately $10\%$ volume expansion during lithium intercalation. The uneven lithium distribution during fast charging leads to localized stress concentration, causing graphite particle damage and delamination, which similarly compromises the conductive network [50].

paragraph_context: Aiming at the kinetic obstacles in the rapid charging process of lithium-ion batteries, a design idea of high entropy solvation configuration by introducing multi-component lithium salts was proposed [51]. This high entropy (HE) electrolyte was prepared by dissolving $0.2\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ , $0.2\mathrm{M}$ LiFSI, $0.2\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{LiPF}_6$ , $0.2\mathrm{M}$ LiDFOB, and $0.2\mathrm{M}$ LiTFSI into the mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC) solvent by ratio of 3:7. The Raman spectrum shows the weaker solvent coordinated peak of Li-ions, which is consistent with the slightly decreased overall electrical conductivity and almost unchanged viscosity of electrolyte. In addition, the 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) chemical shift shows the shielding effect of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ within the shell, and the 19F NMR spectrum indicates the increased $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ -fluorinated anions interaction. For the analysis of SEI, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirms that anions decompose to form inorganic components such as LiF, $\mathrm{Li}_{x}\mathrm{N}$ species. The molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal that the entropy increase effect results in 36 types of diverse $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ solvation configurations (Figure 2a). The radial distribution function (RDF) results show that multiple anion species squeeze into the inner solvation sheath of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ in the HE electrolyte. In addition, the simulated self-diffusion coefficient of HE electrolyte is larger than that of the routine electrolyte, which can be elucidated by the smaller solvated structure. As the result, the capacity retention rate of graphite/LiNi $_{0.5}$ Mn $_{0.2}$ Co $_{0.3}$ O $_{2}$ full battery after 650 cycles at 1 C is $95.4\%$ , and the capacity at high rate of 5 C reaches $82.3\mathrm{mAh/g}$ compared to $45.2\mathrm{mAh/g}$ of conventional electrolyte (Figure 2b).

paragraph_context: Beside the high rate charging issues, the rapidly deteriorated performance of Li-ion battery at low temperature limits its application in cold area. The primary challenges for lithium-ion batteries at low temperatures stem from two key issues: SEI instability and lithium deposition on the anode. Compared to ambient conditions, the anode undergoes more pronounced volume changes during charge-discharge cycles at low temperatures. These fluctuations accelerate SEI film cracking and regeneration, significantly compromising its stability [52]. Additionally, reduced electrolyte viscosity and decreased ionic conductivity at low temperatures slow lithium-ion migration on the anode surface, promoting lithium dendrite formation [53]. The growth of these dendrites not only depletes active lithium reserves and reduces battery capacity, but also poses safety risks by potentially puncturing separators and causing internal short circuits. To meet the low temperature challenge, the high chaotic mixed salt electrolytes were designed by adding four inorganic lithium salts, namely LiF, $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ , $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}$ , and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ , into carbonate based (LP30) and ether based (LDD) commercial electrolytes with $5\%$ fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) additive, respectively [54]. This strategy is aim to regulate the solvation structure of $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ by increasing the system mixing entropy; promote the rapid formation of inorganic rich SEI film on graphite surface. Experimental data shows that the capacity of both high chaotic electrolytes approach $300\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , while commercial electrolytes have almost no capacity at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . In terms of the high rate performances, the 3C rate specific capacities of Li/graphite half-cells in LP30-FEC-4S and LDD-FEC-4S are $219\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ and $165\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , respectively, which are significantly higher than those of commercial electrolytes LP30 ( $120\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ ) and LP57 ( $150\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ ).

paragraph_context: High-entropy electrolytes, as a groundbreaking paradigm for lithium-ion battery performance enhancement, demonstrate significant advantages in improving battery performance and safety through the introduction of multi-component lithium salts (e.g., $\mathrm{LiNO}_3$ , LiFSI) or composite solvent systems (mixed solvents of carbonates, ethers, and ionic liquids combined with functional additives like FEC and TTE). By leveraging the high-entropy effect to regulate $\mathrm{Li}^+$ solvation structures, these electrolytes not only enhance fast charging capabilities and cycle stability, but also improve low-temperature performance. Safety breakthroughs include raised the thermal runaway onset temperature, shortened self-extinguishing time, and high flash points. However, current high-entropy electrolyte research remains in its early exploratory phase, with limited publications and insufficient systematic theoretical frameworks or large-scale application foundations. Future efforts should focus on expanding salt-solvent-additive synergistic high-entropy systems, deepening the structure-activity relationships between high-entropy effects, $\mathrm{Li}^+$ solvation structures, and SEI formation, customizing optimized systems for extreme conditions, and addressing cost and process challenges in large-scale production to accelerate practical applications.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The design of Li-metal electrolytes requires attention to five key elements: (1) High Coulombic efficiency of metallic lithium, particularly ensuring efficiency in the initial few cycles to minimize initial lithium loss [56, 57]; (2) Compatibility with actual high-voltage cathodes [58, 59]; (3) Cycle performance under real-world conditions (low electrolyte concentration, low lithium content, high cathode load) [60, 61]; (4) Cost-effectiveness (low salt concentration) and large-scale production feasibility (simple synthesis and purification processes) [62, 63]; (5) Low flammability and high boiling point, especially gas generation suppression [64]. Recent studies have made great progresses to tackle the above issues. However, the five key elements are hard to be reconciled, some of them are even contradicted to each other. In this context, the introduction of high entropy effect may provide a possible pathway to break the thermodynamic and kinetics limitations and to balance the key factors.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: To address the trade-off between ion conductivity and electrochemical stability in weakly solvated electrolytes, a design concept for HEEs was proposed based on molecular diversity [65]. By increasing the types of solvents/co solvents to enhance solvation entropy, the mesoscopic solvation structure is regulated to reduce ion aggregation, and improved ion transport performance is achieved while maintaining the anion enriched solvation structure. paragraph_context: The challenges faced by lithium metal batteries in low-temperature environments are closely related to the unique characteristics of their metallic lithium anodes, which differ significantly from traditional lithium-ion batteries with graphite anodes [69, 70]. First, the increased viscosity of the electrolyte at low temperatures slows $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ migration, leading to localized over-concentration on the anode surface and irregular dendrite formation. Second, the high chemical reactivity of metallic lithium causes irreversible changes in the composition and structure of SEI due to altered electrolyte kinetics at low temperatures, resulting in a sharp rise in impedance and continuous consumption of active lithium and electrolyte. By contrast, the SEI film on graphite anodes remains relatively stable at low temperature. Third, low-temperature dendrite fractures produce dead lithium that cannot participate in cycling, causing rapid capacity decay. By comparison, dead lithium in lithium-ion batteries primarily stems from incomplete intercalation, which is much less severe compared to that in lithium metal batteries. Finally, the probability of dendrites piercing the separator and causing internal short circuits significantly increases at low temperatures for lithium metal batteries. paragraph_context: A design approach for HEEs based on multi-component salts is proposed to address the issues of low solubility of lithium salts, insufficient kinetic and interfacial stability in traditional electrolytes. This approach breaks through the solubility limitations of single salt systems and regulates the solvation structure to optimize ion transport and interfacial stability. From the Thermodynamical angle, the melting temperature of electrolytes is determined by the Gibbs free energy, which can be reduced by increasing the entropy of mixing $(S_{\mathrm{mix}})$ . Therefore, increasing the $S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ should be a promising strategy to lower the freezing point and increase the battery capacity at low temperature (Figure 5a). When the temperature decreases below the melting point of electrolytes, a phase transition from liquid to solid will occur, which will reduce the conductivity of the remaining liquid phase and block electrode pores, thus isolating sections of the active material and cause capacity loss. Importantly, the Coulombic efficiency at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reaches $80\%$ compared to only $30\%$ for traditional electrolytes. As temperature decreases, the ${}^{7}\mathrm{Li}$ resonance of the $0.75\mathrm{M}$ HE electrolyte shows a smaller shift compared to the $0.75\mathrm{M}$ traditional electrolyte, which demonstrates that introducing multiple salts stabilizes the solution when the temperature changes (Figure 5b, c). The core idea is to use multi-component ion mixing to enhance the system entropy change $(\Delta S_{\mathrm{fus}}*)$ and reduce the melting point [89]. The optimal composition is $45\mathrm{mol}\%$ LiFSI, 15 mol% KFTA, and $40\mathrm{mol}\%$ KFSI (LS45KT15KS40), which achieves an ion conductivity of $0.082~\mathrm{mS~cm^{-1}}$ at $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $0.13~\mathrm{mS~cm^{-1}}$ at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The Li || Li symmetric battery can stably cycle for over $900\mathrm{h}$ , and the Coulombic efficiency of the Li || Cu battery is $96.21\%$ . When matched with the high voltage NCM811 positive electrode, the capacity retention rate exceeded $80\%$ after 200 cycles at $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Moreover, the cell with high loading cathode $(8.7\mathrm{mg~cm}^{-2})$ and thin lithium anode $(50\mu \mathrm{m})$ maintains $87.78\%$ capacity after 65 cycles at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Mechanism analysis shows that the multi ion entropy effect increases $\Delta S_{\mathrm{fus}}^*$ to $1.39R$ , reducing the melting energy barrier. MD simulation shows that $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ mainly coordinates with anions, creating solvent-free environment to promote the formation of rich inorganic SEI. Experimental results from XPS confirm that F element accounts for $22.33\%$ of SEI, inhibiting dendrite growth and side reactions. In addition, the $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ promotes uniform Li deposition through electrostatic shielding effect. Through entropy driven regulation, this strategy provides a new design path for high safety lithium metal batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Significant progress has been made in applying high-entropy liquid electrolytes to lithium-ion and lithium-metal batteries. The general strategy involves enhancing the mixture entropy and configurational entropy of electrolytes through multiple components, regulating the solvation environment of lithium ions, improving lithium-ion diffusion coefficients and ionic conductivity, expanding the electrochemical window, and enhancing SEI stability to prolong battery cycle life. Furthermore, leveraging the cocktail effect by introducing non-flammable components further improves battery safety. To investigate the regulation mechanisms of high-entropy electrolytes, Raman spectroscopy and NMR were employed to characterize solvation environments, while XPS and TOF-SIMS were used to analyze SEI composition and properties. Combining the theoretical simulations such as MD and DFT methods with experimental data, to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms can be elucidated and the structure-property relationship has been proposed. However, current research on liquid high-entropy electrolytes for lithium-ion and lithium-metal batteries remains in its early stages, requiring substantial efforts for deeper exploration. 1. As a complex chemical system, high-entropy electrolytes involve intricate interactions and synergistic effects among multiple components. The complex forms, concentration ratios, and chemical reactions between these components present significant challenges for researchers attempting to establish structure-property relationships. Due to the intricate interactions among components, it is difficult to accurately describe and predict their performance through simple experiments or theoretical models. This complexity has led to relatively slow progress in the research and application of high-entropy electrolytes. Therefore, in experimental research, we must pursue bold innovations in research paradigms to explore new mechanisms for developing high-entropy electrolytes. This requires not only improving existing characterization techniques but also developing novel theoretical frameworks suitable for high entropy systems, aiming to uncover more unknown scientific principles and potential applications during experiments. Furthermore, achieving high standardization in data formats is crucial. By ensuring standardized and unified data collection and documentation, we can provide robust foundations for theoretical calculations while delivering high-quality data for machine learning algorithm training and optimization to accelerate the development of HEE. 2. To further enhance experimental efficiency and ensure result reliability, it is urgently need to adopt high-throughput experimental techniques. These advanced methods enable large-scale, rapid experimentation, significantly improving both efficiency and output. Additionally, it is suggested to validate high-entropy electrolyte compositions by systematically analyzing and testing various formulations. This comprehensive evaluation will assess the practical performance and stability of high-entropy electrolyte in real-world applications. Such measures will not only guarantee the accuracy and reliability of experimental data but also provide robust data support and theoretical foundations for future research and practical implementations. 3. Using machine learning-assisted design to accelerate the iterative development of high-entropy electrolytes. By constructing precise machine learning models, it is suggested to conduct in-depth mining and analysis of massive datasets including electrolyte composition, electrochemical performance, and structural characteristics. These models can rapidly predict key performance metrics for high-entropy electrolytes under different component combinations, such as ionic conductivity, cycling stability, and compatibility with electrode materials. Based on these predictions, we can selectively identify promising electrolyte formulations, significantly reducing the number of trial-and-error experiments in traditional methods and substantially shortening R&D cycles. Additionally, machine learning algorithms can be used to optimize experimental variables like reaction temperature, solvent ratios, and additive types, further enhancing synthesis efficiency and performance. As experimental data accumulates, the models continuously learn and optimize, improving prediction accuracy and reliability, providing robust technical support for the iterative development of high-entropy electrolytes. 4. In theoretical research, molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate unique advantages in studying the mechanisms of high-entropy liquid electrolytes. Functioning as an "atomic microscope," this method dynamically reveals complex ion-solvent interactions, the formation and evolution of polyanion clusters, and ion transport pathways in locally high-entropy environments at atomic scales. It directly correlates microscopic structures (e.g., coordination shells, free volumes) with macroscopic properties (e.g., ionic conductivity, migration numbers), providing critical insights into how "entropy stabilization" regulates ionic behavior. However, this approach faces three major limitations: First, its accuracy heavily depends on empirical force fields, where imprecise models may yield unphysical results. Second, computational costs restrict spatial-temporal scales, particularly hindering the capture of all slow kinetic processes in first-principles simulations. Third, constructing reliable models to accurately reflect electrochemical potential effects remains challenging when simulating complex environments like electrode-electrolyte interfaces. To advance this field, future research should integrate emerging methods like machine learning potentials to expand simulation scales while maintaining accuracy, and validate simulation results with experimental characterization techniques such as spectroscopy, thereby collectively constructing comprehensive mechanistic interpretations.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Lithium batteries are currently the most popular and promising energy storage system, but the current lithium battery technology can no longer meet people's demand for high energy density devices. Increasing the charge cutoff voltage of a lithium battery can greatly increase its energy density. However, as the voltage increases, a series of unfavorable factors emerges in the system, causing the rapid failure of lithium batteries. To overcome these problems and extend the life of high-voltage lithium batteries, electrolyte modification strategies have been widely adopted. Under this content, this review first introduces the degradation mechanism of lithium batteries under high cutoff voltage, and then presents an overview of the recent progress in the modification of high-voltage lithium batteries using electrolyte modification strategies. Finally, the future direction of high-voltage lithium battery electrolytes is also proposed.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: At present, as the concept of carbon neutrality takes root in the hearts of the people and the increasingly serious greenhouse effect, air pollution caused by energy supply urgently needs to be minimized. Compared with the method of burning fossil fuels to obtain energy, the position of rechargeable lithium battery power supply technology with almost no pollution emissions is gradually improving in the field of energy technology.[1] The development history of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries has been since decades. As early as 1991, Sony Corporation developed the first commercial rechargeable lithium-ion battery. In the following decades, a lot of research aimed at improving the performance of lithium-ion batteries has made lithium battery technology increasingly mature. Although rechargeable lithium-ion battery technology has been widely used in our lives, with the increase in the power of portable electronic devices, the desire for long-range electric vehicles (EVs), and the desire for electrical energy storage for the grids (EESs), the current lithium-ion battery technology can no longer meet the demand.[2-4] The state-of-the-art commercial rechargeable lithium-ion batteries are mainly composed of cathode and anode materials, electrolyte, current collector, and separator. Among these components, the main contribution to the specific capacity is the cathode and anode materials. In terms of anode materials, to pursue a higher specific capacity, researchers have shifted their attention from the traditional carbon-based anodes to lithium metal.[5] This is because lithium metal has the lowest redox potential $(-3.04\mathrm{V}$ , vs standard hydrogen electrode) and low density $(0.534\mathrm{gcm}^{-3})$ , resulting in its theoretical specific energy density as high as $3860\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , which is nearly 10 times that of graphite anode.[6-9] Because lithium metal has extremely high reactivity, using it as an anode will cause additional reactions with general commercial electrolytes, resulting in uneven lithium deposition and dendritic growth, and even safety hazards.[10-12] Fortunately, many works in recent years have basically solved this problem through a variety of strategies, including surface coatings, porous current collectors, electrolyte modification.[13-16] In contrast to anode materials, the theoretical capacity of cathode materials with the highest specific capacity (such as lithium cobalt oxide, nickel-rich materials, etc.) is only about $270\mathrm{mA g}^{-1}$ , which greatly prevents the increase in the energy density of the battery. In theory, there are two ways to increase the specific capacity of the cathode. One is to develop a new cathode material with a higher specific capacity (e.g., increasing the nickel content in the layer transition metal oxide cathode material, as the more nickel the cathode can extract more $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ at the same voltage), and the other is to increase the upper-limit charging voltage of the battery. Obviously, the latter is easier to obtain a high specific capacity. (According to the formula, energy = capacity × voltage) Whereas, an excessively high upper-limit charging voltage will cause a series of problems in various components of the battery, such as irreversible phase changes, aggravated side reactions, transition metal dissolution, etc., which will make the battery fail prematurely. Not only that, the inert components that were originally thought not to participate in the reaction, such as current collectors, binders, and conductive carbon, will also degrade at a sufficiently high charge cutoff voltage.[17] This is an aspect that is easily neglected, but it also leads to rapid battery failure.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Among the many cathode materials, their different characteristics determine their application fields, and some of them have been commercialized. Nickel-rich cathode material is a kind of cathode material with broad application prospects, which has been adopted by many electric vehicle manufacturers due to its large specific capacity, high working voltage, and excellent high-power output performance.[18] In addition, increasing the proportion of nickel in the material can increase the specific capacity. $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ is the first cathode material developed. Its volumetric energy density is higher than other cathode materials, and its theoretical specific capacity is particularly high. Portable electronic devices need to store as much energy as possible in a limited volume, so $\mathrm{LiCoO}_2$ is widely used in the batteries of portable electronic devices. $\mathrm{LiFePO_4}$ is a cathode material that has been developed rapidly and practically. It is mainly used in energy storage equipment, high-power electric tools, and light electric vehicles. The most competitive advantage is its good cycle stability (over 2000 times of charging and discharging), and good rate performance. The most important thing is that it is safe, nontoxic, and low in cost. At the same time, low capacity and low bulk density hinder its further development. $\mathrm{LiMnO}_2$ is a cathode material with a spinel structure. Due to its three-dimensional lithium ions channel, it cannot damage the structure under multiple cycles. Its characteristics are cheap, pollution-free, and high discharge voltage platform. As people's demand for battery energy density continues to increase, some cathode materials suitable for high voltage have been developed. Among them, candidates for high-voltage cathode materials worthy of high hope include nickel-rich layered oxides $\mathrm{(LiNi_xCo_yMn_zO_2}$ and $\mathrm{LiNi_xCo_yAl_zO_2}$ $(x + y + z = 1)$ , lithium-rich layered oxides $\mathrm{(Li_{1 + x}M_{1 - x}O_2}$ , $\mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Mn}$ , $\mathrm{Ni}$ , $\mathrm{Co}$ ), high-voltage spinel oxides $\mathrm{(LiNi_{0.5}Mn_{1.5}O_4)}$ , and high-voltage polyanionic compounds (phosphates, sulfates, silicates, etc.).[19] Figure 1 shows the energy density, power, cyclability, cost, and thermal stability of various high-voltage cathode materials. Under high-voltage conditions (usually higher than $4.2\mathrm{V}$ ), these cathode materials can generally reach a specific capacity higher than $200\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ , although there may be a risk of electrolyte decomposition or irreversible phase change of the material. In recent years, great effort has been made to solve the problem of instability at high voltage, such as electrolyte modification,[20,21] electrode surface coating,[22-24] and doping of elements in the electrode composition,[25,26] etc.

paragraph_context: In this review, we first discussed the mechanism of battery degradation induced by increasing the upper charging voltage. Different from other reviews, this review also introduces the use of different electrolyte modification strategies to improve lithium batteries at high cutoff voltage. Then, it briefly reviews the relevant work in recent years, and finally puts forward a summary and prospect.
