Based on LiFEA-based carbonate electrolyte, the Li||NCM811 battery exhibits outstanding cycling performance. The pouch cell maintained $8 1 \%$ capacity retention after 100 cycles (charge: 0.4C, discharge: 1C). In contrast, the blank cell survived only 50 cycles under identical conditions. These results indicate that LiFEA-based carbonate electrolyte has promising potential for widespread application in high-performance LMBs. However, through in-depth research into the physicochemical properties of LiFEA, it has been discovered that the excessively high donor number (DN) of FEA− can lead to high reactivity and poor compatibility with some solvents (such as FEC). Therefore, to address this issue, a new lithium salt lithium, 2-[2-(2-methoxy ethoxy)ethoxy] ethanesulfonyl(trifuoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiETFSI) has been introduced based on FEA− by incorporating sulfonyl groups [73]. Electrolytes containing LiETFSI in carbonate solvents not only ensure high conductivity but also exhibit a higher ${ \mathrm { L i } } ^ { + }$ transference number ${ ( { t _ { \mathrm { L i } } } ^ { + } { \approx } 0 . 8 ) }$ with a moderate DN. The anion facilitates the dissolution of oxygen-containing organic compounds in the SEI while reducing the dissolution of inorganic components such as LiF, confrmed by XPS and TOF–SIMS. Consequently, the electrolyte establishes a SEI interface with a lower impedance rich in inorganic components. The advanced LiETFSI electrolyte (with $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 } ,$ ) enhances the CE to $9 9 . 0 \%$ , indicating a high reversibility of the Li plating/stripping process. In comparison, the CE with advanced LiFEA electrolyte only reaches $9 6 . 6 \%$ , and the addition of FEC does not make a big diference due to the poor compatibility between LiFEA and FEC. When they encounter lithium metal, the FSI− groups are chemically decomposed into LiF and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ , which assist in forming SEI on lithium metal and repairing SEI in the cracks lacerated by lithium dendrite. Furthermore, the FSI− anions exchanged from the flm are electrochemically decomposed to inorganic components to strengthen the SEI. paragraph_context: The solvation structure refers to the arrangement formed when solute ions are surrounded by solvent molecules in an electrolyte solution [79]. This structure directly afects the movement and reactivity of ions in the solution [80]. Solvent molecules interact with solute ions through electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, or coordinate bond, resulting in the formation of a solvation shell [28]. The composition, structure, and physicochemical properties of SEI largely depend on the solvation structure of the electrolyte. To modulate the solvation chemistry in liquid electrolytes, it is imperative to comprehend the interplay between ions and solvents. These interactions are intricately linked to regulating interface stability, expanding the electrochemical stable potential window, controlling kinetics, and suppressing side reactions within batteries.

paragraph_context: The developing of high-voltage batteries has faced challenges such as designing a suitable electrolyte, especially for the LMBs. Ether electrolytes are considered suitable for LMBs due to their compatibility with lithium metal. However, they cannot endure high voltages. Researchers usually apply high-concentrated electrolytes (HCE) [104, 105] or localized high-concentrated electrolytes (LHCE) [11, 106] strategies to improve the compatibility of both sides. Currently, the weakly solvating electrolytes (WSE) [107, 108] are confrmed an efective strategy to modify the electrochemical performance. The HCE strategy increases lithium salt concentration to reduce free solvents (increase the ratio of salt/solvent, Fig. 8a), constructing an anion-rich solvation structure which helps form a stable SEI. However, the high viscosity, low ionic conductivity, and high cost of HCEs limit their practical use. LHCE strategy mitigates these issues by using inert diluents (weak solvent), which can also maintain the anion-rich solvation structure. WSE strategy applies low-solvating-power solvents to encourage ion pairing, enhancing SEI stability but potentially reducing ionic conductivity. It should be noted that the above-mentioned strategies can be achieved by regulating the solvent (solvent chemistry). In comparison, anions can play a prominent role in electrolyte design (anion chemistry, Fig. 8a). By optimizing the structure and properties of anions, the solvation structure can be directly controlled. Unlike traditional methods, the anion chemistry is a new strategy to regulate the solvation structure, enabling the electrolyte good electrochemical performance like high-voltage stability.

paragraph_context: Our group proposed a new strategy to tune the solvation structure of Li-ion by anion chemistry [35]. We utilized the high DN of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ to coordinate with ${ \mathrm { L i } } ^ { + }$ , competing with DME in the solvation process. The $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ weakens the solvating ability of DME, and this competition reduces the number of solvated molecules, thereby lowering the likelihood of solvent oxidation at high potentials. As a result, an anion-regulated weakly solvating electrolyte (ARWSE) is formed (Fig. 8a). paragraph_context: In summary, the anions’ involvement in the solvation structure can greatly infuence the electrochemical stability of the electrolyte. However, characterization methods are not yet sufcient and mature enough to obtain accurate solvation structure and dynamic information, especially during battery cycling. It is also important to elucidate the formation and composition of the interfacial flm generated by anions and solvents. The design of a uniform and stable SEI is crucial for enhancing the electrochemical stability of the electrolyte and stabilizing both negative and positive electrode materials. This requires a comprehensive understanding of the thermodynamics and kinetics of anion decomposition. Furthermore, studying the plating/stripping behavior of metal anodes $( \mathrm { L i } ^ { 0 } , \mathrm { N a } ^ { 0 } )$ is crucial for improving the cycle stability of metal batteries. Analyzing the role of anions in these processes is an efective strategy to achieve the goal, sometimes the combination of the multiple anions is better. In the future, there will be further exploration of novel anion chemistry. Through the structural design of the anions, it will be possible to precisely control the anion chemistry to enhance energy density, cycle life, and safety of the batteries. At the same time, by integrating the popular artifcial intelligence computing technologies, it is possible to better predict and optimize the performance of electrolytes, driving innovation and development in this feld. In conclusion, the future development of the electrolyte feld can be achieved not only through the design, development, and application of anions but also through the development of new solvents, laying a solid foundation for the next generation of highperformance and safe battery technologies.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Li metal batteries (LMBs) have been widely studied due to the unprecedented theoretical specific capacity and ultralow redox potential of Li metal anode (LMA). Nevertheless, out-of-control growth of lithium dendrite and fragile solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) seriously limit their practical applications. Herein, 2D $\mathbf { s } \mathbf { p } ^ { 2 } .$ -carbon-linked covalent organic framework $( \mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathbf { c } \mathbf { - C O F } )$ is prepared and constructed as artificial SEI film on the surface of LMA for impeding the formation of Li dendrite and regulating the interface stability. The $\mathbf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathbf { c }$ -COF is designed to be fully $\pi$ -conjugated along both the $_ { x }$ and $_ { \gamma }$ orientations with high conductivity, which can reduce interface impedance and facilitate the uniform distribution of ${ { \bf { L } } } _ { } ^ { + }$ flux. Consequently, the $\mathbf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathbf { c }$ -COF-modified symmetric batteries exhibit high ${ { \bf { L } } } _ { } ^ { + }$ transference number $( t _ { \mathrm { L i ^ { + } } } )$ of 0.85, excellent cycle life $\mathbf { ( 4 0 0 0 0 ~ h ) }$ and extremely low overpotential $\mathbf { ( 1 0 ~ m V ) }$ at a current density of $5 \mathbf { m } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with 5 mA h $\mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Meanwhile, the Li deposition behavior is analyzed by in-situ light microscopy, indicating $\mathbf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathbf { c }$ -COF significantly enhances interfacial stability of LMA. This strategy possesses potential value for restraining Li dendrite formation and promoting the progress of COF artificial SEI film.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: covalent organic frameworks, Li metal anode, artificial SEI film, lithium dendrites Lithium metal anode (LMA) is qualified with satisfactory theoretical capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } ,$ ) and ultra-low redox electrode potential ( $- 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { V }$ vs. standard hydrogen electrode) [1–3]. Therefore, it is considered one of the most promising materials to substitute graphite anode. However, lithium dendrite generation due to the strong reducing ability of Li, remarkable volume variation, and uneven Li deposition during the charge/ discharge processes hinder the application of LMA [4,5]. The massive Li dendrites lead to the sustaining consumption of Li and electrolyte as well as the accumulation of an insulating solidelectrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, which increases the internal resistance and hinders the transport of Li ions [6,7]. So, uncontrolled lithium dendrites have affected the cycling stability and service life of batteries. To solve this serious problem, researchers have devised a variety of solutions, including constructing multidimensional conductive skeleton [8–11], optimizing electrolyte formulation [12–16], and exploring solid electrolyte [17–21]. These methods confirm that effective interface protection coating can accelerate the migration and uniform deposition of ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ , thus improving the performance of the battery.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: However, there are also some technical bottlenecks. For example, the mechanical strength of the spontaneously formed SEI layers in ordinary electrolytes is generally difficult to adapt to the volumetric strain of lithium metal during electroplating/ stripping. Hence, researchers constructed graphene film [21,22], $\mathrm { { A l } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { { O } } _ { 3 }$ protection layers [23], or Li alloys [24–26] to adjust the interfacial stability of LMA. Compared with inorganic artificial SEI film, organic polymer protective layer has the characteristics of high mechanical strength and uniform diffusion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ . Notably, the covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have several advantages, including unique structural flexibility, permanent porosity and excellent physicochemical stability [27]. Therefore, building the COF artificial SEI membrane on the Li anode surface can facilitate the uniform transport of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , regulation of lithium deposition, and restraint of lithium dendrite growth [28–31].

[32] prepared a highly crystalline S-COF as an artificial SEI film. The S-COF promotes well-distributed sedimentation of Li, and decreases the nucleation barrier of Li. Furthermore, Zhang et al. [33] synthesized a selfexfoliated TpTG-COF with $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ coordination, which can adjust the charge distribution and promote the even diffusion of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ . However, imine-linked COFs generally show poorer conductivity and structural stability, resulting in higher interface impedance, lower electron delocalization, and inferior chemical stability [34]. Therefore, ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ transportation needs a high migration energy barrier. Significantly, 2D fully π-conjugated COFs exhibit remarkable advantages due to high conductivity, which can reduce interface impedance and promote charge transport. Regrettably, few studies on $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ full carbon-conjugated COFs as SEI layers have been reported up to now.

Compared with Py-COF, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF has better chemical stability and highly delocalized electronic structure [35]. The $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF has the following advantages: (i) regular 1D Figure 1 The $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF structure design and stabilizing mechanism elucidation. Hence, this research could offer a valid tactic for restraining Li dendrite growth and stabilizing LMA.

paragraph_context: To further estimate the influence of the artificial SEI film prepared by COFs on the electrochemical performance of LMAs, bare Li, $\operatorname { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c } \mathrm { - C O F } @ \mathrm { L i } ,$ , and Py-COF@Li electrodes were utilized to assemble symmetric batteries. As shown in Fig. 4a, the overpotentials of bare Li symmetric batteries have a pronounced fluctuation at the current density of $2 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $\mathrm { \Omega } 2 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ). The overpotential is over $1 0 0 \mathrm { m V }$ at the first cycle, due to the battery activation course, then decreases and ultimately increases quickly. On the contrary, the symmetric batteries modified by Py-COF and $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF show stable overpotentials and long cycle life at the same current densities. The overpotentials of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c } .$ - COF-modified symmetric batteries are higher at the first cycle, and finally are stabilized at about $8 \mathrm { m V }$ . The batteries can cycle stably for $3 7 0 0 \mathrm { h }$ . The symmetric batteries modified by Py-COF also show similar cycling behavior but a shorter time of stable cycle for $5 3 0 \mathrm { h }$ and an overpotential up to $1 3 \mathrm { m V }$ . For the sake of plenitude proof of the advantages of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF as artificial SEI film in stabilizing LMA, as presented in Fig. 4b, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COFmodified symmetric batteries were tested at a higher current density of $5 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with $5 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , the overpotentials of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified symmetric batteries are only $1 0 \mathrm { m V }$ . Most crucially, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified symmetric batteries can stably cycle more than $4 0 0 0 \mathrm { h }$ , showing superior electrochemical melioration. As shown in Fig. 4c, for visually observing the variation of the voltage curves, the 1000th, 2000th, and 3000th cycles are magnified. The $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified symmetric batteries display steady charge/discharge curves, and possess lower overpotential and excellent cycling performance, indicating that $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF has the effect of stabilizing LMA. The LMA with $\operatorname { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathtt { c } .$ - COF artificial SEI film possesses lower overpotential and longer cycle life than other artificial SEI film-modified symmetric batteries in the former reports (Table S1). For supervising the interfacial ion transport, the cycle-correlation electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was tested as illustrated in Fig. S6. The resistances of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF- and Py-COF-modified symmetric batteries increase marginally during the pre-activation course, due to the low electrical conductivity and the realigning of Li-ion transfer channel at COF|Li interface [36–38]. The interface impedances of the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF- and Py-COF-modified symmetric batteries show a tendency to decrease gradually. While the interface impedances of the bare Li symmetric batteries exhibit an initial decrease and then an increase. Before the 10th cycle, the interface impedances of the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF- and Py-COF-modified symmetric batteries are larger than that of bare Li. Yet, after 30 cycles, the interface impedances of the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF- and Py-COF-modified symmetric batteries are smaller than that of bare Li. Remarkably, the interface impedances of the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COFmodified symmetric batteries are the smallest. The lower interfacial impedance indicates the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF artificial SEI film holds better stability and higher conductivity, thus accelerating $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ion transfer. These enhanced electrochemical performances indicate that the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF artificial SEI film is valid to inhibit side reactions and dendrite growth.

paragraph_context: To better explain the protective effect of the COF artificial SEI layer on LMA, SEM was operated to analyze Li metal batteries (LMBs) after cycling. In contrast to bare Li and Py-COF@Li, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF film is uniformly distributed on the Li surface with a thickness of ${ \sim } 1 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ (Fig. S7). Both bare Li symmetric batteries and COFs-modified symmetric batteries were disassembled after being charged/discharged 100 cycles at $2 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $( 2 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ ). As illustrated in Fig. 5a–c, the surface of bare Li displays a big crack and moss-like Li dendrite after 100 cycles. The reason is that pristine Li has no specific Li-ion appealing sites and the effective charge transfer kinetics cannot be established [30]. For Py-COF-modified electrode (Fig. S8), some Li dendrites appear on the surface of the Py-COF-modified electrode, which is due to the Py-COF with fewer lithophilic sites. In comparison, $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified electrode displays a slick appearance (Fig. 5d–f). The $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF with regular 1D channels, fully conjugated structure, and high conductivity can achieve uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ diffusion and contribute to inhibiting the growth of Li dendrite. Therefore, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF layer lowers the migration energy of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and accelerates $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer. The aforementioned remarkable Li sedimentation behaviors demonstrate a potential value of the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF artificial SEI in restraining dendrite growth.

paragraph_context: The modified electrodes were prepared by coating suspension liquid of COFs on the surface of copper foil to evaluate the interface stability of the COF-modified electrode. Then the modified electrodes were assembled into a battery for systematic electrochemical testing. The Coulombic efficiency (CE) is illustrated in Fig. 6a. The Li|Cu batteries were tested at the current density of $0 . 5 \mathrm { \ m A \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ $( 0 . 5 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ ). Compared with the bare Cu batteries, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF- and Py-COF-modified Li|Cu batteries show both satisfactory CE maintaining rate and cycle life. While the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified Li|Cu batteries have better electrochemical performance than the Py-COF-modified Li|Cu batteries. The CE value of bare Cu batteries markedly decreases after 70 cycles. While for Py-COF-modified Li|Cu batteries, CE values begin to decline after 110 cycles. In stark contrast, the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified $\mathrm { L i } | \mathrm { C u }$ batteries can steadily work for more than 135 cycles and have a high value of CE $( 9 8 \% )$ . Furthermore, $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF-modified Li|Cu batteries can also steadily work for 90 cycles at a greater current density of $1 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with $\mathrm { 1 \ m A \ h \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ , while the performance of Py-COF-modified Li|Cu batteries (60 cycles) and bare Cu batteries (20 cycles) is poor at the same current density (Fig. S9). In addition, the lithophilicity of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF and Py-COF can be characterized via Li nucleation overpotential [32]. The Li|Cu batteries’ voltage hysteresis is shown in Fig. 6b. The Li nucleation overpotential of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COFmodified Li|Cu batteries is $1 5 \mathrm { m V }$ , which is significantly lower than that of the Py-COF-modified $\mathrm { L i } | \mathrm { C u }$ batteries $( 2 4 \mathrm { m V } )$ and bare Cu batteries $( 2 8 \mathrm { m V } )$ . Therefore, the lower Li nucleation overpotential manifests that the Li nuclei can grow evenly and smoothly, which decreases the lithium dendrite formation during the plating/stripping course [41]. Ultimately, $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { c }$ -COF has outstanding lithophilic ability owing to its high conductivity and fully conjugated structure.

paragraph_context: ABSTRACT Developing Li metal batteries (LMBs) with highvoltage cathodes is crucial for realizing high energy storage systems. Thus, advanced electrolytes that can derive stable interphases for both Li anode and high-voltage cathodes are highly desired. $\mathbf { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ has been widely used as an efficient additive for solid electrolyte interphases in ether-based electrolytes, but its poor solubility in carbonate-based electrolytes limits its application in high-voltage LMBs. Herein, trimethyl phosphate was proposed as co-solvent in ethyl methyl carbonate/fluoroethylene carbonate electrolyte to endow the electrolyte with high $\mathbf { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ solubility and flame-retardant properties. Additionally, lithium bis(oxalato) borate was added to improve the interfacial stability at both the anode and the cathode sides. As a result, the obtained electrolyte exhibited high compatibility towards both Li metal anode and high-voltage layered cathodes. After cycled between 2.8–4.3 V at a current density of $1 . 2 \mathrm { \ m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ for 300 times, Li $| | \mathbf { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ and Li| $\mathbf { | L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811) full cells delivered high capacity retention of $8 0 . 2 \%$ and $8 4 . 2 \%$ , respectively. More amazingly, the Li||NCM811 cell with a negative-to-positive capacity ratio of 3.33 still remained a capacity retention of $\sim 8 0 \%$ after 150 cycles under the same charge/discharge conditions. The understanding of this fire-retardant, high-voltage electrolyte enriched with $\mathbf { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ inspires the development of safe and high energy LMBs through interphases regulation.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Keywords: Li metal anode, high voltage cathode, flame-retardant electrolyte, solid electrolyte interphase Considering that the advanced Li-ion batteries (LIBs) are reaching their theoretical energy density limits, lithium metal is widely acknowledged as the “holy grail” material to take the place of graphite anodes owing to its outstanding specific capacity $( 3 8 6 0 \ \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { h } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } ) $ and the most electronegative potential $( - 3 . 0 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } \nu s$ . standard hydrogen electrode) [1–3]. When coupled with high-voltage cathodes such as $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ (LCO) and $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } .$ - $\mathrm { C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811), high energy densities of more than 500 W h $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ can be achieved in Li metal batteries (LMBs), which will be of great significance in prolonging the cycling lifespan of portable devices and electric vehicles [4]. However, the unstable electrolyte-electrode interphases at both the anode and the cathode sides have severely impeded the applications of high-voltage LMBs. For the anode side, high reactivity of metallic Li will lead to uncontrollable parasitic reactions with conventional electrolytes, causing uneven Li deposition, unrestrained Li dendrite growth, and excessive electrolyte consumption, and eventually resulting in early capacity collapse and safety issues [5–7]. For the cathode side, the highly delithiated LCO and NCM811 materials at high cut-off voltage will not only lead to irreversible phase changes, but also accelerate the oxidation of electrolyte components. As a result, the original $R 3 m$ structure collapses accompanied by the dissolution of massive transition metal (TM) ions, and the accumulated decomposition products will greatly hinder the ionic transport at the cathodic interfaces [8,9].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Selection of electrolyte components plays an important role in modifying the electrolyte-electrode interphases. Generally speaking, ether solvents are less participated in the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation structures, thereby rendering high coulombic efficiency (CE) in LMBs [10,11]. However, the comparatively lower electrochemical window $( < 4 \mathrm { V } )$ makes it incompatible with high-voltage cathodes [12]. Carbonate solvents present better electrochemical stability under high-voltage conditions, but the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formed in the carbonate-based electrolytes cannot provide sufficient protection for Li anode, leading to continuous growth of dendritic Li and early exhaustion of the electrolyte [13]. It should also be noted that the conventional carbonate electrolytes are intrinsically flammable, which makes the cell under the risk of thermal runaway or even fire. In that case, there remains an urgent need to develop new electrolytes with high interfacial compatibility and flame-retardant properties.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Adding additives is the simplest way to promote the properties of SEI layer [14]. $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ is an anion-type additive reported to generate an inorganic-rich SEI with high ionic conductivity and rigidity in ether-based electrolytes, but the low solubility makes it rarely involved in carbonate-based electrolytes [15]. Many pathways have been explored to introduce $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ into carbonate-based electrolytes, such as employing high donor number (DN) co-solvents [16], introducing electron-deficient receptors [17], and constructing $\mathrm { T M } { \cdot } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ complex [18]. However, these methods fail to grant the electrolyte flam- retardant properties, and the sole addition of $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ cannot provide sufficient protection for the cathode materials [19]. Furthermore, many high DN solvents are incompatible with high-voltage cathodes [20], and the complex metal depositions on Li metal anode/separator may lead to short-circuit of the cells [21,22].

paragraph_context: Herein, we employed trimethyl phosphate (TMP) as a solubilizer to dissolve $0 . 2 \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { ~ L i N O } _ { 3 }$ in the ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC)/fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC)-based electrolyte. Cost-effective TMP was selected as solubilizer due to its good compatibility with high-voltage cathodes and flame retardancy. In order to promote the interfacial compatibility at both the anode and the cathode sides, $0 . 1 \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ lithium bis(oxalato) borate (LiBOB) was further added to the electrolyte. As a result, a highly conductive SEI film enriched with inorganic species such as nitrides, $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and boron oxides was formed, which could improve the abilities of electrolyte to resist thermal runaway. When coupled with LCO cathodes, a high capacity retention of $8 0 . 2 \%$ could be obtained after 300 cycles with a current density of $1 . 2 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and more than $8 5 \%$ of the $3 ^ { \mathrm { r d } }$ cycle capacity can be preserved when coupled with NCM811 cathode after 250 cycles with the same current density. Even after the Li foil anode was replaced by pre-deposited Li reservoir (negative-to-positive capacity ratio of 3.33), the Li||NCM811 cell still remained a capacity retention of ${ \sim } 8 0 \%$ after 150 cycles.

paragraph_context: Deposition behavior and interfacial chemistry of Li metal anode Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was employed to observe the morphology of the deposited Li on the Cu substrate. As shown in Fig. 3a, the Cu substrate is covered with rod-shaped dendritic structures in the base electrolyte, which will increase the specific surface area of the Li metal anode and intensify the side reactions at the anode side. After the adding of LiBOB (Fig. 3b), nodule-like structures start to appear, indicating that the compatibility between the Li metal anode and the electrolyte is somewhat promoted. In contrast, the morphology formed in the PN electrolyte (Fig. 3c) is mainly dominated by granular shape of the Li deposition with the width of about $5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ with no needle-like dendrite observed, indicating that the addition of $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ can effectively reduce the surface area of Li deposition, suppressing the consumption of the Li metal anode and the electrolyte during cycling. After the incorporation of LiBOB and $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ , the width of Li grains further grows to $8 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , illustrating the formation of a smooth and flat Li deposition morphology in the PBN electrolyte (Fig. 3d). Such results indicate that the introduction of LiBOB and $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ leads to a dense and uniform Li deposition, which is of great significance for achieving high CE [25].

paragraph_context: Rechargeable lithium-metal batteries that are operated based on reversible metal plating and stripping during the charge/discharge process are known for their high energy density far beyond the conventional, graphite-anode-based Li-ion batteries [1]. However, the hostless structural evolution of Li metal during the anode process easily forms dendrites and could lead to a hazardous short circuit of batteries [2]. In addition, Li metal shows strong reducibility and tends to react with the conventional liquid organic electrolytes, which accounts for metal corrosion and flammable gas (e.g., $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ , CO) evolution at the anode [3,4]. To address the above challenges, quasi-solid-state polymer electrolytes (QSPEs) have been proposed in recent years because of their high ionic conductivity, favorable mechanical properties, easy manufacture, and low cost [5–7]. The QSPE is usually prepared by impregnating a polymer substrate (e.g., polymethyl methacrylate or PMMA) with a liquid carbonate or ether-based electrolyte (where the solvent acts as the plasticizer) so that it combines the advantageous features of both liquid and polymer electrolytes [8–10]. However, most QSPEs still suffer from poor thermal stability and compatibility with the use of the Li-metal anode, and the rechargeable Li-metal batteries prepared from the QSPE show inferior cycling stability and safety [9,11– 13]. Therefore, searching for ultra-safe QSPEs with high electrochemical and mechanical stability is crucial for the development of rechargeable Li-metal batteries [14–17].

paragraph_context: In this work, we propose a one-step in situ polymerization approach to obtain a double-network structural hybrid polyester-based flame-retardant quasi-solid-state polymer electrolyte (DN-FRQSPE). Our strategy is to use two networks to construct the DN structure: the first network is a loosely cross-linked flame-retardant P-N containing polyacrylate system. The second network is the PMMA with a highly cross-linked structure. Thus, the DN-FRQSPE was prepared via in situ polymerizing the flame-retardant P-N containing acrylate monomer (N,N-bis(2- hydroxyethyl acrylate) aminomethyl phosphonic acid diethylester, or BHAAPE) in the liquid PMMA system. Benefiting from in situ solidification technology [18,19], the obtained DN-FRQSPE exhibits excellent electrochemical performance, good flexibility, and high flame retardancy. Guided by this flame retardant quasi-solid system, the Li metal anode exhibits a milder and more standardized electrochemical behavior with dendrite-free morphology as demonstrated by a stable cycle more than $2 0 0 0 \mathrm { { h } }$ in Li/Li symmetric cells. Moreover, the allsolid $\mathrm { L i / L i F e P O _ { 4 } }$ full batteries based on this DN-FRQSPE possess ideal rate performance and outstanding cycling stability (a small capacity decay of $0 . 0 3 5 \%$ per cycle over 200 cycles).

However, wild Li dendrite propagations owing to chaotic Li depositions raise challenges for LMB blossoming. Separators with specific demands thus should be involved when smoothly transferring into LMBs. In this research, a fascinating P(TPC@Lys-Li) separator is prepared by the turbulent interfacial polymerization and electrospinning to ingeniously clarify dependencies of Li+ transfer dynamics on double electric layer thickness (DELT) regulations within porous skeletons. P(TPC@Lys-Li) enables negatively charged porous skeleton surface and compresses DELT, which constructs high-efficiency Li+ fast-transfer channels on porous skeletons and accelerates Li+ transfer speed by 18.3 times. Especially, P(TPC@Lys-Li) supplies extra Li+ for stable formations of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, homogenizing nucleation and growth behaviors during Li depositions. Remarkable C-rate capacity and cycle stability thus arise for assembled LMBs, holding 87.2 % capacity retention after 700 cycles at 0.5C even under high cathode loading and lean electrolyte conditions. P(TPC@Lys-Li) also maintains constant physical scale and unabated mechanical strength even at elevated temperatures approaching 200 ◦C, which provides excellent battery security as LMBs encounter uncontrollable thermal runaway. Above attractive features enable P(TPC@Lys-Li) separator to be potentially applied in LMBs demanding sufficient security, high-capacity density, and fast charge technology.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with excellent safety and low selfdischarge features have developed rapidly since their first commercialization in 1991 [1–3]. Revolutionary advances in energy over the past three decades drive LIBs widely used in portable electronic devices and energy storage fields [4]. Presently, LIBs reach energy density limits theoretically and have been unable to meet current high energy density developments [5–7]. Therefore, lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) with extremely high energy density and the lowest electrochemical potential have once again received widespread attention [8–11]. Also, actual manufacturing lines and fundamental battery assembly units of LIBs containing current collectors, encapsulations, shells, and separators can be directly used for LMB fabrications and lower commercialization barriers [11,12]. However, chaotic Li depositions generate wild Li dendrite propagations and erratic solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer owing to dissolution, precipitation, and regeneration, which admits responsibility for degenerative cycling stability and security [13,14].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: As the typical electrochemical inert component, separators function in critical roles during battery operations even though do not directly participate in electrode reactions, which mainly isolate two electrodes and conduct Li+ based on insulating porous skeletons [15–17]. Pliable textures, suitable porous skeletons, and adaptive strength are also equally important [18,19]. Two fabrication techniques based on polyolefin substrates thus predominate in normal LIBs. However, specific needs should be involved as smoothly transferring separators to LMBs. Common separators own poor thermal stability limited by polyolefin melting points, which tend to shrink and cause short circuits at elevated temperatures [20–22]. Whereas, high-power LMB operations inevitably generate immense heat and raise inner temperature. Inferior thermal stability only provides inadequate security and may cause spontaneous combustion or explosion.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Besides, the intrinsic low surface energy feature worsens separator electrolyte affinity [23,24]. $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ can only be transferred in electrolytes filled with porous skeletons. Poor wettability and electrolyte retention generate inadequate filling conditions, which increases ion transport barriers and directly impacts battery performance. Coating ceramic layers on separators can simultaneously optimize thermal stability and electrolyte affinity [25–29]. However, surface coatings cannot optimize related characters of internal skeletons. Even developing the shutdown functional tri-layer separator, in which continuous $\mathrm { { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { { O } _ { 3 } } }$ coatings are online constructed on porous skeletons, the thermal dimensional stability still does not break limits [30]. Most efforts are thus devoted to developing separators with thermally stable and functionalized polymers to replace polyolefin separators, especially based on the simple and easy-on electrospinning strategy [31–34]. Gan et al. [35,36] suggested novel strategies for high-specific energy lithium-metal batteries based on silica-coated silver nanowires in composite single-ion conducting polymer electrolytes and designing lithium powder anode stabilized by electrospinning membranes. Liu [37] and Ding [38] prepared multifunctional separators by electrospinning crosslinked polybenzoxazine and anisotropic semi-aligned polyacrylonitrile, which expectedly brings security and improved battery performances for practical LMBs.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Researchers generally attribute battery performance elevations to the improved separator wettability, while ignoring $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer processes within porous skeletons. Especially, the diameter of separator pores is much larger than the effective ionic radius. Hence, the effects of functional separators on $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer should be mainly concentrated within the range of a few nanometers on the porous skeleton surface, which just fitly matches the double electric layer thickness (DELT) [39–41]. The Gouy-Chapman-Stern model suggests that porous skeletons repulse ions with the same charge and draw counter-ions, generating the stern layer composed of counter-ions [42–44]. Therefore, the DEL can be adjusted by enabling negatively charged porous skeletons to generate a specific stern layer consisting of Li+, which may lubricate Li+ transfer and construct high-efficiency $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ fast-transfer channels. Besides, this alternative ion transfer dynamics holds decisive effects on the nucleation and growth of Li dendrites. Since DELT varies inversely to surface charge density, restructuring surface charge on porous skeletons can precisely regulate DELT, which provides ingenious ways for exploring dependencies between $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer dynamics and particular porous skeletons.

Remarkable thermal stability of P(TPC@Lys-Li) held constant physical scale and mechanical strengths even at temperatures close to $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ which provided sufficient security for batteries to prevent internal short circuits as LMBs confronted thermal runaway. P(TPC@Lys-Li) also enabled negatively charged porous skeleton surface and compressed DELT, which functioned pivotal roles for constructing high-efficiency $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ fast-transfer channels on porous skeleton surface and accelerated $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer speed by 18.3 times. Especially, P(TPC@Lys-Li) supplied extra $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ for stable SEI layer formations, homogenized nucleation and growth of Li dendrites, thus acquired excellent cycle performance and higher C-rate capacity. The above attractive features enable the P(TPC@Lys-Li) separator to be potentially applied in LMBs demanding sufficient security, highcapacity density, and fast charge technology.

paragraph_context: Schematic diagram of turbulent interfacial polymerization and preparation of novel high-performance electrospinning separator are listed in Fig. 1. 2.92 g lysine, 0.84 g LiOH, and 200 mL methyl alcohol were added into a round-bottomed flask and heated reflux for 6 h to acquire lithiated lysine (Lys-Li) as the aqueous phase. Dissolving 4.06 g paraphthaloyl chloride (TPC) in 200 mL n-hexane as the oil phase. The oil phase was added into the aqueous phase at the rate of 20 mL/min. After repeated centrifugation and ultrasonic cleaning three times, P(TPC@Lys-Li) was suction filtrated and vacuum dried at ${ 8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$ for 24 h. The separator was vacuum dried at $8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h and shifted to a drying dish for use. The untreated lysine and TPC were subjected to the same turbulent interfacial polymerization and electrospinning to prepare the P(TPC@Lys) separator. paragraph_context: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) incorporating solid-state polymer electrolytes (PEs) are promising candidates to meet the growing energy demands of advanced energy storage systems. However, polymer electrolytes face several challenges, including low ionic conductivity, narrow electrochemical stability window (ESW), and interfacial instability, which limit their compatibility with high-voltage cathode materials in LMBs. This study presents a novel strategy to overcome these limitations by tailoring the polymer backbone at the molecular level, thereby enabling highly tunable chemical functionalities. A fluorine-functionalized copolymer was synthesized via in-situ polymerization, composed of polyethylene glycol methyl ether acrylate (PEGMEA) and 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl methacrylate (TFEMA). The fluorinated functionality of TFEMA imparts wide ESW, exceeding 5 V vs. Li/ Li+, and facilitates the formation of an inorganic-rich hybrid interphase (SEI/CEI) while ether functionality containing PEGMEA enhances segmental motion and interchain ion exchange. Electrochemical assessments reveal that the optimized fluorinated copolymer achieves an ionic conductivity of 0.329 mS cm− 1 and a lithiumion transference number of 0.64 at ambient temperature, attributed to the anion immobilization effect. The Li|| NCM811 cell, incorporated with optimized fluorinated copolymer, delivers a specific discharge capacity of 181.5 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ at a 0.1C rate and maintains a reversible specific capacity of 118.06 mAh $g ^ { - 1 }$ , having a remarkable capacity retention of 81.47 % after 200 cycles at a 0.5C rate. Notably, it also retains 76.89 % capacity over 300 cycles at a high rate of 1C. This work introduces a new approach for the rational molecular design of polymer electrolytes, achieving excellent electrochemical properties suitable for high-voltage lithium metal batteries.

paragraph_context: In recent years, rapid advancements in emerging high-tech fields such as deep-sea exploration, space missions, aviation, electric vehicles (EVs), robotics, and flexible wearable electronics have substantially increased the demand for high-energy-density battery technologies [1–5]. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) typically use graphite as an anode material, offering a limited theoretical capacity of 372 mAh ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ [6]. However, this capacity imposes a bottleneck for achieving higher energy densities, necessitating the exploration of alternative anode materials. Lithium metal has garnered attention as an attractive alternative due to its exceptionally high theoretical capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ), low redox potential (− 3.04 V vs. SHE), and low density (0.53 g cm− 3 ) [7,8]. These attributes position lithium metal batteries (LMBs) as promising candidates for next-generation high-energy density energy storage systems [9]. Despite these advantages, the commercialization of LMBs, particularly when paired with high-voltage cathodes, is impeded by critical challenges such as dendritic lithium growth induced by uneven lithiumion flux, parasitic side reactions at high voltages, and the limited electrochemical stability of liquid electrolytes. Collectively, these issues lead to safety hazards, electrolyte leakage, and short battery lifespan [10–12]. Consequently, employing solid electrolytes in high-voltage LMBs is deemed to be a more viable approach to mitigate the safety and performance risks associated with liquid electrolytes [13,14].

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Among the primary types of solid electrolytes, inorganic solid electrolytes (ISEs) [15,16] and polymer-based solid electrolytes (SPEs) have been extensively investigated for their potential use in LMBs [17,18]. While ISEs generally offer high ionic conductivity at room temperature $( > 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { \ s \ c m ^ { - 1 } } )$ and a wide electrochemical stability window, their practical application is constrained by factors such as high production costs, inherent brittleness, and susceptibility to moisture and oxygen [19,20]. In contrast, SPEs present several advantages over ISEs, including cost-effectiveness, flexibility, ease of fabrication, scalability, absence of leakage, low density, and improved interfacial contact with electrodes [21–23]. Polyethylene oxide (PEO) based SPEs are among the most widely studied materials in LMBs; however, their employment in high-energy-density LMBs is hindered by significant challenges, including low ionic conductivity at room temperature $( < 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ : \mathrm { S \ c m ^ { - 1 } } )$ ) [24], a narrow electrochemical potential window that limits their pairing with high-voltage cathodes such as $\mathbf { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ (LCO) or LiNi M-$\mathbf { n } _ { \mathrm { y } } \mathbf { C o } _ { 1 \cdot \mathbf { x } \cdot \mathbf { y } } \mathbf { O } _ { 2 }$ (NMC), and difficulties in achieving interfacial stability or compatibility [25,26].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To overcome these limitations, a key strategy has focused on enhancing the electrochemical stability window of polymer electrolytes and developing stable interfacial layers. Recent studies have established that an inorganic-rich hybrid interface containing LiF exhibits mechanical stability, thereby improving the cyclic performance of LMBs by promoting better surface morphology and preventing parasitic side reactions between electrodes and electrolyte [27]. Various fluorinated additives such as fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC), 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropylether (TTE), bis(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl) ether (BTFE), or fluorinated salts and surface coatings of electrodes have proven an effective way to form the inorganic-rich stable interface [28–30]. While these strategies still suffer from several intrinsic limitations, such as additive depletion, inhomogeneous SEI, complicated processes, and challenges for scalability [31–33]. Furthermore, these fluorinated additives are costly, have environmental concerns, and fail to simultaneously address both the potential stability and interfacial issues of polyether-based electrolytes. This underscores the need for polymer electrolytes that inherently form stable interfaces while offering broad electrochemical stability.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Functionalizing polyether-based materials has emerged as a highly effective strategy for achieving the desired chemical and electrochemical characteristics. In particular, fluorine functionalization not only expands the electrochemical stability window but also promotes the formation of thin, uniform, inorganic-rich hybrid interphase by providing the source of fluorine for LiF or by modifying the solvation structure [34,35]. The incorporation of fluorinated segments into polyether-based electrolytes or cationic polymer coatings has been shown to enhance potential stability and interfacial robustness [36,37]. Fluorinated polymer electrolytes exhibit significant thermal and electrochemical potential stability [38,39]. Additionally, integrating a fluorinated crosslinker into the structure of a polymer electrolyte enhances its oxidative resistance and ensures stable cyclic performance in LMBs [40]. Despite these advantages, typical fluoropolymers are often crystalline and function as a non-coordinating host matrix [41,42]. Consequently, achieving the optimal balance of properties in fluorinefunctionalized polymer electrolytes requires precise structural engineering.

paragraph_context: In this work, we have developed a novel in-situ polymerized fluorinefunctionalized polyether-based copolymer electrolyte aimed to address the challenges related to ionic conductivity, oxidative stability, and stable interface formation. The copolymer backbone incorporates both fluorinated and polyether-based bifunctionalities. Polyether-based components facilitate $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ion hopping, thereby enhancing the electrolyte’s ionic conductivity. The inclusion of fluorinated segments ensures a persistent, non-depleting internal fluorine source for LiF rich SEI/CEI formation and reduces the electronic cloud density around oxygencontaining polar groups and effectively lowers the energy level of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). This modification increases the copolymer’s oxidation resistance by raising the energy barrier for electron removal under high-voltage conditions, thus extending the electrochemical potential stability window beyond 5 V vs. $\mathrm { L i / L i ^ { + } }$ [43,44]. Tetraethylene glycol dimethyl ether (TEGDME), which possesses a high dielectric constant, was introduced as a plasticizer to further enhance ionic conductivity, achieving a value on the order of $1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { S } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ at room temperature. Consequently, the optimized fluorinated copolymer exhibited an ionic conductivity of 0.329 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ at ambient temperature. Li||NCM811 LMBs incorporating the optimized copolymer electrolyte demonstrated stable cycling performance over 200 cycles at 0.5C and excellent stability over 300 cycles at $^ { 1 \mathrm { C } , }$ both at ${ } ^ { 3 0 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C } .$ . This remarkable performance is attributed to the formation of an inorganic-rich hybrid interphase, facilitated by the fluorinated segment of the copolymer. Furthermore, pouch-type batteries were fabricated and successfully operated at ambient temperature to demonstrate the practical applications.

paragraph_context: To design a stable electrolyte system for high-voltage applications, the careful selection of salts and plasticizers is equally important to achieving optimal performance. Lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI), recognized for its high chemical and thermal stability [49], facilitates the formation of a TFSI− tethered polymeric network that effectively mitigates the space-charge layer formation. However, LiTFSI alone is insufficient to passivate aluminum foil, leading to significant corrosion when the operating potential exceeds 4 V [50]. To address this issue, the incorporation of lithium hexafluorophosphate $\left( \mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 } \right)$ has been shown to effectively suppress aluminum pitting corrosion [51]. Nonetheless, $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ decomposes at elevated temperatures [52], prompting the selection of LiTFSI as the primary lithium salt in this study. Thus, we strategically used the distinct advantages of these two salts and harnessed their combined impacts [51,53]. TEGDME, a shortchain ether-based oligomer, is utilized as a plasticizer to enhance salt dissociation due to its high dielectric constant. The incorporation of TEGDME into the electrolyte system results in improved ionic conductivity at room temperature. Furthermore, in-situ polymerization ensures intimate contact between the electrolyte and electrodes, thereby enhancing the overall electrochemical performance of the cell. Fig. 1 presents a schematic illustration of the polymerization process alongside a cross-sectional SEM image of the NCM811 cathode infiltrated with the in-situ polymerized electrolyte.

paragraph_context: To evaluate the contribution of each electrolyte component, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed. According to frontier molecular orbital theory, electrons in the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) possess the maximum energy and are prone to donation, correlating with the oxidation potential. Conversely, the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) readily accepts electrons, which corresponds to the reduction potential. The calculated LUMO energy levels of LiTFSI and $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ were − 1.61 eV and − 1.69 eV, respectively, both lower than those of the solvent molecule (TEGDME) and the copolymer of PEGMEA-TFEMA (PT). This indicates the preferential decomposition and participation of lithium salts in the formation of the interface between lithium metal and polymer electrolyte. Notably, the LUMO energy level of the copolymer PT at − 0.623 eV is lower than that of TEGDME $( - 0 . 3 2 3 \ \mathrm { e V } )$ , suggesting that PT is more likely to participate in the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), thereby preventing further decomposition or undesirable side reactions.

paragraph_context: Lithium metal anodes exhibit substantial application potential, featuring an energy density of 3860 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and a low operating voltage (3.04 V compared to the standard hydrogen electrode) [1]. Coupling the lithium metal anode with high-voltage cathodes (e.g., $\mathrm { L i N i _ { x } C o _ { y } M n _ { z } O _ { 2 } ) }$ is a promising approach to maximize the energy density of lithium metal batteries (LMBs). However, the practical applications of LMBs are severely constrained by safety issues such as lithium dendrite growth, liquid electrolyte consumption, and flammable gas generation [2,3]. LMBs employing solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) have garnered significant attention due to the intrinsically high safety and favorable thermal stability. The ideal SSEs possess several key attributes: (1) high ionic conductivity to enable efficient ion transport, (2) sufficient mechanical strength to accommodate the volume changes of lithium anodes and suppress dendrite penetration, (3) excellent chemical stability toward the counter electrode material, (4) low electrode/SSEs interface impedance, (5) a manufacturable process compatible with large-scale production [4,5].

paragraph_context: Among all the reported SSEs, solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) composed of uniform mixtures of polymer matrix and lithium salt hold broad application prospects in the field of high-performance batteries [6,7], owing to the excellent mechanical properties, good interfacial contact with electrodes, and ease of large-scale production [8,9]. A variety of polymer matrices, such as poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) [10], poly (vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) [11], polyacrylonitrile (PAN) [12], Poly (ethylene glycol) diacrylate monomers (PEGDA) [13], and poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC) [14] has been extensively investigated. However, the practical application of SPEs is still limited by the low room temperature ionic conductivity, narrow electrochemical window, and insufficient thermal resilience. To develop composite SSEs for highenergy-density and high-safety quasi-solid-state lithium metal batteries (QSSLMBs), significant efforts are being devoted to optimizing polymer-inorganic component combinations and designing the microstructure of the composite SSEs [15]. In polymer electrolyte systems, typical inorganic SSEs like Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS) [16], Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) [17], and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 . 3 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 0 . 3 } \mathrm { T i } 1 . _ { 7 } ( \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ) _ { 3 }$ (LATP) [18] are utilized as active fillers, leveraging their ability to create additional ion-transport pathways [19,20]. In addition, the incorporation of inorganic ceramic particles offers the following advantages: (1) reducing the crystallinity of the polymer matrix to enhance segmental motion, (2) forming percolation pathways at the polymer/inorganic fillers interface to boost ionic conductivity, (3) acting as a physical barrier to suppress lithium dentrite growth [21]. Moreover, the addition of plasticizers enables SPEs to achieve high ionic conductivity and low crystallinity, which is considered an effective method to obtain high-performance SPEs [22–25]. Propylene carbonate (PC) is one of the common substances in ester electrolytes, which has high ionic conductivity (5.8 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , strong solvation abilities, and stability at potentials above 4.0 V, which can be chosen as a plasticizer in polymer electrolyte [26,27].

paragraph_context: However, the narrow electrochemical window of single SPEs precludes simultaneous stabilization of lithium metal anode and highvoltage cathode, leading to the failure of QSSLMBs during long-term cycling [28–30]. Facing these challenges, various multilayer structured SSEs have been introduced, such as double-layer inorganic electrolytes, double-layer polymer electrolytes [31], asymmetric electrolytes [32,33], sandwich-type electrolytes etc. [34–36]. Recently, Han et al. [37] introduced high-performance PEO/HMO buffer layers between the cathode/electrolyte and anode/electrolyte. Owing to the dynamic and abundant $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ migration pathways within the PEO-based matrix, the PEO/HMO layer achieves a specific capacity of 183.6 mA $\mathbf { h } \ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { - 1 }$ for the high-loading NCM811 cathode and demonstrates excellent rate capability. Inspired by this design, multilayer electrolytes providing stable SSEs/electrode interfaces and excellent ionic conductivity are considered an effective strategy for constructing thin SSEs in highvoltage QSSLMBs [38]. Realizing long-life QSSLMBs requires electrolytes to simultaneously stabilize high-voltage cathodes and lowpotential lithium anodes. In theory, the rigid cathode necessitates an electrolyte layer with high ionic conductivity to create a stable ionconducting interface, whereas the electrolyte layer interfacing with the soft lithium metal anode must possess high stability to inhibit lithium dendrite formation. Designing composite SSEs based on LLZTO with a broad electrochemical window is essential to bolster the chemical compatibility of electrolyte/the electrode [39]. The introduction of plasticizers into PVDF-based polymer electrolytes allows the polymer electrolyte to combine the advantages of a liquid electrolyte and a solid electrolyte, which is conducive to improving the ionic conductivity and forming a tight interface between electrode/electrolyte [40].

paragraph_context: The structure and functional mechanisms of the quasi BCSEs are illustrated in Fig. 1a. The anti-oxidation layer and the anti-reduction layer were constructed by a simple tape-casting method, corresponding to a PPLLP layer on the NCM811 cathode side and a PLLPP layer on the Li metal side. The anode-facing PLLPP layer, establishes intimate contact with lithium metal by releasing PC from PPC to form a protective solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) film, effectively suppressing dendrite nucleation and safeguarding the lithium anode [41,42]. The cathodealigned PPLLP layer, not only provides reasonable ionic conductivity to ensure efficient $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport throughout the layer, but also acts as a soft contact between the positive electrode and electrolyte. The good wettability between the cathode and the electrolyte allows for volume changes of the active material in the cathode during cycling [43]. SEM images (Figs. 1b–d and S1) reveal the visible PPLLP/PLLPP interface in the initial quasi BCSEs. The surface morphologies of both layers (Fig. 1c–d) are smooth and homogenous, which ensures efficient $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport without extra interfacial resistance. The second stage differs between the two composites. For the PLLPP layer, the weight loss between $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 300 ◦C is associated with the decomposition of PPC and DMF. In contrast, for the PPLLP layer, the weight loss between $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 295 ◦C is due to the evaporation of PC. Additionally, TG analysis further confirms the release mechanism of PPC in PLLPP and the in-situ polymerization mechanism of PC in PPLLP. The PLLPP in contact with lithium metal exhibits a mass loss percentage of 17.41 % after 800 h of cycling, which is attributed to the formation of trace amounts of PC (Fig. S2). The mass loss percentage of PPLLP is 32.60 % after cycling with NCM811 cathode, resulting from the electrochemical polymerization of PC to form PPC (Fig. S3). Moreover, the as-prepared functional bilayer quasisolid electrolyte exhibits excellent mechanical flexibility, maintaining structural integrity after repeated bending, twisting, and foldingunfolding cycles (Fig. 1g). The corresponding stress-strain curves of PPLLP, PLLPP, and quasi BCSE are provided in Fig. S4. As shown in Fig. S4, the maximum stress of PPLLP is 0.54 MPa. It was noted that the mechanical strength of PLLPP was 1.57 MPa. After the introduction with PPLLP, the stress of BCSE reached 1.56 MPa. The enhancement in mechanical properties can be attributed to the well-dispersed LLZTO nanoparticles within the polymer matrix [9], which contributes to lithium dendrite suppression. Based on the aforementioned analysis, PLLPP demonstrates dendrite-suppressing capability, rendering it superior for direct contact with the lithium anode [7], whereas PPLLP serves as an effective buffer layer between the cathode and PLLPP electrolyte [15].

paragraph_context: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to determine the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energies of various electrolyte components. Generally, the lower LUMO energy value indicates a greater propensity to accept electrons, facilitating electrochemical reduction. Conversely, the higher HOMO energy value suggests a greater tendency to donate electrons, which can enhance electrochemical oxidation processes [51]. As illustrated in Fig. 2e, the PC exhibits a relatively elevated LUMO energy, implying its capability against reduction, while a depressed HOMO of PPC indicates its ability to resist oxidation. As a result, the complementary properties of these components synergistically broaden the electrochemical stability window of the prepared BCSE. To further investigate the lithium-ion coordination chemistry, the corresponding electrostatic potentials (ESP) of polymer constituents were analyzed (Fig. 2f). Generally, the stronger the electronegativity of the polymers stands for the greater the coordination ability with $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ [52]. In PLLPP electrolytes, the C––O group in the complex formed between PC and PVDF exhibits stronger electronegativity compared to that in pure PC and PVDF, which suggests the enhanced dissociation of Li+. paragraph_context: The electrolyte in contact with the lithium anode should concurrently inhibit lithium dendrite growth and ensure good interfacial contact. Inspired by the fact that PPC can slowly release trace amounts of PC upon contact with lithium as well as a wide electrochemical window (4.6 V), we designed the PLLPP electrolyte for potential application in QSSLMBs. Fig. 3a provides a detailed explanation of the “self-sacrificial” reaction of PPC. PPC polymer undergoes a spontaneous chemical reaction in contact with Li metal, and consequently decomposes into PPC fragments and PC molecules. Fortunately, trace amounts of PC infiltrate the electrolyte/electrode interface, thereby improving interfacial contact and reducing interfacial impedance. In addition, LLZTO filler plays a crucial role in the CSE, such as enhancing ionic conductivity and acting as a rigid barrier to suppress lithium dendrite growth [55]. The effects of different LLZTO loadings, ranging from 5 % to 25 % in PLLPP were investigated to explore the appropriate filler effect. When the LLZTO content reaches 15 wt%, the PLLPP electrolyte exhibits the highest ionic conductivity $( 2 . 3 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { { S c m } ^ { - 1 } ) }$ (Fig. 3b). Additionally, the surface morphologies of PLLPP demonstrate the smooth morphology at the optimal loading (Fig. S8). As the LLZTO content exceeds 15 wt%, excess LLZTO leads to nano-filler agglomeration, resulting in a rough electrolyte surface and lowering the ionic conductivity [56]. Galvanostatic cycling test was conducted on Li|PLLPP|Li symmetric cells to assess the interfacial stability (Fig. 3c). Prior to testing, lithium symmetrical batteries were first treated at $6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h to ensure close electrodeelectrolyte contact. Owing to the uniform contact enabled by the generated PC and the dendrite-suppressing capability of the inorganic fillers, a stable long-term cycling exceeding 800 h at 0.2 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ is observed without short-circuiting. Fig. 3d demonstrates the remarkable stability of the PLLPP electrolyte over 400 to 405 h, maintaining a consistently low overpotential of 35 mV. Furthermore, the PLLPP coupled with Li metal anode demonstrated a more uniform Li plating morphology and a denser interfacial contact between PLLPP and Li, indicating the interfacial stability of PLLPP toward Li anode (Fig. S9). In contrast, a symmetric cell using pure PC-plasticized PLLPP failed abruptly after 150 h cycling (Fig. S10), attributed to excessive PC causing reduced membrane flexibility and accelerated dendrite growth [42]. The time-resolved electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of Li symmetric cells assembled with PLLPP were tested to understand the degradation effect of PPC at the electrolyte/electrode interface (Fig. 3e). The corresponding equivalent circuit was presented in Fig. S11. In the Li|PLLPP|Li symmetric cells, the initial interfacial resistance sharply decreased from approximately 350 Ω $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ to approximately 220 Ω $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ within 48 h and remained stable for 800 h, which attributed to the slow release of PC from PPC upon contact with the Li anode, thereby improving interfacial contact and ensuring the resistance to electrochemical reduction.

paragraph_context: XPS analysis was conducted to investigate the chemical composition of the PLLPP/Li interface. Fig. 3f–g displays the C 1s and F 1s spectra of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formed on the lithium metal surface in Li|PLLPP|Li cells after 800 h of galvanostatic testing. In the F 1s spectrum, the strong peak at 688.2 eV corresponds to the ${ \bf - C F _ { 3 } }$ in the TFSI-, whereas the small peak at 684.8 eV represents LiF production [57]. Moreover, the intensity of ${ \mathrm { - C F _ { 3 } } }$ compared with the corresponding PPLLP/Li is lower (Fig. S22), indicating the PC promoting dissociation of lithium salts. These results demonstrate that the trace amounts of PC released by PPC facilitate LiTFSI dissolution and promote the generation of LiF-rich SEI layers [54,58], which is conducive to the enhancement of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conductivity as well as the good wettability of lithium metal in PLLPP electrolytes. Conclusively, benefited from the structure optimization aroused by mild degradation of the PPC component, the PLLPP is able to present the enhanced electrochemical performance matching with Li electrode.

paragraph_context: To address the issues of suboptimal ionic conductivity and poor contact with the cathode in PLLPP electrolytes, a composite membrane (PPLLP) was fabricated using LLZTO and PC. Fig. 4a illustrates the insitu polymerization mechanism of the PC component in the electrochemical process. Firstly, the alkaline surface of LLZTO induces the dehalogenation reaction of the PVDF polymer during cycling, triggering PC ring-opening to form PPC chains, which then react with dehalogenation products to form copolymers. The synergistic incorporation of LLZTO and $\mathtt { P C }$ enhances ionic conductivity, achieving a maximum of 1.38 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ in the optimized PPLLP electrolyte with 35 wt% LLZTO (relative to PVDF) and 1.5 mL PC addition (Fig. S12). The corresponding SEM images were investigated to examine the surface morphology of PPLLP with different LLZTO proportions and PC contents, ultimately yielding a dense and uniform PPLLP membrane (Figs. S13–S14). As indicated by the FTIR spectroscopy (Fig. S15a), the characteristic absorption band of $\mathtt { C } { = } 0 \mathrm { a t } 1 7 9 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ only appears when the amounts of added PC exceeds 1 mL [22]. LSV measurements showed electrochemical windows exceeding 4.5 V for all PPLLP samples, validating their compatibility with high-voltage cathodes (Fig. S15b). Fig. S16 shows that the ion transference number increases with the addition of $\mathrm { P C } ,$ indicating that the incorporation of PC can improve interfacial contact and reduce interfacial impedance, thereby facilitating the enhancement of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ migration efficiency. The impedance of the buffer layer of PPLLP (Fig. S17) and the corresponding electrochemical performance (Fig. S18) are also measured. Residual PC triggers nonuniform SEI formation in PPLLP-CSEs, leading direct short-circuit failures in Li|Li cells under cycling [59]. This issue can be settled in full battery when combining with the above PLLPP layer at the Li anode. The SEM images reveal the structure of the in-situ polymerized PPLLP composite polymer electrolyte (Fig. S19), where the uniformly distributed LLZTO provides continuous pathways for $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport, ensuring high ionic conductivity after polymerization. SEM test of disassembled Li|PPLLP|Li cells revealed a mossy Li surface and micro-cracks at the PPLLP/Li interface, indicative of unstable anode-side reactions (Figs. S20 and S21) [60,61]. The NCM811||Li metal cell employing PPLLP electrolyte exhibited stable interfacial resistance during cycling (Fig. 4b), which correlates with the formation of a 32 nm-thick LiF-rich cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) on the NCM811 surface (Fig. 4c–e). XPS analysis demonstrates the formation of LiF in PPLLP/NCM811 CEI [62], which serves as a robust protective layer to stabilize the NCM811 interface during the cycling process [63]. The morphology and microstructure of the NCM811 cathode after contact cycling with PPLLP were revealed by HRTEM (Fig. 4e–f). The TEM-EDS mappings revealed a uniform spatial distribution of the elements Ni, Co, Mn, and F on the surface of NCM (Fig. 4e). Furthermore, the cycled-NCM811 in PLLPP presented a compact CEI with a thickness of≈32 nm, which facilitates rapid fast Li-ion transport (Fig. 4f). As shown in Fig. 4g, the HRTEM image shows lattice spacing of 0.234 nm and 0.205 nm, respectively, corresponding to the (111) and (200) planes of LiF in the Fm-3m structure (the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) of the NCM811 cathode after cycled with PPLLP membranes is provided in Fig. S23). Based on the above analysis, the electrochemical polymerization of PC enhances interfacial contact, promotes ion transport, and forms LiF-rich CEI, which improves cycling stability [64].

paragraph_context: To demonstrate the advantages of dual-functional bilayer quasi-solid composite electrolyte, the performance of PPLLP, PLLPP, and BCSE were evaluated. The PPLLP layer constructed continuous $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conduction channels by in-situ polymerization of PC (Fig. S24) and LLZTO packing, with a R.T. conductivity of 1.38 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , significantly surpassing the ionic conductivity of the quasi BCSE $( 7 . 3 9 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { { S c m } ^ { - 1 } ) ( \mathrm { { F i g . 5 a } ) } }$ , as well as the smallest Ea value (0.20 eV) (Fig. 5b). After cycling with lithium metal, the ionic conductivity of the PLLPP electrolyte is enhanced, which is attributed to the formation of a more continuous Li+ transport pathway due to sustained release of trace PC (Fig. S25). As shown in Fig. 5c, the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transfer number of quasi BCSE $( \mathrm { t _ { L i } ^ { + } } = 0 . 7 5 )$ ) is much higher than PLLPP, attributed to the moderate coordination of PPC and $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ in the PPLLP layer (binding energy − 1.03 eV), weakening the strong interaction between $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { P V D F ^ { - } } ~ ( - 0 . 5 5 ~ \mathrm { e V } ) ,$ and promoting ion dissociation and directional migration (Fig. 5d–e) [64]. Fig. S26 presents the current-time curves corresponding to different composite solid electrolytes (PLLPP, BCSE, and PPLLP). Furthermore, the Li|BCSE|Li symmetric cell demonstrates a high CCD of 1.40 mA cm− 2 with low overpotentials at various current densities (Fig. 5f). The interfacial compatibility of the quasi BCSE in the symmetric cell is evaluated by galvanostatic cycling at a current density of $0 . 2 \mathrm { \ m A \ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ (Fig. 5g), and a small and stable polarization is observed over 1000 h with no significant short-circuit failure, indicating a good dendrite suppression capability [65]. This durable performance results from the double-layer structure of quasi BCSE, forming a soft and hard synergistic barrier. Specifically, PPC releases PC to improve the wettability of lithium metal, while LLZTO nanoparticles act as a rigid physical barrier to prevent dendrite penetration and avoid direct short circuits. Therefore, quasi BCSE with unique bilayer structure contributes to excellent electrochemical performance. To evaluate the interfacial stability of the Li|BCSE|Li, the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy was applied (Fig. S27). The detailed equivalent circuit (Fig. S11) and the corresponding values of resistances are shown in Table S3. Due to the continuous release of PPC, the interfacial impedance value gradually decreased from 335.83 to 80.91 Ω $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ (after cycling with Li). During continuous contact with lithium, the PC produced by PPC decomposition can wetting the PPC/Li interface, making it more closely contact and increasing the ionic conductivity of PPC. In addition, the continuous decomposition of PPC leads to a decrease in its layer thickness, which is one of the reasons for the decrease in interfacial impedance. As shown in Fig. S28, the cross-sectional SEM image of BCSE electrolyte cycled with Li metal remains a tight and coherent structure, which is conducive to stabilizing ion transport and inhibiting dendrites. Additionally, our work was compared with previously reported studies in terms of ionic conductivity, ion transference number, and electrochemical window; all of the mentioned aspects demonstrated superior performance (Fig. 5h).

paragraph_context: To validate the practical advantages of the quasi BCSE, three types of full cells were assembled for comparison. As shown in Fig. 6a, the NCM811||PPLLP||Li battery exhibits a polarization voltage of 150 mV during the first cycle, attributed to the in situ formed PPC serving as CEI film, thereby enhancing the oxidation resistance. However, the trace amounts of PC in PPLLP destabilizes the lithium anode, leading to obvious deterioration after 50 cycles [61]. In the NCM811||PLLPP||Li full cell, the sustained releasing process of PPC leads to a gradual decrease in polarization. However, the unsatisfactory ionic transfer and interfacial compatibility with the cathode result in a large polarization voltage (142 mV) and rapid decay in discharge capacity (Fig. 6b) [54]. The quasi BCSE full cell exhibits the lowest polarization voltage (120 mV), owing to the synergistic optimization of both electrode interfaces (Fig. 6c). At 0.2C, it retained a discharge capacity of 148.6 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ after 100 cycles with an average coulombic efficiency retention of 96.56 % (Figs. S29 and S30). As depicted in Fig. 6d, the discharge capacity of the quasi BCSE full cell at 0.5C is 169.0 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ , and133.2 mAh ${ \tt g } ^ { - \mathrm { i } }$ is still remained after 430 cycles. The outstanding cycling stability of quasi BCSE full cell demonstrates the superior features of the bilayer configuration. As shown in Fig. S31, the charge/discharge curves of Li|| NCM811 battery with PC plasticized PLLPP showed that the battery was overcharged in the fourth cycle due to the degradation of PC at 4.0 V [66], further validating the necessity of bilayer configuration for improved high-voltage stability. To further verify the applicability of quasi BCSE, the cycling performance of the full cell was evaluated at the current density of 1C (Fig. 6e), and the capacity of NCM811||PLLPP||Li rapidly deteriorates after 500 cycles. In contrast, the NCM811||BCSE||Li exhibits an initial specific capacity of 160.8 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and a capacity retention rate of 84.15 % after 1000 cycles. As shown in Fig. 6f, the NCM811||BCSE||Li cell has an initial capacity of 133 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at the current density of 2C and experiences 1500 stable charge–discharge cycles. The rate performance is also evaluated in full cells with PLLPP and BCSE quasi-solid-state electrolytes (Fig. S32). Within the current density range of 0.1C-2C, the carefully designed quasi BCSE membrane showed the rate performance to PLLPP. Thanks to the electrochemical polymerization of PC to form trace amounts of PPC (with a low HOMO) on the cathode side, accompanied with the depolymerization of PPC that released trace amounts of PC (with a high LUMO) on the lithium anode side, the bilayer composite quasi-solid-state electrolyte, prepared by a simple tape-casting method exhibits an enlarged electrochemical window (Fig. 6g), and achieves favorable stability for both the cathode and anode in NCM811||Li batteries. In addition, NCM811||Li matched quasi BCSE is assembled into a pouch cell and fully charged to light up the green LED in flat, bending, bending-recovery, and shear states (Fig. 6h).
