paragraph_context: To address the critical challenge of simultaneously accommodating lithium metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes in solid-state batteries, a quasi BCSE was designed to enhance full-cell cycling stability. The mechanism is summarized as follows: as shown in Fig. $^ { 7 \mathrm { { a } , } }$ , the PLLPP polymer electrolyte, when in contact with lithium metal, undergoes mild degradation of PPC to form trace amounts of PC, which constructs continuous ion transport pathways and improves the interfacial compatibility with lithium metal. However, the poor compatibility with high-voltage cathodes, such as NCM811, leads to suboptimal full-cell performance due to insufficient cathode-electrolyte contact and increased interfacial impedance. To improve the contact between the polymer electrolyte and the high-voltage cathode, an additional layer of PPLLP polymer electrolyte was introduced. The PPLLP polymer electrolyte, which exhibits high ionic conductivity and generates in-situ formation of LiF-rich CEI layer, can effectively enhance the overall performance of the battery system. However, as cycling progresses, PC tends to form a thick and non-uniform SEI, leading to direct shortcircuiting in Li symmetric cell (Fig. 7b). Impressively, the quasi BCSE architecture strategically integrates the advantages of both layers while mitigates their individual drawbacks (Fig. 7c). paragraph_context: In summary, the bilayer-structured electrolyte, with PLLPP as the dendrite-suppressing layer and PPLLP as the interfacial buffer layer, has ensured the stability of both the lithium anode and the high-voltage cathode. The PLLPP-CSEs with PPC component slowly degraded to release trace amounts of PC, which can inhibit the Li dendrite growth and form an intimate interface. The oxidation tolerant PPLLP-CSEs, featuring an enlarged electrochemical window, were strategically employed high-voltage cathode/electrolyte interface layer, effectively preventing deleterious interfacial side reactions between the electrolytes and the cathode materials. Through the convenient layer-by-layer tape casting, the prepared quasi BCSE presented an ultra-thin total thickness of \~43 μm, an excellent ionic conductivity (7.39 × 10− 4 S cm− 1 ), and a superb t+ transference number (0.75). Consequently, a distinguished electrochemical performance was obtained for NCM811||BCSE||Li cell, which delivered a discharge capacity of 133 mAh g− 1 at 2C and a cycling lifespan of 1500 cycles. This work offers an effective approach to achieve the commercialization of LMBs through a multilayer electrolyte design strategy.

Ltd, Xi’an, 710025, PR China Increasing the charge cut-off voltage represents one of the effective ways to increase the energy density of Limetal batteries (LMBs). However, this approach is hindered by the poor oxidation stability of conventional electrolytes, which tends to be more severe under high temperatures. To address this challenge, we synthesized a solvent, N-pyrrolidine-trifluoromethanesulfonamide (TFSPY), and formulated an electrolyte using 2 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) salt. This electrolyte enables stable long-term cycling of Li||LiCoO2 cells (≈10.8 mg cm− 2 ) at a high voltage of 4.5 V, demonstrating a capacity retention of 90 % after 200 cycles—significantly outperforming conventional carbonate-based electrolytes. Mechanistic analysis reveals that TFSPY promotes the formation of an FSI− -enriched solvation structure, thereby facilitating the decomposition of FSI− , which leads to the formation of a robust SEI on the lithium metal anode, thereby effectively suppressing dendrite growth. Furthermore, TFSPY is partially oxidative and decomposed, generating a Li3N-enriched CEI that significantly enhances high-voltage cycling stability even at high temperature up to 60 ◦C. The synergistic stabilization of both electrode interfaces—through the formation of protective SEI and CEI layers—enables reliable battery operation under high voltage and temperature conditions. Furthermore, the broad endothermic platform of the TFSPY molecule is key to its application in high-temperature fields. These findings provide valuable insights for the design of advanced electrolytes for high-energy-density LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Since their commercialization in 1991, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have dominated the energy storage market for portable electronics and electric vehicles (EVs), owing to their high energy density, superior efficiency, and long cycle life [1,2]. Among anode materials, lithium metal anodes (LMAs) exhibit the highest theoretical specific capacity (3860 mAh ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and the lowest electrochemical potential (− 3.040 V vs. SHE), making them a promising candidate for next-generation high-energy batteries [3–5]. Although conventional carbonate-based electrolytes remain prevalent in LIBs owing to their well-balanced properties, they are inherently unsuitable for LMAs due to their inability to form a stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [6]. Ether-based electrolytes, especially when matched with advanced film-forming additives, demonstrate markedly enhanced SEI formation kinetics on lithium metal anodes, offering superior interfacial stability relative to carbonate systems [7]. However, critical limitations such as low flash points and inadequate oxidation resistance (typically <4.0 V vs Li+/Li) impede their practical implementation [8–11]. Furthermore, both carbonateand ether-based conventional electrolytes suffer from compromised electrochemical stability at elevated potentials (>4.3 V vs Li+/Li) [12], despite the energy density benefits achievable through higher cutoff voltages [13]. This instability manifests through oxidative decomposition at the cathode-electrolyte interface, leading to: (i) accelerated transition metal dissolution from oxide cathodes [14], (ii) progressive thickening of the cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) [15], and (iii) gaseous byproduct evolution (e.g., CO₂ from carbonate solvents) [16]. These degradation pathways collectively contribute to capacity fade, impedance increases and ultimately, cell failure [17]. Therefore, the rational design of advanced electrolyte systems that maintain exceptional interfacial stability under high-voltage operation (>4.5 V vs. Li+/ Li) represents a critical research frontier in next-generation battery technology.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The electrochemical stability and interfacial characteristics of lithium batteries under high-voltage operation (>4.5 V vs. Li+/Li) are fundamentally determined by electrolyte composition, which governs the nucleation kinetics and structural evolution of the cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) [18–21] Fluorination chemistry enhances electrolyte oxidative stability through the strong electron-withdrawing effect of fluorine atoms, which systematically lowers the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level by 0.4–0.8 eV [22,23]. In terms of high-voltage molecular design, –F groups are introduced to further enlarge the oxidation window and Li metal compatibility [24–26]. For instance, By replacing the central part of the DMB backbone with –CF₂–, the resulting FDMB molecule exhibits enhanced stability against both Li metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes [27]. During electrochemical cycling, fluorinated solvents undergo preferential oxidation at the cathode interface, forming nanostructured fluorine-rich passivation layers $( { \mathrm { e . g . , ~ L i . p O _ { y } F _ { z } } } )$ which enhance interfacial compatibility and suppress transition metal dissolution [28–30]. While sulfone- and nitrile-based solvents exhibit ultrahigh oxidation resistance (>5.5 V vs. $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } / L i ) }$ [31,32], their practical implementation necessitates hybridization with fluorinated solvents to maintain anode compatibility, as their inherent reduction instability would otherwise compromise SEI formation on lithium metal anodes [33,34].

paragraph_context: Sulfonamide electrolytes have excellent thermal and electrochemical stability $[ 3 5 , 3 6 ]$ , making them highly compatible with high-voltage cathode materials such as nickel-rich NCM811 and lithium-rich manganese-based oxides (LRMO) [37]. At the same time, these electrolytes preferentially decompose, forming inorganic-rich interfaces (e.g., LiF, Li₃N, Li₂SO₃) on the electrode surface, effectively inhibiting parasitic reactions while maintaining efficient ion transport [38]. N, N dimethyltrifluoromethylsulfonamide electrolytes, for instance, enable stable cycling of LMBs at extreme potentials up to 4.7 V [39]. Notably, these electrolytes demonstrate exceptional compatibility with high-voltage LCO cathodes, achieving 89 % capacity retention after 200 cycles at 4.55 V [40]. We synthesized a high-purity solvent, N-Pyrrolidine-trifluoromethanesulfonamide(TFSPY),(Fig. S1a) and constructed an electrolyte from it, so as to realize the stable cycling of high-voltage lithiummetal batteries [41,42]. TFSPY promote the formation of inorganic-rich interfaces, which can improve the cycling performance of commercial LCO cathodes at 4.5 V and inhibit LCO surface degradation and side reactions. In particular, the LCO cathode exhibited a high-capacity retention rate of 90 % at 4.5 V after 200 cycles with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.5 % in TFSPY electrolyte. In addition, under these conditions, the battery exhibits superior rate performance and shows good thermal stability with a capacity retention rate of 89 % after 100 cycles at a high temperature of 60 ◦C.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: The solvent’s oxidation resistance governs the electrochemical stability of the electrolyte at high voltages, and a wide electrochemical window is a fundamental prerequisite for its application. Simultaneously, the solvation structure dictates the transport behavior of lithium ions and the interfacial chemistry, where a well-designed solvation structure is key to achieving enhanced stability of the lithium metal anode. Fig. 1a presents a comparative evaluation of the oxidative stability of different solvents based on their highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy levels. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the HOMO energy level of TFSPY is significantly lower than those of conventional carbonate solvents, ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC). This reduced HOMO energy indicates superior anodic stability, suggesting enhanced compatibility with high-voltage cathodes. Fig. 1b explores the oxidation stability of the molecule by LSV testing. It is observed that the oxidation current of 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte initiates at approximately 4.3 V, and its decomposition intensifies with an increase in electrode potential. In contrast, the initial oxidation reaction of the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte occurred at $5 \mathrm { V } ,$ indicating its oxidative decomposition reaction was effectively inhibited. Thus, 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte exhibits a wide electrochemical window and excellent stability at high voltages. Fig. 1c compares the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ binding energies of EC, DMC, and TFSPY solvents. The weaker $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } } .$ - TFSPY interaction $( - 1 7 . 7 \mathrm { k J } \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$ relative to EC and DMC，which is beneficial to the formation of anion-dominated solvation structures. Concurrently, Raman spectroscopy $( 7 2 0 { - } 7 6 0 ~ \mathrm { ~ c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , Fig. 1d and Table S1) reveals $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } { \mathrm { - } } F S I ^ { - } }$ coordination in different electrolytes. While the conventional 1 M LiFSI in EC/DMC electrolyte predominantly forms solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIPs) and contact ion pairs (CIPs), Raman spectroscopy reveals that the TFSPY-based system exhibits a significantly higher proportion of CIPs and ion aggregates (AGGs), indicating that TFSPY promotes more anion entering into solvation structures. Increasing LiFSI concentration from 1 M to 2 M further reduces free FSI− anions, promoting their incorporation into the solvation shell. This anion-rich coordination environment facilitates the formation of an inorganic-rich SEI, enhancing cycling stability [43]. Fig. 1e shows the FTIR test results, The peak intensity of pure TFSPY solvent gradually weakens with the increase of salt concentration, and the peak position undergoes a certain “redshift.” The results demonstrate that increase the LiFSI concentration would decrease the fraction of free TFSPY solvent. The decreased fraction of free TFSPY solvent is beneficial for enhancing electrolyte stability, which are crucial for high-voltage cell applications.

paragraph_context: Experiments were conducted to validate the aforementioned theo retical insight. The electrochemical compatibility and reversibility of lithium metal with TFSPY was evaluated by testing of 1 M LiFSI TFSPY electrolyte in Li||Cu cells (Fig. 3a). The TFSPY-based electrolyte exhibits an average Coulombic efficiency (CE) of 98.7 % after 350 cycles. This result proves that TFSPY has exceptional interface compatibility with lithium metal. Building upon this result, we optimized the system by increasing LiFSI concentration to 2 M to further improve the interface compatibility between electrolyte and lithium metal anode. Meanwhile, Since the 2 M LiFSI EC/DMC system cannot maintain stable at high voltage (Fig. S4), selected 2 M $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ in EC/DMC (3: 7 vol%) as the reference electrolyte. As shown in Fig. 3b, the average CE of a cell using 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte is only 89.8 % after 100 cycles, confirming the poor compatibility of Li with conventional carbonate electrolytes. In stark contrast, Li||Cu cell with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolytes exhibits significant cycling stability, approaching 400 cycles at 1 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with an average CE up to 99.1 %. This finding suggests that the SEI derived from TFSPY-based electrolyte is well-maintained. Meanwhile, the enhanced interfacial stability of the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte is further evidenced by polarization analysis of Li||Cu cells (Fig. 3c).

paragraph_context: Comparative examination of the voltage profiles reveals significantly lower polarization increase in TFSPY systems, with only a marginal increase between the 10th and 50th cycles, whereas the 2 M EC/DMC electrolyte exhibits substantially larger polarization evolution over the same cycling period. This marked difference in electrochemical behavior directly correlates with the superior stability of the TFSPY-derived SEI. Fig. 3d shows the voltage curve of a Li||Li symmetrical cell at a current density of 1.0 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ . The TFSPY system maintains exceptional cycling stability with minimal polarization increase over 1400 h, in stark contrast to EC/DMC electrolytes which experience rapid failure within 200 h. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed to analyze the variations in resistance during cycling (Fig. S5). The observed semicircles in the high-frequency regions represent the resistance of SEI $( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { S E I } } )$ . For the Li||Li cell with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte, the $\mathtt { R } _ { \mathtt { S E I } }$ experiences a lower increase than that of 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte, which can be attributed to stable SEI with low interfacial impedance. Furthermore, the morphological changes of the Li electrode after cycling were investigated via SEM characterizations, the electrode interface in 2 M carbonate-based electrolyte is porous (Fig. 3e) and also shows significant nanoscale dendritic lithium after only 10 cycles (Fig. 3f). On the other hand, the lithium electrode in 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte formed a smooth and dense surface after 10 cycles under the same cycling conditions (Fig. 3g), demonstrating uniform lithium deposition/stripping processes that effectively suppress dendritic growth and dead Li formation, consequently resulting in mitigated RSEI increase and ultimately leading to the observed enhanced cycling stability and higher Coulombic efficiency.

paragraph_context: The electrochemical performance of Li-metal full cells, configured with Li metal anodes paired with high-loading NCM811 cathodes (9.5 mg $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ and cycled at 0.5C, demonstrates the critical role of electrolyte composition in cell stability (Fig. 4a). The capacities of cell in 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte experienced significant rapid decreases, which can be attributed to the formation of extensive dendritic dead Li leads to rapid capacity fading. In contrast, TFSPY-based electrolytes lead to an impressive high-capacity retention of 96 % after 300 cycles, coupled with a high average CE of >99.98 %. At the same time, the charge-discharge curve of the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte shows better repeatability than that of the 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte (Fig. 4b and S6). These results collectively demonstrate that TFSPY-based electrolytes exhibits excellent cathode stability and anode compatibility in lithium metal batteries. For further investigation into the stability of the constructed CEI under high voltage conditions (up to 4.5 V), LCO was utilized as cathode due to the higher operating voltage plateau and better high-voltage cycling stability [44]. As depicted in Fig. 4c, the capacity of the carbonate-based system is almost depleted after 100 cycles, which could be attributed to the poor electrolyte stability at high voltages, resulting in intensified side reactions. Whereas the capacity retention of the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte remains as high as 90.5 % even after 200 cycles with an average CE of 99.5 %. In contrast to the carbonate-based system, the discharge voltage plateau of the TFSPYbased system exhibits remarkable stability throughout the entire cycle, indicating that the polarization of the cell does not increase significantly and excellent interphase formation durability (Fig. 4d and S7). In order to understand the origin of the improvement in high-voltage electrochemical performances, the oxidation stability of the electrolytes on the LCO cathode was evaluated through an aggressive float test with a hold time of 12 h at 4.5 V (Fig. S8), the cell leakage current density using the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte was $4 . 2 \mu \mathrm { A c m } ^ { - 2 } ;$ , which was equivalent to \~12.5 % of the 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte $( 3 3 . 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { A } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ . The lower leakage current density in the TFSPY-based electrolyte indicates that fewer side reactions occur on the cathode surface, confirming that the designed electrolyte has higher oxidation stability compared to the reference electrolyte. Importantly, 2 M TFSPY-based electrolytes exhibit excellent cycling stability even under harsher conditions. at high temperatures $( 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and high voltages (4.5 V). As shown in Fig. 4e, at high temperatures $( 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and high voltages (4.5 V), the capacity retention of cell with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte is still as high as 89.1 % after 100 cycles. However, the cell with 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte failed over 50 cycles and have low Coulombic efficiency. The sharp contrast indicating that the TFSPY-based electrolyte has good interfacial stability at high temperatures. Moreover, the thermal stability of TFSPY is verified through DSC testing (Fig. S9). The EC electrolyte exhibits an endothermic peak at approximately ${ } ^ { 3 4 } \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ corresponding to the melting process of the EC electrolyte. Furthermore, starting from around ${ 1 3 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ a significant endothermic peak appears at ${ 1 8 6 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ which corresponds to the thermal decomposition process of the EC electrolyte. In comparison, the TFSPY electrolyte demonstrates a broad endothermic platform $( 3 0 { - } 1 6 7 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , with an endothermic peak observed at ${ } ^ { 2 4 2 } \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ corresponding to the solvent vaporization process. The thermal stability of the TFSPY electrolyte is a critical factor enabling its application in hightemperature fields. As shown in Fig. S10，cell with 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte shows rapid capacity decay and retains a low specific capacity when the charge/discharge rate is raised to 2C. In contrast, cell with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte shows better rate capability, with a capacity retention rate of 87.5 % after 100 cycles at 2C. In addition to investigate the long-term cycling stability of cells with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte, the rate performance at 4.5 V was also evaluated $( \mathrm { F i g . 4 f ) . }$ . The Li||LCO cell using the TFSPY-based electrolyte exhibits higher reversible capacities compared to that of reference electrolyte at current density of 0.1C to 5C, respectively. label: 结构表征
paragraph_context: The morphology of the cyclic LCO is shown in Fig. 5a-f, where the LCO electrode with 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolyte undergoes electrolyte oxidative decomposition under high voltage conditions, resulting in heterogeneous surface deposits with particulate morphology on the electrode surface and the appearance of cracks (Fig. 5b, e). In contrast, a smooth electrode surface and intact particles without breakage were observed in LCO cycled with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte (Fig. 5c, f), The well-maintained morphology of cycled LCO can be attributed to the formation of TFSPY-based CEI, resulting in ideal cycling performance. It is well known that the properties of the interphase film are crucial factors affecting cell performance. Therefore, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was employed to investigate in detail the main components within CEI. As illustrated in Fig. 5g-h. XPS analysis of CEI formed in 2 M $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ in EC-DMC showed strong signals of C–C (284.8 $\mathrm { e V } ) , \mathrm { C } { \longrightarrow } ( 2 8 6 . 5 \mathrm { e V } )$ in the C1s spectrum, and $\mathrm { C = o } \left( 5 3 2 \mathrm { e V } \right)$ in the O1s spectrum, indicating carbonate electrolyte decomposition. In addition, the decomposition of $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ was confirmed by the presence of LiF (685.2 eV) and POxFy (687.8 eV) in the F1s spectrum. For the CEI formed in the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte, the low content of C–C and C–O attributed to the partial decomposition of TFSPY molecules and the high content of LiF indicate the formation of an inorganic-rich CEI. Meanwhile, the S–F signal is attributed to the partial decomposition of LiFSI, while the C–F signal originates from the decomposition of TFSPY. The higher $\mathrm { C - F }$ peak intensity than the $\mathtt { s - F }$ one implies that the CEI on the LCO surface is mainly derived from the decomposition of TFSPY rather than LiFSI. In the N1s spectrum (Fig. 5i), the peaks observed at 400.2 eV correspond to $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } ,$ which are mainly generated through the partial oxidative decomposition of TFSPY. CEI enriched with LiF and Li N can significantly enhance the stability of the lithium-metal interface [45]. As a result, the cell shows good cycling performance at high voltages. Moreover, A distinct Li3N signal was observed in the electrolyte of 2 M LiFSI in TFSPY, whereas only a trace amount of nitrogen-containing compounds was detected in the 2 M LiFSI in EC-DMC electrolyte. Therefore, this indicates that $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ originates from the decomposition of the TFSPY solvent (Fig. S11). To elucidate the underlying roles of two electrolytes on cathode behavior during cycling, XRD analyses was conducted to examine the structural alterations of fatigued electrodes. As displayed in Fig. S12, all reflections in the XRD patterns of both cycled cathodes are assigned to a hexagonal structure with R3m space group without any impurities. Notably, the reflections from the cathode compatible with EC/DMC-based electrolyte exhibit significant broadening and intensity reduction compared to those from TFSPY-based electrolyte, indicating severe structural degradation during cycling. These findings highlight the beneficial role of TFSPY-based electrolyte in augmenting the structural stability of layered oxide cathodes during cycling. Compared to the conventional EC-DMC electrolyte system, the TFSPY-based electrolyte demonstrated significantly reduced transition metal dissolution (Fig. 5j), indicating effective suppression of cathodeelectrolyte side reactions. Furthermore, increasing the lithium salt concentration led to additional mitigation of transition metal dissolution, confirming the superior interfacial stability of the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte under high-voltage cycling conditions. Apart from the CEI and cycled LCO cathode, SEI and cycled Li anode was also investigated, in conventional 2 M EC/DMC-based electrolytes, the lithium metal anode exhibits pronounced dendritic growth during cycling, as evidenced by morphological characterization (Fig. S13). In contrast, the use of TFSPY-based electrolyte results in a smooth and uniform surface, suggesting significantly improved interfacial stability and suppressed dendrite formation [46]. Futhremore, the XPS results of the lithium metal anode also indicate the formation of a LiF-rich SEI interface with TFSPY-based electrolyte (Fig. S14). Through a comparative analysis of the SEI formed after different numbers of cycles, the primary spectral features and their relative intensity ratios remain largely consistent. This remarkable consistency strongly indicates the high stability of the resulting SEI. In addition, the presence of $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 3 }$ (Fig. S15) can facilitate $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport [47]. These results show that the decomposition products of TFSPY electrolyte successfully stabilize the electrolyte interface. Fig. S16 displays the corresponding mass concentration of elements on the LCO surface. The higher concentration of $\mathrm { F } ,$ N and S elements can be observed in the CEI formed by the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte system in comparison to the EC/DMC-based electrolyte system. Meanwhile, CEI formed by the 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte system displays relatively lower levels of C and O elements. This again indicates that the TFSPY solvent molecules participate in oxidative decomposition to form inorganic-rich CEI films. In addition, the corresponding mass concentration of elements on the Li metal surface also exhibits a higher concentration of F, S elements with 2 M TFSPY-based electrolyte system (Fig. S17). This result shows that SEI formed in TFSPY-based electrolyte exhibits a higher inorganic content. The TFSPY solvent molecules undergo partial oxidative decomposition on the LCO cathode surface, forming a stable CEI enriched with Li₃N and LiF species. This robust CEI layer is instrumental in enabling the superior high-voltage performance of TFSPY-based electrolytes. Concurrently, the increased incorporation of $\mathrm { F S I ^ { - } }$ anions into the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation sheath promotes their reductive decomposition at the anode interface, generating a robust SEI. The synergistic formation of these protective interphases on both electrodes collectively ensures exceptional cycling stability under high-voltage and elevated-temperature conditions.

paragraph_context: In this work, we synthesized a solvent, TFSPY, as a high-temperature and high-voltage electrolyte. The electrolyte composed of this solvent and 2 M LiFSI salt successfully supports the long-term cycle stability of Li || $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ (≈10.8 mg cm− $^ { - 2 } )$ cell at 4.5 V. Commercial LCO cathodes retain 90 % after 200 cycles. Under the high temperature of $6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , the capacity retention can be maintained at 89.1 % even after 100 cycles. Mechanistic analysis reveals that TFSPY promotes the formation of an FSI− -enriched solvation structure, thereby facilitating the decomposition of FSI− , which leads to the formation of a robust SEI rich in LiF on the lithium metal anode. There is no lithium dendrites observed in the SEM images of lithium metal anode, indicating that SEI formation in TFSPY-based electrolyte effectively suppresses dendritic growth. Furthermore, TFSPY is partially oxidative and decomposed, generating a Li3N-enriched CEI that significantly enhances high-voltage cycling stability. The synergistic stabilization of both electrode interfaces—- through the formation of protective SEI and CEI layers—enables reliable battery operation under high voltage and temperature conditions. Furthermore, the broad endothermic platform of the TFSPY molecule is key to its application in high-temperature fields. These findings provide valuable insights for the design of advanced electrolytes for high-energydensity LMBs.

Ltd., Beijing, 100070, PR China  f School of Environmental Engineering, Nanjing Institute of Technology, Nanjing, 211167, PR China Regulating ionic transport, particularly achieving uniform cation-selective transport, is critical for enabling highrate and stable lithium metal batteries (LMBs). Herein, we design an amino-functionalized metal–organic framework composite separator (NS) to tailor ion transport via anion anchoring. Guided by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the -NH groups in NH -ZIF-8 selectively anchor PF− anions, thus promoting Li+ transport. The NS separator exhibits a high Li+ transference number (0.72) and enhanced Li+ conductivity (0.60 mS cm− 1 ). Molecular dynamics simulations confirm the anion-confined and Li+-selective transport mechanism. Consequently, Li symmetric cells with NS achieve ultra-stable cycling over 4000 h at 5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ . Phase-field simulations further demonstrate dendrite-free Li deposition. In full cells paired with LiFePO4 or LiNi1/3Co1/ 3Mn1/3O2 cathodes, NS enables superior rate capability and long-term cyclability, significantly outperforming commercial polypropylene separators. This work provides a rational design strategy for functional separators toward high-energy, high-power LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Developing post‑lithium ion batteries (LIBs) technologies is a cutting-edge and urgent topic due to the rapid development of portable electronics and electric vehicles [1–3]. As one representative of post-LIBs area, lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have drawn considerable attention. Metal lithium possesses an ultra-high theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and a lowest electrode potential of − 3.040 V (vs. the standard hydrogen electrode), which brings great possibilities for highenergy devices [4–6]. Nevertheless, the occurrence of notorious lithium dendrites induced by undesirable ionic transport seriously hinders the advance of LMBs [7–9]. From the essence of ionic transport, restricting the freely transport of electrolyte anions is an extremely important factor. Massive anions migration could result in concentration polarization, joule heating as well as side reactions [10]. More importantly, anion transport could accelerate the nucleation process of lithium dendrite according to the classical Sand's formula [11,12]. Therefore, regulating ionic transport to realize highly efficient transport of Li+ ions has important practical significance for promoting the applications of LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The separators, as the essential intermediate for the migration of cations/anions, offer an ideal platform for tailoring ionic transport [13,14]. Recently studies have proved that functional separators or solid-state electrolytes are efficient routes for improving the Li + transference number [15–17]. Currently, optimizing the transport dynamics of Li+ ions via functional separators mainly including the construction of homogeneous pores and the introduction of electrostatic interaction. For instance, anodized aluminum oxide membranes with the pore diameter for about 100 nm was applied in $_ \mathrm { L i } { - } s$ batteries, which could allow uniform lithium deposition on lithium metal anode [18]. Xian et al. designed a functional separator with honeycomb channel structure, which realized the homogeneous deposition of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions [19]. In the study of An and co-workers, a covalent organic framework based composite separator possessed electrostatic interaction with the freely movable lithium salt anions to suppress their diffusion and stable lithium metal anodes [20], emphasizing the importance of tailoring ionic transport by design functional separators.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Comparing with the above studies to suppress the migration of anions, the immobilization of anions could be a more efficient way. Among which, utilizing functional groups to anchor anions is feasible. It could achieve specific coordination and directional regulation of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions transport, which is expected to increase $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ions transference number $( \mathrm { t _ { L i } ^ { + } } )$ via a more stable and effective way. Besides, it could help to lower the de-solvation energy barrier and realize uniform interface electric field. This strategy could enable a more persistent effect during the cycling process. Previous studies have demonstrated that the incorporation of nitrogen atoms into polymer backbone could decrease the binding energies of cation/anions [21–24]. The interactions of amide to anion could facilitate the dissociation of ion pair to promote $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ ion transport [24,25]. The above reports demonstrated the positive effects of functional groups for immobilization of anions. However, seldom study focuses on exploring the mechanism of functional groups toward immobilizing anions, which is of great significance for realizing ionic selective transport to fundamentally inhibit dendritic formation.

These factors enabled the cells to possess a lower degree of ohmic polarization, thereby presenting higher discharge capacities. In addition, the cells with NS demonstrated higher voltage platform than that of ZS and PP at each rate, especially high rates over 5.0C (Fig. 5d), which confirmed that the NS was beneficial for suppressing the battery polarization when charging and discharging at high current density. paragraph_context: Gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs) have garnered significant attention owing to their high ionic conductivity, improved interface feature, and structural integrity. However, the low thermal stability, poor cycling durability, low cation transference numbers, and inefficient dendrite suppression of GPEs seriously hinder the practical applications. To address such issues, herein, we present a novel amine-functionalized boron nitride reinforced poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) hybrid gel polymer electrolyte (fBN-HGPE) for highperformance, dendrite-free lithium metal batteries. The fBN-HGPE has unique rigid–soft gel matrix and rapid ion-transport pathways, delivering high thermal/mechanical stability, effective lithium-dendrite suppression, an ultra-high ionic conductivity of $2 . 3 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { ~ S ~ c m ^ { - 1 } }$ , a high cation transference number, and remarkable cyclability. As a result, fBN-HGPE-based batteries with various cathodes $\mathrm { ( L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } , }$ LiFePO4, and LiCoO2) exhibit superior electrochemical performance. DFT calculations show that the functional additive–impregnated gel traps TFSI− anions and minimizes concentration gradients at the electrode–electrolyte interface. The present work proposes a rational design and synthesis strategy to construct a rigid–soft hybrid GPE tailored for highperformance lithium metal batteries.

paragraph_context: With the rapidly expanding market for electric vehicles and flexible or wearable electronic devices, there is a relentless pursuit of cuttingedge energy storage systems with long cycle life and high reliability [1,2]. Nevertheless, lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), owing to their ability to deliver exceptionally high energy density [3–6]. Despite that, LMBs overcome LIBs by harvesting high energy from their ideal negative electrode (metallic lithium) owing to its superior theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and low redox potential (− 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode) [7,8]. Unfortunately, it faces some serious challenges, including cycling degradation and safety issues owing to unstable redox of highly reactive Li metal in flammable alkyl carbonate electrolytes, including ethylene carbonate, diethyl carbonate, and dimethyl carbonate [9–11]. Over the past decade, researchers have increasingly sought to replace conventional alkyl carbonate electrolytes with ionic liquid (IL)-based gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs) because of their merits, such as high ionic conductivity, negligible volatility, minimized flammability risk, and flexibility. Nonetheless, the high cost of ILs hinders their practical usage for large-scale deeds [12,13]. On the other hand, the GPEs specifically possess a low Li-ion transference number because of the fortified ionic behavior, which failed to suppress space-charge formation at the surface of Li anodes, and mechanical softness that enables lithium dendrites to penetrate through the gel matrix, thereby compromising operational safety [14,15]. Therefore, identifying scalable, low cost, and safe GPE systems is crucial for realizing high-performance next-generation LMBs [16–18]. Until now, several polymer backbones, such as $- ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - C F } _ { 2 } ) _ { \mathrm { n } ^ { - } } , \ - ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - O } ) _ { \mathrm { n } ^ { - } }$ , $- ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - C } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } ) ( \mathrm { C O O C H } _ { 3 } ) ) _ { \mathrm { n } } \mathrm { - } ,$ and – $- ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - C H } ( \mathrm { C N } ) ) _ { \mathrm { n } ^ { - } }$ have been proverbially employed as GPEs in LMBs. These polymer backbones provide distinct polar functionalities (C–F, C–O–C, C–––N, and C––O), which critically regulate ion–polymer interactions, mechanical robustness, and overall gelation behavior in GPEs [19–25]. Among these, C–F functional group derivatives containing P(VDF-HFP) backbones have gained eye catching attention due to their high dielectric constant, high density of polarizable fluorinated groups, ability to prevent dendrite growth, suppression of lithium pulverization during cycling, and insoluble in many organic solvents [26,27]. Recently, Jing Jie et al. have developed a P(VDF-HFP)-based gel polymer electrolyte that delivers an ionic conductivity of 0.047 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and a specific discharge capacity of 134.8 mAh ${ \mathfrak { g } } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.2C for LFP||Li cells [28]. Similarly, Ahmad Shokrieh et al. designed the P(VDF-HFP)-based electrolyte assembled with the LFP||Li battery, which displayed an ionic conductivity (σ) of 0.21 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ with a discharge capacity of 150 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.2C-rate [29]. According to the prior investigation, P(VDF-HFP) alone is still inadequate for GPEs owing to its sluggish lithium diffusion kinetics, unsatisfactory compatibility with electrodes, and safety problems that do not meet the LMB requirements [30,31]. For example, inert fillers such as $\mathrm { { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { { O } _ { 3 } } }$ [32,33], SiO2 [34], BN [34,35], montmorillonite [36,37], palygorskite [38], halloysite nanoclay [39], and metal–organic framework [40], as well as active fillers such as garnet-type $\mathrm { L i } _ { 7 - x } \mathrm { L a } _ { 3 } \mathrm { Z r } _ { 2 - x } \mathrm { T a } _ { x } \mathrm { O } _ { 1 2 } \ [ 4 1 - 4 5 ] ,$ , NASICON type $\mathrm { L i } _ { 1 + x } \mathrm { A l } _ { x } \mathrm { T i } _ { 2 - x } ( \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ) _ { 3 }$ [46], can optimize the performance of polymer electrolyte by improving the local amorphous domains of polymers and thereby improving the electrochemical features. However, the scalable fabrication of GPEs with high thermal stability, excellent cyclability, elevated cation transference number, and robust dendrite suppression continues to be hinder the real time applications [47–50]. Hence, novel functional fillers are urgently required, and the underlying mechanism needs to be clarified. Inspired by a recent study, functionalization of the BN with amine groups emerges as a promising strategy, serving as an effective anion-trapping media in ion gel electrolyte through Lewis acid–base interactions. According to the findings, aminefunctionalized boron nitride $\left( - \mathrm { N H } _ { 2 } { - } \mathrm { B N } { - } \right)$ impregnated polymer chains significantly enhances thermal homogeneity, which in turn promotes uniform nucleation, suppresses dendritic growth, and improves Li-ion migration and overall electrochemical performance [7,31].

paragraph_context: The fabrication of hybrid GPE was carried out under an argon-filled glove box with 0.1 ppm of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and 0.1 ppm of H2O. The detailed preparation method of amine functionalized BN is presented in the supporting information. Initially, a measured 6 wt% of aminefunctionalized boron nitride powder was dispersed into $N ,$ N-dimethylformamide for 30 min under ultrasonic agitation. Subsequently, 1.0 g of poly(vinylidene fluoride co-hexafluoropropylene) was dissolved in a solvent mixture, followed by magnetic stirring for 3 h at $6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to obtain a homogeneous viscous polymer slurry. Afterward, bistrifluoromethanesulfonylimide salt was added and continuously stirred for 30 min. Then, the resultant viscous slurry was coated onto a clean glass substrate. Finally, the polymer-coated substrate was dried in a vacuum oven at $8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 48 h. Similarly, the P(VDF-HFP)/LiTFSI and BN/P (VDF-HFP)/LiTFSI-HGPE were designed through the similar approach described above. The polymer/Li salt complex was formulated with a 1:1 weight proportion. The resultant gel polymer electrolytes were punched into discs (Φ = 19 mm) for further electrochemical use. For simplicity, P(VDF-HFP)/LiTFSI, BN/P(VDF-HFP)/LiTFSI, and Aminefunctionalized BN/P(VDF-HFP)/LiTFSI were named as PL-GPE, BN-HGPE, and fBN-HGPE, respectively.

paragraph_context: From the practical stand point, the polymer electrolyte should maintain good thermal stability to ensure reliable and safe electrochemical performance. The internal resistive heating and side reactions can elevate the cell temperature during continuous charge–discharge cycling, which causes thermal softening or decomposition of the polymer matrix. Such degradation can deteriorate the interfacial contact, decrease ionic conductivity, and in severe cases, lead to catastrophic failure or short-circuiting, posing serious safety risks. In this perspective, thermogravimetric analysis was performed to explore the thermal resistance of the HGPEs, which influences the battery safety as presented, and the corresponding zoomed version is inserted in Fig. 2b. The thermal degradation of virgin P(VDF-HFP) reveals a single-step degradation of the − CH2− CF2− backbones begins at around ${ \sim } 4 5 0 \ \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Fig. S6). On the other hand, the fabricated material exhibits a drastic acceleration in the degradation kinetics of P(VDF-HFP) segments up to ${ \sim } 3 3 5 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , which can be attributed to the strong polarity of formyl hydrogen (HC(=O)–) solvent molecules impairing the intermolecular interaction of − CH − and − CF − chains, leading to the decrease of thermal stability of the GPEs [75]. However, the inclusion of additives decreased the thermal degradation as compared to the filler-free medium as revealed in the magnified version (Inset). Consequently, the fBN-HGPE framework provides a safer and more thermally resilient electrolyte environment for high-performance LMBs.

paragraph_context: A novel non-flammable electrolyte formulated with lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (LiOTf) in trimethyl phosphate (TMP), synergistically improved by lithium nitrate (LiNO3) and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) additives, is developed to address the critical safety and performance challenges of lithium metal batteries. The additives play distinct roles as FEC lowers the overpotential for lithium plating/stripping, enabling stable cycling for over 500 h in Li//Li cell, while $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ boosts the average coulombic efficiency of Li plating/stripping to 96.82% in Li//Cu cell. Electrolyte-electrode interface analysis reveals that FEC modulates $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ decomposition, forming a composite and robust solid electrolyte interphase enriched with LiF and nitrogen‑oxygen compounds, which is crucial for cycling stability and suppressing dendrite formation. Subsequent EIS and Tafel analysis show a very low charge transfer resistance of 13.65 Ω and an exchange current density of 2.951 mA/cm2 , indicating excellent interfacial charge transfer kinetics. Under high-current and high-capacity tests, this electrolyte outperforms commercial electrolyte, confirming the remarkable stability of the optimized interface. Its practical viability was demonstrated in $\mathrm { L i } / / \mathrm { L i M n } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ half-cells. Notably, the cells sustained over 1900 cycles with \~80% capacity retention while also demonstrating remarkable durability for over 1800 cycles at 500 mA/g. This highlights its suitability for high-power applications and showcases its promising prospects for practical application. The inherent fire resistance of the TMP-based electrolyte addresses critical safety concerns without compromising electrochemical performance. This electrolyte provides a promising and highly feasible solution for durable, high-power, and safe next-generation batteries and energy storage systems.

paragraph_context: Despite their immense potential, lithium metal batteries face significant barriers to commercialization. Conventional carbonate-based electrolytes are volatile and flammable, posing risks of fire or explosion during thermal runaway or internal short circuits, creating serious safety concerns [2]. Furthermore, the high chemical reactivity of lithium metal triggers continuous side reactions with the electrolyte, forming an unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [3]. This fragile SEI fails to suppress lithium dendrite growth, leading to separator piercing, short circuits, and ongoing consumption of electrolyte and active lithium, resulting in reduced coulombic efficiency and diminished cycle life [4].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The stability of the electrode-electrolyte interface is critical for suppressing dendrite growth and minimizing side reactions. Functional additives such as fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and lithium nitrate $\mathrm { ( L i N O _ { 3 } ) }$ have been proven to effectively form stable SEI layers. FEC facilitates the formation of a LiF-rich SEI layer, enhancing mechanical stability and ionic conductivity [5], while $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ contributes to a dense, inorganic protective layer, improving the reversibility and durability of lithium metal anodes [6]. These additives are essential for achieving high-performance lithium metal batteries.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: To address these challenges, this study employs trimethyl phosphate (TMP) as a non-flammable solvent, leveraging its exceptional flameretardant properties to provide intrinsic battery safety [7]. TMP is paired with lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (LiOTf), a thermally stable lithium salt with excellent dissociation properties [8]. A nonflammable solvent alone is insufficient to ensure long-term electrochemical stability [9], necessitating further optimization of the electrode-electrolyte interface to improve performance. The innovative electrolyte design by substituting 20 mol% of LiOTf with $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ in a TMP-based electrolyte and incorporating 5 wt% FEC, forming the Li $[ \mathrm { O T f / N O _ { 3 } } ] { \mathrm { - F E C } }$ electrolyte is developed in this study. This approach leverages the synergistic interaction between $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ and FEC to form a unique and robust SEI layer in situ on the lithium metal surface, enriched with LiF and nitrogen-containing compounds. The electrolyte achieves over 500 h of low-overpotential (\~0.05 V) cycling in Li//Li symmetric cells, sustains over 1900 cycles with \~80% capacity retention and 99.3% Coulombic efficiency in $\mathrm { L i / / L i M n _ { 2 } O _ { 4 } }$ half-cells, and demonstrates excellent rate capability. This salt composition modification strategy effectively addresses solvent‑lithium metal compatibility issues, suppresses dendrite growth, and delivers superior safety, extended cycle life, and excellent rate performance, paving the way for the commercialization of high-performance lithium metal batteries.

paragraph_context: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were performed using Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP, version 6.5.1) to investigate the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation structures in Li[OTf/NO ] and Li[OTf]. Two trimethyl phosphate (TMP)-based electrolyte models were considered. The nitrate-containing electrolyte, $\mathrm { L i } [ \mathrm { O T f } / \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ]$ , followed the composition LiOTf: $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } \colon T M P } = 0 . 8 \colon 0 . 2 \colon 8$ (in molar ratio) and was constructed using an integer-packed model of $5 \mathrm { L i ^ { + } } , 4 \mathrm { O T f ^ { - } } , 1 \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } ^ { - } }$ , and 40 TMP molecules, corresponding to a total of 721 atoms. The nitratefree control electrolyte, Li[OTf], was constructed by replacing LiNO3 with LiOTf while keeping the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and TMP counts unchanged, corresponding to an integer-packed model of $5 ~ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ , 5 OTf− , and 40 TMP molecules, corresponding to a total of 725 atoms. For a consistent comparison, both electrolyte models were simulated under periodic boundary conditions in the same cubic cell with a side length of 20.4 Å. Initial configurations were generated by molecular packing and subsequently pre-relaxed to remove unfavorable close contacts; the relaxed structures were then used as starting points for AIMD.

paragraph_context: All calculations were carried out using the VASP within the projector augmented-wave (PAW) framework. The exchange–correlation functional was described by the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation. Dispersion interactions were included using the DFT-D3 method with Becke–Johnson damping $( \mathrm { I V D W } = 1 2 )$ . A planewave kinetic energy cutoff of 520 eV was employed. Brillouin-zone sampling was restricted to the Γ point (Γ-only) due to the large cell size.

paragraph_context: AIMD simulations were conducted in the canonical (NVT) ensemble at 300 K. The ionic motion was propagated with a time step of 0.5 fs $( \mathrm { P O T I M } = 0 . 5 )$ , and the thermostat was implemented via VASP's molecular dynamics algorithms (MDALGO). Electronic self-consistency during AIMD employed Gaussian smearing $( \mathrm { I S M E A R } ~ = ~ 0 )$ with $\mathrm { S I G M A } = 0 . 1 0 ~ \mathrm { e V } ,$ , an electronic convergence criterion of $\mathrm { E D I F F } = 1 \times$ $1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ . All AIMD trajectories used in structural analyses were taken from equilibrated segments, and radial distribution functions and coordination numbers were computed from the resulting trajectories.

paragraph_context: THE BIGGER PICTURE The application of Li metal batteries (LMBs) is hampered by unstable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) and dendritic Li growth. Electrolyte engineering is an effective way to address these issues. Localized high-concentration electrolytes (LHCEs) are very effective in increasing Li+ -anion coordination. However, the addition of large amounts of fluorinated diluents leads to an increased cost, environmental pollution concerns, and low ionic conductivity. In this study, we present a non-fluorinated electrolyte with a micelle-like solvation structure. The amphiphilic asymmetric ether (AAE), containing a lithiophilic oxygen segment at one end and an alkyl chain at the other end, spontaneously forms micelle-like structures with Li+ during the solvation formation stage. AAE can effectively promote Li+ -FSI coordination through steric crowding and keep the electrolyte with high ionic conductivity. This strategy exhibits a new and scalable design of low-cost electrolytes for LMBs.

paragraph_context: Electrolyte engineering plays a critical role in enabling lithium (Li) metal batteries. However, the simultaneous realization of anion-rich solvation structure and high ionic conductivity of electrolytes via solvation structure design remains challenging. Here, we report a low-cost, non-fluorinated electrolyte with a micelle-like solvation structure by introducing amphiphilic n-butyl methyl ether (MNBE) into Li bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI)/ 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) for stable Li metal batteries (LMBs). MNBE can effectively promote Li+ -FSI coordination through steric crowding. Meanwhile, the inert alkyl chains of MNBE can mitigate the reaction between electrolyte and Li metal due to their lithiophobicity. Specifically, the micelle-like, non-fluorinated electrolyte exhibits an ionic conductivity as high as 12.55 mS cm1 , and its anion-rich solvation structure promotes the formation of LiF-rich solid-electrolyte interphase. We constructed a 7.3 Ah Li||NMC811 pouch cell employing this electrolyte under harsh conditions, exhibiting ultra-high specific energy of 503.7 Wh kg with impressive cycling stability of 84.1% capacity retention after 100 cycles.

paragraph_context: Lithium (Li) metal battery is regarded as the next-generation power source due to the merits of high theoretical capacity (3,860 mAh g1 ), low density (0.534 g cm3 ), and low standard electrode potential ( 3.04 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode).1,2 Nevertheless, the practical application of Li metal anode is hampered by its limited cycle life, mainly stemming from unstable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) and serious dendritic Li growth. In the pursuit of higher energy density batteries, especially for energy densities beyond 500 Wh kg1 , the electrode areal capacity needs to be increased to more than 4 mAh cm2 , while the electrolyte mass/capacity (E/C) ratio will be necessarily reduced to less than $2 . 1 \ \mathfrak { g } \mathsf { A h } ^ { - 1 }$ . 3 These requirements, however, further exacerbate the above challenges.4 Electrolyte engineering is an effective way to modulate the SEI composition and Li morphology, thus greatly improving the electrochemical performance of Li metal batteries (LMBs). It has been well demonstrated that inorganic-rich SEI can relieve Li corrosion caused by the swelling of organic components of SEI during electrochemical cycling.5–7 Increasing Li+ -anion coordination8 and/or diminishing Li+ -solvent coordination9 in the Li+ solvation shell of an electrolyte can facilitate the formation of inorganic-rich SEIs. To date, several promising strategies have been developed involving high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs),10 localized HCEs (LHCEs), mixed solvents,13–15 additive tuning, liquified gas electrolytes,17 single-salt-single-solvent electrolytes,18–20 and micelle-like electrolytes.21,22 In particular, HCEs are very effective in increasing Li+ -anion coordination in the Li+ solvation shell, thus improving interfacial stability and maintaining safe operation.10 Yet, the viscosity, cost, and electrode wettability are compromised in these high-concentration systems. LHCEs are designed to reduce the electrolyte viscosity by adding inert fluorinated diluents, maintaining all the properties required for good battery performance while diminishing Li+ -solvent coordination in the Li+ solvation shell.12 However, the addition of large amounts of fluorinated diluents leads to an increased cost and potential environmental pollution concerns,23–25 and also greatly reduces the conductivity of the electrolyte (e.g., 2.44 mS cm1 for 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-TTE).12 The main reason for this phenomenon is that the highly electronegative fluorine withdraws electrons from oxygen atoms, resulting in reduced binding affinity between Li+ and oxygen atoms of the solvent molecule. Low conductivity leads to inferior Li+ ion transport kinetics, especially when the battery is operated with a high-areal-capacity anode (R4 mAh cm2 ) and a high current density (R4 mA cm2 ).

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Based on the above discussions, an ideal electrolyte for high energy density batteries should possess the following key features: (1) the ability to form an anion-rich solvation structure in the absence of fluorinated diluents/solvents at low salt concentrations to produce a stable inorganic-rich SEI, (2) a high ionic conductivity to ensure fast Li+ transport, and (3) oxidative stability toward high-voltage cathodes. Despite the encouraging progress in optimizing LMB electrolytes, achieving these requirements simultaneously by engaging low-cost and fluorine-free electrolytes through rational solvation structure design, especially for >500 Wh kg1 LMBs, has yet to be realized.

paragraph_context: In this work, we introduced a non-fluorinated electrolyte with a micelle-like solvation structure to realize 500 Wh kg1 LMBs. An asymmetric ether, that is n-butyl methyl ether (MNBE), containing a lithiophilic oxygen segment at one end and an alkyl chain at the other end, is introduced as a cosolvent into the LiFSI/ DME electrolyte system to form a micelle-like solvation structure (Figure 1). MNBE can effectively promote Li+ -FSI coordination through steric crowding and induce more FSI to decompose on the Li metal surface, resulting in LiF-rich SEI. Furthermore, the inert alkyl chains of MNBE located in the outer layer of the solvation shell can also passivate the Li/electrolyte interface, thus alleviating electrolyte decomposition and Li metal corrosion. More importantly, 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE exhibits an ionic conductivity of up to 12.55 mS cm1 . Consequently, a high-capacity (7.3 Ah) Li metal pouch cell has been realized with a high energy density of 503.7 Wh kg1 and good cycling stability (84.1% retention after 100 cycles) based on our micelle-like solvation electrolytes. As a corollary, the micelle-like solvation electrolyte provides a scalable electrolyte engineering strategy and guides the development of electrolytes for advanced batteries.

Significant red shift of the peaks associated with the anion is known to occur upon dissolution as a result of the decrease in coordination between cation and anion.33,34 As in Figure 5A, it is clear from the LiFSI spectra that the S-N-S bending peak of the FSI at $7 7 2 \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ is shifted to $7 1 6 ~ \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ when dissolved in DME, demonstrating a strong dissociation of the Li+ -FSI, consistent with the solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIPs) solvation structure.35,36 By contrast, the shift of FSI (S-N-S bending) peak for 1.5 M LiFSI/MNBE is much smaller (ranging from 772 to $7 4 0 ~ \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ ), an indication of the strong $\mathsf { L i } ^ { + } { \mathsf { - F S l } ^ { - } }$ interaction, which is characteristic of the solvation structures of contact ion pairs (CIPs) or aggregates (AGGs).

paragraph_context: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis is performed on these three electrolytes as well as on the solvents to further verify the formation of micelle-like solvation structure. As shown in Figures 5E and S32, the protons relevant to MNBE and DME are named $\mathsf { H } _ { 1 } , \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } , \mathsf { H } _ { 3 } , \mathsf { H } _ { 4 } , \mathsf { H } _ { 5 } , \mathsf { H } _ { 6 } ,$ and $\mathsf { H } _ { 7 } ,$ respectively. The 1 H NMR of the relevant protons in the DME-MNBE mixture shows almost no chemical shift compared with those in pure DME or MNBE, indicating that there is no direct interaction between DME and MNBE (Table S5). With the addition of LiFSI, the chemical shifts of the relevant protons in all three electrolytes undergo a significant upfield shift. This phenomenon is the result of FSI involvement in the solvation structure, which results in a shielding effect37 and is consistent with the Raman spectra results (Figure 5E; Table S6). At the same time, we find that the $\mathsf { H } _ { 3 } , \mathsf { H } _ { 4 , \qquad }$ and ${ \mathsf { H } } _ { 5 }$ near the oxygen atom undergo larger chemical shifts in 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE than in 1.5 M LiFSI/MNBE, indicating a further increase in electron density, while there are no significant changes in the ${ \sf H } _ { 6 }$ and H7 at the other end of the MNBE, away from the oxygen atom. This result suggests that the lithiophilic oxygen atom of the MNBE is inside the first solvation shell, while the lithiophobic alkyl chain is located outside. The participation of MNBE in the first solvation shell is likely to cause steric crowding, thus enhancing $\mathsf { L i } ^ { + } { \mathsf { - F S l } } ^ { - }$  interaction. Such surfactantlike behavior for MNBE not only demonstrates the involvement of both DME and MNBE in the solvation structure but also provides powerful evidence for the formation of the micelle-like solvation structure. In addition, to confirm the spatial distribution of MNBE in micelle-like solvation structure, two-dimensional nuclear overhauser enhancement (2D NOE) spectroscopy was carried out on the DME-MNBE mixture as well as 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE, which can provide structural information between spatially close protons within a given molecule. It is well known that the NOE interaction between protons is distance dependent: NOE interactions are hardly detected once the protons distance beyond $5 \mathring { \mathsf { A } } . ^ { 3 8 , 3 9 }$ As shown in Figures 5F and S33, no significant crosspeaks are observed between the relevant protons in MNBE with or without the addition of LiFSI, implying that the distances between them are all more than 5 A˚ , which proves that the alkyl chain of MNBE remains straight before and after involvement in the solvation structure and no bending occurs. The MNBErelated Raman spectra as well as the NMR spectra are consistent with the MD simulations in Figures 2D–2F, which jointly validate the formation of the micelle-like solvation structure from both experimental and theoretical aspects. Additionally, the applicability of the micelle-like solvation strategy was further validated by substituting MNBE with the structurally similar n-hexyl methyl ether (MNHE) (Figure S34).

paragraph_context: Cryo-transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) and time-offlight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) resolved the microstructure of SEI. As shown in Figures 6A–6D and S35, the SEI of 1.5 M LiFSI/DME presents an inhomogeneous layered morphology and reaches a thickness of 15 nm. By contrast, the SEI of 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE not only exhibits a uniform amorphous morphology, but the thickness is only 7 nm. This feature not only helps to reduce the diffusion path length of Li ions but effectively reduces the Li consumption from SEI reformation in each cycle. In addition, the three-dimensional (3D) structure of SEI and spatial distribution of each component were further resolved by ToF-SIMS depth profiling (Figures 6E– 6H). The ionic fragments of Li and inorganic components, LiF, were characterized as Li and $\mathsf { L i F } _ { 2 } { } ^ { - } ,$ , respectively. Since the SEI grows on the surface of the Li metal, the time taken for the Li signal to reach its maximum value can be used to analyze the thickness of the SEI. As shown in Figure 6G, the Li signal takes about 150 s to reach its maximum value in 1.5 M LiFSI/ DME-MNBE, only half of the one for 1.5 M LiFSI/DME (300 s), suggesting that the thickness of the SEI is thinner in 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE. This conclusion is consistent with the results of the cryo-TEM. Moreover, at the sputtering time of 50 s, the content of LiF in the SEI of 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE is 1.2 times higher than that of 1.5 M LiFSI/DME, which implies that the MNBE induced more FSI decomposition at the Li/electrolyte interface (Figure 6H).

paragraph_context: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to track the compositional differences in the SEI generated by these two electrolytes.40,41 As shown in Figures 6I, 6J, and S36, the SEI compositions of the two electrolytes are analogous, due to the similar decomposition pathways of the ether electrolytes. However, the relative proportions of the different elements vary considerably, which confirms the influence of the different solvation structures on the formation of SEI. Specifically, a striking S-F (687.7 eV) peak is observed in the F 1s spectra of 1.5 M LiFSI/ DME, which is caused by the incomplete decomposition of FSI at the interface due to a large amount of solvent coordination with Li+ . Furthermore, the incomplete decomposition of FSI is further confirmed by the sharp $\mathsf { R } \mathrm { - } \mathsf { S } \mathsf { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - } \mathsf { R } ^ { \prime }$ peak in the S 2p spectra (169.5 eV) and the faint Li2O peak in the O 1s spectra $( 5 2 8 . 2 \ \mathsf { e V } ) . ^ { 3 6 }$ By contrast, the SEI formed by 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE exhibits an intense Li-F (684.8 eV) peak, while the S-F peak is negligible, indicating a complete decomposition of the FSI. Similar trends are found in the S 2p and O 1s spectra. Meanwhile, the lower C (53.51% to 38.16%) and higher F (6.84% to 13.61%) contents compared with 1.5 M LiFSI/DME indicate that 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE forms a LiF-rich SEI dominated by inorganic components34 (Figures 6I and 6J; Table S7). 1.5 M LiFSI/MNBE also forms a thin and inorganic-rich SEI (Figure S37). Combining the evidence obtained from cryo-TEM, ToF-SIMS, and XPS, it can be concluded that MNBE-based electrolytes are capable of forming ultra-thin, uniform, and LiF-rich anion-derived SEI. Furthermore, the MNBE-based electrolytes could form thin CEIs with higher inorganic components on the cathode surface, similar to SEIs (Figures S38 and S39). This enabled the cathodes using MNBE-based electrolytes to maintain structural stability over longer cycles (Figure S40). In addition, the alleviation of Li reactivity to the electrolyte can be demonstrated by the reduction of corrosion current density at the interface.41 As shown in Figure 6K, the corrosion current density of 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE is 0.085 mA $\mathsf { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ after 10 cycles, which is much lower than that of 0.143 mA cm2 for 1.5 M LiFSI/DME, fully reflecting the passivation effect of MNBE on Li/electrolyte interface. The electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) of Li||NMC811 cells under different cycle numbers also show the same pattern as the above phenomenon (Tables S8–S10; Figure S41), i.e., the impedance of the 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE varies less and the interface is more stable after multiple cycling.

paragraph_context: In this work, we present a class of non-fluorinated electrolytes with micelle-like solvation structures toward the realization of practical LMBs. A series of experimental analyses and theoretical calculations confirm that MNBE with amphiphilic structure can effectively promote Li+ -FSI coordination and passivate the Li/electrolyte interface, forming ultra-thin and inorganic-rich SEI. Benefiting from these features, the practical 7.3 Ah Li|| NMC811 pouch cell with 1.5 M LiFSI/DME-MNBE achieves a lifespan of 100 cycles under ultra-high energy density of 503.7 Wh kg1 . We demonstrate that non-fluorinated and lowcost electrolytes can form an anion-rich solvation structure while maintaining high ionic conductivity through rational solvation modulation. This work exhibits a scalable design of low-cost fluorine-free electrolytes for high energy density LMBs.

paragraph_context: In this paper, electro-thermal behaviour of a Li-ion pouch cell have been analysed using devel oped mathematical model, MSMD-based NTGK and ECM models, and the results compared with experiments. The variations of electro-thermal parameters change under CC discharge and WLTP current profile were investigated. Cell terminal voltage at 1 C-rate discharge can be predicted until the last stage of the discharge process with relative errors less than 1.5 %, 2.0 % and 3.0 % for ECM, NTGK and mathematical models, respectively. The maximum relative error in the variation of terminal voltage for the dynamic current profile is 1.5 %, 2.0 % and 2.5 %, respectively. Consequently, ECM model is more successful in analysing battery behaviour. However, mathematical model has a significant advantage over other models due to the analysis time of a few minutes. The methodology implemented in the single-cell models is applicable at the module level. However, the cells within the module are under pressure. A methodology for mini-module assembly has been developed to investigate the effect of compression on electrothermal properties. Mini-module tests showed that the energy provided by the cells under compression increased by 25 % compared to the single cell. Consequently, it is essential to consider compression and other effects in module-level analyses.

paragraph_context: The transformation of electrification and related technologies in the automotive industry has occurred rapidly due to the low energy efficiency of conventional internal combustion vehicles, the pollution effects of these vehicles and the depletion of fossil fuels. [1–5]. In this context, the number of new generation vehicles with alternative vehicle technologies for sustainable transportation, has increased remarkably [6–8]. Consequently, the prevalence of electric vehicles (EVs) continues to increase due to advancements in high energy density batteries, developments in fast charging technology, and improvements in battery life cycle [9–14]. There are cells with cathode materials of various chemistries that supply a range of requirements such as lifespan, cost, safety, performance, power, energy, electrical and thermal properties [15–19]. Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) performs successfully in all metrics and the battery whose electrical and thermal properties are investigated in this study has this chemistry [20].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: EV battery packs consist of sub-components such as cover, frame, housing, modules, which provide structural strength and ensure safety norms in case of failure and accident [21–25]. In addition, battery management system (BMS) comprises of software and hardware components that provide electrical control and management, data collection, communication, safe charging and discharging. Battery thermal management system (BTMS) is also responsible for maintaining the battery system within the optimum operating temperature range [26–31]. Therefore, it is essential to investigate battery behaviour under various conditions to design and develop these systems.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The battery pack used in EV consists of modules configured to provide the vehicle-specific electrical requirements. The module includes cells and provides them with mechanical strength while also contributing to improve thermal performance. Common types of batteries used in EVs include cylindrical, prismatic, and pouch cells. Pouch cells, in contrast to other types of cells, are sealed with a flexible foil. Consequently, in pouch cells, swelling occurs due to the heat and gaseous by-products generated by entropy change and Joule heating. This results in a decrease in cell capacity and mechanical degradation. Therefore, the module consisting of pouch cells is assembled by placing flame-retardant foam battery pads (FBPs) between the cells. FBPs compensate volume changes caused by swelling and provide protection against deformation. Consequently, the electro-thermal behaviour of a single pouch cell differs from that of a compressed cell. In this study, the changes in the electrical and thermal properties of the single cell were first experimentally investigated, and then modelling studies of the battery were conducted using electro-chemical models.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Electrochemical models used to predict battery parameters with high consistency are critical in the design of auxiliary systems that comprise the battery system. The Multi Scale-Multi Domain (MSMD) approach is frequently favoured for electrochemical behaviour of the battery cell for developing Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) model [32–38]. This approach involves the superposition of the properties of components such as current collectors and porous components, including anode, cathode and separator, which constitute the multilayer cell structure [39,40]. Also, all components are represented at all points on the cell, and calculations are performed at different scales by taking into account the multi-physics structure of the cell in this approach [41]. In other words, used solution method calculate particle-level active material diffusion, electrochemical reactions, and cell-level electrical and thermal performance at various domains [42].

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: There are two models commonly used in the electro-chemical modelling of batteries based on the MSMD approach. One of these is the Newman, Tiedemann, Gu, and Kim (NTGK) model correlates and numerically calculates the thermal and electrical fields of the battery utilizing model-specific parameters determined through curve fitting from experimentally derived discharge curves [43–46]. In this model, the heat generation rate is obtained by calculating the electrical parameters and the temperature distribution is determined from the energy conservation equation [47]. The other model is the ECM model, in which model-specific parameters are obtained by examining the effect of current pulses applied to the cell. The Equivalent Circuit Model (ECM) enables the electrical behaviour of the battery to be modelled as an electrical circuit consisting of resistance and capacitance elements and provides thermal parameters to be obtained by using these parameters [48]. Higher-order equivalent circuits comprising more electrical elements provide more accurate results, but the calculation of values of the circuit components becomes more complex [49–51]. Therefore, the second-order equivalent circuit model (SOEC) was selected for the development of the mathematical model.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Terminal voltage (TV) and heat generation of the battery cell vary depending on temperature, current, state of charge (SOC), and state of health (SOH) [52–56]. Therefore, the numerical values of elements used in the modelling of the battery should be determined experimentally, considering these variable conditions. Several methods can be used to determine battery characteristics. One of these is hybrid pulse power characterisation (HPPC) test involves the application of current pulses to the battery cell at various SOCs. This allows the calculation of internal resistances (IR) from the change in TV, and the test is frequently used to determine cell characteristics [57–60].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The temperature of the cell increases due to chemical reactions, while the SOC and the current change depending on the velocity profile and vehicle characteristics during operation. Furthermore, electrochemical reactions exhibit high temperature dependence, and electro-thermal behaviour of the battery cell varies depending on ambient temperature [61–64]. It is important to determine the IR by considering these boundary conditions to develop an effective battery model. After comparing battery models, the electro-thermal behaviour of the mini module with a 4S1P connection configuration and the single cell was investigated, and the differences between them were discussed.
