paragraph_context: ECM is an electrochemical model consisting of a specific number of resistor and capacitor elements, depending on the order of circuit $[ 4 8 , 6 5 ]$ . High-order ECM provides more accurate results, but the calculation of model parameters becomes more complex. Ansys Fluent adopts the SOEC model shown in Fig. 1. Ohmic resistance, denoted by Ri, refers to the resistance of the components that constitute the battery [66]. Primary factor contributing to equivalent internal resistance (EIR) is the ohmic resistance, which leads to sudden changes in the TV [67]. R1-C1 branch of the circuit is associated with charge transfer process, while R2-C2 branch represents diffusion process [68]. The diffusion process affects the impedance more at low frequencies of the current, while the charge transfer process mainly affects impedance at currents up to several hundred Hz. Consequently, it is understood that the charge transfer process signifies fast dynamics, the diffusion process represents slow dynamics, and both processes are characterised by different time constants [69]. The model parameters are calculated by applying CC discharge method or HPPC test to the cell $[ 5 7 , 7 0 ]$ . Heat generation occurs within the cell during operation [71–76]. Dynamic behaviour of the cell varies depending on this temperature. The BTMS in EVs is responsible for maintaining the cells within their ideal operating temperature range of $1 5 \mathrm { - } 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to ensure safety and obtain optimum performance from the cells. Therefore, if the ambient temperature is initially assumed to be ${ 1 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$ in modelling and experimental studies, it is predicted that the cell temperature will not exceed the ideal operating temperature range under specified current conditions, based on experience. Thus, in terms of representing the electric vehicle application, SOEC parameters were determined in this study by performing the HPPC test at 15, 20, 25 and $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ .

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: During the HPPC test, the cell is subjected to charge and discharge processes in the current profile shown in Fig. 2. Accordingly, changes in TV of the cell are analysed, and the SOEC parameters are obtained [77]. When instantaneous current pulses are applied to the cell, a sudden drop in voltage is observed due to the effect of film resistance caused by the formation of a solid electrolyte interface. The sudden drop in the cell’s TV is associated with ohmic resistance in the circuit. A deviation from the open-circuit voltage occurs during the intercalation and deintercalation of lithium ions to overcome the activation energy. This phenomenon is referred to as activation polarization and the process takes place within milliseconds or a few seconds. A concentration gradient forms during the transfer of ions within the electrode and electrolyte, and the effect of this process on voltage becomes apparent within minutes. These two phenomena, which indicate fast and slow time dynamics, are represented by the HPPC test through changes in TV resulting from the application of a current pulse [69,78]. The cell is initially discharged with a C/3 rate CC up to the lower limit of the operating voltage range. C-rate refers to the current depending on the capacity of the cell. Then, the cell is charged with a C/3 rate CC until it reaches the upper limit of the operating voltage. Thereafter, charging process is continued at constant voltage. Following the preliminary phase, the cycle consisting of current pulses and CC discharge is applied to the cell 10 times. At the beginning of each cycle, a 30-s discharge current pulse is applied to the cell, followed by a 40-s rest period and then a 10-s charge current pulse. The value of the currents applied is determined according to the nominal capacity of the cell. Relative discharge current is 1, while the relative charge current is 0.75. Then, the cell is discharged with C/3 rate so that SOC of the cell is decreased by 10 %. As a result of the 10th cycle, the cell is completely discharged. paragraph_context: NTGK model is a semi-empirical electrochemical model that is based on the MSMD solution approach [86–88]. Within the NTGK model, calculations are performed by solving Equations (9)–(11), due to the physics of electrical, chemical and thermal processes at different length scales. However, in this model, the correlation between the electrical and thermal fields is determined by means of the parameters U and Y, which are determined as a result of the experimental study and are specific to this model [44]. U defines the equilibrium voltage, while Y is the conductivity [89]. jECh is calculated by Equation (16) [84]. $$ j _ {E C h} = \frac {Q _ {\text {nominal}}}{Q _ {\text {ref}} \text {Vol}} Y [ U - V _ {t} ] \tag {16} $$ Compared to the ECM model, the NTGK model has advantage of allowing for more effortless determination of model parameters. This is achieved by applying a discharge current to the cell at various C-rates. Furthermore, due to the increase in cell temperature during operation, performing these tests at different ambient temperatures increases the accuracy of the model. The parameters U and Y can be determined as a function of depth of discharge (DoD) by means of a fifth order polynomial curve fitting method, as demonstrated in Equations (18) and (19) [90]. $$ D o D = 1 - S O C = \frac {V o l}{3 6 0 0 Q _ {\text { nominal }}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} j d t \tag {17} $$ $$ U = \left(\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {5} a _ {n} (D o D) ^ {n}\right) - C _ {2} \left(T - T _ {\text { ref }}\right) \tag {18} $$ $$ Y = \left(\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {5} b _ {n} (D o D) ^ {n}\right) e x p \left[ - C _ {1} \left(\frac {1}{T} - \frac {1}{T _ {r e f}}\right) \right] \tag {19} $$ where $a _ { n }$ and $b _ { n }$ are the polynomial coefficients that can be modelled to best fit the experimental data, while C1 and C2 are the coefficients determined to fit the temperature dependence of the U and Y parameters. T represents the absolute ambient temperature (◦K) and $T _ { r e f }$ denotes 298.15 K. In order to determine all these coefficients, the voltage-time curves obtained from the discharge tests are first converted into voltage-DoD curves. This curve is then converted into voltage-volumetric current transfer rate curves. Finally, the slope and intercepts of this curve are calculated for each DoD, and the U and Y parameters are fitted [89]. However, in this study, the parameter estimation toolbox in Ansys Fluent was used to specify the parameters U and Y. For this purpose, discharge tests were conducted under a range of ambient conditions and various C-rates, so the curves of TV change were transferred to the parameter estimation tool box as a text file. Thus, U and Y parameters for 4 different temperatures were calculated by the Ansys Fluent depending on the experimental results.

Then, the charging and discharging currents are calculated by using Equations (22) and (23) [92]. $$ I _ {c h g} = \frac {- V _ {o c} + \sqrt {V _ {o c} ^ {2} + 4 R _ {e q} P _ {c h g} (t)}}{2 R _ {e q}} \tag {22} $$ $$ I _ {d i s} = \frac {V _ {o c} - \sqrt {V _ {o c} ^ {2} - 4 R _ {e q} P _ {d i s} (t)}}{2 R _ {e q}} \tag {23} $$ where $V _ { o c } , R _ { e q } , P _ { c h g }$ ve $P _ { d i s }$ denote the open circuit voltage, equivalent resistance, and the power demanded from the battery during the charging and discharging processes, respectively. The capacity of the cell exhibits a dynamic change depending on the ambient temperature and current. Consequently, the SOC value consumed in a time step can be calculated using Equation (25) by determining the capacity change under the existing conditions [93]. $$ S O C = S O C (0) \mp \frac {1}{C _ {\text { cell }}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} i _ {b} (t) d t \tag {25} $$ where SOC(0) indicates the SOC value at the beginning, $C _ { c e l l }$ and $i _ { b }$ denote the cell capacity and instantaneous current value, respectively. At the beginning of each cycle, the instantaneous SOC value is determined, and electrical parameters of the battery are calculated accordingly. As stated in the ECM and NTGK model, there is a direct correlation between electrical and thermal properties. Consequently, the calculated parameters are transferred between sub-models. The thermal sub-model allows the heat generated in the battery cell to be determined numerically without using a measuring device such as a calorimeter. The battery cell was discretised into surfaces, and the heat conduction equation, stated as in Equation (26), was algebraised by using the finite difference method [94]. $$ \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(k _ {x} \frac {\partial T}{\partial x}\right) + \frac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(k _ {y} \frac {\partial T}{\partial y}\right) + \frac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(k _ {z} \frac {\partial T}{\partial z}\right) + \dot {q} = \rho c _ {p} \left(\frac {\partial T}{\partial t}\right) \tag {26} $$ The thickness of the battery cell used in the present study is negligible compared to its other dimensions; therefore, the cell is considered planar. Consequently, the heat conduction equation can be expressed as in Equation (27) [95]. $$ \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(k _ {x} \frac {\partial T}{\partial x}\right) + \frac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(k _ {y} \frac {\partial T}{\partial y}\right) + \dot {q} = \rho c _ {p} \left(\frac {\partial T}{\partial t}\right) \tag {27} $$ All heat transfer mechanisms have been included as boundary conditions in the heat conduction equation. The equation has been discretised using the finite difference method, and the heat generation rate per unit volume has been calculated. The experimental study was carried out and the temperature change at the points determined on the cell surface was measured. In the thermal submodel, the heat conduction equation is solved using the experimentally obtained temperature data to calculate the reversible and irreversible heat terms that comprise the heat generation. Furthermore, the mathematical model is able to calculate the dynamic change of the entropic term. For this purpose, Equation (28), known as the Bernardi Equation, was used, taking into account the calculated electrical and thermal parameters [71]. $$ q = q _ {i r r e v} + q _ {r e v} = I (V _ {o c} - V _ {t}) - I T _ {b} \frac {d V _ {o c}}{d T} \tag {28} $$ Thus, the instantaneous change in the electrical and thermal properties of the battery during a dynamic driving cycle can be determined. However, in order to examine the change in battery parameters during a CC discharge process, the vehicle dynamics submodel has been deactivated. Therefore, the blocks where current calculations are performed have been removed and the current is represented as a CC value block.

The application of uniform and sufficient compression force is crucial in practice. Maintaining the compression effect can be achieved using mechanical apparatus, or, when the number of cells is high, by placing the cells in a housing. In this study, following the compression process, the cells were transferred to an environmental test chamber using clamps, thereby maintaining the uniform compression effect. The use of a large number of cells causes difficulties during the module’s transportation process, resulting in the loss of contact between cells or a reduction in the compression effect. paragraph_context: The mini module with 4S1P configuration consists of lithium-ion pouch cells with a capacity of 73 Ah, adhesive film tapes, aluminium cassettes, compression foams, plastic spacers and busbars. The adhesive film tape ensures the contact of the cell with the aluminium cassette. The aluminium cassette is the component that provides heat transfer by conduction, with one surface in contact with the cold plate and the other surface in contact with the large surface of the cell. The busbar is the element that enables the cells to be connected in either a serial or parallel configuration. The plastic spacer fulfils two functions: firstly, it provides the mechanical connection of the cell with the busbar; secondly, it limits the movement of the cell on the vertical axis. However, lithium dendrite is an undesirable phenomenon in the cycling process of lithium-ion batteries, which can have a serious impact on battery safety and cycle life. The lithium dendrite problem is a pressing issue that hinders the development of lithium metal battery applications. In this work, a new binary electrolyte system, PILs-Es, was constructed using [BMP]TFSI ionic liquids intermixed with carbonate-based organic solvents. The optimal solvent ratios were selected by analyzing the ionic conductivity and viscosity studies. It is demonstrated that the PILs-E30-based half-cell exhibits excellent cycling stability and lower charge transfer impedance, which plays a positive role in the formation of a more homogeneous and dense solid electrolyte interfacial film (SEI film) on the surface of the anode. [BMP]TFSI is involved in the film-forming process, forming a more stable SEI film product, slowing down the decomposition of carbonate organic solvents, and inhibiting the occurrence of side reactions between the electrolyte and the electrode surface.PILs-E30 produces a more homogeneous deposition of lithium, which makes the generated SEI film more homogeneous and dense, and inhibits the generation of lithium dendrites, thus protecting the anode material. The LiFePO4| Graphite full cell based on PILs-E30 exhibits excellent electrochemical performance, with a discharge specific capacity of 117.5 mAh g-1, a high capacity retention of 95.0 %, and a Coulombic efficiency of close to 100 % after cycling for 200 cycles at 1 C multiplication rate. This proves the usefulness of PILs-E30 in full batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: At present, the world is facing serious environmental problems such as climate warming and the energy crisis. As people continue to consume traditional non-renewable energy sources such as oil and coal, the transition to new and sustainable energy sources is particularly urgent [1–4]. Lithium-ion battery is an advanced rechargeable battery, which has become a popular choice in energy storage market due to its outstanding advantages such as long cycle life, low environmental pollution and low self-discharge rate [5].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: However, lithium dendrites are currently prevalent in lithium-ion batteries. Lithium dendrite is an undesirable phenomenon in the cycling process of lithium-ion batteries. It can have a serious impact on battery safety and cycle life [6–9]. Lithium dendrites are columnar deposits formed due to uneven lithium deposition of lithium ions on the electrode surface [10–12]. As the battery cycles, the lithium dendrites will eventually puncture the diaphragm, causing direct contact between the positive and negative terminals. This can cause a short circuit within the battery, leading to explosion or combustion [13–18]. In addition, the presence of lithium dendrites will also affect the cycle life of the battery, thereby reducing the capacity and energy density of the battery [19–22]. In short, lithium dendrites are an urgent problem that hinders the development of lithium-ion battery applications.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Electrolyte is an important component of lithium-ion batteries, assuming the key role of migrating lithium ions between positive and negative electrodes. The composition of the electrolyte is closely related to the electrochemical and safety performance of the battery, such as energy density, cycle life, multiplier performance [23–26]. Electrolytes can be categorized into liquid electrolytes, solid electrolytes, and gel-like polymer electrolytes based on their physical form [27–29]. In order to improve battery performance and develop highly safe lithium-ion batteries, it is necessary to focus on the optimization and Ionic liquids (ILs) are a class of substances with unique properties, also known as "molten salts". They have a melting point of ${ < } 1 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and are composed of a wide variety of organic and organic/inorganic anions [12,30]. ILs are characterized by high ionic conductivity, low volatility, excellent thermal stability, non-pollution, and a wide electrochemical window [31–33]. These properties provide possibilities for their application in lithium-ion battery systems.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: The properties of ionic liquids are influenced by Coulombic in teractions between anions and cations, Van der Waals force interactions and hydrogen bonding interactions [12,34,35]. The different combina tions of anions and cations can meet different functional requirements. The passivation of the anode and improvement of the cycling performance of the battery can be effectively achieved by mixing ILs with suitable organic solvents. For instance, Basile et al. demonstrated that immersing Li metal electrodes in N-propyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium bis (fluorosulfonyl)imide effectively stabilized the Li surface, enabling a cell paired with an LiFePO₄ (LFP) cathode to achieve a cycle life of 1000 [36]. Separately, Wang et al. utilized 1-octyl-3-methylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate (Im1(8)PF6) as an additive. By facilitating the formation of an SEI rich in Li₃N on the Li metal anode, they regulated Li deposition and attained a stable Coulombic efficiency of 97.4 % in Li||Cu cells [37]. Li et al. employed a high-concentration fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC)-based electrolyte with LiFSI as an additive. This formulation passivated the highly reactive Li metal surface, suppressed dendritic growth, and achieved a high capacity retention of 89.1 % after 200 cycles at a 1C rate [38].

paragraph_context: This study introduces a binary electrolyte system, denoted PILs-ES, formulated by incorporating the ionic liquid [BMP][TFSI] into a conventional carbonate-based electrolyte. The derived optimal formulation (PILs-E30) markedly suppressed lithium dendrite growth. Furthermore, LiFePO₄||Graphite full cells employing PILs-E30 exhibited exceptional cycling stability, retaining 95.0 % of their initial capacity with a Coulombic efficiency approaching 100 % over 200 cycles.

paragraph_context: First, commercial electrolytes were prepared. In a glove box under a high-purity argon environment (all with water-oxygen content lower than 0.1 ppm), dimethyl carbonate (DMC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), and ethylene carbonate (EC) were mixed in the ratio of 1:1:1 by volume, and then appropriate amounts of lithium salt of lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF ) were added to obtain the initial commercial electrolyte (CE) with a concentration of 1 mol $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ . Next, the preparation of ionic liquids was started. Before proceeding with the preparation, the ionic liquid components were pretreated by drying: firstly, the solvent was dried at $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h using 3A specification molecular sieves, and then an appropriate amount of molecular sieves was added to the ionic liquid solvent in order to remove the residual water. Subsequently, 1- n‑butyl‑1-methylpyrrolidine Pyr14+ cation and bis(tri fluoromethylsulfonyl)imide TFSI-anion were selected and placed in a magnetic stirrer with homogeneous stirring for 24 h to synthesize 1- n‑butyl‑1-methylpyrrolidine bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ionic liquid ([BMP]TFSI). Finally, the binary electrolyte was configured. [BMP]TFSI was added to the initial commercial electrolyte CE at different mass fraction percentages, and after stirring, different mass fractions of ionic liquids|organic solvents co-mingled binary electrolytes PILs-Es were obtained.The composition of the electrolytes was formulated as shown in Table 1.

It was then placed in a blast drying oven for drying to obtain the working electrode. paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries are pivotal to electric vehicles and modern energy systems, playing a key role in global efforts to achieve net-zero CO2 emissions by enabling the storage of renewable energy. However, their safety remains a major concern due to the flammable nature of polymer-based electrolytes and separator membranes. This study leverages a large dataset of published experimental measurements of Total Heat Release (THR) from various polymer materials obtained through combustion calorimetry, aiming to assess the fire hazard potential of such materials. The performance of Support Vector Regression (SVR), Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and Hist Gradient Boosting Regression (HGBR) models was evaluated in estimating THR values. Key input features included density (g/mL), solubility (MPa1/2), molar cohesive energy (J/mol), entanglement molecular weight (g/ mol), and glass transition temperature (K), with THR (KJ/g) as the target variable. Three feature configurations (C1, C2, and C3) were assessed to investigate the influence of solubility and molar cohesive energy on THR prediction. Model performance was validated using multiple statistical metrics and visualized through a 2D Taylor diagram and a 3D bubble plot. The HGBR-C3 model (NSE = 0.9858, CC = 0.9932) demonstrated superior predictive accuracy, with C3 configurations consistently yielding low bias and high reliability, except in the GPR model, where C2 showed improved performance. The integration of artificial intelligence techniques with combustion calorimetry data provides a valuable approach for mitigating fire risks in lithium-ion batteries.

paragraph_context: Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of modern portable electronic devices, providing the energy required for smartphones, laptops, tablets, and many other technologies that are essential to daily life [1–8]. As we transition toward a more sustainable future, the role of Li-ion batteries is expanding beyond consumer electronics into large-scale applications, particularly in electric vehicles [9] and renewable energy storage systems [10]. One of the driving forces behind this transition is the global urgency to address climate change. The adverse effects of climate change, from extreme weather events to rising sea levels, are triggering governments, industries, and individuals to seek more sustainable energy solutions [11,12]. The need to preserve the environment has made the shift to electric vehicles crucial. These vehicles, powered by Li-ion batteries, offer a cleaner alternative to traditional fossil fuel-based transportation, contributing to reduced greenhouse gas emissions and lowering the overall carbon footprint [13]. Furthermore, significant efforts are being made to explore renewable energy sources for both domestic and industrial power generation. Solar and wind energy, among the most promising renewable options, require efficient energy storage solutions to balance supply and demand.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: While Li-ion batteries are indispensable in advancing sustainable energy solutions, their development still faces significant challenges [17,18]. Safety concerns, especially the risk of fire and overheating, are prominent issues [19]. The high energy density that makes Li-ion batteries so powerful can also cause thermal runaway, a chain reaction that leads to overheating, fire, and in severe cases, explosions [20]. Therefore, improving the safety profile of Li-ion batteries is critical to their widespread adoption, particularly in electric vehicles and renewable energy systems, where failure can result in catastrophic consequences.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Despite numerous advancements in developing fire-retardant polymer materials for lithium-ion batteries, several limitations persist [12]. Many existing polymer electrolytes and separators suffer from insufficient thermal and oxidative stability, especially under abusive thermal or mechanical conditions [8]. Conventional materials like polyethylene or polypropylene, while widely used, are prone to thermal shrinkage and ignition at higher temperatures, which can result in thermal runaway. Although the incorporation of flame-retardant additives or ceramic coatings can mitigate these risks, such approaches often face commercialization bottlenecks due to processing complexity, increased weight, reduced ionic conductivity, and limited mechanical flexibility [21]. Furthermore, many flame-retardant materials lack scalability, are cost-prohibitive, or do not meet long-term performance standards in practical battery systems [22].

paragraph_context: In light of these limitations, this study offers a novel contribution by applying hybrid machine learning modeling integrated with combustion calorimetry to evaluate and predict the fire hazards of polymer-based materials using thermophysical descriptors. This data-driven framework provides a predictive pathway for early screening and optimization of safer, high-performance materials, including polymer electrolytes, separators, binders, and other components within battery systems. While this approach is not a comprehensive solution to battery safety, it represents a targeted advancement in data-driven fire-risk prediction for polymer-based components, thereby reducing reliance on costly trial-and-error experimentation and accelerating the development of next-generation fire-safe batteries.

These accidents are typically linked to the flammable nature of the liquid electrolytes, polymer-based separators, and additives used in the battery manufacturing process. For example, mobile phones are known to overheat and ignite due to internal battery failures. Similarly, the growing popularity of EVs has raised concerns, as some vehicles have experienced fires during charging or after collisions [20]. In aircraft, the compact and powerful batteries used can become hazardous if not properly managed, and hoverboards have made headlines for battery explosions caused by poor-quality components or overcharging [44].

External factors, such as exposure to excessive heat, mechanical impact, or even punctures, can also lead to thermal runaway [46]. Furthermore, fires originating outside the battery pack can induce overheating in the cells, causing a chain reaction within the battery and leading to combustion [47].

However, during thermal runaway, this separator can degrade or catch fire, exacerbating the situation. Therefore, the separator’s performance directly influences both the efficiency and safety of the battery. Acting as an electrolyte reservoir, the separator facilitates ion migration, but if the material becomes unstable, the entire battery system can fail [41].

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: The total heat release of a polymer is defined as the heat of complete combustion of the pyrolysis gases per unit of its initial mass [51]. This property provides insight into the potential of the material to fuel a fire during a thermal runaway event. Pyrolysis combustion flow calorimetry, as adopted in this study, is a reliable and widely accepted method for determining the THR of various polymers. The experimental process for THR measurements followed the methodology reported by Walter and Lyon [54], which involves the thermal decomposition of polymer samples under controlled conditions. Small-sized polymer samples were subjected to a pyrolysis probe, which thermally decomposed the materials in flowing nitrogen gas. The temperature was carefully controlled, starting below the onset degradation temperature of the polymer and increasing at a rate of $4 . 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ per second, until it reached a maximum temperature of $9 3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ As the polymer samples decomposed, volatile decomposition products were swept from the pyrolysis chamber by the flowing nitrogen gas. After the initial pyrolysis, oxygen was introduced into the system for 60 s to create a nominal gas mixture of 4:1 $\mathrm { N } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ before entering a $9 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ furnace. The addition of oxygen facilitated the combustion of pyrolysis products, facilitating the measurement of total heat release.

paragraph_context: Vector Regression is a powerful machine learning model widely used for regression tasks across various fields, including technical, scientific, and humanities domains [59]. It is especially known for its ability to handle data categorization in two-dimensional spaces while also being effective in higher-dimensional spaces [60]. Unlike traditional regression models, SVR can operate in both linear and nonlinear modes by utilizing different kernel functions, making it highly versatile for a variety of predictive modeling tasks [61]. SVR can adopt several kernel types, including Gaussian (radial basis function), polynomial, and linear kernels. The choice of kernel significantly affects the model’s ability to capture the underlying patterns in the data [62]. For instance, a linear kernel is suitable for simpler relationships, while Gaussian and polynomial kernels allow SVR to model more complex, nonlinear relationships. One of SVR’s key strengths is its ability to perform well even with a limited number of data points, which makes it useful for small datasets where other models might struggle [63].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: SVR involves several important parameters that influence its performance, including epsilon (ε), regularization (C), gamma (γ), and the kernel type [64]. The epsilon parameter defines the margin of tolerance where no penalty is applied to the errors, allowing for a more flexible model. Regularization (C) controls the trade-off between achieving a low error on the training data and maintaining a smooth model, while gamma controls how far the influence of a single training example reaches. These parameters can be fine-tuned to optimize the model’s performance, typically through trial and error. One of the unique aspects of SVR is its ability to fit both lines and curves to data, making it an effective tool for regression in linear and nonlinear contexts [65]. SVR approximates the target function values using defined mathematical concepts to fit the curve to the data. This approach allows for precise predictions by finding the best regression function that maximizes the margin between the training data and the fitted line or curve.

paragraph_context: Regression is a powerful non-parametric probabilistic model used for regression tasks, which operates under the framework of probabilistic regression [65]. Unlike traditional parametric models that assume a fixed form for the relationship between inputs and outputs, GPR entails a more flexible modeling approach by defining prior probability distributions over latent functions directly [67]. It takes as input a training dataset comprising N pairs of vector inputs and noisy scalar outputs, ${ \tt y } _ { \tt n }$ and constructs a model that generalizes well to unseen input locations, making it ideal for forecasting and modeling in complex systems [68]. One of the key features of GPR is its ability to model the noise in the output, which captures uncertainties arising from external factors, such as observation errors or measurement inaccuracies. This probabilistic treatment of uncertainty is a distinguishing feature of GPR, allowing it to account for the inherent randomness in real-world data. The noise helps to explain variations in the output that are not directly linked to the input variables, adding a layer of robustness to the model [69].

label: 概述
paragraph_context: At its core, GPR defines a prior over the possible functions that could describe the relationship between input and output, which is characterized by two key components: the mean function and the covariance function [68]. The mean function encodes the central tendency of the function and is often assumed to be zero, simplifying the model. On the other hand, the covariance function, also known as the kernel function, encodes information about the shape, smoothness, and structure of the function. The choice of the covariance function is crucial as it defines how points in the input space influence one another, determining the model’s capacity to capture underlying patterns in the data.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: In GPR, some of the most important parameters include the length scale, which defines how far the influence of one data point extends to another, variance, which controls the variability in the function, and noise level, which models the uncertainty in the output. These hyperparameters can be fine-tuned using optimization techniques to improve the model’s performance. Over the past decades, both theoretical and practical advancements have made GPR a serious contender for supervised learning applications. Its ability to provide not only predictions but also uncertainty estimates makes it valuable in fields requiring high confidence in predictions, such as material science, energy storage, and engineering applications. The general expression of the GPR model that links the explanatory vector (x) and the response (y) can be given as: $$ y _ {i} = f \left(x _ {i}\right) + \varepsilon \tag {3} $$ The full mathematical framework for the GPR model has been reported elsewhere [69].

paragraph_context: Boosting Regression is an advanced machine learning technique derived from the gradient boosting family, which builds predictive models by iteratively improving the performance of weak learners, usually decision trees [70]. Gradient boosting is well-regarded for its effectiveness in handling various types of datasets and is one of the best methods for both classification and regression tasks in tabular data [71]. Its key strength lies in its ability to build models in a stage-wise fashion, where each stage focuses on minimizing the errors of the previous model by optimizing a loss function. The concept behind gradient boosting is to combine multiple weak learners (models that individually may not perform well) into a stronger, more accurate predictive model. When decision trees are used as weak learners, the resulting model is referred to as a gradient-boosted tree. This approach enables the model to progressively correct the errors made by the previous trees by focusing on the residual errors, thus improving overall predictive performance. The model is built by training trees one after the other, with each tree learning from the mistakes of its predecessors.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Boosting, a more recent enhancement of traditional gradient boosting methods, optimizes the training process by employing histogram-based techniques [70]. This allows the algorithm to group continuous features into discrete bins, which speeds up the computation significantly, especially for large datasets. The use of histograms reduces the complexity of finding the best-split points for decision trees, making the model more efficient while retaining accuracy. In addition to speed, this method often requires less memory than traditional gradient-boosting algorithms, further contributing to its popularity. One of the main reasons Hist Gradient Boosting tends to outperform models like random forests is its ability to focus on difficult-to-predict examples. Whereas random forests build trees independently and average their predictions, gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, each one aimed at reducing the residual error of the combined trees before it. This stage-wise approach makes gradient boosting a more powerful tool for learning complex patterns in data.

Finally, the glass transition temperature marks the temperature at which the polymer transitions from a hard, glassy state to a softer, rubbery state, affecting its thermal stability [58]. Notably, a strong negative correlation exists between THR and the material’s density. This is because higher-density polymer materials typically exhibit lower thermal diffusivity and reduced porosity, which can suppress flame propagation and limit the extent of combustion. This leads to a lower total heat release.

The uniformly high correlation coefficients, along with low standard deviations and RMSD values, confirm that all models achieved near-perfect fits under these conditions. While this convergence may visually mask the impact of individual features, it underscores the models’ strong capacity to learn patterns from the training dataset. Nonetheless, as emphasized earlier, the true discriminative power of the configurations becomes evident in the testing phase, where model generalization to unseen data is more rigorously evaluated.

paragraph_context: The ratio of training to testing data plays an important role in determining the performance and generalization of machine learning models [74]. In this study, we adopted a 70:30 train-test-split ratio, where 70 % of the data was used for training the models and 30 % for testing. This ratio is commonly used to ensure that a significant portion of the data is available for model training while maintaining enough data for reliable model validation during the testing phase. However, the performance of the developed models can be significantly influenced by the volume of training and testing data. Larger training datasets generally allow models to learn better patterns, while an adequate testing dataset is essential for robust performance evaluation. Therefore, to gain more insights into the effects of varying the train-test-split ratio on model performance, a three-dimensional bubble plot analysis was employed.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: A range of train-test-split ratios from 85:15 to 60:40 was employed. The impact of these ratios on model performance was evaluated by analyzing the Mean Absolute Error and Correlation Coefficient for each model configuration across the different ratios. The corresponding results are presented in Fig. 8, which illustrates how the models performed under varying train-test-split ratios. The performance of the SVR models across the three feature configurations is shown in Fig. 8a, b, and c. It can be observed that the SVR models achieved optimal performance when the test data was split between 25 % and 30 %, as indicated by lower MAE values and higher CC values. This range seems to provide the best balance between having enough data to train the models and a sufficient portion to test their generalization capability. When the test data percentage exceeded 30 %, the model’s performance slightly declined, suggesting that reducing the training data too much can impair the model’s ability to capture complex patterns. On the other hand, using too little testing data can lead to overfitting, where the model performs well on training data but fails to generalize to unseen data. In the case of the GPR models (Fig. 8d, e, f), the results reveal a different trend. For the C2 and C3 configurations, the GPR model performance was at its peak around a 15 %–20 % test data split. At these ratios, the models achieved the lowest MAE and the highest CC values, reflecting their ability to generalize well with a larger portion of data available for training. The performance trend for the HGBR models (Fig. 8g, h, i) closely mirrors that of the GPR models, especially for configurations C2 and C3. The HGBR model, being a tree-based ensemble model, typically benefits from having a larger training dataset, which allows the trees to learn more complex relationships between the input features and the Total Heat Release of the polymer compounds. paragraph_context: To enhance the transparency of the HGBR-C3 model and strengthen the physical interpretability of its predictions, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to quantify the contribution of each input descriptor to the predicted Total Heat Release [73]. The mean absolute SHAP values (Fig. 10) identify density as the most influential variable, followed by glass transition temperature, molar cohesive energy, solubility parameter, and entanglement molecular weight. The SHAP summary plot indicates that higher density values are strongly associated with lower predicted THR, aligning with the expectation that denser polymer structures exhibit reduced fire load. Likewise, higher GTT values tend to decrease THR, consistent with the inverse correlation observed in the heatmap analysis. It is important to note that the negative SHAP sign reflects the direction of association rather than the absence of influence, indicating that increases in GTT are generally linked to reductions in THR. MCE shows a mixed contribution pattern, suggesting a more complex influence on combustion behavior, while solubility and entangle molecular weight exert smaller but measurable effects. Overall, the SHAP results corroborate the earlier correlation analysis and confirm that the model captures physically meaningful relationships between thermophysical polymer descriptors and THR, thereby providing an interpretable and scientifically grounded basis for guiding electrolyte and separator material selection.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: While the machine learning models developed in this study have demonstrated considerable potential in estimating the Total Heat Release of polymer-based compounds used in Li-ion batteries, a few limitations also exist. These shortcomings present opportunities for future research to improve the models’ accuracy and robustness. First, despite the inclusion of a broad range of polymer materials during the training phase, the generalization of the models could still be limited. The models were trained on specific polymer compounds, and while they performed well on this subset, the diversity of polymer materials in the real world is vast. Polymers not included in the training data, especially those with distinct chemical structures or properties, may suffer low prediction accuracy. This generalization weakness highlights the need for expanding the dataset to cover a wider variety of polymer types, which would make the models more applicable to a broader range of materials.

label: 机理/模拟
paragraph_context: Another limitation relates to the in-situ conditions under which the materials are expected to perform. While the models were developed using data from controlled environments, actual Li-ion battery systems operate under varying conditions, such as changes in temperature and operating voltage. These factors can significantly influence the combustion dynamics and thermal behavior of polymer materials, leading to discrepancies between predicted and actual THR values. Incorporating additional features that capture the effects of these dynamic conditions could improve model accuracy in real-world applications.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Finally, regarding separators and thermal runaway, the separator mainly affects when thermal runaway starts, rather than how much heat is released after it begins. Melting of polyolefin separators is endothermic and does not materially reduce post-onset heat release, which is driven by exothermic reactions between electrodes and electrolyte and by oxygen release from the cathode. Ceramic coatings can improve dimensional stability and delay onset, but they do not control post-onset heat-release rate. Accordingly, THR-based polymer screening in this work is most informative for fire-growth propensity and pre-onset mitigation, not for the chemistry that sustains thermal runaway once initiated. The present study demonstrates the feasibility of predicting THR from fundamental polymer descriptors; however, the framework is general and can be adapted to other fire hazard indicators such as peak heat release rate, fire performance index, and fire growth index, which would further enhance its applicability in battery safety design once suitable datasets are assembled.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: This study presents a robust approach for optimizing polymer-based electrolytes and separator membranes in lithium-ion batteries using advanced machine-learning techniques. The research addresses a critical issue of fire risks in modern energy storage systems, posed by flammable battery components, particularly polymer-based materials. Through large-scale combustion calorimetry experimental analysis of the Total Heat Released from various polymer compounds, this study investigated how these materials contribute to fire hazards based on their thermophysical properties, providing new insights into fire safety for Li-ion batteries. The findings revealed that the HGBR ensemble model outperformed both SVR and GPR in predicting THR, particularly in the C3 configuration, where all input features were included. The HGBR-C3 model achieved the highest prediction accuracy (NSE = 0.9858, CC = 0.9932), demonstrating its ability to capture the complex non-linear relationships between input features and THR. The C3 configuration consistently provided the best performance across most models, highlighting the importance of using a comprehensive set of descriptors in predicting material behavior. The following are some notable key points from this study. • Machine Learning as a Tool for Fire Safety: The integration of machine learning with experimental techniques like combustion calorimetry marks a significant advancement in addressing fire safety risks in lithium-ion batteries. These findings demonstrate the potential of AI-driven approaches to optimize material selection and improve the safety of high-energy-density batteries.  • Enhanced Model Performance: The HGBR model demonstrated the best overall performance, especially in the C3 configuration, making it the most effective tool for estimating THR. SVR also showed strong performance, while GPR exhibited limitations, particularly when molar cohesive energy was used as an input feature.  • Feature sensitivity: Solubility emerged as a significant predictor of THR, especially in the GPR model, where the C2 configuration consistently outperformed the others. This indicates the need for careful selection of input features when using different machine learning models to predict material behavior.  • Comprehensive Descriptors Improve Accuracy: The inclusion of a broad set of descriptors, as seen in the C3 configuration, improved prediction accuracy across all models, underscoring the importance of leveraging diverse material properties for more reliable THR predictions.

Further studies should focus on expanding the dataset to include more polymer materials, which would improve the generalization of the models. More advanced deep learning methods should also be employed to gain further insights from the models. Additionally, incorporating in situ conditions such as temperature fluctuations and voltage variations into the models could further enhance their predictive accuracy and applicability in real-world scenarios.

paragraph_context: Pairing high-loading Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes with Li-metal anodes offers a promising strategy toward high-energy Li-metal batteries. However, structural instability and surface reactivity of both electrodes induce parasitic reactions with the electrolyte solution, particularly under high charging rate conditions, leading to rapid capacity degradation. Herein, a dual-additive-incorporated carbonate-based electrolyte solution is developed for the stable cycling of Li-metal batteries, featuring a high-loading Li[Ni0.9Co0.05Mn0.05]O2 cathode under lean electrolyte and high charging rate conditions. The individual and combined effects of lithium difluorophosphate (LiDFP) and lithium nitrate (LiNO3) are systematically investigated to elucidate their influence on the cycling behavior of Li-metal batteries. The synergistic effect of LiDFP and LiNO3 modulates the electrolyte–electrode interphase (EEI) layer to be robust and conductive, suppressing dendritic Li growth and structural degradation of the cathode. This study also highlights the importance of suppressing the crossover effect for Nirich cathode-based Li-metal batteries. The Li||Li[Ni0.9Co0.05Mn0.05]O2 Li-metal full cell with a areal capacity of 4.6 mAh cm–2 and lean electrolyte condition delivers a high discharge capacity of 230.0 mAh ${ \boldsymbol { \mathsf { g } } } ^ { - 1 }$ at 0.1 $\mathrm { C } ,$ maintains stable cycling over 200 cycles with a cycle retention of 85.4 %, and exhibits an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.87 % at high rate conditions.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: One of the biggest challenges facing humanity is rapid climate change. To combat this, the Net-Zero policy aims to reduce carbon emissions to achieve a balance in which the amount of carbon released into the atmosphere equals the amount removed. Current global efforts are focused on achieving this goal by 2050 [1], and these efforts include the use of alternative energy sources to replace fossil fuels, which are the primary source of carbon emissions during energy production, secondary batteries have gained worldwide attention.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Consequently, the growing demand for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems (ESSs) has expanded the market for batteries, increasing the requirement for next-generation batteries with higher energy density than that of lithium-ion batteries [2]. In this context, Li-metal batteries (LMBs), which represent next-generation secondary batteries with high energy density, are actively being developed as promising advanced energy storage technology to enter the future secondary battery market. The Li-metal anodes (LMAs) employed in these batteries are known to exhibit lowest potential (− 3.04 V vs. SHE, standard hydrogen electrode), low density (0.534 g cm–3 ), and exceptionally high theoretical capacity (3860 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } ) _ { : }$ , enabling them to achieve significantly higher energy density than graphite anodes (372 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ . Moreover, as a strategy to increase the energy density of LMBs, the employment of a high capacity Ni-rich layered $\operatorname { L i } [ \operatorname { N i } _ { \mathbf { X } } .$ - $\mathrm { C o _ { y } M n _ { 1 \cdot x - y } ] O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM) cathode is unavoidable. Despite previous efforts to realize high-energy-density LMBs, several intrinsic challenges remain. For example, due to their strong reducing power, LMAs accelerate continuous side reactions with the electrolyte solution, while the formation of Li dendrites increases the reactive surface area, further exacerbating electrolyte solution consumption. Additionally, Ni-rich layered cathodes form a thick interfacial resistance layer owing to side reactions between the highly reactive $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 4 + }$ and the electrolyte solution. Furthermore, the anisotropic lattice volume change during charging induces microcrack formation and transition metal (TM) dissolution, which collectively accelerate the structural degradation of the cathode [3,4]. Consequently, the combination of LMAs and paired with Ni-rich cathodes results in poor Coulombic efficiency (CE), a shortened cycle life, and insufficient safety margins. In the context of liquid electrolytes for LMBs, these are largely classified as ether- or carbonate-based electrolyte solutions. Ether-based electrolyte solutions exhibit high reduction stability and are known to form conductive inorganic-rich solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers (e.g., Li O-rich), which are chemically less reactive when in contact with LMAs, thereby enhancing the reversibility of Li plating/stripping. However, the low upper potential limit (<4 V vs. Li/Li+) due to low oxidation stability of these electrolyte solutions is not suitable for use in high-energy-density LMBs that require high-voltage cathodes (>4 V vs. $\mathrm { L i / L i ^ { + } } )$ . In contrast, carbonate-based electrolyte solutions exhibit high oxidation stability, thereby rendering them highly compatible with high-voltage cathodes. However, owing to their low reduction stability, they inevitably tend to form organic-rich SEI layers on the surface of LMAs, ultimately increasing the interfacial resistance. Moreover, in liquid electrolyte based LMB systems, the use of high capacity cathodes or fast charging rates induces dendritic Li growth, which shortens the lifespans of the LMBs and can eventually lead to short circuiting and serious safety concerns [5]. The dendritic Li growth and the formation of inactive dead Li, which impose critical limitations on LMBs, originate from the uneven Li deposition caused by the formation of an unstable and thick SEI layer. In addition, the unstable and resistive cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) layer, which is formed through the reactions of highly reactive $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 4 + }$ , induces uneven $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ intercalation/deintercalation, thereby accelerating degradation across the entire cathode. To address these challenges, the sophisticated engineering of stable SEI and CEI layers that enhance the interfacial stability between the electrode and the electrolyte is crucial. Recently, various strategies have been reported based on the incorporation of different additives, with examples including the design of LiF- and $_ { \mathrm { L i _ { 2 } O - r i c h } }$ SEI layers, multi-layered SEI structures, and thin conductive CEI layer [6–11]. However, it remains challenging to simultaneously stabilize both the SEI and the CEI layers using a single additive. Therefore, a rational combination of multiple additives with distinct functionalities is required to overcome these limitations. Identifying synergistic effects between complementary additives and quantitatively evaluating their interfacial stabilization roles remains an important research challenge.

This, in turn, prevents the crossover of Ni-ions to the anode and mitigates further electrolyte solution decomposition caused by Ni-ions reduction on the LMA. It was therefore apparent that the $\mathrm { L i D F P / L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution provided enhanced cathode protection by suppressing TM dissolution from the cathode, and exhibited a synergistic effect by preventing further LMA deterioration caused by Ni crossover. paragraph_context: To directly observe the impact of electrolyte-dependent CEI layer composition on the structural degradation of the cathode, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was conducted. For this purpose, the cathodes were recovered from the Li||NCM90 Li-metal full cells using the $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ and $\mathrm { L i D F P / L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solutions after 150 and 200 cycles, respectively. Cross-sectional TEM samples of their secondary particles were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB). Fig. 5b shows a bright-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) image of the NCM90 cathode cycled with the $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ electrolyte solution. The generated microcracks allow the electrolyte solution to penetrate the interior of the particles, exposing fresh surfaces and promoting further side reactions. As a result, undesired CEI layers are formed, which increase the interfacial resistance and accelerate consumption of the electrolyte solution. First, high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) analysis of the primary particles of the NCM90 cathode cycled with the $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution (Fig. 5c) revealed a ≈19 nm-thick NiO-like rock-salt impurity layer along the edge of the primary particle $( \mathrm { F i g } . \ 5 \mathrm { d } ) .$ . This impurity layer is electrically insulating, which hinders uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport into the active material and increases the $\operatorname { R } _ { \operatorname { c t } }$ (Fig. S16). As also reported in previous studies, $a \ \approx \ 4$ nm-thick impurity layer was additionally observed along the lateral side of the primary particle, even though the (001) facets, which are aligned parallel to the Li and TM layers, typically exhibit a greater structural stability than other crystal facets [35–37]. These results demonstrate the high surface reactivity of the Ni-rich cathode with a 90 % Ni content and confirm that cycling under 4.3 V at a 1 C charging rate imposes a highly oxidizing condition. Additionally, the [001] zone-axis diffraction pattern of Region II revealed diffraction spots corresponding to a mixture of rock-salt and layered structures (Fig. 5e), indicating that structural degradation propagated from the surface toward the interior of the particle. As shown in Fig. 3, although the CEI layer formed with the $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution contains decomposition products such as $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } N }$ and $\mathrm { L i N _ { x } O _ { y } , }$ these species appear to be ineffective in protecting the cathode surface, as suggested by the observed structural collapse. Because the NCM90 cathode after 150 cycles with the $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution was developed a thick and resistive CEI layer along with a pronounced rock-salt impurity layer, nonuniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ intercalation/deintercalation was likely to occur. The core of the secondary particle also exhibited structural degradation comparable to that of the surface (Fig. S24a–c). The HR-TEM image and the corresponding Fourier-transformed selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern in Fig. S24c reveal the presence of a ≈ 18 nm-thick rock-salt impurity layer on the particle surface. In contrast, the HR-TEM and related Fourier-transformed SAED patterns of the NCM90 cathode after 200 cycles with the $\mathrm { L i D F P / L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution revealed remarkably different structural features. Thin intergranular cracks were observed in the particles; however, additional side reactions with the electrolyte solution caused by its penetration into the secondary particles were significantly reduced, as evidenced by the slight structural degradation of the particle core (Figs. 5g and S24f). An ≈8 nm-thick NiO-like rock-salt layer was detected in some grains, which was attributed to the formation of a stable LiDFP-derived CEI layer (Fig. 5i). These HR-TEM findings are consistent with the electrochemical results and other analytical observations and confirm that the presence of ≈1 wt% LiDFP in the total electrolyte solution plays a critical role in modulating the surface chemistry of the NCM90 cathode, enabling uniform $\bar { \mathrm { L i ^ { + } } }$ transport and enhancing the structural stability.

paragraph_context: As illustrated in Fig. 6a, the electrochemical performance of the present systems is compared with those of previously reported Ni-rich NCM cathodes (Ni >80 %) and carbonate-based electrolyte solutions containing LiNO3 [14,38–45]. The results presented in the figure highlight the superior performance of the $\mathrm { L i D F P / L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution. In addition, Figs. 6b and S25 provide schematic illustrations of the performance enhancement mechanism achieved by introducing synergistic dual additives into LMBs are based on Ni-rich cathodes. Although FEC-based baseline electrolyte solutions form mechanically robust LiF-rich EEI layers, rechargeable LMBs employing high-loading Ni-rich cathodes exhibit severe capacity fading. This degradation is primarily driven by electrolyte decomposition at the highly reactive surfaces of both the Ni-rich cathode and LMA, leading to the formation of unstable interfacial layers and promoting structural deterioration of the cathode. Furthermore, the substantial volume expansion of the LMA under high charging rates $( \geq 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { C } )$ leads to an increased interfacial resistance. The organic-rich interfacial films formed on both the cathode and LMA, which are composed of species such as ROLi and ${ \mathrm { R O C O } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { L i } } ,$ , increased the interfacial resistance and provided insufficient surface protection, thereby promoting further electrolyte decomposition. The baseline electrolyte solution forms a thick and nonuniform interfacial layer at the interface, which impedes $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport and leads to an uneven $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ distribution. This resulted in localized intercalation/deintercalation into the cathode and localized plating/stripping on the LMA, which are accompanied by spatially heterogeneous volume changes across the cathode and dendritic Li growth on the LMA during cycling. In contrast, the $\mathrm { L i D F P / L i N O _ { 3 } }$ electrolyte solution forms a uniform and highly ionically conductive interfacial layer, which facilitates homogenous $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport and improves the uniformity of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ distribution. As a result, it suppresses microcrack formation at the cathode and dendritic Li growth on the LMA, effectively mitigating volume expansion of the LMA (Figs. S2 and S22). These results indicate that LiDFP preferentially decomposes at the cathode interface to form $\mathrm { L i _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } } ,$ , which effectively protects the cathode surface. In the presence of LiDFP, $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ further decomposes to generate Li3N on the cathode, contributing to the formation of a robust and ionically conductive CEI layer (Fig. 3). At the LMA, Li3N derived from $\mathrm { L i N O } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { \bf p { - } } 0$ species originated from LiDFP collectively form an ion-conductive SEI layer. This suitable interfacial chemistry is highly dependent on electrolyte engineering and contributes significantly to an improved electrochemical performance (Fig. 1), thereby highlighting the importance of both the cathode and anode interfacial design for the development of LMBs operated at high charging rates.

paragraph_context: In LMBs employing high-loading cathodes, the interfacial chemistry of both the cathode and anode plays a critical role in stabilizing the EEI layer. In this study, the incorporation of LiDFP and $\mathrm { L i N O _ { 3 } }$ as dual additives leads to the formation of a stable SEI layer composed of $\mathrm { L i F } , \mathrm { P \mathrm { - } \mathrm { O } }$ species, and Li N on the Li-metal surface, as well as a LiDFP-derived CEI layer on the cathode. The mechanically robust and ion-conductive SEI layer suppresses parasitic reactions on the Li metal surface and promoted dense Li plating, thereby rendering it compatible with a highloading cathode. In parallel, the ion-conductive LiDFP-derived CEI layer reduces interfacial resistance and facilitates uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport, leading to homogeneous $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ distribution. This, in turn, alleviates the local stress on the cathode and enhances its structural integrity. These synergistic effects result in an enhanced cycling stability for the highloading Li||NCM90 Li-metal full cells. Overall, this work underscores the importance of engineering the interfacial chemistry of both electrodes and design of electrolyte solutions for practical realization of high energy density, fast charging LMBs.

Enhanced Li+ transport was achieved through dipole-ion interactions between [VEIm]+ cations and carbonyl groups of PET4A and complemented by dynamic coupling between PET4A and anions. The optimized UiO/PPV-Li exhibited an ionic conductivity of 9.12 mS⋅cm–1 at ambient temperature. The electrochemical stability window was extended to 5.31 V (vs. Li⁺/Li) through coordination of PF– with Zr–O clusters in the UiO-66 structure. The desolvation energy barrier of solvated Li+ was effectively reduced by UiO-66 and optimized hopping sites for Li⁺ transport provided by polymer chains were identified through theoretical calculation. Li ‖ UiO/PPV-Li ‖ LiNi0.8- Co0.1Mn0.1O2 exhibited discharge specific capacity of 154 mAh⋅g− 1 at 1 C (75.7 % retention), enhanced cycle stability at 4.8 V and superior high-rate discharge capacities compared to liquid electrolytes. Significant safety improvements were exhibited through flame retardancy and structural integrity of UiO/PPV-Li. The graphite ‖ UiO/PPV-Li ‖ LiCoO2 pouch batteries exhibited high safety under calendering and nail penetration. The UiO/ PPV-Li in-situ synthesized through γ-ray radiation-induced polymerization and crosslinking is a novel strategy for the development of next-generation lithium metal batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: The demand for high energy density lithium batteries has surged with advancements in smart electronics and electric vehicles [1,2]. Lithium metal anodes (3860 mAh⋅g⁻1 ) present a superior alternative to conventional graphite anodes [3]. However, the practical implementation has been fundamentally limited by safety concerns associated with lithium dendrite growth and electrolyte leakage [4–6]. The challenges are effectively mitigated through the utilization of gel electrolytes, which are characterized by stabilized interfaces and restricted free liquid components [7,8]. Compared with conventional liquid electrolytes, gel electrolytes have been demonstrated to exhibit superior thermal stability, broader electrochemical stability windows, and enhanced safety characteristics [9]. Nevertheless, the intrinsic limitation of low ionic conductivity in gel electrolytes has remained a critical barrier to the widespread application [10]. The limitation has been addressed through the strategic incorporation of ionic liquids (ILs) into the material, where the ionic conductivity and safety of the electrolytes are synergistically enhanced through the superior ionic transport capability, non-volatile and non-flammable nature of ILs [11–14].

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Metal organic frameworks (MOFs) with high porosity and structurally tunable architectures have been demonstrated to effectively suppress lithium dendrite growth through nanoconfinement effects and regulated $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ deposition [15,16]. Moreover, the channels of MOFs have been shown to enhance ionic conductivity through geometrically constrained ion transport pathway. The Lewis acidic sites within MOFs enable anion immobilization through coordination interactions, which increases the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transference number [17,18]. Consequently, MOFs-based gel electrolytes have demonstrated the ability to inhibit dendrite growth and improve batteries performance [19–21].

paragraph_context: Conventional methodologies for fabricating gel electrolytes are associated with inherent limitations. Ultraviolet curing is constrained by photoinitiator dependency and inhomogeneous crosslinking [22,23], solution casting is plagued by solvent evaporation induced cavities and weak electrode-electrolyte interfacial adhesion [24], and electrospinning is demonstrated to exhibit suboptimal production throughput and structural heterogeneity [25]. In contrast, radiation-induced synthesis has emerged as a superior alternative, where initiator-free polymerization is achieved through control of dose rate and duration at ambient temperature. The technology enables in-situ gelation within pre-assembled batteries [26].

paragraph_context: Herein, UiO-66 were initially synthesized via a conventional solvothermal method utilizing $\mathrm { Z r ^ { 4 + } }$ and terephthalic acid as precursors [27]. paragraph_context: Theoretical calculations were conducted by Shenzhen Huasuan Technology Co., Ltd. The methodology was referred to the work of Sheng et al. [22] The desolvation energy $\mathrm { ( } E _ { \mathrm { d e s o l } } \mathrm { ) }$ of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } } .$ –solvates was calculated using density functional theory (DFT). The crystalline structure of UiO-66 was modeled based on single crystal X-ray diffraction data retrieved from the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD: 733458) [28]. Structural optimizations for UiO-66 and guest-incorporated systems (Li(EC)+@UiO-66, Li(EC)+@UiO-66, EC@UiO-66) were performed using the CASTEP module in Materials Studio. Grimme dispersion corrections were applied to account for van der Waals (vdW) interactions, with a plane-wave cutoff energy of 830 eV and a Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid of $1 \times 1 \times 1 .$ . An implicit solvent model with a dielectric constant (ε) of 20.7 was implemented via the DFT-COSMO method (DMol3 module) to simulate the electrolyte environment. The double numerical polarization (DNP) basis set and GGA-PBE functional were consistently employed, with DFT-D3 corrections applied to accurately describe interfacial weak interactions. The desolvation energy $\left( E _ { \mathrm { d e s o l } } \right)$ of Li+–solvates was calculated by formula 5: $$ E _ {d e s o l} = E _ {\left[ L i (E C) _ {3} ^ {+} @ U i O - 6 6 \right]} + E _ {[ E C @ U i O - 6 6 ]} - E _ {\left[ L i (E C) _ {4} ^ {+} @ U i O - 6 6 \right]} - E _ {U i O - 6 6 ]} \tag {5} $$ Among them, $E _ { [ L i ( E C ) _ { 3 } ^ { + } \ @ U i O - 6 6 ] }$ is the energy of Li(EC)3+ in UiO-66, E is the energy of single EC molecular in UiO-66, $E _ { [ L i ( E C ) _ { 4 } ^ { + } \ @ U i O - 6 6 ] }$ is the energy of Li(EC)4+ in UiO-66, $E _ { U i O - 6 6 }$ is the energy of UiO-66.

paragraph_context: Increasing the cut-off voltage of the LiCoO2 (LCO) cathode holds great promise for achieving high-energy-density lithium metal batteries. However, at cut-off voltages above 4.5 V, issues such as interfacial instability and transition metal dissolution severely hinder practical application. Here, we report a quasi-solid-state electrolyte (PCA) constructed from 2-cyanoethyl acrylate (CA) units, which promotes the formation of a high-quality cathode electrolyte interface (CEI) by regulating the composition and structure of the electric double layer (EDL). CA preferentially adsorbs onto LCO surfaces and coordinates with Co ions, stabilizing the cathode structure, while its strong ion–dipole interactions with DFOB– anions promote co-accumulation within the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP), excluding solvent molecules to construct a stable and dense organic–inorganic hybrid CEI. Benefiting from this, the Li|PCA|LCO battery retains 84 % of its capacity after 600 stable cycles at a high cutoff voltage of 4.6 V and also exhibits excellent performance in full cells with high-loading cathodes and pouch cells. Furthermore, by increasing the cut-off voltage, the assembled pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 433.6 Wh kg–1 . This work highlights the critical role of polymers in regulating the EDL/IHP structure and offers a new approach for the development of high-voltage quasi-solid-state lithium metal batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: To address these issues, extensive efforts have been devoted to cathode modification strategies (such as elemental doping and surface coating)[6,8–11] and electrolyte design (including high-concentration electrolytes and functional additives)[12–16]. However, cathode modification often introduces electrochemically inactive components, which reduces the specific capacity and increases production costs [17, 18], while high-concentration electrolytes suffer from poor cost-effectiveness[19]. Although functional additives have shown some progress in stabilizing high-voltage LCO systems[20,21], interfacial degradation remains a major challenge limiting long-term cycling stability. Converting liquid electrolytes into quasi-solid-state polymer electrolytes not only preserves favorable interfacial contact but also eliminates leakage risks, thereby significantly enhancing the safety of lithium metal batteries [22–26]. Previous studies have shown that compounds bearing strongly electron-withdrawing cyano groups not only enhance oxidative stability, but also coordinate with Co ions in delithiated LCO through –C–––N groups, effectively suppressing Co dissolution and optimizing the composition of the CEI [27–29]. However, the regulatory role of such coordination interactions in tuning the interfacial solvation structure and CEI formation mechanism remains poorly understood. Notably, the formation of the CEI primarily depends on the decomposition behavior of anions and neutral molecules adsorbed within the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP) of the electric double layer (EDL) at the cathode surface [30–32]. Polymers possessing polarizable dipoles can preferentially adsorb onto the LCO surface via strong interactions, facilitating the redistribution of interfacial species and playing a crucial role in interfacial chemistry. Therefore, elucidating the intrinsic relationship between the EDL and interfacial stability, and precisely modulating LCO interfacial chemistry via EDL engineering, are crucial for achieving stable operation at high voltages.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: In this work, the cathode-side EDL was regulated using a polymer matrix of 2-cyanoethyl acrylate (CA) containing strongly polar cyano groups. Quasi-solid-state polymer electrolyte (PCA) was successfully fabricated via in situ polymerization. The cyano groups in CA not only impart excellent oxidative stability to the electrolyte but also preferentially adsorb on the LCO cathode surface and coordinate with Co ions, effectively suppressing their dissolution. Meanwhile, strong ion–dipole interactions between CA and $\mathrm { D F O B ^ { - } }$ anions drive the co-enrichment of anions within the IHP, while repelling solvent molecules. This leads to the formation of a dense CEI protective layer synergistically induced by the polymer and anions, effectively suppressing parasitic reactions and structural degradation at the CEI. Benefiting from these advantages, Li|| LCO batteries based on PCA electrolyte retained 84 % of their capacity after 600 cycles at a high cut-off voltage of 4.6 V, exhibiting excellent performance in both high areal capacity (>3 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ full cells and pouch cells. Further increasing the cut-off voltage to 4.6 V enabled the pouch cells to achieve a high energy density of 433.6 Wh $\mathbf { k } { \mathbf { g } } ^ { - 1 }$ . The safety of the pouch cell based on the PCA quasi-solid-state electrolyte was further validated through accelerating rate calorimeter (ARC) and nail penetration tests. This study not only elucidates the key role of polymers in regulating the IHP but also provides new design strategies for achieving interfacial stability in high-voltage quasi-solid-state lithium metal batteries through electric double layer engineering.

paragraph_context: The highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) of the lithium salt, solvents, and polymer matrix were calculated using density functional theory (DFT), as these energy levels are closely associated with the oxidation and reduction potentials [33]. As shown in Fig. S1, CA containing strong electron-withdrawing cyano groups exhibits excellent oxidative stability due to its low HOMO energy level. However, its poor compatibility with lithium metal leads to the formation of an unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), resulting in severe lithium corrosion [34]. To address this, lithium difluoro(oxalato)borate (LiDFOB), which possesses a lower LUMO energy level, was introduced as the lithium salt to undergo preferential reduction and form a boron-rich SEI protective layer. Dimethyl sulfite (DMS), a solvent with a high dielectric constant and low viscosity, was employed to enhance the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte and facilitate lithium-ion transport [35,36]. Fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) was used as a co-solvent; its high LUMO and low HOMO energy levels act synergistically with CA to enhance the overall redox stability of the electrolyte. To investigate the role of CA in the electrolyte and its influence on the EDL structure at the cathode side, a reference liquid electrolyte (denoted as "LE") was prepared by dissolving 1 M LiDFOB in a DMS/FEC mixture (volume ratio 1:1). The optimal amount of CA was added to LE for in situ polymerization to prepare the quasi-solid-state electrolyte (denoted as “PCA”) as the experimental sample. Photographs and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra before and after PCA polymerization are shown in Fig. S2. Details of CA optimization are provided in Fig. S3–S6 and elaborated in Fig. S6.

paragraph_context: The electrostatic potentials (ESP) of DMS, FEC, LiDFOB, CA, and polymerized CA (Poly-CA) were calculated via DFT (Fig. 1a, S7, and Table S1). CA and LiDFOB exhibited comparable negative ESP values (-0.06), while Poly-CA showed the most negative ESP (-0.07), indicating a stronger tendency for interaction between the polymerized CA and the LCO surface. Furthermore, first-principles calculations were performed to evaluate the adsorption energies of DMS, FEC, DFOB– anions, and CA on the LCO surface (Fig. 1b). CA exhibited the lowest adsorption energy (-5.87 eV), indicating its preferential adsorption. This strong interaction arises from coordination between the nitrogen atom in the cyano group of CA and cobalt atoms on the LCO surface, thereby anchoring CA to the cathode. Notably, compared to DMS and FEC, CA exhibits the strongest ion-dipole interaction with DFOB– anions (-0.38 eV) (Fig. 1c and S8), promoting their co-enrichment at the cathode interface and incorporation into the IHP. This facilitates solvent molecule exclusion and leads to the formation of a stable and uniform CEI (Fig. 1h). In contrast, the CEI derived from solvents and DFOB– anions in the LE system is loose and prone to corrosion (Fig. 1g). Based on the above results, we propose that CA regulates the IHP structure and induces the formation of a stable CEI through a dual mechanism involving coordination and ion-dipole interactions.

paragraph_context: In summary, this work precisely regulates the EDL and IHP using a cyano-containing quasi-solid-state electrolyte, successfully constructing a robust CEI that enables long cycle life in high-voltage solid-state lithium metal batteries and high-energy-density pouch cells. The CA polymer monomer preferentially adsorbs on the $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ surface and coordinates with high-valent cobalt ions, stabilizing the cathode lattice and suppressing transition metal dissolution. Meanwhile, strong ion-–dipole interactions between CA and DFOB– anions drive their enrichment in the IHP, displacing solvent molecules and promoting the formation of a mechanically robust and electrochemically stable organic–inorganic composite CEI. The high safety of the PCA quasi-solid-state electrolyte was further verified through ARC and nail penetration tests. The excellent performance of this strategy with NCM811 cathodes further confirms its broad applicability and scalability. This work not only proposes an effective approach for constructing stable interfaces but also offers new insights for quasi-solidstate electrolyte interface design, significantly advancing the development of high-energy-density lithium metal batteries.
