Herein, inspired by the intermolecular hydrogen bonding network in low-viscosity $\mathrm { ^ { * } H _ { 2 } O ^ { * } }$ , we construct a novel DEE through the synergistic coordination of succinonitrile (SN), dimethylsulfone (MSM), and lithium difluoro (oxalate)borate (LiDFOB). The extensive hydrogen bond network between the $S = O$ groups of MSM and α-hydrogens of SN simultaneously improves the Li metal compatibility and salt dissociation, resulting in a low viscosity (18.73 mPa s) and high ionic conductivity (3.14 mS cm− 1 ) comparable to commercial carbonate electrolytes. Crucially, anion-dominated solvation structures induced by the salt concentration promote the formation of a B/F/S-enriched solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) with an organic-rich outer layer and inorganicdense inner layer. This gradient SEI alleviates mechanical stresses, homogenizes Li+ flux, and suppresses dendrite growth. Consequently, the LiCoO2||Li cell retains 87.4% capacity after 1000 cycles at 5C (3.0–4.5 V), and the LiCoO2||graphite pouch cell maintains 90.3% after 2500 cycles, validating its practical viability. The intrinsic safety of the electrolyte and its compatibility with high-voltage cathodes underscore the significant possibilities for next-generation, high-energy-density LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Driven by the accelerating global energy transition and pursuit of carbon neutrality, high-energy-density storage technologies have emerged as pivotal enablers for electric vehicles, smart grids, and portable electronics. Lithium metal anode is crucial for high-energydensity batteries, offering exceptional theoretical capacity (3860 mAh ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and the lowest electrochemical potential (− 3.04 V vs. RHE) [1,2]. However, the practical deployment of Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) is impeded by dendritic lithium growth, parasitic interfacial reactions, and excessive “dead lithium” accumulation [3,4], all of which are exacerbated by the use of traditional organic liquid electrolytes. Carbonate-based electrolytes (e.g., EC/DEC) decompose at the Li-metal interface, forming unstable solid electrolyte interphases (SEIs) that fail to suppress dendrites, whereas the limited oxidative stability (<4.0 V vs. $\mathrm { L i } / \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } )$ of ether-based electrolytes (e.g., DOL/DME) renders them incompatible with high-voltage cathodes such as LiCoO (LCO) or NCM811 [5]. The intrinsic flammability and volatility of these organic electrolytes present serious safety hazards under thermally abusive and fast charging conditions [6]. Although advanced electrolytes, such as fluorinated solvents [7,8], highly concentrated electrolytes (HCEs) [9, 10], localized HCEs (LHCEs) [11–14], and ionic liquids [15,16], partially overcome these limitation, they present practical barriers including high viscosity, poor interfacial compatibility, and high cost. Solid-state electrolytes effectively suppress dendrites but are constrained by low ionic conductivity at room temperature and inadequate interfacial contact [17]. Therefore, exploring electrolytes that facilitate high ionic conductivity, broad electrochemical stability, and inherent safety is crucial for realizing high-voltage, fast-charging LMBs.

label: 理化性质
paragraph_context: Deep eutectic electrolyte (DEE), as a new functional liquid system, is formed through intermolecular interactions resulting from hydrogen bonding, Lewis acid-base acceptance/donation, and van der Waals forces. Typically, DEEs display a significantly lower melting point than their individual components, while also conferring benefits such as high thermal/chemical stability, low volatility, and a broad electrochemical window. Apart from this, DEEs are simple to prepare, cost effective, and non-flammable, as has been demonstrated in the field of electrochemical energy storage, especially in LMBs [18,19]. Nonetheless, the practical application of DEEs is hindered by their intrinsically high viscosity and low ionic conductivity that originates from their robust intermolecular interactions, which severely impede ion mobility and interfacial charge transfer, thereby impacting their fast-charging capability.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: Succinonitrile (SN) has emerged as a promising component in DEEs due to its compatibility with high-voltage cathodes and exceptional thermal stability. Moreover, the high dielectric constant of SN facilitates the dissociation of lithium salts, and its plastic crystal behavior enhances ion mobility at room temperature, to potentially address the key limitations of traditional DEEs [20]. Unfortunately, activation of the adja cent α-hydrogen (α-H) atoms by the electron-withdrawing nitrogen (N) of SN initiates detrimental side reactions with Li metal that disrupt the SEI integrity, accelerate lithium corrosion, and generate “dead lithium,” which impairs the cycling stability and coulombic efficiency of the battery [21]. Thus far, SN-based DEEs with the combined advantages of high ionic conductivity, low viscosity, and satisfactory compatibility with the Li anode for stable, fast-charging LMBs have not yet been reported.

paragraph_context: Herein, we report a rationally designed SN-based deep eutectic solvent (DES) formed by combining dimethyl sulfone (MSM) and SN in a 1:4 molar ratio. Subsequent combination of the DES with lithium difluoro(oxalate)borate (LiDFOB) formed a low-viscosity DEE (18.73 mPa s) with high ionic conductivity (3.14 mS $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ at $2 5 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The hydrogen bonds between the $s = o$ groups of MSM and α-H of SN mitigates the inherent reactivity between SN and Li metal. The optimal concentration of LiDFOB in the DEE (1.2 mol $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ facilitates the aniondominated coordination of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , to generate abundant aggregate (AGG) clusters. This improves the desolvation kinetics and results in the construction of a robust B/F/S-rich gradient SEI, which enables the deposition of dense, dendrite-free Li. The $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 } |$ |Li cell with this electrolyte achieved impressively fast-charging at 4.5 $\mathrm { v , }$ and maintained long-term cycling stability for 1000 cycles at 5C. Subsequently, the practical applicability was proven by successful operation in a highly loaded cathode and a 20 μm Li foil pouch cell. Notably, the LiCoO ||graphite pouch cell retained 90.3 % of its capacity over 2500 cycles. This study establishes hydrogen bonding as a critical design parameter for solvation engineering for fast-charging, high-energy-density LMBs with intrinsic safety.

paragraph_context: To overcome the characteristically high viscosity of DEEs, which arises from the strong coordinative interactions between solid hydrogenbond donors and lithium salts, we engineered a DES using MSM as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Specifically, the polar $s = o$ groups of MSM form an extensive network of hydrogen bonds with α-H in SN molecules to form a fluid-enhanced eutectic system. Mixtures of MSM and SN in molar ratios ranging from 1:2 to 1:6 were heated at $6 0 \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ yielded homogeneous transparent liquids for ratios of 1:4 to 1:6, whereas the ratios 1:2 and 1:3 resulted in partial precipitation (Fig. S1, S2). These DESs, designated MSN-x $( x \ = \ S \mathbf { N }$ molar equivalent), were systematically characterized. The thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) curves in Fig. S3, revealed that MSN-4 exhibited superior thermal stability, indicating maximum MSM-SN interactions at this stoichiometry. Combined with its lower viscosity of 10.31 mPa s (Fig. S4), MSN-4 was selected as the optimal DES and designated as MSN. Mechanistic studies based on 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy revealed an upfield shift of the MSM 1 H signal from 2.95 ppm to 2.58 ppm and a downfield shift of the SN 1 H signal from 2.66 ppm to 2.78 ppm upon the formation of MSN (Fig. S5a). These shifts signify reduced electron density surrounding the hydrogen nucleus in SN as a result of ${ \cal S } = { \cal O } { \cdots } { \mathrm { H } } { \longrightarrow } { \cal C } $ hydrogen bonding (Fig. S6). Furthermore, a significant blue shift of the $O = S = O$ symmetric stretching in Raman spectroscopy (Fig. S5b) was observed, further confirming the presence of this interaction [22]. The DFT-optimized structure revealed that the distance between the O atom of MSM and the α-H of SN is 2.4 Å (Fig. S7), notably shorter than the sum of their van der Waals radii (2.72 Å), which provides definitive quantitative evidence for the ${ \pmb S } = { \pmb O } { \cdots } { \mathrm { H } } { \longrightarrow } { \pmb C }$ hydrogen bond [23].

The surface SEI layer (0 nm) was primarily composed of organic species, as evidenced by the characteristic peaks of C–C (284.8 eV), C–O (286.3 eV), and $C = O \left( 2 8 8 . 7 \ : \mathrm { e V } \right)$ , along with decomposition products including C–SOx (287.1 eV) derived from MSM and C–F (290.9 eV) originating from LiDFOB, which collectively form a protective organic matrix [30,48]. Notably, the preferential reduction of LiDFOB is theoretically predicted by its lowest LUMO energy level (− 2.07 eV) and has been confirmed by LSV curve (Fig. S36) [49,50]. Such a reduction generates chemically stable LiF (684.5 eV) and Li–B–O species $( \mathrm { L i } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ BOyFz, O 1 s at 531.8 eV) [51], effectively passivating the electrode interface and curtailing electrolyte consumption. This reduction mechanism is further corroborated by the gradual decrease in the intensities of the of Li–B–O (192.2 eV) and B–F (193.9 eV) signals in the B 1 s spectra with increasing etching depth. As the etching depth increases to 20 and 40 nm, the inorganic components become progressively more prevalent, as demonstrated by the emergence of Li2O (529.4 eV) and the gradient increase in the Li3N (398.2 eV) content (Fig. 5f). A similar compositional gradient from the outer to the inner SEI layer was observed for $\mathrm { L i _ { x } N _ { y } }$ (395.8 eV) and Li S (162.1 eV) [52]. Moreover, the signal intensity of LiF remained stable throughout the SEI; however, the relative concentration of LiF increased dramatically from 52.4 % to 86.2 % as the B–F species diminished, confirming its preferential accumulation in the inner SEI layer (Fig. 5f). The above-mentioned results reveal a gradient heterogeneous SEI structure in the 1.2 m MSN-LD electrolyte, which evolves from a solvent-derived organic-rich outer layer to an inorganic-dominated inner layer (Fig. 5e, g). The flexible organic components at the surface buffer the interfacial strain during Li plating/stripping and suppress continuous electrolyte consumption, while the dense inorganic inner layer ensures dendrite suppression and rapid $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport. Specifically, anion-derived LiF passivates the Li surface because of its high interfacial energy and electronic insulation, thereby restraining the growth of Li dendrite. Additionally, $\mathrm { L i } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and $\mathrm { L i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N }$ are excellent $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conductors that facilitate a uniform $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux. Briefly, this DFOB- -rich $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation structure promoted the formation of an organic-inorganic gradient SEI, which provides an efficient protective barrier for the Li metal during cycling.

paragraph_context: In summary, we demonstrated a hydrogen-bond-mediated molecular engineering strategy for designing a low-viscosity DEE with enhanced interfacial stability. Specifically, the hydrogen bonds between the $s = o$ groups of MSM and the α-H in SN effectively suppress the parasitic reaction on the surface of the Li anode. Precise control of the LiDFOB concentration (1.2 mol $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 } )$ induced an anion-rich solvation structure that drove the formation of a B/F/S-rich gradient SEI, which enabled dendrite-free Li deposition and rapid Li+ transport. With this design, a high-voltage LCO-based LMB retained 87.4 % of its capacity after 1000 cycles at 5C fast charging. More significantly, practical LCO||Gr pouch cells with this electrolyte maintained stable operation for 2500 cycles at 1C. This electrolyte has the additional benefit of being non-flammable and is thus intrinsically safe under typical operating conditions. This work exemplifies the dual strategy of solvent insertion and interfacial regulation, and provides inspiration for the application of highly active solvents in Li metal batteries.

paragraph_context: Elevating the charging cut-off voltage of nickel-rich layered oxide cathode-based lithium metal batteries (LMBs) is crucial for obtaining high energy density. However, the instability of the cathode electrolyte interphase under high-temperature/voltage condition severely hinders the development of Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 batteries. Here, we propose an anion-enriched solvation strategy for constructing robust cathode electrolyte interphase to enhance interfacial stability between cathode and electrolyte under high-temperature/voltage condition. The strong dipole interaction between 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenylboronic acid and ethyl carbonate promotes the removal of ethyl carbonate molecules from the primary solvation shell, obtaining an anion-enriched solvation structure. This well-designed solvation structure facilitates the formation of $\mathrm { L i B _ { x } O _ { y } / I }$ LiF-rich cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) with excellent mechanical and thermal stability. In consequence, the Li||NCM811 batteries achieve 80% and 76.9% capacity retention after 300 and 150 cycles at 4.6/4.7 V, respectively. Moreover, the batteries deliver a 71.8% superior capacity retention after 150 cycles at 60 ◦C. More importantly, a 6 Ah pouch cell could stably work for 150 cycles under lean electrolyte condition. This strategy offers new insights into the electrolyte design for high-energy LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: With the rapid development of electric vehicles and portable electronic devices, it is urgent to develop rechargeable batteries with higher energy density [1–3]. Among various options, lithium metal batteries (LMBs) employing nickel-rich layered oxide cathodes are particularly promising due to their exceptional capacity and voltage characteristics [4–6]. Although raising the charge cut-off voltage can increase the energy density of LMBs, operating at the elevated voltages introduces significant interfacial challenges. The raised voltage accelerates the decomposition of electrolyte components, initiating parasitic reactions that consume the electrolyte and destabilize the cathode/electrolyte interface [7,8]. This degradation is manifested in structural collapse, particle cracking, and transition metal ions (TMs) dissolution within the cathode, all of which contribute to irreversible capacity loss. Under practical conditions, elevated operating temperatures above 50 ◦C further accelerate these side reactions by lowering the activation barriers, thereby amplifying interfacial instability [9,10]. Consequently, stabilizing the cathode/electrolyte interface under high-voltage/temperature conditions is essential for the successful deployment of high-energy LMBs.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: One of the most effective strategies to mitigate interfacial degradation is constructing a robust cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) [11]. In principle, CEI is typically formed through the oxidative decomposition of electrolyte components located in the solvation sheath of Li+ [12]. In conventional electrolytes, solvent molecules dominate the solvation structure, which leads to the formation of organic-rich CEIs [13]. However, they often possess porous architectures and poor mechanical strength, making them susceptible to cracking or dissolution during operating under high voltage/temperature conditions. The failure undermines the protective function of CEI and promotes ongoing parasitic reactions at the interface. To address this issue, high-concentration electrolytes and localized high-concentration electrolytes have been developed to obtain anion-dominated solvation sheath [14,15]. This approach promotes the generation of inorganic-rich CEIs, which feature high robustness and thermostability [16–18]. Nevertheless, the high cost limits their practical application. An alternative solution involves low-cost, weakly solvating electrolytes which also favor anion-dominated solvation [19–22]. However, their poor oxidative resistance constrains their compatibility with high-voltage cathodes.

paragraph_context: Therefore, it is imperative to develop new strategies to achieve anion-dominated solvation structures in electrolytes with conventional salt concentrations. Although in our previous studies, we introduced strategies involving additive-mediated anion sieving coordination and pseudo-concentrated electrolytes to realize an anion-dominated solvation sheath, which attained remarkable results $^ { [ 6 , 2 3 ] }$ . More diversified strategies still need to be developed.

paragraph_context: Additives are the most cost-effective and scalable levers for tailoring electrolyte performance. Among them, boron-containing compounds have attracted widespread attention because of their low cost and intrinsic high-temperature/high-voltage tolerance. Conventional representatives function via sacrificial oxidation on the cathode surface, depositing B–O-containing species that passivate the interface [24,25]. Although this strategy affords a certain degree of protection, it inevitably consumes the additive continuously and yields an organic-inorganic hybrid CEI that is prone to fracture or dissolution under aggressive cycling conditions.

paragraph_context: Herein, we propose an anion-enriched solvation strategy to construct a robust CEI via weakening the coordination of polar solvents with cations. As a demonstration, 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenylboronic acid (TFMBA) was employed as additive in an ethyl carbonate (EC)-based carbonate electrolyte. The TFMBA molecule establishes a strong dipole–dipole interaction with EC, competitively displacing EC from the primary $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation sheath. Simultaneously, $\mathrm { P F } _ { 6 } { } ^ { - }$ anions enter the solvation layer, creating an anion-enriched solvation structure that subsequently directs the formation of a LiBxOy/LiF-rich inorganic CEI. $\mathrm { L i B _ { x } O _ { y } }$ not only exhibits high $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ conductivity but also strengthens the mechanical robustness and thermal stability of the CEI through its unique B–O–B covalent framework, thereby effectively suppressing CEI dissolution. Besides, the rigid LiF phase within the interphase resists mechanical failure of the cathode during cycling, thereby enhancing the structural integrity of NCM811. The $\mathrm { L i B _ { x } O _ { y } / L i F } .$ -rich CEI effectively alleviates the cathode structure collapse, irreversible phase transitions, and TMs dissolution. Consequently, an anion-enriched solvation structure is realized under a conventional salt concentration (1 M $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 } )$ without resorting to costly high-concentration or localized highconcentration electrolytes. As a result, the $\mathrm { L i } | | \mathrm { L i N i _ { 0 . 8 } C o _ { 0 . 1 } M n _ { 0 . 1 } O _ { 2 } }$ (NCM811) cells employing the optimized electrolyte retained 80.0% capacity after 300 cycles at 4.6 V and 76.9% after 150 cycles at 4.7 V. Even at a high temperature of $6 0 \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ the cells demonstrated an exceptional capacity retention of 71.8% after 150 cycles. Remarkably, the electrolyte can stabilize the operation of a 6 Ah pouch cell (\~498 Wh $\mathbf { k } \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ with a lean electrolyte (1.23 $\textrm { g } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 } )$ for 150 cycle. This work provides an effective reference for the reasonable design of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ solvation structure to achieve high-voltage/temperature, electrolytes for LMBs.

paragraph_context: Li||NCM811 batteries are usually paired with typical EC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ in a mixture solvent of EC, ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC) and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) (2:7:1 by volume, denoted as baseline electrolyte). 2 wt% TFMBA was employed as an additive in baseline electrolyte to obtain anion-enriched solvation structure. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were used to elucidate the impact of additives on the solvation chemistry. As depicted in Fig. 1a, b and Figure S1-S3 (Supporting Information), $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ is inclined to coordinate with oxygen atoms in solvent molecules EC, EMC and FEC. In contrast, the additive TFMBA does not participate in coordinate with Li+. In the electrolyte containing TFMBA, there is a significant decrease in the number of EC solvent molecules coordinating with Li⁺ compared to the baseline electrolyte. Furthermore, the reduced solvation of EC mitigates its oxidative dehydrogenation, which in turn lowers the likelihood of HF formation through reaction with $\mathrm { P F } _ { 6 } ^ { - } .$ . This contributes to the stabilization of the cathode bulk phase at high-voltage [26]. In terms of the distribution of ${ \mathrm { P F } } _ { 6 } { } ^ { - } ,$ , the intensity of the first distribution peak in the electrolyte with TFMBA is higher than that in the baseline electrolyte. This suggests that the interaction between ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { P F } _ { 6 } { } ^ { - }$ has been enhanced. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis also indicated that a higher proportion of $\mathrm { P F } _ { 6 } { } ^ { - }$ anions are bound to Li⁺ in the electrolyte with TFMBA, with fewer remaining in the free Li⁺ state, relative to the baseline electrolyte (Fig. 1c). Moreover, the $^ 7 \mathrm { L i }$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra exhibit a notable upfield shift in the electrolyte containing TFMBA, indicating an enhanced shielding effect from neighboring $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } } ,$ , which is attributed to the coordination of more anions with $\operatorname { L i } ^ { + } \left( \operatorname { F i g } . 1 \mathrm { d } \right)$ . Raman spectroscopy shows that when TFMBA is mixed with EC, the C=O characteristic peak of EC molecules undergoes a blue shift, which indicates that the electron-deficient positive potential region induced by $\mathrm { - C F _ { 3 } }$ in TFMBA forms a core dipole attraction with the strong negative potential region of the carbonyl oxygen in EC molecules. This directional dipole interaction will promote the further shift of the electron cloud of the C=O bond of EC to the carbonyl oxygen, increase the bond order and bond energy of the C=O bond, and thus increase the vibration frequency of the chemical bond (Figure S4, Supporting Information). As illustrated in Fig. 1e, TFMBA exhibits a robust binding energy with EC, which also signifies a pronounced dipole-dipole interaction. This potent interaction empowers TFMBA to sequester EC molecules from the peripheral solvation shell of lithium ions, thereby markedly diminishing the interaction between Li⁺ and the polar solvent EC (Fig. 1f). These results emphasize that TFMBA, leveraging dipolar interactions, realizing an anion-enriched solvation structure, which promotes the development of an inorganic-rich CEI.

paragraph_context: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were used to assess how different solvents tend to break down when oxidized. As indicated in Figure S5 (Supporting Information), the examination of the frontier molecular orbital energy levels shows that TFMBA has the highest HOMO energy level (− 8.0436 eV) of all the components in the electrolyte. This suggests that TFMBA is more likely to undergo oxidative decomposition, which helps to form a passivation layer on the cathode surface. Moreover, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analysis further reveals oxidative decomposition triggered by TFMBA at a low potential (3.16 V), with exhibits a considerably higher oxidation potential than the baseline electrolyte (Figure S6, Supporting Information). To further explore the fundamental mechanisms behind the antioxidant properties of the electrolyte, additional calculations were performed to examine how solvent molecules are arranged on the cathode surface. As shown in Fig. 1g, TFMBA exhibits higher adsorption energy than other solvents, enabling it to gather more readily on the NCM811 surface. This is due to the high polarity of TFMBA molecular (Fig. 1h and Figure S7, Supporting Information). Consequently, TFMBA is more likely to be oxidized first, which helps to create a stable CEI that is abundant in B- and F-containing compounds. In addition, the preferential adsorption of TFMBA decreases the contact between EC and the cathode, thus preventing the oxidative dehydrogenation of EC and reducing the probability of side reactions with $\mathrm { P F } _ { 6 } ^ { - }$ that produce HF.

paragraph_context: The CEI layers generated from various electrolytes were investigated using depth-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Fig. 2a, b and S8-10 (Supporting Information), the CEI generated from TFMBA-containing electrolytes exhibits a lower proportion of C-atoms compared to that from the baseline electrolyte, suggesting that fewer organic components (C=C, C-O, C=O, C-F, C-C/C-H) are produced by solvent decomposition. Interfacial instability, predominantly triggered by the dissolution of TMs, represents a major degradation mechanism for the NCM811 cathode, leading to the migration of $\mathrm { N i ^ { 2 + } }$ ions to the layered $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ sites [40]. A decreased I(003)/I(104) ratio serves as an indicator of cathode degradation and is utilized to evaluate the severity of this degradation [41,42]. The intensity ratio of fresh cathode is 1.93. Obviously, the cathode cycling in the TFMBA-based electrolyte has a higher I /I ratio (1.71) than the baseline electrolyte (1.58) after 200 cycles. Importantly, the (003) peak split in the baseline electrolyte means that an undesired phase transition occurs in the particles during high voltage operation (see Fig. 5a) [43], which results in poor lithium reversibility. In addition, TMs dissolution is also the main factor resulting in the degradation of electrochemical properties, especially under high voltage [44]. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) was used to measure the dissolution of TMs (Ni, Co, Mn) on the lithium anode after cycling. The ICP-MS results in Figure S19 (Supporting Information) demonstrate the CEI derived from TFMBA-containing electrolyte suppressed the TMs dissolution. Then, the TMs dissolution amount in the cathode was evaluated by depth profiling analysis using TOF-SIMS. As depicted in Fig. $5 { \bf g } ,$ the TM fluorides (e.g., NiF− , CoF− , MnF− ) in the CEI layer from the baseline electrolyte, caused by corrosive by-products like HF [45], contrast sharply with the CEI layer from the TFMBA-containing electrolyte. Thus, the TFMBA-based electrolyte facilitates the formation of a thin yet robust CEI on the cathode surface, which can withstand significant volume changes, thereby preventing structural cracking and the dissolution of TMs (Fig. 5i).

paragraph_context: Beyond the cathode, the TFMBA-containing electrolyte also shows measurable benefits at the Li interface, which are reflected in the plating/stripping behavior and the distinct SEI chemistry. As shown in Figure S20a and b (Supporting Information), the lithium metal surface after cycling in the electrolyte containing 2% TFMBA remains relatively dense and smooth, with no obvious cracks or dead lithium, indicating a uniform deposition/stripping process and high interfacial stability. In contrast, the lithium surface cycled in the baseline electrolyte exhibits a large number of loose, porous, sponge-like lithium clusters, with a significantly increased surface roughness, and some areas have peeled off to form isolated dead lithium. This suggests uneven lithium deposition and repeated rupture and regeneration of the Solid Electrolyte Interphase (SEI), which could lead to continuous loss of active lithium and increased interfacial impedance (Figure S20c and d, Supporting Information). In addition, XPS was employed to analyze the SEI components formed in different electrolytes. As depicted in Figure S21, the lower carbon and oxygen content in the SEI formed with TFMBAcontaining electrolyte indicates that TFMBA addition reduces the decomposition of solvents molecules, leading to fewer organic components. Figure S22 (Supporting Information) shows that the signals containing F and P are significantly enhanced in the SEI derived from the TFMBA-containing electrolyte. The reduction in organic components and the enrichment of fluorine-, phosphorus-, and boron-derived species (LiF, $\mathrm { L i _ { x } P F _ { y } O _ { z } }$ and $\mathrm { L i B _ { x } O _ { y } ) }$ indicate the formation of an SEI that is rich in inorganic components, which is more resistant to solvent attack and interfacial fluctuations. This, in turn, significantly enhances the stability and cycling performance of the LMBs.

To meet rising energy demands, it is essential to incorporate key battery parameters, such as cathode type, capacity, N/P ratio, and E/C ratio, into a pouch cell design (Fig. 6a, b). As depicted in Fig. 6c and Table S2(Supporting Information), the cathode and electrolyte components significantly influence the overall weight of the battery, with the cathode comprising 64.2% and the electrolyte 15.4%. paragraph_context: Developing safe electrolytes with an expanded electrochemical stability window (ESW) offers a promising pathway toward practical high-energy-density lithium-metal batteries (LMBs). Here, we propose an intrinsically nonflammable F-rich high-entropy electrolyte consisting of fluorinated ester and phosphazenes. This system strategically integrates the disordered environment of high-entropy design with the low polarization characteristics of fluorination to expand the ESW and regulate the solvation structure. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations and systematic control experimental results demonstrate that the designed electrolyte minimizes Li+- solvent interaction, which on one hand induces an inorganic-rich interface, and on the other hand accelerates the desolvation kinetics, ensuring that solvents rarely exist in the inner Helmholtz layer. The resulting electrolyte enables commercially viable Li||NCM 811 to operate safely and stably under ultrahigh-voltage (4.8 V) and lowtemperature (-20◦C) conditions. We believe the results of this work hold reference significance for the design of electrolytes in sodium/potassium/calcium/magnesium batteries.

label: 概述
paragraph_context: For the convenience of people’s lives and to reduce environmental damage, electric instruments and vehicles have begun to rise. Hence, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are starting to be used in various industries [1]. However, with in-depth research, current LIBs are almost approaching their theoretical energy density [2]. Intending to pursue high-energy density storage systems, it is vital to replace the graphite anode with other anodes with higher specific capacity [3,4]. Lithium metal batteries (LMBs), which have been withdrawn from the stage of history, have regained people’s attention originated from their higher energy density [5]. Because the specific capacity and working voltage determine the energy density [6,7], improving the working voltage or capacity of batteries is the most direct and promising strategy to meet the requirements of high-energy density storage systems. For the anode, Li metal possesses a high specific capacity (3860 mAh g− 1 ) and the lowest redox potential (-3.04 V vs the standard hydrogen electrode) [8–10], and is one of the most promising candidates to replace the commercial graphite anode. As for the cathode, reaching a high cutoff voltage (>4.5 V) for cathode materials that have been successfully commercialized (e.g. $\mathrm { L i N i _ { x } C o _ { y } M n _ { z } O _ { 2 } } ,$ x+y+z=1) can remarkably elevate the energy density [11,12]. However, currently, neither the commercially successful carbonate-based electrolytes nor the widely studied ether-based [13] electrolytes can enable the combination of highly reactive lithium and ultrahigh-voltage cathodes. Furthermore, the employment of ultrahigh-voltage cathodes not only amplifies energy release during thermal runaway but also triggers oxygen evolution, thereby escalating the likelihood of safety incidents when paired with highly flammable electrolytic solvents. To commercialize LMBs, many different strategies have been proposed [14–18]. High-entropy electrolytes, as an emerging modification strategy, have attracted extensive attention from researchers due to their unique solvation structures. Although the recently reported high-entropy electrolytes have demonstrated superior stability in lithium-metal batteries [19–21], their energy density still requires further improvement, while the safety issues faced by lithium-metal batteries have been overlooked.

label: 电化学性能
paragraph_context: Molecular fluorination has always been an effective strategy in the modification of lithium metal battery electrolytes. It can not only weaken the interaction between ions and solvents, inducing a powerful LiF-rich solid-electrolyte interface (SEI), but also introduce nonflammable properties [22,23]. Furthermore, the antioxidation ability is improved due to the strong electron-withdrawing induction effect of -F [24]. Notably, a high-entropy (HE) environment will increase the degree of chaos in the entire system, which means that, compared to an ordered solvation structure, the component of the system tends to exist in a disordered free state according to recent studies [19–21]. Hence, the desolvation energy of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ in the high-entropy electrolyte (HEE) will be decreased. In this work, based on the feature of fluorinated solvents and HEE, we propose an intrinsically nonflammable high-entropy fluorinated electrolyte (F-HE), consisting of 2,2-difluoroethyl acetate (DFEA), fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC), methyl 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl carbonate (FEMC), methyl trifluoroacetate (MTFA), and ethoxy(pentafluoro) cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN). In this F-HE system, fluorinated molecules (FEC, FEMC, and DFEA) with weak solvation ability serve as solvents, we propose the solvent will stay as far away as possible from the electrode surface (Fig. 1a). We believe that weak solvation will enhance the stability of the interface, which can be accounted for as the solvent molecules being hard to approach the electrode interface and decomposition (Fig. 1b). In addition, the decrease in the HOMO/LUMO energy levels caused by fluorination also facilitated the formation of a fluorine-rich interface (Fig. 1c). To further weaken the solvation power, MTFA and PFPN serve as functional diluents to construct F-HE. Notably, MTFA is a good low-temperature solvent and PFPN possesses good fire retardance [25,26]. That is why we chose these two functional solvents to construct F-HE. In F-HE, we suggest that fluorinated solvents can decrease the coordination with $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and contribute to forming the fluorine-containing interface, while the HE environment can further improve the desolvation process, and it can also compensate for the low ionic conductivity caused by fluorination. The synergistic effect of fluorination and high entropy, for one thing, can minimize the coordination of solvent molecules, keeping them away from the inner Helmholtz layer and reducing redox decomposition. For another, influenced by the HE environment, the average size of the solvation clusters decreases. According to the Einstein-Stokes equation, the reduction of the hydrodynamic radius will increase the diffusion coefficient [19], that is, it will enhance the ionic conductivity. This addresses the issue of reduced ionic conductivity resulting from fluorination (Fig. 1e). Consequently, the F-HE achieves high coulombic efficiency (98.2 %) and low overpotential (85 mV) under the high current density (2 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ,$ and 4 mA cm− 2 ). Li||NCM 811 cells with practical conditions (50 μm-Li, areal capacity: 1.9 mAh $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , ultra-high cutoff voltage: 4.8 V) can be cycled stably both at room temperature and low temperature (-20◦C) with the capacity retention about 80 % and 87.4 % after 300 cycles and 100 cycles.

paragraph_context: One of the problems now faced within LMBs is how to consider the ionic conductivity and the ultrahigh-voltage stability of the electrolyte simultaneously [27]. Fluorination can increase the stability of electrolytes to the Li anode, which is attributed to their priority reduction capability [28]. However, fluorination will inevitably affect the conductivity of electrolytes. Notably, a HE environment can dissociate ion clusters and improve ion conductivity [19,29], and the increase in ion mobility can be attributed to the rise in excess entropy $\boldsymbol { \mathbf { S } } _ { \mathrm { e x } }$ (Eq. 1) [30], where D is the diffusion coefficient, a and b are empirical fitting parameters, and $\mathbf { k _ { B } }$ is the Boltzmann constant. $$ \mathrm{D} = \mathrm{aexp} \left(\frac {b S _ {e x}}{k _ {B}}\right) \tag {1} $$ Constructing HEE with fluorinated solvents can stabilize the Li anode while ensuring ionic conductivity. A series of non-fluorinated carbonates, including EC, EA, and EMC are chosen as the control group for studying the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE. First, the charge distribution of molecules before and after fluorination is verified through simulation (Fig. 2a). Compared to EC, EA, and EMC, the reduced electron cloud density around O atoms in FEC, DFEA, and FEMC is observed, denoting the relatively weak binding between $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and fluorinated solvents, which is also proven by the simulation of binding energy. This indicates that fluorination can promote the desolvation process. Therefore, five types of electrolytes with 1 M $\mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 }$ were elaborately prepared to explore the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE. Among them, FEC: DFEA: FEMC: MTFA: PFPN (2: 3: 3: 3: 1 vol %) is referred to as F-HE, FEC: DFEA: MTFA (2: 6: 4 vol %) is referred to as DFEA-base, FEC: FEMC: MTFA (2: 6: 4 vol %) is referred to as FEMCbase, EC: EA: EMC: MTFA: PFPN (2: 3: 3: 3: 1 vol %) is referred to as N-HE, and EC: DEC (1:1 vol %) is referred to as EC/DEC. The melting points of five kinds of electrolytes were tested (Fig. S1, 2), except for EC-DEC, all the electrolytes remain in a flowing liquid state at ${ \bf - 2 0 ^ { \circ } C , }$ which meet the basic conditions for low-temperature operation. In addition, from the results of differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), it can be observed that F-HE is the only electrolyte that does not exhibit any exothermic peak during the process of cooling to -80◦C. This indicates that during the cooling process, neither a transformation from liquid to solid nor the precipitation of salts occurs. The parasitic reactions on the $\mathrm { L i N i } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (NCM 811) at the charged state were characterized through potentiostatic tests using Li/NCM 811 cells (Fig. 2b). Cells using EC/DEC and N-HE exhibited high leakage currents, especially holding at 4.9 V and 5 V, which demonstrates that EC/DEC and N-HE experienced severe side reactions on the NCM 811 and it is probably attributed to the strong catalytic activity of $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 4 + }$ . On the contrary, cells using F-HE exhibited low and stable leakage currents, representing a powerful cathode electrolyte interface (CEI) was induced and prevented the dissolution of transition metal ions. For further studying the oxidation stability window of electrolytes, Li||SS cells were employed to perform linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests at a scan rate of 5 mV s⁻¹ (Fig. 2c). The amount of irreversible current was about 13.3 μA (The detailed calculation process was described in the Methods part). F-HE displays a significantly higher oxidation stability (5.2 V) than EC/DEC and N-HE, and F-HE showed considerable oxidation stability among the reported electrolytes $( { \mathrm { F i g } } .$ . 2e). Furthermore, igniting tests demonstrated that F-HE is non-flammable (Fig. 2d), which is attributed to the release of fluorine radicals from fluorinated solvents during combustion. These radicals quench hydrogen and hydroxyl radicals, thereby interrupting the chain reaction of combustion and ensuring the battery will not catch fire or even explode during thermal runaway. To investigate the role of the HE environment, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) was adopted to evaluate the solvation environment of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 2f). F-HE, FEMC-base, and DFEA-base consist of an equal proportion of solvents, diluents, and the same salt concentration. However, the solvation environment of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ exhibited a big difference. Compared to FEMC-base, $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ in DFEAbase is less affected by solvents and anions, which is confirmed by an obvious downfield shift of chemical shift. Notably, although there is an equal proportion of FEMC and DFEA present in F-HE, the chemical shift of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ is not between DFEA-base and FEMC-base, but towards a lower field shift, which confirms that a weak solvation interaction between $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , solvents, and anions is generated under the influence of the HE environment [20]. Furthermore, a downfield shift also occurred in N-HE with non-fluorinated solvents compared to FMEC-base, which further proves the effect of HE to the solvation environment. The Raman test was also conducted to evaluate the solvation environment of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 2g). Due to the strongest solvation ability of FEC, we select to analyze the coordination of FEC. F-HE has more free FEC than coordinated FEC compared to FEMC-base and DFEA-base, and this is in accordance with the result obtained from the NMR test. All this verifies the superiority of constructing F-HE.

paragraph_context: To investigate the stability of the designed electrolyte toward the Li anode, the reversible plating/stripping behavior of Li was first evaluated through Li||Li cells under a constant current density of 0.5 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (Fig. 3a). In the initial few weeks of cycling, the battery using N-HE exhibited a smaller overpotential compared to the one using EC/DEC, confirming that HE indeed promotes lithium ion migration and reduces concentration polarization. However, a dramatic increase of the overpotential (even to 800 mV) is found in the subsequent cycle using N-HE, which is attributed to severe parasitic reactions that occur between N-HE and Li and generate an over-thick interface layer. The phenomenon suggested that just focusing on creating a HE environment but ignoring the ability to passivate interfaces is infeasible. In contrast, applying fluorinated solvents can stabilize the interface effectively, which is confirmed by the lower overpotential and longer cycling lifespan. Notably, combining FEMC and DFEA to construct F-HE exhibited highly reversible plating/stripping behavior, manifesting as the lowest overpotential (40 mV) and the longest cycling time, which demonstrated that under the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE, lithium can undergo long-term plating and stripping behavior under low overpotential. To further verify the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE, Li symmetric cells with different rates were tested (Fig. S3c). As the current density increases, the Li symmetric cell using F-HE exhibits the lowest overpotential throughout the entire cycle, suggesting the combination of HE and fluorination indeed significantly enhances the charge transfer kinetics [41,42] (Fig. S3e). First, cells using N-HE exhibited a dramatic increase in overpotential, demonstrating that an instability SEI is generated and severe parasitic reactions continuously occur (Fig. S3e), indicating the importance of fluorination, even though it will reduce the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte. Then, we compare FEMC-base, DFEA-base, and F-HE together, although F-HE is obtained by a simple mix of FEMC and DFEA, the stripping/deposition behavior under high current density has been greatly improved (Fig. S3b), suggesting the HE environment affects the solvation structure, improving the desolvation energy and inducing a powerful SEI. The above outcomes demonstrate the synergistic effect of HE and fluorination. The impact of fluorinated and HE synergistic effects on $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ desolvation was further approved by the distribution relaxation times (DRT) analysis (Fig. 3b-d) [9]. This analysis further subdivides different electrochemical control processes. The test results comply with previous reports [43], the charge transfer resistance $\mathrm { ( R _ { c t } ) }$ and SEI resistance $( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { S E D } } )$ exhibited strong temperature dependence. Among them, the charge transfer process is the controlling step at low temperatures, while $\mathtt { R } _ { \mathtt { S E I } }$ prevails at high temperatures [44, 45]. Specifically, the N-HE has a lower $\operatorname { R } _ { \operatorname { c t } }$ than EC/DEC at -20◦C (Fig. 3b, c), demonstrating that the HE environment helps promote the charge transfer process. Notably, the F-HE possesses the lowest $\operatorname { R } _ { \operatorname { c t } }$ (Fig. 3d), suggesting that fluorination further promotes the charge transfer process (Fig. S4a), and under the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE environment, cells are expected to exhibit excellent low-temperature and high-rate performance, which will be discussed later. This is also confirmed by the lowest activation energy of the charge transfer process (Fig. S5), the activation energy for Li symmetric cells with the F-HE is estimated to be 45.03 kJ mol− 1 , much lower than using other electrolytes, and this also proves the advantages of the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE environment. The transference number of $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ is another influencing factor under high-rate conditions. The $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transference number $( t _ { L i } ^ { + } )$ of different electrolytes is measured using the method from Abraham et al [46] (see Supporting Information for details) (Fig.S6, 7). F-HE has the highest $t _ { L i } ^ { + }$ (0.84) compared to other electrolytes, demonstrating that the desolvation process is improved. Furthermore, concentration polarization in F-HE will greatly decrease especially under high-rate conditions. This also explains very well that symmetric cells using F-HE exhibited the lowest overpotential under high current density. Finally, the average Coulombic efficiency (CE) of Li in Li-Cu half cells with different electrolytes under different current densities is tested by applying the Aurbach method (Fig. 3e). As expected, Li-Cu cells using F-HE exhibited the highest CE under different current densities which also confirmed the superiority of the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE environment. Furthermore, the Li plating/stripping CE was tested using Li-Cu cells with different electrolytes (Fig. S8a). Cells using F-HE exhibited the highest platting/stripping CE within 100 cycles (96.9 %) and obtained uniform deposition morphology (Fig. S9), which conforms to the outcome derived from Li symmetric cells, that is, a large overpotential will lead to more severe diffusion limitation and induce the growth of dendrites according to Sand’s time [47].

paragraph_context: With the exception of compatibility with the Li anode, the emphasis on judging electrolytes should also be on compatibility with the positive electrode, specifically under ultrahigh-voltage conditions. Hence, Li|| NCM 811 cells with high-loading positive electrodes and limited negative electrodes were assembled using different electrolytes to evaluate their practicality under high voltage conditions (Fig. 6a). Among five electrolytes, F-HE exhibited superior stability and compatibility with the cathode even under ultrahigh cutoff voltage (4.8 V) manifest as the maximum cycle life (with the capacity retention about 80 % after a 300- week cycle). Demonstrating that F-HE induced a powerful cathodeelectrolyte interface (CEI) to curb the destruction of NCM 811 particles as well as reduce the dissolution of transition metal ions in high valence states. On the contrary, rapid capacity degradation occurs in the cells with N-HE and EC/DEC, which suggests that, for one thing, the cathode material undergoes an irreversible phase transition and even fragmentation under high voltage, for another, the SEI of the anode is also experiencing a continuous process of fragmentation and reconstruction. Notably, despite the batteries using DFEA-base and FEMCbase also exhibiting rather remarkable cycling performance, the electrolyte still undergoes oxidation to varying degrees under high voltage (Fig. S14). To further verify the practicality of the electrolyte, Ah-level pouch cells were assembled and tested under harsh conditions (the cutoff voltage is 4.8 V). As shown in Fig. 6d, e, the carefully designed electrolyte induces robust dual interfaces and can support the operation of 4.8 V Ah-level pouch cells, with an energy density as high as 355 Wh $\mathbf { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ . In-situ EIS measurements were performed to conduct an in-depth study on the effects of different electrolytes on NCM 811 particles under high voltage. The application of N-HE and EC/DEC resulted in a drastic rise in impedance than F-HE, which confirms poor structural integrity in the process of high-voltage charging and discharging [34] (Fig. S16). The corresponding DRT data were gathered to carry out a more detailed investigation into how impedance varies with voltage at different frequencies (Fig. 6f-h). Since at room temperature (30◦C), the charge transfer process is not the controlling step, there is not much difference in the charge transfer impedance (Rct) of the three kinds of electrolytes during the charge and discharge process. Instead, the interfacial impedance $( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { S E D } } )$ is the main rate-limiting step at this temperature. We specifically focused on the variations in the interfacial impedance of the three electrolytes during the charging and discharging process. EC/DEC and N-HE exhibited a much higher interfacial impedance than F-HE, which indicated that cells using EC/DEC and N-HE generate a thicker interfacial layer during the cycling process, causing low coulombic efficiency and dendrite growth. Conversely, there is no discernible variation in the interfacial impedance throughout the cycling process using F-HE, which confirms that a thin interfacial layer with high ionic conductivity is formed and inhibits the decomposition of electrolytes as well as homogenizes the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ flux. Then, the charge-discharge curves of different electrolytes during cycling were analyzed to acquire more comprehensive details regarding the charge-discharge process. As shown in Fig. S15, using EC/DEC and N-HE results in the fast decay of average discharge voltages and capacities, which demonstrates that the energy density continues to decay as the cycle progresses caused by the irreversible phase transition under ultra-high cutoff voltage. Notably, the application of F-HE can protect the cathode material to the greatest extent and slow down the decay of the energy density, even under the condition of an ultra-high cutoff voltage, suggesting that the loss of oxygen was effectively inhibited, hence decreasing the irreversible phase transition [52]. The detailed analysis of the phase transition will be thoroughly discussed in the next section. The cycling performance of the battery at low temperatures was analyzed to further validate the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE in promoting desolvation energy. As shown in Fig. 6i, under extreme conditions of low temperature and a high cut-off voltage, the cells using F-HE exhibit stable cycle performance (retaining about 87.4 % of initial capacity after 100 cycles under -20◦C), which confirms that the synergistic effect of HE and fluorination significantly promotes the desolvation process as well as anti-oxidation capability. To more prominently highlight the benefits of the synergistic effect between HE and fluorination, we compared the performance of previously reported Li/NCM 811 cells, which feature high cathode loading and a limited Li source, across three key parameters: cut-off voltage, cycle life, and decay rate (Fig. 6j). Benefiting from the synergistic effect of HE and fluorination, solvent molecules can be kept as far away as possible from the electrode surface, which ensures the stability of the electrolyte under high voltage. Furthermore, the existence of fluorinated solvents ensures the formation of a fluorine-containing interface, which guarantees the reversible phase transition of the NCM 811, reduces the generation of dendrites, and minimizes side reactions on the anode side. Hence, applying F-HE still exhibited longer cycle life and lower decay rate even under ultrahigh-voltage conditions compared with the previously reported electrolytes.

paragraph_context: Furthermore, the Fourier transform spectrum reveals that, despite cycling under ultrahigh-voltage, NCM 811 particles manage to retain an intact layered structure, which is ascribed to a powerful CEI effectively protecting NCM 811 particles. Conversely, a thick and uneven CEI (5.2\~27.2 nm) was detected in NCM 811 cycled in N-HE, confirming that the electrolyte undergoes severe oxidation decomposition and that the CEI is consistent with conductive organic species during the cycling process. Meanwhile, extensive irreversible phase transitions from layer to rock-salt were detected in the corresponding Fourier transform, signifying that irreversible oxygen and capacity loss were generated in NCM 811 particles after cycling under the ultrahigh-voltage conditions, which further illustrated that the as-formed CEI failed to protect NCM 811 particles [32]. Notably, $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ will be hard to diffuse in the tightly packed rock-salt phase, and this well explains the higher impedance observed in the Li||NCM 811 cell cycled with N-HE compared to that with F-HE [57]. Apart from the phase transformation, the fragmentation of NCM 811 particles also poses a challenge during cycling under ultra-high voltage. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to observe the morphology of NCM 811 particles cycled with different electrolytes (Fig. S17). Except for the NCM 811 cycled in F-HE, all NCM 811 particles exhibited varying degrees of cracking cycled in other electrolytes, which confirms the superiority of the CEI derived from F-HE.

paragraph_context: The differential capacity versus voltage of cells cycled in different electrolytes was analyzed to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the phase transformation process during ultrahigh-voltage cycling. As shown in Fig. 7b, the capacity of NCM 811 is primarily attributed to a four-step phase transition during cycling: from hexagonal (H1) to monoclinic (M), followed by transitions to hexagonal (H2 and H3) structures [52]. The phase transition during the charging process is divided into two parts: before 4.11V (stable region) and after 4.11V (unstable region). Among them, the phase transition from H1 to M usually appears as a split peak attributed to the $\cos ^ { 3 + / 4 + }$ redox couple contributes to a small part of capacities [52]. Notably, the phase transition after 4.11V is termed the unstable region because, within this voltage range, the H2-H3 phase transition readily triggers the precipitation of lattice oxygen. This, in turn, renders the phase transition irreversible. The utilization of F-HE endows the NCM 811 particles with the ability to preserve structural integrity during the entire ultrahigh-voltage cycling procedure. This is conspicuously demonstrated by the reversible peaks emerging in the differential capacity vs. voltage curves. Subsequent analysis of the CEI composition revealed the underlying cause enabling the NCM 811 particles to sustain their structural stability (Fig. 7c-e). Analysis of the C1s and O1s spectra reveals that the CEI derived from F-HE contains minimal organic components and is of thin thickness, which validates the TEM findings. In addition, C-F with high polarity in the F 1s spectra mainly comes from the decomposition of fluorinated solvents, which will promote the desolvation of Li+. In sharp contrast to the application of F-HE, a highly irreversible phase transition was observed in NCM 811 particles cycled with N-HE (Fig. 7f), which is consistent with the observation results of TEM. Furthermore, the CEI composition contains a substantial quantity of organic components and features a relatively thick layer. (Fig. 7g-i).

paragraph_context: To obtain a more lucid representation of the phase transition process during voltage alterations, the in-situ X-ray diffraction (in-situ XRD) technique was employed for analysis (the detailed description of the operation process is provided in the Supplementary materials). The (003) and (101) peaks of NCM 811 particles were analyzed prominently, as these two peaks are highly correlated with the phase transition during the charging/discharging processes [57]. As shown in Fig. 7j and Fig. S18, when NCM 811 is cycled under ultrahigh-voltage conditions with F-HE, the position of both its (003) peak and (110) peak exhibited negligible variation, which verifies that there is less lattice expansion and minimized oxygen loss during the ultrahigh-voltage cycling process [57]. By contrast, the application of N-HE leads to a severe irreversible phase transition caused by lattice expansion and oxygen evolution, which manifests as a greater peak shift during the ultrahigh-voltage cycling process (Fig. 7k and Fig. S17). In this chapter, through a series of in-situ and ex-situ characterizations, it is demonstrated that the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE effectively protects the NCM 811 material under an ultra-high cut-off voltage by minimizing the coordination of solvent molecules.

paragraph_context: In summary, we propose a strategy of an intrinsically nonflammable high-entropy fluorinated electrolyte (F-HE), which systematically integrates the characteristics of fluorination and high-entropy, minimizing the interaction between $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ and solvents. Benefitting from this minimized coordination ability, on one hand, during the charge-discharge processes, solvent molecules are rarely transported to the inner Helmholtz layer by lithium ions (this can be attributed to: (1) The diversity of solvation structures prevents specific solvent molecules from following the migration of Li+; (2)Under the synergistic effect of HE-induced weak solvent-ion interactions and fluorination-induced low solvating power, the desolvation process dominated by anion participation; (3) The decomposition of fluorinated solvents and anions forms a fluorine-rich interface, which prevents subsequent solvent molecules from approaching the electrode surface.), significantly suppressing the electron transfer; on the other hand, facilitating the kinetics of charge transfer, ensuring operability under low-temperature and high-rate conditions. Furthermore, the increase in the diffusion coefficient of Li+ brought about by HE also largely compensates for the low ionic conductivity caused by fluorination. Owing to the synergistic effect of fluorination and HE, high coulombic efficiency (98.2 %) and low overpotential (85 mV) can be achieved at high current densities, enabling commercially viable batteries (high loading cathode and controlled anode) to achieve stable cycling (with about 80 % CR after 300 cycles) under ultrahigh-voltage (4.8V). Meanwhile, a series of in-situ and exsitu tests were conducted to thoroughly analyze the structural and compositional evolution of the NCM 811 cathode during cycling, further validating the superiority of the electrolyte designed in this study. We believe this work can further enhance the energy density while ensuring safety and provide better guidance for the development of electrolytes.
